en: Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śāstraprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Sureśvaravārttika* composed by Bhagavad Ānandajñāna, the disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Śuddhānanda. 1.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 4097.
|| Śrīḥ ||
Now begins the second chapter:
"This world, indeed, [was] that," because its nature as the inner self was not yet known.
That which consists of name, form, and action has arisen like a snake and so forth in a rope. || 1 ||
I am that Truth, which is the Brahman of truth, distinct from both the formed and the formless, consisting solely of consciousness, and characterized as being neither prior nor posterior.

In the third chapter, ignorance (*avidyā*) among knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance was elaborated upon as it was set forth in the aphorisms; now, beginning the fourth chapter to elaborate upon knowledge, the author recalls what has preceded. The phrase "taddha" (that indeed) means that it was stated in the section on the unmanifest (*avyākṛta-prakriyā*) that the world, consisting of names and forms, arose from the unknown Self like a snake from a rope. This example, moreover, is intended to illustrate the theory of illusory transformation (*vivarta-vāda*).
For the sake of the goal. || 1 ||
Just as a rope, when not clearly discerned in the darkness, is falsely conceptualized [as a snake].
In the same way, the self is conceptualized through states such as the appearance of a snake or a stream.
In this regard, he recalls the very authoritative statement mentioned previously: "When [the object] is uncertain," etc. (Verse 2).
Ignorance is the cause of misfortune, and the entire world arises from it.
Fearing that this internal [self] is a source of misfortune, one intensely desires liberation from it.
In response to the inquiry, "What is the purpose of stating that the universe is a manifestation of the unknown Self?", he says: "anartha... (verse 3).
The goal of human endeavor is the complete destruction of all misfortunes for the inner self.
The thorough knowledge of reality is the cause of the goal of human life. || 4 ||
Having restated the previously mentioned "non-purpose" and its cause, and having shown the fruit of attaining that [purpose], he restates the previously mentioned "human purpose" and its cause:
"The human purpose... (sūtra 4).
He whose true nature consists of the attainment of all joy and the total removal of every evil.
Since this transmigrating being is by its very nature ignorant and possesses perverted vision, [it is bound].

He states the reason for right knowledge being the cause of the human goal [puruṣārtha] with the words "nirasta" (dispelled), etc. This inner self (pratyagdhatu), though wandering through transmigratory existence due to false cognition produced by its own ignorance, is in reality free from all evils and has likewise attained supreme bliss; this is certain from the scriptures (śruti).

Therefore, since one's own ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge of oneself, and that [ignorance] being destroyed, it is logical that the knowledge of the inner self is the cause of the human goal—this is the meaning. || 1 ||
1. ga. *ātmani* | *sa* | [vol2, page 594] 888 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Second Adhyāya—]
Because the human goal is obstructed by nothing other than ignorance alone, there is no other [cause].
Since awakening destroys ignorance, no further means is required.
Having stated that right cognition (*samyag-dhī*) is the cause [of liberation], he recalls the refutation of other causes: "Delusion... etc.
The distinction regarding what is to be negated is that the other means—either *prasaṃkhyāna* or ritual action (*karman*)—are excluded. (6)
It was stated previously that "The Self alone" is the aphorism for this knowledge.
Likewise, its introduction together with its purpose has been stated previously. || 7 ||
Anticipating the question, "Where have the human goals (pumartha) and their cause been stated?", he says: "Ātmeti" (as the Self). This means "in accordance with the Sūtra on Knowledge" (vidyāsūtra).

The meaning is: "of that knowledge of the Self which has been aphorized. He states that the purpose was already mentioned at the beginning, following the objection, in the passage starting with "They say...
(tadāhuḥ), etc.; thus he says: "Previously" (prāk). || 7 ||
When the inward-facing witness is directly realized, everything that is to be known is fully accomplished.
The darkness of the sheath is completely dispelled, and the goal of human existence is fully accomplished.

What is the purpose of that? He states it: "The west," etc. The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) expresses non-mediate immediacy (*aparokṣatva*). The meaning of the prefix (*upa-sarga*) is that such knowledge is not assailed by doubt or error; the remainder of the sense is "because there is no other object besides that. When that knowledge—which is the cause of all aforementioned types of knowledge—exists, what would happen? To this he says: "Without remainder," etc. (8).
Therefore, one should thus perceive the non-dual Self within oneself.
The Self alone is considered, according to scripture, to be the object of the knowledge of Brahman.

He cites the *Vidyāsūtra* as authority for the fact that self-knowledge alone is the cause of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). The phrase "since" [is used] because, according to the reasoning already stated—namely, that ignorance is merely an obstacle—the inward intellect is established as the cause of the human goal; thus, in the passage "By 'Self' alone," it is intended that the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should contemplate the Self, which abides in its own majesty, within itself. Otherwise, the *sūtra* would be purposeless; this is the meaning. [The text continues: "In its own majesty..."

He specifies [the object] for the sake of establishing its status as the goal of man by saying "non-dual. He concludes the restatement of the goal of man and its cause by saying "the Self" (ātman). || 9 ||
Then, having likewise referred to ignorance as "that which is other" and as being perishable—
Up to the end of the first chapter, its meaning has been explained clearly.
Anticipating the question, "Where are 'the harmful' and 'its cause' stated?", he says: "Now" (*atha*). The meaning is that *avidyā*, which was indicated in the aphorism "Its distinction...

(*tadbhedam*), and its effects—which were restated in the passage beginning with "But he who [sees] another... (*atha yo'nyām*)—have been explained by the textual sequence extending to the end of the chapter.

That is to say, according to the *avidyā* as indicated and restated therein. By the word "perishable" (*naśvarīm*), its fitness for being sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*) is expressed. By the word "directly" (*añjasā*)...
The propriety of the exposition has been stated. || 10 ||
The internal, the elemental, and likewise the divine.
That which has been, that which is, and that which will be; as well as the goal to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment.
All this that has come into being has arisen from ignorance alone. || 11 ||
Repeating what was stated in the *Annabrāhmaṇa*, he specifies the effect of ignorance with the words: "With reference to the self" (*adhyātmam*). || 11 ||
1 ga. *vastīpu* | 2 kha. *paryayānā* | 3 kha. *tatrāha* | [vol2, page 595] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 889.
And having summarized it, that [subject] is presented once again at the end of the chapter.
This indeed consists of name and action, which take the form "this is such-and-such."
And the summary of the triad is the integration of the subtle body (liṅgadeha) and the self (ātman). || 13 ||

He restates what was said in the *Upasaṃhāra-brāhmaṇa* with the words "In brief" (*saṃkṣipya*). The two *ca*s have the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and are connected to the word *vāc*, which is the effect of ignorance, following the word *tat*. The latter two [conjunctions] have the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). This is also a summary of the summary stated in the passage beginning with "This triad" (*tad etat trayam*).

He recites [the verse]: "Of the triad also. He illustrates that very point: "By the linga," meaning the aggregate of the subtle and gross bodies, which is to say, the collection of the body and the instruments of action. || 12 || 13 ||
This Prajāpati, whose body is the three worlds, possesses the universal form.
Within him are contained all infinite deities; he has vital breath as his very body.

1. Therein, he states the nature of the effect (*kārya*): "The three worlds," etc. He states the nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*): "Within," etc. The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that by which the entire universe is contained within (*antarṇītam*), and infinite deities are likewise contained within. The reason for this is as follows:
"Prāṇa," etc. For it will be stated there that everything is included within it. || 14 ||

One who does not know the true nature of the Self, who possesses the conceit of superimposing [the world] upon it, and who has desisted from outward activity—such a person is the fit subject for this knowledge. (15)
Having restated what has been said, he states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa with the words "avijñātā" (not known). The word "tat" refers back to the two bodies mentioned immediately prior.

The meaning is that Prajāpati—who, due to ignorance of the Self as described, had superposed the notion of "I" upon himself, and who, by virtue of that, became averse to sense objects and free from passion—is himself presented by the Śruti as the qualified candidate for this knowledge; it is to him that Ajātaśatru speaks the Brāhmaṇa in order to impart the wisdom. || 15 ||
This one has directly realized the nature of the self in an object characterized in this way.
Gārgya is introduced by the scripture with the intention of expounding the knowledge of Brahman.

He elaborates on what has been stated with the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*). "Of such characteristics" (*evam-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the one described in the passage beginning with "the embodied self of the three worlds," namely, in Brahmā (*jāpati*). [16]
Because he does not know Brahman in its entirety, he is arrogant; therefore, he is insignificant.
For indeed, no one who possesses complete knowledge ever falls into duality. || 17 ||
One might ask: since Gārgya is a knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*), how can he be raised up as a qualified candidate [for instruction]? To this, the text replies with the words "akṛtsna" (incomplete).

This means that because he lacks the primary knowledge of Brahman, he is unqualified for the status of a teacher (*ācārya*). His pride regarding the acquisition of the primary knowledge of Brahman is the indicative mark [of his lack of qualification]. Therefore, since his status as a teacher is untenable, the sense is that he must indeed be a disciple. [He is] a knower of the primary Brahman—

If it be argued that even he might possess pride like the contemporary knowers of Brahman, the author replies: "Not indeed" (na hi). The meaning is that not even a modern knower of Brahman is fit to be proud, because of the contradiction [between knowledge and pride]. The reason for his lack of pride is stated as: "Because he is non-dual" (nirdvaya). || 17 ||
112 1 ka. kha. 'tyeva rū'; 2 va ṣayaḥ svayaṃ [vol2, page 596]

890. Thus, the supreme Person, having completed all that is to be known and attained the highest human goal, [is established]. *Suresvarācāryakṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtikaṃ* [Second Chapter]—thus ends [the section on] the completion of all that is to be known and the attainment of the supreme human purpose.
Ajātaśatru is designated as the teacher Gārgya because of their identity. || 18 ||

Fearing that Ajātaśatru might also require another teacher because he is equal to Gārgya, [the author] says: "It is concluded. He states "likewise" to show that it was like being a disciple of Gārgya, who was a knower of Brahman only in a secondary sense. The reason for Ajātaśatru’s status is given as "due to his solitary abiding" (aikāramyāt). || 18 ||
Since ignorance has been explained, now, for its cessation:
A clear exposition of the sutra "Ātmeti vā" is now commenced. (19)

Having stated the connection with the *brāhmaṇa*—namely, that this *brāhmaṇa* is for the purpose of explaining [the nature of] Prajāpati, who is the effect of the aforementioned ignorance (*avidyā*), and who, having destroyed attachment to his own body through the meditation on him as the Self, is a seeker of liberation desiring the knowledge of Brahman—he now states the connection with the chapter (*adhyāya*) by saying, "When [ignorance] has been explained. This means: when ignorance along with its effects has been fully disclosed, and when the cessation of bondage—which is required—is to be achieved, its cause [must be addressed].

While being explained, it is elucidated; the meaning is that it is the "Sūtra of Knowledge" (vidyāsūtra). With the word "atha" (now), he shows the occasion for stating the prohibition immediately after the statement of what is to be prohibited. "Sphuṭa" means for the arising of knowledge that is clear, free from doubt, uncontradicted, and possessed of fruit. || 19 ||
By means of the Śruti, which takes the form of the presentation of Gārgī and others as disciples and teachers;
This narrative has been composed for the purpose of establishing easy comprehension. (20)

Anticipating the objection—"If the Vidyāsūtra is intended to be explained, for what purpose is this narrative (ākhyāyikā)?"—he says: "By means of the Śruti. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "regarding the supreme, most subtle, ultimate Reality. || 20 ||
But other wise men explain the connection here in this way.
"This very one" refers to that self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānātman*) which was previously introduced.

Having stated his own intended connection between the chapters, [the author] states the position favored by Bhartṛprapañca with the words "But others. This refers, for now, to the relationship between the preceding and subsequent chapters. He explains the meaning of the word "this" (*evaṃ*) with the word "that" (*sa*). In the verse concerning the entry [of the Self], the individual soul (*jīva*) is indicated as the thread [of the argument].

This is the meaning. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that the individual soul (jīva), which has been stated in the aphorism, is well-known both in common worldly usage and in the Veda. || 21 ||
The determination of that [matter] will be explained by means of the historical narrative of Gārgya and Kāśya.
In this body, the agents and the enjoyers are indeed the deities themselves, and nothing else.
This very Śruti, assuming the form of Gārgī, stated the prima facie argument.

[The text] causes Ajātaśatru to rise and address the Brāhmaṇa as "Gārgya. One might ask: since an undertaking is appropriate only when there is the possibility of uncertainty for the sake of reaching certainty, how can such a possibility exist here? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "Having heard," and supplies the word "beyond" (*ūrdhvam*) after the word "other" (*apara*).

This is to be construed with the term "pūrvapakṣa" (the prima facie view). As they have said: "The deities are both those to be released and the presiding agents of the instruments; what other task remains for the cognitional self? Thus, Gārgya, standing within this philosophical system, is raised up for the purpose of adopting the pūrvapakṣa. ||22||
— for the purpose of establishing the existence, agency, and enjoyership of the self. || 23 ||
1. Kha. *tadvicchi*. 2. *śeṣam*. [Vol.
2, page 597] 9. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 891.
For the sake of establishing the final conclusion through scripture, the form of Kāśya has been conceived.
And that [position] is untenable because it is fruitless and because it does not connect with the subject under discussion. || 24 ||

He states the intention of the Bhāṣya, which says that the Śruti has declared the established conclusion (siddhānta) by means of the word *kāśya*. He explains the phrase "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*) as follows:

the connection is that the form of Kāśya was fashioned by the Śruti for the purpose of establishing the existence and other attributes of that [Self]. He summarizes that very point with the words "the established conclusion.
He refutes the connection proposed by others with the words "because it would be fruitless. [This is because] the vital breath (*prāṇa*), being a deity, lacks the status of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).

The connection [proposed] that the subsequent section of the text is intended to state the means for the self's renunciation is incorrect; for the means to achieve that [renunciation] for the self would be fruitless, and because it would lack connection with the subject at hand—namely, that liberation results from the knowledge of unity through the realization "He knew himself as this alone. Indeed, the establishment of that [agency and so forth] does not pertain to the real agency and other attributes of the individual soul (jīva). This is the meaning. || 23 || 24 ||
Even in the position that deities exist, why is their existence and so forth not accepted?

"If it is desired that the cognizer be distinct from the body, then this effort is fruitless. (25) He establishes the reason for its fruitlessness with the words "the deity," etc. Even in the view that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the beloved [deity] of Gārgī, why is the existence and so forth of the *jīva*—which is distinct from the two bodies—not accepted through that [deity] as the medium? If that is indeed desired, then [it must be accepted] regarding the deity.
The meaning is that, since the existence of the knower has already been refuted, any effort to establish it as a real entity is in vain. || 25 ||
But when one whose true nature as the one Self is unknown is intended to be spoken of here, [then...]
Abiding in the effects of ignorance, he [was awakened] by means of the Vedic revelation embodied in Gārgya.
As the proponent of the prima facie view, for the sake of pacifying all causes of suffering.
Kāśyapa cut through the root of the prima facie argument and became an ocean of established conclusions. || 27 ||
By means of this scripture, one is awakened for the sake of comprehending the meaning of all the Vedāntas without exception.
Then all this effort will bear fruit, and not otherwise. || 28 ||

He states that the two faults mentioned previously do not exist in his own position by means of the passage beginning with "ajñāta" (unknown). When, in this narrative, the ignorant Gārgya—who possesses a sense of "I-am-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*)—is intended by the Śruti as the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) for the sake of pacifying his own ignorance, which is the cause of all suffering; and when Ajātaśatru, having set out to cut through that ignorance which is its cause, acts as the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) for the sake of establishing non-duality (*aikya*); [then the aforementioned faults do not apply].

If the proponent were thus restated [by the opponent], then all efforts—such as the refutation of the selfhood of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and the assertion of a distinct self—would become fruitful; furthermore, there would be no impossibility of liberation here, since that [liberation] is established through the destruction of ignorance and its products by means of knowledge. But in the other case (the Sāṃkhya view), effort is fruitless, nor is it consistent with the context, for if agency and so forth were real entities, liberation through knowledge would not be logical, because a real entity cannot be removed by that [knowledge].

The meaning is that if [agency and so forth] were real, there would be no possibility for liberation—which consists in the destruction of evil—while they remain in that state; and if they were merely imagined, then the various conflicting views regarding agency and the rest could not be established. || 26 || 27 || 28 ||
Alternatively, this narrative may serve the purpose of a rule regarding faith, conduct, and so forth.
Having realized the goal through the vision as it was taught, he has cultivated the conviction that nothing else exists.
Therefore, he was exceedingly arrogant, a devourer of those whose cause for pride remained unknown. || 29 ||
1 Kha. "For the sake of establishing this [point].
[Vol. 2, page 598] 892 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Second Adhyāya—]"

Having set aside the connection stated by others, the connection stated by himself was established; therein it was said that a narrative (ākhyāyikā) is told for the sake of easy comprehension. Now he states another purpose: "Faith" (śraddhā). Since we observe that Gārgya and Kāśya were full of faith, faith is the supreme means for knowledge. It is the established practice that the highest [knowledge] cannot be obtained from the lowest merely by permission, but through formal instruction. This is not [attained] by the power of dry logic alone.

The meaning of the words "she is obtainable" (*sā labhyā*) and so forth is as follows. The phrase "or else" (*yadi vā*) signifies an alternative regarding the result. Having thus explained the connection, he states the meaning of Gārgya’s pride and so on with the words "as stated. The meaning is that Gārgya was once extremely proud because, through the vision of the Self consisting of the three foods, he had attained that state; thinking that there was no Brahman other than that, he possessed the knowledge of reality which destroys the ignorance that is the cause of pride for those who have not yet attained it. Thus, he was at one time exceedingly haughty. ||29||
But having approached one who is faithful, endowed with wealth, and seeking the highest good—
"I shall tell you about Brahman," Gārgya said to the King of Kāśī.

He introduces [the passage] beginning with "saha" (together), [referring to the word] "śraddhālum" (one who possesses faith). These qualifiers are for the sake of ensuring the fitness of the recipient regarding the transmission of the knowledge (*vidyā*).

The word "tu" (but/however) is intended to indicate the meaning that will be stated hereafter: namely, that it is appropriate to provide an answer even without a question from a qualified candidate (*adhikārin*). || 30 ||
From the vision of the oneness of self, there is no enemy born, nor shall there ever be one.
Therefore, Ajātaśatru of Kāśī possessed an intellect contrary to that of Gārgya. || 31 ||
The fact that Kāśya was not born from a foe (*ajātaśatru*) is established by the words beginning with "no" (*na*). The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is connected with the ablative case.
He clarifies the previously stated reason by means of a qualifying statement: "Gārkha... (verse 31).
Because there is no reality higher than Brahman, nor any other entity from which it differs.
I shall declare to you that which is to be venerated, which is the cause for the destruction of all calamities.
Relying on such scriptural passages as "There is nothing else higher than that," he explains the term "Brahman" and so forth. He states the fruit of its meditation: "All... (32).
"One should not [speak] unless asked"—surely the Sage has acted contrary to this.
Being asked, "Whose speech is this?", Kāśya spoke to Yaja. || 33 ||
"One should not become the teacher of anyone unless asked, nor of one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, the wise man should behave like one dull-witted among the people.
[The opponent] raises the objection that the conduct of the Sage (*ṛṣi*) contradicts this *smṛti* rule, using the words "No" (*na*) and so forth, regarding Kāśya’s behavior toward Gārgya.

The word "hi" (for) is used here for the purpose of establishing that, from the very beginning, there is no such question; and the word "yat" (which) signifies "because," while the word "hi" is stated to clarify its meaning. || 33 ||
Or rather, it is the perception of the self as incomplete, because of the observation of pride and other such [defilements].
Therefore, for the sake of completeness, he questioned Kāśya, who was endowed with wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "I shall speak" (*bravāṇi*), a certain partial scholar (*ekadeśin*) says that since verbal roots have multiple meanings, this word means "I shall ask," and thus there is no contradiction with the traditional Smṛti texts. Regarding the phrase "out of pride" (*darpaṭ*), the word "etc.
(*ādi*) is included to signify the desire for gain and so forth. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Gārgya knows his own self as the incomplete Self" (*akṛtsnātmadarśanam*).
1 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
3 "For the sake of totality" means for the sake of the knowledge of the complete reality. It is appropriate that the inquiry proceeds toward him for the sake of perfect knowledge.
The qualification beginning with "wisdom" (prajñā) is intended to indicate this. || 34 ||
The qualified candidate is one who possesses faith, desires to know, and is endowed with humility.
Even if not asked, this knowledge should be spoken by a wise person to him.

In this context, because the literal sense of the scripture would otherwise be strained, he states his own position by taking the text according to its explicit words: "the faithful one" (*śraddhāluḥ*). These qualifiers serve to establish his eligibility (*adhikāritva*). By the term "the wise one" (*vipaścit*), it is stated that the speaker possesses the capacity for attaining that realization.
But he who speaks according to what is not dharma, and he who asks according to what is not dharma—
one of these two dies, or falls into enmity.
Knowledge said to a Brāhmaṇa: "I am your treasure; guard me.
Do not give me to one who is envious, so that I may remain most powerful."

The meaning is that this does not contradict the conduct of the Ṛṣi, because the aforementioned Smṛti passage beginning with "ityādi" intends only to state that knowledge should not be imparted to one who is unqualified. || 35 ||
Where neither dharma nor artha exists, nor even a corresponding desire to hear them.
In that case, knowledge should not be spoken [to one who is unfit], just as a good seed [is not sown] in saline soil (36).

Even if the questioner is unqualified, knowledge must not be given; regarding this, he cites a traditional authority (*smṛti*). [The verse begins with] "Dharma... The two sets of seven [verses] concern the disciple. That is to say, such knowledge conforms to the place, time, and capacity [of the recipient]. In that regard, even if knowledge has been imparted...
An example is given to demonstrate that [the practice] is not fruitful. || 36 ||
And where there may be one seeking the Dharma, or likewise a desire to listen to it.
In that case, it should be called "knowledge" (vidyā), as is indicated by the very fact of its negation. || 37 ||

He states the authority for the claim that she should be instructed even without being questioned, provided she is qualified, by saying: "Dharma and Artha. Now, one might object: there is no such Smṛti statement without a prohibitory injunction; to this he replies: "Because of the prohibition. The meaning is that since the giving of knowledge to an unqualified person is prohibited, it is understood that she may be taught even without a question, provided she is qualified. || 37 ||
O noble one, like those who have lost their horses or whose chariots are burnt, they rely upon a protector of the earth.
He spoke [of one] rich in human wealth and endowed with divine wealth.

If Gārgya proceeded to speak the knowledge to one who was qualified, then why did he approach and speak to the king, bypassing a suitable Brāhmaṇa? To this, he says: "The [union] is lost," etc. As they say: "A union is appropriate when there is a cause for qualification, like the case of the lost horse and the burnt chariot. (38)
For a person who is endowed with these two kinds of wealth is thus qualified [for spiritual practice].
Therefore, Bālāki learned all ritual acts from Kāśya.
1 kha. ga. "nvitaḥ || 38 || 2 kha. 'rmaṇyato | [vol2, page 600] 894 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Adhyāya—]

By the logic already stated, he reveals the fruit of the relationship between Gārgya and Kāśya: "Vitta... and so on. As they say: "For one who possesses both [wealth and learning] has the qualification; therefore, it is appropriate that the statement was made for the purpose of establishing that qualification. || 39 ||
"I shall speak the Brahman to you," said Vāja, while I was occupied with the Yājyā.
Today I give a thousand cows, even without the definitive realization of the oneness of the Self.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "a thousand" as follows: "Brahman," etc. (40).
The Śruti has declared this for the purpose of the gift of a thousand cows.
Through the repeated utterance of the name "Janaka, Janaka," it becomes clearly manifest.
He introduces [the passage] beginning with "Janaka" by means of the words "A thousand cows," etc. (41).
All people desire to serve Janaka, who is ever intent on giving.
Desirous of speaking, they run toward him, seeking to seize him.
He explains that [verse] as follows: "one who is desirous of hearing" (śuśrūṣum). || 42 ||
"Having transcended the bounds of common ignorance, this son of Garga has come to me."
Surely he regards me also as one who desires to give and who wishes to listen. || 43 ||

Fearing that it might be suspected that the mere statement of Gārgī—“How shall I speak of Brahman?”—was the sole cause for the King’s gift of a thousand cows to those desiring to speak and those desiring to hear, he says: “Out of simplicity” (*maugdhīm*). He restates the intention of the visitor with the word “surely” (*nūnam*). Thus, the gift of the thousand cows was made by taking her mere words as the occasion.
The meaning is "accumulated. || 43 ||
The sun is his eye; he is established in the intellect, conscious, all-pervading, and eternal.
One should always worship this very one situated in the center of the sun as Brahman.

The moon shines exceedingly with its nectar; the Brāhmaṇa shines by his royal status.
From this point on, he speaks "Soma is King" with the desire to teach its meditative worship.

He explains the words beginning with "pāṇḍara" by means of the passage beginning with "ambhaḥ. Based on the Vedic scripture stating, "Soma is the king of the Brāhmaṇas," it is said that he "rules over the Brāhmaṇas. He states the purpose of mentioning the four qualities as follows: "One should meditate upon him... (15).
Because it possesses the same property of being denoted by the same name, the *soma* plant is also understood [by that term].
Since the deity of both is one, that which is to be worshipped is therefore twofold.

He states another meaning of the word *soma*: "Equal," etc. The meaning is that not only the moon is *soma*, but the creeper (*latā*) is also *soma*, because both share the commonality of the attributes known as waxing and waning, and because the deity of the moon is one and the same in both. He explains the utility of grasping the creeper: "The object of worship," etc.; the words "having unified with the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)" are to be supplied. || 17 ||
A single deity is manifold, yet she is perceived as distinct objects by each individual.

We worship this Self as Brahman, because it pervades everything.
The explanation is to be understood as exactly the same for all statements, as before. (59)
Fearing the objection that "it is improper to say food belongs to the Brahmin because the Brahmin is not such [an eater]," he says: "The Brahmin.

For whatever quality is attributed to a person here by name, it is indeed [found] therein.
That alone shall be the fruit for him; this is the definitive conclusion regarding all statements. || 60 ||

Anticipating the objection that the qualities (*guṇa*) and the fruits (*phala*) might also be identical for every successive section (*paryāya*), he says: "The quality" (*guṇa*). Here, in the sections already mentioned and those yet to be described, in whichever section a particular quality of the person to be meditated upon is presented by words such as "the firm one," "the king," or "the radiant one," for one who meditates on that [person], there shall indeed be a fruit corresponding to the meditation on that quality—such as "he becomes the firm one of all beings," and so forth—in this manner for all the statements.

The Puruṣa is to be meditated upon. || 69 ||
Space is not like a material object that can be divided into parts, for it is full and does not undergo movement.

The two qualities of the ether-Brahman (*ākāśabrahman*)—that it is "full" (*pūrṇam*) and "non-active" (*apravarti*)—have been stated; he now explains them with the words "in parts," etc. Just as a jar or similar object is divided into parts, space is not so; therefore, it is full and non-active, meaning it does not cause activity. He states another meaning for the word "non-active": "devoid of action. For while all activities exist within the sky (space), it itself does not [act].
Therefore, the meaning is that action likewise does not proceed from it. || 62 ||
He shall be victorious because of his habit of conquering, since he is not defeated by others.

Those born from one mother but from another [father] are declared to be *styā*.
He may even become the husband of another's wife and a destroyer of his half-brothers.

The Victorious One (Viṣṇu) is superior to Vaikuṇṭha by virtue of his qualities, due to the worship of Indra’s qualities.
Because it is called "Unconquered Army" (senā'parājitā), there is the defeat of one's rivals. || 65 ||

Anticipating the objection as to how a single mode of worship can yield manifold fruits, he states that it is due to the difference in the qualities of the object of worship: "The Victorious One," etc. (69).
Since fire endures even when the world is piled upon it, therefore...
Because he reduces everything to ashes, he is called Viṣāsahi by the lords.

The meaning is: by the lords (*īśvaraiḥ*) who are capable of determining the meaning of the Vedas. || 66 ||
In the waters, in the seed, and in the intellect, one perceives the conscious Puruṣa as Brahman.

This prefix *prati* is used according to its literal meaning, because the fruit [of action] is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

Thus:
"Since it is accepted that [the word] *sati* has the meaning of 'being contrary' (*prātikūlya*), that is to say, when it exists. || 69 ||
He who is constantly diligent regarding the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous.

It is radiant, endowed with the secret essence, and beautiful within the cognitions of the mirror, the eye, and so forth.

"Like a flash of lightning," [verse 72].

Struck by the various parts of the body of a man running swiftly toward him, [he was overwhelmed].

Because the destruction of their livelihood [occurs] through the Asuras and Yama, and because their life-force depends upon those two.

He states the meaning of the qualification "of the person consisting of speech" (*śābdapuruṣasya*) as "of life" (*āyuḥ*). He explains the passage beginning with "He who [knows] this," etc., with the words "and of life" (*āyuṣaśca*). || 76 ||
In all directions he is the second, never departing, always accompanied by a companion.

Surrounded by virtuous servants and attendants, he should be a lay devotee at all times.
May there always be stability in the lineage of one's sons and other progeny. || 78 ||

He explains the passage beginning with "sa ya etam" and so forth. Regarding the word "sādhu": its excellence (*sādhutvam*) consists in its accordance with the understanding of the worshipper. Likewise, in the shadow-like ignorance and in the intellect, there is but one single deity.
Before the time of death, not even disease shall approach him.

"In the Virāj-self, in the body, and in the intellect," and so forth, as before.

Previously, there was an enumeration of the individual [factors], but here they are stated collectively.

Having had his instruction rejected, he was [convinced] again and again through corroboration.
Out of great respect, Brahmā spoke various other words until he was completely satisfied.
He makes manifest its conclusion with the words "pratyākhyātā" (was rejected). The ellipsis is: immediately after that, due to ignorance alone, Gāyī became devoid of the desire to speak. || 82 ||
Because particularities are infinite, he declared that Brahman is the totality.
When that too was forbidden, Gāyatrī then became silent.

Having mentioned a few specific qualities, [the author] states the word "entire Brahman" at the end; anticipating the objection as to why this is done without a general summary, he says: "Of the particulars," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "because they are infinite and thus impossible to describe individually. The underlying sense is that all [qualities] are included therein. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "He remained silent," etc., by saying: "In that," etc.—meaning in that which is distinct from both the whole and the parts.

The word "atha" (then) is used to indicate Gārgya’s lack of ready wit regarding the subject matter; his resorting to silence and remaining with his head hanging down is made evident to those standing nearby by the use of the particle "atha. || 83 ||
That which was previously described as the entire Brahman is this very same [reality] through ignorance.
In one way or many ways, it is conceptualized by the ignorant like a rope-snake. || 84 ||

Now, an objection is raised: "If one serves that which is called 'Brahman' by the King, is it not the case that its very non-Brahmanhood is being established? For is it something other than that [which is Brahman], or is it not?

The first alternative is not tenable because it contradicts the remainder of the text beginning with, 'I shall indeed make you know it. Nor is the second, because since it would be something other than that, it would follow—like a jar—that it too is non-Brahman. To this, he says: "That which... Or rather, since the primary Brahman has been indicated as "the Self," why [should one seek] the sun and so forth?

Anticipating the objection that another stage of meditation (*jhāntara*) has been mentioned by Gārgya, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the intention of the Śruti: "That which is whole," etc.
The meaning is: "in one way" refers to both in its entirety (*samastatvena*) and in its parts (*vyastatvena*). || 84 ||
1 ga. *samanvitā* | 2 kha. *sarvaiḥ* | [vol2, page 607] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 901.
Seeing Gārgya with his head hanging downwards and offering no reply, the king...
He said "only this much" to him in order to remove any remaining doubt.

He states the purport of the word "sa" (he) and so forth: "avāk" (not speaking). Here, the abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) is indicated. On the occasion of the subsequent [reply], he mentions the lack of comprehension as "aprati-bhā" (inability to respond). The meaning is that the King’s statement is intended to remove Gārgya’s doubt regarding whether the remaining primary Brahman was already known to him. || 85 ||
And when the yoga of restraint is being practiced, one should point only to the sacred scripture (śruti).
"You have said that speech is Brahman; yet that much alone is Brahman for you. 86.

He explains the meaning of the protracted vowel (*pluti*) in this sentence, stating that it must be expressed when a question is connected with one who is being defeated by means of the loss of a proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) and so forth. He says: "being defeated. For it has been stated [in the *Pāṇini Sūtra*]: "And [the *pluti* occurs] when questioning one who is to be defeated. He clarifies the state of being defeated itself: "Brahman... (86).
Where [the Self] is unknown, the world is unknown; where it is known, the world is known.
That alone is Brahman because of its fullness; that which you have described is not so, due to its incompleteness.

Now, it might be objected: "It was promised that Brahman would be taught in the form of the sun and so forth, yet that is not Brahman, because there is no other Brahman [apart from that]. To this, he says: "The unknown," [verse 87].
In the reality of the self, which is established by itself and is neither excluded nor followed [by others].
The word "Brahman" must have its primary meaning; it cannot apply to what you have described, because that is not the case.

He states the reason for [the statement] "Brahman is indeed full" with the words "avyāvṛtta" (unrestricted). The reason why that [term "full"] lacks its primary meaning in reference to the sun and so forth is given by the phrase "atathātvataḥ" (because it is not such). This means: because the sun and other things mentioned by you possess the nature of being restricted and so forth. || 88 ||
Therefore, for this reason, [the Lord addressed] Gārgya, who had spoken thus: "So far, indeed, [is my knowledge]."
The king said, "It is not merely this," clearly indicating the impossibility of his attaining the status of a Brahmin.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "etāvad dhi" (for this much only) with the words "yasmāt" (because). The reason is that, according to the logic already stated, the sun and so forth are not Brahman. || 89 ||
This statement is difficult to conceive for one who does not know the true nature of Brahman.
"It is not merely this," [says] Brahmā; therefore, it is indicated that Kāśya knows. || 90 ||
He states the intention of one who says, "I have come near you," as follows: "Unknown. || 90 ||
Then Gārgya, having inferred the king's proficiency in the knowledge of Brahman, [spoke].
He spoke these means for the realization of the Supreme Brahman.
Desiring to know the Supreme Brahman, I have approached you with great reverence.
To him who spoke thus, "Instruct me according to the true reality," the king [replied].
If a Brāhmaṇa should approach a Kṣatriya for sexual intercourse when they are of equal caste and no distress exists, [he incurs a penalty].
This conduct is contrary to the natural order and is forbidden by the treatises on Dharma.
1. Of them. 2. *thāvattva* (variant).
[Vol. 2, page 608] 902 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Second Chapter]

He introduces the statement regarding the approaching [of Gārgya] with the words "Gārgya. The meaning of "having inferred" (*anumāya*) is "having reasoned," as expressed by the phrase "this much is not [Brahman].
The sense of the word *atha* (then) is that it is appropriate for one who does not know Brahman to approach one who knows Brahman. "This" refers to the king who knows Brahman.

He states the fruit of approaching [the teacher]. "The Supreme Brahman" [is the object]. He explains the sentence regarding the approach: "Having approached. By this, he excludes an approach motivated by mere curiosity or by an atheistic disposition. "With reverence" [is said]. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "in reverse order" (*pratiloma*). "In this manner" [is the phrase]; the ellipsis is "the King said. He excludes a *brāhmaṇa* who is merely a product of social convention. "By birth" [is the term used]. Dharma—

Regarding the phrase "by means of the treatises": Gautama states that in times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa may acquire knowledge from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, provided he follows and serves him until its completion:
"In times of distress, study from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is ordained."
And following after and serving the teacher for as long as the study lasts.
A student should not dwell for life with a teacher who is not a Brahmin,
nor with a Brahmin who has not mastered the Vedas, if he desires the supreme goal.
Thus says Manu. The meaning is that, because of such prohibitions as these, it is improper for a Brāhmaṇa to seek refuge with a Kṣatriya. || 91 ||
Going forth for the sake of the fruits of security and well-being is not forbidden.
Thinking, "Brahmā will speak to me," the king's act of approaching was forbidden.

Anticipating the objection that his very survival would then be difficult to ensure, he states the point indicated by the word "in times of no distress" (*anāpadi*): "By *yoga*," etc. *Yoga* is the attainment of what has not been attained; *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been attained. For the sake of these, a Brahmin’s approaching a king is not forbidden:
"He should master the meaning of the Vedas and various treatises..."
One should approach the Lord in the month of Caitra for the sake of attaining security and the fulfillment of one's goals.
The meaning is "at the time of death. If so, what is the status of the prohibitory statements? To that he says: "Brahman," etc. (94).
Therefore, I shall leave you just as you are, uninitiated, like a bilva fruit placed upon the palm of the hand.
I shall declare the Brahman, through the knowledge of which one becomes all-knowing. || 95 ||

Since a Brāhmaṇa is superior to a Kṣatriya, there might be a doubt that it is impossible for Gārgya to approach the King for the sake of knowledge; anticipating this, [the author] explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Vyeva tvā" (I will indeed explain it to you). With the words "ataḥ" (therefore), he states the distinction of the Brahman about to be described from the Brahmans such as Āditya and others. By the phrase "yaj-jñāne" (in the knowledge of which), [he shows that] even though Gārgya lacks the status of a higher caste, he possesses superiority in terms of knowledge.
Because of the king's preeminence, it is therefore appropriate that he should carry it.
"Not by years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he among us who is learned in the Vedas (anūcāna) is great."
This is the meaning of the statement "because of the traditional teaching (smṛti). || 95 ||
Having spoken thus, the king took Tarpa’s hand and rose.
And the two of them approached the sleeping man with the desire to speak of their business.
1. Ink-pot.
[vol2, page 609]
Brāhmaṇa 1. Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Verse 901] He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "him [the teacher] in his hand" (*taṃ pāṇau*), etc., as follows: "Having spoken thus" (*ity uktvā*). He explains the section beginning with "Then those two" (*tau ha*) as: "They arrived" (*ājagmatuḥ*). || 96 ||
[The text establishes] that the Brahman described by Gārgya is not the enjoyer, and likewise that these [elements] are not the Self.
Thinking, "I shall awaken Bālāka," the king went to where he was sleeping. || 97 ||
He clarifies this very point with the phrase "by the desire to express the effect" (kāryavivakṣayā). He says "of these," meaning of these [beings] such as the sun and so forth. ||97||
Having approached the sleeping [king], the King of Kāśī addressed him by the names of the deities as previously described.
Then he manifested a disease by means of [mantras] beginning with "bṛhan" and so forth.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "him by these" as follows: "The deity," etc.; the meaning is: "then, during the state of deep sleep. || 98 ||
Although being thus awakened, he who was asleep did not wake up at all.
From this, it is understood that the one intended by Gārgya is not the enjoyer. || 99 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "he did not rise" with the words "even though being awakened. Since the vital breath (prāṇa) does not rise despite hearing its name used for the purpose of awakening and despite being pressed, it follows that the active prāṇa is not the enjoyer; this is the established conclusion he expresses with the words "since.
Why did they abandon the time of waking and go to sleep?
For indeed, the clarity of all phenomena is perceived during the state of waking. || 100 ||
It rejects the state of one who has gone to sleep, saying "while awake. The meaning is that it is improper to abandon what is proximate to reach what is remote.

Anticipating the objection that this transition [to the waking state] is intended to distinguish the Self taught by Gārgya from the Self desired by Kāśya and to instruct [the latter] on that [Kāśya's] Self, he says: "Because of clarity. In that [waking state], every instructed matter can be explained by distinguishing its parts; however, in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because all worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) ceases, that transition is not [possible].
The meaning is "think. || 100 ||
Because of the intermingling of the vital breaths, the deities, and the person.
In the state of awakening, it is impossible to make a distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
He provides the answer: "Even though all objects are perceived while awake, because they are intermingled like milk and water, the vision that discriminates their true nature is not attained.
This refers to the verse beginning with "prāṇānām" (of the vital breaths). || 101 ||
The person possesses only the state of being an enjoyer; even in the slightest degree, he does not possess the state of being an object of enjoyment.
By virtue of the intention regarding Kāśī, the food possesses only the state of being an object of enjoyment, not the state of being an enjoyer.
What is this intended discrimination? He states it: "The state of being an enjoyer," which means the state of being a witness (*sākṣitva*).
"The state of being the object of enjoyment" means the state of being the witnessed (*sākṣyatva*). This refers to the "non-moving one," that is, the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 102 ||
Due to their being mixed together, it would be impossible to distinguish between what is to be consumed and what is to be enjoyed.
Therefore, discrimination went with great care toward the sleeping person in order to act.
