page 610] 904 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Second Adhyāya— ]
One might ask: "Let such discrimination exist while one is awake; why does it not exist in the state of a sleeping person? To this he says: "Because of its being mixed up.
The word "with care" (*ādara*) is used for the purpose of indicating the gravity of the intended task. || 103 ||
Therefore, although the presence of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth exists during the waking state, [it does not constitute their essential nature].
Because they are intermingled with one another, it is difficult to distinguish them.

Regarding the passage beginning with "clarity" (*spaṣṭatā*) and so forth, he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The phrase beginning with "even though" (*yadyapi*) is an explanation of the meaning of that word [“therefore”].
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Therefore, it is logical for [the Lord] to go to the sleeping person. || 104 ||
However, because he is away from home, the enjoyment [of his property] is not granted to him.
When [the Self] is asleep, all the deities together with the organs remain indifferent.

To the question, "Since there is an equal degree of confusion even during sleep, how can there be a cognition of discrimination therein?", he says: "Of the Self. The meaning is that because the presiding deities, together with the instruments of the enjoyer, are withdrawn during deep sleep, there is no confusion; therefore, discrimination is easily achieved there. || 105 ||
Then, due to the exhaustion of the karma engaged in during waking enjoyment.
Its instruments lie within itself together with the self, the enjoyer.

He states the reason for the summary [of the state] as "asleep" and "engaged": "While waking," etc. That refers to the state of being asleep; the meaning is: while the Supreme Self remains unknown. || 106 ||
The vital breath alone remains awake; it is the enjoyer, as agreed upon by Gārgya.
And likewise, it will be explained later in the concluding section with the words, "protecting by means of the vital breath. (107)

Fearing that there might be an implication of enjoyment [of objects] even for the self of Gārgya because of its being withdrawn there [into the heart], he says: "The vital breath" (prāṇa). He states the authority for this: "By the vital breath" (prāṇena). The meaning is that later on, in the passage "Protecting by means of the vital breath the lower nest," its non-withdrawal during sleep will be stated. || 107 ||
It is clearly stated as "consisting of breath" (prāṇamaya), likewise because of the scriptural passage concerning its non-setting.
The breath alone, being untiring, remains awake here day and night.
In this regard, he cites another scriptural passage: "The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) indeed keep watch in this city. This means that the scripture expresses this very point.

Furthermore, from such statements as "It does not tremble, it is not harmed; this is the deity that never sets," he says "likewise" to show that there is no withdrawal [of the senses] during deep sleep. He concludes the result of the aforementioned proof with the words "unwearied. In this context...
The mention of the body. || 108 ||
Just as in the waking state, the vital breath was formerly the enjoyer.
"He remains exactly the same even in dream; if he is a cognizer, let him perceive this.
[Verse 109] He states the object obtained during the constant waking of the vital breath (prāṇa) with the word "yathā" (as). By the word "api" (even) in "svapne'pi," sleep is included as well. [109]
Because the self consisting of the three foods is manifested as the vital breath (prāṇa), the moon (indu), and likewise the waters.
Therefore, oneness has been stated; thus, the vital breath (prāṇa) is awakened by means of the names of the moon. || 110 ||
[Brāhmaṇa 1] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 905.

It is incorrect to claim that the Prāṇa is not the enjoyer simply because it does not hear the word of awakening during sleep while remaining unslumbering; for there is a distinction between the Prāṇa and the Moon.

Anticipating the objection that his failure to wake up was not due to being insentient, but rather because he was addressed by names such as "Candramas," the author says: "Of the vital breath (prāṇa).

The meaning is that this is stated in the passage revealing the nature of the threefold food: "Now, water is the body of this vital breath, its form is light, and that [light] is the moon," and so forth. || 110 ||
Let "bṛhan" and so forth serve here as an illustrative indication.
Or, by the power [of the context], for those deities whose names have not been mentioned. || 111 ||

Furthermore, having raised the objection that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) might be addressed by the name "Candra" alone because it is the self of all, yet could also be addressed by the names of the sun and others since it is the self of all, [the author] says: "Bṛhan" (Great). Here, "iha" refers to the statement of the address. Therefore, the ellipsis is that he addressed him by those names as well. Alternatively, because the vital breath being addressed is one with the *sūtra* (the cosmic thread), by its power, the unmentioned parts of the *sūtra* [are implied].

He states that [the Lord] was also addressed by them using names such as "Diti" and so forth, because of the inclusion of the name "Candra" [among those names]. This is due to the force of the context (sāmarthyāt). || 111 ||
If the vital breath were the enjoyer, it would perceive the sound as it arrives, just as in the waking state.
If he were not an enjoyer, he would not have heard, just like a stone or similar objects. || 112 ||

Having established that there is no addressing by means of names such as "Candra" because those words are not heard [by it], he concludes what was stated regarding its non-enjoyership in the waking state with the words "yadi... (if...). The construction is: "If it did not hear, it would not be an enjoyer. || 112 ||
But surely, even while this person is asleep, he is awakened by his own names?
Only the enjoyer will perceive sound, and not the non-enjoyer, which is other and insentient. || 113 ||

Regarding the claim that "there is no experiencer because the word of address is not heard," he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). Although it is appropriate for the two [the body and the self] to come together during sleep—leaving behind the waking state—in order to distinguish them, and although in that state only the experiencer would be addressed by his own names and thus hear those sounds while the non-experiencer would not, on account of its insentience; nevertheless, the intended cognition of distinction does not arise. This is the meaning. || 113 ||
Even from this, no distinction would arise; what difference, then, could there be between these two?
It is not so, because Gārgī’s position has always been determined as being specific.

Regarding how [the distinction] was not established prior to the authoritative knowledge of the unborn, eternal Brahman, he says: "Not at all. Even from what is seen, there is no discernment between the enjoyer and the enjoyed because of the doubt arising concerning the selves of Kāśya and Gārgya. Dispelling that doubt, he refutes it with: "Not so," [referring to] the vital breath desired by Gārgya.

The meaning is that he who is distinct from Kāśīśa (the Lord of Kāśī) due to his own nature is not the enjoyer; for since his state of constant activity is already established even prior to awakening, it is impossible for him not to hear sounds when the vital breath arises, and thus the absence of movement in the hands would be illogical. || 114 || 115 ||
When speech and the other [senses] have set, that one who has not yet set here is the immortal.
Indra is without rival, possessed of a body of water, and enveloped by name and form. || 116 ||

He demonstrates the very determination of the distinction: "he who has not set. Here, this means "during sleep. The reason for that is: "immortal. He states another distinction: "Indra. Anticipating the objection that sovereignty might belong to Kaśyapa as well due to the absence of any rival, he states another distinction: "in water. This is because it has been stated that water is the body of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
114 [vol2, page 612] 906 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Adhyāya]

The meaning is that for the desired Self, which is the locus of that body, there is no state of being that body, because there is a lack of evidence [for it]. He states another distinction: "Name," etc., based on the Śruti passage, "The vital breath (prāṇa) is concealed by name and form, both of which are real; but the Self is not so, for it is the 'Reality of reality'. || 116 ||
He remains pervading the entire universe, beginning with the internal self.
In whom the world is woven like warp and woof, according to the analogy of the nave of a wheel. || 117 ||
He recalls the threefold pervasiveness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that has been stated: "Adhyātma, etc. Therein he says:
"Woven" (*otam*). The connection is: "Having completely pervaded the universe, it remains. (117)
Producing a tumultuous sound, he performed his own duty in its entirety.
Even while performing [actions] in a dream, the vital breath remains just as it does during the waking state. (118)

Anticipating the objection that the form [of the dream state] is as easily accomplished within the self as has been described, and thus there would be no attainment of a specific distinction, he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "mounted upon its own activity" (*sa svavyāpārārūḍha*). Regarding the word "acting" (*kurvāṇa*): because one observes an excess of sound produced by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) during sleep even over waking, the qualifier "tumultuous" (*tumula*) is used. It does not merely produce sound; rather, it performs every kind of activity.

He says, "Ram" (the syllable *ram*), meaning "his own activity. Since the passage begins with the word "who" (*yaḥ*) in the phrase "he who has not set," the word "that" (*tat*) should be understood here [to refer back to that same subject]. The particle "api" in the phrase "even in dream" (*svapne 'pi*) is intended to include the state of deep sleep (*svāpa*). || 118 ||
Furthermore, Gārgī does not accept any other enjoyer here besides the vital breath (prāṇa).
Whether at that time or at another time, there is nothing other than the vital breath (prāṇa) that is to be enjoyed. || 119 ||

Anticipating the objection that even though the vital breath (*prāṇa*), possessing the aforementioned characteristics, remains present during sleep, there is nevertheless an absence of experience for it at that time because another experiencer has taken its place, he says: "And not... Here, "here" refers to the context of sleep under discussion. The reason for this is stated: "At that time.
Therefore, that which is to be realized must necessarily be understood as being directly present.
Because it has the nature of a cognizer through the vital breath (prāṇa), it burns just as fire would burn. || 120 ||

He states the conclusion regarding its very status as the enjoyer: "Therefore," etc. It has been said that "directly" means its proximity is unobstructed. He provides an illustration for the capacity of that which is capable [to produce] an effect when it encounters its object: "the combustible," etc.
And even though he was being informed, he did not indeed understand it.
Therefore, it is established that the vital breath (prāṇa) is not the enjoyer, because it is not conscious of its own name.

To this, he replies regarding the attainment of the hearing of the word [of the Veda]: "Not so. He states the meaning established by the method of elimination: "prā... [and so on]. The word should be divided as "abhoktā" (non-enjoyer). || 121 ||
And because he did not perceive the connection with the specific excellence of the well-spoken [teaching], he did not understand it;
for there is no possibility of non-perception on the part of an omniscient deity. || 122 ||

He raises the objection that the non-mention of his own name is due to a failure to grasp the relationship [between himself and the deity], not due to a difference in nature. He replies: "svākhyā" (his own name);
there is no failure to grasp the relationship with the deity because [the deity] is omniscient. Thus he says: "agraha" (non-grasping). || 122 ||
1. He states the measure: "O!
[vol2, page 613]
If it is argued that even in your position, the defect of non-apprehension (*agraha*) is equally present, [the following response is given].
It is not so, because there is conceit regarding the whole [body], whereas there is no ego-identification with a single part. (123)

He raises an objection, suggesting that the failure to grasp the name of the one being addressed and the resulting fault of non-selfhood are equally applicable even to the self desired by you; thus he says, "In your own position as well.

Since, according to the Kāśyapa [tradition], the desired self possesses the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding the entire aggregate of effects and instruments, it would follow that this [conceit] is absent in the mere vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is but a single part of that aggregate.
He refutes [the objection] by stating that the non-mention of its name is not due to its being a non-enjoyer; "not so," he says. || 123 ||
For when there is the utterance of a name such as "finger," that which possesses it (the finger) is not what is intended.
Thus, one who identifies with the entire body does not experience the identification with a single part of the body. (124)

He establishes this very point through an illustration: "The finger, etc. Just as when one says "hand," "foot," or "finger," Maitra does not rise up—because he identifies with the entire body and not merely with that [limb] alone—so too, because the one who desires Kāśī identifies with all organs of action and perception, there is no grasping of the name [of the vital breath] when it is merely in the place of the finger; this is not, however, because it is non-self (anātman).
This is the meaning. || 124 ||
But because the vital breath (prāṇa) is fully present within all things, both collectively and individually.
For him, there can be no lack of self-awareness due to his universal conceit, as if it were his very self.

Anticipating the objection that since the moon is also a part of the vital breath (prāṇa), it would not rise when addressed by its name because it possesses the conceit of being the whole—just as the example of the finger and so forth applies here—the author says: "Of the prāṇa... Just as the nature of "cowness" (gotva) is fully present in each individual object, the conceit of "I" is possible for the prāṇa in every instance; therefore, due to this distinction from the Self (ātman), it is improper to claim that there is no perception [of the moon] even when its name is uttered.
This is the meaning. || 125 ||
Awakening and non-awakening do not exist for consciousness, because it consists solely of immutable awareness.
For there is no awakening from another, just as there is none from the sun rising over a vessel of water.

Fearing the objection that, just like the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the conscious self (*cidātman*) also possesses fullness and thus the realization of all things is established, making both knowledge and ignorance equal, he says: "Knowledge... etc.

To the question, "How can there be the state of being a knower if it is merely immutable pure consciousness (*kūṭasthajñaptimātra*)," he replies: "The other... etc. The word "not" indicates that this is not the primary Self.

The meaning is that because it possesses knowledge dependent on the eyes and other organs, it is not the primary conscious self. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of establishing its well-known status as a knower.
Or [one might argue] that sound [is the Self]. Anticipating the doubt that "that alone is the primary Self and no other exists," he says: "Appātra" (the Self here).

The meaning is that there exists the immutable consciousness (kūṭasthabodha), which is distinct from the reflection of consciousness (caitanyābhāsa) arising from the sun in the water, just as the primary sun is distinct from its reflection. || 126 ||
Just as one's own lack of awakening is seen even through one's own conceptualization, so it is with that self.
Likewise, even though there is a state of being an enjoyer, there is likewise no awakening of consciousness in the vital breath (prāṇa).
Setting aside the incidental discussion, he raises an objection regarding the subject at hand: "By its own designation. (127)
Because the principle of the distinction between the states of being asleep and not asleep is applicable here.
This "seizing while asleep" is not logical, nor is it appropriate for one who is not asleep. || 128 ||
1. ka. ga. ‘prahāddoṣa’ | 2. ga. maitraṃ | 3. ka. maivamiti | 4. ka. ‘devābhi | 5. ka. ‘devābhi | 6. kha. nā tvappāṃ | 7. kha. ‘ṭastvadā | [vol2, page 614]
908. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]:

Since the self that has gone to Kāśī is asleep while the other is awake, and since the logic of a distinction consisting of a specific difference between them is possible, it is not proper for the name to be grasped by the one who is asleep when being addressed, whereas its non-grasping by the other is not tenable; thus he says: "supta" (asleep). 128.
Because the ear and other organs are always subordinate with respect to the primary [organ], [they do not perceive it].
When that [intellect] is awake, it is awake; when it sleeps, it sleeps under its influence.
Anticipating the objection that even for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is no grasping of its own name because its organs have been withdrawn and it is not an enjoyer, he says: "Of the ear, etc.
The meaning is that by virtue of that [the senses], the subordinate follows the principal. || 129 ||
The senses would not experience sleep if the vital breath were their primary principle.
For the ministers lie down while their master remains awake.
He clarifies the impossibility of the withdrawal of the instruments if the vital breath were the enjoyer, by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "No," and so forth. 130.
If there is no awakening because of speech using names whose referents are unestablished, [then the following applies].
The mention of that [the deity] is purposeful, because it is intended for the purpose of negating the deity's own self-nature. || 131 ||

He raises an objection, stating that because the person is addressed by names not commonly known as names for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it does not arise [from the breath], since they are distinct entities; this is expressed by the words "not well-known. He replies that the mention of the deity’s name is purposeful, as its intent lies in negating Gārgya’s underlying view that the lunar deity is the experiencer and agent—the Self—within this body; thus he says, "The deity... (131).
The non-enjoyership of the vital breath (prāṇa) is established also from its being mentioned by its own name.
For the purpose of negating the [existence of] deities, it is understood by means of the names of the moon. || 132 ||
Explaining the commentary beginning with "kevala," he elucidates what was stated [in the verse] as follows: "Of the vital breath... (132).
Because the synthesis of memory, cognition, desire, and so forth would otherwise be impossible.
The non-experiencing nature of the instruments is accepted, just as that of bodies and cognitions. || 133 ||

Nevertheless, some maintain that the senses are the self. Having raised the alternative as to whether their individuality constitutes the self or whether it belongs to their aggregate, he refutes the first position with the words "smṛti" (memory). First of all, the senses do not possess the status of an enjoyer individually, like the hand and other limbs;
for otherwise, the unification of cognitions—such as "I who saw a form now hear a sound"—would be impossible, since one [cognition] would belong to one [subject] and another to another.
The meaning is that [this is so] because it is impossible for that [to occur] when [the object] is perceived. || 133 ||
Since that which has been described as such is insentient, how could there be any possibility of its being an enjoyer?
And since consciousness is the object of enjoyment for another, there is no state of being an enjoyer for anything other than that.

He states the second [reason] as "because of insentience" (*acaityanyāt*). Just as a composite whole is untenable as being either distinct from or non-distinct from its constituent parts, so too the group of instruments—which is described as non-different from sentience—is not an enjoyer because it is insentient, like a jar; this is the meaning. He states the common argument for the refutation of both positions: "of that which is other than consciousness" (*cidanyasya*). Therefore, [the objection applies] from the perspective of consciousness (*citaḥ sakāśāt*).
...up to verse 134.
1. *Dātmarṣa* Brāhmaṇa [Vol. 2, page 615], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śākhaprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 909.
By the very logic of the "stick and cake" maxim, the sense organs are non-experiencers.
And no deity other than the vital breath (prāṇa) is logically possible. || 135 ||

He states another reason for the fact that the instruments (karaṇas) are not the enjoyer: "As with the stick" (daṇḍa). Just as when a cake is stuck to a stick and the stick is grasped, the cake is also grasped by force, so too, by that same logic, once the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) as the Self has been refuted, the non-selfhood of the instruments associated with it follows as a matter of course. Even though the vital breath, the instruments, and the lunar deity are all non-enjoyers, one might suspect that some other deity here must be the enjoyer.
He says "no. The meaning is that this is because the statement regarding the inclusion of all deities within the vital breath (prāṇa) serves as the authoritative evidence. || 135 ||
But surely, prior to that, the Sun and others were mentioned as being distinct from it?
How can that distinction regarding the domain of the deities be refuted? (136) In this regard, he raises the objection concerning a contradiction with the initial statement: "But surely," etc. (136)
It is not so for that entire [aggregate], because the vital breath (prāṇa) is the cause of its unity.
Or likewise, due to the predominance of air, as illustrated by the examples of the nave of a wheel and so forth. || 137 ||

He replies: "It is not so. He states the reason for the identity of the various deities within the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with the words "Are" (O friend). By the word "etcetera," passages such as "For he indeed is all the gods" and "Which one is the single deity? are included. Furthermore, because of the preeminence of Vāyu over Agni and the other deities, he says "Verily" (*vāva*), asserting that there is no deity apart from the Self, which is the vital breath. And this is to be seen in the *Saṃvarga-vidyā*.
The measure is one vyāma. || 137 ||
Let the aggregate itself be the enjoyer, because it is directly perceived as being associated with that [enjoyment].
But there is no possibility of an enjoyer existing apart from that [consciousness]. || 138 ||

Having stated that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are not the Self, he raises an objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to state that the gross body is likewise not the Self, beginning with the words "the aggregate" (*saṃghāta*). This means that the gross body is a collection of the four elements. The meaning of the reason is that its connection as a knower with form and other qualities is observed through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such as in the cognition "I, who am fair, see. [The opponent argues this] because of the impossibility of [an eternal] Self, since a Self distinct from these is not perceived, and there is no other means of knowledge (*māna*).
The meaning is: "and because it is not desired. || 138 ||
The state of being an enjoyer is in no way conceivable for that which is insentient.
And because consciousness is the object of enjoyment for another, like a woolen blanket, boiled rice, or water. || 139 ||
He refutes [the objection] with the words "No," and so forth. He establishes its insentience with the word "consciousness" (cit). || 139 ||
Nor is the state of being qualified by consciousness perceived through direct perception.
For the sake of perceiving the connection with consciousness, who is postulated as its knower? (140)

Furthermore, you maintain that the body qualified by consciousness (*cid-viśiṣṭa*) is the enjoyer; and regarding that qualification, there must be either perception or some other means of knowledge (*māna*). [We reply: "No," because consciousness is not an object for that [perception], nor is the other [means of knowledge] accepted [by you]. He says: "And not... Even if that which is qualified by consciousness were an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), the body or something else could not be the knower (*jñātṛ*). First, it cannot be the former, because it is impossible for one and the same thing to be both the knower and the known; nor can it be the latter, because you do not accept another cognition [to know that cognition].
Thus he said: "Consciousness," [140] |||
In this context,
nothing whatsoever is admitted as having its own independent nature apart from consciousness.
Nor could one partake in the fruit of valid cognition apart from its own purpose. (141)

Anticipating the objection that there is no need for a knower because [consciousness] is established by itself, he says: "Not here. The phrase "here" refers to both common worldly usage and the scriptures. Furthermore, since anything other than consciousness is not self-luminous—like a jar—it cannot be the Self; thus he says: "Nor... The meaning is that the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), which is the instrument of cognition, its result (knowledge), and its locus (the knower), do not exist as distinct from self-luminous consciousness. || 141 ||
For no object of knowledge whatsoever is ever observed to exist without being known by consciousness.
And manifestation does not depend on anything else, for that which is insentient cannot be a means of perception.

Furthermore, if consciousness (*cit*) were related to an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), then since consciousness itself would be an object of knowledge, there would have to be another consciousness as its knower, or it would have to be non-consciousness (*acit*). It cannot be the first case, because the plurality of consciousnesses is not established; if it is the second case, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). [The term] *cinmimīte* means that which measures consciousness.

That which is insentient (*jaḍa*) is an object of cognition (*meyam*), just like a jar; therefore, it cannot be the knower (*jñātṛ*), whether it be sentient (*cit*) or insentient (*acit*). This is the meaning. Furthermore, at the time when there is the cognition of a connection with consciousness, one must state the means of knowledge (*māna*) that perceives that [connection]; and having raised the dilemma of whether that [means] is insentient or non-insentient, he states the defect [of both options]. The word "not" (*na*) may be construed either as *na cet* or as *jaḍād ajaḍād iti*. The meaning is: because [consciousness] is itself non-insentient luminosity (*ajaḍaprakāśatva*). || 142 ||
Furthermore, when the production of perception depends upon the body, perception itself is not admitted [to exist].
And since the inferential mark (liṅga) is being inferred, how can there be the status of direct perception (pratyakṣa)? || 143 ||

Furthermore, is it your view that perception alone is the single means of knowledge for an agent possessing a specific body? In that case, is that perception [itself] the means of knowledge, or something else?

It is not the first, because perception has as its objects things such as color and their substrata, but not anything other than those; thus he says: "From the body... He refutes the second alternative with: "Of the mark (liṅga)... (143)
Likewise, when there is a connection with another object, perception is established as residing in the body.
In the accomplishment of thorough investigation, no means of valid cognition whatsoever is required.

Furthermore, he states that the synthesis [of the thought] "this was known by me" is unestablished due to the absence of a proving agent. He says: "In the same way. Just as there is a lack of evidence for the body's being qualified by consciousness, for perception having that [body] as its agent, and for that [body] alone being the means of knowledge, so too—in the case of perception which possesses a subject-object relationship through another object such as sound, and which resides in the body—[the synthesis] "this was known by me" and so forth [is likewise unestablished].

The meaning is as follows: the synthesis [of cognitions] cannot be established by perception as a means of knowledge, because perception has sound and other such objects as its domain; nor can it be established by any other means, since no such means is admitted. Therefore, due to the absence of a means of knowledge, synthesis is not established, and consequently, the enduring entity which is based upon that synthesis is not established. || 144 ||

Furthermore, for one who asserts that inference is not a valid means of knowledge, this utterance of speech would be purposeless until it has been perceived and connected with the cognition of another. (145)

As for the claim that perception alone is the only means of valid cognition, he says [in response] that this is not so, because the validity of inference is necessary. He states: "Speech," etc. Regarding the utterance of sentences such as "Bring the cow," there would otherwise be futility; for is it for one's own sake or for the sake of another? It cannot be the former, because through one's own speech, one does not gain knowledge of anything previously unknown to oneself. Nor can it be the latter, because the fact that another person has gained knowledge of that meaning from one's sentence is not perceptible to oneself. Furthermore, by the speech of another, [knowledge arises] for me...
1. It is being ground. 2. ka. kha. *bhūtiprā*. 3. *pekṣyate*. [Vol.
2, page 617] 1. Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 911.
The meaning is that since it is necessary to employ an inference—namely, "by my statement, he too will come to possess that knowledge"—otherwise the statement would be purposeless. || 145 ||
Even if one conforms to the view of one's own self, only delusion results.
Because of this lack of proficiency, no one among the virtuous wishes to give [it].
Furthermore, he states that even the composition of their own treatises is improper because it causes harm: "svātma... and so forth.

Even if one follows their treatise—which is the vision and teaching regarding their own self—there would only be delusion. For its purpose is not heaven or liberation; rather, it asserts that there is no self belonging to another world, and so on.
Because of such knowledge, no one desires to give anything to a virtuous person, but instead wishes to seize his own property; therefore—
The meaning is that one who knows the scriptures but is outwardly oriented toward sacrifices and the like becomes an atheist and shall go to hell. || 146 ||
Because there is no fear of unrighteousness or other such things, people would kill him without hesitation.
And they would forcibly seize this wealth; this is the result of their lack of discernment.

Furthermore, he states that one who composes a scripture for the sake of harming others would be insane, because through knowledge of your teaching there is an absence of fear regarding causes such as unrighteousness (*adharma*).
He says: "From unrighteousness, etc. This refers to the world of the virtuous. "They would seize" (*ādadyuḥ*) means they would take away.

Nor is it the case that a scripture which teaches the non-existence of dharma and adharma, or of heaven and hell, could be based on inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and have as its object specific individual souls.

It is logical that [the opponent’s position] is equivalent to the speech of a madman; for the diversity of observed effects necessarily depends upon a diversity of causes, as it is impossible to maintain that such [diversity] arises from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Indeed, the diversity of pleasure and so forth does not arise from those [pleasures] themselves, because the state of being an agent of action depends on differentiation. If that state were causeless, it would contradict experience; and thus, one who composes a treatise in such a manner is cast into the category of the insane and should be disregarded.
The intended meaning is "it might be so. || 147 ||
Because a specific change is observed upon pressing, [it follows that] there is a composite body.
It could never be the enjoyer of the fruits of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

He states another reason for the body’s being non-self: "Upon pressing," etc. The word "etc. (ādi) is intended to include its various sub-divisions—meaning, that which is called the gross body is a composite of the four elements. (148)
If, in this context, the status of being an enjoyer is postulated for the mere aggregate alone;
Because the aggregate is not distinct [from its parts], it would never manifest as something superior.

He clarifies what was stated by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "If... Here, the word "here" refers to the enjoyer. If the aggregate were the enjoyer, there would be no distinction in its rising [from sleep] due to the lack of difference between its being pounded and not being pounded; nor would there be a distinction in that [rising] caused by those two [actions], because even in the absence of those, no cause for prior rising is observed. Furthermore, it is not the case that the specific quality produced by pounding alone is the cause of rising, since there is no necessity for a prior rising [to occur].
This is the intended meaning.
|| 149 || Likewise, from merely slightly touching or from pressing with force;
And for that proponent according to whom the enjoyer is of a different nature from the body and so forth, [the following applies]. || 150 ||
It would be consistent because of the multiplicity of connections with causes such as dharma and so forth.
There would be a distinction in the experience caused by grinding and not-grinding. || 151 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 618] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]:
He clarifies that the composite nature is always undifferentiated. Regarding the word "īṣat" (slightly): just as one who has merely been touched by a soft touch [is struck with fear]—

The meaning is that, since there is no difference in its state even when subjected to pounding, there would likewise be no excellence in its awakening. Anticipating the objection—"In your own view as well, how can there be a difference in arising between being pounded and not being pounded?"—you respond with the words "the body, etc. The word "etc.

is intended to include the various sub-divisions thereof. This is because there is a multiplicity of causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, as well as the connection of the self with those [causes] and the resulting connection with the body.

The meaning is that, in my position, the arising [of the effect] and so forth caused by that [cause] is logical. He establishes the very consistency of the arising and so forth with the verse beginning "peṣaṇa" (grinding).
[This occurs] due to the superior, inferior, and middling nature of the causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Then this distinction in its awakening would indeed be logical. || 152 ||

He states the reason for the distinction among the causes that give rise to the aforementioned feelings: "Sukham" (pleasure). The meaning is that because of the varying degrees of the factors—such as dharma and so forth—which are the causes of the causes giving rise to pleasure, pain, perfect enlightenment, and so on, they are designated by the term "feeling" (*vedanā*). He states the result of that distinction: "Tatprabodha" (the awakening thereof). The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the self (*ātman*), which is distinct from the aggregate (*saṃghāta*). At that time...
This means: provided that there exists a specific cause for awakening, according to the principle previously stated. || 112 ||
And there is this distinction here: that by mere contact alone—
Unconscious and fast asleep, he was awakened by being squeezed and pressed repeatedly.

Having stated the possibility of a specific [result] upon awakening within one's own position, he demonstrates the certainty with the words "If it exists... and so forth. It was said that this refers to the mere act of waking from sleep. || 153 ||

Therefore, let it be understood that this [self], which has arisen together with the instruments for the purpose of churning and so forth, is the enjoyer, just as a king is [the enjoyer] along with his ministers. (154)
He states the specific result [of this practice] with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). Here, the word "iha" (here) refers to the body. || 154 ||
As if causing his own mind to enter this body which is like a corpse.
He who rose up as if blazing should be understood as the enjoyer.

He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "as if blazing" (*jvalanniva*), etc., by saying "mṛta," etc. For it is said "as if" (*iva*) because, in reality, there can be no penetration of consciousness (*cidāveśa*) into the body without the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*). Indeed, there is no actual blazing of the conscious self as there is of fire; rather, having apprehended such a manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), it is said to be "as if blazing. || 151 ||
Distinguishing [the self] by means of the qualities of anger, fear, agitation, knowledge, and dharma.
Let it be determined that he who rose up from the body is the enjoyer. || 156 ||
He explains "the piṇḍa" and so forth with the word "krodha. || 156 ||
Moreover, the vital breath (prāṇa) exists for the sake of another because it is composite, like a house and so forth.
And therefore, it is not logically possible for that which is of the nature of an object of enjoyment to be the enjoyer. || 157 ||

Having stated that the body and so forth are not the Self, he states another reason for the fact that the vital breath (prāṇa) is not the Self, beginning with the word "api" (even). He states the result of its being for the sake of another (pārārthya) with the words "tataśca" (and therefore). || 157 ||
1 kha. ga. Saṃghāta [vol2, page 619]
The vital breath (prāṇa),
situated within the body, always supports the body like a pillar.
Just as the wind is gathered within the body, so too is he.
He explains how there is a state of being combined: "of the body. This refers to either the breath of the nose or the primary vital air (prāṇa). || 158 ||
Since this is so, the vital breath (prāṇa) is therefore described as being like a house and other such things.
Therefore, the Self, being of a different nature, is perceived as distinct from the body and the attributes of the body. || 159 ||

Having reflected upon the state of being a composite (*saṃhatatva*), he states the resulting conclusion regarding its being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the body. The phrase "it is accepted as being for the sake of another" is the ellipsis to be supplied. To the question, "What follows from that being for the sake of another? he replies with "and from the body. The meaning is that there is a distinction because the body and so forth are objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*), whereas the Self is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). This is the reason based on difference in nature (*vaidharmya*). The word "non-enjoyer" (*abhuṅ*) [is used] as the reason. The word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) refers to the result of the state of being a composite.
Be patient. || 159 ||
Like a house containing a fruit that is distinct from its own parts and from things of a similar class.
Likewise, because it is composite, the vital breath (prāṇa) effects the experience of the non-composite self.

Anticipating the objection that, although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is for the sake of another like a house and so forth, it nonetheless possesses the status of being the master of the aggregate because houses and the like are seen to have that [status], he says:

"one's own self" (*svātman*). Just as a pillar and so forth are parts of one's own self such as a house, and the house itself is the whole; and just as a house is an object of enjoyment for one who is distinct from and not an aggregate of other similar houses; likewise, the vital breath, because it is an aggregate, is an object of enjoyment for that which is its own non-aggregate [self].
This is the meaning. || 160 ||

Its nature consists of its own purpose—such as existence and so forth—which is obtained independently of any external dharma, and which manifests as birth and the like known as growth, decay, and destruction of its own arising. || 161 ||
For it is indeed by observing that there is an object which is perceived solely by the one who perceives and knows its sphere.
In that same way, let the reality of the vital breath (prāṇa) and its qualities be understood. || 162 ||
Nevertheless, fearing that the Self might be considered a composite entity because it is the "residue" (the beneficiary) just like Caitra, he says: "svajanma... (His own birth, etc.).

That whose existence and manifestation are obtained without depending upon these attributes—the birth, growth, decay, destruction, name, form, and the birth of its direction (spatial orientation) regarding His own house—is independent by nature; and He [is distinct] from those [attributes] such as the house and its...

The meaning is as follows: among various objects of experience, there is one who is independent, both the seer and the knower; having perceived that object, he is the one whose existence and manifestation are attained independently of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and their attributes. It should be understood that the nature of being the object for those [vital breaths] belongs precisely to him who possesses the characteristics of the seer, the knower, and so forth. The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to indicate that the illustrative example is as much a means of proof as the logical reason (*hetu*). [The argument is: the subject under dispute is subordinate to an object untouched by its own specific attributes, because it is a composite entity (*saṃhatatvāt*).
The sense is that through the inference "like a conjoined object," the vital breaths and so forth are established as being distinct from the self. || 161 || 162 ||
But surely, in the established doctrine of Vedānta, no other entity is admitted?
Like the established doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas, [it is based] on the single reality that is the inner self. || 163 ||
In order to challenge the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that distinguish that self, the opponent states the nature of his own tenet: "But surely...
He provides an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): "The Sāṃkhya... (163).
115 [vol2, page 620] 914 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]
Through the ignorance regarding the unity of the Self, everything is imagined within the inner self.
That which consists of the vital breaths and so forth, being born of the non-self—namely, form, name, and action. (164)
Anticipating the objection that "there is no absence of another entity because of the existence of breath and so forth," he says: "In the state of oneness" (aikātmya). || 164 ||
When everything—both the imagined and the unimagined—is accepted as being none other than the Self alone.
Therefore, the statement of positive and negative concomitance is not applicable here due to their identity. || 165 ||

Dispelling the doubt regarding a real distinction between things based on their imagined and unimagined natures, he states the conclusion: "The imagined," etc. That which is established by the world as imagined—such as dreams—and that which is accepted as unimagined—such as space—all that, because it is inherently non-existent due to its insentience (jaḍatva) and other qualities, is simply the Self. Thus, since there is a single uniform essence (ekarasya) within the inner self (pratyagātman), the relation of concomitance (anvaya) and so forth cannot be established with respect to any supposed difference. This is the meaning. || 165 ||
There is neither positive concomitance nor negative concomitance for that which is imagined, because of its falsity.
And because that which is non-conceptualized is a unity, it is not established at all [as manifold]. || 166 ||

Even though there is no other non-conceptualized entity (*avastvantara*), one might suspect that it exists as something conceptualized (*kalpita*). Having raised this doubt, [the author] examines whether positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth depend upon what is conceptualized, what is non-conceptualized, or what is both conceptualized and non-conceptualized; he refutes the first alternative with the words "No," and so on. He addresses the second alternative with the words "Of the non-conceptualized," etc., because positive concomitance and the rest require a pair [of terms], whereas that [non-conceptualized reality] is non-dual (*advaya*) and beyond the scope of objects (*aviṣayatva*). In that case...

The meaning is that it is unestablished. The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of excluding the third [alternative]. The meaning is that because the consequence of duality would follow if the objects were both imagined and non-imagined, there can be no positive concomitance (anvaya) and so forth in that case. || 166 ||
Because the primary focus is on the derivation of masculine nouns, there is no fault in [the use of] *anvaya* and so forth.
But the establishment of the true nature of reality here does not occur through positive concomitance and the like alone. || 167 ||

Or, if one were to accept [the existence of] another [entity], it would follow that a real difference must be accepted; to this, he replies with the word "puruṣa" (the Person). The meaning is that, since the purpose of the statements concerning the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth—beginning with "The Self" (*ātman*) and continuing with "Which is the Self?

(*katama ātmā*) and what follows—is for the sake of knowing the Self by taking recourse to an unreal difference, there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*). Anticipating the objection that the mention of positive concomitance and so forth is redundant because that [non-duality] is established by that very [Self-knowledge], he says:

"But not... Here, "here" refers to the statement of one's own position. "Establishment" means certainty; the sense is that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth are not ultimately real. || 167 ||
Even though this [self] is imagined through ignorance, it partakes in the status of being the object of the notion of "I."
In this world, it is understood that there is an enjoyer; however, there is no proof for the existence of a non-self. || 168 ||

If it is argued that the cognition of the Self arises from the sentence, [we reply: prior to hearing that sentence, the Self has not been perceived; therefore, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the like are not easily established, because they must have a perceptible object. This is the intention. Regarding the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*): it means while this aggregate of non-Self (*anātman*), imagined by one's own ignorance, exists. "Here" means prior to hearing the sentence. It is incorrect to say that the Self was perceived even before that, on the grounds of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), because [the status of being self-luminous] depends upon the establishment of its meaning.
Anticipating the objection that "that [self] is established," he says: "But not... The meaning is: because it would follow that it is not the Self. || 168 ||
Therefore, having restated [the object] as it is established through positive and negative concomitance, [one proceeds].
Through the discrimination between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, the oneness of self is awakened by means of scripture. || 169 ||

Anticipating the objection, "If the Self is established by itself (*svataḥ-siddha*), what is the use of the sentence consisting of the *anvaya* and so forth?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Since the *anvaya* and so forth [occur] with respect to the Self which is self-established, therefore—by means of that [sentence], through the purification of the meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (you) known as the distinction between the enjoyer and so forth—one restates that [Self] without overstepping it and makes its identity with Brahman known by means of the sentence. Thus, the sentence beginning with *anvaya* serves for the purpose of purifying the meaning of *tvaṃ*.
And for the sake of the knowledge of oneness; thus, the meaning is that both [the individual soul and the Supreme Self] possess purposefulness. || 169 ||
For it is observed that in all its effects, there is indeed something other than consciousness.
Even the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established here through the negation (*apavāda*) of the effect.
If one asks, "Then what kind of positive and negative concomitance are those by which the meaning of 'Thou' (*tvam-artha*) is purified? he says: "Consciousness" (*cit*).

The persistence of consciousness is observed throughout all the effects of ignorance (*avidyā*) along with its appearance; and that [consciousness], as well as ignorance and its products, is [realized] through the negation of them within the Inner Self (*pratīci*).

The meaning is that negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also established from this; thus, the Self (*ātman*), which is non-deviating, is the witness, whereas the non-Self (*anātman*), which is deviating, is the object witnessed—such is their nature. The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies that there is well-known recognition of these stated positive and negative concomitances both in the world and in the Veda.
The word "iha" (here) refers to the inner witness (*pratyak*), who is the substratum for the negation of ignorance and its effects. || 170 ||
There would be a fault in the proof of a single self, and that proof is not real.
For its establishment is based on valid means of cognition; therefore, it is not contradicted. || 171 ||

As for the statement that "positive and negative concomitance [are possible] because of identity" and so forth, he accepts the first alternative—namely, that such [concomitance] is impossible whether that identity is known or unknown—by means of the following dilemma. Regarding the term *aikātmya* (oneness): the "defect" refers to the impossibility of positive and negative concomitance. Then, raising the objection that since oneness is always known due to its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*), there could never be positive and negative concomitance, he says: "If its establishment... This refers to the thing (*vastu*).

If it is argued that the perfection which constitutes its own nature (*svarūpa-siddhi*) is not opposed by [the requirements of] positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, then—fearing that it would exist at all times due to the absence of any opposing factor—the author says:

"It is based on valid cognition" (*prāmāṇikī*). The phrase "opposed by positive concomitance and so forth" is to be supplied as the remainder. The word "for" (*hi*) is used to establish that the knowledge derived from valid means of proof (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) is indeed opposed to that [perfection]. The resulting conclusion is that because that [knowledge] is opposed to it, the perfection of its own nature is not contradicted by it, since it is the very means of establishing it (*sādhakatvāt*).
He said: "Therefore," [verse 171].
Nor is there a determination of oneness that depends upon human activity.
Since its fruit has been fully accomplished, any further expectation is fruitless. || 172 ||

Anticipating the objection that "its establishment through a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇikī*) is not in contradiction with it, just as when a jar or the like has been cognized there is no further need for another means of knowledge, so too when oneness has been cognized there can be a requirement for positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the like," he says: "And not... Because once that [oneness] is ascertained from the sentence, its fruit—the destruction of bondage along with its causes—is already accomplished; therefore, since any requirement for positive concomitance and the like after the knowledge of oneness would be useless, [the sentence operates] with respect to a mental auxiliary (*mānasahakāriṇi*).
The meaning is that there is no dependence on that [former cognition]; therefore, only the cognition that contradicts it is authoritative. || 172 ||
As long as one does not directly perceive the non-dual Self through scripture, [one remains bound].
For the sake of realizing the nature of the self through positive concomitance and so forth, who indeed can prevent that? || 173 ||
Having accepted the impossibility of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth once identity is known, he refutes the second [position] with the words "yāvat tu" (as for...). 173.
Ignorance and that which arises from it are indeed the Self itself, whose true nature remains unknown.
Through the awakening to that true reality, there is the sublation of that [false appearance], just like the sublation of a snake [mistaken for a rope] or similar illusions. || 174 ||

If it is argued that there must be an admission of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth because ignorance serves as an auxiliary cause for the cognition of the Self, then one might suspect that duality would also be required by that [ignorance]. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And ignorance... The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that its being of the nature of the Self as described is well-established by scripture. Furthermore, since the sublation of all duality through the knowledge of the Self is admitted—just as the sublation of a snake occurs upon the cognition of the rope—the possibility of real duality does not arise; thus he says: "That..."
Or so it is said. || 174 ||
Even for things such as ropes that are already established, [error arises] through reliance on another imagined [entity].
Just as there is the removal of what was previously established [as a fault], so it is here with respect to the Self.

Anticipating the objection that even the knowledge of the inner self (*pratyag-jñāna*) must be sublated, or else it would be unsublatable—if the former, it could not function as a sublater; if the latter, the sublation of all duality would remain unestablished—he says: "Of those [entities] already established" (*klṛptānām*). The genitive case here has the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*). || 175 ||
Therefore, the enjoyer is that which is to be measured by a single means of valid cognition; the object of enjoyment is other than that.
Even though there may be deviation among the objects of enjoyment, the enjoyer remains non-deviant.

Having taken up the imagined distinction prior to the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he concludes the result [of the inquiry], such as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, with the words "the inward" (*pratyak*).

Having concluded the result that the Self is indeed the self-luminous principle of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*), while the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are non-Self because they are objects of perception, he concludes the positive concomitance and so forth with the words "of the objects of enjoyment" (*bhogyānām*). || 176 ||
Even though the vital breath (prāṇa) is being awakened with effort by means of [the mantras] beginning with "bṛhan,"...
When he did not perceive [the truth] at all, he then made another effort.
Having rubbed him many times with his hand, the King of Kāśī also awakened him as he slept.
Then, due to the agitation arising from the water, he regained consciousness.

Having established the Self as distinct from the two bodies through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and other means, he restates the explanation of the scriptural passage beginning with "Him" (*tam ityādi*).
The phrase "by [the words] 'Bṛhan' and so forth" refers to the effort made through repeated address. Having introduced the passage beginning with "With his hand" (*taṃ pāṇinā*), he explains it.
Regarding the word "wheel" (*cakra*), he restates the meaning of the passage beginning with "He, indeed" (*sa ha*). The term "pressing" (*āpeṣa*) [is explained]. 177–178.
This is the nature of causes: that they depend upon other conditions.
The emergence of its own effect from the sky is like the appearance of clouds. || 179 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the self possesses the agency of rising by virtue of its independence—and since being an agent is defined by such characteristics—what need is there for grinding and the like, the author says: "Of the causes. Just as the sky, though it is the cause for the arising of clouds, still depends on the east wind and other factors, so too the self, as the agent of rising, must depend upon grinding and other means; for the definition of an agent is one who employs other causal factors while not being employed by them oneself. || 179 ||
When the intellect and other faculties arise from the Supreme Self due to its being pressed [by the individual soul], [the following occurs].
The arising of the Seer is never direct, like that of space within a jar.

Anticipating the objection that the "arising" (*utthāna*) of the self is its awakening from sleep and that, since this awakening is its very nature (*svarūpa*), it does not depend on a cause, he says: [Note: The provided text contains manuscript variants for the commentary portion, which have been transcribed as they appear. [Vol. 2, page 623] The arising of the self from sleep is its awakening; because this is its essential nature (*svarūpa*), it does not depend upon a cause—this is the doubt, and thus he says: 1. kha. ...awakening... 2. kha. ...then... 3. kha. ...or here... 4. ka. ...non-occurrence... [End of excerpt]

"From pressing" (āpeṣāt). When the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, which were merged in the unperceived inner self (*pratīci*) during deep sleep, arise from the Supreme Self due to karma and other causes that produce the waking state, the emergence of consciousness is figuratively spoken of as their production;
it is not a direct production of them, just as the production of space within a jar is not the production of space itself. He states the reason for this here.
"Always," [it is said]. || 180 ||
Therefore, through the lack of realization, it should be understood that the vital breath (prāṇa) is not the enjoyer.
But through awakening, the soul is determined to be solely the enjoyer. || 181 ||
Having established the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, he concludes that very meaning of the sentence beginning with the reason with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 189 ||
Just as things that are not themselves burning possess the quality of being burners through contact with that which burns.
Similarly, the state of being an enjoyer belongs to the divine self through its conjunction with the enjoyer. || 182 ||

If it is argued that the state of being an enjoyer belongs to the person alone, then how is the status of the vital deity (prāṇadevatā) established in that regard? To this, he says: "Of those that are not burning," etc. (182).
Having discriminated the Self as solitary from the body, the senses, and the mind.
Then, having pointed out the enjoyer, the king questioned Gārgya.

Having restated what has been said [in the preceding verse], he explains the meaning of the words "sa ha" and so forth. He says "deha" (the body). The word "atha" (now) is used to show the opportunity for the question that will be stated immediately after the [instruction on] discrimination. || 183 ||
He who was awakened by pressing is distinct from the vital breaths and the other [elements].
Who was this person before his awakening, and from where did he come? || 184 ||
He states the nature of the inquiry: "By pressing," [verse 184].
In the sense of connection with the internal organ, "vijñāna" is used in the agentive [sense].
The term *pratyaya* may have the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), or it may be derived from the abstract state (*bhāva*) in relation to an action (*kriyā*). || 185 ||

If one intends to express the relationship between the word "consciousness"—which ends in the *lyuṭ* suffix—as being synonymous with the internal organ, then the suffix would have to denote the agent (since the internal organ is the knower). However, [in the compound *vijñānamaya*], the suffix does not denote the agent. Therefore, it is established that the suffix *mayaṭ* here signifies abundance. Thus, the term "consisting of consciousness" refers to the internal organ characterized by an abundance of consciousness. Because it knows by virtue of being an agent, the internal organ (antahkarana) is "consciousness" (vijñāna). When the word *vijñāna* denotes the eyes and other sense organs, then the suffix (*pratyaya*) must have the sense of an instrument; thus, "that by which one cognizes" is consciousness, meaning the eyes and so forth.
When its connection is with the action, then "cognition" (*vijñapti*) is consciousness; the meaning is that consciousness would then be the action itself. || 185 ||
"When there is a desire to express the object of cognition, the word *śabda* would be derived in the sense of the object (*karman*)."
Because the aforementioned [meanings] do not exist in the inner self (pratyagātman), the word has a figurative sense (*prāyārtha*) there.

When [the word *vijñāna*] refers to things such as a bank (*taṭa*), it means that "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) would be a jar or the like; this is what he states by the word "object of knowledge" (*prameya*).

Since the word "consciousness" is employed for these meanings, and because it is not used in its primary sense elsewhere, [it is absent] in the case of the immutable inner self (*kūṭastha*), due to the absence of the aforementioned agency and so forth.

He states that the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of "consisting mostly of" (*prāyārtha*), because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which is the object of the speaker's proficiency in debate—is subject to modification, whereas the inner self (*pratyak*) is not subject to such modification.
[This refers to] "of those as described," etc. (verse 186).
[Vol.
2, Page 624] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter:
"Due to the delusion of pervasion by the intellect and other faculties, which are manifested by ignorance like one's own reflection..."
Because of the conceit of identifying with that [intellect], the self possesses the nature of being composed of consciousness (vijñānamaya). || 187 ||

Just as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) undergoes modification, the Self—being unattached—cannot possess that same nature due to its lack of connection with the intellect (buddhi) and so forth; anticipating this doubt, he says: "svābhāsā" (having its own reflection). He explains that this is merely an illusion produced by the pervasion of the intellect and other faculties arising from ignorance (avidyā), which possesses the reflection of the Inner Self (pratyagābhāsavatī). He states the result of this delusion: "tadātmatva" (the state of being that [intellect]). He states the fruit of the error: "vijñāna" (consciousness). || 187 ||
Because it is perceived as a witness and because it is the substratum of the intellect and other faculties, [it is called the witness].
Therefore, it is generally intended that [the fruit] has no agent as its cause. || 188 ||

He states another reason for the fact that the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of "mostly" (*prāya*): "By being a witness" (*sākṣitvena*). And because it is impossible for it to have the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), he says "likewise":
"As a non-agent" (*akāraka*). Since it lacks the nature of action and so forth, he states the reason for its being a witness: "Therefore" (*tena*). || 188 ||
For, being conceited in his knowledge, he understands every object.
Therefore, the state of being composed of consciousness [arises] from the non-awakening of the inner self. || 189 ||

Anticipating the objection as to how one who is inherently omniscient could have intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth as primary, he states that omniscience occurs precisely through the door of its connection with ignorance; thus, it is logical that [the scripture] has a general sense. He says: "Since... (verse 189).
Or rather, because it apprehends the object of cognition as distinguished by consciousness.
Therefore, because the internal self is perceived as non-different from that [Brahman], it follows that its nature consists primarily of being the object of knowledge.
He clarifies that the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of "predominance" (*prāya*) by means of another method, [beginning with] the words "by consciousness" (*vijñānena*).

The connection with the second half of the verse is as follows: because the Self (*pratīc*), through its internal organ—which is denoted by the word "consciousness"—pervades objects of knowledge by means of its mental modifications (*vṛtti*), the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of predominance. || 190 ||
Having stated that [the self] consists of consciousness, it is further described as consisting of earth and the other elements.
And because of the prohibition of remedies, its purpose as a means of atonement is appropriate. || 199 ||

By stating that the suffix *mayaṭ* does not have the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*) when there is a direct scriptural indication (*śrauta-liṅga*), he concludes that it has the sense of "predominance" (*prāya*). He says: "vijñāna... etc. For it is not admitted that the inner self (*pratīc*) is a modification of earth and so forth; thus, by virtue of its association with those terms, its being "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) is also appropriate for it. Furthermore, since existence and other qualities are negated in that context by both Śruti and Smṛti, the meaning is that [the suffix] has the sense of predominance. || 199 ||
Since all things whatsoever are without self because they are merely conceptual constructs, [the Self] is non-conceptual.
The Puruṣa fills [the world], just as a girdle [encircles] the snakes and other creatures that crawl before one's eyes. 192.

He states the meaning of the word *puruṣa*: "of the non-self" (*anātmanaḥ*). Just as a rope, being unimagined, fills [the space occupied by] imagined things such as a snake, so too, because non-selves are imagined and an imagination without a substratum is impossible, the Self—remaining unimagined as the substratum for them—exists filling all others entirely; therefore, He is the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. || 992 ||
This very proficiency [is established] here through the examination of the intended meaning (tātparya).
For it begins with "He indeed" and concludes with the determination "not by this," and so forth. || 193 ||

Why is the Bhāṣya beginning with "purīśayanāt" (because of sleeping in the city) disregarded? To this he says: "vyutpattiḥ" (etymological derivation). The meaning is that here only this etymology—"He is called *puruṣa* because of his fullness (*pūrṇatva*)"—is to be accepted, since the purport of the sentence is seen to lie in its being full within itself. In that regard, the purport of the Śruti is as follows:
[vol2, page 625]

He states the reason [for this] with the words: "That indeed, this person... (sa vā ayam puruṣaḥ). Having introduced the person with the phrase "in all [beings]" (*sarvāsu*), his fullness (*pūrṇatva*) is determined by the passage beginning with "nothing whatsoever remains unattained by him" (*nainena kiñcanānāvṛttam*). Thus, the meaning is that the purport (*tātparya*) of the Śruti is established regarding that fullness. [The text continues: "He is... (*saṃdi-*)...
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that the determination [of the matter] occurs from the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the *gva*. || 193 ||
This, then, is the statement of the meaning of the words; now follows the statement of the relationship.
Regarding the question "Who is this? and so forth, what is the purpose of this introduction? (194)
Having restated the discussion concerning the categories such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) that has already occurred, he promises to state the connection with what follows.
Regarding the phrase "this [is]," he expresses the expectancy for the sake of stating the connection: "of the question," etc. (194).
Some explain it as being rooted in the *Coka*, while others say it is from the *Prabha*.
They declare this for one who has arisen for the sake of realizing the true nature of reality. || 195 ||
In that regard, he states the system of Bhartṛprapañca: "The objection," etc. This means "containing that [objection]. He indicates his own view with the words "another," etc. || 195 ||
If this [agency] were the inherent nature of the person, then even though the instruments exist, [agency would still occur].
Tell me, why is there this occasional agitation of his? (196)

Anticipating the question of how they explain the statement containing the objection, [the author] states the meaning of the corresponding commentary (*bhāṣya*)—namely, "of this person" (*puṃso'sya*)—to address the point: if the enjoyer is by nature consciousness, then while the instruments (the senses) are present, why is there only occasional awakening? Furthermore, the meaning is that prior to liberation (*apavarga*), the instruments are always existent. Awakening, moreover, has both the Self and the non-Self as its objects. The word "this" (*asya*) refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

This is the statement of the author: the construction is that, in response to such a question, "let this matter be explained as it is. The sense is that because the Self, whose nature is consciousness and who possesses the instruments [of perception], is always attained to awakening, there is no sleep. || 196 ||
Or, having abandoned this body, a person has gone to another land.
Or, if it were destroyed, from where could it come again to assume a body? Let this be explained. (197)
He says that even upon entering deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is no deliverance: "Having departed," etc. For it has been said:
"But if, having departed from this [body], he were not present [there] or had perished, how could there be a return? (197)
This ought to have been asked by the gatekeeper; however, because he was a disciple, he did not urge him to do so.
Nevertheless, it does not remain indifferent, because it itself accepts [the existence of] cognition. (198)

Anticipating the objection—"Since he has accepted discipleship, all this ought to have been asked by the gatekeeper; why then did he not ask it?"—the author says that it was because of ignorance. He states: "It ought to have been asked. As they say: "This very thing ought to have been asked by the gatekeeper, for it is the disciple who should prompt [the inquiry].
Then, one might suspect that having seen Gārgya as ignorant and his questioning ceased, it would have been appropriate for the king to remain indifferent; anticipating this, the author says:

"Not at all. [The word] *inaḥ* means a master or a king. He says this because the King had previously promised to produce in Gārgya the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Regarding the word *bodhaya*: it has been stated— "When the disciple does not understand the point being urged and the teacher desires to explain that matter, then he himself raises an objection and provides the explanation. (198)
1 [vol2, page 626] 920 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Second Adhyāya]
Having made a vow, one does not turn back without having fulfilled it.
The vow of the true person (satpuruṣavrata) is that which accords with one's request; thus it is called the "true person" vow. || 199 ||

Fearing that the King might abandon him even though he had already made his promise upon seeing that Gārgya was unskilled in answering questions, [the teacher] said, "Under the influence of... (adhina iti).

The meaning is that because Ajātaśatru is a virtuous man, once he hears of the teacher's conduct, it is impossible for him to remain indifferent even upon perceiving that the student is unskilled. || 199 ||
If its consciousness were immutable, how could it be occasional?
If awakening were impermanent, then it would be occasional and thus purposeful.

Having stated the reason for Gārgya’s illumination and for the King’s lack thereof, the author raises an objection regarding the phrase "having left this": "The immutable is his. The meaning is that the consciousness constituting the nature of this person is immutable (*kūṭastha*) and not occasional; therefore, because its knowledge is immutable, the Self has neither gone elsewhere nor perished during deep sleep. [Objection: This contradicts the experience, "I did not know anything at all."

The proponent of the previous position says, "That [is] occasional. Although it is logical that consciousness is occasional because of its impermanence as established by experience, he says, "In the view [of yours]," to show that this does not resolve the impossibility of such occasional knowledge for the person mentioned in the phrase "of this person" (*puṃso'sya*). Alternatively, even though Gārgya did not ask the question, [the author] states the reason for the King’s asking it and [then] explains the inquirer’s intention.

Having proposed the alternative as to whether one’s own knowledge is eternal or non-eternal, [the opponent] adopts the first: "He is immutable" (*kūṭastho 'sya*). [The author] refutes this by contradicting experience: "It is occasional" (*kādācitkam*). He restates the second position: "In your view" (*mataḥ*). In that case, it would be logical for the Self to possess occasional knowledge only if the Self were of the nature of non-consciousness (*acit-svabhāva*); and if it were of the nature of non-consciousness, there would be a loss of its essential nature (*svarūpa-hāni*).
Considering it to be *niriti*, he said: "It is occasional. || 200 ||
His identification with the body and so forth is occasional and has a cause.
Its status as a witness to coming and going is eternally such because it is without cause.
Refuting the statement of another which contains a challenge in the form of a question, [the author] refutes the impossibility of occasional knowledge for this person mentioned here [in the verse].

Regarding the phrase "in the body and so forth": for this Self residing in the body, occasional cognition in the form of various forms of identification (*abhimāna*) is logical, because it has merit (*dharma*) and other factors as its cause; when that [cause] is awakened for the sake of yielding its fruit, such occasional [cognition] for that Self is logical due to the identification with the body and so forth.
The meaning is that it possesses the nature of pure consciousness (*cit-kaja-jñāna*). How, then, is it of that very nature? To this he says: "By scripture" (*āgama*).
The meaning is that the Self's nature as consciousness, by virtue of being the witness of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, is indeed eternal, because it does not depend on any cause. || 201 ||
For this very reason, it has been taken away from those virtuous ones who depend upon causes.
Therefore, arising after having not previously existed is occasional, and thus it does not entail any fault.

One might object: "Let it be granted that the identification with the body and so forth, even when produced by merit (dharma) and the like, is eternal, because merit and the like are always possible; therefore, there can be no state of deep sleep (suṣupti).

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This [is not so]. Because it is the inherent nature of all effects to come into being after not having existed, the identification with the body and so forth—though produced by merit and the like—is itself an effect and thus possesses that same inherent nature. Furthermore, although merit and the like continue in an uninterrupted stream, they are nonetheless subject to interruption at the level of their specific manifestations (vyakti).

The sense is that existence is constant, and since there is no restriction on the effect even when the cause exists, such restriction occurs only within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*); therefore, the state of deep sleep is not unestablished.
The phrase "occasional" refers to the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 202 ||
