Because the reply is contrary to the meaning of the question, it does not have such a meaning.

Regarding the objection that "if his consciousness were immutable" (*kūṭastha*) and so forth, he replies with the word "the inner self" (*pratīcī*). Since it has been stated that at the time of sleep the individual soul (*jīva*) resides in the inner self alone, and that upon waking it returns from that very place—as will be explained in the subsequent refutation—the meaning of the question and the answer becomes clear.

Because, according to your way of explaining, the meaning of the question and the answer would be contrary [to this], it is not tenable for the question to have the meaning you have proposed; therefore, in your position, it is not [the case].
The meaning is that it proceeds as a question containing a challenge. || 203 ||
And since the means for going and so forth reside only in the body, how [could they exist] otherwise?
Neither the movement of the person to another place nor its destruction is logical.

Regarding the passage beginning with "having abandoned this," he says: "movement and so forth. Here, "and so forth" (ādi) refers to arrival; "instruments" (sādhanāni) refers to the feet and other limbs. He says "nor even... because its destruction is not logical, as it would preclude rising again and lead to the fallacy of acquiring what was not earned (akṛtābhyāgama), and so on. || 204 ||
Because the direct realization of Brahman has been promised [as the goal].
Therefore, it is appropriate to explain directly the true nature of both the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment. || 205 ||

Having established the opponent’s view—which was indicated by the aphorism *codyaikamūlām*—through the passage beginning with *puṃso 'sya*, and having refuted it with the passage beginning with *dehādiṣu*, [the author] now begins to state his own view, which was hinted at in the passage *idānīm apare yāthātmyapratipattyartham*. He says: "Directly" (*sākṣāt*).

Since the knowledge of immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) was promised in the words "I shall indeed make you know," for that purpose the nature of the seer and the seen must be explained; therefore, regarding the pure meaning of the term "as it truly is" (*yathāvat*), [he proceeds].
The meaning is: "the cognition of the sentence-meaning. || 209 ||
Form produced by causes such as karma is unreal, because it lacks continuity.
It is signless (animitta) because it is always non-deviating from itself. || 206 ||
"Prior to awakening, its form consists of actions and effects devoid of an agent."
[This] is intended to be made understood by the enjoyer who resides within our sphere of experience. || 207 ||

1.1 He explains the nature of the visible object by distinguishing it from the seer: "Karma, etc. The world is produced by karma, knowledge, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and so forth, [which arise] from ignorance (*avidyā*).

The meaning is that the non-self (*anātman*) is not [the witness], because it deviates due to its absence during states such as deep sleep. He distinguishes the nature of the seer from the seen by saying, "without cause.
The meaning is that the innate, immutable form of the Self is always non-deviating, precisely because it does not depend on any external cause.
Anticipating the objection that the aforementioned reality of deep sleep is not accepted by Gārgī, he says, "prior... [and so forth]. [This refers to] the word *asmat-pratyaya*...

The meaning is that the King’s intention was to make Gārgya understand the unchanging nature of the Self, which exists as the witness therein amidst the beloved ego; therefore, Gārgya’s disagreement is irrelevant to that purpose. || 206 || 207 ||
"Because for him, prior to awakening, there was not even the slightest effect to be produced by karma and so forth."
Because it is perceived by a means of knowledge directed inwardly, this [self] has that as its intrinsic nature. || 208 ||
922 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Adhyāya]:

Since not even the slightest duality, such as the effects of knowledge and so forth, is perceived during sleep and similar states due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this Self is the aforementioned Consciousness— [vol2, page 628] [continues]...the Self which is the substratum of all things. Therefore, the Self is established as being of the nature of pure consciousness, devoid of all distinctions. Thus, the conclusion is reached that the Self is non-dual and eternally free. This concludes the discussion on the nature of the Self as presented in the second chapter. (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be the beginning of a commentary on the second chapter of the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad*, specifically addressing the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and the non-dual nature of the Self.)
The meaning is that this is based on the Vedic scripture stating, "Indeed, seeing its own nature, one does not see [it]. || 208 ||
Who was he before awakening, and from where has he come?
"O Gārgya, tell us this: what is the limit for our stay and for our departure? (209)

Having indicated the intended connection between the preceding and following sections in the commentary, he states the meaning of the two questions with the words "Where? He clarifies the two points with the words "In the case of... (sthitāv iti). || 209 ||
This [self] was not elsewhere than the facing one, nor did it come from anything else.
If there were indeed agency, then this would not be an illusion. || 210 ||

Having explained the literal meaning of those two verses, he states their intended meaning: "abhūt" (it was). If this Self, while remaining in deep sleep, had been elsewhere, or if it had come from another, then the worldly transaction of action, agent, and result would be real;
but if its staying and coming are both self-limiting and there is no other [substratum], then this transaction must be illusory, because such a thing is impossible in a single entity.
The meaning is that these are two questions according to his intention. || 210 ||
Where it is said, "where [there is] another," and where it is said, "but where [there is] this."
Such is the effect of ignorance and knowledge; and thus the Śruti has declared.

He states the proof for the erroneous nature of conventional usage such as action and for the reality of its absence, beginning with the words "Where... The construction is as follows: in that context, the first scripture, following our own explanation, has stated the conventional usage of action and so forth, which is the effect of ignorance; the second scripture, however, has likewise declared the other [effect], namely the absence of conventional usage such as action, which is the effect of knowledge. || 219 ||
Because Vālāki was unable to speak or ask in return, [the king] departed with speed from that place.
Kāśya himself proceeded to explain the meaning of the two questions.
He explains the passage beginning with "tadu ha" and so forth. [The phrase] "vaktum" (in order to speak) introduces the subsequent response. [The word] "tataḥ" (from that) [introduces it]. || 212 ||
Even though you were asked, this which was known by me was not understood by you.
You ought to listen with right-mindedness to this reality as it is being explained. || 213 ||
He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "yadapṛcchāma" (what we asked) as follows: "by that which was asked. || 213 ||
Wherein this one, having become thus asleep, [heard] the sound of his own name being called.
This is not the sign of tears; listen to this sign of the hand.

He restates the sentence beginning with "where" (*yatra*). Regarding "where": he explains the meaning of the phrase "he became asleep" (*supto 'bhūt*) by saying "by his own name. Regarding "where": he explains the meaning of the locative case (*saptamī*) by saying "for which cause. The meaning is that the abiding in Brahman through the withdrawal of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is the cause for the absence of specific cognition. He states that the sentence beginning with "that of these" (*tad eṣām*) is intended to demonstrate that [cause]: "that is the cause for that. (214)
Since a threefold nature is observed in the stages of the vital breaths, beginning with the intellect (buddhi).
The genitive case here, "of these," is employed by way of a metaphorical indication (bhukti). || 215 ||

2, Page 629] 1. *Brahmaṇam* | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 923.

He states the intended meaning of the use of the genitive case of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) in the word "of these" (*eṣām*) with the words "the threefold nature" (*traividhyam*). Among the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—...
The meaning is that the genitive of specification (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed because, among those [many] objects, one perceives three objects and desires to grasp one of them. || 215 ||
There is the appearance of direct perception, and another is the conformity with causes.
And thus, the senses, whose nature is that of instruments, are colored by external objects. || 216 ||

What are those three categories? He states them: "The inward," and so forth. The term *pratyak* means "inward" or "reflected"; *bhāsa* means "appearance," specifically the appearance of the Self (*ātmabhāsa*). Among these, the genitive case in the word *eṣām* ("of these") is used in the sense of "for the sake of grasping" those vital breaths (*prāṇas*). He qualifies them with the words "external," etc., in order to manifest their true nature as instruments (*karaṇa*), which they could not do without their causal nature (*kāraṇātmatva*). || 216 ||
Because the entire range of effects, beginning with cognition, has the person as its cause for manifestation.
Therefore, the projection and withdrawal of the intellect and other faculties are dependent upon karma.

In order to explain that the Self abides in its own nature due to the exhaustion of karma and other factors during the forthcoming state of deep sleep (*svāpa*), the author intends to discuss the bondage caused by karma and so forth;

he first states that karma is the cause of that [bondage] with the words "of the intellect, etc. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because of such scriptural texts as, 'Its upward movement and withdrawal, its arising and submergence, have karma as their cause. (297)
"He is the enjoyer by virtue of the manifestation of his own self, but he is the agent due to the cause of ignorance."
For the supreme subject is said to be both the enjoyer and the agent, being undifferentiated from the two. || 218 ||

He states that both the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*) are causes of bondage: "One's own self," etc. Fearing an objection regarding the contradiction with established doctrine—that there is one enjoyer due to the power of the reflection and another agent due to ignorance—he says: "The two," etc. Because something other than the Supreme exists as either an effect or an object of enjoyment, the particle *hi* is used for the purpose of determining that both of these belong to that [Supreme] alone. It is the enjoyer alone, and not...
The word "ca" (and) is used to refute the view that [the self] is the agent. || 218 ||
When the action of one who applies themselves to the fruit while awake becomes magnified.
Because the causes for emergence are absent at that time, he remains inactive while sleeping.

Since the state of being an enjoyer and so forth exists there at all times, he states [the following] regarding why there is sleep there: "jāgrad" (waking). "Vyutthānam" means awakening. There is a word-break as "akartā" (non-agent). Non-agency is also an indicator for non-enjoyership. || 219 ||
Agency is dependent on an instrument; by the agent, the object is employed.
From that, there is enjoyment impelled by karma, and from that, the arising of formative predispositions (saṃskāra). || 220 ||

In that case, one might argue that because of the absence of both bondage and its cause during deep sleep, there is liberation from which there is no returning; to this he says: "The enjoyer," etc. The meaning is that because the latent impressions of transmigratory existence and ignorance persist during deep sleep, there is no liberation. || 220 ||
This insentient person is conditioned by the formative forces (saṃskāra) such as pleasure and pain.
Impelled by passion, hatred, and so forth, one then engages [in action] once again. || 221 ||

He states that both latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*) are causes for further transmigration through the gateway of passion (*rāga*) and so forth. [The verse says] "happiness" (*sukha*):
the meaning is that an ignorant person, conditioned by happiness and the like, and impelled by passion and so forth, transmigrates once again. || 221 ||
1 ma. cakāra | [vol2, page 630] 924 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter— ]
Furthermore, these [elements] possess both mutual causality and likewise mutual effectuality.
Therefore, prior to awakening, this self possesses unsevered mental formations (saṃskāras).

He restates what has been said regarding the mutual relationship of cause and effect among the states of being the enjoyer and so forth, with the words "mutually. He states the result of their being causes and effects for one another with the words "by that. 222.
It is unconnected with ignorance and established as false cognition.
This supreme being wanders incessantly through the cycle of births from Brahmā down to a stationary pillar.

He states that if latent impressions (vāsanā) persist prior to knowledge, the result is the continuity of saṃsāra: "Ignorance" (avidyā), etc. The meaning is that the Supreme Self itself, being ignorant and having ascended to false knowledge, wanders perpetually through various kinds of wombs. || 223 ||
Upon the exhaustion of the karma of the waking state, he takes up all mental impressions (bhāvanās).
[He is] one whose nature is unawakened, yet who has arisen in the form of mind, intellect, and so forth.
"By that which is born from its own intrinsic nature" refers to the agent of grasping.
"The agent who appears within direct perception is called the field (kṣetrajña).

Having explained the meaning of the word "of these" (*eṣām*) through the passage beginning with "its threefold nature," the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) has been stated by the passage beginning with "of the intellect and so forth.

Now, having restated that meaning, he states the meaning of the phrase "taking up consciousness" (*vijñānam ādāya*) with the verse beginning "waking. [This refers to] the grasping of objects by the external organs.
The capacity known as *bhāvanā*—which bestows all waking experiences—is taken up by the sleeping person when the karma that produces such enjoyment is exhausted; he then lies in the ether (*ākāśa*).

In this context, the meaning is that the agent of "taking up" (*ādāya*) is expressed by the suffix (the gerundive). He states the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*): "not being awakened" (*asaṃbuddha*).

For that ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is consciousness itself, has given rise to the mind, intellect, and so forth; and [the person] is pervaded by that which is born from primordial ignorance and is designated as having the nature of a substrate (*adhi*).

The meaning is that the instrumental case in "by the instrument of the reflection of consciousness" (*cidābhāsena*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇārthe*). He analyzes the agent of the act of taking (*ādāna*), which was indicated by the suffix *-lyap*:

"the innermost" (*pratyak*). The meaning is that this very one who is illuminated—the individual soul (*jīva*)—is the agent of the taking; he is the limit, the end, and the substratum of the manifestation of consciousness, that is, of its reflection. Or rather, it means that he is such because his essential nature is the reflection of consciousness. (224, 225)
Consciousness, being grasped, possesses the capacity to be directed toward its object.
In this context, what is to be grasped from speech and the other vital breaths (prāṇas) is the coloring of their respective objects.

Explaining the meaning of the term "of the vital breaths" (prāṇānām), he clarifies the cognition of the act of taking up, which is called "prior cultivation" (pūrvabhāvanā), with the words "being taken up. The word "here" (iha) refers to the statement within the sentence. He states the meaning of "turned toward the objects" (viṣayonmukham) as "the coloring by objects" (viṣayāñjanam). The meaning is that the capacity of speech and the other organs to grasp while in contact with their respective objects is the act of taking up (ādānakarma). || 226 ||
In this context, the powers (śaktis) are understood as the instruments (karaṇas) by virtue of their causal nature.
In this context, the Supreme Self is the grasper, whose form is non-different from its own manifestation. || 227 ||

The meaning of the sentence has been stated thus: the individual soul (*jīva*), having withdrawn the capacity of the senses to grasp objects through the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), rests in the unperceived Brahman, which is like space. Now, he states another meaning: "The powers" (*śaktayaḥ*). The instruments (*karaṇa*)—that is, the cognitions (*vijñāna*)—which possess the power to grasp objects and are capable [of such action], were mentioned in the second verse; they are the instruments of withdrawal during sleep, acting as the substrate for the unperceived consciousness (*caitanya*) mentioned in the third verse.
1. *Nādisaṃ*. 2. The connection is with *kha*.

And the meaning is that the Supreme Agent, who has attained the superimposition of identity with that ignorance in which His own reflection appears—or who is non-different from the individual soul (jīva) which is His own reflection—abides in the pure space of His own essential nature (svarūpa). || 227 ||
Likewise, in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, the Śruti [speaks] by way of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the wind (vāyu).
It states the inclusion of speech, fire, and so forth, for no other reason.

He states a scriptural indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the dissolution of all effects into their causal state during sleep: "In the same way. Following the principle of the dissolution of effects during deep sleep, in the section on the *Saṃvarga-vidyā* (the knowledge of the absorber), beginning with "Vāyu indeed is the absorber" and ending with "For Vāyu alone absorbs all these," the text describes the absorption of fire and the other elements into the nature of Vāyu; then, beginning with "Prāṇa indeed is the absorber," [it continues] "for Prāṇa alone... [absorbs these].

Furthermore, by the passage ending with "he remains concealed within all," the Śruti declares the withdrawal of speech and the other organs into the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa). Since the effect cannot be withdrawn into anything other than its cause, the meaning is that when the Śruti speaks of the withdrawal of speech and the others into the nature of the vital breath during sleep, it intends to express the withdrawal of the effect into the nature of its cause. || 228 ||
Everything from Name down to Hope is established in Prāṇa.
And because of the statement regarding the binding of the vital breath (prāṇa), that which has been stated is well-said. || 229 ||

He states that the section on the knowledge of the elements (*bhūmavidyā*) also illustrates what has been said: "Name, etc. By the word *prāṇa*, the unknown Brahman is expressed. Regarding the fact that all effects whatsoever are established in the unknown Brahman, preceded by the individual soul denoted by the word *manas*, he cites another scriptural passage on this very point: "Prāṇa, etc. He concludes that during deep sleep, every effect is withdrawn into its causal state.
It is well-spoken. || 229 ||
The conjunction of that which has manifested its own effect with its causal essence.
In this case, there would be the grasping of speech and so forth by the bubbles, just as [they are grasped] by water. (230)

Having explained the meaning of the suffix in the word "ādāya," he states the meaning of the base [prakṛti] as "āvirbhūta" (manifested). The word "sva" (own) refers here to the Supreme Self; it means "during deep sleep. The example is given in order to express that "conjunction" (saṃsarga) is identity (tādātmya). || 230 ||
Or rather, this instrumental case in the word "vijñānena" is used in the sense of accompaniment (sahārtha), as it is heard in the scripture.
The withdrawal of speech and the other [organs] occurs together with the knowledge of the knower. || 231 ||

Having explained the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) and state (*itthaṃbhāva*), he states another meaning with the word "together" (*saha*). He clarifies that very point with the word "together. The meaning is that there is a withdrawal of the instruments along with their respective objects and the knowledge of those objects. || 231 ||
Or rather, let this third case ending be understood as expressing the sense of "being in such a state."
Through the nature of inward-facing knowledge, there is the withdrawal of cause and effect.

He states that there is no fault even regarding the meaning already expressed in the passage, "The powers of the third [state] are the instruments," by saying "Or rather" (*yadi vā*). Anticipating the objection that this would then be a tautology, he says "The inner self" (*pratyak*), etc., because he accepts different meanings for the words *vijñāna* and *śabda*; thus, the meaning is that the dissolution of the world occurs here along with its cause, which is the nature of experience, and therefore the Self abides in its own glory (*sve mahimni*). ||232||
That which is directly perceived as non-different from awakening is called "this."
For the sake of its correct comprehension, there is the internal mental recitation.

He explains the meaning of the two words *ya eṣa* (who this) with the words *ananyā* etc. The meaning is that the self-luminous reality denoted by "that" (*tat*) is the very same as the inner self (*pratyag-bhūta*) denoted by "this" (*eṣa*). He states the purport of the passage beginning with *antara* (within) with the words *tasya*. When it is stated that the heart is the locus of the inner self and that it is the very same for Brahman as well, the identity of truth is established; and for the sake of its perfect realization, it is said that "Brahman is within the heart."
The meaning is that it is stated to be the location of the heart of Brahman. || 233 ||
Having diligently turned the mind away from the spheres of external objects of cognition.
Behold your own self directly with a gaze inclined inward. 234.

Raising the objection, "How can there be identity between the referent of 'thou' (tvaṃ), which appears as bound by non-difference from the body and so forth, and the non-transmigrating Brahman? he states that the referent of 'thou' must be investigated: "parāk... etc. For the mind is naturally diffused among external objects;

therefore, having extracted it from those [objects] through their positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) and having made it abide in the inward Self, one should—by means of a vision directed toward that [Self]—[realize] the attributeless [Self].
The meaning is: "Censure yourself; realize [the truth] directly. || 234 ||
This notion of a self in persons is observed to be unerring.
In the case of erroneous cognitions that do not arise from the self, [they are sublated] by the inner self (pratyagātman). || 235 ||

He explains what that discriminating intellect (*vivekadhī*) is like: "The Self," etc. Consciousness (*caitanya*) is the very nature of the Self for men; it is non-deviant with respect to the inner self (*pratīci*), whereas it is deviant among the non-self cognitions (*anātmadhīṣu*).
Therefore, consciousness is non-deviant while the other [cognitions] are deviant—this is the meaning of discriminating intellect. || 235 ||
Even for one who has realized the nature of the Buddha, that [delusion] persists due to the error of cognizing external objects.
It appears as if confounded for those whose minds are afflicted by darkness.
Raising the objection—“If the consciousness of the Self (*ātmacaitanya*) is immutable and non-deviating, how can there be the notion of agency and so forth?”—the author says: “Buddhi...

The meaning is this: although the perception of the Self’s own nature, which consists of pure awareness, is immutable and non-deviating, it appears to the undiscriminating as possessing agency and other such qualities due to the delusion of identifying the body and so forth with the Self. || 236 ||
When half of the task remains, and when the cause is entirely exhausted through the knowledge of the Self.
Let this Self be realized within itself as having the nature of the unprecedented (apūrva) and so forth. || 237 ||
He states the result of [the fact that] agency and so forth are products of nescience (avidyā): "Devoured," etc. (verse 237).
By means of the words "taking" (ādāya) and "space" (ākāśa), identity is established.
Because the identity of the Knower of the Field and the Lord is directly stated here by Śruti through the destruction of ignorance. || 238 ||

Having explained the distinction between the meanings [of the two words] for the sake of the knowledge of unity (*aikyajñāna*), he states its result with the words "by offering" (*bhādāya*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "by means of offering that meaning. The word "by the Veda" (*śrutyā*) is a statement regarding the verbal form (*ākhyāta*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the knowledge of unity. The meaning is that when that [knowledge] exists, because of the abandonment of false knowledge, its expression is purposeful. || 238 ||
Because of its location therein, the word "heart" (hṛdaya) here denotes the intellect (buddhi).
For the purpose of realizing the identity of the individual soul (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman). || 239 ||
1. Not in the sense of an object; 2. It is said. [Vol.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 927.

Regarding the phrase "within the heart" (*antarhṛdaye*), he states the meaning of the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*). He says "because of its location therein" (*tātsthyāt*). One might raise the objection: why should the term "heart" not refer simply to the lotus-shaped piece of flesh, since the word is used in its primary sense there? Anticipating this, he says: "on account of the identity of the self" (*aikātmya*). Since it is well known that the individual soul (*jīva*) resides in the intellect (*buddhi*), when the Supreme Space (*ākāśa*) is also said to be established therein, the identity of those two is established; for that purpose [the term "heart" is used].
The meaning is that by the word "heart" (hṛdaya), the intellect (buddhi) is intended. || 239 ||
Just as when one says "the space within a jar" and "the great space," there arises the single cognition that they are one and the same.
Likewise here as well, it is explained [in this way] so that there may indeed be an inward-directed cognition. || 240 ||

Fearing that if there were identity (*aikātmya*) between the two, there would either be duality (*bheda*) in the first case, or the redundancy of the other term in the second case, and considering that even in their identity there is no uselessness of the other term because of the difference in what is to be excluded (*vyāvartyabheda*), he says: "A pot," etc.

Here, "here" refers to the sentence under discussion. "The cognition of the inner self" (*pratyagdhi*) means the cognition of its oneness (*tadaikarasya*). Having taken [the pot] from here, [he places it] in space.
The meaning is that it is said "it lies. || 240 ||
Since no object other than the internal witness of the intellect can be conceived.
Therefore, by the word "ether," the inner self (pratyagātman) is denoted. || 241 ||

Anticipating the objection that—since the word "ether" (ākāśa) conventionally denotes the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), which does not have Brahman as its referent—one cannot here attain the cognition of the identity between the individual self and Brahman—he says: "Of the intellect" (buddheḥ). || 241 ||
For it will be explained that the birth of the vital breaths and so forth proceeds from the inner self (pratyagātman).
And therefore, by the word "ether" (ākāśa), Brahman alone is denoted here.

One might suspect that the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) also exists within that [ether], because it is all-pervading; anticipating this, [the author] states: "Of the vital breaths, etc. Since the word "ether" used here refers to this Self—which is drawn forward by the subsequent use of the word "Self"—and since scripture declares it to be the cause of the birth of the vital breaths and so forth, the "ether" here must be Brahman alone; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the remainder of the passage. Thus he says: "Of the vital breaths, etc."—"All these beings, indeed, arise from the ether... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1].
The word "ca" (and) is used here to include other scriptural passages, such as "O Deva," and so forth.
"Indeed, the name of the Existent is 'Space,' O Somya," so says the Śruti.
No other space than the space of Brahman is understood here.
In that very context, he cites another scriptural passage: "Now, space" (*athākāśa*).

Fearing that this might also refer to the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*), and considering it to contradict the logical principle stated as "Space [is Brahman] because of its designation as something distinct and so forth," he cites yet another scriptural passage: "The Infinite" (*santa*).
The meaning is "the Supreme," whether superior or inferior. The locative case in the phrase regarding "lying down" (*śayana*) expresses the sense of location. || 243 ||
In this immutable Self, which is of the nature of consciousness and exists as the causal essence, [there is no change].
The complete cessation of the enjoyer is designated by the term "he lies down" (śete). || 244 ||

He states the meaning of the word "lying down" (śayana): "By itself," etc. Anticipating the objection that it is improper for the enjoyer to rise again after having dissolved entirely into the aforementioned reality, he intends to show that this is not so, because dissolution is accepted in the form of the unknown reality.
He specifies [the subject] by means of the phrase "in the form of the cause. || 244 ||
1. Not by the speech of Brahmā; 2. g. ‘from this ākā’ [vol2, page 634] Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika, Second Chapter—928.
And the example, such as the prince and others, likewise applies directly.
Because it consists of nothing but immediate consciousness, sleep is not appropriate here. || 245 ||
Having raised the objection, "Why is there this mention of 'lying down' when the well-known meaning [of sleep] has been set aside?", he says: "And there is an illustration. Furthermore, he says:

"The inward... (verse 245), explaining that the well-known state of lying down, which is sleep, cannot be attributed to the Self, because the Self, being pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), is by nature opposed to it.
When this [self] exists having abandoned the presiding over the body, then—
If one asks why he remains in his own self alone, it is because he sleeps.
Having restated what was said, he introduces the reason by means of a question: "The body, etc. (246).
Moreover, this person, abiding in the inner self, does not go elsewhere.
It is said that one "sleeps" during deep sleep; this very point is now being explained.
He explains that very point [with the words] "from this. The word "ca" (and) serves to include the passage beginning with "Being, my dear," and so forth.

The word "itaḥ" (from this) is connected with the statement "because he says 'he sleeps'. He introduces the passage beginning with "those [dreams]" in order to establish the meaning already established in another Śruti text. That—
"That" [refers to that]. || 247 ||
Others, amazed, explain it as being by means of the consciousness of the intellect (*buddhivijñāna*).
Having taken up the knowledge of speech and the other [senses], he who has arisen rests in the space of the heart.

Having stated his own intended meaning for the passage beginning with "tadeṣām" and having introduced the passage beginning with "tāni" in accordance with that, he sets forth the view of Bhartṛprapañca. Regarding the word "anye": seeing that our own commentary is flawed and their own commentary is faultless, those whose minds are overcome by astonishment—[referring to] that which has arisen previously to the actual emergence, [perceiving] through the instrument called the cognition known as *buddhi*, the [cognition] in the form of speech and so forth.
The meaning is that others explain this sentence as follows: "Having taken up [the breath], it remains in the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) which is delimited by the heart. || 248 ||
When about to sleep, the self withdraws everything into the mind by means of the mind alone.
The vital breaths, together with their respective powers, as well as the mind, dissolve into the Self.

Having stated that there is a withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*) of speech and the other organs by means of "taking" (*ādāya*), [the author], in response to the expectation as to by what sequence this occurs, says: "One who desires to sleep. This means: while the mind still exists. "Collects" (*samūhati*) means he withdraws them into the form of the mind; or, the instrumental case (*manasā*) may be used in the sense of an instrument. Their withdrawal is into the self of that [mind] alone. The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are the organs of speech and so forth; their own powers are the capacities for grasping objects.

The meaning of "martyam" is the Self (*ātman*), which is the inward-facing reality (*pratyagartha*). When speech and the other organs dissolve into the mind (*manas*) within the mind, then—anticipating the doubt as to where that [mind] itself might abide—it is said:
"the mind also... (verse 249).
With the collection of the senses shattered and endowed with the cultivation of discernment.
Through the movement toward the space within the heart, the self experiences its own dream-state by means of the channels. || 250 ||
The aggregate of consciousnesses such as mind and speech is designated by the term "instrument."
The term "vijānāti" (he cognizes) is derived by means of the abstract noun (bhāva-sādhana) when the action resides in another [the object], while the agent [the self] remains stable. || 251 ||

If the self has withdrawn its instruments (the senses), then one might suspect that it would not see dreams due to the absence of causes; anticipating this, he says: "Viśīrṇa... [etc.]. "Buddhibhāvanā" means the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state. "From the space within the heart" means from the elemental space delimited by that [heart]; this is to be connected with the phrase "returns through the channels. The internal and external organs, such as the mind and speech, are the "cognitions" (*vijñāna*); the self, having those as its limiting adjuncts, [emerges] from sleep...

The meaning is "everything. By the term "instrument," it means by the intellect (buddhi) which is designated as the instrument, as previously stated. Anticipating the objection that the word "by cognition" (*vijñānena*) might refer to an agent or other such factors, he says: "He cognizes" (*vijānāti*). When the word "cognition" (*vijñāna*) refers to an agent, the individual soul (*jīva*) is understood through the etymology "he who cognizes"; however, when referring to the Supreme, the word "cognition"—being derived from the sense of "making known" (*jñapti*)—denotes Brahman, and not [the soul].

In this case, both [meanings] are appropriate to be accepted because of the mention of separate agents and because Brahman has no further expectancy; therefore, by that [word], the instrument is expressed.
As they have said: "In both instances, the word *vijñāna* is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*). || 290 || 251 ||
That luminous activity of the fish, being followed by the properties of the haddā, [is established].
Since it arises from that [source], they know its dissolution to be in the specific heart-center (hṛd-viśeṣa). || 252 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "ya eṣa" as follows: "prakāśa... etc. The word "jñasya" (of the knower) is to be understood as a separate term. Its nature is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) characterized by consciousness (*caitanya*). The attributes of the heart (*hṛddharma*) are desire and so forth. "In the specific heart" means in the space delimited by that [heart]. "Dissolution" (*laya*) means resting there. As it has been said: "For that which is the self consisting of knowledge, its self-luminous modification issues forth through the door of the heart; therefore, the heart is the specific [locus]."
"Restraint. || 252 ||

Having withdrawn, through the intellect of meditative cultivation, the knowledge of speech and the other senses directed toward their respective objects without exception, the Knower rests in the sky of the heart. (253)
By stating that there is a difference in meaning between the two words "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), he concludes the meaning of the sentence: "In its own domain," etc. (293).
When the consciousness whose form is meditative cultivation is manifested within the heart.
Therefore, this statement "it lies in the heart" appears meaningful for the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). || 254 ||
He states the reasoning for the soul’s lying down in the space of the heart during sleep with the words, "By means of mental impression" (*bhāvanā*).

When the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state belonging to the soul reside unmanifested in the heart due to the force of karma that produces dream-experiences, then—because sound and other objects are essentially composed of those impressions—they appear in that form even though they are non-existent in reality.
However, during deep sleep, because both gross and subtle forms of knowledge and its objects are absent, there is lying down in the space of the heart.

The meaning is that the word is purposeful. As they have said: "For in that [state], the cognition of *bhāvanā* remains specifically manifested; it is for this very reason that, having acted thus, one says 'in that' (*tasmin tatra*). || 254 ||
Thus, this scriptural passage has been explained by some with great effort.
Having examined these two, the discerning ones should accept them for themselves.

He concludes the refutation of the opposing position with the word "evam" (thus). By stating that the activity of providing an interpretation proceeds by means of one's own conjecture, transgressing the intended meaning of the scripture (*śruti*), he dispels any suspicion regarding the acceptability of the opponent’s interpretation. With the word "parīkṣya" (having examined), he refers to the two interpretations; the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "the faultless one is to be accepted, while the other is to be rejected. || 255 ||

Together with cultivation, because of the withdrawal of what was heard through the intellect.
Since there would be no such conclusion, this conceptual construction is futile.
Nevertheless, why is it that the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca alone must be rejected as faulty? To this he says: "Together" (saha).

Since the scriptural texts state that the mind is withdrawn during deep sleep along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the withdrawal of speech and the other organs is not established by means of that [mind] alone; thus, in deep sleep...

The conceptualization beginning with "by the mind alone" and so forth is futile; therefore, since the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) alone is the instrument during the withdrawal of speech and the other organs, and since the reflector possesses agency, it is logical that upon the total withdrawal [of all faculties], the individual soul (*jīva*) persists within Brahman which remains unknown—this is the meaning. || 216 ||
When he himself takes up those things that have been relinquished within his own sphere of activity.
At that very time, speech and the other [senses] declare of him: "He sleeps. || 257 ||

Having strengthened his own interpretation by refuting the interpretations of others regarding the passage beginning with "tadeṣām" (of these), he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "tāni" (those), which was previously introduced, as follows:
"In their respective objects. The meaning is that it "grasps," that is, it withdraws [them] into its own self. || 257 ||
Therefore, because it relies upon verbal designation, [the notion of "I"] first arose with respect to the inner self.
If there is even an inconsistency regarding the name, then a logical argument is also set forth. || 258 ||

He states the fruit of the explanation of the name "he sleeps" (*svapiti*): "The designation" (*samākhyā*). He raises an objection: that according to another scriptural passage, *svam apīto bhavati* ("he has merged into his own"), one remains in one's true nature during sleep; furthermore, he argues that the names "ear" and so forth deviate from their primary meanings [during sleep]. To this, he replies:
"Even though there is deviation," the subsequent sentence provides a logical argument (*yukti*) supported by the name itself to establish that one remains in one's true nature during sleep.
"From that," [it is said]. || 298 ||
The word "prāṇa" is understood to refer to the sense of smell within the context of speech and the other [organs] as their material cause.
Because it is not subsumed within the primary [meaning], it is not accepted as denoting that. || 259 ||

In the statement, "The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed grasped," he clarifies the meaning of the word *prāṇa* by revealing the underlying logic: "Speech and so forth. Anticipating the objection that direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), he says: "Of the primary [breath]. This non-consummation should be understood from the perspective of an observer standing by. Because all instruments (the senses) are withdrawn during deep sleep, and because there is an absence of limiting adjuncts that cause differentiation, the individual soul (jīva) exists in the nature of Brahman, which is beyond transmigratory existence.
This is the intended meaning. || 299 ||
In a dream, the basis for the organs of action has as its cause nothing but latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Because all the sense-faculties have become dissolved, their activity is not like that of one who is awake. (260)

Anticipating the objection that even the withdrawal of the organs occurs during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), yet there is no abiding as the non-transmigrating Self because of the deviation seen in the dream state (*svapna*), he says:

"Vāsanā... The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the activities of the substrata of the cognitive organs. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no abiding there as the non-transmigrating Self. The phrase "activity produced by the conjunction of objects and organs" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. It should be understood that this is because [the organs] have dissolved during deep sleep.
The example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is: "like awakening. || 260 ||
Just as the state of being a transmigrator is observed when there is connection with limiting adjuncts such as speech and so forth.
Therefore, all [objects] have been withdrawn; hence, there is no transmigratory existence for the Seer.
1. Yoga; 2. Having discarded the intermediate [state] by means of that; 3. From bondage, [the cycle of] saṃsāra...

He explains the first half [of the verse]: "Speech and so forth. Two states are intended here; among them, the phrase "as it were" (*iva*) is used to indicate that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) is merely conceptual (*kalpita*). He analyzes the second half: "But those... (*te tu*). The word division is *asaṃsāritvam* (non-transmigratoriness).
Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is what is intended here. || 261 ||
But is it not the case that even in a dream, perception is experienced just as it is in the waking state?
Even when separated from all the sense organs, the self possesses the state of being happy or miserable.
He states the doubt regarding the passage beginning with "sa yatra" etc., [introducing it with] "nanu" (But...). || 262 ||
"Do not say so; because cyclic existence—characterized by the pleasure, pain, and so forth arising from dreams—is false, the Śruti declares its falsity. (263)

He refutes the objection based on following [worldly] convention by saying, "It is not so. Anticipating the question, "How is that [convention] false? he says, "Because of the authority of the Śruti," namely, "Therefore... (263).
For him there is neither sleep nor waking; how, then, could the occurrence of a dream be possible?
Its waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states are nothing other than its own essential nature.

He explains the falsity of dreams as intended by the Śruti and the Bhāṣya, beginning with "no" (na). The sense is that the three states do not exist in reality for the unattached Self. He states the way in which their appearance occurs with the word "pratyak" (the inner self). This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti): "The nature of the inner self is ignorance; it is from this nature that [the world] proceeds. || 264 ||
He who, being asleep, perceives a dream while thinking, "I am awake."
This is the conceptual construction of living beings who lie within the night of ignorance.

Having raised the objection as to how the manifestation of the triad [of states] is possible if the three states are merely illusion (māyāmātra), he says "In sleep," etc., indicating that even that [manifestation] is likewise [illusory]. || 265 ||
All this world, both moving and unmoving, is mere illusion.
Just as the rope and so forth are the reality of the snake and so forth, so too is the supreme state "That thou art" [the reality]. (266)

Anticipating the objection that "what is doubted is not false because it is subject to empirical usage, like a jar," he says: "It is illusion. He refutes the doctrine of error without a substratum by stating: "of the snake and so forth. || 266 ||
In this world, people suffer merely from the delusion of the mind.
My consciousness is agitated by confusion regarding the directions, like a traveler who has lost his way. || 267 ||
Having stated that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*), he states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) of the reason (*hetu*): "The mind... (267).
On this matter, the scion of Yadu's lineage spoke these two verses:
The ancient and eternal Viṣṇu [spoke] to the crowned one who had sought refuge.

By stating that bondage arises from ignorance, it follows by implication that liberation comes from knowledge; now, while providing the authority for this, [the author] states the contradiction with scripture regarding the reason under discussion.
"In this... [he says]. By [describing Him as] the embodied one, he sets aside [objections such as] His being non-omniscient. "The Ancient One" (purāṇa). || 268 ||

page 638] 932 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Second Chapter— ]
The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not seek refuge in me.
Their wisdom stolen away by illusion, they have resorted to a demonic nature.
Anticipating the objection—"Since [the Self] is self-luminous, knowledge is easily attained; how then can there be bondage through ignorance?"—he says: "Not me," etc.
For this divine illusion of mine, consisting of the gunas, is indeed difficult to overcome.
Those who take refuge in me alone cross over this illusion.
He says "no" to the idea that they will reach the Lord by transcending Māyā; he says "the Goddess. Then he states what the means for transcending her is: "Me alone. || 270 ||
This entire world, characterized by truth, the prior cause, and so forth, is indeed the Self alone.
"Or rather, from the statement 'you have gone,' his purpose here is already fulfilled.

[Verse 271] Having raised the doubt, "What is the means for transcending Māyā? What indeed would be the means for the realization of the Blessed One?", he explains that means and its fruit, beginning with the word "ātman. The word "brahmapadam" (the state of Brahman) should be supplied and joined [to the end of the previous sentence]. "Iha" (here) refers to the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*).
This is the statement of the established position. || 279 ||
Having completely dispelled the darkness of ignorance directed toward the external, it [the knowledge] is indeed turned inward.
The conceptualization of ignorance as being within the inner self (pratyagātman) is itself a construction of ignorance.

Anticipating the objection, "Why should not perception and the other means of knowledge themselves be the means for that [realization]?", he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*). The meaning is that all perception and so forth, culminating in the duality produced by the ignorance of the inner self, are incapable of illuminating the inner self. Regarding the inner self...

Anticipating the objection, "How can there be a connection with ignorance (avidyā) in that which has knowledge (vidyā) as its very nature?", he recalls what was stated in the *Saṃbandhagrantha*: "In the inner self" (*pratyagātmani*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates that, in terms of the actual state of reality (*vastuvṛttyā*), there is no ignorance therein. || 272 ||
Conceptual constructions such as existence and non-existence are to be understood as pertaining only to their own referents.
If [the existence of the waking state] were established by virtue of its own nature as waking, it would be established only for oneself, and not by itself [for others]. || 273 ||

Having stated that the contradiction with scripture arises from the reason [of being] "empirically treated" by one who asserts that "bondage is through ignorance and liberation is through knowledge," he states a counter-inference: "svārtham" (for its own sake). The meaning is: "The subject under dispute is false, because it is for the sake of another, like that which is commonly accepted. He states the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*): "jāgrad" (waking state), etc.; that is to say, because of reasons such as its insentience (*jaḍatva*). || 273 ||
If a dream, which is perceived as being accomplished through speech and other faculties, were equal to waking consciousness;
Tell me, from what source is the establishment of these three states [attained]? || 274 ||

In order to state the indicator of the subject (*pakṣavācaka*) in the inference for others (*parānumāna*), he restates it: "speech and so forth" (*vāgādi*). This means that because the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) which is to be proven is observed therein. "Cognition" (*bodha*) refers to the object being cognized, such as a jar and so on. The word "dream" (*svapna*) refers to the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], according to the Vedic scripture: "There are three dreamers. Now he states the sublation (*bādhaka*): "the state" (*avasthā*). If this were real, it would have to be so either intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or extrinsically (*parataḥ*).
Not iron, because it is insentient; nor the other, because no relationship can be established; thus, the [proposed] entity remains unestablished—this is the meaning. || 274 ||
In the manifestation of existence [vol2,
page 639].
And because of the statement ending in the suffix -ktvā in "having taken" (ādāya), [it refers to] a single action occurring at a prior time.
But perfection is indeed within oneself, because [anything else] is impossible in the beginning and at the end. || 275 ||

He states another reason for its falsity, beginning with the word "ādāya" (having taken). Since the use of a suffix ending in *ktvā* refers to an action occurring prior in time between two actions performed by the same agent, it is understood that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth exist prior to sleep—whether in the dream state or the waking state. Therefore, because they are absent at the beginning and at the end, they are false due to their variability; the object of dispute is false because of its variability, just like the [consensus] example.
This is the meaning. || 275 ||
Thus, for those whose eyes have been opened by the knowledge of awakening to the reality of things as they are.
There is no disease, there is no old age, and there is no wandering through foreign lands. || 276 ||

He states the fruit of declaring the falsity of the three states: "Thus, having become... and so forth. The meaning is that through the ascertainment of the falsity of the duality produced by the aforementioned reasoning and means of knowledge, when one purifies the categories of existence, the result is the cessation of all misfortunes through the knowledge of the collection of meanings arising from the sentence. || 276 ||
There is no disease, no affliction, and no flow of desire and the like.
There would be no joy, fear, agitation, loss, gain, or death. || 277 ||
There is no sorrow, nor any discontent, neither agency nor the state of being an object of action.
There is neither the object of knowledge nor the knower; yet, their non-existence is not asserted either. || 278 ||
It has been stated that "there is no disease"; this [disease] is of two kinds: adventitious (*āgantuka*) and innate (*naisargika*). The adventitious is twofold: external and internal;
he shakes off both of these, such that "there is no disease. He casts aside the innate by stating "there is no desire and so forth."

The meaning is that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the beginning of desire (*kāma*), and there is no attachment to its association. Alternatively, the absence of contact with desire, anger, and so forth has been stated. He says "they would not exist" to show that when ignorance is destroyed, its effects—the two bodies—are destroyed, and thus their attributes are also destroyed. In the second explanation, however, this is an explanation of the meaning of the word "beginning" (*ādi*): agitation (*udvega*) is the aversion caused by the realization of reality, while [the other] is caused by separation from what is desired.

Grief (*śoka*) is a modification of the mind (*citta*) and so forth; this very same [modification], when caused by the non-attainment of what is desired, is designated as discontent (*arati*); such is the distinction. He refutes the triad of agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, the triad of knowership (*jñātṛtva*) and so forth, and the triad of enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*) and so forth, stating: "There is no agency. One might then ask: "In that case, would the absence of the aforementioned diseases and so forth exist in the knower? To which he replies: "The absence of those too," because the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) lacks any basis in valid cognition, the absence itself likewise [lacks existence].
The meaning is that it is not authoritative. || 277 || 288 ||
Thus, through this knowledge of the connection between words and their meanings, one becomes an eye for the world.
One who is established in the true nature of the inner self [is freed] from ignorance, which is the cause of conceptual construction.
When destroyed by the fire of perfect awakening, conceptual construction does not remain.

Anticipating the objection that "in the absence of a knower and so forth, knowledge itself would be absent, and thus its fruit would not be established," he says: "Thus, even though [knowledge] is joined with duality as its sublater, it arises through the eye of the world consisting of the Śruti, the teacher, and so forth, which are themselves imagined by that very ignorance. (1) [Variant reading: *parikramaḥ*].

The meaning is that when that [knowledge] exists, its fruit is accomplished according to the principle stated above. He concludes the previously mentioned fruit of knowledge with the words "vikalpa" (conceptual construction).
The meaning is that for the knower, there is an abiding in the immutable Self upon the destruction of ignorance and its effects. || 279 ||
Therefore, O King, desiring to make this matter known to Gārgya, he spoke as follows.
He spoke the verse beginning with "sa yatra" regarding the supreme succession of liberations.

Having established, by means of the same reasoning applied to the falsity of dreams, that the waking state and so forth are likewise false, he introduces the scriptural authority for that falsity with the words "desiring to make [it] known. The meaning of the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is that it serves as the reason for the commencement of the subsequent passage, namely, the desire to cause the knowledge of the aforementioned matter to arise. || 280 ||
Because it exists in sleep, it is called "dream"; this is the distinction between waking and sleeping.
It is clearly performed for the sake of practicing falsity. || 281 ||

He says, "It moves by means of the dream-state," relying upon the Mādhyandina recension; the ellipsis is that it moves by means of that function called "seeing. He states the purpose of the qualification: "the waking state," etc. He states the result of distinguishing [the dream] from both: "falsity," etc.; for when the dream is distinguished from the waking state and from sleep, then its [nature as] the body...
The meaning is that through the distinction from the two [realities] well-known as being true, the falsity of the insentient is made clear. || 289 ||
When night had fully set in, his senses were withdrawn by sleep.
When the karma of the waking state has been exhausted and the experience of sleep is present, || 282 ||
By the word "where," he states the time suitable for dreaming: "at night. He states the observed cause of dreaming:

"when [the senses] are withdrawn. He shows that this depends on the absence of an unseen obstacle (*adṛṣṭa-pratibandhābhāva*). "While awake" refers to the very same [absence of an unseen obstacle] as its cause.
He said: "In a dream... [The verse continues: "...enjoyment and its cause. (282)
Having concealed the state of awakening, which is characterized by having the body and so forth as its locus.
There, the formative force (saṃskāra) brought forth by karma arises from the desire for one's own pleasure.
He states the absence of any obstruction from karma and past experience by saying "bodha" (awakening). He mentions another cause by saying "karma.

He explains that for a person possessing awakened latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the waking state, even the desire for pleasure in a dream is a cause; thus he says "tatra" (in that case). || 283 ||
He entered another state by means of his own power of illusion, like a master of magic through his own magic.
He created, and continues to create, many various objects, both high and low, which are unreal.
[They are] fully acquired through the means of ignorance, desire, action, and so forth.
Those things which are common to his awakening are seen by him alone in a dream. || 285 ||

He states the fundamental reason: "the state" (*avasthām*). Fearing the objection that one in the dream state might be inactive like one in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he says: "and high" (*uccaiḥ*). The meaning is that although it is in fact inactive, it is not so from the perspective of appearance (*pratīti*), because that would contradict scriptural texts such as [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9] regarding its being a "station" (*sthāna*) and so forth. The phrase "he creates" implies "for his own enjoyment. If that is so, then let the dream be real, since it is produced by karma and other factors, just like the waking state.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Cognition," meaning that it is not real because it is perceived by nothing other than itself, like a snake in a rope. It does not exist in the Self.

It should be understood that there is no deviation [in the argument], because the absence of falsehood (*anṛtatva*) is intended as the reason. And this has been stated [in the verse]: "of those who are not false" (*anṛtān iti*). || 284 ||
The view that the worlds are the fruits of karma is declared to be their false belief.
By the words "uteva" and so forth, the realization of absolute unity is clearly established. || 286 ||

Having explained that [the phrase] "he will say to them," he states the meaning of the word *loka* with the words "The worlds. Regarding the passage beginning with "become those" (*tadbhūtāḥ*), he states the meaning of the word *iva* with the words "Of these. The meaning is that the falsity of the great kingship and so forth—which are the fruits of karma—is expressed by the word *iva* for the purpose of clearly showing the single-flavored nature of the ultimate reality. || 286 ||
Is it not the case that, just as in awakening, worldly things do not deviate from their state at that particular time?
It is said that even in a dream, they may be non-existent, just as they are not present at their own [specific] time. || 287 ||
He raises an objection: "The worlds are not false, because they do not deviate from their own time, just like the waking world. (287)
But has it not already been established that the world of the waking state is illusory?
The fact that ignorance alone is the cause [of bondage] is established by awakening through the pressing of the hand. || 288 ||

In order to state that the probandum (*sādhya*) is deficient, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) recalls what was stated in the verse concerning the "trembling of the hand" (*pāṇipepa*). He says, "But surely... (*nanu*). Anticipating the objection that falsity (*mithyātva*) cannot be non-existence (*asattva*) because it would contradict the established doctrine, nor can it be indefinability (*anirvācyatva*) because it is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), he says, "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). He clarifies what was previously mentioned [by the word] "previously" (*prāk*) by saying, "the hands... (*pāṇī* || 288 ||).
And that being the case, an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is not possible for you.
Because everything is of a false nature, this is not so; for why is that? (289)
1. He states the conclusion resulting from that falsity: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). He provides the reason for the impossibility of a distinction between the example and the thing illustrated:
"It is false" (*mithyā*). Therein, the proponent (*pūrvavādī*) asserts the impossibility of an objection in order to establish the example: "This is not so" (*na etat*).
He asks for the reason why there can be no objection: "Why? He states the reason for what he wishes to know: "Since... (289).
This is for the purpose of establishing the mere distinction between the two categories of the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
The text beginning with "trembling of the hands and feet" intends to explain purification therein. || 290 ||

He explains that very point [with the words] "By means of discrimination" (*viveka*). This text, beginning with "the clapping of hands," is the sole cause for the discrimination between the two bodies and the Self.

In that context, although the notion of the Self's stoutness and so forth—such as "I am stout"—is false, and thus the falsity of the waking state is established by implication, nevertheless, by treating that [notion] as if it were non-existent, the objection raised by way of that illustration is formulated. And when the objection exists, it is [to be answered] by its refutation.

Having stated the falsity of dreams, he says "purity" (śuddhiḥ) [in verse 290], because by proving that the waking state is likewise false, the purity of one who is liberated from the two bodies is intended in the *Svapnavākya*.
Therefore, having taken a fabricated example, [one might falsely conclude] regarding the self directly.
The purification of internal and other types of defilements is explained here. || 291 ||

Having relied upon the aforementioned classification, he concludes the established point with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Even though the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) does not exist in reality, [it is employed for the sake of understanding].
Thus ends the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the second chapter—] page 642, verse 936.

Having established [the world] as quiescent, one might suspect that the dream is real; therefore, by refuting that, the removal of all forms of impurity from the Self is expressed through the statement regarding the dream.
The meaning is that since even the waking state is likewise illusory, the Self must be of a single essence and pure. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the statement concerning the dream. || 291 ||
Relying upon some slight similarity, one falls into the error of identity.
Since this applies to every logical principle (nyāya), what has been urged here is not correct.

Anticipating the objection that if the purity already stated by implication through the declaration of falsity in the "hand-clapping" passage (*pāṇipeṣavākya*) is stated here as well, it would be a tautology, he says: "Something [is common]. He means: while a tautology resulting from some degree of similarity exists everywhere, the absence of tautology due to internal differences is equally applicable here as well; for whereas in the previous case the means to purity was merely implied, in this case it is expressly stated in the words.
The state of being. || 292 ||
Great kings and others such as these do not fall within the scope of his own direct experience.
They should be known as being identical with it (the self), because they are perceived as non-different from it. || 293 ||

Having stated through the voice of the opponent that a resolution must be given because the objection regarding the reality of dreams arises by means of the analogy of the waking state, [the author], in response to the inquiry "What is that resolution?", says: "The great king and so forth. Here, "of this" refers to the dreamer.
The meaning is: "The objects under dispute are neither the self of the seer nor its attributes, because they are objects of his perception, like a jar. (293)
From the king, who was lying on his couch, [the knowledge was obtained] through direct perception and other means of valid cognition.
The king, having gone to the forest, is seen externally by his own eyes. || 294 ||
Furthermore, he states that dreams are false because they are perceived as objects distinct from those seen while awake: "Upon the couch... and so forth.
It should be understood that this refers to the direct perception and other means of knowledge belonging to the bystanders who are awake. || 294 ||
In accordance with his own experience, the king’s word in his palace is not false.
For those who have awakened from a dream, the forest they had resorted to would be unreal. || 295 ||
Anticipating the objection that "since it is a different state from dreaming, why should the king and other objects seen while awake not likewise be false?", he says:

*svānubhūti* (one's own experience). The word should be split as *amṛṣā* (not false). Anticipating the further objection that "if what is seen by the waking perceiver is real because of the waking perceiver’s experience, then what is seen by the dreamer should also be real because of the dreamer’s experience," he says: *svapna* (in a dream). In that state, [the dreamer] has resorted to a forest.
The construction is: "It would be false that the king was seen by him alone [and no one else] when he had grown up. || 299 ||
What is seen in the waking state is false in the dream; what is seen in the dream is false in the waking state.
Because the states of sleep and one's own waking objects are mutually inconsistent. || 296 ||

Furthermore, he states that there is no distinction between these two by means of the following inference: "Dream and waking—these two are false because they mutually deviate from one another, like [the perception of] a snake [in a rope] and so forth. Thus: "The waking... (verse 296).
And how could there be day or night for one whose eyes have been withdrawn, or how could there be seeing?
In the same way, how could there be life for the dead, or youth for the aged? (297)

And because there is no suitable time, he says that the dream is false: "The day," etc. And because there is no suitable cause, he says it is likewise so: [Brāhmaṇa 1] accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 937.

Regarding the word "withdrawn" (*saṃhṛta*): the word "from what" (*kutaḥ*) is connected to both [parts]. Furthermore, he says it is false because it contradicts valid cognition (*pramā*), stating "of the dead" (*mṛtānām*). || 297 ||
The vision of the eyes and other senses does not perceive what is within the body.
And how could there be an end to the Himavat and other mountains, or their origin within the heart? (298)

And because there is no suitable location [for them], he says "no" in the same manner. The meaning is that it is not supported by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) that the eyes and other sense organs, which function as instruments for perceiving external objects, could perceive objects situated within the body; nor is it possible for large-sized objects such as the Himalayas—which are the objects of those senses—to exist within the heart, which lacks such magnitude. || 298 ||
Nor does it, having emerged from the body, perceive mountains and other such objects.
How did he go, being devoid of a body and lacking the means for movement? || 299 ||

Anticipating the objection that a suitable location is established because one accepts that dreaming occurs outside the body, he says: "Nor also... The reason for this is given as: "The body... Does the dreamer go outside either conjoined with the body or unconjoined? Not the first, because there would be no perception [of the dream] at the place where he lies down; nor the other, because movement is impossible for one devoid of means, and because another body is not perceived—this is the meaning. || 299 ||
If this [Self] performs its effects even without the body and so forth, [then it must be eternal].
Without a doubt, the assumption of a body and so forth by this [consciousness] would result in being purposeless. || 300 ||

He restates the opposing view—that the effects of that [body], such as movement and so forth, might exist even without the body—by the word "antareṇa" (without). He refutes it by way of over-extension (atiprasakti) with the words "vyartham" (it would be useless). || 300 ||
Surely you were seated upon a couch when you went to the forest in a palanquin?
One will not see the Self outside the body, for that is not so.

He raises a doubt regarding the passage beginning with "sa yathā" (just as that), saying: "nanu" (but surely). The meaning is that the statement about dreaming within the body contradicts experience. He takes up the refuting statement as the reason for rejecting that objection: "na tat" (not that). || 309 ||
Having taken hold of ministers and others for the sake of accomplishing enjoyment for his own self.
The king, staying in the midst of his own country, moves about as he pleases.
In this regard, he explains the illustration: "The ministers and so forth. (302)
This [state], characterized by the waking state, resides within one's own body and kingdom.
Having thus taken up the vital breaths as the self, he perceives his own [forms] according to his desire.
He provides an illustration: "In one's own body. The meaning is that, just as in a dream, even in the waking state, the world is superimposed upon the self by ignorance. || 303 ||
1. By means of unreal limiting adjuncts (upādhis), this very one, whose nature is immutable and unattached, [is perceived as such].
The Self, whose impurity is superimposed by ignorance, is purified by knowledge.
he saṃ | 2 kha. ga. śayaḥ || 300 || 3 kha. hāntare sva | 4. nipro'yaṃ | 5. ga. vanaru | 118

If both [the self and the world] were products of ignorance (*avidyā*), how could there be purity of the Self, given the absence of the cause for that—namely, knowledge (*vidyā*)? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Asatyā... (Because it is unreal).
This means by means of the Vedas, the teacher, and so forth. || 304 ||
Of the unattached with the attached, of the immutable with the perishable.
A real union of the self with the non-self is not possible.
He clarifies the statement that the Self possesses a state of impurity superimposed by ignorance through its being immutable and unattached, with the words "of the unattached one" (niḥsaṅgasya).
In a fraudulent transaction, that which is given without permission and that which is rejected, along with its lineage, [is nullified].
Due to delusion arising from other factors such as the grammatical case-role (kāraka), one directs [the notion of agency] toward oneself. || 306 ||

Furthermore, is the impurity of agency and so forth in the Self inherent or extrinsic? It is not the first; thus he says: "As immutable" (kūṭastha). Nor is it extrinsic, for that would contradict such scriptural texts as "Not this, not this" (neti neti). If it were a non-entity, then since it would be nothing other than delusion (moha), the agency and so forth produced by it would likewise not be real entities. Thus he says: "It has been refuted" (pratyākhyātam). || 306 ||
Surely you have stated this reversal of his [position] out of desire?
And if that were so, how could the relationship between the seer and the seen be pure? (307)

Having stated that the seer of dreams and the like is pure because of their falsity, the author now raises an objection against that purity in order to introduce the passage beginning with "Now, when... (atha yadā...). He does so by saying "But surely" (nanu). The word "of this" (asya) refers to the dream-seer. By the word "and" (ca), the continuity of the phrase "is said to be" is indicated. By the word "and the like" (ādi), the states of being things to be heard and so forth are expressed. He states the resulting conclusion: that the seer is not pure when there is a connection with desires and the like. How?
Thus [it is said]. || 307 ||
Since it is self-established, how could there be any association with ignorance?
Apart from association with ignorance, there can be no association with that which is born of it.
He states that there is no connection with desire and so forth for the Self by saying "friendly" (maitram). He provides the reason for this by saying "by itself" (svataḥ).

If it is argued that even in the absence of a connection with ignorance—which is the sole cause of bondage—there might still be a connection with desire and so forth, he says "no," adding "ignorance" (ajñāna). || 308 ||
Thus, because it is pure by its own nature and because there is no association with a second, this [is so].
Therefore, the Self is liberated from its own state [of objectivity] by virtue of being pure, immutable consciousness alone. || 309 ||

He states the result regarding the absence of a relationship between the seer, ignorance, and that which is born from it: "In this way" (evam). Since, according to the manner described, the two are not joined, the Self is inherently pure;
therefore, by its own nature, it is liberated, meaning it becomes eternal, pure consciousness alone. The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative (*prathamārthe*). || 309 ||
It does not come into contact with form in the same way that auditory consciousness does.
In that very same way, the self enters into conjunction with saṃsāra through its state of immutability. || 310 ||
He clarifies the soul's lack of connection with desire and the like by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "not," etc. (310).
Thus, this detailed commentary is introduced in order to determine the meaning.
1. *Sthadaṃ*. 2. *ka. ga. syātvayena*. [Vol.
2, page 645] 1. Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 939.
[He perceives] the purity and the distinction between his own states of sleep and waking.
Having stated the non-duality of the self, it is now explained with reference to deep sleep.

In that context, he takes up the passage beginning with "atha" as an authoritative source. Regarding the phrase "ityarthasya": having restated what was previously said, he explains the passage beginning with "atha.

Regarding the word "viśuddhim": the meaning is that after describing purity and so forth in the two states [of waking and dreaming], it is intended to show that non-dual Brahmanhood is realized in deep sleep. || 311 || 312 ||
By the scriptural statement, "He does not know," the agency of the Self is negated.
For although it sees, the wise one does not perceive [it] due to its immutability. || 313 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "yadā" (when), he states the meaning of the phrase "na veda" (he does not know). He says "no. Anticipating the objection that it is not proper to negate the Self's agency in knowing because, as a witness, it possesses that agency, he says "paśyan" (seeing). The implication is that, therefore, the scriptural negation is not contradictory. || 313 ||
Now, as for the one who knows, in that way the self possesses the status of being the witness of the knower.
The non-agency of the internal self (pratīc) is established by us in every instance. (314)

To show that the Self is the witness of the knower and not its agent, he cites another scriptural passage, beginning with "Now" (*atha*). The word "now" (*atha*) indicates the commencement of the purification of the meaning of "Thou" (*tvam*). The meaning is that the Self has no agency, because according to the scriptural statement—"He who knows the knower who stands [thinking] 'I shall smell this'"—the Self is described as the witness of the knower, following my own interpretation. Furthermore, it is the presiding overseer of all actions... all beings... [etc.].

In the Upaniṣads, it is stated for the sake of those seeking liberation that the inner self (pratīc) is non-dual pure consciousness by virtue of its immutability (kūṭasthatva), as in the passage beginning "That which is the witness" (tādhivāsaḥ sākṣī). To this he says: "Of the inner self," [meaning] that it does not possess agency. || 314 ||
In some cases, the witness is the knower of the subject; in other cases, it is the supreme knower of the cognition.
Or perhaps, for one who knows external objects, the selfhood of that [self] as their agent is being negated.

Fearing that the qualification "the witness of the knower" might imply a limitation, he says: "Sometimes. If it is argued that even when [the Self] is predominant in some place, at some time, or in some respect, its status as the witness of all remains unimpaired, then how can there be a negative statement such as "how could it not know"? To this, he says: "That...
(verse 315).
The capacity for knowing belonging to this inner self (pratyagātman) is considered supreme;
since that [knowing] arises from a relation, it is now stated in response to the question: "To whom does it belong? (316)

He introduces the genitive case in "of whom" (*kasya*).
