Regarding the word "other" (*para*): the meaning is that since the knowing-ness of the inward-facing self (*pratyak*) arises from its connection with an object, because it is born from this connection with an object, the genitive case "of whom" is used here in reference to that connection. || 316 ||
Because the self-sense and so forth arise from karma, they must be abandoned when that karma is exhausted.
This genitive case is logically used in the sense of the object (karma), intended to express the absence of the two [the agent and the instrument]. || 317 ||

He applies that [term] specifically: "action" (*karman*). For this genitive case is indeed appropriate only with respect to action, since [terms such as] *mātrā* and so forth constitute the object (*karman*)—[the various readings being] 1.
*te'thādhu*; 2. *ga. te'pyadhu*; 3. *ka. ga. kartṛtvaṃ*; 4. *kha tatkṣayatvataḥ*. [Vol. 2, p. 646]

The meaning is as follows: because action (*karman*) is something produced, it is destroyed during deep sleep; since that which is born from it is also destroyed therein, the intention is to convey the idea that due to the absence of any second entity, one does not experience even the slightest thing, such as a mother or others.
This is the intended sense of the passage. || 317 ||
This word *cana*, used in the sense of "even," also excludes non-existence.
The disappearance of both the residual and the residual-possessor is here called deep sleep. || 318 ||
The particle *api* excludes the notion that [the state] consists of two parts. He states the intended meaning of the word *api*:
"of the non-existence. The meaning is that in deep sleep (*svāpa*), just as the existence of the world is negated, its non-existence is also negated. Even when existence is negated, non-existence—

Anticipating the objection that "it need not be negated because even in its presence there is no contradiction with sleep," he says: "The remainder," etc. The "remainder" is non-existence (abhāva) because it is subordinate; the "residual" is existence (bhāva) because it is primary. The "disappearance" of these two is the absence of specific cognition; therefore, even non-existence must be negated in sleep. The locative case in "here" (iha) refers to the person as the locus. || 318 ||
Now, by what sequence does this [self] attain deep sleep?
Thus, it is called "the Beneficial" (Hitā) for the purpose of establishing the sequence.
Having described the nature of deep sleep, he introduces the subsequent passage with "Now" (atha), stating its purport while anticipating a further inquiry.
Likewise, from the navel up to the throat, the heart is situated in the middle.
It has a stalk, resembles the calyx of a lotus, possesses five apertures, and is turned downwards. || 320 ||

In that regard, he states the location of the heart: "from the navel. The meaning is according to the Vedic scripture: "It stands above the navel at the end of a span below the *niṣṭyā*. He describes the nature of the heart situated in the middle, starting from the throat down to the navel: "with its stalk. The meaning is according to the Vedic scripture: "The heart is like the interior of a lotus bud and is downward-facing. (Chāndogya...)
Relying on the Vedic revelation, the qualification "having five apertures" [is applied]. || 320 ||
The individual embodied beings have as their own supports the centers within the heart that appear blue and so forth.
Furthermore, his abodes become frequented by gods, mortals, and others;
these various states arise from cognition just as they do in the waking state.
One hundred and one channels have emerged from all sides of these two.

He states that the cavities of the heart are the locus for two states, beginning with the words "In dream. The meaning is that those five apertures within the heart of the embodied being are the substrata for the two states. He describes their specific colors—red, white, tawny, dark, and blue—in the order starting from the east, beginning with the words "Blue and so forth. He then declares the presiding deities of these [cavities] with the words "The locations."

The openings served by gods, mortals, and others are also their respective locations. The Sun, the Moon, Fire, Parjanya, and Space are the gods. Prāṇa, Vyāna, Apāna, Samāna, and Udāna are the mortals. By the word "and others" (ādi), the various vital breaths—eye, ear, speech, mind, and anus—are included. All of these are located in the Pratihāras in the east, south, west, [north, and zenith].

They exist one by one in the apertures above, starting from the passage beginning with "Of this very heart, there are five divine apertures" and ending with "He who knows these five Brahman-persons as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world. This is the meaning [of that passage].
(Note: *ka*, *ga* read *iti ma*).
[Vol.
2, Page 647] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 941.

The meaning is "because they have been explained in detail. He states their function: "And the apertures (suṣayaḥ)," etc. The meaning is that these apertures, as causes for the arising of cognitions consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the form of sound and so forth—just as in the waking state—are likewise [causes] in the dream state. From the apertures... [nirgataḥ]... (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available text.)
He states the primary channels: "One," etc. This means by way of various movements in all directions. || 329 || 322 ||
From each sense organ, ten [rays] have emerged, directed toward their respective objects.
Nothing other than karma and its causes exists for the sake of experiencing the fruits of states such as sleep.

Having stated the number of channels established by other scriptural passages such as "one hundred and one," he describes the manner of their functional application with the words "for each sense. He states the cause of their origination with the words "karma, etc. He states the result of their emergence toward their respective objects with the words "dream, etc. || 323 ||
Just as rivers carry water, so do the channels carry the fruit of karma.
The channel that goes upward alone to infinity; by traveling through it, one is liberated. || 324 ||
He explains how they are the means for enjoyment: "They carry," meaning that they indeed cause the person to experience [objects] by bringing about a connection with sense objects.

Having stated the application of the hundred channels, he states the application of the remaining channels: "Infinite," meaning according to the Vedic scripture: "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality. || 324 ||
Furthermore, subtle subdivisions of each individual channel have been proclaimed.
It is reckoned by those who contemplate yoga to consist of seventy-two thousand [verses].

Anticipating the objection—“If the arrangement of the channels (nāḍīs) is determined in accordance with another Vedic text [which states there are 72,000], how then is the present passage to be understood?”—he says: “Of each one. The meaning is that, according to the scripture: “There are these one hundred and one channels; in each one of them there are seventy-two thousand subsidiary channels. He states the authority for the fixed number of those [subsidiary channels]: “They are numbered.”
Thus it is said:
"Seventy-two thousand [channels] have issued forth from the heart."
"The channels called *hitā* are indeed beneficial; in their midst is a mandala with the luster of the moon, and situated in its center is the Self, motionless like a lamp.
As for the statement that there are three hundred and fifty thousand channels, that refers to the various types of veins belonging to this world.
Twenty-nine hundred thousand and likewise nine hundred.
"One should know that there are fifty-six vessels (śirā) designated as dhamanīs"—this should be understood as referring to their specific classifications. || 325 ||
Like filaments produced from kadamba flowers on all sides.

The channels (nāḍīs) have issued forth from the heart, by which the little body is pervaded. [Verse 326] He states the nature of the channels as they are introduced: "Like the *kadamba*," etc. He describes their pervasiveness with the words "on all sides.
Having raised the doubt that their pervasion extends even outside the body, he says, "by which," etc. [326]
Because they bestow beneficial results, they are therefore known as "beneficial" (*hita*).
Drawn forth from the heart, they emerged just as rays of light do from the sun.
He explains how those [channels] have the word "beneficial" (*hita*) as their name: "Beneficial" means that which has been acquired by those performing ritual actions (*karmin*).
Having thus explained the passage beginning with "named beneficial," he states what is intended in the phrase "from the heart": "From the heart. || 327 ||
By the term "purītat," the sheath of the heart is here denoted.
One should understand that as a general characteristic intended to express its pervasion of the body. (328)
By that [term], he states what is denoted by the word *purītat*: "the *purītat*. Here, the term "here" refers to the sphere of worldly activity (*vyavahārabhūmi*).

However, it is the body that is indicated here, because the wrapping around the heart serves as its indicator, and because it is intended to signify the channels (*nāḍī*) which pervade it; thus he says.
"Having spoken," [it is said]. || 328 ||
The latent impressions arising from one's own karma that reside within the heart.
Having expanded itself through the channels, it sees its own self at will.
He states the intended meaning regarding the section on action (*kriyāpada*) as follows: "In a dream... (329).
Having completely abandoned one's own enjoyments upon the exhaustion of one's own activity.
Having withdrawn [the senses] by means of those very [powers], he who is liberated attains the state of deep sleep.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "by those" (tābhiḥ) as follows: "one's own [forms]," etc.; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "the instruments consisting of latent impressions" (vāsanāmayāni karaṇāni). || 330 ||
Having experienced, without remainder, the enjoyments arising from the processes of waking and dreaming, [he remains].
Having withdrawn the senses, he rests within the self by means of the channels.

Anticipating the objection—namely, that even when the karma [producing the dream] is exhausted through the enjoyment of the dream, how can sleep occur by way of the withdrawal of the instruments (karaṇas), since waking is also possible—he says:
"jāgrad" (waking). || 331 ||
Having pervaded the body internally and externally through general consciousness, one becomes weary from the exertion.
Like a hawk, the Self attains the supreme state of deep sleep.

[Objection: Surely in the waking state one goes about through action, not into sleep; for the attainment of Brahman is not produced by that [action]. How then is there sleep? To this he says: "In common," etc. Just as a hawk, having flown about and become weary, finds rest upon reaching its own nest, so too the Self, in order to destroy the weariness caused by moving between the two states, abandons particularized cognition and [rests] within its own body by means of the common wisdom consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

The meaning is that the grandson [of the Self], having pervaded both the internal and external through the state of being the inner witness (pratyaktva), reaches Brahman and, by means of that form, attains non-attachment and indifference.
In this context, the heart is held to be the location of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) of the intellect (dhi).
In that regard, all the sense organs are always dependent upon the intellect.

If it is suspected that the self possesses limited dimensions because of its coming and going, like a hawk, [the author] replies: "No, because those two [movements] occur through the medium of the intellect.
[Ka. kha. ga. reads *prāha*; ga. reads *nanekaśaḥ*.
He says: "The intellect" (dhiyaḥ). Here, "here" (iha) refers to the body. He states that the external organs are essentially the intellect (buddhitattva): "Therein" (tatra).
This means while the intellect resides in its location, the heart; it is said that the state of existence of the external organs is always [dependent on it]. || 333 ||
Since this is so, therefore those [elements] [enter] through the channels by the power of karma. || 334 ||
The intellect extends its mental modifications outward, like a fisherman's net.
Having extended them, he firmly establishes them in their respective locations.
Therefore, during the waking state, this person possesses a cognition that manifests specific distinctions.
Though devoid of action, he pervades all things, just as the sun pervades the ten directions.

He states the result of their dependence on the intellect (*buddhi*) with the words "Since... The meaning is that the intellect, by means of its own instruments, makes them directed toward objects through the channels of the *nāḍīs* due to the karma that causes waking. He asks what occurs after this expansion and answers with the words "The functions (*vṛttayaḥ*).
This means those [instruments] situated in their respective abodes—that is, located in the cavities of the ears and so forth—[become active] through the doors of their own functions.

The meaning is "the instruments. The phrase "externally toward sound and so forth" refers to this. Having raised the objection that while the movement outward of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the senses is possible due to their being composed of parts and being active, such movement is not possible for the Self (*ātman*), which is partless, he says: "Therefore.
Because the intellect and the instruments move outward, therefore the Self—though naturally partless and inactive—is [perceived as such] when qualified by its own ignorance.

The meaning is that, accompanied by the intellect (buddhi) endowed with the specific quality called the manifestation of manifest consciousness (caitanya-ābhāsa), it pervades all objects through the doors of the ears and other senses; it is like the sun, which is all-pervasive by means of its rays. || 334 || 335 || 336 ||
When those very functions of the senses are permeated by one's own consciousness, [they become the means of knowledge].
At that time, it is said that the inner self withdraws and sleeps.

Having raised the doubt as to how there can be sleep for the self while it is engaged in the experiences of the waking state, he says: "tāḥ" (those). The meaning is that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) occurs when the functions of one's own senses—which are the causes of waking experiences and are permeated by the reflection of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*)—are withdrawn into the Inner Self (*pratīc*). || 337 ||
The origin and dissolution of the inner self (pratyak) occur in accordance with the limiting adjuncts of the intellect (buddhi).
But that which is free from distraction and dissolution is, by its very nature, supreme like the interior of a jar.

He states the reason for the claim that those two [contraction and expansion] belong to the Self through the contraction and expansion of the intellect (*buddhi*). He says "of the intellect" (*buddhi*). One might ask: "Why could these two not be natural to the Self? To this he replies: "distraction" (*vikṣepa*), etc. Indeed, it is not fitting for modifications such as expansion or contraction to occur spontaneously in the Self, which is self-luminous;
rather, just as the sky undergoes contraction and so forth due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as a jar, so too do these belong to the Self due to limiting adjuncts such as the intellect.
This is the meaning of the verse. || 338 ||
Having withdrawn through them, he brought the vital functions back [to himself] by means of the channels.
Pervading its own body like molten iron, it rests within its own self.
He concludes the explanation of the passage beginning with "tābhiḥ" (by those): "tābhiḥ" means bringing [them] together, that is to say, concluding. || 339 ||
The subsistence of the sense faculties is due solely to their own causes, not through the effect.
Therefore, the pervasion must occur through the very semblance of consciousness, by way of its causal nature.
1 Kha. Following the sequence. [Vol. 2, page 650] 944 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Second Adhyāya—]

Anticipating the objection—"Since the body and the senses are withdrawn during sleep, how can there be lying down pervading the body?"—the author says: "By its own [nature]," etc. The connection is: "by its own cause alone," that is, by way of its causal nature (*kāraṇātmanā*). During sleep, the body and the senses do not persist in their own specific forms (*svarūpeṇa*), but rather in their causal form; therefore, because it is possible for the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) to pervade the body which consists of those [causes], [the Self] lies pervading the body.
The meaning is that it is logical for [the Self] to rest within its own self during sleep. || 340 ||
In deep sleep, there is no connection of the inner self with the body.
Nor can it arise through the intellect and so forth, because there is no direct connection with its locus.

If it is argued that the pervasion of the appearance of the body and so forth is intended [even then], then the distinction between waking and the other states would not be established; anticipating this objection, he says: "In deep sleep. The meaning is that there, the consciousness has only a general pervasion and not a specific pervasion; therefore, because of the absence of the conceit of grossness and so forth in the body, and the absence of the conceit of being a knower and so forth in the intellect and other faculties, there is a distinction. Regarding the lack of connection with specific objects in the intellect and so forth during sleep:

He states the reason: "That" (tat) refers to the body, which is the locus of those [faculties] such as the intellect; the meaning is that it is because of the lack of a specific connection with that [body].
For it will be stated later on that "he has indeed crossed over."
"In this state of deep sleep, [there is] 'the father and so forth'"; thus, all relations are excluded. (342)

In this regard, he states the proof: "For he has crossed over," etc. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that here only the connection with sorrow is being precluded, and not the association with the body and so forth?
To this he replies: "In deep sleep," etc. (342)
This supreme state of the Self has transcended the flood of all the sufferings of saṃsāra.
Regarding the term "state" (avasthā), the illustrative example is expressed as "just as that" (sa yathā). || 343 ||
He introduces the scriptural passage beginning with "Just as that" (sa yathā) by first restating what has preceded it: "All... (sarva...). 343.
Just as an infant at the breast is free from attachment and aversion.
Because of the absence of that [object], the mind does not constantly transform into the nature of objects.

Explaining the illustration of the child, he states that from childhood itself there is an absence of passion and the like, using the term "stanaṃdhaya. This means one who sucks the breast, that is, an extremely young infant. The word "evam" (thus) in the illustrative case is connected with the word "yathā" (just as). He states the result of that absence [of passion] with the words "tadabhāvāt" (due to the absence of that). || 344 ||
And because their faculties have not yet fully developed, there is no experience of passion, hatred, and the like.
Like a soft thorn, that cognition is not capable of piercing its own objects.

He states another reason for the absence of passion and so forth, as in the case of a child’s childhood: "not fully developed," etc. Even so, since a child's growth tends toward sense objects, how can there be an absence of passion for women and the like? To this he replies: "soft," etc. (345).
And it is everywhere devoid of limbs because it is the source of that which is to be enjoined.
Or a king who is exceedingly happy in this world, even though possessed of his senses. || 346 ||
1 Who is to fight?
[Vol.
2, page 651] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 945.

He explains the analogy of the great king. "In all cases" refers to that context; the reason for this is stated as "that which is to be enjoined. He states the distinction from what precedes it as "fully grown. || 346 ||
Or a Brahmin who has realized all principles in their entirety, because he has accomplished what was to be done.
Having reached the supreme, unsurpassed pinnacle of bliss, he is utterly tranquil.

He analyzes the illustration of the great Brāhmaṇa: "Having known," etc. The connection is as follows: the Brāhmaṇa, being distinguished, having reached the supreme pinnacle of bliss, lies down at ease because he has accomplished all that was to be done. || 347 ||
These three, beginning with the fool, are intended as a single illustrative example.
It is stated thus for the purpose of removing the blindness caused by the intoxication of childhood and ignorance. || 348 ||

Having stated the literal meaning of the scriptural examples, he states what is intended [by the author]: "The child, etc. (bālādi). The meaning is that these three—the child and so forth—which were mentioned as examples, are not [to be taken] as such; rather, the single example is the great Brāhmaṇa. The word "api" (also) draws in the negative particle from the phrase "that knowledge is not sufficient" (na tad-dhīr alam). To the question, "Why are two of the three scriptural examples being disregarded?", he replies: "The child, etc. (vāla).
The meaning is that the final example is cited for the purpose of removing two defects: the foolishness of a child and the blindness of pride in a king. || 348 ||
Because the fool lacks discernment, the lord of the earth possesses discernment.
To refute the blindness caused by that intoxication, the Great Brāhmaṇa is spoken. || 349 ||

In order to establish the third point, he states the reason for the king’s seizure while excluding the child, [beginning with] "Of the child. The connection is that this is stated as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). He says "That" (*tat*): in the previous case, there was the king’s seizure due to a fault; in this case as well, because of the prohibition of that same fault, the seizure of a great Brahmin (*mahābrāhmaṇa*) occurs, and thus that very same instance serves as the illustration. || 349 ||
Having transcended the causes of suffering, it destroys all sufferings without exception.
It is the supreme culmination of bliss; therefore, it is called "the destroyer. || 350 ||

He states the meaning of the word *atighnīm* (all-destroying) as follows: "Having transcended," etc. The construction is as follows: that supreme state of bliss which has been attained by the knower through his being a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), his tranquility of pride, and so forth—that [state], having transcended the afflictions (*kleśas*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśas*) which are the causes of suffering, completely uproots all sufferings that are their effects; therefore, it is called *atighnī*. || 350 ||
Because, for children and others who possess an unchanging self, [this occurs] within their own self.
An exceedingly great delight arises; that is the intended illustration. || 351 ||
Having accepted the distinction between the illustrations, he states the intended portion [of the meaning]: "Nirvikāra" (without modification), etc. || 359 ||
The self enters into a relationship with others through the forms of cause and effect.
That which is characterized by the nature of oneness is directly called "white. || 352 ||

He states the meaning of the word "lying down" as it applies to the subject of the illustration: "The other," etc. The meaning is that because the self attains identity with the unknown Brahman along with the ego and so forth during deep sleep, its "lying down" consists in its abiding directly in the form of Brahman. || 312 ||
1. ga. Consisting of three meanings.
119 [vol2, page 652]
946 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter:
Even for those things that are extremely close, there is a distinction between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object known (*meya*).
Collyrium and other such substances applied to the eyes are not intended to be seen by the path of vision. || 353 ||

Anticipating the objection that if the individual soul (jīva) has attained oneness with Brahman, it would realize "I am Brahman" and thus never rise again from that state, [the author] provides an illustration for the absence of such knowledge during deep sleep, despite the soul's extreme proximity to Brahman: "Atyanteti" (Verse 353).
How much more so in this case, within the Self, where all distinctions have been utterly destroyed without remainder?
The relationship between the grasped and the grasper [ceases] when all distinctions have been dispelled. || 354 ||

Having stated the illustrative example—that according to the maxim of "extreme distance" and "extreme proximity," excessive nearness is an obstacle to cognition and not its cause—he states the application to the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) by asking, "What [happens]? In a person who has fallen into deep sleep, all identification with the body and so forth—which is the cause of differentiation—is destroyed; for this very reason, it has the nature of removing all differentiation. Therefore, the meaning is that in that state, there is no relationship between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). || 34 ||
Only their state of health is observed as established in the world.
That very state [of deep sleep] is intended to be expressed directly as the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) for sleep. || 355 ||

The illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) have been explained. There, since the illustration consists specifically of the sleep of children and others according to the scriptural statement "he sleeps" (*śayīta*), one might raise the objection:
"In the phrase 'of those whose self is changeless' (*nirvikārātmanām*), how is it that the state of children and so forth is mentioned there as well? Anticipating this, he says: "svastha... (355).
For it is the one who is in deep sleep that is intended here as the subject of the illustration.
Nor is any distinction observed in the sleep of fools and others. || 356 ||

He states the reason why the sleep of children and others cannot serve as an illustration (dṛṣṭānta): "By way of being the subject of the illustration" (dāṣṭantikatvena). The word "here" (atra) refers to that statement [of his].

Therefore, the sleep of children and others is not an illustration because there is no difference between it and the subject of the illustration (dāṣṭantika); this is the implied meaning. Anticipating the objection that there is a distinction—namely, that their sleep is the illustration while the sleep of people like us is the subject of the illustration—he says: "Nor even... (nāpi). || 356 ||
The child, whose intellect was unimpeded, was devoid of all excellence.
He attains the supreme and most exalted culmination of bliss. || 357 ||

One might object: "Since the state of a child lacks discrimination, it does not possess the condition of well-being that consists of supreme bliss; therefore, how can the validity of that illustration be established? [To this, the author replies:
"Unimpeded" (avyāhatā). || 357 ||
To whatever extent the growth of passion and so forth arises in the child...
To that same extent, even suffering becomes fully developed. || 358 ||

It is incorrect to claim that a child, whose intellect is unafflicted by passion and the like, attains a state of unsurpassed bliss free from suffering and its causes; for even such a child is afflicted by passion and the like, as evidenced by the perception of hunger, thirst, and so forth. Anticipating this objection, he says: "As long as... The meaning is that when passion and the like are predominant, suffering is abundant and happiness is meager. || 358 ||
Just as there is thinness here, so long as it pertains to the self.
To the same extent that there is a diminution of suffering, there will likewise be an increase of the nature of happiness. (359)

He states the dissimilarity as follows: "Just as," etc. One who possesses passion and so forth [is not such a person], because of the paucity of suffering and the abundance of happiness, and so on, which have become fully developed.

The meaning is that the illustration refers to one who is a child regarding passion and the like, whose intellect is unimpaired, and who abides in a state of unsurpassed bliss. The word "here" (iha) refers to the sphere of worldly transaction. || 319 ||
Therefore, through progressive increase and through the destruction of the causes of suffering, [this occurs] upon hearing [the teaching].
The culmination of bliss is said to be reached by means of ten thousandths of that [bliss]. || 360 ||

Regarding the statement that "upon the destruction of passion and so forth, there is the destruction of suffering, and thus the abundance of happiness," he states the proof: "In the subsequent [passage]. Starting from "That is one human bliss" and ending with "That is one bliss of Brahman," the scripture declares that in each successive stage, through an increase of a hundredfold excellence over each preceding stage, the culmination of bliss is reached in Brahman; therein it says, "of one who is learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire."

The meaning is that, according to scripture, through the destruction of passion and other afflictions which are the causes of suffering, there follows the cessation of the suffering that is their effect, thereby establishing an abundance of happiness. || 360 ||
Because it is established as the mere ultimate reality, it is neither excluded nor followed by anything else.
"But the supreme culmination of bliss is in the Infinite (bhūman) alone"—such is the statement of the Śruti.

[The author] provides corroboration from another Śruti regarding the fact that the supreme culmination of bliss is in Brahman, by citing the passage beginning with "That which is the Infinite, that is bliss" (*yo vai bhūmā tatsukham*). He says "unrestricted" (*avyāvṛtta*): because everything culminates in the Inner Self (*pratīc*), which is of a single flavor, it is understood that the culmination of bliss is in that very place. Thus, the passage beginning with "That which is the Infinite, that is bliss," etc., [is established].
This is the meaning. || 361 ||
Ānanda is the Self itself, devoid of both difference and association.
Therefore, it naturally attains a state that is free from the causes of suffering and destroys all excesses.

Having stated that "the culmination is in the plenitude of bliss" (*ānandasya bhūmni niṣṭhā*), [the author] raises the doubt that there might be a difference between bliss and the Self, and says: "Bliss. Anticipating the doubt that there might be a connection between that [bliss] and the Self—as in the case of an action and its agent, or as in the case of a blue lotus—he says: "Difference. He states the result of the identity of the Self and bliss: "Suffering," etc.; the ellipsis is "the culmination of bliss is exceedingly great. [This refers to] the state...

Thinking that this state of finality (niṣṭhā) is attained even without knowledge by one who has withdrawn from activity due to the exhaustion arising from the movement of worldly affairs—and therefore a renewed exertion is appropriate—he says: "Therefore, by itself," etc. (362).
Regarding that which Gārgya Kāśya asked—"What did this become then?"—that was [the question].
Everything has been explained completely and correctly, exactly as it is, without exception. || 363 ||

In order to state the connection of the passage beginning with "Just as a spider [spins its web]," he recounts what has preceded: "Gārgya," etc. This means: by adding all the required particulars without exception. || 363 ||
And by this aforementioned [method], for one who has indeed arisen from the pressing of the hands—
The Śruti declares that purification [is attained] from all actions arising from delusion. || 364 ||

In response to the inquiry as to what the fruit of the resolution of the first question is, he says: "By this. The meaning is that by this, the purification of the referent "thou" (tvam-artha) has been accomplished. The sense of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that such a purification is well-known elsewhere as well. || 364 ||
In order to clarify the meaning of the question, "From where did it come?",
the transition from deep sleep to the waking state is now explained, just as [it was previously explained]. (365)
He states the purport of the subsequent [verse]: "Why?"—that is to say, "of this sleeping jīva. (369)
1 [vol2, page 654] 948 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Second Adhyāya]
Indeed, that which is unstable here departs from that very place to another.
Whether from a house or from a village, he shall certainly depart from that very place. || 366 ||

He raises the objection that the latter [verse] has already been covered by the former with the words "But surely" (nanu). The meaning of the word "for" (hi) is that it is well-established in common experience that the very substratum of staying is the point of departure for going. The phrase "from another" (anyataḥ) is a statement regarding the object of the motion. || 366 ||
Therefore, by implication, the resolution of the subsequent question is established.
One should not undertake an action for the sake of a final decision due to the fault of a kinsman. || 367 ||
The limit of [the soul's] staying has alone been determined, but not the limit of its arrival; thus, the subsequent portion of the text proceeds for that purpose. With this intention, he says:

"Therefore" (tasmāt). Since the certainty regarding the limit of staying is established, and since the certainty regarding the limit of the journey is possible by virtue of that very [certainty], it is not appropriate to begin the subsequent portion of the text for that purpose, as it would be redundant. This is the meaning. || 367 ||
Nor is it tenable that the ablative case has the sense of "cause" (nimitta) and so forth.
In the analogy of the spider and the fire, no causal sign (nimitta) or the like is perceived. || 368 ||

He says "no," etc., in response to the doubt that the ablative case in "kutaḥ" (from where) does not signify the *apādāna* (point of departure), and thus there is no tautology; rather, it is intended as a question regarding the cause for one established in Brahman coming here, or as a challenge to that [position]. || 368 ||
If, in response, the cause and so forth are not directly perceived, [then what remains?]
Or rather, let it have the sense of an ablative, because a lamp is seen elsewhere [than its source]. || 369 ||

Having accepted the lack of comprehension regarding the two [types of] rejection—the rejection of the cause (*nimitta*) and the rejection of the [actual] statement (*ākṣepa*)—he raises the objection that the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) serves as the ablative (*apādāna*) because the use of the word *śrīta* possesses its own meaning due to a restrictive rule (*niyama*), and because there is no absence of another meaning. This is expressed by the words "pratyuktau" (in the case of the rejection). "Anyatra" means elsewhere, namely in the case of the cause and so forth.
"Doṣasya" means of the fault, which is the contradiction with the rejection. || 369 ||
But surely, even here the same fault applies: the tautology of the statement.
It is not so, because what is intended to be expressed is the destruction of all effects of darkness.

The proponent of the previous view states that, because of the fault of redundancy in the case of the ablative (*apādāna*), a different meaning must be expressed by the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*). He introduces this with "But surely" (*nanu*).
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with "Not so" (*naivam*). Stating the reason for that, he explains the intended meaning through the first question with "Since" (*yataḥ*).
The meaning is that the pure sense of "Thou" (*tvam*) is what is intended here. || 370 ||
The intended meaning is Brahman, which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else, and is complete.
Since the true nature of each individual [syllable] is identical, there is no fault of redundancy (jāmitā) resulting from that.

He states what is intended by the second question: "avyāhṛta" (unuttered), etc. The result is that there is no tautology, because it is established that the non-dual Brahman, which is the inner self free from all ignorance and its products, is what is sought to be taught by means of the two questions. || 171 ||
Two objects are presented here as the respective domains of knowledge and ignorance.
The object of the knowledge "He is indeed the Self" has been cited previously. (372)
1. *ka*. *vrajet* | 2. *taraḥ pra* [vol2, page 655] 1.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramakaranda* composed by Ānandagiri. 949.
First of all, the object of ignorance is said to be the misfortune of saṃsāra.
Through the distinction between action and its factors, it consists of name, form, and action. || 373 ||

Having raised the doubt as to how it is known that the subject matter intended to be discussed by means of questions is exactly as stated, he restates that third point in order to explain it: "The two objects" (*viṣayau*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to what was stated in the preceding chapter. He analyzes the presentation of the objects: "The Self," etc. He further specifies the very misfortune called *saṃsāra*: "Action," etc. (vv. 372–373).
In that regard, whatever effect arising from ignorance is intended to be discussed;
All of that was previously established with effort by the Śruti itself.

Regarding that, he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "that which is to be said concerning the object of ignorance" (*avidyā-viṣaye vaktavyam*), etc., by saying "therein" (*tatra*). The locative case here is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
The meaning is that the aphorism concerning ignorance along with its effects has been explained up to the end of the third chapter. This effort consists of both summary and detailed exposition. (374)
Now, the subject matter of knowledge, which is the direct antidote to ignorance, [is to be explained].
Therefore, two questions suitable for that purpose are set forth as those to be addressed. (375)

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "But the Self is the object of knowledge" (vidyāviṣayastvātmā) as follows: "Ignorance" (avidyā). The meaning is that since the aphorism on knowledge (vidyāsūtra) has not been elaborated upon, the two questions are raised for that purpose. || 375 ||
The causes, essential natures, and effects are mutually contradictory.
Because, from the singing of questions appropriate to that [subject], there arises ignorance and knowledge. || 376 ||

How is it that ignorance (*avidyā*) has knowledge (*vidyā*) as its counteragent? To this he says: "The cause," etc. The non-discrimination, attachment, and so forth that make ignorance known are the producers and indicators of ignorance, whereas discrimination, dispassion, and so forth are the producers and indicators of knowledge. Their respective natures are illumination and non-illumination; their effects are bondage and its destruction. Since these are mutually contradictory, [knowledge] is fit to be explained as the counteragent to ignorance.
The meaning is that it proceeds non-dually. || 376 ||
This conventional usage of grammatical factors is always the domain of ignorance.
In the case of the support and the supported, their status as grammatical factors (kāraka) is desired when there is a wall [between them]. || 377 ||

Anticipating the question of how the two questions are useful for the explanation of the aforementioned knowledge (*vidyā*), he states their scriptural meaning in brief: "The agent... and so on. The state of its existence is called "being" (*sadā*). Among these, he summarizes the meaning of the first question: "The substratum... (verse 377).
Therefore, that which goes from one place to another does so only when there is a difference [between the two locations].
Thus is established this state of ignorance; knowledge is its opposite.
He summarizes the meaning of the second question with the words "tadvat" (in the same way). He concludes the scriptural meaning of those two with the words "ityavidyā" (thus [is] ignorance).

To state what is intended by those two, he describes the scope of knowledge (*vidyā*) with the words "vidyāyāḥ" (of knowledge). The meaning is that the object of knowledge is a single-flavored reality, which is the opposite of the non-duality that is the object of ignorance (*avidyā*). || 378 ||
1 ka. ga. pūrvaśru | 1 [vol2, page 656]
950. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]:
"The intellect that arose from worldly experience regarding the distinctions between actions, agents, and so forth..."
It is sublated by the correct knowledge of the true nature of the self as it actually exists. || 379 ||

Thus, he states the result regarding the determination of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) with the words "Action" (*kriyā*). The notion of duality is ignorance; it is sublated by the knowledge of the Self as non-dual.
Therefore, the sense is that the two questions concern the object of that knowledge which is to be produced for the purpose of removing that [ignorance]. || 379 ||
This self is not one thing and was not another elsewhere; nor does it become something else from that which it is.
Thus, the destruction of all the effects of delusion without exception is intended [by this]. || 380 ||

Now he states the purport of the reply: "Not another" (*nānya*). If the relationship of locus and subject (*adhikaraṇādhikartavyabhāva*) and the relationship of source and agent (*apādānakartṛbhāva*) are not intended to be expressed, then what is it that is intended? To this he says: "Thus, entirely... (*iti niḥśeṣa*). The meaning is: provided that the distinction between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) is not intended to be expressed in the manner previously stated. By the word "that" (*tat*), the Self (*ātman*) is denoted. [The phrase] "by means of the knowledge of that" (*tadvidyādvāreṇa*)...
The remainder. || 380 ||
Here, another entity [is established] from the Self by means of non-difference and non-exclusion.
By means of scripture, the cause of duality is directly negated. || 381 ||

He states the reason why the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya*) is not intended here, but rather that the destruction of delusion and so forth occurs through knowledge (*vidyā*), by saying "non-difference" (*abhedena*).
The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the statement consisting of the question and its reply. This means: [the destruction] of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the cause of difference. || 381 ||
But surely, since the vital breaths and so forth exist, how can there be non-differentiation of the Self?
It does not exist in the self alone due to that habitual practice, like [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth. || 382 ||
This raises an objection regarding the previously indicated indivisibility of the Self: "But surely... (nanu). The ellipsis to be supplied is "because it is distinct from those [attributes].

He refutes this by stating that the existence of the vital breaths and so forth is not due to their being superimposed upon the Self—as silver is upon mother-of-pearl—saying: "Not upon the Self" (nātmāni) || 382 ||
To explain how that is so, examples such as the spider and others are cited.
This creation of the Self is not real in comparison to that [ultimate reality]. || 383 ||

In that regard, he states that their being imagined (kalpitatva) is not supported by valid means of knowledge (aprāmāṇika). [The questioner asks: "How so? To this, as a response, he introduces the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*) and so forth. [The opponent objects: "Is it not the case that here, by means of the example, a real creation (*vāstavī sṛṣṭiḥ*) of the vital breaths and so on from the Self is being taught? [The author replies: No; for there is no indication of such superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of those [breaths] upon that [Self]. He says: "Real" (*vāstavam*). This is said with reference to the nature of the Self, which is immutable (*kūṭastha*), non-attached (*asaṅga*), and non-dual (*advaya*).
The meaning is that because the creation of the vital breaths and so forth is impossible, it is merely imagined. || 383 ||
There is no connection of the non-existent with birth, nor is existence sought for that which already exists.
In the immutable there is no modification; therefore, birth arises from ignorance.

Furthermore, he states that there is no origination of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, whether they be non-existent or existent. He says "not of the non-existent" to negate the first [possibility], and "of the existent" to negate the second. Having stated the impossibility of origination by examining the nature of the produced (*janya*), he states its impossibility even by examining the nature of the producer (*janaka*) with the word "immutable" (*kūṭastha*). To the question, "What then is the status of the appearing origination?", he replies: "Therefore—"
Thus it is said. || 384 ||
This creation is described under the guise of a pretext for the purpose of bringing about the awakening of the individual soul.
Because the Self is immutable, its creation is not possible in any way whatsoever. || 385 ||

If creation is unreal, for what purpose is it described? To this he says: "Because it serves to awaken the person. If creation is fruitful, why then should it not be real? To this he says: "Because of its immutability. || 389 ||
This has been declared even by those learned in the entirety of the established doctrines of the Vedas.
This matter has been explained by us exactly as it was by the Gauḍācāryas. || 386 ||
He states the consensus of the elders regarding the fact that this creation, consisting of illusion (māyā), serves the purpose of self-knowledge: "Niḥśeṣa... (Verse 386).
The creation that has been described otherwise, by means of clay, iron, sparks, and so forth;
That is a skillful means for entry; there is no difference whatsoever.
He restates that very point: "clay," etc. (387).
But when creation is directed toward something else, there is no possibility for such an objection to arise.
How can there be production from that which is immutable? And how [can there be production] from that which is conscious into that which is unconscious?

Having demonstrated that the accounts of creation and so forth lack scriptural authority because the scripture concerning creation is intended to establish non-duality, he states another resulting point regarding its alternative intent: "In creation... He then states what that improbable objection is: "From that which is immutable... The meaning is that since objects such as jars arise from clay and the like—which possess activity—creation of the universe cannot proceed from Brahman, because Brahman is changeless. Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect [is impossible] if there is identity of characteristics.

Since neither Brahman nor the world—whether conscious or unconscious—is perceived [as a cause], that [cause] does not exist; therefore, the world is not born from it. Thus he says: "Inert" (acitkam). || 388 ||
And how could one perform various kinds of tasks without the necessary means?
How can the arising of manifold forms occur from that which is of a single form? || 389 ||

Having stated the impossibility of Brahman being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe, he states the impossibility of its being the efficient cause (*nimitta*): "And [Brahman] is without means" (*niḥsādhanaṃ ca*). Because it is non-dual (*advaya*), it is without means; and because of its uniformity (*aikarasya*), Brahman cannot be a cause in either way—this is what he states with the word "the universe" (*viśva*). The sense is that this collection of objections is improper, because the scriptural accounts of creation have another purpose and thus creation is of the nature of *māyā*. || 389 ||
Thus, for such objections, [the response] follows from the nature of the person.
The scriptural statement regarding avoidance is not based on the actual nature of things.

If that [creation] consists of illusion (*māyā*), then one might ask: "How is it that [the scripture] says 'just as' (*sa yathā*) and so forth for the sake of refuting that? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this very way" (*ityevamiti*). This means that, without conforming to the nature of reality (*vastu*), but merely in accordance with human cognition, the passage beginning with "just as" is intended to refute the objections raised by you according to the logic previously stated. The word "thus" (*evam*) refers back to the sentence under discussion. The creation of the Lord is not for His own purpose.
The meaning of the word "etcetera" (ādi) in the objection is: "Because it possesses desire, because it is not for another's sake, and because it is non-dual. || 390 ||
The spider, acting as its own agent, applies itself to its work with focused intent.
By means of threads that are self-established and by means of the instrument which is the thread itself.
It accomplishes movement in one place, and likewise within the self as well.
Having thus stated the purport, he explains the passage beginning with "sa yathā" (just as that) by means of the word "ūrṇā" (wool). He asks: what is that action? He says: "threads" (tantūn).

[The word] "by itself" (ātmanā) is stated for the purpose of excluding any instrument other than itself. Having declared the absence of any means external to itself, he describes its manifold nature as a creator by means of an instrument not distinct from itself, using the phrase "from itself" (svataḥ). He applies the analogy of the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) to the Self, stating "in the same way" (*tathā*). || 399 ||
Just as the web of a spider is insentient [while arising] from a sentient being.
Likewise, the world, consisting of effects such as space and so forth, [arises] from the conscious Self.

Having refuted the objection beginning with "and [the argument] is without a means," he addresses the objection beginning with "insentient" and so forth. By the words "insentient," the objection beginning with "the production of the form of the universe" and so forth is refuted. || 392 ||
Just as sparks arise from a fire, possessing the very nature of fire.
In the same way, from the Self in deep sleep, there arises the emergence of the vital breaths and the other faculties. || 393 ||
Dispelling the objection beginning with "How [could it be] from the immutable," he explains the passage beginning with "In another way" as follows: "Like sparks. (393)
That which is illustrated by the example of deep sleep is characterized thereby.
Prior to the manifestation of all things, Brahman is devoid of name and form.

When it is stated that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth arise from deep sleep (*suṣupta*), one might suspect that the locus (*sthāna*) is also a cause; to address this, he says: "From deep sleep...

By stating that the self in deep sleep is the *apādāna* (the point of departure), the unmanifest name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the unknown Brahman prior to awakening, is indicated; the meaning is that that very [Brahman] is the cause. || 394 ||
In all the Upanishads, it is thus stated that there is no cause for the Self other than itself.
Therefore, it is heard that the Supreme Self alone is the ultimate cause of the universe.
Furthermore, since there is no evidence for a cause other than Brahman as ignorance (*avidyā*), he states that it is precisely that [Brahman] which is so; thus he says, "In all...
This refers to Brahman as unknown (*ajñāta*). He excludes the *pradhāna* and others by saying, "Nothing else," meaning because nothing else is heard in scripture. || 399 ||
When the Brahman has set entirely from this world without exception, [what remains?]
What is the cause of the production of the world? It is that [Brahman], because there is no exclusion of anything other than it.

Having stated his own position, he addresses a member of his own school: "In Brahman," etc. The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the locative case. For one who has merged completely [into Brahman], there can be no other cause for re-emergence than Brahman, because that is undesirable; nor can it be Brahman itself, because of its immutability (*kauṭasthyāt*). This is the meaning. || 396 ||
If Īśa exists as something distinct [from the world], by whom has he been impelled?
If the world were created by this [Lord] from himself, why is it not so at all times? (397)

The proponent of a detached God (*taṭastheśvaravādin*) says: "Because of that [God], even though the world is dissolved, its birth occurs by virtue of Him. He asserts: "He exists. First, he refutes the idea that He is detached, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for His existence. Furthermore, even if He existed, one must consider the dilemma: would He create the world being impelled by someone else, or by Himself? He then restates the second alternative and refutes it.
"If [it were] from itself," [it would be as follows]. || 397 ||
Neither sovereignty nor dependence can be conceived of in that which is measured by valid cognition.
Nor does the effect proceed toward its own production, because it has already dissolved.

He states the fault in the first [position] with the words "sovereignty" (*aiśvaryam*). The meaning is that both [attributes] cannot be authoritative for a single [entity] because they are mutually contradictory.
Regarding the proponent of *svabhāvavāda* (the doctrine of inherent nature), who claims that the effect itself is active in its own production and does not depend on a cause, he says "nor...

(*nāpi*). The sense is: if even a latent [effect] were active in its own production, there would be no restriction regarding its time of appearance, since there is no difference in its non-existence at that time. || 398 ||
If the effect were distinct from the cause, then how could there be the relationship of cause and effect between the two?
What kind of relationship can there be between two things established separately, like the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains? (399)
Furthermore, regarding whether there is a difference or non-difference between cause and effect, he says "if it were different" [verse 399] to show that the first case is not tenable.
Moreover, since that [cause] is non-different [from the effect], how can there be the relationship of cause and effect?
Nor does that which is inactive by nature possess the status of being a cause.
[The author] refutes the second alternative with the words "Now" (*atha*). Furthermore, is the cause something that acts or something that does not act?

Is it occasional or not? In the first case, there would be an infinite regress; in the second, the effect would have to exist eternally. To this he says: "Nor... (*nāpi*). If it does not act, then [the objection follows].
The meaning is that if something were a cause even while not performing an action, the effect would arise at all times. || 400 ||
And thus,
how can that which is not being performed be called an "action" (kārya) here?
And that entity which is devoid of action is held to be a non-agent. || 101 ||

Furthermore, he analyzes whether the effect itself is being produced or not. Thus it is said: "And so forth. Regarding the first alternative, since it possesses the nature of an effect, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the action [of producing] must itself be produced, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He refutes the second alternative with the words: "not being produced. The intention is that if it were not being produced, then even the Self (*ātman*) and other such entities would follow as being effects. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the sphere of the conventional usage of cause and effect. [This is stated] because the cause, if it does not perform [an action], [cannot be established].

And he states another fault regarding the non-performance of the action: "The action... etc. The meaning is that since it is accepted that an agent is that which performs an action, there would necessarily be a contradiction with one's own tenets in both positions. || 401 ||
Because it is completed by mere attachment alone, time, karma, and other such causes [are not required].
That manifest [effect] is incapable of producing itself, due to its lack of inherent capacity. (402)

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no fixed order of cause and effect, since time and so forth act as the regulators? [Reply: No; he says "by dissolution" (layena). Since it is heard in scripture that "that [unmanifest] became the year," time is itself an effect. Furthermore, because action and the rest are desired by him [the Lord], they all find their finality in dissolution within that which is designated by the word "dissolution"—namely, the causal Self. Therefore, even for its own production, time and the like lack the capacity, because they are non-existent in their own right.

The meaning is that the capacity to establish order is utterly remote [from such a cause], according to the maxim: "What reason can one who is incapable of even protecting himself have for protecting others?
Anticipating the objection that even that which is unborn—such as time (*kāla*) and so forth—might be an establishing factor because it exists in the form of a cause, he says: "That" (*tat*).
Therefore, that which is unborn cannot be an establishing factor; for a potter does not create a jar merely by existing in the form of its producer.
This is the meaning. || 402 ||
Even in the view that [the Lord's] power is eternal, there would be simultaneous production and so forth.
One attains the result of every action, yet it does not persist in that manner.
(403) [From the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, Second Chapter]

Having raised the objection that if time and so forth are effects, then their cause must be the cause of everything else, while everything else is an effect—thereby establishing a fixed order—he considers whether that [cause] also possesses power (*śaktimat*) or not. If it does not possess power, then everything would result in being the cause of everything. If it does possess power, then one must consider whether that power is eternal (*nityā*) or non-eternal (*anityā*). If it is eternal, then is the cause endowed with it independent (*nirapekṣa*) or not? Having thus formulated the alternatives, he refutes the first [position] with the word "eternal" (*nityā*). [The verse begins: *kalpā-*...

He replies immediately with the words "na ca" (nor). For a causal factor possessing power (*śaktimat*) is not dependent [on anything else], because that would result in its possession of power being rendered ineffective; such is the meaning. || 403 ||
Furthermore, if one accepts that potency arises [in the cause], then the cause would be devoid of potency.
Furthermore, if a power [arises] from another power, an infinite regress would result. (404)
He restates another alternative: "śakti" (power). Does that [effect] arise without power, or from another power?

In the first case, since the effect could be produced just like the power itself, there would be no need to postulate a causal agent possessing power; thus he says: "kāraṇam" (the cause). Having restated the other alternative, he refutes it: "atha" (now). || 404 ||
In relation to what is this present time said to be "passed"?
And it would also attain the state of being future, because of its lack of unity and its lack of parts.
Having raised the objection that the cause resides in the preceding moment while the effect resides in the succeeding moment, he refutes this distinction of time, asking: "Why? (405)
If time is accepted as a substance that is eternal, unitary, and all-pervading;
On what basis could there be a distinction such as pastness, futureness, and so forth? || 406 ||

Raising the objection as to how that [time] can possess parts (*aikatyābhāgavattva*), he considers the alternatives—whether time is a substance or an action—and having stated the first, he refutes it with the word "eternal" (*nityam*). The meaning is that, if it were all-pervading (*vibhutve*), there could be no internal differentiation of its own kind, just like space. || 406 ||
If the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies were time, then time would arise from the unmanifest.
Because the sun and other [elements] have dissolved, their activity is not admitted at that time. || 407 ||

He states another interpretation: "ādityādi" (beginning with the sun). [Objection: If that [time] arises from Brahman which is unknown, then how is time established as having the nature of its support? To this he says: "avyakta" (unmanifest). [Objection: Let it be so; what is the loss there? To this he says: "ādityādeḥ" (of the sun, etc.). At that time...

The meaning is that the determination of the cause as existing in the moment immediately preceding [the effect]—up until the point where the sun and other phenomena arise—is thereby established. || 407 ||
Nor can there be a subsistence of the whole [in its parts], because it is partless and unitary.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in classical Indian textual tradition signify a section break or the end of a chapter. [End of Section] [End of Chapter]
Because of the absence of parts, oneness, and lack of commonality among the portions. || 408 ||
Anticipating the objection that the effect-substance is composed of parts and that its causal substances are those very parts, in which it inheres, he says:

"And not so. Its subsistence in them cannot be either by way of occupying a single part (*ekadeśena*) or in its entirety (*kārtsnyena*). It cannot be the first, because that [effect] lacks other parts distinct from its own constituent parts;

nor can it be the second, because if a single entity were to subsist in multiple locations in its entirety, its effects would have to occur in each individual location. Therefore, it does not [inhere] in them.

This means "subsistence. Furthermore, just as a whole (avayavin) lacks parts and is a unity, so too, because it is neither a universal (asāmānya) nor a relation (asaṃbandha), it cannot subsist in multiple locations; thus he says: "Because of its partlessness" (niṣkalatva). || 408 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 661] 1 Brāhmaṇa, with the commentary titled Śākhaprakāśikā by Ānandagiri. 955
If the substratum is partless, then that which is supported must likewise be of such a nature.
Since they occupy different locations, how can there be a single composite whole (avayavin) in that manner? (409)

Having stated the counter-position, he states the fault: "In the substrata," etc. The meaning is that, just as with color and so forth, its status as a whole (avayavin) is not established within the [constituent] forms and so on. || 409 ||
Therefore, the distinction of place, time, and so forth does not reside in the object for a valid cognition.
Just as there is a distinction of directions and a distinction of different species, so too is there [a distinction] within the Self.

If, according to the reasoning already stated, there is no difference pertaining to real entities (vastu) caused by time and so forth as established by valid cognition, then what is the status of the manifested manifold of difference? To this, he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The word *vat* means "just as" (*yadvat*). || 410 ||
In the same way, the creation and destruction of the world are imagined within the Self.
Having observed the actual state of things, how could there be the occurrence of creation and so forth? || 411 ||
He states that if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is imagined within the Self, then by means of that [imagination], its attributes are also established therein:

"The world," etc. That is to say, "like that," meaning like the world. Since origination and so forth are imagined, he recalls the reasoning stated in passages such as "the creation of the Self" on the grounds of its immutability (*kauṭasthya*): "The reality," etc. (411).
I have previously explained how the agent and other grammatical factors are merely an illusion.
Thus, it is logically consistent that "everything is the Self" and "it is not so. || 412 ||

Furthermore, he states that the imagined nature of the group of non-self factors such as action and its instruments was already explained in the section on their causes and so forth, by saying "kāraka... etc.
He cites scripture as the authority for the imagined nature of duality, saying "sarvam... etc. (412).
Therefore, the arising, subsistence, and destruction of the world occur at every moment.
Because ignorance alone is their cause, no sequential order exists among them. || 413 ||

Anticipating the objection as to how the birth and so forth of the world can be unreal since they are perceptible and possess a fixed sequence, he says: "udbhūtī" (at their arising). The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (hence) is that these [births, etc. are non-existent in reality. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "they would be perceptible at every moment. By this, it is indicated that the world has the nature of appearing and then vanishing. Having refuted the substantiality suspected of birth and so forth due to their perceptibility, he now refutes the second reason.
It destroys [ignorance]. This is called ignorance. || 413 ||
Here, the vital breaths (prāṇas) are considered to be seventeen, consisting of the ten beginning with hearing (śrotra).
The distinction among these, characterized as internal (adhyātma) and so forth, is based on their limitation by the worlds. || 414 ||

Having thus explained the passage beginning with "evameva" (in the same way) along with its supplementary context, he states the meaning of the word *prāṇa* in the phrase "all the *prāṇas*" (*sarve prāṇāḥ*). He says: "The *prāṇas*.

The meaning is that the *prāṇas* intended here are the seventeen constituents of the subtle body (*liṅga*), namely: the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, the five vital airs (*vāyu*), the mind (*manas*), and the intellect (*buddhi*)—beginning with the ear and so forth. These possess numerous divisions according to their internal, external, and other modes of existence.
Anticipating the question, "How is there a state of seventeen?", he says: "The world," etc. The body is the world. || 414 ||
1. This is as follows: [vol2, page 662] 956 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter—]
The various worlds are divided by the different modes of birth, such as the womb-born and others.
Likewise, the gods, who are the selves of the presiding deities, would be the causes of division. || 415 ||

Regarding the phrase "all the worlds," he explains the meaning of the word *loka* with the words "old age" (*jarā*). Regarding the phrase "all the gods," he explains its meaning with the word "likewise" (*tathā*), meaning that they are born from the Self under discussion. || 419 ||
Those vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed common to all; let them remain uncommon only within this body.
This transformation of beings occurs according to their karma and according to their learning. 416.

[The text] clarifies the manifold nature of the gods with the words "te 'pi" (they too). Although Āditya and the others are collective entities (*samaṣṭi*) by virtue of their super-divine (*ādhidevika*) nature, nevertheless, within the individual body (*ādhyātmika*), they themselves become individual entities (*vyaṣṭi*) in the form of the eyes and so forth; this is the meaning. Of these—

Having raised the objection as to how the elements can be material (bhautika) in relation to their own production from the Self, he states the meaning of the verse beginning with "all" (*sarvāṇi*). He says: "Of the elements" (*bhūtānām*).

The sense is that they are effects of the Self through the mediation of those [elements]. To the question of how it is that the quality of producing pleasure, pain, and delusion is observed in them only occasionally, he replies: "Just as" (*yathā*) || 416 ||
He was born from the birth of the vital breaths and other elements, just as a fire is produced by sparks.
Even the Supreme Self was born, just as the ether is [manifested] through the births of jars and other objects.
He states the meaning of the Mādhyandina recension, "all these selves emerge," with the words "prāṇādi" (beginning with breath).

Anticipating the objection that—just as sparks are produced from fire—the Supreme [Self] might also have a real birth in the form of various specific appearances of consciousness, he says "jajñe" (was born). || 417 ||
Apart from the vital breath (prāṇa), no other extraction of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is recognized.
For from scripture, a clear statement has been heard to this effect: "from these [elements]. || 498 ||

Anticipating the objection that "the self is born from itself because it is a real entity, like a jar," and intending to point out the fallacy of this inference in the case of space (*ākāśa*), he says:
"prāṇādi" (beginning with breath). He further states "śruteḥ" (from scripture) to show that an inference of the self's birth apart from its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) contradicts scripture;

that [scripture] will be explained later. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to demonstrate the contradiction with the established principle beginning with "nātmā 'śruteḥ" (the self is not [born], because it is not so heard). || 498 ||
For it is by ignorance alone that the Self assumes the forms of the vital breaths and the knower of the field.
Therefore, he is by himself the Supreme Brahman; his secret name (upaniṣad) is declared [as such].
For the purpose of meditation, that which is pure is called the upaniṣad.
This is his supreme secret; one should worship it according to reality.

In that case, it would follow that there are three [entities]: the individual soul (*jīva*) as conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the unconditioned [individual soul], and the Supreme [Self]. To this he says: "Because...

Having explained the meaning of the Mādhyandina recension just as in the Kāṇva recension, he introduces and explains the passage beginning with "Of that" (*tasya*) and so forth, starting with the words "Of that," etc.
"The secret name of the inner Brahman (*pratyag-brahman*)," namely "the Truth of truth," is the esoteric name of the Upaniṣad.

The meaning is that it is for the sake of worshipping that [Self] and for the sake of realizing identity with it. He elaborates on the very meaning of the first half-verse: "tadasya" (of that, of this). || 419 || 420 ||
In this section on the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), whatever meditation whatsoever [is prescribed]— [this is the beginning of the commentary] titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri.
One should point out that all this is the fruit arising from the knowledge of Brahman.

He establishes that this [name] has the fruit of arising from knowledge (vidyā) by means of an illustration: "Brahman," etc. The meaning is that just as every form of meditation heard in the context of the knowledge of Brahman has that [knowledge] as its fruit upon arising, so too does this name. || 421 ||
Just as in the case of the milking vessel and other such examples, all forms of meditation should be understood in this same way.
Because it is subordinate to knowledge (*vidyā*) and constitutes its life-force, it cannot be an independent fruit [of action].

Anticipating the objection—“How can the meditation (*upāsana*) situated within that specific context have the production of that [knowledge] as its fruit?”—the author says: “As in the case of the *godohana* [vessel], etc. By the word “etc.,” [the following is included]: “He strews [the grass] so that it is not too thick; he thus makes him [the sacrificer] not too conspicuous with offspring and cattle” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.4.3); and “For one desiring cattle, [he should place] the loose earth from the footprint of a horse” (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.8.18.5).

It is understood that one should construct the altar (*vedi*). The *godohana* vessel, which exists as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and depends upon the fetching of water (*praṇayana*), accomplishes the attainment of heaven by way of fulfilling the application of the *darśa* and other rites; it is precisely through this mediation that it also accomplishes the attainment of cattle. Having raised the doubt as to whether that [vessel] is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and having established—on the basis of the requirement of the material used—that it is for the sake of the sacrifice as a subordinate element of the water-fetching prescribed by the very sentence, [the author concludes: "it is for the sake of the sacrifice."

Even though the fact that the *godohana* vessel serves as a means for bringing water—which is required by the sacrifice (*kratvapekṣita*)—and thus constitutes its specific function (*kāryatā*), is established by syntactical connection (*vākyīya*), nevertheless, because the injunction (*niyoga*) requires application (*viniyoga*), it has been established in the fourth book (*caturtha adhyāya*) that it also serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), following its connection with the term "one desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*).

Similarly, every meditation (*upāsana*) situated within the context of knowledge (*vidyāprakaraṇa*) accomplishes that knowledge through the medium of what it depends upon (*upajīvya*), since it subsists upon the created phenomenal world (*sṛṣṭaprapañca*) for its own sake; thus, it also brings about another fruit, just as...

One should establish that instruction; it is not an independent fruit because it would contradict its dependence [on another]. Therefore, the meaning is that meditation (upāsti) is the cause of knowledge (dhī) by way of purification, according to the power of the context (prakaraṇa). || 422 ||
That which is called the Upaniṣad of Brahman is "the truth of truth."
The Upaniṣad of this [text], "The vital breaths are indeed truth," has been explained. || 423 ||
He introduces the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth" by means of the words "of truth" (satyasya). || 423 ||
The vital breaths (prāṇas), which consist of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), are called "truth" because they are united with the supreme truth; their supreme state is Truth itself. || 424 ||

He states its meaning in brief: "The name," etc. He states the reason why they are denoted by the word *satya* (truth): "Because of another," etc. The meaning is: because of the connection with that substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). || 424 ||
The subsequent [section] is the perfect revelation of the meaning of the Upaniṣads as previously stated.
The two Brāhmaṇas beginning with "yo ha vai śiśuḥ" will come to be [hereafter]. || 425 ||

By stating the meeting between Gata and Uttara-brāhmaṇa, he indicates an intervening matter. Regarding the word "spoken" (*ukta*): since the mere disclosure of that [matter] was already established, the word "properly" (*samyak*) is used with the intention of expressing a specific qualification regarding it. || 429 ||
Let it be granted that the two Brāhmaṇas are indeed called Upaniṣads.
Tell me, does this name belong to the transmigrating soul or to Brahman? (426)
1 Kha. Lamu | [vol2, page 664] 958 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Second Adhyāya— ]

Having accepted the connection [between the two views], he initiates an inquiry while remaining in doubt due to the observation of specific differences. The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to establish that the explanation of that [objection] is manifest therein. || 426 ||
If there were indeed a transmigrating being who was not awakened, [then] the crushing by the hand would occur.
Then that very [reality] is to be known; from the knowledge of that alone comes liberation.

Having stated the doubt according to the maxim that "that which is doubtful and fruitful should be investigated," and having restated the first position—which serves as the motive for the investigation—he says regarding that [position]: "In the hands... etc. Anticipating the objection that only that from whose knowledge liberation arises is the object to be known (the Knowable), and not the individual soul (jīva), he says:
"From the knowledge of That... || 427 ||
And at that time, he who is denoted by the word "Brahman" would be nothing other than a transmigrating being.
"At that time, we understand that knowledge of it is 'brahmavidyā' (knowledge of Brahman).
Anticipating the doubt that this [knowledge] arises only from the knowledge of Brahman and not from the knowledge of one who is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*), he says: "Brahman.
Anticipating the doubt that whatever knowledge is *brahmavidyā*, that alone is Brahman and not the transmigratory being, he says: "Knowledge of it" (*tadvidyā*). || 428 ||
Now, it is established by logic that there exists indeed one who does not transmigrate.
Whatever has been stated regarding the transmigrating being will then apply to that [state].
(429) Having restated an alternative position, he states the result: "Now" (*atha*). This is because the primary meaning of the name as previously explained is sublated in that very state.

The principle of "fitness" (yogyatva) and so forth: the meaning of "as it has been stated" is that [the self] is to be known, and that liberation occurs precisely through the knowledge of that [self], and so on. || 429 ||
The defects of those two, who possess distinct natures, are [removed] by those [scriptures] which establish Brahman-hood.
All the Vedas would be contradicted, because nothing could then be other than what it is.

One might suspect that the position of the *Brahmopaniṣad* is correct because of the authority of the scriptures; anticipating this, the author analyzes whether there is difference or non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, and states the fault in the first case. [He says: "If [they were] different. He explains that very point: "In the state of being Brahman... He states the reason for the contradiction with all the scriptures: "There is nothing else... Since it is impossible for something else—whether existing or having perished—to be another, if there were a difference between the individual soul and the Supreme, the scriptural teaching of their identity would be contradicted.
The meaning is that there would be an obstruction. || 430 ||
And since there is no one other than Brahman, likewise there is no sufferer when it does not exist.
