It would follow that the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman is rendered purposeless. || 431 ||

But in another interpretation, since there would be no suffering beings, the instruction [of the Veda] would be as useless as for Brahmā himself; for that instruction is not purposeful for Brahmā because he is eternally liberated, and there is no other [being] to whom it could apply. Thus he says: "Of Brahmā. (431)
Thus, the cause of doubt is the motivator of inquiry.
Therefore, investigation must be carried out, for it effects the destruction of the aforementioned doubts. (432)

Since even the position of the *Brahmopaniṣad* is untenable without inquiry, it has been stated that the non-perception of a specific [reason] is the cause of doubt, and that this necessitates inquiry; thus he states the conclusion: "Thus, because of doubt. Having stated the motivator of inquiry, he concludes its necessity as its effect: "Therefore," etc. || 432 ||
There is no other supreme being beyond saṃsāra, distinct from the one awakened by the pressing of the hand.
For it is heard in the Śruti that its origin proceeds from that which consists of the state of the wise (prājña). || 433 ||

Having introduced the subject matter for investigation by means of doubt and so forth, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words beginning "No" (*na*). Thus, the ellipsis to be supplied is that there is no such thing as its "Upanishad. He states the reason why Brahman is not something other than the individual soul (*jīva*) with the word "the vital breaths" (*prāṇa*). For it is heard in scripture that from the state of sleep, the emergence of the vital breaths and so forth occurs from one who possesses adventitious knowledge; and since Brahman is intended as the cause of the world, it is therefore not other than the individual soul.
The meaning is: because of possessing adventitious knowledge, or because of possessing states. || 433 ||
Having thus made the promise, "I shall speak the Brahman to you," the king then approached a sleeping man and himself attempted to awaken him by touching him with his hand.

Anticipating the objection that the scripture declares its origination from the *prakṛta* (the subject under discussion), namely Brahman, and not from the individual soul (*jīva*), he says: "Brahman. The implication is that, therefore, it is the individual soul itself that is the subject under discussion by the word "Brahman. || 434 ||
Having led him to that other state by way of the path of non-perception of oneself.
Therefore, from that state called deep sleep (suṣupta), he taught the origination of the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the rest.

Establishing its status as the subject under discussion, he declares it to be the cause with the word "him" (*tam*). The meaning of that word is the individual soul (*jīva*) in the state of awakening. "By way of the path of dreaming" means by means of the presentation of dreams, as in the passage beginning, "When he moves about in a dream," and so forth.
The word "thence" (*tataḥ*) refers back to the reasons already stated. || 435 ||
Therefore, no transmigrating being other than this [consciousness] can be conceived here.
And having referred to the beloved self, it is said that "he is to be seen. || 436 ||

Even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is the subject under discussion by virtue of possessing occasional knowledge and so forth, one might suspect that the cause of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the rest could be something else entirely; anticipating this objection, he says: "The transmigrating [soul] (*saṃsārī*). This means starting from the passage beginning with "Those two, indeed" (*tau ha*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the context of the present section.

Having stated that the transmigrating soul is an object of knowledge according to the introductory method, he says "having restated" (*anūdya*) to show that it is so even by way of what remains: "the dear self," which means the enjoyer characterized by dear things such as sons, wealth, and other means of enjoyment. || 436 ||
And in all the Vedantas, it is the inner self alone that is enjoined.

"It should not be seen as different from that by virtue of being an object of knowledge"—this is what is stated. Furthermore, he says "In the Vedāntas" to show that its very nature is to be an object of knowledge. || 437 || || 437 ||
Through connection with another state, it will become transmigratory.
Even if this [self] were transmigrating by its own nature, it would not be so, because such a perception is impossible.

When it is argued that because the Upaniṣads teach the birth of the world from the individual soul (jīva) in the state of deep sleep, and because that [jīva] alone is seen to be the object of knowledge, there is no Lord (Īśvara) known through the Vedāntas who is the cause of that [world], the proponent of the doctrine of a Lord (Seśvaravādin) objects: "In another state" (avasthāntare). The meaning is that this very jīva, who by nature is subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsārī) and connected with two states, becomes the Supreme (para) when he enters another state called deep sleep; thus, the birth of the world is said in scripture to proceed from the Supreme alone.
1 ka. kha. From scripture.
[vol2, page 666] 960

The meaning of the objection is as follows: "Is there not a difference in the entity due to the difference in its states? He refutes this with the verse beginning "neha" (not here), on the grounds that no such difference in the entity is experienced and because it would contradict established doctrine (*aparāddhānta*).
In this world, no object distinguished by another genus ever attains a different genus from its own nature, except through the agency of God. (439)

He states, by means of an illustration, that there is no difference in the substance [of the self] despite the difference in its states, beginning with the words "no" (na) and so forth. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "due to the difference in states such as walking, lying down, and so on. Therefore, the meaning is that even in the case of the Self, there is no difference in its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Regarding the doctrine of a personal God (*seśvaravāda*), one might argue that due to His power, a different class of entity could actually arise from Him—one characterized by qualities such as being a cow; for nothing is impossible for the Lord. To this, he replies:

Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": apart from that cause, nothing else can become something else. The meaning is that if it were to alter the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, then nothing whatsoever would remain established. || 439 ||
If one were to abandon even one's own nature, fire would certainly become cold.
Furthermore, all means of valid cognition would be subverted, and everything would be both inferior and superior [simultaneously]. (440)

He states the contradiction with logic (*nyāyavirodha*) regarding the reversal of essential nature (*svarūpa*) due to differences in state (*avasthābheda*) and so forth, [in the verse] beginning with "svabhāvam. The meaning is: whatever entity is cognized as possessing a certain property, that entity does not deviate from that property, because otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). || 440 ||
Likewise, the Sāṃkhyas and others [establish] the non-existence of the Lord through many arguments.
They strive with effort to bring this about; who else is superior to them in wisdom? || 441 ||

Having stated that because [the Lord] is characterized by sleep only when distinguished by states such as wakefulness, He possesses transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), and thus there is no other Lord, [the author] cites the consensus of the disputants regarding the non-existence of such a Lord. Regarding the phrase "The Sāṃkhyas and others": if He possessed a body, He would be equal to ourselves and others; if He lacked a body, He could not be the creator of the world—just like a liberated soul (*mukta*)—since the agency for the world can belong only to the individual souls (*jīva*) through the medium of their unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). Such are the arguments [advanced against Him], rendering Him irrelevant.
He provides the commentary: "bahiti" (thus). The word "hi" is used for the purpose of indicating that logical arguments (*yukti*) are indeed as effective as scriptural authority (*āgama*).

"Effort" (*yatna*) refers to the presentation of those arguments as being free from defects. [An objection: "But will someone other than them, due to superior intelligence, not also establish the Lord?
[The author] says "no": "tebhyaḥ" (from them) || 441 ||
Even for those wandering in saṃsāra, there is an incapacity for the acts of creating the world and so forth.
If it is argued that its being the cause of the world is illogical, we say no, because of the authority of the Śruti.

The opponent raises an objection: "The subject of dispute (the transmigrating soul) is not the cause of the birth of the world and so forth, because it lacks the capacity for that, like a stone; and its lack of capacity in this regard is due to its being a transmigrating being. [The author] refutes this by pointing out the fallacy of the "missing the time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*):
"Not so, on account of scripture" (Sūtra 1.1.3). The word "even" (*api*) has the sense of the aforementioned example. || 442 ||
Just as that which is within the range of the senses is determined through the treatises.
In the same way, let it be understood from the Śruti that the world is characterized by the activity of transmigratory beings. || 443 ||

Anticipating the objection that even scriptural passages such as "In this very way" do not apply to the transmigrating soul's being the cause of the world—since that is beyond the scope of perception and other means of knowledge—he says:

"akṣādi" (perception, etc.). This refers to dharma and so forth. The sense is that scripture does not require another means of knowledge to convey its own meaning, because it is intrinsically authoritative. || 443 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 667] 1. Brāhmaṇam] Thus, this position has first been established through reasoning, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
Now, another position, different from that established by the logic of the treatises and so forth, is being set forth.
He concludes the doctrine of no Lord (*nirīśvaravāda*) with the word "thus" (*evam*). He introduces the doctrine of a Lord (*seśvaravāda*) with the word "the Teacher" (*śāstrā*). || 444 ||
He who is all-knowing, all-wise, and free from hunger and other such needs.
The scripture states, "He who [is] on earth," and likewise, "Not this, not this. (445)
And because of the scriptural statement that [the Self] has no gross beginning, and likewise from such passages as "not full" and so forth.
There exists a supreme Lord beyond saṃsāra, under whose control all this stands.

Therein, he cites the scriptural passages concerning Īśvara mentioned in the Bhāṣya, beginning with "He who is omniscient. He summarizes their meaning as "the non-transmigrating one. He clarifies the nature of Īśvarahood with the words "of whom... (verse 449/446).
And he alone is the creator of the world, characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth.
Therefore, [the word "ātman"] is used in grammatical apposition with "of itself" (ātmanaḥ). || 447 ||
Regarding that Vedic [text], he states an inference based on the mark of the effect: "That very [Self]... He states its essential nature: "The True One...

He provides the scriptural authority for its being the creator of the world: "Therefore... Beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," it sets forth the definition through "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth; then, having drawn back to the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and employing the term "Self" (*ātman*) therein, it refers to Brahman.

The meaning is that, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "desire" (*chanda*) and the word "Self" (*ātman*), it is stated that the creation of ether and the rest proceeds from the inward-facing Brahman. || 447 ||
Indeed, the non-arising of those who wander in saṃsāra is proclaimed to be exactly like this.
It is not so, because Maheśvara alone is the substratum of space in that case. (448)

One might raise the objection that the Lord is not the cause of the world according to the *Taittirīya* Śruti, because it contradicts the *Vājasaneyi* Śruti. [The author replies: "Of the transmigrating soul" (*saṃsāriṇaḥ*).

Since in the passage "In that which is the space within the heart," the Supreme Self alone is accepted as being the space (*ākāśa*), and since the phrase "from this very one" refers back to the space of the Supreme Self under discussion, it is stated here that the world originates from Him; therefore, there is no contradiction between the *Taittirīya* Śruti and the *Vājasaneyi* Śruti.
He resolves the objection with the words: "Not so. (448)
Having introduced the subject with "I shall declare Brahman to you," [the text proceeds with] the instruction on Brahman.
How could a king who is exceedingly wise speak what is unrighteous and contrary to the Veda? || 449 ||

Anticipating the objection that it is unestablished that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) used in the response refers to the Supreme [Brahman], he says, "Brahman," after first considering the context. The sense is that if the ether were not Brahman, there would be both the abandonment of the subject under discussion (*prakṛtahāna*) and the introduction of something not under discussion (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*); and it is not proper for one who acts with deliberation to speak of what is not the subject at hand. || 449 ||
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with other scriptural passages if it were stated here that the transmigrating soul is [the object of the meditation].
In the phrase "O Somya," by the name "Sat" (Being), Brahman is intended there. || 450 ||

Furthermore, if space were something other than Brahman, one must consider whether it is the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) or the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*); having thus raised this dilemma, he refutes the first alternative.
"By another Śruti," etc. Here, "here" refers to the acceptance of the response. He asks: "Could it not be that even another Śruti has as its subject matter the transmigrating soul?
He replies: "Because of the word 'Being' (sat). The sense is that otherwise, there would be a violation of the introductory context beginning with "Being alone" (*sad eva*). || 410 ||
"That which is called 'space' is indeed Brahman itself, which is without name or form."
In another Vedic scripture, it is heard that [Brahman] is directly [the cause], like the non-destruction of space.

He provides another scriptural passage as proof for the fact that the *prakṛta* (subject under discussion) ether is Brahman: "The ether... There, considering that the word "Brahman" is a clear reason for the ether being Brahman—just as its being a different entity from name and form [is a reason for it being Brahman]—he stated "directly. || 451 ||
And likewise: "Day after day, one should be devoted to the scripture and to the Supreme Self."
In deep sleep, there is no room for any other suffering being apart from Brahman.

Anticipating the objection that even if the aforementioned space were Brahman, the space under discussion—which is associated with the three states—would still be subject to transmigratory existence, he says: "And thus... (tathāca). The words "by the power of which" (yattadvaśāt) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 452 ||
The birth and likewise the dissolution of the self are not due to modification.
It is in no way logical that it should have the elemental ether as its object. || 453 ||

He states another interpretation: "Because there is no modification of that" (*atadvikārataḥ*). By referring back to the subject under discussion with the word "from this" (*asmāt*), the origin of the vital breaths and so forth is stated. If, in passages such as "This [ether] which... (*ya eṣa...*), the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) were the subject under discussion, then this pronoun would refer to that alone;

however, the birth and dissolution of the vital breaths and so forth do not proceed from that, because it is not established that they are modifications of the elemental ether. Furthermore, the word "from this" (*asmāt*) stands in grammatical apposition with the word "Self" (*ātman*).
Therefore, because of that [context], the meaning is that this word "space" does not have the elemental space as its object. || 453 ||
The capacity for the creation of the world and so forth, as well as the causal complex and the like, belong to one who is subject to suffering.
Just as it is not possible for us or those like us who are subject to saṃsāra, so it is [in that case].

Having stated that the Lord is the cause of the world through scripture and inference, he provides the logical justification for that very point: "The world," etc. "Sāmagrī" means the collection of auxiliary causes; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), knowledge and other factors are included. || 454 ||
A bad treatise cannot be the source of the capacity [for knowledge], because it merely manifests that [capacity];
for a means of valid cognition does not function when it contradicts another means of valid cognition. (455)

Anticipating the objection that, based on scriptural passages such as "In this very way," the birth and so forth of the world might belong to the transmigrating soul (saṃsārin), and further fearing that there would be a contradiction with scripture if it were otherwise—just as a mother-of-pearl becomes an illusory appearance—he says: "Not [the power]," and so on.

Anticipating the objection that although the scripture is merely informative and not a causal agent, it will nevertheless inform us that the transmigrating soul is the creator of the world, he replies: "It has no authority in that regard," because the transmigrating soul lacks that capacity.
He says that because it contradicts that [perception] due to its being directly perceived: "By another means of knowledge," etc. (455).
If the transmigrating soul and the Lord were established by their own nature as independent of one another, [then liberation would be impossible].
Oneness of these two is not logical, just as it is not possible for light and darkness. || 456 ||
1. That is its nature.
[Vol.
2, page 669] 1. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 963.

Having raised the objection that the proof of the Lord (Īśa) has been stated through both scripture and reasoning, and that His established conclusion (siddhānta)—that He is the "Truth of truths" according to the Upaniṣads—is [merely] a refutation of the non-Brahman, he says: "paraspara... (verse 456).
Therefore, it is incorrect [to say] "I am Brahman" if one intends to refer to Brahman as the immediate inner self (pratyak).
Because it is distinct [from the self], it would be impossible for the sufferer to grasp [the body]; otherwise, one would incur the fault [of the self being subject to change]. (457)
He states the result of the inference—"They are not non-different from one another because they are mutually contradictory, like darkness and light"—with the words "I" (*aham*).

He states the defect in the opposing case (*vipakṣa*) with the word "defect" (*doṣa*). The sense is that just as a minister, contemplating himself as the king, would incur [the fault of] transgression, so too the individual soul (*jīva*), seeing itself as the Lord (*īśa*), would incur transgression. || 457 ||
But by means of virtuous deeds, one [worships] that God, the supreme cause of the universe.
Having propitiated [the Lord], one attains supreme excellence through His grace. || 458 ||

Anticipating the objection that there is no liberation in the absence of the knowledge "I am Brahman," as stated in such scriptural passages as *tameva* (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1), he says: "By means of good deeds.
For it has been said: "One who performs actions for Me, who regards Me as the supreme," and so forth. And the followers of the Pañcarātra say:
"A person who is devoted to my work attains the state of the Supreme Brahman. "Those contemplators of the inner self who take refuge in Him with devotion [attain that subtle state]."
“They indeed go to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is free from old age and death. Thus [it is said]. || 458 ||
In that case, even those scriptural passages that proclaim the identity of Brahman and the Self would likewise [be contradicted].
They will be merely explanatory statements; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.

If there is an absence of knowledge regarding the oneness of Brahman, what then is the status of those [scriptural] statements? To this he says: "Brahma... He states the contradiction with worldly consensus if those [statements] were taken in their primary sense: "There would be a contradiction. || 459 ||
It is likewise not contradicted by the treatises on logic nor by worldly conventions.
If that were so, then this objection is answered as follows regarding the attainment [of the result]. || 460 ||

He states that there is no contradiction whatsoever in accepting the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman on the grounds that those [scriptural passages] are merely explanatory statements (arthavāda). He says "by reasoning" (tarka); [this refers to] principles established in the world, such as the distinction between the ruler and the ruled. He concludes the doctrine of theism with the words "thus, when [the prima facie view] has been reached. He begins the final conclusion (siddhānta) with the word "here" (atra). || 460 ||
This is not so, because this very [Veda] is measured by its mantras and brāhmaṇas.
The direct entry of the Supreme Lord is heard from all sides.
Regarding the claim that the Upaniṣad concerns an "impersonal" (taṭastha) Lord, he says: "Not this. || 461 ||
And before the two-footed beings, the Person entered the city.
You are every form and every form indeed; you are woman and you are man.
Thus is the collection of mantras, and likewise the Brāhmaṇas as well.
The statement "having entered here" was previously uttered by the Brāhmaṇa. (463)
The sentence "Having created that" is likewise heard in the Taittirīya Śruti. *Sureśvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Second Chapter. [Vol. 2, p. 670] 964.
This very sentence beginning with "seyaṃ" also occurs in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. || 464 ||
He cites the assertions of the proponents of entry (*praveśavādin*) from the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, beginning with the word "in front" (*puraḥ*), etc.
In the same way, because of the scriptural teaching that the two words "Brahman" and "Self" have a single substratum.
Therefore, it is indeed proper to determine that "I am Brahman. || 465 ||

He states another reason for their non-difference: "Brahmātma" (Brahman is the Self). The meaning is that because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such passages as "This Self of theirs is Brahman," the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) must be accepted just as in the case of each single term. Regarding the objection that one would not grasp [the truth] as "I am Brahman," he says "aham" (I). The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that the identity is established as authoritative according to the manner already explained. || 465 ||
And since the position is established in this way, this fault follows.
The state of being in saṃsāra belongs to the Supreme [Self] because of the reason that [the individual self] is non-different from it. || 466 ||
He raises an objection against the position of identity with the words "And when... He states the reason for perceiving the aforementioned defects in the Supreme Self: "That...

The sense is that its being subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva) is not possible, because that would contradict scriptural passages and other authorities declaring its non-transmigratory nature. || 466 ||
Now, how could this [state] of being non-transmigratory possibly be established for him?
In that case, instruction would be useless, since liberation from it [would occur] even without it. || 467 ||

He introduces a consequential argument (*prasaṅga*) to state another fault regarding [the doctrine of] identity. With the words "Now" (*atha*), he says: even though the Supreme is intended to be non-transmigratory, if it were non-different from the transmigrating soul, the teaching that it is "non-transmigratory" would be purposeless, because liberation would be established even without that teaching. Thus [he says]: "Then... (verse 467).
When this has been urged, some offer a rebuttal.
Among those created beings, the Supreme Lord did not directly enter as another.
In these two defects, he arouses attachment to his own [view] and a lack of meditative concentration. "Thus" means: he elucidates that very point.
With the words "in those created," he states the reason why, in the absence of direct entry into it, there is no contact with cause and effect. "The other" [refers to the Supreme]. || 468 ||
Having undergone transformation, it possesses the characteristic of being the nature of consciousness.
The Supreme entered into all beings, from Brahmā down to the level of stationary objects.
How, then, does it enter into its effects? To this he says: "In the modification," etc. (469).
Even the self consisting of consciousness [arises] from the Great One, whose nature is that of the Supreme Self.
It should be understood as both different and non-different from all things, by virtue of their intrinsic nature. || 470 ||

Even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman, one might suspect that if there were a difference from it, the cognition "I am not Brahman" would arise; and if there were non-difference, Brahman itself would be subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*).

Anticipating this objection, he says: "The cognizing self (*vijñānātman*). Since every entity possesses a nature that is both different and non-different, and since the soul is not a [separate] reality, its being both different and non-different from Brahman is like that of the waves and so forth of the ocean—this is the meaning. || 470 ||
In this context, where "to dwell" (avasātum) should be read, "to settle" (avasitum) is certainly incorrect. 1. Ga. reads *murutā*.
By that [other] through which one is distinct, he is held to be a transmigrating being (saṃsārī) entitled to ritual action (karma).
Through the realization "I am Brahman," which excludes any other alternative, one shall attain Brahman.
Nevertheless, he states "by which" (yena) to show how the absence of suspected defects [is established] therein. || 471 ||
When this is so, the connection with the aforementioned faults will not occur.
For if one conceives of it otherwise, there is an encounter with a logical fault. || 472 ||

Having established the matter according to the method stated, he states the resulting conclusion—that Brahman possesses neither the state of being a transmigrator nor that the teaching is rendered useless—by saying, "As stated. Anticipating the objection that it is undesirable for a single entity to be both different and non-different due to their mutual contradiction, he says, "Not so," by means of the analogy of the ocean and its waves. Furthermore, he says, "For this reason," that if either absolute difference or absolute non-difference were postulated, the purpose of the teaching would not be fulfilled.

Nor is Brahman’s state of being non-transmigratory [established] as being either different from or non-different from that [transmigration]; the meaning is that it follows by process of elimination (pāriśeṣyāt). || 472 ||
The connection with limiting adjuncts such as the body is established by relying on other means of knowledge.
Since the status of being the Brahman priest (brahmatā) has not entered [the ritual] through the statement that restates it, on account of the Vedic revelation (śruti). || 473 ||

He refutes the proponent of the partial view (*ekadeśin*) with the words "the body, etc. Having restated that the individual soul (*jīva*), as qualified by two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is established through worldly experience, its identity with Brahman is declared by such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). Since the fruit [of this realization] exists—according to scriptural texts such as "fearlessness, a firm foundation"—there is no need to propound [theories of] entry or creation, because those would not serve the purpose of man (*apuruṣārtha*); therefore, the Supreme has not entered into created things directly, but rather [entered] having undergone modification (*vikāra*).
The meaning is that it is incorrect to say, "In the same way, [the self] has the characteristic of being a living being. || 473 ||
These may be the destinies of the conscious self with respect to modification.
A collection of various substances would be something other [than its parts], like the earth. || 474 ||
For that which possesses parts, there may be a modification of one part.
That which they call the "conscious self" (vijñānātman) is merely a transformation (pariṇāma) of the Self (ātman). || 475 ||

Regarding the claim that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a modification of the Supreme, he offers an analysis in order to refute it. He begins with the words "vijñāna" (consciousness) and proposes three alternative views concerning the transformation of the soul: either the soul is a collection of many substances, like a heap of sesame seeds and so forth;
or it is many substances existing in mutual independence; or else, the Supreme—which possesses parts—has transformed into the state of the soul as one of its constituent portions.
Thus he stated one [view]. Regarding the word "nāna" (various): having stated the transformation, he cites the consensus of the elders. [He says] "vijñāna" (consciousness).
For this [earth], like a jar or similar object, is subject to modification in one part.
Or rather, [it exists] without destroying the configuration, like hair, saline soil, and so forth. (476)

He confirms that very point by means of an illustration: "like a jar, etc. The phrase "for" (*hi*) is stated in order to say that if the Self possesses parts, then a modification of one part is possible; just as there is a transformation of hair, nails, and so forth in a person without the destruction of his prior state, or just as there is a modification of the earth into saline soil and the like, so too, from the Supreme Being in His prior state, there exists a portion called the individual soul (*jīva*).
He states another alternative [view] with the word "transformation" (pariṇāma). He says "configuration" (saṃsthāna) [in verse 476].
1 kha. ... bound... | 2 kha. ga. ...śatvavi... | 3 kha. explains... [vol2, page 672] 966 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Second Adhyāya]...
Or else, the other [the effect] would transform in its entirety, like a substance such as milk.
There can be only these many positions regarding the modification of the Supreme Self.

He shows another alternative: "in their entirety. Fearing that there might be a deficiency on the part of the author of the Bhāṣya—who composes three kalpas within another kalpa—he says: "so many. || 477 ||
A primary unity is not tenable for a collection of distinct substances.
Because they are connected by a single birth, there is oneness in terms of their qualities. || 478 ||

Therein, he refutes the first [position] with the words "bhinnaiḥ" (by distinct [entities]). If the "otherness" (paratva) belongs either to a collection (*samāhāra*) of various substances or to those [substances] themselves as mutually dependent, then there would be no unity; for there is no primary unity among many, nor can there be otherness of a collection, because that [collection], being difficult to describe in terms of either identity with or difference from its constituents, is merely conceptualized (*kalpita*). This is the meaning. [The opponent might argue: "Because many things, such as pieces of sugar-candy and so forth, possess a single genus (*gotva*),"...

Fearing that even though there are many substances, they might be considered one through the medium of a single genus (*jāti*), he says: "of a single genus. Therefore, the connection with the preceding [verse] is that primary oneness does not exist. || 478 ||
And this being the case, the abandonment of your own established doctrine would necessarily follow for you.
And if the whole were eternally accompanied by parts that are inseparably established [from it], [then...]
A portion of him, remaining in that state, attained the condition of transmigratory existence.
Even then, there was a partial manifestation of that Supreme Self. || 480 ||
A fault or a quality belonging to its own category would necessarily follow for this [entity].
In this way, the fault of the transmigratory state would belong to the Supreme Being alone, and it would be difficult to avoid.

In that case, let there be no primary identity with Brahman; to this he replies: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The sense is that such multiplicity is not accepted by anyone. He restates the second [position]: "And eternal" (*nityaṃ ca*). This is not the Supreme of the previously described nature; rather, it is the view that among the mutually connected parts, there is a single composite substance (*avayavidravya*) persisting through them, and the individual soul (*jīva*) is a transformation of one part thereof. To this, he states the refutation.
"Pratyaṃneti. He states the result regarding the contact with qualities and defects residing in the parts of the possessor of those parts: "saṃsāriteti" (479).
Even when there is a complete transformation of the water, the supreme Self remains.
There would be a contradiction with the Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning, and that is an undesirable consequence. || 482 ||

Having explained the third [position], he refutes it with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). Having raised the objection that the contradiction of Śruti and other authorities is acceptable, he says "sa ca" (and he) in response to the Vedic adherent. || 482 ||
The Vedic statement "It is neither born nor does it die," which negates the six modifications of being, serves to exclude any transformation in the inner self (pratyagātman). || 483 ||
In that regard, having cited the scripture, he states its purport with the words beginning "na" (not). "It is never born, nor does it ever die.
1. Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 967.

The Smṛti passage beginning with "This is unmanifest, this is inconceivable" should be considered. He summarizes the purport of the Śruti and Smṛti [with the words]: "The inner self... (pratyag...). || 483 ||
The divine, embodied Person, who is both external and internal, is self-born.
Partless, actionless, tranquil, stainless, and situated like the sky. || 484 ||

To show that there is not only a contradiction with the Śruti and other authorities in the final stage [of dissolution], but in all three stages as well, he cites the Śruti passages, beginning with "For He is divine. Regarding His nature as light, he states the reason for His being a partless substance: "He is formless" (amūrta). Anticipating the objection that this might be inconsistent with atoms and the like, he qualifies it by describing Him as "full" (pūrṇa). To refute a relative fullness such as that of space, he describes Him as "the Person" (puruṣa), who is the cause of all effects.

1.1 He states that [the Self] is the substratum of the battle: "with the external" (*sabāhya*). He states its immutability (*kauṭasthya*), which is the absence of all modifications, by saying: "unborn" (*aja*).

He states its lack of determination with the word "partless" (*niṣkalam*). He states the meaning established thereby with "actionless" (*niṣkriyam*). He states that it abides in a state of detachment and indifference with "quiescent" (*śāntam*). The reason for this is "pure" (*vimalam*). An illustration for this purity is "like space" (*vyomavat*). || 484 ||
Thus, by hundreds of such statements proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti, these [are established].
All such positions are contradictory; therefore, they should be abandoned with effort. || 485 ||

He states the meaning obtained from the words spoken: "ityādi" (and so forth). By the word "ādi," such [scriptural passages] as "like space, he is all-pervading and eternal" and "this very one is the great unborn Self," etc., are included, as well as Smṛti statements such as "he is called unchanging, immovable, firm, and immutable. He states the result of the contradiction: "they are to be abandoned" (tyājyāḥ) || 485 ||
And there would be no occurrence of cyclic existence, because of the partless, immutable nature of the Self.
The field-factor would then follow as being located in the same place as the fruit of its own action. || 486 ||

He states another defect in the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a single part of the Supreme (*para*): "In the state of transmigratory existence... He provides the reason why it would follow that there is no movement for [the soul] in heaven and other realms: "Because it is immutable (*kūṭastha*)... Otherwise, even the Supreme would possess movement; for the point is that when the parts of a cloth move, the cloth itself does not fail to move. || 486 ||
If it be argued that there is movement for the soul when it is separated [from the body], like a spark [of fire] and so forth;
Nevertheless, it would follow that one who is without a wound could still undergo the occurrence of injury. || 487 ||

He raises an objection by means of an illustration with the words "of that which is separated. He refutes the view that the soul is a portion of the supreme Self—like a spark bursting forth from fire—and that its movement consists in this, with the words "even so" (tathāpi). || 487 ||
Just as when fish move through water, there is a continuous threading of gaps.
In the same way, as living beings wander about, they arise from the Supreme Self at dawn. || 488 ||
In that very context, he states another fault along with an illustration: "Of water," etc. (488).
Furthermore, in this way, a contradiction with the words of the *Anuṣṭubh* [or *Araṇa*] would also result.
The activity of an effect does not arise from anything other than its own cause. (489)
1. ‘Ki’ | 2. kha. vimuktaṃ | 3. kha. trimaktaṃ | [vol2, page 674] 968 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Second Adhyāya—]

He states the fault resulting from the acceptance of both the bursting [of the soul] and its entering into another; this is the meaning of "and so" (*tathāca*). Furthermore, even bursting is not appropriate in the case of another [body], because it contradicts the previously cited Śruti and Smṛti—this is the sense of the particle *api*. Having accepted the transmigratory wandering of the individual soul (*jīva*), he says that such [transmigration] does not exist [in the case of the Supreme Self], beginning with the words "by its own cause" (*svakāraṇa*). || 489 ||
Since the supreme self and the individual soul are one consciousness, how can there be transmigration for the individual soul?
Therefore, like the movement of one's own [shadow], the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (jīva) is thus maintained. || 490 ||

Having stated the general principle regarding the object (*vastu*), he applies it to the present case with the words "parama" (supreme). To the question, "How then does that [supreme state] become the cessation of the delusion of the mind of saṃsāra?
he replies with the verse beginning "svapna" (dream). || 490 ||
Even in their own bodies, embodied beings experience great suffering from things such as thorns.
Therefore, there is great suffering for oneself and others even when living beings move about. || 491 ||
If you do not accept that saṃsāra as a real entity, then I too have not entered into it through delusion; therefore, [the opponent] might suspect that they are permanent like Brahman.
Anticipating this, he says: "In the case of permanent things... (491).
If it is thought that there is no fault because of the examples of sparks and so forth, [we reply: no.
It is not so, because the treatise serves as a communicator of objects as they actually exist. (492)

One might object: "There is no fault," arguing that since the scripture uses analogies such as sparks [of fire], it is not improper to conceive of the Supreme as undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) and so forth, nor is it improper to conceive of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being a transformation and so forth, because these are established by that scripture; for even its eternity and other attributes are established therein. To this, he replies: "It is not so.

He states that the conception of the relationship between part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*) and so forth between those two does not arise from scripture. He provides the reason for this: "As it actually exists" (*yathāsthiteti*). || 492 ||
A treatise makes known what was previously unknown, because such is the very nature of valid cognition.
He did not attempt to alter the categories of objects as they were determined by valid means of knowledge.

He states the distinction of that [knowledge] from memory and so forth: "ajñātā" (unknown). He provides the reason: "because perception and the like are seen to make known what was previously unknown.

He says "evam" (thus) [to introduce the next point]. Anticipating the objection that it might be an instrument (*kāraka*) like the eye and other sense organs, he says: "padārthān" (the objects). || 493 ||
Just as objects such as the formed and the formless are determined by means of valid cognition.
An object is made known through examples only in accordance with how it has been perceived. || 494 ||
Then, raising the objection that since even the status of being an indicator is impossible, for what purpose is this scripture? he says: "mūrta... (verse 494).
Thus, this treatise proceeds everywhere by means of illustrative examples.
It does not bring about a cognition of an object that is the opposite of what has been established by another means of valid cognition. || 495 ||

Just as visible entities such as forms and so forth are perceived, so too is the unperceived reality understood through examples in accordance with them; having thus stated the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "evam" (thus). He states the exclusion [of other possibilities] with the words beginning with "na" (not). || 495 ||
Even with hundreds of examples, it cannot be established that fire is extremely cold.
Because it is contradicted by other means of valid cognition, it is not apprehended even by Indra.
Anticipating the objection that scripture may be instructive even regarding what is contrary to human experience by virtue of illustrative examples, he says: "Exceedingly cold," etc.
[Note: The manuscript variants for *saṃcāra*, *dehinaḥ*, and *jīvasaṃ* are noted here as per the source].
The meaning of the sentence is understood—this is the ellipsis. Thus, the meaning is that the scripture does not cause understanding even through an example if it contradicts perception. || 496 ||
Furthermore, that which contradicts another means of valid cognition is not accepted as a valid cognition itself.
For there can be the status of a means of knowledge only when the object of cognition is not already pervaded by another means of knowledge. || 497 ||

Anticipating the objection that a sentence such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is seen to convey a meaning contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge, he says: "By another means of knowledge," etc. The reason for this is stated in the phrase: "by another means of knowledge. || 497 ||
Likewise, words and their referents, as well as inferential marks and objects of perception;
No one can know an unknown object through scripture without disregarding [the need for] various means of cognition. (498)

Having resolved the contradiction by showing that the scripture has a distinct object—namely, the reality which is non-dual in essence and is not an object of perception and other means of knowledge that have as their domain the imagined duality—he states another reason for that very point: "In that way" (tathā). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, there is no contradiction of the scripture with another means of knowledge. (498)
The conceptualization of the relationship between part and whole, and so forth, is based on meanings established by worldly convention.
Therefore, it is in no way logical to postulate another self [apart from this one]. (499)

Having established that the scripture, being the source of livelihood for all, provides a cognition that is not contradicted by other means of knowledge, he concludes the resulting point with the words "loka...

(in the world). It is not proper to accept the imagination of the Supreme Being as having parts and so forth—based on worldly principles such as examples like sparks and the like—just as fire has them;
for this would contradict scriptures stating His partlessness and non-duality. Therefore, the scriptural texts regarding examples do not convey a contradictory meaning.
This is the meaning. || 499 ||
The mention of sparks and so forth [serves as an analogy] for the individual soul (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman).
Therefore, the intended meaning here is the realization of the identity of the self. || 500 ||

If, by hearing the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the relationship of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*) between those two is not intended to be expressed, then what is it that is intended? To this he says: "Like sparks" (*visphuliṅga*). Since this is so, he states that in this scriptural illustration, the intended meaning is the nature of their identity; thus he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 100 ||
The meaning as stated [in the middle] is intended [by the author], as is confirmed by the introduction and conclusion.
Just as the Śruti, having asserted that "the Self is everything beginning with Brahmā," [establishes this]. 501.
This very point is established today by means of examples and logical reasons, beginning with the drum.
The conclusion of the meaning of the proposition is achieved through statements such as "the unprecedented" (apūrva) and so forth. || 502 ||

He states another reason for the fact that the passages concerning creation and so forth have unity as their purport: "upakrama... (beginning, etc.). He demonstrates those two [reasons] with the words "brahmādi... (Brahmā, etc.). This means: "in accordance with the initial proposition. The reasons are "being produced from that" and so on. The meaning is that since the Śruti is observed to be of a single form in its beginning, middle, and end, all Vedāntas culminate—either directly or indirectly—in unity.
122 1 kha. with *saṃ*; 2 kha. says: "That..."; 3 kha. its meaning: "Therefore...
[vol2, page 676]
In all Vedānta statements, the oneness of Brahman is enjoined. *Sureśvarācāryakṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtikaṃ*, Second Chapter.
Thus, there is indeed no disagreement among commentators in its entirety. (503)

He indicates the consensus of those who know the purport of the scriptures regarding the stated meaning with the words "sarva... (all...). Thus, the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that oneness alone is the meaning of the scripture, because it is the consensus of the elders. || 103 ||
For when it is possible for that single expression to convey both [meanings] without difficulty, [one should not resort to splitting the sentence].
And it is logical to conceive of other meanings for the statements concerning creation and so forth. (504)

Anticipating the objection that, although all Vedānta passages have the primary purport (*mahātātparya*) on unity, creation and so forth are also intended by those passages as a secondary purport (*avāntaratātparya*), he says: "tadvidhi... etc. The injunction of unity is the passage beginning with "That Thou Art" (*tat tvam asi*); its connection with them as a single syntactical whole (*ekavākyatva*) constitutes the relationship of principal and subordinate (*śeṣa-śeṣitva*). Since this is possible without effort, it is not appropriate to assume that the passages concerning creation and so forth have creation and so forth as their primary meaning.

The meaning is that it is logical for there to be a single syntactical unity, as a division thereof would be improper; indeed, the very principle [stated] has been intimated by the word "hi" (for/indeed). || 504 ||
Nor is there any means of valid cognition for that [result], and another result would have to be postulated.
Therefore, the statements concerning creation and so forth must have as their ultimate purport the non-dual nature of the Self.

Even if there is no contradiction with the principle of the unity of the great purport (*mahātātparya*), nevertheless, neither the proof nor the fruit [of the Vedas] can be the basis for inferring that the passages concerning creation and so forth have that as their primary purport. He states this with the words "Not [the first]" (*na ca*). He states that the second [alternative] is not the case with the words "And the [fruit] to be inferred" (*kalpyaṃ ca*). The sense is that it is impossible to infer such a fruit, because it would contradict the maxim: "That which lacks a fruit when in proximity to that which possesses a fruit is subordinate to it. [This applies to] the passages concerning creation and so forth—
He states the conclusion regarding the fact that these sentences do not have that as their primary purport: "Aikātmya... (verse 105).
In this regard, some relate a beautiful narrative as follows.
This desired object is clearly perceived exactly as it is conceived.

He introduces the narrative composed by Draviḍācārya regarding the fact that the sentence beginning with "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is intent upon non-duality (*aikya*), while the passages concerning creation and so forth are subordinate to it. He does so by saying, "They relate. He shows that the narrative follows the meaning already stated by saying, "And thus.

By saying, "Just as," he reveals the auspiciousness of that narrative—which takes the form of an illustration and its application—by virtue of its culminating in the final fruit. [The word] "in non-duality" (*aikye*)...

The connection [of the words] is as follows: that which is the desired object, the final conclusion of the Vedānta, they call that [treatise] by which it becomes free from doubt and uncontradicted. || 506 ||
For just as someone might previously have been the son of a universal monarch, a youth;
He became insane due to disease, the application of [poisonous] substances, injury, and so forth. || 507 ||

In this regard, he introduces an illustrative narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) in the form of an example, beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*). He states the cause for that young prince’s separation from his parents and [his own] nature, beginning with the word "disease" (*vyādhi*); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), incidental afflictions (*upadhā*) are included.
Not a statement. || 107 ||
Having lost his pride as a king and being utterly bewildered, he entered the forest.
And being surrounded by vipers, he considers himself to be a tiger. || 508 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 677] 1. Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
He states the fruit of intoxication: "Dhvasta... He describes his entry into the house of the Śabara: "By hunters...
He describes the purpose of that entry: "The hunter... || 108 ||
Through the passage of great time, that karma and that ego-sense came into being.
Having destroyed the residual impressions of royalty, he dwelt in the abode of a Śabara.

Having restated the aforementioned conceit (*abhimāna*), he states its effect: "That action" (*tatkarma*). Fearing the objection that even when the conceit of being a king has been destroyed, the performance of actions conforming to the Śabara caste might continue due to the obstruction of its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), he says: "Dissolved" (*dhvasta*). The reason for this is:
"Dwelling" (*vasan*). || 109 ||
And through the use of auspicious medicinal herbs, his mind became restored to health.
And because it conforms to its own intrinsic nature, the self-awareness has emerged from the exclusions. || 510 ||

Because his mental resolve has naturally turned away from that conduct, appearance, and activity, and because he lacks even mere mindfulness [of them], he does not abandon the state of being a hunter. (511)

To the question of how pride regarding the body (*śarīra-abhimāna*) and so forth can arise in one who is insane, he says: "Śubha... (The auspicious...). Anticipating the objection that if even one of sound mind, such as a prince, were to conceive the state of being a hunter, that state could never be removed, he says: "Svasvabhāva... (One's own nature...).
Anticipating the objection that if, in accordance with his royal caste, he were to rise above the conceit of being a hunter, he would then abandon his status as a hunter, he says: [the following].
Having learned of him from some source of tradition, one who does not deceive should approach him.
He was a friend of his father, who knew the truth regarding their common birth and karmic connection.
"In that case, since there is no cause for it—namely, the absence of any memory of his royalty—he could never abandon his status as a hunter.

To this, he replies: "From some [source]. This means from scripture (*āgama*) or instruction (*upadeśa*). He states the reliability (*āptatva*) of the one who has approached the prince and makes him aware of it, by virtue of not being a deceiver. He shows his capacity to make known the prince's royalty by saying: "He is a savior (*tāraka*)."

*Tajjāti* means: his *jāti* (birth) is his royalty (*rājatva*), and his *karman* (action) is the protection of the learned and so forth; by this [word], he knows their relationship, that is to say, their connection as being present. Alternatively, it means: knowing the prince’s association with the class of hunters (*vyādhijāti*) and with actions corresponding to that.
Regarding how the traveler was to effect the awakening of the prince to his royalty, he says: "Of his father" (*tatpituḥ*). || 112 ||
By activity, by action, by birth, and likewise by those honored as universal monarchs (cakravartin).
Just as someone might awaken [another] to the status of being a prince by means of his physical marks. || 513 ||

He states that regarding the knowledge that the prince resides in the Śabara’s abode, scripture (*āgama*) is not the sole cause; rather, there are other causes as well. He says: "By [his] conduct," etc. The connection is as follows: having recognized his status as a prince through the performance of virtuous deeds inferred from his observed activities, through his possession of the royal insignia, and through the characteristics of a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*) described in the scriptures—just as he was known, so it is: "You are not a hunter; you are the son of the primary king."
He says that [the verse] makes known that he has entered the house by some conversation, as follows: || 113 ||
Then, as soon as he regained his memory through the realization "I am the king," he understood.
Having abandoned his state of being a hunter, he attained the condition of Anibodha. || 514 ||
Having attained his father’s throne, he receives the consecration for kingship.
Because he has already attained the status of a prince, he does not even strive for its attainment.
He states the fruit of the instruction with the words "labdha" (obtained). This means that as soon as the instruction was received, by its power, the king’s memory was restored.

He states that fruit with the words beginning with "atha" (then). The word "atha" is intended to indicate that the authoritative instruction is the cause of right cognition, as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Now, one might object: how can it be that a prince who has lived for a very long time in the abode of the Śabaras suddenly regains his status as a prince?
He states that no other operation is required apart from the destruction of the obstacle through knowledge: "attained," etc. (114) (111).
Because the self is pierced by the arrow of delusion, and because of the complete destruction of that delusion.
Upon attaining the status of a prince, he requires nothing else at all. || 516 ||
If the status of being a prince is inherently attained [by nature], then from where does the notion of being a hunter arise? To this he replies with the word "moha" (delusion).

Anticipating the objection that for the sake of attaining kingship—which requires the sublation of the superimposed state of being a hunter—that knowledge must be repeated, he replies with the words "mohadhvaṃsa" (destruction of delusion). Since that destruction results from knowledge alone, repetition is not purposeful; such is the meaning. || 116 ||
In whatever way this [world] appears, it is indeed Brahman alone, due solely to the lack of realization of Brahman.
Having asserted the nature of self in relation to the intellect, the sense organs, the body, and so forth. || 517 ||

Having restated the illustration, he states the subject of application (*dārṣṭāntika*), beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*). If the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed Brahman itself, how can there be the notion of self (*ātmadhī*) in it with respect to the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth?
To this, he replies: "Brahman... (117).
Thus, due to the lack of awakening to the reality of the inner self, one is occupied with worldly objects.
It distinguishes its own self from non-self entities that are directed inwardly.

He states the result of the cognition of selfhood in what is not-self with the words "This is that. He specifies [the object] as "the Self" (*ātmānam*) in order to refute the idea that the word "own" (*sva*) refers to one's own property;
he qualifies it as "innermost" (*pratīcīnam*) to exclude the possibility that the word "Self" refers to the body and so forth.
Seated upon the plane of saṃsāra, he remains established in the thought, "I am a transmigrating being."
To one who desires liberation, who knows reality directly, and whose longing has emerged from worldly existence; || 519 ||

If the individual soul (jīva), identifying with the two bodies and established in the notion "I am the doer and the enjoyer," [remains thus], then what is the duty of the teacher toward him? To this he says: "Saṃsāra... [and so forth]. Toward that preeminent person who is wandering incessantly through various kinds of births, who somehow follows the feet of a Guru due to the power of merit accumulated over many lifetimes, who possesses the fourfold qualifications (sādhanacatuṣṭaya), and who has cast aside all ritual actions—it is the direct [instruction of] Reality.
The meaning is that the teacher who knows reality awakens [the disciple]. || 119 ||
By means of such statements as "That which is the Self," through the method of agreement and difference, [the truth is established].
The Guru should awaken the disciple by means of the statement "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and other such maxims.

He states that the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence has as its constituent parts the internal and external divisions, beginning with the word "ya" (who). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "by means of the purification of word-meanings through positive and negative concomitance. || 120 ||
1 ka. kha. rājābhi | [vol2, page 679] 1–Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 973.
The great darkness of the ego-sense within has been completely consumed by the fire of right knowledge.
Having abandoned everything arising from delusion, one then attains Brahman through Brahman alone. || 521 ||

He states the fruit of the knowledge derived from instruction with the word "properly" (*samyak*). Anticipating the objection that it is impossible for one thing to become another, he says "Brahman itself. If that is so, it is improper to say "he goes to Brahman," because it is impossible for one's own self to be the destination; to this he replies with "having abandoned.
The meaning of the word "then" (*atha*) is the exclusion of any other intervening action between knowledge and its fruit. || 121 ||
For the sake of liberation, other than through the destruction of the darkness regarding the inner reality (pratyaktattva).
For it does not depend upon any other means whatsoever, even the slightest.
He states the reason for that: "The inward," etc. (122).
Because birth and so forth are impossible [in Brahman], and because [the world] does not exceed the nature of Brahman; [therefore, it is not different from Brahman].
No other purpose can be conceived, and the statement would otherwise be rendered meaningless. (523)

Anticipating the objection that there exists another means for the desire-to-know (*vividiṣā*)—since the injunction regarding sacrifices and so forth serves as a cause for liberation through the *vividiṣā*-injunction—he replies with the words "birth, etc. (*janmādi*). He states this because the fourfold fruit of ritual action is inapplicable there, and because the [injunction] of the sentence prescribes the cause of knowledge; thus, apart from knowledge, there is no other means useful for liberation. If the *vividiṣā*-injunction were not prescribing the cause of knowledge...

However, he states [in the verse] that it prescribes only the means to liberation: "And it is useless," etc. The sense is that, in that case, it has already been stated that there is no connection with the fruit of the action to be enjoined. || 523 ||
If the relationship of part and whole and so forth is intended to be directly expressed in the knowledge of Brahman;
O Goddess Samudrā, at that time, Śakti would not have spoken with such respect. || 524 ||
That which is not expressed by speech, nor that which is conceived by the mind;
Likewise, a sentence, such as "the unprecedented" and so forth, is like a single block of rock-salt.

It has been stated that because the passages concerning *tattvamasi* and so forth have as their primary purport the identity [of the individual soul and Brahman], and because the passages on creation and so forth are subordinate to them, one cannot—on the basis of those [creation passages]—imagine a relationship such as part and whole between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Now, he states the contradiction with other scriptural texts that would arise in the opposing view: "If [Brahman were] a part," etc. If, like a wave from the ocean, it were accepted that in the passages on creation and so forth—which inform us of Brahman—Brahman actually possesses the nature of part and whole, then [its] transcendence beyond speech and mind [would be lost].

The meaning is that the Śruti would not speak of it with such intent, because [the Śruti] has as its object that which possesses distinctions. He says "apūrvādi" (beginning with 'without prior') to show that even such statements as "Brahman is, in reality, without parts or divisions," "like a mass of salt," "consisting of the single essence of consciousness," and "neither before nor after" would be contradicted. The word "tathā" (likewise) is used to draw back the phrase "nāvakṣyat" (he would not have spoken). || 124 || 125 ||
And he spoke these words regarding death: "Do not disparage the view of diversity."
If he had intended to express the relationship of part and whole, he would not have employed such a statement.

He shows the contradiction with the censure of the view of difference for the proponent of partiality (ekadeśin) by means of the words "nānātva" and so on. The construction is as follows: "He goes from death to death"—this censure of the cognition of multiplicity expressed in such statements would not have been uttered in your own position. The word "tathā" has the sense of including the statement, "It should be viewed as one alone. If there were an intention to express a relationship of part and whole in Brahman in reality, then the aforementioned statement—
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter [page 680]:
He states that in your position, such expressions as "the same," "one alone," and "without a second" should not be employed, because they lack the intended meaning.
Regarding the relationship between part and whole: || 126 ||
For the sake of establishing the perception of the cognition of objects as having a single nature and a single essence in each individual instance.
"Therefore, the scriptural passages concerning creation and so forth do not aim at establishing that [creation].

(527) Having established that the sentences regarding creation and so forth have no *tātparya* (ultimate purport) regarding their own literal meaning because they contradict many other statements, he concludes with the result: "One form" (*ekarūpa*).
The word "one form" is used for the purpose of negating both difference and non-difference. (527)
And for the self, which is partless and not inherently subject to transmigratory existence, [bondage] does not occur by its own nature.
The state of being both a part-possessor and a transmigrating entity is established even by logical reasoning. || 528 ||

One might object: "Since the scripture concerns the relationship between part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*) and so forth, and lacks intent regarding [the reality of parts], let there be no conceptualization of such [parts] based on that; for we observe that material causes like clay possess parts, and by the logic that Brahman, as the material cause of the world, must likewise be so, there will be [arguments for its having parts]. Anticipating this, he refutes the first alternative—whether the conceptualization of parts and so forth arises from itself or from another—by stating "And not" (*na ca*). This is because it would result in the cognition of contradictory meanings.

The meaning is that because there is no logical necessity for [the cause to be] the material substrate (*upādāna*), it is possible even in the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*). || 528 ||
The conceptualization of the individual soul and transmigratory existence has as its cause the imagined limiting adjuncts.
Granted that such may be; yet among the wise, there can be no doubt regarding the truth.

If it [the world] were imagined from something else, one might consider whether that [source] is itself imagined or unimagined; thus, he accepts the first alternative with the words "imagined. He rejects the second with the words "no," and so forth. The meaning is that for those who possess discrimination, the status of being "unimagined" does not appear in non-self-objects that consist of parts and part-havers, because that would contradict both logic and scripture. || 129 ||
And if this identity were indeed the intended meaning of all the Upaniṣads, [then...]
"How can the distinction between the conscious self (vijñānātman) and so forth be said to be contrary to that [non-duality]? (530).

Having refuted the conceptualization of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) as part and whole based on those two [distinctions], and having stated that the Vedāntas have non-duality as their primary purport, he says "If this is what is intended" (530) to show that the acceptance of that [non-duality] results in the impossibility of duality.
It is said [this was written] for the purpose of destroying the contradiction regarding the authority of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa).
Some proclaim that there is a commingling of consciousness, the self, and so forth. (531)

Considering the word "kaṃ" to have the sense of a question, he states the view of the dualists: "Karma," etc. Thinking that its [the opponent's] objection has already been refuted, he says "kila" (it is said). || 131 ||
In this world, which consists of nothing but the single Self, all human goals have been fully accomplished.
In that case, your [arguments for] injunction and prohibition would both be without an object.

Anticipating the objection that even if the Vedāntas are devoted solely to the single supreme human goal, there is no contradiction in their authority, and thus what is the use of duality, he says: "Aikātmya... (verse 132).
1 Kha. Definition of Form.
[Vol.
2, page 681] "The Brāhmaṇa," accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramakaranda* composed by Ānandagiri. 975.
Because it is liberated by its very nature, and because there is no bondage, it is likewise [liberated] by itself.
Likewise, the commencement of the Vedāntas would result in being fruitless. || 533 ||

Having stated the contradiction with the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) regarding the position of absolute non-duality (*kevalādvaita*), he states the contradiction with the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*). [The verse begins with] "Inherently" (*svataḥ*). Since the Supreme is eternally liberated and there is no other being—whether bound inherently or by another—the absence of a disciple follows; thus, due to the absence of a qualified candidate (*adhikārī*), the Upaniṣads would not be commenced. This is the meaning. || 533 ||
Thus, such objections and their refutations have been described.
The very relationship has been proclaimed many times in various investigations. || 534 ||

Fearing the charge of tautology, he offers a rebuttal: "ityevamādi" (and so forth). By the word *iti*, there is a reference back to the objections already stated; by the word *evaṃ* (thus), there is a summary of the mutual contradictions and other points to be mentioned; and by the word *ādi* (etcetera), there is the statement that the Upaniṣads have their purpose already exhausted by being devoted to injunctions (*niyoga*) and the like. These objections and their refutations have been explained precisely in the *Saṃbandha-granthas*. [The term] *avyākṛta*...

Although these have been described repeatedly in the discussions on the heavens, the meaning is that this objection is raised in order to provide a refutation by way of a different approach. || 534 ||
And because they are mutually contradictory, like light and darkness.
The authority of both the Karmakāṇḍa and the Upaniṣads is equal. || 535 ||

Furthermore, do you accept that both sections (kāṇḍas) possess validity, or only one of them? It cannot be the first, because they are mutually contradictory like darkness and light; nor can it be the other, because one who accepts the validity of one while asserting the invalidity of the other contradicts the injunction for Vedic study.
Thus he says: "paraspara... (535).
If validity were to exist when there is existence, then both [the cognition and its object] would possess validity.
Let the authority of that very section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) be established. || 536 ||
Anticipating the objection—"If the validity of either one of the two [sections] is impossible, how can there be an establishment of validity even in your own position?"—he says:

"satī" (being). Since the validity of the *karmakāṇḍa* (the section on ritual action) is not contradicted by the distinctions between the taught, the teacher, and so forth, the other section (*jñānakāṇḍa*), which depends upon it, is likewise [valid].
The meaning is that pride is not contradictory in either case, because it has duality as its object. || 136 ||
If the authority of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) constitutes its validity, then that same validity belongs to both of us as well.
That which devours all has here again forcefully proclaimed its lack of self-nature (anātmya).

In that case, one might object: "Just as the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) possesses authority regarding its own subject matter, so too must the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) possess authority regarding its own subject matter. Yet, if duality were its subject matter, it would follow that there is no distinction between the two sections, and it would contradict the introductory and concluding passages [of the Upaniṣads]. Therefore, by the force of the authority of the jñānakāṇḍa, non-duality (advaita) alone—which sublates the duality concerning the subject matter of the other section—returns once again. This is the objection raised in verse 137 with the words "karma... etc.
If this is so, then let there be a lack of authority for the Upaniṣads.
Furthermore, because they contradict other means of valid cognition, their status as authoritative sources is not accepted.
(538) 1. kha. *dorna prāmā* | 2. kha. *api pramāṇavya* [Vol. 2, page 682]
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Two, Verse 976:

He refutes this with the commentary beginning with "If that were so" (*evaṃ tarhi*). Regarding the phrase "If it were thus": thinking that there is no contradiction with the injunction for Vedic study, since that study is established as being for the purpose of recitation (*japa*), he states another reason for their lack of authority: "By other means of knowledge" (*mānāntara*). This refers to the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction of alternatives. || 138 ||
Moreover, it even brings about the destruction of one's own purpose; this is because of its proximity.
Therefore, that [Upanishadic portion] lacks authority, while the authority belongs to the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa). || 539 ||

In that very context, he states another reason, beginning with "api" (also). The sense is this: since it teaches non-duality (*advaita*) by depending on the distinction between disciple, teacher, and so forth, its non-authoritativeness follows from the fact that non-duality is destroyed by the presence or absence of those [distinctions]. || 539 ||
This objection raised by you is not valid, because it has already been answered.
Futility and having another meaning do not apply here, as has been explained previously. (540)

The proponent (siddhāntin) declares the invalidity of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa). He says, "It is not so," and recalls what has already been stated: that the section concerning knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) is neither fruitless nor subordinate to anything else. [He addresses the objection] that it would be useless (vyarthatā). || 140 ||
"I am Brahman"— this realization brings liberation at the very moment of its birth.
Since it is directly experienced, there can therefore be no pointlessness [to this]. || 541 ||
He clarifies that it possesses fruitfulness by stating "Brahman. || 141 ||
The fact that [perception] determines only the mere thing has already been explained at length regarding the relationship [between word and object].
Therefore, the Upaniṣads cannot possibly have any other meaning whatsoever.
He clarifies the state of being non-remnant, which was stated in the *Saṃbandhagrantha* and other works, with the words "the reality" (vastu). || 142 ||
[The two types of non-cognition] have as their sole cause the non-arising or arising of a valid cognition regarding their own respective objects of comprehension.
Validity and invalidity are not established otherwise. || 543 ||

Having recalled what was previously stated, he defines the characteristics of valid and invalid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa* and *apramāṇa*) for the sake of establishing the authority of the Upaniṣads. [He says: "By its own object of cognition" (*svaprameya*). He establishes this through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), stating that validity does not belong to a thing such as a jar unless it produces a valid cognition regarding its own object—otherwise, the consequence would be that even a jar would be a means of knowledge—and nor does invalidity belong to a thing simply because it fails to produce such a cognition—otherwise, the consequence would be that even the eyes and other senses would be invalid with respect to color and so forth. Thus he says: "Not otherwise."
Thus [it is said]. || 143 ||
And what follows from this? That which is indeed thus useful for the subject at hand.
Listen with one-pointed mind to all that is the reality when it is thus.

If this is so, let it indeed have that definition; nevertheless, he asks: "What is established by this much for you regarding its utility as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the subject under discussion, namely the Upaniṣads? He says: "Furthermore... When that definition has been stated, that which is useful for being a means of knowledge is present in the Śruti.
He says that one must become [one] by means of a single blow: "gravi" (144).
In the Upaniṣad, one directly realizes my own [nature], which is its own object of cognition;
how could there be invalidity for it? Otherwise, from what source would its status as a means of valid knowledge arise? (545)
1. Origin; 2a. ‘The Poet.
