2, page 683] [The Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 977.

Anticipating the doubt as to what ought to be heard, [the author] considers the alternative of whether the Upaniṣad produces valid knowledge regarding its own object or not; having restated the first position, he refutes it with the verse beginning "svaprameye" (regarding its own object). || 145 ||
If it does not produce valid cognition, it is called an *upaniṣad*.
Your statement would be contradicted by direct perception. || 546 ||
Having restated the second [position], he refutes it: "If not," etc. (146).
Fire does not burn wood, nor does the sun heat it.
Thus, your statement that it is "as it is" contradicts direct perception.
He clarifies with an example that the opponent's statement—that "it does not produce valid cognition regarding its own object"—is contradicted by direct perception: "Not fire... (147).
The fruit born of the knowledge of Vedānta is direct, like [the relief from] being burned by fire and so forth.
That which is called the abandonment of the miseries of saṃsāra is experienced through direct perception. || 548 ||
Anticipating the objection that, although the Upaniṣads lack invalidity due to their non-originated nature, they remain in that same state because of a lack of fruit, he says:
"As fire... Just as from the burning by fire there is the perceptible fruit known as a blister, and just as from the drinking of water there is the destruction of indigestion—

Just as a physician [directly perceives] the removal of poison and the like through the application of mantras, medicines, and so forth, so too the fruit of the cognition arising from the [Vedic] statement—characterized by the destruction of bondage—is directly perceived; this is the meaning. || 148 ||
And as for what was said—that they obstruct their own welfare—that too is trivial.
As it is being told, you ought to hear it exactly as it is.

Having refuted the lack of authority of the Upaniṣads on the grounds of the absence of [valid] reasons, and having restated what was said regarding their subversion of their own meaning, he sets out to demonstrate its incorrectness by asserting it and then providing a proof for it: "They obstruct," etc. (149).
For the apprehension of their own objects of cognition is said to be the intrinsic purpose of the means of valid cognition.
If the Vedāntas do indeed establish that [reality], how can they be considered invalid? || 550 ||

In order to state that the Vedāntas do not subvert their own meaning, [the author] states the general principle regarding the objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the words "svaprameya...

etc. Therein, the word *hi* is used for the purpose of attaining consensus among both worldly people and investigators. He states that the Vedāntas, which produce the aforementioned objects of their own meaning, do not subvert them; therefore, they are indeed authoritative (*pramāṇa*) in that regard, in the words "taṃ cet... (verse 110).
And there is no sublater here for the knowledge arising from the Vedānta statements.
Even though there are obstacles, because [the Self] consists of the true nature of the inner witness, || 551 ||
Anticipating the objection that those [scriptures] lack authority because they produce sublated cognitions, he says: "And not... Here, the word "here" refers to both the world and the scriptures.

He anticipates the objection that, in the absence of a sublater, there would be a loss of non-duality because that [cognition] would be distinct from the Self—since no produced cognition exists as non-distinct from it—and thus he says: "Of the sublaters... Perception and the other means of knowledge are accepted as sublaters; however, since they are of the nature of the inner self (*pratyag-rūpa*), they do not [sublate themselves].

Alternatively, there is no sublation because the cognition delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) arising from the sentence is its very nature (*svarūpa*); nor is the sublated modification itself perceptible, as it is [immediately] transcended. 123. kha. 'ccāpyape'. 123. (Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary commentary on the philosophical point that the realization arising from a Vedic statement is self-evident and not subject to sublation, as the cognitive state is non-different from the Self, and the mediating mental mode is likewise not perceived as an object.)
[Vol.
2, Page 684] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]:

By means of [the knowledge of] the Self, that very [ignorance] is sublated; for since it is sublatable by the intellect kindled by awakening, even the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is sublated by that same [awakening], because of the contradiction between itself and its opposite, and because of the manifoldness of states.
The meaning is "because of obtaining. || 111 ||
Valid cognition, invalid cognition, and likewise the semblance of valid cognition.
Since they indeed act toward me in such a way, how could there be any lack of conviction? || 552 ||
Fearing that [the Self], while bestowing existence and manifestation upon everything, might itself not exist, he recalls the third resolution:
"The means of knowledge" (pramāṇam).
Is it by virtue of having a single object, or rather by a difference of objects?
Let it be stated that there would be a contradiction among the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas). || 553 ||

Having stated that because there is no difference between the internal self and the perceived means of knowledge such as direct perception—which are accepted as sublaters—those means of knowledge cannot be sublaters of it, [the author] offers an alternative analysis to argue that, due to the difficulty of establishing contradiction, there can be no relationship of the sublated and the sublater among the means of knowledge themselves. He asks: "What? (verse 113).
If there is corroboration by another means of knowledge, then it is a mere restatement.
There is no contradiction among means of valid cognition when they converge upon a single object.

Therein, having restated the first [position], he refutes it with the words "by another means of knowledge" (*mānāntareṇa*). If the corroboration of one means of knowledge by another means of knowledge consists in their having the same object, then it is merely a reiteration (*anuvāda*) and not a contradiction. This is because the word "if" (*cet*) has the sense of restriction; for when multiple means of knowledge converge upon a single object, a contradiction is impossible. Otherwise, they would not have a single object, as this is not observed in cognitions such as that of silver and its absence. This is the meaning. || 114 ||
And just as it is in the case of the ear and other [senses] when their objects of cognition are distinct, so it is here.
Because they are mutually independent, there is an absolute absence of contradiction. || 555 ||

He states another alternative interpretation with the word "bhinnaiḥ" (by different [meanings]). He says that even the report of contradiction does not apply when there is a difference in meaning, using the word "nitarām" (extremely).
And a single existent sentence does not both perform and not perform [an action].
It is accepted that [the means of knowledge] establishes valid cognition and its negation in some cases. (556)

Anticipating the objection that even though the *Tattvamasi* and other such statements do not contradict perception and other means of knowledge, they themselves state a meaning contrary to their own purpose with respect to the teacher and the disciple, he says: "And not... The meaning is this: on the plane of empirical usage (*vyavahāra-bhūmi*), a sentence—whether worldly or Vedic—is observed in some cases to produce valid cognition (*pramā*) and in others not; however, no single sentence is ever seen to both produce valid cognition and negate it regarding its own meaning. Therefore, a sentence does not destroy its own meaning.
Is it not so, from such statements as "fire is cold" and "it is hot"?
This appearance of contradictory objects is observed as it arises. || 557 ||
Following his own experience, he raises a doubt: "Fire," [he says]. || 157 ||
Nor can a contradictory meaning be determined from either one alone or from both together.
By restating [the subject] through a portion of the statement, it is understood that "fire is cold. || 558 ||
1. Having understood; 2. "having regard for one's own purpose"; 3. This determination.

He refutes [the opponent's position] by considering the alternative: "Is 'Is fire hot? Is it cold? one sentence or two sentences? He begins with "No," etc. Regarding the case of being a single sentence, he establishes the absence of the perception of contradictory meanings by stating "by restating," etc. The statement "Fire is hot and cold" is a single utterance; its part, "Fire is hot," restates what is already established by perception as hot fire, while its other part, "Fire is cold," is something new.

Cold fire is not perceived; nor is there a contradiction between the portions of the restating and the perceiving [cognitions], because they do not possess equal strength—this is the meaning. || 158 ||
A cold fire is indeed possible, as it falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition.
And in that case, contradiction with another means of knowledge is likewise not accepted. (559)

Since a cold fire is impossible, how can there be an injunction by way of restatement? To this he replies: "It is possible. The other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) is perception (*adhyakṣa*) directed toward a cold fire. He says that if a cold fire were possible, there would be no contradiction with perception for the sentence that makes it known. The word "also" (*api*) implies that the sentence possesses a referent that actually exists. || 159 ||
Or it may be cold like cold itself, because its coldness has not been removed.
In this way, there would likewise be no contradiction of this [scriptural statement] by other means of valid cognition as well.

If another fire were also perceived as being like a hot fire, then, since both parts of the statement would be equal in being merely reiterative (anuvāda), how could there be a "cold fire" mentioned in the sentence?
To this, he says: "like cold. He states the reason by relying on a specific time: "of coldness.
Even in the case of the simile, the lack of contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge regarding the phrase "cold fire" is established through its partial identity with "hot fire."
Thus he said: "In this way. || 160 ||
The fire of the cold season becomes cool, and likewise, the earthly fire becomes hot.
There is no contradiction between the two statements, because they are understood to have different meanings. || 561 ||

It has been stated that "cold fire indeed exists"; he now provides an illustration of that very existence with the words "the winter [fire]. Although it originates from lightning, clouds, and so forth, the divine, fuel-less fire intended here is the winter fire. He mentions the nature of the hot fire incidentally with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).

Having established the absence of contradiction when there is a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), he establishes its absence even when there are separate sentences (*bhinnavākyatva*) with the word "distinct" (*bhinnena*). || 169 ||
There is no contradiction when there is a single meaning, nor is there one when there is redundancy, because it does not depend on that [redundancy].
And there are no other means of cognition, because [the object] is not within the scope of another means of cognition. || 562 ||

Having stated that there is no contradiction whether there is unity or plurality of sentences, he applies the point established in the example to the subject at hand: "In the case of having a single meaning" (*aikārthya*). This is its meaning: regarding the sentence *tattvamasi*, whether there is unity or non-unity [of the sentence], and even within the first case (unity), whether it has a single meaning or multiple meanings—in neither case is there a contradiction; for we observe both a single and a manifold meaning by relying on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and what is established by valid means is not contradictory.

[The author] refutes the position that there are multiple sentences with the words "mānāntarāt" (from another means of knowledge). The meaning is: there is no contradiction between one sentence and another sentence because they have different objects; otherwise, [if they did refer to the same object], there would be no contradiction due to their mutual agreement (*saṃvāda*). || 162 ||
This has been stated by way of concession; however, it is not the method of those who know the science of sentences.
That which is the capacity of a single word, while existing as such, to convey multiple meanings.

980. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Adhyāya]:

Having provisionally accepted the position that even if there were unity of the sentence (*vākyaikya*), it would be purposeless, he says "merely a verbal assertion" (*vāṅmātra*). He uses the term "having accepted" (*abhyupetya*) [to indicate this]. The reason for this is stated as "but not... (*na tu*). || 163 ||
"Because there is unity of purpose"—thus is the definition of a sentence stated.
If it were to convey multiple meanings, its statement would not possess the character of a definition.

What, then, is their principle? He states it: "Now, because of unity [of meaning]. Just as there is an absence of multiple meanings for a single sentence, so too is the definition of a single sentence stated by those who know it:

"A sentence is one because of the unity of its meaning, provided that if it were divided, there would be a mutual expectancy"—this is the sense of the statement "a sentence is one because of the unity of its meaning. This applies to a single sentence, whether worldly or Vedic, which has a single purpose—
He says "aneka" [in verse 164], meaning that because it possesses the nature of being multiple, it is pervaded by the definition stated therein; thus, it would not constitute a single sentence.
When the entire Veda is accepted as being a single sentence alone.
Since no other statement is possible at that time, by what could there be contradiction? (565)

Anticipating the objection that even if the sentence beginning with "That thou art" (tattvamasi) forms a single syntactical unity as a whole, it might still contradict other sentences, the author considers the alternatives—whether the entire Veda is a single sentence or consists of two sentences—and refutes the first alternative by stating: "One" (ekam). || 169 ||
Or else, there are two statements, due to the distinction between the established fact and the matter to be proven.
Even then, there is no contradiction here between the two [statements], as they convey different meanings. (566)
Having restated the second [point], he states the lack of contradiction: "vākya... etc. Here, the phrase "in this" refers to the two sections (kāṇḍa). || 966 ||
Nor does the Upaniṣad ever destroy one's own interest or the interest of others.
And listen with one-pointed mind to how that is being explained. (567)
It has been stated that the Vedāntas, which convey their own uncontradicted meaning, neither subvert that [meaning] nor contradict other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, he begins to establish that very point by way of another method. Regarding the phrase "nor indeed" (*nāpi*): the expression "in some cases" (*kvacit*) was used with the intention of referring either to a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) or to a difference in persons (*puruṣa-bheda*). How can the Upaniṣad, while teaching non-duality (*advaita*), not subvert its own purpose and the purpose of others?
He asks: "How so? To that end, he states the preliminary ground for explaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*): "It is being explained... (167).
If one were to maintain that "all is the self," it would produce a valid cognition whose object is a knowable thing.
"This destroys the meaning of the Upaniṣads"—this is the speech of the shameless. (568)
Regarding its "destruction of its own purpose," does this mean the destruction of its own object or the destruction of its own fruit? It is not the first; thus he says: "All... (968).
It is the attainment of all human goals without exception and the perpetual transcendence of all misfortunes.
If one's own purpose is achieved through the knowledge of Vedānta, what other [purpose] could be desired beyond this? || 569 ||

He says it is not the second [alternative], stating "without remainder. Even though this does not strike down its own fruit, he says "no" because there is no possibility of its striking down another of its own fruits, stating "for its own sake. || 169 ||
Nor does it either prohibit or enjoin any ritual action belonging to the Upaniṣads.
Because that [scriptural] statement is exhausted upon the realization of the one Self within oneself. || 570 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 687] 981 1 Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
Nevertheless, fearing that because it subverts the authority of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), it might also subvert the welfare of others, he says: "It negates... (verse 170).
Nor does the statement in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) fail to produce valid cognition regarding its own meaning.
And how can that [cognition], while producing a valid cognition regarding its own object, be said to be invalid? || 571 ||

Fearing that, once the statement regarding the non-dual inner self (*pratyagātman*) has been set aside, a ritual injunction (*karmavākya*) would no longer produce valid knowledge regarding its own subject matter due to contradiction with that [non-dual self], he says:
"Not so" (*na ca*). Fearing that it might lack authority because of contradiction even while producing valid knowledge of its own subject matter, he says:
"And if [it were] regarding its own subject matter" (*svārthe ca*) || 171 ||
And because valid knowledge arises from direct perception, as well as from sentences such as those concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
It is impossible to say that valid cognition does not arise. || 572 ||

Anticipating the objection that no valid cognition (pramā) arises with respect to its own object from ritual injunctions due to a lack of means of knowledge (māna), he says: "Because of directness" (prātyakṣyāt).
The particle *na* is used here for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the admission [of the opponent's point]. || 172 ||
If, however, the arising of valid knowledge occurs through the statements of the Vedānta for one who has been carried away by sense objects, [then it is established].
No, because direct perception is more powerful than the awakening of inference. || 573 ||

He raises an objection: since the unity [of the Self] is made known by the statement concerning Brahman, the meaning of the ritual (karma) statements is sublated; therefore, no valid cognition (pramā) arises from those [ritual] statements. He answers this with the words "viṣaye" (regarding the object): "The subject under dispute does not produce valid cognition, because its object has been sublated by another means of knowledge (pramāṇa), like a statement that fire is not hot. He refutes this by stating "no," on the grounds that perception, which possesses a cognition dependent upon inference, is more powerful; thus, when there is a conflict with it, inference does not operate.
to give || 573 ||
"Having taken up whatever [objects] are already established, one follows the power of desire and hatred."
May that which is desired always be mine, and may even the slightest undesired thing not come to pass.
The means of accomplishment are for the sake of attaining what is desired and for the removal of what is undesired.
The Śruti, when speaking of a person, does not state anything for any other purpose.

Anticipating the objection that, because the *karmakāṇḍa* is authoritative as a means of valid knowledge regarding its own subject matter, its object must therefore be real, and thus the Upaniṣads would be sublated, [the author] states "Just as... (*yathā*), considering that the previously mentioned reason is unestablished. Just as one perceives objects and, through the superimposition of beauty or ugliness upon them, generates attachment or aversion, and being dependent on those, thinks, "May what is desired be mine," and "May what is not desired not be mine"—[so too is the case with the world].

The meaning is this: one who desires what is not yet attained seeks only the means to achieve it; thus, the scriptural injunction regarding action is satisfied by the mere mention of those means, and does not concern itself with whether those means and so forth possess ultimate reality or not. || 174 || 171 ||
Just as in the case of the optional Agnihotra and other rites, there is a connection between the means and the end to be accomplished.
In some places, it speaks of desires as being characterized by falsehood and other such qualities.

He supports the stated point by means of an illustration, beginning with "Just as": the scripture, which impels one toward optional rites (*kāmya-karma*), [is effective] when its connection [to the goal] is unknown.

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Two:

The meaning is that the scripture, while making known desires along with their fruits and their means, does not state that there is truthfulness or the like in any of them; likewise, even regarding the obligatory *agnihotra* and other rites, the scripture, while teaching their specific details, does not speak of their truthfulness or the like. || 176 ||
Nor, however, do men refrain from performing actions that yield desired results.
For this reason, desire never ceases for those who do not know reality.

Anticipating the objection—“If the truthfulness of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and so forth is not stated, how can qualified persons engage in ritual acts?”—the author says: “Not [so],” etc.

By the force of the word “also” (*api*), it is understood that this applies even to obligatory rites (*nityakarman*). The meaning is that for those who are ignorant, there exists a desire that impels them to act. || 577 ||
Nowhere in this world is any action ever seen to occur without desire.
For whatever one does, all that is the activity of desire.

Having raised the doubt that, although one engages in optional rites (kāmya) out of a desire for results, one might not engage in obligatory rites (nitya) due to the absence of such a desire, he states the proof that engagement in those [obligatory rites] is likewise motivated by desire: "Not out of desire" (akāmataḥ). || 178 ||
"According to his desire," and so forth—this is the detailed explanation of that meaning.
It will be stated that one who does not desire and likewise does not act is liberated. || 579 ||

In that very context, he cites scripture as authority: "sa yathā" (just as that...). In connection with the fact that activity proceeding from the power of desire constitutes bondage, he states "akāmayamānaśca" (and one who is without desire), relying on such scriptural passages as "athākāmayamānaḥ" (now, one who is without desire), etc., which teach that cessation [from activity] due to the absence of desire constitutes liberation. The word "akurvann" (not acting) is to be understood as a separate syntactical split. || 179 ||
[This is] for one who has destroyed all authority [over worldly matters] and possesses complete self-realization.
Whether in the state of active involvement or in the state of cessation, the subordinate status of the qualities is always maintained.

Anticipating the objection—since activity is observed even in the case of a knower who is free from desire, how can there be liberation for one who is desireless and non-active—the author says "All... and so forth.
*Adhikāra* refers to the relationship between the person and the injunction, and so on; *guṇabhāva* refers to agency. (180)
Therefore, because it lacks an objective referent, that which was stated regarding the oneness of Brahman and so forth [is established].
All that should be understood as avoided by following exactly the path described above. || 581 ||

Having established that the connection [of the Upanishads] is understood through their indifference toward the truth of the *karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section), he concludes the critique of the inference under discussion with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the pointlessness of the other section (*kāṇḍāntara*) due to its lack of purpose if [the Upanishads] were for one's own sake, and the absence of fruit in the grasping of the teaching, just as there would be no object if they were identical [to the ritual section]. He states the meaning of the word "therefore" with the words "Just as... (*yathā*). For the ignorant person—

The meaning is this: since one who is dispassionate engages in ritual action, there is a connection [between the two]; therefore, the authority of that [ritual] section is established through the cognition derived from its statements.
Furthermore, because that [section] maintains neutrality regarding the truth and so forth of the Self, the Upanishads are also authoritative as they are not in contradiction [with it]. || 189 ||
It is not possible to turn back one whose mind is drawn away by passion and the like.
582. No one whose mind is dispassionate is capable of engaging with the treatise.

Since the treatise on action (karma-śāstra) teaches connection and is intent upon engagement and so forth, it follows that [such engagement] arises from the power of passion and the like, because it is incompatible with [dispassion]; thus, there is engagement according to the treatise.
Anticipating the objection that this would result in the object becoming real, he says "no," and so forth; the meaning is "because it is not an agent. || 182 ||
1. Of someone. 2. ka. ga. mayāna.
[vol2, page 689] "1 brāhmaṇam" accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 983.
One should explain that the means of accomplishment yield both desired and undesired fruits.
The scripture does not effect either the cessation or the engagement of the person.
What, then, does the treatise do? To this it says: "Desired," etc. It states what is to be excluded: "Not," etc. || 183 ||
Even by transgressing the scripture, due to the strength of passion and other afflictions.
Even today, men are seen to be active while still possessed by desire. || 584 ||
He states another argument for the claim that there is no engagement [with activity] based on scripture, beginning with "api" (even/also). || 984 ||
The relationship between the goal and its means, and the arising of desired and undesired results.
But the scripture, like the sun, always directly illuminates them.
He concludes the task of the treatise on action with the verse beginning "sādhya... (verse 185).
In those [treatises], which are the sole lamps for the scriptures and which constitute the paths to the goal and its means.
"Men act according to their own inclinations, and not according to the scriptures. (586)
He concludes that it is desire, not the scripture, which is the motivator: "In those [cases]," etc. (186).
Therefore,
the Vedāntas are never sublaters of the ritual scriptures.
And that [cognition] cannot be without an object, because there is a distinction in the objects of knowledge, as in the case of the sense of touch and the others. || 587 ||
He states what follows from its being the initiator [of worldly activity]: "vidhi... and so forth. The meaning of the word "tat" (that) refers to the two sections [of the Veda].

Since the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) has as its object imagined karma and the like, while the Brahman section (*brahmakāṇḍa*) has as its object the non-dual, unimagined reality, there is no contradiction between the two; this is the meaning. || 987 ||
But some who consider themselves wise [assert] things that are mutually contradictory.
All honors accord due respect to the reality of the single self-nature. (588)

Having stated that the Vedāntas possess authority regarding their own subject matter by means of refuting all contradictions within its own position, he states the position of the logicians (tārkikas), beginning with "But some [say]... This means: provided that the reality of non-duality, which is accessible through scripture, has been apprehended. || 188 ||
Since these objects, such as sound and the rest, are mutually distinct from one another by means of the auditory and other senses.
The claim that "everything is measured as the Self" contradicts direct perception. || 589 ||
In this regard, he states the contradiction of the Śruti concerning Brahman with perception, beginning with "by the ears and so forth. (189)
The perceivers of the objects of sound and their respective agents are each distinct.
Because they are inferred here [in this world], therefore there is a contradiction with the logical mark (liṅga). || 590 ||
He states the contradiction with inference regarding that [scriptural claim]: "From sound, etc. The connection is as follows: "In these bodies, they are inferred individually.

The sense is that the scriptural teaching of oneness is contradicted by the following inference: "The activity observed in other bodies, which is similar to the activity inherent in one's own body, must be preceded by an effort, because it is a specific kind of activity, just like the [activity] under consideration. || 190 ||
1. Regarding entities.
Likewise, there is a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) due to the distinctions between those desiring a village and so forth.
Being greatly delighted and not detracting from the oneness of Brahman, they illuminate it. || 591 ||
In that very context, he states the contradiction with scripture. [He says] "tathā" (so it is). He states the reason for their joy: "brahma" (Brahman), etc. || 199 ||
How indeed can there be a contradiction regarding the oneness of Brahman for those whose cognitions perceive distinct objects?
Thus, those who propound duality should be approached and questioned by the knower of Brahman.
When it is argued that the oneness of Brahman is not possible because it contradicts the three measures of knowledge, he asks: "Regarding the oneness of Brahman... (992).
O friend, does the diversity of sound and the other [objects] contradict the oneness of the self?
If it is not contradicted, then why is a contradiction stated so emphatically? || 593 ||

Is that oneness contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge, or is it that non-duality [itself] [is contradicted]? Having raised this dilemma, he refutes the first alternative by means of an illustration.

"What?"—the connection is: "if, however, it is not contradicted. Just as when it is said that "the one ether resides in all beings," there is no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge which apprehend distinctions such as sound, because their objects are different; so too, when it is said that "the one Brahman resides in all beings" [there is no contradiction].
The meaning is that even so, there is no contradiction with direct perception (pratyakṣa). || 593 ||
Nor can Brahman be known even by means of perception and other instruments that distinguish existing objects.
Exclusion is merely the absence [of something] from another, [occurring] somewhere by means of something.

He addresses the position that the non-duality of Brahman is contradicted by those [means of knowledge] with the word "sat" (Being). Since perception and the other means of knowledge apprehend only Being (*sanmātra*), they cannot establish through them a mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*) consisting of differentiation from anything, anywhere, or by anyone; for such would involve defects such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Therefore, the meaning is that the non-duality of Brahman is not contradicted by them. || 994 ||
There does not exist any means of valid cognition whatsoever that apprehends duality.
In the same way, I shall explain [this] regarding the Sun; therefore, there is no contradiction with the *Manu-smṛti*.

Furthermore, he states that their grasping at duality has been refuted in the discussion on the relationship [between the means and the goal] and elsewhere, saying "dvaita... He says "tathā" (likewise) because that will also be explained later in the investigation of creation and so forth. He concludes that non-dual Brahman is not contradictory, saying "nātaḥ" (not from this). || 195 ||
As has been stated, they are inferred to be distinct for each individual body.
They are the perceivers of objects such as sound, and they are also the agents of actions.
He restates the contradiction with inference [with the words] "And that which... (yac ca) || 196 ||
If, when asked by whom these [differences] are inferred, one should say, "By us who are skilled in logical marks," this too is not reasonable. (597)

One might argue that since every movement is preceded by effort, there is no distinction between selves; however, this does not establish a difference between selves, because it is also possible for a movement to be preceded by one's own effort—just as the movement of one's own body is preceded by one's own effort. Furthermore, if the movement of another's body were preceded by one's own effort, then the distinction between self and other would have to be established at the very outset. Yet, this distinction cannot be established through perception, because the other person is not perceived; nor can it be established through inference, because that would involve circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*). Bearing this in mind, he says: "They are distinct."
He raises a doubt with the intention of stating another defect: "Thus asked. To that, he states the refutation: "And this... (197).

It demonstrates the lack of logical consistency [in the opponent's position] with the words "ananyā" (not other). The meaning is as follows: that self whose difference is to be proven must be either self-luminous or perceptible. In the first case, since it is not an object of cognition, its difference cannot be established through valid means of knowledge (*māna*). "Explain this: who among you are skilled in inference? || 599 ||
[The Lord resides] separately within the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
To begin with, skill in inference does not exist in each of those [senses] individually. (600)
Therefore, we ourselves are indeed the means for [attaining] the body and so forth.
Because actions are to be accomplished by numerous means, there is no difference [between them]. || 601 ||

Regarding the phrase "by us who are skilled in inference," he asks here for the meaning of "us. [The opponent replies: "The body, or the collection of organs, or something other than the two bodies. [The author says: "Neither the first two, because they are insentient and thus incapable of being an inferer; nor the last, because it is changeless"—this is the sense. Considering that the word *kim* has the sense of a question, the proponent (pūrvavādī) says: "The body... etc. You yourself have admitted that the capacity to infer resides in each one of those [individually].

Since skill in inference is individually excluded from those [bodies], therefore, because the actions of inference are accomplished by many factors (kārakas) characterized by numerous instruments such as the body, the cognition of the distinctness of the self for each body arises from an inference whose agent is of such a qualified nature. This is the meaning. || 999 ||
If it be argued that this is because actions are to be accomplished by means of abundant resources (bhūrisādhana), then [the following response applies].
For you as well, the consequence follows that even a single [cause] would possess multiplicity. || 602 ||
He refutes the opponent’s statement regarding our position with the word "bhūri" (abundant). || 602 ||
Because the self and so forth possess action, each of them is an agent.
Consequently, there would follow a plurality of selves, just as in the case of fire and other such [entities]. || 603 ||

If it is argued that the distinct self is the agent of inference because actions are accomplished by multiple factors (*kāraka*s), then [the author] explains what was stated—that in that case, even each individual entity such as the body would have to be manifold—by saying "of the self and so forth. This means that for the self and the body and other factors of inference, there exists a subordinate action for each one; just as all the factors such as fire and the rest possess such activity.

Since you have accepted this, does the intermediate action of the self (ātman) require multiple factors (kārakas) for its accomplishment, or not? If the first [alternative is true], is it accomplished by multiple factors distinct from the self, or by those that are not distinct from it? Not the first, because it would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā).

In the second case, however, there would be the consequence of the self being manifold; and thus, due to the attainment of multiplicity in the cognizer—just as in the case of fire and other causes of cooking—the selflessness (nairātmya) of the soul would follow.
This is the meaning. || 603 ||
Even inference is admitted by you yourself to be an action.
The body, the sense organs, the intellect, and so forth, would each possess multiplicity. (604)
Because ritual actions are accomplished by means of many instruments, for this reason—[Vol. 2, p. 692] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter.
Therefore, the indicative mark (liṅga) consists of the statement of such characteristics and causes. || 605 ||

Anticipating the objection that "there is no intermediate action for the inferrer at all, because that [action] is admitted only in its causes, and because inference, being a form of knowledge, is not an action," he says: "Inference also... The meaning is: "because it is the meaning of a verbal root" (dhātvarthatvāt). Alternatively, the meaning is: "because in the Bhaṭṭa school, knowledge is accepted as being an action. He extends the aforementioned reasoning to the body and so forth: "The body... [The meaning is: "of that [body], there is no intermediate action..."

The sense is as follows: if [the intermediate action] does not exist, then there is no agency; if it does exist, then there would be a multiplicity [of actions] for each [agent] due to the reason you have stated, because that intermediate action is accomplished by many factors (kārakas), and if it were to be accomplished by multiple factors distinct from those [primary ones], there would be an infinite regress. Thus, when the qualified self is the cognizer, one who states the reason—that actions are accomplished by multiple factors—[is refuted] by the aforementioned logic, even by a learned person.
He says that there should be laughter: "In this way," etc. (604–605).
Because all qualities and actions depend solely upon the agent.
In that case, the reason [you provide] would likewise entail for you the fallacy of being inconclusive (anaikāntikatā). || 606 ||

Having refuted the view that the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of an agent is accomplished by multiple agents, he refutes another alternative with the words "guṇa" etc. The meaning is as follows: if the intermediate operations of agents were to be accomplished by multiple agents, then because those operations would reside solely in their own respective agents, the probans "being an action" (*kriyātva*) would exist even in the absence of the property to be proved—namely, being accomplished by multiple agents—and thus there would be a logical fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). || 606 ||
The reason lacks the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*apakṣadharmatā*), because name and form have the internal self (*pratyagātman*) as their substratum;
since there is no such property [in the self], how can there be causality with respect to its distinction? (607)

Having stated that inference does not arise because there is no logical connection for the inferrer, he considers even its probans (*liṅga*) to be difficult to state, and thus refutes the Sāṃkhya-proposed probans such as "birth" based on their specific restriction (*pratiniyama*), etc. [The verse begins with] "Not in the subject" (*apakṣa*). The meaning is that birth and so forth are not suitable as proof for the plurality of *puruṣas*, because they reside in the body—which consists of name and form—and do not apply to the *ātman*. [The *ātman* is of a different genus than substance...]

Anticipating the objection from the logicians that [the self] must possess the specific quality of hearing because it possesses hearing, like a pot, he says: "Dharma... (verse 607). For it is not the case that [the self] is perceived as possessing qualities, since the scripture states, "He is alone, devoid of qualities," and because pleasure and so forth are qualities of the mind, and the scripture declares, "All this is indeed the mind. Therefore, the reason—that of possessing the aforementioned qualities—does not apply to the distinct self; the point is that it suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddhi*). || 607 ||
Bodies possess a single self, even though disputes exist regarding them.
Because there is no difference in their being bodies, just like the body of the opponent. || 608 ||
Having stated the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) in the inference of difference, he states a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*): "Aikātmya," etc.
The meaning is: bodies other than the body of the opponent possess identity with that [opponent's] self, because they are living bodies, just like the [opponent's own] accepted body. (608)
In the same way, one should apply this to the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the objects of the senses as well.
The identity of the Self with all beings is likewise established through direct perception.

He extends the aforementioned reasoning to the sense organs and so forth by saying "likewise" (*tathā*). One should infer as follows: "The disputed objects are the instruments of experience for the opponent, because they are sense organs, just like the sense organs of the opponent. Having thus made the mind, intellect, and objects the subject of the inference, [the conclusion] is that the sense organs and so forth belong to that body.

That from which the birth, maintenance, and destruction of the world are accomplished is the Supreme.
Having previously promised "Brahman," it has been demonstrated exactly as it is. || 1 ||

It has been stated that "its secret doctrine" (upaniṣad) [is this]; its explanation is now being given here.
For the realization of the truth of the supreme Brahman by means of Maitreyī. || 2 ||

Having recalled the previously mentioned alternative meaning, he states the purport of the two subsequent Brāhmaṇas with the words "tasya" (of that). The referent of the word "that" is Brahman as the inner self (*pratyagbrahma*). He states the fruit of the explanation of the Upaniṣad with the words "para" (supreme). || 2 ||

The connection between the preceding and the subsequent sections, as well as their sequential order, has already been stated. "Yo ha vai" is the statement of the question; "tasyāyam" is the conclusion.
The vital breath (prāṇa) is placed within the body, and likewise, it is established in the head.

He states the division of the portion preceding that [verse] which begins with "brāhmaṇam avatārya tam": "yo ha" and so forth. Those [afflictions] residing in the head and the mind, characterized by attachment to sound and the other sense objects.

The body shall be its receptacle, since it is situated within the body.

For the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the support of the body, is that upon which speech and the other [senses] depend.
They are sufficient for the accomplishment of their own tasks, but they do not depend solely on the vital breaths.

Regarding this, he states another reason: "The body," etc. The sense organs, which perform their functions by depending on the vital breaths (prāṇas) situated within the body, are arranged in five ways; however, in states such as fainting, they do not function because that [vital breath] is absent. Therefore, the meaning is that the body is the substratum (ādhāna) for them. || 12 ||
And because it is placed back again, they know the head to be the "re-deposit" (pratyādhāna).
He was placed individually in each of the specific regions of the head. || 13 ||
He states the meaning of the term *pratyādhāna* (counter-support) with the word "pratīti" (perception). He further clarifies that very point with the words "śiraḥ" (the head). || 13 ||
For vitality, life-force, and strength indeed arise from food and drink.
Upon this support of strength, the vital breath remains established in the body.

Having thus bowed to the Lord of the Unborn, the departure of the vital breath (prāṇotkrānti) will now be explained.
Some declare that the wind, characterized by activities such as inhalation and exhalation, is the pillar.

In this regard, he states the proof: "weakness. When the self, having brought the body to a state of weakness, enters as it were into a state of delusion, then the vital breath (prāṇa) departs; this will be explained in the sixth [chapter] in accordance with the meaning already stated regarding that departure. He says "exhalation, etc. in order to accept the interpretation of Bhartṛprapañca concerning the passage on the pillar. For it has been said: "The vital breath is exhalation..."

[vol2, page 696] 990 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Second Adhyāya]— [The text continues: ...the wise one, having understood the nature of the Self as it truly is, does not perceive any distinction between the cause and the effect, nor does he see the world as something other than the Self. Therefore, the knower of Brahman, remaining established in the Self, transcends all dualities and attains the state of absolute peace. This is the final conclusion of the inquiry into the nature of the Self. [End of Second Adhyāya]

Speech, though being of a single kind, is divided by the distinction between the speaker and the enjoyer.

"By way of being the speaker" (*vaktṛtvena*). He explains that while it is divided into two, it is the seventh by way of being the speaker and [the eighth] by way of being the utterer. And he says: "And the seventh... (verse 28).
The accomplishment of color is by means of speech, and likewise, the experience of the primary taste.
Through the combination of two syllables, there may arise the seventh and eighth speech.

Anticipating the objection—"Even though speech is the effect of the organ of speech, since the tasting of flavor is the effect of the organ of taste, how can there be a twofold division of speech?"—he says: "Varṇa... The perception of flavor is the act of chewing (carvaṇa). || 29 ||
The subsequent Vedic revelation was for the sake of establishing the superiority of the sages over [others] in the accomplishment of giving.
And likewise, meditation would bear fruit only when [the object] is understood as "these two indeed. (30)
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "these two indeed" as follows: "qualified," etc. To the question, "For what purpose is their designation by names such as Bharadvāja and so forth?
he replies there: "In that manner," [verse 30].
The phrase "of all" would be a statement of the result for the aforementioned practice of meditation.
In order to negate the absence of a self, it is said that "all this belongs to him. || 31 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "of all" (*sarvasya*). Regarding the word "all" (*sarvasya*), fearing that the meaning of the phrase "all of this" (*sarvam asya*) and so forth has already been explained, he states its intended purport: "By this," etc. For one who is being worshipped, there is no state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) toward another; rather, [that other] is solely an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*).
This is the meaning. || 31 ||
Thus ends the second Śiśu Brāhmaṇa of the second chapter in the Commentary on the Vārttika to the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. || 2 ||
Now begins the third Brāhmaṇa.
The Upaniṣads of the vital breaths have been declared, and the vital breaths themselves have also been explained in brief.
That which is their ultimate truth is now being investigated. || 1 ||

In order to state the connection [of the present section], he recounts the preceding narrative: "The vital breaths," etc. The meaning is that, in connection with the *Brahmopaniṣad*, the *Upaniṣads* of the vital breaths—consisting of meditations on specific names—have been explained; and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is also stated that their number is limited to those [already mentioned]. Which are these vital breaths?
He says "And the vital breaths (prāṇāḥ)" because that expectation has been removed. Since they are infinite, they cannot be determined in their entirety;
nevertheless, they have been described in brief by way of the ears and so forth, and by the word "and" (ca), their nature as the Word (śabda) has also been stated—this is the meaning.
He states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa: "But that which... (yat tu). || 1 ||
Of what nature are these vital breaths, and how is their reality maintained?
The meaning is that such things as these should be stated; this is the subsequent scriptural authority (āgama). || 2 ||

One might object: "If the commencement of the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of defining the Supreme Brahman—which is the 'Truth' denoted by the term *satya* consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*)—then the passage beginning with 'Two indeed... is redundant, since that [Brahman] is not defined therein; rather, one should have begun simply with 'Now, therefore, the instruction' (*athāta ādeśaḥ*). Anticipating this doubt, he states the purport of the section preceding the word *atha*: "The vital breaths... [He continues: "They must be either conscious or unconscious; in the second case, they would be either causal selves (*kāraṇātman*) or modifications (*vikāra*)."

Nor is there volition, because they are not the Self; nor are they of the nature of causes, because according to the scriptural teaching on birth, if they were modifications, they would be "mere matters of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*) and thus not real. The word "iti" is for the purpose of restating the manner of these expectations. The word "evam" refers back to their essential nature. By the word "ādi," their reality is included. All of this is stated without exception for the purpose of destroying [all] expectations; therefore, from the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) onwards—
The meaning is that the textual passage beginning with "the two indeed" (dve vāva) and so forth, which provides a definition, is purposeful. || 2 ||
Of the hundred beings consisting of the five elements, whose nature is the formation of bodies.
The supreme Brāhmaṇa was commenced for the purpose of ascertaining one's own true nature.
Anticipating the objection that their true nature or reality is not being stated because only the elements (*bhūta*) are being described, he says: "But later" (*paścāt*).

The meaning is that since the elements—which consist of effects and instruments—are denoted by the word "real" (*satya*), the subsequent statement is not contradictory insofar as it describes the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) which have those [elements] as their essence; thus its nature and so forth are being explained. The term "Brāhmaṇa" refers to a portion of that [subsequent section]. || 3 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 699] [Regarding the Brāhmaṇa: Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
"By means of the statement negating its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), Brahman is clearly indicated as 'not this, not this' (*neti neti*)."
That very reality which was intended to be investigated is now being stated.

Anticipating the objection—"Since Brahman, which is the Truth of truth, is what is to be expressed, why is there this description of the vital breaths as previously stated? It is useless"—the author says: "That which has as its limiting adjunct... In the expression "the Truth of truth," the word *satya* ending in the genitive case denotes that which is to be abandoned (*heya*), while the word *satya* ending in the nominative case denotes that which is to be accepted (*ādeya*). The passage preceding the word *atha* (now) is for the purpose of stating the original nature of these two; the subsequent portion, up to the end of the Brāhmaṇa, [is for the purpose of explaining the means of attaining it].
The collective meaning is: "for the purpose of defining what is to be accepted from the wings [of the argument]. || 4 ||
The supreme Brahman is by its own nature formless; it [appears otherwise] due to causes such as ignorance (avidyā).
It is described as having two forms, like the sky [appearing dual] due to its dependence upon a jar.
One might raise the objection: "Brahman is unattached; how can it have a connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and why, then, would one wish to reveal it by removing those adjuncts?

To this, he says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes its effects. The phrase "as pointed out by Śruti and Smṛti" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. An illustration for how that which is formless (*arūpa*) appears to possess form through the medium of limiting adjuncts is given: "like space" (*viyadvat*). || 5 ||
Or one should know the forms and formless aspects of Brahmā, together with their latent impressions, within matter.
Brahman alone is described by those two; for the state of being Brahman is not possessed of form.

Having taken for granted the twofold nature of Brahman as "with attributes" (*sopādhika*) and "without attributes" (*nirupādhika*), he states that the one with attributes alone possesses two forms: "or the two forms. The word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and). Anticipating the objection that there might even be a third form consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*), he says: "together with the impressions" (*savāsane*). He explains how those two constitute the nature of Brahman: "Brahman itself," because it is "defined" (*rūpyate*), meaning it is specifically known.

Up to this point, having raised the objection that those two (the individual soul and the internal organ) possess the nature of Brahman just like consciousness and so forth, [the author], intending to speak of Brahman as devoid of limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), says: "The state of being Brahman" (brahmatvam).
The abstract suffix (*bhāva*) has its own primary meaning here, because of the scriptural texts such as "without form" (arūpa) and so on—this is the sense. || 6 ||
This Brahman, having only ignorance as its limiting adjunct, is called the cause.
That very [Self] attains the state of being a knower by relying upon the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect.

One might object: "Is there not another form of Brahman called 'causality'? If so, how can it be said that there are only two forms? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Ignorance" (avidyā). The meaning is that causality is not an independent form, because it is dependent upon effects such as the formed (mūrta) and the like. If it is argued that "knowership" is another form, he says: "That very same [ignorance]. Since knowership has its cause in the intellect (buddhi), which is included within ignorance, knowership is not a separate form.
This is the meaning. || 7 ||
Abiding within the limiting adjuncts of those functions, it is called "Being" (sat) and "Knowledge" (jñāna).
The specific connection between each deity and its respective faculty is thus designated as such.

If it is argued that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a different form (*rūpāntara*), he says "no," [explaining] "its function" (*tadvṛtti*). Having raised the doubt as to whether the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-devatā*) or the presided-over sense organ (*adhiṣṭheya-indriya*) is a different form, he says "the deity" (*devatā*). The meaning is this: that very [self], having become the presiding deity such as Brahmā, is called the "deity"; and that same [self], when conditioned by the presided-over sense organ, is designated by that term [i.e., "means of valid cognition"]. || 8 ||

Likewise,
the connection with the body and so forth would be characterized by suffering, birth, and other such conditions.
In this way, one who possesses the conceit of divine wealth and so forth is called "wealthy" or "possessor of cows. || 9 ||

Anticipating the objection that the gross or subtle body might be a different form [of the self], he says: "Likewise" (tathā). If it is argued that being a cow and so forth is a different form, he says: "The wealth of cows," etc. (godhana), [implying] "no. || 9 ||
The Inner Controller, the Witness, and the Omniscient— thus is the conviction.
And by means of false superimpositions and their effects, the immeasurable is measured.
If it is argued that the nature of the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) and so forth constitutes another form [of Brahman], he says "no," beginning with the word "antaryāmī.

Whether by way of the qualified and the unqualified, or by way of the conceptual and the non-conceptual, the distinction between those two is indeed insubstantial; for the entirety of the aforementioned form is intended to be expressed as such.
It has been stated [that Brahman is "not this, not this"]. Anticipating the objection that there exists another form of Brahman which is an object of knowledge, he says: "It is false" (*mithyā*).
By the word "that" (*tat*), ignorance (*avidyā*) is denoted. The instrumental case is used in the sense of "being in such a state. || 10 ||
Ākāśa:
First of all, this form of Brahmā is born from the cause of delusion.
The true nature of the self is that which is cognizable by a single cognition consisting of pure consciousness alone. || 11 ||
He concludes the description of the conditioned form with the word "one" (*ekam*). He indicates its unity with the word "delusion" (*moha*).

He begins to manifest the unconditioned form with the word "innermost" (*pratyak*). The meaning is that the true nature of the Self is that which shines forth as the innermost reality of a single essence—pure consciousness (*jñapti-mātra*) independent of anything else for its existence or manifestation. || 11 ||
It is neither excluded nor followed after, being unborn due to the impossibility of a second.
Nor is there a meaning for the sentence and the word, because they are devoid of particularity and generality. || 12 ||
He states its reality by means of its being devoid of both universals and particulars: "not excluded" (*avyāvṛtta*). The reason for this is given as: "the second" (*dvitīya*).
Furthermore, he says that whatever is born is unreal, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, whereas this [Brahman] is not born and is therefore real:
"unborn" (*aja*). Moreover, whatever is expressible is false, like silver and the like; but this is not so expressed, and therefore it is real.
He says "No," and so forth. He states the reason for its being inexpressible with the words "Because of difference" (bhedāt). || 12 ||
It is not to be apprehended by other means of valid cognition, because it is not connected with anything external.
The [self] does not require [external] means such as sacrificial materials and the like, because it is already endowed with that ignorance. || 13 ||
Furthermore, he says "No" to the claim that whatever is known is false, whereas this [Reality] is real because it is unknowable. He states the reason for its being beyond perception and the like:

its lack of sound and other qualities. Moreover, he says "independent" to show that whatever depends on parts and the like is false—just as a snake [superimposed on a rope] is—whereas this is real because it does not depend on them. He states the reason for that: "unborn" (avi-).

However, it is not the case that this [non-existence] possesses independence or is itself non-existent, because [this objection] has been resolved in the *Saṃbandhaparīkṣā*; such is the intended meaning. || 13 ||
The oneness of the self is based on the conviction of the self; indeed, a second [self] would exist only for the sake of the self.
Therefore, having the realization of non-self, I am by myself alone, solitary. || 14 ||

Having raised the objection as to how there can be cognition of that [the Self] if it were independent of the means of knowledge such as the sense organs (*mātra*), he recalls its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), stating that it is cognizable solely through the single cognition of the *pratyagātman* (the inner self). He says "The Self" (*ātmeti*). By stating that being the Self (*ātmatva*) is the reason for this, he implies that what is not the Self is imagined (*kalpita*)—like a silver shell—because its manifestation is dependent on something else. Regarding the second [point], he states the consequence of its being imagined: "Therefore" (*ata iti*).
It means that it is absolute, free from conceptual proliferation, and independent. || 14 ||
This is expressed by way of negation as "not this, not this."
Taking ignorance as the limit, these two forms of Brahman exist.

Having stated the connection and prepared the ground for the explanation of the words, he joins the phrases: "Two indeed are the forms of Brahman. With the word *yat* ("that"), there is a reference to Brahman as the subject to be established. Fearing that if these two were its forms, they might—like consciousness—not be subject to negation, he says: "ignorance" (*avidyām*). In that state, those two exist having that very ignorance as their limit; however, by means of knowledge (*vidyā*), that [ignorance] does not [exist].
When that [ignorance] has been removed, there is an opportunity for those two; therefore, the meaning is that because ignorance exists, it is to be negated. || 15 ||
Or rather, the word "vāva" is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that these two alone are determined [as such].
When combined with subsequent qualifiers that are of the same class, [the compound is called a *dvandva*]. || 16 ||

He states the purpose of the particle (*nipāta*): "for the sake of restriction" (*avadhāraṇāya*). The meaning is that the particle is used for the purpose of illuminating the certain determination that "there are only two forms of Brahman. Anticipating the objection that if two forms of Brahman are restricted [to being only these two], then the qualifiers to be mentioned later—such as "mortality" and so on—are improper because they would contradict that restriction, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "the embodied" (*mūrtaṃ ca*) etc.: "in the case of a conjunction" (*samuccite*). This implies that [the particle] contains within itself...
The meaning is that since those two alone are determined as the specific qualifiers of the *uttara*, there is no contradiction with the remainder [of the text]. || 16 ||
And by drawing back the word "vā" with the word "ca," it is expressed [as follows].
And that form of Brahman is indeed both embodied and unembodied.

[Objection: But since it is "only the formless" (*amūrtam eva*), how can the commentary (*bhāṣya*) say "and the formless" (*amūrtaṃ ca*)? For in that case, the particle *eva* (only) would not apply to the word "formless. To this, he says: "Indeed" (*vāva*). By drawing the word *vāva* toward the word "formless" in the phrase "and the formless," it is stated in the commentary that "it is indeed the formless" (*amūrtam eva*); the meaning is that this is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). He concludes the meaning of the sentence beginning with "the formed" (*mūrtaṃ ca*) by saying: "The formed" (*mūrtam*). This refers to the nature of Brahman under discussion.

The meaning is that there is no third form; one is indeed "mūrtam" (the formed), characterized by such attributes as mortality, while the other is indeed "amūrtam" (the formless), characterized by such attributes as immortality. || 17 ||
The Supreme Brahman, accompanied by ignorance, is characterized by the attributes of having form and being formless, and so forth.
It is distinguished; the mutual conjunction of phenomena is not admitted. || 18 ||

Anticipating the objection that the qualified nature belongs to the formed and the formless, while mortality, immortality, and so forth are the qualifiers—since these are taught with reference to the formed and the rest—the author says: "As [the case] of one possessed of ignorance. This means that because the others follow what is primary, and Brahman possesses that same state. He refutes the opposing view with: "No. (18)
Because dharmas are entirely dependent upon the object to be qualified, they do not [function] mutually.
Likewise, for those who are indifferent, their association might occur at some time.
In this regard, the reason is stated: "by way of distinction. The connection is that there is no mutual association. However, in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the authority...

The sense is that a subsequent (pauṣṭhikī) mutual connection among the nine qualifiers has been accepted. [An objection: "In that case, let there be such a connection here as well.
To this he says: "tathā" (so). The word "tathā" is for the purpose of drawing in the negative particle (nañ). || 19 ||
Of Brahman, the Supreme Self, who is the limit of the person consisting of consciousness.
Furthermore, there are two forms of the quality of darkness (tamas), because they are not distinct from the others.

Anticipating the objection that, even though there is no mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between them, Brahman might still be the qualified (viśeṣya) as a neutral substratum, he says: "Vijñāna... [and so on]. Regarding the statement that the two forms of the Supreme and the individual self are qualifiers, he states the reason indicated by the word "atha" (now/therefore): "tadanya... [and so on]. This means: because of the distinction from that—namely, from the Supreme which is desired as other than the Self, or from the Self which is desired as other than that Brahman.
The meaning is that [the identity] is established because of the scriptural statement regarding their origin from the same source. || 20 ||
Just as [fear arises] from imagined snakes and the like regarding a garland that is not actually known [to be such].
Whether real or unreal, there is neither exclusion nor inclusion. || 21 ||
In the same way, apart from that [unmanifest], the two [ego and intellect] are always inherently existent within Brahman.
Nor, however, are they non-different [from it]; rather, they are indeed Brahman itself, free from duality.

One might raise the objection: "Let it be that the inner Brahman (*pratyagbrahman*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and the two forms are the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*); nevertheless, because there is a distinction between the form and the bearer of the form (*rūpa-rūpin*), non-duality (*advaita*) is lost. Anticipating this, he says: "Established" (*kṛpta*). There is no real distinction or non-distinction between the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—such as a rope—and the imagined [snake] and so forth, because what is imagined cannot be a property of the unimagined; nor can those two [distinction and non-distinction] be unreal, for that would be undesirable to you. Therefore, of those...

The meaning is that because the relationship of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is impossible, Brahman possesses only the nature of a locus; thus, in reality, it does not have two forms that are distinct, for that would entail the impossibility of the relation between form and the possessor of form (*rūpa-rūpin*), nor are they non-distinct, as the same fault would apply. Anticipating the question, "What then is the status of the two forms as they appear?", he says: "But those... (verses 21–22).
The corporeal [body] consists of parts beginning with atoms; it is plump, possessed of configuration, and firm.
That which is formless would be contradictory to that [spatiality], as it possesses no parts nor occupies a location.

In the passage beginning with "mūrta ca" (and the corporeal), having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*) after first explaining the meanings of the two *ca*s as denoting both conjunction and restriction, he states the meaning of the word "mūrta":

"aṇvādi" (atoms, etc.). Having raised the objection that the definition "that which possesses parts is corporeal" would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to air (*vāyu*), he qualifies it by saying "pīna" (dense/solid). He states the meaning of the word "amūrta" (incorporeal): "tadviruddham" (the opposite of that). He clarifies precisely what is meant by being the opposite of the corporeal: "niraṃśam" (partless).

Having raised the objection that a partless whole (avayavin) might possess parts like its own components, he says: "as in the case of space" (deśavat). The sense is that even though air possesses parts, it does not manifest [its parts] in the same way as earth and the other elements do. || 23 ||
A mortal is subject to death, characterized by perishability.
That which is opposed to it is certainly not nectar, for it inevitably leads to ruin.

He states the meaning of the word *martya*: "The mortal" (*martyam*). Anticipating the objection that this [term] might not apply to the earth and so forth, he says: "That which... He states the meaning of the word *amṛta*: "The immortal" (*amṛtam*). He establishes the contradiction [between the two] by saying: "The eternal" (*dhruvam*). || 24 ||

That which is dependent remains here; having gone there, it stays without pervading it.
That which is contrary to it likewise arises in such a way that it does not remain.

He explains the passage beginning with "and [what is] situated" (*sthitaṃ ca*) by the word "dependent" (*āśritam*). The word "here" (*atra*) is a reference to the sentence. He follows the commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "preceded by going" (*gatipūrvakam*).

Regarding the word "having gone" (*gatvā*), he speaks having raised an objection concerning the mention of the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) with the word "that which" (*yat*). [He says] "that is contradictory."
It establishes the contradiction with persistence: "It comes indeed," [so it is said]. || 29 ||
That which is perceived as having a manifest form, while its specific qualifiers are not being grasped, is denoted by "sat."
That which is perceptible is called "direct," while that which is not perceptible is likewise called "indirect."

Having raised the objection that the word *sat* means "existing," he explains it with the words "It is *sat*. He clarifies the very contradiction with existence by stating "not perceptible" (*apratyakṣam*). || 26 ||
Earth, water, and likewise fire—this is called the embodied [form].
The two elements that are formless are air and space alone. || 27 ||

Having stated that the inner Brahman (pratyagbrahma), when unknown, is qualified by attributes such as "formed" (mūrta) and so forth, and having thus explained the meanings of the words, he says "Earth" (kṣitiḥ) to show that the triad of elements is directly qualified by attributes such as "formed" and so forth. The mention of "formed" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for "mortal" (martya) and the rest. He says "Elements" (bhūta) to show that the dyad of elements is directly qualified by attributes such as "formless" (amūrta) and so forth. The mention of "formless" is an elliptical indication for "immortal" (amṛta) and the rest. || 27 ||
They know the triad of earth, water, and fire to be embodied, mortal, stable, and existent.
The pair consisting of air and space is traditionally known as "formless" and "immortal. || 28 ||
He analyzes "earth" and so forth with the words "the corporeal. He elucidates "the two elements" and so forth with the words "the incorporeal. ||28||
Precisely because it possesses form, it is mortal; and precisely because it is mortal, it is subject to persistence [and decay].
Because it is stable, it can be determined as distinct by way of "this-ness" (idantā) and grasped by the senses.
He explains the relationship of cause and effect among the qualifiers, beginning with "mūrtatva" (corporeality) and so forth, starting from the very beginning: "Because of corporeality," etc. (29).
Because it possesses a specific designation, it is not all-pervasive, since it exists in some places as a single part.
And because it is stationary, it is mortal; and because it is mortal, it is indeed material.
He demonstrates this very point by beginning from their end: "Because they possess a designation" (*sopākhyatvāt*). This means: because they are objects of sensory cognition.

Even so, how is there non-pervasiveness? To that he says: "In some places. That is to say, because they exist in a limited form in a location accessible to the senses. Nor is there a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) on the grounds that although qualities such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) exist, immortality (*amartyatva*) is absent in atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like.
The meaning is: "because of the desire for dwelling. || 30 ||
Because it is formless, it is immortal; that which is all-pervading is beyond the reach of the senses.
Because it transcends the senses, it is all-pervading; and because it is all-pervading, it is therefore immortal.
He applies the aforementioned reasoning to such qualities as incorporeality and so forth. "Because of incorporeality" is the explanation of the word "yat," which may also be read as "yattu.

"Omnipresent," etc. Having stated the relationship of cause and effect beginning from "because it is formless" (*amūrtatvāt*), he begins again from "that" (*tyat*) and states that [reason]: "because it is beyond the senses" (*atīndriyatvāt*). || 31 ||
Because it is devoid of form, it is immaterial and free from the manifestation of any such shape.
The mutual connection between form and the rest occurs by way of cause and its effect. (32)
Like a rosary of beads, because their mutual capacity is not lost.
The connection even of material objects and the like, by way of being the cause and that which possesses the cause; || 33 ||
*Sthitatva* (stability) consists in being delimited, while *asthitatva* (instability) is the absence thereof; thus, the meaning is "because of its imperishability.
He concludes with an illustration regarding the relationship between corporeality (*mūrtatva*) and the others as cause and effect, stating: "hetu... [and so on]. In those cases, it is just so.

He states the reason for their fitness with the words "of capacity" (*sāmarthyasya*). He concludes the mutual connection even among [qualities] such as formlessness (*amūrtatva*) and so forth with the words "because of the cause and effect" (*hetu-phalāt*). || 32 || 33 ||
Because when even one among them occurs, there is the occurrence of all.
Therefore, for the sake of restriction, the word "only" (eva) has been employed in that very [context]. || 34 ||

He states the reason for their mutual association with the words "origination" (*saṃbhava*). Regarding the fact that when any one among the material (*mūrta*) and immaterial (*amūrta*) categories exists, the remaining three are necessarily present, he provides the proof for this with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). In that context, in the passage beginning with "the material," after mentioning only the material or only the immaterial, the use of the particle *eva* (only) is intended for the purpose of restriction; for, according to the stated principle, [the presence of] the other... of the aforementioned qualifiers [is implied].
The meaning is that in the absence of one, the other three exist. || 34 ||
Of those two that have been mentioned, the embodied one is first described.
