Primarily, it would be capable [of action] there; in that very state lies the characteristic of the formless.

He states the subject matter characterized by formlessness: "Ākāśa," etc. The term *ākāśa* refers to the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: Brahman is the cause of all; that very [Brahman] is the cause which bestows existence and manifestation upon the entity called the unmanifest. In that regard, because it is partless and not an effect, it possesses formlessness, immortality, pervasion of all effects, and transcendence; thus, these are stated as the primary characteristics of that which is formless.
This is the meaning. || 77 ||
And on earth as well, that which has been described as the defining characteristic of a physical form is preeminent.
Those situated in the interval between both possess mutually blended characteristics. || 78 ||
The characteristic would be merely secondary in the intermediate stages between the two extremes.
Likewise, the conventional usage of "formed" and "formless" is also observed there.

He states the subject matter regarding the characteristic of having a form (*mūrtalakṣaṇa*) with the words "And in earth," etc. Regarding what the status is for the four intermediate [elements], he says: "Of both," etc.

The construction is as follows: since water and the others situated between the final two—the effect and the cause—possess characteristics that are mutually mixed in terms of being both formal (*mūrta*) and formless (*amūrta*), therefore the two characteristics in them are merely secondary (*gauṇa*). If there were an absence of the usage of both [terms] for those situated in the middle, from what would its [secondary] nature arise?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "mūrta" (material), etc. The meaning is: "just as in the case of the final effect and its cause. This implies that it is so even in the case of those situated in between. || 78 || 79 ||
This is brought forth for the purpose of grasping the primary function, in order to establish the definition of pervasion.
From earth up to space, this constitutes the characteristic of the formed and the formless.

He concludes the view of Bhartṛprapañca with the words "mukhyā" (primary). The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (hence) is that the literal sense [of the opponent's position] is untenable. Because the definition of "formed" (*mūrta*) and so forth is fully present only in earth—both for the purpose of grasping the primary application and for the purpose of pervading the objects to be defined—it refers to that alone.
(Note: Variant reading *ka. 'pyapa'*).

In the sky, which is the root cause, there is the formed (mūrta), while that which is characterized as the formless (amūrta) is all-pervasive; thus, the subtle element (tanmātra) is formless, appearing here and there among the intermediate stages.
[Vol. 2, Page 712] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter.

The formed exists in the sky, the root cause, while that characterized as the formless is pervasive; thus, the subtle element is formless, appearing in some measure here and there among the intermediate stages.
The meaning is that because the moment exists, there is the state of being both [the cause and the effect]. || 80 ||
This [is so] because of the reason that it is seen in the scriptures as being in the right eye.
A certain specific distinction is desired for the right eye of the Liṅga. || 81 ||

Having stated the supreme doctrine that is to be accepted, and considering the purpose of the passage beginning with "Now, as for the formless" (*athāmūrta*) to have already been explained, he states the intended meaning of the specific mention, "This which is in the right eye" (*yo 'yaṃ dakṣiṇe 'kṣan*). He says: "This which... The meaning of the reason is: because the scripture has been seen; that is, because by means of that [scripture], the specific [nature] of the one in the right eye has been seen. || 81 ||
Therefore, such vigor as yours has not been seen anywhere else in this world.
The statement "in the right eye" is emphasized with effort because of the Vedic scripture.

The distinction there is not derived from scripture alone; rather, it is also due to inference, namely: "The subject under dispute possesses excellence because it is the right member [of the body], just like the right hand. Thus he says, "possessing vigor" (*vīryavat*). The word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) is connected here with the word "thus" (*ittham*). By that, the right eye is indicated. The ellipsis is: "Vigor is desired [for it]. Therefore, according to the statement of scripture, in comparison to the other eye, [excellence resides] in the right eye.
He says that it proceeds from afar: "The right," [verse 82].
For, through the division of the body (piṇḍa) and the vital breath (prāṇa), [this occurs] both with respect to the internal self (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaivata).
The distinction between the embodied and the unembodied aspects of the two forms of Brahman has thus been explained.
With the intention of explaining the relationship between that [individual soul] and the rest, he restates what has preceded: "The body," etc. This means "in the form of cause and effect.
The meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that although there are many intermediate limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), only two limiting adjuncts of the Supreme Lord are well-known.
"Vibhāga" means "distinction. || 83 ||
Now, however, [we shall discuss] that very same [organ], which consists of action, as it has been described.
We shall describe the form of the *liṅga*, which consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the self. (84)
He states the connection [of the following section] with the words "Now" (*atha*). This means: of that which has been described as possessing the aforementioned divisions;

[that is,] of the subtle body (*liṅga*) superimposed as the very nature of the Self—this is the ellipsis. Of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the essence of the formless, there is indeed the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of passion and so forth.
The meaning is that the statement beginning with "for what reason" (tasya hetu) is intended to express that it is not so. || 84 ||
Due to their connection with the embodied soul, the apūrṇa state, and so forth, the latent impressions (vāsanās) reside in the subtle body (liṅga).
Through the defect of the delusion of its own manifestation, the Puruṣa is considered to be composed of those [impressions]. (85)

He states the reason why that [internal organ] alone is its substratum: "mūrtā" (embodied), etc. Since the internal organ alone has a connection with all objects, such as the embodied and so forth, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and the like, caused by that [connection], spread while depending upon it alone; this is the meaning. To the question, "How then is the *puruṣa* seen to be composed of passion and the like?", he replies: "svābhāsa" (self-manifesting), etc. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is that in which there is a manifestation (*ābhāsa*) of itself; [the state] produced by that is...
The delusion that [the self] is "one possessed of passion" and so forth arises; by that defect, the person becomes composed of passion and the like—this is the meaning. || 85 ||
1. And the Deva.

2, page 713] 3. The Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śākhaprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1007.
Variegated by manifold latent impressions (vāsanā), that [mind] is like a painted canvas or a wall.
It is like a magical illusion or a conjurer's trick, a source of delusion for the self.

Now, is the mind's being constituted of latent impressions (vāsanā) superimposed or non-superimposed? Not the first, because since that [nature] exists in the person (puruṣa) as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of referring to him by that term [of "mind"]. Nor the other, because it would follow that even the substratum (dharmin) would possess a non-superimposed form. To this he says: "aneka... [and so on].

He qualifies [the self] with the word "vyāmoha" in order to clarify the connection of the self with latent impressions, which was mentioned in the passage beginning with "svābhāsa... [verse 85]. || 86 ||
Where those devoid of scripture are deluded, thinking that this alone is the full extent [of reality].
The Buddhist Vijñānavādins as well as the Naiyāyikas and others [hold this view]. (87)

Clarifying that the very locus of one’s own delusion is the *liṅga* (the subtle body), he states the delusion of the Vijñānavādins with the words "only this much. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows:

we shall describe the nature of that in which they are deluded—the view that the Self is nothing other than mere cognition (*buddhi*) characterized by the mental modification of "I" (*ahaṃ-vṛtti*), which is naturally fragile and defiled by passion and so forth, and which is neither a permanent nor a momentary entity. Regarding their such delusion:
He states the reason: "those who lack scripture. By saying "likewise," he indicates that even among logicians there is delusion, just as among Buddhists. || 87 ||
This which consists of latent impressions belongs to the self as a substantial entity.
The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that form (rūpa) is its quality and that this is transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). || 88 ||

He reveals their delusion with the words "of the self" (ātmanaḥ). The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which is grasped by the notion of "I," possesses attributes such as passion (*rāga*), and so forth—is the self.

Of that substance, its form consists of the impressions (*vāsanā*) [of those attributes], and that is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). The connection [of the sentence] is as before: we shall describe the nature of that [self] regarding which they are deluded. || 88 ||
The Pradhāna, consisting of the three guṇas, exists for the sake of the Puruṣa as its purpose.
The followers of Kapila (the Sāṃkhyas) also maintain that "this existent [principle] proceeds independently.

[The author] states the error of the Sāṃkhyas: "consisting of the three guṇas," etc. It is not the internal organ alone that is the Self; rather, the Self is something else—omnipresent, devoid of all activity, and self-luminous. For the sake of that [Self's] experience and liberation, the primary cause consisting of the three guṇas is postulated; that is the Self...

The connection is as follows: we shall describe the nature of that [object] regarding which you are deluded—that the internal organ, not remaining [as it is], proceeds with properties similar to those [objects]. || 89 ||
Even some who consider themselves experts in the Upaniṣads, due to their extreme proficiency, [may fall into error].
Having constructed this process, those who are unskilled in the meaning of Vedānta say thus. || 90 ||

Having stated his own view—that "that wherein the various delusions of the wise arise is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and not the Self"—he introduces the system of Bhartṛprapañca with the words "Moreover" (*api*) and so forth. [He argues that] because they lack knowledge regarding the reality intended by the purport of the Vedānta, those who call themselves followers of the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣada*) are not truly so; nevertheless, out of mere self-conceit, they measure the Self—which is the subject of the Upaniṣads—by means of their own imagination.
The construction is as follows: having devised some procedure devoid of reasoning, they assert the consistency of that [procedure] with the reasons and so forth. || 90 ||
Whatever external modification there may be that surrounds the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), [that is the field].

Whether with respect to the internal (adhyātma) or the divine (adhidaiva), [this occurs] through the differentiation of name and form. 99.1 (Note: The variants provided indicate that the reading *tattvam* is found in manuscripts kha and ga, while *atra evam* is found in manuscript ka; furthermore, manuscript kha reads *yadvaita*.)
In this context, that which is both unmanifest and manifest is indeed only this much, according to Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter.
Whether it be embodied or formless, it is called "being" (sat) and "non-being" (tyat). || 92 ||

Anticipating the doubt as to what the process [of creation] is like or how its connection [to the preceding] is established, and intending to state that the process will be explained later, the meaning of the commentary— which serves to establish the connection— is as follows: whatever modification of *māyā* there is that envelops the *vijñānātman*, whether pertaining to the internal self (*adhyātma*) or the divine realm (*adhidaiva*), and which has been differentiated through the division of name and form— all this, whether it be manifest (*mūrta*) or unmanifest (*amūrta*), is the subject matter of the explanatory restatement of its nature as "the existent" (*sat*) and "the non-existent" (*tyat*).

He says: "The journey," and so forth. The meaning is that as long as the individual soul (jīva) exists as a limiting adjunct (upādhi), everything born from the unmanifest (avyākṛta) is just this much—namely, that which was previously described in the preceding text by the word "Real" (satya), consisting of the five elements, and explained as both the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta).
The reality of the vital breaths also arises from their connection with the reality of the elements.
How is it that all these vital breaths are characterized by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)? || 93 ||
Being devoid of name and form, they exist by virtue of the cause that is the conjunction with reality.
The embodied beings, possessing name and form, became manifest as if they were their very vital breaths.
And their lives are fit for being commanded; it cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, in this matter, everything has been clearly and thoroughly purified by means of the sacred revelation (Śruti). || 95 ||

Having raised the objection, "If the elements (bhūtas) are indeed real (satya), how is it said that 'the vital breaths (prāṇas) are real'?", he states the meaning of the commentary— that the prāṇas are real because of their connection with them— beginning with the words "of the prāṇas. [The prāṇas are real] by virtue of being effects together with the elements denoted by the word "real," which serve as their causes.

The meaning is that because of the relationship of identity (*tādātmya*), these [prāṇas] also possess reality; therefore, the Vedic scripture stating "the prāṇas are indeed reality" is not contradictory. To demonstrate this very point, he states the inquiry found in the commentary: "How so? It is not only their reality that depends on such a relationship; rather, wishing to show that even the names and so forth residing in them [depend on it], he says: "In that regard, the prāṇas are the conscious selves (*vijñānātman*) which are devoid of name and form; they are conjoined with another..."

He provides the answer in the Bhāṣya: "But because... (yatastviti). All eleven vital breaths (*prāṇas*), like the principal one, are adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*); although they are by nature devoid of name and so forth, through their association with the real [elements], they become as if possessed of effects and instruments, endowed with names and forms, and thus they are directly fit for designation.

And by the very logic previously stated, the scriptural passage "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed truth" is established as true; it is not appropriate to interpret it otherwise, because they [the vital breaths] are inherently free from sublation—this is the meaning. Thinking that this truth has been thoroughly purified, he concludes the restatement of what was previously told by connecting [the text]: "That here... In the phrase "the truth of truth," everything denoted by the word "truth" in the genitive case is [referred to] by "tasya ha" (of that).
Therefore, the meaning is that it has been correctly demonstrated by the preceding scripture. || 93 || 94 || 95 ||
But for one whose mass of truths has been dispelled, it belongs indeed to the self consisting of consciousness alone.
That which is its own essential nature remains now to be explained. || 96 ||
Desiring to introduce the subsequent statement, he provides a transitional summary (*pātanikā*), extracting the nature of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) from [the category of] reality (*satya*).
1. Variant *kha*: "by them";
He states the meaning of the phrase "it must be explained" with the words "vyāviddhā" (devoid of). Whatever form there may be for that which is excluded from the aforementioned mass of reality—
The meaning is that it remains as something to be expressed by two [words]. || 96 ||
In this state, differentiation ceases.
This experiencer is the conscious self, and likewise are these deities. 97.
The phrase "having consciousness as their self" [is used] because of the cessation of the cause of differentiation.
For this [world], characterized by name, form, and so forth, has that as its substratum. || 98 ||
There is no distinction from its own nature, and that name, form, and so forth have been purified.
Having purified all this, the conscious self (vijñānātman) is revealed. || 99 ||

In this context, while explaining the commentary’s statement that “in this state there is no distinction such as ‘this one is the enjoyer’ or ‘these are the conscious selves (vijñānātman) and the vital breaths (prāṇas),” he states the result of extracting the true aggregate from the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). He says: “In that [state]”; the meaning is that when the knower of the field remains in the state characterized by the exclusion of the true aggregate, there is the cessation of division. He describes the division appropriate for that:

He leads. "This" refers to the deities—the speech and other organs presided over by deities, which are essentially consciousness (*vijñānātman*) and have those [deities] as their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). He states the reason for the cessation of differentiation with the word "bhedeti. He establishes this reason with the commentary: "For this distinction, consisting of name and form, resides in the substratum.
He restates the meaning of the word "yataḥ" found in the commentary with the words "yataḥ," [referring to] all experience of past and future...
The meaning is that because [the self] is reached through three limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it does not exist in itself; and by the removal of those [adjuncts], the aforementioned division ceases.

Having prepared the ground, the commentary introduces the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) with the words: "Having purified all this here as truth, and having entered within, the *vijñānātman* (the conscious self) is pointed out. [This is followed by the verse: "having purified... (vv. 97, 98, 99).
Therefore, this characteristic would be common to all of them as well.
For in this case, no distinction among the knowers of the field (kṣetrajña) can possibly be established. || 100 ||

He states the meaning of this: that all of this constitutes the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the conscious selves (*vijñānātman*). He says "of all" (*sarveṣām*). To clarify what was stated by the word "thereby" (*tena*), he says: "the distinction (*viśeṣa*) is here. The meaning is that the form which is described here as being excluded from the aggregate of the real (*satya-rāśi*) is common to all living beings, because there is no cause for any distinction [among them]. || 100 ||
Now, the form of this person is being pointed out.
The form of the person (puṃs), which is the substratum of both the formed and the formless, has been exhausted.

The commentary (*bhāṣya*) is intended to explain the sentence, "The form of this very person, whose self is consciousness (*vijñānātman*), is now being described. It states its meaning as follows: with the words "of this" (*etasya*). One might object: "When the form of the Supreme Self (*parātman*) is to be stated, the presentation of the form of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) is like an untimely dance. Anticipating this, he states the meaning of the phrase "all form is exhausted in the fundamental embodied [form]" with the words "of the person" (*puṃsaḥ*). There are indeed two...
The meaning is that by these and other such words, the nature of the "other" (the opponent) has been stated. || 101 ||
But by whatever specific quality its nature as consciousness is asserted, [that same quality must belong to the Self].
While it is being differentiated from the supreme Self, which is non-dual. || 102 ||

In this context, that form which is beyond the five elements is what is intended to be indicated by those [words].
The word "yathā" (as) refers to *māhārajana*, which consists of the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 103 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-different from the Supreme, that [nature] has already been stated, the author says "by which" to explain the meaning of the phrase "non-material" (*apāñcabhautika*), which intends to point out that specific form by which the Supreme Self, when being delimited, attains the state of being the conscious self (*vijñānātman*).
Anticipating the question of what kind of nature is here described— which is not driven by the elements and is common to all living beings— the author cites a scriptural illustration.

Regarding the phrase "yatheti": the meaning is that by this sentence, it is intended to indicate in the Śruti a form common to all living beings, consisting of a collection of various passions and so forth, like a cloth colored with turmeric and other dyes. || 102 || 103 ||
Regarding this very [subject], some explain the connection as follows.
Therefore, this which is being stated is improper, for it is as illogical as any other [absurdity]. || 104 ||

He summarizes the relationship stated by Bhartṛprapañca with the words "tasya" (of that). He refutes it with the words "tadayuktam" (that is improper). Anticipating the question, "How is the statement of the opponent's relationship devoid of logic? he says "yathā" (just as). The meaning is: "Just as that relationship is devoid of logic, so too is this established conclusion (siddhānta) being stated; listen with attention. || 104 ||
For the perfumes of flowers and the like adhere only to things such as clothing.
It is observed to be restricted to those of its own kind, and not to other kinds. || 105 ||

Regarding the claim that the individual form (*jaiva-rūpa*) consists of the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one must consider the following alternative: is the individual soul (*jīva*) of a different genus from the cloth and other objects which serve as the causes for those impressions, or is it of the same genus? In the first case, its connection with them cannot be established; thus he says: "puṣpādī" (flowers, etc.).
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that perception is a conventional means of valid knowledge (*vyāvahārika-pramāṇa*). || 109 ||
Indeed, no latent impression whatsoever is observed even in a substance, such as space.
And how could there be a latent impression (vāsanā) in consciousness, which is neither a substance nor of a similar class? || 106 ||

The second [alternative] is not tenable; for even if there were a commonality of genus (*sājātya*), a connection with that [genus] is unestablished because, like space (*vyoma*), it is unattached (*asaṅga*). Thus he says: "Even in the case of a substance" (*dravye’pi*). Furthermore, neither a higher nor a lower genus exists in the Self, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); since its very commonality of genus is unestablished, there can be no latent impression (*vāsanā*) therein. Thus he says: "And in the case of a non-substance" (*adravye ca*). || 106 ||
If consciousness were to assume the form of latent impressions, it would be like a skull.
The latent impressions would be fruitless, because they do not exist apart from consciousness.

Furthermore, having raised the dilemma as to whether the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is non-different or different from the Self, [the author] refutes the first alternative by stating: "The latent impression... If the Self assumes the form of the latent impression—just as clay assumes the form of a jar or the like—then, because that impression exists without distinction from consciousness (*caitanya*), it cannot be a differentiator of the Self; for the Self itself does not bring about its own differentiation from something else.
Because the latent impressions would otherwise be rendered purposeless, that [identification] is not the self; such is the meaning. || 107 ||
For consciousness arising from the auditory faculty is not perfumed by the latent impression of form.
Even though there is no difference in their status as objects, [the mind is not affected] because consciousness is unattached. || 108 ||

In the second case, however, is that [activity] unconnected with the Self or connected? If the former, considering it to be futile, another alternative is rejected.

[The text] says: "No, for... The meaning is as follows: knowledge of sound produced by the sense organ of hearing is not perfumed by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of form; even though there is no distinction between those two in terms of being objects [of cognition], they lack the mutual relationship of object and subject. Furthermore, because consciousness (*cit*) is unattached (*asaṅga*), it does not possess the status of an object at all; thus, there is no connection with the latent impressions of passion and so forth. || 108 ||
And there is the negation of the six modifications of existence for the conscious self.
Furthermore, the expression "unattached" is heard repeatedly in the Śruti.

He states that because consciousness (*cit*) is immutable, there can be no latent impression (*vāsanā*). He says "six" [referring to the six sheaths]. To establish that it is not an object due to its non-attachment, he cites the authority for the first [point] with the words "and 'unattached'. In that regard, he uses the term "repeatedly" to show the repetition found in scripture, which serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the scripture's intended meaning (*tātparya*). || 109 ||
That which is obtained through the conjunction of the elements is not itself composed of the five elements.
Speaking thus, one is laughed at even by children in this world. (110)
Having discarded the latent impression (vāsanā) regarding the self, he refutes the claim made by others that its nature is non-material (apāñcabhautika), stating: "The elements...
In the division between the formed and the formless, his own division ceases.
Thus, not forgetting what you yourself have said, how can there be talk of a distinction between latent impressions?

Regarding the claim that the individual soul (jīva) acquires its state as a limited entity from the Supreme through latent impressions (vāsanā), he replies with the verse beginning "mūrta" (the embodied).

He does not forget what was stated by the opponents in this context—that upon the discernment of the individual soul, which consists of both [the real and the unreal], the distinction between the enjoyer and so forth is destroyed;

therefore, to speak of the soul's differentiation from the Supreme and from other selves due to latent impressions is incorrect, because the distinction between the enjoyer and so forth [would have been eliminated].
Since those [means] would also be destroyed upon the destruction [of the object], the meaning is that there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. || 111 ||
In that same way, they compose an improper method devoid of logic.
It is indeed held that there is one external aggregate consisting of both the formed and the formless. (112)

Having refuted the connection stated by others beginning with the words "of that" (*tasya*), he introduces his own method of analysis (*prakriyā*) which was indicated in the phrase "having composed the method. He says, "They compose," meaning "possessing the aforementioned connection. The word *asādhvīm* (ungrammatical/incorrect) is the division [of the compound]. The reason for this is given: "by logic" (*nyāya*). Stating the conceptualization of three heaps, he first mentions the debtor heap (*adhamarāśi*). He says, "embodied" (*mūrta*), etc., regarding that conceptualization.
The word "kila" is used, it is said, for the purpose of indicating that this is outside the scope of the Vedas. || 112 ||
1. Here, the supreme heap called the Paramātman (Supreme Self) is designated.
This third group, however, is intermediate and is the motivator for those two.

He describes the "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭa*) heap as "the highest" (*uttama*). Here, the meaning is that it is either the best among the heaps or the first of the two, and so forth. He states another heap: "the middling" (*madhyama*). As they have said: "These three things are the formed (*mūrta*), the formless (*amūrta*), and the essence of the self (*ātmatattva*) such as saffron-dye and the like. He states the specific characteristic of the middling heap: "the motivator" (*prayojaka*). ||113||

1012. By this agent and enjoyer, the Self, who has arisen from the clapping of hands, the aggregate consisting of volition, knowledge, action, and so forth, acts as the motivator. (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika, Second Chapter)
In response to the inquiry "What is this?", he says: "The hands," etc. The word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to objects such as passion and so forth. || 114 ||
The aggregate of the formed, the formless, and so forth, as well as the means of accomplishment, should be employed accordingly.
They seek to make peace with the logicians according to their strength.

The state of being a prompter (*prayojakatva*) is the state of being a producer; since that cannot exist without an object, he states the object [in the verse] beginning with "embodied" (*mūrta*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the mention of the mortal, the immortal, and so forth. He further states that the means (*sādhana*)—the collection of causes consisting of knowledge and action, as well as the aggregate of effects and instruments—is also that which is prompted, [in the verse] beginning with "the means" (*sādhana*). As they have said: "This very thing, consisting of knowledge, action, and prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*), is the external, embodied and unembodied aspect of this action."

He says "by the logicians" (tārkikaiḥ), meaning that they formulate another conceptualization after having postulated a triad [of agent, instrument, and object], based upon which the accomplishment of enjoyment occurs for one who possesses the instruments of action. || 115 ||
This instigator has indeed resorted to the very characteristics of the zodiacal signs.
Having said this, out of fear of being classified as Sāṃkhya, they then imagine it otherwise.

He elaborates on that very point with the words "this" (*ayam*). First, there is the motivating aggregate (*prayojaka-rāśi*) consisting of action and so forth, which rests upon the *liṅga* (the subtle body);

the word "it is said" (*kila*) is used to indicate that this is [merely] his own accepted position. If it is argued that since this [aggregate] resides within the intellect (*buddhi*), it belongs to the Sāṃkhya school, then the meaning is that, out of fear of that [consequence], he conceives of it otherwise because of its association with that [intellect]. || 116 ||
Just as fragrance, which resides in a flower, persists by depending upon that nourished [flower].
In the same way, even when the flower has disappeared, the latent impression (vāsanā) remains in the self as its characteristic mark.
To explain how this is so, he says: "Fragrance," etc. (117).
Latent impressions, desires, and karmas reside only in the subtle body (liṅga), not in the Self.
They approach the Self by means of the indicative mark, just as fragrance [indicates] a vessel of perfume. || 118 ||

Raising the objection as to what proof there is for the claim that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) acquired during the state of being a *liṅga* persists in the self even when that *liṅga* has disappeared, [the author] considers the statement of others—that just as with the contact of a flower and oil, that impression exists even when separated from the mind, and it is by means of that [impression] that the differentiation of effects occurs through the mind—to be the proof here; thus he says: "The impression... (verse 118).
Although devoid of qualities, he is a portion of the Supreme, having arrived from the outside.
They declare that through action, he becomes manifest with his attributes.

Anticipating the objection, "How can there be latent impressions (vāsanā) and so forth in the Self which is devoid of qualities?", he says: "Even though it is without qualities. The meaning is that although the Self is directly devoid of qualities, it becomes as if possessed of qualities through karma and other factors acquired in the proximity of the body and organs from the collection of external forms and the like. || 119 ||
And from that, one becomes the agent and the enjoyer, and is likewise bound and liberated.

Those who rely on this doctrine praised by Kaṇabhuj [the Vaiśeṣikas] maintain that the self is consciousness; it is the agent and the enjoyer. [120.1] [Note: 1. ka. ga. read *kartā bhoktā sarvaḥ*; 2. sa. reads *rūpasya*;
3. reads *kāra*.]

Having explained the commentary beginning with "That [Self] is indeed a part of the Supreme Self," he now explains the passage beginning with "He is the agent" and so forth, starting with the words "Then... (tataḥ). || 120 ||
The sign of the aggregate of elements is derived from the presence of the aggregate of karma.
From the *liṅga*, he attained the Self; that is, from the cause of connection with the *liṅga*. || 121 ||

Anticipating the question of how the causal aggregate (prayojakarāśi), having entered the subtle body (liṅga), comes to reside within the self (ātman) by what sequence, he says: "of the aggregate of elements" (bhūtarāśeḥ).
The meaning is that the aggregate of karma, having entered the subtle body from the aggregate of elements, has then entered the self because of its identity with the subtle body. || 121 ||
Even ignorance, which is the power of Kṛṣṇa, has arisen from the Supreme alone.
Having transformed a portion of the Supreme Self, it abides within the individual self (vijñānātman).

He states another system of others, following the very mindset of the logicians, beginning with the word "Kṛṣṇā. The meaning is that he follows the view that the individual soul (jīva) is ignorant, according to one who asserts that the Lord’s power, though innate ignorance, having become manifest from Him alone, modifies a portion of Him and resides in that very soul. || 122 ||
Just as a defect consisting of impurity arises from the earth itself.
Just as a portion of the earth remains after being transformed [into something else], so it is with the Supreme Self in relation to ignorance.

Anticipating the objection that if ignorance arises from another [the Supreme Self], it would reside in that alone and not in the individual soul (jīva)—since an effect cannot exist elsewhere apart from its cause—he says: "Just as... (verse 123).
Those who assert that ignorance is a phenomenon devoid of self-nature are like those who speak of barren soil and the like.
Thus, out of delusion, they follow the tenets of the Sāṃkhya school.

It was previously stated that [the opponent] follows the Sāṃkhya system by asserting that the causal aggregate (*prayojakarāśi*) is dependent upon a mark (*liṅga*); now, it is stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not a property of the Self (*anātmadharma*). He says: "Not-Self" (*anātma*). Just as rust and so forth are properties of a specific portion of the earth and not a property of the entire earth, so too is ignorance.

The meaning is that those who say, "This is not the dharma of another," follow the Sāṃkhya system because they lack the discrimination between their own position and that of others, [claiming] that knowledge and ignorance are not attributes of the Self (*anātmadharman*). The form *anuvartante* is a Vedic (archaic) usage. Now, one might ask: how can those following the logicians (Tārkikas) follow the Sāṃkhya, which is contrary to them? To this he says: "Out of delusion" (*saṃbhramāt*). || 124 ||
It is not proper to conceive in this way, because it contradicts the established tenets of the Veda.
Moreover, this has been stated previously regarding the sublation of the Vedānta.

He responds to the claim that ignorance (avidyā) resides in the individual soul (jīva), which is a part of the Supreme Transformation (paravikāra), by stating "not so. He provides the reason for this by citing the contradiction with scriptural passages such as "neither coarse" (asthūla). Furthermore, even in the *Bṛhad-vicāra*, the relationship between the individual soul and the Lord as part and whole (aṃśāśitva) and so forth has been refuted due to its contradiction with scripture.
It establishes the reason: "even previously," [as stated in verse] 125.
If the Supreme were possessed of parts, then the characteristics such as being subject to transmigratory existence and so forth would be attributed to it.
All defects, indeed, converge upon the solitary inner self.
He clarifies that very point: "In the state of being possessed of all parts" (sakalatva). || 126 ||
And in the case of the identification of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) with the Supreme Self, it occurs spontaneously.
The absolute impossibility of oneness between the individual soul (kṣetrajña) and the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 127 ||

The individual soul (jīva) is neither a part nor a modification of the Supreme; rather, it is a distinct entity from Him. Thus, one might suspect that states such as transmigratory existence and being subject to wounds would not manifest in the Supreme. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the knower of the field" (kṣetrajñasya). The connection is with the phrase "in absolute identity" (atyantasaṃbhitau).
The meaning is that, in that case, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural texts as the *Tattvamasi* (That thou art). || 127 ||
Now, by way of metaphorical designation, the very characteristic mark (liṅga) is considered the location of the self.
At that time, when the mark (liṅga) has been destroyed, it is not logical for latent impressions (vāsanā) to persist in the self. || 128 ||

He raises an objection: "The supreme part (*parāṃśa*), having the subtle body (*liṅga*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), is the Self. [This begins with] "Now" (*atha*). "By way of metaphor" (*upacārataḥ*) means by way of conceptual construction (*kalpanayā*). The meaning is that the Self is the supreme part which has that subtle body as its adjunct. He refutes this: "No. If it is said that the individual self (*jīvātman*) is the supreme part imagined through the limiting adjunct of the subtle body, then in states such as deep sleep, when the subtle body has dissolved, there would be no latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the Self; for in the absence of the subtle body, the individual self—which is dependent upon it—would also be absent, and consequently, those [impressions]...
The meaning is that even in the state of yoga, the latent impression (vāsanā) remains in the individual soul (jīva); thus is established the process [of its persistence]. || 128 ||
The reasoning that was previously set forth regarding the basis of latent impressions (vāsanā).
All of that should be connected here for the purpose of refuting the prima facie argument.

Fearing that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) might reside not in the conditioned self, but rather in the supreme Self which is like a reflection, he recalls what has been stated by saying "the principle" (*nyāya*).

In this context, the principle regarding the substratum of impressions— which was stated in the passage beginning with "for [impressions] such as those of flowers," namely the impossibility of homogeneity (*sājātya*) and so forth— must all be followed here for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that the inner self (*pratīc*) is their locus.
This is the meaning. || 129 ||
Furthermore, the arising of ignorance is neither from the supreme Self nor from itself.
The conceptualization beginning with "like saline soil" and so forth is not tenable. || 130 ||

Having refuted the relationship of part and whole between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), he now refutes the arising of ignorance from the Supreme. Regarding the phrase "and its arising":
by the word "etc. (ādi), conceptualizations such as ignorance having the individual soul as its locus are included. || 130 ||
If ignorance were inherent in the Supreme Self, there would be the consequence of no liberation.
And in this world, attachment to the doctrine of selflessness leads to the destruction of delusion. || 131 ||

He clarifies the impossibility [of liberation] with the words "anirmokṣa" (no liberation). If ignorance were produced from another [entity], then that [other entity] alone would be subject to saṃsāra, because the two [ignorance and saṃsāra] would have a common locus.

Consequently, as long as ignorance exists, there is no liberation; nor is there liberation when it has been destroyed, because an effect cannot be absolutely destroyed while its cause remains. Thus, upon the destruction of the effect—ignorance—the cause must perish; and in that case, since the one seeking liberation would no longer exist, liberation itself would be unestablished.
This is the meaning. || 131 ||
Nor is it accepted that the latent impression exists apart from the locus of the impression itself.
Departing for another country results from the avoidance of virtuous substances. || 132 ||
Regarding the claim that even when the *liṅga* has departed, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) residing therein remains in the Self, he says: "The impression... [vol2, page 721]. The impression—
The example is that of a person arriving from another country. Regarding the term "possessing qualities" (*guṇavat*): for a quality cannot exist independently by abandoning its substance;
even in a flower-basket, because the parts of the flower persist, there is no transgression of the property by the property-bearer. This is the meaning. || 132 ||
They proceed with consistency, and even the very syllables of the Veda do not contradict them.
For since that [other] conceptualization is not tenable within the conceptualization already described, that [second] conceptualization is not logical. (133)

He states another reason for the fact that the self is not the locus of latent impressions (*vāsanā*): "In a consistent manner" (*sāmañjasyena*). This means: in the aforementioned conceptualization, that is, in the conceptualization of the self as the locus of latent impressions. He states the consequence of the contradiction with scripture and reasoning: "No" (*na*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) reiterates the aforementioned contradiction. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "of the self being the locus of latent impressions. || 133 ||
Desire, volition, and so forth are heard in scripture as the attributes of the mind, which is their substratum.
But the phenomena do not belong to the self, for in the scripture it is stated that "non-attachment indeed [is the means of liberation]. (134)

In that regard, he cites scriptural passages, beginning with "Desire. Anticipating the objection that the Self, like the mind, might possess the status of a substrate (dharmin), he says, "But not [so]. The reason for this is stated: "For in the scripture... The word *hi* found in the Vedic text is carried over by the word *hi* here; its meaning is expressed by the fifth case ending (*pañcamyā*). || 134 ||
For it is said: "In the heart alone one meditates, as it were, upon forms," and another [scriptural passage] likewise.
"Desires [are those] which are in his heart," and so forth; likewise, there is the statement, "For he has crossed over. (135)

And because of the restrictive hearing [of the text], he says that desire is not a property of the Self: "For in the heart... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.1]. Then, as to how there is the perception of properties in the Self, he says: "It meditates, as it were... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7]. Regarding the fact that desire and so forth belong to the mind alone, he cites another passage: "Desires... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7]. And regarding the point that they do not belong to the Self, he cites yet another passage: "He has crossed over... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22]. || 135 ||
For there is no meaning other than that which is heard from the words as they have been spoken.
It can be correctly conceptualized; therefore, [a conceptualization that is otherwise] is not tenable. || 136 ||

Fearing the objection that the Self alone is denoted by words such as "mind" (manas) and "heart" (hṛdaya) found in the cited scriptural passages—and that what is intended here is simply the arising of desire and so forth in the Self due to its conjunction with that mind—the author says: "From what has been heard," etc. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "of the Self's being the locus of desire and so forth. (136)
This entire Upaniṣad is for the purpose of establishing the nature of the innermost Brahman.
Because the Vedāntas reach their conclusion by having that alone as their ultimate purpose. || 137 ||

He states the reason for the claim that no meaning other than what is heard in the stated scriptures (śrutis) should be postulated: "The inner self" (*pratyak*), etc. Having raised the doubt as to how the stated scriptures can have the nature of being subordinate to the fact that the inner self is Brahman, he says: "Only that much," etc. To begin with, the Vedāntas are one—

Therefore, since the unity of Brahman is established in accordance with the six marks [of inference], the intended meaning of the aforementioned scriptural passages situated therein also culminates in that very point; thus, there is no need to postulate any other meaning. || 137 ||
Furthermore, even in the view that there are three aggregates, no meaning here is logically consistent.
By which a conceptual construction is made that contradicts all principles of logic. || 138 ||

Even though the gender-distinction is absent in the case of the person (*pums*), having refuted the existence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he now refutes the conceptualization of the three aggregates (*rāśitraya*).
[Vol. 2, page 722] 2016 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]...
'The two heaps'—here, this is a statement introducing the presentation of forms. The word *artha* signifies the word *eva* (only/indeed).

By the word *ca* (and), the lack of consistency regarding the restriction (*avadhāraṇā*) in the phrase "and indeed the formed" is understood. By the word *api* (also), the impossibility of applying the restriction drawn by the particle *ca* in the phrase "and the formless" is understood."

He states that one should not assume a triad of groups because it lacks conformity with the literal words of the scripture: "It is done," etc. The negative particle (*nañ*) found in the first half-verse is connected here as well. He provides the reason why this assumption—which he will describe as contrary to many principles—should not be made: "By which," etc. (138).
But when there are only two forms—the formed and the formless, together with their latent impressions—then [the state of liberation occurs].
And then it is joined with the third, which has the form of Brahman; thus it is said. || 139 ||
For you, it is precisely the cognizing self (vijñānātman), which constitutes a single part of Brahman, that [is the object of knowledge].
"In form"—this statement is then appropriate, as it conforms to conceptual construction. (140)
He states how there is consistency with the word "verily" (*vāva*) and so forth even in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Two.

Having raised the doubt as to how there is no contradiction with various principles in the view of three groups, he considers the alternative—whether the individual soul (*jīva*) is included among the forms or among those possessing form—and, regarding the first case, considering it falls within the category of things to be negated, he teaches the scripture regarding the second case: "Brahman. At that time, [the soul is] among those possessing form.
That is to say, in the case of the conceptualization of the inclusion of the individual soul (jīva). || 139 || 140 ||
Now, whether by way of the nature of consciousness or by way of the supreme self;
If the conceptualization were based on direct audition (śruti), he would have said "in form" (rūpe) at that time. || 141 ||

Alternatively, if the conception of three groups were based on direct scriptural statement (śruti), or if the individual soul (jīva) were included among those possessing form, then the scripture would have stated "the form of the other" by means of that [soul]; thus he says: "The self of consciousness" (vijñānātman). || 141 ||
Furthermore, the statement "and [the reason] has two forms" is likewise incorrect, because here the three characteristics [of a valid reason] are possible.
There are two forms, the embodied and the unembodied, since the third is the latent impression (vāsanā).

Let it be granted that, according to the scriptural passage beginning with "two indeed," there is this instruction regarding the entry of the individual soul (*jīva*) into the midst of form; what is the harm in that?

To this he replies: "And because of the dual number. If the soul were included within the aggregate of forms, then the dual number in the word "two" (*dve*), the restrictive particle "indeed" (*vāva*), and the emphatic particle "only" (*eva*) would be inappropriate, since a threefold nature is possible within the midst of form. He clarifies this threefold nature:
"Embodied," [it is said]. || 142 ||
Brahman is always intended to exist in both embodied and incorporeal forms.
But for the field, it is not characterized merely by the form of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 143 ||
He raises the objection that there is no contradiction with the dual number and so forth due to the difference in the objects [of the senses], stating: "It is held... (143).
Even then, the All-pervading Lord undergoes modification through the medium of the individual soul (jīva).
The statement that there is a connection with latent impressions (vāsanā) and so forth is a meaningless utterance. 144.

In such an arrangement, the statement that the form of the Supreme Being, as it undergoes modification through the medium of the individual soul (jīva), consists of the "formed and the formless" (mūrtāmūrte), would be improper; for even latent impressions (vāsanā), karma, and so forth, are present there through that same medium.
To this he says: "Even then... (tadāpi). || 144 ||
For even among latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is not the slightest distinction whatsoever.
Since the field-knower (kṣetrajña) is beyond the three states, therefore it is non-existent [as such] when conceptualized.

To the question, "How can there be an attachment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) to the Supreme through the medium of the individual soul (*jīva*? he replies with the words "of the latent impressions. The ellipsis to be supplied is "the distinction [is made] by way of the forms of the embodied and the unembodied. He states the conclusion: that to establish a distinction—namely, that those two forms belong to the Supreme which undergoes modification through the medium of the *jīva*, whereas the form of the latent impressions belongs to the *jīva* itself—is merely a confusion out of place. Furthermore, it is not...

The sense is that it must be stated that the two forms of the other [the Lord] exist even without being the door to the individual soul (jīva), because the same contingency would apply to the form consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) as well. || 145 ||
And an entity is not directly transformed into another entity.
It can be said that even in this world, [the word "Brahman"] is used here in its primary sense (mukhyā vṛtti). // 146 //

Let it be then that even the form consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) belongs to the Supreme Self as transformed into the individual soul (jīvātman). Anticipating this objection, he says: "The thing" (vastu). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in this world, everywhere, it cannot be said that a thing is actually transformed into another thing. The word *añjasā* is explained by the phrase "in its primary sense" (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*). For such [a transformation] does not exist.
It transforms due to contradiction, not otherwise, because [otherwise] there would be no stability; this is the intended meaning. || 146 ||
Nor is this knower of the field (kṣetrajña) other than the supreme self (paramātman).
And in such a conceptualization, there would certainly be a loss of one's own established tenet. || 147 ||

Furthermore, regarding whether the individual soul (jīva) is absolutely or non-absolutely a different entity from Brahman: he states that it is not the first case, because it would result in a contradiction with one's own established doctrine (*aparāddhānta*). He says, "a different entity. The meaning is also that the second case is refuted by the rejection of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*). || 147 ||
Therefore, by those great-souled ones desiring to reveal the meaning of the Vedānta, [this work was composed].
Such a conception is improper to entertain for those who seek the welfare of others. || 148 ||

He concludes the refutation of Bhartṛprapañca with the words "by those desiring to investigate thoroughly. The meaning is: "of this kind" refers to the triad of aggregates, the soul's being the locus of desire and so forth, and so on. The word "ayuktā" (untenable) is to be supplied as the predicate. || 148 ||
In the phrase "a male in the right eye," the self consisting of the subtle body (liṅgātman) is intended.
1:332 Because that very [subject] is the topic under discussion, [the terms] "with respect to the internal self" (adhyātma) and "with respect to the divine" (adhidaiva) [are used]. || 149 ||

Having refuted the connection and the method of interpretation belonging to that [opponent] regarding the passage beginning with "His" (*tasya*), he states the meaning of the word *tat* according to his own view:

"In the right eye" (*dakṣiṇe 'kṣan*). In the phrase "Of him indeed" (*tasya ha*), the word *tat* refers to the subtle body (*liṅga*). Thus, "this which is in the right eye" refers to the internal (spiritual) realm.

The meaning is that because "this which" (*ya eṣa*) refers to the divine realm (*adhidaiva*), the word *tat* (that) relies upon what has been previously mentioned, as it is that very subject under discussion. Furthermore, the word *atha* is a synonym for the word *tathā*. || 149 ||
"Let there be the grasping of the individual soul (jīva) here, since there is no difference in its being the subject under discussion."
Why is it not said that these are the very forms of that [Self]? Let this be explained. (150)

Since the subject under discussion is the grasping of the marks (liṅga), and because the individual soul (jīva) is likewise present in the passage concerning the trembling of the hand, it follows that the soul alone would be grasped here by the word "that" (tat).
1. 'tāyāṃ syā | 2 ka. tataḥ | [vol2, page 724]

He raises the objection: "Let it be so. [The author] replies with the word "jīva" (the living self). Even though that [self] is the subject under discussion, he says "tasya" (of that) because, although it is the topic at hand, it does not possess the nature of being conditioned by latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
thus, it is not the referent of that term. || 110 ||
For it is not intended here by the Vedic revelation that [the self] has a single father.
Therefore, it is the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), whose nature is that of the instrument (*karaṇātman*), which is intended here. || 151 ||

Because it is intended to make known that the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-different from Brahman, [the author] states that its form as transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is not logically tenable in reality. He says, "Not so. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the present context. He states the resulting conclusion regarding the impossibility of the soul being characterized by latent impressions: "By the instruments," etc.; this means the passage beginning with "For him, indeed... (*tasya ha...*) [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3]. || 151 ||
The subtle body (liṅga), accompanied by latent impressions (vāsanā), [proceeds] toward those whose natures are characterized by mild or very mild modifications.
Because the knower perceives it as the witness, the object of knowledge takes on the form of the field (kṣetra). || 152 ||
For this reason as well, he states that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) belongs not to the individual soul (*jīva*), but rather to the mind (*citta*): "The latent impression... (verse 152).
If the form [of the world], such as saffron-colored cloth and so forth, were to belong to the Witness, [then...]
If he had not then given the instruction regarding the Self as "not this, not this," [the world would have remained ignorant]. (153)

He states another reason for the fact that the latent impressions (vāsanās) of agency and so forth do not constitute the nature of the Self: "māhārajanam" and so on. Here, the word "atha" has the sense of restriction and connects with the negative particle "na. || 113 ||
Furthermore, it cannot be established by means of valid cognition that this [result] belongs to anyone other than [the agent].
"Not so, not so"—this [negation] concludes that very [Self] at the end of the sixth [chapter]. || 154 ||

Anticipating the objection that this instruction does not concern the individual soul (jīva) but rather the transcendent Brahman, he says: "Of another. Since at the conclusion of the sixth [chapter], having introduced the Self with the words, "O, by what means is the knower known?", the text concludes with the word "Self" in the passage, "This very Self is 'not this, not this'"; therefore, the meaning is that here too, the instruction concerns that very Self and not a transcendent entity. || 154 ||
By the statement "vyava tvā," the meaningfulness of the proposition would likewise be established.
If this instruction regarding the tiger were to apply even to one who has arisen from the mere clapping of hands. || 155 ||
For this reason as well, he says that this instruction refers only to the inner self (pratyagartha): "vyeva" (he indeed knows). 119.
Another arose from the clapping of hands, and yet another from the sound "cemetī."
At that time, the notion "this is something else" would be a false cognition, arising from the cause of delusion.

He establishes the very point already stated by means of the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). [The verse beginning with] "pāṇi" [means]: "Dhī" refers to the knowledge "I am Brahman. Therefore, this instruction pertains only to the inner self (*pratyag-artha*); consequently, since the scriptural realization of the identity "I am Brahman" is established, the purpose of the proposition is fulfilled. || 156 ||
There would be no arising of the realization "I am Brahman," which consists in knowing oneself alone.
Right understanding destroys all darkness and bestows liberation. || 157 ||

Regarding the claim that the individual soul (*jīva*) is one thing and the Brahman being pointed out is another, he states another fault: that it would contradict such scriptural passages as "Then he knew himself alone" (*tadātmānam evāvet*). This is expressed by the words "It would not be so" (*na syāt*). || 197 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 725] 3 Brāhmaṇa:
Only for that which is non-self, namely the instrument-self (karaṇātman), can there be the grasping of weapons.
But it is not logical for [the cognition] to have the object as its witness, because of the negation of its form. || 158 ||

Since the individual soul (jīva) is non-different from Brahman, it is impossible for it to be characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā); therefore, it is established that the mind alone takes on those forms and those words.
This is stated in the verse beginning with "karaṇa" (verse 118).
Those latent impressions (vāsanās) are of manifold forms; they reside in the subtle body (liṅga), yet the witness of that subtle body is the Self.
They manifest manifold forms, just as a gem displays its surface. || 159 ||

Having raised the objection—“If the *liṅga* (the subtle body) is colored by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of agency and so forth, how can that [agency] appear in the Self?”—the author recalls what was stated in this context: “by the force of the delusion of its own reflection. Regarding the term “impressions,” the word “covering” (*āstaraṇa*) is used as an illustration for limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as blue, yellow, and so on. || 199 ||
In this context, the term "māhārajana" refers to a yellow color.
Because the saffron color has passed away, it is compared to the indragopa insect. || 160 ||

Having explained the passage beginning with "tasya" (of that), he states the meaning of the word *māhārajana* in the section beginning with "yathā" (as). Regarding the phrase "māhārajanamiti" (the word māhārajana):

one might object, "Since the word is well-known in the sense of saffron (*kausumbha*), why should it not be understood here as such? For it is said: 'Kusumbha, vahnishikha, and also mahārajana'. To this, he replies: "Indra... [160]
Just as a yellow garment appears as such to a witness, so too does that mark appear.
The visual faculty is permeated by latent impressions arising from objects such as names and so forth.

Having stated the meaning of the individual words, he states the meaning of the sentence: "It is drunk," etc. The connection is with "of the witness-consciousness" (sākṣiṇo dṛśeḥ). He states the cause for the transformation of that [witness] into such a state, namely the mind (liṅga), as "naming and so forth. || 169 ||
Like wool and such things that are slightly pale, so does the liṅga shine forth.
The indragopa insect is intensely red, and likewise, the mind is exceedingly red.

He explains the meaning of "pāṇḍvāvikam" with the word "īṣat" (slightly); by the word "ādi" (and so forth), "kambala" (woolen blanket) is included. He explains the meaning of "indragopa" with the word "indra" (Indra). || 162 ||
In some cases, an excess of rajas is observed; in others, an excess of tamas is intended.
In the same way, an excellence of the sentient being also arises from some cause. || 163 ||

When it is asked what the cause is for the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the mind, he says that it is the diversity of the *guṇas*. Regarding the phrase "of rajas," the expression "in some cases" refers to the objects [of experience] caused by the predominance of a particular *guṇa*. || 163 ||
In some cases, there is primacy of one [of two figures], while in another subject, there is [primacy] of both.
And for all three [of these], elsewhere [than in the case of the Lord], there is variety due to knowledge, action, and so forth. || 164 ||

Having raised the doubt as to what is the cause for the increase or decrease of the qualities (*guṇas*) with respect to each respective object, he restates that variety and states its cause, beginning with the words "In some cases" (*kvacit*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), passion (*rāga*) and so forth are included. || 164 ||
OT SA [vol2, page 726]
Just as the brilliance of fire arises from the excellence of its luminous quality (*sattva*), so too does the mind [arise from the excellence of its own quality].
Just as a white lotus is gentle and brings delight, so too [is he]. || 165 ||

Having explained the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he states the meaning of the phrase "like the flame of a fire" with the words "of fire. He states the meaning of the phrase "like a lotus" with the words "lotus"; the word "mind" is to be understood as the remainder [of the comparison]. || 165 ||
Just as a single flash of lightning utterly dispels the dense darkness.
It was exceedingly radiant, having entered our eyes and mouths. || 166 ||

He analyzes the phrase beginning with "at once" (*sakṛt*). Regarding "at once": it means that it robs—that is, obstructs—the activity of our eyes, which are like blind eyes, toward their object. Likewise, he states the application to the case at hand (*dārṣṭāntika*): due to the excellence of the illumination of knowledge, for someone, a latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises, shining forth intensely all at once from every side. Thus: "the true path" (*sadgati*). 166.
Of the principle of Hiraṇyagarbha as it was being born from Keśava.
The form of that great-souled one, it is said, flickers like lightning.
Desiring to offer praise for that [meditation] in order to establish the injunction for meditating upon the Sūtra as distinguished by the final impression (*vāsanā*), he says: "Hiraṇyagarbha.
The word "kila" is used to indicate that its being born from the Supreme and its luminosity are well-known from Śruti and Smṛti. ||167||
Therefore, he who meditates in this very form day and night—
May the Goddess Śrī, the destroyer of all darkness, always take refuge in the lightning.

Explaining the statement regarding the fruit—beginning with "once" (*sakṛt*) and so forth—while teaching the meditation on the Sūtra as qualified by the aforementioned latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [the author] says "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The meaning of the word "therefore" is that the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, as previously described, is fit for meditation. The phrase "day and night" is stated with the intention of specifying three qualifications for the meditation.

The sense is that the visible fruit of meditation has been stated, whereas the invisible fruit is that which is scriptural, beginning with "him according to... (*taṃ yathā...*) and so forth. || 168 ||
Since there is no middle, nor indeed an end, nor any measure to be found for it.
The illustration [of the variety of experiences] is due to the accumulation of latent impressions over infinite eons. || 169 ||
The phrase beginning with "māhārajanam" and so forth does not intend to specify a fixed quantity.
It is intended as an illustration by him precisely for the purpose of showing the various types. || 170 ||

Anticipating the objection that the impressions (*vāsanās*) must also be limited because of the statement of limited examples—since there is a similarity between the example and the thing exemplified—the author says: "It has no beginning. This provides the reason for the fourfold negation. The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is its explanation. The word "infinite" (*ananta*) [is used] to answer the question: "If so, why was an example provided? He replies that it is by way of illustration (*upalakṣaṇatvena*). Thus he says: "An example..."

Regarding the word "heart" (*hṛti*): anticipating the question, "If the demonstration of the extent of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is not for the sake of providing examples, then what is its purpose?", he clarifies what has already been stated. Regarding the phrase "in various ways": the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) is the possibility of such an extent. || 169 || 170 ||
Having thus explained the nature of reality in its entirety, [the author] now...
An effort is made to provide an instruction on the true nature of ultimate reality. || 171 ||
[Vol.

2, Page 727] 3 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: Having recounted the conduct from the *Āśiśu-brāhmaṇa* up to the "Instruction" (*ādeśa*), the subsequent portion is for the purpose of explaining the word "Satya" (Truth) ending in the nominative case.
He says "the statement" [referring to] "without remainder. || 171 ||
Since all things, whether manifest or unmanifest, have been explained herein, therefore—
An instruction is subsequently given to him who is free from pride. || 172 ||

The two words [of the verse] explain [the matter] by fulfilling the expectation [of the questioner]. Regarding the word "yataḥ" (from which): anticipating the objection that since its establishment is easily accomplished even through perception and other means of knowledge, what is the use of this instruction, he says: "ananya... (172).
Then, for the manifestation of the Truth whose nature is both embodied and unembodied.
Since no other entity remains apart from Brahman. || 173 ||
This instruction regarding Brahman is said to be for that which is beyond all instruction.
Of that which is designated as "excessive pride," whose nature consists of the non-duality of the individual measure (pratyaṅmātrā). || 174 ||

He states what it is in relation to which the proximity (*ānantarya*) of the instruction (*ādeśa*) [is established]: "mūrta... [and so on]. He explains why Brahman alone is intended to be pointed out immediately after the explanation of the aforementioned Truths: "brahma... [and so on]. He demonstrates its dependence upon an instruction: "nirādeśasya... [and so on].
He provides the reason for the claim that Brahman is devoid of any other instruction: "atimāna... [and so on]. Regarding its being beyond speech and mind (*vāṅmanasātītatva*):...
The cause is "the inward" (pratyak). || 173 || 174 ||
This word "ādeśa" may refer either to the object of the action or to the instrument of the action.
Alternatively, the instruction or the teaching regarding the non-dual Self is "not this, not this" (neti neti).
Having explained the two words *atha* and *ataḥ*, he states the meaning of the word *ādeśa*: "In the matter of action," etc.

By the etymology "that which is pointed out" (*ādiśyate*), Brahman is the *ādeśa*; by the etymology "that by which [Brahman] is pointed out," the word is the *ādeśa*; or by the etymology "the pointing out itself," knowledge is the *ādeśa*.
This is the meaning. || 175 ||
How can the reality of Brahman be [described] by means of the two words "not this, not this"?
The reality intended to be pointed out would be beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition.

[The opponent] objects: "Surely the two derivations as 'action' (bhāva) and 'state' (bhāva) are not tenable, because starting from the instruction, the two words 'not this, not this' (neti neti) are employed; however, in the case of the 'instrument' (karaṇa) interpretation, the instruction consists of two words, and by that [instruction], Brahman cannot be pointed out, since it is not denotable by them. Thus he raises the doubt: "Not this... (176).
Listen, all of you, to the refutation of that which arises from ignorance.
Because that non-cognition is excluded by means of the single nature of each individual moment. || 177 ||

He says, "Listen," meaning that although the two words are not denotative [of Brahman], they are said to be the cause for the cognition of Brahman; therefore, because of their extreme subtlety, they must be heard with focused attention. He states the same point concisely: "Through the ignorance of That... The meaning is that the two words are the cause of the cognition [of Brahman] by way of removing the ignorance superimposed on the Inner Self (pratīc) and its products. An objection is raised: "If the negation of form and so forth from the Inner Self were something other [than the Self], there would be a loss of non-duality; otherwise..."

He says "no" to the claim that even negation (niṣedha) is of the nature of non-existence. He says "the inner self" (pratyak). Since the destruction of one's own ignorance and its effects culminates in [realization] as being nothing but oneself, how could there be duality? Or how could there be the existence of negation? For negation itself enters into that [reality]. This is the meaning. || 177 ||
The supreme state of the formless, which is the causal self, has been described previously. *Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter. [Vol. 2, Page 728] 1022.
And likewise, for that which has form, there is spatial confinement within the earth; such is the nature of those two. || 178 ||

Even though the Self lacks duality due to negation, one might suspect what that [negation] is, since it possesses a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); anticipating this doubt, he recalls the previously mentioned view of Bhartṛprapañca as being faultless. "Of the formless" (*amūrtasya*). Alternatively, even if there is an absence of duality through negation, one might suspect that its state remains unchanged due to the root cause (*mūlakāraṇa*) and so forth; therefore, he says "of the formless" to show that such is not the case, because that [root cause] is itself the object of negation.
The meaning is that everything existing between the primal cause and the final effect is to be negated. || 178 ||
Whatever object whatsoever is intended for both pride and verbal designation, [it is all subsumed therein].
This [intermediate state] exists precisely between the two aforementioned [states of] cause and effect. (179)
Nevertheless, suspecting that the Self might be accompanied by something else—an entity distinct from cause and effect that is not subject to negation—he raises the dilemma:

"Is that [companion] beyond speech and mind, or not? Assuming the first alternative—that it is not distinct from the Self—he refutes the second alternative with the verse beginning with "māna" (measure). || 179 ||
Likewise, name-and-form, karma, the vital breaths, the worlds, and so forth [are all likewise].
Neither the agent, nor the action, nor any other cause, nor even the effect [exists]. || 180 ||
Having raised the objection that [Brahman] possesses duality because of [the existence of] name and so forth, he states that even those must be negated because they reside within cause and effect.
He says, "Name," etc. Some claim that since the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are not to be negated, Brahman possesses duality through them; to them he replies, "The vital breaths," etc.
Since the worlds and their presiding deities are also not to be negated, the state of possessing duality remains as before; to this he replies, "The worlds and so forth," etc.
Fearing that [Brahman] might be subject to duality because factors such as the *kārakas* (instrumental causes) are not to be negated, he says: "And the *kāraka*," etc. This means "another result.
He dispels the charge of duality by means of intermediate causes and so forth, saying: "The cause," etc. (180).
Genus, quality, action, substance, relation, and even existence itself.
Existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and likewise the state of being neither—these are all merely your own self.

Anticipating doubts regarding [the categories] such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, he says: "Genus," etc. Connection is inherence (*samavāya*). Particularity (*bhāva*) is the ultimate particular (*viśeṣa*).
By means of conceptual constructions such as "existence" (*sat*), he loosens the state of being dual with existence. Thus: "Existence. (181)
The knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and then the action and its fruit.
By means of such negations, which rely upon the cognition [of the object], [the object is negated]. || 182 ||

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "My self" (*mamātma*). The word *atha* has the sense of conjunction and is a synonym for *tathā*. "Action" (*kriyā*) is an operation conducive to the arising of valid cognition (*pramā*). The "result" (*phala*) is valid cognition itself. Now, one might object: having begun with the aim of making Brahman known, that Brahman is not made known by the aforementioned negation;
for mere negation is not the making known of that [Brahman], and thus there would be a loss of the initial proposition (*pratijñāhāni*). To this, he says: "Thus—" (*ityā-*)...

"Deriti" (Thus). By the word "na" (not), there is the negation of both that which has been stated and that which has not been stated. By means of this, having negated everything, the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of Brahman is understood through the remaining [reality] that stands firm. That very thing is its reality (*tattva*); in that regard, there is no abandonment of the initial proposition (*pratijñāhāni*).
[Vol.
2, Page 729] 3 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1023
The "indicator" (upapradarśaka) is intended as the designation for all [categories] beginning with name (nāman).
Is this negation being made of that which has been presented, or not?

[The author] says "upeti" (beginning with 'upa'), having raised the doubt: "In the absence of something to be negated, there can be no negation, because that is impossible without a prior apprehension.

He concludes the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the words "tasya" (of that). The meaning of the word "atha" (now/then) is the possibility of the negation being preceded by a prior apprehension. 183.
The form of a material object, once extracted, does not exist separately.
If even that which is unimagined does not exist in the world, how much less so that which is imagined through delusion and the like? || 184 ||

Having raised the objection that "what is prohibited in Brahman might, out of delusion, remain elsewhere—just as a prohibited jar remains here [elsewhere]," he states the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument: "Drawn forth," etc. (184).
Even though a cloth is negated in a jar, it remains elsewhere than the jar.
Because that [property] exists elsewhere as well, there is no prohibition of the subject (dharmin) which is not [otherwise] negated. || 185 ||

He refutes the example with the words "the jar" (*ghaṭa*). The meaning is as follows: although a cloth or the like is excluded from a jar and so forth, it is logical that it should exist elsewhere, because it is not imagined there; for even setting aside the jar and so on, the substratum (*dharmin*) consisting of threads and the like remains unexcluded. || 185 ||
Of that entity which is negated in the ultimate sense and arises from delusion regarding it.
Or else, how could there be a separate existence for that [world] from the perspective of the ultimate self? (186)

He states the disparity regarding the object of discipline (*dāntika*) with the words "from the supreme reality" (*paramārthāt*). The meaning is that the self, which has been negated, does not exist—either as distinct or non-distinct—from what is other than the non-self, because it is merely imagined, like silver and so forth. || 186 ||
Because all things that are to be negated are mutually inconsistent with one another.
Therefore, since there is no deviation of cognition [from its object], that which is superimposed upon it is negated. || 187 ||

Anticipating the objection that the status of being imagined (*kalpitatva*) is unestablished, he says: "Of the things to be negated. Anticipating the objection that there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) in the argument "the subject of dispute is imagined because it is variable, like a snake," with respect to the inner self (*pratīci*), he says: "Of the inner self.
