He states the resulting conclusion: "In that [inner self], that which is imagined is not born of itself; being negated therein, it does not exist elsewhere, like silver. || 187 ||
The negation of those things designated by the word "thus" (iti) occurs within the nature of direct experience.
Let it be determined that Brahman is that wherein there is an end for those things that have an end, yet which itself is infinite. || 188 ||

One might object: "If space and the like, which are superposed upon the Inner Self (pratīc) and denoted by the word 'prakṛti,' are negated by the word 'iti,' then Brahman is not established because there is no word to denote it;

therefore, the negation is useless. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the word *iti*. Even in the absence of a word directly denoting Brahman, the negation culminates in that [Brahman], because it is impossible for [negation] to be absolute; for every collection of perishable modifications ends in the Puruṣa.
The meaning is that a person perishes [only] through the absence of a cause for destruction, according to the principle that [what lacks a cause for destruction] is indestructible. || 188 ||
Both existence and perception [are established] on the basis of direct perception of their own objects.
The Vedic mantra regarding the formless and so forth ceases [to apply] to that which is indefinable. || 189 ||
The word "prakṛtam" (the subject at hand) refers to that which has been introduced; since it is included by virtue of being the subject at hand, its inclusion follows accordingly.
[Vol. 2, page 730] 1024 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter—]

Anticipating the doubt that [the Self] might be voidness (*śūnyatā*), he says: "It exists" (*sad*). The meaning is that because the word "I" does not denote the inner witness (*pratyagātman*)—which bestows existence and manifestation upon both being and non-being, which is self-luminous, and which transcends mind and speech—it cannot be negated; therefore, it is not voidness. || 189 ||
The one who seeks to negate negates by the power of the partless conscious self.
Having destroyed everything else by means of consciousness alone, the Self-awareness proceeds as fullness from itself.

Furthermore, he states that the word "not" (nañ) does not negate duality, such as the corporeal and so forth, because it negates that which has already attained existence and manifestation through the power of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), thereby resolving [the object] into the conscious Self (*cidātman*).

He says: "It negates. One might raise the objection that if the negative particle negates duality by the power of the Self, then because the negative particle and the Self would always exist together, duality would never exist at all. Anticipating this, [the author] explains that the conscious Self, by means of the knowledge arising from the sentence itself, completely sublates everything.

He says, "By means of higher knowledge," [meaning] that because it persists through its own nature as being uninterrupted, the realization of non-duality is established prior to that [final] knowledge. || 190 ||
For in this [Self], which perceives only the inward-facing, throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, [there is no change].
That which appears as something other than that [object] is not denied. || 191 ||

Having stated that the Self is not something to be negated, he concludes that duality is what is to be negated with the words "pratyak" (the inner Self). The meaning is that even during the three states [waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], whatever is an effect or a cause in the presence of the Witness, and which possesses the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), that is to be negated. The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies that such [duality] is fit for negation because it is merely imagined (kalpita). || 199 ||
When direct perception and inference are always established without being critically examined, [they lead to error].
With eyes wide open and the intellect turned inward, one blows away [impurities] within oneself by means of the measures (māna). || 192 ||

He states the fruit of the prohibition: "Āvicārita... etc. One whose mind has blossomed through the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth with the resolve of offering them to the Lord, having attained knowledge of the inner self (*pratīc*) from the heard Vedic statement, and by the power of that [knowledge] having destroyed ignorance and its effects, remains forever free from activity within the Self alone.

The meaning is that [the Self] abides in its own majesty. By the cessation of ignorance, there follows the cessation of its effects; thus, the state of being established in one's own majesty is described as being free from all opposition. || 192 ||
Therefore, because it is the cause of the cognition of dependence, it is the entity that is both effect and cause.
When investigated, that does not exist, like blackness in the sky or in the self.

Anticipating the objection that even if ignorance regarding the inner self (*pratyagvidyā*) has been destroyed, how can there be the destruction of the world, and that if it is not destroyed, the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is not accomplished, he says: "Dependent" (*apekṣā*). Just as there is dependence on causes and dependence on effects, so too with that knowledge; by reason of that, the manifested effect and so forth do not exist in reality within the Self. Therefore, like the blue color in the sky, the world is also false when investigated.
The meaning is that it is the exertion of knowledge. || 193 ||
Because the grounds for the application of words are impossible in the inner self (pratyagātman).
And because those things which are the objects of the means of valid cognition are established by themselves, there is no need for inference.

Although the world, like the blackness of the sky, is to be negated because it arises from delusion, the Self cannot be established by that negation; for the object to be established is not pervaded by the negation of its effects. [Regarding the word] "śabda": [it refers to] the unattached [Self]. 1. Established.
[Vol.
2, Page 731] 3 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1025.

Since the genitive case and so forth are inapplicable to the inner Self (*pratīc*), which is immutable and non-dual, it cannot be taught by way of positive injunction; rather, it is taught by way of its negation—this is the meaning. As for that which...

Regarding the point that this [Self] is not established by means of negation in the same way as space, he says: "By means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, because that [space] falls within the scope of inference and other means of knowledge, it is not established through negation. However, the inner Self (*pratyagātman*) is devoid of sound and other qualities, is not an object of other means of knowledge, and even scripture does not apply to it by way of affirmation; therefore, its establishment is by way of negation. This is the meaning. That which is not [established by] affirmation...

If it is argued that [the self] does not exist because it is not expressed by way of affirmation—just like the son of a barren woman and so forth—then, with the intention that the self would likewise be non-existent due to its not being expressed by way of affirmation, he says:
"By itself" (svataḥ). || 194 ||
As long as the object of the designation "I" does not [perceive] itself within itself, [it remains unawakened].
One attains the inner self; the negative particle does not cease its function until that point. || 195 ||

This very point—that the inner self (pratyak) is not non-existent because its existence and manifestation are independent of anything else—is clarified by the verse beginning with "māna" (means of knowledge).

For this [self], in empirical usage, possesses adjuncts (upādhi) and is the object of means of knowledge other than verbal testimony; however, as long as it does not attain its state of abiding in its ultimate nature through the exclusion of all particularities, so long the negation regarding the objects of its adjuncts does not reach its final conclusion. This is the meaning. || 195 ||
Then, having discarded ignorance and its effects, one attains the Self by means of the self within the Self.
When that which is to be negated has been utterly destroyed, the negation itself also ceases. || 196 ||

How, then, does the negation [of ignorance] occur? To this he says: "It is discarded" (*nirasta*). He clarifies the meaning of the first quarter [of the verse]: "That which is to be negated" (*niṣedhya*). Ignorance and its effects are that which is to be negated; they alone serve as the cause of the negation by way of being its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). The meaning of the word *atha* is that when that [ignorance] has been destroyed, there is an absence of the cause for the persistence of the negation once the object of negation has ceased. || 196 ||
Whatever is intended here, such as the state of being a knower (pramātṛtva) and so forth—
And the absence of that [world] is negated by the statement, "All that is not this. || 197 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if the "other" (the subject) is not negated, there would be an infinite regress if there were another negator for the duality that is to be negated—and that in the absence of such a negator, the persistence of the negation would imply the Self possesses attributes—the author says: "By means of the state of being a knower, etc. (197).
All this is to be negated, for it pertains to the reality of the self which is itself not to be negated.
Therefore, one should not be intent upon non-existence, because even non-existence must eventually cease.

Anticipating the objection, "If there is a negation even of the negation itself, how is there not an infinite regress? he says: "The object to be negated" (*niṣedhyam*). By this, he states that the view that negation is ultimately grounded in non-existence (*abhāva*) is also refuted. He says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The words "there would be a negation" (*syāt niṣedhaḥ*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 198 ||
The repetition "not this, not this" is used because of the desire to negate everything that might be grasped.
Therefore, repetition (vīpsā) alone is what must be negated regarding everything that is intended to be understood.

Having raised the objection—"Since duality has been negated as being merely the inner self (*pratyag-mātra*), why are there two *na*s even when the meaning of the sentence is the inner self?"—he says "neti" (not this, not that). The meaning is that because whatever is perceived is negated, this is a repetition (*vīpsā*). He further states "evam" (thus) because it results in the cessation of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth. He clarifies that very point with "jighṛkṣita" (that which is intended to be grasped) and "bubhutsi" (that which is desired to be known).

Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): since the repetition (*vīpsā*) of everything desired is what must be negated, it is therefore logical that that [repetition] alone [is negated]; such is the meaning. || 199 ||
129. 1 kha. by oneself; 2 kha. this self is not; 3. of the prohibition.
Through knowledge and action, this [Self] is fully pervaded; thus, the inquiry comes to rest.
Without being measured, one reaches completion in that which is not intended to be done.
Anticipating the objection, "Even in that view, how is there the cessation of all expectancy? he says: "jñāna... (knowledge...). This is the meaning to be understood:

the expectancy "this is to be done" ceases through the repetition [of the word], because everything that has been attained is negated; and since it is not within the scope of either knowledge or action, the knower abides in a state of identity (*tādātmya*). Thus, the repetition is appropriate—this is the sense. || 200 ||
Through the knowledge of the true nature of the rope, [the world] ceases from its causal self, just like the snake.
A prohibition cannot be established by any other means, even in hundreds of years.

Having raised the objection that—since the destruction of duality and its cause occurs through the very cognition of the non-existence of the gross and so forth, the realization of Brahman would be purposeless—therefore there is no distinction between the position of non-existence (*abhāva-pakṣa*) and the position of repetition (*vīpsā-pakṣa*), he provides an illustration for the point that the cognition of the reality of Brahman alone is the sublater: "In the case of the rope... (201).
Whatever is obtained in this world, all of that is negated.
And this being so, even the suspicion regarding what has not been specified is removed.

[The author] states the fruit of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) with the words "whatever... whatever" (*yadyad iti*). He then explains what occurs when everything that is to be specified is negated, with the words "and thus" (*evaṃ ca iti*).

When the entirety of that which falls within the domain of speech and mind is negated by the two negatives (*nañ*), it follows by implication that Brahman is the substratum transcending those—[Brahman] which is without limit.
The meaning is that because negation is impossible, the doubt regarding its not being specified is likewise destroyed. || 202 ||
If there is no repetition (vīpsā), then these two sentences are intended [to be taken] as distinct.
By the negation of the two [positions] mentioned, and because that [middle position] is thereby exhausted, it would [not exist]. || 203 ||
There is a suspicion regarding subjects not explicitly mentioned, because there is no prohibition against anything whatsoever.
Or else, if it has non-existence as its object, then existence is not being negated.

Having stated the merit in the case of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), he states the defect in the alternative view with the words "If not" (*na cet*). He explains what the defect is in the case of two separate sentences with the words "It has been said" (*uktā*). The meaning is that, because the two sentences would terminate with the negation of the formed and the formless, there would be no negation of everything that can be designated; thus, a doubt might arise that Brahman is indeed something that can be designated as having some unspoken portion remaining. He states another doubt with the words "Or if" (*yadi vā*). By these two [words]...

The meaning is that the doubt might arise that the sentence is restricted to those [entities] because the two negatives negate only the manifest and the unmanifest forms, rather than negating non-existence itself.
Among those things established by direct perception, there is the apprehension of what is other than that which has been negated.
When that which is unestablished negates those things that are established, there is the apprehension of emptiness. || 205 ||

He establishes that very point with the words "directly" (*sākṣāt*). In the case of perceived things such as the ground, since only those perceived things like jars are grasped as the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), both of these remain directly non-vacuous. However, if the perceived world were negated within the unperceived Brahman, the statement would result in nihilism (*śūnyāvasāyin*); for there is no means of knowledge regarding Brahman, and the perceived world has been negated.
This is the meaning. || 205 ||
1. ga. paṃtaskāraṇātmanoḥ | ni | [vol2, page 733] 2 brāhmaṇam ] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1027.
Having begun with the word "injunction" (ādeśa), this prohibition is now stated.
That by which [something] is directly pointed out is called such an "instruction" (ādeśa). || 206 ||

Anticipating the objection that the statement might be grounded in emptiness (*śūnya*), he says: "The instruction" (*ādeśa*). Having stated that this is the instruction regarding Brahman, the meaning is that because it is expressed as a negation, this instruction—known as a negation—is solely intent upon establishing Brahman. || 206 ||
Therefore, by way of negation, [the Self] is realized through the witness whose nature is not subject to negation.
Having negated both the known and the unknown, it then remains eternally established in pure perception.

He states the conclusion regarding the impossibility of the sentence being established in emptiness: "niṣedha... (negation...). The meaning is that by means of the teaching of negation, the wise one remains in his own essential nature after having negated the world of cause and effect—which is unfit for negation—by way of the Brahman who is the witness.
The sense of the word "atha" (then) is that it is appropriate for the wise one to abide in his unconditioned form once the limiting adjuncts have ceased. || 207 ||
Just as form is not perceived by the auditory cognition, because it lacks the causal connection with form.
And it has not been grasped, is not being grasped, and will not be grasped, just like sound. || 208 ||
When the inner reality has been fully realized through the statement "not this, not this," [the Self is known].
In the same way, the selfless (anātman), together with its cause, has not existed, does not exist, and will not exist. || 209 ||

Fearing that what has been once prohibited might nevertheless arise again and again—as is observed in the case of snakes and the like—he refutes this by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "Just as... (yathā). This means that there is no connection of the ear with [the object] by way of its form (*rūpa*), which serves as the cause.
The existence of a second self does not exist apart from ignorance, just as [the appearance of a second moon].
"Likewise, its cessation is not something other than the realization of the Self.
Anticipating the objection that the cessation of duality, along with its cause, might be something distinct from the Self, he recalls what was stated previously by saying, "not other."
When that absolute oneness, which is not dependent on anything else, is directly established;
then this proposition, "It is indeed so," would be rightly declared as fruitful. || 211 ||

Since it is impossible for the statement to be established in the negation of speech, [the author], having stated that "the wise man remains as that Self after having rejected everything superimposed by means of repetition (vīpsā) in the form of a witness," states another reason for the position of repetition: "ananyā" (not other). || 219 ||
Because of the possibility of repetition in the form "not this, not this," the aforementioned reality [is indicated].
Thus, there would be the fulfillment of the purpose; otherwise, it would not be possible.

He concludes that position with the words "not so" (*neti*). The meaning of the reason is that by resorting to the repetition (*vīpsā*), the intended matter—the meaningfulness of the proposition and so forth—is possible. Fearing that the establishment of the stated meaning might not occur, he says: "the state of having accomplished one's purpose" (*kṛtārthatā*).

It is only upon the establishment of the stated meaning—namely, that absolute unity (*aikātmya*) is not dependent on anything else—that a person has accomplished their purpose, and not otherwise; for it is said: "If one has known this here, then [one becomes] immortal... (*iha cedavedīdatha satyam...*) and so forth.
The meaning is that [this is established] from such scriptural passages as "I am" (mastīti). || 212 ||
The intellect, though attached to external objects, [becomes pure] through its coloring by the inward-facing reality.
Therefore, being excluded from the external object, it finds its stability in the inward Self.
[Vol. 2, Page 734] 1028 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Adhyāya]:
He concludes the result of the negation with the word “parāk” (outward). By its very nature, the mind is directed toward external objects; somehow, through the power of destiny—
The meaning is that [the mind], being withdrawn from sense objects through renunciation and being prohibited [from them], will, by process of elimination, abide in the inner Self (pratyak). || 213 ||
For the negative concomitance (vyatireka) has already been established prior to the statement of the injunction.
This instruction is now stated for the purpose of establishing the state of being Brahman directly.

Having explained the negative statement (*niṣedhavākya*) through reasoning based on the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), [the author] now states that this very same [statement] is intended to convey a different meaning by way of affirmation (*vidhimukhena*). He addresses the position that it has the purpose of expressing "distinction" (*vyatireka*) with the words: "Of the distinction" (*vyatirekasya*). The word *hi* is used to indicate that the establishment of distinction is shown by the use of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśe*). Since the distinction of Brahman from the formed (*mūrta*) and so forth was already obtained previously, [it is not]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

If it is argued that the instruction is for that purpose [of purification], then for what purpose is it? To this he says: "Directly" (sākṣāt). The meaning is that the instruction is given so as to directly awaken the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) to his state of being Brahman immediately after the purification of the meanings of the words. || 214 ||
The negation does not have the purpose of negating [the object], because it is intent upon the meaning of its definition.
Since no internal interval of Brahmā is established, it follows that he is nothing but emptiness. || 215 ||
Some, reflecting on the two [previous] positions stated, say that the instruction (*ādeśa*) has the purpose of negating form and so forth; to them he replies with the words beginning "No" (*na*).

For the instruction of a negation does not have the purpose of negating the form and so forth which are to be negated, because its primary purport is the meaning of "Thou" (*tvam-artha*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

He states the fault in the contrary case: "Of Brahman," etc. Since form and so forth, being cognized, are negated, whereas Brahman is not cognized [in that context], [the negation would imply] a real [negation of Brahman].
The meaning is that the universe would be nothing but emptiness. || 215 ||
The distinctness of the embodied form and so forth from Brahman is established solely through the use of the genitive case.
Consequently, there would be no attachment to the principle of *jāmitā* (avoidance of repetition), and the statement of *pāriśeṣya* (residual method) would be untenable. || 216 ||

Fearing that—since the position of negation is untenable because it is impossible for Brahman to possess form and so forth—the position of non-difference might follow by exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), yet that has not been established previously due to a lack of proof—he says: "The genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning is this: in the very passage "There are indeed two," the distinctness of the mortal body from Brahman was established by means of the genitive; therefore, if there were a statement of distinction again in the sentence concerning its instruction (*tad-ādeśa*), it would be a tautology. As for that which [remains] by exhaustion...

Regarding the claim that [the sixth case-ending] signifies the meaning of difference (*vyatireka*), he says: "No. The meaning is this: since the non-difference of the formed (*mūrta*) and so forth from Brahman has been negated by the statement of negation, it is incorrect to say that difference is established through the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*); for if that [non-difference] is already established by the sixth case-ending itself, there is no room for the method of exhaustion. || 216 ||
And it cannot be refuted, because it relies upon perception and the other means of valid cognition.
Even some desired purpose would not be accomplished through a prohibition. (217)

Having refuted the position of exclusion (*vyatireka*), he states another defect in the position of negation (*niṣedha*) with the words "it is possible" (*śakyate*). The meaning is that it is impossible to negate that which exists as the object of that [negation] by depending upon it—namely, form and so forth—because of the contradiction involved. Even if one were to argue that the negation of the object of perception and the like is appropriate because they are illusory (*ābhāsa*), like the cognition of silver and so on, even then the statement of the "instruction" (*ādeśa*) does not have negation as its purpose, because the mere [negation] is fruitless; thus he says.
"Because of the prohibition," [it is said]. || 217 ||
And if it were restricted solely to negation, there would be no instruction from the Lord.
When it is stated that Brahman is not form and so forth, there is no negation of form and the rest [in general]. // 298 //

Furthermore, is the sentence concerned solely with negation, or does it, by means of that negation, culminate in Brahman? It is not the first, because it would contradict the initial context; thus he says:
[vol2, page 735]

"Niṣedhati" (he negates). The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that in the second case, our own position would be reached. Even in the view of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the sentence does not have that [negation] alone as its purport, because it would contradict the opening statement (*upakrama*); if it is argued that it has Brahman as its purport by means of that [negation], he says: "Brahma... || 218 ||
And thus, the establishment of Brahman-hood occurs when there exists a second entity.
"Vyeva tvā" (I will surely separate you) is the meaning of the proposition, nor would it be made manifest. || 219 ||
Therefore, by the method of elimination, there would be a failure to establish the intended object.
Therefore, the explanation of what has been stated should be made directly, in accordance with its accomplishment.

Anticipating the objection—"What loss is there if the sentence concludes by means of a negative statement (vyatireka) even when the negation of the corporeal and so forth has been established?"—the author says "tataśca" (and therefore). He states a defect common to both positions with the words "vyeva" (it would indeed be excluded). If the negation of the corporeal and so forth, or the negation of its non-difference from Brahman, implies by the method of residue (pāriśeṣya) a positive injunction of its being something other than that, then the meaning of the proposition would not be revealed by the statement of location.

The meaning is that because there exists either another established entity (*siddhavastvantara*), or a negation (*niṣedha*), or a second thing such as something corporeal (*mūrtādi*), the non-dual reality (*advayārtha*) cannot be established.

How, then, is the statement of negation to be justified? To this he says: "Just as... The construction is as follows: since the desired Brahman is not established under either of the two positions, one must provide a direct explanation of the statement of negation regarding that very Brahman in such a way that it is established.
The negation of every entity that is not the Self has already been established.
Because of the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self, and because of their mutual deviation from one another. || 221 ||
In order to explain that very point, he restates [the argument] that the negation and its counter-positive are established even prior to the statement of the injunction: "It is established.
He states the reason for the negation of the non-self: "Mutually... (229).
Mutual deviation is observed in this non-self entity.
Even the deviation from one's own nature [is known] through its own witness during deep sleep and so forth. (222)

He establishes this through experience. Regarding the phrase "mutually": not only is the non-self (anātman) imagined as something to be negated by cognition due to its mutual variability, but he says "of its own nature" [svarūpa-] because the variability of the self is established by one's own experience in states such as sleep. ||222||
Just as this existence of mother and others is established by direct perception, so too is this [existence of the self].
Even the non-existence of the knower and so forth arises likewise from the substratum of inward consciousness.

Under the guise of restating [the opponent's view], he rejects a different meaning and offers his own interpretation consistent with his position; wishing to show that the inner self (pratyagartha) is indicated by the meaning of the negative particle (nañ), he states the relationship between the witness and the witnessed through an illustration: "Just as... (yathā). || 223 ||
The self is established without deliberation, due to its being of one form with ignorance.
The entire non-self becomes established through its dependence upon the self that is established by itself. || 224 ||

Anticipating the objection that "if the non-self (anātman), consisting of existence and non-existence, is established by experience, then it must likewise possess reality," he says: "unexamined" (avicārita). The meaning is:

every non-self appears as if manifesting only through the grace of the self-luminous Self; yet, because it is indefinable, its very nature is the ignorance of the inner witness (pratyagavidyā). Therefore, how could this [non-self] possess reality? || 224 ||
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Chapter Two:
One whose consciousness is not obscured and from whom all modifications have been cast away...
Because it consists of mere vision, there is no [cognition] such as the mother or the measure that is other [than that vision]. || 225 ||

Having raised the doubt as to how the Self is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), he says "because it is of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpatvāt*). Even so, having raised the doubt that if the Self were to manifest the non-self (*anātman*) like a lamp, it would be subject to modification (*vikārī*), he says "free from [all such] limitations" (*vyapāsta*). He establishes its nature as pure consciousness (*saṃvidrūpatva*) by saying "not other" (*ananya*). Having raised the doubt that it might possess manifold flavors (*nānārasatva*) by appearing in the forms of the knower (*mātṛ*) and so forth, he says:
"View" (dṛṣṭi); the remainder [of the meaning] is that there is no diversity of flavor (nānārasatā). || 229 ||
Whatever accomplishment there may be, consisting of existence or non-existence, all of that belongs to the non-self.
Since it is considered to have a nature contrary to that [duality], it is established in me alone. || 226 ||

An objection is raised: since it is observed that a lamp or similar object, which possesses form and other qualities, serves as a means of manifesting objects such as a jar, the Self too, if it were to manifest duality, would necessarily be subject to the same defects of insentience and so forth; therefore, its capacity to manifest must belong to something else entirely. Anticipating this, he says: "bhāva... (The meaning is: for the Self is not the manifestor [of itself], because that would result in its being non-Self. || 226 ||
"By means of non-dual experience alone, [one abides] within the stages whose nature consists of existence and non-existence."
Perceiving the inner, immutable Self, he remains as the Self of the fruit.
Fearing the charge of infinite regress—that it [the Self] would require another agent because it is an agent, like a lamp—he says: "Not other" (*ananya*).
Fearing that by the statement "seeing," the Self would incur the predicament of being a non-eternal agent of seeing, he says: "The fruit" (*phala*). || 227 ||
Therefore, wherever the differentiation of the mother and so forth ceases, [that is the state].
In each and every case, being solitary, he achieves success through his own inherent greatness alone. || 228 ||

He concludes the discussion on the relationship between the witness (sākṣin) and the witnessed (sākṣya)—namely, that between the inner self (pratyagartha), which is the immutable, non-dual essence of consciousness, and the meaning of the negative particle (nañ)—with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).

The meaning of the word "therefore" is the state of being the nature of the fruit (phalātmatva) as previously mentioned. The term "avasthābheda" (difference of states) is understood through the repetition [of the word]. ||228||
Therefore, the non-existence of the knower and so forth is established through the awakening to one's own Self.
Non-arising always characterizes that Buddha as having non-dual cognition.

Having restated the previously mentioned relationship, he states that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) indicates the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the subject and so forth":

the function (*vṛtti*) of the negative particle consists in its denotation (*vācakatvena*) of that [absence] in which it occurs; thus, the "function of the negative" (*na-vṛtti*) is the absence of the subject and so forth. That [absence] indicates the inner self (*pratyañcam*), which is the singular essence of consciousness (*bodhaikarasam*) and the means of establishing itself.

Therefore, the meaning is that in a prohibitive statement, the word "na" (not) has the sense of "you" (tvam). He explains this [phrase] "always perceived as non-different": "apṛthakpramitam" (perceived as non-distinct). || 229 ||
And because pride and the like are not distinct from the nature of self-experience, they do not exist as something other than that.
The activity of that which possesses a cause would consist in the awakening to eternal consciousness.

Why is it not characterized by its opposite? Because that [Self] is established through the very force of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge; therefore, he says: "Because of distinctness" (*vaiviktyāt*).

It is impossible for the "measurer" (*mātr*) and so forth—accompanied by their own cause, which is ignorance—to exist within that which has the singular essence of immediate experience (*pratīcyanubhavaikarasa*), since the insentient and the sentient are absolutely distinct.

Therefore,

the meaning is that the inner self (pratyag-vī) is not known through perception or other means of knowledge. Furthermore, it is not [known] as a means of realization even for the means of knowledge and so forth.
He says that its function is such: "eternal," etc. (230).
Apart from ignorance and the rest, it possesses characteristics distinct from those of causes and the like.
The object whose nature is the Self is attained as non-different from the inward-looking consciousness. || 231 ||

Anticipating the objection that the reason—namely, "distinction" (*vaiviktya*) and so forth—is unestablished, he says: "ignorance and so on" (*avidyādi*). Because of its difference from that [Self] due to the dullness born of it, the reality which is distinct from duality and constitutes the very nature of the inner Self (*pratīc*) is obtained through one’s own direct experience; therefore, the meaning is that there is a distinction between the Self and the non-Self. || 231 ||
This reality is established by itself, independent of the knower and other such factors.
Since everything is established from that [very source], how could it be established from anything else? (232)
Anticipating the objection that non-difference is unestablished, he says: "This [is so]. He states the reasoning for this: "Of everything," etc. (232).
The establishment of the objects of knowledge has been stated as being due to its own inherent power, and not from scripture.
To bring about the realization of its nature as Brahman, it is described as "Not this, not this" (neti neti). || 233 ||

He restates the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*): "It has been stated. The inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the referent of the term *tvam*, is established by its own majesty; therefore, the establishment of the object of the negative particle has already been stated—this is the purpose of the restatement. Stating the meaning of the word "iti," he declares the meaning of the sentence: "Of that," etc.

The sentence "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) is said to be the authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) for making known the Brahmanhood of the witness (*sākṣin*), who is the referent of the negative particle, [and] by the word "iti," [the negation of] the formed and so forth...

By retaining the remainder and discarding the qualifiers, Brahman alone is indicated; therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that Brahman, as conveyed by the word "It" (tat), is the meaning of the negative particle (nañ), namely, the Witness. || 233 ||
That which is characterized by the negative particle (*nañ*) as being directly [denotative] of the immeasurable self-evidence (*ātmapratyaya*).
Because ignorance and the rest have that as their very nature, it is understood as Brahman. || 234 ||

Raising the objection that it is improper to claim the sentence "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) is the authority for the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—on the grounds that what is limited cannot be the unlimited—the author says: "The Self" (*ātmeti*). Although the primary denotation (*vācya*) is limited, the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) lacks such limitation; and since there is no other reality apart from that, the sentence is understood to teach that Brahman, indicated by the word "not," is nothing other than the mere negation of the object of the negative particle. This is the meaning. || 234 ||
[This occurs] through the realization of the inner true nature of that which arises from delusion and its products.
Because it has been sublated, he therefore said, "It is Brahman," in order to dispel delusion.

It might be objected that it is illogical for ignorance and the like to be identical with the Self due to their mutual contradiction; therefore, the statement [of scripture] cannot be intended to teach that the inner Self (pratyak) is Brahman. Anticipating this, he says: "The inner Self" (*pratyak*). Because there is no cause for limitation, the meaning of the word "not" (*na*)—namely, Brahman indicated by the term *iti*—is the inner Self;
thus the sentence "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*) declares this fact, and through the intellect, it destroys delusion. This is the meaning. || 235 ||
"Therefore, there is great agitation regarding the command, thinking 'Now, indeed!'"
Therefore, this dissimilar instruction that is being uttered is surely improper. || 236 ||
Having explained the sentence of instruction (*ādeśavākya*), he raises a doubt in order to introduce the passage beginning with "na hi" (*na hīti*). He says: "The instruction...
[Vol.
2, page 738, verse 1032]. This is from *Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter.
The word "ati" is used with the intention of expressing his great intensity, the gravity of his purpose, and the excellence of this [work] through its distinction from other treatises. || 236 ||
This instruction is indeed appropriate, for there exists nothing higher than it.
Therefore, this very instruction regarding Brahman is intended here as the authoritative teaching.

He states that the grammatical substitute (ādeśa) is improper because it lacks similarity in its mode of progression (*prakrama*). He says, "It is proper. He concludes its propriety with the words, "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 237 ||
He desired to instruct him in that reality which is beyond Brahman.
The reason for this is: "No," because all those objects that could have been designated therein have been negated. || 238 ||

Anticipating the objection—how can there be an absence of other designations for that [reality] since it is possible for it to be described in a positive form—he says: "That which is intended to be taught. The meaning is this: regarding that supreme reality, Brahman, which is desired to be pointed out, there are as many designatable things as there are, such as the formed (mūrta) and so forth; by the negation of all these through the word "not," its realization occurs, rather than being taught by way of a positive injunction. || 238 ||
And their cessation is precisely as previously described, characterized by their identity with the One Self.
However, in this case, an actual existence in different locations is not tenable. || 239 ||

One might object that even by way of negation, there can be no teaching of non-duality, because the cessation of form and so forth would result in duality; anticipating this, he recalls what was stated in passages such as "there is no existence other than knowledge. He says, "by cessation," and so on. Furthermore, regarding the status of existence and non-existence elsewhere than Brahman—whether taken superficially or in reality—he first accepts the former and then refutes the latter, saying, "distinct," etc. (239).
The meaning of the word "Brahman" is held to be neither excluded nor followed.
For when something else is present, the primary meaning of the word "Brahman" cannot be determined. || 240 ||

Regarding the point that existence and non-existence do not truly abide apart from Brahman, he states the reason for this after first explaining the meaning of the word "Brahman": "avyāvṛtta... (verse 240).
Because the grounds for the application of words are exhausted within a single essence.
Likewise, this is considered the supreme instruction regarding those things which are denoted by that [instruction]. || 241 ||
Furthermore, he states that the instruction regarding Brahman is more logical by way of negation alone, beginning with the words "śabda... (verse 241).
Since, having accepted the relationship between the signifier and the signified, [the meaning resides] in the syllable.
Not even a single word here refers directly to Brahman.

He concludes that a positive injunction is impossible here with the words "abhidhā" (denotation). The meaning is that because the [Self] is immutable, unattached, and non-dual, there is an absence of a cause; therefore, the primary function of words does not apply. || 242 ||
The instruction is "not this, not this" alone; by that, it is directly applicable here.
[This is] for the purpose of negating the desires produced by the ignorance of that [reality]. || 243 ||
1 ka. ga. māptataḥ | 2 ka. ga. 'śo'yama' | [vol2, page 739] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri; 1033.

He concludes that the injunction of a prohibition is applicable there with the words "the injunction. Having stated the reason for the impossibility of an injunction being directed toward a positive act, he states another reason with the words "because of the non-comprehension of that. || 243 ||
For both the formed and the formless are real; the vital breaths are real because they have that as their self.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is designated as "real" because of its having that [intellect] as its limiting adjunct. || 244 ||
Having explained the passage beginning with "na hi," he now states the meaning of the word *satya* (truth) in the genitive case in the verse beginning with "atha. He says: "mūrta" (the formed).

The particle "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that this matter is well-known from another Vedic scripture (*śruti*), namely, "It became both *sat* (being) and *tyat* (becoming). The meaning is that the five elements, their effects, and consciousness conditioned by them constitute "truth" (*satya*). || 244 ||
Those definable distinctions of that which is indefinable are characterized by their effects.
The name "having gained a foothold" is applied metaphorically to the other [the object]. || 245 ||

One might object: "Let the entire world, including the Lord (Īśvara) and the individual soul (jīva), be that which is denoted by the genitive case; nevertheless, the meaning of the nominative case—the unconditioned Brahman—is not present there, because the application of words to it has been refuted.
Anticipating this doubt, he asserts the occurrence of the word "satya" (the Real) there through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā): "Of the indefinable," etc. (245).
Reality consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, [comprising] the vital breaths and so forth in their forms as effects.
For him as well, that which has been determined as "it does not go" is the supreme truth.
He states the intended meaning of the nominative case by restating the sense of the genitive: "mūrta" (embodied), etc. || 246 ||
For these have no reality apart from the objects already described.
Nor is there any unreality in them; therefore, their supreme state is the Truth.

This is because it is taught that knowledge arises from renunciation. Thus, it is established that renunciation is an ancillary part of knowledge. Therefore, having placed knowledge at the forefront, a wise person should renounce in this world. This is the meaning.
