Thus [ends the section]. || 32 ||
1. And the Self... 2. ...the followers of Śiva. 30. 3. ...not here. 6. [Vol. 2, page 746] 1040 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter—]
And by means of speech and actions, O Noble One, throughout many births in the cycle of existence.
The one of purified soul indeed attains liberation in the first stage of life.
Anticipating the objection that this statement concerns the renunciation of stages (krama-saṃnyāsa), he says: "By those who have cultivated [the mind]" (bhāvitaiḥ). || 33 ||
But for the wise man who has attained that [state] and is liberated, having seen the goal, [there is no further rebirth].
Among the three stages of life (āśramas), which would be the true goal for one who desires the supreme?

Anticipating the objection that even for one who has gone forth as a renunciant from the very practice of *brahmacarya*, there might again be a return to the life of a householder or other stages by his own desire, he says:
And there are thousands of such accounts in the Purāṇas and Smṛtis regarding this matter.
The texts that establish renunciation exist as direct perception itself. || 35 ||

He concludes the proof by stating that there are numerous scriptural passages (*śruti*) which serve as the source for the Smṛtis that provide authority for the fact that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is an auxiliary to knowledge (*jñāna*). [Thus he says: "The scriptural passages... (35).
Alternatively, it was previously stated that the term "Brahman" has its primary meaning in the perception of Being (sat).
Thus, it is maintained that the primary meaning of the word "Self" refers to Brahman. (36)

Having stated that the Brāhmaṇa is intended to enjoin renunciation as an aid either to the nature of knowledge or to its fruit, [the author] restates the meaning of the preceding Brāhmaṇa with the desire to explain a different point: "The primary," etc. This means that the import of the word *tat* (That) has been enjoined as extending up to the import of the word *tvam* (Thou).
He summarizes the meaning of the forthcoming Brāhmaṇa: "Now," etc. The import of the word *tvam* as extending up to the import of the word *tat* will be stated immediately thereafter.
This is the meaning. || 36 ||
Then, there is the realization "This is that" regarding those two things denoted by the terms Brahman and Ātman.
The entire essence of the meaning of the Madhu-kāṇḍa is established by means of this statement. || 37 ||

Raising the objection, "If the meaning of the two Brāhmaṇas is exhausted by the meanings of the individual words, then by what is the meaning of the sentence expressed?", he says, "By the Madhu-Brāhmaṇa. The connection is: "by the sentence beginning with 'That this Brahman is without prior... This means that the primary denotations of the words "Brahman" and so forth—referring to their respective implied (lakṣya) meanings—are [unified]. The sense is that the entire essence of the Madhu section is non-duality (aikya). || 37 ||
Therefore, the Śruti itself [provides] for the arising of the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self.
Desiring to practice renunciation in this world, Maitreyī begins [to speak]. || 38 ||

Having explained the matter for the sake of the Brahmins in various ways, he introduces the Brāhmaṇa passage—while maintaining the position that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is an auxiliary to knowledge (jñāna)—by setting forth a narrative (ākhyāyikā) for the sake of easy comprehension. [The word] "pratyak" [is used]; the word "ataḥ" is intended to refer back to the fact that renunciation is an auxiliary to knowledge; and the word "iha" indicates the discourse concerning one who is dispassionate. || 38 ||
For renunciation is prescribed in the Śruti as being preceded by the permission of one's wife and others.
Therefore, for the sake of granting permission, the Sage spoke thus to Maitreyī regarding himself. (39)
[Vol. 2, Page 747] 4 Brāhmaṇam. Accompanied by Ānandagiri’s sub-commentary, the Śāstraprakāśikā. 1041.
Having raised the doubt as to why the sage, being detached, addressed his wife at the time of indifference, the following is the purpose of that address:

He states the intended meaning [of the text] with the words "wife, etc. By the word *saṃnyāsa*, the gradual renunciation (*krama-saṃnyāsa*) is understood. Having obtained the permission of his mother, father, wife, sons, friends, and kinsmen, as well as all those who are his officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and having performed the *vaiśvānara* sacrifice as before, he should give away his entire property; thus [the author] quotes the *Kauṣītaki Śruti*. With the words "in the Śruti," he completes what was required by the particle *hi*. Therefore...
Thus [ends the verse]. 39.
Or rather, one who is about to depart from this station characterized by the householder's life.
"You ought to grant me permission for renunciation, as I desire to perform it."
He explains the words of the seer: "Intending to depart. To counter the wife's apprehension—"Let it be; what is to be done by me in that regard?"—he says: "Those who desire to act. (40)
"You have spoken rightly; you wish to do what is appropriate for us."
Since this is the case, quickly instruct me as to what must be done. || 41 ||
He provides the introductory context for the words beginning with "Hanta" (Well then). "It is fitting" means it is appropriate for your knowledge, your age, and the place and time;
this is the completion of the sentence. The ellipsis to be supplied is "it must be done by me. || 41 ||
Then, having been granted permission, he spoke these further words to her, beginning with "Hanta."
"I shall make a division of property for you with your co-wife Kātyāyanī."

Having introduced the passage beginning with "Hanta," he explains it: "Anujñātaḥ" (Permitted). The word "atha" indicates that the permission is the cause for the subsequent engagement in the following statement. || 42 ||
A woman who is destitute, when appointed by a wealthy man to the performance of duties, [is considered equal to him].
Since I have gone forth into homelessness, there can be no further union of purpose between you two.
[The opponent objects: "If you indeed intend to renounce the world, then let it be done; why do you seek a separation from us by dividing our property?
We ourselves shall divide the property and effect the separation after your renunciation. To this, he replies with the verse beginning with *niḥsva*:
"Wife, son, and slave—these three are declared to be without property."
"Whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong; that is his wealth."
This is the meaning of the traditional authority (smṛti). How, then, is she entitled to perform ritual action? To this he replies: "as one who possesses property" (svavatī). || 43 ||
Formerly, [this] was indeed entrusted by you two to me; now it is [returned] by me to yourselves.
"Let us divide [the property]," his wife urged him. || 44 ||
Anticipating the objection that even for you, who are dispassionate and have renounced, the state of being destitute is the same, he says: "Possessing [his own]. (44)
Having shared one's own means with others through various modes of livelihood, one should renounce; thus it is enjoined.
For it is on the basis of that scripture that this classification is being made by me.
Even though he was our master prior to his renunciation, we who desire to perform that [rite] must not effect a division of the property between us two.
Anticipating the objection that there might be an absence of a specific rule, the author clarifies what was stated by the word "by him" (*tena*) with the phrase "by means of functions" (*vṛttibhiḥ*).
The meaning is that the scriptural injunction—"having distributed them among corresponding functions, one should renounce"—is the regulating authority in this matter. || 49 ||
It is fitting that you have resolved not to give away this wealth.
Your wealth, consisting of the essence of renunciation, brings about the welfare of others.
In that regard, Maitreyī says: "It is fitting. The reason for this is: "Because you... (46).
For whom is association with those of great majesty not a cause of supreme benefit?
Even impure water, having reached the Gaṅgā, attains purity. || 47 ||

[The opponent objects: "Surely, you have no right to wealth for the sake of accomplishing your own welfare, because women, being of sinful birth, are a heap of impurity; for the Smṛti says: 'Women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras are of sinful birth. Therefore, wealth that brings about your welfare should not be given to you. To this, he replies: "O Mahānubhāvā! [He provides] an illustration regarding the fact that association with great souls is a cause of excellence.
He said: "It is impure. || 47 ||
There is no other human goal than union with the Blessed One, because of its immortality.
Therefore, I ask: how might wealth be a means for attaining immortality? (48)

He introduces the verse beginning with "yamviti" by saying "bhagavaditi. The construction is as follows: since it appears to me that there is no human goal other than liberation (mokṣa) solely through connection with You, I ask You how wealth could possibly be a means to that liberation. || 48 ||
Even if this entire earth were filled with wealth as its very essence, it would not suffice.
By that much alone, would I become immortal? Or would I not? Let it be told as it truly is. (49)
Clarifying the very question, he connects the statement with the word "by the essence" (sāreṇa). || 49 ||
For wealth does not truly benefit the wealthy by its mere existence.
Since they are beneficial by way of action, therefore action is being inquired about.

Anticipating the objection—"How can the Bhāṣya statement 'the earth [is purified] by ritual action accomplished with abundant wealth' be consistent, given that there is the perception of the question: 'Is wealth a means to liberation or not?'"—he says: "With that... (sasa iti). || 10 ||
Being questioned, he replied to his wife: "Immortality does not come from wealth. (51)
If this wealth leads to immortality, why do you wish to give it away?
Thus questioned, he spoke of the purpose for which wealth is acquired.
He states the meaning of "not so" and the rest with the words "he replies. He introduces [the next passage] beginning with "just as," preceded by a sense of inquiry, with the words "if wealth.
Just as the life of men depends upon perishable means,
so too your life, through your wealth, does not consist of the nature of immortality.
He explains this with the words: "In perishable things," etc. (53).
1 21° 1 [vol2, page 749] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1043
"Since immortality results from knowledge alone through the total destruction of ignorance."
There is not even a hope for immortality through ritual action accomplished by means of wealth.
He explains the passage beginning with "of immortality" and so forth as follows: "ignorance. || 54 ||
How can the attainment of immortality come about through knowledge alone as its sole cause?
Action is not the cause of liberation, nor is fire the remedy for heat.
Birth is determined by karmas; and if there is birth, how can there be sustenance through these [karmas]? (55)
He establishes the stated point by means of a question: "Why? He clarifies that actions are contrary to liberation with the words: "From actions. (59)
The activity of the virtuous is beneficial by its very nature.
If [he is so] even toward a person who has done him harm, how much more so toward his own devotees? || 56 ||
Demonstrating a censure against that [position], he states a general principle: "From its own nature," etc. (56).
Surely this must be my own fault, that even you have acted thus toward me.
They wish to act in opposition; who else could be a benefactor to me? (57)

This suggests his suspicion that he himself might have committed some offense against his own domain. The word "nūnam" (surely) implies that even though they are bestowers of grace upon all beings, [he suspects otherwise]. Anticipating the doubt—"If we desire to act unfavorably toward you, then go to someone else who acts favorably toward you"—he asks: "Who? (verse 57).
How can you bind me with wealth— me, who am devoted, beloved, and virtuous?
And those like you renounce the world without having brought about the destruction of desire. || 58 ||
Fearing that the time for our renunciation has arrived and that there is no longer an opportunity to act for your benefit, he says: "Anuraktām" (to her who is devoted). || 58 ||
If this immortality were something to be attained through deliberation, then the desire to abandon it would not be logical.
"Immortality might come from wealth; tell me, what would that do for me? (59).

Anticipating the objection—namely, "Is this very wealth being given to you not itself the means to immortality? What need is there for another means?"—he states the intended meaning of the verse beginning with "yena" (by which), starting with "vittāt" (from wealth).
Anticipating the further objection—"By that [wealth] I shall not attain immortality"—and thus expressing a desire to renounce it, he says "vittā-" (from wealth...).
Thus [it is said]. || 19 ||
If you have such a desire to favor me, or if compassion for me is intended;
Whatever the Blessed One knows, with that please share with me.

Having brought her husband under her control through reproach and reasoning, she displays her discipline. As for the word "yadi" (if): the ellipsis is "share [the wealth] from the presence of your co-wife Kātyāyanī. || 60 ||
1 kha. ga. *tukā* | na | 2 ga. *mura* | 3 ka. *nyasyanti* | [vol2, page 750] 1044 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter—]
By virtue of which knowledge, having completely abandoned all means of wealth and resources, [one attains liberation].
You desire sovereign power; therefore, grant that very wealth to me.
Anticipating the objection, "I too do not possess the knowledge that is the means to liberation; how then can it be given? he says: "That which... (verse 61).
For that wealth of which neither beginning nor middle nor end exists.
Wealth does not go to waste; let that very same treasure be given away. || 62 ||
Anticipating the objection that "it is impossible for me to give you my own means of knowledge because it would result in its depletion," he says: "Not beginningless" (nādiḥ). || 62 ||
For you possess infinite wealth; how could that which is infinite be given away?
What kind of gift can there be for that which is non-existent? Therefore, let that which exists be given. || 63 ||

Furthermore, since your wealth is finite, you are not able to give it to me; because it does not exist for you, there can be no gift of what is non-existent, like a flower in the sky—thus he says, "Ananta. Therefore, he states the resulting conclusion: "Let knowledge alone be imparted to me"—thus [he says], "Sadeva" (Being alone). || 63 ||
For one whose self has not yet emerged from the worldly pursuits of saṃsāra, [there is no liberation].
This knowledge, which is the sole means to liberation, can be given by me;
yet, fearing that you might lack the desire for liberation, it was intended to be bestowed upon you [only after such a desire arose].
"You are disenchanted with saṃsāra; receive the unsurpassed nectar. || 65 ||

He said: [the author] states the purport of this [passage] as "saṃsāra... etc. Since one who is not dispassionate has no inclination toward the knowledge that is the cause of liberation, there arises the doubt of a lack of qualification because of the absence of dispassion, and thus a lack of the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutā*). To address this, the meaning is: "I merely wish to give you wealth for the sake of my own livelihood. Then, suspecting that she might become qualified for knowledge due to her desire for liberation by thinking, "Therefore, I am dispassionate," he says:
"From saṃsāra," [thus it is said]. 64 || 65 ||
You do not speak words that are contrary to what is appropriate for women.
As before, you continue even now to speak what is agreeable to me. || 66 ||

He states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "O beloved" (*priye*) as follows: "Of women. For this is the speech appropriate for women: words that are favorable toward their husband. As they have said:
Whether he is of bad character, addicted to sensual desires, or devoid of virtues,
a husband must always be honored by his wife like a god.
"A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, whether he be living or dead, should never do anything disagreeable.
Thus, you speak even regarding the state of liberation as if it were the state of worldly existence; you do not transgress the established doctrine by speaking contrary to it.
The meaning is that he joins the path. || 66 ||
All beings, even those born together with him, abandon a man who is going toward liberation.
Because of your excessive devotion, you do not wish to abandon me even for the sake of liberation.
[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled *Śākhaprakāśikā*:
"She who is the wife is indeed half of one's own self," according to this Vedic scripture; therefore, I am always your innate companion and favorable to you, so do not be adverse toward me.
Anticipating the objection that this might lead to worldly talk, he says: "Liberation. || 67 ||
As if unable to endure separation because of my great affection.
Do you wish to follow Muktā, desiring to attain identity with me alone? || 68 ||
He says: "Not only do you not wish to abandon me, but out of a desire to attain me, you follow me even into liberation.
Regarding the word *vibhāgam*: it means "not enduring," that is, "unable to bear. The elision of the letter *s* in the verbal form is a Vedic archaism. ||68||
Due to excessive affection, Umā was drawn away and took refuge in the other half of the body of the one who suffers from pain.
But you desire to measure me, the complete Self, with your entire being.
He says that your excellence is not only over all ordinary men and women, but even over Pārvatī herself: "Excessive affection," etc. (69).
Since this is so, I shall therefore describe to you the means for attaining the immortal.
Therefore, reflect upon that which I am explaining with your mind.

By explaining the passage beginning with "O beloved," it was stated that the praise directed toward her was intended by the husband, who was pleased upon seeing her dispassion (*vairāgya*). Now, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "Come here" (*ehi*): "Since" (*yataḥ*). Since both your dispassion and desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*) are observed to be just like mine, I shall therefore speak of the means to liberation—knowledge—preceded by an expression of that dispassion; and as I am explaining that, my speech concerning that subject [is intended].
Having taken hold of a one-pointed mind, you desire to meditate with certainty upon the meaning; that is to say, because the meaning is profound. || 70 ||
One whose intellect is purified does not become dispassionate toward this cycle of existence, even up to the level of Brahmā.
For as long as that is not the case, a person shall not be qualified for knowledge.
Showing the purport of the passage beginning with "Verily, she is not [the husband's]," he states that one who is not dispassionate lacks the qualification for knowledge: "Up to Brahman.
Even though this is a cause for dispassion, one who is attached to it does so because of its being a cause for dharma and other such goals.
Therefore, one whose self is purified by action becomes dispassionate toward this worldly existence.

Anticipating the objection that—since bondage has a nature that vanishes as soon as it is seen, and since there is thus no cause for attachment to it—dispassion (*vairāgya*) is established by itself, making the scripture that teaches it redundant—he says: "Dispassion... (verse 72).
Therefore, this scripture [teaches] with effort the causes of detachment within saṃsāra.
He began to speak with the reasoning, "Or rather, no. || 73 ||

Since a person is attached to the cycle of transmigratory existence due to the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma and its enjoyment, this Śruti proceeds with the primary intent of explaining—through the passage beginning with "Not this, not that" (*neti neti*)—the causes of that [attachment], such as its perishability, in order to establish detachment (*vairāgya*) in those of purified intellect by means of [the performance of] karmas.
It introduces the Śruti thus. The word "for" (*hi*) indicates the necessity of understanding those causes for the sake of attaining detachment.
1046 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]:
"In that very thing where supreme attachment exists, there is likewise disregard for everything else."
Having performed an action with supreme effort, one seeks the fruit from another.

In order to establish dispassion through pure understanding, the worthlessness of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) is being described. Anticipating the question, "In what manner must actions be performed so that they produce purity?", he says: "In which... etc. In that [world] such as heaven where the transmigrating soul has excessive attachment, one should perform obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*) and the like with the intellect dedicated to the Lord, in such a way that there is a lack of regard for the incidental purity resulting from the performance of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*).

The meaning is that, having performed [the duties], having become pure-minded, and being dispassionate while desiring the unsurpassed fruit of knowledge, one becomes a seeker of Brahman (brahmajijñāsu). || 74 ||
Just as one does not obtain the juice of sugarcane without pressing it, so too [one does not obtain the goal] without exertion.
However, the mental impression arising from intense suffering persists only for as long as it endures in the consciousness.
Its opposite is pleasure, which is indeed slight; when that [pleasure] perishes, there is destruction. || 76 ||

Anticipating the objection that even through the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) and so forth, the desire to know Brahman (*brahma-vividiṣā*) does not arise for people like us because it is not observed in such cases, he says:

"Why? Just as a person pressing sugarcane in a machine obtains its juice, so too one who performs obligatory rites and the like with the intention of offering them to the Lord obtains the fruit of those actions—namely, the desire to know—in this world or the next, according to such scriptural texts as "by whatever means [one may attain it]."

This is the meaning. [The author] states this with the intention that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) does not arise through purification resulting from the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) and so forth, because detachment (*vairāgya*) is impossible as long as pleasure is perceived even within *saṃsāra*.

He says: "Intense... and so on. The exertion involved in performing the means for pleasure is intense suffering; as long as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) born thereof persists in the intellect, sensual pleasure—which is the opposite of that suffering—continues to exist. That [pleasure] is slight, and it perishes when the suffering ceases, being inseparable from it.
The meaning is that since it is devoid of essence, it is appropriate to cultivate detachment toward it. || 75 || 76 ||
In summer, little cold is pleasant; in winter, little heat is pleasant.
That very [suffering] causes suffering, because there is no finality in its causes. || 77 ||

Furthermore, because the causes of pleasure and pain are not constant, pleasure—along with pain—is accompanied by its own causes and is therefore not to be sought; thus he states another reason for dispassion: "Cold," etc. He states the reason for the non-constancy of the causes of pleasure and pain: "Because of their causes," etc.
This means that there is no fixed rule regarding the times of the emergence and non-emergence of those two causes, namely *dharma* and *adharma*. || 77 ||
In this world, there is no sound that is inherently pleasant or unpleasant by its own nature.
Attachment and aversion of the mind are the cause of the pleasant and unpleasant aspects of objects such as sound. (78)

Anticipating the objection that there must be a fixed determination of the causes for the fact that some objects such as sound are pleasant while others are the opposite, he says: "The sound exists. To the question, "How then is the perception of this fixed determination possible? he replies: "Attached," etc. It is the mind, defiled by passion and the like through the prior superimposition of beauty or ugliness upon sound and other objects, that is the cause for the perception of them as pleasant and so forth.
This is the meaning. || 78 ||
Everything is by its own nature unpleasant and non-self, because it arises from causes that are themselves unpleasant and non-self.
Because it causes inward delight, even that which is unpleasant is considered pleasant.

It has been stated that neither dearness nor lack of dearness exists inherently in non-self-objects; now, it is explained that because they are born from the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the inner self (*pratyak*), they do not exist inherently in them. [Vol. 2, Page 753] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1047. It has been stated that neither dearness nor lack of dearness exists inherently in non-self-objects; now, because they are born from the ignorance of the inner self, they do not exist inherently in them.
He states that [the Self] is dear by saying "by itself" (*svataḥ*). Having stated that dearness arises from the superimposition of excellence, he states another reason: "the inner self" (*pratyak*).

According to the reasoning previously mentioned, even though the non-self (*anātman*) is not dear by itself, it is treated as dear because it is the object of a mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) that manifests the bliss which constitutes the nature of the inner conscious Self (*pratyak-cit-svarūpa*). This is the meaning. || 79 ||
Everything, beginning with one's wife, is unpleasant by its very nature, causing suffering from beginning to end.
Because of that cause—the self's own pleasure—a wife and so forth are called "dear. (80)

He states another reason for the fact that things which are by nature non-self are not dear: "The wife and so forth. Then, raising the doubt as to how there can be a notion of dearness toward them, he clarifies what was stated—that it is because they cause delight to the inner self—with the words: "Because of that cause" (taddhetoḥ). || 80 ||
In no state whatsoever is the self considered unpleasant to anyone in this world.
Just as one's wife and others, whether beloved or unloved, are repeatedly seen to be non-self; || 81 ||

Anticipating the objection that even the self’s state of being dear is not constant—since one is sometimes seen to desire its destruction—the author says "No," and so forth. The meaning is that because the love for one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is never absent even when one afflicted by disease and the like desires the destruction of the body, the self is of the nature of bliss (*sukha*). The word *apriyaḥ* should be read as a separate term [in the verse]. In that regard, he provides a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) for the rule regarding this love: "dear... [and so on].
Thus [ends verse] 81.
For the non-self is inherently unpleasant, precisely because it serves as a means for achieving the pleasure of the self.
Through devotion, even a paramour may become as dear to a harlot as her own husband and kin. || 82 ||
If it is argued that [the self] is not dear in itself, then it cannot be dear even as the object of the self, because one thing cannot possess the nature of another; anticipating this doubt, he says:

"In itself" (*svataḥ*). The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that we observe the figurative usage of "fire" applied to a boy who, though not fire in himself, is treated as such due to his connection with its qualities. A *bandhakī* is a cause of bondage, that is to say, an unchaste woman. For it has been said:
*Puṃścalī*, *dharṣaṇī*, *bandhakī*, *asatī*, *kulaṭā*, and *itvarī* [denote an unchaste woman]. Even when *vardhakī* is read in place of [one of these], the meaning remains the same. || 82 ||
Since joy arises spontaneously from within oneself, it is therefore without external cause.
Having abandoned the secondary beloved, one should resort to the primary beloved.
Having established that the self is dear by its own nature and that which is not the self is not dear by its own nature, he states the resulting conclusion: "without cause," etc. (verse 83).
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall.
Unions end in separation, and life ends in death. || 84 ||
Furthermore, because Vedavyāsa has stated that both sensual pleasure and its causes are unstable, he says "kṣaya... (verse 84) to indicate that one should cultivate detachment toward them.
There is no such happiness in the world that does not become a source of suffering.
Because they cause unhappiness in the states of non-attainment, separation, and destruction. || 85 ||
2048 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]:
It was stated previously that even a small amount of pleasure is suffering because its cause brings about pain; now, he says that this [suffering] exists even in that [pleasure] itself.
"Not so," etc. (Verse 85).
If this is so, then whatever pleasure is produced by a means [of attainment] is considered [to be suffering].
Having renounced those entirely, one should take refuge in absolute happiness. || 86 ||

Let it be; what of it? To this he says: "If it were so. The construction is: if whatever pleasure exists whatsoever is considered to be caused by suffering, then that very [pleasure] is regarded as producing suffering. || 86 ||
Because this worldly happiness is, for the reasons stated, nothing but suffering.
Having extracted [the mind] from here and there, one should establish it in the West (the heart) alone with joy. || 87 ||

Regarding the concern that the attachment to the pleasure of sense objects—which is remembered as an "infallible attachment to sense objects" for those lacking discrimination—is therefore not to be rejected, he says: "pertaining to worldly existence" (*sāṃsārika*). This means that, for the reasons already stated, such as the fact that the manifold world of non-self (*anātma-prapañca*) is produced by delusion and so forth. The word *ataḥ* (therefore) is to be construed with the preceding ablative case. Consequently, [it refers to] worldly pleasure...
The examiner explains the process of eliciting the essential point. || 87 ||
Just as the staff and other attributes in a garland are caused solely by the cognition of the garland.
The husband, wife, son, and so forth, arise in this way from the cause of ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyag-ajñāna). (88)
He clarifies that this [universe] is indeed the effect of one's own ignorance by means of an illustration: "The body," etc. (88).
The cessation of all misfortune and the attainment of all joy.
If [liberation] occurs through mere knowledge of the Inner Self (pratīc), how could anything other than that be sought? || 89 ||

It is not only because it arises from ignorance that there is an absence of affection for the non-self; rather, since both types of human goals are accomplished through the mere cognition of the Self alone, one should abandon the non-self and cultivate affection for the Self alone. Thus he says: "All... (verse 89).
Depending on whose relationship, even that which is dear acts as if it were dear.

Even a friend becomes an enemy because of association with someone [else]. He says that [the desire for happiness] is properly directed toward that [Self alone], because it is the human goal by being the cause of the Self’s delight in what is not-self. Regarding the words "of whom" (yasya):
the meaning of the word "for" (hi) is that one observes a mass of iron pervaded by fire to take on the form of that [fire]. But as for the non-Self, it is not the cause of the Self’s delight—

He says, "Even though it is dear," [etc.], because since it possesses three causes, it does not constitute the supreme human goal (apumartha), it is therefore appropriate that one should feel no attachment toward it. || 90 ||
Having seen it, experience the reality of the two categories: the self and the non-self.
The desire to acquire and the desire to abandon, being produced by that [ignorance], should be maintained as such. || 91 ||

Validating his experience regarding the point already stated, he declares the conclusion: "Having seen," etc. The meaning is that, having experienced the true nature of the Self and the non-Self according to the method described, there arises in the Self a desire to acquire it—caused by the cognition of its being the supreme human goal—and a desire to abandon the other—caused by the cognition of its not being the supreme human goal. || 91 ||
1. Kha: yasyāssaṃ; 2. Kha: syate || 91 ||
Various kinds of attachment and clinging that he has toward external objects.
For the reasons stated above, one should establish everything facing westward. || 92 ||

He concludes the intermediate subject matter with the verse beginning "nāna" (not manifold). The meaning is that, for the reasons stated, the state of being the supreme human goal resides in the Self alone and nowhere else, and so forth. || 92 ||
A person remains as long as he is not weary of everything from the hells up to the world of Brahmā.
For the time being, there is no qualification for the path of the knowledge of liberation. || 93 ||

Having stated that detachment from what is non-self must be cultivated, he concludes that one devoid of this [detachment] lacks the qualification for knowledge (vidyā), beginning with the words "from hell. The construction is as follows: as long as a person has not become disillusioned with the entire cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), up to the realm of Brahmā, as if it were hell, so long does he lack the qualification for knowledge—the means to liberation. || 93 ||
Completely liberated from all attachments, he has liberation alone as his purpose.
Therefore, one who possesses passion is not qualified for the arising of the knowledge of the inner self.

He concludes the qualification for knowledge (vidyā) belonging to one who is dispassionate with the word "all. The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is that dispassion is conducive to the arising of knowledge, whereas attachment is opposed to it. || 94 ||
The self exists because it is established through direct perception; for therein lies the experience of the self itself.
Thus should the exposition of the objects of cognition be understood; that is valid cognition (pramā). 95.

The section of the text preceding the statement "one should see" (draṣṭavya), beginning with "Verily, not for the sake of the husband," has been explained. Now, he explains the meaning of the word *ātman* found in that very statement. He says: "The Self. He establishes the well-known usage of the word *ātman* as referring to the Inner Self (*pratīc*). He says: "Therein. Having stated the literal meaning, he states what is intended. He says: "Thus. He states the meaning of the word *draṣṭavya*. He says: "One should be seen."

The meaning is that what is intended here is that the Vedic vision is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which is the inner self (*pratīcyātman*). || 95 ||
First of all, this notion of a self arises spontaneously for everyone.
Therefore, that very cognition which [erroneously] apprehends "all is the Self" when it has not been attained is what is here enjoined. || 96 ||

The suffix -tavya has been understood as being injunctive; it enjoins either the perception of the self as established in common worldly usage, or the knowledge that "Brahman is the Self. Having thus raised this alternative, the proponent of injunction (vidhivādin) refutes the first with the words "the Self [is already known]. He accepts the second with the words "not [already] attained" (aprāpta). || 96 ||
When there is indeed a distinction between the seer and the seen, it is in this way that cognition is established.
Since an injunction is not possible when there is no distinction between the person to be enjoined and the object [of the action], [it follows that it does not apply here]. || 97 ||

The proponent of the final conclusion (siddhāntin) says: "The seer," etc. The meaning is that [the injunction] is not applicable when the identity of Brahman as the Self is unknown, because there would be no object for the injunction; nor is it applicable when that knowledge is already known, because there would be an absence of distinctions such as the person to be enjoined (niyojya). || 97 ||
The names and so forth increase progressively, each subsequent one being greater than the preceding, according to their respective order.
Having introduced the true nature of the Self, the Śruti proclaimed that very reality.
132 1 Who are you?
[vol2, page 756]
1050 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter:

Once the identity of Brahman and the Self is known, the scripture establishes the absence of difference. Regarding the word "subsequent" (*uttareti*): having taken up the principles beginning with Name and ending with Breath, and without deviating from the order of recitation, it describes each subsequent principle as greater than each preceding one, and then [explains] their true nature.
The meaning is that the Śruti beginning with "But the Bhūman alone is to be desired to be known," which spoke of the mere Self designated by the word 'Bhūman,' has stated this. ||98||
And he himself established the definition of the Infinite (Bhūman) as that wherein nothing else exists.
Now, [the verse] beginning with "atha yatra" provides the definition of both the minor [offense] and that which ends in death. || 99 ||

"Who is that Bhūman? To this he replies: "And of the Bhūman. Fearing that [the definition] might over-extend to Prāṇa and so forth, he says: "Now (atha). One *ca* (and) is for conjunction; the second is for the removal of doubt. || 99 ||
For by the phrase "Now, therefore," there is indeed the ascertainment that "I alone [am all]."
Having negated that which is not of the nature of the Self, there follows the negation of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 100 ||
By the statement beginning with "The Self alone," which brings about the realization of the perfect Brahman.
Therefore, there is no darkness that has not been dispelled, nor is there any knowledge that has not arisen.
In that way, misfortune does not cease, nor is happiness attained.
The completion of what is to be done and what is to be known arises from the awakening to the true nature of the inner self. || 102 ||

Having stated that the entire world, from name up to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is nothing but Brahman and that Brahman is non-dual—and therefore, because there is no distinction between the person to be enjoined and other factors, there can be no injunction—he states another reason for the absence of an injunction, beginning with "Now, therefore... (*athāto*). By means of the passage beginning "Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the *ahaṃkāra*," and so forth, one reaches the certainty that "I am indeed Brahman. Having thereby negated everything that is of the nature of the non-self, [the text continues]: "Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the Self" (*athāta ātmādeśaḥ*), meaning that the Self alone is the reality.

By the passage beginning with "dityādi," it is stated that through the realization of the non-dual Self (*advayātma-dhī*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is also sublated; therefore, the meaning is that one whose ego-sense has not been destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman is not fit for the performance of ritual injunctions. Indeed, the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) in the passage beginning with "ahamevādhastāt" is that the ego-sense, by virtue of being the Self of all, is unfit to be Brahman. He further states that not only is the ego-sense destroyed by the cognition of identity, but this constitutes the attainment of the entirety of human goals (*puruṣārtha*): "na... [etc.].
"From this knowledge"—that is to say, from that [knowledge]. He states its fruit in brief: "The effect," etc. || 100 || 101 ||
In all the Upaniṣads, it is thus [taught] that the subject and so forth are non-self.
The reality of each individual atom is heard [in scripture] along with its logical justification. (103)

He states the consensus of all the Upaniṣads regarding the meaning declared in the Chāndogya Śruti with the words "In all [Upaniṣads]. This means, for instance, in those beginning with "Brahman alone is this immortal," and so forth; that is to say, just as in the Chāndogya Śruti. By the phrase "supported by reasoning" (sopapattikam), he indicates the non-contradiction of the authority of the Śruti, which is strengthened by its auxiliary sciences (upakaraṇa). || 103 ||
Here too, by the statement "not this," that which is not of the nature of the inner self [is negated].
Having restated the [opponent's] position, he says: "Our Śruti declares that 'all is the Self. (104)
In that regard, he states the dialogue from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, beginning with "here" (iha). || 104 ||
There is no abiding of an object to be negated by way of either existence or non-existence.
Therefore, the Śruti has directly declared that everything is indeed the Self alone.
He states its purport: "bhāva... [verse 105]. This is from the *Brahmaṇa* 4, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1051.
No one whose mind has not emerged from its state [of absorption] perceives anything other than the inward-facing Self.
Even when emerged from that state, one perceives the self while indeed perceiving other things as well. || 106 ||

Having established that the Vedic texts (*brahmāṇi*) apply to one who is either ignorant or has known [the Self], and that they are dependent upon that [knowledge], he states another reason for the fact that the worldly knowledge of the Self is not something to be enjoined, beginning with the words "no" (*na*). "One whose mind is not withdrawn" (*avyutthitamanāḥ*) means one whose notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) does not function as having itself as its object;

that is to say, [he is one] for whom there is no injunction, because he lacks any knowledge other than that [of his own self]. This is the remainder [of the sense]. [This refers to] the state of the soul when it has withdrawn from the two-fold [worldly] condition.

The meaning is that [the self] is bound, i.e., possesses the notion of "I" regarding its own objects. Even with respect to such a person, there is no injunction; the remainder of the sense is that for him, the realization of his own nature is established even without an injunction. || 106 ||
Where there is independence for the agent, there the agent is enjoined.
Through positive and negative concomitance, one discriminates between the self and the non-self. || 107 ||

Having raised the doubt as to which [element] possesses the status of being enjoined by the suffix *tavya* when two cognitions of the self are not themselves subject to injunction, he states the general principle:
"Svātantryam" (independence). He states the object of the injunction in the present context: "Anvayeti" (through connection), with "vidhiḥ" (the injunction) being the understood remainder. || 107 ||
But for one who has understood the meaning of the words, there is simply ignorance of the meaning of the constituent parts.
Since an obstacle exists therein, one is enjoined to that [practice] for its removal. || 108 ||

Anticipating the objection—"What is the use of an injunction for the purification of word-meanings through syntactic connection (*anvaya*) and so forth, since that [sentence-meaning] is already known from the sentence itself?"—he says: "The word 'speech' (*vacas*)," etc. This means: when that [obstacle] is removed—that is, when the ignorance of word-meanings, which is an impediment to the cognition of the sentence-meaning, has been destroyed—it is by means of that injunction for the purification of word-meanings. || 108 ||
Having thus understood the meaning of the matter, I shall speak as I previously declared.
"Indeed, this was Brahman"—thus, by means of the reasoning that leads to oneness. (109)
One who is free from obstacles understands the meaning of a sentence directly from the sentence itself.
Because of the contemplation of the inner reality (pratyaktattva) which is neither excluded nor followed [by conceptual constructions]. || 110 ||

In that case, one might object: "Since the cognition of the sentence-meaning will be established through the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) and so forth of the word-meanings already known, what is the use of the sentence? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Thus. Just as the purification of word-meanings was described in the section on Brahman according to the logic following from [the realization of] unity, so too the qualified seeker—who has known the word-meanings, who has ascertained the meaning as being devoid of generality and particularity, and who is free from the obstacle called ignorance regarding that—[attains the goal] through the sentence.

O King, he understands the meaning of the statement because of his perfect intellect; that is to say, because there is no arising of [faults such as] pride or [logical defects like] lack of positive concomitance (anvaya) and so forth. || 109 || 110 ||
The realization of eternal liberation arises directly from the sentence alone.
And the cognition of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the recollection of the meanings of the individual words. || 111 ||
The meaning of a word is certainly remembered through positive and negative concomitance.
In this way, one realizes the self to be free from suffering and inactive. || 112 ||

He states the Bhāṣyakāra’s agreement regarding the point already mentioned: "Nitya... etc. Then, raising the objection—"In that case, why is there a purification of the word-meanings through [methods such as] *anvaya* and so forth?"—he replies: "Of the sentence-meaning... etc. He indicates the fruit of knowing that [sentence-meaning] with: "Thus... etc. The meaning is that, by means of the knowledge of the meanings of *tat* and *tvam*, when the sentence-meaning is known, the immutable reality remains as the remainder (*avaśiṣṭam*). || 111 || 112 ||
[vol2, page 758] 1052 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Adhyāya]:
"Because of the predominance of the non-self arising from the delusion regarding the Self, there is a continuity with darkness (*tamas*)."
In the past, the Self was indeed the Self prior to the arising of the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic sentences. (113)

One might object: "Even though the cognition of the meaning of words is the cause of the cognition of the sentence-meaning, that cognition does not depend on syntactic relation (*anvaya*) and so forth, because the cognition of the Self as 'I' is always established. Anticipating this doubt, he says: *pratyak* (the inward). The meaning is that prior to the knowledge of the sentence-meaning, the Self has known itself as qualified by the body and other such things arising from ignorance due to its connection with ignorance, and not as being fit for syntactic relation with the sentence-meaning. || 113 ||
Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance, one should seek the Self within that which is non-self.
Then, having withdrawn the self into the Self, one perceives that "the Self is everything. || 114 ||

Since he does not realize the pure Self without [the means of] positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, it follows that by means of those [means], having extracted the Self from the body and other such things and known it to abide in its own majesty, he experiences it through the statement "I am Brahman. This is what is stated in the phrase "by means of the nameless" (*anāmakena*). Here, the word *atha* (then) signifies the subsequent destruction of ignorance along with its effects, following the attainment of knowledge. || 114 ||
And because it makes known what was previously unknown, an injunction (vidhi) is therefore declared here.
And the arising of what has not yet arisen is not tenable, because there is no logical basis for it. || 115 ||

The injunction (*vidhi*) has been stated for the purification of word-meanings through the process of syntactic relation (*anvaya*) and so forth; now he says that there is no fault even in accepting an injunction for making known what was previously unknown regarding the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). He states the reason expressed by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) with the words "not previously known" (*ajñāta*). The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to provide an illustration based on the purification of word-meanings achieved through syntactic relation and so forth. He states the reason indicated by the word "therefore" as "not having [previously] engaged" (*apravṛtta*). || 115 ||
That which has no coming into being is eternal, or that which has the nature of being eternally existent.
It does not possess the quality of being produced, just as [the qualities of] fragrance and space do not belong to the body. || 116 ||

How is there an absence of injunction (*nyāyābhāva*) in that case? [The opponent might argue: "There is an injunction for either knowledge, or the object of knowledge, or both. Thinking that the first alternative is untenable because it has already been stated that an injunction is impossible whether ignorance remains or that ignorance has been known, [the author] states a general principle with an illustration in order to refute the second alternative: "It is eternal," etc. (Verse 116).
That which has its own origination and so forth from itself, or that which absolutely does not [have them], [is unarisen].

Because it is established independently of any action, that is said to be "self-established" (svataḥ-siddha). He applies this to the subject at hand [in the analogy]: "origination and so forth. That reality which is the Self (ātmavastu) does not possess origination and so forth inherently like a jar or similar objects, nor does it exist even through limiting conditions (upādhi) like space; therefore, its existence is independent of action and is self-established.

Therefore, the meaning is that there is no room for an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding that which already exists. Alternatively, "origination" (*utpatti*) is the beginning of an entity’s existence; thus, that which possesses existence by its own nature, and that which lacks existence altogether—such as space (*ākāśa*) and a sky-flower—are unfit for an injunction because they do not depend on action, whether they are inherently existent or non-existent. This is an elaboration of the previous point. || 117 ||
But that which is capable at the very beginning of arising depends upon a mere cause.
For it is that [consciousness] which brings about the manifestation of action there, thereby making it fruitful.
1. ...of the mind || 113 || 2. ...other [readings]; 3. ...from this; 4. ...from the self; 5.
...of the injunction; 6. ...the praise is logical.
[Vol. 2, page 759]

[Brāhmaṇa] Having raised the doubt as to what, then, is the injunction (*vidhi*), and intending to refer to action (*kriyā*), he states the relevant passage concerning it: "By way of origination... (*utpattyā*)—1053.1.

Regarding the word *dāvi*: the two words *yat* and *tat* have the sense of "result" (*phala*). "Action" (*karman*) refers to human effort (*puruṣavyāpāra*). The reason for this is given by the phrase "that which effects its manifestation.
The second occurrence of the word *tat* has "action" as its referent. || 118 ||
The effect would then be dependent upon the cause, because it derives its very existence from that cause.
No other cause is observed for what is another's duty or what is not to be done. || 119 ||

In order to refute the injunction regarding the self and its cognition, he states the accepted position: "The effect," etc. Regarding the stated point, he states the negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"Otherwise," etc. || 119 ||
The notion that "everything is the Self" must arise from the power of the object of cognition itself.
If that [cognition] were dependent on a cognizer, it would follow [the same status] as the cognition of fire in the world.

Nevertheless, he explains what occurs when there is an absence of injunction regarding the Self and the knowledge thereof, by saying "all. Since Brahman and the Self are not effects, they do not depend on an injunction; likewise, the cognition of them—arising from the force of valid means of knowledge and so forth—is not dependent on the person. Therefore, it is not something to be accomplished through human will and effort subject to an injunction. Anticipating the objection that the independence of that cognition from the person is unproven, he says:
Third: 120.
Therefore, because it does not depend on a person, there can be no injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self.
1. However, the activity of affirmation and so forth regarding this [object] is established because of its being that very reality. || 121 ||

Considering that the cognition of the Self does not possess the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—unlike a treasure found in the world of heaven—because it lacks the quality of being a delimiting factor (*paricchedakatva*), he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This means:

with respect to the Self and the knowledge thereof. Having established the impossibility of injunction (*vidhi*) regarding knowledge and so forth, he concludes the subject matter of injunction, which was described by the words "wherein there is independence," by saying: "From connection, etc. (*anvayādīti*). This means: of this operation consisting of connection and so forth. || 121 ||
Likewise, there are hearing, reflection, as well as tranquility, self-control, and so forth.
Whatever a person is capable of doing, that is what is prescribed for him. || 122 ||

He specifies that very [hearing] with the words "śravaṇam" (hearing). He clarifies this very point—that the activity of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth is enjoined because it does not depend on the person—with the words "pumān" (the person). || 122 ||
And since the fruit of all means of valid cognition consists in a specific, qualified experience.
And the fruit would not be something to be enjoined; therefore, this is not enjoined.

He states another reason for the fact that the Self cannot be an object of injunction: "viśiṣṭa... etc. The meaning is as follows: experience, which is the fruit of all means of knowledge and is characterized by reality, bliss, and so forth, is the very nature (svarūpa) of Brahman, the Self; and since a fruit—unlike heaven—does not require an injunction, the Self is not something to be enjoined. || 123 ||
That which may be a valid means of knowledge, an invalid means of knowledge, or a fallacious appearance of knowledge.
All of that indeed manifests as having the very form of consciousness.

In that very context, he states another argument: "The means of valid cognition," etc. The meaning is this: since all this—beginning with the means of valid cognition—is manifest within consciousness (*caitanya*), it appears as something superimposed (*kalpita*). Therefore, the reality of consciousness (*cid-vastu*), which is present everywhere as the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), is not subject to injunction (*vidhi-yogya*). || 124 ||
Though assuming various forms, it remains essentially of the nature of pure consciousness alone.
Among these, one is invariably concomitant with the probandum; the others are deviant. || 125 ||

In that very context, he states another reason: "Not manifold" (*nāna*). The meaning is that the existent reality, which is an undivided form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is thus the locus of various particularities;
therefore, that which is inherently devoid of particularity is not fit for injunction (*vidhi*). In that same context, he states another supporting argument: "The inner self" (*pratīcī*). The Self...

The consciousness of one's own nature (*svarūpacaitanya*) is of a single flavor and non-deviating; whereas the non-selfs (*anātman*), both in their own forms and mutually, are deviating. Therefore, the meaning is that there is never an injunction regarding their forms. || 125 ||
Even when there is deviation regarding the mother and other [objects], consciousness remains non-deviant.
But even though it exists throughout the entire world, it is nevertheless subject to deviation from others.

Anticipating the objection that self-consciousness (*ātma-caitanya*) is also subject to deviation during states such as deep sleep, he says: "mātrādi" (beginning with the mother). The meaning is: because it is the means of proving that [consciousness]. He states another reason for its non-deviation: "mithaḥ" (mutually). The meaning is: in the entire world, every non-self entity is seen to be mixed with others and is indeed subject to deviation in its own nature; therefore, the consciousness that proves them is itself non-deviant. || 126 ||
Even though true knowledge has arisen, it [remains obscured] due to the persistence of the sense of being a knower and so forth.
Therefore, prior to the awakening of men, that [reality] appears as if it were unarisen.

If the Self is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), then that knowledge is eternally established; thus, one might fear that injunctions for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth would be purposeless. Anticipating this, he says: "It has arisen. Although knowledge is eternally established in the inner self (*pratīci*), due to its association with the state of being a knower (*mātṛtva*) and the like, and due to the conceit of limitation, it appears as if unattained by everyone prior to the arising of knowledge through the enjoined hearing and other means; therefore, hearing and the rest must be performed according to scriptural injunction.
The meaning is "that which. || 127 ||
When it is directly elucidated by means of the path of reasoning as previously stated, [it is understood].
At that time, one considers the consciousness as already arisen, even though it had not yet arisen previously. || 128 ||

He states the fruit of that practice: "It is made manifest" (vyutpādyate). The meaning is this: when the referent of "thou" (tvaṃ-padārtha) is awakened as the non-dual Self by means of hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth—having abandoned the conceit born of the connection with being a mother and so on—one realizes: "Even previously, this knowledge was indeed attained as the Self itself, though it was veiled by Māyā; and that concealment has now been removed. || 128 ||
Even the notion that "nothing at all exists" is itself witnessed by its own subject.
How much more so, then, would the intellect of one who knows this be unwavering? || 129 ||

Anticipating the objection that intrinsic self-awareness (*svarūpajñāna*) is merely adventitious—since it is not observed prior to linguistic instruction (*vyutpādana*) and is observed after it—one says: "Witnessed by itself" (*svasākṣika*). The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that [self-awareness] is the means of establishing both the state of being knowledge and the state of not being knowledge. || 129 ||
"Self" is the designation of the object of knowledge; the word "vai" (indeed) is used here for the sake of recollecting that [object].
It is said that "one should see" means pervasion by the activity of valid cognition. || 130 ||
First of all, based on the requirements of the words, such a [meaning] arises here.
Is the direct experience resulting from sacred scripture in accordance with reality, or not? || 131 ||
1 ka. ga. tat | [vol2, page 761] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1055
When examined, experience is like the experience of silver in the case of mother-of-pearl.
Whether it be valid or invalid, [it depends] on the connection or lack of connection with the object of cognition (meyasaṃgati).

Having refuted the view that the sentence "draṣṭavya" (to be seen) has a prescriptive intent (vidhiparatva), he restates [the opponent's position] in order to reject the meaning struck down by the words: "ātme—" etc. "iha" refers to the statement of the sentence; "atra" refers to the stated object of cognition. He sets aside the superficial meaning with "yathā."

The meaning is that the cognition of distinctions such as the knower (*mātr*) and so forth with respect to the Brahman-Self, being perceived through the power of words, is false—just like the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl. Anticipating the objection that "even though the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl is false because it is sublated, the cognition of distinctions such as the knower is not false because it lacks such sublation," he states the point accepted by the disputants: "Valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇam*). A valid means of knowledge is that which makes known an object that is unsublated and not already known; that which makes known otherwise is invalid (*apramāṇa*).
This is the meaning. || 130 || 131 || 132 ||
In this case, the distinction between the subject (mātṛ) and the object (meyabheda) is not at all apprehended by the means of knowledge (miteḥ).
Since it is certain that the Self is the object accessible solely to the inward-turned intellect. || 133 ||

Let it be so; what has occurred in the present context? To this he says: "The knower," etc. Here, the phrase "in Brahman, which is the Self" is intended. The ellipsis is "because of its non-duality. The sense is that the object of dispute is false because it lacks authoritative evidence, like a commonly accepted [illusory] thing. He states another reason for the falsity of the notion of difference regarding the Self: "the inward," etc. Consciousness is the inward intellect (*pratyagdhi*), and [the Self] is cognizable by that alone.
The meaning is that since the self is determined to be self-luminous, the cognitions of "me" and so forth directed toward it are false. || 133 ||
If it is not the object of the inward-facing intellect, then this is not the Self, just like a jar or other such objects.
Consequently, it follows that this [world] must fall within the interval beginning with Brahmā and ending with him. || 134 ||

Anticipating the objection that the self-luminosity of the Self is unestablished, he says: "The inward cognition" (*pratyagdhī*). He states that if it were not the Self, it would result in its being merely imagined: "Brahmā and so forth" (*brahmādi*). || 134 ||
"The attainment [of an object] through the vision of a distinct perceiver does not apply to the Self, as it does to a jar or similar things."
And there is no pervasion when there is non-difference, precisely because of the reason that they are of one and the same nature. || 135 ||
As for the claim that there is a pervasion by the activity of the knower (*pramātṛkriyā*) and so forth, that too has been refuted by [the doctrine of] self-luminosity; thus he says: "By distinct...
Furthermore, regarding the pervasion of the Self's act of seeing, is it the Self itself that is the seer, or another? It is not the first; thus he says: "Not...".
The meaning of the reason is that the conclusion [of the act] occurs either as the object (*viṣayatvena*) or as the subject (*viṣayitvena*). || 135 ||
And there is no seer other than the Self, because of the negation of any other seer.
Moreover, in this world, no relationship of seer and seen exists between two distinct seers. (136)

He refutes the second [position] with the words "na ca" (nor). The ellipsis to be supplied is "because of such scriptural texts as 'There is nothing else but this'. Having granted the difference between the two perceivers, he says "na ca" (nor). The meaning is: there can be neither equality nor inequality between them; it cannot be the first [equality], because—as in the case of two lamps—it is impossible for them to stand in the relation of object and subject; nor can it be the other [inequality], because there is no evidence to establish the status of one as a subordinate quality and the other as the primary conscious entity. || 136 ||
A contradiction with action would arise for the seer in the act of perceiving his own self.
Because that [state] is eternally attained through such a view, there would follow the consequence of the injunction being purposeless. || 137 ||

Regarding the statement "it is the self alone that sees," he states another defect: "Action" (kriyā). In a single action, there would be both agency (*kartṛtva*) and the state of being a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*).
[End of Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika by Sureśvarācārya, Vol. 2, p. 762, verse 1056].

The meaning is that there is a contradiction because [the self] would have primacy as the object (*karman*). He states another fault in that very context: "Because of the perception of that" (*taddṛṣṭeḥ*). Since one's own perception of oneself by oneself is established at all times through its own independence even without an injunction, the injunction is of no use therein; such is the meaning. || 137 ||
Even when the transmigrating self is perceived, there is no purpose whatsoever [in such perception].
And this alone is our misfortune: the perception of a transmigrating self.

Anticipating the objection that even one’s own vision of oneself might require an injunction for its own production, the author refutes the first alternative—that such a vision belongs to a transmigratory being—by stating "saṃsārī" (the transmigrator). He further states "ayameva" (this very [one]) to show that not only would the injunction for seeing that [Self] be futile, but it would also lead to undesirable consequences. || 138 ||
Since anything other than that is unestablished, how could there be a perception of it?
Now, if this self is already well-known, why is the vision of it enjoined? (139)

He states another alternative: "of something other than that. Anticipating the objection that [the term] is not well-known from common worldly usage, he says "Now" (atha), [indicating its establishment] through the scriptures. || 139 ||
Since the seer, the seeing, and the seen are perceived through direct experience, there is no need for reliance on scripture.
If the self of the seer were distinct [from the body], it would be difficult to say that "the self is separate. (140)

He states another reason for the fact that the view of a transmigrating self cannot be subject to injunction: "Because it is [already] desired" (*iṣṭi*). The meaning is that regarding a matter already established in the world, that view does not depend upon scriptural injunction. Having raised the objection that since the Self is established as the seer in the world, there might be an injunction for that view, he says: "Of the seer" (*dṛṣṭuḥ*). The sense is that what is divided, like a jar, is not the Self. || 140 ||
And if the self were not established, there could be no establishment of transmigratory existence.
A relationship whose connection is not already established is never accepted anywhere. (141)
Even if that [Self] were indeed the Self, since it transcends hunger and so forth, one might suspect that the scriptural injunction applies only to the perception of it as something extraordinary;

anticipating this, he says "And not... The meaning is that because transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) is well-known to be dependent on another, the Self is also known by virtue of its connection to it.
The word "connection" refers to the sphere of transmigratory existence. || 141 ||
If there were no connection with a self, this cycle of existence would not be observed.
Tell me, from what cause has this desire for liberation arisen? || 142 ||

The Sāṃkhyas maintain that even though it resides in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it does not belong to the Self (*ātman*). To them, he replies with the words "If not" (*na cet*). The point is this:

if the Self were not subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*) would be impossible, because bondage and liberation must have a single locus. Nor can it be possible for these to occur in the Self through the medium of the intellect (*buddhi*), since that which is unattached (*asaṅga*) cannot be joined with such states; and if the connection were merely imagined (*kalpita*), it would result in the doctrine of Māyā. || 142 ||
The rule regarding falsehood is as lost as the birth of the son of a barren woman.
Likewise, this method does not apply to the direct perception of the mother-tantra.

The non-subservience of the cognitions of both the transmigrating and the non-transmigrating self is to be established; since the cognition of the self does not belong to a non-person (apuṃstantu), it is not subject to injunction, as this is observed [to be the case] elsewhere.
1. From [the word] "dṛṣṭa"; 2. from "ka. kṣaṇāt" || 143 ||
He establishes this by means of the subsequent [verse]: "anṛtatra... He states that even in the opposing case (vipakṣe), the deficiency of an injunction remains as it was: "mātra... etc.
The meaning is "because of its being eternally attained. || 143 ||
In the conjunction and disjunction of various constituent substances, the nature of the jar [remains].
The all-pervasiveness of space is eternal, because the power of space cannot be avoided.
Likewise, when there is a connection with external objects such as sound, or when there is a distinction [between them], [the cognition arises].
The connection with immediate consciousness is eternal, witnessed by the eternal Self.

Anticipating the objection that even in the absence of an original injunction (apūrvavidhi), there must be either a restrictive injunction (niyama) or an exclusive injunction (parisaṃkhyā), he states, by way of an illustration, the eternal attainment of the knowledge of the Self through the words beginning with "not manifold" (nāna). He provides the proof for its eternity in the verse beginning with "the eternal Self" (nityātmā). || 144 ||
Therefore, there is no possibility of an alternative view here in the realization of the identity of the Self.
Therefore, neither a restrictive injunction (niyama) nor an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā) is tenable on that account. || 146 ||

He states the fruit of its constant attainment: "Since," etc. According to the principle already stated, because there is constant attainment in the knowledge of the Self, there is no occasional attainment; therefore, there is no restrictive rule (*niyama*) here. A restrictive rule applies when there is the possibility of an alternative (*pākṣika-prasaṅga*); since that [alternative] is excluded by it, there is no exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) here either. This is the meaning. || 146 ||

Since it is established that [the term] "being" (sat) refers to that which exists, and since it is not possible for it to exist elsewhere than in that [Self], it follows by logical necessity that the authority [of scripture] regarding the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is exactly the same as that regarding the Upaniṣads.
Only the injunction [is authoritative] because it is independent; the literal expression of words is not so, because it is dependent. (147)

One might object: "Since knowledge arises from the word alone, even in the absence of an injunction, an injunction is required for the sake of its authority in producing that [knowledge]. To this, he replies with the words "karma" and so on. Just as in the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), only the injunctive sentence is the means of valid knowledge while everything else is employed as subordinate to it, so too in the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*), because the meaning of an injunction is incapable of being apprehended by any other means of knowledge, the sentence resting upon that [meaning]—such as "This Self" (*ayam ātmā*) and so forth—establishes independent authority.

However, an injunction that is devoid of a [corresponding] means of knowledge is not authoritative regarding its object, because that object is capable of being established by other means of knowledge; since that which rests upon it would then be dependent, the injunction exists in the Vedāntas solely for the sake of establishing their authority. This is the meaning. || 147 ||
Not so; for there is the realization of the true oneness of the self, which is not attained by any other means of knowledge.
The authority of the manifestation of the denotation is like that of a sentence which awakens one from sleep. || 148 ||

He replies to the claim that "the verbal testimony [of the Upaniṣads] lacks authority" by saying, "Not so. The meaning is that even though identity is established, because it lacks form and other such qualities, it is unfit for other means of knowledge; therefore, the sentence that conveys it [is authoritative]. || 148 ||
Validity is appropriate,
as in the case of awakening from sleep or worldly speech.
For it is maintained that the object of cognition is a reality consisting solely of the non-agent and the single self.
Because, apart from that, no exclusion from the means of valid cognition is obtained for anything else. || 149 ||

Anticipating the objection that identity cannot be the object of verbal expression or auditory perception because it is incompatible with the presence or absence of the states of "measuring" (mātrā) and so forth, he says: [The text continues: "Because of the non-occurrence... (akāra-vṛtteḥ).
1058 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Adhyāya]:

"It is called ‘Raka’" means that although the mother and so forth exist as entities, because they lack scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇikatva*), the reality denoted by the word "Tat" (That) is the immutable, single-flavored essence.
Since sound is one, it is therefore a synonym for sound.
For, apart from ignorance regarding the oneness of the self, there is no other obstacle whatsoever.
Since that which is dependent on injunctions is something to be accomplished, it has no power over what is not known.

In the Vedāntas, although there is no injunction for the sake of establishing authority, one might suspect that an injunction exists there because knowledge is required to destroy the veil between Brahman and the Self. Having raised this doubt, the author refutes the first alternative—namely, that the veil is something other than ignorance—by saying "having abandoned" (*muktvā*). The ellipsis is: "Having abandoned [the idea that] there is no injunction regarding knowledge for the sake of destroying that [veil]. He addresses the second alternative—that the veil is ignorance itself—by saying "injunction" (*vidhi*). If it is ignorance...
The meaning is that, at that time, because their intellects are dependent on inference, they lack validity; therefore, they are not capable of refuting it. || 150 ||
Struck by darkness, she abandoned the knowledge of the reality of the self as it truly exists.
Since there is no other cause for this, therefore the injunction is not a means of valid cognition regarding the three [Vedas].

If it is asked what, then, is the remover of this ignorance, he says: "Just as... Since even the purpose of destroying the obstruction is impossible through injunction, he states the resulting conclusion: "Because... || 111 ||
Furthermore, the lack of autonomy in the person to be enjoined implies the correctness of their cognition.
Because it has the object of cognition as its sole cause, it could not possibly possess the nature of a cognizer. (152)

Anticipating the objection that it is incorrect to say [the scripture] does not destroy ignorance because the injunctional system lacks authority—since authority is attributed to the enjoined knowledge by an intelligent person—the author says: "Of the one to be enjoined" (niyojyasya). Then he states what causes the correctness of that cognition: "It does not perish" (naśyati) || 152 ||
Just as there is independence for an injunction, so too is there independence for the expressive scripture within the Vedāntas.
Likewise, that which is beyond the senses [is established] due to the commonality of not being subject to human composition. || 153 ||

Regarding the objection that the scriptural statement [of Brahman] is not authoritative because it has an already established object (*siddhārtha*) and is thus dependent [on other means of knowledge], he replies with the word "vidheḥ" (of the injunction). He states the reason for the equality of independence between the sentences concerning ritual action and those concerning knowledge with the words "anṛtatva... (unreality...). Furthermore, he states another reason—namely, that it makes known an object incapable of being apprehended by other means of knowledge—just as [the Veda] is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), with the word "tathā" (so too). || 153 ||
That which is not an object of the senses and so forth is not established by its own nature, and therefore it is not proven by any means of knowledge.
This denotation, while making [the object] known, does not depend on anything else.

Anticipating the objection that, like the earth and other elements, the Brahman-Self must also be accessible through other means of knowledge (māna), and therefore how it can be considered beyond the senses (atīndriya), he says: "akṣādī" and so forth. The meaning is that Brahman—being devoid of form and other qualities, self-luminous, independent of any means of proof, and unfit for perception and other such means—is the subject of the scriptural texts (abhidhā-śruti) which declare it, and these texts do not depend upon injunctions (vidhi). || 114 ||
Therefore, the authority of an injunction lies in its communication of both the goal to be accomplished and the means for its accomplishment.
Because that which is beyond the senses cannot be known by anything other than that [supersensory means]. || 155 ||
Procedure [vol2, page 765]
[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

1059. Since the authority of an injunction (*vidhi*) is not accepted regarding an already established fact, and since its authority has been refuted in relation to a mandate (*niyoga*), he states as a corollary that its validity belongs only to that which is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*). He says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*); for the means to a desired end is obtained even without an injunction.

Anticipating the objection that its authority lies therein, he says: "by something other than that. The remainder of the sense is that, therefore, authority resides solely in the injunction regarding the means for accomplishing the desired end. || 155 ||
Just as the relationship between the probandum and the probans cannot be expressed by means of verbal denotation.
Likewise, that which is established by itself cannot be brought about through the word of an injunction.
