Anticipating the objection that "the subject under dispute is established by scriptural injunction because it is the meaning of a scripture, like the Agnihotra," he says: "sādhyā... The sense is that the inference is contradicted by the verbal testimony of the Śruti, which provides an uncontradicted, certain, and non-doubtful cognition regarding Brahman. || 116 ||
Since the unity of the self is established by itself, it does not depend upon action.
And consequently, there is an absence of cultivation because cultivation depends upon action. (157)
And in the absence of meditative cultivation, the injunction has no authority there.
The status of expression as a means of valid cognition, however, arises from its capacity to convey an object already established by itself.

Having established that [the object] is already accomplished and existent, he states another reason for this: "Of the identity" (*aikātmyasya*). The meaning is as follows: where there is action, there is productive activity (*bhāvanā*), because the latter has action as its object to be accomplished; and where that [productive activity] exists, there is an injunction (*vidhi*). However, since neither action nor the like exists in the case of an accomplished entity, there is no authority for an injunction therein. Anticipating the objection that even verbal expression (*abhidhā*) might be an authority there—on the grounds that it is a Vedic statement just like those [other accepted ones]—he says:
"From itself" || 157 || 158 ||
If it is argued that verbal expression is not a valid means of knowledge because it is dependent [on other factors], provided it functions according to the worldly path;
Direct designation, such as "That thou art," is like the statement regarding fruits on the bank of a river. (159)
Even though the objection has already been answered, he raises it again by means of an analogy: "Because of its dependence. He clarifies that very point with the word "denotation" (abhidhā).
The connection is as follows: denotation, such as [the Mahāvākya] "That thou art," is not a valid means of knowledge because of its dependence. || 159 ||
Furthermore, the combination of words is untenable when there is the direct hearing of their denotative power.
Because a collection of words everywhere has as its cause a verb-form. || 160 ||
He states that in the Vedāntas, an injunction (vidhi) serves not only for the sake of establishing authority, but also for the sake of the mutual syntactic connection (anvaya) of the words:
"In combination," etc. (160).
The collection of words would indeed exist simply because of the presence of verbal forms.
In this context, when the verbal root is heard in its denotation, there certainly exists a verbal suffix such as *asmi* (the present indicative).

He refutes the claim that "the injunction [is established] for the sake of connecting the words" by saying "no. Then, anticipating the objection that "in that case, by the occurrence of the word 'injunction,' our own position is attained," he says "it is not," etc. The word "etcetera" (ādi) is intended to include such expressions as "he knows" (veda) and "it becomes" (bhavati). || 169 ||
"Because of the scriptural statement, there is a logical expectation that 'fruits [are to be eaten] on the riverbank.'"
Because it is apprehended by the means of direct perception, and because there is a connection with the fruit, the shore, and the object. || 162 ||
1. Kha-ban-ma-tā | Arauṃ!

Regarding the argument that it is like the statement about fruits on the bank of a river, he says "sara" (river) [in verse 162], asserting that there the presence of a subject matter accessible through other means of knowledge (*mānāntaragamyārthatva*) serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
This object is to be grasped by direct perception; it is not established by any other means of valid cognition.
Therefore, in such a matter, certainty does not arise from scripture alone.

He refutes the impossibility of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) with the words "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*). The meaning is that since the object denoted by the word *phalītarasaṃbandha* (the connection with the juice of the fruit) is perceptible to the speaker, the sentence depending upon it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), and thus lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in that regard. || 163 ||
But with regard to the meaning of words such as "unprecedented" (apūrva), it does not depend upon perception or other means of knowledge.
Because the reality known as the oneness of the self (aikātmya) cannot be apprehended by means of perception and other such instruments of knowledge. || 164 ||

He addresses the pervasion of the means of proof (*sādhanavyāpti*) with the words "apūrvādi" (beginning with the unprecedented). The meaning is that such statements as "that which is unprecedented and has no other [cause]" do not depend upon perception and the like for their own object, because their own object is unfit for such [empirical] means; therefore, there is no pervasion by the means of proof. || 164 ||
The quality of being a non-human-authored statement is common to both the expressive word and the revealed scripture.
The capacity to cognize objects beyond the senses is common to both [the Veda] and the utterances of the *codanā*. (165)

Furthermore, he states a counter-inference (pratyanumāna): "The Vedāntas are authoritative with respect to their own meaning because they are not of human origin, like injunctive sentences. [He says] "because they are not of human origin" (*apauruṣeya*).

Anticipating the objection that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," he says: "The Vedāntas are authoritative with respect to their own meaning because they convey a matter devoid of [need for] corroboration and the like, like what is commonly accepted. [He says] "beyond the senses" (*atīndriya*). || 165 ||
If there is any difference between those two, it is at most the distinction of being established, that which is to be established, and the object of cognition.
But as for its being a valid means of knowledge, no excessive coldness whatsoever is observed. || 166 ||

He concludes the objection regarding the inference based on dependence with the words "siddha" (established). The phrase "of those two" refers to the two sections: the section on action (karma-kāṇḍa) and the section on knowledge (jñāna-kāṇḍa).
First, there arises the extraordinary [realization]: "I am Brahman."
Immediately following the hearing of such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and others, || 167 ||

Anticipating the objection that the Vedāntas' capacity to produce valid knowledge (*pramā*) is itself unestablished, and thus how they can possess authority (*prāmāṇya*), he says: "Valid knowledge" (*pramā*).
The sense is that the verbal realization (*vākyīyā pramitiḥ*) of an eligible seeker (*adhikārin*) cannot be denied. || 167 ||
And thus, why is the status of having the moon as its measure mentioned here in the scriptural statement?
Nevertheless, even for those [scriptures], their status as a means of valid knowledge here is not established by a logic other than that which has been stated. || 168 ||

Anticipating the objection that [the Veda] would lack authority just like [the words of] one's mother and so forth, he says: "If it were thus. The meaning is that if it produces valid cognition regarding its own object, it cannot be non-authoritative, as there is no reason for such a conclusion. He states: "Of the injunction," [meaning] that in the opposite case, even the injunction would lack authority. "The production of valid cognition" refers to the reasoning already stated. "Here" is a statement regarding its own object. || 168 ||
The capacity of all means of valid cognition is such that it brings about the comprehension of things as they truly are.
And since that denotation certainly exists, why should there be invalidity? || 169 ||
1. There is no "ni" in the sense of "gartha. 1. Because of its connection, there is a distinction. 1. Ka. Ga. "kike". Ta. [Vol. 2, page 767] 4.
Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1061.

Furthermore, he states that the Vedāntas are valid with respect to their own meaning because they possess the capacity to produce knowledge of that [meaning], just like perception: "Its own power," etc. (169).
Nor does a means of knowledge depend upon a mark (liṅga) or other such factors when the object to be established is beyond the reach of the senses.
Or [it is not established] by the means of direct perception of a yogi, because those two are not its objects. || 170 ||

Anticipating the objection that even though Brahman is not amenable to perception, the Vedāntas cannot be authoritative regarding their own subject matter because inference and other means of knowledge are possible there, he says: "Nor [is it so]. Even when the operation of inferential marks (*liṅga*) and the like occurs with respect to an object possessing limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*), they do not operate with respect to an object devoid of such adjuncts (*nirupādhika*).
This is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that Brahman, although beyond the range of our senses and so forth, might still be perceptible to yogins who are superior to us, he says:
"The yogi. The word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of drawing back [the preceding] verbal elements. The reason for this is stated in the words: "of those two. || 170 ||
The meaning that is understood from such statements as "not this," "not coarse," and so forth, [is Brahman].
This is accessible through the direct perception of yogis, not because of its being an internal object. || 171 ||
They establish the reason [for this] with the words "no," and so forth. The term "perception of the yogi" is intended as an illustration for [other means of knowledge such as] inference and the like.
This is because, by virtue of being its own nature, the Self provides existence and manifestation to perception, inference, and so on; that is to say, it is their very essence. ||171||
And because it does not enter the domain of direct perception, it is not measured by inference.
For as long as the relationship between the property and the possessor of the property has not been apprehended, there can be no inference. || 172 ||

He states another reason for its being inaccessible to inference: "pratyakṣa... (perception...). Even though it is not an object of the two types of perception, why should it not be an object of inference? For one means of knowledge does not depend upon another means of knowledge; to this he replies: "dharma... (dharma...). Therefore, because it is imperceptible and ungraspable, there can be no inference, as the necessary factors are absent—this is the remainder of the sense. || 172 ||
By whatever kinds of means of valid cognition there is the perception of objects of whatever kind;
It may exist for the world now, and likewise it existed in other times as well. || 173 ||

Anticipating the objection that Brahman, though imperceptible to those living in the present kalpa, might be perceptible to those residing in other kalpas due to their superior capacity for such perception, he says: "That which... The meaning is: the subject under dispute does not apprehend Brahman, because it is a sense organ, like any other [accepted] sense organ. ||173||
Even where an excellence is observed, it does not transcend its own inherent object.
There would be no functioning of the auditory organ with respect to form for the perception of things distant, subtle, and so forth.

Since our sense organs lack such excellence, one might suspect that Brahman is not their object; however, considering that this lack of excellence is equal even in the case of other objects that are unsuitable [for those senses], he cites the Vārttika, beginning with the words "yatra" (where). Even regarding objects such as Dharma and Brahman, for some...

If it is argued that the sense faculty operates [on its own object], then there would be an over-extension (atiprasakti), such that the ear would also operate upon visible form; thus he says "No" [to this].
And if there is no identity between the means of cognition, such as the yogi’s perception, and its object;
Even if that [attainment] were reached, what could one do on planes unsuitable for one's own self? || 175 ||

Having raised the objection that, according to the logic already stated, even though the Brahman-Self is not an object of the yogi’s perception and so forth, it might nonetheless be subject to [the influence of] excellence therein, he states its irrelevance: "The yogi... (verse 179).
1062 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika, Second Chapter:
On account of the similarity between the senses and the objects of cognition, there would be identity; that is not valid knowledge.
Just as there is non-difference from the object to be enjoined, so too there is non-difference from the injunction itself.

One might raise the objection: "Even if perception and other means of knowledge do not apply to Brahman—the Self—on account of the reasoning already stated, since it is to be known through injunctive statements (vidhi-vākya), how can the Vedāntas be an independent authority regarding it? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "akṣādī" [etc.]. || 176 ||
If it is argued that the sense organs and so forth are possible for the sake of the single self, just as fruits and the like [are possible for a tree].
It cannot be prevented in this world even by hundreds of injunctions.

A person does not proceed to act even by means of hundreds of injunctions without first considering his own capacity; how then could there be independence from external factors in the case of injunctive statements? (178)

Furthermore, one who desires to assert that the Vedāntas possess independent authority regarding Brahman as the Self must state whether or not another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) is possible in respect to that knowledge of identity—just as in the case of a fruit on a riverbank and so forth. In the first case, it cannot be dispelled even by such an injunction; thus, even in that position, the establishment of independent authority remains unproven. In the second case, since such authority is established even without it, the injunction is useless.

He says, "It is possible. The meaning of the word *hi* (for) is that if there were a removal of what has been brought forward by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be a contradiction with that very means of valid cognition.

Having stated that the Vedāntas possess independent authority (*anapekṣa-prāmāṇya*), he says, with the words beginning with "no" (*na*), that dependence exists only in the case of injunctions (*vidhi*).
"Even when appointed to prepare foods that must be cooked externally, one should cook the kṛṣṇalas."
Without that power, no person whatsoever desires to act therein. || 179 ||

He clarifies, by means of an illustration, that an injunction (*vidhi*) is dependent upon the capacity for activity residing in the qualified person (*adhikārin*). [The verse begins with] "In the case of those unfit to be cooked" (*apākyeṣu*).

Just as one who is enjoined [to perform a rite] with *kṛṣṇala* seeds—which are unfit for the process of cooking—does not cook them while disregarding his own capacity, but rather acts according to his own ability; even though they are unfit for cooking, he performs only the heating (*saṃtāpana*) required for their preparation.

The meaning is that, by the force of the statement "he cooks," one proceeds toward an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha); likewise, in every case within the scope of an injunction, human capacity is required. || 179 ||
If this is so, why is it said that an injunction is independent?
This injunction does not proceed independently of cultivation (bhāvanā). || 180 ||

Anticipating the objection that it is indeed accepted that an injunction depends upon human capacity, he says: "If this were so. Having stated that an injunction does not possess independent authority because its efficacy as a motivator depends upon the capacity of the qualified agent, he provides another reason for that very point: "No."
Therefore, for this reason as well, the establishment of independent validity is not achieved; this is the remainder [of the argument]. || 180 ||
This is neither a distinct form of cultivation nor likewise a distinct means of valid cognition.
The scripture, by means of figurative expression based on mutual dependence, brings about the realization of identity.

Anticipating the objection that even in the theory of the reality [of the Veda], the dependence on the capacity of the qualified person (*adhikārin*) is equally present— since it is established that the Veda generates valid knowledge [only] by depending on such capacity— he says, "No," and so forth. Although the dependence on human capacity is equal in both cases— namely, in the capacity of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and in the creative urge (*bhāvanā*) which is the object of the injunction (*vidhi*)— nevertheless, because injunctions lack dependence on other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), they constitute an independent authority (*anapekṣa-pramāṇa*).
Anticipating this objection, he says: "And not... Because an injunction (niyoga) is insentient, another means of knowledge is possible therein; otherwise, [the capacity would be lost].

Since the self is not an object of cognition due to the impossibility of grasping it [by other means] and because it is self-luminous, the apprehension of its power has been established therein; therefore, the Śruti, by means of a statement devoid of an injunction, while making known the identity [of the self], does not require another means of knowledge, another performance, or the capacity for activity apart from being grounded in Brahman, but rather makes that known to the qualified seeker solely by its own majesty—this is the meaning. || 181 ||
Therefore, it is logical that the hearing of the expression is always independent [of anything else].
It depends solely upon the knowledge of the signifier, the signified, and their referent. || 182 ||

He concludes the distinction [of the Vedāntas] from the ritual injunctions with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). By stating that there is always independence (*anapekṣatā*), he anticipates the objection: "If even in the apprehension of the word's power (*śakti*) there is no requirement for external support, then even for one who is unlearned, the cognition of identity [between the individual soul and Brahman] would arise from such words as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*). Anticipating this, he says: "In denotation... (*abhidhāna...*). Since a word possessing both power (*śakti*) and intention (*tātparya*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and since that [word] is independent, the expression of independence [applies to it].
The meaning is "ciriti. || 182 ||
Knowledge and action residing in the subject do not bring about an understanding of things as they truly are.
This [cognition] has the object of knowledge as its agent; it is that which brings about an understanding of things exactly as they are.

Since it is impossible for injunctions to be independent [of other means of knowledge], and since their dependence cannot be avoided by accepting them [as such], he states—after establishing that the Vedāntas possess independent authority even without those [injunctions]—that there is no injunction regarding knowledge, because knowledge that is not authoritative cannot accomplish its purpose. He says: "jñāne" (regarding knowledge). This means residing in the knower, that is, within that very person; the meaning is "like the cognition of a woman as fire," and so forth. [Knowledge] has the object of cognition as its agent, and is the means of valid cognition...
"Dependent on me" means [dependent on the Self]. "This one" refers to what was called knowledge and action. || 183 ||
For one person cannot be enjoined to perform the activity of another due to a lack of capacity.
For a mandate for water is not appropriate regarding drying and such effects that are to be accomplished by fire. (184)

Anticipating the objection, "Why should there not be an injunction for a person even with respect to such knowledge?", he says, "And not" (na ca). The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that even when a son is enjoined to perform the duties of his paternal uncle, there is no injunction where the person lacks independence.
He provides an example for the fact that there is no injunction for a person regarding the operation of the means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth, due to incapacity: "For not" (na hi).
Even that limitation of the Self which may arise through the ignorance of Brahman [is likewise unreal].
Once that limitation has been destroyed, it does not depend upon any further means of proof.

Having raised the objection that there must be an injunction regarding knowledge because scriptural knowledge is fruitful, and having proposed the alternatives as to whether that fruit is the destruction of duality, the cessation of ignorance, the attainment of Brahman by the individual soul (jīva), or something else entirely, [the author] considers the first position—that there is an injunction for knowledge because the duality between the jīva and Brahman is destroyed by the enjoined knowledge—and asks: is that [duality] illusory (āvidya) or real (vāstava)?

To the first case, he states that the injunction would be purposeless, beginning with the words "Of Brahman... *brahmaṇaḥ...* [The text continues: ...[of Brahman... [The argument is that if the duality were merely illusory, it would vanish upon the dawn of knowledge regardless of whether an injunction exists, rendering the injunction redundant.]
The meaning is that the means of accomplishment is the ritual procedure, because its success arises from knowledge alone. || 189 ||
Due to ignorance regarding the identity with Brahman, whose true nature is undivided, [the self is perceived as limited].
The knower of the field (kṣetrajña) appears as if delimited, like a snake [perceived] in a rope. || 186 ||
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "unrestricted" (anavacchinna). || 186 ||
And there is no ignorance to be dispelled here other than through the knowledge of the true nature of the inner Self.
In some cases, a means of accomplishment must depend on something else, as is the case with sacrifices and the like for the sake of attaining heaven. (187)

Anticipating the second objection—that even though the body born of ignorance is destroyed by the destruction of ignorance, there is still an injunction for knowledge because it is required for the purpose of destroying that ignorance—he says: "Or not," etc. Here, "in this" means in the inner self (*pratīci*). "In some place or time" is the meaning.
The phrase "other than from awakening" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 187 ||
Nor indeed is there, even in this world, any goal to be accomplished through that primary [agency].
In both worldly and Vedic usage, that which accomplishes something is called a "means" (sādhana). || 188 ||

Raising the third objection—that since the realization of the soul's identity with Brahman is accomplished through enjoined knowledge, there must be an injunction regarding that knowledge—the author says: "And not so" (na ca).

Even if being Brahman were to be accomplished by means of knowledge, it is not accomplished in the primary sense; and when no primary object to be accomplished exists, nothing can be called a "means" in any worldly transaction. Therefore, because there is no object to be accomplished, there is no injunction. This is the meaning. || 188 ||
Furthermore, the fourfold set beginning with origination is established from worldly convention.
It is not logical for that [scripture] to be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it merely manifests an already established fact. || 189 ||

Having raised the fourth objection—that what is to be accomplished (sādhya) is something other than those already mentioned because of the injunction regarding it—he states the true nature of the sādhya in order to show that [objection] is non-existent: "And that which is to be accomplished...
He says this anticipating the objection that one among arising and so forth might also be the sādhya of the enjoined knowledge;
thus he says: "...of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 189 ||
There is not even the slightest [contribution] from the manifestor beyond the acquisition of its own self-nature.
Another form is conceived [as the means] for removing the state of being unknown. (190)

Having set aside the injunction regarding verbal knowledge, he speaks [the verse beginning with] "Not the Self" (nātma) in response to the doubt that there might be an injunction for the practice of that [knowledge], since it destroys ignorance. The meaning is that the destruction of ignorance occurs from the very moment knowledge arises; thus, no further practice is enjoined. || 190 ||
Arising from the nature common to the self, it does not come into being after having previously been non-existent.

[Objection: "Like the cognition of a jar or similar objects, cognition does not depend on distinct causes. Therefore, whether it pertains to the means of knowledge (*māna*) or its repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), there may be no injunction; however, it might exist in regard to the cognition of its own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*). Anticipating this, he states another fault: "The Self," etc. Cognition manifested by that which is the unique, specific form (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*) of this [Self] is not an effect—because it does not depend on causes—and thus it cannot be enjoined.
This is the meaning. || 199 ||
Because the entities of cause and effect consist merely of a stable experience.
Therefore, the arising of what has not previously existed is not tenable within the nature of experience. 192.
Regarding how there is no dependence on a cause external to itself, he says: "Let it remain," etc. Here, the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is connected with the ablative case. || 192 ||
[Vol.
2, page 771] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1065
This mental construction arises from the cause of ignorance regarding the inner self, and not of its own accord.
How could that [scripture] be the object for one who desires to know the true nature of the inward Self? || 193 ||

Furthermore, for one who desires to know Brahman (brahmajijñāsu) or for one who already knows it, there is an injunction; regarding this, one may inquire whether it concerns the means of knowledge or something else.

Having accepted the first alternative, the author refutes the second with the words "pratyak" (the inner self). The meaning is that for one who seeks knowledge, there can be no effort toward anything other than the means to that knowledge, because they have no desire for such things. || 193 ||
This distinction between action and its factors arises from the reality of the single Self being unknown.
In that knowledge, this [defilement] is impossible, because its cause has been eradicated.
He speaks with reference to another interpretation: "The action" (kriyā). || 194 ||
And there is no cessation of ignorance other than the arising of knowledge.
The destruction of saṃsāra is not distinct from the destruction of ignorance. || 195 ||

One might raise the objection that there can be no eradication of ignorance—the cause of differentiation—because ignorance that has not yet arisen cannot be removed due to its non-existence, and that which has already arisen cannot be removed because it is not in contradiction [with itself] simply by virtue of having arisen. Anticipating this, he says "And not... (na ca), asserting that this is not so, because its destruction is possible just as darkness is destroyed by a lamp. Furthermore, one might object that although ignorance is destroyed immediately upon the arising of knowledge, there must still be an injunction for the practice of knowledge in order to destroy its effects; anticipating this, he says "saṃsāra... (transmigration...).
Thus it is said. || 199 ||
Nor is there here the destruction of ignorance as a conjunction within the causal self.
Because its destruction is a real occurrence of the thing itself, like the destruction of a clod of earth by a stone. || 196 ||

Just as the destruction of a clod of earth and the like is a merging into the clay, so too the destruction of ignorance along with its effects is a merging into the Self; [anticipating the objection that] there must therefore be an injunction for practice in order to effect the absolute (niranvaya) destruction of that [ignorance], he says: "Nor also... The meaning is that the destruction of ignorance together with its effects is nothing other than the Self, which is devoid of cause and effect. || 196 ||
Having grasped the true nature of reality, knowledge brings about the destruction of ignorance.
By the functioning of the true nature of things, darkness is always dispelled.

Anticipating the doubt as to how that [knowledge] can consist of the mere self as previously described, he says: "Having taken up" (ādāya). The meaning is that because knowledge destroys ignorance in accordance with the true nature of the object, nothing remains apart from that reality. He provides the experience of the enlightened ones as proof in this regard, stating:
"The reality... (vastu) || 197 ||
Therefore, since it makes known what was previously unknown, an injunction (vidhi) is appropriate here.
Furthermore, in this context, an injunction (vidhi) consisting in the performance of what has not yet been done is simply not tenable.

Having refuted the injunction (*vidhi*) consisting of the instigation of one who has not yet engaged in the Vedāntas, he concludes what was stated in the verse beginning with "Therefore, it is an injunction" by means of the words "The unknown... [Verse 198]. Here, the word "here" refers to the Vedāntas. He states the reason for the meaning of the pronoun "that" (*tat*) as: "Of that which is unperformed... [Verse 198].
Furthermore, the twofold nature of ignorance is not established by reason.
Because the reality consists solely of the one Self, it is logical that ignorance alone exists. || 199 ||

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is twofold, consisting of non-apprehension (*agraha*) and apprehension otherwise (*anyathāgraha*); therein, the cessation of the first occurs merely through birth, while that of the second [occurs through knowledge].
(Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter, Verse 1066).

Some maintain that it arises from "knowledge of what has been enjoined" (*vihitajñāna*). To them, he says: "And its twofold nature. The word "also" (*api*) implies that it is like the nature of that [knowledge]. The particle *ca* (and) is used to conjoin it with the means of valid cognition (*māna*) through reasoning (*yukti*). Anticipating the objection that even oneness does not belong to it because of the absence of both means of valid cognition and reasoning, he says: "Oneness of identity" (*aikātmya*).
The meaning is that since there is no distinction between the locus (*āśraya*) and the object (*viṣaya*), and thus no differentiator exists, there is oneness. || 199 ||
The state of being differentiated by the diversity of objects of cognition serves as the differentiator, just as it does for cognitions themselves.
Since ignorance does not possess this twofold nature here, it is therefore difficult to establish.
He establishes this by means of that very same illustration: "the object of knowledge" (prameya). Here, the word "west" (pratīcī) refers to this [object]. || 200 ||
In this context, it is precisely the ignorance regarding the inner self that is the cause of other entities.
Since there is no other cause for it, how can there be a twofold nature of darkness? || 201 ||

Objection: Ignorance of the Self (ātma-ajñāna), while concealing [the Self], cannot be the cause of the world, because it is impossible for one thing to have two functions [simultaneously]. Therefore, there must be another ignorance as the cause of the world, which is the substrate (vastu) of that [world], [established] by means of the knowledge prescribed [in scripture]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The innermost" (pratyak). According to such scriptural passages as "Indra by means of his powers of illusion" (indro māyābhiḥ), that which is the non-self entity (anātma-vastu) has as its cause precisely the ignorance of the innermost Self. As for the contradiction regarding one thing having two functions, that is resolved by the analogy of a water-channel (kulyā) and so forth.

The meaning is "having cast aside. The word "here" (*iha*) expresses a distinction in worldly convention. He states the conclusion regarding the absence of any cause other than the ignorance of the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*):
"other than that" (*tadanya*). || 201 ||
Nor is there any dependence on practice and so forth, because it is liberated by its very nature.
The "pot-ness" and so forth of a pot and other such objects do not depend upon the repeated practice of the cognition of a pot and so forth. (202)

Lest there be a twofold nature to ignorance, [the author], anticipating the objection that the liberation of the self results from the practice of knowledge, states: "And not... The word "etcetera" (ādi) includes the mention of yoga and so forth. He provides an illustration for the point that the liberation of one who is eternally free does not depend upon practice, beginning with the words "not... (na). || 202 ||
And consciousness that lacks an object is not cultivated, nor is that which is devoid of an aspect.
Because the universal form is the inner self of the one who perceives it, and because [the external] form is denied. || 203 ||

Furthermore, knowledge of Garuḍa and the like is practiced as having an object and a mental form (*sākāra*); otherwise, it is the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). Therefore, because that [knowledge of the Self] is not a practice of yoga, there is no injunction regarding it; thus he says: "And not... He establishes the objectlessness (*aviṣayatva*) of the Self with the words: "The agent of cultivation (*bhāvaka*). The "cultivator" (*bhāvaka*) is the one who practices. He states the reason for the formlessness (*anākāratva*) of the Self: "And because of the form... [and] "It is without sound (*aśabda*)," etc.
The meaning is: "because of the scriptural statement" (diśruteḥ). || 203 ||
It has no apprehension by means of a sense organ that follows after objects such as sound.
And like suffering and so forth, the self is not [an object] of consciousness, because it has the singular nature of being solely for its own sake. (204)

If it is argued that while practicing the knowledge of Garuḍa and the like, one also practices self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), and if the self is said to be perceptible, then one must consider whether it is grasped by an external sense organ or by the mind; to refute the first [option], he says "No. To refute the second, he says "Suffering," etc. (the full phrase being "suffering, delusion, and so forth, generally by the mind"). The reason for this is: "Of consciousness" (*citeḥ*), because of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).
1 11 [vol2, page 773]
The mind, accumulated through mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), is not the cause of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
Because its total eradication occurs right here, due to the abandonment of the ignorance that is its cause. || 205 ||

However, some maintain that the mind, when accompanied by practiced cultivation, is the cause of liberation, and thus they desire a formal injunction regarding the practice of knowledge; to them, he says: "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). For that [cultivation] would have to be either the material cause (*upādāna*) or the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) therein. It is not the first, as he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). Here, the term "here" (*iha*) refers to the state of the purity of knowledge (*jñānasattva*). || 205 ||
The conformity with their respective purposes belongs to meditative cultivation, gnosis, and action.
Since it does not possess the nature of cause and effect, how could there be any persistence in the state of liberation? || 206 ||
He says that it is not the second [alternative], stating "its own effect," etc.; the ellipsis is "as a cause for the inclusive application" (anugati). || 206 ||
And when the self is established through direct perception, there is no need for repeated practice, because its fruit has already been attained.
And if [the means] are not established due to the absence of knowledge, what indeed would depend upon repeated practice? (207)

Furthermore, one might inquire whether the injunction for practice applies when the Self has been realized as immediate (*aparokṣa*), or when it has not been realized; having thus raised this dilemma, he refutes the first alternative with the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*).

He rejects the second alternative with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*). The meaning of the particle "and" (*ca*) is that there can be no injunction for practice toward immediacy regarding the Self if it is known only mediately (*parokṣa*), because immediacy cannot result from mediate practice. || 207 ||
Knowledge arising from the generic form of the self is ignorance with respect to the self.
If that which has arisen once does not destroy [the afflictions], then it would not truly be knowledge. || 208 ||
Anticipating the objection that "knowledge, having arisen once, does not destroy ignorance; therefore, there must be a rule for repeated practice," he says: "The Self...
The meaning is that it is well known that knowledge and ignorance are mutually contradictory. || 208 ||
When right knowledge is relied upon, even that delusion takes it as its support.
The statement, "Uncontradicted darkness exists here," is one uttered by an insentient speaker. (209)

Anticipating the objection that knowledge might possess the nature of knowledge even if it does not destroy ignorance merely by its birth—because that [ignorance] might occasionally exist [alongside it]—he says:

"perfectly" (*samyak*). The meaning is that it has never been observed that darkness remains unremoved in the very same place where light shines. He states the flaw in the opposing view: "unsublated" (*abādhitam*). Here, the term refers to one who is "knowing" (*viduṣī*). || 209 ||
Thus, and so forth, that which was previously stated at great length.
All of that should be thoroughly investigated, for it causes the loss of all opportunities.

One might object: "Has not every form of injunction (*vidhi*) already been refuted in the context of the connection [between the means and the end] and so forth in the Vedāntas? Why then is it refuted here again, like grinding what has already been ground? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this manner" (*ityevam*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the sixfold refutation of injunction regarding verbal knowledge (*śābda-jñāna*) is included. He states the fruit of this investigation: "All," etc. The particle "ava-" refers to the mode of injunction being suspected; even though the injunction has already been refuted—
The collective meaning is that [this objection] is refuted here as a consequence (*prasaṅga*). || 210 ||
Therefore, one who knows the distinction between the self and the non-self should perceive everything as the self.
For by the statement "the Self is to be seen," this very meaning is expressed here. || 211 ||

Having raised the objection as to what the status of the statement "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) would be in the absence of an injunction according to the method stated above, he concludes that point for its sake:
*Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Second Chapter, [page 774, verse 1068].

"Everything. He introduces the statement there with the word "Self. The meaning of this scriptural passage is that the discerning person perceives, through this sentence, that Brahman—which is the supreme bliss because it is desired by all—is the Self worthy of being seen. The word "hi" (for) is used to establish the reason previously stated, namely, the impossibility of any other meaning. || 219 ||
And because all means of valid cognition depend upon the results of all means of valid cognition, even when all means of valid cognition are under investigation.
Therefore, with the desire to enter into the Vedānta, he said: "It is to be heard. (212)

Having stated the meaning of the sentence—that the Self is "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) rather than "to be heard" (*śrotavya*), and that it is not injunctive but rather denotes fitness (*arhatva*), such that the sense is "the Self is fit for seeing"—he introduces the sentence concerning what is "to be heard" with the words "All... (*sarva-*). By relying on the very vision which is the fruit of the means under discussion, all means of knowledge are suggested as being causes [of that vision] regarding the Self; therefore, when a doubt arises that [the Self] might not be known through the Upanishads (*aupaniṣadatva*), he [proceeds] for the purpose of dispelling that [doubt] by means of the Vedantas...

Or rather, the Śruti says that [the Self] "is to be heard" because of the desire to accept it as the cause of the vision of the Self; therefore, the meaning is that its status as being known through the Upaniṣads (aupaniṣadatva) is established. || 212 ||
Since vision itself cannot be enjoined, its means is what is enjoined.
The hearing of the Vedānta with effort, as well as reasoning itself, is the means. || 213 ||

He states the meaning of the sentence concerning what is to be heard: "Of the vision," etc. It is proclaimed with effort that the hearing which is being enjoined must be performed repeatedly, like the Agnihotra sacrifice. He takes up the sentence concerning what is to be reflected upon: "The means," etc. (213).
The principle of direct statement, indicative mark, and so forth, effects a discernment of the power of words.
It is said that one should reflect in order to ascertain the meaning of the scriptures. || 214 ||

He states the nature of *śravaṇa* (hearing) regarding those two: "By means of *śruti*, etc. The meaning is that *śravaṇa* is the determination of the purport of the Vedānta texts concerning the Self as Brahman by means of logical principles (*nyāya*) such as *śruti*, which establish the [inherent] power and the intended meaning [of the texts]. He states the nature of *manana* (reflection): "By means of *āgama*, etc.

This refers to the reasoning (*tarka*) that establishes the falsity of duality for the purpose of reaching certainty regarding the reality known through *śruti* and so forth, by removing doubts such as the impossibility [of the truth of non-duality]. Following that...
The meaning is that "reconnection" (saṃdhāna) is what is intended by the term "to be contemplated" (mantavya). || 214 ||
For it is taught in the scriptures that here, one must understand the intended meaning according to the actual reality of things.
For the injunction regarding the visualization of women, fire, and so forth is certainly not an injunction concerning the object of meditation itself. (215)

Some maintain that the Vedāntas do not have reality as their primary purport, but rather are concerned with injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā*); in response to them, he says: "Reality" (*vastu*). How is it known that the purport of the Vedāntas lies in reality? He explains this by means of the injunction for reflection (*manana*): "As in the case of a woman" (*yoṣit*). Where only the act of seeing is intended and not the actual object, there no injunction for reflecting upon what has been heard exists; however, in this case, because of the injunction for reflection, the purport lies in the reality itself.

The meaning is "it is established. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of establishing the common agreement regarding the absence of an injunction to reflect upon [the Upanishads] in the case of the illustrative example. || 215 ||
In this matter, reasoning is also employed in conformity with the words of the Veda.
Its status as the cause [of linguistic usage] lies in the fixed relationship between the signified and the signifier.

Fearing that it might be contradictory to say "not by reasoning" (*naiṣā tarkeṇa*) and so forth if all that is called "reasoning" (*manana*) were to be a means here because of its abundance, he says: "By the Veda" (*veda*). Here, "here" refers to the determination of the meaning of what has been heard in scripture. "Not indeed" (*naiva*) is a censure of non-Vedic reasoning; following that [Vedic authority]...
[Vol.
2, Page 775] 4 Brāhmaṇam], accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1069.

The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that there is no contradiction even when reasoning (*tarka*) is accepted. Since it is the Vedic word alone that determines reality, what utility does reasoning have?

To this he replies: "The denoted object (*vācya*)," and so forth. The denoted object of the term *tvam* (thou) is not the body and such, but rather the conscious Self (*cidātman*) that is their witness;
likewise, the denoted object of the term *tat* (that) is not primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the like, but rather non-dual Brahman whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*).

Such is the rule governing the relationship between the signifier and the signified. Although the Word (*śabda*) is the determiner of reality, nevertheless, because of [the presence of] doubt regarding its possibility and so forth—

The meaning is that even the deliberation called *manana* is employed as the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), because that which possesses an *itikartavyatā* functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). || 216 ||
In this context, nididhyāsana is said to be the realization that is independent of anything else.
The mention of those two [the first two moments] is intended as being the limits (avadhi) for the preceding ones. || 217 ||

He states the nature of *nididhyāsana* [meditative reflection]: "The other," etc. Having performed hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities, for one who stands free from obstacles to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, the effortless comprehension of the meaning of the sentence arising from the sentence is called *nididhyāsana* in the passage concerning *nididhyāsana*. However, in the passage concerning that which is "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), it was stated that the knowledge which prompts inquiry is merely provisional; or rather, this very [knowledge] is the means.

The sense is that [the author] intends to explain what has not yet been stated. He states the result of the mention of *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) with the words "of the two preceding" (*pūrvayoḥ*). || 127 ||
In this world, one must first diligently perform the practices of hearing [the teachings] and so forth.
Until the consciousness described above manifests as radiant.

This very point—that it constitutes the final stage of hearing and so forth accompanied by tranquility (śama) and the rest—is clarified [by the verse]. "Hearing and so forth" (śravaṇādi): here, "here" (iha) refers to the Self (ātman).

"Effort" (prayatna) indicates the accompaniment of tranquility and the rest, and therein suggests repetition (āvṛtti). "As long as" (yāvat): luminosity (bhāsvaratva) means having the fruit as its culmination. || 218 ||
First, vision arises from scripture; then, understanding arises from scripture and from the teacher.
It is firmly established through the union of the three: the scripture, the teacher, and the self.

He sets forth the sequence of perception and the other stages according to the order of the text. Regarding the phrase "from scripture" (*āgamāt*): from the Veda studied together with its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), first arises the knowledge that prompts inquiry; following that, from scripture and from the teacher comes hearing (*śravaṇa*); from that, reflection (*mati*, i.e., *manana*); and from that, [meditation].

The meaning is that through the hearing [of the scriptures] as enjoined by the treatises and so forth, which serves as the cause for the knowledge of the Self, and through the reflection designated by the word "ātman" (contemplation), which follows from that hearing, there arises—by means of its complete practice—a firm knowledge of Brahman called *nididhyāsana* (meditative absorption), which is free from such obstacles as the impossibility [of the Self's existence]. || 219 ||
Prior practice is merely verbal as long as one does not contemplate what has been heard.
Having heard and reflected upon it, one then realizes that very Self directly.

He states that this sequence is not merely scriptural (*śrauta*), but also logical (*ārtha*), by saying "realization" (*pratipatti*). The ellipsis is: "as long as one does not reflect upon what has been heard, so long does one hear. The word "then" (*atha*) is intended to indicate that the specialized acts of hearing and so forth constitute the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) for the direct realization of the Self. || 220 ||
When knowledge is not otherwise attained, through the means of hearing and so forth, [one should practice].
Once it has arisen, it does not depend on anything other than the experience of the inner self.
1. Established.
[Vol. 2, page 776] 1070 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter—]

If it is argued that even when that [knowledge] has arisen from the word, one still requires hearing and so forth, then one might likewise require something after the cognition born from that [word]; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Ananya" (not other). When the knowledge whose form is the self-established Self is obtained from that [scripture], because the immediate intuition of the inner Self is attained immediately thereafter, the knower requires nothing further, since the Self has been realized; such is the meaning.
Regarding the relationship between the probandum and the probans, there is indeed dependence on the treatise alone, and nothing else.
There is dependence on a logical mark (liṅga) regarding the object to be inferred, and dependence on a person regarding what is appropriate for a person.

Furthermore, having raised the dilemma as to whether the dependence belongs to liberation or to knowledge once it has arisen, he refutes the first alternative with the words "sādhyā" (to be accomplished).

The sense is that, according to the rule that whatever is appropriate for a given end is what must be depended upon therein, knowledge alone is what must be depended upon in the case of liberation. || 222 ||
In the cognition of a broken measure and so forth, the ascertainment is indeed dependent.
But when this [collection] consists of only one or more [such factors], what would depend on what, and for what reason? || 223 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "bhinna" (distinct). The meaning is as follows: for that non-self (*anātman*) which is distinct—that is, for which the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and so forth are different—the result of ascertainment arises in relation to the knower and the rest. However, in the case of that [Self] which is one, non-distinct, and for whom there is no knower and so forth, dependence on the knower and the rest is not logical when knowledge arises from a sentence; for by the very birth of that cognition, the knower and the rest are sublated. || 223 ||
By virtue of relying on the form of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the valid cognition (pramā) arises first.
Subsequently, it is indeed grounded in the object of cognition, conforming to the nature of that object.

[The author] explains how the cognition of non-self arises without destroying the [notion of] the "me" (mātra) and so forth. Regarding the word "pramāṇa": the meaning is that a valid cognition (*pramā*), having first arisen in accordance with its cause, follows its object and results in the ascertainment of it; subsequently, it persists precisely without destroying the notion of the "me" and so forth. || 224 ||
The self knows itself there, by means of the authority of the Veda and other sources.
In that regard, not even the slightest distinction between mother and others can be found. || 225 ||
It reveals the arising of the cognition of the Self through the sublation of the [notions of] the knower and so forth. "The Self" refers to the state of purity of cognition;
"therein" refers to the state of its fruition. || 225 ||
Inference would likewise have as its object the individual thing (padārtha) itself.
But the comprehension of the sentence-meaning arises from the sentence itself. || 226 ||

Fearing that the status of the Self as being known through the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadatva*) might be contradicted because other means of knowledge (*māna*), such as inference, could also apply to the Self—as suggested by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "from the authority of sentences and so forth"—he says: "The object of the words" (*padārtha*). The term "inference" (*anumiti*) refers to an inference belonging to others (non-Vedantins) that is not in conflict with the Vedānta. By the phrase "in that very way," he states that [the Self] is the object of the words. He then says "sentence" (*vākya*) to show that if the Self were the object of mere reasoning (*tarka*) and the like, its status as being known through the Upaniṣads would be appropriate.
Thus, [it is] for the sake of the goal. || 226 ||
For it is only the state of being self or non-self that is understood regarding entities through an inferential mark.
The Self, which transcends all measures of cognition, is understood through the Vedic word alone.
[Vol.
2, Page 777] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1071.
How is it that reasoning (*tarka*) and the like have only the categories of things as their object? To this he says: "The Self," etc., regarding objects perceived without distinction.

Why is it that through reasoning (*tarka*) and other means one merely understands the distinction—that for some there is selfhood (*ātmatva*) and for others there is non-selfhood (*anātmatva*)—but why is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) not understood as well? To this he states the intended point: "All... (verse 227). For it is not the case that because the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is the object [of cognition], the sentence-meaning must likewise be so; the meaning is that the indivisible, single-flavored (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*) sentence-meaning is unfit for such [conceptual] treatment. || 227 ||
Surely knowledge would be incomplete if only the self were perceived.
It is absolute, because no entity other than the inner self (pratīc) is ever perceived as non-self. || 228 ||

Even in the case of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) arising from the sentence alone, that [knowledge] must either have the non-Self as its object or the Self alone. Not the first, because it would entail that the Self possesses attributes (*saviśeṣatva*). Thinking thus, he adopts the second alternative and refutes it with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). The reason why knowledge is incorrect due to having a limited object is stated as "the non-Self" (*anātmanaḥ*). || 228 ||
This [world] is neither different nor non-different from that, because it is born of ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyagātman).
Because, like a staff or a snake [superimposed] upon a rope, it is recognized as being inherently devoid of prior existence and so forth.

He says "not so" because the otherness or non-otherness of the internal (pratyak) non-self is unestablished. The reason for this is given as "the internal" (pratyag). Therein, the illustration is "the staff," etc. He supports the point that the very nature of the non-self is the ignorance of the Self with the words "by itself" (svataḥ). Since the Self is by its own nature devoid of prior, posterior, and simultaneous [limitations], the meaning is that duality is merely avidyā (ignorance). || 229 ||
For when this absolute inner self has been seen, [all else ceases].
There is no knowledge that has not arisen, nor is there such darkness that has not perished.

Since it has been established that the Self is non-dual and duality is merely due to ignorance, he states the resulting conclusion with the words "yataḥ" (since). Kaivalya is the state of being without any limiting adjuncts (nirupādhitva). || 230 ||
Because the reality of the causal and effected entities consists solely in their identity with the individual self (pratyagātman).
Tell me: by the knowledge of that [Self], is darkness destroyed, or is it ignorance of the Self? (231)

Since [the author] clarifies the reason stated in the words, he explains the portion beginning with "therefore" (*ataḥ*) as follows: "from the knowledge of that" (*tajjñānāt*). The word division is also "ignorance has been destroyed" (*adhvastam ajñānam*). || 239 ||
In the restatement of those things already mentioned, such as seeing and so forth, when they have been introduced.
If it is by means of consciousness, then how can it be called "nididhyāsana" (meditative contemplation)? || 232 ||

When the passage beginning with "it is to be seen" has been explained, he asks about the result in the restatement (*anuvāda*)—wherein the word "vaśa" does not appear regarding seeing and so forth—in which meditation (*nididhyāsana*) is restated by means of the word "knowledge" (*vijñāna*). [The question is: "It is a restatement"? || 232 ||
To eliminate any doubt regarding meditative absorption, it is said: "by means of consciousness."
For by the word *nididhyāsana*, meditation (*dhyāna*) is intended. || 233 ||

In that regard, he states the result: "Dhyāna," etc. When it is said, "It is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*), there may arise the doubt that this refers to *dhyāna* (meditative concentration); in response to that, [the text says...
[Vol. 2, page 778, line 1072].
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Second Chapter.

The meaning is that the term "knowledge" (vijñāna) is restated for the sake of the essence (rāsa), because a doubtful point is determined by the remainder of the sentence, as in the case of the injunction, "One should place the pebbles smeared with ghee.
He states the occurrence of a doubt to be set aside: "nididhyāsana... (233).
I have previously stated that meditative absorption and so forth are the causes for the arising of consciousness.
But consciousness, having only its own nature as its object, is traditionally held to have liberation alone as its fruit.

When it is suspected that *nididhyāsana* (meditative reflection) is synonymous with *dhyāna* (contemplation) because of its association with hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other stages, he says "vijñāna" [in the verse] to address this. If it were merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that [reflection] by the word "knowledge" (*vijñāna*) for the sake of understanding the meaning of the sentence, then since meditation is not stated to be a means [to liberation] in the injunction "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*), one might suspect that its status as a means has been neglected; anticipating this, he says "vijñāna. The meaning is: "in various places," beginning from the section on the relationship [of the means to the goal]. Not here...

It should be understood that if there were no injunction, the status of [hearing and so forth] as a means to that [knowledge] would not be established; however, its establishment follows from the scriptural text "having become composed" (*samāhito bhūtvā*), etc., and from the statement "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), which indicates that the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—which is the fruit of hearing and other means accompanied by meditation—is what is intended. If it is argued: "If meditation is accepted as a means, why is that very thing not stated here as well?"—the answer is: "Because it would contradict the remainder of the passage" (*vākyaśeṣavirodhāt*). He says: "For its own sake" (*svārtham*), which refers to liberation. *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "yanmuktimā-". The translation reflects the available portion.*
The connection [of the words] is as follows: "That very independent knowledge which bears three fruits is remembered as *nididhyāsana*. || 234 ||
Nothing other than the destruction of the ignorance regarding the identity of the Self is accepted [as liberation].
For that fruit of the knowledge of the unity of the Self is indeed already attained by itself. 235.

Fearing the objection that if liberation were a fruit, it would be non-eternal because it would depend upon a means of accomplishment, he says: "Aikātmya... He states the reason for not accepting a fruit of knowledge other than the destruction of ignorance: "Prāptam... The meaning is this: absolute oneness (aikātmya), which is isolation (kaivalya), is eternally attained; therefore, since ignorance—which veils it—is dispelled by knowledge, liberation is only figuratively said to be its effect. || 235 ||
Because it is exactly without parts, like a rope-snake and so forth.
This self enters into association with that which has a form superimposed through delusion.

Fearing that if the cessation of ignorance along with its effects were different from the Self, duality would result, whereas if it were non-different, the Self would remain subject to dependence on a means of attainment, he says: "Because... Just as the rope is the reality of the snake and so forth, the Self alone is the reality of ignorance along with its effects;

therefore, even its cessation does not differ from the Self. Nor, by this much, does the Self become an effect of knowledge, for since the cessation depends upon that [knowledge], it is not distinct from the Self.
For even when the nature of a rope is destroyed by the knowledge [that it was not a snake], the snake and so forth—which were its effects—do not persist; such is the meaning. || 236 ||
The Self is the essence of that which is differentiated as the non-Self, such as the subject and so forth.
It is established by itself [as the witness] of that which is false in nature, arising from ignorance of it. || 237 ||
How can there be identity (*tādātmya*), which is a non-distinct union of the Self with the non-Self? He explains how the Self is the reality of that which is imagined:

"The Self," etc. Because it is distinct and because it is not the non-Self, the Self alone is the form of the ego and so forth—which are born of ignorance regarding the Self and are false in nature—since the Self's existence is not dependent on anything else and it is possible for it to be the substratum of all imagination; this is the meaning. || 237 ||
And because there is nothing other than the object of knowledge regarding the self that produces the knowledge thereof.
Therefore, the inner self, which dispels darkness, possesses no conceit of being other than the Mother.

One might raise the objection: "Even if there is an absence of duality consisting of the object, the ignorance, and the path, is the knower different from that [knowledge] or non-different? If he is different, then it is not the Self; if he is non-different, then there is the difficulty of its immutability. Anticipating this, he says: "The Self. Therefore, there is no loss of non-duality (advaita).

Nor is there any difficulty regarding immutability (*kauṭasthya*), because [the Self] possesses the nature of a knower during the state of ignorance; this is the meaning. Nevertheless, knowledge is distinct from the Self—

[The opponent] objects: "Is [the ignorance] different [from the Self] or not? In the first case, there would be a loss of non-duality (advaita); in the second case, because ignorance would always exist, there would be a perpetual destruction of ignorance. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "ananyā" (not other). The meaning is: the non-dual inner Self itself, having ascended to the fruit of the cognition arising from the Great Sentence (mahāvākya), burns away its own ignorance along with its effects;
therefore, the aforementioned defect does not arise. || 238 ||
Thus, having restated that which arises from ignorance, [the scripture] has completely refuted what is falsely attained.
With the words "This is Brahman," he told us that the Self is everything.
The statement to be explained below—that "the non-dual Self alone is the reality of everything"—is supported as the authoritative source [for this view]. Regarding the verse beginning with *ajñāna*:

since the Self is the reality of everything, it is stated that this [world] is false precisely because it is born of ignorance regarding that [Self]. Having restated this in the passage beginning with "This is Brahman," the Śruti tells us, "It is nothing but the Self. This is the meaning. || 239 ||
An object other than that [self], which is not grasped as an object accessible solely to the cognition of a self, appears [as such].
To prohibit the perception of that [duality], the supreme Śruti says "Brahman. (240)

Having stated the purport of the explanatory passage (*anuvāda*), he states the purport of the section beginning with "Brahman, that... and ending with "...knows all," starting with the word "Ātmā" (the Self).

The meaning is: the subsequent scripture, the sentence beginning with "Brahman," speaks in order to negate the perception of any object whatsoever that might appear as other than the self-luminous Self. || 240 ||
Therefore, neither collectively nor individually do they possess authority here based on the sacred scriptures.
For it is with effort that one negates whatever is the object of the cognition of non-self. || 241 ||
By negating the view of non-self (*anātmadṛṣṭi*), the conceptualization of those belonging to one's own school (*svayūthya*) is also refuted; thus he states the fruit of this negation: "All... etc.
Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the Self (*ātman*). He clarifies the meaning of the pronoun "that" (*tat*): "non-self," etc. (241).
The self consisting of effects and the self consisting of causes are the two aspects of the supreme self.
Arising from delusion regarding the true nature of the inner self, these two perish when that [delusion] is destroyed; therefore.

Anticipating the objection that "the effort consisting in the repeated practice of negation is impossible to effect because that [duality] exists as both cause and effect," he says: "kārya... (as the effect). He states the result of those two being born from delusion: "tannāśa... (their destruction). The ellipsis is: "therefore, there is the oneness of reality" (*vastvaikarasyam*). || 242 ||
For the nature of cause and effect belongs to that which is neither prior nor subsequent.
From what source of valid cognition (pramāṇa) could [the existence of] that which devours cause and effect be conceived?

Anticipating the objection that it is unestablished for those two [cause and effect] to arise from ignorance, he says: "apūrva... (unprecedented). The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is this: a means of valid cognition does not establish an object contrary to other means of valid cognition, because its nature as a cognizer depends upon non-contradiction. || 243 ||
Nothing whatsoever is born from this, nor is this born from anything at all.
The Śruti declares "the Self" in this way, effecting the negation of [causes] such as the primal cause.

He states that the scriptural authority for the absolute Brahman—which is described in passages concerning the unprecedented (apūrva) and so forth, and which has the nature of swallowing [all] effects such as "to be done" (kārya)—is found in such texts as "It is neither born nor does it die" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.18), by saying: "Not from this... (244).
135 [vol2, page 780] 1074 Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika) [Second Chapter— ]
I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality.
"The Brahman, which is without beginning and supreme, is not said to be existent or manifest.

(245) Regarding that very point, he cites a Smṛti passage: "It is to be known," etc. He states the fruit of its exposition: "That which," etc. What is that which is to be known? He says: "Without beginning," etc. He describes its distinction from the formed and the formless: "Not existent," etc., meaning it is free from cause and effect.
And this is stated by him [the author]. || 245 ||
Because I transcend the perishable and am even superior to the imperishable.
Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 246 ||
Regarding that very point, he states another sentence: "Because... [and so on]. "He is the Supreme Person" (sa uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ) is the meaning of the Vedic word according to the Śruti. || 246 ||
He who, being thus undeluded, knows me as the Supreme Person.
O Bhārata, that all-knowing one honors me with his whole being.
Thus is the direct statement of the Veda-soul, as approved by the Śruti.
O one such as you, there should be no disregard for Śauri, the inner controller of all.

He states that the intended meaning has been declared because knowledge of it possesses fruit: "He who [knows] Me... He indicates the authority of the stated Smṛti by its being spoken by an authoritative person (āpta): "The Veda... He further states its authority because it is rooted in the Veda: "The Śruti... He gives the reason why this [Smṛti] is not to be disregarded: "All... Some even disregard the words of the Blessed Lord; regarding that, he says: "The Lord said..."
"By the *śaiḥ*" means by those belonging to the Veda (*vaidikaiḥ*). || 247 || 248 ||
In that case, he who is deluded and perceives cause and effect is a fool.
One should direct [the mind] away from that person who perceives the Self as incomplete.

Having stated the purport of the passage beginning with "brahma," he briefly explains the literal meaning, saying "therein. The meaning is as follows: when that Self has been freed from duality in the manner described, one who lacks such discrimination perceives both effect and cause as belonging to itself; [the scripture] thereby excludes that ignorant person—who perceives difference and holds false views regarding Brahman, Kṣatriyas, and so forth—from the goal of human life. || 249 ||
"Brahman" here is a designation for the caste (jāti), because of its proximity to the "kṣatra."
A person of the Brahmin caste may supersede a man who lacks right vision.
Having raised the doubt that the word *brahman* refers to the Supreme (Brahman), he states the contradiction with the immediate context: "He says, 'as Brahman'.

He states the meaning of the sentence as obtained from the mention of the genus: "He says, 'Brahman'. He states the reason for setting aside [the other meaning]: "Because it is not correct," etc. (290).
That which exists, he knows; that which does not exist here, he perceives.
Thus, as if possessed by anger arising from an offense, she addressed the fool. (251)

He explains what is correctly seen: "That which exists. The word "brahma" (Brahman) is used in the locative sense. The meaning is that "that which exists" is selfhood (*ātmatva*), while "that which does not exist" is non-selfhood (*anātmatva*); "foolish" means unskilled in discrimination. || 251 ||
One of a different caste should cast away that person who has turned his back on liberation, as if he were a mere corpse.
He who perceives me, the reality of Brahman which is unborn, as having the nature of birth; || 252 ||

He states the counter-agent to the act of rejection: "from isolation" (*kaivalyāt*). He explains the intention of the agent of rejection: "not born" (*ajāti*), etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "I reject him from his human goal. || 252 ||
What sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self?
He who represents the Self as being one way when it actually exists in another way. || 253 ||

He cites the consensus of Vyāsa regarding the propriety of rejecting that [view] with the verse beginning "What is the use of him? He asks, "Who is this thief of the self? and answers it with the verse beginning "He who [sees] otherwise. || 253 ||
He who does not know the true nature of the Vedas, but perceives them as possessing such qualities as birth and so forth.
If he were to bestow that [status] upon a dull-witted man based on his birth, then that birth would be rendered useless. || 254 ||

He analyzes the second part [of the verse] with the words "yo na" (he who does not). For if someone who does not know the true nature of the Self were to know the Self as being associated with Brahminhood, Kṣatriyahood, and so forth, then that false view regarding caste would cause him—who perceives things incorrectly—to fall away from this absolute liberation (*kaivalya*);
therefore, it is not logical to say that the Self is taken away [by such views]. This is the meaning. || 254 ||
It is always one and non-deviating, while it deviates within the cognitions of objects.
That very reality which is reached as the inner self (pratyak) is indeed the non-self entity (anātmavastu). || 255 ||

Fearing the objection that if the Self (ātman) were distinct from Brahman, the Kṣatriya, and so forth, non-duality (advaita) would be lost; whereas if it were not distinct, there would be the perception of the non-Self (anātma-dṛṣṭi) in that which possesses those attributes—the author says: "All this... The meaning is as follows: since the non-Self and the notion of "that" (the objective world) mutually deviate from one another and also from their own essential nature, that single entity which is observed to be eternally non-deviating therein is the innermost reality (pratyaktattva) of the non-Self. For there is no non-Self apart from that [reality]. || 255 ||
Knowledge arises from internal power, having as its basis the delusion born of the individual self.
Because it is non-deviant, it sublates that which follows from darkness, even though the latter is deviant.

If the Self is the reality of everything, why is it that everything else is sublated by the knowledge arising from the [great] sentence, while that very [Self] is not sublated by time and so forth? Anticipating this objection on the grounds that there is no distinction between them, he says: "Antarmeya... etc. By the power of the non-dual blissful inner Self, knowledge takes on its form and sublates the duality—which resides in the intellect accompanied by the appearance [of objects] produced by ignorance—because that [knowledge] possesses unerring validity.
The meaning is that the knowledge arising from such a statement is stronger in terms of its objective reality. || 296 ||
Because of the cause of his lineage and his true nature as the most inward [consciousness] consisting of pure existence alone.
Therefore, its absence at certain times and so forth does not constitute a refutation of cognition. || 257 ||

Anticipating the objection that this [status] applies equally to time and so forth—since they too have no nature apart from the inner self (pratyak)—he says: "The inner self... The absence of that [nature] means the absence of the power of being an object of knowledge (meyabala) within. Although there is no difference in their being born of ignorance (ajñāna), the phrase "therefore" (ataḥ) refers to the fact that for time and so forth, there is an absence of the power of being an object of knowledge. || 257 ||
1 kha. ga. 'paṃ caure'| [vol2, page 782] 1076 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter—]
For a cognition is not accepted as a sublater when it is independent of that which is to be sublated.
Because these two are mutually opposed, right knowledge dispels darkness.

Anticipating the objection that "this distinction is not tenable because there is no difference in their being born of ignorance," he says: "It is not sublated. The fact that a cognition arises from ignorance is not the determining factor for its capacity to prove [an object]; for we observe that cognitions such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell do not possess the power to sublate [their objects]. Therefore, a cognition is sublatable based on the nature of its object; since time and other factors lack that [nature], they are not established [as sublatable]. Nor does the mere fact of being born of ignorance entail a failure to establish a disparity in the objects of knowledge (*meyavaiṣamya*), as even among earthen things, there is a difference between stones and...

The sense is that this is because one perceives a difference within [the cognition] itself. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of illuminating the aforementioned perception. He says, "Of those two," to show that knowledge alone is the sublater. Nor can there be a reversal [of the roles] on the grounds of an equal degree of opposition, because we follow what is observed in experience; for it is not the case that light is dispelled by darkness.
This is the sense. || 298 ||
He who knows himself, whether correctly or otherwise.
A human being obtains the fruit of these very according to how they are perceived. || 259 ||
Thus has the summarized meaning of the passage beginning with "brahma tam" been declared.
One wanders through cyclic existence due to false knowledge; through right knowledge, one is liberated.
Having dispelled the objection that arose incidentally from the claim that "the Self alone is the reality of everything," he concludes with the passage beginning with "Brahman.
With the words "the Self," he clarifies what was stated previously—that the fruit [of knowledge] is according to one's understanding—by saying, "it wanders [in saṃsāra]. || 259 || 260 ||
Since the perception of rasa and so forth has already been refuted, what more is there to say?
"Therefore, the Śruti declares to us: 'This very consciousness is Brahman,' and that it is to be perceived as such. || 261 ||

He takes up the passage beginning with "this" (*idam*) and so forth, preceded by a question. Regarding the phrase "because it has been refuted" (*apoditatvāt*): the first *iti* is intended to refer back to the sentence beginning with "Brahman" (*brahma*), while the second marks the conclusion of the question. || 261 ||
That which shines as inwardness, having the inward intellect as its means of valid cognition;
Let it be understood that Brahman is said to be that which has as its sole reality only that much. || 262 ||
Showing that which is to be seen, he states the meaning of the sentence as it has been brought down [into the commentary]: "By way of being the inner self" (pratyaktvena). || 262 ||
Thus the venerable Self has been heard; the rule for hearing is completed.
Now, the further elaboration of that which is to be thought upon (mantavya) is stated. || 263 ||

He introduces [the next section] by first restating the preceding topic, beginning with "As [the sound of] a drum," and so forth. Regarding the word "thus" (*evam*): the injunction for hearing—that "this Self is to be heard"—is concluded according to the method already explained; for the investigation following the capacity and intended meaning has been completed.
