Immediately thereafter, the subsequent section concerning the injunction for reflection (*manana*)—beginning with "As... and so forth—is commenced as an expansion of that injunction, stating that "it is to be reflected upon."
The meaning is that he follows reason. || 263 ||
Furthermore, how is this world, which is intermingled with name-and-form and so forth, [produced]?
In this world, it is possible to see directly that "the Self alone is everything."
1. M. Koga | [vol2, page 783] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri | 1077

Having introduced the subsequent section with the words "all this" (*idaṃ sarvam*) and so forth, [the author] raises the objection regarding contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge. [The word] "namely" (*nāma*) is used. Here, the term "here" (*iha*) refers to the sphere of human linguistic convention. The word "all" (*sarva*) pertains to the word "world" (*jagat*). (264)
Because [the self] is pervaded by a subjective cognition that is non-exclusive and non-contradictory.
For it is indeed possible [to explain] this very same way for those whose intellects are opposed to this. || 265 ||

He refutes [the objection]. Regarding the term "non-excluded" (*avyāvṛtta*): the meaning is that because the world is pervaded by the non-distinct, uncontradicted consciousness of the inner self (*pratyagbodha*), it has no existence apart from that. Anticipating the objection that the realization "everything is pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*) does not arise for people like us because it is impossible for them, he says:

"This... This means that for those whose intellects are inclined toward the non-dual inner self, which is opposed to this duality, [the realization] occurs in this very way: "everything is pure consciousness."
Therefore, the meaning is that the entire world can be known as being merely this much. || 265 ||
Among cognitions that are subject to error, that cognition which is non-erroneous [is the valid one].
The object of knowledge, when presented by that means of valid cognition, can be apprehended directly.
He says that the fact that everything is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is not only established by the experience of the wise, but is easily known even to people like us:

"In all changing cognitions... Since all cognitions are changing, that cognition which is unchanging—by means of that unchanging [cognition], the object brought forward by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) because it is non-imagined (*akalpita*); however, that which is presented by a changing cognition is imagined (*kalpita*) due to its very changeability.

The meaning is that it is not a real entity, nor can it be directly known that "this entire world is consciousness alone," because that which is imagined has no existence apart from that which is unimagined. || 266 ||
Just as [one perceives] distinct sounds arising from the general property of being the sound of a drum.
"No one would be able to grasp its specific notes, like those of a drum's interior.
(267) He explains the illustration regarding this point—that everything is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and that without it, [reality] is difficult to know—by saying "just as": of a drum...
The term "of that which is being perceived" (*nyamānasya*) indicates the nature of sound; from that [nature] arise external particular sounds.

Even one well-trained to draw them out—like a sword from its sheath—is not able to do so; therefore, they are imagined within the universal (*sāmānya*), just as a snake and so forth are imagined in a rope.
This is the meaning. || 267 ||
In the same way, there is not even the slightest object belonging to a self apart from the self itself.
Since it can be scrutinized, it is therefore like a rope-snake.
He states the application [of the analogy]: "In the same way," [verse 268].
Nor is there a concomitance with particulars anywhere, as there is with the concomitance of the universal.
Since a universal is devoid of specific distinctions, there is no apprehension of a universal through this [means]. || 269 ||

Anticipating the objection that because the relationship of universal and particular exists in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it must also exist in the subject of the argument (*dārṣṭāntika*) due to their similarity, and desiring to refute that state of affairs, [the author] considers the alternatives—whether the universal is non-different from or different from the particulars—and refutes the first by means of the verse beginning with "viśeṣaiḥ.

Just as there is no identity (*tādātmya*) of the particulars with the universal, such [identity] of the latter with them does not exist anywhere; for that [identity] is merely a conceptual construction (*tatkalpa*).

The meaning is that there can be no non-difference [between the universal and the particular], because it is impossible for the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) to be merely a conceptualized particular; otherwise, since the universal would not exist, the cognition of it and its apprehension would not occur.
Therefore, in relation to that [universal], the particulars would not exist, and thus there is no non-difference. || 269 ||
If there were no connection with specific qualities,
then individual objects would not be mutually related to one another.
That which is called "the universal" (sāmānya) with respect to a specific [particular] and so forth would be a fragmented [universal]. || 270 ||

He restates the second [objection] with the words "by the particulars" (*viśeṣaiḥ*). He refutes it as follows: if the universal were distinct from those [particulars], then that [universal] which is desired to exist in them would itself be a particular, just like a "broken pot" (*khaṇḍa*) and so forth, because it is distinct [from them]. Therefore, since the substratum (*dharmin*) does not exist, difference is not established. He provides the example "like a broken pot. The phrase "in the particulars" (*viśeṣādau*) means "among the particulars" (*viśeṣeṣu*). || 270 ||
Because the positive concomitance also resides in both [the subject and the example], there is a mutual relationship between the pervaded and the pervader.
Therefore, apart from negative concomitance (vyatireka), mutual pervasion (vyāpti) is not established. || 271 ||

Having refuted both difference and non-difference between the universal and the particular, he refutes the pervasion (vyāpti) desired by the opponents [with the words]: "Because it resides in two. A particular is the pervaded (vyāpta) and the universal is the pervader (vyāpaka); without their difference, there can be no mutual pervasion, because a relationship of that nature depends upon difference due to its dual substratum. Therefore, since difference is refuted, there is neither pervasion nor any other relationship between the two; thus, their existence is merely conceptualized.
This is the meaning. || 271 ||
An object that has not been sublated by the inward-facing consciousness is indeed established by the inward-facing consciousness.
Nor is the selflessness [of the visual faculty] characterized by non-existence; therefore, it is not perceived through positive concomitance (anvaya) either. || 272 ||

Anticipating the objection that "it is not imagined because it appears, like the Self," he says: "The inner" (*pratyak*). The meaning of this is as follows: Is the non-self (anātman) existent or non-existent? If it were existent, would it be different from eternal consciousness (*nityabodha*) or non-different? If it were different, its establishment would have to be either through itself or through another; however, nothing other than eternal consciousness is established by itself, for that would entail the loss of its insentience (*jāḍya*), nor is it established through another without conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

Because that [world] has no connection with another, it is not non-existent, for that would contradict its immediate cognition; nor is it existent, because it is not cognized as such. Since there can be no identity between the insentient and the sentient, and thus there is an absence of both positive and negative concomitance, the world is merely imagined within the Self, being nothing more than that. || 272 ||
Because it possesses a single nature as mere consciousness, the Self does not possess multiplicity by its own essence.
Furthermore, that which is without self does not endure, nor is it established for any purpose other than its own. || 273 ||

Even though there can be no connection (anvaya) or the like between the Self and the non-Self, one might suspect that a connection or the like of the Self could arise from the non-Self; thus, [the author] refutes such a connection with the word "pratyak" (inward). The phrase "āvidyam" (unreal, born of ignorance) refers to the identification of the body and so forth as the Self, which [ignorance] approves of. With the word "svataḥ" (by itself), he states the exclusion (vyatireka). The phrase "nāpi" (nor even) means that it is stated because that [connection] is not established either by itself or through another. || 273 ||
In the case of an insentient object, its state of being "this" does not differ from its state of being "that."
And because it consists of the nature of distinction, the self does not follow after another. || 274 ||

Having excluded the self from that [non-self] by observing its lack of the nature of a non-self (*anātmasvabhāva*), he states its impossibility [of being related] to that even by observing its own nature (*svasvabhāva*). He says "non-self" (*anātma*). Having refuted the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the self with the non-self, he states another reason for the impossibility of their connection: "from another" (*parāt*). The self follows the knower, and he too follows it.

The sense is that if it were otherwise, there would be no connection of the non-self with the self, nor would there be a connection of the self with the non-self, because in reality there is no meeting between the internal (pratyak) and the external (parāk). He states another reason for the fact that the non-self is not truly connected to the self: "Because of exclusion" (vyatireka), meaning because the external is superimposed upon the internal. || 274 ||
1 [vol2,
page 785] 4 Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1079
Because the sound accompanied by the drum is invariably present everywhere.
In those [beings] whose self-nature has been acquired through effort such as that involving pus, and which are subject to deviation from the self. || 275 ||

Having set aside the relationship of generality and particularity that applies to the example and the subject of the illustration, he provides the reasoning for the apprehension of "soundness" (*śabdatva*) in the phrase "of the drum being struck. [He says] "the drum," etc. He states the meaning of the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*): "by the effort of a person," etc. The implication is that in the sentence under discussion, there is the inclusion of the general property (*sāmānya*). || 275 ||
Among the various distinctions such as high and low, which are mutually inconsistent;
The sound of the drum alone is present everywhere without exception.
It clarifies that the generality of being a sound produced by a drum does not deviate from its particular instances: "And [it is] loud," etc. (276).
Therefore, those [sounds] exist apart from the generality of the sound of a drum.
Being devoid of self-nature, their specific distinctions cannot be perceived.

He states the result of their non-deviation [from the general] and their deviation [from the particular], beginning with "the drum. He provides the reason for the non-perception of particulars apart from the general: "they are soulless" (nirātmaka). || 277 ||
From where was this qualification "the sound of a drum" obtained?
By the mention of the drum, this qualification is obtained. || 278 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the drum being beaten," one might object that since only the word "drum" (*dundubhi*) is heard there, it is improper to qualify it with "sound" (*dhvani*), as there is no means of establishing such a qualification. [The author] raises this doubt with the words: "The drum... He states the means for obtaining the qualification with the words: "Of the drum. This is obtained from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). For the apprehension of a specific sound does not arise from the wooden frame called a "drum," because the two are distinct; therefore, just as in that case the word "drum" indicates the sound through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), so too here—
This is the meaning. Furthermore, this [qualification] is to be understood from the specific attribute "of one being killed. || 278 ||
When there is such a perception as "these are the sounds of a drum," [the cognition arises].
Their specific qualities would also be apprehended, because of their identity with them.

Having explained the passage beginning with "Just as" and ending with "for the sake of grasping," he states the meaning of the phrase "but by the grasping of the drum" [in verse 279]: "But of the drum... || 279 ||
Or rather, from the perception of the striking of a drum, there may arise the perception of its specific qualities.
That which is joined with the heroic and other sentiments is called the *dundubhyāghāta*. || 280 ||

He explains the passage beginning with "of the beating of the drum" (*dundubhyāghātasya*) and so forth. He says "kettledrum" (*bherī*). The meaning is that because of the apprehension of the lower-level generality (*avāntarasāmānya*) of "soundness," there is the apprehension of its particulars. He further analyzes the "beating of the drum" itself as "heroic and so forth" (*vīrādi*). Here, the "beating of the drum" refers to the sound of a kettledrum or similar instrument occurring in the context of battle and so on, associated with one or another of the nine aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*); upon the apprehension of that [general sound], there is the apprehension of its particular [sentimental] qualities due to identity (*tādātmya*).
This is the meaning. || 280 ||
A pot with its lid has been found, along with a long-lipped man who knows both place and time.
No subsequent object is experienced as being superior to each preceding one. || 281 ||
Having explained the illustration, he states the point to be illustrated: "It is perceived that it exists. (281)
Thus,
because of its difference from consciousness,
everything is observed as being superimposed upon it.
Whether it be the universal or the particular, [it arises] from the cause of the non-awakening of consciousness. || 282 ||

If it is argued that since the object of cognition (*cetya*) does not exist apart from consciousness (*cit*), how can there be a perception of difference? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this way.

Since there is no distinction between consciousness and the object of cognition, everything—beginning with universals (*sāmānya*)—is superimposed upon that [consciousness] through ignorance; because of its identity with that [consciousness], it appears as such.
This is the meaning. || 282 ||
In the perfect realization of the innermost Self, there is no cause other than the Self itself.
Even that [self], being devoid of selfhood, would exist as a qualification of the self. || 283 ||

If it is argued that the non-self (anātman) shines by means of the conscious self (cidātman), then that [self] too must shine by means of another, like a lamp; anticipating this objection of infinite regress (anavasthā), he says:

"The innermost" (pratyak). He states that while there exists another entity in the form of a knower (pramātṛ) as a means for establishing the non-self, such is not the case for the establishment of the Self.

He says: "Unlike the non-self. If one were to accept another distinct object as the establisher of the non-self, it would result in the abandonment of the established doctrine (siddhānta) that the Self is the establisher of everything.

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That too. The meaning is that even that which establishes the non-self (anātman)—namely, the nature of the cognizer (pramātṛ)—establishes it only as subordinate to the Self;
for it is the Self itself, having assumed that form, which establishes the non-self. Thus, there is no abandonment of our established tenet (siddhānta). || 283 ||
When the parrot of agency perceives itself as the Self, [it is liberated].
Because it is merely the immutably fixed witness-consciousness, it does not perceive the Self in that manner. || 284 ||
Then, fearing that the Self, having become the mother, might likewise bring about its own self-realization due to the lack of distinction, he says: "Because of agency," etc. (284).
Just as a composite object is always perceived by direct perception as being without a self, so too is it understood.
Then that non-composite Self is realized by the inward-turning intellect through the self.

Anticipating the objection that its being "purely of the nature of immutable perception" is unestablished due to its association with the state of being a knower (*mātṛtva*) and so forth, he says: "It is composite.
The meaning is: the Self would be dualistic, non-self, perceptible, as well as subtle, inactive, and established by the consciousness that is its own essential nature. || 285 ||
Because the purpose of the illustrative example is accomplished by the single [verse] alone, there is no need for further elaboration.
It is explained why many examples are stated: it is for the sake of illustration. (286)

He objects to the statement of numerous examples with the words "dārṣṭāntika" (the illustrated point). The meaning of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) is that everything is nothing but the Self (*ātman*). Since its unity is established by a single example alone, the mention of many—such as the drum, the conch, and the lute, and the sounds of the drum-beating and so forth—is fruitless; this is the sense. He declares the result of that [objection] with the word "īryate" (it is moved/undertaken).
Thus [ends the section]. || 286 ||
The great universal [resides] in a single particular in its entirety.
How indeed could there be dissolution for those things whose nature consists of both exclusion and inclusion? (287)

He clarifies that point with the words "mahāsāmānya" (the great universal). The meaning is that, since there is a single Brahman which stands in the place of the great universal, various examples are stated in order to express the manifestation of particulars, of the universal, and of both, respectively. || 287 ||
1 [vol2,
page 787] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1081
The sound of a drum is cited as an illustration of the great universal generality (mahāsāmānya).
The striking of a drum is held to possess both a general and a specific form. || 288 ||

To demonstrate the logical sequence (*layakrama*), he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the three illustrations with their respective three subjects of illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), beginning with the words "mahāsāmānya" (the great universal).

Just as there is no particularity of sound produced by a drum and so forth without the universal of sound, so too, since even the root cause does not exist apart from Brahman— which is neither effect nor cause— there is an intermediate illustration for the dissolution of the cause, which occupies the position of the great universal, into the non-dual Brahman.

The meaning is that the ground of the final dissolution of the commonality of *rasa* (sound) is merely sound, such as that of a drum. By the term "the sound of a drum being struck," there is grasped a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*)—namely, soundness (*śabdatva*)—which is pervaded by the general property of being sound; and this [sound] is the locus for the convergence of particular sounds.

He states [in the verse] "commonality" (*sāmānya*) etc., to show that this is an illustration of how the five elements, which consist of both universals and particulars, reach their final dissolution in the root cause. || 288 ||
"The external ones"—thus it is said, referring exclusively to the particularities (viśeṣas).
These three examples are given for the purpose of establishing the meaning thus stated. (289)

The finality of all mortal things consists in their merging into the elements, both those that are common and those that are specific; in this regard, the external world of sound is cited as an illustration. He says "the external" because they dissolve into the specific sub-universal of "soundness" (*śabdatva*) upon the striking of a drum.

The phrase "and so too" means that it is like the illustrations of the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*) and so forth. [This applies] to the merging of the elements into the non-dual Brahman, which is the cause.

He concludes with the three examples, stating "Thus it has been said," in order to establish the meaning already explained: that for material things, their dissolution occurs within their causes. || 289 ||
Either by means of positive and negative concomitance, or else by way of its non-existent nature.
But an object that is far removed from the reach of the senses cannot be determined by direct perception. || 290 ||

Having stated that everything is nothing but Brahman by declaring the fruit of numerous illustrations, he says the following in order to establish that very point through another illustration: "Anvaya... etc. A thing called a particular (*viśeṣa*) cannot be established by means of valid cognition as being distinct from its universal (*sāmānya*), nor as being identical with it, nor as being devoid of both difference and non-difference; for if there were absolute difference or absolute identity, the relationship of universal and particular would be impossible, and in the case of voidness (*śūnyatva*), it likewise could not be established.
The meaning is that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of constant non-duality. || 290 ||
Therefore, since the existence [of the object] precludes the possibility of an accusative case, there can likewise be no possibility of a genitive case.
One should know it to be exactly as it exists, when it is perceived as non-different from itself.

Anticipating the objection, "What would follow from that non-duality?", he states [the verse beginning with] "The genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning that in the absence of multiple individuals, the status of being a universal and a particular cannot be established due to the lack of such a relationship. Having restated the example, he states the application to the subject at hand with "Just as" (*yathā*). The meaning is that just as non-duality and non-attachment have been described, so too should they be understood regarding the Self-luminous Inner Self (*pratīc*), which is the object of knowledge. || 299 ||
Of all the particularities that consist of the forms of generalities, without exception.
Just as a great generality (mahāsāmānya) may belong to many things in one place, so it is here.
Of mutually distinct entities, by way of name, form, and action;
When there is no connection with grossness and so forth, for those things characterized as cause and effect.
He concludes the illustration with the words "sāmānya" (the universal): just as all particular existents [subsist] within a single universal of existence (*satsāmānya*).
136 [vol2, page 788]
The meaning is "salutation. He explains the application of the principle (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).

According to the aforementioned illustration, because effects and other categories—which possess mutually distinct meanings through names and so forth—dissolve into Brahman, which is characterized by "not gross" (*asthūla*) and other such qualities, there arises the non-dual and unattached experience of the inner self (*pratyag-anubhava*).
The interpretation. || 292 || 293 ||
Subtlety and pervasiveness are to be understood as increasing successively from the earth element onwards.
In those cases where the inner self is the ultimate limit, [the stages are established] by the successive abandonment of each preceding one. || 294 ||
He states the consensus of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) regarding the fact that every modification dissolves sequentially into the Inner Self (pratyagātman): "Sūkṣmatā" (subtlety).

The construction is as follows: among the objects beginning with earth and ending with the Self, one should understand the subtlety and so forth of each subsequent element—such as water—in relation to the abandonment of each preceding ground, such as earth. || 294 ||
And likewise, the principles beginning with Name and ending with Vital Breath reside within the Self.
By the successive abandonment of each preceding [level], they set in the absolute non-duality.
In that very context, he cites the agreement of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Name and so forth. The word "likewise" (tathā) expresses the principle stated immediately prior. ||29||
First, three examples have been cited regarding the duration of stability.
Even though it is not the self of all, its dissolution occurs spontaneously, like a great universal generality.

Having explained the passage beginning with "Just as [the sound] of a drum," etc., he recites the preceding context in order to introduce the passage beginning with "As from a fire fed by two pieces of wood," etc. The phrase "In the examples" (dṛṣṭānta) serves as a restatement of the fact that, during the period of manifestation, the gradual reduction of everything to the Self alone was stated individually for each of the three examples, such as the drum and so forth. He restates the result of stating the three examples, saying: "Like the great universal generality" (mahāsāmānyavat).

The meaning is that since all particularities of existence culminate in the one Reality, and because everything that is not the inner Self (anātman) is dissolved into that single Inner Self (pratyak), there exists nothing whatsoever apart from the Inner Self. || 296 ||
Just as during the time of its persistence, its oneness can be easily known.
In the same way, according to the logic already stated, it is possible [to establish this] even regarding origination. || 297 ||
He states the intended meaning of the subsequent statement: "In the state of stability," etc. The three examples constitute the logical principle (nyāya). || 297 ||
Just as smoke, flame, sparks, and so forth, appear in succession according to their prior differentiation.
Indeed, no distinction whatsoever, such as smoke and so forth, is perceived apart from fire itself. || 298 ||
He states the literal meaning of the illustrative sentence cited: "Smoke," etc. (298).
In this same way, the vital breath, the worlds, and so forth are also non-self prior to their differentiation;
there remains only the absolute inner Self, which is without before, without after, and without end.
He states the application to the subject at hand: "Prāṇa," etc. By the word "division" (vibhāga), birth is expressed in both cases. || 299 ||
For among words derived from a single source, it is indeed the word itself [that is the cause].
If it is argued that there is no such lack of friendship among friends born of the same lineage, we say: no. || 300 ||

He raises an objection in order to state another intended meaning of the passage beginning with "yathā" (as): "Eka... [In this context,] it refers to the specific nature of that [Brahman] within mere sound. Identity of name is observed [in some cases], but not so for things of different classes such as jars and the like in relation to vīraṇa grass and so forth; therefore, the meaning is that there is no identity of the world—which is distinct from the Self in terms of name and other attributes—with the Self, because of their difference in nature (vaijātya). || 300 ||
Just as there is unity in fire, despite its being divided by the distinctions of smoke and so forth.
Just as there is a single identity among those things distinct from name-and-form and so forth, so it is with the self.
He explains the example as being for the sake of the subsequent [point] with the words "smoke, etc. He analyzes the application to the case in hand with the word "name.
Or rather, because there is no distinction in awakening, no difference exists at all.
The reality of both cause and effect is non-different from each other.

By saying "of those distinct from name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth," it was intended that their mutual exclusion is accepted; now he says that this very [exclusion] does not exist. He states: "It shines forth" (prodgheti). The meaning is that because they are pure consciousness (cinmātra), there is no mutual exclusion among them. He establishes the reason: "The effect... (kārya).

The essential nature of both of them is the same—pure consciousness alone, devoid of cause and effect; therefore, because there is no mutual difference between them, there is likewise no mutual difference among their effects. This is the meaning. || 302 ||
Just as one would renounce [the body], disregarding the means of accomplishing one's own ends and so forth; |||
Just as the moon consumes smoke and the like, so the inner Lord consumes the vital breaths and the rest. || 303 ||

If [the Lord] were the cause of another, there would have to be a fruit [for Him], because it is impossible for one who acts with prior intelligence to engage in activity without a result; furthermore, since He is without assistance and beginningless, no further proof can be stated [to establish His causality], and thus there would be a loss of His state of having all desires fulfilled. Some [hold that] this very sentence is the answer, and the author states the intended meaning [of the verse] as "svārtha... (verse 303).
Regarding the statement "it is to be heard from the words of the Vedas," a doubt is raised here because:
Sound is impermanent because it follows upon effort, just like a jar and other such objects. || 304 ||
He states the doubt that arises from the path of the preceding breath: "It should be heard.

Regarding what was said—that the Self is to be heard on the authority of Vedic statements—the doubt is raised: "The Self is not to be heard on the authority of the Śruti and so forth. The reason for this is given by the word "yataḥ" (because).

The meaning of the reason is that since the [Veda] was created by God, it would be non-eternal like the words of the Buddha and others, and thus it would be unfit to be an independent authority. || 304 ||
This illustration of a sigh is given for the purpose of refuting that [objection].
The Veda, being unarisen through effort, would be eternal by its own nature, like space.
He cites the scriptural passage regarding "exhalation" (*niḥśvāsa*) as the answer. Regarding the phrase "of this," he states its intended meaning in order to clarify the refutation:

"without effort," etc. For that [space] is not non-eternal, because it is merely a movement from the Supreme (the Self) of something already existing—just like the space within a well—and therefore it must be eternal by its own nature as the conscious Self. || 309 ||
And because it is not preceded by conscious intent, it conforms to the state of things as they actually are.
In this context, it is established that the Veda possesses the authority of being a source of valid knowledge through its nature as the Buddha’s wisdom.
As for the claim that validity is not independent because it is non-eternal due to being produced (*kṛtakatvena*), he says in response: "Not [dependent on] cognition" (*abuddhi*).
For non-eternality is not the cause of validity, since it is absent in space (*ākāśa*); nor is non-eternality the cause of invalidity, as it applies even to the eyes and other sense organs.
Therefore, the meaning is that because the Veda determines unknown objects, its independent authority (*anapekṣa-prāmāṇya*) is established.

Since the relationship between word and meaning is conventional (*sāṃketika*), the Veda—by its own inherent power, like the eye and other senses—is a means of cognition; thus, it does not depend upon the intellect of a person who establishes the convention.

Anticipating the objection that [the Veda] lacks authority because it is dependent on [human] cognition, he says: "Just as... For the Veda is not preceded by human intelligence, since no other means of knowledge can apply to its subject matter; even if there were such knowledge regarding it, it would not be useful for the composition of the Veda. This is because of the scriptural statement that it was "breathed forth" (*niḥśvasita*). Therefore, just like the Veda itself, the relationship between the words and their meanings—characterized by *śakti* (denotative power)—exists eternally, like the capacity of the sense organs, and is derived from the Supreme Being; it is not conventional (*sāṃketika*), for the Veda follows the nature of those realities.

The meaning is that [the Veda] is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) like a supervisor (adhyakṣa) and so forth. He states the conclusion regarding the eternality of the Veda and its connection [to the author]: "like the Buddha" (buddhivat).

The meaning is that once its eternality and so forth are established, it is improper to claim the Veda lacks authority—just as one would not accept the lack of authority of the words of the Buddha and others, which arise from [their own] intellects. Alternatively, the meaning is: the Veda is a means of valid cognition regarding its own object because it makes known what was previously unknown, just like the accepted cognition of the Lord (Īśvara). || 306 ||
In every respect, that which has been stated by him should be accepted with faith by one who desires to attain spiritual welfare.
Like the light of the sun, this sound is eternal and not artificial. || 307 ||

He states the established fact regarding its authority: "It leads everyone," etc. This means [the Veda] is to be known either as something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*) or as something to be understood (*jñeya*). "By one desiring to become" (*bubhūṣatā*) means by one seeking the highest good (*śreyorthin*). Anticipating the objection that, although it proceeds like the breath of God, it cannot be eternal because it is a product (*kṛtaka*), he says: "Like the sun's rays. Since the Veda has the Lord as its material cause (*vivarta*), it is identical with Him and is therefore eternal, like the rays of the sun.
The meaning is "it might be so. || 307 ||
The Śruti, having established the Self for man by means of the Supreme Self, [is fulfilled].
Having drunk [the nectar] like cause and effect, it remains as its own self alone. || 308 ||

Fearing that the qualification [“supreme”] might be redundant because such eternity exists elsewhere as well, he states the distinction regarding the Veda: “Supreme. Having established—through methods such as anvaya—that you, who identify with humanity and so forth, are in fact the non-dual Brahman, the Śruti, by means of knowledge, sublates the world and remains as the Self of Brahman itself. Thus, although all means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and so forth, are indeed the Supreme Self alone...
Nevertheless, the meaning is that there is a preeminence in the Śruti. || 308 ||
Or rather, the Vedas are attached to the Self, according to the scriptural statement, "All this is the Self."
The supreme traditional teaching beginning with "Just as" (sa yathā) is for the purpose of removing the misconception that [the Self] is the Veda. || 309 ||

Having explained "sa yathā" and so forth in three ways, he states another meaning of that very passage: "veda" (he knows). From the statement "All this is what this Self is," the lack of authority for the Veda would follow; for unless there were falsity [of the world], everything could not be the Self. If that [world] were false, then the Veda situated within it would also share that status, becoming non-authoritative like a reflection of the Infinite (bhūmābhāsa). It is to refute this that the sentence [is spoken]; such is the meaning. || 309 ||
That is incorrect, because the human purpose [of the scripture] is already accomplished by that very statement.
Since every means becomes a non-means once the goal to be attained has been reached. || 310 ||
And if one's own goal is not established, the means do not possess the status of being means.
Nor is there even a general rule and its exception, because the direct hearing of the Veda is taught.
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how can there be a negation? he asserts that it is impossible for that [negation] to lack validity: "That is incorrect.
For while in the case of running, there is a counter-argument such as the production of a part by striking, such a thing does not exist here in the case of what is heard.
The sense is that because the cognition arises from the sentence, doubt and the like do not exist. Nevertheless, the cognition arising from a false Veda is fruitless—

Anticipating the objection that [the Veda] lacks authority because it is sublated by perception, he says "pumarthasya" (of the human goal), meaning: "It is not so, because it contradicts both scripture and experience. The referent of the word "That" (tat) is the non-dual reality of the inner self, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss. Anticipating the objection—"Since the Veda does not exist apart from the Self according to the scripture 'All is the Self,' how can it have authority?"—he considers whether this non-existence apart [from the Self] occurs before or after knowledge. Rejecting the first alternative on the grounds that it contradicts experience, he addresses the second alternative as follows:

"All" [means this]: since the means such as the eye and so forth cease to be means once there is the certain knowledge of a jar and the like, therefore it is intended that for the Vedic sentences as well, their status as a means ceases upon the self-revelation of the Self, which is their own object of measurement. By the Śruti statement "All is indeed the Self," the Self-nature of everything is stated as a general rule; however, by the passage beginning with "Just as... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1), there is an exception to that in the Veda, wherein its manifestation appears as distinct from the Self, like smoke from fire.

Anticipating the objection that there might therefore be a suspicion of its being a mere figurative designation (āmnātatva) and so forth, he says: "And not [so]. The meaning is that since the Veda itself is directly grasped in the statement "These are the Vedas," and because of the scriptural hearing in the sixth [chapter] that "all this is what this Self is," there is no sublation (apavāda) of that [Self]. || 310 || 311 ||
And like the speech of a child or a madman, I shall respectfully state this refutation.
Since this has been stated by us many times here, we shall desist from further elaboration. || 312 ||

Anticipating the objection that—just as there would be a contradiction with the statements to be mentioned later in the case of the general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*)—there would likewise be a contradiction regarding the authority of the Veda if one were to admit, on your view, that it was preceded by the breath of [an author], like the speech of a child, he says: "Like a child. He feels shame to say that the Veda is equal to the speech of a deceiver and the like, since, being the cause of certain, uncontradicted, and unknown cognition, it is not equal to that.

The meaning is that, beginning from the *Mahe-sambandha*, its authority has been stated repeatedly and with emphasis in various places. Furthermore, he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*), indicating that since this matter has been vigorously argued by many according to the maxim, "But it must be eternal, because perception is for the sake of another," we shall not exert ourselves further on this point. For it has been said:
"Therefore, sound is uncreated and never perishes,
because it has an eternal connection with [the word-meaning], like space and atoms."

Nor does the scriptural statement regarding [the world] "breathing forth" contradict its eternity, because what is intended to be expressed is that it is preceded by [divine] intelligence. As they have said:
"The independence of persons is what we must strive to negate. (392)
The words beginning with the Rigveda, characterized as Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman, are spoken [of].
Likewise, the mantras of the Atharvāṅgirasa, extracted from the Brāhmaṇas, should be [recited]. || 313 ||
Indeed, the Brāhmaṇa alone is divided into various categories such as the Itihāsas and others.
In this context, however, what is intended as the object of apprehension is that which is well-known [to the world], and not history and so forth. || 314 ||

Having explained the passage ending with "this was breathed forth," he now explains the section beginning with "the Ṛgveda. He says "the Ṛgveda and so forth. To avoid redundancy, he states that these were "extracted from the Brāhmaṇas. By the word "here," he refers to the sentence under discussion. Anticipating the objection that if one were to take this as referring to well-known epics and the like, it would contradict the scriptural statement regarding "breathing forth," he says: "But the well-known [epics], etc. (313, 314).
For even that which arises from the meaning of the denotable object is [included] by virtue of the statement regarding the possibility of denotation.
The designator can never exist anywhere without the designated object.

Anticipating the objection as to why only the creation of the proliferation of names (*nāma-prapañca*) is mentioned and not the creation of the proliferation of objects (*artha-prapañca*), he says: "The denoted...
The word "for" (*hi*) signifies that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the designator and the designated. He clarifies this very pervasion with the words: "Not... (verse 315).
Because both the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa portions possess the name "Veda" as their designation.
Therefore, by the expression "the Ṛgveda and so forth," both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas are included. (316)
Just as it is established, the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth are also included.
For to grasp it otherwise than it is is unjust, as it transgresses what is well-established in the world. || 317 ||

Having explained the passage beginning with "That which is the Ṛgveda" according to the Bhāṣya, he states another meaning: "Mantra... Anticipating the objection—namely, how the eightfold Brāhmaṇa is included in the Bhāṣya by means of words such as "itihāsa" and so forth—he refutes it with: "Loka... The sense is that, in the absence of a subverting factor, the well-established usage of the elders is not to be disregarded. || 316 || 317 ||
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Since this has also been stated by Manu and others, how could he deserve the reception of [the Veda]? 318.

In order to include those works well-known by the term "itihāsa" and so forth—which are placed alongside the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas—he states a traditional indicator (*smārta-liṅga*) [from the Smṛtis]: "Itihāsa... etc. Another portion [of the Veda] says: "The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He will strike me. The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) means up to the *Vṛddhamanu-smṛti*.
The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "by Atri also" (*atriṇāpi*) has that sense. (318)
Because the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth have their root in the Veda.
Otherwise, its status as a valid means of knowledge would not be tenable. || 319 ||

If one were to argue that the determination of the meaning of the Veda depends upon *itihāsa* and other such sources, then—given its dependence on them—the Veda’s independent authority (*anapekṣa-prāmāṇya*) would be compromised. Anticipating this objection, he says "itihāsa... etc., asserting that this is not so because the opposite is the case. For, according to the maxim "the specific meaning is understood from the commentary," when the meaning of the Veda is determined through the words of a commentator, the Veda does not thereby lose its independent authority in relation to that commentary.
The state of being. || 319 ||
Whatever statement among those is contrary to the words of the directly perceived Veda, [is not authoritative].
Like the words of the Buddha and others, such [a view] must be abandoned because it contradicts the Vedas. || 320 ||

Anticipating the objection that since even the *itihāsas* and other such texts possess authority like the Veda, why should there be a dependence on them [the Vedas], given that they are connected to truth intrinsically (*svataḥ*), he says: "Perception," etc. (320).
And no creator whatsoever is accepted apart from Īśvara.
Likewise, [one may study] the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other such works here on earth for the sake of their practical application.

Regarding the doubt as to how it is established here that there is a recollection of other authors when accepting the Itihāsas and so forth—given that the Lord is heard of as the author here—the [author] says:
"And not... and "here... This is the statement of the final conclusion (siddhānta). || 321 ||
That whose status as a cause has been directly and definitively determined by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, even in the case of performing that action, that very same [nature] is admitted.
1. Let it be measured. || 312 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 793] 4 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1087.

He establishes that the Supreme Being alone is the cause of the Purāṇas and other scriptures through forms such as Vyāsa and others. Regarding the phrase "the state of being the cause": of the Supreme Being—

The meaning is as follows: since it is established by the Śrutis and other authorities that [Viṣṇu] is the cause of all through his knowledge, and since there is also a traditional remembrance (smṛti) of his authorship of the Mahābhārata and so forth—which are effects of that [knowledge]—he alone is Brahman, acting as the cause in various forms in those respective instances; for it is said: "Who could be more blessed than the lotus-eyed one, the author of the Mahābhārata? || 322 ||
Just as the seed alone is accepted as the cause of rice and other crops.
In the same way, the seed alone is the cause, [manifesting] in the form of the sprout and so forth.

The remainder of the sense is that the seed itself, through the form of that [sprout], is the cause even of the leaves, flowers, and so forth. Likewise, Brahman alone, through those respective forms, is the cause in each respective instance.
He states the reason: "In that same way. || 323 ||
Since the seed at the beginning and the end is perceived through direct observation.

Regarding the requirement for a determining factor in the case that the seed itself, through its nature as the soil and so forth, is the cause of the leaf and other parts, he elaborates upon an illustrative example with the words:

Nor is the Veda accepted as having a credible meaning merely because it is stated in the Veda.
However, this is because the reasons for non-authoritativeness are impossible in the case of Vedic statements. || 325 ||

Anticipating the objection that there is no contradiction with the Smṛtis regarding other agents, and that the authority of the Itihāsas and so forth is dependent [on other means of knowledge]—unlike the Veda, which, being "breathed forth" (niśvasita), is non-intentional like the Veda itself—the author says: "And not... The meaning of this is as follows: by the Vedic statement "it was breathed forth," it is not intended that the Veda is an independent authority because it is spoken without prior reflection; rather, it is because the grounds for lack of authority, such as having an object perceived through other means of knowledge, are absent therein.
However, since works such as the *Bhāgavata* and the *Itihāsas* serve to supplement the Veda, there is no lack of authority regarding their perceived (empirical) content;

nor is there any contradiction with the *Śruti* concerning the "breath-like" origin of the *Itihāsas* and so forth, because that refers to their manifestation from the Supreme Being in the form of Vyāsa and others without effort. || 325 ||
The authority of Vedic statements does not depend upon other means of valid cognition.
The validity of the senses and other means of knowledge also arises from the very same cause as previously described.

Anticipating the objection that—on the principle that "a word whose capacity is understood from worldly usage is also expressive in the Veda"—the Veda’s status as having an object not perceived by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) is unestablished, he says: "Validity" (*prāmāṇyam*). The meaning is this: although the cognition of the power (*śakti*) of individual words depends upon other means of knowledge, the validity of the sentence does not depend upon them, because it is a rule that [validity] belongs to that which has an unknown object. This state of having an unknown object is the cause of validity.
"How is it determined that it is *jaka*? Because it is observed as such among well-known means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," he says: "Of the sense organs, etc. (326).
