He states that the eye is composed of light (*taijasa*). [The verse says: "By its own object," etc. The meaning is: "The subject under dispute is composed of light, because among color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects], it manifests only color-form, like a lamp. He states a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) [against the opponent]: if the eye did not share the same genus (*sājātya*) as the color-form it grasps, then, just as color-form is not grasped by the ear, it would likewise not be grasped by the eye. [The verse says: "If not," etc. (364).
Otherwise, there would be no apprehension of all objects that belong to the same class as the object [in question].
Just as it is for each individual sense organ here, so it is for the mind and the intellect. || 365 ||

He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) regarding the intended object (*viṣaya*) in the aforementioned inferences, beginning with the words "No" (*na*). Here, the term "here" (*iha*) refers to the sphere of conventional discourse (*vyavahārabhūmi*). || 369 ||
However, because they consist of the essence of all beings, those two grasp all objects.
It should be understood as "of the mind and the intellect," for otherwise that [result] would be impossible. || 366 ||
Anticipating the doubt as to how those two [the mind and the intellect] can also grasp all objects, he says "sarva" (all), because they are composed of the five elements (*bhūta*). The point is this:

the subject under discussion (the mind and intellect) belongs to the same class as the five elements, because they are graspers; for whatever is a grasper is of that nature, just as a lamp, which grasps form, is of the same nature [as the elements].

Nor is the reason unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*), because the non-self (*anātman*), which is not an object of the mind and intellect, does not exist [independently]; and their belonging to the same class is accepted as being within the sub-class of substance (*dravyatva*).

The point is that since being produced by sleep, the grasping of that [object], and being its cause do not apply to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). He states, "Otherwise," [verse 366], asserting the impossibility of a cause established by experience as a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*).
Intellect (buddhi) is said to be the commonality of the cognitive powers directed toward the skin and other sense organs.
1.1 Prāṇa alone is said to be the commonality of the power of action, just like that [the individual breaths]. || 367 ||

Having stated that the skin and the other [senses] are composed of the elements (*bhautika*), he describes their common characteristic form, which is distinct from light (*prakāśa*). "The skin and so forth"—the meaning is that for the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) along with their powers, illumination (*prakāśa*) is the common characteristic form. Considering the organs of action (*karmendriya*) to be elemental like the others, he states their common characteristic form: "Prāṇa. The meaning of this is: speech is a modification of space (*nabhas*), consisting of an aperture...

Since sound is manifested when grain exists, the two [ears] are bound to the auditory organ and consist of air (*vāyavīya*), because they invariably do not depend on light and possess the specific instrumentality of conveying touch, and because strength in the form of wind is observed there; for the Śruti says, "Breath indeed is strength.

The two feet are fiery (*taijasa*) because they generally possess a hot touch, like a lamp. The anus is watery (*āpya*) because of its unctuousness, like clarified butter (*saṃmata*). The generative organ (*upastha*) is earthy (*pārthiva*).

Because it possesses fragrance, like that which is commonly agreed upon [to be earth]. Thus, the common characteristic of these elemental derivatives (bhautika) possessing the power of action is that their activity is like light, as in the case of the skin and so forth. Speech is composed of fire (*taijasa*), according to such scriptural texts as "Speech is made of fire. The hands are, as before, composed of air (*vāyavīya*). The anus is composed of earth because it possesses fragrance, according to such scriptural texts as "The bladder is wealth" and so forth. The organ of generation is composed of water; by process of elimination, the feet are composed of space (*nābhasa*).
Or rather, this is the meaning. || 367 ||
The powers of cognition, such as hearing and the rest, exist for the purpose of accomplishing the enjoyment of sound and other objects.
In the same way, the powers of action, such as speech and the rest, exist for the purpose of experiencing [the results of] karma.

Regarding the question, "For what purpose do the organs of knowledge (jñānendriyas) exist?", he says: "Sound, etc. For it has been stated: "The function of the five [organs] with respect to form and the other [objects] is held to be mere perception. Regarding the question, "For what purpose do the organs of action (karmendriyas) exist?", he says: "In the same way."
And it has been said: "Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure belong to the remaining [senses]. (368)
The specific power as previously described, preceded by the mind and the intellect— [Brāhmaṇa 4, with the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā by Ānandagiri]. 1095.
Furthermore, there is also a twofold distinction between those two based on intention (saṃkalpa) and determination (adhyavasāya). || 369 ||

To the question of by what all these are impelled to function therein, he says: "As stated. By the word *śakti*, the substances possessing power (*śaktimat*) are understood. How is there a distinction between the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*), since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is indeed said to be twofold? To this he says: "Volition" (*saṃkalpa*). || 369 ||
Whatever [capacity] belongs to a particular suitable sense organ is observed even in relation to something other than that.
That should be understood as its very mode of existence, not a change in its intrinsic nature. || 370 ||

As for the claim that the ear and other organs are modifications of space (*ākāśa*) because they manifest sound, that is incorrect; for it is observed that the eye, though composed of fire (*taijasa*), also manifests [sound], as is well known from the proverb "the serpent has ears in its eyes. Furthermore, the argument that the hand and the skin are composed of air (*vāyavīya*) because they are the instruments for grasping and feeling what possesses touch is invalid, due to the deviation found in the feet and so forth; nor can it be established merely by possessing a specific kind of touch in the absence of a necessary connection.

The faculty of speech possesses luminosity (*taijasatva*) because it exists even in the hands and so forth; nor does the anus and so forth possess fluidity (*āpyatva*) simply because they are moist, as this would lead to an over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and similar substances; nor is the generative organ (*upastha*) and so forth earthy (*pārthiva*) merely because they possess odor, since that quality also exists in the anus and other organs. Therefore, the elemental nature of the sense organs cannot be established by their specific functions. To this, he says: "appropriate" (*yogya*). That which is the appropriate function—such as hearing and so forth—of each [organ], such as the ear and so forth...

The meaning is this: although that [consciousness] is observed in the eye and other [senses], it must be understood as belonging to the ear and other [senses] as well, because it is impossible for its nature to be otherwise; for even in the absence of a difference in location, the distinction between the senses—which is discernible through the difference in their effects—is difficult to deny. || 370 ||
Thus, from the dispersion of the powers of knowledge and action belonging to the Self of the universe, [the world arises].
The manifestation of the self as a body is for the sake of providing the basis for the sense organs.

Even if the arrangement of the instruments [of action] is thus established, the creation of the body remains irrelevant, because the bondage of the Self is accomplished through the operation of the senses even in the absence of that [body]. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In this way. According to the stated principle, for the sake of providing a locus for the instruments of that transmigrating soul who is the self of the world through the two-fold operation of the senses, there is the creation of the body; and indeed, the operation of the senses is not possible without a substratum.
For [the senses] are indeed the aged; and the body is composed of the five elements, because the pentad beginning with sound is perceived therein—this is the intended meaning. || 371 ||
And this being so, if from that [cause] the effect previously manifested, [then...]
That [effect], however, undergoes dissolution right there into its own cause.
Since the body and the instruments [of action] are composed of the elements, they attain the fruit [of their actions] by dissolving back into those elements. And so it is. || 372 ||
The dissolution of all these occurs in the primary cause alone.
Because effects have that [cause] as their cause, there is no dissolution into another effect. || 373 ||
If it is argued that even when the elements have dissolved into their effects and instruments, their dissolution might still occur elsewhere than in Brahman, he says: "In the Root" (*mūle*).
This means that because Brahman is the cause of those [elements], the elements are the effects of the Root Cause. Even so, one might suspect that their dissolution could occur elsewhere than in That;
anticipating this, he says: "Of effects," because [Brahman] is not distinct from its effects, and because it is impossible for an effect to dissolve into another effect, such [a view] is not tenable.
Thus [it is said]. || 373 ||
1 ka. 'kāra' | [vol2,
page 802] 1096 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Second Adhyāya— ]
Because the letters beginning with *aṭ* are directly perceived within the *piṇḍas* and so forth, this [process] consists of their dissolution (*laya*) and so on.
Delusion regarding previous actions leads to this state of dissolution through ignorance. || 374 ||

It is not only in Brahman that there is the dissolution of all effects, for the dissolution of a jar is observed in clay and so forth, and you yourself have accepted that the dissolution of effects and instruments occurs within the elements; thus, suspecting that there might likewise be a dissolution of effects within other effects, he says: "In the lump [of clay] and so forth.

Since the dissolution of a jar and the like is admitted in the primal cause (mūlakāraṇa) which has attained the state of clay and so forth, there is no dissolution of one effect within another effect.

The meaning is that, even though the dissolution of a jar and so forth into clay and so forth occurs during tasks such as making a lump [of clay], because this dissolution is not perceived by those who lack discernment, the delusion arises that the dissolution into other effects occurs only within the immediate [clay and such] due to a lack of discrimination. || 374 ||
In this same way, the objects of touch and so forth are to be understood as residing respectively within the skin and the other sense organs.
There is dissolution into the subtle measures (mātrās) beginning with touch, and likewise, there is dissolution of those [measures] as well.
Even for that [mind], there is the dissolution of cognition when it reaches the generality of mental objects.
Just as rivers [merge] into the ocean within the single commonality that is their own domain. || 376 ||
And even the commonality of the consciousness of the objects of cognition resides within the self.
In that which is free from dissolution and distraction in another, and is immutable; || 377 ||

Having established the dissolution of the elements and their derivatives into Brahman, the fundamental cause, he applies this principle to the meaning stated in the commentary beginning with "of all touches" (*evaṃ sarveṣāṃ sparśānām*). The word "thus" (*evam*) means that one should understand the dissolution of specific touches into the mere category of touch, and the dissolution of specific forms into the mere category of form denoted by the eye, and so forth. [The dissolution] occurs in the unchanging Self.
This is the remainder [of the sentence]. The qualification beginning with "laya" (dissolution) is for the purpose of establishing its state of being untransformed. || 375 || 376 ||
Likewise, there is dissolution into the objects of one's own generalities, such as "largeness" and so forth.
Of all the organs of action, [the dissolution occurs] into their five common [elements]. || 378 ||

The textual passage beginning with "Just as [the modifications] of all [the organs]" and ending before "of all actions" has now been explained through both summary and detail. Now, he states the purport of the section beginning with "Thus, of all actions": "Speech, etc. The meaning is that the dissolution of the organs of action and their respective objects occurs in their common generic forms such as "speaking-ness" (vadanatva) and so forth; these, in turn, dissolve into the vital breath (prāṇa), and that [breath] dissolves into its causal self.

Just as there is a dissolution of the sense organs and their objects into the five universals, such as tangibility (sparśatva) and so forth, so too is there a dissolution of the organs of action and their objects into the objects that consist of the universals within the domain of speech and the rest; such is the construction [of the verse]. 378.
Vibration exists within the powers of knowledge as manifestation.
But pure vibration alone, within the powers of action, is devoid of luster. || 379 ||

He provides the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) in order to state the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the commentary beginning with "prāṇaśca" and so forth. He states the meaning of the word *kevala* [in the verse] as "devoid of radiance" (*niṣprabha*). || 379 ||
IR 1 ka. ga. as from clay, etc.; 2 sa. having made a promise to him.
All this movement, moreover, has its basis in the intellect and the sense organs.
"He is to be known as having the vital breath (prāṇa) as his self," and "He is indeed its slayer," according to the Śruti. || 380 ||

The commentary states that *prāṇa* is indeed nothing but knowledge (*jñānamātra*). He explains the purport of the [Bhāṣya] with the words "sarvo’pi" (all...). Since movement (*parispanda*) is of the nature of *prāṇa*, and since the various sense organs are also of the nature of movement, and because of the Vedic scripture stating "That which is *prāṇa* is *prajñā*," the meaning is that the status of being *prāṇa* is established for both types of sense organs due to the identity of *prāṇa* and *buddhi*. He provides the authority for their being *prāṇa* with the word "hanta."
From the analogy of the axe and the peg, it follows that these are indeed the powers of the vital breath alone.
All the organs of action, as well as the organs of perception, [are likewise]. (381)
He cites another scriptural authority (*śruti*) as proof for the fact that the two types of sense organs have that [Prāṇa] as their essence: "paṭṭīgā" etc.
Just as even a noble horse tears up the four pegs that serve as its foot-tethers by means of a single spike, so too does Prāṇa tear away speech and the others;
thus, the meaning is that the sense organs mentioned in the scripture are of the nature of Prāṇa because they are dependent upon it. || 381 ||
When the person, with the collection of organs rendered yellowed, abides in his own self;
Likewise, there is the statement of the Śruti: "The pure vital breaths are awake. (382)

Since those [senses] are dependent on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and have it as their essence, he states another scriptural passage regarding their dissolution: "They merge into breath" (*āpīta*); that is to say, in accordance with the dissolution of the senses as previously described. || 382 ||
Together with the power of action, that power of knowledge dissolves.
And the Śruti, with reverence, asks "In whom? regarding the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa). 383.

He states the result regarding their identity with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the words "together indeed. Intending that the dissolution of the vital breath occurs in the Supreme, he cites the scriptural authority for its being the cause of that [dissolution] in the passage beginning, "In whom shall I depart? The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the experience concerning the vital breath; the second "and," however, refers to the meaning of other scriptural passages such as "He created that vital breath. (383)
This dissolution is common and is designated as having a common end.
This dissolution is not absolute, because it arises merely from contact with its own cause. || 384 ||

Furthermore, he states that there is conformity with the remainder of the passage [in the fifth chapter] by noting that the ordinary dissolution (laya) common to all living beings—which ends in the cause denoted by the word "samāna"—will also be discussed at the end of the fifth chapter. He says: "sādhāraṇa" (common). He provides the reason for this commonality between the dissolution described in the fourth chapter and that in the fifth: "svahetu" (by its own cause). || 384 ||
The supreme imperishable is characterized by the sovereignty of the powers of knowledge and action.
Having arrayed itself as the world, it withdraws [the world] back into its own self alone.

To the question of how the dissolution ending with the fifth [element] is said to end with the cause (*kāraṇa*), he says: "By knowledge," etc. The meaning is that because Brahman possesses all powers, it expands itself alone into the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and having withdrawn that back into its own self, it remains as itself; thus it will be so according to the remainder of the fifth [chapter]. || 385 ||
1. ka. ga. tadā; 2. ka. ga. yataḥ. [vol2, page 804]
By the scriptural statement "having crossed over," the causal self (kāraṇātman) is thus designated.
The phrase "he has transcended" (atyakrāmat), however, expresses his state of being seedless (nirbīja). || 386 ||
In this regard, raising the doubt that although words denoting effects such as the vital breath (prāṇa) exist there, no word denoting the cause exists, he says:
"By etymology" (nirukti). The meaning is that the cause has been stated in accordance with the previously explained sense: having extended the vital breaths and entered the Self therein, He remains.
If it be argued, "Then let that alone be the real reality," he says: "Because He transcended" (atyakrāmat). || 386 ||
Since this is so, therefore, following the dissolution of the power of all-encompassing knowledge, [the state of Śiva is attained].

The single *prāṇa*, which withdraws all functions, remains. Since the root cause has been stated here by the words "having withdrawn," it is for that very reason that the sequence of withdrawal is described by the Śruti passage beginning with "In what, then, are you and the Self established? occurring in the context of the fifth [question]. Thus, even though the cause has been mentioned there, from where does that [withdrawal] arise?
He states that there is no room for the suspicion that this is a figurative expression (layokti), because [of the following reason]. || 387 ||
The prāṇa dissolves into the apāna, and likewise the apāna dissolves into the self of the vyāna.
Vyāna also enters Udāna, and Dāna likewise goes to Samāna. || 388 ||

The *prāṇa* is a specific modification [of the vital breath], because of the scriptural statement regarding its dissolution into the *apāna*; for it is not possible for the primary [breath] itself to undergo such dissolution. Nor is there any impossibility of its being the withdrawer of all effects, since it possesses both the presence and absence (correlation and exclusion) of all worldly activities; thus he says: "Prāṇa. Just as the *prāṇa* dissolves into the *apāna*, so too the *apāna* dissolves into the *vyāna*, the *vyāna* into the *udāna*, and that [the *udāna*] also dissolves into the *samāna*; thus he says: "Likewise. The meaning of this is explained in the fifth [chapter].
The word "hi" (for) indeed indicates a proven fact. || 388 ||
The very self that is the cause of the world is designated by the term "equal" (samāna).
This common primordial dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya) is considered to be universal. || 389 ||
Fearing that the word *samāna* might also have a specific technical sense (like the words *prāṇa* and so on), he says: "the causal self" (*kāraṇātman*).
Having briefly explained the meaning of the remaining part of the passage in accordance with the context, he concludes with its natural dissolution: "all... (verse 389).
Even its state of being a mass of pure consciousness is not said to consist of the intellect.
The self is said to consist of the connection with the manifestation arising from the perception of the present.

Now, is there a dissolution of all effects in the *prākṛta* [laya], or not? If not, then there would be no distinction between deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and dream (*svapna*), because even in a dream there is a dissolution of some effects. If [it is argued that] there is [such a distinction], then the statement "the *prājña* is bound by the cause" and "the *prājña* is liberated through bliss," and so forth, would be contradicted; for the state of being *prājña* is impossible in the absence of the functioning intellect (*prajñā*) due to the dissolution of those respective cognitions. Therefore, he says: "by means of *prajñā*"—referring to the *prākṛta* dissolution.

The word "also" (api) is used to provide an illustration for the absence of dependence on the intellect. How then is the state of being the Knower (prājñatva) taught in the Śruti? To that he says: "The Inner Self," etc. (390).
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) bear validity here [in this world] by virtue of being mutually consistent.
This, whose true nature is not understood, is called the cause. || 391 ||

Fearing that the established doctrine (siddhānta) would be abandoned because the cause [the unmanifest] becomes the "knower" (prājña) through its association with the reflection of the Self—since there is a distinction between the cause and the Self—he says:
"That which is the cause," meaning that the reality of the Self, when unknown, becomes the object [of cognition] on the plane of empirical transaction (vyavahārabhūmi).
It is direct perception...

The meaning is this: since that which is declared in the discourses of the Śruti and Smṛti to be the cause of the world— such as Brahman and the like— attains its authority [therein], how then can there be duality?
When that is known, this entire world, including all that is moving and stationary, becomes known.
And when it is unknown, that which is thus unknown is said to be this very thing. || 392 ||

He cites the scriptural text concerning the "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" as proof for the point that the Self alone is the cause by way of ignorance. Regarding the verse beginning with "In which":

the meaning is that that very thing—known when [the Self] is known and unknown when it is unknown—is this cause established by the Upaniṣads, because there is no effect that exists apart from its material cause. || 392 ||
But surely, here the dissolution of the object itself is stated by the scripture.
But why has [the cause] of the instrument not been stated? To this it is replied: || 393 ||

Although you have established that the dissolution of the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties occurs during the elemental dissolution (*prākṛta-laya*), he asks: "Even so, why is this not [explicitly] stated in the Śruti? He states the reason for the fact that the dissolution of the instruments (*karaṇa-laya*), though intended, is not mentioned directly by the Śruti:
"It is said... (393).
The scripture considers the instrument to be of the same genus as its own object-domain.
By the mention of the dissolution of the object, the dissolution of the internal organ is stated. || 394 ||

He elucidates that very point with the words "svagocara" (within its own range). The homogeneity of the instrument has already been made manifest. He shows the fruit of that homogeneity with the words "viṣayasya" (of the object). || 394 ||
Thus should this Self be understood through reasoning, as previously described.
One should strive diligently by means of the logical method of the examples mentioned, such as the drum and so forth. || 395 ||
Because it is the basis for the causes of the arising and dissolution of the self and of commonality.
"The self alone is everything"—this meaning of the proposition has thus been established. || 396 ||

He concludes the elaboration on the method of reflection with the word "evam" (thus). The construction is as follows: just as this Self is to be reflected upon through reasoning, so too was it previously stated. He demonstrates that very manner which was mentioned by saying "dundubhyādi" (the drum, etc.). The presentation of numerous reasons by means of various illustrations is an effort toward the substantiation of the matter as it has been described. || 399 || 396 ||
The Paurāṇikas have declared that this dissolution is natural (svābhāvika).
But dissolution preceded by conscious intent is preceded solely by perfect knowledge. || 397 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "sa yathā" (just as that), which is intended to clarify the understanding of the meaning of the sentence, he cites the consensus of the Paurāṇikas for the sake of specifying the scope of the dissolution already mentioned:
"svābhāvika" (inherent). Dissolution is threefold, distinguished as occasional (*naimittika*), inherent (*svābhāvika*), and absolute (*ātyantika*). For it has been said:
"The dissolution of all beings is indeed threefold."
"Dissolution is likewise occasional, natural, and absolute."

Among these, the first is the intermediate dissolution (avāntara-laya) caused by Brahmā. As it is said: "The occasional (naimittika) dissolution of those [beings] at the end of a kalpa is that of Brahmā. The second, however, is the cessation of effects within their primordial cause (prakṛti). The absolute (ātyantika) dissolution is dependent upon knowledge.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Two:
He says that liberation (*mok�sa*) is preceded by intelligence (*buddhipūrva*). And it has been said: "Liberation, known as absolute, lasts for two *parārdhas* of the *prakṛti*. (397)
The state in which effects exist within their own cause as mere potentiality is called non-absolute dissolution (anātyantikilaya), which provides the occasion for further birth. (398)
He states the distinction between natural dissolution (*svābhāvikalaya*) and dissolution preceded by wisdom (*dhīpūrvaka*). Regarding the word "power" (*śakti*):
since it is maintained that in natural dissolution the effects abide within their cause in the form of power (*śaktyātmanā*), therefore this [dissolution] is not final; such is the construction.
He clarifies its non-finality with the word "again" (*bhūyaḥ*); because it leaves room for birth once more, it is "natural" (*prākṛta*).
This is the meaning. || 398 ||
It is the cause for the destruction of past, future, and present births, and so forth.
But as for that destruction which is preceded by wisdom, it is for its sake that this supreme scripture exists. (399)

He introduces the subsequent statement for that purpose, speaking of the distinction regarding the dissolution preceded by intelligence (*dhīpūrvavilaya*). The meaning is as follows: the destruction of ignorance—which is the cause of birth and so forth throughout the three periods of time—is indeed a destruction preceded by intelligence; therefore, the subsequent scripture is intended to demonstrate the knowledge of its means.
This example is stated here for the purpose of establishing the matter as it has been described.
Just as a lump of salt, cast here into the ocean, its own source, [dissolves]. (400)
Following the dissolution of the hard water, the residue dissolves; once dissolved, there is no one who can take it up by drawing it out from the waters. (401)
Even a skillful man is capable [of this] in the form of a remnant, as before.
No one at all is capable of grasping it by means other than its ocean-like form. || 402 ||

Having introduced that [subject] without distinction, he introduces the scriptural illustration specifically with the words "as has been stated. The meaning is this: for the purpose of establishing that reality—namely, that the dissolution of the phenomenal world of cause and effect occurs through knowledge in Brahman, which is of a different nature from it—the scriptural text provides an illustration. He explains the words of that [passage] with the word "yathā" (as). By the word "evam" (thus), which refers to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the word "yathā" [is connected].

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: that which is a lump of sea salt (*saindhava-guḍikā*), when thrown into its own source, water, dissolves immediately after the hardness of the water has subsided.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "na hy asya" (for there is no...): "of that which has dissolved. The phrase "as before" means as in the state prior to being thrown into the water.
He restates the proposition (*pratijñā*) in order to state the reason for that: "sāmudra" (oceanic). Its form is merely water. || 400 ||
One who desires to grasp it may take water from the ocean from whichever source one wishes.
Then and there, that salt is consumed; no residue remains anywhere.

He states the meaning of the causal statement beginning with "from whichever [direction]" with the words "he should take. "Desiring to grasp him" means having the desire to seize that fragment (*khilya*). || 402 ||
The ocean water reaches the state of a solid residue through the heating power of the sun.
Since he came from the ocean (sindhu), for that reason he is called Saindhava. || 404 ||

Briefly summarizing the meaning of the illustrative statement and elaborating upon it, he states the reason for its being a fragment: "sāmudram" (oceanic) and "sindhoḥ" (of the ocean), which explain the meaning of the word "saindhava. || 404 ||
That which has its own parts undivided is then called a *khilya*.
This very one is like a fragment of rock salt cast here into the great ocean. || 405 ||

He states the meaning of the word *khilya*: "asaṃbhinnena" (by that which is not mixed). The non-mixture of its own parts means their firmness due to mutual cohesion. The word "atha" (then) means in the state prior to being cast into its source, the water. Having explained the meaning of the two words, he states the meaning of the sentence: "so 'yam" (this very same). The meaning is that he abandons the residual form of light. The word "atha" (then) serves to indicate that the attainment of the opposing state is the cause for the abandonment of that light. || 405 ||
Then, having encountered a contrary nature, it abandons its fiery state.
Due to the separation from heat, solidity is destroyed; that is its destruction.
Fearing that even when the digestive heat has been relinquished, it might persist in the form of a residual fragment, he says: "The heat... (verse 406).
When the cause of solidity has been destroyed here in the great ocean, there remains only the void.
Following the destruction by the water of the hard [mass], the solid residue dissolves. || 407 ||

He clarifies this very point with the words "hardness" (kāṭhinya). The meaning is that when the cause of hardness—the contact with heat—is destroyed by throwing a solid mass into the great ocean, the solid mass itself is also destroyed through the destruction of the hard water. || 407 ||
Only that form which is unconditioned remains for him.
That which arises from the connection with the constituent parts of fire ceases.

He states the remaining point with the words "yadeva" (that which...). This refers to the aforementioned solid mass (*khilya*). That is merely water. Anticipating the objection that being uncreated (*akṛtrimatva*) is equally applicable to hardness as well, he says: "tejaḥ" (fire). || 408 ||
Connection with fire and the other elements is the cause of its assuming a fragmented form.
Because it exists when that exists, and likewise perishes when that is destroyed. (409)

In that case, one might object that conjunction with that [fire] alone is the cause of the state of being a remnant (*khilyatā*), and thus the mention of earth and so forth is redundant; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Fire and so forth.

He states the reason why even living earth and the like are causes for that [state]: "In the absence of that... For a cause is postulated through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and these two are equally present in the case of earth and so forth as they are in the case of fire; therefore, the status of being a cause is indistinguishable [between them]. || 409 ||
Or thus, [the word] *ara* [is explained] by way of its nature as cause and effect.
The actual conduct of one who turns back is said to be contradictory. || 410 ||

Having stated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) both briefly and in detail, he now explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "evam" (*thus*) in order to expound the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Thus—[Vol. 2, page 808] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Second Chapter.

The literal meaning is as follows: by the word "this" (*idam*) in this sentence, the real nature of this internal self (*pratīc*), which is contrary to its causes and so forth, is being expressed. || 410 ||
For the sake of realizing Brahman-ness, which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else.
The designation "Great" (mahat) would exist for the sake of its immutability, and the word "element" (bhūta) is used for the sake of its being a product. (411)
He states the meaning of the two words "mahat" and "bhūta" [as follows]: "avyāvṛtta... (verse 411).
Relying on the actual state of affairs, [this applies] to the internal subject prior to awakening.
For the sake of making known that which is established by itself, the words "great" and so forth are spoken. || 412 ||

Anticipating the objection that the greatness and other attributes of the inward Self (pratīcaḥ) belong only to the state of liberation, he says: "real" (vāstavam). The word "even" (api) should be supplied [to read] "even before" (prāg api). The ellipsis is to be completed as: "of that which is established by itself in the form of greatness and so forth. || 492 ||
The statement that "it is infinite" is an expression of the negation of its cause.
"The non-far shore" refers to the effect; "the far shore" refers to the cause of the effect. || 413 ||

He states the meaning of these two terms, "endless" (*ananta*) and "shoreless" (*apāra*), with the words "of the cause. He asks: how is the status of the Supreme as an effect (*kāryatva*) refuted by the term "shoreless"? To this he replies: "The shore" (*pāra*). The meaning is that once "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*)—that is, the cause—is negated, it becomes easy to refute its being an effect. || 413 ||
Likewise, the effect of a cause is established as having an end, even though it is beginningless.
Even the expression "a mass of consciousness" is used for the purpose of negating other types of birth.

Nevertheless, how is its causality negated by the word "ananta" (endless)? To this he says: "Of the cause," etc. For the cause is indeed beginningless; otherwise, there would be a lack of continuity and an infinite regress. Its effect has an end, for it is well known that it has an end. Indeed, clay and the like, once transformed into a jar, do not produce a bowl and so forth [from that jar]. Therefore, by the exclusion of the effect through the term "anapara" (having nothing beyond), the causality of the Supreme is established.

The meaning is that it is possible to negate [it]. He states the referent of the term "mass of consciousness" (vijñānaghana): "of a different genus" (jātyantara). A different genus is that which is other than cognition (jñapti). || 414 ||
In this way, there is a conjunction of cause and effect between the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and space (ākāśa).
Having attained the state of oneness that is to be realized through direct realization (abhiṣyānīya), one turns back from speech. || 415 ||

He states the meaning of the word "eva" (only/alone): "The Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña). Having realized the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) from such statements as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), by the power of that realization, the world known as cause and effect indeed ceases to exist; thus, the ultimate conclusion is the absolute uniformity of Reality alone—this is the meaning. || 415 ||
Through the awakening to the oneness of Brahman, which destroys the notions of cause and effect.
There is no attainment of a distinct self-nature, just as there is none for a small fragment within the great ocean. 416.

Fearing the consequence that even though the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) has been destroyed by the destruction of cause and effect through knowledge, it might arise again, he says "kārya... and so forth. For there is no further state of being a living soul due to the absence of a cause; indeed, there is no re-emergence of that very same thing which was destroyed and cast into the great ocean. This is the meaning. || 416 ||
Just as water, having come into contact with heat, becomes solidified into a clod.
In that very same way, he who is beyond those who are characterized by ignorance attained the state of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

Anticipating the objection that through knowledge only ignorance is destroyed—and not the relationship of cause and effect or the state of being a living soul (jīvatva)—the author introduces the verse beginning with "from these" (*etebhyaḥ*), stating that since everything that is non-self is born of ignorance, its destruction through knowledge results in the destruction [of all those things]. Thus he says: "Light...
(verse 417).
The self consisting of action, undergoing diminution, reaches its final consummation therein.
Those who are established in the Vedānta declare that those elements are ignorance (avidyā). || 418 ||

Since the word *bhūta* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the "great elements" (*mahābhūta*), how can the Supreme be designated as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) in relation to these elements whose nature is ignorance? To this, he says: "The body is called *mati*. That in which all effects dissolve—that root cause, Ignorance—is denoted by the word *bhūta*. As the teacher Vācaspati Miśra has stated: "The unmanifest subtle element of the elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) is that which exists as the potential power of the seeds of name and form (*nāmarūpa*). This refers to the well-known [gross] elements.
The meaning is that it is untenable for [the Self] to be the arouser of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). || 418 ||
The Self is beyond causes and effects, because of its nature as the absolute fullness.
From these elements, which are of the nature of ignorance, the state of cause and effect arose. || 419 ||

Then, suspecting that the elements (*bhūta*) here might simply be the causes and effects that give rise to those [gross bodies], he says: "The Supreme" (*para*). Because He is the Self (*ātman*), due to His fullness, He is distinct from limited causes and the like. Under the influence of the elements consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*), He assumes their state; thus, the meaning is that here the word "element" (*bhūta*) refers to the root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) which consists of the effects and so forth. || 419 ||
Since ignorance alone is its cause, it does not exist once that ignorance has been destroyed.
This distinction between cause and effect [vanishes] through the awakening that "I am Brahman. (420)
He states the result of the fact that everything which is not the Self is born of ignorance: "Since... (420).
Then, when that [ignorance] is destroyed through perfect awakening, there remains only the absolute unity of the Self.
For him, there is no specific designation other than the mere state of being fulfilled. || 421 ||

However, some maintain that the cessation of activity is the ultimate goal of emptiness; refuting them, he states the result of the cessation of duality, beginning with the word "In that" (tasmin). The word "atha" is intended to establish that the realization of unity is the cause for the destruction of the bondage of ignorance. Anticipating the objection that liberation would lack purpose for man in the absence of consciousness, he says: "Of this" (asya). || 421 ||
I have declared that those things which are established without critical inquiry are ignorance (avidyā).
From these elements which have become causes, [the self] is neither effect nor cause. || 422 ||
It is designated as "arising" because it brings about a form that possesses cause and effect.
Through its association with ignorance, this [self] comes to possess manifold forms. || 423 ||
Having restated the meaning of the word *bhūta*, he explains the meaning of *samutthāya* with the words "unexamined," etc. This is the supreme awakening (*bodha*) which is neither cause nor effect.
In the passage, "Having arisen from those aforementioned elements, it assumes its respective specific forms," the term *samutthāna* (arising) signifies this very process.
Elaborating upon that, the author states that through ignorance (*avidyā*), the Self acquires manifold forms. Thus he says: "Ignorance" [vv. 422–423].
The appearance of consciousness and unconsciousness is characterized by the nature of self and non-self.
This darkness consists of mutual dependence in the form of cause and effect.
Clarifying its nature as possessing manifold forms, he describes its distinction as a reflection of consciousness: "Cetanā" (consciousness).
In this way, even the self becomes a cause and effect through the power of darkness.
"Indeed, it enters [into the state of being an agent] through its own manifestations, namely the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the mind (manas) and the intellect (buddhi).

(425) Anticipating the objection—"Even though ignorance (avidyā) possesses these manifold forms, what does this have to do with the inner self (pratīcī)?"—the author says: "The effect," etc. It is not only by virtue of ignorance that the Self assumes the state of cause and effect; rather, it is through the limiting adjuncts such as the intellect, which are produced by ignorance and characterized by its own manifestations.
He says that [the Self] has attained states such as motherhood by virtue of its own power, in the words: "By its own manifestations. (425)
"I do not know the cause of the arising of darkness"—this [cognition] consists in non-apprehension.
It produces false knowledge, as if it were creating darkness. || 426 ||

Having thus stated the origination [of ignorance], he describes the sequence therein with the words "tamaḥ" (darkness). There is no dispute that the entire origination of the self is rooted in ignorance; and that darkness, which is ignorance, at the very outset—consisting of the non-apprehension [of reality] in the form "I do not know," "I am deluded"—while producing that false knowledge, produces another subsequent false knowledge similar to it. This is the meaning. || 426 ||
It is like the nature of the internal reflection (pratyagābhāsa) residing in the intellect, which is the product of ignorance.
"The arising of [the notions] 'I am the knower' and so forth is said to belong to the Supreme Self.

(427) Having stated that the arising [of the ego-sense] has ignorance alone as its cause, he now describes how it is produced by the intellect and other faculties which are its effects. He says "ignorance" (avidyā); by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the mention of being an enjoyer and other such attributes is intended. (427)
The hearer would likewise be of a distinct form through the activities of the sense organs.
"One who is suffering, fair-complexioned, or a twice-born is distinct from the body," so it is said. (428)

He states the arising [of cognition] as having the sense organs as its cause: "Through hearing," etc. That is to say, it is by means of those functions which have the sense organs themselves as their gateway. He describes that which is produced by the gross body: "Suffering," etc. (428).
Whether one is wealthy, a possessor of cattle, or poor, it is due to the union of the self with wealth and other such objects.
Even though he did not possess those [qualities], through the aforementioned practice of concentration and so forth, he attained the state of a Māka.

He states that [the notion of "I"] for one possessing a body is produced by the connection with wealth and so forth, saying: "The wealthy. Here, the word *ātman* refers to the body. He concludes the discussion on the false arising of the self, saying: "One who does not possess that. (429)
Arising from delusion regarding the true nature of the inward Self, it is false, like the [cosmic egg] of Brahmā at the beginning of creation.
For from the distinction between the field and the knower of the field, there arises [the cycle] up to the state of a stationary pillar (sthāṇu).

In order to explain the passage beginning with "those very [elements]," he recounts the preceding context: "The inward Self," and so forth; from Viriñca down to a stationary post—dvi-... [the text continues].
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that the very fact that the arising [of the world] is produced by delusion is the reason for its falsity. || 430 ||
When there arises an understanding of reality as it is, according to the supreme Vedic revelation of the Vedānta;
Then those elements from which he attained the state of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) perish.

He explains this with the word "yathā" (just as). The meaning is that when a cognition conforming to reality arises from hearing the Vedānta texts, then the elements—designated by the term "ignorance" (avidyā)—perish; consequently, due to the absence of their cause, even the emergence of the state of being a knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and so forth perishes. || 431 ||
By the mere attainment of its own true nature, perfect knowledge completely dispels all darkness.
Since he kills from that [distance], he does not look toward his practice.

In this context, he refutes the view of certain partial thinkers (ekadeśin) who maintain that "enlightenment depends upon repeated practice and destroys ignorance along with its effects," by stating: "Its own nature... (432).
In the case of suggested meanings, the suggester does not destroy that darkness by means of repetition.
This is the nature of a manifestor: it does not depend upon application.

He states, by way of an illustration, that knowledge is independent of any obscuration and is the destroyer of ignorance and the like: "In the case of manifested objects," etc. The meaning is: "The subject under dispute is independent of obscuration and dispels darkness, because it is a manifestor, like a lamp. Desiring to express the pervasion (vyāpti) of the stated reason, he says: "Of the manifestor," etc. (Verse 433).
That which is the nest of delusion and its effects arises from the conjunction with ignorance.
Even the inner self became that Brahman, yet it was falsely perceived as something remote.

If it is argued that the destruction of ignorance results from the knowledge of unity, then since that unity always exists in Brahman—which is non-different from the inner self—how can there be remoteness (*pārokṣya*) regarding Brahman, and how can there be transmigratoriness (*saṃsāritva*) regarding the self which is non-different from Brahman? Anticipating this objection, he states that the remoteness in Brahman is caused by ignorance, beginning with the word "moha. That Brahman, though immediate and consisting of the oneness of the inner consciousness, becomes remote due to delusion (*moha*); for the object residing in delusion and its effects is [conceived] through delusion.

Because it possesses positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) and because it is impossible [to apply] to a real entity in reality, the meaning is that mediacy (pārokṣya) is false with respect to Brahman, whose characteristic has been stated as "that which is immediate" (sākṣāt). || 434 ||
In the same way, although the reality is non-dual, it appears so due to the cause of its lack of realization.
The self has entered into the state of transmigratory existence, just as darkness pervades the sky.
Regarding that Self which is non-different from Brahman, even though it is beyond perception, he states by means of an illustration that its state as a transmigrating being is due to nescience:
"In the same way," [verse 435].
Since the state of Brahman belongs to the self, the state of the self also belongs to Brahman by its very nature.
Because it is obstructed by the mere presence of darkness, it is attained only when that darkness is destroyed.

He concludes the purport of the passage beginning with "those very [words]" with the words "of the Self. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, there is no difference in meaning. 1. "Knowledge alone...
139 [vol2, page 812] 1106 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Second Adhyāya]

Anticipating the question, "How then does the cognition of mutual difference arise?", he says: "Only darkness" (*tamomātra*). The meaning is that when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, [the individual soul], having abandoned its state of possessing distinctions, remains as the Self that is Brahman. || 436 ||
All darkness is destroyed solely by the birth of the correct cognition that all things are of the nature of the Self.
Consequently, that perception perishes, and nothing arising from ignorance remains. || 437 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "not after death" (na pretya) as follows: "All" (sarvam). || 437 ||

In the Self, which is eternally arisen, the cognition of being causeless and so forth must first be produced; thereafter, from that cognition of causelessness and so forth, arises the cognition of Brahman within the innermost Self (pratīci).

How could that [notion] not remain, given that it arises from the cognition of Brahman in the Inner Self? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Always" (*sadā*). The phrase should be divided as "the cognition of [the Self] as being without cause, etc. The notion of agency and so forth regarding the Self is natural; however, the notion of non-agency and so forth must be instilled through the [Vedic] sentence.
Thus, through the knowledge of unity derived from the sentence, the notion of agency and so forth is first destroyed, and thereafter—like a fire without fuel—[it ceases].
The meaning is that even the cognition of Brahman perishes when it is directed inward like the sound of a bell. || 438 ||
That form of the one who has cast off all duality, which is nevertheless perceived as differentiated—
By that very knowledge, all else is known without exception.

Nevertheless, since the perception of distinctions such as space (ākāśa) still exists, he says "apāsta" (cast aside) to explain how there remains no trace of cognition born of ignorance therein. Whatever form of the single-flavored inner self (pratīc) is perceived as possessing distinctions such as space, that is known by the very knowledge of the inner self; for that [form] is merely the play of ignorance and nothing more than that. Therefore, at the time when agency and other attributes are destroyed by the knowledge of the inner self, the cognition of distinction is also destroyed.
This is the meaning. || 439 ||
It is perceived as having the nature of cause and effect, yet it is distinct from those characteristics.
Having consumed [the world] like cause and effect, the Seer alone remains.

Having destroyed specific designations, he states the remaining reality: "Not a cause," etc. The meaning is that the world, which possesses manifold forms, is withdrawn into the state of being a single uniform cognition, and thus the one conscious Self alone remains. || 440 ||
Because it rejects the production of a self from the perception of the individual soul (ātman) as its material cause.
Because a second [self] is impossible, may I be one who possesses such unprecedented qualities.

Anticipating the objection that it is incorrect to say "in the form of non-cause and non-effect" because the internal Self (pratyag) possesses the number one and thus the possibility of having cause and effect, he says: "The internal... (441).
"Free from darkness, the true nature of that which is the witness to the coming and going [of phenomena]."
It is apprehended directly by a cognition that conforms strictly to that [object] alone.

Since there is no distinction in the fact that mere conceptualization (*saṃjñāmātra*) must be discarded because it is non-intelligent by nature, one might raise the objection: "Why is it that the removal of delusion and so forth occurs through the perception of the inner self (*pratyagīkṣaṇa*), but why would it not also occur from the cognition of jars and other objects? Anticipating this, he states the distinction [in verse 442]: "Free from... (*vyapeta...*).
Because the true nature of the entities consisting of cause and effect is merely the perception [of them].
There is nothing whatsoever unknown, nor any unworthy recipient; therefore, even darkness [is dispelled].
[Vol.
2, Page 813] 4 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1107.

He states the fruit resulting from the distinction shown between the knowledge of the inner self (*pratyag-jñāna*) and the knowledge of objects such as a jar, beginning with the word "dṛṣṭi": "By the word 'ataḥ' (therefore), the inner self..."
The expression of knowledge. || 443 ||
No distinction of designation exists here between the knower of the field and the Lord.
When that cause, darkness, has been destroyed, how could there be a designation [of it], since it lacks a basis? (444)

He concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "no" (na) with the words "the knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). The word "here" (iha) refers to the state of knowledge. He clarifies that very point with the phrase "in its cause" (taddhetau). The word should be divided as "animittataḥ" (without a cause). The connection is: "Or from what cause would there be a designation? (kuto vā nimittataḥ saṃjñā). ||444||
Having heard that there is no self after death, Saṃjñā urged him [to act].
Fearing her own destruction, Maitreyī spoke to her husband with great respect.

Without perceiving the qualification "arisen from ignorance" regarding that which has reached the state of being a name (saṃjñā), he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "She [is] Ha... as follows: "The name," etc. (445).
And by the expression "a single mass of consciousness," as well as by the term "devoid of perception."
Because these two statements are mutually contradictory, my mind is utterly bewildered.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "atra" [in verse 446] as follows: "vijñāna... etc. He states the cause for the delusion regarding the Self by means of the two aforementioned statements: "uktyor...
I have spoken to you that which is non-contradictory and very clear.
But due to your own transgression, you perceive my words as having a contrary meaning. || 447 ||

Desiring to make the qualification explicit, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "together" (*saha*), etc.: "It is not contradictory. To the question, "How then does the cognition of contradiction arise there? he replies: "Due to one's own fault. || 447 ||
By the expression "the single mass of consciousness," I have declared that your entire being is one with the Self.
And likewise, through the destruction of perception, he brings about the cessation of the arising caused by ignorance. || 448 ||

Having stated "it is indeed a mass of consciousness," he says "there is no perception" (saṃjñā); anticipating the objection as to how this was stated without contradiction, he says: "vijñāna... (verse 448).
That specific designation which he had, characterized by the nature of consciousness and so forth, [ceased].
For one whose delusion has been destroyed by right vision, that [ignorance] ceases entirely. || 449 ||
He elaborates on the meaning of "uttarādhara" [superior and inferior] as follows: "viśeṣa... (verse 449).
But that which is beyond the other shore, infinite, and the actual knowledge of the self—
Since that [Self] is immutably established by its own nature, why would it ever cease to be? || 450 ||
He clarifies what was stated in the first half [of the verse]: "As for that which... He states the reason for its immutability (*kauṭasthya*): "Because it is established by itself.
He states the result of that: "Why is that? || 410 ||
Thus Yājñavalkya spoke this to his wife. || 451 ||
1. ka. "Because of being the mind, it is the two *auras*. [vol2, page 814] 1108 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Adhyāya—]
Even upon the destruction of cause and effect, it is self-established, non-dual, and immutable.
Whatever entity it may be, that is sufficient for the self-awareness [of consciousness] by virtue of its independence.

He summarizes the meaning of the passage beginning with *saha*: "Thus this... Having raised the objection—"If designations such as 'the self of consciousness' (*vijñānātman*) have been destroyed, how can there be knowledge of reality, given the absence of a cause?"—he states the meaning of the passage beginning with *alam*: "The effect... The term *ananya* ("non-dual") is stated for the purpose of establishing that [reality] is established by itself (*svataḥ-siddhatva*). || 459 || 452 ||
In this state, the self, whose true nature is unknown, has its intellect enveloped by ignorance.
Therein, one who is seized by false grasping possesses the cognition of distinctions such as the seer and the seen. || 453 ||
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "yatra hi" as follows: "yatreti. One whose very self (*ātman*) is reality (*tattva*) that is unknown is thus [described]. || 453 ||
In this state, one whose vision is veiled by the darkness [of ignorance] has not realized the true nature of the self.

In that regard, when a person whose self-knowledge has become subordinate to qualities such as the intellect—which are manifested by ignorance—does not know his own true nature because his spiritual power is impaired by ignorance, he is said to be a "perceiver of duality. This is explained in detail in the following passage: "Where... [454.1]
By [the words] beginning with "tyādi" || 44 ||
I have previously declared that the world consists of nothing but the residue of ignorance.
In the verse, the word "for" (hi) is used as a reason, [showing] that this world is indeed the effect of ignorance. || 455 ||

Having stated the purport (*tātparya*), while explaining the words, he states the meaning of the particle *hi* [in the verse]: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). This refers to the beginning of the inquiry into the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and so forth. He declares the reason for the stated point, known as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), with the word "not" (*na*). Since it has already been stated that duality is merely ignorance (*avidyāmātra*), he says that the word *hi* is used here to provide a supporting reason for that very point. Thus he says: "The word *hi*. (Verse 455)
The nature of measurement would be that which manifests the existent.
This is the very nature of ignorance: that it falsely constructs what does not exist. (456)

Now, one might object: "Does the phenomenal world (prapañca) exist or not? In the first case, ignorance (avidyā) would have no utility; in the second case, how could even ignorance be capable of manifesting that which is non-existent?
Anticipating this doubt, he states [the answer] with an illustration: "Of the existent," etc. (Verse 456).
The word "iti" is a particle used here to illuminate the meaning of the reason already stated.
That which was once a single being becomes two; that state is called duality (dvaita). || 457 ||
The word "upamārtha" means "the sense of a simile," and "bhavati" is the verb meaning "it becomes."
In that very state of ignorance, this notion is appropriately considered false. (458)
Anticipating the objection—"Even if duality is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), how can the word *hi* (for/indeed) signify its cause?"—the author says: "It has been stated. The meaning is this:

since the world is merely ignorance (*avidyāmātra*), like a piece of silver [mistaken for real silver], by reason of its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*) and other such grounds, the word *hi* serves to illuminate that very cause.

If it is asked, "Why should the word *hi* not simply express the aforementioned reason itself?", he replies: "Of that... [referring to the fact] that particles (*nipāta*) are illuminators (*dyotaka*).
1. Satkāra | [vol2, page 815] 4 Brāhmaṇa | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1109.

For "you alone" is indeed the established tenet of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). He explains the passage beginning with "duality" (*dvaita*) and so forth as "dvīta. In order to support the meaning of the word "iva," he states the final sense of the sentence beginning with "yatra hi," namely, "tatra. (Verses 457, 498)
But how can this expression "as it were duality" function as a simile?
If duality does not exist as a real entity, because everything consists solely of the nature of the one Self (ekātmya), [then how can there be bondage or liberation]? || 459 ||

He raises an objection: "Is duality present or not? Not the first, because it contradicts monism; nor the second, because it is impossible for one and the same thing to be both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, and thus the word 'iva' (like) would be unestablished. (459)
This is not a fault, because it is observed even with respect to a single object.
The absence of the relation between the object compared and the standard of comparison is like the quarters of the sky in the firmament.

He says [in the passage beginning] with "No," etc., that even though there is no duality between the Self and anything else, the word *iva* does not fail to have the sense of a comparison, because the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is observed even in a single entity. He explains this very observation [with the words] "the notion of direction" (*digdhīḥ*). Just as there is no direction other than space (*ākāśa*)—since there is a lack of evidence for it—nevertheless, the cognition of similarity is seen in space in the form "it appears like direction"; likewise, the Self...
The meaning is that even in the absence of non-duality, the establishment of the statement "he becomes as if dual" is achieved. || 460 ||
The battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa was like the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
Just as it is well-established in the world, so too should it be understood here.
He states the possibility of the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison in a single instance by means of another example: "Rāma... (verse 461).
Or rather, even the non-duality of māyā is accepted as being derived from the ultimate non-duality.
Because the meaning of the analogy is thus established, as in the cases of a dream and a magical illusion.

Anticipating the objection that there is no intention here to express a comparison between the two, since the intent is the meaning "the battle of these two is incomparable," he supports the comparison by another means: "Because of non-duality" (*advaitāt*). The word *iva* implies "it is possible. [The battle is compared] with imagined duality (*kalpitadvaitena*).

He clarifies the [attainment of] perfection with the words "as follows" (*yathā*). The meaning is that in a dream and in a great magical illusion (*mahendrajāla*), the Self appears as if possessing duality—taking the form of a duality consisting of an agent and so forth arising from its own ignorance—by means of the dreamer or by the magician who has created it. || 462 ||
It is even said in the world: "Though real, it appears as if false."
No one at all is capable of saying that the state of falsity does not exist. || 463 ||

Anticipating the objection as to how false dreams and the like can serve as examples for the nature of reality, he says: "It is false" (*mithyā*). The first particle *api* is used to express that just as a false object appears as if it were real, so too [is the case here]. The second *api*, however, serves to include the scriptures.
Anticipating the objection—given the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is perceived is real"—as to how a false entity can serve as an example since it lacks existence, he says:
Regarding the phrase "false existence": the meaning is that it contradicts the established consensus regarding delusion and sublation. || 463 ||
He who here declares that the Self possesses the nature of being both collective and distributive according to the Śruti;
This refutation of that position is stated in the passage beginning with "yatra hi," and so forth. || 464 ||

The purport of the passage beginning with "For where... is as follows: having stated that the perception of duality occurs only during the state of ignorance and not otherwise, he declares its result with the words "All this...". The scriptural passage beginning with "For he is the seer" and the Śruti text beginning with "All this is indeed this Self" are what is referred to here.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Two:

The word "here" (*iha*) is stated for the purpose of determining the observer. The sense is this: if such a form of the Self were unreal, there would be no contradiction; however, if it were real, then the Śruti—which teaches the perception of duality—would be contradicted precisely during the state of ignorance (*avidyāvasthā*). || 464 ||
Just as one who has entered the state of sleep during that stage of ignorance.
The other [sense] smells a more subtle fragrance with the nose. || 465 ||
He explains the passage beginning with "that" (tad) and so forth: "In that" (tasyām). || 465 ||
The extraction of the *bhāṇa* and other forms is desired due to their connection with the beloved of the brother-in-law (*ghrātṛpriya*).
The designation "one who smells" (jighrati) may also apply to both the action and its result.

Since only the words denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the action (*kriyā*) are heard [in the text], one might suspect that the statement "by means of smelling" (*ghrāṇena*) is improper; therefore, the intention of the Bhāṣya is to state that the phrase "the one [smells] the other" (*itaro itaram*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the *kāraka* (participant in an action). Regarding the word "smeller" (*ghrātṛ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes everything that serves as the cause for the connection between the sense of smell and its object. Nevertheless, one might suspect that the fruit [of the action] is not mentioned here because there is no word expressive of it; anticipating this, he says: "he smells" (*jighrat*).
"Even so" (tītyapi) means that it is just as there is a designation of "one [factor] for another" among the causal factors (kārakas); such is the meaning of "even" (api). || 466 ||
This same application as previously stated should also be employed in the subsequent statements.
In this context, it is said that the subject and so forth arise solely from the ignorance regarding the inner self.

In the passages beginning with "Then one sees the other," he extends the previously stated reasoning [to these cases]. Regarding the phrase "in the subsequent ones": where [the text] concludes the meaning of the sentences concerning killing and so forth, he says "the inner self" (pratyak). 467.
This has been declared to be the domain of the technical designations of action and its factors.
Therefore, with the complete destruction of ignorance, the perception of vigor ceases. || 468 ||
He states the result by restating that [point]: "Action," etc. The word "therefore" expresses the fact of being produced by ignorance. || 468 ||
Now, the object of the statement "a mass of consciousness" is being explained.
Or rather, by the phrase "wherein," it refers to the wise one in whom ignorance has been destroyed. || 469 ||

He introduces the passage beginning with "Wherein, indeed, for him" (*yatra vā asya*) with the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). The meaning is that this follows the explanation of the sentence beginning with "From these" (*etebhyaḥ*) by means of the words "wherein" (*yatra*), and so forth. He explains the syllables [of the verse] with the words beginning with "destroyed" (*dhvasta*). When the knower (*vidvas*) has attained the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), wherein everything has become the Self alone (*ātmaiva*), who is there to act, by what instrument, and what object would he smell? What indeed could he desire? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15)
The connection is that one should say "the direction of Śrī" (śrīdikam). || 469 ||
But where, through the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, this limb of the Self [is realized]... || 470 ||

When all ignorance has been utterly scorched by the rays of the sun-like light of the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self, tell me: who is there, by what means, and what [is to be known]? Speak!
Because this entire universe consists of nothing but the Self, it is [perceived] solely through the oneness of the one who desires to eat.

He clarifies that very point with the words "wherein" (*yatra*). For the ignorant self, once the knowledge of reality has arisen through the power of the scriptures and so forth, [the ignorance] is destroyed—[this is the meaning].
1. [The word *artha* means] purpose; 2. [it refers to] that which is spoken of here.
When the nature of knowledge exists, in that state of knowledge wherein everything becomes the Self alone—the connection here is as before.
He states the meaning of "everything became the Self alone" as a supporting reason: "aikātmya... (470, 471).
The entire world, like the sixth object of cognition, is like cause and effect.
For the wise one whose self-blindness has been destroyed, it occurs upon the arising of perfect knowledge. || 472 ||

Having raised the objection that if everything—including the agent and so forth—is nothing but the Self, then it must exist in exactly the same way [as the Self], he summarizes the purport of the passage beginning with "all" (sarvam) with the verse starting "the sixth" (ṣaṣṭhī). || 472 ||
The cause of cognition is always single, being neither excluded nor inclusive.
It abides as a single unity, a mass of consciousness and bliss. || 473 ||
Anticipating the objection that if duality is insubstantial, then non-duality must also be so because it is non-different from it, he says: "avyāvṛtta" (unrestricted).

The meaning is that there remains a single reality consisting of pure consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), which is devoid of commonalities and particularities, self-luminous, of a single nature, and identical with the supreme goal of human life; thus, duality does not culminate in emptiness. || 473 ||
In this [state], there is no division into subject and so forth, because the cause for such [division] is impossible.
Because pure consciousness is established by itself, according to the teaching that it is a mass of pure awareness. || 474 ||

Anticipating the objection—namely, that since whatever is established arises solely from the distinction between the measure (mātrā) and so forth, how can self-luminosity and the like be attributed to it—the author says:
"grāhakādi" (the grasper, etc.). Here, "atra" refers to that which resides within knowledge (vidyā).
Without relying on the ignorance of the Self (ātmāvidyā), the status of being an agent (kārakatva) is not obtained. [Verse 474]
For indeed, without depending upon an agent, [an action] cannot be established. || 475 ||

Anticipating the question, "What is the cause for the distinction between the grasper and so forth, or how is it that such [distinction] is impossible?", he first demonstrates that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the causal agent (*kārakahetu*). He says, "The Self" (*ātmeti*). He states that the causal agent is the cause of action by saying, "And the causal agent" (*kārakaṃ ceti*).
The meaning of the locative case is the conventional usage of "action" and "causal agent. (Verse 475)
In the same way, without action, the fruit does not come into existence at all.
This very ignorance manifests itself in the form of the agent and so forth. || 476 ||

He indicates that its status as both fruit and cause [is established] by the word "without" (*antareṇa*). Anticipating the objection that since many causes are admitted there, the position that ignorance alone is the cause is undermined, he says: "the agent, etc. (verse 476).
Since this is so, therefore, upon the total destruction of ignorance, this world [ceases].
Through awakening, the entirety of the determinate and the indeterminate attains the state of the Self.

Having stated the cause for the division into subject and so forth, he says "yataḥ" [verse 477] to explain that when that [division] is destroyed by knowledge, the destruction of the division occurs through the state of being the Self alone.
Once again, it regains consciousness when dissolved within the causal self (satkāraṇātman).
Just as this world exists, so it would become upon the dissolution of ignorance.

Furthermore, that which is under dispute will arise again because it is established by the Self alone, just as in deep sleep and so forth, like the perceiver who has reached a state of completion. *Sureśvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Second Chapter. Anticipating that objection, he states the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of having a cause, beginning with the words "bhūyo'pi" (even further). || 478 ||
Let it suffice for now that there is no perception regarding the self when knowledge arises.
Even though ignorance exists, there is no such notion of a self.

He states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "by which" (yena) as follows: "By knowledge," etc. The meaning is that such [knowledge] conveys the distinction between the grasper and so forth. || 479 ||
By which immutable witness all the world, beginning with the subject who perceives, is seen.
The entire world knows [this]; tell me, by what means could it know that? 480.

Having stated that this statement is based on the principle of *kaimutika* (a fortiori), he applies it to that very point: "The perceiver and so forth. The meaning is: if even in the state of ignorance the witness of all does not depend on anything else, how much more so in the state of knowledge? || 480 ||
In this insentient world, the conscious one alone is here as the witness.
Even in that case, a subject-apprehender and so forth are not required for establishment by means of direct perception.

One might object: "Since the world, like the witness, will be established as independent [of anything else] without distinction, how can it be said that the world knows the world through the immutable witness?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The insentient," etc. Here, the word "here" refers to the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). As for the witness...

One might then object: "Why should there not be a dependence on another means of proof even for that which is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), since we observe that the knowledge of one person's consciousness is established through dependence on another person? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The grasper and so forth. The meaning is that in the case of the unconditioned Self, which is pure consciousness (cidātman), there is no establishment through dependence on another, because that would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthiti). || 481 ||
How much more so this notion [of self] regarding that which has destroyed the causes of the misfortunes of saṃsāra?
When the sun of perfect knowledge regarding the true nature of the unity [of all things] has risen, || 482 ||

In that context, the word "also" (*api*) indicates the logical principle summarized by the phrase beginning with "by which," etc. Regarding the term "designation" (*saṃjñā*): since there is no conscious being other than the Witness (*sākṣin*), even in the state of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no distinction such as the subject who grasps and so forth within the Self; how much less so in the state of knowledge (*vidyā*)? This is the meaning. || 482 ||
Moreover, even with respect to the knower, there is no conceptualization regarding the inner self.
Since the cognizer is not apprehended by means of the objects of the cognition that has arisen. || 483 ||

He states the purport of the verse beginning with "vijñātāram" (the knower) as "boddhāram" (the cognizer). The meaning is that even with respect to the cognizer, there is no cognition of distinctions such as the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) and so forth; how much less, then, could there be such a distinction for the Witness (*sākṣin*)? He states the reason for the absence of knowledge of distinctions like the subject of apprehension in the cognizer with the word "boddhṛ" (the cognizer).
The specific characteristics of the knower and so forth are established without being critically examined.
This notion is proclaimed as "great" when it is certain regarding the object. (484)

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, where is the cognition of the distinction between the grasper and so forth intended to reside?", he says, "It is determined in what is not the self," namely, "without investigation. (484)
Since this is so, it is established that the vision of the inner self (pratyagātman) is thus accomplished.
It has been declared that everything, including the means such as hearing and so forth, is directly the Self. (485)
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the second Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

He concludes the meaning of the *brāhmaṇa* with the words "Since" (*yataḥ*).
