In the very same way, that which is perceived through direct observation in the form of conduct;
That very dharma would be truth, which serves as the cause for establishing [the distinction between] states.

He states the meaning of the word "truth" (*satya*) in the phrase "this is truth" with the word "thus" (*tathā*). That is to say, just as the *apūrva* of Hiraṇyagarbha is the originator of the world...
[vol2, page 827]

Likewise, that very thing which is perceived through conduct being practiced as seen by direct perception is the meaning of the word *apūrva*, namely *dharma*. It is called "truth" (*satya*) in the world;
for it is well known in the world that truth is that which establishes the system of the social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*). This is the meaning. || 50 ||
Like the property-bearer, that [property] is also twofold, by way of being common or specific.
Because it is the cause for establishing the distinction between common and specific objects. || 51 ||

In this context as well, there are many words for "truth" (satya); in order to distinguish their meaning, he states their twofold nature with the words "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) and so forth. He states the reason for this twofold nature with the words "common and particular" (*sādhāraṇaviśeṣa*). The distinction is that what is of a general form in the passage "And this which is in this [world] is truth," and what is of a particular form in the passage "And this which is within the self is truth," should be understood as combined in the passage "This is truth. || 51 ||
This [person], engaged in the truth of the Dharma, possesses the specific characteristics of gender and physical form.
And Virāṭ was Hiraṇyagarbha, endowed with all castes. || 52 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "this is human" [in verse 52]: "Dharma," etc. The two bodies impelled by dharma and so forth, designated by terms such as "sūtra" and the like, which are characterized by a specific genus (jāti) and are capable of all worldly transactions—that genus is what is entirely denoted by the word "human. This is the meaning. || 52 ||
The mention of the human species is an illustration intended to include all species.
"This is human"—the explanation of this is as before. (53)

If it is argued that because of the qualification "this is human" (mānuṣam), there is no connection with all castes, he says in response: "Manuṣya. The connection is that by the phrase "this is human," the human caste is grasped. That [caste] is also indicated as twofold—external and internal—just like *dharma* and so forth; therefore, by the phrase "this is human," there is the inclusion of the entire aggregate of castes, and furthermore, regarding the external variety, that which is expressed as "that which is in this... [and so on].
He states that the expression "the internal" (*madhyātmam*) is a statement regarding the internal divisions [of the body], saying: "The explanation. (13)
"The earth is the body"—thus has that which was previously described been set forth in its various parts.
"This Self is Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Śveta"—such is that statement. (54)

He states the purport of the synonym "this is the Self" as follows: "The earth. Beginning with "This earth," and continuing through the section ending with the synonym "human being," [the text] proceeds in this sequence—from the earth as the body (*śārīra*)—to that which is called the whole (*avayavin*) known as the Virāj-sūtra.

The meaning is that this definition of the whole (avayavin) possessing those [parts], beginning with "the Self" (ātman), is now being set forth, following the division explained according to the barley-corn (yava). || 54 ||
Of the various emanations of Hiraṇyagarbha and of the elements, each separately.
Since its state as honey has been described, its totality is now being explained.
Anticipating the objection that there would be tautology since this [meaning] is already conveyed by the word "embodied" (śārīra) in the first instance, he says: "Hiraṇyagarbha. || 55 ||
"This is the Self" is considered the first instruction regarding the Virāj.
Therefore, that which has the nature of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) to it is denoted by a word ending in the seventh case.

Regarding the phrase "this is the Self" (*ayam ātmā*), he explains the meaning of the word "Self" (*ātman*). The term "this" (*ayam*) refers to that which is the combined form of the Virāj and the Sūtra;

thus, in the expression "this is the Self," the word *ātman* is in the nominative case (*prathamānta*), or this is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in this Self" (*asmin ātmani*), [the same applies]. (Note: Variants *vāśarī* and *vīrī* appear in manuscript *ka*.)
141 [vol2, page 828] 1122 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Second Chapter— ]
He states that by the word *ātman* ending in the locative case, only the Virāj is being spoken of: "by [the word] ending in the locative.

The connection with the preceding [verse] is: "the mention is of the Virāj. He states that the internal aspect of the Virāj, which is the *liṅga-ātman*, is expressed by words such as "consisting of light" (*tejomaya*): "that [is] within it. This means: from the words "consisting of light," and so forth. || 16 ||
The nature of the effect and the nature of the cause always exist for the sake of that [Purusha].
And that which is called "the self" here is what they know as the "conscious self. (57)
Regarding the phrase "this which is the Self," he states that the word "Self" here denotes the individual soul (jīva) as the reflection of consciousness. [He says] "the effect," etc.;

the ellipsis is that this [soul] is designated by the word "Self" here as the "residual" (śeṣī). He dispels the objection regarding the non-establishment of the residual by saying "consciousness," etc. ||17||
In that Self whose nature consists of the destruction of both the manifest and the unmanifest...
By the statement of the simile of the scrap of food, the self consisting of consciousness is introduced. || 58 ||

Regarding the phrase "This indeed is the Self" (*sa vā ayam ātmā*), he explains the meaning of the word "Self" (*ātman*) with the words "In which... The meaning is as follows: in the final section of the text, the individual soul (*jīva*)—heard of as "this Self"—is taught to be one with the Supreme, who is devoid of ignorance and its products, through the analogy of the lump of salt and other examples, and by such statements as "Verily, this [is] the same. That [Supreme], and not the individual soul, is the "Self" intended here. || 58 ||
When he, having destroyed the darkness by means of the knowledge of Brahman, is firmly established in Brahman;
Because of the absolute impossibility of darkness and its effects arising from that [source]. (59)

Anticipating the objection that Brahman is devoid of ignorance and its products, whereas the individual soul (jīva) is the opposite, and asking how there can be identity between them, he says: "Brahman... The meaning is this: when that Brahman is firmly established in the individual soul, and ignorance has been dispelled by the knowledge of it, then—because of the total non-contact with cause and effect and the absence of any obstruction—it is logical that its natural identity with Brahman exists. || 59 ||
He who was formerly a transmigrating embodied being due to ignorance—
Thus, by means of this knowledge, he now dwells directly as the Supreme Brahman.
Having explained the meaning for his own sake, he states the meaning of the three words "sa," "vā," and "ayam" with the phrase "yo'sau. This means: "now, in the state of knowledge (vidyā). || 60 ||
This [world], which has arisen from ignorance and its products, is destroyed; its only reality is that of pure consciousness alone.
The self alone is infinite and boundless, established in its own majesty.
He elaborates upon the Self, which is the fruit of knowledge and was mentioned immediately prior, in the verse beginning with "dhvasta. (61)
For the sake of knowing the true nature of that which is without before, without after, and without middle, and which is not an object of the internal sense.
That very passage beginning with "sa vā" is stated along with an illustrative example. || 62 ||
He introduces the statement regarding the point already explained with the words: "Apūrva... (62).
Because the darkness [of ignorance] has been destroyed by the thorough knowledge that "I am Brahman."
He is called "King" because he has not lost his vision of the Self through the limbs of kingship.
1 ka. ga. rī cāpya 2ka. kha. vastre meṃ | [vol2, page 829] 5 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1123.

He explains the meaning of the word "king" (rāja) as it applies to that [knower]: "Brahman," etc. The meaning is that because ignorance is dispelled through knowledge, and because [the Self] shines forth by the manifestation of its own nature without obstruction, the knower of Brahman is worthy of being called a "king. || 63 ||
Likewise, by the word "adhipati" (sovereign), independence is denoted.
The self-interest [of the Lord] consists in the realization of the inner Self, because the world-soul possesses that as its cause. (64)

Fearing that the word *adhipati* (lord) might be redundant with the word *rāja* (king), he says "tathā" (likewise). By the word *rāja*, the meaning is "like a king. He establishes [the master's] independence with the words "svārthe" (for its own sake). || 64 ||
By the mere realization of the inner Self, one attains the completion of the world-soul.
Desiring to reveal it directly to us, another Śruti says: "Just as... (tadyathā). || 65 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "tadyathā" (just as): "pratyag" and so on. The meaning is that the supreme Śruti proceeds by means of an illustration, desiring to demonstrate that the phenomenal expansion of cause and effect culminates in Brahman alone. || 65 ||
Just as [spokes] are fixed in the hub of a wheel and on the outer rim of the wheel.
In the same way, the spokes, beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa), are woven lengthwise and crosswise within the Supreme Self.
He explains those words: "The wheel," etc. (66).
Some explain this illustration regarding the self in an entirely different way.
For the sake of establishing the meaning of the entire initial proposition, the proponents of Brahman [state]: || 67 ||

He introduces the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca on the passage beginning with "tadyathā" (just as). Regarding the phrase "they explain": the mention of the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is intended to indicate the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*). He points out the result of this alternative interpretation with the word "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*):

the proposition that "this Self is possessed of manifold expansion" (*saprapañca*) is established in the text "all this is what this Self is"; it is for the sake of proving that point that there is this alternative interpretation.
This is the meaning. || 67 ||
Having unified one's own self with the imperishable Supreme Self.
Having conceived of himself as the nave of a wheel, the wise man [should proceed]. || 68 ||
This body is like the rim, and the world, beginning with the deities, is like the spokes.
Having performed this visualization, one should always practice meditative reflection with a mind permeated by that very state.
He clarifies that very point with the words "having unified. First of all, the Self does not differ from the Supreme, because of the scriptural texts on unity.

Having conceived the body—which consists of the five elements—as the rim of a wheel, and the Self as the hub of that wheel, and having projected the world of deities and so forth upon the Self and the elements, one should always perform meditation with a mind fixed upon that very projected object. This is the meaning.
For one who always meditates by means of this path of meditation, [the goal is attained].
Like heated iron, their oneness becomes difficult to undo once it has occurred. || 70 ||

Anticipating the doubt, "What is the use of this meditation?", he says: "By this. Anticipating the doubt that eternal oneness is not the fruit of meditation, he qualifies it [with "āvṛtti"], considering that its [the meditation's] result is the destruction of bondage. || 70 ||
Having reached this state, one desists from being a meditator.
It becomes an object of meditation for those blinded by the cataract of ignorance. || 71 ||

If it is argued that one should extend meditation even after attaining oneness, he says "no," with the words "etām" (this). He states that the fruit of oneness is not merely the cessation of being the meditator, but also the attainment of being the object of meditation, with the words "avidyā" (ignorance). || 71 ||
Having ascertained this inconceivable supreme abode of yogins, [one should remain there].
Having reached which they do not return, having attained the supreme Nirvana. 72.

He defines the nature of the object of meditation. Regarding the word "having ascertained": having ascertained through direct identity that very one who, when known, being liberated, does not transmigrate again—that aforementioned inconceivable Supreme Self, the refuge of the wise—he who remains [in that state]...
The meaning is that it becomes an object of meditation for those who are ignorant. || 72 ||
For this wheel of Brahmā is established within each and every living being.
But because they lack awakening, this is not experienced by all those living beings.
Having presented the system of others—that [the wheel] consists of its arrangement and meditation as well as their fruit—he states another system belonging to those very same people:
"Each individually," etc. The meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that the presence of Brahman in the hearts of all living beings is well-known from all the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
If the wheel called Brahman is always situated in the heart of all living beings, why then is it not experienced by everyone?
Regarding this, he says: "Because of non-awakening. (73)
Some clearly explain it in this way, due to the boon granted by Vaiśvānara.
Even such a [text], though correct, must be explained as being beyond the literal sequence of syllables and not to be rejected. || 74 ||

He concludes the prima facie view with the words "vaiśvānara" etc. He states that this interpretation, though seemingly attractive at first glance, is not to be accepted because it deviates from the literal sense of the scriptural text, using the word "akṣara" (literal sense). This means it is characterized by the aforementioned method of exposition. || 74 ||
Even if it were obtained through implication, it would not be preceded by anything else.
"Those indeed should be worshipped," so say those who know the scriptures. || 75 ||
Anticipating the objection that "since the self is seen to possess various tastes by the force of the illustration, our intended meaning is not outside the scope of the Śruti," he says:
"by the force [of the illustration]. Although your intended meaning appears by the force of the illustration, nevertheless, it is not scriptural (śrauta).

In the section concerning ripening (*smin-prakaraṇa*), because there is no word expressive of that [multiplicity], and because it would contradict statements regarding the *apūrva* (unseen potency) and so forth, this illustration cannot serve to establish a multiplicity of forms for the Self.

Thus, even an implied meaning (*ārthika-artha*) should not be accepted; for it is an established principle that "that which is a meaning derived from implication is not the subject matter of the Vedic injunction (*codanā-artha*)," otherwise there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasakti*). This is the meaning. || 75 ||
Even if they are very numerous, unseen things that possess valid means of cognition must be postulated.
Not even a hundredth part of what has not been seen should be postulated, as it lacks any means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, he states that even other things besides Brahman do not possess multiple flavors (nānārasa), because there is no basis for such a distinction; otherwise, it would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga): "Those who possess valid means of knowledge... (76).
The arrangement of the wheel as described has not been heard previously in the sacred syllables.
Furthermore, the term "upāsana" (meditative worship) is not heard anywhere in the entire Brāhmaṇa.

Now, it might be argued that Brahman is not imagined as having the form of the entire [diagram] and so forth, but rather that the arrangement of the circles (cakravinyāsa) is thus taught by the Śruti itself; to this he replies:
"As stated... As for the statement "one should meditate" (nididhyāset), regarding that he says: "And not... || 77 ||
In the two locations of the hub and the rim, they are accepted as being by way of illustration.
For in the statement concerning the illustrative example, the Self alone is directly heard here.

Furthermore, not every feature present in the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is applicable to the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika), because that would contradict its very nature; therefore, he says "not the navel" [in verse 78] to show that Brahman does not possess the form of having a beginning and so forth.
The surrendering of the vital breaths and so forth is heard in scripture as being directed toward the inner self (pratyagātman).
How can that [deity] among the elements, such as the gods and so forth, be understood when it is not heard [in the scripture]? (79)

Regarding the claim that the world, consisting of deities and so forth, is not supported by the inner Self—which stands in the place of the nave of a wheel—nor by the elements constituting the body, which stand in the place of the rim of the wheel, he says in response: "The state of being supported. (79)
Its division into external and internal, as well as its state of cause and effect, [is likewise].
By the phrase "that very [Self]" (tadetad), the inner Self (pratyañ) is restricted to this very place;
thus, because it contradicts the principal statement, he says that Brahman does not have the form of the aggregate and so forth, using the word "outside" (bahiḥ). || 80 ||
Now, regarding the phrase "that which is other," it is likewise for the purpose of eliminating the perception of duality.
It is my conviction that the rule for the object of worship and the act of worship is not complete [in this way]. || 81 ||

For this reason as well, he says that Brahman does not have the nature of being the "entirety" (samasta) and so forth: "Now," etc. [Objection: But since meditation on another deity is censured, it is not desired; however, meditation on Brahman is appropriate because it is uncensured, for the injunction for worship proceeds with respect to That. Therefore, it must possess manifoldness (saprapañcatva), for that which is devoid of manifoldness (niṣprapañca) is not worshipped. To this, he replies: "Upāsya" (the object of worship), etc. For without difference (bheda), the possibility of the modes such as the object of worship and so forth is not possible; and in the present context, there is the perception of difference.
It is refuted; the meaning is that there is no injunction for meditation here. || 81 ||
[This is] because the only obstruction is ignorance, and the fruit is the identity with Brahman.
Apart from the knowledge of Brahman, there is no other action for attaining it. || 82 ||

Having stated the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the argument that "Brahman is an object of worship because it possesses phenomenal expansion (*saprapañca*), like the vital breath (*prāṇa*"), he then refutes the first alternative by raising the dilemma: "Is this worship for the sake of the Self's attainment of Brahmanhood, or for some other fruit? He refutes the first with the words "Through ignorance," etc. It is not the second, because there is no other fruit; for nothing else is desired by the individual soul (*jīva*) apart from the attainment of Brahman upon the destruction of ignorance, and since that [attainment] is achieved through knowledge alone, the worship of it is useless.
And this is the meaning. || 82 ||
That which is not expressed by speech, nor that which is conceived by the mind;
Know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which they worship.

Having stated that the reason for being an object of worship is unestablished in its pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of possessing a fruit brought about by worship, he states the contradiction with scripture (*śrutivirodha*) with the words "That which... (verse 83).
1126 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]
Pervasion by the activity of a female lay follower is the definition of non-celibacy.
Since such a thing was performed by Śruti, how can Brahman be meditated upon as being like that? || 84 ||

Now, one might object: "Even if Brahman is not to be rejected because it is not within the scope of unrefined speech and the like, its being an object of meditation (*upāsya*) is not contradictory, since it is refined and accessible through that [refined speech].
Anticipating this doubt, he states the meaning of the scripture: "One should meditate" (*upāsīta*). The word "such" (*tādṛg*) means pervaded by the act of meditation;
that is to say, it is meditated upon, attended to, and accepted. || 84 ||
As for the statement, "It is seen by you through the intellect, indeed by the mind alone," [it is as follows].
Therefore, it is for the purpose of enjoining the knowledge of the Self, not for enjoining meditative worship. || 85 ||

[Objection: But surely there is also an injunction for the meditation on Brahman in some places; and since the scripture itself has thus set aside [the objection] by means of scripture, Brahman must be the object of meditation. To this, he says: "But it is seen," etc. (Sūtra 1.1.12).
For by that which is permeated by rajas, Brahman is not attained.
Therefore, through the purity of one's consciousness, one should seek knowledge within the inner self.

Anticipating the objection—“Since the ritual procedure for knowledge (vidyā-vidhāna) has already been set aside, how can this [text] have that as its purpose?”—the author replies with the words “rajaḥ” (passion).
The meaning is that the aforementioned statement is intended for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman, specifically for the purpose of enjoining the purification of the intellect. || 86 ||
Or rather, because it was previously established in identity with the non-Self through its connection with that which is not the Self.
The meaning of the word would be "the intellect of all living beings. (87)

To the objection—namely, that since there is no word expressing a rule for purification (*śuddhi*) in the aforementioned statement, how can it have that as its meaning—the author replies with the words "Or else" (*yadvā*). The meaning is that, because of the consistency with the qualification "foremost" (*agryā*), the intended sense of the statement is that the intellect of all beings is of the nature of consciousness (*cidākārā*) by the mere fact of its birth, even prior to its attachment to objects. || 87 ||
This is the meaning of that statement; it is not, however, an injunction for worship.

Since there is no injunction for meditation when the absolute unity of the Self has destroyed all distinctions, [the author] concludes with the verse beginning "This" (eṣa) another possible interpretation for the scripture that was suspected of enjoining the worship of Brahman. || 88 ||
Therefore, the doctrine that [the world] has the form of a wheel is incorrect, because it contradicts the cognitions derived from the Vedas and other sources.
Therefore, this very meaning of the sentence is "the village," because it is possible based on valid cognition. (89)

He concludes that the views of Bhartṛprapañca and others are untenable, because there is no evidence for Brahman having the nature of being both the whole and its parts, and because such a view contradicts scripture.
[The word] "cakre" [indicates this]. Having stated that the opponent's position is to be disregarded, he declares that his own position is to be accepted with the word "tat. That very...

The meaning of the passage beginning with "Brahmā was first" (*brahmāpūrvam*) is to be understood as intended in the passage beginning with "It is as follows" (*tadyathā*), because other alternative positions are untenable and because there exists no authoritative scripture that teaches [anything] other than this uniform [view]. This is the sense. || 89 ||
By the phrase "so they say," the purpose of the knowledge of Brahman is stated.
This is the resolution made for that which was previously presented along with its objection. || 90 ||
"Therefore, all that became"—this result of knowledge was stated in the third [chapter], and it is here concluded; thus he states another position with the word "that" (tat). || 90 ||

The correct explanation of the Self according to the aphorism "Ātmaiveti" (It is the Self indeed) is provided here, accompanied by the commentary known as the *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. [Vol. 2, Page 833] 1 Brāhmaṇa. 1127.
By means of the five Brahmins, [the king] acted according to the Śruti for the sake of attaining the realization of the all-pervading Self.

Having explained the passage beginning with "tadyathā" (just as), the author introduces the section beginning with "idaṃ vā etat" (this indeed is that) by referring back to what has preceded: "ātmeti.

The thread of knowledge (*vidyāsūtra*) was introduced in the third [chapter]; this is its explanation, which has been perfectly provided by the five preceding Brāhmaṇas through the Śruti. And that [explanation] is the cause for the direct realization of the identity of the Self—the referent of "thou"—with Brahman, which is the entire, complete reality.
The structural interpretation. || 91 ||
This entire knowledge of Brahman, for the attainment of absolute liberation, is completed.
That which Yājñavalkya spoke at great length to his own wife.
Fearing that even though the Sūtra has been explained, the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) has not yet been made clear, he says: "It is completed" (samāptā). ||92||
From this point onward, the aforementioned knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is being expounded.
This narrative is for the purpose of praise, serving as a further means for engaging in practice. (93)

Fearing that if this [work] were completed as fruitful [in itself], the subsequent text would be rendered purposeless, he says: "As stated... Anticipating the objection that praise might be fruitless, he says: "In order to engage... (93)
Out of reverence, the Śruti explains the meaning of the narrative by means of two mantras.
For an object that is praised merely by scriptural revelation attains the status of being worthy of acceptance. || 94 ||

He explains the commentary beginning with "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) and so forth, which is intended to state the purpose of the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) brought forward for the sake of praising the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

Regarding the phrase "the purpose of the narrative": [it refers to] the two mantras that are about to be stated. Anticipating the objection that stating the meaning already expressed by the Śruti through the mantras would be redundant, he says: "by the Śruti. The word "for" (*hi*) indicates that the reason for the excellence of the praise lies in its being worthy of acceptance. ||94||
Even though he had attained the goals of human existence, Śacīpati protected Yama.
Therefore, by means of that very inward knowledge, there shall be the accomplishment of the noble fruit. || 95 ||

Anticipating the question, "In that case, what kind of praise is this?", he says: "Avāpta... (Having attained...). This should be construed as "that very [attainment] is the knowledge of the inner self" (*pratyagvidyā*).
Therefore, the meaning is: even for one who has accomplished all that was to be done, [this praise is offered] by means of the preservation of that [knowledge]. || 95 ||
For it was acquired in the past by the Aśvins through great exertion.
Therefore, the knowledge of Brahman is the supreme means for his liberation. || 96 ||
He states another praise of knowledge with the words: "And by the great... (96).
Just as among all human goals, liberation (kaivalya) is the highest.
Just as it is with all means of accomplishment, so too is this the supreme means of accomplishment for that Vidyā.
He states another praise: "Niḥśeṣa... (verse 97).
The account of Aśva and Atharvaṇa [is told] because of their attainment of the knowledge of Brahman.
That which was previously unmanifested is directly brought forth by means of the two mantras. || 98 ||

Having demonstrated the manner of praising knowledge (*vidyā*), he restates what was said in the verse beginning with "by means of two mantras regarding the meaning of the narrative" (*ākhyāyikārtham*): *avīti* || 98 ||
1128 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Second Chapter]:
It is said that Atharvan, being requested by the Aśvins, [taught] this Madhu-vidyā.
Then Atharvan said: "May Indra sever my head if I speak [otherwise]. (99)
Therefore, out of fear, I shall not speak this vidyā to you two.
They both said to him: "Previously, we two [offered] our heads for the sake of Indra's cutting. (100)
Having cut off your horse's head and joined it [to his own], we shall then hear from him.
From Brahmā, with his horse-headed form, [he received] the Madhu-vidyā for the sake of liberation. || 101 ||
When he had granted permission, saying "So be it," he then cut off that head of his.
He placed his head upon the horse, and because of that, he imparted the knowledge to him.
Then, on the following day, that Indra also [honored] the two Aśvins upon his head.
Then he placed that knowledge, which was upon his head, upon his own head.
He spoke the remainder of his own words to the Aśvins, seeking immortality.
Since this is so, therefore truth must be protected with diligent effort. || 104 ||

Summarizing the meaning of the narrative as it is being revealed by the two mantras, he states the meaning of the scriptural narrative found in the first chapter of the Pravargya section, beginning with the words "By the Aśvins," and so forth. The particle *kila* expresses the indirect nature of the subject matter, indicating that it is established solely through scripture (*śruti*).
The phrase "therefore, by means of the head of the horse" is the intended sense. The meaning of the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is the absence of fear caused by Indra. [The word] *brāhma*...

The word *atha* (now/then) signifies that the cutting off of his head was faultless because it was dependent upon [the teacher's] permission immediately following the command. Furthermore, the meaning of the word *punaḥ* (again) is the immediate sequence after the commencement of the instruction in knowledge (*vidyā*). The meaning of the word *atha* is the immediate sequence after the cutting off of the head. The word *atha* is stated as the cause for the bestowal of the remainder of the knowledge, which follows the rejoicing immediately after the rejoining of his own head. To the question, "For what purpose did the Brāhmaṇa proceed toward the risk of losing his life? he says: *ṛtā-* (from truth...).

Regarding the word "yan" (which), he states its purport with the words "yataḥ" (since). Since the sage protected the truth even when he had fallen into a life-threatening crisis, the meaning is that those who seek their own welfare must protect the truth even at the cost of their lives. One should exert effort to avoid untruth even when there is an occasion for it to arise. 99 || 100 || 101 || 102 || 103 || 104 ||
This indeed is that honey which was proclaimed in another section.
"Indeed, it is heard from the words of the Brāhmaṇa that [the gods] said this to them. (105)
This is clearly that Madhu-Brāhmaṇa which was previously mentioned.
That which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the Aśvins concerning the awakening to the Self; || 106 ||
Having seen this ritual act of Aśva and Atharvan, he spoke it with a Ṛgvedic verse.
This very thing is stated by the seer himself, based on his own vision as a seer. || 107 ||

Having explained the purpose of the narrative, he explains the passage beginning with "This," and so forth. "This" means that very Madhu which was indicated but not made explicit in the section on the Pravargya; it is that which has been described in the words "this earth," and so on. He asks: how was Madhu indicated by another context? To this he says: "Dadhyañ," and so forth. This is heard from the Brāhmaṇa statement in the first [section] beginning with "By these two."
1. The Explanations (Pravacanāni). 2. Ga. As for that which is proclaimed...
[vol2, page 835] 1.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1129.

The connection is that one should meditate on the Madhu Brāhmaṇa. Anticipating the objection—"In that case, since its purpose has already been served by that [previous section], what is the use of this Madhu Brāhmaṇa?"—the author says: "This" (etad). The meaning is that this very Madhu Brāhmaṇa, which was the means for the knowledge of the Self and which the Brāhmaṇa had previously taught to the Aśvins in an unmanifest manner in the vicinity of the Pravargya rite, is now being stated clearly through the passage beginning with "If this" (yadidam) and so forth. He then states the meaning of the passage beginning with "That this, the seer... (tadetadṛṣiḥ).

"Aśvī" (the one possessing horses). The meaning is that the seer of the mantra, having a vision of the Ṛṣis, perceiving through a subtle object a preeminent dharma-born image, spoke by means of the mantra while beholding the subject at hand—the relationship between disciple and teacher. In that context, he introduces the verse beginning with "tadvām" (that [work] of yours).
"Tadetad" (this very thing): the meaning is that this work which has occurred is expressed by the mantra as seen through that vision. || 105 || 106 || 107 ||
O two men, I shall reveal that deed of yours.
For the sake of gain and acquisition, they employ cruelty against those who travel in secret on the yoke of the wheel.
Just as thunder awakens the sight of one who has arrived.
I shall reveal that secret deed of yours both; I am making it manifest.
When the seer, with the head of a horse, spoke to you both concerning the honeyed drink.
Having cut off Dadhīca's horse-head and severed his head, the Aśvins [restored it].
Then that horse-headed one spoke this honey-word to the Saṃgha through you two.
Desiring to make himself true to the cosmic order (*ṛta*), that sage wished to become truthful. || 111 ||
And from that very circumstance, it is understood that he has fallen into a life-threatening danger.
Truth must be protected with effort, even at the cost of one's own life. || 112 ||

He explains the mantra words beginning with *tadvām* by means of the passage beginning with *āviṣkaromi*. The connection is: "I shall reveal that which he spoke. He explains another mantra beginning with *atharvaṇāya* by means of the passage beginning with *dadhīcaḥ*.

The word *atha* is intended to indicate that the fulfillment of one's promise is essential for those possessed of wisdom. Even though he had fallen into a state where his life was in danger, [he remained steadfast] regarding himself...

The connection is that, desiring to make [his word] true, he spoke "honey. The intended meaning of the term *ṛtāyan* has already been stated in the passage beginning with "since it is thus"; he restates it here as the occasion arises. And therefore... || 108 || 109 || 110 || 111 || 112 ||
The Atharvan spoke of the honey pertaining to Tvaṣṭṛ, which has the sun as its object.
O you two doers of marvels, even that which is like a girth—namely, the perception of the reality of things as they truly are—is [to be attained]. 113.
He explains the passage beginning with "tvāṣṭram" and so forth. The connection is as follows: "āditya... and so on, up to "yattadapyavocad. || 113 ||
Therefore, the two Aśvins are like the twin gods Dasras who bring about the destruction of disease.
He spoke of honey not only as belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, but also as being within the bark itself.
He states the meaning of the word *datra* [in the verse] as "by means of exhaustion. He states the meaning of the word *api* [in the verse] as "not. || 114 ||
Thus [is described] the conclusion of the knowledge of Tvaṣṭṛ in the two chapters concerning the Pravargya rite.
Then, having performed [the rite] with the two mantras, there is the withdrawal of the knowledge of the armor. || 115 ||
Thus, having been composed across these two chapters, the Madhu-kāṇḍa is completed.
For that reason, an object taught merely through scripture is held in high regard. || 116 ||
In order to introduce the passage beginning with "in front" (*puraḥ*), he restates what has preceded: "The Pravargya," etc. He then states the purport of the two subsequent mantras.

Regarding the word "atha" (now): the word "atha" is used to indicate that the knowledge of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son (Vidagdha Śākalya) serves as the cause for the knowledge regarding the "stages" (kakṣya). When the two types of knowledge have been pointed out through the chapters, he states the resulting conclusion with the word "evam" (thus). As to why there is a summary by means of two mantras of the meaning already stated in the chapters, he says: "śruti... (the Veda...). The remainder [of the sense] is: therefore, a summary by means of a mantra is appropriate. || 111 || 116 ||
In former times, he created bodies of bipeds—both birds and humans.
Then, by his own power, he created four-footed animals and wild beasts before him.
That bird is here called the *liṅga* because it was previously consumed by the body.
He entered nine new bodies before him, like the moon reflected in water. || 118 ||

Regarding the word *pura*: the term *atha* is a synonym for *tathā*. He states the cause for the creation of a body by the *kūṭastha* (the immutable one) with the words "by its own *māyā*. The meaning is that the bird is the possessor of a subtle body (*sūkṣmabhoga*). The meaning of the word *atha* is that, for the ignorant person, the attainment of a subtle body immediately after the abandonment of the gross body, followed by the attainment of a new gross body, is an inevitable succession as long as ignorance persists. This is the reality.
An illustration is given in order to refute the theory of bodily conjunction (dehayoga). || 117 || 118 ||
If it is asked why he is called "Puruṣa," the scripture itself [states] that it is for the sake of the Puruṣa's purpose (puruṣārtha).
He explains this with the words beginning "all" (savā) for the sake of realizing the identity of all as one. 119.

He states the purport of the sentence beginning with "sa vā ayam" by way of fulfilling the expectancy [of the reader]. He asks, "Why? and states the purpose of explaining the meaning of the word "puruṣa": "All... (119).
This person (puruṣa) must be the Self, because it lies within the body (puruṣa).
Because of that, this person is called "Puruṣa" in all these worlds. || 120 ||
Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he analyzes the words: "This person" (*puruṣo 'yam*). He concludes that point with the word "therefore" (*tena*).
Do not say this, for it would lead to the consequence of [the world] being limited, since this world—
Nothing whatsoever remains unenveloped by this woman, nor is anything left unpenetrated by her, like the threads of a web.

He raises a doubt regarding a distinction based on the description of the substratum and the superstratum with the words "pariccheda" (delimitation). He provides the answer with the sentence beginning with "no" (na). He explains that [the definition] is "maitram" (friendly/appropriate), and clarifies it by stating "not non-pervasive" (nāvyāptam). || 121 ||
Nothing is uncovered by the self in that way, like a thread woven through a cloth.
Because he is full, he is Puruṣa; therefore, this one Brahma is Puruṣa. || 122 ||

Avoiding the charge of tautology regarding the subsequent statement, he states the meaning with the words beginning "No" (*na*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that the resolution of the tautology is evident when the meaning of the two statements is explained by means of the two examples. Since it is established—according to the principle of the *Akṣarādhikaraṇa*—that the entire world is pervaded by the Self as warp and woof, he states the resulting conclusion: "Because of its fullness" (*pūrṇatvāt*). Brahman is full; how [then] can there be a person? (*puruṣa*)... [text fragment ends].
Regarding its existence therein, he says: "Brahman. (122)
1. *Rau-mantrōpayu* | [Vol.
2, page 837] 1. *Brāhmaṇam*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
Than whom there is nothing further,
than whom there is nothing smaller or greater.
Like a tree, he stands alone, steadfast in heaven;
by that Puruṣa all this is filled. || 123 ||

Regarding the statement "Brahman is full and of a single essence," he cites another mantra: "From which... The meaning is that there is no distinction therein between effect and cause, or between internal and external. The word "kaścit" (some) is a Vedic usage. He states its immutability with the word "vṛkṣa" (tree).
He states that [the Self] is not established within its own majesty by saying "in heaven. He states the resulting conclusion by saying "therefore. || 123 ||
The entire world has been made his own by him through a mere utterance.
"That which is concealed is prohibited, appearing as if it were non-self.

[Verse 124] He states another meaning for the sentence beginning with "not by this" (*nainena*). He says "covered" (*āvṛtam*). He provides another explanation for the second sentence: "concealed" (*saṃvṛtam*). [Verse 124]
There is no cause or effect that has not been assimilated by Him as His own self.
There is no cause or effect that has not been offered by this Self.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "āvṛtam" by way of its contrapositive (vyatireka), saying "tanna. He also clarifies [the passage] beginning with "saṃvṛtam" by that same method, saying "tat. || 125 ||
For he became a counterpart to every form;
having entered body after body, he assumed the very shape of each of those bodies.

Taking up another mantra, he explains it with the words beginning with "form" (rūpa). The two particles are used to state that the possession of manifold forms conforms to worldly discourse and experience. 126.
Either by means of illusions, which are forms of ignorance regarding the inner self, or by means of false cognitions.
Though it is one, it is perceived as having many forms, like the sun reflected in water. || 127 ||

Raising the doubt as to what the cause is for the other [the Lord] having manifold forms, the author considers two alternatives—whether it be the material cause (*upādāna*) or the instrumental cause (*nimitta*)—and answers the first with the words "by means of *māyās*. Anticipating the objection that the use of the plural number is inappropriate for a single entity, and considering its justification through a diversity of modes, he states the second alternative and refutes it with the words "or if... (verse 127).
The form of the All-pervading Lord, consisting of Māyā, exists for the purpose of awakening to the true nature of the inward Self.
In this world, it is not possible to know a reality without relying on the scriptures, teachers, and so forth. (128)

Anticipating the objection as to why this multiformity exists, [the author] states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tadasya" (that belongs to him), because the order of meaning is more powerful than the order of the text. He says:
"pratyak" (reflexive). Anticipating the objection that this [Self] can be known by itself even without a form produced by *māyā*, he says:
"śāstra" (scripture). || 128 ||

Bṛhadāraṇyakopani
The reason why this [deity] possesses manifold forms is stated here.
"Because of the statement 'to whom [the world] is joined,' [it follows that it arises] solely from false cognition. (129)

Having stated the cause for the manifold nature of the "other" (the external world) in the phrase "or if," [the author] now takes up the passage beginning with "for it is logical," preceded by an inquiry, in order to prove that very point.
[The question is: "Whence is this? [The answer is: These senses, denoted by the word *hari*, are connected to this internal self (*pratīc*) prior to knowledge due to ignorance;
and that connection—by which the self becomes manifold in form—is caused solely by the false cognition arising from those connected senses.
He explains the statement regarding the "cause" (hetu) as being the "occasion" (nimitta) for [the designation] "figurative" (bhākta), [stating]: "It is false" (mithyā). || 129 ||
Just as punishment and the like are appropriate for one's own son due to his lack of knowledge of reality.
Likewise, due to the lack of realization of the inner reality of the Self, there are fears.
He explains the connection of the inner self with the senses due to ignorance by means of an illustration: "As a garland," etc. (130).
The senses themselves are the monkeys, because they carry one toward sense objects.
These amount to ten thousand one hundred, according to the classification of living beings. || 131 ||
Anticipating the objection—"What follows from the connection with the senses, even if that connection is based on ignorance regarding the self of the *hari*s (the senses)?"—he says:
"The senses. He explains the meaning of "ten" and "a hundred" by saying: "Ten. He then addresses the contradiction in accepting that there are eleven of them.
He said: "It is the vital breath (prāṇa). || 131 ||
In this world, there is no other cause for the non-cognition of the self than the [defects of] the sense organs and so forth.
For as many monkeys as there are, so many are dependent upon him.

The connection [between the Self and the body] has been stated as "for they are joined" (*yuktā hi*); how then can identity (*tādātmya*), which is contrary to that, be asserted by the words "this [is that]" and so forth?

... : [The text continues as follows: Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-svabhāva). Among these, Mahāmati, the imagined self-nature consists of the various appearances of objects that arise from the discrimination of names and signs; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. The dependent self-nature, Mahāmati, is the causal conditionality of all dharmas, which arises from the habit-energy of beginningless false discrimination. It is like a dream or a reflection. The perfected self-nature, Mahāmati, is the state of things being eternally free from the imagined nature within the dependent nature; it is the realization of suchness (tathatā) through non-discriminative wisdom. And the self-nature of the ultimate truth, Mahāmati, is the realm of the Tathāgatas, which is attained when the dependent nature is purified of the imagined nature, transcending all dualistic conceptualizations. Thus, Mahāmati, by understanding these four kinds of self-nature, one enters into the stage of the Bodhisattvas and realizes the non-arising of all dharmas. Therefore, you should practice with diligence to abandon the imagined nature and realize the perfected nature. Thus it was said.

[The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in perfect wisdom, does not perceive a self, nor a being, nor a soul, nor a person; he does not perceive form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor formations, nor consciousness; he does not perceive the eye, nor the ear, nor the nose, nor the tongue, nor the body, nor the mind; he does not perceive forms, nor sounds, nor odors, nor tastes, nor tangibles, nor mental objects; he does not perceive the element of earth, nor the element of water, nor the element of fire, nor the element of wind, nor the element of space, nor the element of consciousness; he does not perceive the limit of past time, nor the limit of future time, nor the present time; he does not perceive the conditioned, nor the unconditioned, nor the limit of reality; he does not perceive the dharma, nor the non-dharma, nor even the state of all-knowledge. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in perfect wisdom, he does not perceive anything at all, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in perfect wisdom, trains in the perfection of wisdom. [Subhūti asked: "Is it possible, O Blessed One, for one who does not perceive any dharma to produce the thought of awakening? [The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, it is indeed so. [Subhūti asked: "If, O Blessed One, all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having produced the thought of awakening, train in the six perfections, mature beings, purify the buddha-field, and finally attain supreme perfect enlightenment? This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in perfect wisdom, trains in the perfection of wisdom. [Subhūti asked: "Is it then, O Blessed One, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in the perfection of wisdom, will reach the place of awakening and turn the wheel of Dharma? ... 1031: [The text continues with the following: Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva), the self-nature of dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva), the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the ultimate reality (dharmatā-svabhāva). What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of false discrimination? It refers to the attachment to names and forms (nāmarūpa) based on the various appearances of objects, such as the grasping of "this is a cow," "this is a horse," "this is a man," "this is a woman," and so forth, according to their respective characteristics. This is called the self-nature of false discrimination. What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of dependent origination? It refers to the manifestation of the various appearances of objects arising from the habit-energy (vāsanā) of false discrimination, which, though devoid of external objects, appear as if they were real due to the power of beginningless ignorance. This is called the self-nature of dependent origination. What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment? It refers to the realization that the self-nature of dependent origination is, in its true nature, devoid of the characteristics of false discrimination; it is the state of non-duality, free from the duality of grasper and grasped, and is the realm of the Tathāgatas. This is called the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of the ultimate reality? It refers to the fact that all phenomena are, from the very beginning, unborn and unceasing, being like a dream, a mirage, or a reflection; it is the suchness (tathatā) of all things, which is the object of the noble ones' wisdom. This is called the self-nature of the ultimate reality. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself in this way:

by thoroughly understanding these four kinds of self-nature, one shall not fall into the views of the philosophers and shall quickly attain the stage of a Bodhisattva. Thus it is said: The self-nature of false discrimination, The self-nature of dependent origination, The self-nature of perfect accomplishment, And the self-nature of the ultimate reality— These four kinds of self-nature Are taught for the sake of the wise. Thus ends the section on the four kinds of self-nature. 1031.

Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of false discrimination? It is the attachment to names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) as having an intrinsic nature, based on the objects of the five sense-faculties and the mind. This is called the self-nature of false discrimination. What is the self-nature of dependent origination? It is that which arises from the causal conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma; it is the manifestation of the body, the abode, and the objects of experience. This is called the self-nature of dependent origination. What is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment? It is the realization of the non-existence of the self-nature of false discrimination within the self-nature of dependent origination, by means of the wisdom of non-discrimination and the wisdom of insight. This is called the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. What is the self-nature of the ultimate reality? It is the suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), signlessness (*animitta*), the absence of desire (*apranihita*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). This is called the self-nature of the ultimate reality. Mahāmati, these are the four kinds of self-nature. By means of these, all the various teachings of the Tathāgatas are established. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself in the discernment of the self-natures so that you may transcend the views of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the philosophers (*tīrthakara*). Thus it is said: "The self-nature of false discrimination, Dependent origination, Perfect accomplishment, And the ultimate reality— These four kinds of self-nature Are taught by the Buddhas."

The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if a noble disciple possesses four qualities, he is one who has reached the ultimate destination, one who has completed the journey, one who has laid down the burden, one who has attained his own goal, one who has utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, one who is liberated through perfect knowledge, and one for whom birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence beyond this. What are the four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. Ānanda, if a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, he is one who has reached the ultimate destination, one who has completed the journey, one who has laid down the burden, one who has attained his own goal, one who has utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, one who is liberated through perfect knowledge, and one for whom birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence beyond this. ... : [The text continues as follows: Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). Among these, the imagined self-nature is that which is grasped by ordinary people through names and signs (nāmanimitta) regarding objects that have no intrinsic reality. The dependent self-nature is the manifestation of various appearances based on the causal conditions of ignorance and the habit-energies (vāsanā) of false discrimination. The perfected self-nature is the state in which the dependent nature is seen as being eternally free from the characteristics of the imagined nature. The self-nature of the Great Vehicle is the realization of the non-duality of subject and object, the absence of self in phenomena (dharmanairātmya), and the attainment of the stage of Tathāgatahood through the purification of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna). Mahāmati, you should understand that these four kinds of self-nature are the gateway to entering the profound meaning of all the Buddha's teachings. By means of this, one transcends the views of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and externalists, and realizes the stage of Buddhahood.

... : [The text continues as follows: Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva), the self-nature of dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva), the self-nature of perfected reality (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-svabhāva). Among these, Mahāmati, the self-nature of false discrimination refers to the attachment to names and signs (nāmanimitta) regarding objects that do not exist. The self-nature of dependent origination refers to the manifestation of various appearances based on the causal conditions of false discrimination. The self-nature of perfected reality refers to the non-existence of the former two within the latter. The self-nature of the ultimate truth refers to the realization of the non-duality of subject and object through the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (prapañca). 528 …… [The remainder of the text follows] …… 528.136. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent self-nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the perfected self-nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-vyavasthāna-svabhāva*). Among these, Mahāmati, the imagined self-nature consists of the various names, signs, and conceptualizations regarding the body, possessions, and abode, which are based on the dependent self-nature. The dependent self-nature, Mahāmati, arises from the causal conditions of ignorance, desire, and karma, and it is characterized by the non-duality of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*). The perfected self-nature, Mahāmati, is the state of the dependent self-nature being eternally free from the imagined self-nature; it is the realm of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that transcends all linguistic expression. As for the self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of all phenomena, Mahāmati, it refers to the fact that all phenomena are established through the power of the Tathāgata’s vow and the mastery of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-vaśitā*); it is not something produced by causes and conditions, nor is it something that has arisen from the dependent nature. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should cultivate your practice by relying upon the perfected self-nature and abandoning the imagined and dependent self-natures. Thus it is said: The imagined nature is like a barren woman’s son; The dependent nature is like a dream or an illusion. The perfected nature is the eternal absence Of the imagined within the dependent. The basis for the manifestation of all phenomena Is the power of the Tathāgata’s vow; It is not born of causes and conditions, Nor does it arise from the dependent. Thus, one should abandon the two natures And rely upon the perfected nature. By practicing in this way, One shall quickly attain Buddhahood. 528.140. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, please explain to me further how the various forms of consciousness manifest, and how the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) occurs. The Blessed One replied: "Mahāmati, there are eight kinds of consciousness. What are these eight? They are: the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), the mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*). Among these, Mahāmati, the storehouse consciousness is the root of all phenomena; it is the support for the arising of the seven evolving consciousnesses. The mind-consciousness, Mahāmati, arises in conjunction with the storehouse consciousness and the mental objects, and it is characterized by discrimination. The five sense-consciousnesses, Mahāmati, arise simultaneously with the mind-consciousness, depending upon the sense organs and their respective objects; they are characterized by the grasping of external marks. When the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) of the false views of a self and what belongs to a self is thoroughly purified, the transformation of the basis occurs, and the seven consciousnesses cease to function. This is called the attainment of the Tathāgata-knowledge. Thus it is said: The storehouse consciousness is the root; The mind-consciousness arises from it. The five sense-consciousnesses Arise together with the mind. When the habit-energy of false views Is completely purified, The basis is transformed; The seven consciousnesses cease. This is the Tathāgata-knowledge, Which is attained through this transformation. 528.145. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, please explain to me the characteristics of the three kinds of liberation (*vimokṣa*) so that I and other Bodhisattvas may understand them and quickly attain the supreme enlightenment. The Blessed One replied: "Mahāmati, there are three kinds of liberation. What are these three? They are: the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*), the liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*), and the liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*). Among these, Mahāmati, the liberation of emptiness means that one realizes that all phenomena are devoid of a self and what belongs to a self, and thus one is liberated from the view of a self. The liberation of signlessness means that one realizes that all phenomena are devoid of the characteristics of form and appearance, and thus one is liberated from the grasping of marks. The liberation of wishlessness means that one realizes that all conditioned phenomena are suffering and impermanent, and thus one is liberated from the desire for existence. However, Mahāmati, these are merely gateways to liberation; the true liberation of the Tathāgatas is the realization of the equality of all phenomena, which is beyond thought and expression, and is the cessation of the duality of subject and object. Thus it is said: Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— These are the gates to liberation. But the Tathāgatas' true liberation Is the equality of all things. Beyond thought and expression, It is the cessation of duality. By realizing this, one attains The supreme enlightenment. 528.150. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, please explain to me the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*) so that I and other Bodhisattvas may understand them and proceed without confusion. The Blessed One replied: "Mahāmati, there are ten stages of Bodhisattvas. What are these ten? They are: the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the stage of purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the stage of radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), the stage of brilliance (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), the stage of difficulty to conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), the stage of presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), the stage of far-reaching (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*), the stage of immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*), the stage of good intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), and the stage of the cloud of dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). Among these, Mahāmati, when a Bodhisattva has perfected the practices of the first stage, he enters the second stage, which is characterized by the purification of precepts. Having purified his conduct, he enters the third stage, where he masters the concentrations and wisdoms. Entering the fourth stage, he burns away the defilements of the afflictions with the fire of wisdom. Entering the fifth stage, he overcomes the difficulties of the world. Entering the sixth stage, he faces the reality of dependent origination. Entering the seventh stage, he proceeds far beyond the reach of ordinary beings. Entering the eighth stage, he becomes immovable because he is free from effort and conceptualization. Entering the ninth stage, he attains mastery over the powers and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Entering the tenth stage, he is like a great cloud covering the sky, raining down the Dharma for all sentient beings. Beyond these ten stages, Mahāmati, is the stage of the Tathāgata, which is the fulfillment of all vows and the perfection of all qualities. Thus it is said: Joy, purity, radiance, and brilliance, Difficult to conquer, presence, and far-reaching, Immovable, good intelligence, and the cloud of dharma— These are the ten stages of the Bodhisattvas. Having perfected the practices of these stages, One attains the stage of the Tathāgata. Free from all faults and afflictions, One fulfills all vows and qualities. 528.155. 127a7. 爾時，世尊說是法已，告諸大眾：「汝等當知，此法甚深微妙，難可測度。若有菩薩摩訶薩能信受奉行，則於未來世中，必當成就無上菩提。」 127a9. 爾時，會中有一菩薩摩訶薩，名曰文殊師利，即從座起，合掌白佛言：「世尊！云何名為信受奉行？云何名為成就無上菩提？」 127a11. 佛告文殊師利：「信受者，謂深信諸法皆空，不生疑惑。奉行者，謂依教修行，不違正法。成就者，謂證得諸法實相，永離一切戲論。無上菩提者，即是究竟涅槃。」 127a13. 爾時，文殊師利菩薩聞佛所說，歡喜踊躍，即白佛言：「世尊！我今當往娑婆世界，為諸眾生演說此法，令其信受奉行，速證無上菩提。」 127a15. 爾時，世尊讚言：「善哉，善哉！文殊師利！汝能如是發弘誓願，利益眾生。我今隨喜。」 127a17. 爾時，文殊師利菩薩禮佛足已，與諸大眾辭別而去。即時，娑婆世界六種震動，天雨妙華，地涌甘泉，一切眾生皆得安樂。 127a19. 爾時，世尊復告阿難：「汝當受持此經，廣宣流布，令一切眾生皆得聞知。」

543: The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivered all suffering. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness and emptiness is form; form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form. What is form is emptiness, and what is emptiness is form. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; likewise, no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; transcending all inverted dreams and delusions, he attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on this *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra. It relieves all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: *Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.* Thus spoke the Blessed One. With these words, the Venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, including the *bodhisattvas*, *śrāvakas*, gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Buddha had taught. They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā-svabhāva*). Among these, Mahāmati, the self-nature of false discrimination refers to the attachment to names, signs, and characteristics, based on the grasping of objects through the power of beginningless habit-energy. The self-nature of dependent origination refers to the manifestation of various appearances, which arise in succession from the seeds of the Ālayavijñāna, like waves upon the ocean. The self-nature of perfect accomplishment refers to the non-duality of the object and the subject, the cessation of the grasping of characteristics, and the realization that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, and reflections. The self-nature of the ultimate reality refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, which is free from the duality of existence and non-existence, and is the realm of the Tathāgatas.

745. ... [The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature as the ultimate reality (dharmatā-svabhāva). [Mahāmati asked: "What, Blessed One, is the imagined self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the attachment to names and signs (nāmanimitta) by those who do not understand that they are merely the manifestation of their own mind. [Mahāmati asked: "What, Blessed One, is the dependent self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the manifestation of the various objects such as form (rūpa) and so forth, which arise from the habit-energies (vāsanā) of false discrimination. [Mahāmati asked: "What, Blessed One, is the perfected self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the non-duality of the imagined and the dependent, which is the state of being free from the characteristics of grasped and grasper (grāhyagrāhaka-lakṣaṇa). [Mahāmati asked: "What, Blessed One, is the self-nature as the ultimate reality? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the Tathatā (Suchness), the Bhūtakoṭi (the limit of reality), and Nirvana; it is the nature of all phenomena that is unchanging and undifferentiated. [The Blessed One continued: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, the imagined self-nature is like a person with cataracts seeing hairs or a net of flies where there are none. The dependent self-nature is like a mirage, a dream, a reflection, or a city of the Gandharvas. The perfected self-nature is like gold, silver, or lapis lazuli found in the ground, which remains unchanged even when fashioned into various ornaments. And the self-nature as the ultimate reality is like the ocean, because it is the source from which all the dharmas of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emerge. [The Blessed One concluded: "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself to abandon the imagined self-nature and realize the dependent and perfected self-natures, thereby attaining the realization of the self-nature as the ultimate reality. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Hearing this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati was delighted and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had taught. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Examination of Self-Nature," in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra in ten fascicles.

... : [The text continues: Furthermore, O Blessed One, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor a being, nor a soul, nor a person; he does not perceive form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor formations, nor consciousness; he does not perceive the eye, nor the ear, nor the nose, nor the tongue, nor the body, nor the mind;

he does not perceive forms, nor sounds, nor odors, nor tastes, nor tangibles, nor mental objects; he does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor the ear-consciousness, nor the nose-consciousness, nor the tongue-consciousness, nor the body-consciousness, nor the mind-consciousness; he does not perceive contact, nor feeling, nor craving, nor grasping, nor existence, nor birth, nor aging and death. He does not perceive ignorance, nor the formative forces, nor consciousness, nor name-and-form, nor the six sense-bases, nor contact, nor feeling, nor craving, nor grasping, nor existence, nor birth, nor aging and death. He does not perceive the attainment of the fruit of a Stream-enterer, nor that of a Once-returner, nor that of a Non-returner, nor that of an Arhat; he does not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood, nor the state of a Tathāgata, nor Arhatship, nor even the state of a Samyaksambuddha. Why is this? Because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty, they cannot be apprehended. Because they are unapprehendable, they are not produced, and because they are not produced, they do not cease. That which is neither produced nor ceased is neither past, nor future, nor present. That which is neither past, nor future, nor present is beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). That which is beyond conceptual proliferation is the perfection of wisdom. Thus, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, and because he perceives nothing, he does not become attached to anything. Being unattached, he is liberated through non-clinging. This is called the "perfection of wisdom" of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

[Then the Blessed One, having spoken these words, rose from his seat and entered the great parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees. [At that time, the earth shook in six ways; the sun and moon were eclipsed; and from the sky there fell a rain of celestial flowers. All the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, wept with tears falling like rain, wailing and lamenting: "Alas! The World-Honored One has passed into parinirvāṇa too soon! Alas! The Eye of the World has been extinguished! [Then the Venerable Ānanda, having wiped away his tears, addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa: "Venerable sir, the Tathāgata has now entered parinirvāṇa. How shall we perform the funeral rites for the body of the Tathāgata? [The Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied: "Ānanda, just as the funeral rites for a universal monarch are performed, so should the funeral rites for the body of the Tathāgata be performed. What are those rites? They are as follows: wrapping the body in five hundred layers of fine cotton cloth, then in five hundred layers of fine silk cloth, placing it in an iron coffin filled with oil, covering it with another iron lid, and setting it on a funeral pyre made of all kinds of fragrant woods. Then, after the fire has been lit, the pyre should be extinguished with milk. This is how the funeral rites for the body of a universal monarch are performed; and it is in this same manner that the funeral rites for the body of the Tathāgata should be performed. [Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, took the body of the Tathāgata and proceeded to the city of Kuśinagara. Having arrived at the city, they placed the body in the Malla hall. Then the Mallas of Kuśinagara, hearing that the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, were overcome with grief and sorrow. They adorned the city with various kinds of banners, canopies, and perfumes, and prepared a great funeral pyre of all kinds of fragrant woods. Then they took the body of the Tathāgata, wrapped it in five hundred layers of fine cotton cloth and five hundred layers of fine silk cloth, placed it in an iron coffin filled with oil, covered it with another iron lid, and set it upon the funeral pyre. When the pyre was lit, the fire would not burn. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa then said to the Mallas: "O Mallas, you must first pay homage to the body of the Tathāgata with music, dance, song, and various offerings before the fire will ignite. The Mallas then offered music, dance, song, and various offerings to the body of the Tathāgata. Only then did the fire spontaneously ignite and consume the body of the Tathāgata. When the body was consumed, only the relics remained. The Mallas then divided the relics into eight portions and built eight stūpas over them. [This is the Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra.]

He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm.
