Now begins the third chapter:
[herein] is the meaning of the Madhu-kāṇḍa contained within the Yājñavalkya-kāṇḍa.
Henceforth, it will be clearly explained by the Śruti with great effort. || 1 ||
That non-dual knowledge of bliss which is directly and immediately perceived—that immortal Brahman, the ultimate refuge of all, I am. (1)

Having explained the Madhu-kāṇḍa, which has the primary focus on the principal subject matter (*pradhāna*), [the author], wishing to introduce the Muni-kāṇḍa, which has the primary focus on reasoning (*yukti*), states the connection (*saṃgati*). The words "the meaning belonging to the section" (*kāṇḍaga arthaḥ*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The repeated statement through questions and answers constitutes the effort in the exposition. He states the purpose of repeating what has already been said with the word "clearly" (*sphuṭam*). || 1 ||
The section belonging to Śaṅkha and Likhita follows immediately after this Madhukāṇḍa.
Now begins the supreme section (kāṇḍa), which abounds in investigation.

Koṇḍa states the reason for the Westerner’s [position] as follows: "Yājñavalkīyam" (the work of Yājñavalkya). The meaning is that since the statement by Kokka occurs immediately after the citation of the authoritative source, the sequence of these two works—which primarily consist of scripture and reasoning—is established accordingly. || 2 ||
The very same meaning that was stated previously is now being expressed here as well.
It is neither etymologically justified nor logical for two things that do not reside in the same word to be expressed as one.
The ignorant [opponent] raises the objection of tautology with the words "nanu" (but surely).

To the question—"What fault is there in stating the very same thing again even through a difference in sections?"—he replies: "It would be a tautology. For in both cases, non-tautology is desired only by virtue of the remainder (*śeṣa*); otherwise, it would contradict the principle of the "cognition based on all recensions" (*sarvaśākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), which applies to a single recension.
The meaning is that since there is no difference in the sense between the two *gaṇḍa* [sections], repetition is not appropriate because it would be fruitless. || 3 ||
And even though they have the same meaning, there is no redundancy in this at all.
And because the section of Yājñavalkya primarily concerns logical justification. || 4 ||

He speaks of only one single samādhi. Regarding the phrase "even though the meaning is the same": the sense of the word "well-known" (prasiddhi) is that there is no tautology because of the difference in the supporting factors (upapādaka), which constitute the primary elements. || 4 ||
This has been described by you as stated in the Āgama, in the section concerning the honey.
In order to purify the meaning of the scriptures, he will set forth logical arguments here. || 5 ||

And the independence of scripture is not refuted by the statement of reasoning.
Because the arguments [concerning] being a different object and so forth are distinct from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 6 ||
1kha. Regarding the predominance of action and knowledge.

The meaning is that, in accordance with the refutation of that [position], reasoning (*yukti*) is accepted within the Veda. "What is death, by which action along with its means is conjoined and brought under control, and through the attainment of what one becomes a seeker of liberation?

To this he says: "Limitation," etc. The meaning is that death is the erroneous cognition—which is the cause of the distinctions such as Brahmin and Kshatriya—accompanied by passion and other afflictions. He takes up the passage beginning with "By what," etc.: "By what? (19).
Whatever mortal means of accomplishment there is, that which is to be accomplished is likewise born as a mortal.

As it has been said: "If death were destroyed along with its means, then every action would have to be abandoned; yet, the abandonment of action—which is the cause of the supreme human goal—is not appropriate.

Therefore, this question is not tenable. To this, he replies: "By me... [and so on]. The sense is that the perishability of the object to be accomplished is necessarily inherent in it. Now, when Āśvala proceeded to engage in debate (*jalpa*) in order to defeat Yājñavalkya, it was appropriate for him to employ fallacies (*chala*) and the like; for according to the maxim that "the responses of those with insincere speech are themselves insincere," a response based on the actual truth (*yathātattvam*) would have been inappropriate.

This is because debate (*jalpa*) cannot result in the determination of truth (*tattvanirṇaya*); regarding this, he says: "The proponent" (*pravaktā*). Here, the term "here" (*atra*) refers to the discussion of debate (*jalpakathā*).

The significance of *vicāra* (investigation) lies in its fruit, which is the determination of truth (*tattvanirṇaya*). This is because we observe questions posed by those possessing knowledge, such as Aśvalāyana and others, with the intention of victory and so forth, and because refutations are subsequently brought forward; thus, this constitutes *jalpa* (disputation). 1146 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]: Having explained the passage beginning with "atha" (now), he addresses the concern that there is redundancy between the questions "by how many? and "which ones?", as well as the redundancy between the answers "by three" and "the Puronuvākyā," etc.; thus he says: "By three..."
Thus [ends the section]. || 51 ||
Because it shares the same numerical value as the three worlds, there shall be victory over all living beings.
For it is within these three alone that all living beings originate. || 52 ||
To the question "What is the use of them?", he states the meaning of the response beginning with "Whatever [is there]... as follows: "The three worlds" (*trailokya*).
The three worlds constitute the *trailokya*; therein, in the sequence beginning with the earth (*bhūḥ*), there is the number three, and likewise in the *puronuvākyā* verses and so forth.

Therefore, because of the similarity of number between those three worlds and the *puronuvākyā* verses and so forth, by effecting the three worlds through the *puronuvākyā* verses and so forth, there would be the conquest of all living beings—this is the meaning. [This is the] result...

Anticipating the objection that since the meditation on the worlds follows the meditation on the self, the conquest of those [worlds] is appropriate, but not the conquest of all living beings, he says "all" (sarva) to show that because living beings are included within the worlds, their conquest is not something other than the conquest of the worlds. || 12 ||
Because of commonalities such as brilliance and so forth, there is the attainment of prosperity in the world of the gods and other realms.
These are indeed the perfections of the fruit; here, action (karma) is not intended to be discussed. || 53 ||

The two kinds of perfection—perfection of action and perfection of fruit—have been mentioned; regarding that, as to what kind of perfection is desired in the passage beginning with "only the world of the gods," he says: "on account of its brilliance, etc. (53).
Radiance, sound, lying on the ground, and clarified butter, meat, milk, and water [are the offerings].
The attainment of the celestial realms and so forth occurs because of the possibility of possessing radiance and other such qualities. || 54 ||

He elaborates upon that: "Radiance," etc. Radiance belongs to the oblations of clarified butter; sound belongs to the oblations of meat and so forth; and lying down below belongs to the oblations of milk, Soma, and the like.

Since radiance and other such qualities exist even in the worlds of the gods, the ancestors, and humans, these oblations—clarified butter and the rest—result in the attainment of the world of the gods;
meat and the rest result in the attainment of the world of the ancestors; and milk, Soma, and the rest result in the attainment of the world of humans. Indeed, these are the oblations.
The meaning is that when [the mantra] is brought to completion, the worlds are produced; by contemplating this, the conquest of the worlds occurs. || 14 ||
The mind is infinite because its functions are infinite, due to the infinity of objects such as sound and the rest.
Having brought about the Viśvedevas as mental functions (manovṛtti), due to their equality with infinity. || 55 ||
By means of that right knowledge, he perceives only the infinite.
One who possesses the aforementioned vision, while renouncing the world, [attains] the fruit for himself.
He states the meaning of the phrase "the mind is indeed infinite" with the words "by its modifications. The cause for its infinity is stated as "of sound and so forth.

He states the meaning of "infinite" and so on with the words "the Viśvedevas. He states the meaning of the word "world" with the words "the fruit. This indicates that this meditation has the sacrificer as its agent. [He says] "himself," and not that this is a meditation connected to a subsidiary part (aṅga) because of the word "sacrificer."
The sense is that it should be stated as "dam" (the syllable *da*), because the mind is common to all [the letters]. || 55 || 56 ||
The three verses beginning with the Puronuvākyā have been recited previously.
Those very [verses] mentioned here are to be understood as the stotriyas, and no others. || 57 ||
Regarding the phrase "one's own *stotriyas*," he explains the meaning of the word *stotriya* with the words "three. || 17 ||
Regarding the verses on the sacrifice within the deities (*adhiyajña*), which ones are those concerning the self (*adhyātma*)? What are they?
Internally, they are said to take the form of prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna.
He clarifies the meaning of "Which are those eight that are internal? by way of a question: "The Gītās, however. He states the meaning of "Prāṇa alone," etc., as follows: "Prāṇa... (58).
Victory [is attained] over the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, due to the similarity in their number and other such qualities.
Then Aśvala also desisted, because the resolution of the question he himself had posed had been provided.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 5,689.
Thus ends the first Aśvala-Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter in the *Śrībṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*. || 1 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "What [is the use] of them? as follows: "Victory. By means of the correspondence of the number three, and through the correspondences of being first, middle, and last, one identifies the worlds such as Earth and so forth with the *puronuvākyā* verses and the rest; by that identification (*saṃpad*), there is victory over the worlds—this is the meaning. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then indeed... as follows: "Aśvala too... The word "too" (*api*) indicates arrogance. [It implies: because he did not know that Yājñavalkya was beyond his own sphere of competence...
The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is immediate succession. || 59 ||
Thus ends the first Aśvala Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. || 1 ||
Now begins the second Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding liberation from death and supreme liberation, these two were treated in the preceding Brāhmaṇa.
The supreme Brahmana is said to be for the purpose of ascertaining the true nature of death. || 1 ||

He recites the narrative: "From death," etc. The meaning is that by explaining liberation from death—which consists of time, from karma born of false knowledge accompanied by passion and other afflictions, and which is the cause for the delimitation of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth—the purification of the referent of "thou" (tvam-padārtha) has been accomplished. He introduces the Ārtabhāga Brāhmaṇa with the words: "Death-formed," etc. || 1 ||
When it was asked, "By what characteristic is this one seized by death? [the answer follows].
It is said that this [individual] is seized by means of the form of the graspers (graha) and over-graspers (atigraha). || 2 ||
Anticipating the question, "What is that form of Death which you wish to determine?", he speaks with a sense of inquiry: "What? (verse 2).
It consists of the nature of the results arising from the discernment of the elements, the sacrifice, and so forth.
It is the locus of delusion and attachment, characterized by death, the grasper, and that which is grasped.

If it is argued that even for death in the form of the planets and so forth, there is a specific characteristic (asādhāraṇa-rūpa) expressed in the statement, he says in response: "With reference to the objective world" (adhibhūta).

The meaning is that death, as previously described, consists of the limitation of the subjective self (adhyātma) and so on, being composed of action, its factors, and its results, and supported by attachment and other passions caused by delusion, taking the form of the senses and their objects. || 3 ||
1148 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]:
The forms of one liberated from this world— namely fire and the others— were previously described.
In the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa and likewise in the Aśvala Brāhmaṇa.

Having raised the objection that it was already stated previously that [the gods] were seized by the grasp of death before the attainment of the deity, [the author], considering that there exists a state of being seized by the aforementioned death because fire and the others possess birth and so forth, recalls what was said. "Hence" (itaḥ) means from death in the form of attachment and evil, which arises from the conceit of limitation. He clarifies the very statement "previously" (pure) with the words "Udgītha... (udgītha). || 4 ||
And this is held to be the fruit of those actions that are conjoined with knowledge.
Therefore, because it possesses the sequence of arising and so forth, it must be impermanent, like a jar or similar objects. || 5 ||

One might object that even though states such as being fire and so forth are seized by death, the attainment of the fruit of the Sūtra—which is their combination—is not seized by it; therefore, liberation is simply the attainment of that [Sūtra], making effort for the sake of perfect knowledge (samyagjñāna) useless. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And the fruit... The meaning is: since the desired fruit of the combination is impermanent—like a jar—because it possesses birth and other characteristics, the attainment of the Sūtra is not liberation. || 5 ||
Therefore, from this aforementioned definition of the probandum and the probans:
Liberation from the blinding cycle of existence must be achieved through the cause of knowledge.

The conclusion is stated as follows: "Therefore... (6). This Brāhmaṇa is intended for this purpose: since the fire and so forth, as well as the Sūtra which is of that nature and the Self of the world, are subject to birth and other states and are seized by death, liberation from that [death] must be achieved through knowledge by means of the removal of ignorance. Thus the result is expressed.
Even if the divine fruit of knowledge and action has indeed been described previously;
Even so, it remains white despite being bound by the grasp and over-grasp.
He states another reason for the rejection of the *Samuccaya-phala-sūtra* due to its pervasion by death: "By knowledge," etc. (7).
Because speech, mind, and breath exist even within the nature of the threefold food.
Therefore, even Prajāpati was not liberated from those things whose forms are the graspers and the over-graspers.

To explain how the thread is bound by means of the form of the planets and so forth, he says: "Speech," etc. The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is that those [senses], together with their objects, exist within Prajāpati. || 8 ||
Speech and the other senses are known as the "seizers" (grahas), and the group of four is not intended to be emphasized here.
Now, following the statement regarding the extension of the Prātimokṣa, its specific distinctions are being explained. || 9 ||

Having explained in the preceding Brāhmaṇa liberation from death in the form of Time (Kāla) and so forth, it was stated that since everything is pervaded by that death in the form of the planets and so on, liberation from the world-soul—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—must be declared for the sake of purifying the meanings of the words that constitute the sense of the entire passage; with this purpose, the connection of this present Brāhmaṇa has been stated. Now, beginning the explanation of the meanings of the individual words, [the text] says: "Speech, indeed, is the sacrifice... and so forth.

Fearing that the question "How many are the *grahas*? and the reply "Eight," etc., would be untenable—given that speech, sight, smell, and mind are already included among the *grahas*, as are name, form, odor, and desire among the *atigrahas*, along with the four [elements] residing therein—he accepts the well-known status of the *grahas* and *atigrahas*. He states: "Speech and so forth. If that is so, then the number four, which resides therein [in the elements], [is also known].

To the question of how there can be both a query and a response regarding [the number] being already known, he says: "And the tetrad. Anticipating the objection that, as in the case of the singularity of the animal (*paśu*), the tetrad might also be intended to be significant, he says: "Regarding the *atimokṣas*. Because the logic stated for speech (*vāk*) and so forth is extended (*atideśa*) to the skin (*tvac*) and so forth, the tetrad is not intended to be significant, just like the singularity in the phrase "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), since [singularity] is a qualification of the thing to be enjoined (*upādeya-viśeṣaṇa*).

The point is that, just as in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the singularity residing in the cup is not intended to be expressed because it serves merely as a delimiter; otherwise, if the cleansing were enjoined with reference to both the cup-ness and the singularity, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) because two things being simultaneously qualified cannot be related to one another—resulting in the sentence meaning "he cleanses the cup" and "and he cleanses that one. Therefore, just like the singularity of the cup, the fourfold number here is also not intended to be expressed.

[Objection: But surely, since the *grahas* (seizers) and *atigrahas* (over-seizers) have already been known, questions and answers are not appropriate, as there would be no further rest [in inquiry] therein. To this he says: "The particularity thereof.

The word *atha* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since the *grahas* and so forth have been known in a general way, the meaning is that the question and so forth are for the purpose of determining the specific number desired regarding them. || 9 ||
The sense organs, such as the nose and so forth, are to be known as the *grahas*; their objects, such as smell and so forth, are the *atigrahas*.
The odors and other objects are seized by the planets, and the self is seized by the planets through their transits.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed a grasper" as follows: "The graspers. He explains the mutual relationship between the graspers (graha), the over-graspers (atigraha), and the grasper (the subject who grasps): "By means of the graspers," etc. (10).
Just as an odor brought by the out-breath comes under the control of the sense of smell.
In the same way, the planets such as the eye [and other senses] here [function] together with their attendants, such as the vital breaths (prāṇa).

Establishing that very point by means of an illustration, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "by the out-breath" (*apānena*). [He says: "By the out-breath. Just as an odor impelled by exhalation remains under the control of the sense of smell, so too color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest, impelled by their respective corresponding airs, are dependent upon the eyes and other senses.

Likewise, the apprehensions (*graha*) of the eyes and other senses, together with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), etc., remain under the control of the objects of apprehension such as color-form; and even though they are bound to one another, [they do not function independently].
The meaning is that they are bound by him as well, because [the bondage] possesses fruit without being tied to a grasper. || 11 ||
For objects such as odors, which reside within the intellect, are awakened by karma.
For they employ the nose and the other senses; therefore, those [objects] are the *atigrahas* (seizers).

Although the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are called *grahas* (seizers) by virtue of their etymological derivation as "those that seize," he explains how odors and the rest are also *grahas*: "Odors and so forth. Indeed, objects rooted in beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within the intellect—whether auspicious or inauspicious—[are what are seized].

Impelled by karma, they impel the sense organs, such as the nose and so forth, for the purpose of manifesting cognitions of their own respective forms; thus, because they transcend the graspers (the senses) and bring them under their own control, they are called "over-graspers" (*atigrahas*). The word "hi" signifies that the fact of objects being the impellers of the sense organs is established by experience. || 12 ||
"This death which has been described here—does that death also have another death?
Tell me truly, O Yājñavalkya, whether it exists or does not exist. (13)
He explains the passage beginning with "All this is [subject] to death" and so forth with the words "This which... (yo'yam). || 13 ||

If it exists, there would be an infinite regress; if it does not exist, there would be no liberation.
Considering this reply to be distressing, he questioned him further.
He states the intention of the questioner: "It exists. He concludes the question with the word "iti" (thus). || 14 ||
No fixed state whatsoever is taught to be death.
For death is called the destroyer with respect to those things that are to be destroyed. || 15 ||
Anticipating the objection that the reply "Agni indeed is death" is improper because the word *mṛtyu* is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) as referring to Vaivasvata, he says: "No. (15)
I declare that even for one who is subject to death, there is indeed yet another death.
And it does not incur an infinite regress here, because everything has death as its cause.
He states that the commentary beginning with "there exists" (*asti tāvat*) is appropriate even if the word *mṛtyu* lacks a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) like that of *aśvakarṇa* and so on.

Regarding the phrase "of death" (*mṛtyoḥ*): the meaning is that the direct realization of the identity of the Self is the death of death consisting of [the cycle of] falling and so forth, along with its cause.

Having raised the objection that if there were a death of death, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), he says: "And not... (*na ca*). The direct realization of the Self [sublates] all duality.
The meaning is that, like a fire without fuel, having consumed [the object], it subsides without requiring another burner; thus, there is no infinite regress. || 16 ||
By eating all kinds of food, Agni likewise becomes death itself.
Having become food for the waters, he was seen with a body of many forms.
Having stated the intended meaning of the reply, he explains the literal meaning of its words: "Not all," etc. (17).
For Agni or Hiraṇyagarbha, or indeed Water, is considered to be the cause of that.
Death is renowned on earth as the cause of the destruction of all effects. || 18 ||

Having raised the objection as to how fire and water can be death when it is knowledge that is the death of death, he states another point: "Fire," etc. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the fact of water being the cause with respect to Hiraṇyagarbha is well-known from such passages as, "He created the waters at the beginning; into them he cast his seed. He states the reason for the status of the Sūtra and the Unmanifested (avyākṛta) as death: "Of effects," etc. Or rather—

Although water, which is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta), is the cause of Hiraṇyagarbha—who is called the "thread" (sūtra)—one might still ask: how can it be his death? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the effects," etc. (Verse 18).
The direct realization of one's true nature is death for that which consists of ignorance.
Nor would there be an infinite regress here for death, which is the cause of saṃsāra. || 19 ||

Fearing that the objection—that if there is death for the indeterminate (avyākṛta) there would be an infinite regress, and if there is not, there would be no liberation—remains as it was, he says: "The inner self... (19).
Just as it obstructs birth, so too does it bring about its destruction.
The realization of the true nature of the inward Self does not lead to an infinite regress; therefore, no such fallacy occurs.

Although knowledge removes ignorance, its effects, and itself, there might still be the suspicion that because cessation is distinct from the self, it requires another remover, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Anticipating this, he says: "It brings [it] to rest. That is, that very cognition.

The meaning is that there is no infinite regress. || 20 ||
Other than these, there are secondary forms of death; through them, upon dying, there is rebirth.
Even past births do not destroy our perfect knowledge.

Fearing that it would be improper for a single word to have multiple meanings—given that the Sūtra, the knowledge of reality (*tattva-dhī*), self-restraint (*yama*), and so forth are distinct types of "deaths" (*mṛtyu*)—the author says: "Others. He states the reason why these others are secondary deaths (*gauṇa-mṛtyu*): "By them... He provides the reasoning for why right knowledge (*samyag-dhī*) is the primary death: "The previous... [This refers to] the removal of the cause of births occurring throughout the three periods of time.
The meaning is that, because it is devoid of hope, the state of being the primary death of right-mindedness has been described by him. || 21 ||
In the very explanation already stated, this declaration of the fruit would be logical.
But not so in the realization of the Self, which utterly destroys the entirety of saṃsāra. || 22 ||

Having raised the objection—"By supplying (*adhyāhṛtya*) the word 'knowledge' (*jñāna*), how can it be explained? For there is no basis for such a supply," he replies that the scriptural mention of the fruit, beginning with "again" (*apa punar*), is what provides that basis. He says "as follows. He states the reason why it is appropriate to explain by supplying the word "knowledge": "But not... Since death does not exist when there is such realization of the Self, the scriptural mention of the fruit is indeed appropriate.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, the meaning of the first half [of the verse] is that if explained according to the literal text, the mention of the fruit would be improper due to the absence of the word "knowledge" (jñāna).

Anticipating the objection, "How is that [mention of the fruit] possible in your view?", he says: "But not... (na tu). The meaning is that when the aforementioned realization of the Self is supplied [as the context], the scriptural mention of the fruit is not improper, because when that [realization] exists, there is no further death. || 22 ||
The complete awakening to the Self is the total destruction of the darkness of death.

It does not admit of being a positive concomitant, nor does it admit of being a negative concomitant.

Therefore, prior to that destruction, [the Self] is indeterminate...

With the intention of asking, "Since that [dissolution] occurs in its own cause for effects such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), why is the qualification 'in the two views' (*dṛśau*) used?

he says, beginning with "No" (*na*).
