Even though it has been created, how can that food remain undiminished while it is being eaten every day? To this he says: "Therein.
When that food has been created in the manner shown, because its creation occurs at every moment just as its eating does, its imperishability is established.
Such is the meaning. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that enjoyment is inseparable from creation. || 69 ||
Just as the self constantly consumes food through speech, body, and intellect, so too does it experience [objects].
In the same way, it also brings about birth through the unexhausted continuums of karma. || 66 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the creation of food is for the purpose of enjoyment, and since there is a restriction regarding enjoyment, there must likewise be a restriction regarding its creation—how then can it be inexhaustible? [The author] says "eternally" (nityam), establishing the invariable concomitance [between the two]. || 66 ||
The elements, being diminished by the karma of the Supreme Self, [perish].
Since they are produced here by the Puruṣa, therefore that Puruṣa is imperishable.

He cites the statement "The person (puruṣa) indeed is the imperishable" as the authority here. Regarding the phrase "the elements": since things such as rice and other grains, which are being consumed daily through enjoyment, are produced from a further material cause by the enjoying person on the ground of experience, with karma as the instrumental cause;
therefore, the meaning is that the person is the cause for the non-destruction of food. || 67 ||
The experience of past karma by persons, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is what [occurs].
Therefore, due to the specific nature of attachment, there is again the process of another. 68.4.

He states another reason for the non-exhaustion of food: "pūrva... and so forth. The present experience of pleasure and the like, which belongs to living beings, is impelled by karma from previous births; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [experiencing] results not performed by oneself (*anyathākṛtābhyāgama*) and so on. Therefore, even while this experience exists, because of the diversity of desires for objects of a similar kind, there arises another birth characterized by further experience through the medium of ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). This is the meaning. || 68 ||
This being so, living beings for the most part are generally possessed of attachment.
Therefore, by the power of the latent tendencies of desire, food is created again and again.

Nevertheless, he explains how food remains inexhaustible there with the word "tatra" (there). The meaning is that while that enjoyment arises through the diversity of desires, because it predominates for the ignorant who are generally the majority, food is created again and again in accordance with the aggregate of those desires; thus, its inexhaustibility is established. || 69 ||
Some are exhausted through experience, while others are accumulated through action.
The elements are like the flames of a lamp through its continuous succession. 70.

One might raise the objection that since the mere elements (*bhūtamātra*) which constitute the aggregate of cause and effect are themselves effects, they perish; and because the person (*puruṣa*), who is intended [to be eternal] as the enjoyer and the agent, would also perish upon their destruction, food cannot be imperishable. To this, he replies: "They perish. He provides an illustration for the creation of the constituent elements in the form of a continuous stream: "As of a lamp," meaning that just as its flame undergoes decrease and increase through its continuity, so too do the elements...
The meaning is that those two would belong even to the constituent elements (mātrās), and because the enjoyer is not a product, there is no fear of his destruction. || 70 ||
It is based on the ritual refinement that establishes the state of being mutual eaters and drinkers.
Initiated by those whose nature is consciousness, the entire world wanders about.
1. Vaiśiṣṭya; 2. Kha. dṛṣṭau.
[Vol. 3, page 27] 1160 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Third Adhyāya]

If the individual soul (*jīva*), the progenitor of the world, were liberated after having consumed the created world, how could the world be imperishable? Otherwise, the authority of the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) would be undermined. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Mutually... The world, joined with mutual relationships of enjoyer and enjoyed, as well as with desires, actions, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*), has been commenced by the souls under their own influence; therefore, even when one soul is liberated, because other creators remain—as in a dream—the world does not cease to exist.
The meaning is that the world wanders excessively due to that [ignorance], and therefore it is "inexhaustible" (akṣaya). || 71 ||
For whoever possesses a conscious self performs by whatever action whatsoever.
It is the cause of the creation of the world, together with its constituent elements and its presiding deities.

How is this world begun by living beings? Since it is accepted that the field-knower (*kṣetrajña*) alone—possessing powers such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—is its creator, [the author] says: "By consciousness," etc. This means: even by someone who is lowly; "by whatever" implies even by one who is not distinguished. The word "for" (*hi*) is used to state that the mere field-knower's status as the cause of the world's creation has been previously explained. || 72 ||
Having heard this, it was stated by the Lord himself: "In such a way, karma is not exhausted."
Likewise, for one who perceives the Self as consisting of the three foods, there is the attainment of divine speech and other such perfections. || 73 ||

Raising the objection, "If karma perishes at every moment, how was that world created by it?", he says [the answer] by relying on such scriptural texts as "For him, it does not perish" (*na hy asya...*). The connection is as follows: he states this very point himself through scripture so that karma does not perish. Furthermore, in the Sūtra, for one who meditates with the *ahaṃgraha* (identification) upon the threefold food, there is the attainment of that which is the Sūtra—the world-self consisting of speech and the rest.

By the passage beginning with "And for the earth," it is stated that she (the earth) does not perish; furthermore, because of the Vedic revelation stating, "Then these divine, immortal vital breaths enter him," he says [in the verse], "divine," etc., thus establishing the non-destruction of the world. || 73 ||
"This is that, and this is that"—thus [one perceives] permanence throughout the three times.
But for that which exists, there is merely modification.

He states that even the scriptural passage expressing the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "That" and "this"—namely, "That indeed is this"—is a proof for the non-perishability of the world.

He says: "This. To the question, "If the world existed even prior [to creation], how can its birth be spoken of?", he replies: "Of that which exists. Manifestation is a modification (*vikriyā*). The word "but" (*tu*) is used to state that there is no production of what is non-existent. || 74 ||
And whatever one desires from this [state], it arises from ignorance, desire, and action.
Even for one established in Brahman, the Śruti has proclaimed imperishability.
He states that the scriptural passage beginning with "Whatever [he desires] from this Self" is also proof for the non-destruction of the world. Regarding the phrase "whatever":
the connection is that the scripture—"whatever he desires from this Self, that he creates"—declares the non-destruction of ignorance and the rest, even though they reside within Brahman. || 75 ||
Destruction does not occur through the attainment of totality; therefore, desire and karma do not cease.
Therefore, because no means of valid cognition is possible, that which is stated is incorrect.

Since that non-destruction has been established, he states the resulting conclusion—that there is no destruction of desire and so forth through the combination of the sutra’s [teachings]: "Entirely," etc. [Vol. 3, page 28]. Prior to this...
[end of fragment]
[Brāhmaṇa 2] With the commentary known as *Śākhaprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri: 1161.

Since there is no evidence for the destruction of desire and so forth through the attainment of the Sūtra, it is argued that the statement regarding the destruction of the two bodies and so on is improper, as it would merely result in the fruit of the initial conjunction.
He concludes: "By means of valid cognition. || 76 ||
That which is heard of as the destruction of manifestation by way of its being of the nature of the cause;
We do not at all deny that such a cessation occurs even in deep sleep. || 77 ||

[Objection: But surely the non-destruction of the world is not tenable, because, being an effect, its destruction within its own cause is heard in scripture in the passage, "Whatever they depart from here, into that they all enter. To this, he says: "Of manifestation" (*vyaktatāyāḥ*). The meaning is that since the destruction of the effect within the cause is established even in the state of deep sleep (*svāpa*), the performance of the combined practice for that purpose would be useless. || 77 ||
The very birth of the thorough knowledge of the innermost reality serves as the cause for destruction.
The human goal arises from this duality; nothing other than this is desired. || 78 ||

How, then, is liberation attained in your view through the destruction of duality? To this he replies: "The inner self... Although the destruction of duality is brought about by knowledge, one might suspect that the attainment of Brahman is accomplished through ritual action; anticipating this, he says: "And the goal of man... For there is no means to liberation other than knowledge itself; ritual action is connected to it only by way of that [knowledge]. This is the meaning. || 78 ||
And likewise, for all ritual actions as well, [the rule is] "this very one."
The application [of this] has been demonstrated for the arising of the knowledge of the inner self. || 79 ||

He states the authority for its connection with liberation through the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). [The verse says] "that" (*tam*); that is to say, in accordance with the connection with the channels of the vital breaths (*prāṇāḍikā*). || 79 ||
The knot of the heart is severed, and all doubts are cut asunder.
And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.

Now, regarding the statement concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*), which asserts that action has a direct connection to liberation by way of being an auxiliary to knowledge, [the author] says: "Not so, because it would contradict other Śruti texts," and states: "It is split" (verse 80).
"By the exhaustion of the enjoyment [of results], there is the destruction of desirable and forbidden actions."
Even for the wise, there is no destruction of those undertakings already commenced, due to their prior awareness. || 81 ||

If one were to argue that since karma is destroyed by knowledge, even those actions whose effects have already begun would be destroyed, resulting in the impossibility of *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) and thus contradicting the Śruti and Smṛti, he addresses this objection with the principle "but the others [are exhausted] through experience, and then one attains [union]" (*bhogena tvitare kṣapayitvā sampadyate*), stating: "Through experience... (81).
"But for all karmas acquired throughout the entire course of existence,"
The destruction of those [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun occurs through the arising of perfect knowledge. || 82 ||

Anticipating the objection that knowledge would be useless because other past actions, like those already begun, cannot be revoked by knowledge, he says "until the end of worldly existence" (ābhavāt), according to the principle: "But only those prior [actions] whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed, for that is their limit. This means until the grasping of the present body. || 82 ||
1 kha. yādyanu | 2 kha. tatvajñānā' | 146 [Vol. 3, page 29]
1962 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]:
Just as there exists a means of knowledge for the destruction of karmas upon the arising of knowledge...
Through the attainment of totality, when [defilements] are destroyed, no such conceit regarding anything whatsoever is admitted. (83)

To the objection that just as karma is destroyed by knowledge, there would be no harm even if it were destroyed through the attainment of the *sūtra*, he says: "Upon the arising of knowledge... (verse 83).
Furthermore, ignorance is not the discerning [agent], because it is of the nature of darkness.
Therefore, she is appropriately called Ācchādikā, as she consists of all [the letters] both collectively and individually. || 84 ||

By the initial conjunction (*ādyasamuccaya*), the destruction of karma and so forth through the attainment of the Sūtra has been refuted. Now, regarding the claim that ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes the individual soul’s (*jīva*) limitation from the Supreme, he refutes the first alternative—namely, that this ignorance is either non-apprehension (*agraha*) or misapprehension (*anyathāgraha*)—by stating: "the limiter" (*paricchetrī*).
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the quality of being a coverer is well-known in the case of external darkness. || 84 ||
Nor is false cognition admitted to be determinative.
Does the cognition of blue determine space even in the slightest degree? 85.
He states the second [reason]: "And not... The meaning is: "The subject under dispute is not determinative, because it is false cognition, like that which is commonly accepted as such. ||85||
For the manifestor is indeed dependent on [the material cause], but it is not like a potter.
The determinative nature of cognition follows from its conformity with the object to be measured. (86)

He says "sato hi" (for [the cognition] of the existent) to show that even if it is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), its status as a determinative cognition (*paricchedaka*) does not suffer loss, just like right knowledge (*samyagdhī*).
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that although it manifests an object that is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), it does not manifest an object that is sublated (*bādhita*). Of that...

It clarifies its nature as a manifestor. But it is not [the case that it manifests itself], for he says: "Furthermore, the subject of dispute is not a determiner, because it does not conform to the means of knowledge, like the cognition of the sky-flower. Thus he says: "The means of knowledge" (meyeti). 86.
If it is argued that even ignorance conforms to the actual state of things, then [the following applies]:
If I am liberated, liberation shall always be mine; or bondage shall be mine in the opposite case. || 87 ||

He raises the objection that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), saying "As for example... [and so on]. Is its object of knowledge (*meya*) always liberated or always bound? Not the first, because if it were always liberated, there would be an absence of bondage, which leads to the consequence that the scripture (*śāstra*) need not be commenced. Nor the second, because if it were always bound, there would be no liberation, resulting in the aforementioned fault. Therefore, he says "liberated," [implying] that the reason is not unestablished. Furthermore, its bondage and liberation cannot be adventitious; for if bondage were a real entity (*vastu*), liberation would consist in its destruction.

The sense is that if [the object] were non-substantial due to its connection with yoga, then because the destruction of that [object] depends upon knowledge, if knowledge is constant, that very [knowledge] must conform to the real entity. || 87 ||
It could not be the material cause of that which is neither self nor belonging to a self.
For threads do not produce a jar here, because they lack identity with it. (88)

Furthermore, in your view, is Brahman or avidyā the material cause (upādāna) of the world? It is not the first [option], as he says: "Not the Self" (nātmā). The meaning is that because of non-identity (atādātmya)—that is, due to the contradiction between insentience (jaḍatva) and consciousness—identity (tādātmya) is impossible. He states: "For not... (na hi), implying that if causality were possible even without identity, then it would also exist between a thread and a jar. || 88 ||
1. Kha. and Ga. read *'dhitvaṃ pari*. 2. Kha. reads *yānu*. [Vol.
3, page 30] 2. Brāhmaṇa, together with the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri. 1163.
Ignorance belongs to the Supreme Self by its very nature, while desire and action reside externally.
This very thing has been stated by you yourself upon the arrival of ignorance. || 89 ||

In the second [verse], he states the contradiction with his own accepted position. Regarding the phrase "from the Supreme Self" (*parātmanaḥ*): Bhartṛprapañca himself asserts that ignorance (*avidyā*) arises from the Supreme Self by its own nature, like saline soil (*ūṣara*) from the earth; whereas desire (*kāma*) and action (*karman*), along with their latent impressions (*savāsana*), arise in each subsequent stage from the force of desire and so forth in each preceding stage within the Inner Self (*pratīci*), and are not produced by ignorance. Therefore, the claim that ignorance is the material cause (*upādāna*) of desire, action, and the world consisting of ignorance is contradicted by his own statement.
The meaning is "it is established. || 89 ||
Nor can desire and action [operate] when ignorance is non-existent.
Therefore, it is impossible to create clay, elephants, horses, and so forth without a cause, just as [it is impossible to create them from nothing]. || 90 ||
As for the claim that "if desire and action remain, they produce [the world] even though ignorance has been destroyed," he says: "Not so.

The phrase "being non-existent" is stated as the reason. He states another reason for the non-arising of ignorance: "That," meaning that just as prepared clay produces artificial things such as elephants and the like, desire and action do not produce ignorance in that way, because ignorance lacks a cause, just like the Self.
Such is the meaning. || 90 ||
Furthermore, even in the world, a cause does not produce that which is absolutely non-existent.
Even with a keen glance at the earth, the lotus-born [Brahmā] did not appear from the sky.

Fearing that the reason [stated] for desire and action being the causes [of ignorance] might be unestablished, he says: "Not so. Even if it exists, a cause does not produce ignorance, because that which has been destroyed is in every way non-existent; for in the world, no cause is seen to be the producer of the non-existent.
He provides an example for the principle that a cause is not the producer of the non-existent: "As in the case of dancing," etc. (91).
If Brahman alone is considered the cause of birth through ignorance, [then...]
While that exists, how could there be the total eradication of ignorance? (92)

Now, one might raise the objection: "If Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), just as the earth is for a lotus-pond, and desire and so forth are its efficient cause (*nimitta*), like rain, then how can it be said that ignorance lacks a cause? To this he says: "Brahman... [Verse 92]. He then states: "In that case, since Brahman exists, there would be no absolute destruction of ignorance, and thus there would be no liberation. Thus he says: "In that... [Verse 92].
If there were an absolute eradication of delusion regarding its cause, [then liberation would occur].
Tell me, while this perishable thing already exists by its own nature, what is the use of means? 93.

Having restated the opposing view, he states the fault: "If it were absolute" (*ātyantikī*). The meaning is that if delusion (*moha*) were absolutely severed while its cause still exists, then, because it would be subject to destruction by its own nature, it would be illogical for it to require a separate destroyer; consequently, the practice of means aimed at destroying *saṃsāra* along with its causes would be rendered futile. || 93 ||
And desire and karma are not able to protect these [beings] from ignorance, even by means of Śakra.
But how can you two possibly make that which exists become destroyed? || 94 ||

Having refuted that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of Brahman, he states another reason for refuting that desire (*kāma*) and so forth are its instrumental cause (*nimitta*): "If not," [verse 94].
1164 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]: Even when desire, action, and so forth have been abandoned, if ignorance (*avidyā*) remains...
If that were the case, it would contradict the explanation of the statement "not so. (95)

He restates the objection that, due to the initial conjunction [of means], there is no destruction of ignorance even when desire and the like are destroyed, with the words "kāma" (desire), etc. The result of the initial conjunction is either the destruction of desire and the like through contact with their cause, or their absolute destruction without a trace. It is not the first, because that would apply even during deep sleep, rendering the practice of the means futile; nor is it the second, because as long as ignorance exists, such [absolute] destruction is impossible. And let it not be argued that [the means] should simply not lead to ultimate [destruction].
Intending to show that [the view] beginning with "desire" (kāma) is ruined because it contradicts your own explanation, he says: "Not so," and so forth. || 91 ||
The first word, "not this," effects the negation of both the formed and the formless.
The second [position] is "no," which serves as a negation of cultivation (bhāvanā).

He restates that [opponent's] explanation in order to state the contradiction: "No. The meaning of the word "then" (atha) is that when the category of material objects and so forth is negated, the category of cultivation alone remains as the object to be negated. || 96 ||
That which remains when the specific qualities such as cultivation and so forth have become tranquil.
That supreme Brahman is partless; it is taught as "not this, not this."

Having stated the meaning of the individual words (*padārtha*), he states the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*): "The creative urge" (*bhāvanā*). Thus, the sense is that if there were no absolute destruction of desire and so forth, there would be a contradiction with the explanation of the "Instruction" (*ādeśa*) given by others in the *Mūrtāmūrta-brāhmaṇa*. || 97 ||
Brahman has been known exactly as it is, and darkness has not departed from him.
This shall be consistent through the grace of Jātavedas (Fire). || 98 ||

Anticipating the objection that even when desire and the like are absolutely destroyed by the knowledge arising from the instructional sentence (ādeśavākya), the Supreme Self must still be meditated upon because a residue of ignorance remains in order to destroy that [residue], he says: "It is known" (jñātam). || 98 ||
And what kind of purification of the dualistic object is intended here?
There is either non-connection with non-duality, or destruction, as in the case of the purification of impurity. || 99 ||

And since non-duality cannot be perceived as long as the reality of duality remains unpurified, [the author] here analyzes the purification of the reality of duality, beginning with the words "Duality...
The word "here" refers to the statement in the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca. || 99 ||
When both the whole and the parts are perceived, non-duality and duality are not separate.
Because of their identity, [the destruction of one] is not logically tenable, nor is such destruction admitted.
When all duality has perished, there can be no perception of things as either whole or parts.

He refutes the first [position], that purity is the non-connection of duality with non-duality, with the words "samasta... (the whole, etc.). In this view—that a single reality consists of both the whole and the parts—duality is not an entirely different entity from non-duality, because the two are mutually intermingled; therefore, there is no establishment of their lack of connection. He rejects the second [position], that purity is the destruction of duality like the removal of impurity, with the words "nāpi" (nor also), as it is not accepted...
The cause for [the state of] being made is "destroyed. || 100 || 101 ||
1. Kha. Its non-connection; 2. Ka. It is stated that it is not so.
[Vol.
3, page 32] Brāhmaṇa 2, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1165.
How can two things that are mutually contradictory, like cold and heat, [exist together]?
In one place, there would be a co-inherence (samavāya) of both the collective and the individual properties. || 102 ||
Having accepted that the single reality is both "the whole" and "the parts," it was previously maintained that the purification of duality serves as the cause for non-dual knowledge;
now, however, he refutes this by stating that it is improper for a single thing to be both the whole and the parts, beginning with the verse starting "cold... (102).
While the Vedic statements concerning the *apūrva* and so forth remain extant, it is possible [to establish their meaning].
Nor can even the Lord describe the nature of the Self as being either identical with or distinct from it.
And because it would contradict scripture, he states that there is no single [principle] that is both collective and distributive: "In the case of the apūrva and so forth," etc. (103).
And there is no perception [of the self] like that of a jar and so forth, because [the self] is non-different [from consciousness].
There would follow the consequence of non-selfhood [of the seer] due to the non-difference between the seer and the seen. || 104 ||
Furthermore, regarding the claim that the Self exists both as a whole and as its parts, there is no proof—neither perception, scripture, nor inference—to support it.

He states this with the words "And not... Just as a jar or other object is perceived as manifold through its general and particular aspects, such is not the case for the Self; for the Self is non-different from everything because it is the inner witness (pratyak) of all. Since anything extracted from the inner witness would be devoid of essential nature, perception cannot grasp multiplicity within that single-flavored (ekarasa) reality.

The meaning is that perception exists. Anticipating the objection that the Self cannot possess oneness because the distinction between the seer and the seen is accepted, he says: "Because it is nameless," etc. (104).
If it were not so, the perception of the individual parts would be subsumed by the perception of the whole alone.
Otherwise, the scriptural statement "in the self" would result in being invalid. || 105 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "If not," stating that scripture does not provide knowledge of the Self as being either identical or distinct; rather, it is contrary [to such a view]. || 101 ||
"By what means is the unheard heard?"—to this question, there is the following statement: "In what [manner]?"
Such [a position] would be utterly contradictory, and there is no other means of valid cognition here either. (106)

He states that there is not only a contradiction with the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* regarding the view of the whole and the parts taken together and separately, but also a contradiction with the *Chāndogya* and the *Atharvaṇa*.

[He says] "By which," etc. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the collection of scriptural passages teaching uniformity (*ekarasya*) is included. The ellipsis is: "the view of the whole and the parts is contradictory. He replies to the third [objection] with "And not," etc. For there is no means of valid knowledge, such as inference, that establishes its being both the whole and the parts.
The meaning is that [inference] is not applicable because of the absence of a probans (liṅga) and so forth that would be pervaded by that [object]. || 106 ||
When both the whole and its parts are examined, nothing at all is perceived.
Because they have exclusively ignorance as their cause, like the perception of a rope-snake and so forth. || 107 ||

He concludes the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the opponent's view with the words "samasta... (all...). The ellipsis to be supplied is "not even a slight means of valid cognition.

Since the opponent's view lacks a foundation in a means of valid cognition, it is caused by the ignorance of the undivided reality; thus he states the result—that it is rooted in an error dependent upon that [ignorance]—with the words "pūrṇa... (complete...). 107.
1 ka. ‘And Vyāsa [is the authority] regarding non-perception. 2 kha. ‘Or Vyāsa’s perception.
[Vol. 3, page 33] 1966 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Adhyāya—]
He would have to grasp all atoms individually and without exception.
He who does not perceive all these various dualities as being one within each [individual]— || 108 ||

Furthermore, as for the multiplicity of the self being stated [in scripture] either as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) or an object of meditation (*dhyeya*), it cannot be the former; for it would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of a non-omniscient person possessing knowledge whose objects are all the various distinctions of duality. Thus he says: "The atoms... (108).
And among all the various forms of duality that are perceived by anyone, [there is no such thing].
If that were the case, its infinity and its nature as Brahman would be impossible to establish.

He states the second [objection]: "In all [cases]," etc. For that meditation belongs to one who possesses that knowledge; and it has been stated that a partial aspect cannot be known in its entirety by one who is not omniscient. Or, even if there were cognition of the partial aspects of the whole, nevertheless, if all dualistic distinctions were subsumed under a single essence, there would be no infinity of the reality (vastu).

Likewise, due to the absence of limitation, the state of being Brahman is not logical; since Brahman is the unsurpassed Great, it cannot exist as the Self in either a collective or distributive sense even as an object of meditation—this is the meaning. || 109 ||
Just as phenomena such as blue and so forth are perceived through the view of substantiality.
In the same way, various non-selves are perceived through the view of a self, because of contradiction. || 110 ||

He states another reason for the impossibility of both positions being true: "Substance," etc. Just as there is no contradiction between the perception of blue and the like and the perception of the lotus and the like, such that by perceiving the lotus and so forth, one perceives blue and the like as being identical with it; in the same way, the non-self cannot be perceived as identical with the self through the perception of the self, because there is a mutual contradiction between those two and their respective perceptions. This is the meaning. || 110 ||
And likewise, in this case, the scriptural statement "turning away" would constitute a contradiction.
He has clearly demonstrated to us the distinct views regarding the self and the non-self. || 111 ||
He establishes the contradiction with scripture [by the words] "And thus" (tathāca). The word "here" (iha) refers to the statement in the Kaṭhaka Upaniṣad. || 111 ||
When it is stated, "The Self, indeed, is this 'ara'," there is no injunction for the perception of the non-Self.
Having merely restated [the self] as it is already established, the view of the self is enjoined. || 112 ||

In the passage concerning "that which is to be seen," the perception of the Self—both collectively and individually—is enjoined. Anticipating the objection that, because of such an injunction, the Self must be accepted as manifold either as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) or as an object of meditation (*dhyeya*), he says: "The Self. Here, the injunction itself has already been refuted; even if it were admitted, the meaning is that such an injunction does not exist regarding the perception of a manifold Self. To the question, "What then is enjoined here? he replies: "Having restated... This...

The meaning is that, by first restating the duality established in the world through the words "Brahman" and so forth, and then declaring its non-existence apart from this Self with the words "that which is this Self," the fitness of the Self for being perceived is here stated. 112. Furthermore, wherever an injunction is observed, in each such case, the Self is the object [of that action].
By means of the teaching that the entire [universe] is not the Self, the vision of the inner Self (pratyagdṛṣṭi) is enjoined. || 113 ||

Anticipating the objection that there is an injunction regarding the perception of the whole and the parts in passages such as "This is its self-nature" (*aitadātmyam*), he says: "Where... [The commentary notes: *ātmatvena* (as the Self) in manuscript *ka*;
*katvena* in manuscript *kha*; *stutaḥ* (praised) in manuscript *kha*.
End of page 34, volume 3.]

Wherever in the region of the Vedic scriptures there exists a subject matter and a method of instruction, in each such instance, this knowledge of the Self is produced through the means of hearing and so forth by way of restating all that is non-Self; the meaning is that there is no injunction regarding the perception of the non-Self. || 113 ||
The knowledge of the relationship between the probandum and the probans does not arise from anything other than scriptural revelation.
In other objects, however, [this is established] through means of valid cognition such as direct perception. || 114 ||

Having stated that "the vision of the inward Self is enjoined," one might suspect that, like ritual injunctions (*karmavākya*), the Brahman-injunctions (*brahmavākya*) are also intended to be centered on *niyoga* (an obligatory mandate). Anticipating this, he refutes the analogy with the words beginning "sādhyā" [in the original verse]. Even a ritual injunction is not centered on *niyoga*, because the relationship [of the suffix] *liṅ* and so forth is not grasped when that [mandate] is unknown; rather, since the knowledge of the relationship between the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) is not obtained from the Veda through any other source, that very [knowledge] is dependent upon the sentence.

The meaning is "namely. [An objection is raised: Since the cognition of the relationship between the means and the end depends upon perception and other means of knowledge, how can there be no attainment [of that relationship] from any other source? To this, he says: "In the case of others than that" (*tadanyeṣu*). The very nature of the sacrifice and so forth, which is distinct from the relationship, is what is cognized through perception and the rest; however, the fact that it possesses the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) and so on—which is mentioned in reference to that nature—is cognizable solely through scripture (*āgama*). Therefore, the cognition of the relationship is not produced by another means of knowledge. Similarly, in reference to the non-Self (*anātman*), only the Self (*ātman*) itself is made known.
The intended meaning is "by the word of Brahmā. || 114 ||
Therefore, the scripture [teaches] the realization of the Self as that which transcends all measures.
It is honored as a causal sign (nimitta), like the statement made by one who has awakened from deep sleep. || 115 ||

Raising the objection that since the Self itself is not an object of any means of knowledge, it is impossible to grasp its relationship [with words] just as one does with a *niyoga* (an injunction), and therefore how could it be the meaning of the scripture?—it is established that a word, having its relationship perceived in a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), makes known the attributeless Self through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, [the following is stated]: *vāmam...* [etc.]

He says: "All," etc. The connection is that scripture (*śruti*) is the authority regarding realization. Having raised the objection—how can there be authority for that [scripture] with respect to the Self, which is self-luminous and the fruit [of knowledge]—he says: "Therefore," etc. The meaning is that scripture becomes an authority regarding the reality whose nature is existence (*sadrūpa-vastu*) by being the cause for the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna-nivṛtti*) through the knowledge produced [by it]. Thus, the validity of the statement lies in its function as a remover [of ignorance].
He states an illustration: "In deep sleep," etc. (115).
Even the instruction of the mother has been presented so that it may not be contradicted here.
Likewise, we shall explain the *Sarvabhadra* in the subsequent section; therefore, may this [conclusion] be auspicious.

It has been stated that seeing [the Self] both collectively and individually is neither authoritative nor purposeful; now, in response to the claim by others that the Vedic injunction beginning with "vidyāṃ ca" (knowledge and...

prescribes the combined application (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action—which have different functions but a single goal—the author says: "The mantra... Here, the phrase "in this world" refers to the position that the reality is of a single essence (*ekarasa*). Since a plurality of the reality is impossible due to the impossibility of combination, that reality is of a single essence, and [liberation] comes from the knowledge of it alone.
With the words "Kaivalya" (isolation), he concludes the excellence of his own doctrine: "All... (116).
Two types of knowledge have been proclaimed, distinguished by the categories of higher and lower.
In this context, knowledge and ignorance are said to terminate in the state of darkness.
Although the meaning of the mantra beginning with "vidyāṃ ca" will be explained later, he states it here in brief for the sake of ease of understanding: "The higher," etc.

Regarding the statement, "Two kinds of knowledge are to be known: the higher and the lower," those two knowledges which were mentioned as being distinguished by the categories of higher and lower—[the text says] "vidyām" (knowledge).
(Note: The manuscript reading "panokti" is noted in the source.)
In the passage "nescience and knowledge" (*avidyāṃ ca vidyāṃ ca*), the terms *vidyā* and *avidyā* denote knowledge and action respectively; for action culminates in darkness (*tamas*).
[Vol. 3, p. 35] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Third Chapter. 2168.
In the phrase "nescience and knowledge," the words *vidyā* and *avidyā* refer to knowledge and action, because action ends in darkness.

The meaning is that because knowledge possesses the fitness for the term "knowledge" (vidyā), it is so called due to its determination of the reality of things and its suitability for the word "knowledge. || 117 ||
"Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for attaining the highest good for a Brahmin."
Through austerity one destroys impurity; through knowledge one attains immortality.
Having explained the meaning of "knowledge and ignorance," he demonstrates the meaning of the word *saha* (together) and the meaning of the second half of the verse by means of Manu’s statement:
"Austerity... The meaning of the first half of the verse is the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action as means and end, which is the sense of *saha*.

The meaning of the second half of the mantra is that through action there is the destruction of the sins that obstruct knowledge; thereafter, by means of fully matured knowledge, one attains liberation (*nirvāṇa*).
This very thing is what is meant by "austerity. || 118 ||
Cognition, in which the distinctions of the internal organ and so forth have been destroyed, partakes of oneness alone.
How could an insentient being engage in an injunction such as "it should be seen"? 119.

The meaning of the mantra to be explained hereafter is summarized by both Śruti and Smṛti. Regarding the point that one who is in the intermediate state is qualified for the practice of seeing the Self, he says: "Dhvasta... (verse 119).
Such refutations as these have already been stated against those whose minds are corrupted by faults.

"In 'the Self alone'—this very point is not stated again here" (verse 120). Anticipating the objection that this is a tautology because the opposing view has already been refuted in the passage beginning with "the Self alone," he says: "and so forth. This refers to those by whom the Self has been defiled—meaning those who have defiled it both collectively and individually through its various aspects. [The word] *kalu-*...

Or, [the phrase] "pitadhiyām" may mean: the collection of faults mentioned here is not being referred to by the word "iti," for that was not stated there; however, as for the refutation of them which was stated right there under the term "ādi" (and so forth), that is not stated here. Thus, the meaning is that there is no tautology. || 120 ||
This commentary, whose meaning is perfectly clear, has no need for a sub-commentary.
Therefore, let the remaining meaning here be understood from the very words of the Commentary itself. || 121 ||

Having introduced the commentary beginning with "Now it must be stated therein" regarding the refutations of the opponent's positions—which were raised by them as their own faults while remaining unrecognized as such—the author says: "Suvispaṣṭa" (very clear). The meaning of the remainder is that the rest is the [remaining] refutation.
Up to this point, there has been the statement refuting the position of Bhartṛprapañca. || 121 ||
By what means is there bondage, consisting of the graspers and the over-graspers, which is brought about by that?
He spoke thus, "O Yājñavalkya," in order to determine the motivating cause.

Having concluded the investigation (*vicāra*) and connecting it with the exposition of the scripture (*śruti*), he introduces the passage beginning with "where" (*yatra*) by way of fulfilling the expectancy [of the reader]. He says:
"The word *graha*. This particle (*nipāta*) indicates the necessity of determining the causal agent (*prayojaka*). || 122 ||
On the basis of the mark consisting in being the substratum of karma, it is the ignorant person who is understood here.
And because the original case-ending is replaced by the adoption of another case-ending. || 123 ||

In this regard, having raised the objection that the word "person" (*puruṣa*) refers to the knower because of its proximity to him in the immediately following sentence, he states that proximity is set aside by an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
He says: "Action" (*karman*). Although it will be stated later that this [person] is the substratum of action, and that indicative mark is stronger than proximity—[as stated in Vol.
3, page 36].

Anticipating the objection that the word "person" (puruṣa) will refer to the proximate knower because of the use of the pronoun "his" (asya), [the author] states: "Because of the difference in case-endings between 'this' (ayam) and 'his' (asya), the use of the pronoun does not have a proximate referent; rather, like the injunction 'that which belongs to Agni' (yad āgneyaḥ), it refers only to the well-known non-knower. This is the intended meaning.
He said: "Of the one under discussion. || 123 ||
Where, for this ignorant man who has died due to the exhaustion of his lifespan—
Speech returns to its own source, and the vital breath follows after the wind.

Having explained the meaning of the word *puruṣa*, he connects it with the passage beginning with "where" (*yatra*). Regarding "where": the connection with what follows is, "at that time, what does this *puruṣa* become? || 124 ||
Those portions of deities such as Agni and others which have been acquired through karma for the sake of experience.
These very things are denoted here by words such as "speech" and so forth, and they are not products of a person.

One might raise the objection that because speech and the other organs do not dissolve for the ignorant person—based on the reasoning of "speech [merges] into mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6) and so forth—and because scripture here refers to the wise person alone, as seen in passages such as "the fifteen parts of his dissolve" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.7), it follows that this applies only to the knower; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Agni, etc.

The sense is that the entities consisting of the instruments, denoted by words such as "speech," do not exist when presided over by the person as the enjoyer—the word "only" (eva) being used to exclude this possibility.
He states the meaning [of this] with "No" (na). || 125 ||
Upon the exhaustion of the individual's karma, they withdraw their respective portions according to their due.
This is stated to be the withdrawal (upasaṃhāra) of the deities beginning with Agni.

Let the portions (aṃśa) beginning with Agni be expressed by the words "speech" and so forth; for they too have karma acquired for the sake of experience, and thus there exist karmas for that purpose. How then is their dissolution? Who is the agent of that dissolution? And what is the dissolution of those portions which are non-different from the possessor of the portions (aṃśin)? To this he says: "Of the person... (puṃsaḥ).
Thus [ends the verse]. 126.
Furthermore, the deities reside within the various locations of the human body.
Each deposits its own portion for the successful accomplishment of the experience of its respective karma.

Anticipating the objection that, upon the fall of the present body, if the presiding deities were withdrawn, then the sense organs would be devoid of their presiding deities in the assumption of another body and thus could not serve as instruments for experience, he says: "Of the person" (puṃsaḥ). || 127 ||
"Let us dwell here in the space within the heart," so it is said, because [the self] dissolves into space.
Because the self consisting of consciousness is applicable as the subject matter of the question. || 128 ||

Having explained the meaning of the words "speech" and so forth, he now states the meaning of the word "Self" (*ātman*) in the passage "The Self is space" (*ākāśa ātmā*). He says: "In the heart. He provides the reason for using the word "Self" to denote the space within the heart (*hārdākāśa*), setting aside the primary (transcendent) Self: "Because of space," etc. The meaning is that, according to scriptural testimony, the primary Self merges into the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*); however, since the primary Self is not of the same nature as that [elemental] space, such a merging is impossible for it. Furthermore, [the space within the heart is intended] because it is the object of the question, "Where is this? (*kvāyaṃ*)...
He says that because it arises from yoga with the Self, the word "Self" does not apply to that [mind] here; this refers to the question. || 128 ||
For they are devoid of a presiding controller, like tools that have been laid down.
The instruments, such as speech and the rest, are not sufficient for the accomplishment of the enjoyment of the person. (129) [Note:
1. kha. *karmanirvartitā*] (147)
1170 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:

Even upon the departure of the gross body, because the individual soul (*jīva*) continues to rely on the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*) prior to liberation, the question "Where is this [soul]? is untenable. Thus it is said—

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The presiding [deity]. Although the *jīva* is dependent upon the subtle body (*liṅga*), nevertheless, in the absence of the gross body, that [subtle body] would not grant experience if deprived of its presider; therefore, since even though existing, it is equivalent to non-existent, it is logical that the Lord is the substratum for the cause of experience.
This means that even if a conscious presider exists, the subtle body has no utility for experience without the gross body.
This is the meaning of the word "hi. || 129 ||
"This person is the deity of Videha; such is his function."
He asked that best of sages, "What is the support of this person? (130)
Having introduced the interrogative statement, he explains it: "videha" [means] "this one"; "ayam" (this) is explained by "eṣa" (he). || 130 ||
Does it attain the nature of the cause, or rather, does it exist by means of some other nature?
Does he simply remain as he is, or has he taken refuge in action itself? || 131 ||
Whether it be the qualities, or Īśāna, or Time, or indeed Destiny;
Let it be stated whether [the world] is accidental, a continuous stream, empty, or subject to destruction. || 132 ||

He elaborates on the question itself with the words beginning "What? [and so forth]. Those of our own school who maintain that the individual soul (*jīva*) is also an effect state that it assumes the nature of the causal form characterized by objective ignorance (*avidyā*) along with its reflection, once it has abandoned the gross body.

Others, however, say that when the gross body is discarded, due to the absence of any obstruction, the soul remains in its own uncommon, essential nature; thus, this one "state of supreme serenity" (*saṃprasāda*)—from this [body]...

The meaning is that this is based on scriptural passages such as "from his body," and so forth. He states the views of the Mīmāṃsakas, Sāṃkhyas, and Tārkikas with the words "Or rather. He describes the method of the *Jyotirvids* (astronomers) with the words "Or time. He expresses the intention of the *Devatākāṇḍa* (the section on deities) with the word "Divine. He states the views of the Lokāyatikas, Yogācāras, and Mādhyamikas with the words "Chance," and so forth. [He speaks of] the destruction of the soul (*jīva*) which previously existed, without...

"He goes as one who is praised"—this states another opinion held by those who maintain that [the self] performs the functions of a living being. "Destruction"—this concludes the question by stating that which is intended to be expressed in the aforementioned sections: "Let it be so stated. || 131 || 132 ||
Pleased by the inquiry, the Ṛṣi took her hand.
He was astonished that [the other] had asked a question not shared by anyone else. || 133 ||

He states the meaning of "bring it," etc., with the words "by means of a question. "Cultivated" (bhāvita) means "brought under control" (vaśīkṛta). Having stated the satisfaction as the reason for taking her hand, he states another reason with the words "any [reason]. || 133 ||
He said "only we two" for the purpose of establishing exclusivity.
Furthermore, the concealment of knowledge is observed many times even in the Śruti. || 134 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "the two of us" (*āvām*) as follows: "By the term 'uncommon' (*asādhāraṇya*)," which means that the knowledge of the meaning of the question and the answer must reside in the questioner and the respondent alone. Therefore, the meaning is "after the taking of the hand in marriage. For what purpose is this knowledge uncommon? Indeed, it is not something to be hidden, as there is no evidence for such a requirement; thus he says: "Knowledge" (*vidyā*). "Knowledge indeed approached the Brahmin, saying to him—" *Note: The final sentence is an excerpt from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (11.5.3.1).*
1 1 ka. kha. ...ṃttamaḥ || 130 || 2 kha. explains.
[Vol. 3, page 38]

"I am he; protect me. Do not give me to one who is unworthy or to one who is arrogant. Guard me, for I am superior to you. Let me not die along with your knowledge, nor let it wither away in barren soil. [He who is] a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), a giver of wealth, wise, learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), and beloved—"
"The one who proclaims knowledge as knowledge—these six are my sacred fords (tīrthas)," so says the Śruti.

The son of the teacher, one who is desirous of learning, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, capable, a donor of wealth, a seeker of wealth, one's own kinsman, and a virtuous person— these should be taught according to the prescribed dharma.
A knower of Brahman should die together with his knowledge at his own will;
even in the midst of terrible calamity, he must never sow it in barren soil.
"Knowledge, approaching a Brahmin, said: 'I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to one who is envious; thus may I become most powerful.
This is also the meaning of the Smṛti. 134.
Our very consciousness was exactly as it was before this [moment].
The two of us alone shall likewise know [the truth] hereafter, exactly as it has been declared.

He connects the words of the sentence beginning with "āvām" (we two). Regarding "of us two": the phrase "this cognition" refers to the object of the instigator; the meaning is that it is the aforementioned nature of this cognition belonging to the instigator. || 135 ||
While this question was being explained by you in the presence of people.
"This purpose stated by us two would certainly not be accomplished.

[The author] states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the verse beginning with "not [in] 'na'": "In a place with people" (*sajane*). This means that if your commentary were being explained in this region filled with a multitude of various people, the knowledge that serves as the basis for our bond would not be exclusive to us two; therefore, one must depart from the company of people.
This is the meaning. || 136 ||
But Yājñavalkya did not say this out of fear of being outwitted by another's speech.
In debate, since no one speaks other than the proponent himself, [the opponent's position is not established]. || 137 ||

He speaks [the following] out of the apprehension that, for the sake of making the knowledge of the prompter unique, there might be no exit from it, but others too might ask questions in the midst of it, and thus a definitive conclusion would be impossible; hence he says: "But not so. The word "this" refers to the statement of the subject matter at hand. He states the reason why there is no fear caused by the questioning of others: "In debate (jalpa)," for one who desires victory is the one qualified for that.
It is said: "With one who desires victory, there are *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*. Thus, the meaning is that until his power has been determined, one does not engage in other [debates]. || 137 ||
He answered even the remaining questions, skipping over them in due order.
Because it comes from a virtuous person, there can be no cause for fear regarding this indirect speech (anyokti). || 138 ||
He states another reason for his departure from virtuous people—not out of fear of indirect speech (*anyokti*)—in the verse beginning with "pariśiṣṭān" (those remaining). [Variant readings:
1. *vaped*; 2. *yā vi*].
Regarding the statement that the Ṛṣi, having departed from there and gone out, explained the question of Ārtabhāga—that was not due to a fear of speaking otherwise;

for, having returned to that very same place, he explained to him the remaining questions of Bhujyu and others. Therefore, his departure outward was not caused by fear, as he possessed the knowledge [to answer them].

Going [to the assembly] was desired solely for the purpose of maintaining [the teaching]; otherwise, having departed from that place, he would not have answered the remaining questions, yet he does answer them. Therefore, the meaning is that his departure was not caused by fear of being outshone by another's speech. || 138 ||
Judging that this was excellent, they departed from the company of virtuous people.
Then Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga, having stepped aside, conversed together.
He states the meaning of "therefore" (*hetoḥ*) and so forth: "It is well," [verse 139].
Then, having departed from that virtuous person, they spoke thus to one another there.
The Śruti has declared all of that out of a desire to do what is pleasing to us.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Those two, when... as follows: "From that place" (*sajanāt*). The meaning of the word *atha* (then) is the immediate succession to the desire to favor the listeners.

The word "there" (*tatra*) indicates a secluded place. The point is that the statement beginning with "those two, having departed" is not the speech of either the questioner or the speaker, but rather belongs to the *Śruti* for the purpose of favoring the listener. || 140 ||
Because it is dependent upon karma and other factors, this [self] is not accepted as its own substratum.
Because it abides on the plane of saṃsāra, the self is not dependent upon a cause. || 141 ||

In order to purify his own position, he refutes the view held by some that [the self] becomes the cause through its own nature, and so forth, with the words "karmādi" (action, etc.). Regarding the claim that it "attains the state of being the cause," he replies with the word "saṃsāra" (transmigration). The meaning is that because it resides on the planes of experience, it is the enjoyer. || 141 ||
Because it is insentient, Pradhāna and the like are not accepted as the locus of the Person (puruṣa).
It does not know the action nor its fruit, nor does it have any connection with anyone. || 142 ||

Regarding the views that it is the qualities (*guṇas*), time, or destiny alone [that act as the cause], he says: "Because of its insentience" (*acitkatvāt*). The meaning is that the insentient cannot, by its own independence, serve as the locus of experience for an enjoyer. Regarding the view that it is karma itself that is relied upon, he says: "Not karma. Furthermore, karma does not even understand the relationship between the fruit and the one who possesses the fruit—namely, whose this fruit is—therefore, it cannot be the substratum [of the self].

He says "no" regarding the one who enjoys [the fruit]. Alternatively, suspecting that Hiraṇyagarbha, the knower of the fruits of karma, might be the locus of the enjoyer, he says "no. The sense is that there is no evidence for the claim that the disembodied deity—the individual soul (jīva)—attains another body by depending upon the *sūtra* (the subtle body). || 142 ||
Nor can it reside in Īśvara, because that would entail the futility of composing the treatise.
If that were the case, there would be the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done. (143)

Regarding the objection that "if [the Lord] were the controller," he replies: "Not so. The meaning is that if the Lord were the cause of bondage, then since heaven and liberation would be dependent upon him, and since he is independent, the scripture—which would otherwise be useless—would not be commenced. In that very case, a fault must be considered;
here, however, a merit is to be reflected upon.
1. Having approached the region. 2. But. 3. *vakyiṃ*. 4. Whose? [Vol.
3, page 40] 2. Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1173.

He states the subsequent point: "Having been created," etc. The meaning is that since the enjoyer would have the Lord as his substratum, the accomplishment of enjoyment would occur solely by His power; thus, the two faults are unavoidable. || 143 ||
This [world] is indeed presided over by destiny, following the power of karma and time.
If it is argued that the person continues to exist, even this is not tenable.
The previously mentioned fault, namely "due to insentience," also exists here. || 144 ||

He raises the objection that the enjoyer, presided over by Īśvara and governed by time and karma, transmigrates for the sake of his welfare; therefore, there is no loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāni*) and so forth. [The author replies: "By destiny" (*daiva*). Having raised the alternatives—whether these two (time and karma) alone, or both together with destiny, or whether they are supported by Īśvara and Pradhāna—he refutes the first: "Not so. Even though deities such as Agni possess consciousness, they lack independence; therefore, time and the rest associated with them cannot be the substratum of the enjoyer.
The meaning is "you. || 144 ||
If it is thought that the previously mentioned [argument] is valid along with the gods, || 145 ||
Activity or non-activity always proceeds from the sovereign power of the deity.
1. Because the cause for restriction does not exist, there would be no restricted state. || 146 ||

He restates the second [position]: "sadevatākam" (accompanied by a deity). The meaning is that the two—namely, time and what is called karma—together with deities such as Agni and others, are capable of impelling a person toward activity when the Lord is the primary factor. He provides the answer to the objection of over-extension: "pravṛttiḥ" (activity). The word "deity" refers to the Lord. Why is there not a fixed rule—that activity occurs at one time and cessation at another—even if His sovereignty is admitted?
Therefore, he says: "The restriction. || 145 || 146 ||
Nor, moreover, would action alone be the support for a person, since—
It has been previously stated that [the opponent's position] is corrupted by the defects of insentience and impermanence. || 147 ||
Fearing that karma and the like might not be the primary cause of the Lord, but rather the sole motivator, he recalls what was stated in the verse "Not karma" (2.3.40): "And not... (147).
"I must follow him, for he has become my creator."
How can there be knowledge of objects such as time with respect to an action that is perishable? (148)
And with the words "nor of anyone," etc., he clarifies another reason stated [by him] with the word "by me. || 148 ||
Since this is so, therefore all [factors] such as time, fate, and the Lord, etc., [are subordinate].
For men, action is paramount; this [body] is the unsurpassed support. || 149 ||

Anticipating the objection—how can that [cause] be determined if neither the individual nor the collective [factors] are capable of being the motivator—he states his own view with the words "yataḥ" (since). || 149 ||
"Chance, necessity, and destiny have not been accepted as the causes."
Furthermore, because there is no stability in the continuum, it cannot be established by valid means of knowledge that [the body] is the substratum.
1 kha. ...from the substratum, there is connection. 2 ka. ...not of the isolated one.
[Vol. 3, page 41] 1174 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Adhyāya]...

Anticipating the objection—"How can one's own position be established when the positions of chance (*yadṛcchā*), continuity (*saṃtati*), and emptiness (*śūnya*) remain unrefuted?"—he addresses the position of chance with the word "Haṭha" (Force). The meaning is that these words denote "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), and that [nature] is not a motivator, because it would render the employment of fixed causes and materials purposeless. He addresses the Yogācāra with the words "And in the continuity" (*saṃtatau ca*). For the continuum of cognition (*jñāna-saṃtāna*) is not the cause of bondage, as there is no proof for it.
The meaning is that because it is non-substantial (avastu), its persistence (sthiti) is untenable. || 110 ||
Karma is not possible in the preceding aggregates because they have already perished.
And in this case, there could be no transformation upon the connection with the subsequent aggregates.

If it is argued that even though the aggregate of cognition (*jñānaskandha*) is momentary, it must be the instigator of action because it is a real entity (*vastu*), we respond as follows: Is that action supported by a substratum (*sāśraya*) or without a substratum (*nirāśraya*)? In the first case, does it reside in a momentary aggregate as its support, or in some other stable support? Regarding the first alternative, one must choose between whether the action resides in the preceding aggregates or in the succeeding aggregates within the series of present aggregates existing in temporal succession. He refutes the first of these with the words: "Not action... (*na karma*).

For present karma is not established in the aggregates (*skandhas*) that precede the abandonment of the body, because those [past aggregates] have perished and thus cannot serve as a basis; this is the meaning. He addresses the second [position] with "Nor... [i.e., *na ca*]. If karma were to be connected by being supported in the subsequent aggregates, its production would not occur in the present moment, because it is impossible for karma to arise without a basis. Furthermore, if the basis existed at that very [moment of production], then [the doctrine of] momentariness would be lost.
The meaning is "injury. || 151 ||
Even an action that is not completed would never be capable of yielding a result.
Nor can there be existence in one place at one time, because of the contradiction between birth and destruction. (152)

He refutes the position that [the self] is without a substratum with the words "not established. The meaning is that action which is not supported by anything whatsoever cannot even be established; and even if it were established, because its very nature is one of perpetual dependence [on something else], it would not bear fruit. Having stated that action cannot serve as a substratum for the aggregates of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) on the basis of their momentariness, he says "nor" to show that momentariness itself is untenable. And thus, in a single moment—

The meaning is that because arising and perishing necessarily exist together in one and the same locus, the substratum of those two must be connected to at least two moments; therefore, the intended momentariness is not established. || 152 ||
Nor is any stable entity admitted to exist apart from the aggregates.
This [teaching] proceeds with reference to one who is connected to both enjoyment and liberation. || 153 ||
Having rejected the two positions—that karma has as its basis the momentary aggregates or that it is without a basis—the author states another position with the words "And not...

The word "this" refers to karma; the underlying sense is that [the former position] is refuted because it contradicts established doctrine due to the refutation of the theory of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). || 113 ||
And just as this non-undertaking is perceived even in the case of emptiness.
Because a limited breath is impossible, emptiness is not tenable in any way. || 154 ||

He refutes the positions of emptiness (*śūnya*) and annihilation (*nāśa*). [The phrase] "and the non-commencement" means that if either emptiness or annihilation were the motive, the commencement of the treatise would not be logical, because there would be no purpose to be accomplished. He states another fault: "Just as... Just as this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is perceived, so it is not with emptiness or the annihilation of the living being; nor is there any other means of valid cognition (*māna*) for either of these two. Thus, the notion of the annihilation of the living being has been explained as being merely adventitious (*aupādhikī*).
1 ka. ‘tāni trīṇi jñānam | 2 kha. sya pakṣadvaya | 3 ka. states another point. [vol 3, page 42] 2 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1175

The meaning is that neither emptiness nor destruction are the causal factors [for the cessation of bondage]. The mention of "emptiness" is an elliptical expression for the destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*). "In every way" means both by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and by means of reasoning (*yukti*). || 114 ||
Since this is so, it is therefore logical that action alone is his refuge.
On the plane of saṃsāra, for a person, [the experience] arises from time and so forth, because of their predominance.

Having refuted the external positions, he concludes his own position with the words "yataḥ" (since). The syntactical connection should be understood by supplying the word "iti" after the verb. Anticipating the objection that a restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) is inappropriate because time and other factors also exist, he says: "of time and so forth. || 115 ||
Therefore, the Śruti itself has declared that karma alone is preeminent.
[The world arises] from Kāla, Daiva, Īśvara, and so forth, because of Time and the rest, and through their impulsion. || 156 ||

Having stated the matter, he introduces the scriptural passage beginning with "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth. [He says] "karma. He clarifies the meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) with the words "of time, etc. (156).
When there is action, the diversity of beings is logically established.
By the word "karma," both knowledge (vidyā), meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), and ritual action (karman) are expressed. || 157 ||

He states the reasoning for time and so forth being dependent on karma, beginning with the word "satī" (when existing). The meaning is that the diversity of time and so forth—such as their acting as motivators—is logical only when karma exists as the impelling cause; otherwise, there would be the aforementioned lack of order, such as activity occurring or not occurring at random. Regarding the phrase "karma haiva," he explains the meaning of the word "karma" [in verse 197].
"At the commencement of the body, the efficacy of pure karma is not admitted."
Therefore, all three of these are designated by the word "karma. || 158 ||
One might ask: why could the word *karman* not refer to action alone? To this he replies: "The body," etc.; the meaning is that it is so according to such scriptural passages as "As action...
He concludes the meaning of the word *karman* with the words: "Therefore," etc. (158)
Having thus deliberated upon this [path], which is not overwhelmed by the aforementioned defects, they [acted].
They both declared that for one desiring to go to the other world, action alone is the support.
He concludes the meaning of the sentence with the word "evam" (thus). That is to say, ritual action (*karman*) is untouched by the defects stated regarding the positions of others. || 159 ||
And as for those causes which were previously mentioned, and that which the two of them praised;
They both praised karma with reverence among all those things that had been mentioned.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "atha" [and so forth]: "Of the causes... (verse 160).
Even though there is no difference in their status as causes, [the inquiry remains] as to which one is the primary cause when one observes them.
Thus, there may be praise for karma, because its predominance is logically established. || 161 ||
Raising the objection, "Since the causality of many factors is indistinguishable, why is there praise for action (karman)? he says: "In the state of being a cause," etc.

The meaning is that although the causality of all [factors] is equal, when an inquiry arises as to which is primary and which is secondary, the praise of action is purposeful because its primacy is thereby established. || 169 ||
Having brought under control causes such as Īśvara and others, as if acting independently—*Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Third Chapter. [Vol. 3, p. 43] 1176.
It is observed that for one whose action succeeds, action is the primary factor; therefore, it is [called] *karman*. || 162 ||
Even Īśvara and the like cannot be established if they are subordinate to an action.

"Therefore, among all these [causes], karma is said to be the primary one" (163). He establishes both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as proof for its primacy by means of the words "having brought under control. For it has been stated [in the Sūtra]: "The inequality [of the world] is not due to partiality, because [God] is dependent [on karma]" (VS 4.1.21). He concludes with the result of the aforementioned proofs: "Therefore, karma... (162–163).
Since this is so, therefore, even in the absence of a deity, the deceased [receives the offering].
Falling away from this body due to his reliance on the predominance of karma, [he is reborn]. (164)
One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and evil through evil action.
Thus, this Vedic statement is to be understood solely on the authority of scripture. || 165 ||
The cumulative number of verses from the beginning is 5854.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa, the Ārtabhāga Brāhmaṇa, of the third chapter in the *Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*. 2.
He states the meaning, along with its supplementary implications, of the passage beginning with "By merit, indeed, one becomes meritorious," starting with the word "yasmāt" (because).

Since it is established that the appropriation of the body and organs—consisting of the gross and subtle elements—is impelled by karma, he concludes by providing the proof for the following: that a person who has departed from the gross body after death transmigrates repeatedly through the power of karma assisted by time and other factors, even in the absence of the presiding deities of the constituent parts.

Regarding the phrase "iti": the meaning is that since the idea that karma alone, assisted by factors such as time, is the cause of bondage for one who has died is something extraordinary and can therefore be known only through scripture (*āgama*), the aforementioned statement is the authoritative source (*māna*) for this point. || 164 || 165 ||
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa, concerning Ārtabhāga, of the third chapter in the *Śāstraprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*.
Now begins the third Brāhmaṇa:
concerning those who are being liberated from saṃsāra, as well as those who are transmigrating here.
Although the destruction of the body and so forth is equal for all, some among them undergo rebirth. || 1 ||
In that cause where there is the absolute abandonment of the body and other such things for others;
Whether it exists or does not exist, that which acts as its instigator is thus described. (2)

He recounts the narrative in order to explain the connection [of the verses], beginning with the words "From cyclic existence" (*saṃsārāt*). Although the destruction of the effect and the cause is the same at the time of death for both those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and those not yet liberated, among them, for all except the *jīvanmuktas*, there is the re-assumption of a body and so forth, as is observed [in scripture].
1. *nyadarśanāt* | 2. *ka. 'kāra'* | 3. *ka. 'kara'* |
[Vol. 3, Page 44] 5 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1177.

It may be argued that for those who are liberated, there must exist that in the absence of which there is the absolute cessation of the body and so forth; for bondage and liberation consist in the presence or absence of that [state].

The meaning is that, when the question "What is that [cause]? arises, it has been determined after deliberation—according to the method already stated—that it is indeed karma accompanied by the latent impressions of knowledge (vidyāvāsanā). || 1 || 2 ||
It is certain that karma belongs to death, which takes the form of the seizers and over-seizers.
It is now stated: to what extent would the pervasiveness of that karma extend? (3)

This very point—that "that which impels it has been declared"—is now elucidated by the word "graha" (the vessel). The meaning is that action accompanied by knowledge has been stated to be the impeller of the bondage consisting of objects and the senses. He states the connection [of the following section] while anticipating a question: "How much?
In response to the inquiry as to what the extent or pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the present action is—namely, the measure of its fruit—he proceeds to define it.
The meaning is that it refers to the *Antarabrāhmaṇa*. || 3 ||
The determination of the fruit of action is established through both commonality and particularity.
The specific state has been described previously; now, however, the general [state] is being discussed. (4)

The measurement of the fruits of Vedic actions has already been stated; therefore, one might ask, "What is the purpose of this [present section]? Anticipating this doubt, the author distinguishes the fruit of action in order to state its non-redundant subject matter. The phrase "in common" (*sādhāraṇyā*) means that the status of the fruit of action exists in two ways: as a collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) and as an individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*). The status of its fruit as an individual manifestation was stated in the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa in the passage beginning with "He became Agni," and so forth. Thus, by elimination—*pariśeṣāt*—[the present section concerns the collective fruit].

It reminds one of Pārtha. [The author] says "viśeṣa" (particularity) and so forth. Then he states its non-redundant subject matter: "sāmānyaṃ tu" (but the universal). The meaning is that this is stated in order to define the fruit of action in its collective form as presented in the Sūtra. || 4 ||
To what extent does manifest karma pervade within saṃsāra?
"This [reality] is described by Bhujyu as consisting of both the universal self and the particulars. (5)

[Objection: Is it not the case that the fruit of Vedic action described here in the Sūtra is said to be of the nature of *saṃsāra*, and since that consists of both the collective (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), the distinction [you have stated] is not tenable? Nor is it appropriate to say that this [Sūtra] teaches the collective aspect after having taught the individual aspect, for it has already been stated that "death becomes his very self" even with respect to that [individual aspect]. To this, he says: "In *saṃsāra*. Even though two states have been mentioned, [the reference is to] that which has begun...

In response to the doubt as to how extensive the range of the fruit of karma is—whether in its collective or individual form—it is stated in this *Bhujyu Brāhmaṇa* that its measure is precisely that which is included within *saṃsāra*; the meaning is that the specific point of that matter is established by this. || 1 ||
The extent of the effects of delusion regarding the true nature of the inward Self is here described.
When this has been correctly explained, nothing remains unsaid.

Now, one might object: "Has it not already been stated that the fruit of karma is essentially of the nature of saṃsāra, since that Sūtra [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.7] declares that the Self possesses hunger and other such traits?

Anticipating this doubt, he states the specific meaning intended [by the present passage]: "The Inner Self" (pratyag). The point is that in this Brāhmaṇa it is taught that everything to be accomplished arises solely from one's own ignorance; therefore, because there is a difference in the subject matter, this does not merely repeat what has already been said. He states the purpose of the statement regarding the effect of delusion: "In this [state]" (etasyām).
The ellipsis is that "what has not been mentioned falls within the category of duality. || 6 ||
Of the entity; 2. No *ka* in manuscript *kha*.
