1178 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:
There is nothing superior to the killing of an embryo and the Aśvamedha sacrifice among sins and merits respectively.
Thus, there are indeed tens of millions of such statements from the authors of the Dharma.

It has been stated that this Brāhmaṇa is intended to show that the fruit of Vedic action falls precisely within the bondage arising from ignorance. Anticipating the objection—namely, how it can be intended here that *all* the fruit of action constitutes transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)—the author says: "The embryo... and so forth. Among sins and merits, the killing of a Brahmin and the Aśvamedha sacrifice are the two greatest; nevertheless, how is it that all the fruit of action is transmigratory existence? [The answer follows:]...

He says: "Thus" (*ityevam*). By the word *iti*, there is a reference back to the aforementioned killing of a Brahmin and so forth; by the word *evam*, there is a statement regarding the types of merit and demerit similar to those. And thus, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is produced by the killing of a Brahmin and by sins similar to it, as well as by the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and by merits equal to it. As they have said:
"The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, a camel, a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, a bird, a Caṇḍāla, or a Pulkasa."
And as it is said: "By the rope of dharma one goes upward; by the rope of sin one goes downward.
By the word "also" (api), the meaning is that this includes such scriptural passages as, "Those whose conduct here has been pleasant," and so forth. || 7 ||
For the effect of an evil deed is limited even in other circumstances.
For this reason, it is not further elaborated here; moreover, it is disregarded because it serves no purpose.

One might object: "Let it be that there is the fruit of action and thus saṃsāra; nevertheless, just as there is the fruit of merit, so too must the fruit of sin be described here, otherwise detachment from it would be impossible. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of sin... The meaning is that since the experience of various sufferings among animals, ghosts, and so forth—which constitutes the fruit of sin—is already established in the world, there is no novelty (apūrvatva) to it, and therefore it does not require a formal definition. Furthermore, for the sake of the human goal, the Śruti...
He says "bhūyaḥ" (furthermore) to show that because the fruit of evil is a greater disadvantage, the Śruti does not pay heed to it. || 8 ||
And since that desire to abandon [suffering] is established by itself, it is not discussed here.
The fruit of the ritual known as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) is indeed most exalted.

Anticipating the objection that—even though it is *adharma*—it ought to be investigated for the sake of its avoidance, and thus its definition is appropriate because one desires to abandon it, he says: "And by itself" (*svataśca*). If that were so, then since there is no difference in being the fruit of action, the Śruti’s disregard even for the fruit of the Aśvamedha would be appropriate; to this he replies: "Supreme" (*parama*). Because the Aśvamedha and other such rites possess fruits that are not unsurpassed (*anatiśaya*), detachment from them cannot arise by itself.
The intended meaning is that for that purpose, it must be demonstrated that [the world] has entered into the category of misfortune by way of being cyclic existence (saṃsāra). || 9 ||
For indeed, meritorious action is the means for attaining all human goals without exception.
Thus say all the Śrutis and the Smṛtis as well, in numerous places.

Having stated "the Brāhmaṇa," he provides an introductory transition (*pātanikā*) in the form of a doubt and its resolution, in order to declare that all ritual action prescribed by the scriptures has *saṃsāra* as its fruit alone.
He states [the verse beginning with] "niḥśeṣa... He expresses the well-known fact indicated by the word "hi" (for) with the words "thus they say.

[He explains: "The scriptural texts are twofold—the passage concerning the desire for heaven (*svargakāmavākya*) and the passage concerning the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣāvākya*)—and thus [they teach] that both happiness and knowledge arise from dharma, and that dharma arises through action alone."
He states the purport of those Smṛti texts, such as "For those who have attained perfection, Karma-yoga is superior," by the words "repeatedly" (anekaśaḥ). || 10 ||
[Vol.
3, Page 46] 3 Brāhmaṇa: Together with the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
1179 Because it shares the commonality of being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), like the human goals such as heaven (*svarga*).
Therefore, there is a suspicion that even liberation might not have the Sage as its means of accomplishment.
To remove that apprehension, this subsequent Śruti passage has been commenced.
Now, having restated the doubt, the Brāhmaṇa proceeds as a response: "If it were for the sake of the human goal," etc. (11).
"Even for the king of rituals, which is action augmented by knowledge,"
In liberation, there is not even the slightest attainment of the objects of saṃsāra.

He states how doubt is removed in that regard: "By knowledge," etc. "That" refers to the attainment mentioned. The meaning is that even ritual action accompanied by knowledge has saṃsāra as its fruit alone; this will become clear in this Brāhmaṇa. || 12 ||
The delusion regarding the true nature of the inward Self takes the form of action and its agents.
It expands upon that reality in which all actions, factors of action, and entities have been entirely cast aside.

If it is argued that ignorance (*avidyā*) is accepted as existing here and there within *saṃsāra*, and if that [ignorance] is stated here to be the result of karma, how could there not be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows?
To this, he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*). The meaning is that in the undifferentiated conscious Self (*cidātman*), that ignorance manifests itself in the form of karma and so forth;
thus, even though bondage is born of karma, there is no loss of its being born of ignorance. || 13 ||
However, that which is asserted here by certain individuals who have not realized the true nature of the self;
Action devoid of attachment to results should be known as leading to liberation.

Even though ritual action accompanied by knowledge has saṃsāra as its fruit, [the author] deliberates—refining his own position that knowledge alone serves the purpose of liberation—and thus sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). "Unascertained" (*anirjñāta*): he refers here to the commencement of the *Brāhmaṇa* established by the aforementioned method. "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) means that which is conjoined with knowledge (*vidyā-samuccita*). || 14 ||
Just as even bondage can produce a result contrary to its nature for the sake of liberation.
"Just like poison, curd, and so forth"—thus is the illustrative example stated. (15)

Anticipating the objection—"How can action, which is the cause of bondage, be the cause of liberation? They are contradictory"—the author says: "Bondage... Although action is indeed the cause of bondage, as the Smṛti states, "A living being is bound by action," nevertheless, when accompanied by knowledge (*vidyā*), it becomes opposed to bondage and produces a fruit consisting of its own destruction; thus, for the sake of liberation, it is illustrated in the Commentary by the example of poison mixed with curd and so forth. Therefore, just as [poison] alone...

Just as curd and other substances, though they cause death, fever, and so forth, bring about life, nourishment, and the like when combined with mantras, sugar, and other ingredients; likewise, the meaning is that even action which by its very nature has bondage as its fruit is capable of leading to liberation when it is conjoined [with knowledge]. || 19 ||
In order to refute the response stated above, it is said: "This is not correct."
The statement regarding the lack of a beginning is for the purpose of removing the cause thereof.

He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Regarding the phrase "it being thus stated," he introduces the commentary (*bhāṣya*) with the words "because liberation is not something to be commenced" (*anārabhyatvāt mokṣasya*). || 16 ||
If liberation is accepted as something that must be undertaken, then it would be as has been stated.
But this liberation is not something to be undertaken [as a new effort], because its accomplishment results from the cause that is knowledge. || 17 ||
[Vol. 3, p. 47] 1180 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]:

He explains that [point] with the words "ārabhyatve" (in the case of being something to be commenced). If liberation were admitted to be something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then it would follow that it is accomplished by combined ritual actions (*samuccita-karma*).
The meaning is that it may exist, but it does not have the status of being something to be accomplished (sādhya), because it depends solely upon cognition. || 17 ||
For it has been stated that even prior to the arising of knowledge, "this [universe] was indeed Brahman."
Since the realization that the world, Brahman, and the self are one is established, liberation does not arise from ritual action.
Fearing that liberation might be something to be accomplished through action just as it is accomplished through knowledge, he offers a counter-example by saying "Brahman.
Even prior to the arising of knowledge, the state of being Brahman is established for the transmigrating world, according to such scriptural texts as "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman.
Therefore, the meaning is that liberation is not to be accomplished by knowledge—because there is no example to that effect—and it is likewise not to be accomplished by action. || 18 ||
If it is maintained that a thing is liberated by its own nature but bound by another, [then...]
Then the effort for liberation would be fruitful; not otherwise.

Furthermore, liberation is not something to be accomplished; for instance, is the inner self (pratyag-vastu) liberated by itself and bound by another, or is it bound by itself and liberated by another?

Regarding this, he restates the first position with the words "If [it be so]... Therein, he first addresses whether the cause of bondage—another—is non-existent or existent. With the words "For the sake of liberation... he shows that if the cause of bondage is non-existent, then the destruction of bondage along with its cause is easily accomplished without effort.

The meaning is that liberation is established as not depending upon karma. He refutes two possible alternatives: first, that the cause of bondage is a real entity, and second, that the inner self (pratīc) is inherently bound; for if either were true, the undertaking of effort for the sake of liberation would be fruitless. "No," he says. || 19 ||
This [knowledge] is merely the manifester of a reality that is established by itself.
Its status as a creator in the world is simply not tenable. || 20 ||
He states another reason for the fact that liberation is not something to be accomplished by knowledge (*vidyā*). [The verse says: "Knowledge... Why is its nature restricted to being a manifestor?
To this he replies: "It is a producer. The meaning is that if it were a causal agent (*kāraka*), it would not be an illuminator, like clay and other such materials. || 20 ||
The operation of valid cognition occurs with respect to an object when it is separated from it only by ignorance.
Knowledge regarding an object that has already begun [to exist] is fruitless, because it merely reveals what is already there, like a lamp. // 21 //

Anticipating the objection that manifestation is also untenable because it would be self-established—since manifestation is co-natural [to the object]—he says: "Through ignorance," etc. The meaning is this: although manifestation is self-established, when the Self is veiled by ignorance, it is only through the entry of knowledge in the form of a mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) arising from the sentence that the destruction of that [ignorance] is conventionally designated as such [manifestation]. He states another reason for liberation being unachievable: "Having begun," etc.

If liberation, characterized as the fruit, is accepted as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then knowledge would have no role in it, as it would be rendered useless; for, like a lamp, knowledge functions as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and thus enters into that which is manifested (*vyaṅgya*), not into that which is to be accomplished. Therefore, since it is logically untenable for it to possess such a fruit, liberation is not something to be accomplished—this is the meaning. || 21 ||
And apart from ignorance, no other bondage for liberation is admitted.
The cessation of that [karma] for which [the rite] is performed by means of this ritual action is brought about here.

3, page 48] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1181

Lest it be thought that [liberation] might not be accomplished by knowledge alone, but rather by action combined with knowledge—since the removal of ignorance and other obstacles requires a combination (samuccaya)—the author raises this doubt and says: "And not... (*na ca*). "Bondage" (*bandhaḥ*) means obstruction or intervention (*vyavadhiḥ*).
"By knowledge" (*vidyayā*) means by knowledge accompanied by [action]. "Here" (*iha*) is an expression for the inner self (*pratyagartha*). || 22 ||
And liberation for the self is held to be merely the destruction of ignorance.
For if liberation were to exceed that [state], it would certainly be impermanent. || 23 ||

He states another argument for the fact that liberation cannot be accomplished through a combination [of knowledge and action]: "Ignorance" (avidyā). The meaning is that if liberation were dependent upon means other than the destruction of ignorance, it would necessarily be non-eternal; therefore, since liberation is simply the cessation of one's own ignorance within the inner self (pratīci), there is no room for a combination [of means]. || 23 ||
There is no sublation [of reality] other than through the excellence of right knowledge;
therefore, there can be no combination of knowledge and action for one whose delusion has been destroyed. (24)
Anticipating the objection that this very [knowledge] is what is to be accomplished through the combination [of means], he says: "Properly" (samyak). || 24 ||
And because the power of action within the world has its object already fully determined.
For the fourfold effect of action—namely, origination and so forth—is indeed observed. (25)

Anticipating the objection that if liberation were thus unattainable, it would follow that it must be attainable through action alone, he says: "Nirjñātā" (known). The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. The sense of "api" (also/even) is "in all cases. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "liberation is not something to be accomplished by that [action]. He clarifies its nature as having a known object: "For it is seen," etc. (Verse 29).
For origination, extreme transformation, conditioned phenomena, and the fruit of action [are the objects of knowledge].
There is no other task to be performed than this through action; nor is liberation sought through anything other than this. || 26 ||

He clarifies that very point with the words "In [the case of] origination" (*utpattau*). Anticipating the objection that there might be some fifth effect of action, he states what is indicated by the word *hi*: "No" (*na*). The meaning of the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is the fourfold fruit of action. The impossibility of being an effect of action is expressed by the second *ataḥ*. The word *tat* (that) refers to action (*karman*). || 26 ||
And liberation for any one of these [views] is not logically tenable.
Because the various modes such as arising and so forth are invariably associated with impermanence. || 27 ||

[The opponent] raises the objection: "Even if liberation is established by scripture and reason for others, action (*karman*) is still the cause [of liberation], because it is one of the four [possible causes]. To this, he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). How is it that its being one of the four is impossible according to reasoning? To that he replies: "Because of origination, etc. (*utpattyādi*).
Alternatively, the connection is with "these modes of origination, etc."; in that case, the remaining [part of the verse] is the reason. || 27 ||
For it is accepted that liberation is separated from [reality] by nothing more than ignorance.
For indeed, when there is an intervention by something other than that, no means of valid cognition is established. || 28 ||

"In that case, let liberation be eternal; what is the harm in that? To this he replies: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). The ellipsis is: "Therefore, being of the nature of one's own essence, it is not logical for it to be non-eternal. Having raised the objection that since other intervening factors are also possible, the veil is not merely ignorance, he states another solution: "Other than that" (*tadanya*). The word "for" (*hi*) is intended to indicate the previously mentioned resolution. || 28 ||
If it is argued that the state of having a perishable fruit belongs to action alone, independent [of knowledge], [then...]
But for that very person who possesses this knowledge, the fruit shall be stability. || 29 ||
Having briefly provided the objection and its resolution, he explains the objection [with the verse]: "If it is perishable... Here, the word *cet* ("if") is connected with the word *iti*. || 29 ||
Through the cessation of the previous power, there arises another power. || 30 ||
For it is observed that poison and the like [lose their potency] through contact with another substance.
Do not speak thus, for there is no means of valid cognition [for it], just like worldly objects. || 31 ||

How is this established? To that he says: "The former," etc. Therefore, because action is connected with knowledge, there arises another power through the removal of the previous power; this is the remainder [of the sense]. He provides the resolution: "By means of authority," etc. The meaning is that, like poison, curd, and so forth, action does not initiate a different effect due to a difference in auxiliary factors, as there is a lack of evidence for such a thing. || 30 || 31 ||
No authority other than scripture is accepted for liberation.
Therefore, this statement would not be well-said, being like [the claim that] poison, curd, and so forth [are beneficial]. || 32 ||

In order to state that there is no evidence for the claim that "action conjoined with knowledge is the constant initiator of liberation," he provides an introductory transition: "Not from scripture" (nāgamāt). The meaning is that, because it is supersensuous (alaukika), it is like dharma. He states the consequence regarding the absence of other means of knowledge: "Poison" (viṣa). Since there is no other means of knowledge regarding liberation, statements such as "like poison, curd, etc. are improper; for liberation does not depend merely on an illustrative example. || 32 ||
Cognition occurs beyond the stated causal factors, as in the case of [the perception of] poison and so forth.
When another effect arises, even action does not exist. || 33 ||

Having provided this introductory transition (*pātanikā*), he establishes the absence of evidence for the claim that liberation is achievable through ritual action (*karma*). He states: "It has been said. Regarding the production and so forth of effects as previously described, there is no means of valid cognition (*māna*) for the existence of the capacity of ritual action—whether combined with knowledge or not combined—to bring about the production of another effect called liberation; whereas in the case of poison and the like, such capacity exists for the production of other effects.
The meaning is that this very [consciousness] is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it is directly perceived. || 33 ||
Knowledge whose nature consists in the non-exclusion of the probandum is merely an action, because it lacks substantial reality.
For knowledge must be dependent upon the object itself, and not dependent upon its causal factors.

Furthermore, regarding the combination of meditation (*upāsti*) or means of knowledge (*māna*) with ritual action (*karman*), [the author] says "meditates" (*upāste*) in order to state that there is no combination of knowledge and action in the first case;

he states the absence of the nature of knowledge [in meditation] with the words "that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhya*). The meaning is that meditation, which consists of the repetition of mental impressions (*pratyaya*) directed toward an object to be accomplished—the thing to be meditated upon—is merely action because it does not depend on the reality of the object. Having raised the doubt that it might still possess the nature of knowledge even in the absence of the reality of the object, he says "for knowledge... [and continues with] "means of knowledge" (*māna*).
For knowledge depends on the object (*vastutantra*), not on the agent (*kartṛtantra*); whereas meditation depends on the agent, therefore it is not knowledge—this is the meaning. || 34 ||
This is action; by that [action], such a result is found in no other way whatsoever.
Therefore, this is a compendium of ritual actions (kriyā), and not a compendium of vidyās. || 35 ||

He states the consequence of its not being knowledge: "Karma" (verse 35). By "such," he refers to action conjoined with meditation (*upāsanā*). He clarifies the aforementioned consequence: "Action" (*kriyā*). By the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), he declares that meditation is a mental action.
The relationship between the probandum and the probans has scripture as its sole means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, action is not at all heard of in the Śruti as a means for liberation.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that action—whether combined with knowledge or not—is the cause of liberation, he first refutes it by stating "sādhyā" (to be accomplished), etc.; the word "pāralaukika" (pertaining to the next world) is to be supplied as the remainder. He refutes the second [position] by stating "mukteśca" (and of liberation), etc.

The meaning is that passages such as "We have drunk Soma," etc., do not constitute valid authority for their own literal sense because they are merely praises of ritual action (*karma-stāvaka*), owing to contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 36 ||
Liberation for us is the destruction of ignorance; action is not the means to that.
For action does not destroy darkness, just as darkness that has arisen cannot destroy darkness.

He states another reason for liberation not being achievable through action: "By ignorance," etc. Anticipating the objection as to why action is not the cause for the destruction of ignorance, he clarifies what was stated in the passage "apart from perfect knowledge" by means of an illustration: "For not," etc. This means that when there is darkness regarding a rope—i.e., when there is ignorance of the rope—the darkness that arises is the cognition of a snake and so forth. || 37 ||
Even though knowledge and action may arise from ignorance, [they do not constitute bondage].
Nevertheless, the excellence of cognition consists in its conformity with the oneness of the object of knowledge. (38)

One might object that it is incorrect to say "action does not remove ignorance because it is born of ignorance, like the cognition of a snake in a rope," since such an inference could also apply to knowledge. Anticipating this, he states that "lack of conformity with reality" is the limiting condition (upādhi), saying: "Ignorance... (Verse 38).
For action, which conforms to the identity with the self, does not transcend the ignorance of the self.
Because it originates from a mere portion of *tamas*, it does not destroy that ignorance. || 39 ||

Anticipating the objection that such a limiting adjunct (upādhi) is impossible, he says: "Not the Self. He states the reason implied by the word "for" (hi): "Consisting of darkness alone" (tamomātra).
The meaning is that without the conceit of agency and so forth, there can be no action, nor knowledge—which is the sublater of that [action]—and thus the distinction between them is not established.
He states the conclusion regarding the fact that action does not conform to reality: "Therefore not... (nātaḥ). || 39 ||
Because it arises solely from the single reality of the Self, which is established by itself.
Knowledge destroys all darkness without exception, but action does not, because it follows after that darkness.

Anticipating the objection that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) might pervade the probans (*sādhana*), he says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). The meaning is that knowledge arises from the sentence in the form of the non-dual, single-flavored reality whose nature is self-luminous Being-Consciousness-Bliss; that [knowledge] then removes all darkness (*tamas*). He concludes regarding the result of the limiting adjunct: "But not... Because it follows after darkness and does not follow the reality (*vastu*), ritual action (*karman*) does not destroy darkness.
Although the triad beginning with ignorance is held to be a reflection within the inner self (pratyagābhāsa),...
It is accepted that [the object] is apprehended precisely by means of a cognition produced from the cognition of the cognition itself. || 41 ||

Now, it might be argued that whatever conforms to a real object destroys ignorance; however, there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) seen in the case of ignorance itself and so forth. Therefore, the negative concomitance— [The text continues with the argument regarding the nature of knowledge and its relationship to the destruction of ignorance.]

Since there is no impurity of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-aśuddhi*) [in this case], he says: "ignorance, etc. Ignorance consists of the triad of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), doubt (*saṃśayajñāna*), and [the absence of] knowledge;

even though these are permeated by consciousness (*caitanya*), prior to the arising of [true] knowledge, they are not accepted as the cause for the destruction of bondage along with its causes. For although they partake in the form of consciousness, because they are the cause of erroneous manifestation (*viparīta-prathā*), they lack conformity with reality (*vastvanusāritva*). Therefore, there is no impurity of negative concomitance in the case of the subject under dispute, which is ignorance.
The meaning is that this follows from the inference: "It is perishable because it conforms to a perishable object, like the cognition of a rope. || 41 ||
Therefore, it is in no way logical that karma is the cause of liberation.
The direct destruction of ignorance is not possible; however, it is appropriate [to speak of its destruction] through a traditional succession.
He states the conclusion: "Karma... Since the aforementioned conditions have been established and a counter-inference is impossible, the previously stated inference stands firm.
Anticipating the objection—"If actions do not directly contribute to liberation, how can passages such as the *vividiṣā-vākya* be justified?"—he says: "Ignorance... (42)
And since liberation is to be accomplished through karma, does each [deity] bestow liberation individually?
Do they destroy the cycle of worldly existence by acting individually, or do all the actions together effect this? || 43 ||

If it is argued that even in the absence of a counter-inference, the reason "being an effect of ignorance" deviates with respect to knowledge, we say no; for the intended meaning of the reason is "the state of not being luminous. With this in mind, he examines the possibility of ritual actions being the cause of liberation, stating: "And in liberation... (verse 43).
Either through a single repeated application or through practice throughout one's entire life.
In this way, an equal option is accepted regarding the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) starting from one. || 44 ||

He states three alternatives regarding the performance of both parts [of the ritual]. "Once," etc.; the word "liberation" (mukti) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He also provides an alternative for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), corresponding to the performance: "One, etc. The meaning of the alternative is that liberation results from giving a sacrificial fee consisting of either one, or many, or all [of the items], such as cows and so forth. || 44 ||
Whether by means of optional rites, or by the obligatory ones, or by all of them together, liberation is sought.
Whether by those [deeds] based on Śruti, or by those based on Smṛti, or by deeds belonging to both.
While performing the very rites that are to be practiced, he introduces alternative options, such as "or by means of optional rites" (kāmyaiḥ). || 49 ||
And regarding their conjunction with knowledge, there is a distinction based on the predominance of the qualities.
Conceptualization should be understood as threefold for the sake of accomplishing the fruit of liberation. || 46 ||

Having considered actions alone, he now considers them in combination. Regarding the phrase "of these": when there is a combination of knowledge with actions for the sake of liberation, there are three alternatives due to the distinction between both being equally primary, or one being primary and the other secondary.
That is to say, they are either equally primary, or action is primary and knowledge is secondary, or the reverse. || 46 ||
If each individual [repetition] were to effect liberation, it would be like the oblation of barley, rice, and so forth.
Since one's purpose is accomplished by that alone, one does not perform anything further than that.

He restates [the teaching] beginning with "each single action bestows liberation. Regarding the word "each single": it is just as each individual oblation of rice, barley, and so forth [is efficacious].

The meaning is that, for the same reason as before, each individual act such as the *agnihotra* is an alternative cause of liberation. In that case, other ritual acts would be rendered useless.

[The opponent] objects: "Even by one [action]. [The author replies: "And there is no purposefulness through optionality as in the case of rice and so forth, because with respect to liberation, no such [optionality] among actions is heard in scripture; rather, that [optionality] is resorted to only as a last resort. This is the intended meaning. || 47 ||
In both the ritual application and the sacrificial fee, this circumambulation is the same.
Then, having come together, they all perform the rites for liberation. || 48 ||
One attains a single, fixed result for all actions whatsoever.
Because, like the New Moon sacrifice and others, there would be a single result, and that [consequence] is undesirable. || 49 ||

He extends the critique to the two positions—that liberation occurs through a single performance (*sakṛtprayoga*) or through a single sacrificial fee (*ekadakṣiṇā*)—by stating "in the performance" (*prayoge*).
The meaning is that in those cases, neither a further performance nor a further sacrificial fee would be purposeful. Having restated the alternative view, he refutes it:

[The author] concludes [the previous argument]. Now, with the word "atha" (now), he states the reason for the unity of action (*aikakarmya*): "because of the unity of the fruit" (*phalaikatvāt*). The illustration has already been explained previously.

To the question, "What is the harm in the unity of action?", he replies: "And that... (*tacceti*). The point is that there is no unity of action among the *Bṛhaspatisava*, the *Rājasūya*, and so forth, because they have different qualified performers (*adhikārin*). This is because [the sacrifice] may be performed repeatedly, or throughout one's life (*yāvajjīvam*), or because many things such as cows and so forth are involved.

Alternatively, if liberation were achieved through a single sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it would not be established; or if liberation resulted from the performance of a single act throughout one's entire life, then the performance of other actions would be useless. Furthermore, it is impossible for a single person to perform all ritual acts, nor is there any authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to suggest that a multitude of fees or every fee constitutes the cause of liberation. Nor is the Vedic scripture, "Those who give gold attain immortality," a proof for this, because its intent is merely to praise the act of giving; otherwise, [it would contradict other scriptural passages].
And the meaning [of the sūtras] is that a prohibition [of this] would contradict the Śruti. 48 || 49 ||
For indeed, it is heard in scripture that the fruit of optional rites is something other than the fruit of liberation.
But their status as having liberation as their fruit follows neither from scripture nor from any other source.

He refutes the position that [the rites] may be performed for the sake of desired results (*kāmyaiḥ*) by stating "another" (*anyat*). Having raised the objection that even though the scriptures declare that optional rites (*kāmyānām*) have fruits such as heaven, it is not contradictory for them to also have liberation as their fruit—since we hear of curds, for example, being used both for obligatory purposes and for optional ones—he replies with "of those" (*teṣām*).

Having raised the further objection that liberation might be accepted even if it is not explicitly stated in scripture, on the grounds of traditional law (*smṛti*) or logical reasoning (*nyāya*), he says "nor even" (*na api*). || 10 ||
Furthermore, the analogy of the *godohana* vessel is not applicable to optional rites (*kāmyakarman*).
For there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to establish that these have liberation as their fruit. || 51 ||

Now, it may be argued that just as in the case of the injunction "one desiring cattle should fetch water in a milking vessel" (*godohanena paśukāmasya praṇayet*), the milking vessel is seen to produce the fruit of cattle through the fulfillment of the fetching required by the sacrifice— wherein the application [of the vessel] occurs swiftly through the Vedic injunction (*niyoga*) by means of a visible intermediary, since the purpose of a subordinate injunction (*viniyoga*) is to serve the primary injunction— and where even the word expressing desire (*kāmapada*) merely restates the contextual qualification (*adhikāra*) by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); so too, in accordance with the requirement of the material cause (*upādāna*), the sentence...

When [the text] enjoins the *godohana* vessel as a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to the carrying of water for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), it follows that, because it is prescribed by depending upon that [sacrificial act], it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) while also serving the purpose of the sacrifice.

As they say: "Even that which is intended for another purpose, when present nearby, may be connected with something else. Similarly, even rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarma*) have liberation (*mokṣa*) as their ultimate goal by way of heaven and so forth; regarding this, he says: "And not... The intention is as follows: [concerning] the word *kāma*...

Since, by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), there would be the consequence of it being a mere restatement (anuvāda) if it were directed toward the subject matter at hand, it is understood from the context of application (viniyoga) that this constitutes a distinct injunction (niyoga). And that [injunction] is: 1. with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); 2. as in the case of the *ka* manuscript, "like a forest" (*vaṇavat*).

1186 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]: It brings about the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*) of the *godohana* vessel with respect to both one’s own self and the fruit; thus its status as a human goal (*puruṣārthatva*) is based on its inclusion (*aupādānika*). Nor does there occur a disruption of the application (*viniyogabhaṅga*) due to the force of such inclusion, because that [inclusion] is dependent upon it. For the injunction (*vidhi*) employs the means for the sake of benefiting the self. Upa-

Furthermore, the understanding of the specific function (*kāraviśeṣa*)—namely, that the accomplishment of the fetching [of water] required by the sacrifice is achieved through the *godohana* vessel—is understood from the sentence itself via its application (*viniyoga*).

Thus, since the injunction (*niyoga*) depends on the application, and the connection with the word denoting desire (*kāmapada*) cannot be abandoned when it depends on that [injunction], the *godohana*, although prescribed as part of the ritual, is established as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). As it has been said: "In the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika*), because it is a modification, the primary element is the sacrifice; [otherwise,]..."

"It could not be so. This means that ritual acts performed with desire (*kāmyakarman*), which have heaven and the like as their fruits, cannot have liberation (*mokṣa*) as their fruit, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*māna*). The word "nyāya" (reasoning) refers here to the reasoning of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The particle "hi" is used to indicate that the reason stated in the passage beginning with "of those... serves to establish the reasoning of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). || 51 ||
And all that has been stated as the definition of difference would also be immeasurable.
If all actions together were to bring about liberation, [then there would be no need for knowledge]. (52)
Alternatively, he will refute the position that [liberation results] from "eternal" rites later on; for now, he refutes the fourfold set of positions beginning with "from all.

Regarding the phrase "and all": the meaning is this—if all actions, whether eternal, optional, Vedic (śrauta), or Smṛti-based, were to have liberation as their fruit, then everything that was stated in the earlier Mīmāṃsā regarding the differentiators such as difference in words, repetition, procedure, and name—[all that would be undermined].

That [Vedic injunction] would then be non-authoritative, because if the fruit were one, a distinction between rituals would be untenable; therefore, if liberation were the fruit of all rituals, there would be a contradiction with the defining characteristic of ritual distinction due to the unity of the ritual act. || 52 ||
Our understanding of what is to be proven and the means of proof regarding the world beyond does not arise from verbal testimony.
Sai, mi 127 53.
Nor have I heard from the words of the Vedas anywhere that ritual action has liberation as its fruit.
He states a defect common to all positions, such as the claim that "each single action bestows liberation," in the following verse: "sādhyeti."
No sacrificial gifts go there; it is attained by knowledge alone.
And the mantra "I know" (vedāham) dispels other paths through knowledge.

Having reminded [the opponent] of the absence of scriptural authority [for the view that mere action leads to liberation], he states the contradiction with scripture regarding the claim that mere action is the cause of liberation: "Not there" (na tatra).
By the locative and the nominative cases, *kaivalya* (isolation) is referred to. In the mantra, however, the phrase "knowing him thus" (*tamevaṃ vidvān*) is to be supplied as the remainder. || 94 ||
Neither by action does the inner self undergo diminution or increase.
"His greatness is eternal"—thus it will also be declared later on. || 55 ||

Furthermore, because liberation—which is of the nature of the inner self—cannot be the locus for the addition of any excellence by action, he states that it is not to be accomplished by that [action]: "Not by action.
He also states from the remainder of the scriptural passage that liberation is not to be accomplished by it: "For him, it is eternal" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9). || 11 ||
The world acquired through action is perishable, but that which is won through knowledge is eternal.
Why, then, do you not heed this clear statement of the Śruti? (56)
And for this reason, he says that it is eternal and not something to be accomplished: "It is subject to decay. (56)

Furthermore, the theory of aggregation has already been thoroughly refuted more than once before.
We shall explain this further here as well, in connection with the context, without excessive detail. || 57 ||

Having refuted the view that action alone is the cause of liberation, [the author] now refutes the threefold synthesis mentioned in the verse beginning with "and their union with knowledge" (jñānasaṃyoga).
The phrase "and synthesis" (samuccayaśca) refers back to the previously mentioned connection. We shall also refute that synthesis later on in the context of the relevant discussion;
however, here too, rather than being overly prolix, we shall state its refutation in brief—this is the construction of the argument. || 17 ||
Even when combined, knowledge does not dispel ignorance regarding karma.
Because they stand in the relationship of the probandum and the probans, they cannot exist at the same time. || 58 ||

In this context as well, demonstrating what was already stated—that we reject the combination [of knowledge and action] without excessive detail—he rejects the combination of the knowledge of the means (*pramāṇajñāna*) and action as being related as the auxiliary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*). He says: "by coming together" (*saṃnipatya*). Knowledge that comes together as an auxiliary to action does not remove ignorance;
he states the reason for this: "the goal" (*sādhya*), etc. Action is the means by way of purification, while knowledge is the goal; and thus...

The meaning is that because there is no coexistence at one and the same time between the prior and subsequent periods, there can be no relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin); nor can that which is to be accomplished [by knowledge] be subordinate to it, since they do not enter into a single ritual performance, and because it is accepted that even actions belonging to another birth serve as a means to knowledge. || 18 ||
And because of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, like that between a lion and a ram.
Because they do not abide in the same location, there is no conjunction between the two. (59)

He states the synthesis [of the two means] by way of their equal primacy: "The sublated... and so forth. "Pañcāsya" means a lion. "Uraṇa" means a ram. The meaning is that because they do not abide in one and the same part, they cannot coexist in a single substratum. || 19 ||
Granted, there may be a combination [of these views] by way of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator.
"Without relinquishing their respective capacities, as in the case of the donor and the recipient.

(60) Now, is there a relationship between knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*karman*), or not? In the first case, the establishment of their conjunction (*samuccaya*) follows; in the second, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakatva*) is not established. To this, you reply: "The sublated..."—that is, by not abandoning the power of sublation inherent in knowledge and the power of being sublated inherent in action.

If their conjunction is intended as a combination by way of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, then that is indeed accepted, just as in the case of wood and fire; such is the meaning. || 60 ||
Ignorance (avidyā) would be the cognition of things as they are not; its opposite is knowledge (vidyā).
Thus, there is a conjunction of those two, like that of the sun and the moon.
He demonstrates the aforementioned synthesis along with its logical justification through another example: "Not as it is," etc. (61).
Knowledge depends upon the object, and likewise, action depends upon the agent.
The status of being an agent and so forth arises from delusion regarding the self; by its very nature, the self is not an agent.
He states another reason for the absence of combination: "The entity," etc. To the question, "How does this much [of an argument] establish its absence? he replies: "By the agent," etc.

The meaning is that because the self is immutable (*kauṭasthya*), agency and so forth are products of ignorance (*āvidya*); therefore, since they cannot coexist with the knowledge of that [self], there is no combination. || 62 ||
Just as a kṣatriya does not participate in the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice.
Whether a Brahmin or a Kṣatriya, one who lacks pride regarding his status as a Brahmin may engage in the duties of a Kṣatriya.

Furthermore, since the knower of reality (*jñānin*) is devoid of the conceit of agency (*abhimāna*), there is no injunction (*niyoga*) for him; therefore, how could there be a combination (*samuccaya*)? To state this, he provides an illustration with the words "Bṛhaspati," etc. The word "or" (*vā*) is used to indicate one who lacks the conceit of being a Kṣatriya. (63)

Likewise, one who perceives the body and so forth as not-self does not even observe activity [belonging to them]. He states the application to the subject at hand: "one who is disembodied" (videha). Even the slightest capacity for universal victory is conceivable therein.

there too, having set aside the doubt regarding the qualification of those desiring all fruits, since only one assumption is necessary even when many might be possible—and because the requirement is satisfied by that much alone—it was proved that the qualification belongs to only one person, and specifically, that qualification was determined to belong to one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*). The same applies to the obligatory (*nitya*) rites.

He says "no" to the claim that even for those obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), a fruit distinct from liberation (*kaivalya*) is postulated; he states: "like the Viśvajit. There is not even the slightest capacity for the production of a fruit characterized by origination and so forth; therefore, that person is not the one to be enjoined. [This is understood] from the injunction "one who is living should offer the oblation," which specifies the person to be enjoined as being qualified by the state of being alive.

The meaning is that [the result arises] from the attainment of that [result] there. Now, even if one assumes a fruit based on the performance [of rites] while living, since living is unavoidable, it is proper for it to be a qualification of the person entitled [to the rite] (*adhikāri-viśeṣaṇa*); nevertheless, when assuming that the performance is prompted by what is enjoined, because men act out of desire, the entitlement belongs only to those seeking a fruit, according to the Smṛti: "Whatever a living being does, that is the activity of desire. This applies even to obligatory (*nitya*) rites.

He says "liberation" (mukti) to show that the fruit of actions does not possess such qualities as origination and so forth. Although those lacking discrimination do not seek liberation characterized by the absolute cessation of the body, nevertheless, for those possessing discrimination who desire liberation and are entitled to perform obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), it is logical that liberation is their fruit; this is the intended meaning. || 76 ||
If there were no human goal as a fruit, an injunction would not be tenable.
For it is only when that [desire] exists that the performance of obligatory rites (nitya-karma) is possible. || 77 ||

If it is argued that there is no fruit for the obligatory rites (*nitya*) as heard in scripture, then they would be fruitless; yet, because they are enjoined, they must be performed—anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "It is for the purpose of man" (*puruṣārtha*). He states the reason why an injunction is impossible without a fruit: "In that... (verse 77).
For those who act with prior reflection upon things that are eternal yet consist of suffering, [there is no sorrow].
Men would not engage [in action] if there were no fruit resulting from these [actions]. || 78 ||
To the question, "How can an injunction be applicable when there is already a fruit [of action]?", he says: "In those things whose nature is suffering," and so forth.

An injunction has activity as its fruit, and there is no activity without a fruit; since there is no other fruit in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), liberation is therefore their fruit—this is the meaning. ||78||

The fruit is not [obtained] from the sentence in this way, because not even the slightest fruit is obtained therefrom; since there is no hearing of its capacity [for such a result], we maintain that there is no cognition of the fruit [arising] from it.

Therefore, this relationship of the sublated and the sublator is not tenable between those two. || 96 ||

Anticipating the objection, "Could there not be a contradiction between these two, ignorance and karma? he says: "Contradictory. The ellipsis to be supplied is "because they are established by both common experience and the Veda. He states the result of the absence of contradiction: "Sublated," etc. (Verse 96).
If it is argued that the unseen potency of karma is dispelled by knowledge;
Because ignorance is destroyed by knowledge through direct perception, that [opposite] statement is false. || 97 ||

One might object that because there is no contradiction with ritual action (*karman*), the fact that knowledge removes ignorance is not established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), but is rather something unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). To this, he replies: "By knowledge... [Verse 97]. He refutes this by stating that when a visible cause exists, it is improper to postulate an unseen one.
For the husks produced by threshing are indeed directly perceived within the rice grains.
Its accomplishment occurs through that capacity, not through rituals such as the Agnihotra.
In this case as well, it is conceptualized in exactly that manner through the cognition of direct perception. || 99 ||
Because of the capacity of obligatory karma to destroy the ignorance regarding the inner self.
It is not logical for you to forcibly imagine the destruction of ignorance [as occurring] through power.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the words "tuṣa... (husk...). The construction is as follows: when there is the perceptible separation of the husk from the grain produced by the threshing of rice and so forth, the arising of the aforementioned effect [of liberation] through the power of the Agnihotra and other rites is not postulated. He states the application to the subject of the analogy with the words "tadvat" (in the same way). This means: by force, that is, without a means of valid cognition (māna). || 98 || 99 || 100 ||
150 [Vol. 3, Page 61] 1194 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Chapter]
And that which is not contradicted by ritual actions, which pertains to the true nature of deities and substances.
That knowledge should be accumulated, for it is not in contradiction with ritual action.

Granted that ignorance is destroyed by knowledge; however, one might object that—based on such scriptural passages as "That alone which one performs" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.11)—just as ritual action is to be combined [with knowledge], so too knowledge combined with it possesses a superior fruit. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And by actions. In passages such as "That alone which one performs," the combination [of knowledge and action] is appropriate because the knowledge of deities and so forth is not in contradiction [with action]; however, the knowledge arising from sentences such as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) is in contradiction with action, and therefore [no such combination is possible].
Therefore, the meaning is that this combination alone is the destroyer of ignorance. || 101 ||
And since the efficacy of the eternal rites was not perceived by you yesterday;
Or is it something contradictory to actions, or that which is devoid of perception and so forth? || 102 ||

It has been stated that, whether permanent rites (*nityakarman*) are performed collectively or individually, no unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*) need be postulated for either their maintenance in their own nature or for the destruction of the ignorance that obstructs liberation. Now, even while conceding the existence of such an unseen potency, he states that it is not to be postulated for liberation: "Or, if it were to be postulated... The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is not to be postulated for liberation. He investigates this point for that purpose.
"Contradictory" means he demonstrates the contradiction. "That which... [102]
There is no produced or producing entity, nor anything consisting of substance, quality, or action.
Let such a fruit as that which is produced [by other means] be conceived as the result of obligatory ritual (nityakarman). || 103 ||

By means of [the discussion on] actions, that very [reality] is manifested as being neither effect nor cause. [The author says] "No" [to the objection]. To explain how that is so, he says: "Not a substance," etc.

Because it is distinct from substances and the like, and because it is not produced by them, it is neither effect nor cause; it is something other than the fourfold set beginning with origination (*utpatti*).
The literal meaning is: "Is that fruit called liberation, which is the opposite of [worldly] bondage, to be postulated as the fruit of eternal things? (103)
Or rather, do you perceive some capacity whatsoever belonging to that which has a beginning, wherein action [might reside]?
May such a fruit be ordained; let it be here in accordance with what is right. || 104 ||
He states another alternative with the words "Or rather" (kiṃvā). To the question of how the determination is made in such an investigation, he replies with "Just as" (yathā). || 104 ||
If it must necessarily be postulated as that which motivates human activity, [then this is the case].
It is logical to postulate that the fruit [of action] belongs only to those things which possess origination and so forth. (105)
He shows the conclusion that follows reason with the words "necessarily" (*avaśyam*). For conceptual construction must set aside contradiction;
for even if a contradiction exists, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if one were to still entertain a conceptual construction—this is the sense. || 105 ||
And because presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted precisely there in the conceptualization of liberation.
Since there is no capacity [for action], therefore the conception of liberation is not tenable. || 106 ||

Having raised the objection—"Since it has been stated that the impossibility of the injunction for obligatory rites (nityakarman) leads to the assumption of liberation as its fruit, how can there be such a definitive conclusion?"—he says:
"And because of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). Therein, the word "there" refers to any one of the fruits beginning with origination. || 106 ||
The performance of the obligatory rite [is established] by relying on the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).
It is logical to conceive of liberation [in this way], since no other possibility exists. || 107 ||
[Vol.
3, Page 62] 3 Brāhmaṇam, accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā: 1195.
Although that [knowledge] alone does not postulate liberation as the fruit of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), nevertheless, when combined with the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it does so.
He raises the objection, "It will conceptualize," with the words "of the eternal" (nityasya). || 107 ||
The connection of optional rites with results other than liberation exists because it is so stated in the scriptures.
The connection with obligatory rites must belong to liberation, by the method of elimination.

He states how there is a conclusion by elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) due to the absence of any other result: "From liberation" (*mokṣāt*). He provides the reason: "Because no result is heard in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), and because an injunction without a result is impossible. [Thus it is] "by way of elimination" (*pāriśeṣyataḥ*). || 108 ||
Do not say so; for it is untenable because the manifestation of the fruits of karma is infinite.
By way of the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya), liberation consists of the fruit of karma.
He refutes this, saying: "Not so. || 109 ||
But as for objects of desire for those who long for men, no limit can be established.
For it is likewise [the case] regarding the fruits of action and their means of accomplishment. || 110 ||

He clarifies the statement regarding the infinity of the manifestations of the fruits of action, intended to show that there is no possibility of exhaustion. He says, "The desires of men," etc. Here, "here" refers to the sphere of the fruits of action. The phrase "of objects" is explained as "of the fruits of optional (kāmya) actions. The word "for" (*hi*) is used to corroborate this infinity of fruits with one's own experience. He states, "Likewise," to show that there is no limit to the means of attaining those fruits, just as there is none to the fruits themselves. || 110 ||
Because there is no restriction regarding place, time, and so forth, the desires of persons are infinite.
Likewise, there is [the application] of their means through the pursuit of desired objects in rites performed for specific wishes. || 111 ||

He states the reason for the infinity of the two [desire and its means] with the words "deśa" (place). He states another reason for the infinity of desire with the word "tathā" (so). That is to say, it refers to the distinctions in the superimposition of excellence regarding the means of achieving that—namely, the means of desire. The expression "so" (tathā) indicates infinity. Even though there is a distinction in the results which are the objects of desire due to the distinction between desire and its causes, how can there be a distinction in the actions that are its means? Why should one excellent action alone not accomplish everything desired?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "kāmyā" (desiring). For means are employed after having recollected what is desired;
therefore, when there is a difference in that [object], there is a difference in the means, otherwise the difference in that [object] would result in being accidental—this is the sense. || 111 ||
And because of the diversity among individual beings, due to causes such as place, time, and so forth.
And if that were the case, there would be an infinity of desires and their means.
The method of elimination would not apply even to an omniscient being, because [the objects of knowledge] are infinite.
Nor is the status of being the fruit of karma established through the method of elimination. || 113 ||
Because even liberation is included as a fruit of obligatory rites (nityakarman).
Nevertheless, the establishment [of the object] through the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya) is not tenable here either. || 114 ||
He states another reason for the infinity of desires (*icchā*) and the means to their desired fruits (*iṣyamāṇaphala-tatsādhana*): "In every living being" (*pratiprāṇi*).

Even though there is an infinity of desires and so forth among all living beings due to their diversity based on place and other factors, he asks what follows from this in the present context and replies:

"Thus" (*tathā*). The word "also" (*api*) has the sense of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"). He clarifies the very reason already stated—"that being so"—by the word "infinitude" (*anantatayā*).
Thus, although the causes of the fruits of desire are infinite, since the state of being a fruit of action is common to all of them, liberation is not a fruit of action.

1196 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]—anticipating the objection that the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) is appropriate because [the other options] have been excluded, he says: "And not... He establishes the non-establishment of that [elimination] with: "No... and so forth.

The word "here" (*iha*) refers to liberation (*mokṣa*). The phrase "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) means even though the state of being a fruit of action is equal in all cases, such as heaven and so forth. || 112 || 113 || 114 ||
If it is admitted that liberation also has the nature of being the fruit of obligatory rites (nityakarman), [then...]
Since it belongs to the same class as the effects of karma, how can the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya) apply? || 115 ||

Anticipating the objection that, since the fruit of optional (kāmya) action exists in everything other than liberation, whereas it is absent in liberation, liberation must be established by the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya), he says: "The obligatory (nitya)," etc. (115).
Therefore, there would be an exhaustion of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), because [the fact in question] can be established otherwise as well.
Furthermore, liberation is not accepted here as being any one of these, such as origination and so forth. || 116 ||
Because liberation is eternal, it is contradictory for it to involve origination and so forth.
It is neither something to be produced nor something to be modified, because modification is prohibited. || 117 ||

The conclusion is stated: "By means of *arthāpatti*... This refutes the claim that, since no other possibility remains (*pāriśeṣya*), an *arthāpatti* supported by that [absence] must postulate that eternal injunctions have liberation as their fruit. The meaning is that since the eternal injunctions are justified even by having any one of the four fruits—such as origination (*utpatti*) and so forth—as their result, there is no *arthāpatti* that establishes liberation as their fruit. It is true that the eternal [injunctions] have any one of origination and the rest as their fruit...
One might suspect that liberation (*mokṣa*) is also one of those [categories]; anticipating this, he clarifies what was stated there [in the verse] with the words "nor any one of these.

The phrase "of arising and so forth" refers here to the statements in the treatises on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*). The reason for their being contradictory is given by the word "eternality" (*nityatva*).

He states another reason for the absence of both being produced (*utpādyatva*) and being modified (*vikāryatva*) with the word "no. This is because of the prohibition of modification in both Śruti and Smṛti.
The remainder. || 116 || 117 ||
Nor is liberation desired as something to be refined, like rice in a vessel or similar objects.
Nor is it attainable because it lacks any means of attainment, owing to its nature as pure inwardness alone. || 118 ||

Another reason for the absence of being something to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is stated: "The rice-grains," and so forth. Another reason for the absence of being something to be attained (*āpya*) is stated: "Nor even," and so forth. || 118 ||
And because the eternal is distinct from all actions for that reason.
If it is argued that the effect must likewise exist because it conforms to its cause, [we reply: so be it. || 119 ||

He raises an objection based on the designation [of the act] as "eternal" (nitya), arguing that because the obligatory daily rites such as the Agnihotra are distinct from other types of ritual acts, their fruit must also be eternal; thus, by virtue of the name, he questions [the claim]: "Of the eternal... (nityasya). || 119 ||
Why should there not be a commonality of characteristics [between them] due to their similarity in being objects of action?
Let it be stated that [the obligatory rite] has as its fruit that which is eternal, [as opposed to] the fruits of rites performed for specific desires.
He provides a resolution by means of another designation: "Not so," [verse 120].
