3, page 64] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1197
If it is argued that there is a distinction because of the cause, we say no, because the effect must be similar to its cause.
Why should [the self] not be eternal, like the *mānavī* and other [entities], while possessing its own characteristics? (121)

One might object: "There is no distinction between the Agnihotra and other such rites on the basis of their designation as 'obligatory' (nitya), by which one could claim that they differ from other rites designated as 'occasional' (kāmya) in terms of having fruits; rather, [the distinction] is due to the force of conditions such as being alive. To this he replies: "Even though there is a distinction caused by the [different] conditions, obligatory rites do not have liberation as their fruit, because they share the same fruit as occasional rites and thus do not have that [liberation] as their fruit."

"No. To the question of how their status as being equally *naimittika* (contingent) is established, he says: "kṣāma," etc. The meaning of this is as follows: In the injunction, "If the fire of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should burn his house, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa*) to Agni Kṣāmavat," the word "should burn" (*dahet*)—being a prescriptive suffix (*vidhi-vibhakti*) joined with the well-known referential pronoun "yaḥ" (*yasya*)—indicates the occasion (*nimitta*) known as the burning of the house; thus, [the text continues] with "to Agni Kṣāmavat, a cake... and so forth.

By the word "dinā," the *kṣāmavatī* [offering] is prescribed. In the passage, "He whose two oblations (*havir*) should meet with misfortune (*ārti*) must offer a five-platter (*pañcaśarāva*) of rice for Indra," the phrase "should meet with misfortune" (*ārddhet*)—by means of the injunctive suffix (*vidhivibhakti*)—announces the misfortune of the oblation as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the offering that is about to be enjoined by the injunction "he should offer" (*nirvapet*), and thus the offering itself is enjoined.
Similarly, in "He offers when [the vessel] is broken; he offers when [the grain] has spilled," and "Now, Varuṇa seizes that sacrifice of him whose two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are scorched."
When he takes that oblation, then that very oblation should be completed; for it is said, "The sacrifice is indeed the expiation for the sacrifice.

Thus, an expiation has been prescribed for causes such as a breakage, yet that [expiation] does not have liberation as its fruit. Likewise, even when there is a difference in the cause, the constant fruit is not liberation. || 121 ||
For it cannot be established [as such] because of its distinctness from the eyes of worldly beings.
In some cases, those with owl-like vision perceive taste and other qualities even from what is not a visible form.
He provides an illustration for the point that obligatory ritual (*nitya-karma*), although distinct from other types of action, does not have liberation as its fruit: "For not... (verse 122).
The meaning is: "because it is formless, [and thus] devoid of that [liberation]."
In the world, the capacity to perceive tastes and so forth is not observed in the eye.
Therefore, because its capacity is not apprehended, it is not conceived as being contradictory. || 123 ||
In this regard, the reason is stated: "from taste and so forth. The remainder of the sense is that the capacity directed toward objects such as taste is contradictory. || 123 ||
The capacity of whatever [cause] is observed to exist in a particular [effect], that capacity belongs to it only in that [effect].
For even if one goes very far away from here, excessive cold is indeed encountered. || 124 ||

How, then, is its capacity established? To this he says: "The capacity. The meaning is that even if one leaves behind humans and goes as far as the owl and other such creatures. How could the eye of an owl and others, which does not depend on light, perform its function like the eye of us and others? To this he says: "In this world. Even for the eye of an owl and others, which does not depend on light, it is only with respect to its own object, such as color-form (*rūpa*), etc., [that it functions].

The meaning is that there is no excellence of capacity in [the perception of] rasa and so forth. In this context, the word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to refer back to the reason stated, namely, "because the capacity of the eye is not apprehended. || 124 ||
The activity of karma is constant and certain, like poison, curd, and so forth.
As for what was stated regarding "that which one undertakes," let that too be so within its own domain.
[Vol.
3, page 65] 1198 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter—The Application of the Analogy].

He states the application of the analogy: "Action," etc. Just as the eyes of an owl and other such creatures function without depending on light, so too action, even when conjoined with knowledge, [functions independently].
The meaning is that it is the initiator within its own sphere of activity, being one of the four [causes]. || 125 ||
The statement of the scripture as well, beginning with "By knowledge alone," is likewise [to that effect]. // 126 //
And there is a distinction between one who sacrifices for the gods and one who sacrifices for the self.
Thus it is heard clearly from the words of the Śruti: "So they say. (127)

Having raised the objection that the conjunction with knowledge (*vidyā*) would be useless, and considering that this is not so because it is useful for initiating a specific result, he states the authority for this: "That which indeed... Following the principle that action conjoined with knowledge produces a specific result, he cites the Śatapatha Śruti: "The sacrificer to the gods... Beginning with "They say," from the passage starting "The sacrificer to the gods is better than the sacrificer to the self," [the author speaks] regarding the performer of optional rites (*kāmya-kartṛ*).

The meaning is that the distinction of the "sacrificer for the Self" (ātmayājī)—who performs ritual action for the sake of self-purification rather than from a desire for rewards from the gods—is thus clearly indicated as being superior. Furthermore, the sense is that the sacrificer for the Self is distinguished above all performers of sacrifices, and this is also supported by the compendium of Smṛti texts.
Manu also stated in another system of thought that one who sacrifices to the Self is an "ātmayājī."
And even there, seeing with equanimity, he becomes a sacrificer to the Self.
This is either a praise of equal vision, or it is based on what occurred in the past.
But surely Manu, beginning with "Learn this rule of action leading to the supreme good for a Brahmin," continues:
"The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, and restraint of the senses..."
Non-violence and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good.
Having thus described specific types of ritual action with these and other words,
and having instructed as follows:
"Vedic ritual action is to be known as always more conducive to the highest good."
"Perceiving the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self,
he who sacrifices to the Self indeed attains self-sovereignty."

By saying this, it is intended that action conjoined with knowledge has liberation as its fruit; therefore, he says: "Also by Manu. The meaning is that if a person, being unmodified, were to see [all things] equally, then, having become one with the Supreme Self, he becomes self-ruling (*svarāṭ*); thus, what is intended here is a praise of the knowledge of the Self. He provides another interpretation for the term *ātmayājī* (one who sacrifices to the Self) when it possesses the sense of "seeing another": "Or else... [the beings...].
The meaning is that the term "one who sacrifices for oneself" (ātmayājī) refers to the wise woman, in relation to her previous state. || 128 ||
He who performs action according to the prescribed rule for the sake of self-purification.
"He who sacrifices to the Self"—it is he indeed who is referred to here by Manu. (129)
He elaborates upon this: "The Self," etc. By the word "here" (*iha*), there is the citation of the passage beginning with "seeing as equal," and so forth. 129.
[Vol. 3, page 66]
3 Brāhmaṇa: For a person of well-refined intellect, together with the aforementioned ritual acts—[this is] accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
In this world or in the next, knowledge that certainly effects liberation arises. || 130 ||
Having stated the intention of Manu, he explains that very statement right there with the words "well-purified" (*susaṃskṛta*).

What is intended by this statement of Manu is that for one whose intellect is purified by actions pertaining either to this world or the next, knowledge in the form of a single essence arises through the power of hearing and so forth, and this results in liberation.
The meaning is that this is because it was stated by that very same [author]: "By means of the great sacrifices and the [other] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman. || 130 ||
Furthermore:
"Brahmā [is established] from the words of the creators of the universe and from the excellence of the gods."
Manu himself directly demonstrates that the bliss of the elements is imperishable. || 131 ||
"Know that sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities (guṇas) of the self.
Having introduced this, [it continues]:
"Sattva is knowledge, tamas is ignorance, and passion and aversion are recorded as rajas."
Having thus stated their characteristics and so forth, [the author says]:
"I shall explain in its entirety the arising of the fruits of those three qualities— whether superior, middling, or inferior."
Having thus analyzed and described the arising of those fruits with these and other verses—
“This secondary course of transmigration is to be understood as threefold and indeed of three kinds:
inferior, middling, and superior, according to the specific nature of one's actions and knowledge”—

Having thus declared the threefold division, and having taught the threefold paths of the *tāmasī* and *rājasī* types, and having described the inferior and middling paths of the *sāttvikī* type, he sets forth that very same [path] as the supreme by means of the passage beginning with "Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat," and so forth.
“Thus has been fully described the threefold cycle of karma pertaining to all living beings,
which consists of the three types of action in their threefold manner.”
Concluding thus, Manu considers that action joined with knowledge has only saṃsāra as its fruit; so he says: "Brahman...
Furthermore:
"Vedic action is of two kinds: active (pravṛtta) and withdrawn (nivṛtta)."
Desire-driven action, whether for results in this world or the next, is described here as "pravṛtta" (active engagement).
Action performed without desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as the path of cessation (nivṛtti). By practicing active (pravṛtta) action, one attains equality in power with the gods.
[Vol. 3, p. 67] 1200 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]:

Thus, beyond the attainment of sovereignty similar to that of the deities who are the fruits of ritual action, there is the combined [attainment] among the five elements, both manifest and unmanifest.

"One who, while remaining [in this world], practices [the path] with dependence, even though he possesses destruction, attains the five elements"—thus [the scripture] states directly. To the objection that this does not mean liberation is the fruit of the combination [of knowledge and action], he says: "O Deva" (deva). || 131 ||
But those who read the text as "atyeti" are unwise.
Because it is tainted by the faults already mentioned, there is no transcendence of suffering through any means other than awakening.

If it be argued that liberation alone is intended [as the result] from the performance of the combined practice—on the basis of the reading "but one who serves the withdrawn [state] transcends the five elements"—the author replies to that:
"But as for 'transcends'... This indicates the contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "There is no other path for going.

Furthermore, there is no transcendence of the elements through action, because action is not opposed to them; therefore, since that [transcendence] is established through knowledge alone, [the combination is not intended].
Intending that the reading "he goes even to the elements" (*bhūtāny apyeti*) is to be understood as following from the impossibility of accumulation (*caya*), he says: "as stated.
This very state of being corrupted by the aforementioned defects consists in the fact that karma is not opposed to delusion and its effects. || 132 ||
The subsequent commentary, being of clear meaning, does not require further explanation.
Therefore, the subsequent portion of the text is now correctly explained.

Furthermore, after the commentary beginning with "Moreover" (*kiṃcānyat*) has been explained, and when the occasion for explaining the commentary beginning with "And not" (*na ca*) arises, he says: "It is clear" (*spaṣṭā*). [The opponent objects: "If it is clear, then it need not be explained; in that case, it would be more appropriate to conclude the Brāhmaṇa right here. What is the purpose of the subsequent textual section? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] proceeds to explain the words of the Brāhmaṇa, which was commenced in order to demonstrate that all fruit of action is of the nature of *saṃsāra*. Relying upon that commentary on the words of the text...
He states the subsequent composition [beginning] with "yataḥ" (since). || 133 ||
For that which instigates the bondage of the one to be bound is what has been declared here.
In this context, action alone is primary, while everything else is subordinate.

In order to state that all action—whether accumulated or unaccumulated—is for the purpose of bondage, while right knowledge alone is for the purpose of liberation, [the author] says "Brāhmaṇa. Having thus stated the connection by way of the inquiry, he recalls what has preceded so that there may be no forgetfulness due to the intervention of the inquiry. Prayo—

Regarding the word "jyāyasaḥ": the particle *hi* (for) indicates that it necessarily requires an efficient cause (*prayojaka*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the passage in the Ārtabhāga section. What is that efficient cause? For when many things converge, there is no determination of their specific distinctions; to this he replies: "by way of predominance. The word "here" (*iha*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). As for the question of how one can be certain that time and so forth are not also efficient causes, he replies: "because it is other than those. || 134 ||
And that action is, by its very nature, both determinate and indeterminate.
However, the pervasive pervasion of that which is delimited has already been explained previously.
The unbounded pervasiveness is declared by means of the question posed by Bhujyu.

He recalls the twofold nature of action (*karman*)—as that which is excluded and that which is included—by the words "paricchinna" (limited). Among these, it has already been shown in the *Udgītha* section that the pervasion of excluded action extends from the sun up to the limit of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); thus, he says "paricchinnasya" (of the limited) for the purpose of leaving [only] the object to be explained. Having summarized what has occurred, he states the purport of the Brāhmaṇa: "apari... (unlimited...).
[The word] *cchiti* || 135 || 136 ||

3, Page 68] 3 Brāhmaṇam. Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
"Existing both outside and inside the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), in the form of the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual parts (*vyaṣṭi*)."
The pervasion of Hiraṇyagarbha is proclaimed for the sake of knowing bondage. || 137 ||

Regarding the statement that the pervasion of both kinds of karma is being described, one might ask: "To what purpose does this serve? For it does not assist either in worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) or in liberation (*apavarga*.
To this, he replies: "From the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). For bondage is of this extent—neither more nor less—and thus [the author] excludes other possibilities.

The pervasion of the two kinds of karma is stated for the purpose of delimiting the measure of bondage; and the meaning is that such delimitation, by means of dispassion (*vairāgya*), is the cause of liberation. || 137 ||
In order to demonstrate the disparity [between the two], for the sake of generating fear regarding the question.
The story of Bhujyu is told with effort for the sake of the opponent's understanding. (138)

Anticipating the objection—"Even though the Brahmin had proceeded in this manner, why does Bhujyu relate his own completed story?"—the author says: "Because of the disparity," and so forth. The disparity (*vaiṣamya*) refers to the fact that the subject matter of the question regarding the fruits of the vision of the Self as both the aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) is extraordinary (*alaukika*).

For the sake of understanding that, Bhujyu relates his completed story; and furthermore, it serves to delude Yājñavalkya’s intellect during the debate (*jalpa*), so that [Bhujyu] may achieve victory over his opponent.

The meaning is that it is because [the teacher] desires the pupil's victory. By the word "with effort," it is indicated that the narration of the story serves as an introduction (upodghāta). || 138 ||
When we questioned him about the ends of the worlds, we asked that very thing.
At that time, O Gandharva, who were those who became his attendants? || 139 ||
Having stated the purport of the two stories of the Brāhmaṇas, he explains the words of the passage beginning with "Then, when... (*atha yadā...*). Regarding the phrase "of the worlds" (*lokānām*):

the meaning of the word *atha* there is "time. When many people, having set out for the purpose of knowing the dimensions of the universe, were cutting themselves down to size, they asked a Gandharva about the destination of the performers of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), saying, "Where did the Pārikṣitas go? And he—

The meaning is that since the Gandharvas imparted all this knowledge to us, your claim that "we have not obtained that [knowledge]" constitutes a failure of your proposition; for when questioned on that point, you were unable to provide an answer. || 139 ||
By using an expression with an unestablished name, for the purpose of achieving the confusion of the opponent.
Bhujyu says that they were performers of the horse sacrifice, the sons of Parikṣit.

Anticipating the objection—"If it is the destination of those who have performed the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) that you wish to inquire about here, why do you employ an unfamiliar designation instead of their well-known name?"—the author says: "Unfamiliar... It should be understood that the *pārikṣitas* are those who performed the horse-sacrifice known as *parikṣit*, so called because by it everything, including the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), is completely destroyed (*paritaḥ kṣīyate*). || 140 ||
The question, "Who were those Pārikṣitas? has been stated here three times.
This utility of the threefold statement is now described in detail according to its divisions. || 141 ||

One might raise the objection that the statement "Where were the Pārikṣitas? is redundant because it is a repetition of what has already been said three times. The word "Pārikṣitas" refers to the subject matter under discussion here. The answer is: "Because it was stated three times. (141)
The first statement may be for the purpose of a question, while the subsequent one is for the purpose of a reply.
One should state that the third [speech] was addressed to Yājñavalkya, and thus all three speeches have been declared.
He shows the application by way of division: "Regarding the meaning of the question," etc. First, [the question is]: "Where were those Pārikṣitas? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.1).
[Volume 3, page 69]

In Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Three, verse 1202: The first statement is for the purpose of posing a question to the Gandharva, while the second is for the purpose of providing a corresponding answer. That which was asked of the Gandharva—namely, "Who were those who became the Pārikṣitas?"—its reply is intended to be expressed there: "He told us everything."
The meaning is that there is no tautology because of the distinction made by the threefold statement, wherein the third [statement] has the purpose of posing a question to the Sage. || 142 ||
The path measured by the movement of the sun's chariot during the day and night is as follows:
To that extent, it is pervaded by the rays of the sun multiplied thirty-two times.
The Sage, desiring to explain their movement, defines the dimensions of the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*). Regarding that, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "thirty-two" and so forth.
[He says] "by the sun": the distance traversed by the chariot of the sun in one day and night is multiplied by thirty-two;
the region pervaded by its rays, together with the region pervaded by the rays of the moon, is called "the earth."
"As far as the earth is illuminated by the rays of the sun and the moon— including its oceans, rivers, and mountains— so far is it traditionally held to extend."
Such is the intended meaning. || 143 ||
In thirty-two days and nights, as much space as the sun traverses while moving across the sky, that much distance is covered by the light propagated by the lamp.
This great body of Vairāja is the instrument of the deities.

Regarding the phrase "this world" (*ayaṃ loka*), he explains the term *loka*. By the expression "with thirty-two," he means that which is uttered, spoken of, or made the object of the word *loka*—that is, the sound "world. He describes the nature of this world as being encircled by the Lokāloka mountain. He states that its form is the body. Relying on such scriptural passages as "Fire is the head," he qualifies it as a deity (*devatā*). Its greatness [is as follows]:...
Its nature is that of a gross aggregate.
This region alone, however, provides the means for the accomplishment of the enjoyments of living beings.
And the pervasion of the deities beginning with Agni is considered to be of this extent. || 145 ||

He shows that this very [world] is the ground of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*) with the words "only this much. By the qualification "of living beings," he anticipates the doubt that the pervasion by the deity might exist elsewhere than there, and thus says: "fire and so forth. (141)
Beyond the world is the lightless realm, devoid of all living beings;
it extends twice as far as the world previously measured, encompassing the earth.
He states that its nature is light with the words "from the world" (*lokāt*). He precludes its being a place of enjoyment with the word "all" (*sarva*).

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "it encompasses all around" (*taṃ samantam*) with the word "it pervades" (*paryeti*). There is no contradiction with the statement beginning "twice the size of the world" (*lokaparimāṇād dviguṇaparimāṇā pṛthivī*), because that refers to a specific portion of it, whereas this [light] pervades the world on all sides.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the passage beginning "nor [the light] of the sun and moon," because that refers to a particular part of it.
The state of being. || 146 ||
The region of the Lokāloka mountain is devoid of all living beings.
The ocean stands twice as large as the earth beyond it. || 147 ||
Revealing what was stated in the passage "beyond this world" (lokāt param), he clarifies that this portion of the earth which encircles the world serves as the ground for its vast expanse.
Regarding the word "loke" (in the world): he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "tām" (her) and so forth as "samudra" (the ocean). || 147 ||
Those learned scholars who are knowers of the Purāṇas call it Ghanoda.
Therefore, the shell of the cosmic egg extends everywhere beyond that.
In this regard, he states the consensus of the Paurāṇikas: "Yam" (referring to the verse). For it is said:
"The ocean of nectar is situated all around this cosmic egg."
Supported on all sides by dense water, it remains stationary;
outside the dense water, it extends horizontally and upwards in a circular form.
"Being maintained on all sides, it remains with dense brilliance;
like a ball of iron, the fire stands circular in shape on every side."
He provides the introductory context for the passage beginning with "tadyāvatī" (to that extent) by saying "brahmāṇḍa" (the cosmic egg). This means "from that ocean designated as 'ghanoda'. || 148 ||
Immediately after the earth, the ocean itself is heard mentioned in the Veda.
But in the Purāṇa, regarding what is outside the cosmic egg, there is a contradiction wherein the Smṛti is sublated.

But do not the Paurāṇikas maintain that there is an ocean called Ghanoda outside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and that many other cosmic eggs situated within it undergo the process of rising and sinking? For it has been said:
"O one of great intelligence, from the elements arises the egg, which is vast and rests upon the waters."
Thus, by means of this cosmic shell [of the universe], [it extends] across, upwards, and likewise downwards.
"Just as the seed of a wood-apple (kapittha) is completely enveloped on all sides by its husk, so too, Maitreya, is the egg (aṇḍa) enveloped by water ten times greater [in volume]. Thus it is said.
How, then, is there agreement with the Purāṇas in this matter? To that he says: "The earth," and so forth.

If it is heard [in the Śruti] that after the earth there is an ocean within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa), then there would be a mutual contradiction between the Śruti and the Smṛti, since the Purāṇa speaks of it being outside. Anticipating this objection, he says: "There is no contradiction. The meaning of this is: [just as in the case of] "One should wrap the entire Audumbarī post... [the two texts are reconciled].

There arises a doubt as to whether the Smṛti rule—"one should sing the Udgītha while touching the Audumbarī post"—is contradicted by the Śruti, and if so, whether it is rooted in Śruti or rooted in error.

In this context, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is as follows: because the agent is the same, one might infer a Śruti for this Smṛti just as in the case of the Aṣṭakā and other Smṛtis; however, since there is a contradiction between the inferred Śruti and the perceived Śruti, and since they are not equal in status due to being respectively perceptible and imperceptible, a choice (vikalpa) between them is impossible, and thus both lack authority. This is the prima facie view regarding the contradiction with the perceived Śruti.

Just as no inference for "non-hotness" arises regarding fire, so too, by distinguishing that the Smṛtis such as the *Aṣṭakā* are rooted in Śruti while Smṛtis contrary to them are rooted in error, it was established in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*—in the section on contradiction (*virodha*) under the sūtra "But in case of contradiction, there would be non-reliance; for when [the contradiction] is absent, there is inference"—that the Smṛti regarding the "veiling of all [the sacrificial post]" is sublated by the Śruti regarding touching. Likewise here, the Purāṇic statement is to be sublated in the event of contradiction with Śruti.
Thus [it is said]. || 149 ||
1204 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:
This commentary is now undertaken here upon the path of those who have performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
And this can be stated thus, based on the measurement of the Lokāloka mountain and so forth. || 150 ||

Anticipating the objection—"If the destination of those who perform the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is what is intended to be expressed here, then let that alone be stated; what is the use of a description of the universe (*bhuvanakośa*)?"—he says:

"The explanation" (*vyākhyā*). Although the explanation of the path for those who perform the horse-sacrifice was indeed the subject under discussion in the Śruti, nevertheless, by determining the dimensions of the worlds (*loka*), the non-worlds (*aloka*), the Lokāloka mountain, the earth, and so forth, through the investigation of the cosmic structure (*bhuvanakośa*), that [destination] can be ascertained. Therefore—
The meaning is that those words are applicable to the subject at hand. || 150 ||
According to the aforementioned measure, with the intention of describing the practice of meditation.
Therefore, there is a statement regarding the dimensions of the effects, such as the Lokāloka mountain and others. || 151 ||

He states the fruit [of meditation] by means of another method, based on the description of the *bhuvanakośa* (the cosmic egg), beginning with the words "as stated. The meaning is that the scriptural passage beginning with "thirty-two" is intended for meditation (*dhyāna*) upon the thread-soul (*ātmasūtra*) of the world—including the light, the world-and-non-world (*lokāloka*), and the earth situated within it—according to the dimensions already described; therefore, the discourse on the *bhuvanakośa* is purposeful. || 151 ||
This world indeed exists with the dimensions as previously described.
This is the expansion of Virāj, pervaded by the light of the sun. || 152 ||
He restates the meaning of the phrase "this world" with the words "it exists. The word *bhānu* (light) is also an elliptical designation for the moon. || 112 ||
Emerging from that world, the earth stands doubled in size;
and the ocean, twice as large as the earth on all sides, stands surrounding it. (153)
He restates the meaning of the passage beginning with "that" [tam] as follows: "From that" (tataḥ). || 113 ||
Having crossed that ocean, whatever else lies beyond it.
Now, an illustrative comparison is being made for that which is to be understood. || 154 ||

He introduces the passage beginning with "tadyāvatī kṣurasya" (as large as the edge of a razor). Regarding the word "tam": the meaning is that this [simile] expresses an analogy for the fissure in the joint of the shell of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍakapāla*), which is required for the movement [of the soul] toward that destination which lies beyond the cosmic egg, outside the world and so forth, having transcended the ocean under discussion. || 154 ||
The space situated within the joints of the skull is [to be understood] by implication according to its measurement.
Whatever has been stated here by way of comparison is now being elucidated by this [verse]. (155)

One might object: "The phrase 'that much' refers only to the internal space of the ether (ākāśa) and not to the cavity of the shell [of the cosmic egg], as there is no restrictive evidence for the latter; therefore, this comparison does not apply to it. Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "The shell... Since nothing extremely subtle can be logically established beyond the ocean other than the cavity of the shell of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa), the ether situated precisely at the junction of the shell of the cosmic egg is what is referred to by the words "that much" and so forth. Therefore, it is indeed that which is situated at the junction.

The meaning is that, by the scriptural mention of the sky as an illustration, it is clarified as being characterized by a specific dimension; there is no other space [implied], because that would contradict logical necessity (*arthāpatti*) and so forth. || 155 ||
By that [means], he [led] the Pārikṣitas, who had attained the state of being the Self of the altar (cityātman), by his own [power].
Having established it within, the vital breath leads it toward both the state of totality and individuality.
He states what is intended by the verse beginning with "tān indra," using the word "tena" (by that). || 196 ||
In this context, the Self of consciousness (cittātmā) may be the "fair-winged one" (suparṇa), or else it is said to be the Self of the sun (ādityātmā).
For from this place we have arrived by the path described by Āditya. || 157 ||
He states the meaning of the word *suparṇa*: "In this sentence... [he says]. Regarding the point that either the Virāj or the Sūtra might be the *suparṇa*, he provides the reason:

"This... [he says]. Since the capacity to lead those who have reached the vicinity of the shell of the cosmic egg—having attained the world of Brahman by the path described as beginning with light—to the outside belongs only to the Sūtra and the Virāj, the meaning is that one or the other of these two alone is the *suparṇa*. || 117 ||
Thus Agni and Indra [carried] all the Pārikṣitas along the path of the sky.
Having extracted it from the egg, he gave it to Vāyu, who possesses a subtle form.

One might object: "Even though the power of the eye (the capacity for seeing) pervades both inside and outside the *sūtra*, since the *virāj* exists only within [the body], how can that power belong to it?

Anticipating this doubt, the author explains the meaning of the word "Indra" and states the significance of the phrase "he gave them to Vāyu. He says: "Thus... Because Indra, who consists of the *city* (the sacrificial altar) and takes the form of the *virāj-sūtra*, possesses the fitness of being the one who causes [the breath] to go outward, he gave them to Vāyu; such is the meaning. Now, as for the *sūtra*...

Regarding the statement that "the wind [is] indeed the thread (*sūtra*) of the wind, O Gautama," because of this scriptural testimony of identity, one might ask: how could the Thread-Self (*sūtrātman*), having brought them out from the external egg, have bestowed those winds?

To this, he says: "Subtle... [and so on]. [He means: from the Thread, which possesses the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), [he brought forth] that which possesses the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), his own self...
The sense is that it is indeed appropriate for those possessing both action and knowledge to direct their gaze toward the wind. || 158 ||
In this context, Agni is said to be the deity of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
And this encasement by wind, which has been described here as something unprecedented; 159.

Now, having raised the doubt as to how Indra—despite being described as such—can be the bestower of the fruit for those who perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice, the author clarifies the meaning of the word "Agni" in the context at hand: "The Aśvamedha... Here, the word "here" refers to the sentence under discussion. If it is argued that the deity in the form of Agni is what is denoted by the term "unseen potency" (*apūrva*) produced by the Aśvamedha, and that therefore he alone should be the giver of the fruit according to the principle "Jaimini [holds] that merit [is the cause]," rendering Vāyu redundant, the author says:
Regarding "the envelopment by air": the meaning is that whatever is unprecedented here is indeed the very body of the wind. || 199 ||
Therefore, it is held that the wind itself is the manifestation of a previously non-existent form.
Immediately following this, the function of the unprecedented (apūrva) is now being pointed out. || 160 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the wind (*vāyu*) and the unseen potency (*apūrva*) are distinct—one being the embodied agent and the other the body—it is possible for a single entity alone to bestow the fruit, why then two? He says: "The wind. The meaning is that the unseen potency produced from the horse sacrifice, which manifests its power for the sake of granting the fruit, is indeed the wind itself; thus there is no difference between these two. He states the purport of the passage beginning with "them" (*tān*): "Immediately thereafter," [referring to] the offering made by the performers of the horse sacrifice to the wind.
The word "not" (na) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Effect" (kārya) means the result (phala). || 160 ||
Then Vāyu, having taken up the sons of Parikṣit, established them within his own self.
Having brought them there, he caused those whose sole form was their vital breaths to depart.
1 ga. pūrvade | [vol 3,
page 73] 1206 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Third Adhyāya— ]
Where those who performed the horse sacrifice in former times have gone from here and stand.
The one whose self is wind caused [them] to go for the sake of attaining both the collective and the individual states.

He explains the syllables: "The descendants of Parikṣit. The meaning of the word *atha* (now/then) is the immediate sequence following the offering (*pradāna*), as indicated by the *virāj* meter or the *sūtra*.
In response to the expectation of where he led them, he says: "Therein. By means of meditation (*upāsti*) upon those whose sole form is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they attained the state of gods.

He demonstrates this through such scriptural passages as, "Having become a deity, one attains the state of Vāmā," and so forth. Having restated the path therein, he declares its fruit: "The self of the wind" (vāyvātman). || 161 || 162 ||
That [which occurs] by means of proclaiming the unprecedented fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) ritual.
This narrative, having been set forth, is now completed without remainder. || 163 ||
He states the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) in order to introduce [the passage] beginning with "Thus" (*evam*), etc., [with the words] "The horse-sacrifice" (*aśvamedha*). || 163 ||
Now, the Śruti itself has proclaimed the remainder of the answer.
Or else, it is the very statement of Yājñavalkya that [is true], namely the words: "It is exactly so. (164)
Therefore, one should cite the sentence beginning with "tasmāt" and indicate it as being from the Śruti.
That Gandharva, filled with great wonder, praised Vāyu alone. || 165 ||

Anticipating the objection, "If the narrative (ākhyāyikā) is concluded, what is the purpose of what follows?", he says: "By means of the question," etc. The meaning is this: when it is merely stated that Vāyu led even the moderns to that place where the ancient performers of the Aśvamedha sacrifice had gone, there arises a desire to know where those ancients resided.

It is to satisfy this inquiry that the Śruti itself, through its own voice, provides the specific detail—the remainder of the current question beginning with "Where" and so forth—by saying "Thus" and so on.
He joins those syllables [as follows]: "Vāyu" (wind). 164 || 169 ||
Since nothing other than the wind exists outside, there is no exterior apart from it.
The movement of the deity is from that [wind]; therefore, Vāyu is greater than Anila. || 166 ||
To the question, "Even though fire and the other elements are present, why praise Vāyu alone? he says: "Vāyum.

Since there is no movement of any other deity outside or inside the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) as there is for Vāyu, but rather [movement] only within the egg, the meaning is that among the deities, Vāyu alone is the greatest; therefore, he praises him. || 166 ||
Since this is so, it should be understood that it is indeed wind and nothing else.
Thus, through individual manifestation (vyaṣṭi) and collective manifestation (samaṣṭi), he exists both within and outside the cosmic egg.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore" (tasmāt) as follows: "Since... Because it is praised for being greater than air, that very [element] is the aggregate (samaṣṭi) through its external pervasion and the individual (vyaṣṭi) through its internal pervasion; this is the meaning. The explanation of the terms "individual" and "aggregate" begins with "the egg" (aṇḍa), and so forth. || 167 ||
Pervasion in its specific form is designated as "individual manifestation" (vyaṣṭi).
In its general form and as a collective whole, the wind itself exists in two ways. || 168 ||
1 kha. 'riha ca | [vol 3, page 74] 6 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 1207.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "vāyureva" (only air) as follows: "pervasion" (vyāpti). The connection with what precedes is that it refers to pervasion in a general sense. Having stated the meaning of the individual words, he states the meaning of the sentence: "vāyureva. || 168 ||
Some entity is perceived here in this world, consisting of both the mobile and the immobile.
Whether in general or in particular, it is indeed the wind that is consecrated. || 169 ||
Anticipating the objection that since other things also consist of both [aspects], how can there be such a restriction, he says: "The reality... (119).
Nor is there any other entity besides wind [to be established] by means of either a universal or a particular.
"Or rather, the connection is air alone," according to this restrictive statement. (170)
Anticipating the question, "How is this meaning established? he says, "By virtue of the restriction," beginning with the words "not" (na), etc. (verse 170).
This praise would belong to the Lord [Śiva] alone, in the exclusion of connection with others.
But the exclusion of non-connection is not accepted as such excellence. || 171 ||

Now, [the author] says "no" to the view that this might be intended even by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*): "other," etc. "Such" means possessing excellence produced by the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). || 171 ||
This is the summary and detailed exposition of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The greatness of one endowed with knowledge has been revealed by the Śruti out of its own wonder.

Anticipating the objection that the description of wind as having a dual nature is irrelevant to the answer to the question at hand, and that praise for it is therefore futile, he says "Aśva... [etc.], implying that this is not so because the fruit of the specific Aśvamedha sacrifice itself is what is being stated by the Śruti. By departing from the narrative (ākhyāyikā) and speaking in its own voice, the Śruti declares the aforementioned greatness; thus, he indicates that such is the purport of that passage.
"Out of agitation," [it is said]. || 172 ||
He who has taken refuge in the Self as the wind, which exists in both collective and individual forms.
He paints death once again; he thus returns to death as his own self.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 6027.
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa, the Bhujyu Brāhmaṇa, of the third chapter in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣyavārtika*. 3.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "What else... as follows: "The aggregate," etc. He provides the reason why the worshiper, having died once, does not take on a body for further death: "Death," etc. (173)
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa, the Bhujyu Brāhmaṇa, of the third chapter in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
1. Let this be observed.
[Vol. 3, p. 75] 1208 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter—]
Now begins the fourth Brāhmaṇa.
The task of the realization of the oneness of the Self has been explained in its entirety.
Now, the subsequent section is introduced for the purpose of destroying that very root. || 1 ||

He summarizes and follows up for the sake of the three Brāhmaṇas with the words "aikātmya" (oneness of self). With the phrase "tanmūla" (having that as its root), he promises the commencement of the subsequent six Brāhmaṇas for the purpose of the knowledge that destroys ignorance, which is the root of all evil. The meaning of the word "atha" (now/therefore) is that once evil has been described, there arises a need for its cause and the means to destroy it. The word "ūrdhvam" (afterwards) serves to exclude the reference to the immediately preceding Brāhmaṇa alone. || 1 ||
Being engaged in merit and demerit, he is bound by the fetters of grasping and attachment.
He who wanders incessantly through the cycle of rebirth from Brahmā down to a stationary pillar is one of deluded intellect.
Thus has this supreme excellence been described, and the merit thereof has been proclaimed.
The subsequent section is introduced to determine whether one who desires liberation exists or does not exist.

Having stated the connection for the remainder of the chapter, he recounts the preceding narrative in order to explain the meaning of the Upastabrāhmaṇa. [The word] "puṇya" [refers as follows]: He who, through ignorance, has superimposed the state of being a mother, is possessed by ignorance and the like, is seized by the graspers (graha) and over-graspers (atigraha), and is born and dies in various wombs, is always bound; this was previously stated, and it was also said that the fruit of action belongs only to the transmigrator—this is the meaning. [This is] the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa.

He says: "one who desires liberation" (*mumukṣu*). The meaning is that here the referent of "thou" (*tvam-artha*)—the witness of the mother (the intellect), through which the cycle of transmigratory existence is superimposed upon the Self—is determined as one who desires liberation. || 2 || 3 ||
Because it is not distinct from the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and sensation.
For when its existence is established, one strives for its liberation. || 4 ||

Liberation is required by one who desires liberation (mumukṣu), and it must be explained; however, the determination of its existence is not self-evident. Therefore, he says: "The body... [and so forth]. Sensations consist of suffering and the like, which are modifications of the intellect (dhīvṛtti). Once the existence of the Witness (sākṣin) as distinct from the witnessed has been established, effort toward liberation from that [bondage] becomes possible; thus, the meaning is that His existence must be stated. || 4 ||
Those whose [existence] is understood through scripture as pertaining to the future world.
For them, O wise one, this undertaking is indeed already accomplished.

To whom, then, is it said that there is a state of being distinct from the body and an existence [therein]—to the mother or to someone else? It cannot be the first, because her existence is already established by the authority of the *karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section of the Veda); nor can it be the other, because one who is unestablished does not enter the intellect and thus cannot be made known. Anticipating this objection, he accepts the first flaw [by stating]: "He will be" (*bhaviṣyat*). [This refers to] the agent of the afterlife, distinct from the gross body and so forth.

The meaning is that this Brāhmaṇa is not intended for those for whom [the existence of] the knower is already established by the force of the section itself, because it is already established for them. || 5 ||
"Because prior to the establishment of the agent-self, [the self] is not distinct from the intellect and so forth."
The self as witness shall now be described according to what is seen and what is desired.

He refutes the second objection with the word "katra" (where). Since the mother is established in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) by virtue of her association with the intellect and other faculties—
[as found in] the *Brāhmaṇa* [text], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri, volume 3, page 76, line 4].

The witness is defined in the immediately following Brāhmaṇa as being qualified for knowledge; and it is not the case that he cannot be established because he is unknown, for there is no contradiction in explaining him in a specific form when he is already known in a general sense—as possessing dharma—by virtue of his being the prover of the existence or non-existence of the state of being a mother and so forth. This is the intended meaning. || 6 ||
It is now considered who is a fit subject for the knowledge of Brahman.
For when the object has been determined, instruction becomes meaningful.

The Teacher, by stating "from Brahmā down to a blade of grass" and so forth, has shown that a qualified candidate for the teaching is easily found; likewise, the *Nyāyavārttika* states: "He proclaimed this scripture for the sake of the world's tranquility. Anticipating the objection—"In that case, what is the need for deliberation regarding the qualified candidate?"—he says:
"The subject matter. In the passage beginning with "from Brahmā," the mere existence of a qualified candidate is intended, not universal qualification. For it is not the case that...

The sense is that since this scripture has universal eligibility (*sarvādhikāra*), it is therefore appropriate to define the qualified candidate for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*); thus, the Brāhmaṇa section begins. One might object: "In the imparting of knowledge, one will naturally proceed with faith; what is the use of considering the qualifications? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The subject matter" (*viṣaya*). The meaning is that consideration of the qualification is purposeful because that [knowledge] is applicable only toward a qualified person and would otherwise be futile elsewhere. ||7||
It may be the instruction of a Brahmin, or it may be that of one who is not a Brahmin.
Since the state of being Brahman is established by its own nature, [the teaching] regarding Brahman would be purposeless. || 8 ||

He deliberates on who here is the fit candidate for authority: "Or [is it] Brahman? Regarding the first alternative, he states that the instruction would be useless: "Because of the state of being Brahman. (8)
Even by means of a hundred instructions, the state of being Brahman cannot be attained in any way whatsoever.
Since it is not Brahman by its own nature, it is therefore not accepted as being [produced] from that which is non-Brahman.
He states the second [objection]: "In the case of instruction," etc. (9).
Because of the true nature of the single self of all, nothing here is found that is not Brahman.
This is stated in order to prevent the suspicion that there might be a confusion between the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara). || 10 ||

He states that this very position is untenable with the words "of all. The word "śāstram" (the scripture) has the sense of the locative case. It might be argued that the *Brāhmaṇa* is commenced in order to determine the qualified candidate for that [scripture]; to this he replies with the words "kṣetrajña" (the knower of the field). By dispelling the doubt regarding a real difference between the individual self (*pratyak*) and Brahman, the *Brāhmaṇa* is intended to establish the certainty that Brahman itself—when veiled by ignorance—is the fit object for knowledge; and this is not accomplished by the "Brahma-section" (*brahmakaṇḍikā*) alone.
The meaning is that its purpose has already been stated, because this [work] is a commentary upon it. || 10 ||
By the word "yat," the intended reference is to the qualificand.
"Because there is no cognition of the particular from the cognition of the mere universal.
(11) Commencing the explanation of the meaning of the word *padārtha*, he states the meaning of the word *yat*: "By the word *yat*," etc. The reason for this is given as "the universal," etc.
The meaning is that since the word *yat* denotes the substantive (*viśeṣya*), it refers to the perception of the mere universal and the non-perception of the particular. (11)
"All [the words] beginning with 'directly' (sākṣāt) are said to be qualifiers of that."
Because it makes known a specific object, like [the words] "blue," "red," or "lotus.
12.11.0 1kha. 'satattva'.
[Vol.
3, page 77] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:
He states the purport of the five words beginning with "directly" (*sākṣāt*). For what purpose is this division made?

"You are afraid. Regarding the word "distinct" (*viśiṣṭa*): the meaning is that this distinction exists because these words, like the words "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) and so forth, denote a qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*). || 12 ||
And because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words beginning with "that" (*yad*).
The relationship of qualifier and qualified is determined here by the Vedic text itself. || 13 ||

Establishing that [the Veda] conveys a distinguished meaning, he states another reason for the aforementioned division, beginning with "yad" (that which). This means: "by direct statement" (*śrutyā mukhataḥ*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the expression of the word-meanings. The meaning is that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) among words indicates the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*) among their respective meanings. || 13 ||
By the expression "directly" (sākṣāt), a perceptible object is denoted.
The non-perception of the mind [is established] because its [perception] is not seen, as has been refuted. || 14 ||

Having explained the division of the words, he states the meaning of the term "directly" (*sākṣāt*). Regarding the phrase "directly," one might raise the objection that if the referent of the word "that" (*yat*) is intended to be expressed as directly perceived by the word "directly," then it would follow that the Self is held to be graspable by the mind; anticipating this doubt, he says: "of the mind. The reading should be understood as "non-grasping" (*agrahaṇam*). || 14 ||
Or else, it is because when the seer is reached, there is the qualification "directly."
To prevent that undesirable consequence, it is stated that [the knowledge] must be "immediate" (aparokṣa). || 15 ||

He states the meaning of the term *aparokṣāt* (from that which is non-indirect) with the words "Or rather" (*yadi vā*). There is an alternative interpretation based on what is about to be said: since the word *sākṣāt* (directly) would imply a direct perceiver of the visual act, the term *aparokṣāt* is used to exclude that possibility; for its directness is not figurative, as it is known by the Witness (*sākṣin*)—this is the meaning. || 19 ||
Because the first qualification [of the scripture] is established by the fact that it possesses the purpose of the seer, the seeing, and the seen.
The term "not indirect" (aparokṣa) and so forth is stated for the purpose of negating worldly conventions. || 16 ||

He states another alternative view hinted at by the word "or" (*yadi vā*): "The seer," etc. Since in the world the triad beginning with the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) is well known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), when the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used here, that triad might be understood; therefore, to exclude that, the word "immediate" (*aparokṣāt*) is used. The meaning is that the triad is not directly perceived in its primary sense. || 16 ||
For [this applies] to that which has as its object the convergence of the seer, the seeing, and the seen.
"But the word [serves] for negation and for the apprehension of an object that is not distinct from direct perception. (17)

If it is argued that the word "immediate" (*aparokṣāt*) is intended to negate the perception of the triad [of seer, seeing, and seen], then its purpose must be stated; anticipating this objection, he states its purpose by way of restating the negation: "The seer... He uses the word "for" (*hi*) to indicate that [the negation] pertains to the act of seeing whose object is that [triad]. || 17 ||
Because of the negation of the conflation of the seer, the seeing, and the object seen.
Mere perception is established by itself; it constitutes the result of the qualification. || 18 ||

What is the fruit of that negation, which is designated as the apprehension of an undifferentiated object? He states this [in the verse]: "The seer, the seeing... and so forth. The word "seeing" (darśana) is to be understood as referring to the "fusion" (saṃbheda).
The term "immediate" (aparokṣāt) serves as a qualifier. || 18 ||
[Volume 3,
Page 78] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
If that which is called "existent" were indeed of a single nature and possessed the characteristics previously described;
Whether it be non-dual or dual, that is not observed because of the reason already stated. || 19 ||
Therefore, for the sake of establishing non-duality, this term "Brahman" is qualified.
That reality which is unutterable and non-conceptual is called Brahman. || 20 ||

The term *brahma* removes doubt regarding the word "one" (*ekam*). Even if a single, common object is perceived—and even if it appears through the two words as being immediate and of a single essence—nevertheless, because of the three words, it remains undetermined whether that stated object is non-dual or dual; therefore, in order to resolve that doubt and determine that it is indeed non-dual, the referent of the word "that" (*tat*) is qualified by the word *brahma*.
This is the meaning. He explains the word "Brahman" [as follows]: "unrestricted" (avyāvṛta). || 19 || 20 ||
This has resulted in what is not the goal of man, unless it were the Self itself.
Because it has the nature of the self as its object, it is thus qualified as "the self. || 21 ||

He states the intended meaning of that which is taken up by the word "yat" (which) as the substantive, which, having been restated by "yaḥ" (who), is qualified by "ātma" (Self). [The phrase] "not the human goal" means:

since heaven and the like do not possess the nature of the ultimate human goal, the qualification "Self" is applied to the Self for the purpose of determining, through the certainty that Brahman is the Self as previously described, that it possesses the unsurpassed nature of the human goal. This is the meaning. || 21 ||
It is not overwhelmed by a second object, whether of a similar or dissimilar kind.
According to the established doctrine of the Sāṃkhya, that [agency] is obtained as being like that of the Spirit (puṃvat), because of the perception of manifoldness. || 22 ||

He states what is excluded by the other qualification: "of the same class" (*sajātīya*). The meaning is that [the object] is untouched by non-self (*anātman*) in every respect, like the Sāṃkhya concept of the Self (*ātman*), and is denotable by the word "That" (*yat*); thus, it follows that because it is limited (*paricchinna*), it is not Brahman; yet it is not the case that the non-self does not exist at all, because that would contradict the cognition of it. || 22 ||
Therefore, for the purpose of negating that [notion], it is declared to be "the innermost of all."
How can that which is the internal object for all be said to be manifold? || 23 ||

Having restated the doubt, he adopts a qualifying attribute that removes it, beginning with "yataḥ" (from which). Even though [the Self] is the innermost of all, fearing that it might still be limited, he says: "of all" (sarveṣām). || 23 ||
Because the cognitions produced by garlands, serpents, and so forth are of a single uniform nature.
By the obstruction of the inward-facing reality, manifoldness does not remain. || 24 ||
Having stated "of all," one might suspect a contradiction for someone who asserts the absence of limitation; therefore, he says: "Like a garland," and so forth.
Just as the imagined serpents and other things have the single form of the garland, so too for non-selves, the only independent form is the mere inner self (pratyagātman).
Thus, because duality does not remain once one follows the inner self which is the substratum, there is no limitation—this is the meaning. || 24 ||
"For one who has realized the true nature [of reality] regarding entities that consist of existence and non-existence,"
Because it is non-deviating everywhere, the Self must be the innermost of all. || 25 ||

Anticipating the objection, "In the absence of manifold objects, how can there be the state of being within all? he states its justification by taking recourse to imagined duality: "The inner self," etc. (25).
1212 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:
That Brahman which is here distinguished as being directly and immediately present—
And through the inclusion of everything within, there is a connection with the innermost self. || 26 ||

Having stated that a word denoting the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) has other words that provide its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), he states another alternative view, beginning with "yat. In this sentence, the mention of "that which is Brahman" is the statement of the qualificand; its qualifier is "directly and immediately perceived" (*sākṣād-aparokṣāt*). Then, "the Self" (*ya ātmā*) is another qualificand, and its qualifier is "the innermost of all" (*sarvāntaraḥ*). Nor does a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) occur here due to a difference in meaning, because these are intermediate sentences whose scope is limited to the meanings of the individual words.

The meaning is that even though there is a difference [in the constituent parts], there is unity because the great sentence (mahāvākya) has the meaning of the [entire] sentence as its object. || 26 ||
"Directly" means immediately, non-figuratively, and through non-intermediacy.
Thus, this pair is said to be conceivable only within Brahman, which is directed toward the West.

He states the meaning of the two qualifiers of Brahman with the words "directly" (sākṣāt). Now, if both [qualities] are possible only for the Inner Self (pratīc), then how can this be a qualifier of Brahman? To this he says: "Thus, the pair. Although the aforementioned pair is possible only in the Inner Self, nevertheless, it is stated as a qualifier of Brahman; such is the sense. || 27 ||
Likewise, because being the innermost of all is incompatible with existing as a distinct entity.
Because of the non-duality of all things, the self is established in Brahman alone. || 28 ||
How can "being within all" (*sarvāntaratva*) be an attribute of the inner self (*pratīc*), given that it is possible only in non-dual Brahman? To this he replies: "In that way" (*tathā*).
Although, because Brahman is non-dual and because duality is opposed to its very existence, the possibility of "being within all" resides in that [Brahman] alone;
nevertheless, since it abides in the Self as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), it is intended that this [Self] alone possesses that as its attribute. This is the meaning. || 28 ||
[This applies] to the two categories known as Brahman and the Self, which are absolutely identical.
Through the sublation of duality and its associations, the full reality is perceived. || 29 ||

To explain why the qualifiers are presented here in such an inverted order, he says: "Because... (yataḥ). The meaning is that since the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of Brahman and the Self is understood through the sentence by means of the negation of difference and relation—given that the passages beginning with "That which is directly" (*yatsākṣāt*) and "This Self" (*ya ātmā*) constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*)—therefore, the reality as an undivided whole is established through the purport of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*). || 29 ||
Or if there is a conjunction with a single qualificandum by way of being its qualifier.
For [the categories] beginning with "directly" (sākṣāt), there would be mutual independence from one another. || 30 ||

It has been stated that Brahman and the Self are the subjects (*viśeṣya*) while the others are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) as appropriate; now, with the words "directly" (*sākṣāt*) and so forth, he says that everything is both a qualifier and a subject of everything. Regarding the phrase "or rather" (*yadi vā*): the construction is that among the meanings of the words beginning with "directly," there may be a mutual connection between each one as a qualifier and [the others] as the subject. This occurs when each one is taken as the subject.
The reason is: "mutually. || 30 ||
Because they determine a single object and because they conform to one another's meanings.
All qualifiers qualify [the subject], just as [the word] "lotus" [qualifies the word] "blue. || 31 ||
1. ka. kha. by *kṣā* and *bhyāṃ*. 2. kha. *brahmaiveha*; ka.
*brahma ceha*. 3. kha. *'rabhe*. 4. kha. *'mitya'*. [Vol. 3, page 80] 8. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1213.

If it is argued that by stating their mutual independence (*mitho'napekṣatva*), the primary importance (*prādhānya*) of each is indicated, then how is it that they function as mutual qualifiers? To this he replies: "One... and so on. Since these [words] terminate in an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*) by following one another's meanings, they become mutual qualifiers; therefore, just as "blue" and other such qualities qualify "lotus" and the like, so too do these [words] mutually exclude [one another].
The meaning is that it is impossible for two [words] to terminate in a single referent without conforming to distinct referents. || 31 ||
For [the words] "directly" and so forth have their own qualifiers already implied.
By mutually obstructing one another, they abandon their own contradictory meanings. (32)

If it is argued that because there is a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*) based on a difference in meaning, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), and thus terms such as "directly" (*sākṣāt*) and so forth do not have an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*), the author states the manner in which the sentence conveys its own meaning to address this doubt: "Upātta... [and so on]. Terms such as "directly" are connected with their respective qualificands; in accordance with those respective qualificands, by means of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), they abandon their own internal parts that are incompatible with the connection to the sentence-meaning, and thus [convey] the undivided [meaning].

The meaning is that they culminate in the sense of being impartite (akhaṇḍārtha). The word "hi" is used to state that their status as having an impartite meaning is necessary due to the function of indication (lakṣaṇā) and the overall purport (tātparya) of the sentence. || 32 ||
By means of the path that does not abandon one's own welfare, through the subduing of various associations.

By the very birth of the intellect that realizes the true nature of the Self— which is the cause for destroying the delusion of difference— one attains through the hearing of the words what is inherently unmeasurable, even though it was already attained.

One might raise the objection: "If the meaning of the sentence is indicated by words such as 'directly' (*sākṣāt*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then, just as the bank indicated by the word 'Ganges' is not itself the Ganges, this [sentence-meaning] would likewise lack properties such as being directly perceived. Anticipating this, he says: "Its own meaning" (*svārtha*). The meaning is that, like the word *śoṇa* (red), these words terminate in the sentence-meaning precisely by taking up their own primary meanings. If these words indicate the sentence-meaning by means of recollecting their own meanings, then [in the case of the sentence] "Bring the cow... (*gām ānaya*)...

Anticipating the objection that—just as in the case of "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*)—the sentence-meaning might consist of either a distinction (*bheda*) or a relation (*saṃsarga*) being indicated, he says: "But not... The meaning is this: for here, distinction and so forth are not the sentence-meaning, because they are not what is intended to be known and because they do not serve the purpose of man; therefore, it is logical that the sentence terminates in an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) reality. [Objection: But surely knowledge of the sentence-meaning is fruitless without practical application (*anuṣṭhāna*), just like the knowledge of the meaning of sentences such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).

To this he says: "No," [meaning] "due to difference. Liberation, which is already attained as one's own inner self (*pratyaktvena*), is merely obstructed by ignorance; it is said that through the mere arising of knowledge—which destroys the cycle of transmigratory existence at its root—upon hearing the statement, the wise person attains it once the obstruction has been destroyed, not [that they attain it] inherently through sacrifices and the like.
This object of proof is fruitful, because of the scriptural statement regarding its eternality; such is the meaning. || 33 ||
Because of the statement of grammatical coreferentiality, by way of qualifier and qualified.
Through the process of understanding the characterized and the characteristics, one attains the meaning as it has been described. || 34 ||

He concludes the final position with the words "sāmānādhikaraṇyena" (by way of grammatical coreferentiality). Since the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence is thus fruitful, therefore—due to the coreferentiality of the words, the relation of qualifier and qualified between their meanings, and the relationship of the indicated and the indicator for each individual word and for them collectively—the seeker of liberation ascertains the undivided Self from such sentences as "That thou art," and so forth; this is the meaning. || 34 ||
If this were for all purposes, then the qualification "directly" (sākṣāt) would be [necessary].
Alternatively, [the sequence] ends with *aparokṣa* or ends with *brahman*;
however, the qualifier *sākṣāt* (directly) serves to exclude everything else, while all other terms are the qualificands—this is another position he states. All— [vol 3, page 81]

[The commentary] states that [the passage] has this meaning. He mentions another alternative interpretation: that the qualifiers "directly perceived" (*sākṣāt*) and "not indirect" (*aparokṣāt*) have as their qualificands Brahman, the Self, and the Inner Controller of all.

He mentions yet another possibility: that the two qualifiers ending with "not indirect" (*aparokṣāntam*) have as their qualificands the Self and the Inner Controller of all, while everything else is a qualifier.
Or it extends up to Brahmā. || 35 ||
The two qualifiers of Brahman are "witness" (sākṣin) and "immediate" (aparokṣa).
Because of the connection with Brahman in the sentence, and because nothing other than that is heard there. || 36 ||

Anticipating the objection that "how can there be a difference in meaning within a single sentence, for in that case the sentence would be split," [the author], considering that a multiplicity of meanings is introduced by way of possibility, states the intended position with the word "yad" (that which). For here, Brahman has two qualifiers— namely,
"the Self" and "the innermost of all"— which, being conjoined by the two *ca*s, are presented as qualifiers of that very same subject, as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) of the sentence under discussion.
The meaning is that it is [the Self] alone that belongs to another, because nothing else is heard here as the substantive, as is the case with Brahman. || 36 ||
That which is not separated from the seer by any intervening obstacle.
Because Brahman has the nature of being immediately present to each individual, it is without mediation. (37)

Since Brahman is imperceptible and remote, how can it be said to be "directly perceived"? To this he says: "That which... The connection is: "Explain that. He establishes its non-remoteness with the word "pratyak" (the inward-facing). || 37 ||
They declare that Brahman is non-exclusive, non-inclusive, and not figurative.
Such [a result] arises from direct perception; it can never be otherwise than that.
He states that the qualification [of being] "immediate" is possible only with respect to Brahman: "avyāvṛtta... (verse 38).
Then, through the negation of all [objects] within the self, consciousness abides as one within the self.
For negation is not intended unless the ultimate reality has been attained. (39)

If duality exists, how can Brahman be neither excluded from nor inclusive of anything? To this, he provides the answer by means of the qualification "Self" (ātman): "All... [etc.]. He raises an objection: if there is a negation of all cognized non-Selfs without distinction, then by that same logic, the Self would also be subject to negation; thus, cognition would become objectless. He replies: "Not so," because a negation without a limit is impossible. Therefore, the Self serves as the limit.
The remainder is as follows. || 39 ||
An effectual entity is designated through the states of presence and absence.
By negating the state of being a cause, one takes refuge in Brahman as the Self. || 40 ||

Furthermore, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the other [logical criteria] apply only to that which is an effect (*kārya*), and the inner Brahman (*pratyag-brahma*) is not an effect; therefore, it is neither excluded from nor included within them. To this he says: "By exclusion" (*vyatireka*). One might object: "If Brahman is not an effect, then it must be the cause, and thus the problem of positive concomitance and so forth remains as before. Anticipating this, he says: "In the state of being the cause" (*kāraṇatva*). By negating its status as an effect and so forth, Brahman attains the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*); therefore, positive concomitance and the like have no scope there.
Such is the meaning. || 40 ||
Because the reality of the causal substance is merely this much.
Brahman, which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else, is therefore the Self itself. || 41 ||
1 ga. kṣādapaṃ | 2 ka. 'yābhyāṃ vai kā | [vol 3, page 82] -4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 1215.

If that which is to be negated, such as the effect (kārya) and so forth, were different [from Brahman], it would not be excluded [from reality]; if it were non-different from Brahman, then Brahman itself would also be subject to negation. Anticipating the objection that there is a persistence [of Brahman] due to its being the cause and an exclusion [of the world] due to its being the effect, he says: "This much" (etāvat). The sense is that because that which is superimposed—like a snake [upon a rope]—is negated, Brahman, which is the non-dual substrate and the inner self (pratyagātman), is established in its uniform oneness. || 41 ||
He alone is the eternal, the witness, and likewise the innermost self within all.
You ought to describe that very [reality] of such characteristics to me exactly as it is. || 42 ||

Having explained the passage beginning with "yat," he now explains the passage beginning with "tam. The phrase "yaśca" means the Self that is Brahman, characterized by such attributes as direct perceptibility (*sākṣāttva*) and so forth. Just as in the world one points out a cow by seizing its horn and saying, "This is it," so too [the request is]:
"Show me the Self that is Brahman directly, right here! || 42 ||
Because of the statement of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the two terms denoting Brahman and the Self.
It is logical that these two have a single purpose, since they mutually establish their respective meanings. (43)

Anticipating the objection that an inquiry into their identity is not appropriate because the difference between Brahman and the self is perceived through direct perception, he says: "By virtue of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*).

The meaning is that because of the coreferentiality of the two words "Brahman" and "self," there is non-difference between their referents; for it is accepted that such a relationship exists when words with distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) denote a single object. Anticipating the further objection that this might be based on a figurative identity—as in the case of "Name is Brahman" (*nāma brahma*)—he says: [the following].
"Mutually" (mithas); "so be it" (tathā) is the statement that their identity is non-figurative. || 43 ||
Brahman is directly qualified as having the singular nature of the Self.
Because, for that reason, the state of being Brahman is impossible elsewhere than there. || 44 ||
He explains how the meaning of the word "Brahman" culminates in the Self: "Brahman," he says.

Since Brahmanhood is impossible for anything other than the Self due to its being distinct from it, and because [the text] specifies that "Brahman is directly the Self," the meaning is that the referent of the word "Brahman" culminates in the Self alone. || 44 ||
For even the self is not conceivable apart from Brahman.
Therefore, the expression of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the two words "Brahman" and "Self" [is established]. (45)

He establishes that the referent of the word "self" (ātman) culminates in Brahman alone with the words, "The self also... The meaning is that anything else, such as a pot and so forth, is not the self. He states the resulting conclusion: that the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the two words "Brahman" and "self"—in which each terminates in the other's own referent—is intended as primary identity (mukhyaikya). This is shown by the words, "Since... (yataḥ). || 45 ||
Therefore, there is a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between Brahman and the Self.
Through the negation of non-Brahman and the non-Self, there arises the realization of the oneness of the Self as being unassociated [with the world]. || 46 ||

Nevertheless, one might ask: how can there be a cognition of oneness from a sentence when there is the perception of non-Brahmanhood in the Self and non-Selfhood in Brahman? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By means of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇa*). Since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is primary, and since the two referents stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified, by the power of the word *ātman* which conveys a qualifier of Brahman, non-Brahmanhood is [negated] in the Self; and by virtue of the word *brahman* which conveys a qualifier of the Self—
The meaning is that, through the destruction of the notion of non-selfhood, the cognition arises from the sentence with reference to that unity which is devoid of difference and association. || 46 ||
