Even for Brahman, the state of being non-Brahman arises from delusion regarding the Self; it does not exist in reality.
The self is also beyond perception, as is Brahman, due to its association with darkness.

He states that the self possesses the fitness for the destruction of its non-Brahmanhood: "Of Brahman also... He states that even in Brahman there is the fitness for the destruction of its non-selfhood: "Of the self also... (47)
"Because the destruction of the non-Brahman and non-Self [notions] occurs through knowledge that dispels darkness."
One attains Brahman, which consists of the unprecedented and so forth, and is free from all association. || 48 ||

He states the resulting conclusion regarding the two [factors] being fit for sublation by virtue of their being characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*): "Of darkness... It should also be understood that [the Brahman is] "devoid of association" and "without differentiation. The words "the wise one attains" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 48 ||
Because the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self sublates that [notion] as well as the notion of the non-Self.
Because only the individual measure remains within me, I am the primordial measure of the sacrificial cake and other offerings.

Anticipating the objection—"Since non-Brahmanhood and so forth are destroyed, and since emptiness (śūnyatā) is the ultimate limit, how can there be a cognition of an object that has a single flavor?"—he says: "The inner self" (pratyak), etc. [This means] "by way of sublation," that is to say, "of the sublated. || 49 ||
Having fixed one's vision upon the Self, which is uniquely colored by inward-facing awareness.
"He is answering," said Yājñavalkya, whose intellect was noble-minded, to him.

Having explained the question both concisely and in detail, he takes up the reply with the words "having concentrated" (*praṇidhāya*). This refers to the questioner, Uṣasta; [the answer concerns] the sublime (*udāram*), that is, the supreme (*utkṛṣṭam*) Brahman. || 50 ||
Because here, the self, the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth, exist in manifold ways.
We do not know who is intended by this [statement] "of the perceptible object. (51)
He asks in order to determine the meaning of this word: "The self," which has been described as the sphere of empirical experience. || 11 ||
In order to make known his intended meaning, he then said, "That is the self."
The inclusion of "all" is an elliptical reference (upalakṣaṇa) to what was previously stated. || 52 ||

He takes up two words as the answer: "vivakṣitā" (intended). The word "of this [pronoun] *eṣa*" is to be supplied. The meaning of the word "tataḥ" (from that) is immediate sequence following expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Anticipating the objection that by specifying "the innermost of all" (*sarvāntara*), there might be a disregard for the other qualifications present in the question, he says: "sarvāntara... (12).
The commencement from the earth up to the sky is designated by means of the sixth case-ending.
And it is called the "Self" because it is the witness to the arrival and departure of the knower and other such factors. (53)

He states the meaning of the genitive case [in "ta-"] with the word "kṣoṇī" (the earth). The meaning is that here, the world—beginning with the earth and ending with space, together with its cause—is understood through the word ending in the genitive case.
He states the meaning of the word "ātman" with the words "ātmeti ca. The particle "api" (and) has the sense of restriction (emphasis). || 53 ||
Even though there is a distinction between the cognizer and the means of cognition, it does not differ with respect to each individual body.
Because it is the witness of external objects, it is therefore called the Self (ātman). || 54 ||

3, Page 84] 4 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1217.
How can the Witness be grasped by the word "Self" while setting aside the well-known mother? To this he says: "Not indeed... (*na hi*). It is not so.

Just as a pot or similar object ceases to exist once it is broken, so too does the selfhood of the divided [universe] vanish; thus, the meaning is that the Self is none other than the non-dual Witness. || 54 ||
Just as mutual deviation among the knower and so forth is witnessed by one's own self-awareness, [so too is the deviation between the two].
Because the Self is the witness of the absence of all measures (mātrā) and so forth, it is not like that. || 55 ||
Fearing that this [consciousness] might also be distinct for each body—just like the mother and so forth—due to its variability, he states the non-establishment of the reason:

"Because of variability. The meaning is that since it is the witness of both existence and non-existence, variability is impossible; therefore, there is no distinction of it per body, because it too is the witness. || 55 ||
That which is perceived through direct observation by means of [the words] "directly" and so forth;
Apart from the inward reality, no other self is perceived. || 56 ||

In that case, one might suspect that because the mother and others are the objects of perception (sākṣya) and the Self is the perceiver (sākṣin), duality would result; anticipating this, he says "directly," etc., following upon direct experience. || 56 ||
Because the self, nescience, and that which arises from it have as their sole reality the inward-facing dimension alone.
Therefore, because of their correct cognition, those two [the means and the result] terminate in that alone.

Anticipating the objection that even if [the world] is not perceived apart from the inner self (pratyagātman), its existence might still be possible—just as a jar hidden behind a wall—and that therefore duality remains as it was, he says: "The inner self... (verse 17).
Because, through the complete absence of a self, there is a connection with that which has another as its object.
Everything beginning with "directly" (sākṣāt) and so forth may be considered a qualifying attribute (viśeṣaṇa). || 58 ||
How is it established that the cause, together with its effect, is nothing but the inward Self (*pratyag-mātra*)? To this he says: "Of the Self.

Since that which is desired as distinct from the Self cannot exist separately from It in its entirety—because anything other than the Self would lack its own essential nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*)—the true reality (*yāthātmya*) of the world is simply the inward Self alone. Furthermore, the previously mentioned qualification [of the Self] follows from the impossibility of any other explanation.
He says "sākṣāt" and so forth, meaning that [the scripture] establishes the non-duality of Brahman and the Self. || 18 ||
Because there is no apprehension of any other entity apart from the inner self as such.
For that which has the single form of exclusion, no exclusion is obtained. || 59 ||
Nevertheless, suspecting that there might still be a difference whose counter-correlative is the non-self (anātman), he says: "By way of being the inner self" (pratyaktayā). || 19 ||
Because of contradiction, there is no positive concomitance for this [universal], just as there is none for "cowness" in a broken part of a cow and so forth.
Even difference is not tenable on account of the true nature of non-duality. || 60 ||

If it is argued that since difference is difficult to find for the inner self (*pratīc*), whose nature is both different and non-different, its lack of difference [from the world] would entail insentience (*jaḍatā*), he says "due to contradiction" (*virodhāt*) to address this doubt. Just as a universal is non-different from the individual, there is no non-difference of the inner self from the various selves because of the contradiction between consciousness (*cit*) and insentience (*acit*); thus, just as there is difference between them, so too there is no non-difference between the two. If it is then asked whether, in that case, only the unreality (*tucchatā*) of duality remains, he says "even the distinction" (*vyatireko 'pi*).
Exclusion is emptiness. || 60 ||
Therefore,
by way of being nothing but the inward Self (pratyag-mātra), the non-Self dissolves into the Self.
Even if it were determined that "this is your self," there would still be no determination regarding the question [of the self]. || 61 ||

What, then, is the destination of the world? To this he says: "The inward" (*pratyak*). The meaning of the word is that [the destination] cannot exist because of the impossibility of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Having explained the meaning of the passage beginning with "this one" (*eṣa*), he provides the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) to introduce the question beginning with "which one" (*katama*). [He says: "Of you. (61)
Because of the lack of awakening, there arises the notion of "mine" and "self" with respect to many [objects].
First, the one Self is within the *piṇḍa*, and likewise, the other is within the *liṅga*.
The third would be the witness of the intellect, which is likewise what is being doubted.

Anticipating the contradiction that "there is no determination even when determination exists," he says, "My... He elaborates on how the manifold world arises from ignorance regarding the possibility of multiple selves, ending with the words, "...within the body. This diversity [is explained] by means of the distinction between the gross and subtle bodies and their witness.
This is the meaning. || 62 || 63 ||
Since this is so, tell me: which one among these is intended here?
The Self, which is directly perceived through such means as direct perception, is determined as "this" by being distinguished from everything else.

He states the nature of the question with the words "yataḥ" (from which). Since there is the possibility of many selves, [the meaning is: from among those, please point out—which one is intended as being directly [the self]—by isolating it from others, just like a cow or other objects, and state it as something perceptible. || 64 ||
Yājñavalkya also spoke to him [the questioner] by means of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the words, "He who [breathes] with the prāṇa."
Desiring to make the inner self easily understood through the vital breath and other faculties, [he spoke]. 65.
Yājñavalkya also adopts the reply beginning with "He who [breathes] by means of the vital breath," and so forth. || 65 ||
Having caused the intellect to grasp that which is beyond [the senses] by means of inference from the vital breath and so forth.
Thereafter, I shall cause [him] to understand according to the specific qualifications as they have been acquired.
Having taken this to heart, Yājñavalkya spoke thus to him.
That which is expressed by the words "he who [acts] with breath" and "with speech" does not convey the stated meaning through its indicative mark (liṅga).

Why does [the author] proceed to make the Self known through an inferential mark (liṅga), while disregarding the Self which is to be directly understood by means of qualifiers such as "directly" (sākṣāt)? To this he replies: "By the act of breathing, etc. The meaning is that, thinking "I shall clarify the aforementioned qualifiers—namely, the state of being Brahman—after having purified the referent 'thou' (tvam-artha) by means of inference," he composed the passage beginning with "He who [breathes] by means of breath," and so forth. [This concerns] the meaning of the words.

If it is argued that the cognition of the sentence-meaning, like the cognition of purity, also arises from *liṅga* (indicative power) alone, [the author] says "no. The meaning is: because oneness is cognizable solely through syntactical connection (*vākya*). || 66 || 67 ||
That which moves through the mouth, which is perceived by the vital breath (prāṇa), and which is the most inward of all—this is the Self (ātman), the ultimate limit within everything. 68.
And that [is] the end.

Taking up the reply with its underlying intention (*sābhiprāya*), he explains its words: "The mouth," etc. The word *aprāṇaḥ* is to be split [as *a-prāṇaḥ*].
It is described as "the most inward of all" in order to show that, by virtue of being the innermost of everything, it is the ground of the manifestation of all things. || 68 ||

While this collection of instruments is asleep, he remains awake, his vision unimpaired.
Perceiving the forms of latent impressions (vāsanā), one breathes through the vital breaths by means of the wind. 69.
Since the functions such as breathing arise from the very collection of the eye and other organs, and not from a self (ātman), how can it be said "he who [breathes] by means of breath," and so forth?
To this, he says: "When asleep. || 69 ||
Therefore, the lack of selfhood (anātmatva) of the vital breaths and so forth is established by their being described as instruments (karaṇa).
And because everything from the intellect down to the physical body is of the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), it too is not the Self.

Anticipating the objection as to how discrimination can be established even regarding the activity of breathing and so forth—which is dependent on the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the like—the author says: "The state of being non-self" (*anātmattvam*). The connection is with the phrase "because of the statement regarding the instruments" (*ataḥ karaṇoktitaḥ*). The meaning is that the vital breath and so forth are non-self because they are instruments, just like a lamp; nor is the reason unestablished, since that [instrumentality] is stated by the third case-ending (the instrumental case). Anticipating the charge of an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, he says: "The vital breath... and so forth.

First, with respect to the intellect (*buddhi*), there is identity (*tādātmya*) [with the vital breath], because of the Vedic revelation: "That which is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is wisdom (*prajñā*); that which is wisdom is the vital breath.

Furthermore, there is such identity for the sense organs, because of the Vedic revelation: "Therefore, they are called 'vital breaths' (*prāṇāḥ*) by this name. And there is identity for the body because it is dependent upon that [the vital breath], according to the Vedic revelation: "The vital breath alone, being the self of wisdom (*prajñātman*), having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise up. Since it possesses the designation of the word "vital breath," it is as well-established as...
The meaning is that [the elements] beginning with earth are not the self. || 70 ||
"The body [is not the self] because it is visible, and because the vital breaths and so forth are instruments."
Therefore, the establishment of the selflessness of both the mark (liṅga) and the body (piṇḍa) would follow.

He states another argument for the body being non-self: "Because it is an object of perception" (*dṛśyatvāt*). Having restated the reason for the non-selfhood of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, he concludes that both bodies are non-self: "Of the vital breath and so forth" (*prāṇādeḥ*). || 71 ||
By means of the instruments of action such as the vital breaths, he is naturally uncombined and solitary.
It performs that activity even while remaining inactive, just like a magnet.

Anticipating the objection that even in the state of isolation (*viveka*), if the Self were the cause of vital functions such as breathing, it would follow that the Self is composite and active, he says:
"prāṇādi... (breathing, etc.). The word should be divided as *akurvan* (not acting). A simile is given for how something can be a cause of action elsewhere by mere proximity:
"ayaḥ-kānta" (the magnet). || 72 ||
"By no sentient being whatsoever established here in this world."
The activity of an insentient object, such as a chariot and the like, is not observed to be constant.

Anticipating the objection that there is no conscious self (cidātman) distinct from the aggregate [of body and mind], and asking how such qualities as its lack of action could possibly belong to it, he says: "In the world...
The meaning is: the activity of the insentient is preceded by a conscious controller, because it is the activity of the insentient, just like a chariot and so forth. || 73 ||
1 kha. "These two are coming. 2 ka. "Associated. 3 kha. "But the Self. [Vol.
3, page 87] 1220 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]—
The body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and so forth, are observed to be governed [by Him].
Therefore, by means of that very [cognition] through which activity occurs, the self must be admitted as distinct from these [objects]. || 74 ||

He infers by first stating the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*): "The body," etc. The meaning is: "The disputed activity is preceded by a conscious controller, because it is an activity of an insentient thing, like [the case of] a [chariot] agreed upon. It should be observed that in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the term "restricted" (*niyata*) is for the purpose of establishing that the activity of chariots and so forth is preceded by a conscious controller; however, in the case of the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*), it is for the purpose of the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*). || 74 ||
"Having previously made a direct promise, 'I shall show myself to you,' [I have now fulfilled it]."
If one is unable to act in that manner, one should awaken [the disciple] by means of a ritual mark (liṅga).
Just as someone else might do, so have you made a promise regarding another's self.
Without having personally accomplished that [realization], you merely indicate it to this person by means of an inferential sign.
He explains the passage beginning with "yathā" (as... by saying "pratijñāya" (having promised). That is to say, "to act accordingly," meaning to perceive [the object] in accordance with the promise.
By "liṅgena" (by a sign), he means by such signs as running and so forth. In the case of the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*), "by a sign" means by such signs as breathing and so forth.
Therefore, it is exactly as promised; it is precisely as it was asked.

A reply must be given to me; otherwise, there would be a fault.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "yadeva" (whatever it may be) as follows: "In accordance with the proposition. This means that you must provide an answer for my sake, following both your own proposition and my inquiry; otherwise, there would be a loss of your proposition and your words would become unworthy of attention. Therefore, both that proposition and the inquiry must be followed. || 77 ||
We have repeatedly offered our response to you, exactly as we had promised.
Yet, dissatisfied even with that, you desire to know otherwise.

He states the purport of the reply with the words "Just as... etc. Following your proposition and your question, I have repeatedly stated the reply: "This is your Self, which [is known] by means of prāṇa. The meaning is that the Self can be known only as something non-objective (*aviṣayatayā*), and not otherwise. He says this because, despite being told so repeatedly, you remain dissatisfied and wish to understand the Self as an object, like a jar or other such things. Therefore—
The reality of the Self is not like a jar or other such objects, as it does not exist apart from the path already described.
It is impossible to point it out specifically, because it lies beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition. || 79 ||

Anticipating the objection that it should be stated in accordance with the desire for knowledge (*mumukṣā*), he says: "It has been said" (*uktā*). He states the reason for the claim that while the Self is known as the inner self (*pratyak*) by way of non-objectivity, it is impossible to speak of the reality of the Self as an object distinct from that [non-objective] knowledge.
He says: "By means of the instruments of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*); || 79 ||
Because of which power you say "the piercer," and because of which power you say "not the piercer."
Having seen him here with that very vision, you behold that which is to be realized as Brahman.

If it is asked how that [Self] can be the object of knowledge since such knowledge is impossible, he says "I know" and so forth. This is from the *Kūṭasthānuvākabrāhmaṇa*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. Page 88, Volume 3. 1221.

By whose grace knowledge and ignorance proceed at different times regarding objects such as sound and the rest—having seen that very [Self] through the vision of its true nature, if you then cast the fault of objectivity upon the Self, then speak; for in the vision of the Self by way of the aforementioned vision, there is no occasion for objectivity.
This is the meaning. || 80 ||
For that entity which is immeasurable cannot be established by means of valid cognition.
It is explained as follows, so that it may be illustrated by way of comparison with a jar.
Anticipating the objection as to why that which is not an object cannot be made into an object, he introduces the Bhāṣya with the words "because of the very nature of the thing" (*vastusvābhāvyāt*).
He explains: "It is immeasurable" (*aprameyam*); for the meaning of the particle *hi* is the impossibility of the destruction of its own nature. Thus it is stated by the Bhāṣya.
The remainder. || 81 ||
Of the seer, the seeing, and the seen, which are conjoined with one another;
The self's constant state of being a witness is said to be the very nature of reality.
In response to the inquiry "What is that?", he explains the Bhāṣya passage, "the state of being the seer of seeing and so forth," as follows: "The seer" (draṣṭṛ). || 82 ||
Prior to the emergence of the knower and so forth, she is eternally neither subsided nor arisen.
With inward vision, he remained unattached, abiding in his nature as the non-agent. || 83 ||

[Objection: But since the witness (sākṣin) is also a real entity, it must be perceivable by the subject and so forth; why then is it not perceivable by the subject and others? To this he says: "The subject and so forth... The meaning is that the inward vision is eternally devoid of rising and setting and is immutable; thus, even prior to the activity of the subject and so forth—such as during sleep—it shines forth, and therefore it is not perceivable by them. Regarding the witnesshood of the inner self (pratyak)...
Anticipating the objection that the Self is not immutable because it possesses activity like a witness with a body, [the author] says "akāraka" (without agency), etc.

Since it is impossible for the inward-looking vision to possess activity either by itself or through another, and since it remains established in all Śruti and Smṛti as an immutable Self due to its being unattached, it is not so [as the opponent claims].
This real nature of the self is characterized by being neither cause nor effect.
It is once-for-all manifest, of the nature of oneness, free from darkness, and non-dual.

And because it is other than cause and effect, he says that the inner self (pratīc) is devoid of action: "akārya" (not an effect). If it is argued that the Self is said to possess activity because the Self attains the state of being a sacrificer due to its capacity for action, we say no; for while that state exists for the Self as conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it does not exist for the Self in its other [unconditioned] aspect. Bearing this in mind, he says: "etad" (this). Furthermore, [the purpose of the scripture] is either for the sake of illumination, or for the sake of Brahman, or for the sake of the destruction of darkness.

He says that there is no activity of the Self for the purpose of destroying difference, using the word "once" (*sakṛt*). He says it is not the second [alternative], using the word "oneness of self" (*aikātmya*). He says it is not the third, using the word "free from darkness" (*vitamaska*). And he says it is not the fourth, using the word "non-differentiating" (*abhedaka*). || 84 ||
It attains the state of being a witness through its connection with this darkness (tamas).
And the association of the self with delusion has as its sole cause the quality of darkness (tamas).
1. He says: "No.
[Vol. 3, page 89] 1222 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya—]

If it is asked, "Whence does its status as a witness derive?", he says [in response]: "This... [referring to the verse]. Likewise, does the Self's connection with darkness exist in reality or not? Not the first, because it would contradict its quality of being unattached (*asaṅga*); nor the second, because of the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For if the connection with darkness were unreal, one would have to admit yet another darkness. He says: "Only darkness" (*tamomātra*). The meaning is that the infinite regress regarding the connection has been refuted. || 81 ||
The immutable witness-consciousness, its delusion, and the semblance of that consciousness—these three constitute the triad.
He is called the cause of the world, the witness, and the controller. || 86 ||

If it is argued that even the status of being a witness (*sākṣitva*) is as real as causality (*kāraṇatva*) and so forth, he says [in response]: "The immutable" (*kūṭastha*). This triad is spoken of in three ways according to the mutual relationship of subordinate and principal; thus, the meaning is that causality and the rest are merely products of ignorance (*āvidya*). || 86 ||
Causality does not arise from immutability; rather, it occurs through the absence of that delusion.
And because intellect and the like possess the quality of inertia (jāḍya), the inference of their cause is logical. (87)

But regarding those proponents of transformation (*pariṇāmavādins*) who assert that the pure Brahman is the cause and claim that this causality is real, [the author] says to them: "Causality... Since the pure conscious self (*cidātman*) alone cannot be the cause, he states another reason for its being the cause: "Due to insentience (*jāḍya*). Because the effect is insentient, an element of insentience must be inferred in the cause as well, since the effect conforms to its cause; therefore, there is an insentient power (*jaḍaśakti*).
The meaning is that because it exists only for that which is qualified [by conceptual construction], it is not real. || 87 ||
Even the distinction from the knower and so forth belongs to the reality whose nature is consciousness.
It is appropriate for one who is the witness of his own darkness regarding an unknown object of knowledge. || 88 ||

If the distinction or non-distinction between the Self and the knower (mātr) and so forth exists in reality, let it be; likewise, let witnesshood and the rest also exist [in that way]. If, however, it does not exist, then—fearing that the Self would be as indefinable (anirvācya) as the knower and the rest—the author says: "The knower and so forth... The word "also" (api) serves to include non-distinction. Distinctions and non-distinctions such as the knower and so forth are superimposed upon the Reality, which is pure Consciousness (cinmātra), conditioned by beginningless and indefinable ignorance (ajñāna).

Those two [difference and so forth] do not belong to the pure [Self], because they are absent in the state free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi); therefore, the meaning is that difference and the rest are merely conceptual constructions (kalpanāmātra). Anticipating the objection that if "being an object of knowledge" (meyatva) belongs to that which is unknown, then ignorance (ajñāna) would also be an object of knowledge by virtue of being a qualifier, he considers that this is not the case because ignorance is a mere adventitious indicator (upalakṣaṇa), and thus he qualifies [the subject] with the word "own" (sva). || 88 ||
For one whose vision is immutable, being a witness— like that of an insentient entity— is not tenable.
Because there is no connection with the object of perception, consciousness does not arise even when that [object] exists.
Furthermore, regarding whether the witness (sākṣin) is conscious or unconscious: in the first case, is it pure or ignorant? It is not the first; thus he says, "kūṭastha" (the immutable).

He refutes the other alternative with "tasmin" (in that). The meaning is that even when there is a connection with the objects of witnessing, an unconscious entity cannot be a witness, just like a jar. || 89 ||
Therefore, the status of being a witness for another occurs through the path of the manifestation of one's own ignorance.
Because the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is conjoined with the relationship between cause and effect. || 90 ||
He accepts the position that it belongs to the ignorant one. Therefore, how can there be for another a manifestation of his own delusion by means of the appearance of the witness?
[Vol. 3, page 90]

Regarding the lack of connection with the meaning of "Thou" (tvam) therein, he says: "The effect," etc. Because of dependence, the connection belongs only to the effect and so forth; however, since the reflection enters into that [effect], the Self is the witness—this is the meaning. || 90 ||
The relationship with the mother and so forth is established exactly as it is experienced.
In the same way, its non-existence is also established by mere experience alone. || 91 ||

Having stated that the state of being the object, such as the mother and so forth, is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*), he now states that its absence is likewise so cognized. [He says] "the knower and so forth. The term "connection" (*abhisaṃbandha*) here means existence (*bhāva*). || 91 ||
First of all, these three as they have been described have no other cause.
But the categories of entities, such as the cognizer and so forth, have dharma, adharma, and the like as their causes. || 92 ||
Anticipating the objection that being the witness, the inner controller, and the cause are not due to ignorance (avidyā), but rather produced by merit (dharma) and so forth, he says:
"ananyā" (not other). Since merit and the like are impossible for the Supreme, if these three [states] are caused by ignorance alone, then what is the utility of merit and the rest?

To this he replies: "pramātrādi" (the knower, etc.). The word "ādi" (and so forth) in "adharma-ādi" is intended to include passion (rāga) and the like; the "ignorance" mentioned is the material cause (upādāna) of the knower and the rest.
The meaning is that the sign (nimitta) consists of phenomena (dharma) and so forth. || 92 ||
The connection of the intellect and so forth occurs through birth alone with the conscious self.
The connection with the womb has as its cause dharma, adharma, and so forth. || 93 ||

If it is argued that, just as the Self possesses the nature of the mother and so forth, its connection with them is also produced by merit (dharma) and other factors—and therefore, even though that connection exists, it might at times be non-existent—[the author] says "no," stating: "of the intellect (buddhi), etc. If it is suspected that if the Self always possesses the form of consciousness (cidākāratā), then it must likewise possess the forms of jars and other objects, and consequently there would be no distinction between the manifestation and non-manifestation of jars and the like, [the author] states: "of the jar, etc."

The meaning is that the connection of the intellect and so forth with objects such as a jar is adventitious and depends upon a cause; and when that [connection] exists, merit (dharma) and so forth are the cause for the perception of pleasure and the like therein. || 93 ||
In this context, there is a single perspective of the knower that devours objects such as sound and the rest.
It depends upon many means and bestows the fruits of pleasure and pain. || 94 ||

The commentary (*bhāṣya*) stating "because of the very nature of things" has been explained. As for the claim that the statement "the seer of seeing is indeed the Self" is intended to show that the Self is not an object of seeing—that is incorrect. Regarding the Buddhists who maintain that "it does not exist," the commentary beginning with "seeing is twofold" and so forth explains, therein, the worldly seeing (*laukikī dṛṣṭi*). [The word] "knower" (*pramātṛ*) refers to this. Between the worldly and the ultimate (*paramārtha*) seeings, the modification of the intellect (*buddhi*) accompanied by its appearance (*sābhāsa*) is the worldly seeing.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, she does not take herself as an object, because her purpose is fulfilled by another object; thus he says: "Sound and so forth. Having stated the distinction from the perspective of objects—namely, between the ultimate view and the worldly view—he also states it from the perspective of the cause:
"Abundant... He states the distinction from the perspective of the result: "Happiness... || 94 ||
And this [consciousness] perishes in an instant, because its cause is fragile.
And it is distinct in each body because of its uncommon causes. (95)

He also states [the nature of the cause] by way of its own form: "momentary," etc. Its causes consist of attachment to objects that are the basis for worldly perception and so forth. In another manner... [Vol. 3, p.
91] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Third Chapter. [1224]

He states the distinction [between the individual souls]: "In each body," etc. The word *tu* (but) is used to state that this [distinction] does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*).

The reason for this is given: "Because it is uncommon," which means that it is accepted that [the merit, demerit, etc. produced by Caitra and others are generated individually [for each soul]. || 91 ||
This [reality], which has the nature of action and agent, exists by way of the essence of non-action and non-agent.
Because its true nature consists solely of that much, it arises as being entirely pervaded by that [consciousness]. || 96 ||

He states another distinction: "Action" (*kriyā*). For action is perception (*dṛṣṭi*) as it is defined by the agent and other factors; this is the meaning. He explains the second kind of perception—that which is ultimate (*pāramārthikī*), which is not an action because it abides as the immutable Self (*kūṭasthātman*)—with the word "non-action" (*akriyā*). If that is so, then...

Regarding the objection that accepting two types of vision would result in the loss of non-duality (advaita), he says: "merely that much" (*tāvanmātra*). The meaning is this: the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārthadṛṣṭi*) alone is the true nature of worldly vision;
therefore, worldly vision, being pervaded by that [ultimate vision], is included within it, and thus there is no consequence of duality. ||96||
Where there is a complete occurrence of both the pervaded and the pervading entities, that is [pervasion].
In that very case, pervasion would be primary, as in the case of an object such as a rope-snake. || 97 ||

Anticipating the objection that, because it is impossible for two things to be both the pervaded and the pervader in a single locus—as is seen with smoke and fire—there must be a difference between them, he says: "In its entirety. Pervasion is of two kinds: primary and secondary. The first is of the nature of identity between the pervaded and the pervader, like that of a rope and a snake; since this pertains only to what is perceived [as identical], there is no loss of non-duality (advaita). This is the meaning. || 97 ||
Due to the distinction of place, time, and so forth, the two [entities] are unique in their essential nature.
Pervasion does not hold directly, like that between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains. || 98 ||

He states the case where pervasion is not primary: "deśa" etc. Pervasion that occurs between two things distinct in their own nature (*svarūpa*) due to the non-difference of location and so forth is not primary, because such [pervasion] is never observed between two absolutely distinct things; therefore, the meaning is that in the case of smoke and the like, pervasion is not primary. || 98 ||
This worldly perception of the self depends upon the knower and so forth.
But the vision of that inner self should be understood as the ultimate reality. || 99 ||
This worldly view of the self is a view of the self as being the ultimate reality.
It undergoes the sixfold modification of existence, being all-pervasive like space within a jar. || 100 ||
And because it is independent of merit and demerit with respect to its manifestation as consciousness.
Therefore, like the appearance of a jar or other objects, the appearance of the Self is not perishable. || 101 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that, just as in the case of those two [the seer and the seen], the difference between the two types of vision is also real and not merely imagined like the snake in the rope? How then can there be a primary pervasion (*vyāpti*) there? To this he says: "The knower, etc. The meaning is that the worldly vision of the Self is imagined—like the snake and so forth—because it is dependent;

therefore, no real difference exists therein. [Objection: If that is so, then because it is a type of vision, the other [vision] must also be imagined, leading to nihilism (*śūnyatā*). To this he says:

Regarding the word "tat": the sense is that being imagined (*kalpitatva*) is the determining factor for being non-self (*anātmatva*). Having stated the two divisions, he states the conclusion—that a primary pervasion (*vyāpti*) is appropriate there, as in the case of the rope-snake—by saying "paramārtha" (in reality). An objection might be raised: the restriction "pervaded alone" is improper, because just as worldly perception (*laukikadṛṣṭi*) is pervaded by objects, so too the pervasion of the Self (*ātmavyāpti*) is perishable. Anticipating this, he says "dharma" (attribute), [meaning] the pervasion of the Self by worldly perception...
1 Kha. ṃnaḥ || Ṣa. ṃ | 2 Ka. tū || 100 || But this vision, which pervades that [reality], is eternal because it is free from birth and the like.

Therefore, the state of the ultimate reality (paramārtha-daśā) arises as always pervading that which is other than this. [Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1225.

There is also pervasion by objects (*arthavyāpti*) therein; the first is innate (*svābhāvikī*), while the second is produced by attributes (*dharmādikṛtā*). Because those attributes and so forth are perishable, there is a destruction of the pervasion by objects. The meaning is that the pervasion by consciousness (*caitanyavyāpti*) persists as long as perception exists. || 99 || 100 || 101 ||
The conscious self is inactive and a witness; the active [body] is unconscious and turned away [from the Self].
And the witness existing in deep sleep is established as being distinct from "I" and so forth. || 102 ||
Fearing that the other [supramundane] vision might not be distinct from mundane vision because it is not perceived, he establishes their distinction through direct experience: "It is inactive," etc.
If it is not admitted that there is a pervasion by experience for one who is in deep sleep;
By what power could the cognition "I did not know [anything] in deep sleep" arise? (103)

How is that witness, distinguished from the instruments of perception (*mātra*) and so forth, experienced? One might object that there is no experience of it because there is no cause for such experience.

To this, he raises an objection with the words "If not" (*na cet*). There is indeed the cognition of one who has awakened, "I did not know [anything]"; since this is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it requires a prior experience.

Therefore, if a constant experience during deep sleep were not admitted, that [awakened reflection] would be unestablished; thus, the witness distinguished from the instruments of perception and existing in deep sleep is established. This is what he states.
"No," and so forth. || 103 ||
Because the intellect and so forth have dissolved, and because the body and such are insentient.
Just as in the case of a clod of earth or similar objects, there would be no such perception as "I did not know. || 104 ||

Fearing that [the subsequent] reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) might depend solely on the mental states such as dreamless sleep (*sauṣupta-dharma*), he says: "of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth.

He provides another reason for the claim that dreamless sleep-consciousness is not produced by the two bodies (the gross and subtle): "and of the body and so forth. Consequently, he states the established conclusion: that in the absence of the constant experience of dreamless sleep, reflective awareness cannot be established. || 104 ||
The establishment of darkness occurs solely through the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), not through a knower.
Through the reflections of consciousness, ignorance, and the intellect, there is direct perception of that which has the nature of the agent.

By stating that reflection (parāmarśa) is impossible apart from constant experience, he also refutes the status of the ignorance called "deep sleep" as an object of knowledge (meyatva); thus he says: "The consciousness...
Having explained the establishment of ignorance through consciousness and its manifestation, he describes the manner in which the knower (mātṛ) is established: "The awareness...
The meaning is that the knower is immediate (āparokṣya) by virtue of consciousness, its manifestation, and ignorance. || 109 ||
In those selves who are distinct from memory, certainty, doubt, passion, and so forth.
He who follows along through the form of the "I" is considered the supreme subject (pramātā). || 106 ||

Who is that "knower" (mātā) therein? To this he says: "smṛti" (tradition/memory). The meaning is that the knower is the substratum of mental modifications such as knowledge and the like. He says "the supreme" (para), according to the principle: "The knower alone, when sought after, is free from evil, defects, and so forth. || 106 ||
That which is distinct within a single cognizer through the divisions of recollection and so forth;
That cognition, which has the knower as its agent, manifests with the appearance of many forms. (107)

What, then, is that knowledge? He says: "recollection and so forth. Since it exists not only by its own nature as something distinct, but also by way of its object, he says: "manifold. Therein, he provides experience as the proof: "it manifests. [This refers to] that knowledge which, in a single knower—154...
That state is equal even in another knower; this indicates that it is characterized by the agent who knows, being distinguished by its object.
The collective meaning is that knowledge has as its form that which resides in the agent. || 107 ||
Appearing externally as distinct, it possesses genus, form, action, and so forth.
That object of perception is distinct from the knower’s experience and from his knowledge itself.

(108) He asks: "Of what nature is that object there? and answers: "Distinct" (*vibhinna*). He establishes its distinctness by using the term "external" (*bahiḥ*) to exclude [the categories of] knowledge and so forth. By the word "born" (*jāti*), he clarifies what was stated as "appearing as distinct" (*bhinno bhāti*). Thus, it is "distinct" (*vibhinna*) [from the witness-consciousness]. The witness-consciousness...

It turns back from existence. Regarding the word "of the knower" (*jñātuḥ*): the meaning is that whatever appears as distinct from the knower and so forth—such as knowledge which consists of the activity of the knower—that is the object (*viṣaya*). || 108 ||
[The self] is qualified by consciousness, delusion, mental modifications, the body, and so forth.
When that which appears here to the enjoyer manifests, it is traditionally held to be the fruit of valid cognition.

In this context, he states the nature of the fruit of valid cognition (*māna*). Regarding the verse beginning with *saṃvit*: the meaning is that the manifestation within the Self, which appears as qualified by consciousness (*caitanya*) and so forth—as expressed in the phrase "consciousness shines"—is the fruit. || 109 ||
Agency, instrumentality, and objectivity exist through the witness of the Self.
Therefore, since the agent and so forth are established as distinct [from the self], they do not possess the nature of the self.

He states that the fourfold [set] mentioned is established by constant experience: "agency," etc. One *ca* (and) serves to aggregate the results. "Appears" (*ābhāti*) is to be connected with what precedes. He states the consequence regarding the fact that the "measurer" (*mātrādi*) and so forth are objects of witnessing (*sākṣyatva*): "by way of distinction" (*vyatirekeṇa*). "Therefore, of the witness" (*ataḥ sākṣiṇaḥ*) is the statement of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*). || 110 ||
The self is established as a witness by virtue of its distinction from the objects of cognition and the rest.
There is no agency on the part of the knower and so forth, because that [agency] ceases precisely through the state of being an object of witnessing.

He states the result [of the argument] regarding the witnessing nature of the inner self (*pratīc*) with the words "by being a witness. Because the inner self is a witness distinct from the objects of perception such as the *mātrā*s, its establishment as the Self is achieved;

therefore, the meaning is that the fruit of being a witness is Selfhood (*ātmatā*). He concludes that the *mātrā*s and so forth do not possess Selfhood with the word "no" (*na*). That is to say, they are not the Self. || 111 ||

The agency of the Self is appropriate due to its primary nature as the insentient intellect (buddhi) and so forth, which are produced by the conjunction [of the Self with the intellect]; and its state as an enjoyer is due to its primary nature as consciousness (cit). || 112 ||

In that case, there would be a distinction such that the mother and so forth are one, their witness is another, and the immutable seer (kūṭasthadṛṣṭi) is yet another; to this he replies with the word "pratyak" (the inward-facing).

The meaning is that the state of being a knower (mātṛtva) and so forth belongs to the Self through the predominance of the intellect and other faculties produced by its own ignorance, while the state of being a witness (sākṣitā) arises through the predominance of its own reflection; but in its own nature, it is the immutable one—thus, there is no real distinction. || 112 ||
Everything that was stated regarding the explanation of the indeterminate [questions] is exactly so.
In this case as well, the reality of the matter should be connected [to the previous discussion] for the sake of purification. || 113 ||
Having explained the commentary beginning with "The view is two-fold," he states that the third principle (*tātayanyāya*) serves as a supporting factor for the point already expressed.
[Vol.
3, page 94] 4 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1227.

Regarding the term "avyākṛtā" (indeterminate): it refers to the meaning of the commentary beginning with "the reality of things, due to the inherent nature of things," and so forth; that is to say, its purpose is the purification, which is to say, the definitive determination of that [reality]. || 123 ||
By its own power, that which is by nature non-cognitive cannot be established through itself.
When existence and non-existence are rejected by their very nature as not being real entities, [then that is established]. (114)

In this regard, he recalls what has already been stated for the sake of ease of understanding: "By its own majesty," and so forth. An insentient object does not establish itself by its own nature, because it is insentient;

and that very [insentience] is seen to be subject to birth and destruction, whereas the Reality (vastu) is not so. Since both of those [birth and destruction] are excluded from it, the meaning is that it is immutable (kūṭastha). || 114 ||
Therefore, though not being born at all, she appears as if being born.
Consciousness, arising from the birth of the self through the emergence of the cause of non-awakening to that [reality],
appears as if it were perishing even when that [cause] is destroyed, because it is witnessed by that [witnessing consciousness].
Therefore, even the Lord could not establish its status as an effect.

Raising the objection, "If birth and so forth belong only to that which is non-self (anātman), how can there be the cognition of them as belonging to the self (ātman)? he says, "Therefore," etc., [answering] that it is by virtue of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). He states the result of the falsity of birth and so forth for the conscious self (cidātman): "Since," etc. || 111 || 116 ||
An object situated on the plane of ignorance attains association with the mind.
It attains the state of being an object of knowledge (meyatva) and nothing else, once it has abandoned the two levels of earth.

Anticipating the objection that although the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is not an effect, it must nonetheless be insentient because it is an object of knowledge, and consequently it must have a cause, he says: "ajñāna...
(ignorance). By the word "earth" (kṣiti), which denotes a portion of the effects, the Cause is also indicated by implication. || 117 ||
Because the arising of the effect from its cause is established even prior to consciousness.
Therefore, let consciousness be understood as being devoid of the relationship between cause and effect.
Since there is no evidence for the existence of consciousness apart from either the category of cause or effect, how can it be said that it is non-inert and distinct from both?

To this, he says: "From the cause... The meaning is: because consciousness is established even prior to the distinction between cause and effect, as in deep sleep and so forth, it is certain that it is non-inert, being devoid of duality and transcending both [cause and effect]. || 118 ||
For even the emptiness of that which is empty is perceived only when its witness exists.
If emptiness were without a witness, it would be like a witness that is itself without a witness. (119)

But the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins) do not tolerate that very [emptiness]; how then can it be devoid of causes and so forth? To this he says: "Of the empty" (śūnyasya). Although emptiness is not possible because it would entail the contradiction of all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), nevertheless, if it were admitted, its reality would depend upon a witness (sākṣin), since it cannot be established without a prover; this is the meaning. Now, it might be objected that the witness is not accepted as the prover of that [emptiness].

Since the manifestation of that [void] is possible even without it, one might wonder whether it is self-luminous or not; having thus raised this alternative, he refutes the first by stating, "not witnessed" (*atākṣikam*).

The meaning is: if the void were to manifest without a witness (*sākṣin*), then, being without a witness, it would—just like the witness postulated by the opponents—be self-luminous; therefore, there is no disagreement on this point. || 119 ||
1 kha. "That which was said as 'not this' is explained.
[Vol. 3, page 95] 1228 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Adhyāya—]
Even the witness and the non-witness may be established because they are for one's own sake, but emptiness is not.
Because it exists for the sake of another and lacks its own purpose, it would be like the object of a sixth [sense]. || 120 ||
He sets aside another alternative with the word "sākṣi" (the witness).

Our desired witness, being independent, is established by virtue of its self-luminosity and autonomy; however, the void (*śūnyatā*) favored by you is not so, because, being insentient, it requires a sentient establisher.
Therefore, in the absence of an autonomous establisher, the void would remain merely a void. Thus, consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is of the nature of pure Being and immutable, must reside within me.
This is the meaning. || 120 ||
This inner self within the body is understood to be fivefold through valid means of knowledge.
By virtue of being a single cause, a witness, an agent, and one who experiences suffering. || 121 ||

Having raised the doubt as to how there can be a state of uniformity (aikarasya) even when the existence of consciousness as previously described is admitted, he states its fivefold abiding in order to refute the notion of difference within it, beginning with the words "deha" (the body). The meaning is that this innermost essence (pratyagdhātu), which exists within the world starting from the gross body up to the unmanifest (avyākṛta), is experienced in five ways; "miti" here means experience. He clarifies that very fivefold nature with the word "eka" (one).
In that regard, there is a distinction: one [unity] is real, while the other is merely apparent. || 121 ||
The connection between cause and effect is established through scripture, through indicative marks, and through direct perception.
Therefore, because it is experienced [as such], the Supreme Self possesses the nature of being the cause.

If it is argued that it is not logical for the supreme Self, which has become the inner witness (*pratyagbhūta*), to be the cause because of the conflicting views of disputants, [the author] says "no," citing scripture (*śruti*).
The two ablative endings are in apposition. The "mark" (*liṅga*) is the indicator; the effect, such as space and so forth, indicates that Brahman is the cause of the world.
Thus, the meaning is that because of the scriptural statement regarding the relationship between Brahman and the world, Brahman alone is the cause. || 122 ||
Apart from what is perceptible by the senses, even non-existence (abhāva) is not established.
How much more so, then, is existence in this world, which is both a witness and established by nothing else? || 123 ||

Nevertheless, how can there be witnesshood [of the Self] without a subject (mātṛ), since that [witnesshood] is not perceived without it? To this he says: "The inner" (pratyak). The meaning is that the witness, who establishes both the existence and non-existence of the subject, is established as distinct from the subject. Anticipating the objection that, like the subject, the witness would lead to an infinite regress by requiring another establisher, he says: "And the witness... (sākṣī ca) || 123 ||
Even the culmination of the intellect, when ascended upon the aforementioned experience, becomes perfected.
From the measure arises the measurer, and from the measure the measurable is established. || 124 ||

Anticipating the objection that this would result in the duality of both the witness (*sākṣin*) and the mother, he states that the inner self (*pratīc*) possesses the agency of knowledge produced by its own ignorance. The word "also" (*api*) serves as an illustration for its causality and so forth. To explain how that very self becomes subject to suffering through ignorance, he provides the introductory transition (*pātanikā*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used to draw out the fact that this is established through direct experience. || 124 ||
Happy, fair-complexioned, wealthy, and possessing cattle, he becomes so by resorting to the immeasurable external [objects].
Standing upon the ground of valid cognition (pramāṇabhūmi), all this is established. || 125 ||

Having accepted that "being subject to suffering" (duḥkhitva) is an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa), he states its essential nature (svarūpa) in relation to the object of cognition: "one who is happy," and so forth. He concludes the fivefold state [of the self] with the words: "by means of the instruments of knowledge" (pramāṇa). || 125 ||
[Vol.
3, Page 96] 4 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
1229 That which is the cause of the knower and so forth, prior to the emergence of the knower and so forth.
That which has the nature of being experienced by none other than itself is the valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for the eternal Seer.

Granted that causality and so forth are non-real (avidyam), and likewise that reality is non-dual; nevertheless, although that [causality] is established in the form of the knower and so on during the time of empirical transaction (vyavahāra), it is not established in states such as deep sleep because of the absence of a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) there. To this he says: "Prior... Even in states such as deep sleep, ignorance (ajñāna) manifests; otherwise, for one who has awakened, the retrospective reflection (parāmarśa) "I did not know" would be impossible. Therefore, the impossibility of establishing ignorance is itself the proof (sādhaka) for it.
The meaning is that he establishes himself within them. || 126 ||
In that state, no distinction between the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the act of knowing is perceived.
Because it obstructs the reality that consists solely of the true nature of inward consciousness. || 127 ||

If it is argued that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the means of knowledge regarding the Self, [the author] says "not so," for there must be a subject (*mātrādi*) therein; he states "it is mine" (*meyeti*). The reason for this is given as "the inner witness" (*pratyagiti*). || 127 ||
And in this regard, the fruit, as well as the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth, are exactly like this.
How could there be any room for differentiation within the non-dual, singular Self? (128)

Fearing the objection that "if the desired fruit arises in the Self from scriptural knowledge (*śrauta-jñāna*), then in the first case [that it does arise], there must be an acceptance of the distinction between the means of knowledge and their objects, and in the second case [that it does not arise], liberation would be unestablished," he says: "Of such a kind" (*īdṛk*). This means it is conceptual (*kālpnika*), like a snake [superimposed] on a rope. The word "thus" (*tathā*) expresses its being conceptual. The reason for the absence of distinction in reality is stated by the question: "Why? (Verse 928).
This [work], arrived by way of valid cognition, is for the removal of delusion.
In reality, this is not sufficient, because it results in the failure to undertake the treatise. || 129 ||

If the Self were of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*), it would dispel its own ignorance by itself; what then would be the use of an imagined means of knowledge (*māna*)? To this he says: "By the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*). This non-dual consciousness is referred to by the word "this" (*idam*). If this [consciousness] did not dispel delusion by its very nature, then the commencement of the Upaniṣads would be useless, because there would be nothing for the intellect arising from them to remove. Thus he says: "The reality" (*vastu*). || 129 ||
By not relinquishing the meaning already stated, [one remains] on those stages born of ignorance regarding that.
The empirical transaction involving the knower and so forth is like a dream, a magical illusion, or a conjuring trick.

Furthermore, since all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is dependent upon experience, and since that [experience] by its very nature establishes ignorance and so forth, it cannot destroy them without a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus he says: "Regarding the stated object" (*uktārtha*). This means that the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is of the nature of consciousness, does not dispel its own ignorance by that alone. Just as in dreams and the like, a transaction involving a mother and so forth is seen to be caused by the witness of that dream, so too here in this world, one's own...

The conventional usage of terms such as "dyotthamātra" (the mere arising) is appropriately dependent upon that [ignorance]; likewise, the meaning is that the Inner Self (pratyagātman), which establishes its own ignorance and so forth, does not destroy that [ignorance] by its own essential nature. || 130 ||
That which arises from that [ignorance] would be like darkness, established through non-investigation.
Therefore, when delusion is destroyed, the entire world is destroyed within consciousness. || 131 ||
[Vol. 3, page 97] 1230 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]:

Anticipating an objection regarding the disparity of the illustration, he says: "Unexamined," etc. This refers to the fact that the duality consisting of cause and effect is merely imagined (*kalpita*).

He states the result: "Therefore" (ataḥ). The meaning is that when the bondage together with its cause is destroyed by the mental modification (dhīvṛtti) in the form of non-duality arising from the sentence, pure consciousness alone (cinmātra) remains. || 131 ||
In the case of things that are cause and effect, such as pride and its basis, etc.
The Self alone is non-dual by its very nature, undivided from the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth. || 132 ||

If it is argued that because ignorance is destroyed, its residue remains thereafter, and since other things also existed previously, non-duality of consciousness (*cidadvaita*) is not established—anticipating this objection, he says:
"By [the destruction of] difference. The meaning is that the non-duality of consciousness is never, at any time, impaired by itself. || 132 ||
The self has no dependence whatsoever on place, time, state, or the like, by its very nature.

Since [space and so forth] are established only in dependence on something else, whereas the conscious self (cidātman) does not depend on them for its own establishment, there arises this doubt: "In the first case [if it depended on space], it would possess duality like a jar or other objects; in the second case [if it did not depend on them], its manifestation would be impossible as something restricted. Anticipating this, he says: "No. The reason for that is: "By itself" (svataḥ). [This refers to] the existence of space and so forth in relation to the Self.
And because it is the cause of manifestation, there is no dependence upon that [external object]; thus he says: "Of place and so forth" (deśādeḥ) || 133 ||
Whatever object there may be that depends upon place, time, causes, and so forth;
That very [object] would be dependent upon that [subject], but it does not bestow the establishment of place and so forth.
What then? It is dependent upon that; thus he says: "Place," etc. (134).
Whatever object whatsoever is perceived by virtue of its causes and conditions, [is empty].
That result of action should be understood as being independent of the underlying reality.

If it is asked, "In that case, does this not lead to duality—the view that some things depend on space and so forth while others do not?"—he says "kārakādi" (beginning with the causal factors) to show that this is not so.
Since every effect is imagined like a snake in a rope, duality does not exist in reality; such is the meaning. || 135 ||
Since knowledge depends on the object, all action depends on the agent.
The agent and so forth arise from delusion regarding the self; the reality is established as inherently non-dual.

Anticipating the objection—“Why should the result [of knowledge] not also be imagined in the same way as action and its factors?”—he says: “The reality,” etc. Since knowledge conforms to reality, and since action and its factors are products of ignorance (avidyā), when they are destroyed by knowledge, their effects—action and so forth—are also destroyed; thus the reality of the Self remains immutable and inherently non-dual. This is the meaning. || 136 ||
It destroys the causal factors, just as salt soil destroys a seed.
Because its cause has been destroyed by birth itself, it does not even form a bud. (8-8-252) 7.8932. 137.

He clarifies, by means of an illustration, how through knowledge (*vidyā*) there occurs the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), and consequently the cessation of its effects, such as the agent and so forth. Regarding the word "agents" (*kārakāṇi*): one might raise the objection, "Knowledge merely manifests the reality; it does not produce existence or non-existence. How then does it bring about the cessation of ignorance and the rest? Anticipating this, he says: "by birth" (*janmanā*). For that [knowledge], by its mere arising, while making the reality manifest, necessarily removes that ignorance.
The meaning is that it causes [the object] to cease by its very nature, and not through any other operation. || 137 ||

1. *ka*. *ma*. *yā* *buddhimitoṣare* || *ta* | *kha* *dhā’ḍuddhimitrauṣare* || *ta* | 2. *ka* *kārakāt* | [Vol. 3, page 98] 4. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1231.
The establishment of valid cognition occurs in the cognizer, because it is a transformation of the cognizer.
[This occurs] through the intervention of the object, by consciousness itself, and not by the mental modifications (vṛtti). || 138 ||

Now, [the opponent argues that] even though knowledge destroys ignorance and the like, it must reside in the self (ātman); thus, the self would possess specific attributes (saviśeṣatā). To this, he replies: "By the knower" (pramātṛ). The connection is that the establishment of valid cognition (pramā) is consciousness (saṃvit). Some maintain that because knowledge is inferable from its effect as its logical mark (liṅga), it is not directly perceivable by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin); to them, he says: "Without the intervention of the knower. The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) along with its appearance (sābhāsa) and the knowledge residing therein are eternal— [The sentence continues: ...[and thus there is no need for a substrate other than consciousness].* *(Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available portion.)*
The meaning is that it is established by experience. || 138 ||
If there is dependence on another means of knowledge for the mother, then for the mother, there must be measurement by another means of knowledge.
Because attachment to the self is difficult to restrain, an infinite regress would result. || 139 ||

He establishes the absence of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) for both the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*māna*). Regarding the phrase "in another knower" (*mātrantare*): the meaning is that if there were a requirement for a knower to depend on another knower, and for a means of knowledge to depend on another means of knowledge, then an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would be unavoidable at every such instance; thus, there would be a twofold infinite regress. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that an identical infinite regress would likewise follow if the result (*phala*) were to require another result. || 139 ||
The knower, too, would become a cause solely by means of an excellence of cognition.
Thus, a means of knowledge possessing certainty would be established as having a superior consciousness.

Having recalled the explanation of the process of the unmanifest (*avyākṛta-prakriyā*), which was stated for the purpose of supporting the meaning of the commentary beginning with "because of the very nature of the thing" (*vastu-svābhāvyāt*), [the author] now states the process of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-prakriyā*) during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra-daśā*), relying precisely upon that nature of the thing in order to explain the form belonging to it which is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). He says: "The knower" (*pramātṛ*). The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), together with its appearance (*sābhāsa*), is postulated as such because its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) toward the knowledge of the knower would otherwise be untenable.

The meaning is as follows: by means of that very excellence of the manifestation of the object as it truly is (*yathābhāvākhyāti*), immediately after the excellence [of the object] arises, that same cognizer is established as being distinguished by the excellence of the manifestation of knowledge (*jñānākhyāti*).
Consequently, the means of valid cognition (*māna*), designated as "knowledge," comes to be crowned with the fruit of the ascertainment of the object.
The particle *api* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). The word *tathā* draws in the verb from the previous verse. (140)
Just as a determination possesses a form arising from its own uncommon nature.
When the external object of cognition is predominant, there is a cognition of an uncommon object. || 141 ||

Having first stated the form of the ascertainment (*niścaya*), he declares that cognition possesses a form identical to it by means of the words "meyeti. Just as the ascertainment— which is the fruit of the means of knowledge— is characterized by a form manifested through the unique nature of the object of knowledge (*meya*) such as a jar, so too, when cognition proceeds by making the jar and so forth its primary object, the intellect (*dhī*) arises as if possessing the unique form of the jar and so forth, such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth."
"Thus" means that the cognition and its fruit have an identical form. || 141 ||
At the time of human activity, there may be the subordination of the external object of cognition.
It extends from the initial manifestation up to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because of the arising of its specific fruit. || 142 ||
When the object is predominant and the means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth are subordinate, he says: "The means of knowledge...

When the means of knowledge (*māna*) is active toward producing its own fruit, then that means of knowledge, its agent, and the reflection residing therein—this triad—is made primary, while [the object] becomes subordinate and oriented toward it; for it is intended that the fruit arises as qualified by the jar and other such objects. This is the meaning. || 142 ||

But one who is engaged in the means of valid cognition [proceeds] further for the sake of establishing latent predispositions.
The cognition, in which the object is subordinate, is directly perceived by memory. || 143 ||

When there is the subordination of the object and the predominance of the intellect, he says: "By means of the instrument of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*). Having ceased its activity immediately after producing its own result—namely, ascertainment—the instrument of knowledge, having fulfilled its purpose, remains in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited upon its substrate, either the object or the knower.

That [impression], remaining in that state, when awakened by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors, arises in the form of memory at the time of recollection; at that time, the object of knowledge...
The meaning is that the intellect becomes subordinate, while the object of cognition possesses primacy and the intellect possesses the status of a quality. || 143 ||
When, while directly realizing its own self, it becomes the state of being an object of focus;
That very [consciousness] is considered the objective support (ālambana) for that which consists of the nature of cause and effect. || 144 ||

If it be argued that sometimes the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is primary and sometimes the knowledge (*jñāna*) is primary, then how can one's own doctrine—that the single reality alone is primary—be established? To this, he says: "Directly" (*sākṣāt*). The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), together with its mental modifications (*vṛtti*) and accompanied by the reflection of consciousness (*sābhāsa*), designated by the term "knower" (*pramātṛ*), brings about a direct perception of its own object through the superimposition of identity with the immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthacaitanya*). That which is the support of this immutable, immediate consciousness— [The text continues: ...is the Self. Therefore, since the Self is always the primary subject, there is no contradiction in the doctrine that the one reality alone is primary. Furthermore, because the Self is of the nature of pure consciousness, it is not an object; thus, there is no possibility of a conflict between the knower and the known. Moreover, since the Self is eternal and unchanging, it is not subject to temporal distinctions such as past, present, or future. Consequently, the Self is ever-present and does not depend on anything else for its manifestation. This is the intended meaning. Thus, it has been established that the Self is the one reality, free from all distinctions. This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with "Directly. Now, the author proceeds to explain the nature of the Self as the witness (*sākṣin*). [End of excerpt]

Having accepted [the Self] as such, it attains dependence; that very consciousness, as described, is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the manifold of cause and effect, just as a rope is for a snake and the like, because that [manifold] is a manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding it. Therefore, the position that there is only one primary principle (*pradhāna*) suffers no injury—this is the meaning. || 144 ||
This is due to the error of memory, which arises from the mental impressions of previous perceptions.
This activity, common to all the world, transcends the actual nature of things. || 145 ||

If it is argued that even though the fault of admitting multiple primary objects is absent, by stating that "cognition has the object of knowledge as its subordinate," one has abandoned one's own position—that memory does not embrace an external object—[the author] says "no," beginning with the word "pūrva" (previous). Memory, which arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of its own object, appears through delusion as if it possessed an object; therefore, all empirical activity based on memory is not [based on an external object] in reality.
The meaning is that there is no loss of the established doctrine (siddhānta), because [the cognition] conforms to the actual nature of the object. || 145 ||
Prior to the contact with the object, cognition resides in the knower.
Knowledge exists for the sake of establishing the state of being a knower, since the state of being a knower is produced by that [knowledge]. (146)

Anticipating the objection that if memory were devoid of an external object, then because there would be no distinction from other cognitions, even valid knowledge (*māna*) would be dependent upon it, he says:
"It is mine" (*mama*). Prior to the connection with an object, cognition abides by depending on the knower, for the sake of establishing the state of being a knower residing in the subject;

this is because the state of being a knower is produced by that [subject]. Nor is it the case that cognition unconnected to an object does not exist at all, since it is manifested as a specific modification of that which exists in the form of its material cause (*upādāna*).

The meaning is that because of its connection with that [external object], the linguistic usage regarding the object cannot be established by cognition alone without such a connection; therefore, it possesses an external referent. || 146 ||
That which, by the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), stands clearly in the mind as if it were external;
The knowledge whose sphere is meditative cultivation has external objects as its support. || 147 ||
