In that case, one might argue that memory also has an external object because it is a cognition, just like perception; otherwise, there would be a contradiction in its having that as its object. To this, he says:

"Vāsanā" (latent impression). That cognition called "experience," which arose at its own time with an external object as its content, remains in the intellect in a subtle form due to the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by itself; then, in accordance with an awakener such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), it becomes clearly awakened and arises in the form of memory, [cognizing] the previously experienced object—

The meaning is that there is no difficulty whatsoever: although the sphere of mental formations appears as if it were an external object, because there is in reality no external referent, it is not grasped as an external object; and since the cognition of its having an object is established through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is no contradiction in such statements [as those cited]. || 147 ||
Whatever object is perceived exists only through the function of mutual dependence.
That [consciousness] would have as its support only the measure of the mother; it is not established by way of its own inherent existence.

Having described the state of the measuring subject (*māna*) during the time of ignorance, he concludes by stating the inherent nature of reality: "In dependence" (*apekṣā*). The entire inert world is dependent; its mother is the Measurer, the Witness, and it is established as having that [Witness] alone as its support. It cannot, however, be established by itself due to its very inertia.
Therefore, the meaning is that pure Consciousness alone—non-dual, unknowable, and ultimate—is real, while everything else is illusory (*māyika*). || 148 ||
That modification of the internal organ which rests upon the eyes and other sense organs.
The worldly vision is said to be that which has the appearance of objects such as form and so forth. || 149 ||

Having explained the commentary beginning with "due to the intrinsic nature of things" (*vastusvābhāvyāt*) and ending with "and the ultimate" (*pāramārthikī ca*), he analyzes the section beginning with "therein" (*tatra*).

Regarding the phrase "internal organ" (*antahkarana*): the meaning is that worldly perception (*laukikadṛṣṭi*) is a transformation of the intellect (*buddhipariṇāma*) which has the eyes and other senses as its instruments and has form and other objects as its domain. || 149 ||
And because that [birth] is being produced, there is a conjunction with birth and destruction.
But this view of self is eternal, devoid of birth, destruction, and the like. (150)

He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "sā kriyate" (that is performed), saying "tasyāśca" (and of that). He explains the commentary beginning with "yā tu" (but that which) by saying "ātma" (the Self). The word "tu" (but) serves to distinguish this from the previously mentioned perception. || 150 ||
For the reality of cause and effect is the inner self, which is consciousness.
Therefore, the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is eternal within the intellect and its objects.

(151) Regarding the reason for its eternity—namely, its being devoid of birth and so forth—he states the reason: "Because it is an effect," etc. Now, if it were not eternal, because it is a perception...

[The opponent argues: "Just like the vision residing in the eye, even the vision residing in a jar and so forth would be eternal; therefore, [the author] says: 'Therefore' (*tasmāt*). Even that [vision] residing in the intellect and so forth, being indicated by the term 'vision,' is indeed eternal; thus, there is a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). Nor is there a sublation (*bādhā*) consisting in the undesirable consequence of the eternity of the vision residing in a jar and so forth, because that is accepted [by us]; however, due to the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), it is sometimes not manifested. Furthermore, the vision to be expressed cannot serve as an example, because [the property of] being a vision (*dṛṣṭitva*)..."

Since the reason [of being expressible] is unestablished if it is the denotable object (*vācya*), and since the example would lack the probandum if it were the indicated object (*lakṣya*), one should understand that the same logical consequence applies here as well; therefore, the meaning is that the light of consciousness is eternal everywhere. || 151 ||
When the intellect is colored by direct perception, [the notion of a self] arises with dharma and other factors as its cause.
An impermanent form arises, characterized by suffering, sound, and so forth. || 152 ||

Even though the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is eternal, because of the qualification "view" in the phrase "the worldly view is impermanent," it follows that there is another mode of activity (*vṛttyantara*) which is eternal.

Anticipating the objection that there might be attainment [of the Self], he says: "The inward" (*pratyak*). Since the mention of "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) is illustrative, the meaning is that every modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) is impermanent. || 112 ||
In this state, which has the form of direct perception, [the cognition] is based on an external cause.
An aspect arises from the intellect, possessing the nature of coming and going.

Fearing that even the coloring (*uparāga*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) by the forms of sound and so forth might be caused by *dharma* and the like, he clarifies what has already been stated with the words:
"In the stable [intellect]," (113).
Having perceived [it] through the limiting adjunct consisting of the forms of rejection and appropriation.
Because it has a single substratum, it arises as if stable and conjoined. || 154 ||

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to say "the ultimate vision is the Self alone" even though worldly vision is impermanent—since such a statement would entail the impossibility of designating a distinction by calling [the Self] the "seer"—he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "That" (*sā*). [He says: "Due to limiting adjuncts" (*upādhi*). The "single locus" (*ekāśrayatva*) of the two visions means their presence within a single cognition. Agency and the state of being an action, which reside in the witness-consciousness and its modifications, are attributed through superimposition (*āropa*) to that which is of the nature of eternal vision and are thus used in common parlance.
The ellipsis is "by that designation. || 154 ||
Because he is the witness of the intellect and its modifications, the Unborn is not affected by the intellect or its cognitions.
O Lord, it is perceived through ignorance, just as a gem is [perceived] by means of its settings. 155.
To the question of how such designations as "sees," "does not see," "is born," or "perishes" can apply if there is the view of permanence (nityadṛṣṭi), he says:

"Buddhi... etc. Just as a crystal is made to appear in various forms by means of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), so too the Self, though non-different [from pure consciousness], is designated as possessing modifications such as seeing due to its own ignorance (avidyā), because it is the witness of the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties; thus, by their influence, it is conventionally described as being characterized by such activities. || 115 ||
Because it manifests as agent and action, [the self] is [denoted] by words expressing agent and action.
The witness is indicated by names, but he is not directly denoted by them. || 156 ||

Raising the objection: "Why should impermanence not belong to sound by its very nature, through its connection with the view of impermanence [which follows] from the view of self?", he refutes the first alternative—after having proposed the alternatives that the reason is either being denotable (*vācyatva*) or being indicated (*lakṣyatva*)—with the verse beginning with "katra" (where). 156.
Because it is the witness of that [individual's] birth and destruction, it is unborn, indestructible, and self-luminous.
Even that witness is described in such terms as "it is born" and "it perishes."

He states the second [point]: "tajjanma" (its birth). The sense is that even though it is the object of definition (*lakṣya*), there is no establishment of birth and so forth in reality, because it has been stated that the perception of such [birth] is merely due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*). By this, the reason "because it is a perception" (*dṛṣṭitva*) is refuted. || 197 ||
Of vision, which is insentient by nature and exists for the sake of another, [one perceives] consciousness within itself.
You would not perceive the inner self, the seer, by means of this which is seen.
Having stated the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "Not from sight," he explains its words: "From sight" (dṛṣṭeḥ). || 118 ||
With respect to the beginning, middle, and end that are sought after and delimited.
How could you perceive that which is contrary to it by means of a vision that has become its very object? (159)
And because it is distinct from the visible, its being made an object by that [cognition] is untenable; thus he says: "dikṣita" (pointed out). || 119 ||
The activity of the eye is directed toward seeing when the object of sight, such as color-form and so forth, is present.
"How can one perceive that inner self by means of those two [the body and the senses]?"—thus [he asked]. "By itself. (160)

He states another argument for the fact that the Seer is not an object of vision, beginning with the words "of the Seer" (*draṣṭuḥ*). The meaning is as follows: an agent possesses the capacity to produce an action, and that action brings about a result in its object; however, for that which is inwardly present as the fruit of the agent’s action, there is no being pervaded by the action. For the Inner Self (*pratyak*), who is by nature consciousness, there can be no pervasion by vision. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates universal consensus regarding this stated point. || 160 ||
One should not perceive an agent apart from the seer, the seeing, and the object of sight.
Apart from ignorance, how could there be agency for the immutable Self? (161)

It has been stated that the Self is the witness of the intellect and so forth, and possesses the view of eternity. Now, [the author] states with the words beginning "no" that its agency as well belongs to that very same [Self]. The meaning is that immutable consciousness, due to its indifference, does not desire to see the seer and so forth; yet, it possesses the status of being an agent for that [seeing]. He then says "agency" to show that there is no real (vāstavam) agency. || 161 ||
One never perceives an agent as being identical with the true reality in any way whatsoever.
Because it does not follow from ignorance, the luminous inner light is, by its very nature, the true reality. || 162 ||

Raising the objection that even if agency (*kartṛtva*) is rooted in ignorance (*āvidya*), the perception of self and others produced by its connection [to the Self] must be real, he says: "The agent" (*kāra-kam*). Just as the Seer and so forth perceive [objects] through superimposed agency despite being of the nature of one Self (*ekātmya*), so too, having become a non-agent (*akāraka*), one does not produce the perception of self and others, because the connection with ignorance is also non-existent in reality; this is the meaning. The reason for this is stated: "Luminous" (*bhāsvat*). [This refers to] the obstruction...
The meaning is that it consists merely of the vibration of the *vidhura* (the differentiated). || 162 ||
That by which this eye is seen, and that eye by which one sees.
Know that alone to be Brahman, and not that which people worship as such.
He corroborates the meaning of the scriptural passage "not by sight" with another scriptural passage, beginning with the words "by which. || 163 ||
That which the mind does not conceive by means of that [mind] which they call the "conceived" mind;
For you are that which the knowers of Brahman realize, and not this which they worship.

Anticipating the objection that even if it is not an object of the external senses, it might still be an object of the mind, he cites the agreement of another scriptural passage beginning with "na mateḥ" (not of the intellect), stating: "By the mind... (164).
Such statements as these serve to establish the meaning as it has been explained.
There are hundreds of Vedic passages for the purpose of establishing that [the Self] is beyond the reach of the senses. || 165 ||

He concludes with the corroboration from another scriptural passage by saying "ityevamādi" (and so forth). The word "dṛk" (the Seer) is itself an explanation of the phrase "for the sake of supporting the aforementioned meaning. || 165 ||
Because this [notion] of "I" and so forth arises from delusion, it does not exist even in the slightest degree.
It is not possible to assert identity [between cause and effect], because there is no sublation of the established cause.
1 kha. Not that; 2 ka. ga. to see.
[Vol. 3, page 103] 1236 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Third Adhyāya]

Having cited scripture regarding the immeasurability of the Self, he now sets forth the logical argument, beginning with the words "This [is...]. The cause of that [Self] is ignorance (ajñāna), which consists of the constructed [notions] such as the "measurer" (mātrā) and so forth. Because of the non-sublation of that [ignorance], the state of being the Brahman-Self cannot be known through the "measurer" and its like, due to the obstruction posed by ignorance and the rest. However, when ignorance has perished, there is an absence of the "measurer" and other factors arising from it; thus, the Self is not easily known by means of that [instrument]. The meaning is that it is immeasurable with respect to the individual knower (prati-brahma). || 166 ||
Without even making a distinction between views, [he disregarded] such scriptural passages as "of the view," and so forth.
Some wise men explain that this arises from the grace of Jātavedas.
Having explained [the passage] beginning with "not from seeing" (*na dṛṣṭeḥ*) in accordance with the *Bhāṣya*, he restates the explanation of Bhartṛprapañca: "dṛṣṭi... (verse 167).
O L,
you would not perceive the Self as the agent of seeing by means of that which is being seen.
By means of a vision that does not pursue forms, there is no action possessing an agent and an object.

Anticipating the objection, "How can that be its explanation?", he states the intended meaning of the words of the scripture beginning with "no," namely: "Because of seeing" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*). For vision, having arisen through the door of the eye, takes the form of a mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) and perceives color; yet, by that very vision, [the Self] cannot be made an object. He states the reason for this: "Because of form" (*rūpa*). Furthermore, it does not make that [Self] an object because it is an action, just as motion does not make the mover an object; thus he says.
And this genitive case in the word "dṛṣṭeḥ" is used because of the reason of its being currently performed.
But it should be understood as residing in action alone, since it does not exist in any other object. || 169 ||

He states the intention of those who explain it thus: "And because of [the word] 'dṛṣṭeḥ'. He provides the reason why the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*) by stating that the vision (*dṛṣṭi*) is to be accomplished by the self. He uses the word "tu" (but) to indicate that, among transitive actions, the object is more intimate (*antaraṅga*). He explains the meaning of the particle "eva" (only/just) with the word "na" (not), [referring to] another meaning in the form of a residual relation (*śeṣa*) for the vision being performed.
He says it is because it is external; for this reason, [he states] "yataḥ" (169).
In that same way, he declares the self's status as the agent of seeing by means of a word ending in the suffix -tṛc.
Therefore, from the perspective of action, one does not perceive that seer.

Having explained the genitive case, he explains the accusative case with the words "dṛṣṭi" (view). The word "tathā" (likewise) was used to provide an illustration for the meaning of the genitive already stated.
[An objection is raised: "Let it be that the view is the object and the seer is the agent; what follows from that? To this, he says: "yataḥ" (since). || 170 ||
The form that is most desired by the agent is the object of vision, because it is the effect [of the act of seeing].
The eye, the mind, or the intellect is held to be the instrument of the agent. (171)
He clarifies that vision is an object of action. Regarding the term "object" (*karman*): as they say, "Vision is an activity;

that which is its form is the object, for it is that which is most desired to be attained. If that [vision] is the object of the Self, then what is the instrument? In response to this question, following the commentary which states that the eye, mind, and intellect are the instruments, he says: "The eye," etc. (Verse 171).
But the conscious self is the agent here, due to its autonomy in all actions.
The fruit and the perception of form arise from the agent's vision and its final determination.
To one who is doubting whether the seer is the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme (para), he replies with the words "vijñāna" and so forth. The word "dṛṣṭi" has the sense of the locative case.
In that regard—[as found in] Brāhmaṇa 4, Volume 3, page 104—this is accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1237.

The reason is: "because of independence" (*svātantryāt*). Independence is the state of being the instigator of an action while not being prompted by another agent; this exists for the individual soul (*jīva*) in all activities. Thus, the meaning is that its status as the agent of seeing is logical. By stating that the fruit of the act of seeing—which is accomplished by the conscious self (*vijñānātman*)—is the perception of form, he declares that fruit of that seeing with the word "fruit" (*phalam*). || 172 ||
In this context, the agent has reached a state of finality as the means for perception.
It is maintained by some that the fruit [of an action] occurs at a time subsequent to the completion of the action. || 173 ||

In this established framework, in order to clarify that the seer is not an object of seeing, he explains that the culmination [of the process] lies in the seeing itself, by way of its being an instrument and a subordinate factor. He says, "as an instrument" (*sādhanatvena*). For it has been stated that [the self] is employed as an instrument for the action. Having described its subordination through agency in the action, he declares its primacy as the result. He says, "the action" (*kriyā*). For it has been stated that the result occurs after the completion of the action.
"It will belong to someone. || 173 ||
If the action belongs to the master or to someone else, then the action itself must be shown; however, the seer is not seen by means of seeing. (174)

He clarifies the meaning of the word "what" (*kiṃ*): "of the master" (*svāminaḥ*). The master is the individual soul (*jīva*), while the other is its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), known as the intellect (*buddhi*) accompanied by the reflection of consciousness (*sābhāsa*). The meaning is that the perception of form and so forth belongs to one of these two; this is the result. Anticipating the objection that the action, like the result, might also be attributed either to the form or to the self, he says: "the object" (*karma*). For an action is directed toward the object (*karman*) which is most desired to be attained.

Because it has been stated that [the Self] is "become exhausted" (khībhūta), knowledge has cognition as its fruit; action, however, has form and so forth as its object, not the Self—this is the meaning.
He clarifies this very point with the word "karma. As they have said: "That [Self] is to be seen, not to be acted upon. || 174 ||
This being so, that seer of seeing should [be seen] by means of seeing which has become an object.
One should not perceive one's own self as an agent in any way whatsoever through [theoretical] vision.
Having established the division according to the manner stated above, he concludes the result [of that analysis] with the word "tatra" (therein). || 175 ||
This explanation of the great ones does not appear sound to us.
Because it is not included among the syllables of the formal argument (nyāya), it is explained as follows: || 176 ||
He begins to refute the interpretation of others that has been stated: "The explanation... (verse 176).
Thus, this response does not appropriately address the question as it was asked.
For this reason, every specific qualification of the question is impossible in relation to the seer.

In that regard, he establishes the fact that [the meaning] is not conveyed by the literal words of the scripture, beginning with "Just as" (yathā). He states the reason for the answer "No" to the objection that the passage beginning with "That which is directly" (*yatsākṣāt*) follows the authority of the sacred texts (*pramā*), whereas the rebuttal beginning with "Not of seeing" (*na dṛṣṭeḥ*) proceeds with reference to the agent of seeing: "Because" (*yataḥ*). || 177 ||
Because [the attributes] such as "directly" and so forth are not applicable in the slightest degree.
The aforementioned qualification applies to that kāraka which produces [false] views. || 178 ||
Regarding how the collection of qualifiers present in the interrogative sentence is impossible in the case of the agent of seeing, he says: "Directly," and so forth.
[Vol. 3, page 105]
"The answer provided by the other school does not follow the question, because the state of being the innermost of all has been stated [in that way]; this is the remainder of the sense. (178)
Nor are the individual soul (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman) intended here as the two lights.
But surely, because a sentence is connected to a single meaning, there would be no falsity in the statement of only one [of its parts]. (179)

Regarding the two, the higher and the lower, intended within the light (*prabhā*), he states that the application of the qualifiers is appropriate there according to their respective fitness, beginning with the words "the knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*).

The reason for this is given by the words "having a single purpose" (*ekārtha*); the meaning is that, according to the maxim "a sentence is one because of its unity of purpose," [the two terms form a single syntactical unit]. || 179 ||
Furthermore, there could be no state of being most desired [by the agent], because the perception of a desirer is impossible.
There is no other vision for the vision, nor likewise another seer for the seer.
If that [infinite regress] were admitted, there would be an unavoidable infinite regress for the bird.
Because perception is in some way pervaded by another perception. (181)

Regarding the question of what fault there is in admitting both a vision and a distinct seer in both cases, he says: "That" (tad). He provides the qualification "unavoidable" (anivāraṇā) to reveal that this [admission] is a defect because it results in the destruction of the root. He states its consequence with the words "by another vision" (dṛṣṭyantareṇa). It should also be understood as "by another seer" (draṣṭrantareṇa), and the word "vision" (dṛṣṭeḥ) is an elliptical expression for "seer" (draṣṭuḥ). || 181 ||
Likewise, by the very destruction of the seer, there is the fulfillment of the desired object.
And this which is stated—that "this would be purposeless because of [the nature of] perception"—[is also incorrect]. || 182 ||

As for the argument that [the word] "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) implies the status of being the agent of seeing, and so forth—that is untenable. "In the same way" means: just as it was stated that the genitive case in "of seeing" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*) does not denote the object, so too the term "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) cannot possibly denote the agent. The meaning is this:

if one intends to express the status of being the agent of seeing by using the word "seer," then since that very status of being the agent of seeing is already established by the word "seer" itself, the addition of "of seeing" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*) would be redundant. The particle *ca* (and) serves the purpose of emphasis. ||182||
Because the seer and the seeing are always inseparable from one another.
The relationship between qualifier and qualified is accepted when there is deviation [from the universal]. (183)

He states another reason why the qualification of "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) is superfluous in the opponent's position: "Always" (*sadā*). While it is observed that between a blue lotus and a lotus there is mutual deviation—that is, a lotus is qualified by "blue"—there is no such mutual deviation between the seer and vision.
For the seer does not deviate from vision, nor does vision deviate from him; therefore, the word "of vision" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*) is redundant. This is the meaning. || 983 ||
Nor is this a reading resulting from negligence, since it is accepted by all without disagreement.
Nor is it accepted as being a mere figurative statement (āryavāda), because it is not subordinate to any injunction (vidhi). || 184 ||

Fearing that [the passage] might be recited erroneously even though it is meaningless, he says "na ca" (and not). The word "sarveṣām" (of all) means of both groups of followers of the Vedic branches. He says "vidhi" (injunction) to show that this is not accepted as being merely an explanatory supplement (arthavāda). || 184 ||
1 ka. draṣṭṛdṛṣṭe | 2 ka. ca | 3 kha. 'rākaroti | ta ~ | [vol 3, page 106]
Even the state of being cognizable through non-perception is accepted as belonging to the seer.
"In that case, it would follow that [the doctrine] contradicts direct perception, because of what has been stated.
Regarding the point that "the action is to be shown, not the agent," he says: "I... [and so on]. If the seer were accessible to the notion of "I" in common worldly experience—

Even though it is agreed upon by experts in gems that [the gem] cannot be seen, etc., one might think that its being an object of vision can be refuted in such scriptural passages; [anticipating this, the author says: "Perception," etc. (185).
The perceptibility of the object, the means of knowledge, and the knower has already been explained above.
Therefore, this explanation which was provided here regarding the phrase "of the vision" has been refuted.

Having stated the contradiction with the logic of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the opponent, he states the contradiction with his own statement: "meya" and so forth. The meaning of "likewise" (*api*) is that it is just as has been stated [previously] regarding the fact that the Seer (*dṛṣṭi*) is accessible to the notion of "I" (*aham-dhī*). The words "stated by Bhartṛprapañca" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 186 ||
Whatever exists other than the Self as described above, which takes the form of cause and effect—
That which destroys one who is afflicted is trivial, like the silver [perceived] in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like. || 187 ||

Having refuted the interpretation of others regarding the passage beginning with "na dṛṣṭaḥ" and having established his own interpretation, he states the meaning of the phrase "ato 'nyad ārtam": "yathoktāt" (from what has been described). This negates perishability in the form of conjunction with a cause. He says "tuccham" (insubstantial) to avoid the fallacy of contradicting his own tenets. He says "śukti" (mother-of-pearl) [to illustrate]. || 187 ||
This very [consciousness] would thus be unlearned, because it is established by itself.
It is eternally and uniquely unarisen, its true nature being the realization of the inward-turned vision that has been extinguished [of duality]. || 188 ||
Having stated the literal meaning of the words, he now states the implied meaning with the word "this" (etad). For it has been said that this alone is one, non-perishing, and immutable. || 188 ||
Alternatively, this may be a statement of the reason (hetu) because of the nature of the logically consistent entity.
Since the existence of anything other than that is not established, the state of being afflicted (ārta) would possess a logical reason. || 189 ||
The sum of verses from the beginning is 6,216.
Thus ends the fourth Uṣasta Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter in the *Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*. 4.

Therefore, having restated the word [from the previous verse], he states another meaning: "the statement of the reason" (*hetūkti*). This clarifies the meaning in the form of a reason. Regarding the word "stated" (*ukta*):

because a reality characterized by attributes such as directness (*sākṣāt*) exists everywhere as the nature of the inner self (*pratyak*), its existence as something distinct from that [nature] is not established.

The meaning is that everything appearing as a separate entity would be utterly void; thus, the unreality of the phenomenal world of non-Self is established, and the reason expressed by the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is logically consistent. || 189 ||
Thus ends the fourth Uṣasta-brāhmaṇa of the third chapter in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
1240 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya —
Now begins the Fifth Brāhmaṇa].
Everything previously mentioned is a bond that causes attachment.
And once it is determined that the bound [soul] is distinct from existence, || 1 ||

He proceeds to state the connection by referring back to what has already occurred: "In the beginning," etc. The meaning is that in the first three chapters, transmigratory existence along with its causes, such as ritual action, was described;
in the fourth, the immutable consciousness, the inner self, was determined to be the seeker of liberation. || 1 ||
Now, for the sake of utterly destroying the cause of attaining the miseries of saṃsāra.
The knowledge of the true nature of the Self, having renunciation as its sole companion, is thus described.

He states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa: "In the cycle of existence," etc. The meaning is that the fifth Brāhmaṇa is intended to explain perfect knowledge (samyagjñāna) together with renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which destroys bondage along with its cause. || 2 ||
For renunciation is the defining characteristic of one who has produced right knowledge.
And since renunciation is the means for its arising, it is therefore described here.

[Objection: Surely it is knowledge alone that must be expressed, because it destroys ignorance; renunciation is not [required], since it is of no use prior to or subsequent to knowledge. To this, he says: "Once arisen... and so on. The word "and" implies "the means for knowledge. The word "here" refers to the present context of the discussion on knowledge. (3)
Yoga is characterized by active engagement; knowledge is characterized by renunciation.
Therefore, placing knowledge at the forefront, a wise person should renounce in this world.
He states the proof for its being the means to that [liberation] as follows: "In [the case of] activity," etc. (4).
This very question that was asked by Uṣasta is now being asked by Kahola as well.
Why, then, is that very same question asked again, when its resolution has already been established?
Having stated his own intended interpretation of the connection, he raises an objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to state the interpretation intended by Bhartṛprapañca. He says, "Upastā—" and so on;
that is to say, provided there is no difference in meaning in those cases. || 5 ||
If it is argued that there is no fault because of the difference between the questioners, it is not so, because of the difference in the answers given.
For a single question concerning one matter, only a single answer is desired. || 6 ||

He raises the objection regarding the avoidance of tautology: "Because of the difference between the questioners. He refutes this: "Not so. Even for a single subject matter, it is appropriate that there be only one answer, even if the questions are posed by different authors, provided there is no difference among the respondents;

however, in this case, since there is a difference in the answers—such as "He who is not subject to hunger" and so forth—there is no difference among the questioners that could avoid the charge of tautology. This is the meaning. || 6 ||
Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a redundancy anywhere within a single teaching.
And here there is no worldly discourse from which a distinction among questioners might arise.
1. "Of one who desires to know" (nijhāsor iti). 2. *kha* reads: "questioned" (pṛṣṭaḥ). 3. *ka* reads: "'do'sti yato". [Vol.
3, page 108] 5. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1241.

"Let it be then; however, repetition itself is observed, for repetition is seen when there is a difference between the recensions (śākhās)," [the opponent] says. [The author] replies: "It is not repetition. The word *pravacana* refers to the subject matter of the scriptures. He states another reason why the avoidance of repetition through the difference of questioners is not possible: "And not...
For in the Śruti, there is no such thing as worldly chatter (*jalpa*), by which a difference of questioners might serve to avoid repetition, since the scripture is not of human origin (*apauruṣeyā*).

The meaning is that in the Śruti, a real distinction between questioners is undesirable, and an imagined one is useless for avoiding the fault of redundant repetition with the non-imagined [questioner]. || 7 ||
Therefore, although these two words are identical in form, they may express different meanings.
It is determined that in the speech of Kahola and Uṣasta, there are two questions. || 8 ||
He establishes the conclusion: "It is the same. The meaning of the word "that" (tat) is tautology when there is identity of purpose. || 8 ||
Uṣasta questioned him regarding the self that knows the field, but not the supreme state.
Kahola also questioned the Supreme Self, which is free from suffering.

How is there a difference in meaning between these two? To that he says: "The Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña), etc. As they have said: "The former question concerns the Supreme Self; this one concerns the individual self (vijñānātman). The sequence [of the questions] is to be inferred from the Mādhyandina recension in the commentary. || 9 ||
From the presentation of a single part, their identity of purpose is determined.
When dharmas are stated as being mutually intermingled, they are to be established according to their appropriate application. || 10 ||

For those who maintain that the absorption of this conscious self (vijñānātman) into the Supreme Self must be taught, the identity of the two is intended; however, that [identity] is not logical if the two questions have different meanings. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In one... By the statement of both within a single context, their identity is established by the context itself. Therein, in the section concerning Uṣasta, the conscious self is defined as a constituent part of the meaning of the sentence, whereas in the section concerning Kahola...

The meaning is this: however, that portion [of the two questions] which pertains to the other [the Supreme Self] has the same locus because it is presented together, and it possesses the same function, as has been stated. Having raised the objection that the two parts of the sentence-meaning—the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para)—are the objects of the two questions, since one observes a single purpose despite the transposition of their attributes, he says:
"mutually" (mithaḥ). || 10 ||
That which was previously described as being the most proximate [to the Self] resides in the Supreme Self.
Because a portion of that [Self] has been expressed, one will understand it as the conscious self (vijñānātman). || 11 ||

Although the attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*) are said to be mutually intermingled, it is nevertheless intended that they be established according to their respective possibilities; this very point he demonstrates with the word "that" (*yat*). That which is stated as an attribute of the Supreme Self in the dialogue of Kahola—namely, being the innermost of all (*sarvāntaratva*)—will, because it is an attribute of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), apply to that very same one who was the subject of Uṣasta’s question. Since both are mentioned within a single context, the state of being the innermost (*antaratamatva*) belongs to the Supreme Self.
The meaning is that it will be established as residing in the conscious self (vijñānātman) when it is being explained; such is the sense of that statement. || 11 ||
The state of having transcended sorrow, delusion, and the like, as well as the nature of being luminous consciousness;
And even though it has been described as having consciousness as its essence, it will attain the Supreme Self. || 12 ||

He applies the method demonstrated regarding the nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman) to the nature of the individual self (vijñānātman) as well. [The verse begins with] "śoka" (sorrow). Although there is a difference in wording between [the two], [the meaning remains the same]. 2. kha. Therefore, of those two.

Although its state of being beyond the senses and its self-luminosity were explained in the *Jyotir-brāhmaṇa* as pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*), nevertheless, that [nature] will lead one to the Supreme [Self] discussed in the fifth chapter.

The meaning is that because it is connected to that very nature of his, the state of being beyond sorrow, delusion, and so forth, as well as the state of having the nature of pure luminosity, which are predicated of the self of consciousness, will be established for the Supreme Self; such is the sense of that statement. || 12 ||
By the remainder of the fifth chapter, there is the definitive determination of the Supreme Self.
But in the sixth chapter, the determination of the nature of consciousness will be explained. || 13 ||

Having stated the difference in subject matter between the two questions, he declares that the remainder of the fifth [chapter] forms a single syntactical unit with the section on Kahola. He says: "In the fifth...

For it has been stated that the determination of the Supreme Self is to be explained by the remainder of the fifth chapter. He states that the *Jyotir-brāhmaṇa* and so forth form a single syntactical unit with the section on Uṣasta. He says: "But in the sixth... as they have said: "By the sixth [chapter], [the teaching concerns] the individual self (*vijñānātman*). (13)
In this context, there is a presentation of two: the conscious self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (parātman).
The absence of redundancy was made manifest by resorting to the path of logic. || 14 ||

He states the reason why the two questions have different meanings: "The presentation," he says. For it has been stated that there must indeed be a second question that is not a mere repetition. || 14 ||
Thus some explain it, saying that these two are as they have been described.
This explanation is not correct; how it [should be] stated is as follows. (15)
He summarizes the opposing position: "Thus they explain. He states that it is incorrect to claim that two meanings are intended by the two Brāhmaṇas, saying: "Not correctly. || 19 ||
This [is the response] "to you" for both questions as well.
The individual soul (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman) are not the two "selves" intended here.
It reveals incorrectness. [This is] because of the response. || 16 ||
The question is directly recognized as being of one form, and the answer is "Your very self"; how can these two statements have different meanings? (17)

He states that there is no difference in meaning because of the recognition of the identical form between the two questions, as if they were a question and its answer. He says, "The statement of the question.

He concludes by showing the result of the identical form of the question and the answer: "And the answer. The word "and" (ca) serves to combine the identity of the question with this [identity of the answer]. || 17 ||
And two selves cannot possibly exist together within a single body.
The term *ātmapratyaya* has the same meaning as *śrutivacana*. || 18 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the two sentences do not have different meanings: "In one place," etc. Now, even if two enjoyers are impossible in one [place], there is no impossibility of an enjoyer and a non-enjoyer [being present] due to the logic of the *guhādhikaraṇa* (the cave-section) and because of the difference in aggregates between Uṣasta and Kahola; therefore, he says: "The Self," etc. The cognition "Self" has indeed a single object, for there is no evidence that its objects are in reality distinct.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, because it would contradict such scriptural passages as "The one God in all beings," he states that in reality there is no difference between selves:
"Likewise" (tathā). || 18 ||
1 [Vol.
3, Page 110] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1243.
All bodies consist of a single self, even though disputes arise concerning them.
Because there is no difference in their being bodies, like the body of an opponent. || 19 ||
He recalls what was stated in the *Bṛhad-vicāra*—that there is no difference [between them] because it would contradict the inference proving the identity of the self—by saying: "One... (verse 19).
And of everything that ends within [the body], such as the direct [perception] and so forth.
Since the sentence has a single purpose, two selves are not intended [to be expressed]. (20)
He restates what was said regarding the impossibility of the two questions having two selves as their object, once the oneness of the self has been established: "All... (verse 20).
The relationship between qualifier and qualified is characterized by non-figurative status, lack of intervention, and other such specific attributes.
It is not logical for a single self to be manifold, because that [manifoldness] is impossible.

He states another reason for the impossibility of the two questions having different meanings: "Not figurative" (*agauṇa*). This means that [the subject] is qualified by these attributes. He provides the reason: "Because of the impossibility of those," meaning because it is impossible for multiple qualities such as being non-figurative and being the innermost of all (*sarvāntaratva*) to coexist [in a single entity]. || 21 ||
If there were a difference between these two, the undertaking of the Upaniṣads would be in vain.
And there would follow the consequence of no liberation for the individual soul (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman). || 22 ||

He states another defect regarding the distinction between the meanings of the questions: "In vain," etc. The commencement of the Upaniṣads is for the purpose of knowing the identity of Brahman and the Self; in reality, if there were a difference between them, it would not be commenced, because the cognition of identity is impossible between two distinct things. Thus, even if there is an imagined difference, the two questions do not have different objects. Furthermore, if there were a real difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), liberation—defined as the individual soul's attainment of Brahmanhood—would not occur, nor would there be the destruction of ignorance, for that [liberation] too...
He states that, because of the very absence of a reason in your position, [liberation] is impossible; therefore, the scripture is fruitless and not to be undertaken: "anirmokṣa... (verse 22).
Even a negation whose scope is not perceived in its entirety is not tenable.
If it is not admitted that the conscious self, having entered [the body], exists in its entirety, || 23 ||

He states another reason for the absence of a real difference between the selves: "Not as a whole," etc. This refers to the prohibition beginning with, "He who meditates on one or the other of these does not know it, for this [Self] is not a whole," and so forth. || 23 ||
Therefore, in accordance with the actual nature of things, no distinction exists anywhere.
Because they are ignorant of the actual nature of things, their distinction is like a dream or a magical illusion.

Having refuted the distinction of the Self, he now dispels the distinction of the non-Self as a secondary consequence. He says, "The reality" (vastu). The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is the indivisibility of the Self. If the reality is indeed indivisible, how can there be any measure of division therein? To this he replies: "The reality" (vastu). || 24 ||
Therefore, there is only one question; two questions are not intended.
Having been questioned regarding a certain specific point, he is questioned again. || 25 ||

He states the result regarding the identity of the self as being the unity of the question: "One. [An objection is raised: "In that case, the redundancy remains as it was"; to this he replies: "A certain... (25).
The subject matter of the instruction consists of the sentences of question and reply.
His true nature was determined in the past; however, it is being inquired about here.
1 kha. ‘gauṇavyaṃ | 2 kha. ga. ‘di bhittirbhave | [vol 3, page 111] 1244 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Adhyāya—]
He shows that very distinction [of the teaching] with the words: "of the instruction" (upadeśasya). || 26 ||
The witness, who exists as distinct from the intellect, is the object of the question.
The word "pratyaṅ" (facing inward) should be understood as appropriate; it is a summary of the meaning of the preceding question. || 27 ||
He clarifies the subject matter of the first question, which was stated in the [first] three quarters [of the verse], with the words "from the end of the intellect" (*buddhyantāt*).

The meaning is that it has been established by means of the preceding questions and answers that there exists a seeker of liberation, the inner self (*pratyagātman*), who is the subject appropriate for the question beginning with "the witness distinct from the knower, directly" (*pramātṛvyatirikta-statsākṣī sākṣād iti*). || 27 ||
The state of being beyond hunger and so forth belongs to that very reality previously described.
By the second [verse], reality is stated for the sake of removing individual delusion. || 28 ||

He clarifies what was stated by the words beginning with "tasya" (of that) with the phrase "aśanāyādi" (hunger, etc.). He states the fruit of the detailed exposition of reality with the word "pratyak" (the inner self). || 28 ||
Previously, the answer to the question was not stated correctly.
Thinking thus, he again questioned the sage regarding the matter he had asked about.

Having stated that the commencement of another question arises from a desire for specific knowledge regarding the previous question, he describes its commencement by way of another method, beginning with "Just as" (yathā). || 29 ||
By the words "directly" and so forth, that which is characterized as "directly" and so forth is questioned.
Just as it is so conceived, nothing at all is observed in such a response.
Regarding how the answer was not given according to the question, he says there: "Directly" (sākṣāt). || 30 ||
Because of his lack of contentment, Kahola [asked]; therefore, it was indeed Uṣasta’s question that followed.
The learned one questioned the sage further for the sake of understanding the true nature of reality.

Having stated the cause of discontent, he describes its result with the words "from discontent" (*asaṃtoṣāt*). If the answer had not been given according to the question, the sage would have had to ask it himself; as for why anyone else asks, he says: "the learned one" (*vidvān*). He states the purpose of Kahola’s question with the words "in accordance with reality" (*yāthātmya*). || 31 ||
"This is the Self" is one response, and "that which is by means of breath" is another.
Until that much has been stated, the meaning of the question would not be fully determined. || 32 ||

Anticipating the objection that there is no reason for dissatisfaction because Uṣasta’s question has already been resolved through repeated answers, he says: "This... The implication is that since the matter asked about has not been properly determined, it is appropriate to ask again regarding that very same point with the desire to ascertain it definitively. || 32 ||
Surely, the state of being beyond the six waves and the state of suffering [would apply] to the non-dual Self.
Just as light and darkness cannot exist together in one place at one time. || 33 ||
Regarding the statement that these two questions concern the single reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). || 33 ||

1. Ka. Ga. read: *ṛṣiḥ* || 29 || 2. Kha reads: *tadāha*. 3. Kha reads: *nmunividvā*. 4. Kha reads: *cāparaḥ*. [Vol. 3, page 112] 5. *Brāhmaṇam*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1245.
This is not a fault, because that ignorance is the cause of false cognition, delusion, and error.
The transmigratory state of the Self is imagined, like a black streak in the sky.

Regarding the argument that "the two who seek answers are mutually distinct because they possess contradictory properties, like darkness and light," [the author] states "No" [to the first alternative], meaning that their possession of contradictory properties cannot be established by means of valid cognition (*māna*). This is because the first [alternative] is unproven (*asiddhi*). || 34 ||
This has also been thoroughly investigated in the *Bṛhadvicāra*.
This follows from the context of distinguishing the objects of contradictory scriptures. || 35 ||

To the question, "How can it be stated as an established fact that the transmigratory state of the Self is merely imagined due to the delusion born from ignorance of the inward-facing consciousness (pratyag-jñāna)? he replies with the word "bṛhat" (the Great).
The two particles "ca" and "api" are used to indicate that this has already been stated in various other investigations on those respective occasions. Furthermore:

In the course of explaining the distinction between the scopes of the scriptural texts concerning the possession of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) and the absence of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*), he states that the falsity of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) has been demonstrated at the conclusion of the Madhu Brāhmaṇa: "Contradictory... This is to be connected with the preceding phrase, "this has been investigated. (35)
Just as the states of being a rope and being a snake [exist] even in a single object;
Just as [the appearance of silver] arises from its own nature and from delusion regarding it, so too does [the appearance of bondage] arise in the Self;
likewise, liberation and whiteness [purity] belong to two things that are mutually contradictory.
There would be an inherence of two properties, but not as in the case of a blue lotus and so forth. || 37 ||
It gives rise to another conceptual construction (*kalpa*). Regarding the phrase "as being a rope" and "as being white," one must supply the word "iti" (thus) after these.
The statement that there is no real coexistence of liberation and bondage in a single entity serves as a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). However, it is not [the case]... ||36||
Thus, there is no fault whatsoever in the state of having contradictory properties.
If it is argued that the existence of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth constitutes a fault here, [we reply: 38.

Regarding the reason "having contradictory attributes that are merely apparent," the probandum—difference—is either imagined (*kalpita*) or non-imagined (*akalpita*). It is not the first, because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*); nor is it the second, because it would lead to the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in the case of a rope and so forth. Thinking thus, he refutes [the argument] with the words "In this way" (*evam*). He has stated that there is no contradiction insofar as the state of being non-transmigratory (*asaṃsāritva*) exists in its unconditioned form, while the state of being transmigratory (*saṃsāritva*) exists in its conditioned form. Now, however, if one admits the existence of conditions (*upādhi*), [the Self] would possess a second entity (*sadvayatva*).

He raises an objection, saying "nāma," because one observes that only real things such as a jar can serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the position of non-duality (*advaita*). || 38 ||
Because of the statement "not here, not manifold" and because of the declaration "it is indeed one," [Brahman is one].
It is not so, for that [objection] has not been refuted by means of examples, reasoning, and the like. || 39 ||

If that were so, what would follow regarding the existence of duality? To this he says: "Not thus" (*neha*). The ellipsis is "there is a contradiction from the statement. By the force of reasoning known as the example of "not thus"—namely, that modifications such as bowls do not exist apart from clay and so forth—he refutes [the objection] by stating "not thus," because the aggregate of cause and effect fashioned by name and form through ignorance is merely ignorance, and that ignorance is dispelled by knowledge. Thus: "Not thus. (39)
The true nature of reality, when not being grasped, appears as if it were its opposite.
But when it is examined according to its actual state, it is seen exactly as it is. || 40 ||
He clarifies the very rebuttal with the words "not being perceived. Why is it said to be "as if contrary"? Because it is indeed dualistic.
[End of Volume 3, page 113, Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Third Chapter] 1246.

One might ask: why should that not be the reality? To this he says: "according to the actual state of things. The meaning is that since the cycle of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) is produced by name and form, which are the manifestations of indefinable ignorance (anirvācyājñāna), there is no loss of non-duality (advaita). || 40 ||
Whatever needs to be said regarding this objection has already been stated many times previously.
All that has been correctly stated here should be remembered with reverence by those who are diligent. || 41 ||

He reminds us of what was said in response to those who, unable to accept that saṃsāra is characterized by ignorance (avidyā), assert that reality consists of duality alone. He says, "In this [work]," anticipating the objection that this might be unintended because it is merely incidental. He says, "Repeatedly," to show that it has been stated in various places throughout the work. Anticipating the difficulty of grasping the meaning due to its being scattered here and there at the beginning of the connection and so forth, he says, "Extensively. He indicates its lack of contradiction by the word "properly" (samyak).
The word "here" (iha) refers to the doubt regarding the reality of duality. || 41 ||
For those whose minds are afflicted by delusion that is established without critical inquiry.
Even though the supreme Brahman is non-dual, it falsely appears as if dual.
In response to the inquiry, "What is that solution which was stated?", he summarizes it as follows: "Unexamined... (verse 42).
Just as a person afflicted by cataracts perceives the pure sky [as otherwise].
One should perceive it as if variegated by diverse measures. || 43 ||
In the same way, this stainless Brahman, though changeless, [appears otherwise] through ignorance.
It manifests in the form of differentiation, as if it had attained a state of turbidity. || 44 ||

By means of an illustration, he alters the dualistic cognition that serves as the cause for the suspicion that the Veda is useless, starting with the words "Just as" (yathā) and so forth. "By the *mātrās*" means by the objects such as blue, yellow, and so on, which are being measured [perceived]. || 43 || 44 ||
Even that single consciousness of his is divided into many parts.
It was marked with glowing coals, like the water of the ocean during a portentous upheaval.

He states, by means of another illustration, that the one Brahman alone appears in various forms through ignorance: "Of that," etc. "Marked by embers" (aṅgārāṅkita) means behaving like embers, that is to say, perceived as such. || 45 ||
Self-delusion is indeed that which is sublated, for it is not itself the sublater.
The direct realization of one's true nature is not sublated, because it is that which sublates [all else]. || 46 ||

Anticipating the objection that even though Brahman appears as a duality due to ignorance (*avidyā*), there would be no destruction of evil once knowledge (*vidyā*) has gained a footing within that ignorance, he says: "It is sublatable" (*bādhya*). This is the reason for the rule. He says: "But not... By the rule that ignorance is necessarily sublatable—just like darkness—it follows as a consequence that knowledge is necessarily sublatant—just like light. He says: "The inner self... because knowledge is not...

The construction is: "Therefore, that which is sublated is indeed the sublator. For it is not the case that the sun does not rise while darkness exists; likewise, while ignorance exists, knowledge finds no scope. Thus, the meaning is that by its very arising, knowledge shakes off non-awareness and, as a consequence, shakes off that which is born from it as well. || 46 ||
