3, page 114] 5 Brāhmaṇa, together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
Therefore, there would be a conjunction between those two without the abandonment of their intrinsic natures.
Having thus resolved in his mind, the Lord of all masters of yoga [acted].

In order to introduce the words of the Lord regarding the relationship of sublation between knowledge and ignorance—which is established through experience—he provides the introductory transition with the verse beginning "svabhāva-". The word "tataḥ" (therefore) refers to that which is established through experience. || 47 ||
For the removal of delusion, I bow to the one who wears a crown and has taken refuge in me.
And [the author] demonstrates that the nature of the sublated and the sublator does not cease to exist. || 48 ||

Regarding the phrase "the conjunction [of knowledge and ignorance] without the abandonment of their respective intrinsic natures," [the author] states "moha... [verse 48], intending that such a word does not exist in the sentence to be explained hereafter.
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man remains awake.
That in which all beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.

What then did the Blessed One say? He said: "That which is night. For those who lack knowledge, the state of Brahman is like night; therein the wise man is awake, whereas that state in which all beings are awake—that does not appear to the knower of Brahman because it has been destroyed by knowledge.
This is the meaning. || 49 ||
Therefore, this conventional usage regarding the self depends upon knowledge and ignorance.
Therefore, neither a scriptural nor a worldly contradiction can be established here. || 50 ||

He states the result [of the argument] regarding the connection between knowledge and ignorance through the non-abandonment of their respective natures: "Knowledge... and so forth. The meaning of the word *tataḥ* (therefore) is due to the aforementioned connection between those two. The distinction is that the conventional usage "I am Brahman" depends upon knowledge, whereas all other [usages] depend upon ignorance;
thus, in our position, there is no contradiction with any conventional usage whatsoever—this is the meaning. || 50 ||
For those in whom self-awakening has arisen, [there is the cessation] of ignorance regarding the self and that which arises from it.
It is constantly being consumed by the fire of right knowledge; thus it is born. || 51 ||

[Objection: Even for the knower (*jñānin*), since all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are observed, there is the transaction "I am Brahman. How then can it be asserted that any other transaction is produced by ignorance? To this, he says: "Having arisen... The sense is that because all his transactions are sublated (*bādhita*), their persistence has been stated more than once. || 51 ||
Therefore, the subsequent [passage] is intended with reference to the true nature of the reality of the single Self.
The question beginning with "directly" (sākṣāt) and so forth is preceded by the words "that which indeed" (yad eva).

Having described the two kinds of worldly discourse based on knowledge and ignorance, he concludes the introduction to the Brāhmaṇa with the words "aikātmya" (oneness of the Self). The meaning is that the Brāhmaṇa is intended to establish that reality which transcends all that is characterized by ignorance, such as hunger and the like; the word "the subsequent text" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Having introduced the Brāhmaṇa, he introduces the question with the words beginning with "sākṣāt" (directly). || 12 ||
"Yājñavalkya replied as before: 'This, indeed, is your self.'"
For it is precisely here that the characteristics such as "directly" (sākṣāt) and so forth are possible. (53)
1248 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Chapter – 1] [Volume 3, Page 115]
He receives a reply; he says "he replied. The meaning is that just as in the previous question of Uṣasta, so too here [the answer] begins with "Ādīvāha.
The reason for the reply being as before is stated: "It is possible. Here, "ātman" refers to the Self. || 13 ||
Desiring a definitive explanation that leaves nothing remaining, Kahola also spoke as before.
"Which one, Yājñavalkya? he asked; the pure-minded one replied to him. (54)

He states the purport of the second question with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). The meaning is that this question has as its object that reality which transcends hunger and other such conditions. He takes up the passage beginning with "yo 'śanāyā" (He who is beyond hunger) with the words "sa tam" (He [the Teacher] said to him). The meaning is that, because the pure, unconditioned Brahman—which transcends hunger and the like—is always the object of his cognition, he speaks desiring to provide the very answer intended by Kahola. || 14 ||
He who, by means of opposition, [overcomes] all such states as hunger, thirst, and the like;
Having transcended by the very nature of things, he abides in his own majesty. || 55 ||

He summarizes its meaning with the words "yo'śanāya" (he who [is not] for eating). Because of the contradiction between the nature of the aggregate of waves—consisting of hunger and so forth—and the true nature [of the Self], which is characterized by non-attachment, changelessness, and the like, that which stands in its own essential form having transcended that [aggregate] is the innermost Self (pratyagātman), free from transmigratory existence along with its cause;
this is the meaning, as its nature consists in being the innermost of all. || 55 ||
He who, for that reason, is always beyond hunger and thirst;
In reality, he transcends [the world]; let him be perceived as such directly. || 56 ||
Having stated the collective meaning of the reply, he now wishes to explain the meaning of each individual word; thus, he states the meaning of the phrase "aśanāyāpipāse" as follows:
"aśanāya" [means hunger]. || 16 ||
For those two were born from the seed of attachment and grief, just as previously described.
And from those two, thousands of other specific desires were born.

If it is argued that the cessation of those two follows from the cessation of their cause, he states what the cause of those two is: "from grief" (*śokāt*). Based on the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "desire arises from attachment" (*saṅgāt saṃjāyate kāmaḥ*), the construction is that hunger and thirst arise from desire—which is designated by the word "grief"—which is itself the effect of attachment.
The word "hi" (for) indeed indicates the aforementioned traditional teaching. He mentions the effect of those two as a digression: "longing" (*icchā*). || 17 ||
The connection is that the Self transcends those things characterized by hunger and so forth.
If it is argued that the word *ati* has the sense of an action, then the sense of an action is not intended [in this context]. (58)

In order to explain the meaning of the verbal root (kriyāpada), he first states the syntactical connection (anvaya): "The Self" (ātma). The construction is to be joined as follows: "He who transcends attributes such as hunger and so forth—that is the Self. If the word "transcends" (atyeti) were intended to express an action, then one might object that the agent, the Self, would possess activity; to this he says: "Not an action" (na kriyā). || 58 ||
Just as heat and cold always transcend one another according to the nature of things.
In this case, it is not established by means of valid cognition, as it would be in the case of [falling] into a pit or similar [catastrophes]. || 59 ||

How, then, can there be the employment of a verbal form, for there is no word that is without an object? He says [the answer] is "heat. Just as in the expression "Caitra crosses over a pit," why should the verb *atyeti* not be used in its primary sense? For when the primary meaning is possible, a secondary meaning is not [to be accepted].
1 kha. 'dāyā''he'; 2 kha. viśeṣataḥ.

Regarding this, he says: "In that case, [it would be] like a pit," and so forth. Here, the term "here" (*atra*) refers to the objects such as hunger and thirst. This is the reason for the impossibility [of the soul's existence].
"From the means of knowledge" (mānāt) means: because there exists a means of knowledge that makes known the actionlessness of the Self. || 19 ||
He does not transcend these two alone: hunger and thirst.
And he also transcends that sorrow which is the seed of those two.

Having spoken of the transcendence of hunger and so forth, he now speaks of the transcendence of sorrow and so forth, beginning with the words "aśanāya. Alternatively, one might ask: how was that transcendence stated through the transcendence of its cause, since it is not perceived here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "aśanāya. || 60 ||
Grief here is that excessive state of the mind which is instability.
And he transcends delusion, mental instability, and the mind's deprivation by sense objects. || 61 ||
1.1 He states its essential nature: "Sorrow is here. He explains *arati* (discontent) with the words "of the mind," beginning with "sorrow and so forth."
He declares that [ignorance] is the transcendence of delusion (*moha*). Regarding the term "and delusion," he states its essential nature: it is "bewilderment.

Furthermore, he explains that it is a state of mind contrary to that [knowledge], saying: "of objects" and so forth. The meaning is this: by means of objects connected to their respective sense-faculties, there is a "seizure" of the intellect, which turns it away from the Self and brings about its inclination toward itself. || 61 ||
When that which is inherently non-differentiated is perceived as having a differentiated nature due to ignorance, [that is delusion].
False knowledge that appears as the non-Self is taught to be delusion (moha). || 62 ||

He elaborates upon the nature of delusion (*moha*) already mentioned: "From itself" (*svataḥ*). The meaning is this: since there is knowledge of duality within the non-dual, that is false knowledge because it perceives what is not there; thus, in this context, that which is called delusion is the effect of one's own ignorance (*svājñāna*). || 62 ||
Hunger and thirst are all-pervasive because they are properties of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Or rather, there may be a brief statement because it is the effect of sorrow. || 63 ||

He states the reason for the compounding of hunger (*aśanāyā*) and thirst (*pipāsā*) with the word "sarva" (all). [The term] *prāṇa* means that which swallows or withdraws everything, such as speech and so forth; or, because it shares the single characteristic of being the root of sorrow, there is a compounding of those two. The sense is that in this context, the *prāṇa* is the material cause (*upādāna*), while desire (*kāma*) is the efficient cause (*nimitta*). || 63 ||
The teaching is given without compounding because their functions and causes are distinct.
The activity of one who lacks passion is the cause of delusion, which results in a flood of misfortune.

Since it follows that *śoka* (sorrow) and *moha* (delusion) should likewise be treated as a compound, why is there a statement of their separate mention? To this he says: "Not as a compound. How is it that they have different functions? To that he says: "Activity," etc. (64).
If there were transformation, it would be characterized by wrinkles and gray hair.
Death is the dissolution of the body; it is the separation of the body and the subtle signs (liṅga). || 65 ||
He states the difference in meaning between the words *jarā* (old age) and *mṛtyu* (death): "Old age," etc. He clarifies the distinction [of the former]: "separation," etc. (69).
In the previous section concerning the vital breaths, it was stated that sorrow and delusion reside in the mind.
But it is a settled conclusion that old age and death are the inherent properties of the body. || 66 ||
1 kha. The destruction of the intellect. 2 ka. Because of that, the sentence is one; kha. Because of that, the sentence is a unity. 3 ka. ...for indeed...
157 [vol 3, page 117]
1250 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]:
He shows the specific substratum of the aforementioned hexad. Regarding "prāṇa" etc.: [it refers to] the experience of the aforementioned certainty.
The word "tu" (but) indicates a qualification. || 66 ||
The connection with hunger and other such states is not considered to be real for the Self.
Furthermore, there would follow the consequence of non-liberation for that [agent], because of its lack of uniformity.

[Objection: But surely, since those [attributes] are properties of the Self (*ātman*), they cannot be properties of the intellect (*buddhi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth; for they do not appear apart from consciousness. To this, he says: "Hunger and so forth. He states the fault in the contrary case: "There would be no liberation. Furthermore, he says: "And of that," meaning that the connection of hunger and so forth with the Self does not exist in reality. || 67 ||
Since this is so, therefore, due to the lack of realization of the true nature of the inward Self...
Therefore, the connection with hunger and so forth is completely negated by perfect knowledge. || 68 ||

Or how is liberation possible in your own view? To this he says: "Since... The meaning is that because hunger and the like do not exist in the Self in reality, and because they arise from delusion, liberation is easily accomplished through the destruction of that [delusion] by means of knowledge. || 68 ||
That which is the conjunction with its own causes is the passing away of effects.
Because it is not absolute in its nature as form, this destruction is not perceived. || 69 ||

Anticipating the objection that "the passing away" (*atyaya*) of an effect is its destruction, and that for hunger and the like, their "passing away" is likewise merely their conjunction with their own causes, he says: "He who... (verse 69).
The negation of the cause of that [object] which occurs through the very nature of the thing itself.
The knowers of that [reality] declare that very transcendence to be the method for liberation. || 70 ||

If the transgression well-known in the world is not accepted here, then what kind [of transgression] is intended? To this he says: "tatkāraṇa... (By that cause...). By the word "tat" (that), hunger and so forth are meant. The meaning is: when the exposition of liberation—that is, its demonstration—is intended. "Tadvidvāṃsaḥ" refers to those who know that, namely, the knowers of liberation. || 70 ||
Because of hunger and thirst, therefore there is the grasping of their cause.
Because it transcends the self that is the absorber (saṃvargātman), there follows the transcendence of its effects. || 71 ||
He states that because the absolute cessation of an effect is impossible once its cause has passed away, the word "hunger" (*aśanāya*) indicates its cause by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

He says: "By 'hunger'. He states the result: that the cause is established by a word denoting the effect. Since the transcendence of its cause, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is established by the statement regarding the transcendence of hunger and so forth, it is logical that its effects—hunger and the rest—are also extinguished.
The meaning is "the grasping of the cause. || 71 ||
Beginning with the words "by death alone," the Śruti has likewise declared:
For the characteristic is indeed for the sake of eating, in order to awaken from the death of the vital breath.

He states that even the opening of the passage is consistent with the apprehension of its cause as hunger and so forth, by saying: "By death. For [the word] *mṛtyu* (death) indeed [denotes] the cause.
[Variant readings: *kāra-tī hiśa*; *kaduṣṭatvā*; *kadṛṣṭatvā*.
1 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandajñāna: 1251.

Following the principle that "that which is to be characterized is the subject here," starting with the statement "this was indeed enveloped by death" (*mṛtyunāvedamāvṛtamāsīt*), when the expectation arises as to what this "death" is, the Śruti has stated its definition—"for hunger is death"—in order to show that breath (*prāṇa*) is the grasper (*graha*) of death; thus, it is appropriate here [to take] the cause—
The meaning is "of the feet. || 72 ||
It is characterized by the ignorance regarding the inner self, which is established without being investigated.
They declare the Lord to possess the nature of hunger, thirst, and so forth. (73)

In response to the inquiry as to whether the object indicated here (*lakṣya*) is an intermediate cause or the root cause, he says: "unexamined" (*avicārita*), etc. The meaning is that the root cause to be understood here is the Lord (*īśvara*)—who possesses the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācya-ajñāna*) and is characterized by hunger and other such qualities—which is what is intended by the term "hunger" (*aśanāyādi*) in this context. || 73 ||
From the arising of that radiant knowledge of the true nature of the inner self, darkness [is dispelled].
When this self has been destroyed, it transcends that which arises from it, according to the actual nature of things.

[Objection: Since the Lord (Īśvara) is already attained [by all], there is no lack of attainment; and since there is no lack of attainment, it is impossible for Him to transcend hunger and other such effects. Therefore, enough with this grasping at a cause. To this, he says: "That [Self] is the innermost" (*tat-pratyak*). The meaning is as follows: that [Self], which is free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), is eternally attained, yet through ignorance (*ajñāna*) it is as if unattained and will be attained [in reality]; and that ignorance is removed by knowledge (*jñāna*).
Thus, because the nature of the Lord characterized by limiting adjuncts is transcended, the transcendence of its effects—hunger and so forth—is also established.
But surely, knowledge whose nature is not ignorance cannot remove ignorance and its effects; to this, he says: "The reality," etc. (74).
The darkness residing in the self is dispelled by that which arises from the nature of the self’s unique consciousness.
Having been consumed entirely by pride, it remains incomplete.
Fearing that if the Self were merely the cause and effect, it would transcend [the world] and result in a state of nihilism, he says: "The Self.

The connection is with "the innermost Self" (*pratyagātma*). There is a word-break at "asāmānya. By means of the knowledge derived from the scriptural statement—which refers to a reality that is neither excluded (particular) nor concomitant (universal)—the ignorance residing in the Self, along with its effects, is dissolved entirely within the Self itself; thus the innermost Self becomes full. And so it is said:
The meaning is: from what [could] emptiness [arise]? || 75 ||
Because he is by his very nature enlightened, he is therefore by his very nature free from ignorance.
Therefore, because it is pure and non-dual, it is consequently established by itself.
In order to describe the fullness of the nature of the inner self (pratīc), he states it through the relationship of cause and effect, beginning with "yasmāt" (because). || 76 ||
Thus, for one whose delusion regarding the self has been destroyed, how could there be [attachment] to objects arising from ignorance?
The inward-facing [Self] possesses a connection with those characterized by hunger and so forth. (77)

He states the fruit of knowledge—that through the knowledge of the reality already described, ignorance and its products are destroyed, and his state of perfection becomes firmly established—with the word "evam" (thus). This means: by the knowledge of the aforementioned nature of things. The particle "hi" is used to express that when the cause is destroyed, the destruction of the effect is evident. || 77 ||
Just as the pure sky remains so whether impurity is present or absent.
In the same way, the Self [is not perceived] within the causal and effected entities, such as mist and the like.
1252 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:
Anticipating the objection that if the Self is complete due to the destruction of ignorance along with its effects, it must have been impure previously because of its limited nature, he says:
"Yathā" means "as. || 78 ||
Through the vision of the true nature of the inward Self, the Self is the cause that brings its own darkness to an end.
Having sublated ignorance and transmigratory existence, it attains the nature of the unprecedented (apūrva) and so forth. || 79 ||

Anticipating the objection that if the Self is eternally pure, it cannot possess causality, and if it does not, its nature as the "unprecedented" (apūrva) and so forth would be unestablished, he says: "The inner [Self]," etc. (79).
Sorrow and delusion would arise; this is an indication of the function of the thread.
Old age and death, as well as the withdrawal of all activities, belong to Virāj. || 80 ||

Having grasped its cause through hunger and so forth, it was shown that upon the destruction of that [cause] by means of knowledge, only the Full remains; now he says that its cause must also be grasped through grief and so forth. By the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), it is stated that grief and the rest are mentioned in the same sentence as hunger and the rest. With respect to the root cause, the Sūtra is an effect. Through old age and so forth as well, its [cause]...

He states that "battle" is the target. Regarding the word "old age," he explains the purpose of it being an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). He says "of all": the meaning is that in this view, the withdrawal of every effect along with its cause is obtained; therefore, it is appropriate that it be an indicative mark. || 80 ||
The nature of the internal and so forth, the sacrificial and so forth, and the divine and so forth [is as follows].
In this case, all that was previously stated will certainly become meaningful. || 81 ||

Having stated that by grasping the primordial cause—the Sūtra and Virāj—through words such as "hunger" (*aśanāyā*) and so forth, the absolute cessation of the effect is established because of the transcendence of the cause, and thus liberation is established; he then states the scriptural indicative mark (*liṅga*) for that very point: "Adhyātmam, etc. That which was stated in passages such as "He became that fire," regarding the fact that speech and the rest—which exist in various forms—are essentially identical with their causes such as fire—all that [cessation] occurs through the transcendence of the cause.

When there is an absolute cessation of the effect, the statement that the cause—such as fire—is present when the effects such as speech are fruitful, indicates that with the cessation of the cause, there is the cessation of the effect. Furthermore, the meditation on the *udgītha* situated within the context of knowledge would be fruitful only through its specific result; this would not be appropriate unless there were an absolute destruction of speech and the other organs. Nor can there be an absolute destruction of them while their cause still exists. Therefore, [it follows] regarding speech and the rest...

The meaning is that when there is absolute destruction through the destruction of that [cause] by way of its falling back into its own cause, liberation-in-stages (*kramamukti*) is the fruit of the meditation on the *udgītha*; thus, the statement regarding the transformation of speech and so forth into fire and so forth indicates the absolute cessation of the effect due to the passing away of the cause. || 81 ||
Thus, all forms of worship are indeed connected to the knowledge of Brahman.
Because they have been mentioned in the section on knowledge (vidyā), it is certain that they are purposeful. || 82 ||

Just like the meditation on the *udgītha*, other meditations situated within the context of a specific knowledge (*vidyā*) also bear fruit through that very fruit by virtue of their connection with it;
for [the scripture] indicates, based on the context, that when the cause ceases, the effect also ceases. Thus he says: "All. (82)
Because the nature of the inward Self is non-attachment and because delusion and the like are unreal.
Since only the individual measure remains as the opposite, how can there be the possibility of a genitive relation? || 83 ||
And not so; 1. kha. ga.
omit *vi*; 2. ka. ga. read *hṛteḥ* ||80|| 3. kha. states this with the apprehension (*atyāśaṅkā*); 4. ga. reads *vadityuktam* [vol 3, page 120].

Having stated that the passage beginning with "He who [is] beyond hunger" (yo 'śanāya) refers to the inner self (pratyak) which transcends cause and effect, he now states another reason for its actual freedom from hunger and so forth, preceded by a restatement of the previously mentioned reason, beginning with the words "of the inner self" (pratīcaḥ). The meaning of the genitive case is a relationship; that [relationship] does not reside in a single [entity].
The meaning is that it is joined because of its twofold nature. || 83 ||
This triad [of cause, effect, and action] within the self is to be explained by means of the statement regarding cause and that which possesses a cause.
Or rather, the statement beginning with "he who [is not] hungry" was spoken out of a suspicion that it might imply [the presence of] bliss. (84)
Although it is established here that, in reality, the Self has no connection with hunger and the rest due to the transcendence of their primary causes, one might still ask:

what is the mutual relationship between those transcendences such that they are presented in a single sentence? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the cause," etc. The meaning is that from the transcendence of the cause [the Unmanifest] follows the transcendence of the Sūtra [Hiraṇyagarbha], and from that, the transcendence of Virāj. Let it be granted that hunger and the rest are not attributes of the Self; however, let there be no [confusion regarding] their being of the nature of that [Self].
One might raise the objection that it could be like bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth; therefore, he introduces this very passage [beginning with] "like bliss" (*ānandavat*). || 84 ||
Let it not follow that sorrow and the like are intrinsic, as is the case with the happiness of the self.
When X exists, Y will exist; but when X does not exist, Y does not exist. (85)
He states the purport of the scripture that responds to the doubt: "It is inherent. He provides the reasoning for the fact that sorrow and so forth are not of the nature of the Self:

"In which... The meaning is that because sorrow and so forth follow the presence and absence of ignorance (*ajñāna*), they consist of that [ignorance] and are not of the nature of the Self, like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope. || 85 ||
Therefore, [one should know] those characterized as cause and effect, such as hunger and so forth.
By destroying it through the cognition of the Self, which is its opposite, one becomes the one Self. || 86 ||

He concludes the meaning of the sentence, which results from the fact that hunger and so forth are not attributes of the Self and thus do not constitute its true nature, with the words: "Hunger and so forth... (86).
This very nature of the Supreme Self has been elaborated by the Śruti itself.
Having known this very Self, one proceeds by the path described.
Having emerged from that state, the Brahmins indeed wander for alms with great effort.

He restates the meaning of the passage already explained: "The Supreme Self," etc. Having set aside the idea that the aforementioned nature [of the Self] is merely a matter of fact (*ārthatva*), he uses the word "himself" (*svayam*) to state that it is a matter of scriptural revelation (*śābdatva*). He then introduces the subsequent sentence in order to enjoin renunciation for the sake of knowing that [Self]:
"This," etc. Having known this very Self by means of the transcendence of cause and effect, one should emerge from worldly life and lead the life of a mendicant.
The structural interpretation. || 87 ||
The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of identifying the specific qualified person.
For there is no rule for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas in the Śruti.
Regarding the statement that prescribes renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), he explains why the word "Brāhmaṇa" is used for the qualified candidate there: "The qualified [candidate]," etc.
As to why it is made known that he alone has the qualification for renunciation, he says: "Not," etc. (88).
* This half-verse is not found in the manuscripts Ka and Ga. 1 Kha: "tasminnasa" [Vol. 3, page 121]
1254. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [Third Chapter]:
Renunciation is heard of in the Śruti as applying without distinction to all three [classes].
If the mention of the Brāhmaṇa were intended to serve as an illustration, then... || 89 ||
Having stated the intention of the Commentary, he explains the purpose of the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" according to his own view with the words, "Of the three.

In such scriptural passages as "One should renounce even from the stage of studentship," the renunciation of all three castes is heard in a general sense; nor can this general scriptural statement be restricted to a specific case by following the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa."

The meaning is as follows: since there is no justification for restricting the general Vedic injunction—which is supported by specific Smṛti texts stating, "A Brāhmaṇa, or even a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya may renounce from the home"—to Brāhmaṇas alone, when both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas likewise possess the qualification for saṃnyāsa, the qualifying term [Brāhmaṇa] must be taken as an illustrative indication (upalakṣaṇa). Thus, the view based on mere custom is refuted. || 89 ||
If it is accepted that knowledge severs one's entitlement to [the results of] karma, [then what follows?]
Whence can there be a restrictive rule regarding authority when one is forcibly emerging from [meditative absorption]? (90)

He states the reasoning for the impossibility of a restrictive rule regarding the eligibility of Brāhmaṇas alone for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). [The verse begins with] "Karma" (action). The connection is: "How [could it be] by force?

Renunciation, as a result (*phala-ātman*), is not something to be enjoined because it depends upon direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*); however, that which consists of the means (*sādhana-rūpa*)—whether it depends on the knowledge that motivates action or is produced by indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*)—may indeed be enjoined. Nevertheless, since knowledge, which is the cause of renunciation, is already established, there can be no restrictive rule regarding eligibility for it.
The meaning is: "because of the absence of a reason. || 90 ||
If it is established that its very nature is the direct knowledge of the true reality of the Self;
Whoever may have the occasion for rising, that person is entitled to rise.
He states the reason why there is an absence of a cause for that: "The inward" (*pratyak*).

If it is argued that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is necessitated by the nature of knowledge as described—namely, being one or the other—then the desired restriction is not established; for the meaning is that whoever among the Brāhmaṇas and others possesses the knowledge that prompts renunciation would be the qualified person (*adhikārī*) for renunciation. || 91 ||
If this were the statement of a Brahmin, it would be for the purpose of grasping that which has destroyed ignorance.
And at the end, the Śruti will clearly state that he is a Brāhmaṇa. || 92 ||

If it is argued that since the right to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) belongs to all three castes (*traivarṇika*), for what purpose is the mention of the Brahmin? Anticipating this objection, he states another interpretation because [the term "Brahmin"] is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). "If it is thus" means: if the renunciation is authorized for all three castes, then the fruit—which is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) preceded by that [renunciation]—is...

The word "brāhmaṇa" is appropriate for the purpose of restating the true nature (svarūpa) which is devoid of ignorance; moreover, even a Kṣatriya or others may possess the status of a Brāhmaṇa in a particular state, as in the Rājasūya sacrifice and so forth, because that very term [Brāhmaṇa] is used there—this is the sense. He asks: how is the state of fruition expressed by the word "brāhmaṇa"? He replies: "He," on account of the remainder of the sentence. || 92 ||
The vital breath, the mind, the body, and their attributes are characterized by hunger and the like.
These which exist within all beings like the flow of water. (93)

The intended meaning of the mention of the term "Brāhmaṇa" in the passage beginning with "etam," which is devoted to the injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), has been stated; now, the meaning of the word "ātman" [is to be explained].
5 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1255.

Having described liberation from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), [the text] now restates the nature of transmigratory existence—including its basis in hunger and other such states—in order to explain the emergence of one who has become detached from it through knowledge of that [reality]. It says: "The vital breaths... [and so on]. It declares its continuity through the state of being channels (*srotas*) within all living beings. "Ya... [and so on].
"‘These’ refers to those [states] such as hunger and so forth mentioned previously; the construction is that these exist ‘always’ among living beings, like a stream of water. (93)
The conviction that "saṃsāra is a misfortune" has this alone as its cause.
"From whom even those beings who have attained excellence are afraid.
(94) If it is objected: "If the nature of bondage is being restated, why not state hunger and so forth?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "In saṃsāra.

If it is argued that it is not an evil (anartha) because it is a real entity (vastu) by virtue of being saṃsāra, he says: "The inner self... How can saṃsāra be an evil? For surely not everything... [is so].

Therefore, he states the true nature of that which is to be desired: "Because... Even beings such as Brahmā and others, though they have attained the highest state, are filled with fear because of it; how then can that not be a source of misfortune?
For it is the undiscerning who long for it, while others seek to abandon it—this is the meaning. || 94 ||
The cause is said to be the ignorance of the inner self, and the effect is called transmigratory existence.
Its nature is the opposite of that [worldly cognition], as established by Vedic statements concerning Brahman, the Unseen Force (apūrva), and so forth. || 95 ||
Having stated [the definition], he analyzes *saṃsāra*. "The cause" [is mentioned]; the effect is the thread and so forth; the point is that both of these are indeed *saṃsāra*.
Having restated the nature of *saṃsāra*, he states the meaning of the word "Self" (*ātman*): "contrary to that. Its nature is the opposite of the bondage consisting of cause and effect.
Regarding the word "pratyaṅ," he states the authoritative proof: "Brahman. || 99 ||
By the statement "This is That," the Śruti [reveals] the Witness of seeing and so forth.
Having restated [the previous point], he spoke of a direct union with that which has its suffering removed. || 96 ||

Having explained the category of the Self (*ātman*), [the author] states the meaning obtained through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by first explaining the meanings of the words "this" (*etaṃ*) and "that" (*tam*).

Regarding the word "this": the construction is that the Śruti, having restated the meaning of "you" (*tvam-artha*) as "that" (*tam*), declared through the sentence of coordination the connection of that [meaning] with the meaning of "this" (*etaṃ*)—which is pointed out by it—as being directly of one essence. Or else, "this" refers to the meaning of "you," and "that" refers to the meaning of "that."
This is his statement. || 96 ||
One perceives that very Self, which is the object of vision and so forth, as being directly present within those who have imagined a [limited] self.
Having recognized this very one as possessing the characteristics explained above, || 97 ||

He states the meaning of the word "viditvā" (having known) with the words "tam" (him). The first half-verse is a restatement of the meaning of *tvam* (the "thou"); "this one, as previously explained, who has transcended hunger and so forth" is a restatement of the meaning of *tat* (the "that"). The sense is that, having understood this [Self] even superficially, they emerge [from worldly life]. The word "iti" refers back to this act of emerging. || 97 ||
In this context, the one addressed by Uṣasta is the substantive (viśeṣya), while the one addressed by Kahola is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).
In this way, there is the destruction of saṃsāra through the abandonment of that cause, which is ignorance.

In the passage "This is That," he explains the determination of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified. He says, "O Uṣasta. Thus, regarding the state of being the qualifier and the qualified, he states the fruit—which is the destruction of the bondage born of that [ignorance]—through the destruction of the ignorance of the Self by means of the knowledge of its Brahmanhood. He says, "In this way. || 98 ||
1256 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Chapter— 1] [Volume 3, Page 123]
When one says "the space within a jar" or "the great space," it is merely the sky itself.
Just as it is realized, so too is it characterized by such qualities as being directly manifest and so forth. || 99 ||
An object devoid of differentiation and conjunction [is realized] by way of the destruction of its causes.
This alone is to be understood from this statement, and not from any other means of valid cognition. || 100 ||

Anticipating the objection that if *tat* and *tvam* were related as qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*), the meaning of the sentence would not be indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*), like the case of "blue lotus," he says: "Like a jar" (*ghaṭa*). If it is argued that because the jar is already established, it is accessible through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) and thus cannot be the intended object of the sentence, he says: "Because that is its cause" (*taddhetu*). Through the destruction of ignorance—the cause of distinctions and so forth—it is possible to know the indivisible meaning from the sentence alone; in that regard, there is no scope for other means of knowledge.
The meaning is: because of the repeated crossing over of existence. || 99 || 100 ||
The entire passage beginning with "directly" (sākṣāt) pertains to the subject matter of Uṣasta’s question.
And when "to him who eats" is uttered here, that [offering] should be understood to include everything without exception. (101)
Furthermore, he states that what was spoken by Kahola is the qualifier and the other is the qualified, beginning with the words "directly" (*sākṣāt*).
Therefore, the remainder [of the meaning] is that our stated relationship of qualifier and qualified must be accepted. || 101 ||
Because only a generality was answered, there is no cognition of the object as it was asked about.
In the previous case, the cognition [arose] as if it were direct, according to the response. || 102 ||

[Objection: Surely the statement of Kahola is not required, since it is the statement of Uṣasta alone that makes known the true nature of the Self through the words "He who [is perceived] by means of breath," and so forth;

therefore, this is not a relationship of qualifier and qualified. To this he replies: "sāmānya... (referring to the general). The implication is that, since the statement of Uṣasta depends upon that [general definition], the aforementioned systematic arrangement is appropriate. || 102 ||
The sequence of the two words ending in the suffix *ktvā* is according to their logical connection.
If it is understood as "having previously known," then there is a twofold conceptualization. || 103 ||

Having explained the passage beginning with "etam," the author speaks in response to one who, having understood [the text], wonders about the sequence—whether it should be taken literally as heard or otherwise—saying: "The sequence. In that regard, if the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama) were followed, then he says that knowledge would be possible in two ways: "First... (verse 103).
Emergence from the non-dual nature of gnosis occurs through the obstruction of the object of knowledge.
In the state of emergence, there is dependence on exhortation, not because of the destruction of one's qualification. || 104 ||

How is that? Is it the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkaraṇa*) or the motivating knowledge (*prayojaka-jñāna*)? Regarding these, he first addresses the former with the words "jñāne" (in knowledge). Arising from the power of direct realization, one remains in the very nature of that [Self] by following the true nature of the thing; therefore, there is no injunction (*vidhi*) therein. This is because there is no injunction regarding the essential nature which is itself the fruit, and because the relationship between the injunction and the person is eliminated by direct realization, resulting in the absence of a qualified agent (*adhikārin*).
And this is the meaning. || 104 ||
Or rather, the verbal comprehension [of the scriptures] would be the motivator for emerging from meditative absorption and so forth.
For the meaning of the injunction is seen to apply to childhood and so forth, as well as to the period beyond that. || 105 ||

3, page 124] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1257.

He states the second [view] with the words "śābdī" (arising from verbal testimony). The meaning is as follows: if the cognition arising from words in one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs—which prompts the practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)—is what is expressed by the word "viditvā" (having known), then the injunction for renunciation and so forth for the sake of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is logical. [Objection: There is no injunction in this sentence, because an injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) or the like is not heard; how then can there be an injunction for renunciation and so forth here?

He says: "vidhi" (injunction). Although no injunction is seen here, nevertheless, according to the principle that "even if there is no injunction here, there is an injunction for another auxiliary [to be performed] regarding what is already enjoined, such as childhood and so forth," the injunction is clear later in the phrase "he should remain standing. This is the meaning. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the aforementioned principle. || 105 ||
Then, having emerged and understood, that which is intended as the sequence of what precedes and what follows [is established].
If this were the meaning, namely that knowledge is the means for emergence [from meditative absorption], then... || 106 ||

In the view that the order follows the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*), having explained the established arrangement by dividing the process of realization, he states another sequence—namely, that the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the textual order (*śrautakrama*)—with the words "having renounced" (*vyutthāya*). The word "then" (*atha*) serves to exclude the textual order. In this context, it is stated that renunciation is the means for knowledge through the gateway of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth; thus he says, "by renunciation" (*vyutthāna*). || 106 ||
Having understood this, the subsequent Vedic revelation is intended as a response to the question "How so? (katham).
Therefore, the verse beginning with "tasmāt" and so forth should be applied for the purpose of establishing the reason for the ritual placement (nyāsa). || 107 ||

Anticipating the objection that since renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is established as a means for knowledge (*dhīsādhana*) according to the order of the text, it need not be pursued [separately], he says: "Having known" (*viditvā*). To refute the challenge—namely, how renunciation can be a means for knowledge under the view that "renunciation occurs after [knowledge]" (since what exists later cannot be the cause of what is already established)—he cites the scripture beginning with "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa [should cultivate] scholarship" (*tasmād brāhmaṇaḥ pāṇḍityam*). For in that [scripture]:

Since scholarship and other qualities are prescribed for the renunciant who possesses the knowledge that prompts [renunciation], the meaning is that there is no fault even if the sequence is reversed from the usual order, because renunciation serves as a cause for wisdom. || 107 ||
Therefore, it is said "one who knows thus," and so he will explain further below.
The Śruti declares that the renunciation of all actions without exception is the means for knowledge.

Even though renunciation occurs earlier or later, its status as a means to knowledge through the gateway of hearing has been stated; therein, he provides the remainder of the scriptural passage as proof:
"Therefore," etc. The connection is: "Thus says the Śruti. In that context, by the word "uparata" (restrained), renunciation will be enjoined as a means to knowledge. || 108 ||
And here too, the Śruti explains the knowledge that is the means for renunciation.
In whatever manner one examines this matter, there are millions of scriptural authorities here. || 109 ||
He states that the injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is not only for the purpose of attaining knowledge of the Self according to the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka-śruti*, but also in other *śrutis* as well.

Regarding the words "renunciation" and so forth: the particle *api* and the word *ca* are intended to refer back to the preceding and following sentences, both of which he will demonstrate briefly further on. (109)
Just as the activity of living beings here conforms to their knowledge, so it is.
Likewise, here too, the Śruti declares this for those who know the true nature of the inner self.
1 kha. ga. rā hyatra | [vol 3, page 125] 1254 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya—]

Now, one might ask: why is renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which is also authoritative, undertaken by those possessing the knowledge that motivates it, rather than the performance of action since the desired goal is attained through that? To this, he says: "By knowledge," etc. Just as in this world those desiring [results] engage in ritual action based on scriptural knowledge, so too does scripture declare the engagement of those possessing the motivating knowledge in its abandonment; thus, just as with action, engagement in renunciation is likewise inevitable.
The meaning is: "except for those who possess discernment. || 110 ||
With the aim of obtaining a son, he desires to take a wife.
Since the exertion for the sake of a wife follows, thereafter the desire for sons is spoken of. || 111 ||

Having understood this and having explained the sequence of emergence as appropriate, [the author] speaks of the meaning of the term "desire for a son" (*putraiṣaṇā*) in the passage beginning with "of the desire for a son," etc., in order to demonstrate the counter-correlate to that emergence. [He says: "A son... (verse 111).
Even though it has attained its own nature, that which is incapable of serving the purpose of man is like an axe.
Without having entered into the practice, that is taught as "knowledge. || 112 ||

Regarding the phrase "and of the desire for wealth" (*vittaiṣaṇāyāśca*), he explains the meaning of the word *vitta* (wealth): "for the sake of human goals. For just as axes, even though they exist in their own form, do not split wood without being applied to an operation, so too, even though it exists, [wealth] such as gold and the like does not produce a fruit without being put into practice; this is the meaning of the well-known term *vitta*. || 112 ||
That which, by the mere acquisition of its own self, brings about the fulfillment of the goals of human existence.
Emergence occurs solely by the power of that [meditative state], and not like that of a cow or other animals. // 113 //

Anticipating the view of Bhartṛprapañca—who, taking the word *vitta* (wealth) as including even meditative worship (*upāsti*), argues that emergence from it [is taught] by the best of the commentaries, and who claims that emergence from that [meditation] would be misplaced because there is no cause for such emergence once one has emerged—[the author] says: "As for what...

Emergence occurs solely through the power of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmadhī*), not by the force of meditation; for the latter, like a cow or other such things, is not a means to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) merely by its own production.
The meaning is that, just as one must eventually emerge from the state of being a cow or similar [lower forms], so too must one emerge from that [state of samādhi]. || 113 ||
Arising from desire produced by ignorance of the inner self, it consists of the means [to its fulfillment].
The thorough knowledge of the deity and so forth is said to be wealth, just like the mantra. || 114 ||

In this context, renunciation from wealth (*vitta*) is heard [in scripture], but the term "wealth" is not commonly established in the sense of meditative worship (*upāsti*). Therefore, how can there be renunciation from that?
To this, he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*). The meaning is that although worship lacks human wealth like that of the mantras and other ritual factors, it possesses divine wealth;
therefore, renunciation from that [divine wealth] must also be intended here. || 114 ||
One does not find oneself in action, since action is impossible without wealth.
The certainty is this: the desire for wealth is for the sake of ritual action, not for the sake of worldly enjoyment.

He establishes the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) in order to state another meaning for the word *vitta*: "not the self," etc.; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "not directly for the sake of the worlds. || 115 ||
Therefore, wealth is desired here for the purpose of accomplishing one's obligatory duties.
If it were not so, the statement would be distinct due to the grasping of worldly desires. (116) [Vol.
3, page 126]
5 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary known as the Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri:

1259. Even so, how can the word *vitta* have another meaning? He says: "Because [it is] eternal," etc. Since worldly action (*laukika-karma*) is not possible without wealth due to a lack of capacity, the word *vitta* occurs in this sentence for the sake of understanding the obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*); if, by that, the world—

If "wealth" (dhana) were understood here as only cattle and the like, and not as obligatory ritual action (nitya-karma), then the desire for the world (loka-eṣaṇā) would have been mentioned separately from the desire for wealth (vitta-eṣaṇā); for by the word "world" itself, its means—wealth—is already included. Furthermore, if only that [material wealth] were intended by the phrase "and of the desire for wealth," there would be a redundancy. Therefore, the meaning is that by the term "desire for wealth," what is intended is the exertion for the sake of obligatory ritual action. || 116 ||
That desire which is directed toward the worlds is based upon the means for accomplishing them.
They call that "worldly desire" (lokaiṣaṇā), which is the exertion for the sake of rites performed with a desire for rewards.

Regarding the phrase "and from the desire for the worlds" (*lokaiṣaṇāyāśca*), he explains the meaning of the term *lokaiṣaṇā*: "The worlds" (*lokān*). The connection is as follows: that desire which has the cause [of the worlds] as its object, arising from a longing for the fruit, is called the "desire for the worlds" (*lokaiṣaṇā*); and they say that this [desire] is undertaken for the sake of actions performed with a view toward rewards (*kāmyakarman*). || 117 ||
Since that inner self is not to be accomplished by means of any instrument, [one realizes it] by means of the self itself.
With the words "directly" and so forth, he understood [the opponent] to be contradicting the probandum and the means of proof. (118)

Having stated the three types of seeking that are the opposites of renunciation (*vyutthāna*), he restates their motivating cause with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). The two instrumental cases [in *sādhanena*] signify "by means of this state. He establishes that it is not something to be accomplished by a means. He says "contradictory" (*viruddham*); the meaning is that it is so because it is already established and because it is the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). || 118 ||
Therefore, for one who understands the meaning thus stated, [the proof] consists of the forms of the probandum and the probans.
They emerge from the objects of pursuit because their nature is opposed to them. || 119 ||
Fulfilling what is required by the word "yataḥ" (from which), he concludes that renunciation (*vyutthāna*) possesses a counter-correlative (*sapratyogika*). [He says] "sādhyā... etc.

Anticipating the objection—"How can there be renunciation from desires for those who perceive the Self as distinct from action, its factors, and so forth, since that [renunciation] too is a desire due to its being rooted in ignorance?"—he states: "tadviruddha... etc. For those who see only superficially, [renunciation] is observed to be intolerant of desires.
The meaning is that emergence occurs through the desire to directly perceive one's own true nature. || 119 ||
Or rather, [the nature of] verbal, mental, and bodily actions is that they are produced by ignorance and desire.
"He desired," thus was it said even in the past regarding that one enveloped in darkness.

Furthermore, he states that for one who is thus detached and desirous of knowledge, it is proper to renounce all pursuits (*eṣaṇā*). He says, "From ignorance... The meaning is that even the threefold types of action arise from desire preceded by ignorance; therefore, for one who is detached and seeks to know, renunciation of these pursuits is appropriate. If it is asked, "If one who is detached renounces them, then who is qualified for ritual action? he replies with the words, "He desired... (so 'kāmayata).

The meaning is that the eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) has been explained in the third [chapter] as belonging to the ignorant and non-detached person, who is like a beast among the gods; the particle *api* serves to include the non-detached. || 120 ||
From what absence of knowledge does that activity arise, and from the knowledge of that [reality], how could it come to be?
Therefore, upon the arising of the knowledge of the inner Self, there shall be the cessation of all actions.
1 ka. 'sya ka' | [Vol.
3, page 127] 1260 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya—]

If even the man of knowledge is seen to perform action, how can there be an entitlement to action for the ignorant person? For indeed, even men of knowledge such as Janaka and others are seen to be performers of action; to this he replies: "Because of ignorance" (*yadajñānāt*). Since knowledge and ignorance are mutually contradictory, when knowledge exists, ignorance cannot coexist; therefore, activity prompted by that [ignorance] is also untenable. This is because it has been stated more than once that such activity is merely a persistence of what was previously sublated. Thus, the man of knowledge is without action—
He states the result regarding the subject matter: "The inner," etc. (121).
And even one who merely desires to know this very reality of the Self as it has been described.
Only through the cessation of all seeking will one fully attain that knowledge. || 122 ||

Anticipating the objection that there might be an "emergence" (vyutthāna) from knowledge for one who possesses knowledge, the author considers the alternatives—whether for one who is dispassionate or one who is not—and refutes the first with the words "jijñāsuḥ. The meaning is that even for an ignorant person who is dispassionate, an emergence must be undertaken for the sake of attaining knowledge. || 122 ||
"But he who is unable to abandon passion and the like due to the weakness of his faculties..."
However, for that very reason, one must perform action in order to destroy the causes of passion and the like.
He speaks with reference to another alternative: "But he who... (verse 123).
For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means.
For that very person who has ascended to yoga, tranquility (śama) is said to be the means. || 124 ||
He states the authority for one who is not dispassionate having the qualification for ritual action (*karma*): "For one desiring to ascend," etc. Here, *yoga* means the purification of the mind;

for it has been said that "yoga is the restraint of the modifications of the mind. He states the authority for one who is dispassionate having the qualification for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*): "In yoga," etc. (124).
Transgressing the proper course of conduct and persisting in its opposite.
The great-minded call that "emergence," and emergence [is defined] as such. 125.

What is that "emergence" (vyutthāna) which must be performed by one who is detached? To this he says: "That which is proper" (nyāyyām). The meaning is that the discerning ones call that state "emergence" which, by virtue of being contrary to [the state of] seeking (eṣaṇā), transcends the state established in accordance with that seeking. || 129 ||
The vassal has risen in revolt and stands in opposition to the king.
The word "emergence" (vyutthāna) is well-known in the world as well; it is used in that very same sense here.

In this regard, he establishes what is well-known in the world by means of the term "neighboring king" (*sāmanta*). When a neighboring king stands in opposition to a king, being hostile toward him, he is said in common worldly usage to be "rebellious" (*vyutthita*);
in this sentence as well, that word "rebellious" is to be understood exactly as in the world, because there is no difference between the word and its meaning in the world and in the Veda.

However, according to the maxim that "the meaning of a sentence [is what remains] after [all other meanings] have been set aside," the meaning here is that this is an emergence characterized by remaining in a state of non-activity through opposition to the pursuit of desires. || 126 ||
For one's conduct is characterized by begging, having its sole refuge in the state of possessing nothing.
Because he is free from "mine-ness" and grasping, the sage is said to be beyond action.

brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1261.

Now, regarding the term *bhikṣācaryā* (the practice of begging), he states the intended meaning of the word *bhikṣā*: "by means of *bhikṣā*. The particle *hi* is used to indicate that this is well-known in both worldly usage and the scriptures. One might object: "Let the word *bhikṣā* denote by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) a mode of life connected solely with being 'nothing-at-all' (*akiñcana*); however, we do not know what that state of 'nothing-at-all' is. To this, he replies: "free from the sense of 'mine' (*amama*)" (verse 127).
Seeking is a synonym for desire, and desire is that which has not yet attained its object.
Even though all his desires have been attained, he would still exist due to delusion regarding that [attainment]. || 128 ||

Having stated that one who is called a *muni* and possesses nothing attains freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*) by virtue of sacred revelation, he provides the logical justification for that very point with the verse beginning "eṣaṇā" (desire).

The meaning is: when the Self has attained all desires, any desire that arises is born of delusion regarding it and does not exist in reality; and since there is an absence of action in the absence of desire, there is freedom from action. || 128 ||
Because the self has bliss as its sole intrinsic nature, it does not desire happiness [as something external].
Because of their mutual opposition, that which is of the nature of happiness cannot coexist with suffering. || 129 ||

Anticipating the objection that even in the absence of a desire for non-self (anātma-kāma) within oneself, that [desire] might exist in supreme bliss (paramānanda), and thus the performance of ritual acts motivated by it might also occur, he says: "Bliss... etc. Then, regarding the performance of acts performed out of a desire for the cessation of suffering, he says: "Because of contradiction" (virodhāt). || 129 ||
Nevertheless, this negation of hunger and other such states is predicated of the Self.
For the sake of abandoning the individual delusion, which is the sole root of all misfortune. || 130 ||

If it is argued that the absence of suffering in the Self is already established by the passage beginning with "He who is without hunger" (*yo 'śanāyā*), then the prohibition of hunger and so forth would be a prohibition of what has not been previously attained;

anticipating this objection, he says: "Hunger and so forth. Although in reality there is neither suffering nor its cause in the Self, nevertheless, its connection with hunger and so forth is produced by delusion (*moha*); therefore, for the purpose of dispelling the delusion that is the cause of that [connection], the negation of the six waves of existence (*ṣaḍūrmis*) by the passage beginning with "He who is without hunger" is not [redundant].
The meaning is that a prohibition has been established. || 130 ||
When the true nature [of reality] is solely characterized by the absence of desire, there is no cognition of objects according to their actual state.
Therefore, because it is self-aware through the absence of desire, this [consciousness] must indeed be the substratum. || 131 ||
Having negated the six waves within the inner self by means of negating their causes, he states that they are also negated because they are unfit to exist in their own nature, saying:
"Free from desire" (nir-eṣaṇa). || 131 ||
Therefore, the Śruti [teaches] for the sake of the desire for the fruit and for the sake of establishing oneness.
He began to speak of the unity between the desire for sons and the desire for wealth.

Anticipating the objection that if the self were free from desire (*nireṣaṇatva*), there would be no engagement even with liberation because engagement is impossible in the absence of desire, [the author] states the purport of the passage beginning with "yā hi" etc., as follows: "The fruit... The ellipsis to be supplied is "of the desire for means for the sake of realizing oneness. In that context, the meaning is that according to the authority of the scripture, there is only one kind of desire. || 132 ||
For this desire for wealth becomes meaningful only for one who has taken a wife.
Therefore, the desire for sons should be known as non-different from the desire for wealth and the desire for one's own self.
[Vol.
3, page 129] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "yā hi" along with its supporting reasoning: "yataḥ" (because). For wealth does not constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) without ritual performance.
And since there is no performance [of religious duties] without taking a wife, the meaning is that these two are one because of the aforementioned connection between them. || 133 ||
Because there is no difference in their being means [to an end], between the desire for a son and the desire for wealth.
And thus, those who are respectful should explain the oneness of these two here. (134)
In this regard, he states another reason: "By being a means," etc. The connection is with the word "oneness. He concludes that point with: "And thus," etc.

Here, the word "here" refers to the subject matter of the present scriptural passage (*śruti*). The meaning is that the two desires for a son and for wealth are one because they stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect, because they are alike in being causes for results seen in this world, and because it has been stated that they are equal in being means for attaining visible fruits. || 134 ||
Because he is occupied with the desire for what is to be accomplished, his self consists of the desire for sons and wealth.
This is actually a single desire for worldly existence; it is designated as threefold for this reason. || 135 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "that which is the desire for wealth" (*yā vittaiṣaṇā*) by saying "sādhya" (the end). The construction is as follows: that which is described in three ways by the passage beginning with "the desire for a son" (*yā putraiṣaṇā*) is in fact this one alone, namely the desire for the world (*loka-eṣaṇā*), because the others are prompted by it. For it has been said: "Indeed, it is only when prompted by the purpose of all fruits that one acquires all means. || 135 ||
For its accomplishment occurs through its own majesty alone, and not without a means.
Therefore, the presentation of the means of proof must conform to that which is to be proven. || 136 ||

He states the meaning of the verse beginning with "ubhe hi" (both indeed) as "by its own power. For it is not the case that an effect arises from its own nature without a cause, since the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*) has already been refuted; therefore, thinking that a cause must be accepted in accordance with the effect, he proceeded to state "ubhe hi," etc.—this is the meaning. || 136 ||
Because it has spontaneously attained the human goal through the total elimination of all that is harmful.
Therefore, this [search] for the inner self arises solely from delusion. || 137 ||

One might object: "Granted that there are two kinds of desire, nevertheless, they are not appropriate for the Self, since it is said to be free from desire; therefore, liberation remains unestablished.

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Apāsta... (It has been discarded). The sense is that although the Self is naturally free from desire, it possesses a longing for liberation due to the influence of desires produced by ignorance. || 137 ||
Since ignorance of Brahman is the cause of desires, they do not exist in reality.
For those who know the ultimate truth, these aforementioned forms of seeking do not exist. || 138 ||

One might ask: "Why should these desires be considered products of ignorance; why could they not be real? To this, he says: "Brahman... The meaning is that, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), ignorance is the cause of desires; therefore, they are not real. He explains the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) mentioned by the phrase "not in reality" (*na vastutaḥ*):
"In the ultimate sense... (138).
Because its purpose is entirely fulfilled, there is no dependence upon a means of proof.
