Now, in the subsequent statement, the realization of the inner self (pratyagdhi) is enjoined by means of hearing and so forth, and not renunciation; therefore, he explains the injunction regarding that [renunciation] in the phrase "having withdrawn" (vyutthāya). The word "sādhya" means: when the attainment of the realization of the inner self is the intended goal.
The meaning is that wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya), which consists of the abandonment [of all duties], is to be accomplished through this very means. || 167 ||
Having emerged from these aforementioned cravings, he is free from craving.
Then, having become proficient in scholarship, one should bring childhood to its conclusion.

He takes up the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Regarding the word "having renounced" (*vyutthāya*): since self-knowledge is incompatible with ritual action and its fruits, their abandonment must be practiced; therefore, the meaning is that one should perform hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth for the sake of knowledge after having renounced. The word "then" (*atha*) indicates that renunciation is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) to hearing and the other means of knowledge. || 168 ||
First there is the comprehension of the individual word-meanings; thereafter follows their mutual connection.
Next follows the offering of a contradictory meaning, and from that, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. || 169 ||

He states the meaning of the term "pāṇḍitya" (scholarship). Regarding the phrase "padārtha": for one who has studied the Veda (*svādhyāya*), upon hearing words such as "That" (*tat*) and "Thou" (*tvam*), there first arises knowledge of the word-meanings through the investigation of their respective potencies (*śakti*). Next, there occurs a connection between the meanings expressed by those words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikṛta*) by way of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*). Then, when contradiction manifests, the elimination of the contradictory elements—such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth—occurs. Thus, from the capacity of the words, there arises knowledge of three stages of meaning.

The meaning is that scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) consists of what is called "hearing" (*śravaṇa*), which is the fourfold knowledge consisting of the determination of the power (*śakti*) and the purport (*tātparya*) of the Vedāntas regarding Brahman as the Self; this involves first the comprehension of the literal meaning of the sentence and then the ascertainment of its purport. || 169 ||
Then, having brought each one individually to the culmination characterized by wisdom, [he should proceed].
And childhood likewise, according to its application, through positive and negative concomitance. || 170 ||

He states the meaning of "having become disgusted" as follows: "one by one. The meaning is that after having established a firm conviction in the form of the fourfold knowledge through a gradual process, one subsequently possesses the capacity to practice "childlikeness" (*bālya*). He states the purport of the passage beginning with "by childlikeness" as follows: "And childlikeness...

Having performed scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), one has attained the state of possessing the power of knowledge regarding the objects of inquiry, such as the categories of reality, by means of the strength of the fourfold method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
The meaning is that one should desire to remain after having brought [the mind] to rest as much as possible. || 170 ||
"The non-dual reality is the ultimate referent of both the word and the cognition of the Self."
And thus, the state of being solely established in the Self belongs to that which is non-dual, according to valid cognition.

Showing the result of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, he elucidates the nature of the non-Self (*avastu*): "As non-dual" (*advitīya*). The meaning is that, because anything other than that [Brahman] is non-Self, like a pot. He states that just as the cognitions and words "Self" and "Brahman" have Brahman as their ultimate referent, so too the cognitions and words "Brahman" and "Self" have the Self as their ultimate referent: "In the same way" (*tathā*). He states that it is because the status of being Brahman is untenable for that which is not the Self: "On account of the means of knowledge" (*mānataḥ*). || 171 ||
Because they have a single purpose, there is no mutual connection here, just as there is none between two things that have contradictory meanings.
Of the vision that transcends hunger and so forth, and of the entity that is the seer. || 172 ||

Having explained the state of being a beginner (*bālya*) regarding the meaning of individual words (*padārtha*), he now speaks regarding the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*): "Because of having a single purpose" (*aikārthyāt*). This refers to the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the sentence.
1 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1269.

Just as there is no association between the two—namely, agency and so forth which are contradictory, and being beyond perception and so forth—so too here, in the case of Brahman and the Self, who are the witness of the vision that transcends hunger and the like, there is neither association nor difference, because their essential nature is one of single flavor (*ekarasa*). Therefore, the realization of their indivisibility constitutes the meaning of the sentence.
The meaning is "childhood. || 172 ||
"Paṇḍā" is a name for intelligence; it arises in one who possesses pride.
They call him wise; he is here enjoined by means of sacred revelation.

Having briefly explained childhood and wisdom (*pāṇḍitya*), one might ask: "How can wisdom be fourfold, given that it is not well-known? Anticipating this doubt, he explains the meaning of the word *pāṇḍitya* by distinguishing between its root and suffix: "He is called *paṇḍita* because he possesses *paṇḍā*. For one who has studied the Vedānta and desires liberation, the knowledge that arises from that [study] which impels inquiry is *paṇḍā*; since that has arisen for him, he is a *paṇḍita*. His activity is *pāṇḍitya*.

The meaning is that one who possesses the knowledge of the fourfold means (prayojaka-jñānin) is enjoined by the scriptural passage beginning with "therefore" (tasmāt) and so forth to that [fourfold knowledge]. || 173 ||
That which is the action of a wise person is declared to be wisdom.
Therefore, one who has not yet attained stability in reality is directed toward scholarship. || 174 ||

He clarifies the meaning of the word "here" (*atra*) with the words "that which" (*yad iti*). Regarding those who maintain that there is an injunction for one who possesses knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*) toward the aforementioned form of scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), he says in reply: "not being attained" (*aprāpta*). By the word "this" (*etad*), the motivating cognition (*prayojakajñāna*) is expressed as "scholarship" (*paṇḍā*). || 174 ||
Having brought his realization to its culmination through the scriptures, the teacher, and his own self, the ascetic attains personal conviction.
Alternatively, one may remain in the state of a child; for by means of childhood, there is the offering of all thoughts regarding the self.
That which is designated by the word "childhood" should be brought to completion, after which one becomes pure-minded.
Then, by attaining the state of a sage, the Brāhmaṇa becomes Brahman itself. || 176 ||
Having restated the meaning of "having realized panditya," he introduces the subsequent sentence in order to elaborate upon its meaning: "The scripture...

He uses the word "atha" (then) to indicate that childhood (*bālya*) is the cause of *pāṇḍitya*. For *bālya* is the action of a child, such as standing, urinating, and so forth; anticipating the objection as to how that term can be applied in the presence of the power of knowledge regarding the meaning of words and other categories, he says: "In its entirety... (*kṛtsna...*).

For the action of a child consists in the total absence of the cognition that "all is not-self," since they say a child is one whose faculties are not yet matured. According to the principle that "one is not [considered] such as long as one does not manifest [the state]," childhood (*bālya*) is the state of lacking the power of knowledge regarding categories of existence and so forth; therefore, the destruction of the aforementioned lack of the cognition that "all is not-self"—which is of the nature of the power of knowledge—is called "childhood" (*bālya*), as it depends upon reasoning. "Power" (*bala*) indeed means the setting aside of all objective perceptions through the knowledge of the Self.

The meaning is that one should remain in the state of a child, as stated in the passage beginning with "one should remain in that state through childhood. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "and childhood" by saying "that [state].

Then he states the meaning of "then a sage" by saying "one of pure intellect. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "and non-sagehood" by saying "a sage. The word "then" (*tataḥ*) signifies the immediate succession following the completion of scholarship and childhood. He states the meaning of "then a Brahmin" by saying "Brahman itself. || 175 ||
It is enjoined that one should effect the complete awakening of the self.
The connection "he should remain" (tiṣṭhāset) applies everywhere through the prescriptive rule (vidhi). || 177 ||
1 kha. The meaning of the sentence. 2 kha. He states its meaning: ya. 3 kha. ...ti. It does not exist, bā. [Vol.
3, page 137] 1270 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Chapter]—

Now, if it is argued that only the triad beginning with scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) is enjoined here and not renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), and therefore the reproach "why is it useless when that [renunciation] exists? is groundless, the author replies: "In its entirety" (*niḥśeṣam*). Since it is enjoined here that one should practice the means such as scholarship for the purpose of attaining self-knowledge, tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), cessation (*uparama*), and so forth are also intended here as things to be enjoined; in their absence, [the practice of] childhood (*bālya*) and the rest would be—

The meaning is that [the state of being a child] cannot be established as the primary object of the injunction because it arises from [the context of] yoga. Anticipating the objection that since the injunction is heard in relation to childhood (*bālya*), that alone must be the thing enjoined, he says: "He should remain... and so forth. The connection with the injunction "he should remain" applies everywhere: "Having attained it through scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), he should remain; having attained it through the state of a child, he should remain; then he should remain through silence (*mauna*); having become a silent sage (*muni*), he becomes a Brahmin. Thus, the injunction "he should remain" is linked to each stage.
The application [of the commentary]. || 177 ||
"He is called 'one who breathes by means of the vital breath,' and he is designated as 'the seer of seeing.'"
That Self is established through self-experience, from the body up to the Supreme Self.

Having thus explained the section beginning with "Therefore" and ending with "O Brāhmaṇa," he provides the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) to state another meaning for the term *pāṇḍitya* (scholarship).
He says: "By means of the vital breath (*prāṇena*). The meaning is that the subject matter concerning Uṣasta has been introduced. || 178 ||
Indeed, for this perceptible object, [the rule] is prescribed until its completion.
Wisdom is directly [revealed] by the speech of the learned through positive and negative concomitance. || 179 ||

He says that the purification of that [intellect] is "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*). Regarding the word "of this": the particle *hi* is used to state that the discussion of the meanings of words is the cause for that purification. "Until the end" means until the completion [of the work], that is, until the point of comprehension through the connection with the meaning of the sentences. The cognition consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is of the nature of purification; this is what is meant by the term "scholarship," according to the scriptural statement: "One should remain in scholarship."
This is the meaning. The connection is with the phrase "directly until the completion. || 179 ||
In the same way, that which is called "to him who eats" (aśanāya) is also designated as the Supreme Self.
For the purpose of establishing its conclusion, there is the further statement beginning with "by means of childhood. (180)

He states another meaning of the phrase "one should remain in childhood" with the word "tathā" (so). The meaning is that just as the purification of the "thou" (tvam-artha) was enjoined by the instruction "one should remain in scholarship," so too is the purification of the "That" (tat-artha) enjoined by the instruction beginning with "in childhood. || 180 ||
Nowhere else here is the realization of the Self possible except through the meaning of non-duality.
Thus, this meaning should be understood as the object to be enjoined here, based on positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). || 181 ||

He states how the purification of the meaning of "thou" (tvam), which is intended by the statement concerning wisdom, is to be accomplished: "Not elsewhere," etc. Here, "here" refers to the meaning of "thou"; "therein" refers to the statement concerning wisdom. For when the meaning of "thou" is being purified through methods such as syntactic connection (anvaya) and so forth, the nature of being a witness and so on cannot possibly belong to Brahman elsewhere; for that which is limited, like a jar, is incapable of being the Self and so forth. Therefore, [it belongs] to one's own...

The meaning is that, because whatever remains after [the negation] can only exist as Brahman, the purpose of the purification in this statement regarding scholarship is to establish that "the Self is indeed Brahman. || 181 ||
Just as there is no second entity [for the world], so too there is nothing other than the Self.
The existence [of the result] is the meaning of the injunction; thus, it is stated that "one should remain" in the causative form.
1 Kha-ga is being recited.
[Vol.
3, page 138] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Demonstrating the method for purifying the meaning of that word (*tatpadārtha*), he concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "by childhood" (*bālyena*) with the words "without a second" (*advitīya*).

Just as there is no possibility for the object "Self" (*ātman*) to exist elsewhere [than as the Self], so too there is no logical possibility for the object "Brahman" to exist apart from the Self; for that which is non-Self (*anātman*) [cannot exist independently].

The meaning is that, because [the self] is not Brahman—just like a pot—the statement "Brahman is indeed the Self" (brahmātmāiva) is enjoined as the purport of the sentence regarding childhood, consisting in the purification of the referent of "Thou" (tvam-artha) up to its identity with the referent of "That" (tat-artha). || 182 ||
Furthermore, there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two word-meanings.
Because he has turned away from contradictory objects, he is called a sage (muni). || 183 ||

He states another meaning for the word *muni*: "By the qualification," etc. The meaning of the word *atha* is the immediate sequence following the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words. || 183 ||
The non-association of Brahman and the self is like that of two things whose meanings are mutually contradictory.
Due to the oneness of the object, the distinction ceases upon the destruction of darkness. || 184 ||

Now, regarding the word *muni* in the phrase "atha muniḥ," one might raise the objection: if the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva*) is expressed by the word *muni* through the removal of contradictions such as remoteness and duality in the meanings of *tat* and *tvam*, how can there be a non-dual referent (*akhaṇḍārthatā*)? Anticipating this, he says: "Brahman. When a contradiction arises between two things standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified, that contradiction is destroyed; thus, by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a non-dual referent—devoid of both difference and relation—is conveyed. Therefore...
The meaning is that when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, distinctions and the like are destroyed due to the resulting unity of all things. || 184 ||
And there is grammatical coreferentiality, as well as the relation of qualifier and qualified.
The relationship between the signified and the signifier, as well as between objects and the inner self; 185.
He clarifies the process by which a sentence establishes an indivisible (akhaṇḍa) meaning: "Co-referentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya), etc. || 189 ||
This is because of their grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and so forth, just as in the case of "pot" and "that which is other than a pot."
The meaning of the sentence would result from exclusion; for us, it is not directly [the meaning] of the two terms "That" and "Thou. (186)

Now, one might object that because of the inference—"The subject of dispute has a composite meaning, because it is a sentence, like the sentence 'Bring the cow'"—the indivisible (akhaṇḍa) meaning is not established from sentences such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi). Anticipating this, he states the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra): "Because of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), etc. (verse 186).
Because the elements to be dissolved have consciousness and ignorance as their sole causes, they are to be dissolved into the conscious Self.
Once delusion is destroyed, nothing other than the inner Self remains as an object here; therefore, no further purpose remains. || 187 ||

If it is argued that the non-establishment of the sentence-meaning results from the exclusion of contradictory elements, then those contradictory elements would have to reside elsewhere once they are discarded from the conscious self (cidātman); this would result in the loss of non-duality (advaita). To this, he says: "Consciousness and ignorance" (cidajñāna). The meaning is: since agency and other such qualities to be abandoned reside in consciousness because they are born of ignorance regarding the Self, when that ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, there is nothing other than the inner witness (pratīc); thus, there is no loss of non-duality. || 187 ||
It does not become the object of the cognition of a self, for its sole cause is ignorance.
Since the object of knowledge is devoid of a self, therefore there is the state of pure Selfhood.
In that case, since their difference has been refuted and they abide non-differently within the Self, the integrity of that [Self] as an undivided whole would be compromised; therefore, he says:
"The Self. (188)

Having completed the entire state of silence characterized by both childhood and scholarship.
And having become weary [of the world], one should likewise realize the union of the two categories within silence.

The acts of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) were first mentioned by means of the terms "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*), "childhood" (*bālya*), and "sagehood" (*muni*); thereafter, another point was stated—that through those very same acts, there is the purification of the two categories [the Self and the Not-Self], and that between these two purified entities, there exists the relationship of qualifier and qualified. Now, he restates the meaning of the passage beginning with "or [he remains] non-silent" (*amaunaṃ vā*). [The phrase] "having completed" (*samāpya*) refers to the connection between the two categories, which is meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), because it is either that knowledge itself or the cause thereof. Having thoroughly understood this connection...
The connection is that "he becomes a Brāhmaṇa. || 189 ||
Now, by the statement "O Brahmin," his state of fruition is being described.
The reality, devoid of differentiation and conjunction, is established in its own glory.
Furthermore, Brahman is called "Brāhmaṇa" in the form of the direct [manifestation] and so forth. || 190 ||
Now, he states the purport of the word "atha" (then). Regarding the word "atha": the phrase "of this" refers to the statement of the knower.

He specifies what that state of fruition is by saying "bhedā-" (the cessation of difference). The word "atha" is used to express that the state of fruition follows immediately after the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*). || 190 ||
Having attained this state, everyone is called a Brāhmaṇa.
The status of being a Brahmin is secondary elsewhere; in the preceding stages, it is not direct.

How can the word *brāhmaṇa*, whose referent is [specific] caste (*jāti*), be applied to this state of fruition? For even among Kṣatriyas and others who possess knowledge, there exists the aforementioned state of fruition; to this, he replies: "This... [referring to the verse]. One might object: "How can the single word *brāhmaṇa* apply to both the liberated one who possesses knowledge and the bound one who lacks it, since when a specific meaning is established, it is improper for a single term to have multiple meanings? Anticipating this, he says: "Brāhma—" [referring to the following verse].

The meaning is as follows: when the status of being a Brāhmaṇa resides in those devoid of knowledge, such as students (brahmacārin) and others, the word "Brāhmaṇa" is used in a secondary (gauṇa) sense; however, in the case of the liberated man of knowledge who is a Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka, it is used in its primary (mukhya) sense. Therefore, there is no polysemy (anekārthatā) for a single word, because there is no difference in its underlying power (śakti). || 191 ||
Then he asked this question: "By what means would one become a Brāhmaṇa?"
Beyond the aforementioned means, another means of accomplishment is being asked about. || 192 ||

He introduces the statement "By what would he be a Brāhmaṇa? as being intended for inquiry with the words "By what? Anticipating the objection that since it is already established that knowledge is the means [to Brāhmaṇahood], an inquiry regarding its object is inappropriate, he says: "Brāhmaṇya..."
Thus it has been said. || 192 ||
First of all, that which is characterized by sacrifice and so forth is a means [to liberation] through a traditional succession.
Since that [object] is already known from scripture, another means of proof is being asked for.
Let it be then that sacrifices and the like are the subject of the question; regarding this, he says: "sacrifices and so forth. This means from scripture, specifically from the *vividiṣā* passage.
The ellipsis is "the means to liberation. The sense is that [the rule] "but the Agnihotra and so forth are for the sake of that [liberation]" follows from such principles. || 193 ||
"By which of the four?"—such a question is not appropriate here.
Taking up the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalyāśrama) until the completion of the state of Brahmanhood.
° 1 kha. ga. reads *arthaḥ svam ma*; 2 kha. reads *saṃprāptaḥ*.

If it is asked whether the stage of life (*āśrama*) is then being questioned as a means toward liberation, he says "no": "Of the four," etc. Liberation is the meaning of the locative case [in the verse]. || 194 ||–
And it is not appropriate for a sage who has renounced [worldly life] to enter another stage of life (āśrama).
Whether his purpose has been accomplished or not, for him there is no other stage of life.

Anticipating the objection—"From where [does this] distinction [arise], since liberation is established even through another stage of life (āśrama)?"—he says: "And not... A sage who has accomplished his purpose (*kṛtārtha*), having realized Brahman directly, for whom all desires have been abandoned, does not have another stage of life as a means to liberation; indeed, one who has risen above desires cannot resort to another stage of life. But for one who has not accomplished his purpose, though he possesses the knowledge that prompts action (*prayojaka-jñānī*), for him too there is no [other stage of life].

The meaning is that there is no other means for liberation than this [discipline], because knowledge cannot arise through other means such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth for one who is not detached from saṃsāra, according to the principle beginning with "not to one who is not detached from saṃsāra" (nāviraktāya saṃsārāt), and so on. || 199 ||
This question is asked here of the Brāhmaṇa for the sake of making known the means of attainment.
"What would be the means by which one becomes a Brāhmaṇa? Let that means be explained. (196)

"In that case, since there is no object [of the question], let there be no question; but there might be a censure," [the opponent suggests]. To this he says, "This is a question. The word "here" (iha) refers to the statement of the sentence. Thinking, "This is not a censure because there is no reason for it," he demonstrates the manner of the question by saying, "What? (kim iti). || 196 ||
By means of that questioning and answering, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa as described.
By which even one who has not attained knowledge would become exactly like this, O King.

When asked about the cause of liberation that is distinct from right knowledge, ritual sacrifice, and other stages of life (*āśrama*), he provides the answer beginning with "by which" (*yena*). Regarding the phrase "by [the method] of questioning":
even a person whose knowledge has not yet arisen attains the primary state of being a *brāhmaṇa* through that means by which he becomes free from activity;
this is the meaning. (197)
The similarity with the aforementioned Brāhmaṇa [is established] by virtue of the abandonment of all ritual actions.
By the very means of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya), one becomes a Brāhmaṇa as described.

To the question "What is that?", he says: "It has been stated. *Naiṣkarmya*, which consists in the cessation of all activity, is the state of a *paramahaṃsa*; it is distinct from [mere] knowledge, and by means of that alone one becomes a true *brāhmaṇa*. That means is obtained through the renunciation of all ritual action (*sarvakarmatyāga*). Its status as a means toward *brāhmaṇya* is logical because of its similarity to the goal; for there is no distinction between the two in terms of being devoid of activity, and thus the identity of cause and effect is appropriate.
The meaning is "you," O Āditya. || 198 ||
Thus, this meaning must be understood here from the scriptural statement "by which."
The Smṛtis also declare this very same meaning here and there.

He explains how that state of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*) is attained with the words "Thus this... Here, the word "here" refers to the statement regarding liberation as the goal. He provides the authoritative proof for the fact that the stage of the Paramahaṃsa, when conjoined with wisdom, is the means to liberation, with the words "The Smṛtis also... The word "also" (*api*) is intended to include the Śruti as well. || 199 ||
1 kha, 'It is therefore so.
160 [vol 3, page 141]
1274. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]: "O sinless one, two kinds of steadfastness were previously declared by me in this world:
that of the Sāṃkhyas through the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), and that of the Yogins through the yoga of action (*karman-yoga*). (200)

In this regard, first citing the Smṛtis, he states the words of the Lord [Bhagavadgītā]: "In this world... Here, "world" (*loka*) refers to the multitude of living beings (*prāṇinikāya*). The word "formerly" (*pura*) is a reference to what was stated in the second chapter, or it denotes the time of creation and so forth. To the question "What are those two paths?", he replies: "Knowledge... The Sāṃkhyas are those for whom right discernment (*samyagdhī*) is primary; for them, the Paramahaṃsas, there is the Yoga of Knowledge (*jñānayoga*), which is free from activity (*nirvyāpāra*).

The state of being free from action (*naiṣkarmya*) is subtle in form; by that alone is there final consummation (*niṣṭhā*). For those who are both performers of action and yogis, the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) and its performance constitute their means;
by that alone is there final consummation—thus the Blessed One spoke, meaning that he intended for *naiṣkarmya* when endowed with knowledge to be the instrument for liberation. || 200 ||
There are indeed only two paths, characterized by the performance of action and its renunciation.
These two have emerged from their own kind and have followed one another most closely. || 201 ||

In that very context, he cites the words of Vyāsa: "These two," etc. By excluding any other connection, he distinguishes the two paths to the goals of human life. "Karma," etc., states their mutual dissimilarity. "From the homogeneous," etc., states their authoritative status because they are repeatedly mentioned in the Śrutis: "Anukrānta," etc. || 201 ||
And renunciation (saṃnyāsa) especially transcends both of those.
Likewise, the path beginning with "What is the use of offspring? is heard in the scriptures for those who have renounced ritual action.
Fearing that these two might be considered identical due to their being mentioned together, he says: "Renunciation.
He states: "Likewise," meaning that even though renunciation is well-known and celebrated among those who have renounced, it is observed on the path of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya). || 202 ||
"One should go forth from the very stage of the religious student (brahmacarya)," so it has been stated many times.
They declare that renunciation alone is the means for liberation from all actions.
The Śrutis and Smṛtis [speak] loudly, relying upon pure logic.
Then, by the relinquishing of all karmic actions, one attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the aforementioned path is intended here for one who renounces in due order; however, we do not tolerate renunciation at all in the first stage of life (brahmacarya)? To this, he says: "Brahmacarya... The word "iti" is connected with the phrase "the path heard in the Śruti."

Anticipating the objection that there is an option—since the scripture states, "Some have attained immortality through renunciation," implying that for some action is the cause of liberation and for others renunciation is—the author says: "Renunciation" (*saṃnyāsam*). He shows the indicative mark (*liṅga*) known as repetition by using the word "repeatedly" (*bhūriśaḥ*), in order to illuminate the intended meaning expressed by the word "highly" (*uccaiḥ*).
Furthermore, he says "purified" (*śuddha*) to show that these [passages] do not have any other purpose, because they are supported by uncontradicted reasoning.

The logical principle [is that] liberation, being the very nature of the Self, is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*). Having established that the cause of liberation called "renunciation" (*naiṣkarmya*) is nothing other than knowledge, he concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "by which" (*yena*) and so forth: "All... (vv. 203–204).
"By what?"—this may be an objection, because [the origination and so forth] are impossible.
For the means of proof are of one essence here; as I have stated previously. (205)

He states another meaning for the passage beginning with "sa" (he). With the words "by what," he clarifies the objection. He explains [the objection] regarding "origination and so forth. [This concludes] the fifth Brāhmaṇa on liberation, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. Page 142, Volume 3. 1275.

The meaning is that there is an objection as to by whom causes such as karma—other than knowledge—are [the cause], because it is impossible for [liberation] to be the effect of the fourfold karma, and that impossibility has been stated regarding the relationship and so forth. || 205 ||
By whatever means one desires to achieve identity with this through the practice of sādhana;
Therefore, in this very state, the Self is not even slightly too cold.
Having accepted that all causes other than knowledge are sublated [by it], he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "by which" (*yena*), namely, "by the means" (*sādhanena*).

The meaning is as follows: since liberation is uniform like space both before and after the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites, and since the destruction of ignorance depends solely on knowledge, and since the state of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*) does not exceed—either in essence or in its result or its cause—the knowledge itself, no other cause need be sought for the sake of liberation. || 206 ||
Or rather, it may be a statement of the characteristics of one who knows Brahman as previously described.
Let the Brāhmaṇa be identified by that very same mark. || 207 ||

With the words "sa" (he) and so forth, he states the meaning in the form of another question: "Or else," meaning that it is asked by what means the characteristic of the liberated one who possesses knowledge is [known]. The word "ukti" (utterance) here signifies a question. He explains the meaning of "by which" and so forth with the words "yeneti" (by which): the meaning is that the very nature of the liberated one is the characteristic; there is no other characteristic. || 207 ||
He transcended the attributes of the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect.
Since it is the realization of the innermost identity with the Self, how can it be characterized by those attributes? || 208 ||

Now, one might object: "Since qualities such as possessing odor belong to earth and the other elements, and are distinct from them, how is it that for the liberated soul there is no other defining characteristic?

Is tranquility (*śama*) and so forth its characteristic, or is it the absence of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)? Having raised this alternative, he refutes the first with the words "deha... (the body...). The liberated one has transcended the body and its attributes through the knowledge of reality; therefore, a quality of the intellect (*buddhi*) such as tranquility cannot be his defining characteristic, because they reside in different substrates (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
The meaning is "from the root *ṇī* (to lead). || 208 ||
The nature of his entire saṃsāra is not as it appears according to its characteristics.
Even the total non-existence of all things cannot be the characteristic of one who knows Brahman. || 209 ||
He refutes the second [position] with the words "sarva" (all), etc. || 209 ||
Because the definition of logic for those who know it conforms to the nature of the object to be known.
Brahman, which destroys the duality of existence and non-existence, is the object of knowledge for those who know it.
In this regard, the reason is: "because it is to be experienced. || 210 ||
"Therefore, the Śruti clearly states: 'By that very [means]...'"
Such is the characteristic of one who desires liberation, as those endowed with faith have declared.

Now, since the characteristics of the liberated knower have been stated—based on such scriptural passages as "Just as a sloughed-off snake [is cast aside]," "As if with eyes, yet without eyes," and so forth, as well as the Smṛti texts describing the attributes and states beyond the senses of one whose wisdom is steady—the question arises: why is no other characteristic mentioned there? To this he replies with the words "By which... For the answer was given precisely because of the absence of any other characteristic; whereas the Śruti and Smṛti describe these characteristics from the perspective of the knower's empirical dealings (vyavahāra), not from the standpoint of ultimate reality.

1 kha. ‘Because of the connection’; 2 kha. ga. ‘properly’ [vol 3, page 143] 1276 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Third Adhyāya]— [The text continues: ...the connection [is established]; [it is] proper... [end of fragment].

The intended meaning is that, in reality, what is meant here is the absence of those [qualities]. Now, one might object: "The knowers of the tradition maintain that tranquility (*śama*) and so forth are the means prior to knowledge and the characteristics of the knower thereafter; it is not proper to alter this. To this, he says: "Of the seeker of liberation" (*mumukṣoḥ*).

Whatever characteristics such as tranquility the traditionalists have described while being themselves believers, all of that pertains only to one who remains in the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), and not to one who has transcended it.
Such is the meaning. || 211 ||
Even in deep sleep, for one who is utterly deluded, there is the cessation of the entire cycle of worldly existence.
One who is understood through such characteristics is not considered a knower of Brahman. || 212 ||

He states another reason for why the absence of saṃsāra cannot be the defining characteristic of liberation: "Even in deep sleep," etc. The point is this: since even those who do not know Brahman experience the absence of saṃsāra [in deep sleep], that absence is not the defining characteristic of liberation; nor is the absence of ignorance its defining characteristic. For if that [absence of ignorance] were the very nature [of the Self], it could not be a separate defining characteristic; and if it were not the nature [of the Self], it would be indistinguishable from the absence of saṃsāra [experienced by the ignorant]. || 212 ||
The word "brahman" is declared to denote the Self, but it is not said to denote that which is not the Self.
Destruction [of the afflictions] occurs through the knowledge as previously described; this is stated because of the hearing of the [Noble] Truths regarding suffering. || 213 ||

One might object: "Even though there is no other characteristic for the liberated one, how can it be said that 'anything other than this is afflicted,' since the statement would be devoid of an object because nothing exists apart from the liberated self? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the Self. By the word "here," the passage beginning with "pāṇḍitya" (scholarship) is referred to. || 293 ||
Therefore, that which is other than Brahmanhood, characterized by action and its factors, [is not the self].
That which destroys affliction should be known as Brahman, because it is therefore free from affliction.
The cumulative total number of verses from the beginning is 6430.
Thus ends the fifth *Kahola-Brāhmaṇa* of the third chapter in the *Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika*. || 5 ||

He states another meaning of the scriptural passage beginning with "other than this" (*ato 'nyat*). [The word] "from this" (*ataḥ*) refers to that. He states the reason for the perishability of what is other [than this]: "Brahman," etc. Alternatively, since whatever is other than this is subject to affliction (*ārtam*), therefore Brahman alone is free from affliction; this is the statement of the result. || 214 ||
Thus ends the fifth Kahoḷa Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth Brāhmaṇa,
intended to provide a definitive determination of that which was previously described as "the one who is within all."
The portion of the text beyond Śākalya is now being explained from this point onward.
He states the connection [of the text] as follows: "The previous two Brāhmaṇas have declared that the Self is within all; the subsequent three Brāhmaṇas are for the purpose of determining that.
[Volume 3, Page 144] 6 Brāhmaṇa: Accompanied by Ānandagiri’s sub-commentary, the Śāstraprakāśikā.
Of every qualification, such as "directly" and so forth...
"How indeed could there be a definitive conclusion when all internal [positions] have been thoroughly examined? (2)
1277. Objection: Surely other qualifiers have also been introduced; why, then, is "being the innermost of all" determined [as the defining characteristic] while setting those aside?
To this he says: "Of the qualifier," etc. For, in determining that the Self is the innermost of all, its being the Witness and so forth has already been established.
The meaning is that since this is the case, the manner in which it is the innermost of all is now specifically investigated. || 2 ||
By means of the transcendence of hunger and other such states, the meaning of the question has been revealed.
Thinking that it was not correct, Gārgī questioned him again.

One might object: "Since the determination of that [Self] leads to the determination of its inseparable attributes such as directness (sākṣāttva) and so forth—and since qualities like being the innermost of all have already been determined by the passage beginning with 'He who is beyond hunger' (tannirṇayāt)—what is the purpose of undertaking this again? Anticipating this doubt, he introduces the question beginning with "Now" (atha). [The text says: "Hunger and so forth... (3).
As long as the identity of everything from the earth up to space is not asserted, [the world remains manifold].
A question stated directly would not yet have its meaning determined. (4)

Anticipating the doubt as to why the manifestation of the meaning of the questions beginning with "That which is directly perceived" (yatsākṣāt) by means of the passage beginning with "He who is free from hunger" (yo'śanāya) is not complete, he says: "Of earth and so forth" (kṣityādeḥ). || 4 ||
Because hunger and so forth are denied as residing in a single body, their non-denial [in other bodies] follows.
Therefore, from [the analysis of] the earth up to space, there is no determination of the meaning of the question.

Since the five elements have also been negated by the very negation of hunger and so forth, and the mere inner self (pratyagātman) has thus been determined, how can it be said that the question remains unresolved? To this, he says: "Hunger and so forth... (Verse 5).
Those which are considered to be these earthly entities, such as clods of earth, jars, and so forth.
Their internal and external pervasion is perceived here by means of the earth alone.

Anticipating the objection—"Gārgī asks because she perceives that the question has not been correctly resolved; but what is the basis for her questioning?"—the author states that it is based on pervasion (*vyāpti*), and thus declares the pervasion well-known in the world: "Those who... (6).
Just as earthy entities consist of earth alone, so too does the earth itself.
This [earth] is perceived here as being pervaded by water both internally and externally.
Although [the soul] is all-pervading like the earth, he states what kind of pervasion (vyāpti) you intend in that case: "Just as... (verse 7).
Since it was seen in this way, Gārgī therefore questioned him by means of its indicative mark.
He thus posed this question to the highly intelligent Yājñavalkya.

Having stated the pervasion— that whatever is pervasive when non-selfhood is present is necessarily pervaded by something else, as in the case of earth— he shows the question that is rooted therein with the words "In this way. The reason for asking him specifically is indicated by the phrase "of great intelligence," which refers to his capacity to definitively resolve what has been asked.
Maturity is great intelligence. || 8 ||
1 kha. "But" (tv iti). 2 ga. "Wealth" (dhanam). kṣiṃ. [Vol. 3, page 145] 1278 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Third Adhyāya—]
Whatever object is completely permeated by that which has itself as its warp and woof, [that is the cause].
In the world, it is observed that each of those [elements] is pervaded by another, just as the earth is [pervaded by water].

He recalls the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in order to state the inference (*anumāna*) designated by the word *liṅga*. [The verse begins with] "Ota" etc. An effect—which is gross and limited—is pervaded internally and externally by a cause that is subtle and all-pervasive; the pervasion of that [cause] by something even subtler is observed in the world.

For example, just as there is pervasion by water in the case of the earth, which pervades clods of earth and the like; otherwise, there would be the consequence of scattering, like a handful of flour.
This is the meaning. || 9 ||
The earth is pervaded by water; therefore, it is also held to belong to them.
Pervasion by something else exists because of its being a pervader, just as [the quality of] earthiness [pervades] the earth. (10)

He states the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) for the reason of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) with the words "by water" (*adbhiśca*). He states the inference (*anumāna*) with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 10 ||
The reply is, "In air, O Gārgī"; and it is exactly the same for the subsequent questions as well.
The course of replies and questions is to be understood within these statements. || 11 ||

He replies regarding the surface that pervades the waters. "The reply" (pratyukti) refers to this. He extends the principle of the first indirect expression (*paryāyokta*) to the subsequent instances by saying, "in the same way. || 11 ||
Since light is manifested by depending upon the earth and water elements.
The elements do not exist independently; therefore, they do not manifest as fire and so forth. || 12 ||

If it is argued that since the scripture states "from fire, water," one should have said "in fire" rather than "in air," the author replies with the word "pārthiva" (earthy). Although fire pervades water, because fire is dependent on wood, lightning, and so forth, it is not independent; therefore, setting aside fire, it is stated to be "in its cause, air. Furthermore, although air is dependent on its own cause, it is not dependent on water.
The meaning is that the pervasion of that [reason] is established. || 12 ||
Subtlety and pervasiveness are to be known as increasing successively from the earth element onwards.
[This occurs] through the successive abandonment of those [states] ending with the nature of the syllable. || 13 ||

He states the reasoning for the pervasion of each preceding stage by each succeeding one: "Subtlety," etc. The construction is as follows: among the stages beginning from the earth and ending with the innermost Self (pratyak), by the successive abandonment of each preceding one, the subtlety and other qualities of each succeeding one are to be understood. || 13 ||
And because there is a multiplicity of initiators, the term "many" is understood here.
For they know that everything other than the self consists of the five elements.

Regarding the phrase "in the worlds of the intermediate space" (*antarikṣalokeṣu*) and so forth, one might raise the objection that the use of the plural number is improper because each intermediate space and the others are singular; anticipating this, he says: "consisting of the originators" (*ārambhaka*). One might further object that it is improper for there to be such multiplicity in them, since the Self alone is their cause through its own ignorance; anticipating this, he says: "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*). For it has been stated that there is no other entity whatsoever prior to or apart from the Supreme Self. || 14 ||
The path of the sun is thirty-two yojanas in width, with the gait of a chariot.
By the stabilization of that which was spoken, the deities beginning with Indra remained steady. || 15 ||
1. Kha: "In the water of the *ḍresa*"; 2. Kha: "Therefore, by way of independence.
[Vol. 3, page 146] 6. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1279.

He states a further specific detail regarding the elements beginning with earth and ending with Indra—which were previously described as being woven warp and woof—namely, that they exist within the worlds situated between the Lokāloka mountain and the end of the universe: "Thirty-two," etc. (Verse 11).
All these exist in a state of gradation, consisting of both gross and subtle forms.
They are mutually pervasive and pervaded, being perfectly circular in every respect. || 16 ||
And regarding those deities residing within the worlds, he says "gross" (*sthūla*) and so forth: in comparison to each subsequent one, each preceding one possesses grossness and pervasiveness;

conversely, in comparison to each preceding one, each subsequent one possesses subtlety and non-pervasiveness. Furthermore, their movement is unimpeded everywhere within the world, and they are spherical in every respect. || 16 ||
He who is established within the cosmic egg is Prajāpati, the Virāj.

By him, the principles (tattvas) were previously woven together in every way within the worlds of Prajāpati; regarding this, he explains "Prajāpati. He states "Prajāpati" to specify the distinction of Virāj—who pervades the cosmic egg—from the aforementioned deities. He says "woven" (ota). 17.
This state of being woven warp and woof within the worlds of Brahmā is thus described.
The elements that initiate the egg are designated as the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka). || 18 ||
By explaining [the term] as "in the worlds of Brahmā," he states the meaning of the word *brahmaloka*. [He says] "of that" (tasya). || 18 ||
This very creation of the world has arisen from the Self, which is more subtle than the most subtle.
The interior of the egg has thus been explained; what else remains?

He provides the introductory context for another question with the words "tad etat" (this very thing). The meaning is as follows: this abiding of the earth and other elements, which was previously asked about in terms of their internal and external pervasiveness, has been clarified according to the stated method up to the end of the Brahma-world; however, one need not inquire by means of inference regarding what lies beyond the cosmic egg. || 19 ||
In ancient times, Vāyu was the support of all, existing both as the collective whole and as individual manifestations.
That which has been explained must be stated; for that purpose, there is the question and the answer. (20)

He states the subject matter of the question made out of ignorance regarding the intended meaning already expressed: "The aggregate," etc. The word "previously" refers to the statement of Bhujiyu’s question. || 20 ||
In what, then, are the worlds of Brahmā woven across and lengthwise? Let this be told.
Being thus questioned, [Bālāki] said: "O Vārgya, do not question me further in any way.
Having stated that the subject matter of the question pertains to the Sūtra, he explains its syllables: "The woven threads" (*otāḥ*). He takes up the response:
"Being thus questioned," etc. (21).
"O Gārgī, you have somehow overstepped the scope of the question;
lest your head shatter, I therefore restrain you from this. (22)

He explains that [sūtra]: "Mā'tītyeti" (Do not go beyond). The meaning is: do not, by means of inference, make a question at all concerning Indra and others who are the objects of inferential inquiry, having bypassed the present sūtra. He states the purport of "mā te mūrdhā vyapaptat": "mā te". The form "vyapaptat" is stated as the root "vyapapt" with the elision of the augment *aṭ* due to its connection with the prohibitive particle *mā*; the absence of that elision is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). || 22 ||
1. *parvatalo* | 2. ka. *uttarotta* | 3. kha. *rvyāpakena vyāpta* | 4. kha. *naprakṛ* [Vol.
3, page 147] 1280 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]
It would be appropriate for her mind that she should question the deity by whom she is being asked.
"That which proceeds [is established]; having transgressed that, this 'excessive question' (atipraśna) is answered.

Regarding the phrase "anatipraśnyām" and so forth, he states the meaning of the word *atipraśna* in order to explain its sense: "It is appropriate," etc. [This refers to] the [intended] arrival of the Sūtra.

Because it is not accessible to the intellect (*mānasa-gamya*), a question concerning it is appropriate; a question that goes beyond that is an "over-question" (*atipraśna*), which means inference (*anumā*). || 23 ||
That deity which was previously described as "She who desires darkness" is the very deity to be questioned here.
But because it is distinct from that and so forth, this [reality] is called "that which cannot be over-questioned. (24)
He states the meaning of the suffix: "thā tam" (it is not to be questioned). The meaning is that the deity residing within the egg is one who is not to be questioned excessively (*anatipraśnyā*).

He says "because it is other than that" (*tadanyatvāt*) to explain that she is the deity of the Sūtra, who is not to be questioned excessively because she is accessible solely through scripture (*kevalāgamagamya*). || 24 ||
This very [matter], which is not to be over-questioned, [he asked] through the rashness of over-questioning.
If you ask [further], your head shall surely fall due to your own transgression. || 25 ||
Lest it be suspected that the deity of the Sūtra is not to be questioned further, he states the meaning of the sentence [beginning with] "That" (tām) to address this doubt. || 21 ||
It is appropriate to inquire at will about the gross principles through the method of inference.
But this deity whom you ask about is not so gross as that.

Anticipating the objection that there is no fault in questioning the Sūtras by means of inference—just as one does regarding Indra and other deities—since they are all equally divine beings, he says: "The gross [elements]," etc. (26).
It exists as inconceivable, as immaterial, and as the vital breath of living beings.
Therefore, the deity should not be questioned by any means other than through the sacred scripture (āgama). || 27 ||
He states the purport of the conclusion beginning with "O Gārgī" as follows: "Inconceivable. He wards off the doubt that this [Brahman] might be non-existent by saying: "Prāṇa," etc. (27).
For this very reason, logicians [investigate] that [reality] within the treatises on logic.
Just as [people] do not infer the existence of the earth and other elements due to fear, so it is in this case.
He establishes its inconceivability with the words "from this. That is to say, from fear—namely, the fear of the head falling off. || 28 ||
For this vital breath is indeed undefined; who is able to define it?
Therefore, this statement [is made] so that one might not inquire by means of another authority or through scripture. (29)
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning is 6459.
Thus ends the sixth Gārgī Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika. || 6 ||

And because it is well known from the Vedic sound that this *prāṇa* is the *sūtrātman*, it cannot be inferred; thus he says: "This *prāṇa*... He concludes the meaning of the concluding statement with: "...by another means of knowledge. || 29 ||
Thus ends the sixth Gārgī-brāhmaṇa of the third chapter in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

The Seventh Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
1281 Now begins the Seventh Brāhmaṇa.
That which was desired to be asked by Gārgī, characterized by both the collective totality and its individual manifestations.
Then Uddālaka questioned him about that thread based on his outward signs and from traditional scripture.

In the preceding Brāhmaṇa, that which is pervasive and situated prior to the Sūtra was described; now, desiring to explain the Sūtra itself and the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) contained within it, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then, indeed, him... by means of the word "yat" (that). The word "atha" (then) is used to introduce the opening of the question. || 1 ||
And likewise, its controller, the cause of the birth and so forth of the world.
The noble-minded Āgama Gautama questioned Yājñavalkya.
He states that he did not inquire about the Sūtra alone, but also about the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) contained within it; thus: "And so...

Anticipating the objection that a question regarding an object—whether known or unknown—is either useless or impossible, he says "udāra" with the intention of establishing its validity in the first case for the sake of examination. || 2 ||
Then, by means of the singular path of narration, he [attained] the full acquisition of the scriptures, beginning with the Sūtras.
Gautama explained that he had obtained it directly from the Gandharva.

Having stated the purport regarding the Brahmin, he now states the purport of the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*). Regarding the phrase "sūtrādi": the meaning is that he [the teacher] stated his own attainment of the knowledge of the *sūtra* and the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) by means of the narrative, following the instruction [received]. The word "atha" (now/then) serves as the reason for the impossibility of that knowledge being inferential (*ānumānika*). He explains the method of exposition with the word "sākṣāt" (directly): "I [attained] the knowledge of the *sūtra* and so forth from the instruction of the Gandharva."
The meaning is that he attained it directly, that is to say, immediately. || 3 ||
In this context, Brahman is said to be the Supreme Self (Paramātman), as are the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
The gods are to be known as Agni and the others, and the Vedas likewise according to their well-known status.

Having stated the intended meaning of the words "brāhmaṇa" and so forth, he explains the meanings of the terms "brahman" and the rest in the passage beginning with "He is a knower of Brahman," etc., starting with the word "brahman. || 4 ||
And the beings beginning with Brahmā are strung together like beads on a rosary.
When held by a cord, they always remain suspended.

He states the non-redundant meaning of the phrase "knower of beings" (*bhūtavid*) as follows: "Brahmā and the others. The meaning is that he who knows the Sūtra and the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) knows the beings as they have been described. "Governed by the Lord" (*īśayatāni*) means "regulated by the Lord" (*īśvareṇa niyamitāni*). || 5 ||
It is held by the thread and likewise restrained by the inner controller.
He knows himself as the enjoyer, and likewise knows the entire world.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "he is a knower of the Self" by means of the aphorism. || 3 ||
He who, in the form of the Antar-yāmin, knows these [principles] previously described;
He alone knows [the world] up to the end of the Brahma-world; this is the summary of his knowledge.

Fearing that the phrase "he is all-knowing" (*sa sarvavit*) might be a tautology with what precedes it, he states its intended meaning: "By the aphorism" (*sūtreṇa*).

He who knows the earth and the other elements up to the world of Brahman—which were described in the preceding Brāhmaṇa, held together by the aphorism [of the body] and regulated by the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*)—he alone is said to know everything from Brahman onwards; this is the summary of the section beginning with "He is a knower of Brahman" (*sa brahmavit*), which is expressed as "he is all-knowing."
The meaning is that there is no tautology in that. || 7 ||
This sutra is the most internal, even extending as far as the Brahma-world.
For that is said to be exceedingly subtle, the common refuge of all sentient beings.

Even though knowledge of the *sūtra* and so forth has been introduced, why is it said that it should not be inquired about through inference because it is accessible solely through scripture (*āgama*)?

To this he says: "It is the innermost. The meaning is that the *sūtra* is accessible solely through scripture because it is the innermost of all and because it is extremely subtle. If one asks how these two reasons [are established], he says: "It is stated," referring to such scriptural passages as "This is the inner self of all beings. He thus establishes its status as a *sūtra*.
The ascetic [says]: "All... || 8 ||
That which is intended as manifested is the collective karma common to all.
Distinguished by its nature as air, it then remains within the causal self.
In the passage beginning "Vāyu, O Gautama," he performs a purification of the context in order to explain the meaning of the word *vāyu*. Regarding the phrase "common to all":
that which is common to all living beings, accomplished by means of the sacrificial thread during the state of being a sacrificer, is an action consisting of both general and specific elements—

The meaning is that what was previously manifested for the purpose of bestowing its fruit at the end of the sacrificer's body remains in the root cause during the time of dissolution, existing in the form of the *sūtrātman* (the thread-self) as something delimited. || 9 ||
Karma does not attain its own nature without depending upon the means of accomplishment.
Therefore, action, being dependent [on the self], attains its own essential nature. || 10 ||
Why is it specified that at the time of dissolution, action (*karman*) is delimited by the nature of air? To this he says: "Not itself.

For action, being that which is to be accomplished, does not maintain its own self independently without depending on an agent (*kāraka*). Therefore, because air is its cause, it obtains its self by depending upon it; for there is no other specific cause for vibration (*spanda*) than the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth.
The meaning is that this qualification is purposeful. || 10 ||
It is the wind that sustains both the common and the distinguished.
The fruit of action is held to be experienced by all through both collective and individual states.
Having approached that wind and that action, one remains established here.
The male being who possesses the conceit of the activity of wind is called Vāyu.

Let it be so; what happens in the present case? To this he says: "Of the common [air]," etc. That air which is always understood through valid cognition as the substratum of action—which consists of both the general and the particular—does not, indeed, transcend the air that possesses the power of motion.

Elsewhere, action is appropriate; having reached that wind which is the substratum of action and the action itself which depends upon it as its correlate, he who stands among men as the one possessing the conceit of ownership toward those two is the *jīva*; the meaning here is that the wind takes the form of the fruit. || 11 || 12 ||

This very one is Vāyu, the Sūtrātman, the god who is the support of all and the Lord.
The deities, their emblems, rituals, and all else are entirely dependent upon this very [reality]. || 13 ||

Regarding the phrase "that thread," he explains the term *sūtra* [as follows]: "This very one. He states how Vāyu possesses the nature of a thread: "The support of all. He establishes his divinity: "The Lord. He clarifies his being the support of all: "The deity. || 13 ||
By this [breath] is birth sustained; by this wind is this little body maintained.
Even that supreme birth which was desired to be taken was assumed by Vāyu.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "by the wind" (vāyunā) etc., [using the words] "by this" (anena). || 14 ||
The obstructive [element] of earth and the other [elements] exists subtly, like space.
Of what nature is this linga, which is said to be the seventeenth? || 15 ||

He explains "all these" and so forth. Regarding "the obstructor": he asks what that is which remains like space, and answers, "that of which it consists. He specifies the *liṅga* (subtle body) with the word "that which. || 15 ||
Of whom the divisions—Svaha and the others—are like the waves of the ocean.
And that which is said to be the substratum of all latent impressions (vāsanās). || 16 ||
This is another qualification of *vāyu* (wind). Regarding the word "of which" (*yasya*): [these are] the *āvaha*, *pravaha*, *nivaha*, *saṃvaha*, *udvaha*, and so forth.

To refute the difference in meaning between the two expressions "the thread that is wind" (*vāyuḥ sūtram*) and "by means of the thread that is wind" (*vāyunā sūtreṇa*), he recalls its status as the substratum of the aforementioned actions. Regarding the phrase "of the latent impressions" (*vāsanānām*): the remainder of the sense is that this very principle of wind is the thread that supports all things. || 16 ||
Since this world and the next are thus entirely [dependent] upon one another.
And all beings indeed are strung together by the wind. || 17 ||

He concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "by air" (vāyunā) with the words "since" (yataḥ). Since this air, according to the manner described, is the sustainer of everything, the construction is as follows:
"Therefore, by means of air, this world, the other world, and all beings are bound together on every side. (17)
Upon his departure, his limbs would no longer be capable of action in the face of death.
In this sense, the Śruti has declared the well-established worldly consensus.
He states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore" (tasmāt) as follows: "Of that" (tasya). This refers to the wind whose nature is prāṇa. || 18 ||
"The limbs are supported by the wind alone"—this is a well-known fact even in this world; therefore, he states that [well-known fact] with the words beginning "tasmāt" (therefore). // 19 //
He cites a scriptural passage that restates what is well known: "By air," [meaning] "the elements whose limbs are supported. (19)
Since the subtle body (liṅgadeha) and the rest are sustained by the vital air alone, therefore kinsmen say of a deceased person that "this death has occurred. || 20 ||

He states the meaning of "therefore" as "by means of the wind. He states the meaning of "the person," and so forth, as "the kinsmen. Since the wind is the support of all, the meaning is that upon seeing the deceased person, they say this as a sign of the departure of the vital breaths. || 20 ||
Just as her limbs are observed to be drooping, no longer as they were before.
I thought him dead; for such a thing as this cannot occur without death. (21)

In response to the inquiry "What is that?", he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "vyassraṃsiṣata" (they fell apart). He says "yathā" (as follows). The use of the first-person singular verb is intended to show that each of the kinsmen spoke these words individually regarding the deceased. || 21 ||
Just as when the limbs are stirred by the vital air alone, at that time—
His actions become effective, yet not in that same way as before. || 22 ||
Therefore, his life-force has departed; he is dead, of this there is no doubt.
When such sūtras as have been described exist, this kind of conventional renown arises. (23)

He elaborates upon the characteristics of death already mentioned: "By the vital air," etc. The meaning is that when the limbs were sustained by the *prāṇa*, they were capable of their respective functions; but now, since his limbs no longer perform those actions, people say, "This one is breathless and dead. He states the purpose of the concluding summary beginning with "For by the vital air," etc.: "As has been stated," etc. (22, 23).
O Yājñavalkya, this Sūtra has been correctly stated by you, exactly as it is.
Within that [heart], I perceive myself as the Self, the inner controller (antaryāmin) of Brahman.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "evameva" (even so) as follows: "samyak" (properly). The connection is: "just as it was stated in the Sūtra, so too [I perceive] my own Self which is contained within that. || 24 ||
Now, based on scripture as well, the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), who is even more internal than that, is being described.
This relationship of cause and effect is concluded when that [condition] is stated. || 25 ||

He states the purport of the textual passage beginning with "He who on earth... with the words "from the Sūtra. Even though that has been stated, he says "the effect," etc., raising a doubt regarding what remains to be said. This is connected with the preceding [statement] "this very one is being described. || 25 ||
Let it be understood that he who exists here within the earth as its inner controller is the Antaryāmin.
When this was said, and the consequence of over-extension had arisen, the following speech was uttered. || 26 ||

He who joins together the syllables beginning with "He who stands on the earth" and so forth. Regarding the word "standing": when it is said that the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) stands on the earth, since everyone likewise stands [on the earth], the status of being the Inner Ruler of all would not be established; therefore, he states the subsequent sentence as a response to this. Thus it is said: "When this was spoken... (26).
One who is internal to the earth—that is, one who is indeed within the ground.
In that case, the Earth is the deity, because it conforms to the meaning of what you have stated.
To remove this fault, it is said: "That which one does not know. (28)
Taking that up, he explains it with the word "antara" (within). The particle "hi" is used to indicate the earth's need for a controller due to its insentience.
The syntactical connection is: "He is the inner ruler" (*antaryāmī*). He introduces the passage beginning with "whom the earth" (*yaṃ pṛthivī*) preceded by a doubt. Regarding the word "earth":
the meaning is that the quality of being internal to the earth—which you have described—belongs to its presiding deity (*tad-devatā*). || 27 || 28 ||

Supported by this thread, she possesses a body composed of the great elements.
I am the one Earth; I sustain the imperishable universe.
That which possesses such conceit is called the "inner controller" (antaryāmī). || 29 ||

Having first stated the meaning of the word "earth," he declares by means of the aphorism that she is not the inner ruler (antaryāmin): "It is indeclinable" (*avyayam*), which is an adverbial modifier of the action. || 29 ||
And even the earth does not know that deity who abides within its own self.
He is to be understood as the Inner Controller; however, this deity is not the earth. || 30 ||
He confirms that very point by connecting it with the statement: "The earth... (verse 30).
If [the world] were produced by a causal instrument, would there not be another [creator] who likewise possesses such an instrument?
It is not so, because [the Lord] has the earth itself as his body and nothing else.

Regarding the doubt concerning the statement "whose body is the earth," he says: "In the earth. For that [earth] possesses effects and instruments; if there were another controller within it, like a king, then he too would have to be described as possessing a body, and thus he would not be the Lord, being like us and others.
Such is the meaning. He states that the Lord does not possess that [power] by his own nature: "Not so. He cites the scriptural passage as the reason for this:
"Because... (31).
He who is both possessed of purpose and the means to act, solely by performing the duties of the earth.
Nor is any effect or instrument of his own admitted to belong to him. || 32 ||

He explains that [verse]: "The earth," etc. The words "he, the Inner Controller" are to be supplied as the subject. Anticipating the objection—"Why should he not possess that [earth] by his very nature?"—he states, "No," citing another scriptural passage: "Neither action nor instrument belongs to him. || 32 ||
The Inner Controller is supreme, directly manifest, bodiless, devoid of qualities, and non-dual.
Therefore, he should be understood as distinct from the earth, the deity, and the self. || 33 ||
Nevertheless, from what [source] is it known that he is distinct from the deity? To this, he says: "The Inner Controller" (antaryāmī). || 33 ||
He [perceived] that very earth, which was his own effect, through the medium of delusion.
Having attained excellence, he brings that very [mind] under control. || 34 ||

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who [rules] the earth" as follows: "By means of his own effects," etc. The construction is as follows: for the Supreme Lord creates the earth only through the medium of his own delusion (moha), and having created it, he enters into that very earth and, being present there as the one who has attained the status of the agent and instrument, he rules over it. || 34 ||
Fire, though not itself combustible, becomes so by depending upon the substance to be burned.
In that case, once it has acquired its own nature, that which is to be burned cannot be burned by itself.
Just as it is known, so indeed is the Self, proceeding toward its effects consisting of the deity and so forth.
By means of the bodies and other attributes of deities and so forth, he controls the deities and others. || 36 ||
1. Kha, Sa, and Sa read *pṛthivīdeṃ*. 2. Ga reads *vāntarniyauṃ*. [Vol. 3, page 153] 1286 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Third Adhyāya]

Now, one might object: "Does the Supreme Controller possess control by its own nature, or not? In the first case, the dependence on the body and organs as objects of control is untenable; in the second case, even with that dependence, such control remains unestablished. Anticipating this doubt, he provides an illustration: "Even though it is not a burner... This refers, for instance, to wood and the like.
"Having attained its own nature" means being in a state of blazing. He states the application of the illustration: "The Knower... following the aforementioned example.

The construction of the meaning is as follows: the conscious element (*cid-dhātu*), which is the deity to be governed, having entered into its own effects produced by delusion—namely, the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth—governs those deities and others precisely through their respective instruments of action (*kārya-karaṇa*). || 35 || 36 ||
By means of self-existence, non-agency, and the absence of qualities, there is indeed non-duality.
The reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), through the effects arising from its own ignorance, appears as if it possesses those [attributes]. || 37 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the status of being a controller is possible through its own instruments and so forth, what is the need for dependence on another, he says: "But by itself" (svatastu).
To the question, "If it is by itself devoid of effects and the like, how can there be the cognition of its possessing them? he replies: "Consciousness" (cit). || 37 ||
Having divided him into four parts, the Sātvatas worship him.
Likewise [there are] those of Hiranyagarbha, as well as the Pāśupatas and others. || 38 ||

Having spoken of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), he states the consensus of the Pañcarātrins with the words "caturdhā" (fourfold). This means [the Lord] whose nature consists of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. For it has been said:
"The Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, is imperishable and fourfold in essence."
And: "One should gratify Vāsudeva, who is endowed with the three forms."

Another also says: "That which is indeed the sovereign power of all, called Īśvara, the regulator, [is present] through the primordial fourfold nature, differentiated by the distinctions of knowledge and so forth."
And [it is said]: "The Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) of all the gods.

Furthermore, he states that those who know the Yogaśāstra, like the Bhāgavatas, meditate upon Him by dividing Him according to the relationship of cause and effect through the sequence taught in their own scripture. Thus it is said: "Or, by devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna), [the yogin attains samādhi], being untouched by afflictions, actions, their ripening, and their latent impressions... Puruṣa...

"God is without distinction; therein lies the unsurpassed seed of omniscience; He is the teacher even of the ancients," and so forth. In that very context, he states the consensus of the Māheśvaras: "Thus. As it has been said:
"In the stainless, supreme void, the cause is eternally situated and imperishable."
Śaṅkara presides over the power-bestowing instruments together with the collyrium.
"Remaining there, he overcomes these causal agents with his own splendor and,
unobserved by beings, joins them together for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), all proponents of theism are included. || 38 ||
Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, whose essence is the Vedas, dispels the darkness [of ignorance].
Indeed, out of a desire for the welfare of living beings, he has proclaimed this very thing many times.
