In that very context, he states the agreement of Vyāsa: "Kṛṣṇa," etc. (39).
Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest; [he created] the staff born from the unmanifest.
Within this egg are these worlds and the earth with its seven continents.

To explain how he spoke thus, he says: "Nārāyaṇa. How then is his causality established? He says it is by means of ignorance (ajñāna). He says: "the egg" (aṇḍa). By saying "of the egg," he precludes any other cause for the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ. He shows those very [worlds] specifically: "seven. The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of including the worlds not explicitly mentioned. || 40 ||
Salutation be to that God, who is beyond attributes and yet the soul of all attributes.
To Nārāyaṇa, the universal one, the supreme self of the gods. || 41 ||
Why is Nārāyaṇa, the inner controller (antaryāmī), specified as the object for the manifestation of the cause of all human goals? To this he says:
"To him" (tasmai). || 41 ||
It was with reference to this very [teaching] that the sage Nārāyaṇa likewise [spoke].
It is employed by men of great wisdom who are learned in the Vedas. || 42 ||
He states that He is not apprehended through the Purāṇas and Āgamas alone, but also by the very syllables of the Śruti: "Etameva" (this very one).

The mantra beginning with "The thousand-headed God, the all-eyed, the source of all happiness, the universe, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable, the supreme state," is employed by those who know the meaning of the Vedas with reference to the Inner Controller; therefore, the meaning is that He is Vedic. || 42 ||
The internal darkness is the manifestation of consciousness, whose nature consists in the regulation of its own effects.
This supreme controller is said to be such only through that limiting adjunct (upādhi), and not by his own nature. || 43 ||

However, some maintain that the Supreme Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) is indeed devoid of adjuncts (nirupādhika); in response to them, he says: "The inner self" (pratyak). The meaning is this: it is accepted that ignorance (ajñāna), when permeated by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), has the nature of governing its own transformations; and the Supreme Self (Paramātman), as conditioned by that [ignorance], is called the Controller, for His status as a controller does not exist inherently due to His being devoid of activity (nirvyāpāratva). He now clarifies that the status of being the Inner Controller belongs only to the one with adjuncts (sopādhika).
He increases. || 43 ||
He is omniscient, omnipotent, the self of all, all-pervading, and eternal.
This Lord is the eternal cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world. || 44 ||

Raising the objection that the state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmitva*) might also belong to the unconditioned [Brahman] just as omniscience and other qualities do, he states the failure of the supporting example:
"Omniscient," etc. In this case, "being the Self of all" is the reason for omniscience and so forth; "the world" is the reason here for being the inner controller.
The word "always" (*sadā*) is to be connected with every instance. (44)
This very one is the inner deity, the cause of all causes.
He always, in all circumstances, restrains the goddess Earth. || 45 ||
Having explained the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who [rules] the earth," he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "This is your Self" as follows: "This very one...
[The commentary notes: 1. *prabhā*; 2. *kha* reads *śvākhyaṃ vi*; 3. *kha* reads *vasambhava*].
[Vol. 3, page 155]

The Sūtra is the cause; and the Lord who exists as the cause even of that, who, being internal to the deity Earth, always governs her in all her functional states— he is the Antaryāmin you wish to know, and he is the Self of all.
This is the meaning. || 49 ||
The presiding deity of that [element] would be the mere generality of fire.
In the same way, this should be understood regarding darkness as well; and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is designated as the Self (ātman).

Considering that the subsequent passages are identical to the first passage and thus need not be explained, [the author] states that the word *tejas* in the phrase "he who [does not know] in light" refers to light in its general sense. Regarding the phrase "that light which he does not know," he explains what is intended by the word "that.
In the phrase "he who [does not know] in darkness," the word *tamas* denotes merely the absence of light—that which is the opposite of light. "Whom darkness does not..."

And he says that it is the presiding deity who experiences that [pleasure], using the word "thus" (*evam*). Regarding the passage "He who, dwelling in the self... from the Mādhyandina recension, he states the meaning of the word "self" (*ātman*) there as "the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajña*). || 46 ||
The triad of deity, locus, and instrument is called the vital breath and speech.
Since the Lord restrains even these three with respect to odors. || 47 ||

In the passage "He who, dwelling in the breath... [the text] explains "breath" as "deity. By the word "breath," the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) is intended. He provides the reason for this even in the case of the deity and so forth by saying "he restrains. By this, the section beginning with "He who, dwelling in speech... is explained. || 47 ||
This is the definitive explanation of what was said regarding "that which the earth does not know."
By the statement "unseen, unheard," [the mind] is purified for the sake of knowledge. || 48 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "the unseen seer" (*adṛṣṭo draṣṭā*) as follows: "The earth," etc. By the passage beginning with "whom the earth does not know," it is stated that the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) of the earth and so forth does not know the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). Raising the objection—"For he is highly fortunate; why should he not know the Inner Controller who resides within his own self?"—the subsequent scripture determines that [the Inner Controller] is not an object of cognition, even in the absence of being an object.
The meaning is that this is intended to make it known that its true nature can be understood. || 48 ||
"When the seer, the seeing, and the seen are scrutinized by the inward-looking vision,"
Due to the reasons of insentience and subservience to another, there is not even the slightest capacity [in it]. (49)
To the question, "Why is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) not an object [of perception] like ourselves and others? he says: "The Seer" (draṣṭṛ). || 49 ||
Nor is there such a mutual relationship between the seer and the object to be seen, nor likewise between the two acts of seeing.
The relationship between the grasped and the grasper is not perceived by its witness. || 50 ||
Furthermore, because the seer and the others cannot be grasped by one another, the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) is not grasped by them; this he states with the words beginning "no" (na).

Neither between two seers, nor between two objects of sight, nor between two acts of seeing, is there a mutual relationship of grasper and grasped, because those [three], such as the seer and so forth, are equal [in nature].
The meaning is that the Witness, the Inner Controller, is not seen by those objects. || 50 ||
"Abiding within the range of vision of forms and so forth, he is the witness of their coming and going."
How could the earth perceive that which is pure consciousness, the eternal vision of the Self?

In that very context, he states another reason: "rūpādi" (form, etc.). The meaning is that the individual soul (kṣetrajña) of the earth and other elements is not capable of perceiving the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), because [the latter] is the witness of the knowledge of one's own form and so forth, the witness of their arrival and departure, internal, pure consciousness (cinmātra), and possesses the vision of the eternal Self. || 11 ||
Because it does not transgress its own sphere of activity, and because of its uncommon perspective.
Because there is no other seer besides him, the deities do not see him.

Furthermore, he states that this [Self] is not an object: "māgocare" (not within the range). The meaning is that because it is devoid of sound and other qualities, because it is self-luminous, and because there is no other seer, it cannot be grasped by the witness (sākṣin). || 52 ||
Regarding the phrase "the seer of the seen," that witness who was previously cited—
Therefore, it is said that even here [in this context], there is no one other than He who is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī). || 53 ||

Having explained the meaning of the statement "the unseen seer," [the author] introduces the passage beginning with "there is none other than this" (nānyo'to'sti) in order to dispel the doubt that there is a distinction—namely, that those who perceive are distinct from the one who governs, and that the inner controller (antaryāmī) is another. Thus: "of the seer" (dṛṣṭeḥ). || 53 ||
The supreme Self within the intellect is called the "conscious self" (vijñānātman).
The Supreme is said to be the controller, the witness of the arising and passing away of the intellect.

If there is no difference [between the Self and the intellect], then who is the knower? To this he says: "ending with the intellect" (*buddhyanta*). If the status of being a knower belongs to the Supreme [Self] through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the intellect, then how can He be the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), given the absence of anything to be controlled? To this he says: "the intellect," etc. The word *eva* (indeed) is connected with the word *para* (Supreme). || 14 ||
Neither excluded nor followed by anything else, it is complete, established within its own self.
The cessation of all connection with the causes of saṃsāra is called Brahman. || 55 ||

How, then, is it that this [consciousness] is without distinction? To this he says: "avyāvṛtta" (unrestricted). The meaning is that when the conscious substratum, having set aside agency, controllership, and so forth, abides in its own majesty as the undivided form of Brahman—this being what is intended—then the conscious self, devoid of connection with bondage and its causes, deserves to be designated as "Brahman without distinction. || 55 ||
Of this saṃsāra, which consists of cause and effect and is illusory in nature.
Through the statement of the scripture, Brahman alone is the reality that is without before, without after, and without end.

Having stated that [the Self] is unconnected with bondage and so forth, he anticipates the objection that it might exist separately and says: "The effect," etc. The meaning is: from such statements as "All this," and so on. || 56 ||
And likewise, the scripture declares that the inner controller (antaryāmin) is the seer of the earth and the other elements.
Therefore, since the consequence of difference arises, it is said: "There is nothing other than this. (57)

He concludes the purport of the statement beginning with "no" (na) with the words "of the earth, etc. (pṛthivyādeśca). The meaning is: therefore, because the world, consisting of cause and effect, does not exist apart from Brahman. || 17 ||
This alone is the one seer, devoid of agents and the like.
That is conceived by the ignorant as being merely the effect of ignorance.
To the question, "In the absence of anything other than the seer and so forth, how can there be the cognition of their difference?", he says: "This... (verse 18).
162 [Vol. 3, page 157] 1290 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]
It approaches me alone here with exclusivity, just as it does the sun.
Those who see [it] as well as those who are ignorant honor it with [the fruits] born from their lack of understanding of that. 59.

The non-dual element of consciousness (ciddhātu), though partitioned by the intellect and other faculties born of its own ignorance, is superimposed in many ways upon it by the deluded; this he establishes through the following illustration. Regarding the word "me" (mām): just as in the world, although the sun is common to all, observers superimpose upon it the quality of being directed specifically toward them alone, so too do the deluded [superimpose] [diversity] upon it through the intellect and other faculties arising from their own ignorance.
The meaning is that they conceptualize themselves as manifold. || 59 ||
The view is everywhere one and the same, being in all cases distinct from the nature of the self.
This [consciousness] shines forth in many ways due to causes arising from that ignorance.
The cumulative total number of verses from the beginning is 6519.
Thus ends the seventh section, the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa, of the third chapter in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣyavārtika*.
He concludes what was stated—that the non-dual inward vision appears as manifold due to ignorance—with the verse beginning "The vision... (verse 60).
Thus ends the seventh Brāhmaṇa, the Antaryāmin-Brāhmaṇa, of the third chapter in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Now begins the eighth Brāhmaṇa:
[It describes] that which is free from hunger and other such states, and characterized by being directly manifest as "this" and so forth.
Therefore, the Imperishable (akṣara), which abides in the Self free from limiting adjuncts, must be explained.

In the preceding Brāhmaṇa, the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) was determined through questions and answers; now, the author states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa: "Aśanāyādi" (beginning with hunger, etc.). Since the form of the Inner Controller, being characterized by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), is subject to rejection, and since the human goal is not fully accomplished by the knowledge of that [conditioned form], it follows that the goal is fulfilled only through the knowledge of the unconditioned Imperishable (Akṣara). Therefore, the non-manifest Imperishable—characterized by attributes such as "directly perceived" (sākṣāt) and so forth, and constituting the meaning of the sentence—is what must be expressed.
The meaning is: "the emergence of the Mityakṣara Brāhmaṇa. || 1 ||
With reference to which [subject], this entire commentary has been composed for the sake of the Innermost Self.
Therefore, that syllable must be proclaimed; for this reason, the subsequent Vedic scripture [states so]. || 2 ||

Fearing that once the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) has been explained, nothing remains to be explained because there is no other syllable besides him, he explains what was summarized [in the previous verse]: "That which [he] aims at," etc. (2).
In the past, Gautama asked about the subject matter within the Sūtras.
O Gārgī, she then inquired about the state of being woven like warp and woof belonging to those two very [elements].
1. Kha. *rvāntare'nta*; 2. Kha. Ma. *na paripṛ*. [Vol.
3, page 158] 8. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1291.
He states that the latter [section] has its purpose already attained by the former with the words, "By Gautama. The essential nature of the Sūtras and so forth was indeed determined previously;

however, the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) therein was not established. Now, it is determined that the Unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), which is the Sūtra, is pervaded by the Imperishable (*akṣara*) up to the ether (*ākāśa*);
thus, the distinction between their respective meanings is established—this is the sense. || 3 ||
Whatever object may exist above the sky, whether it be existent or non-existent, it is thus specified.
And that which is below the skull, and that which is between the two skulls. || 4 ||

Having stated the Brahmana's intended meaning and its purpose of conveying what has not been understood before, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "yat" (that) as follows: "Of the sky," etc. The connection is: "In what is all that, consisting of the Sūtra, woven across and lengthwise? || 4 ||
That which is above the sky, beginning with the skull, and that which is below, from the lower cavity;

That which is within the skull, and that which is characterized by the elements (bhūta) and so forth—having explained that the word "above" (ūrdhva) and the others have as their object things situated in those respective locations, he states another meaning regarding location: "Above," etc.
Here too, the grammatical connection is as before.
Or one might explain the progression of the categories in this way, without contradiction.
That which has passed away is the past; that which exists now is the present.
And that which is yet to come will not be past, nor is it present.
By the statement "so they say," the defect of inference is removed.

Fearing that the second meaning is not present because it is not mentioned in the Bhāṣya, he says: "padārtha... (regarding the word-meaning). The meaning is: even if a word-meaning is not stated in the Bhāṣya, there is no harm if it is observed [in the text], provided it does not contradict the meaning of the sentence. He clarifies what was said regarding the definition of the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth with the words:
"bhūtam" (the element). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*), however, is as before. He states the meaning of the phrase "they say" (*ityācakṣate*) with the word: "iti" (thus). || 6 || 7 ||
Those who know the scriptures declare that such a sūtra as this is of this very nature.
"Tell me, when asked: 'In what, then, are those woven warp and woof? (8)

Having stated the intended meaning—that this [verse] is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that a Sūtra, which is accessible solely through scripture (*āgama*), cannot be an object of inference (*anumeya*) as is the case with the world of Prajāpati and so forth—he explains the literal meaning of its words, beginning with "This" (*etad*). The meaning is: those who know the sense of the Śruti declare that the entire universe, consisting of the elements and so on, is the Sūtra. He explains the meaning of "In what" (*kasmin*) and so forth, beginning with "Woven" (*otam*), saying "Tell me."
"Recite it according to the Vedic style"—this is what is meant. || 8 ||
In the Sūtra, moreover, all this is both woven together and interlaced.
It is well-established that the time of the world is present. || 9 ||

Here, the locus of the world together with its thread (the *sūtra*) is questioned; and since there is a doubt as to whether that question refers to the present time or to the past and future, the author refutes the first [option] in order to adopt the second. Regarding the word "thread" (*sūtra*): because it is observed that the limbs of the body fall away when the thread called *prāṇa* departs from the body—established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—that which precedes it [in time] is its locus, and that [locus] is always dependent on [the Self].
The meaning is that since, for the time being, a certain perception of existence is observed in the air (*vāyu*) at the present time, the [opponent's] previous argument is not tenable;
the second *tāvat* indicates the formal proposition (*pratijñā*). || 9 ||
And the world, previously unmanifest, now becomes manifest.
This manifestation is logical for that which exists, since it is not possible for that which does not exist. || 10 ||

Anticipating the objection that the substratum of the world need not be questioned even at another time—since it does not exist after destruction or before origination—the author says: "And the world. Although the world exists prior to its origination, it is unmanifest; at the time of birth, it is manifested through name and form. Therefore, the meaning is that it was not non-existent in the past. To the objection that it might be manifested while being non-existent, he says: "And manifestation... (Verse 10).
And this, though manifest, returns once more to the state of the unmanifest.
His present form is sustained by the wind.

Having dispelled the doubt regarding the absolute non-existence of the world prior to its origination, he now dispels that same doubt even after its destruction, stating: "And [it is] manifested. Having stated the existence of the world during the past and future times, he restates what was previously said in order to state the resulting answer to the question: "By means of the wind. || 11 ||
But regarding the past and future times of the world-soul...
Tell me, by what self (ātman) and in what [substratum] is existence (sattā) woven across and lengthwise? || 12 ||

He explains that which remains as the light that is the substratum of the world during both time-periods. Regarding the word "past": the meaning of the question is this: by which Sūtra-self was the existence of the world ordained in the present time, and in what does it abide during the past time through being woven as warp and woof? || 12 ||
Then, having repeated what was spoken by the cow, the seer spoke into the sky.
He [attained] the state of being woven through and through with the wind of the world through diligent effort.

He takes up the response. Regarding the phrase "having repeated [the opponent's statement]": the word "atha" (then) is used to show that repetition is necessary, because the consequence of defeat would follow in the absence of such repetition. Effort, however, consists in the practice of responding through the medium of questioning and rehearsal. || 13 ||
From the earth up to this sūtra, [the period] after destruction and before birth.
In space, that is unperceived, yet it exists by virtue of its mere being. || 14 ||
He analyzes that [nature] as follows: "Earth and so forth" (kṣmādi). || 14 ||
For as long as there is anything that has birth, it possesses distinctions such as name and so forth.
Space is intended here as the reality of all that exists.

He states the intended meaning of that [verse] with the words "yāvad dhi" (for as far as...). The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that no effect is established apart from this world, which consists of name, form, and action, and which possesses birth. || 19 ||
This does not obtain a distinction from existence, because it lacks self-nature.
Nor is there positive concomitance, because that [reason] does not pervade it; nor is its absence admitted when [the probandum] exists. (16)

In order to establish that the unknown Brahman alone is the reality of the world, he proves its status as a mental construction (*kalpita*). [The commentary states: "vyatireka... [and so on]. [Variants: 1. *sva. ga.
gārgyukta*; 2. *ka. ga. protārthatāṃ*; 3. *kha. ga. tiṣṭhati*.
"What is it?

[The answer is: because of its being non-self, which would entail the consequence of it having no essential nature (niḥsvarūpa). The meaning is that, due to the lack of pervasion by that [self], identity with the insentient is impossible for the sentient, because they are mutually contradictory. If it is not insubstantial, then "being an object of perception" (dṛśyatva) is the reason. || 16 ||
The reality of being born from a cause is like the rope for a snake and so forth.
Apart from the seven principles, there is no other destiny for those subject to birth.

Having resolved the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he states the conclusion that the reality of the world is indeed Being (*sat*): "Being" (*sad iti*). He clarifies the meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*): "And because of existence" (*sattvāt ca iti*) || 17 ||
Therefore, all this is indeed Brahman alone during its emergence, persistence, and dissolution.
Thus, the statement of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad is clearly expressed as "All this is indeed Brahman. (18)
Fearing that the world might possess the nature of existence during its period of persistence but not at other times, he says: "Being alone" (*sadeva*).

The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is the absence of any other alternative. He states the proof for the fact that the reality of the world is Being alone throughout the three periods of time:
This existence, prior even to the Imperishable, is the storehouse of the world.
For it will be explained that the Imperishable (akṣara) is free from cause and effect. || 19 ||
Lest one should suspect that the reality of the world is merely unknown and that there is no reality beyond it, he says "arvāk" (below). "Nidhiḥ" means the primary cause. || 19 ||
This power, which is designated as "Being" (sat), is all-powerful.
Nor is "being" (sattā) a universal (sāmānya), because its status as the referent of a cognition is not observed. (20)
Anticipating the objection that "there is no being which is the source of the world, for there is no evidence for its being the cause," he says: "All-powerful.

Beginning with the passage, "Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning," that power denoted by the word "Being" [is the cause], because it possesses the capacity for creation preceded by reflection (īkṣaṇa) regarding fire, water, and food.

The meaning is that it is not stated that *sattā* (Being) is the causal material (*upādāna*) of the entire world on the basis of scriptural authority (*āgama-prāmāṇya*). Anticipating the objection that—given the etymological derivation *sato bhāvaḥ sattā* ("the state of being existent is Being")—*sattā* cannot function as a material cause because its nature is that of a universal (*sāmānya*), and therefore the scripture must have another intent—he says:
"And not... (verse 20).
Apart from the non-existent, no other existent entity is perceived.
O Blessed One, does even non-existence not possess any state of excess? (21)
Regarding the question of how there can be no perception of that entity which is distinct from existence—the meaning of the suffix *pratyaya*—he says: "No.
Having stated the absence of experience as the reason for the non-existence of any entity other than existence, he states the logical argument: "Even non-existence... (21).
Therefore, the Veda is the source for that which is accessible to the intellect of the virtuous in manifold ways.
He declared that [the world] is mere illusion, using examples such as clay and so forth. || 22 ||

This indicates the measure by which [the world] is to be favored. "Being" (sat): the meaning is that the scriptural passage beginning with "an origin in speech" (vācārambhaṇa), by stating that the world does not exist as something distinct from its primary cause—just as a jar and so forth do not exist apart from clay—declares it to be mere illusion, since it is impossible for anything consisting of existence or non-existence to be distinct from Being (sat). || 22 ||
1294 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Chapter]:
By the word "space," the Self alone is to be known; there is nothing else whatsoever here.
For it is not logical that anything other than the Self should possess the quality of being the innermost of all. || 23 ||

Regarding the statement, "In that [Brahman], space is woven as the warp," it has been said that by the word "space" (ākāśa), the unknown Brahman is intended. However, others, taking the word "space" to mean the unmanifested (avyākṛta) and conceiving the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) as being within that, assert that the Supreme Self is a distinct principle other than those two. To them, he replies: "Space... Space, which is heard in scripture as being internal to the world together with its threads, is not the unknown [Brahman].
The meaning is that it is something other than Brahman, because the quality of being the innermost of all cannot belong to anything else. || 23 ||
"Or rather, it is space"—thus indeed did the Śruti declare Brahman alone.
And no cause for the self other than this is found in the Vedas.

Now, one might argue that since the term "ether" (ākāśa) is used in its conventional sense for the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), it is more appropriate to take that very thing here, setting aside the indicative mark (liṅga) of being the innermost of all; to this, he says:

"The ether... He anticipates the objection—"In the passage, 'Ether, indeed, is the revealer of name and form,' why should the word 'ether' not also refer to the elemental ether?"—and replies: "And because it is the cause... For here...

The causality of space is stated [in scripture], and it is established in the Vedānta that "the Self itself, when unknown, is likewise [space]"; furthermore, by the two marks of being the cause of all and being untouched by name and form, and because of the Śruti stating "That is Brahman," and because it has been stated in the sūtra *ākāśo 'rthāntaratvādivyapadeśāt* (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.42) that the word *ākāśa* refers to Brahman in another scriptural passage, its reference to Brahman must also hold here; for indeed, when possible, [one should not resort to a secondary meaning].

The sense is that while it is appropriate to set aside [the literal meaning] of internality, the word "ether" (ākāśa), due to its frequent usage, can also apply to Brahman; this was considered in the Dahara-adhikaraṇa, as stated in the sūtra: "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks. || 24 ||
He is also the one whose purposeful activity consists of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, as well as its regulation and other such functions.
Nothing other than the Self can be conceived as the cause, according to the Śruti.

One might object: "The word 'ether' (ākāśa), even when referring to Brahman unknown [as such], does not refer to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), because that is distinct from it. To this, he says: "The world... (verse 25).
He is the inner controller; He is the source of all, the origin and the dissolution of everything.
The words of the Māṇḍūkya-śruti are clearly recited thus. || 26 ||
Having stated that there is no evidence for a difference between the cause and the inner ruler (antaryāmin), he cites scripture as proof of their non-difference: "This... (26).
Therefore, the wise should not postulate any other unmanifest principle (avyākṛta) distinct from the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin).
Because among the principles (tattvas) ending with the imperishable (akṣara), there is no mention of the unmanifest (avyākṛta). || 27 ||

"He is the Lord of all, He is the All-knowing, He is the Inner Ruler, He is the Source of all; for from Him comes the origin and dissolution of all beings"—thus he states the fruit [of this knowledge] as established by scripture. "Not other than this" (nātaḥ): the meaning of the word is that there is no evidence for difference, whereas such evidence exists for non-difference. He provides another argument for the fact that the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta) is not other than the Inner Ruler: "In the sections ending with the Imperishable" (akṣarānteṣu); that is, even in the three Brāhmaṇas.

The meaning is that since the term "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta) is not heard in the context of the elements beginning with earth and ending with the syllable (akṣara), it is impossible to conceive that the "undifferentiated" is something other than the inner ruler (antaryāmin), who is indicated as the substratum of the world by means of the word "ether" (ākāśa) along with its governing aphorism. || 27 ||
And here too, in the phrase "that is the Veda," it is the world itself that is being designated.
Because of his speech not being made by another, and because of its being either determinate or indeterminate. || 28 ||

One might raise the objection that even though the term "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta) does not appear here, the undifferentiated mentioned in the scriptural passage "From that, indeed, this [was]" is intended here by the word "ether" (ākāśa), thereby establishing a distinction between the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), the Undifferentiated, and the Imperishable (akṣara). To this, he says: "From that, indeed... This means that the reality intended is not something other than the Inner Controller and the Imperishable as you claim; rather, it is simply that the manifest world is denoted by the word "differentiated" (vyākṛta) and not by the word "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta).
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of that" (tasya). || 28 ||
Having stated that "He is the controller of all," it follows that He alone is the object to be known.
Wherein the Self is described by the Śruti, therefore that which has both a beginning and an end is called the unmanifest (avyākṛta). || 29 ||

If it is argued that in the phrase "That from which" (*taddhetoḥ*), the world in its causal state was denoted by the word "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*), and here too, having denoted that very same thing by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), the world in its effected state is woven as warp and woof within it—even so, one might suspect that the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is something other than that; therefore, he says:

"Of all. Having described the Controller through such passages as "He is the ruler of all, the lord of all, [who does not become better] by good deeds," etc., [the text speaks] of that very [Controller].

Through the *vividiṣā* statement, the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) is heard; and that is not tenable without its being unknown. Furthermore, "the unknown" (*ajñāta*) and "the undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*) are synonyms; therefore, the meaning is that the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) alone is the undifferentiated. || 29 ||
Knowledge, action, and the formative predispositions have their essence in the ignorance of the inner self.
Regarding those [karmas] which our Śruti has declared to be the cause for taking up a body.

Even according to the system of Bhartṛprapañca, it cannot be said that there is no distinction between the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and the inner controller (antaryāmin); thus, he states that karma and the rest are merely the play of one's own ignorance. [The verse begins with] "Knowledge" (vidyā). One might object: "Since those [karma, etc. are ineffective, what is the point of saying they are products of ignorance? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The body" (deha). The scriptural passage beginning with "Knowledge and action, as well as one's prior experience (pūrvaprajñā), follow him" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2] is the authority for this. || 30 ||
The persistence of ignorance regarding the inner self is established without being investigated.
This triad should always be accepted; there can be no effect without a cause.

Nevertheless, he explains how these [three] are of the nature of ignorance (avidyā): "Unexamined," etc. To the question, "Why is this triad—which is difficult to define even as existence and so forth—accepted as the effect of one's own ignorance? he replies: "No," etc. The meaning is that there is no cause corresponding to the triad that transcends one's own ignorance. || 31 ||
These three are indeed karma, and that [karma] does not attain its own selfhood because it lacks an agent.
Without the causal factors (kārakas), one does not conform to the application [of action] in its arising.

Having stated that the triad [of body, speech, and mind] is characterized by ignorance (avidyā), the author states the opinion of Bhartṛprapañca, demonstrating its relevance to the present topic: "It is action alone.
As they have said: "Even this triad—consisting of the nature of the innermost consciousness-ātman and characterized by [the colors] mahārajana and so forth—is indeed action alone. And action...
He says "And that" (tacceti) because, being dependent upon causal factors (kāraka), it requires their operation for its own production.
Therefore, action remains enveloped by its very form as application.
Because [the self] is conjoined with the agent within itself, and not otherwise; therefore, its persistence [is established]. || 33 ||
1. Of them; 2. Ga. reads "rakātma"; 3. Kha. reads "to'sti saṃ".
[Vol. 3, page 163] 1296 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Third Adhyāya]—
He states that the performance of action depends not only on the causal factors at the time of its origination, but also during its duration.

He says: "In application... This means: because there is a rule that action is dependent upon causal factors. He points out the defect—that such action would lack its very essence if it were not conjoined with those causal factors—by saying: "No... As has been stated, [action] which is not grasped by an external qualification...
It remains in its own state of application, devoid of a location, yet refined by the material derivative that is co-existent with its production and serves as its efficient cause.
The entire group of those engaged in the practice, indeed, by means of supreme subtlety.
Having ceased prior to the arising of the fruit, it abides in the state of the inner self. || 34 ||

Raising the objection that although action (*karman*) is dependent upon causal factors (*kāraka*) during its time of origination and duration, it does not exist at the time of its destruction because it has ceased to be, [the author]—relying on the view of others who maintain that after destruction it persists in a subtle state as mere existence—says: "With its application," etc. For every aggregate of action, together with the collection of causal factors, exists in an unmanifest and non-gross form as a fruit...

The meaning is that because it exists within the inner self (pratīc) prior to manifestation as something previously non-existent, it is never at any time dependent upon causal factors (kāraka). || 34 ||
This [self], being established in the object of direct perception, is devoid of any [other] means of valid cognition.
It is not known like a jar, nor is it [non-existent] like the horn of a donkey, because it abides in consciousness. // 35 //
If it persists in the self even after destruction, why is it not known as before? To this he says: "The inner [self]...
Then, suspecting that it might not exist at all due to a lack of means of knowledge (pramāṇa), he says: "Nor is it...," because it is established by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin). || 31 ||
And this [Brahman] is not referred to here by the words "not this, not this" because it is the cause and so forth.
Because the specific difference is not apprehended, that [object] is apprehended even as "this is not that. || 36 ||

Raising the objection that "just as duality existing even within the conscious Self (*cidātman*) is negated by prohibitive statements, so too should the mass of karma residing therein be negated," he says: "And not [so]. It is not stated that the mass of karma is negated in the inner Self (*pratyak*) in the same way that duality is negated by the "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) formula;
for since it remains as the cause with respect to subsequent effects, the designation "it goes into that" (*eti tasmin*) is not tenable, especially because it is not distinct [from the Self].

The meaning is that this is because it has been stated [in the previous verse] "because it is being experienced. One might object: "If action (karman) persists in its own nature within the inner self (pratīci) even during dissolution (pralaya) and so forth, why is it not perceived?

For it would be apprehended by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) itself. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the particular" (viśeṣasya). During sleep and similar states, action—just like its cause—is not grasped as something determinate (savikalpaka), because at that time there is no perception of the particularity consisting of the "I-form" (ahaṃ-rūpa); however, its perception as indeterminate (nirvikalpaka) certainly exists.
The meaning is that the commentary states: "Nor is there a designation such as 'this is that,' because the specific distinction is not being apprehended. || 36 ||
The sequence beginning with earth and ending with the thread is stated in relation to the objects to be regulated.
Nor is there a controller or a cause, for such [a view] does not exist in the Sūtrāntika school. (37)

Having stated the opponent's view, he concludes by showing its relevance to the present topic with the words "kṣityādi" (earth, etc.). When there exists the internal self-consciousness accompanied by objective appearance (*sābhāsa-pratyagajñāna*), the designation of the "controller-cause" (*niyantṛ-kāraṇa*)—in relation to the "controlled effect" (*niyamya-kārya*)—is appropriate in the terminology of the Sautrāntikas, and not otherwise. Thus [says] Bhartṛprapañca.
1. kha. ga. naṣṭvā | 2. kha. [End of fragment]
Of the object.
[Vol.
3, page 164] 8 Brāhmaṇa] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1297
For even the followers of other schools maintain that all three are indeed karma; and it has been established that this [karma] is dependent on the agent and is rooted in ignorance (avidyā).

Therefore, even according to other doctrines, since the state of being the controller and so forth depends upon the world—which is the effect of karma governed by one's own ignorance—there is no difference between the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmī), the Cause, and the Imperishable (Akṣara).
This is the intended meaning. || 37 ||
Because it is dependent upon one's own self-experience, it cannot be denied.
Deep sleep is experienced through both the forms of exclusion and affirmation. || 38 ||

[Objection: But surely ignorance (*avidyā*) itself is not possible with respect to the inner self (*pratīc*), because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). To this, he says: "The self" (*svātma*). The word "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. [Question: How can there be an experience of ignorance regarding the self-luminous inner self? To this, he says: "Exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), etc. Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is ignorance. (38)
Darkness is experienced as distinct from white, yellow, and other colors.
Likewise, even by way of affirmation, darkness is like the interior of a *dvirepha* (a bee).

He states an example for experience in the form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) with the words "excluded" (*vyāvṛtta*). He states [an example] for experience in the form of affirmation (*vidhi*) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). || 39 ||
Likewise, at that time, due to one's own lack of awakening, the object is experienced as if it were distinct [from consciousness].
Even the thought "I am deluded" is experienced directly as this very delusion. (40)

He states the perception in the case of the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-rūpeṇa*), saying "In a dream... and so forth; the word "then" (*tadā*) refers to his own statement. He also shows the cognition in the case of the subject by way of affirmation (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*), saying "I am deluded," and so forth. || 40 ||
Prior to the arising of delusion, delusion was already inherent in the innermost reality.
Upon its arising, delusion accompanied by consciousness has ignorance as its primary constituent. || 41 ||

If it is argued that ignorance is established through experience, [the author] says "mūḍha" (deluded), anticipating the objection: "In states such as deep sleep (*laya*), that [ignorance] cannot be established because of the absence of experience. The meaning is: the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is deluded; prior to its arising, there was ignorance due to the incapacity for empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*); subsequently, that which is perceived becomes capable of such transaction, because it is rooted in that ego. || 41 ||
This very delusion, which contains within it the notion of a single self, is the cause of everything.
And the substratum (dharmin) of all phenomena is not beyond perception; therefore, it is like a horse.

Having established that knowledge is directed toward the Self, he states the conclusion with the words "so 'yam" (this is that). This means being situated within the womb, or the midst, of the single Self—that is to say, [within the Self] which possesses the qualities of being the controller of all things, omniscience, and so forth.

Since it has been established that the cause of the world is the non-apprehension of the inner Self, which appears as the objective world and is to be realized through one's own experience, even the claim made by others that "the cause of the world is inferable from its effects as its logical mark" is thereby refuted.
He says: "No. In that regard, there is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): "like a horse. As it is said:
"For one who sees the white color and hears the sound of neighing..."
"And from the sound of the trampling of hooves, there arises the cognition that 'a white horse is running.
In that case, these objects—being invariably concomitant with the specific horse—infer it; however, the cause of the world is not perceived in this manner.
[Vol. 3, page 165] 1294 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopani�sbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]:

This is the meaning. Or rather, let there be an analogy based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), such that the cause of the world is not remote (*parokṣa*) in the same way that cows, horses, and so forth are not remote. An ignorant person—
The word "I" refers to the direct perception of ignorance; therefore, that is the meaning of the term. || 42 ||
When the state of being a driver is destroyed by the cause, this becomes the imperishable.
The connection of the immutable with a second [entity] is caused by ignorance. (43)

Having raised the doubt—given that the single conscious Self (cidātman) is established as both the controller and the cause—how can ignorance (ajñāna), which is accompanied by its own appearance (sābhāsa), possess such a nature? To this he says: "Controller-ship... etc. The controller-ship and causality of the inner self (pratīc) are produced by ignorance; when that [ignorance] is destroyed through knowledge, it becomes the imperishable (akṣara) which is neither effect nor cause. Thus, the meaning is that the controller-ship and other attributes of the Self are merely imagined and do not exist in reality.

And because the relationship between the internal controller and its effects is imagined, he states that the nature of being a controller and so forth is also imagined, with the words: "Of the immutable one" (kūṭasthasya). || 43 ||
This question cannot be the third, because two [other questions] have already been promised.
This question is asked again for the sake of explaining the inheritance of that which was previously mentioned. (44)

Having explained the meaning of the passage beginning with "That is woven in space," he addresses the doubt that the second sentence beginning with "That which is above" constitutes a different question, stating: "This is a [repetition of the] question. The meaning is that this follows from the initial statement: "I shall ask two questions; I shall rise up by means of these two questions. Anticipating the objection as to why there is a restatement of what has already been asked, he says: "Of what was previously stated. (44)
Having been questioned, he asked again, his intellect firm in its conviction regarding what had been said.
For even one whose awakening is dependent on another is capable of speaking from whatever source it may be. || 45 ||

He clarifies that very point: "It was asked. Anticipating the objection that a further question would not be appropriate—since a firm conviction regarding the stated matter already exists, as that certainty has been reached through the previous answer—he says: "Dependent on another. [The text continues with: "bhūta..."

Since even the argument based on dependence upon spirits and the like can be refuted, one’s understanding of the stated matter is not determined by that; for we see even Śūdras and others studying unprecedented scriptures through possession by spirits (bhūtāveśa). This is the meaning. || 45 ||
Or rather, because of the restrictive particle "eva," it is a supplement to the meaning of the preceding question. (46)
Could there be a merging of even a thread in many places, as in the case of the earth?
"Or could it be space itself?"—thus [the question] remains connected to what precedes. (47)
Having stated that this repetition, in the form of a question and answer, serves to strengthen what has already been said, he explains another purpose for the repetition:

"By the word 'evam' (thus), because of its restrictive force. Having restated the meaning of the preceding question, [the author asks] how the status of the subsequent sentence as a supplement to it is understood; [the answer is] through the restrictive force (*avadhāraṇa*).

Regarding this, he asks: "What [is the case]? The meaning is as follows: intending to ask whether the thread, like earth and the other elements, dissolves into space through a succession of stages (*pāraṃparyeṇa*), or whether it does so directly (*sākṣāt*), he poses the question again. By the restrictive emphasis that the thread does not dissolve into multiple locations like earth and the others, but rather directly into space alone, it is established that the latter [answer] is a supplement to the former. || 46 || 47 ||
The eradication of delusion arises from the correct knowledge of things as they truly are.
Therefore, this subsequent [section] concerning the mind is for the purpose of establishing right knowledge. || 48 ||
He states the intended meaning of the question, "In what, indeed, does space [rest]? and so forth, with the words "moha... (verse 48).
From the subtle thread (*sūtra*) down to the earth, everything prior to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is insentient.
Since it is being produced from that [source], it is therefore questioned along with its authoritative basis. || 49 ||

Anticipating the objection that the previous question is likewise intended for that same purpose, he says: "The thread, etc. This means that [the former] is without authority, being accessible only to false cognition; whereas the latter is with authority, being accessible through right cognition. || 49 ||
The Sūtra is indeed difficult to understand, but space is even more so than that.
Therefore, that reality which is even higher than that is difficult to describe, even for Bṛhaspati.
Having stated the intended specific purport, he states the gross purport: "The aphorism," [he says]. || 10 ||
The subject matter of the sūtra, which is to be explained, has been introduced within that which is beyond explanation.
Even that which moves within the sky is difficult to describe because of its extreme subtlety.

He establishes the difficulty of knowing both the sutra and space. "The end of the sutra" (sūtrāntam) means that the word "also" (api) is for the purpose of including the sutras situated therein. || 51 ||
It is the one that transcends all measures, liberated, and consisting of immediate consciousness.
It is neither excluded nor followed; therefore, it is designated as "the Imperishable" (akṣara).

[The author] brings about the difficulty of knowing the Imperishable (akṣara). [He says] "all," etc. These qualifiers are each a cause for the difficulty of knowing the Imperishable. Furthermore, [it is] subtler than even the Sūtras and so forth; this is the ellipsis. || 52 ||
Because it is other than that which is known through the unknown, that syllable is not to be designated.
Nor can there be a denial of that [reality], because it exists in the form of direct perception and so forth. || 53 ||
Regarding the ineffability of the Imperishable (akṣara), he states another reason for its distinction from cause and effect, beginning with "ajñātā" [verse 93].
Anticipating the objection that ineffability implies a lack of intrinsic nature (naiḥsvābhāvya), he says "sākṣāt" and so forth.
Moreover, if one should somehow express that which is inexpressible due to delusion and confusion, [it would be so].
Likewise, there would be a misconception [regarding the meaning], and if it were not stated, one would be defeated. || 54 ||
Having resolved thus in his mind, Gārgī questioned Yājñavalkya;
and he (Yājñavalkya) spoke this to her regarding that indefinable syllable.

He summarizes the broad purport with the words "api cet" (even if). This means: on account of delusion, confusion, and the force of thirst for existence. He introduces the reply with the words "tām ca" (and that). || 54 || 55 ||
"This indeed is that," he said, [pointing to] the imperishable which is directly perceived before one's eyes.
That which has cast aside all descriptions and for which there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 56 ||

He states the meaning of the word "this" (*idam*) with the word "etad. He explains the referent of that term with the word "pratyak" (the inward-facing). He excludes its being a literal denotation (*vācyatva*) with the word "apāsta" (cast aside). The reason for this is given in the phrase "yadananya" (that which is non-different). || 16 ||
"That which is specified as Brahman and the Self, both directly and not indirectly."
Let that identity with it be realized by oneself through the state of inwardness. || 57 ||
[Vol. 3, p.
167] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]: He establishes that [point] with the words, "That which directly... (17).
It is neither excluded from particulars nor does it persist [in them], like "cowness."
Let consciousness be perceived as awareness that is neither differentiated nor sequential.

Anticipating the objection that "on account of being a real entity (vastutva), even the oneness of the Self (aikātmya) must be an object of knowledge (meyam) like a jar," he states the distinction with the words beginning "no" (na). 18.
Because there exists no other established [reality] that is established for anyone.
The word "vai" (indeed) is used to establish that the meaning of the sixth case is "non-otherness. (59)

Having stated that the witness-consciousness described in the *Uṣasta-praśna* is intended here by the term "this" (*etad-pada*) as the indicated meaning of the word "thou" (*tvaṃ-padārtha*), he explains the meaning of the word "verily" (*vai*). He says, "Because... [referring to the verse beginning with *yasmāt*]. Anticipating the objection that it might be merely worldly because it is well-known to oneself despite the absence of its being known to anything other than itself, he says, "It is well-known. Then, lest it be thought that it is therefore a void (*śūnyatā*), he says, "It is not other. The reason for this is as follows:

"Regarding the phrase 'not in the sense of the sixth case' (aṣaṣṭhyartham): the meaning is that the word 'vai' is used to illuminate the reality that is free from cause and effect, non-dual, self-luminous, and unattached. || 19 ||
By the statement beginning with "directly" (sākṣāt), as well as by [the description] of hunger and so forth;
Since it has been diligently stated that [the suffix] *pratyaṅ* is applied here, that [suffix] is joined to this [word] *virāj*. || 60 ||

He states the meaning of that word [“tat”]: “Directly” (sākṣāt). This means by the presentation of the means for knowing that [reality] through effort. The meaning is that the referent of the word “tat” here is the referent of the word “that” as stated in Kahoḷa’s question. || 60 ||
Because this word refers to that which is perceptible and proximate, like the word "jar."
Let this which is "this" be understood directly and exactly as it is. || 61 ||
Now, one might ask: why not take that which was presented by Uṣasta through the word *tat* (That) and [take] what was spoken by Kahola through the word *etat* (This)?

To this, he says: "Perceptible," etc. That which was stated as the referent (*lakṣya*) of the term *tvam* (you) in Uṣasta’s question—by means of the passage beginning with "That which is immediate" (*yatsākṣāt*)—is precisely what is to be understood here by the word *etat*.
Because it is proximate due to its being directly perceived (*aparokṣa*), like a pot, and because the word *etat* has such a meaning, [it refers to that]; but here, the word *tat* does not [apply].

The meaning is that the Blessed One perceives the object briefly stated [by Kahola], because it is logical that his [the Blessed One's] cognition of that object pertains to a hidden (parokṣa) mode of operation, as was stated by Kahola. || 61 ||
Even an object that is worldly cannot be [established] if it has perception as its sole means of valid cognition.
Why [should one teach] that which is stainless and within every limb, as if to awaken it through direct perception?
Anticipating the objection that if the innermost Self were present, it could be pointed out as "this is the pot," you say: "Perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*).

Even ordinary people, such as mothers and others, can perceive the immutable experience (*kūṭasthānubhava*), yet they cannot point it out like a pot because it is internal and thus unfit for such indication.
If even this is so, what need is there to mention that the innermost Self, which is unattached (*asaṅga*), cannot be made known as "this"?
The meaning is: because it is not an object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 62 ||
Because it possesses attributes contrary to the perishable, the imperishable is called Brahman.
In this context, a perishable entity characterized by cause and effect is what is being negated. || 63 ||

Demonstrating that which is contrary to that, he explains the word *akṣara* [the Imperishable], beginning with "from the perishable" (*kṣarāt*). He states the primary meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) as "that which is not an effect" (*kārya-*) and so forth. || 63 ||
By its very nature of decrease and increase, it exists as the causal self alone.
That inward Self is dependent on that [intellect], yet it is immutable and does not undergo any change. || 64 ||

If it is argued that although the effect is subject to decay, the cause is not so, he says "hāni" (loss) in response. Anticipating the objection that the inner self (pratīc) might also be the cause and thus be subject to such a possibility, he says "tat" (that). || 64 ||
"The Brahmins say so" is merely a song intended to conceal one's own transgression.
That [scripture] is not intended for the sake of knowing the Self, for the Self perceives it directly. || 65 ||

Regarding what was stated in the passage beginning with "even if he speaks," he says: "The Brahmins. Fearing that there might be the misconception that "if one speaks what should not be spoken, there is contradiction; if one does not speak, there is no understanding," and thus [the questioner] attributes it to his own fault, [Yājñavalkya] says "not the Self" to show that this statement is not intended to remove that [misconception], but rather to illuminate his own ignorance. Otherwise, it would contradict the remainder of Yājñavalkya’s statement concerning the Imperishable (akṣara).
Intending this, he states the reason: "For that," etc. (69).
In order to avoid the consequence of the faults associated with inference regarding that which is to be explained.
The designation "they say" (vadanti) is used because [the Mīmāṃsakas] hold scripture alone to be the means of valid cognition.
He states the intention behind the explanation: "Insofar as it is to be designated," etc. (66).
This alone is the direct perception of those who know the true nature of all things.
Therefore, this is appropriate for the Brāhmaṇas who culminate in the fruit [of realization].

Since [the Truth] is accessible solely through scripture, how can there be a mention of "speakers" when they say "the Brāhmaṇas speak"? For they are not capable of speaking about that which is not their own object-domain;
to this he says: "This much," etc. [It refers to those] who know the reality of the entire world as the Imperishable Brahman through its identity with their own inner self (*pratyak*).

The meaning is that since these Brāhmaṇas have reached the ultimate goal of human endeavor, every single syllable of this much [text] is directly perceived by them from the scripture; therefore, it is appropriate to mention the speaker. || 67 ||
Those whose ignorance of the Self and its effects have been destroyed through the realization of the true nature of the inner Self.
Therefore, those Brahmins say that it is the abode where all passion has been abandoned.

Establishing that [the word] leads to the attainment of the fruit, he concludes the meaning of the two words with the verse beginning "dhvasta" (destroyed). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, there is no suspicion of defects such as being inexpressible. || 68 ||
But having realized this very point, they emerge from the threefold pursuit.
Therefore, O Gārgī, that immutable and eternal Brahman is self-evident.

He summarizes the meaning of the passage beginning with "This" and ending with "O Gārgī" by saying "This. Having understood the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (the self) superficially, they renounce worldly life out of a desire to know it; therefore, for those intent on hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which is the referent of the term *tat*, becomes fit for their own direct experience as the innermost self (*pratyagbhāvena*). This is the meaning. || 69 ||
If that [consciousness] of theirs were self-cognizable and expressible, it would be like a water-jar or other such objects.
"Because it is not gross, it cannot be pointed out," he said. (70)
1 kha. is called; 2 ka. ga. have *ṣaṇāḥ padaṃ*; 3 kha. has *masi*. [Vol. 3, page 169] 1302 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]—
He states the meaning of the term "not gross" (*asthūla*), preceded by a doubt, with the words "Of these... (verse 70).
If the syllable is neither gross nor subtle, then let it be accepted as such.
Therefore, for the purpose of refuting that [view], he said to her, "Not minute" (anaṇu).
He explains the qualification "not atomic" by way of an objection: "The Imperishable. || 71 ||
Dimension, the great elements, life-force, name, and lineage, and so forth.
The [theories of] causation and so forth are refuted in sequence, with respect to their attainment. || 72 ||

He summarizes [the arguments] by means of the "heat" (tāpa) [of the arguments] beginning with "not short" (*ahasvam*). Regarding the phrase "measure" (*parimāṇa*): by the first "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of taste (*rasa*) and the rest;
by the second, there is the mention of light (*tejas*) and the face (*mukha*) and so on. He states the reason for the negation in sequence: "because of attainment" (*prāpti*). || 72 ||
Between the absolute negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha) and the relative negation (paryudāsa), which meaning of the negative particle is intended here?
Coarse denial (sthūlāpahnuti) occurs when, in the context of an exclusion, one thing is identified as being something other than that.

Regarding all these qualifiers, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādī*) analyzes the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). First, he states that in the case of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), the sentence would result in a mere non-existence. Then, under the heading "sthūla" (gross), he says that in the second case—namely, relative negation (*paryudāsa*)—there would be a loss of non-duality (*advaita-hāni*), because the gross and other qualities would be different from the Imperishable (*akṣara*). Thus ends [verse] 73.
In this case, there would be a gross negation (sthūlāpahnuti) of that object which is ultimately real.
A negation does not terminate in non-existence even elsewhere, much less in the Imperishable (akṣara).
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) resolves the first position with the words "sthūla" (gross). He clarifies the meaning of the locative case with the word "vastu" (entity).
Then, he states that it is not the case that the sentence is restricted to non-existence with the words "nābhāva" (not non-existence). || 74 ||
Even in the case of a relative negation (paryudāsa), there is no separate existence for those things already established.
Therefore, like the case of a rope-snake and so forth, there is no fault in either instance. (75)

In the second [verse], he states the meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the term "paryudāsa" (presuppositional negation), he concludes that the sentence does not result in a state of mere non-existence, nor does it entail the loss of non-duality; thus he says, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 79 ||
In this world, an exception is observed when there exists a general rule.
How can this negation of grossness and so forth be applicable in that which is non-dual? (76)

He refutes the first position with the words "It is seen" (*dṛṣṭa*). For while a general rule (*utsarga*) such as "one should not kill" is observed, an exception (*apavāda*) such as "one should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma" is also seen; however, in the case of the non-dual (*advaya*), there is no such distinction of subject matter. Therefore, the meaning is that [the teaching of] the gross and so forth is not an exception [to the non-dual]. || 76 ||
"There exists a domain for renunciation, which consists of that whose nature is not yet realized as the Self."
The object of negation is that which has as its sole reality the known Self. || 77 ||

He offers a rebuttal, stating that even though the reality (*vastu*) is non-dual, the systematic arrangement of general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*) is appropriate therein. Regarding the phrase "of the general rule" (*utsargasya*): when the [reality] is not known, grossness and so forth are apprehended; when that very same [reality] is known, they are negated. And it is observed that when a rope is unknown, a snake and the like are apprehended, but when it is known, they are negated. The meaning is that this *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (negation by implication) is more sound. || 77 ||
1. Ka: ‘The mantra of the vital breaths. 2. Kha: ‘He states the purport. Ca. 3. Yo-pa-ni. [Vol. 3, page 170] 8.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1303.
And just as the negation of the beginningless is practiced with respect to a single void, so it is [in all cases].
General rules, exceptions, injunctions, and prohibitions [reside] within the single Self. (78)
He clarifies this by means of an illustration: that both attainment and prohibition apply to the gross form and so forth within one and the same Self. [The verse says: "Superimposed...
(Verse 78).
Or rather, the true nature of the syllable (akṣara) as being beyond the gross and so forth is stated here.
Just as there is no delusion regarding the true nature of a garland [when it is seen clearly], so too [there is no delusion] regarding this [reality] from even a single syllable.

Having explained the meaning of the passage beginning with "not gross" (*asthūla*) in accordance with absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), he states another interpretation by following exclusion (*paryudāsa*). He says, "Or rather," and expresses that very point through an illustration: "A garland," etc. The meaning is that the sentence is intended to reveal the non-duality of the world consisting of the gross and so forth; it is not intended as a mere negation. || 79 ||
Or rather, there is a burning away of darkness within the inner self by means of causes such as grossness.
By the fire of the knowledge of the true nature of the self, which arises from the teaching on non-materiality, || 80 ||

Alternatively, the sentence may be intended to sublate the ignorance regarding the cause of grossness and so forth with respect to the Inner Self (pratīc) by means of the knowledge arising from the sentence; thus, adopting the first alternative, he states another meaning [of the verse], beginning with "sthūlādi" (gross, etc.). || 80 ||
Indeed, within this [universe] beginning with earth and ending with space, there is the manifestation of gross objects and so forth.
By that statement, which is woven through and across [the entire argument], all of that has been refuted. || 81 ||

The opponent raises an objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to state another point regarding the negation: "In earth, etc. [He replies: "Let it be so; let there then be a negation of grossness and so forth in earth and the rest, ending with the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). To this he says: "That. Because of the restrictive determination that "all this"—beginning with water—up to earth and ending with the unmanifest, does not exist apart from the Imperishable (*akṣara*), there can be no negation of grossness and so forth therein, due to the absence of a substratum (*dharmyabhāva*).
This is the meaning. || 81 ||
What relevance does that [impermanence] have to the syllable, such that it would be negated therein?
Even in the sky that would be impossible; how much more so in the inner self? 82.

Raising the objection that it might then be negated in the Imperishable (akṣara) because the aforementioned defects would not apply there, he says "tasya" (of that), implying "it is not so" because there is no possibility [of its application] there. He states the absence of such possibility by way of a *kaimutika* argument (an argument from the obvious): "api" (even). "Kham" refers to the unmanifest (avyākṛta). || 82 ||
Some maintain that Brahman exists both collectively and individually.
In order to prohibit such [a view], that which has already been prohibited is being prohibited once again. || 83 ||

Thus, in response to this objection, he states that the sentence possesses meaningfulness by means of its purpose of refuting the views of those belonging to his own school: "The entire... (verse 83).
Or rather, their manifest state is denied within the causal self.
This negation of the state of power (śakti) is made with respect to the nature of the Imperishable (akṣara). 84.

He restates what was said—that there is a burning away of the cause such as the gross body—in order to state the result of the negation of that cause: "The manifest," etc. [This refers to the verse: "Whatever this is... [ka. ga.
...tratā || 79 || ka. ga. ...na tu | Vol. 3, p. 171].

The meaning is as follows: by the passage beginning with "all" (*sarvam*), the gross state (*vyaktāvasthā*) of things such as the gross elements was negated within the cause; now, their potential state (*śaktyavasthā*) must be negated within the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which is distinct from both cause and effect. For that purpose, the passage beginning with "not gross" (*asthūla*) is intended. 84.
And this being so, it is logical that Brahman is both full and all-pervading.
Otherwise, it would be as if it were never done at all, and bondage without liberation would ensue. || 85 ||

He states what follows from the negation of the cause: "If it is so" (*evaṃ ceti*). When the cause and its effect are negated, the terms such as "Brahman" heard in relation to the inner self (*pratīci*) would have their primary meaning; if they were not so negated, because of the limitation of the object, they would have only a secondary meaning, and liberation—consisting in abiding as the nature of the undivided reality—would not be established. Consequently, the scriptures concerning liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) would be contradicted; this is the meaning. || 81 ||
Nor is there a negation of gross objects and the like, since they have already been established.
By means of the restatement of those negations, Brahman is made known within the inner self. || 86 ||

By asserting a different meaning—that passages such as "not gross" (asthūla) teach by way of affirmation like the "That" (tat-tvam-ādi) passages—one abandons their status as being intent on negation. [The opponent asks: "Is it not so? [The author replies: No; for the reason is that the negation of grossness and so forth is already established by the passage concerning the warp and woof (otaprotavākya). He states what the purpose of the sentence would be in the absence of its intent toward negation: "the negation of that," etc. (tanniṣedha...), verse 86.
Know that one's own nature (svabhāva) has as its fruit the negation of the gross and other objects of cognition, as well as the cognizer;
it is Brahman, which is within all, characterized by such descriptions as "directly manifest" (sākṣāt). || 87 ||

Having restated the negation of the gross and so forth, he demonstrates the method for realizing Brahmanhood within the "thou" (tvam-artha), which is its witness. Regarding the verse beginning with *sthūlādi*: the construction is as follows—"Know that very Self, characterized by the aforementioned attributes, to be Brahman; for He exists in three ways, and the result of that negation is the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), which, being understood as His own nature, is self-luminous and is the referent of the term 'thou' (*tvaṃpadalakṣya*). || 87 ||
This being the case, it is impossible for all the gardens to exist as well.
Let every such explanation here be examined as being like the teaching "not this, not this" (neti neti). || 88 ||

He demonstrates the benefit [of his position] by showing that objections such as "if a sentence conveys knowledge through a positive approach (*vidhimukhena*), it would lack the status of being centered on non-existence (*abhāva-niṣṭhatva*)," or "the syllable would possess duality," have no place here. He says, "Of all [sentences]," and then addresses how a sentence containing a negative particle (*nañvat*) can convey knowledge through a positive approach with the words beginning "No" (*na*). || 88 ||
For magnitude such as "large" and so forth depends solely upon substance.
Therefore, this is a negation of substance [rather than a negation of existence] because of the negation of dimension. (89)

Having stated that the purport of the sentence is manifold, he explains the intermediate purport of the fourfold qualification, beginning with "sthūlādi. Having restated the reason conveyed by the word "hi," he states the resulting conclusion: "tasmāt" (therefore). || 89 ||
In every respect, however, whatever has come within the range of speech—
And all of that is refuted in the Imperishable (Akṣara) by means of valid cognition. || 90 ||

Even though substantiality is denied in the case of the Imperishable (akṣara), there arises the possibility of its possessing qualities such as being a *guṇa*; when that is denied by the passage beginning with "not red" (*alohita*), it serves as the definition of another specific attribute.

Fearing that [the objection] might remain unrefuted here, he says: "In every way" (*sarvathāpi*). The meaning is that the negation of the specific cases already mentioned serves as an indicative mark for the negation of all unspecified particulars. || 90 ||
And when there is a negation of a specific instance, a sequence is certainly resorted to.
The certainty is that it arises from capacity alone, and not from any other cause. || 91 ||
In that case, since it would be possible to negate everything simultaneously, the employment of multiple qualifiers would be useless; to this he replies with the word "viśeṣa" (qualifier).

The reason for resorting to a sequential approach is stated as "sāmarthyāt" (by necessity). The meaning is that because speech functions sequentially, the negation of everything cannot be established all at once. || 91 ||
And the sequence of the preceding and succeeding negands follows from their very capacity alone.
When the former [alternative] is prohibited, another necessarily presents itself by the force of the context. || 92 ||

He states that the order of negation must follow the order of the objects to be negated, saying "pūrva... (in the preceding). He demonstrates this very capacity [of the argument] by saying "pūrvasmin...
(in the former). The meaning is that since the negation of a contradictory is impossible unless its opposite has been attained, there is consequently an order among the things to be negated. || 92 ||
Because it is not gross, it is subtle; because it has attained that [subtlety], it is not non-subtle, since the Imperishable (akṣara) is so.
Since it is not short, it is therefore not short; since it is not long, it is therefore not long—such is the syllable.
Because it is not long, the imperishable syllable would not be a substance. || 93 ||

Fearing that, since the negation of grossness implies the negation of all remaining [qualities] by way of illustration, the other qualifiers would be redundant as they merely indicate the sequential negation [of those], he concludes the meaning of the fourfold set of qualifiers, thinking that they are purposeful for the sake of negating [the qualities] such as subtlety which would otherwise follow by implication once grossness has been negated. Thus: "Not gross, etc. (93).
On account of the statement that it has the color of the sun, let it be of the nature of redness.
It is not so, because that which is non-red is devoid of all form and the rest. (94)
He explains the term *alohitapada* by way of doubt: "The sun," [he says]. (94)
In this context, the quality of water is moisture (sneha); shadow is considered to be radiance (dīpti);
darkness is to be known as obscurity (dhvānta); and that which is not darkness is called the imperishable (akṣara). || 95 ||

In the phrase "asneham" (without moisture), he excludes the grasping of a specific kind of passion by means of the word "sneha. Regarding "apām" (of waters): while stating the difference in meaning between the two words "chāyā" (shadow) and "tamaḥ" (darkness), he explains the two terms. "Chāyā" [is explained]; the division is "adīptiḥ" (non-luminosity). The sense is that because there is a difference in the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) due to the prohibitions and injunctions, there is a difference in the negations. || 99 ||
That [self] is not the elements such as earth, nor likewise are it the qualities of the elements.
For, because the context concerns everything internal, there is likewise a negation of both. || 96 ||
He states the meaning of the two terms "without air" and "without space" as "not an element. He states the meaning of the two terms "without taste" and "without smell" as follows:
[Note: The commentary indicates that the text contains variants, such as *taccāna* in manuscript *ga* and *rūpavitraṃ* in manuscript *kha*.]
