Regarding the phrase "nor indeed" (*nāpi*): since the negation of wind and ether, as well as of taste and smell, is heard [in the text], how can it be explained that there is a negation of all elements and their respective qualities? To this he replies: "Because it is within all" (*sarvāntara*). For this is the context of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) which is within all; therefore, the negation of wind and so forth, which was stated for the purpose of establishing its being within all, serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the negation of the unmentioned elements and their qualities.
The meaning is that it is the perishable, the most internal of all, devoid of the qualities of all beings, and undivided; that is, it is joined [with the Self]. || 96 ||
In that case, let it be of the nature of attachment, since attachment to latent impressions is observed.
"This is not non-attachment; for he will say, 'This is indeed non-attachment. (97)

He states the counter-example for the term "unattached" (*asaṅga*), saying: "Let it be so. The meaning is that this [self] possesses a concomitance with subtle passion and the like, which are observed in the self.
He refutes this by resorting to the remainder of the sentence, saying: "This is not so. (97)
Nor is this to be known as a sense-faculty, because it is eyeless and imperishable.
Neither do its sense-faculties exist, nor is it itself a sense-faculty.

He explains the four terms beginning with "not having eyes" (*acakṣuṣkam*). With the words "nor even" (*nāpi*), he refutes [the notions of] connection with a sense organ and identity [with one] by means of two compounds. This is done with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). || 98 ||
The characteristic of consciousness is fire; it is negated as being non-fire.
Why is all this so? Because that which is immeasurable is the Imperishable (akṣara). || 99 ||

Since it will be stated later that "it is indeed light," one asks: "How can it be devoid of light? To this he replies: "Consisting of consciousness" (*vijñāna*). The meaning is that it does not consist of adventitious knowledge. He takes up the subsequent word as the reason for the point already stated, preceded by a question: "Why? (99)
Because by negating the cause, the entirety of the effect is negated.
O Pūrṇa, that imperishable [reality] is to be known as having characteristics such as being directly manifest and so forth. || 100 ||
He performs it by means of that; thus it is called "the cause. || 100 ||
The syllable is that by which a gross object is negated.
By that very [means], everything beginning with the atom is entirely [negated] for him, because it is in total contradiction with it. || 101 ||

Anticipating the objection that because grossness and other qualities are denied in the inward-facing [Self], it would follow that it possesses many forms contrary to those various things being denied—and thus it could not be of a single uniform nature—the author says: "The Imperishable" (akṣaram). || 101 ||
Just as fire destroys opposing things by means of various different forms,
so too in this world is the action of the destruction of gross objects and the like performed by that which is opposed to them.

He clarifies that very point by means of a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). "By another" means: it is not like being situated within the cavity of a belly or being fixed upon the back of a wooden board, and so forth. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the syllable. || 102 ||
There would be a negation of pride and so forth, just as there is [a negation] based on the nature of a single action.
Likewise, by its nature as the directly perceived immutable reality, it effects the negation of everything else. || 103 ||
1 kha. ga. will be stated; 2 kha. establishes; 3 ka. ...thaivāki... [Vol.
3, page 174] 8 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1307.

Anticipating the question of how that Imperishable (akṣara) can be of a single form while being opposed to everything else, he states [the answer] by means of an analogy based on common properties: "Mānitva, etc.
The term "pratyak" is a designation for the agent. || 103 ||
The state of being full of immutable consciousness and the quality of inwardness belong to the Reality by its very nature.
This is its opposition to things that exist as cause and effect. || 104 ||
To the question of how that [Immutable] possesses the quality of being opposed to everything in the manner described, he says: "The Immutable" (kūṭastha).

The meaning is this: the non-duality of the immutable consciousness—which is the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (thou)—and its aforementioned immediacy (*pratyaktva*), which is the referent of the term *tat* (that), as realized through sentences such as "That Thou Art" (*Tattvamasi*), constitute the opposition of the Immutable to all distinctions consisting of cause and effect. || 104 ||
Whether it is called the door, the mouth, the face, or the sign;
Thus, the negation of all three is designated as "amukha" (the faceless). || 105 ||

Regarding the term *amukham*, he explains the meaning of the word *mukha* as "door. The sense is that the word *mukha* is observed to be used for openings, supports, and signs. He explains the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) as "negation. || 109 ||
They maintain that "mātra" means the measure; the object is the thing to be measured, by which it is measured.
Therefore, that [reality] is inconceivable within the syllable, because it is without measure (amātra).
He states the meaning of the term "amātra" as follows: "mātrā," etc. (verse 106).
Where a causal complex characterized by the mother and so forth is accepted with respect to an entity.
Therefore, it is logical that it is the object of cognition, but not that the non-dual reality exists by itself.

If it is argued that [the Self] is immeasurable because of the impossibility of applying a measure to the Immutable (akṣara), then where, indeed, does measurability reside? To this, he replies: "The measure, etc. (mātrādi). || 107 ||
Furthermore, the relationship of pervader and pervaded does not exist in the case of the imperishable reality.
For neither of those two [faults] is excluded by the statement "he does not eat at that time. (108)

He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "he does not eat at that time" as follows: "Pervaded," etc. The distinction is that in that context, by the first statement there is a negation of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), and by the second, a negation of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*). || 108 ||
Whatever object whatsoever is seen in the world is entirely forbidden.
And that which remains has not been established by means of valid cognition. || 109 ||

Having stated that there is no distinction, he raises the objection that this leads to the consequence of emptiness (śūnyatva). [The opponent says: "It is not so, because the Imperishable (akṣara) remains. To this, he replies: "And even if it remains... (109)
If the syllable is thus of such a nature, how can it be understood as "existing"?
For it is not observed that a thing exists simply because it lacks a means of valid cognition. || 110 ||

Anticipating the objection that it might exist even though unperceived—like a jar or other object concealed by a wall or similar barrier—he says: "If it were so. He provides the reason why that which is entirely unperceived lacks reality: "For not... (110).
1 ga. observes.
[Vol. 3, page 175] 1308 Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika) [Third Chapter—]
This is not so, because [the reason] is either established or yet to be proven, and because an answer has already been stated to that effect.
Since it does not exceed beyond existence and non-existence, that which is accepted by you is being stated [as such]. || 111 ||

One might raise the alternative: is it merely the immeasurability (*aprameyatva*) of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) that is being established, or is its non-existence (*nāstitva*) also being proven? Having accepted the first [alternative], he establishes the final position with the words "It is established" (*siddha*). He refutes the second [alternative] with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The meaning is: even if it is immeasurable, the Imperishable does not lack existence, because it has been stated more than once that it is established by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatā*). He proves that [the argument commits] the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*) with the words "In the case of an entity" (*bhāva*...).* 111 *The Sanskrit text for this section is provided in the prompt. The translation reflects the structure of the commentary on verse 111.)*
And since there is an absence of pride, how can there be extension? Where is the positive concomitance (anvaya) when there is negative concomitance (vyatireka)?
Have you perceived the absence of pride, such that you speak in this manner? || 112 ||

Furthermore, he states that the assertion of the absence of the Imperishable (akṣara) is untenable because there is no means of valid cognition (māna). He says "māna... and clarifies the objection with "mānābhāvam...".

The point is this: is that [means of cognition] perceived or unperceived? In the first case, there is no absence of the Imperishable, because only that which establishes both existence and non-existence can be such a means.
In the second case as well, there is no absence of it, because the absence of a means of cognition that would establish it remains unperceived. || 112 ||
For in this world, every means of cognition is a means for the manifestation of an object;
in its absence, it is difficult to maintain that an unmanifested object does not exist. (113)

Having accepted the absence of the object of knowledge (*meyābhāva*) upon the absence of the means of knowledge (*mānābhāva*), he abandons his own provisional position (*upetyavāda*) by saying "for all" (*sarva hi*). The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that it is certainly not easy to say that a jar or other objects—which are manifested by a lamp—are non-existent when they are shrouded in darkness simply because the lamp is absent. || 113 ||
Because of the effort involved in negating numerous properties such as grossness and so forth.
Thus, the existence of the imperishable Self is established here for now. (114)

Now, even the claim that "it exists" is difficult to establish due to the absence of any means of certain determination; therefore, he says: "from the gross, etc. The meaning is that the self-luminous Imperishable (akṣara) is established as the substratum and the limit by virtue of the impossibility of conceiving the object to be negated and the impossibility of its negation. || 114 ||
But even non-existence, by its own power, is not capable of supporting itself like a self-existent entity.
Likewise, the absence of cognition is equal [to the absence of the object] due to both being for the sake of another and being insentient. || 115 ||

If it is argued that, just as the syllable (akṣara) is self-luminous, the same applies to the absence of both the means of knowledge (māna) and the object of knowledge (meyābhāva), and therefore it is improper to speak of the "absence of a means of knowledge" (mānābhāva) and so forth, he says in response: "By its own majesty" (svamahimnā). The words "of the object of knowledge" (meyasya) are to be supplied [to complete the phrase]. The word "likewise" (tathā) refers to the sequence beginning with being for the sake of another (pārārthya). It is equal.
The meaning is: "by the absence of a self. || 115 ||
Because of its absolute cessation from those [objects], this [cognition] exists only as the mere presence of itself.
And since it is established by its own greatness, how could non-existence possibly exist? || 116 ||

Having set aside the similarity of syllables [with the word "akṣara"] on the grounds that it might refer to insentience (*jāḍya*) and so forth—which lack measurement (*māna*) and other attributes—he states another argument for the non-existence of the syllable *a* being absent [in the case of the Immutable]. He says:

"I measure. The meaning is that because the Immutable is unattached and indifferent, it is superior to vessels and the like due to its absolute withdrawal from them; thus, since those objects are not reached by it, and because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), there is no suspicion of its non-existence. || 116 ||
• 1 ka. kha. bhāvācca ta | kha cetyapyayuṃ | [vol 3, page 176]
Since it is by its very nature the form of the fruit of knowledge, it is not an object to be produced by means of valid cognition.
But "it does not exist" cannot be established by itself without a means of knowledge, just like a jar.

Anticipating the objection that "the object of knowledge (meyam) is finite because it is an entity (vastutvāt), like a jar," [the author] refutes this by means of the limiting condition (upādhi) of insentience (jaḍatva). Regarding the word "svataḥ" (by itself):

since the Self is of the nature of consciousness (saṃvidrūpa), another consciousness cannot be produced therein by a means of knowledge (māna); thus, it cannot be said that [the Self] is known through a means of knowledge—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, anticipating the objection that "even the absence of the Imperishable (akṣara-abhāva) does not have its manifestation dependent on a means of knowledge, because it is one or the other of the two—the Imperishable or its absence—just like the Imperishable itself," he says:
"No," and so forth. The intention is that the object under dispute is an object of cognition because it is insentient, like a jar; otherwise, its very nature would be lost. || 117 ||
Just as light is placed within a jar through its connection with the sun.
In relation to the manifestation of light, the sun requires nothing else. || 118 ||

Regarding the point that the existence of the syllable is established by itself, whereas its non-existence is not so, he provides an illustration: "In the case of a jar" (kumbha). For in the case of a jar, it is superimposed that "it shines because of its connection with the sun"; however, it is not the same for the sun, such that one could say "this [sun] shines. Just as [the jar] depends on the jar and other things for its connection with self-luminosity, such is the meaning. || 118 ||
In the same way, non-existence is understood through its own connection with cognition.
Likewise, there is no dependence on another for the connection with comprehension, because comprehension is self-evident.

He states the refutation [of the opponent's view]: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). From the aforementioned example, both non-existence and existence are understood through their connection with cognition; they are not understood by themselves. For cognition, like the object to be cognized, has no dependence on anything else in its relation to cognition; rather, the meaning is that cognition exists by itself alone. The word *nañ* (negation), which occurs in the second half of the verse, is also connected with the first half. || 119 ||
Even this absence of such a state of going cannot be understood without a self-awareness [of that absence].
Therefore, existence here is established by the syllable itself, which is of the nature of the imperishable.

If the self-evident nature (*svatastva*) of cognition were established, then its absence would also have to be self-evident, because it is one or the other of the two states—its presence or its absence—just like its presence. Anticipating this objection, he says "Therefore" (*ataḥ*), meaning that it is not so, because it would contradict the foundational state [of ignorance] upon which [the world] depends. Furthermore, he states "Cognition" (*avagatim*) to show that in the opposite case, the absence of cognition would result in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of universal blindness in the world. Finally, he concludes the result with "From that" (*tataḥ*). || 120 ||
Thus has been explained the absence of continuity (niranvaya-abhāva), which does not arise from the adoption of Buddhist or other [non-Buddhist] views.
In some cases, this occurs due to the absence of the higher knowledge arising from such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi). || 121 ||

Since the syllable is established by its own nature, its non-existence is difficult to assert; therefore, even when gross objects and the like are negated, one does not arrive at emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

To this effect, he states another reason for that very point: "It has been said. The meaning is that we do not claim an absolute non-existence of gross objects and so forth—unlike the externalists—without a cognition that possesses the form of the object as expressed by words; thus, it is not emptiness. || 121 ||
The existence of a second self does not exist apart from ignorance, just as [the appearance of a second moon].
In the same way, its cessation is not something other than the realization of the Self.

[Verse 122] Anticipating the objection that if the absence of grossness and so forth constitutes the Self, then that itself would be nihilism (*śūnyatā*); whereas if it is not the Self, then non-duality (*advaita*) is lost—the author says:
"Not anything else. [Verse 122]
1 kha. °pekṣyate | 2 ka. na bāhyādi | 3 kha. ga. no'nyataḥ || 122 ||
1310 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]:
"That which is directly devoid of cause and effect," and so forth, is the definition of its attributes.
The immutable, immovable, and absolute state exists as the destruction of darkness. || 123 ||
Anticipating the objection that if ignorance were not distinct from the Self, it would lack insentience (jaḍatva), whereas if it were distinct, it would entail duality, he says:
"akārya" (not an effect). The meaning is that when ignorance is removed entirely through perfect knowledge, the reality remains non-dual alone. || 123 ||
There is no means of knowledge for its existence, because it is of the nature of the single, imperishable syllable.
And even though that [object] does not exist, those two are nonetheless established in that manner. || 124 ||

Fearing that if the measure (māna) were not distinct from it, there would be no connection with the object of measurement (meya), and if it were distinct, there would be the same loss of non-duality (advaita-hāni), he says: "Not of this...
Whether the Imperishable (akṣara) exists or does not exist, there is no means of knowledge (māna); for both its existence and non-existence are established solely through the Imperishable itself.

Furthermore, although it is self-luminous, it has no dependence on a means of knowledge like a lamp, because it consists of the single essence of consciousness (saṃvid-ekarasa) and destroys ignorance (ajñāna).

The meaning is that even though it is required by him, duality does not bring about [his] realization; for according to the maxim, "she who is ashamed of killing a dead man might as well burn up her own being. || 124 ||
Whether it be existence or non-existence, [this applies] to the entities of cause and effect.
This is established as if it were cognition itself, though not by its own nature.
And because everything that is non-self is imagined within the internal, conscious element (cit-dhātu)—which is neither effect nor cause—there is no loss of non-duality; thus he says:
"Or it is being. || 129 ||
Since this is so, therefore no one here disputes this point.
Therefore, the statement of a reason is accepted regarding the non-existence of that which has the nature of a syllable. || 126 ||

Since the existence of each individual syllable is established by the manner stated above, and since there is no dispute among disputants regarding its existence, it is argued that the statement of reasons for its existence—which will be presented later—is not required; thus, one raises the objection that the subsequent section, which aims at setting forth an inference, is superfluous. This is expressed by the words "yataḥ" (since). || 126 ||
For it is regarding the inner controller (antaryāmin) that disputants disagree.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing that [point], an inference is formulated here by means of the words of others. || 127 ||

He provides the following resolution: although the scriptural statement is purposeless because its object is the attributeless (nirupādhi) Imperishable, it is meaningful as having that [Imperishable] as its object when considered with respect to attributes (sopādhika).
This he states beginning with the words "yataḥ" (from which...). 127.
Because of its relationship with the objects to be ruled, this Imperishable is the Inner Ruler.
Only by way of the path known as the delusion that reflects consciousness, and not by itself. || 128 ||

Since it has been stated that the Imperishable (akṣara) is indeed the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), one might suspect that whether these two are objects of inference or not is the same for both, and thus there is no contradiction between the earlier and later [statements] due to a distinction in their respective definitions; anticipating this, he says: "The object of rule" (īśitavya). || 128 ||
Therefore, the scripture of inference has come forth for the sake of establishing that very [reality].
Since everything becomes accomplished once the causal self is fully realized. || 129 ||
1. *Lakṣita*.

Since it is established that while there is a conceptual difference, there is in reality no difference, he states the resulting conclusion: that the operation of inference proceeds with reference to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) who possesses this conceptual difference. He says "anumāna... [etc.]. Even though the Inner Controller is established by inference, he asks how the non-sensory [Self] is established through inference; to this he replies: "kāraṇa... [etc.]. This is because, as established in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, the cause of the world serves as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The meaning is that when [the existence of] the All-pervading is established, the Immutable (akṣara) which is free from all limiting adjuncts (anupādhika) is also established; thus, through the medium of the "indirect definition" (taṭasthalakṣaṇa), inference regarding the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) serves its purpose in establishing the "essential definition" (svarūpalakṣaṇa) of Brahman. || 129 ||
This being so, under the governance of this very syllable.
This world revolves, its boundaries fixed and stable in every respect.
He explains the words of the scriptural inference with the phrase "of this" (etasya). || 130 ||
Just as under the governance of a king, the subjects do not transgress the boundaries of propriety.
In the same way, these [elements] beginning with earth abide under the governance of the Imperishable.
He clarifies the stated point by means of an illustration: "In the governing" (*praśāsane*). The word should be divided as *abhinaiti*. || 131 ||
The state of the world, which has come under dispute, was preceded by a creator.
Because the world is established in its order, the state of affairs is like that which is preceded by a king. || 132 ||
He establishes the stated point by means of inference: "In the dispute," etc. (132).
The sun and the moon are preceded by those who possess knowledge of the effects arising therefrom.
Because it benefits all living beings, like a lamp situated within a palace. || 133 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "the sun and the moon," he states the intended inference: "The sun... (verse 133).
The sun and the moon, as lords, do not overstep their appointed boundary.
By whom these two are perpetually sustained here—let him be understood as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin). || 134 ||
He states the fruit of that: "The sun and the moon," etc. (134).
The two halves of a granary do not break apart even when it falls, because they possess constituent parts.
That the earth is heavy like iron, and that the sky is likewise, is a source of great wonder.

He states what is intended in the second turn of the argument, beginning with "of this" (etasya): "like a granary" (kusūlavat). The meaning is that, although the splitting and falling [of the world] would necessarily follow, both of these are not observed in the case of heaven and earth. || 135 ||
Because they possess volition and autonomy, and because they are the cause of the nature of the deity.
Without a controller, this established order of those two would not exist. || 136 ||

Anticipating the objection that because those two [the eyes] are insentient and lack independence, there can be no bursting [of the eye], etc., [the author] states "as if sentient" (*cetanāvat*); for, by virtue of being deities (*devatātva*), they possess sentience and independence. Nevertheless, he says that such a fixed arrangement is observed. Even so, how is it that [the Lord] is established as the controller? [The text continues: ...of the very [controller-ship]... [Note: The provided fragments indicate a commentary on the relationship between the divine controllers and the physical organs].
Thus it is established. 6. Kha. Ga. read "evaṃ vya".
[Vol. 3, page 179] 1312 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Third Adhyāya]— [The text continues with the commentary on the third chapter.]
To this, [the author] replies: "Not without. The meaning is that the arrangement of earth and so forth is impossible without a controller; therefore, it implies the existence of such a one. || 136 ||
Even the separation of those two who are joined together is not observed anywhere.
Without the instruction of the Teacher, such an arrangement would not come to pass. || 137 ||
In this world between heaven and earth, this is not seen to be otherwise.
They transcend intrinsic nature and abide in the teaching of the Teacher. (138)

He states another instance of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*): "Of the two conjoined," and so forth. In the word "praśāsana" (governing), the prefix *pra-* is also connected with the root *śās-* (to rule). The meaning is that such [governance] exists even when separation would otherwise occur; it consists in the absence of such separation. Although conjunction must end in separation, the fact that heaven and earth, though conjoined, are never seen to separate is inexplicable without a controller; thus, this [non-separation] leads to the postulation of that [controller].

He states that the existence of a controller is established even from worldly experience, saying: "In this world... The word *iyam* refers to the aforementioned order (*vyavasthā*). He concludes what is established through experience and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), saying: "Its own nature... The ellipsis is: "Therefore, there exists a Ruler. In the compound *asaṃjñāyām*, the prefix *pra-* should be understood as part of the word for "ruler" (*śāstṛ*). [The argument is: "The two [worlds] under dispute are supported by one possessing effort, because they possess weight yet do not fall, like a hand..."
The sense is that it is like a stone or similar object that has been cast away. || 137 || 138 ||
The establishment of the divisions of time, such as the blink of an eye and so forth.
That which, by not abandoning its own characteristic, is the governance of its Lord. (139)

In the third formulation, he states what is intended to be expressed: "nimeṣādi" (winking, etc.). This means that there is no abandonment of the operation of one's own characteristic mark—namely, the act of winking and so forth—which consists in being a perceiver (*kalayitṛtva*), because it is not relinquished through non-deviation (*ajahadvṛttyā*). The underlying sense is: "Winking and so forth must be preceded by a controller (*niyantṛpūrvaka*), because they are acts of perception, like [the winking of] a person who is currently agreed upon [to be such a controller]. || 139 ||
And the flow of even the greatest rivers is indeed constant.
It should be concluded that [the world] cannot be conceived of without a controller. || 140 ||

He states the meaning of the fourth formulation: "Niyata" (determined). The sense is that the subject of dispute is preceded by a controller, because its activity is determined, just like the activity of servants and so forth. || 140 ||
And the world is seen to be intent upon the accumulation of wealth acquired through suffering.
This is not logical, because [the Lord] is unestablished as the one who bestows the fruits of those actions.
He states the meaning of the fifth formulation: "Suffering," etc.; the word division is "not well-known" (*aprasiddha*). || 141 ||
And likewise for the donor and the recipient, as well as for the action and the relinquishment.
Dissolution is indeed perceived immediately by all people of the world.
Anticipating the doubt that "the giver, the receiver, the gift, or the fruit—what need is there for a Lord? he says: "The giver," etc. (142).
1 kha. ga. govakṣyaṃ | 2 kha. tyāgenu | [vol 3, page 180] 8 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1313
Nevertheless, they praise those who renounce wealth acquired through hardship.
Even those who possess correct knowledge of the means of valid cognition [do not exist] without Maheśvara.

In that case, one might object: "Since there is no giver of the fruit, the praise of the giver would be baseless according to the maxim that 'foolishness indeed consists in the ruin of one's own interest. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even so. Anticipating the further objection that "the praise of something not established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) should not be accepted by those who follow valid means of knowledge," he says: "And even correctly. Furthermore, to the question "Even so, how is the existence of God (Īśvara) established? he replies: "And that... [referring to] the fruits of those who have perished.
The meaning is that, because of the incapacity of giving and because of the view that [merit] is praise, there must exist a Lord who bestows the fruit. || 143 ||
Directly perceiving the connection between actions such as giving and their results.
And whatever those who know the means of valid cognition praise, that is true when there is a Lord.

He confirms this through inference with the words "dānādi" (beginning with giving). How is there the application of the term "sees" (*paśyati*) regarding the connection between an action and its fruit? Anticipating the objection that the relationship between a means and an end in the other world is based on scripture (*śruti*), he says: "those who know the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇajñaḥ*). The sense is: the subject under dispute possesses a giver endowed with specific knowledge, because it is the fruit of an action, like the fruit of service (*sevā*). || 144 ||
Since there is no Teacher who knows the diversity of the fruits of those actions.
In one who is omniscient, it would be impossible for there to be the fruit of karma that is devoid of knowledge. (145)

Considering that very point to be an implication (*arthāpatti*), he says: "In the case of the Teacher" (*śāstari*). For that praise of the giver would be untenable unless there were a distinguished Controller;
thus, it is that which leads to the postulation [of such a Controller]. This is the meaning. || 145 ||
Nor can a non-independent and unprecedented agent be postulated for the attainment of the fruit.
No means of valid cognition is established for the prior existence [of the effect]. || 146 ||

Some maintain that since the *apūrva* alone bestows the fruit, there is no need for a Lord (*īśvara*). To them, he says: "Nor... The meaning is that the *apūrva*, being itself insentient and not presided over by a sentient being, cannot be postulated as the bestower of the fruit. If it is argued that it might bestow the fruit when presided over by the sentient individual soul (*jīvātman*), he says: "Because... The ellipsis is: "therefore, it could not be the bestower of that fruit. [The opponent]—parā...
And here, in the introduction to the connection and so forth, there is a transition. || 146 ||
If it is argued that there must also be a controller, we say: "Not so," for the Śruti is certain even regarding the nature of reality.
Because validity has been stated previously, and because that [validity] is established through inference. || 147 ||

[The author] weakens the doubt raised by those who hate God with the words beginning "niyantṛ" (the controller). The connection is that no proof for [the existence of] a perfectly established [controller] is possible. Furthermore, he states that even if a controller were established, there would be no perception of a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for that; thus, [such a means] is unestablished. This is expressed in the words "tatsiddheśca" (and because of the establishment of that). || 147 ||
Even the postulation of an apūrva through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is not tenable.
Because presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is undermined since it can be accounted for otherwise. || 148 ||
For the procedure of ritual action is not logically tenable unless it yields a fruit; nor is an action, which perishes immediately, capable of conforming to a fruit that occurs at a later time.
Anticipating the objection—"How can there be proof for the *apūrva* (the unseen potential) established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)?"—the author says: "From presumptive testimony.
The attainment of the fruit would otherwise be inexplicable except by means of the *apūrva*. (148)
165 [Vol. 3, Page 181] 1314 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Adhyāya]
It should be understood from the observation of the attainment of the fruit of service through serving [a master], and not from anything else.
And because service consists of action, giving, sacrifice, and so forth are also action. (149)

He establishes that very point [with the words] "from service" (*sevyāt*). Because the attainment of the fruit is possible from the Lord, there is a *arthāpatti* (presumption); the remainder of the sense is that it cannot be established otherwise. To the question, "How is the attainment of the fruit dependent on the Lord? he replies with "and of service" (*sevāyāśca*). The remainder of the sense is that the fruit of giving and so forth is like the fruit of service. || 149 ||
The attainment of the fruits of generosity and the other perfections must arise from that which is to be served.
Because giving and the other [perfections] consist of action, [their result is attained] like obtaining the fruit of service to a king. || 150 ||

Regarding this, he states the inference: "From giving, etc. The meaning is: the object of dispute [is] fruitful when performed by one possessing distinguished knowledge, because it is a distinguished action, like that which is commonly accepted. || 150 ||
The attainment of the fruits of all actions comes from the Lord alone, and not from anything else.
Thus spoke the Blessed Vyāsa, the omniscient one of great intelligence. || 151 ||
Having raised the objection that "the Lord is not the giver of the fruits of Vedic rites because He is a Lord, like a worldly lord," he states the contradiction with Smṛti: "All... (verse 151).
From whom the activity of all beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded.
By worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection.
He cites the words of the Blessed One as composed by Vyāsa, beginning with "yataḥ" (112).
But even without setting aside the capacity of the nature of things as observed in their functioning, [the following holds].
If the establishment [of the result] were achieved through the conceptualization of its attainment, the logical principle would otherwise be violated. || 153 ||

An objection is raised: "Surely it has been stated that the fruit of service comes from the one served and so forth, because it is observed; however, the fruit of giving and other such acts does not come from God, because that is not established.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Also, [the fruit is] seen... (153).
It is characterized by the relinquishing of the efficacy of actions and dharmas as perceived by the world.
Therefore, an improper method is not tenable, because it does not conform to the path of logic. || 154 ||

He elucidates the improper nature [of the opponent's position] with the words "loka... and so forth. The observed efficacy (*sāmarthya*) of service as a religious duty (*dharma*) consists in its capacity to bring about a result from the one served;

following that [observation], since the attainment of a result is possible through giving and other such acts, it is not logical to postulate that [result] arises from the *apūrva* by setting aside the [observed] cause. The meaning is that when a postulation follows what is observed, it is impossible to postulate something that contradicts it. || 154 ||
Furthermore, because it involves an excessive conceptualization, this unprecedented [position] is not tenable.
Or rather, is it the Lord who is to be postulated? What else is it that could reasonably be postulated? || 155 ||

Having stated that presumption (*arthāpatti*) can be accounted for in another way, he points out another defect in the view that the *apūrva* is the cause of the fruit, saying "kalpanā" (postulation). He refers back to that statement in order to explain it, saying "kalpyaḥ" (to be postulated). || 111 ||
The attainment of the fruit of action is observed to result from the performance of the rite itself, and not from an unseen potency (apūrva).
Nor has anything unprecedented been seen anywhere here, because of the impossibility of any means of knowledge [for it].
[Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1315.

Anticipating the objection that "one need not postulate something unprecedented because it has already been established, so there is no excessive conceptualization," he says: "Because of the one to be served" (sevyāt). Here, the word "here" (iha) includes both the scripture and the world. || 156 ||
Furthermore, he possesses the power to bestow that which is unprecedented and beyond all measure.
Likewise, when there is the capacity to bestow the fruit, giving is even more superior. || 157 ||
Having provided the introductory context, he clarifies the abundance of conceptual construction with the words "something unprecedented. || 157 ||
But here, nothing whatsoever is postulated other than the transcendence of Īśa.
Because the remaining [element] that is to be postulated must be experienced as something to be served. || 158 ||

Anticipating the objection that "the conceptualization is equal even in your own view," he says: "But here... Anticipating the objection that "its capacity to grant the fruit and the granting [of the fruit] when that [capacity] exists must be postulated," he says: "Of what remains... In his own position, only the substratum (*dharmin*) is to be postulated; in the opponent's position, there is an excess, as both the substratum and its attribute (*dharma*) are required. Therefore, according to the principle "The fruit is from Him (the Lord), because it is logical," the fruit belongs to the Supreme alone.
The sense is that [he is] a giver. || 198 ||
Both the gods and the ancestors are indeed subject to the authority of human beings.
Those seeking offerings to gods and ancestors would not have existed, had there not been a ruler. (159)

Having explained "dadata" and so forth, he explains "yajamānam" and so forth with the words "devāśca. The meaning is that even for the gods and other lords, because they desire offerings (*havya*) and the like, their dependence on humans—which is termed a "subordinate mode of existence"—is what leads one to postulate [the existence of] a controller. || 159 ||
From ignorance of which there arises in this world a succession of intense misfortunes.
And since liberation from saṃsāra comes from knowledge, why is there no such instructor? (160)
He states another argument for the existence of God: "Because of the ignorance of which... (160).
Is it not the case that this destruction of saṃsāra is desired precisely through action?
It is not so, because liberation from actions is not possible, as it is not heard [in scripture]. || 161 ||
One who desires to establish that liberation arises from knowledge objects as follows: "But surely... He answers: "Not so.
The reason for this impossibility is: "Because it is not heard [in scripture]. || 161 ||
And just as liberation by means of action is in no way tenable;
Since it has already been stated thus, it is not intended that it should be spoken further here. || 162 ||

He recalls what was stated previously—that liberation from those [Vedic texts] is not impossible solely because of the supreme revelation (śruti), but also because it contradicts reason—as follows: "And just as... (162).
Just as liberation is impossible because it depends upon the means of action.
This Vedic revelation also states so through such passages as "He who," and so forth. || 163 ||
Regarding the point that there is no liberation from actions, he introduces the immediately following passage with the words: "Because it is impossible. (163)
1 kha. Likewise here: [vol 3, page 183] 1316 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter—]
They yield noble fruits even when performed many times.
For actions performed out of ignorance necessarily possess fruits that are subject to decay. (164)

He explains those words: "It is declared. The meaning is that it is illogical to say that there is no unknown reality, because if that were so, it would follow that saṃsāra does not exist; for if one lacks knowledge of that [reality], then all actions—even those performed repeatedly with distinguished results—bear saṃsāra alone as their fruit. || 164 ||
And thus, through the thorough knowledge of which there is liberation from all wretchedness.
O Gārgī, how can such a thing as this be called a non-existent syllable? || 165 ||
Since it is established that liberation from actions is impossible and bondage results from the lack of knowledge of the Imperishable (akṣara), he states the conclusion: "And thus," etc. || 161 ||
All would be possessed by wretchedness if that Imperishable did not exist.
Moreover, those who are not miserly are seen [to prosper], and that occurs only when there is a driver.
He states another reason for the existence of the syllable: "All," etc. Anticipating the objection that this might be an unintended consequence, he says: "And they are perceived," etc. (166).
Or rather, the Śruti itself has clearly stated this with effort, saying "yo vā etat."
Through the knowledge of the syllables, men are freed from wretchedness.

Having stated the purport of the two preceding sentences, he explains the literal meaning of the subsequent sentence, beginning with "Yo vā" (or who). The meaning is: "clearly," that is, preceded by the employment of expressive words. The intention is that through the knowledge of reality, there is the cessation of wretchedness; this is the effort [of the text]. ||167||
He who, having known the Imperishable, departs from this world, goes forth [to liberation].
He turns away from that state of wretchedness due to the knowledge of that [reality] which subdues darkness.
He now explains the words of the passage beginning with "atha" (now). Regarding the word "akṣaram" (the imperishable): [it means] from this world, that is to say, from the body;
for it perishes, is destroyed, or dies—this is the meaning. || 168 ||
But he who, through the thorough knowledge of the Imperishable, passes beyond death by means of death itself—
Let it be understood that he alone is the Brāhmaṇa, and no other, in this world. || 169 ||

Anticipating the objection—"For those who know the Imperishable, it is proper that there be no wretchedness; since wretchedness is caused by ignorance, and that ignorance is removed by the knowledge of the Imperishable, how can Brahminhood be stated as the fruit [of such knowledge], given that Brahminhood is equally present in others as well?"—he says: "But he who... (verse 169).
He is omniscient and the creator of all, with the remainder of saṃsāra cast off.
And one who has attained all human goals is here designated as a Brāhmaṇa. || 170 ||
This makes manifest his primary Brahminhood: "He is omniscient. || 170 ||
In order to establish that [the world] is knowable, he spoke by means of the path of the Lord as previously described.
The direct scriptural revelation of the Imperishable is through such passages as "That indeed is this," and so forth. || 171 ||
0 1 ka. ga. nor even yu | 2 kha. ga. 'tiḥ | ātāṃ | [vol 3, page 184]

If it is argued that liberation results from the knowledge of the Imperishable (akṣara) which possesses adjuncts (sopādhika) and attributes such as omniscience, then one might suspect that the Imperishable devoid of adjuncts (nirupādhi) does not exist at all; anticipating this doubt, the author introduces the subsequent passage beginning with "jñeyatva" (the state of being knowable). [This refers to] the Imperishable Self, which is neither effect nor cause, with respect to the Lord who has been superimposed upon it.

The meaning is that, for the sake of realizing [the Self] as immediate through the exclusion of "thou" and so forth, the Śruti declares that [Self] as being free from limiting adjuncts by means of the sentence "That thou art" (tad vā). || 171 ||
This is his state of being a Praśāstṛ, caused by the appearance of his own delusion.
From such statements as "not this, not this," [it follows that] the reality of the self is pure perception alone.

Just as the capacity to illuminate is inherent to fire, so too is lordship (īśvaratva) inherent to the Imperishable (akṣara). How, then, can the unconditioned Imperishable be established by means of negating that [lordship]?
To this, he says: "This... He states the reason for the fact that lordship and the like are superimposed: "Not...". (172)
For the purpose of establishing this very point, the Śruti states: "That, indeed, is this."
Because it transcends the range of the senses, that syllable would be unperceived. (173)

Once its status as a superimposition is established, it is appropriate that the subsequent scriptural passage exists for the purpose of perceiving the unconditioned Imperishable by means of its removal; thus he says, "This [is]...
Having stated the purport, he explains the word "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) with the words, "beyond the range of the senses," etc. (māgocara). 173.
In order to negate its state of non-existence, the imperishable seer is spoken of here.
Because it is merely the immutable witness, it is not called a "seer. || 174 ||

Since it would follow that [the Self] is non-existent due to its immeasurability, [the text] adopts the term "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*). [The opponent objects: "In that case, because it is the agent of seeing, it must possess activity. To this, [the text] refutes the first alternative—that the seeing has itself as its object—by stating: "immutable" (*kūṭastha*) [verse 174].
By means of speech that penetrates from end to end, all visible objects are utterly discarded.
Due to its being both non-agent and non-dual, the nature of the Imperishable Self does not possess the quality of being a seer. 175.
He states the second [objection]: "otā" etc. He states another reason for the impossibility of both positions: "akāraka" etc. || 175 ||
The utterance of "not other" and so forth is for the purpose of negating multiple perceivers.
By means of the negation of other entities, whether of a different class or of the same class.
The one, immutable consciousness is established in accordance with the sacred scriptures.
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Not this" (*neti*) [in the verse]: "Much," etc. He concludes the meaning of the section [with the verse]: "Of a different class," etc.

By the statement regarding the warp and woof (*otaprotavākya*), the insentient (*jaḍa*) distinct from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is refuted; and by the statement "nothing else," etc., the non-insentient (*ajaḍa*) is likewise refuted. Therefore, the meaning is that the indivisible reality (*akhaṇḍa-vastu*), which is the intended purport of the Śruti, is established. || 176 ||
In this syllable, O Gārgī, one is like a king of serpents whose hood is expanded.
Therefore, the entire space woven therein [rests] within the causeless Self. || 177 ||
He joins the syllables of the passage beginning with "in this" (*etasmin*). Regarding the word "in this": it refers to [the world] together with its effects, without remainder. || 177 ||
Due to delusion regarding its own nature, the Imperishable (akṣara) assumes the state of being the cause.
Likewise, this very nature of being an effect is also faultless when it stands alone.
[Vol. 3, page 185] 1318 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:

How can there be a distinction between cause and effect regarding the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which is of the nature of a non-cause? This is because it is accepted as the substratum of all things. Thus he asks: ...because of its being the substratum of everything. Thus he asks—
One should sit with the syllable. Thus [ends verse] 178.
Since everything consists of nothing but syllables, there is nothing whatsoever that has not been withdrawn [into them].
Because it is not in contradiction with the inward-facing [consciousness], that forest is neither something nor is it concealed.

The phrase "faultless and single" clarifies this very point. Regarding the word "of all": there is no other entity not subsumed within the syllable (*akṣara*), because everything lacks any nature other than that; nor does it exist as non-different from that, because of the contradiction between the inward-facing and the outward-facing. Therefore, the meaning is that its being of one flavor (*aikarasya*) is logical. || 179 ||
Likewise, [this applies] to all that is knowable, which is divided into the known and the unknown.
Since it is determined to consist of the nature of the spoken syllables, nothing remains [unaccounted for]. || 180 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if there is no relation of cause and effect through either difference or non-difference with respect to the internal (pratīcaḥ), there might still be some other entity, he says: "In the same way" (tathā). That [entity] must be either knowable or not. In the first case, because it would be included within the cause and so forth, it would be non-existent in the same manner as those [causes], whether by way of difference or non-difference. In the second case, if it were manifest by itself, it would be included within the Imperishable (akṣara); otherwise, due to a lack of evidence, it would be non-existent. This is the meaning. || 180 ||
Nothing whatsoever remains unarisen apart from this gnosis.
Nor is ignorance destroyed [by mere knowledge], because there is no completion of all that is to be known. (181)
The total number of verses from the beginning is 6,700.
Thus ends the eighth Brāhmaṇa of the third Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika. || 8 ||

If it is argued that the knowledge one wishes to produce (*utpipādayiṣita*) is a distinct entity (*vastvantara*), he says "no," [explaining] "not [something] unarisen. Then, if it is argued that the ignorance one wishes to dispel (*nirācikīrṣita*) is a distinct entity, he says "no" again. The point is that this imperishable (*akṣara*), which is the subject of the section on space (*ākāśādhikaraṇa*), does not consist of specific phonemes (*varṇaviśeṣātman*), because that would contradict the subject of the section on the imperishable (*akṣarādhikaraṇa*). || 189 ||
Thus ends the eighth Brāhmaṇa of the third Adhyāya in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Now begins the ninth Brāhmaṇa: The state of being a controller [of the world] belongs to the causal Self by way of its effects, such as the threads [of the cosmic web].
Having restated exactly what was previously declared by scripture, [the author] proceeds as before. (1)
The true nature of the self is stated once again, beginning with the words "directly" (sākṣāt) and so forth.
By way of the detailed and concise treatment of the distinctions between the deities to be restrained. || 2 ||

Having introduced the passage beginning with "that which is directly perceived" (*yatsākṣāt*), and having determined through three Brāhmaṇas—by way of defining its state as being within all—that directness and so forth are its inherent nature, he now states the connection for this present Brāhmaṇa: it is intended for the determination of that very nature directly. He says: "The thread, etc. (*sūtrādīti*).
9 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1319.

That which was stated in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa* through the scriptural passage beginning with "He who is in the earth," etc., regarding the Self as the cause being the controller in relation to all that is controlled—that very same [fact] is here restated by means of the words *prāṇa* and *samāna* according to the previously mentioned method, and taking hold of that very [point].

The meaning is that this Brāhmaṇa section is intended to provide a final determination regarding the nature of the Self—such as its directness and so forth—which, although previously mentioned in connection with the Self by way of describing the expansion and contraction of specific deities to be restrained, requires further clarification. || 1 || 2 ||
Having united its own ignorance with the reflection of consciousness, that imperishable [Self]...
Being existent, the cause attains the state of a controller over its own effects. || 3 ||
Anticipating the objection that it is impossible for the Self—which is immutable, unattached, and non-dual—to be a controller, he restates what has been said: "Consciousness... (3).
The Self of Prāṇa, existing in the states of deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, is called the Imperishable (akṣara).
"That is Brahman"—thus the Śruti also clearly declares that.

It might be argued that it is illogical for the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which has been defined as such, to become the controller by being the cause of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of manifesting ignorance (*sābhāsājñāna*); for in passages such as "Speech merges into breath" (*prāṇam...

vāgapyeti*), scripture declares that breath alone is the cause when one has entered states such as deep sleep. Anticipating this objection, he says "In deep sleep... to show that this is not so because of the non-difference between breath and the Imperishable. He cites the remainder of the passage as proof of their non-difference: "That is Brahman" (*sa brahma*). That is Brahman.

The meaning is that even the Śruti passage, "They call it *tyat*," by employing the word *brahman* with respect to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) after having drawn it in by means of the word *sa*, clearly declares the identity of the cause called *prāṇa* and Brahman according to our own explanation. || 4 ||
Thus, remaining in the state of the inner controller (antaryāmin), [one perceives] the single deity of breath (prāṇa).
By virtue of delimiting [the object] as a thread and so forth, it governs all of this.

Having raised the doubt—namely, that although the Imperishable (akṣara) alone is the cause because of its identity with the cause called Prāṇa, by what sequence does it exercise control—he says: "Thus, the Inner Controller" (antaryāmī). Since the status of the Imperishable as the cause has been established according to the stated method—as the substrate for the limiting adjunct of ignorance accompanied by appearance—that very same [Imperishable], abiding in the state of the Controller, first controls the ignorance accompanied by appearance known as the deity Prāṇa; thereafter—

The meaning is that, by delimiting itself through the Sūtra and other [subtle bodies] which are its immediate effects, it remains as their essence and thereby governs each of them; thus, the Imperishable (akṣara) is the ruler of the entire universe. || 5 ||
Furthermore, that deity of breath exists in the forms of both multiplicity and unity.
Pervading this entire world, she remains here by the power of the karma of living beings.
He restates that very [subject] which possesses sequential controllership in order to distinguish the scope of the subsequent question: "In manifoldness," etc.
He states the reason for the controller's pervasion of the entire world: "The vital breath," etc. (6).
Śākalya questioned him regarding the dispersal and withdrawal of that [speech].
In order to establish the relationship between the object to be controlled and the controller. || 7 ||

He raises a question concerning the nature of the previously mentioned vital-deity (prāṇadevatā) with the words, "Of her" (*tasyāḥ*). He states the result of the inquiry regarding the expansion and contraction of that deity with the words, "To be restrained" (*niyantavyā*). The meaning is that he asked in order to understand such a relationship as that the gross form is the object to be restrained (*niyamya*) and the subtle form is the restrainer (*niyantṛ*). || 7 ||

Being thus questioned regarding the number of the gods, he attained [the answer] through the *nivid* itself.
As many gods as are enumerated in the Nivid of the Vaiśvadeva hymn. || 8 ||
He would possess as many vital breaths as there are beings in this world, both moving and unmoving.
The sage declared to the gods that [the world] is infinite by means of many words.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "saha" (together): "O Deva! This means: by that speech consisting of mantra-padas through which the number of deities is announced (*nivid*). He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "as many as": "The gods. The meaning is: as many deities as are present there in the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra* connected with the *nivid*, standing as those being praised, so many are the gods. How, then, is there oneness with the vital breath (*prāṇa*)?

Regarding that which is asserted there, he says: "He is 'asau' (that one). The meaning is that the proposition of their identity is that the various deities are indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone.
He states the purport of the plural number used in the words of the *nivid* beginning with "three" and so forth: "infinity. || 8 || 9 ||
Starting from thirty-three, these [deities] are assigned to the six [realms] and so forth, respectively.
Withdrawal is by way of reverse order, while the array extends until the end of calculation.
Explaining the purport of the passage beginning with "thirty-three," he states the limit of the contraction and expansion of the gods: "Thirty-three," etc.

Of the three thousand six hundred and thirty-six deities, their withdrawal occurs according to the order of recitation into the thirty-three gods; from them into six; from those into three; from those into two; and from those two into one and a half; and from that into the *prāṇa*. Their expansion, however, occurs in the reverse order.
The meaning is "extending as far as the infinite gods. || 10 ||
When asked "Which one?", he then pointed to Vasu and the others.
Then, being questioned further, he spoke of the Vasus, beginning with Agni.
He explains the meaning of "Which ones? and so forth: "Which ones? He explains the meaning of "Which Vasus? and so forth: "The Vasus.
The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is: after the determination of the thirty-three gods by way of their groups. || 11 ||
For that very same single deity of breath, having withdrawn its own various manifestations, remains as one.
Divided eightfold, she sustains the state of the Vasus for the maintenance of all living beings.

Now, fearing that this might contradict the identity [of the deity] by suggesting that the Vasus are one thing and the presiding deity of the vital breath (prāṇa) is another, he says: "Constricted," etc.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the contraction and expansion of the deity are possible. || 12 ||
They say that wealth is the fruit of action, and wealth is the means for performing action.
Because that [wealth] is deposited within them, they are therefore known as the Vasus. || 13 ||
In the passage beginning with "eteṣu hi," he explains the meaning of the word *vasu*. He says: "*vasu*. He then expounds upon the section beginning with "tasmāt" by saying: "yasmāt. The meaning is:
"because [the world] is dependent on that, karma and so forth [are included]. || 13 ||
The ten vital breaths (prāṇas) in the person, together with the self (ātman) as the eleventh—these they have declared to be the Rudras. || 14 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "eleven" as follows: "The person. He states the meaning of the word "prāṇa" as follows: "the sense organs. [End of] Brāhmaṇa 9, Volume 3, page 188, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā by Ānandagiri. 1321.
He states the meaning of the word "manasā" [with the mind]: the construction is that those eleven who exist in the body in the form of a person are here called Rudras. || 14 ||
Causing others to weep, they run about and weep themselves here and there.
The eleven vital breaths that have arisen are designated as the Rudras. || 15 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "te yadā" (when they... as follows: "rodayantaḥ" (causing to weep). || 11 ||
For from these they take away that which is the cause of stability for mortals as they depart.
The gods who take pride in the month are the Ādityas; therefore, they are so remembered.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "ete hi" as follows: "ādadānāḥ" (taking up). || 16 ||
Longevity, vigor, mindfulness, wisdom, delicacy, physical form, and splendor—
Since they go taking [the light] from there, those are known as the Ādityas. || 17 ||
Explaining the cause of their persistence, he clarifies what was stated [in verse 16] with the words: "Life-span" (āyuḥ). || 17 ||
Indra is to be known as the deity presiding over Meghanāda.
In this context, the thundering cloud is to be known as Prajāpati, the Lord of Creatures, who is the sacrifice. 18.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "stanayitnu" (the thunderbolt/thunder): "And Indra... Here, the construction is as follows: it should be understood that *stanayitnu* itself is *indra*, and *stanayitnu* is to be understood as the deity presiding over the sound of the clouds. Just as *indra* is here described as *stanayitnu*, so too should it be construed that *prajāpati* is here the *yajña* (sacrifice). || 18 ||
The thunderbolt of vigor, the thunderbolt of the lightning bolt—this is what is here called the roar of the clouds.
Since the sacrifice is accomplished by means of an animal, it is therefore remembered as "paśu."

He states the meaning of the word *aśani* (thunderbolt): "Vīryam" (the virile power). Although previously the thundercloud was said to be the deity presiding over the sound of the clouds, nevertheless, the use of the word "here" (*iha*) is intended to show that in this context it is designated by the term *vīrya* and so forth. He states the meaning of the word *paśu* (animal/victim): "Paśu" || 19 ||
For within the six [deities] beginning with Agni, all the aforementioned deities are present.
They proceed according to the number of their steps; therefore, they are remembered as the six beginning with Agni.
He explains [the passage] beginning with "these indeed are... as follows: "in fire and so forth. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "are included within" (antarbhūtāḥ). || 20 ||
Due to the identity of the container and the contained, [this applies] to the three—earth, fire, and so forth.
Therefore, there are three deities beginning with Agni, because they encompass everything within themselves.

He explains "these very [elements]" and so forth. He glosses "as the support" with "for in these," and so forth. Regarding "entirely," the word *tataḥ* (from that) should be construed with the ablative case of the preceding term. || 21 ||
0 1 ka. likewise, [the word] agni-ā; 2 kha. he explains. 166
Food and Prāṇa are the two deities; this is the definitive conclusion regarding these two.
Therefore, the true nature of the entire world is just this much.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "And food," etc., by saying "Food. To the question of how there are only these two deities, he says: "Only this much. || 22 ||
The statement "he who blows" is used for the purpose of determining the Adhyardha [Prastha].
"Because the Pavamāna is one, they say that [regarding it] as such"—this is the injunction.

He explains the passage beginning with "yo'yam" (this which...). Regarding "yo'yam," he states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the section beginning with "tat" (that) as follows: "Because of oneness" (ekatvāt). || 23 ||
"Since there is only the number one and no other, such as the number two, the wise sage, being questioned, replied with derision, 'It is one and a half. (24)
He introduces the response beginning with "That which... by saying "One" (*ekā*).

Since there exists only the number one prior to the number two, and no other number [exists in between], the word *adhyardha* cannot logically have a number as its referent. Nevertheless, having accepted that it does have a number as its referent, the sage—seeing that the question pertains to an impossible object when asked, "How can this, being one, be *adhyardha*?"—responds with derision...
The meaning is that he spoke the verse beginning with "yadasmin" (that which is in this), and so forth. || 24 ||
Or rather, the deity is the entire wind, which is other than that [individual] self.
There would be a state of being "half" because that which is pervaded—consisting of fire and so forth—is subordinate. (25)
Having accepted that the word "adhyardha" refers to a number, he states an external resolution to the scriptural objection: "Or rather, Vāyu... (25).
For one who attains supernatural power, everything, both moving and unmoving, becomes like the wind.
Therefore, the wise call Vāyu "Adhyardha" (the one and a half). || 26 ||
He explains the syllables of the Vedic text beginning with "In this" (*yad asmin*) and so forth: "Prosperity" (*ṛddhim*). || 26 ||
In the case of "one and a half" (adhyardha), the intention of the learned speaker is to emphasize the numerical value.
"By means of that [breath], one prospers in everything"—this is what is found in the Śruti.

Since the context establishes that the word *adhyardha* refers to a number, how can there be this statement of derision? To this he says: "Number... [referring to the verse]. How then is the etymological meaning stated there? To this he says: "Everything... [referring to the verse]. The meaning is that one should reject the view of Śākalya, who speaks falsely, and instead rely upon the view of the sage who possesses right knowledge. Because when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) exists, the entire world attains prosperity (*ṛddhi*), it is therefore called *adhyardha*.
The construction is: "He" [is] the view of the Śruti. || 27 ||
Just as linguistic derivation is taught for the purpose of establishing the status of being an eater of food.
The application [of the rule] is the same even for the one and a half [syllables], namely: "not heard by another. 28.

He states the etymological nature of the word *adhyardha* by means of an illustration: "In food," etc. This is because, according to the Aitareyins, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the eater of food. [Note: 1. ka. ...; 2. ka. having reached the air; 3. kha. in that [text], "he ate food" is the reading.]
[Vol.
3, Page 190] 9 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
1323. Just as the etymological derivation is stated in such a manner—"It is liberated; for the sake of its accomplishment, this Prāṇa indeed pervades everything through food"—so too...
The meaning is that there is also an etymological derivation for the word *dhyardha*. || 28 ||
Because all living beings are included within the vital breath (prāṇa) by virtue of being born from it.
Therefore, Prāṇa alone is the one God; his supreme majesty is indeed this.
He states the meaning of the word *prāṇa*: "That which is born," etc. (29).
Because it sustains all activities, the vital breath (prāṇa) is called Brahman.
Therefore, they call the vital breath (prāṇa) "That" (tyat), [referring] to Brahman in an indirect manner. || 30 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "That is Brahman" as follows: "Because of supporting. || 30 ||
For the purpose of explaining [the teachings] directly and for the realization of their causality.
Those of great intelligence call the vital breath "Brahman" by means of the remote designation "That" (tyat). || 31 ||

To the question, "Why is the Brahman-nature and the indirectness (parokṣatva) of Prāṇa stated? he replies with the word "directly" (sākṣāt). The meaning is: in order to avoid a direct designation of Prāṇa, he designates it indirectly as "That" (tyad); and in order to establish its status as the Cause, he calls it "Brahman," for those who know it speak of it thus. || 31 ||
In all these instruments as well as in those things consisting of effects, [it is likewise].
It abides completely within each of those [categories], beginning with the internal (adhyātma). || 32 ||
In order to introduce the passage beginning with "The earth indeed," he restates the fact that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the self of all, [saying]: "Among the organs... (32).
Furthermore, its eightfold division is described as follows.
Now, by way of a specific qualification, [the text] begins with "earth" and so forth. (33)

Having stated that the vital breath (prāṇa) exists as one's own essential nature within all the instruments of action—whether internal and so forth, or divided into gross and subtle adjuncts—the author states the purport of the subsequent sentence, beginning with "eightfold. The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is its being the self of all. Now, an objection may be raised: since unity and infinity have been asserted of the vital breath through its contraction and expansion, how can it be eightfold? To this, he replies: "by way of functions" (adhikāra).
The meaning is that even for a single living being, there is an eightfold nature due to the specific relationship of ownership over the earth and the other elements. || 33 ||
Furthermore, that which is divided into infinite varieties is said to be eightfold.
The differentiation of the assembly of deities is characterized by its concise definition. || 34 ||

Having explained that *prāṇa* has infinite divisions, one might ask: "Since its eightfold division has already been stated, why is it mentioned again? Anticipating this doubt, the author elaborates on it with the words beginning "ananta-". The meaning is: of *prāṇa*, which consists of all deities and is a collection of deities.
The intention is that this is a concise statement for the sake of making meditation easy. || 34 ||
For that deity whose abode is the earth and whose fire resides therein, as well as the world itself,
Agni shall always be the cause of its illumination.

He states the literal meaning of the passage beginning with "the earth": "The earth," etc. By the word "and" (ca), it is connected to the phrase "of whom. He who should know that—[he would be the knower of all gods].
[Vol. 3, page 191]

1324 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Third Adhyāya]: "It is to be known"—this connects with what follows later. How is fire his world? To this he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). Therefore, the remainder is: "that world is fire. || 35 ||
And the mind is the light of discernment, characterized by its own nature as volition and so forth.
Or rather, the nature of that deity whose light is said to be the mind (manojyotis) [is described]. || 36 ||

He explains [the mantra] "manojyotiḥ" as "manaśca" (and the mind). The meaning is: he who knows that which is the cause for the cognition designated by the word "light" (*jyotis*), which is the mind consisting of volition and so forth, is a "knower. He states another interpretation of this: "his own nature" (*svarūpam*). Of whom...
The wise one is he who knows that light which has the form of the mind and the nature of the self; "the knower" means precisely this. || 36 ||
He whose body is the earth, whose eyes are fire, and whose mind is the instrument of volition.
He who is the presiding deity of the earth here is the ultimate refuge of everything.
Of all that is internal, both effect and instrument.
Such a state should be one's final resort and the support for the self.
O Yājñavalkya, whoever here knows this, he alone shall be a knower.
A wise person is not like this, as you imagine yourself to be wise. (39)

He summarizes the meaning of the three statements with the word "earth" (*kṣiti*). The meaning of "the knower here" is: the deity previously mentioned who possesses the conceit "I am the earth"—he is the one who knows. He explains the passage beginning with "of all. [The phrase] "of all indeed" [is explained]. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who indeed that... with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). Here, the locative case in "here" (*iha*) has the sense of specifying what is under discussion. Regarding the particle *vai*, its restrictive sense has already been stated as "that very one" (*sa eva*). The meaning of the word "person" (*puruṣa*) is explained. It means "one who has become great," because he has attained greatness through his own nature. Or else, it means "one who is full," because he is filled by the qualities of sovereignty and so forth. The meaning of the word "immortal" (*amṛta*) is explained. It means "one who is not subject to death," because he is free from the cause of death, which is ignorance. The meaning of the word "Brahman" (*brahma*) is explained. It means "one who has become Brahman," because he has attained the state of Brahman. Or else, it means "one who is characterized by Brahman," because he is characterized by the qualities of Brahman such as omniscience and omnipotence. The meaning of the word "immortality" (*amṛtatva*) is explained. It means "the state of being immortal," because it is the cause of immortality. The meaning of the word "liberation" (*mokṣa*) is explained. It means "the state of being liberated," because it is the cause of liberation. The meaning of the word "highest" (*para*) is explained. It means "the supreme," because there is nothing higher than it. The meaning of the word "goal" (*gati*) is explained. It means "the destination," because it is the place of arrival. The meaning of the word "supreme" (*parāyaṇa*) is explained. It means "the ultimate resort," because it is the final support. The meaning of the word "Brahman-world" (*brahmaloka*) is explained. It means "the world of Brahman," because it is the abode of Brahman. The meaning of the word "attains" (*anveti*) is explained. It means "he goes to," because it denotes reaching.
