It destroys; but not so [as previously stated]. || 37 || 38 || 39 ||
If wisdom is obtained by this much alone, then let that [wisdom] be the Veda.
In this earthly portion, the embodied deity possesses the conceit of being the individual self (adhyātma).

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "veda" [in the verse] starting with "iyatā. Regarding the phrase "ya evāyaṃ śārīraḥ," he explains the meaning of the word *śārīra* [as follows]: "śārīra iti.

Here, the construction is as follows: that deity who, within the earthly portion consisting of the triad of flesh and so forth born of the mother, becomes identified with that (*tanmaya*) and possesses the conceit of being the internal self (*adhyātmābhimānavān*), is the *śārīra*. || 40 ||
He who is established in such self-conceit as "I belong to the earth," [is a fool].
The aggregate of hair, skin, and flesh is its effect, and this very [aggregate] is its cause.

He states the difference in meaning between the two statements concerning the body of the earth: "The earth," etc. For in that [previous] case, the deity whose abode is the general was mentioned by Śākalya; here, however, the deity whose abode is the particular is spoken of by the sage—this is the distinction. || 41 ||
"This is that very god you asked about; speak further, you fool!"
This philosophical system you wish to expound remains indeed unfinished. || 42 ||

He states the meaning of "sa eṣa" (this is he) with the word "sa" (he). He states the meaning of "vadaiva" (speak indeed) and so forth with the word "vada" (speak). [The phrase] "pṛcchaiva" (ask indeed) [is followed by] "ku vedeti" (where does one know?). [Variants: 1. ku; 2. ka, kha, ga: 'tistasya; 3. ka: 'vidhaḥ || 38 || yā! .
[Vol.
3, Page 192] 9 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

1325. Up to this point. The reason why the question must be performed is given by the word "yataḥ" (since). Because the subject to be expressed is connected with the aforementioned deity, the reason has not been asked—
The meaning is "you" (tvad). || 42 ||
Agitated by anger, he asked him: "Who is his deity?"
To him Yājñavalkya replied, "It is the nectar, the deity. (43)
He introduces the question beginning with "tasya" (of that). Regarding "tasya," he takes up the response: "taṃ prati" (toward him). || 43 ||
For whoever attains accomplishment, that very deity belongs to him alone.
In this context, it should be understood that the definition [of the word] "immortality" and so forth is intended to be expressed.
He states the meaning of the word *devatā*: "Since... The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the present context. || 44 ||
The essence of food consumed by a woman arises from its transformation.
The cause of the mother-derived blood is nectar; that is what is spoken of here. || 45 ||
He explains the "immortal" (amṛta). By the word "woman" (yoṣit), it is stated that the context here refers to the subject matter under discussion. || 49 ||
From the nutrient essence (rasa) arises blood; from blood, which is the substratum of the seed, [arises flesh].
The body is produced directly by that [karma], for which reason it is called "bodily" (śārīra).
To the question, "How is this nectar the cause of the bodily [self]? he replies: "From the essence (rasāt). By the word "directly" (sākṣāt), its status as being perceptible is expressed. || 46 ||
Others call this nectar the divine lunar water.
That [body] arises from rain and other factors, serving as the cause for the solidity of wood and the physical form of the earth.
He states another meaning of the word "amṛta" with the words "anya" (another). To the question of how that [amṛta] can be the cause of the body, he replies with "tat" (that).
In the phrase "parjanyādineti," the word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to rain and other such factors. || 47 ||
In the subsequent statements as well, one should establish the point as it has been explained.
The general rule applies to all; however, the specific details shall now be explained. || 48 ||
He extends the logic already stated to the subsequent sections with the words "in the subsequent ones. The reason for this is given as "the logic. An objection is raised:

"In that case, why is the explanation of the terms 'desire' (kāma) and so forth provided immediately after the passage beginning with 'Then he said, "O Śākalya"'?"; to this he replies: "But there is a distinction. || 48 ||
In this world, the desire for union with a woman is designated as *kāma*.
The heart is the intellect and the light; for by it one sees everything. || 49 ||

While explaining the passage beginning with "For whom desire alone... he states the distinction: "A woman," etc. By the word "here" (iha), a synonym for desire is understood. The reason for its being "light" (āloka) is stated as: "everything," etc. (49).
And that god consists of desire, being anointed by the cultivation of desire.
Its deities are to be known as women, for desire is born from women. || 50 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "That which is this very one" (*ya evāyam*) as follows: "And he" (*sa ca*). The meaning is that the deity whom you asked about as the abode of desire (*kāmāyatana*) is precisely this one who possesses the specific abode known as the latent impression of desire (*kāma-vāsanā*). He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Of him" (*tasya*) as follows: "The deity" (*devatā*). He establishes that women are the cause for a man consisting of desire by means of their own experience. [He says: "Desire" (*kāma*). || 10 ||
In this [world], forms such as white and so forth are luminous, but in the higher [realm], they are otherwise.
The person belongs to Savitṛ; his eye has both truth and the deity as its presiding power. || 51 ||

He states that there is no tautology in the repetition of "the forms themselves" (*rūpāṇyeva*) and so forth by saying "white, etc. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "that which is this very sun" (*ya evāsāvādityaḥ*) by saying "belonging to Savitṛ" (*sāvitra*). The deity whose abode is form in general possesses a specific abode in the form of the solar orb; his eye, designated by the word "truth," is the cause and the object to be presided over, for upon its production, the sun arises as the presiding agent in relation to it.
This is the meaning. || 51 ||
This [path] is also established in three ways within the truths of the Sun of Form (Rūpabhāskara).
As before, so too in all subsequent cases, each [element] is threefold in three ways.

He concludes the purport of the first section beginning with "forms" (*rūpāṇi*) with the word "form" (*rūpa*). The particle *api* is used for emphasis. The meaning of the scriptural passage is that this very Deity alone is established as the forms and so forth, by way of being their general abode (*sāmānyāyatana*), their specific abode (*viśeṣāyatana*), and their cause (*kāraṇa*).
He extends [the analysis] to the passage beginning with "space alone" (*ākāśa eva*) by saying "as before" (*pūrvavat*). Just as in the previous section, it is the general abode—

The meaning is that just as the deity was described in three ways, so too in the sequences beginning with space (ākāśa) and the others, he is to be seen in each case in a threefold manner—as the general locus (sāmānyāyatana), the specific locus (viśeṣāyatana), and the cause (kāraṇa). || 52 ||
At the moment of hearing, that which is present in the ear [is the witness].
Satvaya is designated as his [region], and Devatā is the deity of that direction as well. || 53 ||

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "That which is this ear" as follows: "Pratiśravaṇa," etc. The meaning is that for the deity whose abode is space (ākāśa), the ear—characterized by the act of hearing—is the specific locus, and the quarters (diśaḥ) are its cause. The word "iha" is a synonym for space (ākāśa). The particle "api" is used here, as before, for the purpose of emphasis (avadhāraṇe). || 13 ||
Darkness is to be known as *tamas*, and likewise, the person (*puruṣa*) consists of shadow.
And death is his deity, since death arises from darkness alone.

Regarding the phrase "tama eva" (it is indeed darkness), he states the meaning of the word *tamas* as "darkness. By saying that ignorance—which is called "shadow"—is the specific abode for the abode of nocturnal darkness, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "anya eva" (it is indeed other). He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "mṛtyuḥ" (death) as "and death. To the question of how death can be the cause of the abode of ignorance, he replies: "by means of darkness," that is, by means of extremely firm non-comprehension.

The meaning of the entire chapter is summarized as follows: the Self, which is the witness of all objects, is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the body, the senses, and the mind; therefore, it is distinct from them. Furthermore, because the Self is the witness of the three states—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—it is distinct from those states as well. Moreover, since the Self is the witness of the aggregate of the waking state and so forth, it is distinct from that aggregate. And because the Self is the witness of the cessation of the waking state and so forth, it is distinct from that cessation as well. Consequently, the Self is eternal, pure, enlightened, free, and non-dual. This is the purport of the entire chapter. By the scriptural passage beginning with "He knows the quarters," the fivefold nature [of the deity] according to the divisions of the directions has been stated for the purpose of meditation. Now, he explains the intention of that scripture which speaks of such divisions, starting with the words "In the eastern [quarter]. By the first section, the withdrawal of the manifold of forms (*rūpa-prapañca*) into the heart is shown, based on the scriptural text, "For in the heart alone are forms. By the three subsequent sections beginning with "In the southern [quarter]," the withdrawal of action (*karman*) into that very same [heart] is shown.

The meaning is as follows: by the sequence beginning with "The necklace is said to be in the *dhruvā* [ladle]" and ending with that very same [verse], the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of names occurs within that [heart]; for it has been stated that speech, which is established in fire, is itself established in the heart.
Thus, the withdrawal of the entire world—consisting of name, form, and action—is presented in the heart according to the scripture under discussion. || 76 ||

The collection of actions has been described in three directions; therein, he states the internal subdivision [of that collection] with the words "only," etc. By the passage beginning with "in the south," it is understood that action alone is withdrawn into the heart, because it is stated that sacrifice is established in the heart by means of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth. And by the passage beginning with "in the west," the action known as the birth of a son is likewise withdrawn there, according to the Vedic text: "For semen is indeed established in the heart."

By the passage beginning with "In the north," action conjoined with knowledge is included therein by way of remainder; for it is heard in scripture that [knowledge] is established there through the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other means of the deity Soma.
Thus, the meaning is that all action is withdrawn into the heart within the three directions. || 77 ||

He explains the passage beginning with "In Dhruvā" and so forth. With the words "And of the name," he concludes what was stated as "the withdrawal of all" by saying "Thus.

Just as the locus of the name and so forth was stated by means of the word *hṛdaya*, one might suspect that the support of the heart (*hṛdayādhāra*) is likewise intended by the word *ahaṃlika* due to the similarity in the tone of the sentence; anticipating this, he says: "The word *ahaṃlika*... Then, fearing the question "In that case, what is its meaning?", he first states its status as a technical name (*saṃjñātva*), saying: "Because it has the acute accent on the first syllable... [He explains: having analyzed [the etymology] as "it dissolves during the day" (*ahani līyate*), [the suffix] *kvip* is applied.

When the *kvip* suffix is applied, the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā bahulam* allows for a compound; then, by *tor li*, the *t* is changed to *l*; and by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ kan*, the suffix *kan* is added; finally, by *ke’ṇaḥ*, the vowel is shortened. Thus, according to *nityādir nityam*, the first syllable is udātta. Therefore, the meaning is that the word *hallika* is his name.

An illustration for this is given as *vidagdha-vat*. From the root *dah* (to burn), with the *kta* suffix in the passive sense and the prefix *vi*, there is a *gati-samāsa* by the rule *gatir anantaraḥ*.

Thus, according to the rule regarding the accent of the original form (*pūrvaprakṛtisvara*), the word *vidagdha* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*); the meaning is that this too is its designation because it is stated as such in the Bhāṣya. The particle *hi* is used to support the aforementioned grammatical convention regarding both being technical names (*saṃjñā*). || 82 ||

This means that it has been explained in eight ways and five ways through both unity and multiplicity, as previously described. This second instance of the word "idam" (this) refers to the subject matter of the syllables. || 93 ||
Setting aside the form of a narrative, the Śruti [speaks] by its own words alone.
And he said, "This very person is one who desires to attain the goals of human existence. || 94 ||

Now, one might object: this narrative consists of a dialogue between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya, yet Śākalya did not ask about the syllable (akṣara) here; so how could Yājñavalkya’s engagement be for the purpose of explaining that? To this, he says: "Having abandoned... [the world]. Since it will be stated later that the conclusion occurs at the passage concerning "knowledge" (vijñāna) and so forth, how can there be a statement of the attributeless (nirviśeṣa) meaning here for that purpose? In response to this doubt, [it is said] that this is the intention of the Śruti.
The word "ca" (and) is used to indicate that [the term] "remainder" (śeṣaḥ) is to be supplied. || 94 ||
This world remained under the governance of Him who exists as the inner controller (antaryāmin).
This very [Self] is described as "not this, not this" even in the Madhu-kāṇḍa. || 95 ||

He explains the meaning of the word *praśāsana* (ruling): "In whose ruling," etc. The meaning is that He in whom—He who is the mere witness (*kūṭastha-dṛṣṭi-mātra*) and the substratum for the conceptualization of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*)—the heaven, earth, and so forth abide by virtue of His command, is the Supreme Self; that is to say, He is this very inner self (*pratyagātman*).
He states that the double negation (*neti*) has been explained in the Mūrtāmūrta Brāhmaṇa: "Not this, not this. That same [negation] will be further discussed in the Kūrya Brāhmaṇa.
And the meaning is also [as follows]. || 95 ||
Objection: Since this concerns Brahman, how can it be that the term "Self" (ātman) is merely restated?
This is not a fault, because the nature of Brahman does not consist in being something additional to the Self.

It implies the word "ātman. [The objection begins with] "nanu" (but surely); the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) is to be supplied as the remainder. He refutes this with the words beginning with "na" (no). || 96 ||
The state of being an object of perception, taking refuge, attachment, and fear are the causes of ignorance.
Because that [ignorance] has passed away, there are no ends of fear within the inner self.
He explains the words beginning with *agṛhya*: "The state of being graspable" [refers to] slackness, fear, distress, and destruction. || 97 ||
Free from ignorance, unattached, radiant, and possessing an undiminished nature of consciousness.
Since this is so, there is no modification of this Self, such as destruction or anything else. (98)
He elucidates what was stated as "upon the passing of that" with the words "free from ignorance. He states the fruit of transcending ignorance with the words "since...
(verse 98).
Having transcended these properties of the effect, one also transcends their cause.
Without before or after, he alone is complete, established within his own self.

If the effect is not realized because the cause has been transgressed, how can there be the attainment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) which lacks any excellence? To this, he says: "The effect," etc. (99).
The Śruti, by its own words, directly [describes] the characteristics such as "beginning with 'not this'."
Having completed the knowledge of the Self, he further [taught] that which takes the form of a narrative.
Having taken hold of him, he questioned the conceited Śākalya.
Having become Yājñavalkya herself, she [restrained] him who was acting with excessive persistence.

Anticipating the objection that the sentence beginning with "these eight" lacks connection with what precedes it, he offers a resolution: "The Śruti... The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that it was appropriate for [Yājñavalkya] to question Śākalya because of his pursuit of knowledge and his persistent insistence.
For wealth has been bestowed here by the king for the sake of those most devoted to Brahman.
Therefore, one who is not most devoted to Brahman has no authority whatsoever here to inquire. || 102 ||
[Vol. 3, page 201] 1334 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:
Here, Śākalya is the questioner; how is it that he asks him? Anticipating this objection—that it belongs to another—the author establishes Śākalya’s entitlement to ask the question.

He refutes this with the words "wealth. Here, the word "here" (iha) refers to a sacrifice with abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). The compound should be analyzed as *abrahmiṣṭhasya* (of one who is not most devoted to Brahman). However, the second occurrence of the word "here" (iha) has as its object the assembly of those who know Brahman. || 102 ||
Therefore, filled with rage, he questioned [the teacher] for the purpose of proving his own non-Brahminhood.
That Yājñavalkya [acted] toward Śākalya in order to establish his state of having committed an offense. || 103 ||

How was Śākalya lacking in the highest Brahman-knowledge? To this he says: "Regarding his lack of being the most learned in Brahman" (*abrahmiṣṭhatve*). The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that one who is not the most learned in Brahman has no right to ask questions.

If the Sage, filled with anger toward Śākalya—who, despite having no right to ask questions, proceeded to do so—had then pronounced a curse upon him, why would he have instead asked him questions for the purpose of establishing his lack of being the most learned in Brahman?
Anticipating this doubt, he says "sāparādhatve" (in the case of being guilty) in order to make known the cause of the curse. || 103 ||
Let this very question, beginning with "Not this, not this," now be examined.
In the middle [of the sentence], because there is no interruption of the syntactical connection, the word "iti" functions as before. || 104 ||

The distinction has been stated thus: "sa eṣa" and so forth is a scriptural statement (*śrauta-vākya*), while "etāni" and so forth is an interrogative statement. Now, [the author] speaks by resorting to their status as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). He says: "sa" (he). This is the reason for their being a single unit. Regarding the word "madhye" (in the middle): when there is a division of sentences, such as in "kasmin nu hṛdayam," the particle "iti" seen in the middle serves as the reason for that [division]; however, this is not the case here in the passage "na ca na riṣyaty etāny aṣṭau."
The meaning is that because the word "iti" (thus) is seen in the middle, this constitutes a single interrogative sentence. || 104 ||
That which Śākalya asked in the form of both summary and detailed exposition.
After that, Yājñavalkya also questioned Śākalya.

Even though the statement is a single unit, with the question of Śākalya being intended for determination, he says "samāsa" (compound) out of the consideration that there would be no room for another's question. The meaning of "tataḥ parastāt" is "after the resolution of Śākalya’s question. || 105 ||
In the state of oneness, all this characterized by cause and effect is indeed [one].
It should be brought to complete conclusion, entirely free from both brevity and prolixity. || 106 ||

Having revealed Śākalya’s lack of supreme Brahman-knowledge and having established his state of culpability, the author states the intention of the questioner—anticipating the concern that even the Sage, by bestowing a curse while overcome with anger, might himself incur a lack of supreme Brahman-knowledge: "In the case of the identity of the Self" (aikātmye). || 106 ||
Moreover, this connection with the meaning of the scripture belongs to the subsequent revelation.
For if that were not stated, everything would be like the threshing of chaff. (107)

He establishes the stated intention through reasoning with the word "api" (even/also). The meaning is that this alone is the connection between the subject matter of the scripture (*śāstrārtha*) and the preceding and succeeding scriptural passages (*pūrvottara-śruti*):

namely, that because everything culminates in the one-flavored inner Self (*pratīci*), it is its particularization. [Objection: Let there be no connection between the subject matter of the scripture and the preceding and succeeding passages;

to this he replies: "tadanuktāv" (in the absence of that being stated). It should be understood as "the preceding and the succeeding"; for indeed, in the absence of stating the connection between the subject matter of the scripture [and those passages], the preceding... [is not established].

Thus, there is purposefulness for both the subsequent scripture and the hearing [of it]; and so, for the sake of their success as being subordinate to the knowledge of reality, the intention of the questioner is logical—this is the meaning. || 107 ||
[Volume 3,
Page 202] 9 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
"One should point out the eight abodes here, beginning with earth."
Likewise, the worlds beginning with Agni, and the deities beginning with Amṛta. || 108 ||

Having stated the intention of the questioner, he explains the passage beginning with "these," etc., starting with "eight. Here, the locative case in "in these" (*atre*) and so forth is used for the purpose of determining the abodes and other categories. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "the earth, etc.," the desire-form, space, darkness, water, and semen are included. He states the meaning of "the eight worlds" as "Agni and the others. By the word "etcetera," the heart, eye, ear, and heart [are included].

The eyes and the hearts have been grasped. He states the meaning of the phrase "eight gods" as "Amṛta and the others. Here, by the word "and others," these deities are intended: Strī, Satya, Diś, Mṛtyu, Asura, Varuṇa, and Prajāpati. || 108 ||
In the same way, the eight [senses] beginning with the body should be understood as they have been described.
All these eight persons are again brought together for the sake of initiation. || 109 ||
All the directions are in the heart, and the heart and so forth are in the samāna breath.
Thus, while it is the same, there is contraction, expansion, and infinite deities. || 110 ||
He states the meaning of the phrase "nine persons" as follows: "The embodied one," etc. Those for whom the embodied one (*śārīra*) is the foremost are [the nine];

by means of the genitive case, [these are] the person consisting of desire (*kāma-maya*), the person in the sun, the person in the ear (*śrautra*), the person in the echo (*prātiśrutkara*), the one consisting of shadow (*chāyā-maya*)—which is the reflection in a mirror or the like—and the one who identifies with ponds, wells, and so forth.

The remaining seven are said to consist of the son and so forth. He states the purport of the passage beginning with "He who [knows] those" [with the words] "all indeed. The meaning is that the eight categories, beginning with the abode (*āyatana*), are indicated within each of the four [sets]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the heart and so forth," the body is included. He concludes that Śākalya’s knowledge extends only up to the cause and not beyond it, with the words "Thus. (109) (110)
This greatness of the delusion regarding the true nature of the inward Self has been described by you.
It is ignorance alone that manifests itself in the form of cause and effect.
And this indicates that Śākalya’s knowledge is born of ignorance and is false knowledge. [The word] "pratyak" [means] "inwardly. || 111 ||
In accordance with the knowledge of its own self, it has assumed both concise and expanded forms.
But the Self is by its own nature luminous, pure consciousness alone, full, and stainless. || 112 ||
Fearing that the restriction "it is only ignorance" might be untenable because [the Self] manifests itself in the form of cause and effect for another, he says: "Its own self...
He states the intended meaning of the phrase "transcended" as follows: "But by itself... (112).
He who [answered] these four Aṣṭakas that were questioned by you here;
Having dissolved it and brought it to the state of being an effect, one should then counter-act it by means of its own cause.

Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "He who [knows] those," he explains the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) starting with "He who. Since the Vedic word *puruṣa* (person) serves as an indicator for the deities, the worlds, and the abode, it is said "even all four. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the plane of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*). The meaning of "having led out" (*niruhya*) is—
"Let it be done," [he said]. The meaning is: "Having remained on the plane of ignorance (avidyābhūmi), establish the stability of the world through the aforementioned abodes (āyatana) and so forth.

Having understood the connection—that he asks about Him who remains after having withdrawn the entire universe into His own cause, the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin)—he repeats the word *pratyūhya* and states its meaning. Regarding *pratyūhya*: the word *atha* is intended to indicate the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsārāvasthā). || 113 ||
1336 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Three [Volume 3, Page 203]
Having repeatedly analyzed and elevated it from its cause toward the nature of the effect.
In accordance with the actual state of things, [he perceives] all those characterized as cause and effect without exception.
He who has transcended manifoldness and is free from differentiation and conjunction.
That very God of the Upaniṣads, characterized by the attributes "directly perceived" and so forth. || 115 ||

He restates the meaning of the two preceding words with the phrase "having analyzed. The sense is: having made a distinction between the bases (*āyatana*) and so forth from ignorance accompanied by its fallacious appearances, and having established that [ignorance] as the cause for the persistence of the world, he asks about Him who remains after having withdrawn all of that back into His own Self. He clarifies the meaning of the word "transcended" (*atyakrāmat*) with the word "reality" (*vastu*). The connection is with the subsequent phrase, "I ask about Him."
It is understood from the qualification "in accordance with the nature of reality" that there is no literal transcendence. The reason for this is given as "because of non-differentiation.
He takes up the passage beginning with "But him," etc. The connection here is: "I ask about that too. (114, 115)
For the wise explain this very [truth] within these Upaniṣads themselves.
Because it was contradictory to the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), they did not explain it at all. || 116 ||

He explains the term "aupaniṣada" [as one who is known through the Upaniṣads]. [The phrase] "āsveva" [means] "only in these. He states the reason for this restriction: "karma" [and so forth]. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "therefore, he is aupaniṣada. || 116 ||
The wise declare that Brahman, which is the Self, to be that which is known through the Upaniṣads.
I ask you that, Śākalya; tell me that according to the truth. || 117 ||
Here, he establishes the consensus of the learned as the authority. Regarding the phrase "But him," having stated the meaning of the individual words, he joins them into a sentence:
If you do not show him to me, your head shall shatter.
And Śākalya did not recognize that Self as it had been described. || 118 ||
He states the meaning of "If he [does not]" and so forth with the words "And if not. He explains "Then indeed," etc., with the word "No. This is a particle used in the sense of dejection. || 118 ||
Then, by the fire known as the words of the curse uttered by Yājñavalkya, [he was consumed].
Burnt instantly, he who was a knower of Brahman died, overcome by intense fever. || 119 ||
He states the meaning of that [word] "tataḥ" (from that) and so forth: "tataḥ" || 119 ||
This has never been heard before in the section on karma.
For this is indeed constantly heard in the Vedic Upaniṣads alone.

As for the statement that the Person (puruṣa) is known through the Upaniṣads, that is incorrect, because he is well-known even in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa); nor is there any contradiction with ritual action, since as the agent (kartṛ), he is in accordance with it. As they say: "He whose this body is, he too, by means of those sacrificial implements, is one equipped with sacrificial implements. To this, [the author] replies: "Karma... (verse 120).
Because it is excluded from the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), it is therefore spoken of in this very [section].
Although it was established in the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), he did not state it because of its contradiction with the virtuous.
[Volume 3, Page 204] 9 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

If it is argued that even there [in the Upaniṣads] the person is not indicated as such because of the Śruti [which speaks of him] as an agent, he says in response: "From the Karma-kāṇḍa. Although the form of the person is obtained as an agent in the Karma-kāṇḍa, nevertheless, his nature characterized by non-transmigration and so forth is not applicable there, because it is opposed to ritual action—as has been stated, "because of its lack of utility and because of the contradiction with the qualification for action. Therefore, having been excluded from the Karma-kāṇḍa, this [person] is pointed out only in the Upaniṣads.

Thus, the meaning is that it is logical for this [self] to be "known through the Upaniṣads" (*aupaniṣada*). Furthermore, in the *Sūtra on Origination* (*Autpattika-sūtra*), regarding the passage, "This sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world," once the self as distinct from the body and so forth has been established, its true nature (*tatsatattva*) follows as something that ought to be stated;

nevertheless, the Commentator did not state it precisely because knowledge of that [nature] is incompatible with ritual action (*karma*). Therefore, even the Mīmāṃsakas accept that the person (*puruṣa*) is known through the Upaniṣads.
He says: "It is indeed attained. For it has been stated: "Through the study of the Vedānta, this firmness and the cognition of its object come to pass. || 121 ||
Therefore, there can be no combination of ritual action with the knowledge of the inner Self.
For the realization of the reality of the one Self is indeed contradicted by ritual acts.

With this, he says "pratyak" (the inner), thereby refuting the theory of their combination (samuccaya). He clarifies the reason expressed by the word "ataḥ" with the words "aikātmya" and so forth. || 122 ||
Others, considering themselves wise, believed they had correctly realized the true nature of the self.
Regarding those afflicted by karma, they bring about self-awakening according to the actual state of things. || 123 ||
Furthermore, from where does the possibility of a combination [of knowledge and action] arise, such that it must be refuted? To this he says:

"Others," with the words "they speak of a combination" as the ellipsis. He states the justification for the combination: they practice knowledge in accordance with the reality of things at times other than those prescribed for ritual action, while performing the prescribed action at the time ordained for it; thus he says, "properly. || 123 ||
In reality, knowledge is not an agent, unlike an action.
For, by the obstruction of the path of karma, it indeed undergoes transformation. || 124 ||
He refutes that [objection] with the words "the thing" (*vastu*). For knowledge is dependent upon the thing (*vastutantra*), not dependent upon an agent as an action is.

If the practice of knowledge were to occur at a time other than the time prescribed for the ritual act, then it would abandon its dependence on the thing; and in that case, its status as knowledge would be unestablished, like the visualization of fire in a woman. If knowledge were not dependent on the thing, its lack of validity as knowledge—being like a mere action—would be all too evident.
The repetition of the word "hi" [is for the purpose of emphasis]. ||124||
That which can be done, or done otherwise, or even not done at all;
Therefore, by virtue of your sovereignty, let that be done by you as you desire.
Furthermore, regarding whether there is a combination of practice or knowledge with action, he first addresses the former [with the verse]: "That which is to be done...
The sense is that since practice is an action, there is no contradiction even in its combination with ritual action. || 125 ||
However, that cognition which occurs here must indeed conform to the actual state of things.
It never deviates from its course due to the influence of human will.

[The author] states the second [point]: "In accordance with the nature of things" (*vastuvṛtta*). Here, "here" (*iha*) refers to the qualified practitioner (*adhikārin*), while "in some cases" (*kvacit*) expresses the object of the counter-example for deviation.
The sense is that because the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is not dependent on the person (*apumtantra*), there is no such combination as described above. 126.
160 [Vol. 3, Page 205] 1338 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]—
"In this world, a wise person should never be a reviler of anyone at all."
Even though he was such a person, he became [known] from the proclamation of his enemy's form. || 127 ||
Having concluded the incidental discussion, he explains the sentence introduced in the Bhāṣya, "Therefore, one should not be a reviler," with the words "upavādinā" (by a reviler).
This means by one who causes humiliation. "Iha" (here) means in this world, in some place or at some time.
He states the meaning of "uta hi" and so forth with the words "evaṃvid" (one of such a kind). || 127 ||
Even Yājñavalkya, having burned away the cause of his anger, became an enemy.
Even for Śākalya, there was a gathering [of censure] solely due to the fault of his disparaging remarks. || 128 ||
He elaborates on the meaning of the reason [in the verse]: "Burnt," etc. The second "api" (also) has the sense of "even for a Brāhmaṇa. || 128 ||
Therefore, even Yājñavalkya should not be a detractor or harbor enmity.

Because there is no reproach more painful than this, [the author] concludes the point he has promised to prove with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Thus, from this contempt shown through speech and body—

Thinking that there is nothing more difficult than this, he says "more difficult" (kaṣṭataram) for the purpose of instructing the disciple that one should be intent on the renunciation of all things. || 129 ||
Even the destruction of the next world [is brought about] by reason of hatred toward the learned.
Because, due to a curse, he did not receive the consecration of the Agnihotra fire.

He states the intention of the word "api" (even) and so forth: "paraloka... (regarding the next world). The phrase "attained by Śākalya" is the ellipsis to be supplied. The reason for this is given as "vidvat... (by the knower). Anticipating the objection that his success in the next world is established through the performance of the *agnihotra* fire-sacrifice, the purification of sins committed through hatred by means of the ritual consecration of sons and others according to rule, he says: "agnihotra... (the *agnihotra*). This is because of the observation of the curse, such as "you shall die in the city of Atithya," and so forth.
This is the meaning. Therefore, the ellipsis is "the destruction of his [existence] in the next world. || 130 ||
For robbers, driven by the suspicion that there might be wealth, have taken away the bones.
They also took those away from him because of his hatred toward the knowers of Brahman.
He explains the words beginning with "api" [even] as "parimoṣiṇaḥ" [robbers]. The implied meaning is that, therefore, one should not harbor hatred toward those who know Brahman. || 131 ||
That which was previously stated as "not this, not this" by means of the negation of the meaning of non-self—
Furthermore, another Vedic revelation is intended to provide a detailed exposition of that very same [Supreme Being] by way of injunction;
and for that reason, He must also be described as the root of the universe through narrative accounts.
"Having conquered, cows should be given to the twice-born"—this is the meaning of the subsequent Vedic revelation. || 133 ||

Having concluded the narrative of the dialogue between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya, he states the purport of the textual sequence beginning with "Now, therefore" (*atha ha*) and ending with its conclusion, starting with the words "The non-self" (*anātma*). The connection is as follows: the root of the world must be stated, and for that reason, the supreme Śruti [is required].

To the question, "For what purpose is the narrative? he replies: "Even from the narrative" (*ākhyānato 'pi*). For what is being told is easily understood through it; therefore, that [narrative] is [necessary].
The meaning is that it would indeed be purposeful. He states its gross purport [tātparya]: "Having conquered," etc. (vv. 132–133).
Thus ends the [first] section. [Vol.
3, page 206] 9. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1339.
Since dissimilarity can be questioned only when similarity exists, for that reason [it is so stated].
The similarity between the tree and the mortal is declared by the Vedic scripture. (134)

He states the purport of the mantra beginning with "yathā" as follows: "In terms of similarity. The meaning is that since negative concomitance (vyatireka) depends upon positive concomitance (anvaya), it is appropriate to state the similarity first. || 134 ||
The birth of a tree is from a seed, yet its presence is perceived here at the root.
"O Brāhmaṇas, tell me that which is the root of a mortal's birth.
He states the purport of the verse beginning with "yad" (what): "from the seed," etc. (verse 135).
The root of semen must not be spoken of by you, for it arises from that while one is alive.
In this world, no one's semen exists anywhere once they have died.

He states the meaning of the phrase "Do not say 'of semen'" with the words "semen. He introduces the subsequent [verse] as a reason with the words "because while living. He demonstrates its meaning by way of contrast (vyatireka) with the word "not. || 136 ||
Even a tree that grows from grain is seen to have its birth from a seed.
Of one who has died, nothing whatsoever is observed here that could serve as the locus for a seed. (137)

Let it be; however, one might suspect that just as a tree arises from a seed, so too does another [being] arise from the semen of a living person after the other has died. Anticipating this, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "a tree growing from a seed" (*dhānāruha*). The word "also" (*api*) implies "even a tree growing from a cutting" (*kāṇḍaruha*). Since it was asked what the cause of the world's rebirth is once the entire universe has dissolved, semen—which falls within the category of effects—cannot be the cause of that [rebirth]. Or how could it be?

The meaning is that since a "primal person" (mānapuruṣa) is not established, another person is likewise not established; therefore, the semen contained within such a person cannot be the cause of the universe. || 137 ||
Just as a tree growing from seed appears directly and without any interval.
Since human birth is likewise [the means] for that direct [realization], let that be explained. || 138 ||
He states the purport of the verse beginning with "añjasā" as follows: "dhāna... (verse 138).
Just as the seed of a tree is seen here possessing its inherent power according to how it has been experienced.
And for one who has died in such a manner, there is no further rebirth. || 139 ||
Anticipating the objection that "the cause of the world must be accepted in accordance with experience, so its description is useless," he says: "Just as... (139).
Even a tree growing from a seed-sprout is seen here; likewise, it is accepted in that statement.
Once hands, feet, and so forth have been severed, there is no rebirth for one who has died.

One might raise the objection: "Even when the seed is no longer perceived, the rebirth of a cut tree is experienced; why then should the birth of one who has died not occur without a seed? Anticipating this, he says: "It is seen. He elaborates upon the illustrative example: "Just as from the root and from the seed, the tree's direct emergence occurs... [140]... "just as from the root and from the seed, the tree's direct emergence occurs."
In that same way, it should be spoken regarding one who has died, but not as one would speak regarding a son or grandson. || 141 ||
1. kha. *ṣasya re* | 2. ga. *yate* || 138 ||
[Vol. 3, page 207] 1340 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Chapter]:
He summarizes the meaning of the passage beginning with "growing from seed" (*dhānāruha*). From the root—meaning from the semen of the father and so forth, as in the case of a son and so forth.

He states the exclusion [of the alternative view] by saying "But not," on the grounds that the birth of semen from one who is dead is not possible, precisely because that [death] was what was being questioned. || 141 ||
Just as they would cut down a tree together with its roots and seeds, so it is with both.
When a mortal is indeed cut down by death, from what root does he sprout again? || 142 ||

One might object: "Is it not observed that even a tree, once destroyed, sometimes does not grow again? Likewise, let there be no rebirth for the world once it has died; thus, what is the use of investigating its cause? Anticipating this doubt, he explains the meaning of the verse beginning with *yatsamūlam* (that which, together with its root) by saying *samūlabījam* (together with its root and seed). If the effect known as a tree is uprooted along with its cause, then neither the tree nor its cause will exist; likewise, if the world were [uprooted] along with its cause—
When conflict is thoroughly sublated by perfect awakening, it does not arise again; however, when it is not so sublated, its cause must necessarily exist—this is the meaning. || 142 ||
It is held that that which is being born does not exist, for the very reason that it has already been born.
Or a male being about to be born from the stream of saṃsāra. || 143 ||
He states the meaning of the phrase "born indeed" with the word "is held. To the question, "How then does the notion of saṃsāra arise there? he replies with the words "of saṃsāra. || 143 ||
Samsara, in the form of a continuous flow, persists like the flame of a lamp.
Nothing is born, nor will anything ever be born; therefore, nothing at all exists here.

He clarifies its constant existence in the form of a stream by means of an illustration, beginning with the word "pravāha" (stream). He concludes the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*) with the word "na" (not). || 144 ||
Therefore, what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view— that "it is produced as soon as born"— is incorrect.
Everyone dies after being born, and having died, one is born again.

He states the meaning of the word *śrutisthanam*: "jātaḥ" (born). By explaining the word "jāyate" as the reason, he clarifies the meaning of the word "ataḥ" found in the first half-verse: "janitvā" (having been born). || 149 ||
Furthermore, birth for one who is seedless occurs neither according to scripture nor through logical reasoning.
Speak now of the root of the world, from which everything is born again and again. || 146 ||

Even so, if it be argued that birth and destruction could occur even without a cause, he says "no," by the words "of that which is seedless" (*nirbījasya*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include destruction. Since such scriptural passages as "Being alone, my dear... refer to a cause in which name and form are unmanifest, whereas there is no fixed rule for birth and destruction that lack a cause, the theory of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*) is not tenable; this is the meaning. The result of that impossibility is stated as follows:

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "What indeed does one say about this? by saying "Speak! [The meaning is as follows: The non-false similarity between the tree and the person—that is, their commonality which is not untrue and is accepted as a factor in worldly transaction—is as follows: the *utpāṭikā* is said to be the outer bark attached to the tree;
the *utpaṭa* is the resin emerging from that bark; the *śakarāṇi* are the fragments or pieces; and the *kināṭa* is the very fine, bark-like substance adhering to the inner part of the wood.
The meaning of these words from the scripture must be analyzed. || 946 ||
1 Kha. Punarjanī | [Vol.
3, page 208] 9 Brāhmaṇa] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1341
For the Brahmins do not know that which was asked, the root of the world.
Therefore, the cows have been won and taken; they have all departed according to their respective ways. || 147 ||
He analyzes the commentary beginning with "That is not so" (tanneti) as follows: "That" (tad). || 147 ||
That which was asked by Yājñavalkya, and that which the Brāhmaṇas did not know—
By means of the independent Śruti, that supreme Brahman is revealed to us.

He introduces the passage beginning with "consciousness" (vijñāna) and so forth. Regarding the word "asked": independence (*svātantrya*) is the emergence from narrative exposition (*ākhyānataḥ*). ||148||
He who is declared by the words "directly" and so forth, and likewise he who is the innermost of all;
"The Self in the form of the Imperishable is determined to be neither gross nor subtle;
it is the Person of the Upaniṣads who is described here as 'not this, not this. (149)
Now, this [nature] of his is directly indicated by means of scriptural revelation (śruti). || 150 ||

Having restated the subject matter, he clarifies its purport with the words beginning "directly" (*sākṣāt*). The meaning is that this sentence is intended to provide a definitive determination, once again by way of affirmation, regarding that inner Brahman which was previously described both through affirmation and through negation. || 149 ||
That which is called consciousness (vijñāna) is designated as the immutable sentience (caitanya).
It is neither an agent, nor the meaning of a verbal root, nor even that which would be the fruit of an action. (151)
He states the meaning of the term "consciousness" (vijñāna): "Consciousness," he says. To the question, "How is it called immutable? he replies with the words beginning with "not," etc. || 151 ||
Nor is it the case that even its non-existence does not exist, because of scriptural texts such as "not gross" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).
Since even non-existence is witnessed by that [consciousness], from what means of knowledge could its non-existence be established? (152)

Anticipating the objection that "in the absence of the nature of being an agent (*kāraka*) and so forth, there would be an absence of that [agenthood], because existence and non-existence are mutually antagonistic," he says:

"And not... The word "also" (*api*) is used to provide the state of being an agent and so forth as an illustrative example. The word "and" (*ca*) is used to state that we do not accept the total lack of any other mode [of being] due to the mutual opposition between existence and non-existence; rather, [we deny it] by negating the duality of existence and non-existence.

The meaning is that because it is made known by scripture (*śruti*), it is logical for consciousness (*cit*) to possess immutability (*kauṭasthya*). Anticipating the objection—"Since consciousness itself is non-existent, how can there be a specific cognition characterized by immutability? For according to the scriptural statement, 'There is no consciousness after death,' consciousness does not exist"—he says: "Of the non-existence... The intention is that this [point regarding] scripture has been settled in the *Maitreyī* [Brahmaṇa]. || 112 ||
Because the reality of the entities consisting of cause and effect is limited to just this much.
Therefore, by the statement "That thou art," identity is established. || 153 ||

For this reason as well, he states that consciousness (*caitanya*) is immutable (*kūṭastha*). [He says] "only this much" (*etāvanmātra*). The intention is that it has been stated more than once that a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) cannot exist without a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Alternatively, having raised the objection that even if consciousness exists, it lacks immutability because it must be one or the other of cause or effect, he states that it is distinct from both, since those two are superimposed upon it; thus he says "only this much. This is according to the reasoning already stated.
[Vol. 3, page 209] 1342 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:

The sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is cited as the authoritative means of knowledge for the existence of immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthacaitanya*). Thus, it is said: "Therefore," or alternatively, let there be immutable consciousness.
But what follows for the opponent? To this he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 113 ||
Because it has shaken off all causes for the flood of suffering, that is indeed happiness.
Now, according to the scripture, this very one is the supreme, namely, "That which is indeed the Plenum (Bhūman). || 154 ||

He states the meaning of the word "ānanda" (bliss). Regarding the phrase "nirdhūta" (shaken off): since the word "ānanda" commonly signifies sensual pleasure, one might wonder how the consciousness under discussion can itself be bliss. Anticipating this doubt, he provides the authority for its being supreme bliss with the words "atha" (now). || 114 ||
But that which arises from the contact of the sense objects with the senses appears as pleasure, though it is actually suffering.
Because it has a beginning and an end, that suffering is likewise born from the formative forces of suffering.

Regarding what [the opponent] said—that pleasure is indeed sensual happiness—he replies with the words "sensual" (*viṣaya*). Having stated that sensual happiness is not primary because it is a mere semblance due to being permeated by suffering, he states another reason for its being suffering with the words "beginning and end" (*ādyanta*).

He further combines another reason for that very point with the words "suffering" (*duḥkha*). The pain of performing the means [to achieve it] is the latent impression of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃskāra*), and [sensual pleasure] is dependent upon that.
The meaning is that worldly happiness is nothing but suffering. || 155 ||
From the state of luminous consciousness alone, which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else.
Because it is free from ignorance and non-duality, that is directly designated by the word "Brahman. || 156 ||
Having employed the aforementioned qualifiers as the cause, he states the word *brahma* in order to express the qualified object (*viśeṣya*); thus he says: "unrestricted" (*avyāvṛtta*).

Being free from duality due to ignorance means being characterized by the absence of contact with ignorance, its effects, and suffering, and consisting solely in the unity of indivisible bliss. [Verse 116: That which is devoid of ignorance is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which has been described as knowledge (*vidyā*).
He alone manifests falsely in the form of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) and so forth. || 157 ||

How, then, can it have the status of being a cause and so forth? To this he says: "It is with nescience" (sāvidyaḥ). The inner self, characterized as previously described, is said in the Vedāntas to be the cause of the world due to the power of nescience; therefore, the meaning is that it appears falsely as the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), the omniscient, the omnipotent, and so on. || 117 ||
For one who seeks the fruit that is unseen and who abandons the fruit of seen actions.
This Brahman should be the ultimate refuge for the giver of wealth and possessions. || 158 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "rātri" [and so forth]: "adṛṣṭa... || 158 ||
While this [Self] exists as the ruler, there occurs the connection between action and its fruit.
This restriction is logical and applicable to those who perform ritual actions. || 159 ||
Since it is possible for karma itself to bestow its own fruit, why is Brahman said to be the giver of that fruit? To this he replies: "In this...

Since it is impossible for insentient karma to act as a regulator, the restriction regarding the connection of actions and their fruits for those who perform them is logical only when there is an omniscient, omnipotent Controller; therefore, the meaning is that Brahman is the giver of the fruit of those actions. || 159 ||
1 Kha, "Just so, indeed.
[Vol.
3, page 210] 9 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1343.
Thus one wanders in saṃsāra until the Supreme Brahman is reached as the ultimate refuge.
And it is also the material cause of the world, due to its association with ignorance regarding itself. (160)
He recounts the narrative in order to explain the passage beginning with "of one who stands," etc., thus: "In this way. (160)
But for the sage who has become weary of saṃsāra and has renounced all desires, [there is liberation].
For one who stands firm in that knowledge, there shall be completion and the ultimate refuge. || 161 ||

He takes that up with its supplementary explanation: "For one who possesses the *nivida*. This means that for one who is dispassionate, who has performed renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), who practices hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, who realizes the reality, and who is established in that—Brahman is the supreme goal (*parāyaṇa*), which is to say, the final consummation. || 169 ||
Of the sage whose darkness of delusion has been burnt away by the fire of inward awareness.
For one who abides in this oneness, the Self of Brahman is the supreme goal.
He elaborates on what was stated [in verse 161] with the words "dagdha" (burnt), etc. || 162 ||
For those who know that [Brahman], there is no possibility of a cause for difference, because Brahman is devoid of such causes.
The Brāhmaṇa is indeed Brahman itself, the ultimate refuge, both directly and by figurative designation. || 163 ||

Anticipating the objection, "If the wise one is identical with Brahman, how can there be a supreme goal (parāyaṇa) [since there would be no distinction]?", he says: "Of him who knows that" (tadvidas). The word "here" (iha) refers to the discourse on the science of liberation (mokṣa-śāstra). || 163 ||
Or rather, [the distinction is made] by the scriptural passages "where there is another" and "but where for him."
One should explain the ultimate refuge in such a way as not to contradict the meaning of what has been stated.

One might object that it is improper to say that for those who perform ritual actions (*karmiṇaḥ*) Brahman is the supreme goal (*parāyaṇa*) through difference, whereas for the knower (*viduṣaḥ*) it is through non-difference, because it is impossible for a single term like "supreme goal" to have two different meanings. Anticipating this, he says: "Where... (the verse). The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "In the state of ignorance (*avidyā-daśā*) there is difference, while in the state of knowledge (*vidyā-daśā*) there is its absence.

He states the resulting conclusion: that, in accordance with the difference and non-difference understood from the two respective passages, the nature of being the supreme goal must be described in both ways.
Thus it is said: || 164 ||
Therefore, for those immersed in darkness, Brahman is the supreme goal only through the perception of difference.
And for one whose ignorance has been destroyed, because of oneness with the Self, liberation is the supreme goal. || 165 ||
He summarizes the two kinds of ultimate resort with the words: "Therefore... (165).
This word "Brahmānanda" (Bliss of Brahman) is employed as a synonym for happiness.
And in the world, the designation "bliss" (ānanda) is applied to pleasure that is experienced. || 166 ||

It has been stated that Brahman, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), is the locus of bondage and liberation through ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*). Now, desiring to investigate the bliss of Brahman, he states the accepted meaning: "In Brahman," and so forth. An objection may be raised: "If the word 'bliss' is applied to Brahman, does not the intended blissfulness of Brahman thereby become established? He replies, "Not so," because that [bliss] is an object of cognition (*vedya*), whereas Brahman is not an object of cognition (*avedya*). Thus he says: "In the cognizable... (*saṃvedye*).
And so [ends the section]. || 166 ||
The word "bliss" (ānanda) is also seen elsewhere as a qualifying attribute.
Therefore, this bliss should be investigated with diligent effort within the Vedāntas. || 167 ||
1344 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]:
He states that the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) is not heard here alone as a qualifier of Brahman, but is also found in another Śruti passage.

"By way of being a qualifier" means, in other [texts] such as the Taittirīya and so forth. Having stated the consensus, he declares that it is the task of the investigator [to determine this], beginning with the words "Therefore. The meaning is: because of the scriptural statement that the bliss of the object of knowledge (vedyānanda) is a qualifier of Brahman, which is not an object of knowledge (avedya). || 167 ||
Likewise, it is heard in the Taittirīya Śruti: "Bliss is Brahman."
And this very [point] will be explained later in the sequel with the words "atha eṣa eva. || 168 ||

He clarifies that the word "bliss" (ānanda) also occurs in another Vedic text as a qualifier of Brahman, stating: "Bliss. The word "likewise" (tathā) serves to include other passages such as "Knowing the bliss of Brahman," or it may serve as an illustration based on this scriptural evidence. He states: "Now," indicating that the scriptural mention of bliss is also seen in the remainder of the passage as a qualifier of Brahman; this is a Vedic usage.
Causing a fracture in the joints. || 168 ||
"The Infinite is bliss"—such is the statement of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
It is investigated whether this bliss is something to be experienced or not.

He takes up the passage beginning with "That which is indeed *bhūman*," etc., stating: "*Bhūman*. It was stated that bliss (*ānanda*) is to be investigated within Brahman; regarding that, he describes the nature of the investigation: "This is to be known" (verse 169).
If the bliss of Brahman were perceivable in the same manner as worldly bliss, then these words would appropriately be denoters of the bliss of Brahman. (170)

He wishes to demonstrate the result in both cases with the words "in Brahman. The sense is that otherwise, because there would be a difference between the word and its meaning in worldly usage versus the Veda, it would contradict the logical principle that the meaning of a sentence is uniform. However, it should be understood that if [Brahman] were not an object of cognition, the scriptural teaching of non-duality (advaita) would be free from contradiction. || 170 ||
If that [reality], whose nature is the bliss of direct experience, is ascertained through the words [of the teacher], [then one attains it].
If it is thought that nothing further needs to be considered there, since [the object] has already been understood through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); || 171 ||
It sets aside [the need for] deliberation. "It is experienced" means that; "that" refers to Brahman. A statement has been cited. Therein, bliss is indicated. || 171 ||
For in that [system], one observes statements whose meanings are mutually contradictory.
Brahman, whose object is beyond all measure, is renowned everywhere.

He states that an inquiry into that Brahman must indeed be undertaken, because one observes scriptural passages with mutually contradictory meanings regarding it, and such an inquiry is necessary for the purpose of determining its true meaning. He begins with "No" (na) and so forth. To the question, "How is there the observation of contradictory-meaning statements regarding Brahman?", he replies: "Because it transcends all means of knowledge" (atipramāṇa). Brahman is heard of in all the Vedas as existing beyond those [means of knowledge].
And the meaning is that knowability in that [Brahman] is surpassed by the word "bliss" (ānanda). || 172 ||
"But where [it is said] 'But as for that' (yatra tu asya), and furthermore, 'not from seeing' (na dṛṣṭeḥ)."
And the Śruti declares that it is something entirely other than both the known and the unknown. || 173 ||
1 ga. *niṣṭhita* | 2 ka. *yama* | [Vol.
3, page 212] 9 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1345.

He clarifies that very act of hearing with the words "where... (yatra). The sense is that because there is a conflict of scriptures (āgama-vipratipatti)—due to the employment of words that indicate bliss as being beyond the scope of objects and words that indicate Brahman as being an object of knowledge—the investigation must be undertaken. || 173 ||
Likewise, some maintain that liberation is devoid of bliss.
Therefore, an investigation must be carried out for the purpose of refuting those [objections] as well. (174)

He states another reason for the existence of that effect, namely the disagreement among disputants, with the words "devoid of bliss" (*nirānandam*). The meaning of the word "likewise" (*tathā*) is that others [hold it to be] "with bliss" (*sānandam*).

He states the result of this disagreement with the words "of them. The particle *api* is used to indicate that even for those who argue that liberation is devoid of bliss, there would be a contradiction with scripture (*śruti*) if [the state] were not to be rejected. From this disagreement arises doubt; hence [the word] "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
The meaning of the word [is as follows]. || 174 ||
And here, the impossibility of conceptual construction arises because of the nature of the actual reality of things.
This alternative applies to action, but not to a real entity, because [alternatives] are impossible in the case of a real entity. || 175 ||

The objection that "an investigation must be conducted because of the two conflicting views" is incorrect, since an option is possible—just as in the case of the *udita* (post-sunrise) and *anudita* (pre-sunrise) fire-offerings. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the case of an option... Here, the term "here" (*atra*) refers to the statement regarding the bliss of liberation (*muktyānanda*). [The opponent asks: Even if it is a reality (*vastu*), why is it [restricted] to bliss?

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not accepted there; to this he says: "In action. The impossibility [of conceptual construction] is due to the fact that a real entity (*vastu*), being established as it is, is unfit for conceptualization. || 175 ||
And because of the disagreement among disputants; for some disputants maintain [this view].
Some declare that in liberation there is a bliss that is not to be experienced. 176.
Having established that [the opponent] must engage in investigation due to the two types of misconception, he states another reason for that very point: "The proponent," etc. (176).
Therefore, an investigation into this matter must be diligently undertaken by means of logical reasoning.
For the sake of establishing a correct conclusion regarding both sides of the argument. || 177 ||

Anticipating the objection that there is redundancy because a similar disagreement was already stated previously, [the author] says "it must be performed," considering that since the disagreement as to whether bliss exists in Brahman or not has been resolved, the doubt remains as to whether that bliss in it is knowable or unknowable; thus, in accordance with that, inquiry must be undertaken. Here, "Brahman-bliss" is the meaning of the locative case. [The purpose is] the refutation of the opposing view.

Effort. Regarding both the preceding and subsequent positions, the distinction is that in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the certainty [of the opponent] is incorrect and thus not to be accepted, whereas in the other [the final position], it is to be accepted. || 977 ||
First, let it be understood here that Brahman is that which consists of the bliss of being experienced.
From such scriptural statements as "eating, playing, and rejoicing," and so forth. || 178 ||

Having stated the investigation along with its purpose and fruit as the task to be performed, he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "saṃvedya" etc. Here, "here" refers to liberation (*mukti*). || 178 ||
But surely, if there is oneness, there can be no division here that rests upon causal factors.
Moreover, even in the world, it is observed that an action is accomplished by many agents. || 179 ||

[Vol. 3, Page 213] 1946 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) raises an objection: "But surely," etc. Even though Brahman is non-dual and there is an absence of the distinction between the factors of action (*kāraka*), its being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*)— [The text continues: ...is not impossible, because it is seen that even in the case of a single entity, such as the sun, there exists a distinction between the knower and the known. For instance, when one says, "I see the sun," the sun is the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the self is the knower (*vedaka*). Similarly, in the case of the cognition "I know myself," the self is both the knower and the object of knowledge. Therefore, since the distinction between the knower and the known is observed even in the case of a single entity, there is no contradiction in Brahman being both the subject and the object of knowledge. Thus, the objection is raised: "But surely, even if Brahman is non-dual and lacks the division of causal factors, its status as an object of knowledge is not untenable."
He states what the inconsistency in that case is: "bhūri" (abundant). The particle *api* has the sense of pervasion (*abhivyāpti*). The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). || 179 ||
Furthermore, because consciousness is an action, it cannot be established without causal factors.
Therefore, it is not logical that bliss should be an object of cognition within Brahman here.

Even though action is to be accomplished through a variety of causal factors (*kāraka*), what does that have to do with knowledge? To this he says: "Of knowledge" (*vijñānasya*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also of knowledge. He states the conclusion regarding the impossibility of knowledge in liberation: "Not from this" (*nātaḥ*). || 180 ||
This is not a fault; consciousness would indeed have bliss as its object.
Because of the authority of the scriptural statement, "Consciousness is bliss. (181)
Relying on the authority of scripture, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) says, beginning with "No" (na), etc. [Verse 189].
But surely, even though such sentences exist, this [meaning] is not determined from them.
When the opponent's statement is heard, which brings about the realization of the truth of the oneness of the Self.

Having stated that bliss is knowledge within non-dual Brahman on the authority of scripture, [the author] raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). The meaning is: even though there are statements such as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and so forth, there is no cognition whose object is bliss, because those texts intend to convey the identity between bliss and knowledge. Furthermore, he says "contradictory" (*pratyarthinī*), meaning that if Brahman were an object, it would contradict statements such as "not coarse" (*asthūla*). Moreover, in the *tat tvam asi* and other such sentences...
He asks: how can there be objectivity in that which makes known the inward, single-flavored [Self]? He says: "When... (verse 182).
For indeed, even in the world, nothing whatsoever [is established] by contradiction with another means of valid cognition.
Therefore, pride arises; hence, this is not definitively established.

Furthermore, the distinction between the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, for one who asserts their non-distinction within the Self (*ātman*), there is a contradiction; hence, he states that knowledge does not have the bliss of the essential nature (*svarūpānanda*) as its object, beginning with the words "mānāntara... (by other means of knowledge). The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even in the world" (*loke'pi*) serves to indicate pervasion, or it may serve to provide the example of the Veda.
This is what is meant by the statement that bliss is an object of consciousness (*saṃvedyatva*) in Brahman. || 183 ||
And because means of knowledge are manifestors, they must be employed with respect to an already established entity.
Even if it were an agent, since it would not be an effect, what you have stated is difficult to conceive.

Furthermore, regarding whether a means of knowledge (*māna*) is a revealer (*bodhaka*) or a producer (*kāraka*), he first addresses this by stating, "And because of its being a revealer" (*vyañjakatvāt*). If it were a revealer, then prior to its own arising, it would manifest its object either as something already established or as something not yet established. In that case, the inner Self-Brahman, which consists of bliss, could not be manifested as an object, because of the scriptural teaching on its non-objectivity (*aviṣayatva*); therefore, the meaning is that the bliss of Brahman is not an object of cognition (*vedya*).

He refutes the second [position] with the words "even if it were a causal factor" (*kārakatve’pi*). The meaning is that if the means of knowledge (*māna*) were a causal factor, then since bliss already established as Brahman cannot be produced, the means of knowledge could not produce the bliss of Brahman; therefore, your desired view—that it is knowable by such a means—would not be established. Furthermore, the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is that it is improper for the means of knowledge to be a causal factor, as that would entail the consequence of its being a non-means of knowledge (*amānatva*). || 184 ||
Is it not the case that the cognition "I am happy" is indeed experienced?
Perception does not contradict an object that consists of posterior bliss, because of the contradiction [otherwise]. || 185 ||
1 kha. Therein he says: 2 kha. ‘yakṣa’. [Vol. 3, page 214] 9 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1347.

The proponent of the prima facie view says: "But surely" (*nanu*). Since the fact that bliss is an object of cognition is established by one's own experience, no contradiction with perception or other means of knowledge should be suspected regarding its being an object of cognition; for no other means of knowledge arises when there is a contradiction with one's own experience. This is the meaning. || 185 ||
This is not so, because consciousness is not possible in liberation.
For this liberation is the absence of the body; therefore, the instruments [of action] do not exist.

When it is urged that "Bliss is to be known in Brahman," the author establishes the final position (siddhānta) by saying, "This is not so. He states that the first alternative—that adventitious or non-adventitious knowledge perceives bliss in liberation—is not tenable. He provides the reason for this with the word "yataḥ" (because). Therein, he states the reason for the impossibility of adventitious knowledge with the word "deha" (the body). Therefore, due to the absence of a cause, there is no establishment of occasional knowledge in that state; this is the remainder of the sense. || 1.86 ||
Furthermore, consciousness cannot arise independently of the sense organs and other such factors.
If that were the case, the appropriation of a body and so forth would be purposeless.
Likewise, because it would contradict its unity, the supreme [consciousness] cannot consist of bliss that is an object of cognition.

Anticipating the objection that even in the absence of the body and its instruments (kāryakaraṇa), the knowledge of the bliss of Brahman will arise in liberation—since in transmigratory existence there is indeed a dependence upon causes—he refutes this by way of an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) with the words "the instruments, etc. He refutes the second [objection] with the word "tathā" (so too). Just as the bliss of Brahman is not the object of adventitious knowledge, so too it is not the object of non-adventitious knowledge; for Brahman is not something whose nature as bliss is to be known by itself.
The meaning is: because of the distinction between the object and the subject. || 187 ||
If Brahman, whose nature is bliss, eternally [perceives] itself by itself;
Because that consciousness is eternal, one should know that it is indeed eternal. || 188 ||
Furthermore, whether it be Brahman, the liberated soul, or the transmigrating soul, [the text] restates that it would experience the bliss of Brahman; this is expressed by the word "yadi" (if).
The meaning is that Brahman always knows itself as being of the nature of bliss through its own self in all states, because its own knowledge is eternally present. || 188 ||
Just as water in that [water] becomes one with it, so too the transmigrating soul attains oneness.
"All things become one; they do not exist as separate entities. (189)
Therefore, for the sake of even a slight realization of Brahman, whose nature is bliss—
One who possesses even that [bliss] does not know his own innate bliss of Brahman in such a way. || 190 ||
Even though liberated, he is not a transmigrating being, because of the identity of those two.
"The liberated one experiences supreme bliss"—therefore, that statement is false. (199)

Regarding the second [view] as well, [the author], while restating the position of non-difference—that the liberated one is non-different from Brahman—says "in water": just as water poured into water does not exist separately, so too the liberated one, having previously been in saṃsāra, upon reaching oneness with Brahman in liberation, does not remain in any way as something separate from Him to know His bliss; rather, being non-different, he experiences the bliss of Brahman in the supreme, imperishable state.

The meaning is that this follows from the Vedic scripture stating, "All become one. In that context, he refutes the view that Brahman takes its own bliss as an object: "Not [so], for it is independent," and "Nor [is there an object]. (Variant readings: 1. *apekṣasya na ca*;
Pra.
[Vol. 3, page 215] 1348 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Third Adhyāya]

"Regarding the word 'tat' (that): it means that [the liberated soul] does not know that Brahman as the bliss of its own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*), because due to their identity (*aikya*), the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayitva*) is untenable in a single locus.
By the aforementioned reasoning, he refutes the possibility of the liberated one—who is non-different from Brahman—taking that bliss as an object. Likewise, the third [alternative]..."

He states: "And not... Because of the identity between the liberated one and the transmigrating soul, the other [the transmigrator] is also Brahman like the liberated one; therefore, due to the contradiction between the object and the agent [of knowledge], there is no knowing of the bliss of Brahman—this is the meaning. He concludes the impossibility of the three positions with: "The liberated one... That statement is an elliptical illustration for both the transmigrating soul and Brahman. (189) (190) (191)
Then another, being liberated like a jar or other objects, perceives the bliss of Brahman through the mouth of the Vedas.
If another were to know the state of Brahman, then that oneness would be contradicted. || 192 ||

He restates the position that there is a difference between the liberated one and Brahman, beginning with the word "Brahman. He refutes it by citing the contradiction with such scriptural texts as the *Tattvamasi* ("That thou art"), beginning with the words "Brahman-hood. || 992 ||
"Regarding the notion that 'there is no consciousness after death,' it is scripture itself that negates this."
In liberation, the cognition of distinction arises solely from the cause of oneness. || 193 ||
Furthermore, he states that in liberation, the bliss of Brahman is not an object of adventitious knowledge: "Having departed... (193).
The statement regarding the analogy of woman and man, and that which is expressed as "that indeed."
He declares the impossibility of a knower and so forth, due to the cause of being an unchanging unity.

In that very context, he states another passage: "A woman," etc. This refers to the statement using the analogy of a man and a woman, beginning with: "Just as one embraced by a beloved wife knows nothing external nor internal," and so forth. Another passage begins: "That which he does not see there, though seeing indeed, he does not see," and so forth. He summarizes the meaning of these two: "The knower, etc. (Verse 194).
Furthermore, numerous scriptural statements such as "not this, not this" would be contradicted.
In the acceptance of [categories] such as the agent (kāraka) and so forth, there would be liberation in the absolute Brahman alone. || 195 ||
