He states another reason for the absence of distinctions between action and its factors within Brahman: "Not so," etc. (199).
And because consciousness and bliss are one, there is neither conjunction nor disjunction.
This conceptualization whose object is bliss and knowledge is a futile exertion. || 196 ||

Now, since there is no contradiction with the aforementioned scripture because bliss is not experienced through adventitious knowledge in the state of liberation, it may be accepted that Brahman knows the bliss of the Self only through eternally established knowledge; thus, its status as an object of knowledge is secured. Furthermore, although there is a contradiction between the object and the agent elsewhere, such a contradiction does not exist in the case of the omniscient Brahman.

There is no such flaw; therefore, he says: "In consciousness" (*vijñāne*). Since bliss (*ānanda*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) must be coreferential, and because they are non-different from Brahman, it is impossible for them to be mutually different. Consequently, the conceptualization that bliss is the object and knowledge is the subject—as in the statement "one knows Brahman as bliss"—is not tenable.
Indeed, there can be no contradiction in one instance while there is no contradiction elsewhere; nor does the Omniscient One turn what is non-existent into something existent.
Such is the meaning. || 196 ||
It is only logical that ignorance occurs when there is an attachment to the cognition of an object as something other than what it is.
One knows "Brahman is bliss," but not [the bliss] within the Self that is a mass of pure consciousness.
[The text continues: ...from the poison of worldly existence, O venerable one...
[kha.
'jñatvam |] [Vol. 3, page 216] 9 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1349.
He states another reason for the fact that Brahman’s own bliss cannot be an object of cognition: "Through ignorance," etc. (197).
"Even if one accepts the consequence that there would be cognitions of other objects due to ignorance,"
Otherwise, Brahman would certainly incur the state of being bound by birth and the like, as well as the quality of insentience. || 198 ||

One might raise the objection: "Even for Brahman, who is a mass of knowledge (*jñānaghana*) and whose nature is self-luminous (*svaprakāśātman*), there exist ignorance and the cognition of other objects; for we observe that even the sun, though self-luminous, has both non-shining and shining aspects. Therefore, it is not illogical to say that Brahman knows its own bliss. Anticipating this, he says: "Ignorance... (verse 198).
Therefore, [the statement] beginning with "consciousness" refers to the object as it actually exists.
The explanatory discourse is to be accepted, not that which prescribes knowledge and so forth. || 199 ||

If it is objected that the relationship of object and subject is untenable in the case of Brahman as the knowledge of bliss (*ānandajñāna*), one might ask how such statements as "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) are to be understood. Anticipating this doubt, the author concludes by saying, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He states "No" (*na*) to exclude the notion that these [scriptural passages] do not teach that consciousness possesses subjectivity, bliss possesses objectivity, Brahman possesses the status of a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), and the other two possess the status of qualities (*guṇa*). || 199 ||
Furthermore, that which was stated beginning with "eating" (jakṣat) and so forth is also not contradictory.
Because the Knower consists of all things, he possesses hands and feet on every side.
Having restated the claim that the bliss of Brahman is to be known in liberation based on scriptural passages such as "eating and playing," he refutes it: "Regarding 'eating and playing,' etc.

The meaning is that just as the text "having hands and feet everywhere, having eyes, heads, and faces everywhere" declares the identity with all things (*sarvātmatā*), so too here, because the sage's identity with all is intended to be expressed, there is no contradiction in the bliss being unknowable [in its ordinary sense]. || 200 ||
In the bodies of yogis, gods, and others, eating and other such activities will be possible.
Because the wise one is the self of all, there may be the praise of liberation and the removal [of obstacles]. || 201 ||
He explains how the scriptural mention of eating and so forth can be reconciled even for the wise one who is the Self of all: "The yogi," etc.
He states the purpose of restating the attainment of eating and so forth: "It may be," etc. (209).
The highest Self is considered to be like one who eats in liberation, because it is the self of all.
Even the state of suffering has been attained by embodied beings in such places as Kumbhīpāka.

He raises an objection, fearing that if there were a restatement of the attainment of eating and so forth by the wise one through his identity with all (sārvātmya) in the context of the "eating" section and others, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasakti):
"It is held... (matam iti). || 202 ||

It is not so, because [the self] is caused by the superimposition of suffering born from the delusion produced by contact with the support of the aggregates, vital breaths, and so forth, which arise from name and the rest. || 203 ||

He refutes [the objection] as follows: "No, because the perception of bondage in the Self is due to the superimposition of suffering—which is dependent on false knowledge caused by the connection with the two-fold limiting adjuncts (upādhi) fashioned by ignorance and name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Therefore, suffering does not exist there in reality, nor do eating and so forth; for while the mention of liberation is for the sake of praising the one who is free from ignorance, there is no mention of suffering—even though it is based on ignorance—because that would result in [the Self] being inferior. Thus he says: "Not at all..."
Thus [it is said]. || 203 ||
1 kha. *payate* | 2 kha, *bhūtapi* | [Vol.
3, page 217] 1350 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Third Adhyāya]...
And there is no distinction among the objects of those whose statements are mutually contradictory.
This has already been stated by us previously, exactly as it is, through logical arguments.

As for the objection that the meaning of the scripture remains undetermined because of the perception of contradictory scriptural statements, he replies to that with the verse beginning "viṣaye" (regarding the object). The word "prāk" (previously) refers to the statement in the Madhu-brāhmaṇa. || 204 ||
Because of the identity of the meanings of the terms "bliss," "Brahman," and "consciousness."
Therefore, a relation [of identity] in Brahman is not accepted here, as it is in the case of a blue lotus and the like. || 205 ||

It has been stated that the Brahman-bliss expressed by sentences such as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and so forth is non-objectifiable (*avedya*). Some, however, maintain that the meaning of a sentence is either a relation (*saṃsarga*) or a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), and thus do not accept that sentences like "consciousness" have an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*). To address them, he says: "Bliss," etc.

For these words terminate in a single referent—the meaning of the nominal stem *brahma*—which is what is desired to be known, just as in the case of words such as "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*). And thus, [they function] through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The sense is that because a sentence is a valid cause for [the cognition of] reality only when there is no relation [of syntactical connection], it possesses an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*); otherwise, a sentence that does not convey what is intended to be known would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*). The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is connected with the fifth case of the preceding [verse]. The mention of "relation" (*saṃsarga*) is intended to indicate the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) as well as the indicated (*upalakṣaṇa*). || 205 ||
From the mortal [state], there is a hundredfold increase, progressing further and further upward.
The ultimate state of that which consists of cause and effect is considered to be supreme bliss. || 206 ||

He states the supremacy of Brahman-bliss, which consists of the single flavor of non-objectifiable consciousness, with the words "from mortal... and so forth. Bliss, being the fruit of action, arises from that [action]; furthermore, through desire and other such factors, another bliss arises. For the followers of the Veda, unlike the Vaiśeṣikas, there is no fixed rule regarding the production of heterogeneous effects from pleasures and the like. Thus, for bliss existing in the form of cause and effect, beginning from human bliss and proceeding further and further—

The meaning is that because it culminates in the bliss of Brahman—which is devoid of all differentiation and possesses excellence through its preeminence across the stages (bhūmis)—this [bliss] is considered the supreme one in the Vedas. || 206 ||
The experience of bliss is held to depend precisely upon the means of accomplishment and so forth.
Even that worldly [bliss] is perishable and likewise born from the formative forces of suffering.
But in the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), it has no further dependence, being free from all desire for spiritual means.
The Self alone is the true nature of bliss; therefore, there is no need for means such as knowledge and the like.

Anticipating the objection that if the bliss already described were non-objective (*avedya*), there would be no performance of spiritual means for its direct realization, [the author] replies: worldly awareness of pleasure, which consists of a modification of the intellect (*dhīvṛtti*), is held to depend on causal factors (*kāraka*), to be perishable, and to be produced by passion and the like; however, in the case of the unity of the Self (*aikātmya*), there is no dependence on causal factors, because the awareness of bliss therein is beginningless and endless and independent of everything, whereas the performance of rites serves merely as a removal of obstacles.

He states that [liberation] is due to its being the destruction [of suffering], using the words "by means of the proof" (*sādhanāt*) and so forth. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is for the purpose of including the prover (*sādhayitr*) and others. "The impression of suffering" (*duḥkhasaṃskāra*) refers to passion (*rāga*) and the like. Regarding the statement that in liberation the experience of bliss is independent, he states another reason: "the Self alone" (*ātmaiva*). Therefore, he concludes that neither in regard to knowledge nor in regard to bliss is any means (*sādhana*) to be required: "not from this" (*nātaḥ*). || 207 || 208 ||
It is not insentient because it is of the nature of knowledge; it is not devoid of bliss because it is bliss itself.
"Because its nature is Brahman, which has no end," according to the authority of the scriptural statement. || 209 ||

If the sentence beginning with "vijñāna" were intended to convey the meaning as previously stated, then since that would be established by a single word alone, the other words would be redundant. Thus it is argued.

Anticipating the objection that even if the referents indicated by words such as "consciousness" (vijñāna) are one and the same, they still possess meaningfulness due to the difference in their excluded referents (vyāvartyabheda), he says:
"Not insentient" (na jaḍam). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the established, indivisible Brahman. || 209 ||
In deep sleep, its nature as pure bliss is determined.
[It is known] by means of a nature that is the experience of nothing other [than itself], from which all [external] measures and so forth have been excluded. || 210 ||
Thus ends the ninth Brāhmaṇa of the third Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.
In this fifth [chapter], thirteen [topics] are to be known in brief.
I shall explain hundreds [of points] in the Vārtika treatise; hereafter, in the sixth [chapter].
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣyavārtika*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Sureśvarācārya.
The fifth chapter, according to the sequence of the Upaniṣad. || 5 ||

Stating another reason for the fact that the bliss of Brahman is not an object of cognition, he concludes the meaning of the Brāhmaṇa passage with the words "Ānanda... etc. The meaning is as follows: because one who has awakened possesses a reflective awareness (parāmarśa), and because there is an exclusion of the objects of perception and so forth, it is established—even in the absence of adventitious knowledge—that during deep sleep there is an experience of happiness; thus, the reality consisting of pure consciousness and unsurpassed bliss is proven. || 210 ||
Thus ends the ninth Brāhmaṇa of the third Adhyāya in the Commentary on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Vārtika-Ṭīkā.

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śāstraprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Sureśvaravārttika*, composed by the venerable Bhagavadānandajñāna, disciple of the venerable Śuddhānanda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya*). 3.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 6,910.
Previously, some verses numbering 100,000 (khakhāmibhūmitāḥ) were recited by someone; those do not exist in this chapter today, but there are now 1,980 verses (khādvibhūmitāḥ).
[Volume 3, Page 219] [Volume 3,
Page 220] Now begins the fourth chapter.
Brahman is bliss, consciousness, and characterized by such attributes as being directly manifest.
This has now been determined at the end of the fifth [chapter] by means of the method of debate (jalpanyāya). || 1 ||
Furthermore, by means of the deities of speech and so forth, it is for the sake of his very acquisition of that [knowledge].
The sixth chapter is now commenced with effort, by means of the *Vādanyāya*.
It is known that there exists Brahman— free from the entire range of internal limiting adjuncts, pure, supreme, luminous, full of bliss, and having cast aside the manifestation of duality.
In that state, which is the source of both intellect and speech, my mind is forever established.
In me, who am the realization of the Self, whose greatness is being comprehended through the Vedantas; || 1 ||
Having determined that the inner Brahman is existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*) in the preceding chapter, the author, beginning this new chapter, recapitulates what has been discussed:

"Bliss," etc. The word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) refers to the limit of the fifth [member], just as words such as *buddhānta* do; or, according to the logic of *jalpa*, it refers to the primary argument concerning victory and defeat accomplished by four members—this is the meaning. He states the purport of the subsequent chapter:

"Presently" (*sāṃpratam*) means by way of superimposing the vision of Brahman upon the deities such as Agni, who preside over speech and the other organs. "Of that very [Brahman]" refers to the fivefold Brahman characterized by "directly" (*sākṣāt*) and so forth. "By the method of debate" (*vādanyāyena*) means by the method primarily concerned with determining the truth through the sequence of disciple and teacher. "Effort" (*yatnaḥ*) is the establishment of one's own position by refuting the positions of others. || 1 || 2 ||
The mention of "a group of months" is for the purpose of understanding the appropriate time.
Then, having understood that [was the] right time, the sage approached the lord of the earth.

Having explained the relationship between the two chapters as that of the "instigator" (*utthāpaka*) and the "instigated" (*utthāpya*)— inasmuch as one who has rightfully attained victory over others and self-conquest achieves mental composure in the determination of reality— and having accepted the connection of the Brāhmaṇa as stated in the Commentary, namely that this [chapter] is for the purpose of explaining that [composure] once the desire to know the specific means for the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman-as-Self has arisen; [the author], wishing to explain the meaning of the words, proceeded with the following.

He states what is intended [by the author]: "The appropriate," etc. The meaning is that in the sentence beginning with "Janaka gave" (*janako ha*), etc., what is intended is that the king granted an audience to the petitioners in order to inform them of the opportunity suitable for seeing him. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then" (*atha*):
"The ritual procedure" (*kalpam*), which means "having known the time suitable for the audience. The word *atha* is used for the purpose of imitating the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). || 3 ||
"Have you come seeking cattle, or are you seeking questions for subtle determination?"
"What have you come to say? the king asked that sage.

He explains the passage beginning with "taṃ ha" (to him, indeed) as follows: "paśūn" (animals). The meaning of the phrase "ending with the atom" (aṇvantān) has been stated: that your arrival was for the purpose of either hearing from me the questions whose fruit is the determination of subtle matters, or for speaking their answers. || 4 ||
170 1 ka. gha. ‘rūpasaṃ’; 2 gha. ‘tmakajñā’; 3 kha. ‘deśata’; gha. ‘deśe ta’. [vol 3, page 221]
It is appropriate that Brahmins go to the king for the sake of wealth.
But in times of non-distress, O best of the twice-born, seekers of knowledge do not go to him here.

Some, desiring that Yājñavalkya go to the king for the sake of his welfare (*yogakṣema*) and for the sake of knowledge, have asked questions ending with the determination of subtle matters, thinking either, "We shall resolve them from him," or, "Your coming is for this very purpose. To them, he says: "For the sake of wealth. The meaning is based on the traditional law (*smṛti*): "And one should approach a lord for the attainment of welfare (*yoga*) and security (*kṣema*). Now, Gārgya—

He says "no" to the claim that Brahmins such as Prabhṛti are seen going even to a king for the sake of knowledge; he states, "But not [in this case]," meaning that the sphere of scriptural practice is what is intended here. || 1 ||
Knowledge is not found anywhere else except among the Kṣatriyas, where it may be found.
Brahmins always wait upon the Kṣatriyas right there.

He states the purport of the qualification "in times of distress" with the words "not elsewhere. The construction is as follows: where knowledge is never possible from anyone other than a Kṣatriya, there Brāhmaṇas, being seekers of knowledge, approach learned Kṣatriyas. || 6 ||
Even the mere shadow of a text is not accepted as being in the discipleship of Yājñavalkya.
In his status as a disciple of Janaka alone, the shadow of the [original] text is discernible. || 7 ||

Now, in this regard, even the Guru, the Sage, might become a disciple of Janaka. And it was said [by some] that he abandoned his status as a teacher; to this, [the author] says "no," stating "of Yājñavalkya. Nor is there any lack of fitness for him to be a disciple, for he is omniscient.
The meaning is "from you, O Āditya. Anticipating the objection that his status as a disciple appears from the scriptural statement, "Listen to that," he says, "of Janaka.

Through the use of the singular and plural numbers, the roles of disciple and teacher are manifested for the king and the sage respectively; and the sense is that it is possible for even a teacher to pose a question to a disciple for the purpose of purifying the disciple's intellect. || 7 ||
This word "ending with atoms" (aṇvantān) could not be a qualifier of the sacrificial animal.
But because of the phrase "both," the remaining two [questions] must therefore be asked. || 8 ||

One might object that because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "animals with atoms" (*paśūnaṇvantān*), the word "with atoms" functions as an adjective qualifying "animals," and thus there can be no cognition of an option here; anticipating this, he says: "With atoms. He states the remainder of the sentence as the reason for that: "Both.
Even though the word *vā*, which indicates an option, is absent from the king's statement, the perception of an option here arises from the doubt regarding the remaining words of the sage's speech.

The meaning is that, at the commencement [of the section], the determination of the remaining [terms] is established. He states the result of the fact that the word ending in *aṇu* does not convey a specific qualification of the animal: "the two. (8)
Then, for the sake of establishing the cause of that cause, he spoke as follows.
"I desire both of these," for he would have spoken otherwise [if it were not so]. || 9 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "both indeed" as follows: "taddhetu" (the cause of that). The word "tat" (that) is understood from the sense of the question and the mention of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*).
[Vol. 3, page 222]

The meaning is that the Sage stated "both indeed" (ubhayaṃ eva), excluding the word "desire" (icchā), in order to demonstrate respectively the status of being the cause and the status of having a cause for those two [the knower and the known]. Although the word "desire" was reached through the consideration of the question, it was omitted because of the intention to specify a particular result.

The word *atha* has the sense of illumination. One might raise the objection: "When the word 'desire' (*icchā*) is employed, the relationship of cause and effect between those two is established; therefore, the verbal root [of the action] should not be omitted. Anticipating this, he says: "I desire" (*icchāmi*). If one were to say "I desire both of these," then, because both would be primary as objects of desire, the relationship of cause and effect would not exist; for that [relationship] does not arise except through the distinction of subordinate and principal.
The meaning is "steadfastness. || 9 ||
In this context, there should be the goddess of speech (Vāgdevatā), as well as the abode and the sense organ.
Brahman is the ether and the foundation; this is what is called the Upaniṣad. || 10 ||

Regarding the statement "Speech is indeed Brahman," he explains the meaning of the term "speech" with the word "vāk. Regarding the statement "Speech itself is the abode," he excludes [the notion of] the deity as before, using the word "tathā" (so too). He explains the meaning of "Space is the foundation" with the word "brahma" (Brahman). And he explains the meaning of "One should meditate on this as intelligence" with the word "nāma" (name). || 10 ||
He went to the worlds of the Karaṇāyatana gods, who are established in their own self-nature.
Through meditation, one becomes a god here, having wisdom and the like as his secret foundation.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "having become a god" (devo bhūtvā) as follows: "By the instruments," etc. Here, the term "here" refers to the state of being alive. || 11 ||
And likewise, the installation and the secret doctrine in the temple of the deity.
In all these six cases as well, this very same tetrad is to be understood.

He states that, as in the first section, the fourfold group beginning with the deity is to be known as the object of worship in each of the subsequent five sections as well, by saying "the deity. He concludes that this same fourfold group is identical across all six sections by saying "in the six. || 12 ||
The statement "one who possesses a mother" is a statement of the reason (hetu) for the purpose of establishing that [the person] has performed [the action] correctly.
Likewise, the supreme word exists for the purpose of attaining rightness. || 13 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "one who possesses a mother" (*mātṛmān*) as follows: "The phrase 'one who possesses a mother'... The meaning is that the statement "one who possesses a mother," etc., is intended to make known that Śilini and others—who maintain that Brahman consists of speech and so forth—possess perfect eloquence. He introduces the passage beginning with "for [he would be] one who does not speak" (*avadato hi*) as another reason for that very point. "Perfectness" refers to the quality of being an eloquent speaker, such as victory over opponents and the like.
The remainder. || 13 ||
For in this world, there is no human goal whatsoever for one who does not speak.
Whether seen or unseen, let it be understood from this [text] as the *āra* of Brahman. || 14 ||
He explains this with the words "yasmāt" (because). || 14 ||
If that were not so, then Brahman would be described as having its abodes and so forth, like a single foot.
This Brahman is non-dual; it is not fit to be worshipped as something composite.

He states the meaning of "ekapād" and so forth with the words "na cet" (if not). If it is argued that even such meditation on Brahman will produce a fruit, he says "no," with the words "asamastam" (not combined). || 19 ||
Knowing this, you ought to explain to me the four-footed Brahman.
"Speech alone is the abode," Yājñavalkya also said to him.

Thus, he states the result of this distinction: "The cause, etc. Since the entire world, consisting of both effect and cause, is declared to be nothing but the deity, therefore, by means of the vision of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*) upon deities such as Fire, the entire world is intended to be meditated upon in this section as the object of worship; the meaning is that it is not a meditation limited to a single part. "Having become a god"—that is, while still living as a human, through the accumulation of meditative cultivation.

In order to state another intended meaning (*tātparya*) for the passage beginning with "having become a god," he restates the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) [with the words] "as a god. In the same way, there would be a verbal expression such as "having become a god," because of its possibility.
And many statements in response [are made] for the sake of establishing the oneness of the six. || 25 ||

Here, he states the conformity with the literal words of the scripture: "Thus" (*tathā*). According to the stated purport, it is appropriate for the statement "having become a god" (*devo bhūtvā*) to express the fruit of attaining the state of a god, because that [state] is possible as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Anticipating the objection—how can there be the plural expression "the gods" (*devān*) in every section when Agni and the others are seen to be worshipped individually?—he says: "In each sentence. This refers to the six sections (*paryāya*).

The plural number is used everywhere for the purpose of indicating the plurality of meditations (*upāsti*); otherwise, it would follow that "he goes even to each god," which is impossible since a single meditation cannot result in the attainment of multiple deities. Therefore, the meaning of the scriptural statement "to the gods" (*devān*) everywhere is that the meditation occurring in one section is non-different from the meditation occurring in another section. || 25 ||
Just as it was before the realization of Brahman, so too has one become Brahman itself.
Prior to the worship of a deity, there was no such thing as a devotee of a deity. || 26 ||

Having raised the doubt—given that there is identity in the object of worship (*upāsti*) across all alternative modes (*paryāya*), why does that [worship] not yield fruit like the cognition of Brahman (*brahmadhī*)?—the author states the distinction between the two by way of their respective qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*). The phrase "even previously" (*prāgapi*) means that even prior to the knowledge of the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), it is Brahman alone that exists, while ignorance (*ajñāna*) is merely an intervening obstacle;
however, the practitioner (*upāsaka*) was not a "god" (*deva*) prior to his worship, because that state is something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*). || 26 ||
But by the accumulation of cultivation, having become a wise deity even in this very world, one attains [liberation].
Upon the abandonment of the body, he goes to the gods, beginning with Agni, to the supreme state.

He states the disparity even by way of the results: "The cultivation... etc. One must distinguish that during the state of being alive, the "divine state" is the direct realization of identity with That; after death, it is the dissolution into That, which is oneness with It. The meditation on a result that is temporally remote requires repetition until the moment of death (*āprāyaṇāt*); however, the knowledge of Brahman is not like this, because the result of knowledge—expressed as "one who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—is characterized by immediate succession. This is the intended meaning. || 27 ||
The effect, consisting of origination and so forth, is that which is to be accomplished by every action.
Therefore, it is rightly said that even meditative worship (upāsana) is indeed action (karma). || 28 ||

Because no other entity exists that is distinct from the Self.

I know nothing further that must be gone to beyond this fruit of the worship already described. || 32 ||

To the question, "Why do you not understand even what has been said there?", he replies: "Upon the attainment of the deity," etc. The meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that you have stated only that much. Anticipating the objection that he intends to describe something further—namely, the fruit of meditation known as Brahmanhood, which is attained through a succession of stages—he says: "Not from this," etc. For a matter of such profound depth cannot be conveyed by mere intention alone without actual words.
The sense is that it is difficult to understand. || 32 ||
To him who had spoken thus, he replied: "I shall now tell that to you."
O lord of men, when you are released, you shall go wherever you wish.
"Then," and so forth, he takes up [the passage]. Regarding the phrase "to him who had spoken thus": the meaning of the word *atha* is the immediate succession to the King's desire to know. || 33 ||
Since, upon the destruction of mere ignorance, [the goal] is attained as if it were already reached.
Therefore he says, "You shall go," just as one who has attained composure [speaks].
Anticipating the objection that the statement "you will go" is improper because movement to another location has been refuted, he says: "Ignorance.

In this regard, he provides a worldly illustration: "Health. Health is indeed self-established, yet when it is obstructed by fever or the like, it is said that Caitra has attained it upon the removal of those obstacles by means of medicine and so forth; likewise, although Brahman is eternally attained, [it is spoken of as such] due to the removal of obstructions.
The meaning is that the sage said to the king, "By dispelling [the notion of] knowledge, you shall attain [it]. || 34 ||
In this context, comprehension itself is intended by the term "going."
For he will declare that "you have attained [it]" merely upon the arising of knowledge. || 35 ||

If it is argued that the attainment of Brahman results from the destruction of ignorance, then how can there be the application of terms such as "going" (*gati*) in that context? To this, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is that going is impossible for that which is already established [as the Self]. The phrase under discussion refers to the locative sense. When "going" is used to denote knowledge, he cites the remainder of the passage as supporting evidence: "Having attained" (*prāptaḥ*). || 35 ||
This person named Indha who resides in the right eye—
The deity residing within the sun, whose abode and other attributes have been explained, [is present there]. || 36 ||

Having first made the promise to explain that which is to be gone to by means of the words beginning with "atha," and having considered the objection—"Why is there an explanation of the waking state and so forth without that [destination]?"—he shows Viśva, who possesses the conceit of being awake, for the sake of that very purpose. The phrase "He is named Indha" [is explained] with the remainder of the text: "The eye itself is his abode," and so on;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), what is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhā* and *Upaniṣad* sections is included. || 36 ||
1. *ka*, *sva*, *ga*: in the eye. [Vol.
3, page 232] 2. Brāhmaṇa: accompanied by the commentary known as the *Śākhaprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1365.
Because he consumes fuel day and night, the Puruṣa is therefore called "Indhana" (the Fuel-eater).
Some excellence may be observed here in the right eye through scriptural revelation.
Generally, among men, it is observed that the right arm is more powerful than the left.
Therefore, the seizing of the right eye is for the purpose of attaining the state of being the enjoyer.

Regarding how the word *indh* (the kindler) applies to the one who identifies with the waking state (*viśva*), he says: "It is kindled" (*idhyate*). The meaning is that because it always manifests during the waking state as the enjoyer of gross objects. He states two reasons for the specification "in the right eye" (*dakṣiṇe'kṣan*): by means of scripture (*śrutyā*).
The enjoyment of Viśva, the lord of the city, must be stated as being manifest in some particular place, just as in the worldly case; that manifestation occurs in the right eye.
Therefore, he states the conclusion: "The specific statement is for the sake of establishing its status as an enjoyer," since that [status] is established by scripture and experience.
In the right eye, this person known as "Indha" is recognized as the enjoyer;
though he is indeed Indha, they designate that Self by the name Indra. (39)
Having avoided mentioning [the person] by name directly, [one speaks] indirectly.
Since the gods are fond of being addressed by their names when they are out of sight, therefore—

Introducing the passage beginning with "him" (tam), he states the meaning of the word "this one" (etam) as "the right one" (dakṣiṇa). Alternatively, taking up the sentence, he explains it as "kindling" (indham). He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "those who love the indirect" (parokṣapriyāḥ) as "the indirect" (parokṣa). The connection is: "Therefore, they call him by the name Indra. (39–40)
For the deities take pleasure when their names are invoked in their absence.
Therefore, human beings address him by name only indirectly. || 41 ||
Here he states the worldly consensus, which is indicated by the word "hi" (for/indeed): "it is called the name of the unperceived. || 41 ||
Do not worry about how people outside [the tradition] might understand the true nature of the Name.
Therefore, the mention of the deity's name in the absence [of the person] is pleasing to him.
With what intention do the deities delight in the mention of their names in absentia? To this, he says: "Lest you should recognize us. (42)
Even in this world, people harbor hatred toward those who utter their names directly.
And they desire to be addressed with the words, "Śreyāṃsa, such-and-such a gentleman, is here. || 43 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "those who hate what is perceptible" with the words "pratyakṣa... etc. The word "api" implies even deities. He further states that they feel pleasure when their names are mentioned indirectly with the words "amuka... etc. || 43 ||
The wife of that very Lord of Food (Annapati), who is situated in the left eye, is called Virāj because she is the object of enjoyment; he who is in the right eye is her enjoyer.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Now this," etc., [in the words] "Of that. Being the lord of food (*annapati*) means being the enjoyer; for this very reason, it is said that he is its enjoyer.
He states the reason why the wife is designated by the term *virāj*: "Because she is the object of enjoyment" (*bhogyatvāt*). || 44 ||

For indeed, the division of the one and only God is according to his stations and deities.
It is described here for the purpose of meditation by means of the Vedic scripture, in the form of Agni and Soma.

Now, [the author] says "no" to the claim that a distinction between enjoyer and enjoyed has been accepted for Indra and Indrāṇī. He says, "of the one. The word "hi" is used to state that the well-known distinction between the two states—the eye as the locus and the two conditions—is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) due to the difference in location. He states the result of this explanation of the division: "Agni... (verse 45).
There is no separation whatsoever between these two, which consist of the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
These two are established everywhere according to their status as primary or subordinate.
Anticipating the objection, "If the distinction is for the sake of meditation, why does it not exist by itself?", he says: "Not of these two.

With the intention that, although there is no actual difference, the perception of it arises through the power of adventitious limiting conditions (upādhi), he says: "The primary [nature]," etc. The word "everywhere" refers to both states. || 46 ||
And the meeting of those two occurs mutually within this heart, in the subtle state.
That which is praised here is "saṃstāva"; it is said that the space within the heart (hṛdyākāśa) is this [saṃstāva]. || 47 ||
He explains the passage beginning with "Of those two" (*tayor*). Regarding the phrase "of those two": the ellipsis is that "the space within the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) is the *saṃstava*.
He states how its nature is such: "It is praised together" (*saṃstutaḥ*), meaning that they enter into mutual union. || 47 ||
Of these two, that which is the lump of red salt here is food.
"One should give food" refers to that previously explained binding of the child. || 48 ||

Now he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "athainayoḥ" (then of these two), starting with the words "ūrdhvāsya" (of him whose mouth is upward). Here, the word "atra" (here) refers to the heart. He states that food [as the essence] of Indra and Indrāṇī, as well as Agni and Soma—the Viśva and Taijasa—is also mentioned in the *Śiśu-brāhmaṇa*, saying "annam" (food). The connection is that it is precisely this which is called "food" here. || 48 ||
Likewise, their covering is composed of hundreds of channels interconnected with one another.
It appears like a spider's web due to the similarity of having many apertures. || 49 ||

Now he explains the passage beginning with "of these two" (*athainayoḥ*). Regarding the word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*): the meaning is that just as the aforementioned food serves as the sustainer for those two, so too does that very [food], which is connected to many channels, serve as their clothing, according to the scriptural text beginning with "one hundred and one" (*śataṃ caikā ca*). He states the reason why the lump of blood appears like a window: "many" (*bahu*). It is well known that the heart has many apertures; of that, indeed...
The meaning is: "from such scriptural passages as 'Of this heart' (etasya hṛdayasya)," and so forth. || 49 ||
The path by which those two move upward from the heart is this [channel].
The channel that leads from the state of waking to the ground known as the dream state.

Now he explains the passage beginning with "of these two" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of those two": fearing that the path would be useless because there is no fruit for wandering [between them], he says "waking," etc. It should be understood from the subsequent passage beginning with "now this" that this is an explanation of the Taijasa state. ||10||

3, page 234] 2 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
This is for the sake of the seer’s solitude and for the sake of subtlety itself.
Now, the circumference of the channels is correctly described here.

1.1367 He states the purport [of the verse] beginning with "yathā": "Of food" (*annasya*). This means that for the enjoyer, there is a specific state of food [in the form of] Viśva and Taijasa, which constitutes their subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*).

The meaning is that the subsequent scriptural passage states the measurement of the channels by means of an illustration for the sake of explaining [the nature of the Self]. The word "atha" (now/then) signifies the sequence following the description of Viśva and Taijasa. The word "iha" (here) refers to the statement of the present context. || 11 ||
The channels of this person are exceedingly subtle for the sake of accomplishing worldly activity.
They are as subtle as a single strand of hair divided into a thousand parts.

He explains the words of that [verse]: "The channels" (*nāḍyaḥ*). "Activity" (*vyavahāraḥ*) refers to the going to one's own waking state and so forth. In the compound, they are explained as "beneficial" (*hitāḥ*); in the non-compound form, the word *hi* is used for the purpose of establishing their well-known subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*). || 52 ||
There is nothing in this world that can serve as a comparison for them, because of their extreme subtlety.
Therefore, this division of hair is mentioned for the sake of illustrating the subtlety of the channels (nāḍīs). || 53 ||
Since a hair is extremely subtle, how can it be divided a thousandfold, and how much less so can a single division serve as an illustration for the subtlety of the channels?
To this he says: "It is not a comparison. This means that it is being stated, that is to say, it is being postulated. || 53 ||
Just as this channel is called the "moving one" (saṃcaraṇī) for both the deity and the self.
Likewise, the channels of other deities are to be known by the thousands.
Having introduced a single channel with the words "That which... and so forth, he explains how those [channels] are shown to be numerous by means of an illustration, saying: "Just as...
For it has been stated:
"One should know that there are twenty-nine hundred thousand and nine hundred and fifty-six vessels known as *dharmanis*.
This refers to the deities Indra and Indrāṇī, and to the Viśva and Taijasa selves. [It also refers to] the deities, which are the sense organs such as the eyes.
This is the meaning. || 54 ||
The subtle elements, which carry sound and the other objects, serve as the substrata for the sense organs such as the ear.
In this world, those deities always gratify their own divine selves.

He describes the manner in which the channels (nāḍīs) are employed: "Sound, etc. These subtle channels, resting upon the instruments [of perception], convey objects to the enjoyer; by means of them, they nourish their own substrates—the instruments—which in turn nourish the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and through that, the Self as delimited by it, within the sphere of empirical experience. This is the meaning. || 55 ||
By these extremely subtle [channels], what has been eaten flows into the food.
"The deity pervades this, it extends throughout this as described.

He explains the passage beginning with "by these" and so forth. [He says] "by those which are exceedingly subtle. For this food that has been eaten transforms into three parts; this is what is stated. (Variant readings: 1. *ga* reads *bhaṇyate*; 2. *gha* reads *khyātam*).
In this context, the meaning is that this previously mentioned subtle food, pervading the body through these aforementioned channels (*nāḍī*), causes all the aforementioned deities to pervade it.
The explanation of the term "āsravati" is "it pervades. || 56 ||
In all these beneficial [deities], all the internal deities are indeed present.
They move about in those [waters] filled with abundant essence for the sake of the enjoyment of the person. || 57 ||
Fearing that if the food-essence were to pervade the deities, those very deities would become the eaters [of it], he says: "In all...
The words "in the hitā-nāḍīs" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 97 ||
The pervasion by the manifestation of one's own consciousness is the individual soul’s experience of pleasure and pain.
That [digestive fire] is his deity-abode, and the deities are dependent upon food. || 58 ||
"How can there be experience for a person who is changeless?"—as it has been said: "The Self, situated in the center of its [the body's] orb, is motionless like a lamp.
To this, he says: "His own... What is the cause of the experience shown there? To that, he says: "That too... What is the cause of the sense organs? To that, he says: "And the deities... (18)
Food, which is subtle and resides in the channels, is described here on the basis of scripture.
The injunction [is expressed] from "by these" up to "from the bodily. 59.

He states the substratum of that food which is based upon [the body]: "Food. He cites the scriptural passage concerning the aforementioned food with the word "That" (*tat*). The meaning is that the sentence beginning with "That food here, in the state of the fiery [element], sustains [the body] by means of these... and ending with "...from the embodied self," is what is being discussed here. || 59 ||
The most refined portion of food satisfies the deities of the vital breaths.
The food that reaches the subtle body (liṅga) is said to be its nourishment. || 60 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "therefore" (*tasmāt*) as follows: "The subtle" (*pravivikta*). That which is the aforementioned portion of food nourishes the deities of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the sense organs, and the internal organ known as the *liṅga*. Therefore, for whomsoever the food becomes more subtle, that *taijasa*—the self consisting of the *liṅga*—is likewise [nourished]. The meaning is that, by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is understood that "that" refers to the food of the *liṅga*. || 60 ||
From this physical body, which is composed of the elements and built up from the very beginning through the vital fluids and so forth.
This embodied self (liṅgātmā) has a more refined diet than that previously mentioned.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "asmāt" (from this) as follows: "cīyamānāt" (from that which is being accumulated). This means by that [substance], namely food such as *rasa* (nutritive essence), which is its cause. || 61 ||
The rasa and so forth would be subtle in comparison with the feces and other such waste products.
This subtle food, consisting even of tastes and so forth, produces signs and satisfaction.
He explains how food is "separated" (pravivikta): "from taste and so forth. Nevertheless, he explains how it is "more separated" (praviviktatara): "from taste and so forth. || 62 ||
Since this is so, he therefore said that its characteristic mark is distinct from the gross body.
The sacred tradition holds that food which is most secluded [from impurities] is subtle for one established in the state of *anna*.

3, page 236] 2. Brāhmaṇa, together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1369.
He states the result of its being even more secluded: "Since... He clarifies the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ): "Subtle... (verse 63).
Since the subtle body (liṅga-ātman) is exceedingly subtle, it is not like this gross physical body.
As it passes from one body to another, it is not obstructed by anything. || 64 ||

One might object that since the subtle body (*liṅga*) is also a body, just like the gross one, it cannot be considered subtle; therefore, how can it have "food other than the refined" (*praviviktāhāra*)?
Anticipating this doubt, the author states the proof for its subtlety: "Because... (verse 64).
Some say that the word "iti" is meaningless because it contradicts the actual sense.
In this way, the word *iva* is considered a simile for the meaning [of similarity], and it also expresses restriction in the sense of "as if. (65)

In order to explain the word *iva* occurring in the present sentence, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "The word *iva* is meaningless. To that, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) as expressed by Bhartṛprapañca: "Of the sense of 'only' (*eva-artha*). The construction is as follows: it is determined that the self of the subtle body (*liṅgātman*) is "indeed more refined in its food" (*praviviktāhāratara eva*); they say that the meaning of the word *iva* is a comparison (*upamā*) for that [refinement]. For it has been said: "Just as indeed for the purpose of the growth of the external body..."

"His food is likewise subtle"—on account of this similarity, it is said "he is, as it were, one whose food is even more subtle. Regarding the phrase "as it were" (*ivaiva*), he states its intended meaning: "and in the sense of 'as it were' (*iva-arthe*). The particle *eva* is a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) which should be understood in the sense of "as it were" (*iva*). And thus, just as the Viśva [state] has subtle food, so too this Taijasa state does not have merely subtle food, but rather has food that is even more subtle (*praviviktāhāratara*).

The meaning of the two particles *iva* and *eva* is as follows: the causal self (*kāraṇātman*) is not exactly "one who subsists on even more refined food" (*praviviktāhāratara*), but rather "as if one who subsists on even more refined food"; however, the subtle body (*liṅgātman*) is indeed "one who subsists on even more refined food.
Thus is the sense of the two words *iva* and *eva*. || 61 ||
It is subtler than even the subtle body (liṅga), because it is more refined than that conscious self.
The word "iva" (as if) is employed here for the purpose of providing a simile. || 66 ||
To the question, "Why is it that the taijasa [self], though possessing the nature of a cause, does not have even more refined food? he replies with the words "liṅga" and so forth.

The word "food" is to be supplied as referring to the prājña self. Therefore, the meaning is that the liṅga [self] does not have even more refined food. He concludes by showing that the word "iva" (as if) possesses its intended meaning: "for the sake of comparison. || 66 ||
Like the flower of the Kadamba tree, this deity has its abode in the heart.
They are attached to the outward-tending channels, extending from the heart.

Explaining the pervasion of the aforementioned Sūtra throughout the entire world according to the system of Bhartṛprapañca, [the author] analyzes his commentary, which states: "This subtle deity, within the heart, is attached to the channels that have issued forth from the heart in all directions like the filaments of a Kadamba bud. This is [verse] 67. "Kadamba... [etc.]
Just as this deity is all [pervading], so too are all other deities.
Because all [of them] are common to both the effect and the instrument. || 68 ||

Thus, he states the meaning of the commentary’s phrase "each individual deity" with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). The meaning is that just as the deity named Sūtra is said to be attached to the channels (*nāḍī*) that extend outward starting from the heart, so too all other deities are likewise attached to them.

He states the meaning of the commentary on the reason—"because it is common to all"—in the words "sādhāraṇatvāt" (because of being common). By the word *kara*, the physical locations such as the eyeballs are meant; by the word *devatā*, the sense organs are meant. || 68 ||
In that case, when the function of one [sense], such as seeing and so forth, is present;
At that time, all those deities become subordinate to her. || 69 ||

Anticipating the objection that if all the sense organs pervaded the entire body, the cognitions of form and so forth would become confused, he explains the Bhāṣya: "In that case... (verse 69). The meaning is that when a particular deity performs its function, such as seeing, at a particular time, then all the other deities are subordinate to it.
Likewise, in the other channels as well, because all of them are gathered together.
This very sequence should be understood as applying to both primary and subordinate status. || 70 ||

He states the meaning of the commentary—that even within other channels, whichever deity is required at a particular time appears by assuming the manifestation of the entire divinity—with the words "in the other channels," which means "in the sense-organs not previously mentioned. || 70 ||
And this being so, however many channels there are that bind the heart, [they all arise from it].
And for as many years as there are those Prajāpatis, they are the fires. || 71 ||

Having explained the attainment of the deities through the internal channels (*nāḍī*), the text recalls another form of meditation located in a different place by means of the context of the channels, specifically through their connection with the heart. "In this way" (evam ca): since the channels are introduced as being connected to the heart, one should perform the visualization of the bricks called "Fire" in the form of Prajāpati upon those channels viewed as consisting of day and night; for as many as are the various divisions of the channels, so many are all [the bricks].
The meaning is that this is because it has been stated: "The years are the Prajāpatis, the fires. || 71 ||
Because the subject matter previously mentioned is completed here in each respective section.
Just as she exists with respect to the deities, so too does she exist with respect to the self (adhyātma) and the elements (adhibhūta).
And this pervasive power (vibhvī) exists in the divine sphere as both duality and unity;
just as the channels of this person extend everywhere within the individual sphere (adhyātma). || 73 ||
Likewise, its objective correlate (adhibhūta) consists of the all-pervading winds composed of air.
Having emerged from this very body, they have gone forth in every direction.

Having reminded [the student] of the incidental worship for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), and taking as an illustration the previously mentioned pervasion of the deities within the self (*adhyātma-devatā-vyāpti*), he states that this same pervasion exists also in the spheres of the elements (*adhibhūta*) and the divine (*adhidaiva*). He says: "In every part. The word "of the object" (*vastunaḥ*) implies "of the thread" (*sūtrasya*). He concludes the aforementioned pervasion of the deities with the word "all-pervading" (*vibhvī*). As they have said: "Because the whole is completely present in every single limb..."

"This [is] just as it is with respect to the self (adhyātma), so it is with respect to the elemental (adhibhūta) and the divine (adhidaiva)," and so forth. Having thus stated the all-pervading nature of the deity, he now declares the pervasion of the channels (nāḍīs) in the elemental and other domains by means of the same illustrative example of their pervasion within the self. "Just as... For it has been said:
"Just as the channels exist everywhere within the body with respect to the self, so too do the divine channels belong to this very person who is the self."
"By itself, the channels of that which is about to be described consist of air. He elaborates upon the second half [of the verse]: "From this...
[Note: The manuscript variants regarding the specific terms are noted in the source]. [Vol. 3, page 238]
And it has been stated: "Having emerged from this very body, they remain pervading the entire universe. (Verses 72–73)
1108 11 This very [self], by means of the elemental self alone, follows the path characterized by the channels (nāḍī).
Having filled this entire world, the person who abides within the self remains established.

Raising the doubt as to why the channels (nāḍīs) extend outside the body, he states that it is for the sake of the pervasion of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) by means of them: "Adhibhūta... (verse 79).
For just as there are channels for the internal self, so too are the rays of the Virāj—the divine self—to be known; they are likewise established as individual portions.

He states the pervasion of the rays—which correspond to the channels (nāḍīs)—of the cosmic person (*ādhidevika*), just as there are channels for the individual person (*ādhyātmika*). He says, "The channels," and the meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that the pervasive extension of Virāj’s rays in all directions is logical, since we observe the pervasion of the rays of the suns that are his parts. Furthermore, he states that one should understand the complete presence of Virāj’s rays in every single individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*).
"Regarding 'one's own share' (pratyaṃśa): || 76 ||"
Just as [the knowledge] of the internal person [is complete], so too is that of the entire internal and external worlds.
The completion of the divine self occurs amidst its infinite and distinct effects.

He concludes that just as there is a pervasive presence of the internal person (*ādhyātmika-puṃs*) through the channels (*nāḍī*), so too for the cosmic person (*ādhidaivika*) it occurs through the rays (*raśmi*). He states: "Of the internal [person]"—just as the internal [self] is fully present in its entirety in every limb, so too the Vairāja Self is present in every limb within the internal, elemental, and cosmic spheres.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh [verse].
The internal discernment by means of the path of vision already described.
Having thoroughly withdrawn the deities, he also caused the deities to shine forth.
And having withdrawn the Virāj into the embodiment of the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa).
And that [power] is also in Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the self and the cause of all.

Having stated that the system of others is to be accepted, he shows the sequence of the causality of knowledge according to his own view through the exposition of the universe (*viśva*) and so forth, beginning with the words "ādhyātmikam" (the internal). By means of the aforementioned pervasion, one should dissolve the bodily limitation into the deities such as Fire, those [deities] into the Virāj, that into the Sūtra, and that into the Cause; having further dissolved even that into the non-dual Inner Self (*pratīc*), one should abide as the Full Self—this is the meaning. || 78 || 79 ||
Then, having brought all the internal deities into one's own heart;
One should connect [the breath] from the heart through the channels with the rays of the sun.
Then, surrounded by rays of light, one should go to the center of the sun.
Then the wise one [perceives] Hiraṇyagarbha as the Self, and thereafter that cause.
Elaborating upon what has already been stated, he speaks for the purpose of dissolving the Virāj—designated by terms such as Vaiśvānara and so forth—into the Taijasa, which is the Sūtrātman.

1372 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya] states the sequence: "Regarding the internal self (*adhyātma*)... Having withdrawn the deities, such as Āditya, together with the eyes and other organs, into the heart which is the form of Prajāpati, and then, by means of the channels (*nāḍī*) and rays that have emerged from there—these being the instruments that have become mutually identical with one another—the subtle body (*liṅga*) residing in the sun and the subtle body residing in the heart are unified.

One who is intent on this should not [merely] connect [the breath], but rather, through the channel of the rays of the aforementioned nāḍīs and by means of discriminative awareness (*vivekabuddhi*), the thread—the Self—residing in the heart reaches the mandala; this is the meaning.

The connection is "from the heart of the Self. Following the contemplation that the universe consists of nothing but the *taijasa* (the dreaming state), the discerning one goes to its cause, which is designated by terms such as the *avyākṛta* (the undifferentiated); thus he describes the dissolution of the *taijasa* into the *prājña* (the deep sleep state). From that...
Thus [ends verses 80 and 81].
Then, for one who has attained that Self from Vaiśvānara, [the Taijasa state arises] in the heart.
And one should also dissolve that Hiraṇyagarbha into the self of the vital breath (prāṇātman).
He summarizes the sequence already stated for the sake of ease of understanding with the words "from Vaiśvānara" (*vaiśvānarāt*). The word "that" (*tat*) refers to Vaiśvānara.

The remainder of the sense is that for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), the limitation consisting of the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth, which had been attained, is removed. And that [sequence] should be understood as withdrawn into the Cause of the Sūtra. || 82 ||
And here, by the word "prāṇa," the causal self is also designated;
he is defined as the "Prājña" (the Conscious One), the seed of every effect. (83)

Anticipating the objection that the withdrawal [of the subtle body] into the self of the vital breath (prāṇa) is stated here in the Sūtra, and not into the causal self, he states the meaning of the word "prāṇa":
"By the word 'prāṇa'... Since the dissolution of the Taijasa into the Prājña is accepted, he explains how its dissolution occurs in the cause: "The seed... (83).
Since there is no dissolution of effects anywhere other than in their cause.
Therefore, because it arises from the attainment of its causes, one should understand that it is not without cause.

One might object: "Since the attainment of the fourth state (turiya), which is a mass of pure consciousness like a lump of gold, is the desired goal, let that alone be stated; what is the use of describing the dissolution of Viśva and Taijasa—whose forms are the gross and subtle worlds—into Prājña? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the effects... (verse 84).
Deprived of his supports and instruments, he is seized by that which pertains to the self and the divine.
The self of vital breath exists as one alone, its form being a solid mass of consciousness.

He elaborates upon the true nature of the wise one who has attained the fourth state (turiya), which is beyond cause and effect, with the words "sāśrayaiḥ" (along with their supports). This means that the Self is the cause of vital breath (prāṇa), being its very existence and manifestation; for the Chandogas, moreover, sometimes permit even the absence of euphonic combination (visandhi). || 89 ||
Of that [Self] whose nature is indivisible, those vital breaths (prāṇas) which were formerly his...
The eastern direction itself became [the locus], due to the abandonment of its limitation.
The vital breaths (prāṇas) are directed southward in the south, and likewise westward in the west.
The northern direction, those who dwell in the north, and likewise all the directions in their entirety. || 87 ||

The states of Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turīya have been mentioned; therein, one might raise the objection that only the first two are explicitly stated in the Śruti, and not Prājña and the others. Anticipating this, [the text proceeds by] realizing the oneness of that...
[text fragment]. [Vol. 3, page 240]

Having introduced the passage beginning with "the eastern" (*prācī*), he explains it as follows: "Nirvibhāga... (without division). The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) delimited by the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth are designated by the term "prāṇa" and are situated in all directions. For the wise man, however, because the delimitation of his causal form has been destroyed, those [prāṇas]— [The text continues: ...prāṇas... [are integrated]. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that this is well-known. The meaning is that for one who knows the truth, there is no distinction between the prāṇas belonging to the body and those belonging to the external world; rather, they are all understood to be of the nature of Brahman. Therefore, the statement "the prāṇas are indeed Brahman" is made. This is the sense. Next, he explains the subsequent portion of the text, beginning with "the eastern quarter. He states: "The eastern quarter is the out-breath (*prāṇa*)," and so on. The meaning is that the eastern quarter is the out-breath, the southern quarter is the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the western quarter is the in-breath (*apāna*), and the northern quarter is the upward-moving breath (*udāna*). The intermediate quarters are the pervasive breath (*samāna*). The zenith is the mind (*manas*), and the nadir is the intellect (*buddhi*). The earth is the body (*śarīra*), and the sky is the trunk (*ātman*). Fire is speech (*vāk*), and the sun is the eye (*cakṣus*). The moon is the ear (*śrotra*), and the quarters are the mind (*manas*). Lightning is the hair, and the stars are the pores of the skin. The day is the opening of the eyes, and the night is the closing of the eyes. The bright fortnight is the forward movement, and the dark fortnight is the backward movement. All beings are the lower breath, and the sacrificial formulas (*mantras*) are the higher breath. The Sāman chants are the joints, and the Rig-verses are the bones. The Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the heart, and the Imperishable (*akṣara*) is the mouth. Such is the explanation. Now, he provides the summary of the meaning of this section: "Thus, the prāṇas... and so forth. The meaning is that in this manner, the prāṇas, which are differentiated by the internal self and so forth, are all subsumed within the single prāṇa of the knower, who is of the nature of the cause. Because the distinctions of the prāṇas have been dissolved, they are all understood to be of the nature of Brahman. Therefore, the statement "the prāṇas are indeed Brahman" is made. This is the sense. Furthermore, he explains the subsequent portion of the text, beginning with "the eastern quarter. He states: "The eastern quarter is the out-breath," and so on. The meaning is that the eastern quarter is the out-breath, the southern quarter is the diffused breath, the western quarter is the in-breath, and the northern quarter is the upward-moving breath. The meaning is that this is the knowledge of Brahman, which consists in the realization that the prāṇas are of the nature of Brahman.
