Form has become reduced to its respective respective dimensions, and those [dimensions] dissolve into the Wise One (prājña), the root cause, which is the vital breath mentioned in the final stage; the meaning is that they dissolve into the Cause, the Fourth (turīya), the Inner Self (pratīc). || 86 || 87 ||
The proof of darkness is observed through that which witnesses it, as well as through its effect.
In the presence or absence of that [object], the self is neither an effect nor a cause. (88)

[The author] anticipates the objection: "The cause does not dissolve into the inner self (pratīc), because that [inner self] is itself the cause; for it is impossible for something to dissolve into itself. To this, he says: "That which... (verse 88).
By that very same self-knowledge, all that darkness born of ignorance was likewise dispelled.
Having consumed [all] through the eternal Self, the wise one remains as the Residue by means of the vision of fullness. || 89 ||

Since the establishment of ignorance and its conquest, as well as their respective presence and absence, depends upon that [Self], he states the resulting conclusion once its distinction from those has been established: "By that very [Self]," etc. By this, passages such as "This is not it, not it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6) are explained. (89)
This path has been set forth for the sake of generating the knowledge of the identity of the self.
But unlike [the ascent through] the *arcis* and so forth, there is no postulation of a path for its attainment.

He concludes the result of the entire preceding argument with the words "This" (eṣa). The meaning is: by means of that [knowledge], for the sake of liberation. He excludes the primary path [of ritual action] with the words "But not" (na tu). || 90 ||
Because he possesses the nature of the Self, this one has realized reality and is not subject to obstacles such as distance and the like.
Apart from knowledge, nothing else is required for its attainment thereafter. || 91 ||

Some maintain that even for one who knows [the Self], the destination which is to be described will be reached before long; and thus, they argue, a channel (nāḍī) corresponding to that has been taught.
[The author] anticipates this objection with the words "Because of being the Self" (*ātmatvāt*). Here, the knower (*vidvān*) is the subject qualified.

Then, fearing the objection that "in that case, knowledge itself would not be required," he states "Knowledge" (*jñānam*), intending to show that knowledge is required in order to remove the intervening obstacles. || 91 ||
Having thus made himself understood by the other's self, the sage spoke to the lord of men.

"Thou hast attained fearlessness"—thus, by the destruction of the cause of fear, Brahman has been made known without distinction through the means of wakefulness and so forth. Now, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "fearlessness" (abhayam) and so on, [saying]:
"having made it understood. || 92 ||
The cause of fear is manifold, and its establishment is precarious.
Even prior to the realization of the identity of the one Self, [this notion] is established without being critically examined.
"His fear is gone there. Regarding "fear," it excludes the state of ignorance (*avidyā*).
As for "and that": if it is argued that although [the world] remains poorly established after knowledge (*jñāna*), it was not so before, he says "no," [adding] "even before. || 93 ||
Therefore, by the mere arising of the sun of radiant self-knowledge, which is the true nature of the inner Self, its destruction shall become absolute. || 94 ||
1 ga. is obtained | 2 na. "is disregarded" | 3 gha "thāstrata" | 4 ka. kha. "yamātmānaṃ bhauṃ" | [Vol. 3, page 241] 1374 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]—
He states the result of the constant wretchedness of ignorance: "Since... (verse 94).
And because of the instruction, "Thou hast attained," knowledge alone is the destination of the self.
If there were a destination other than knowledge, he would have told you simply, "You shall attain it. || 95 ||

He states the intended meaning of the instruction "you have arrived" with the words "prāptaḥ" (you have arrived). If it is argued that such an instruction would apply even in the case of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-gati*), he says "jñānāt" (from knowledge); this refers to the phrase "that king. || 95 ||
Considering the sacrificial fee to be equal to knowledge, the king [gave it] to the preceptor.
That king said to Yājñavalkya, "Fearlessness unto you."
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "saha" [and so forth]: "jñāna... || 96 ||
This very gift of safety, characterized by the granting of fearlessness, is the appropriate sacrificial fee for this teaching.
For, compared to the gift known as right knowledge, all other worldly existence is [nothing]. || 97 ||

Since other sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) exist, how can there be an absence of a fee suitable for knowledge? To this he says: "Appropriate" (*ucitā*). Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the Teacher (*ācārya*). He states the inappropriateness of other fees with the words: "other than that" (*tadanyā*). For even in the case of knowledge with attributes (*saguṇavidyā*), there is no fee that is truly suitable; what then need be said regarding the other [knowledge without attributes]? Even though [the text says], "to him [the teacher] he gives this [earth] surrounded by water... regarding wealth...
The intention is that one should offer the full [oblation], for the scripture states: "This indeed is more than that. || 97 ||
And the king replied, "I shall experience that which is free from fear."
Because it is obscured by tamas, it is inferred that there is no other effect [than this]. || 98 ||

He states the purport of the verse beginning with "yo na" (he who does not) as follows: "And that which... The meaning is that since there is no fruit for knowledge other than the cessation of ignorance—such as the reaching of another place—that [reaching] is not "going," as established by the statement in the present tense. || 98 ||
Indeed, because he is the bestower of fearlessness, the Guru has attained fearlessness himself.
How can the king's blessing, "May you be fearless," be understood as a command? (99)
He rejects the benediction offered by the king with the words, "Of one who is fearless" (abhayasya). || 99 ||
Some wise ones declare this to be the statement of the refutation thereof.
He obtained fearlessness from the sound, but he did not manifest it directly.
He states the refutation offered by Bhartṛprapañca: "of this," etc. He clarifies that very point: "from words," etc. (100).
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing direct realization, the king spoke to the sage.
The words "I grant you fearlessness" are spoken because that [fear] has not yet reached him.

He states the conclusion—that the king’s blessing is fruitful even when the Guru possesses indirect knowledge—in the verse beginning with "sākṣāt" (directly). One might object that such [knowledge] is already obtained simply by virtue of being a teacher, according to the Smṛti: "The knowers of truth, who perceive reality, will instruct you in knowledge. Anticipating this doubt, he says "taddhi" (for that...). For he has not directly attained fearlessness; otherwise, it would be impossible for him to provide instruction to one who is already liberated.
1. Kha: This is not present. 2. Gha: Of liberation and knowledge.
[Vol. 3, page 242] 2. Brāhmaṇa: Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1375.
For it has been said: "Fearlessness was attained by Yājñavalkya; it was not unattained, yet it was not directly realized. Therefore, the meaning is that the king's blessing is appropriate. || 101 ||
Or if liberation is of two kinds, it exists indeed even while the body still lives.
One who has directly realized Brahman attains absorption into it after death. || 102 ||

He states another solution offered by those very [authorities]: "Or rather" (*yadi vā*). As they say: liberation in this very body is called "liberated" when one has directly realized Brahman; merging into Brahman after the fall of the body is the second liberation, and that is what is to be aspired for. || 102 ||
Thus they desire to avoid [the objection], but such is not the expression of logical reasoning.
When the Sage has said, "You have attained [it]," a rebuttal is not appropriate. || 103 ||

Thinking that for ultimate liberation there must be some other means such as blessings (*āśīrvāda*) and so forth, he summarizes the refutation of the opponent’s reply with the words "Thus" (*evam*). He then rejects it with "But not" (*na tu*). To the question, "How can this twofold reply be stated outside of logic? he says: "You have attained [it]" (*prāpto'si*). || 103 ||
For he said, "Since you have attained it by merely knowing that."
It is held that there is no other [means] than the direct realization of that, nor its dissolution. || 104 ||
Nevertheless, he explains how the two [other] ways of avoiding [the objection] are improper: "tajjñāna" (by the knowledge of That).

Since the identity of the inner self with Brahman is established by its very nature, there is no possibility of the direct realization of Brahman or its absorption [into it] apart from the destruction of ignorance through that knowledge;
therefore, the meaning is that liberation does not depend on other means such as benedictions and the like. || 104 ||
One is not appointed to the office of a teacher by verbal knowledge alone.
"One should approach a teacher who is learned in the Vedas and established in Brahman," so says the Śruti. || 105 ||
Regarding the claim that the Sage did not directly realize the fearless Brahman—which was obtained from scripture only through indirect knowledge—the author says:
"Śābda... He cites scripture as proof for the fact that one cannot possess the status of a teacher by means of mere indirect knowledge: "śrotriyam...
"You experience fearlessness"—this [statement] is not [appropriate] when the Supreme has not been directly realized.
It is appropriate for the king to speak only when there is a thorough understanding of the mere words. || 106 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the sage has indeed realized Brahman directly: "Fearless. When it was said, "You know Brahman," the King's direct realization of it was understood, because knowing is of the nature of experience (*anubhava*); by that very fact, the teacher's [realization] is also inferred, since the Blessed One qualified him with the term "seer of reality" (*tattvadarśin*). This is the meaning. || 106 ||
Cognition arising from unique characteristics (asādhāraṇadharma) regarding an object is valid knowledge (pramā).
"But that which arises from mere verbal testimony is not a valid means of knowledge, because it does not depend upon the actual object.

[107] To the question—why is it not said that the verbal cognition concerning Brahman, such as "you know," is indeed a mediate (parokṣa) knowledge regarding Brahman—he replies: "Because it is uncommon... [The manuscript notes:
kha. 'nyattalla']
[Vol. 3, p. 243] 1376 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Thus, even when such a general rule (*utsarga*) is established, he states what occurs at that time: "By the word," etc. For indirect knowledge does not [directly] apprehend the reality—
The meaning is that it conforms [to the Upanishads] because its characteristics are defined by such passages as "directly and non-mediately" (sākṣād aparokṣāt). || 107 ||
Even for one who has directly realized the single reality, regarding the dissolution of the impurity of non-duality...
What is being suspected, such that a blessing for it is employed? || 108 ||
As for the claim that liberation is twofold—the first being the dissolution into Brahman after the fall of the body, and that this second type is what should be prayed for—he says [in response]:
"Directly" (sākṣāt). This means that the prayer is directed toward that very dissolution into Brahman. || 108 ||
Therefore, desiring to give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) commensurate with his knowledge, he spoke.
"O Fearless One," said the king, recognizing him by the signs of the knowledge he had described.

Having stated the impossibility of the opponent's position, he states his own position with the word "jñāna" (knowledge). To the question, "Why did the king speak thus when the sage had attained fearlessness?"—anticipating the doubt that perhaps another sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given, or that silence would otherwise be appropriate—he says "yathokta" (as previously stated). The meaning is that he spoke in this way precisely to make it known: "Knowledge, culminating in my own direct experience, has arisen regarding the previously mentioned Brahman-Self. || 109 ||
Apart from direct knowledge, nothing else is sufficient for liberation.

We have stated this repeatedly at every step as before. He refutes the claim that in the case of ultimate liberation there must be some other means, such as a benediction or the like, with the words "directly" (sākṣāt). || 110 ||
When there is the direct certainty that "you are indeed I," [then one is liberated].
In that case, tell me: to whom does the world, including Videha and the rest, belong? (111)
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "these Videhas" as follows: "You too... The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "other than you. || 111 ||
This belongs to you just as much as it does to me, and there is nothing at all inconsistent in this.
And because there is nothing other than you, according to the teaching that "all is the Self. || 112 ||

He states the King’s intention: "This was said from the perspective of conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), but in reality it is not so. With the words "mine" (*mama*), he refers to another object indicated by the pronoun "this" (*idam*); having provisionally accepted that, he says that very thing does not exist, adding: "And because of its non-existence" (*abhāvāt ca*). || 112 ||
When the ignorant cognition of "I" and "mine," along with its causes, has been destroyed;
When the full Self is then perceived, who would wish to give anything to whom?
Thus ends the second Kūrca Brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter in the *Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 7058.

Anticipating the objection—"Since you wish to give me these Videhas as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth, how can there now be a statement to the contrary?"—the author elaborates on the answer, saying "I am [Brahman]. Therefore, he speaks of "these Videhas" and so forth, relying solely upon the perspective of conventional worldly usage (*vyavahāra*).
The words "the king's speech" are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 113 ||
Thus ends the second Kūrca Brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

Now begins the third Brāhmaṇa:
He who has entered into this effect, which consists of name, form, and so forth, and is born of His own ignorance;
The Supreme, through ignorance, attained a state of incompleteness, like the sun reflected in water.
Since the King has been granted fearlessness by Yājñavalkya through the exposition beginning with the state of waking, what remains for which a further answer is required?

Anticipating the objection that [the subject] might be a Brahmin, he recounts the narrative, beginning with the word "nāma" (by name). The meaning is as follows: it was stated in the passage beginning with "Do not see him" (*na taṃ paśyeḥ*) that the Supreme Being, who is the qualified subject, having entered into the intellect and other faculties born of His own ignorance, has attained a state of limitation through His own nescience (*avidyā*). || 1 ||
For the purpose of dispelling that ignorance, [the Lord acted] under the pretext of Gārgya, Kāśya, and others.
This [reality], whose intrinsic nature is the unprecedented and so forth, has been entered into and established. || 2 ||

Having restated the third illustration—that upon entering [the body], one acts through that door as water and the sun do—he restates the fourth: "That is ignorance. By the word "etcetera" in "Kāśyapa, etc.," Yājñavalkya and others are included. || 2 ||
Having thus established the self through scripture, one should now do so through reasoning.
That very same [reality] is also taught in the fifth [chapter], directly, by means of the single path of discourse. || 3 ||

Having explained the meaning of the section on the Honey (madhukāṇḍa), he recalls the commencement of the section on the Sages (munikāṇḍa) with the words "from scripture" (āgamāt). The word "atha" (now/then) is intended to indicate that it is appropriate for the section on reasoning (tarka) to follow immediately after that, since reasoning serves as an auxiliary to valid means of knowledge (māna). The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "the section on the sages has commenced in order to demonstrate that. He restates the subject matter of the fifth chapter (pāñcamika) with the words "that very same [Self]" (sa eva). By the word "directly" (sākṣāt), the Self is further qualified.
The meaning is that [the Self] possesses the characteristics described in the passage beginning with "directly and not indirectly" (sākṣādaparokṣāt) and so forth. || 3 ||
For the sake of correctly understanding that very [point], by means of the *vādanyāya* (the logic of debate).
In the sixth [chapter], the four states beginning with waking are presented in their proper sequence.

He causes [the student] to remember what was stated regarding the sixth [chapter]: "In speech," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "when the sixth [chapter] has commenced. He follows the meaning of the two preceding Brāhmaṇas with the words "in sequence" (*kramāt*). The meaning is that Brahman—which is to be understood through the discourse on the waking state and so forth by means of the meditation upon speech and the other deities as being Brahman—has been declared. || 4 ||
The states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turiya) are indeed my present reality.
Relying upon that very same prior meaning, it is now directly manifested here.
Having restated what has been explained, he states the connection with the subsequent Brāhmaṇa: "Indha" (1).
Furthermore, by the refutation of non-correspondence, the existence of the self is established once again.
Distinctness, purity, self-luminosity, and eternity. || 6 ||
The self possesses eternality through its identity with a nature that is inherently non-superior bliss;
and its non-duality is established by mere perception, not by great logical reasoning. (7)

That which is to be clearly discerned is here being investigated with great effort by means of the logic of debate.
And here, there is a narrative intended to establish the rules for the transmission of knowledge and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that a further analysis of what has already been stated is useless and that "directness" (*sākṣāttva*) cannot be the distinguishing feature because it would entail the same lack of utility for the former [analysis], he says: "visaṃvāda... (regarding contradiction). Although the existence of the Self and so forth was established previously, it is now elucidated with a specific intent by relying on reasoning whose fruit is the determination of truth, through uncontradicted and non-restricted logic, and by dispelling the disputes of opponents; and thus:

The meaning is that the understanding of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) may descend with extreme clarity upon the Self as it has been described. "Eternality" (*nityatā*) means immutability (*kūṭasthatā*). "Certainty of oneness" (*aikātmyaniyatā*) means its perpetual existence. Having stated the purport of the *Brāhmaṇa*, he states the purport of the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) with the words "of knowledge" (*vidyāyāḥ*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the giver, the act of giving, and so forth are included. And the meaning of "and" (*ca*) is that there is also an injunction (*vidhi*) and an instruction (*bodhana*) for the sake of praising knowledge (*vidyāstuti*). The words of the Brahmin. || 6 || 7 || 8 ||
Then Yājñavalkya approached Janaka for the sake of securing his spiritual and material well-being.
"Indeed, having taken a vow, saying 'I shall not speak with the king,' [he remained silent]."

Having stated the purport of the two [statements], he explains the syllables of the causal phrase beginning with "hetu" (the reason), starting with "Yājñavalkya. The meaning of the word *atha* is "immediately after knowing the time suitable for an audience with the king. He states the meaning of the sentence "He thought, 'I will not speak,'" beginning with the word *na*. The particle *kila* is used to indicate that the aforementioned matter is something reported from another source (*parokṣa*). Since the root *vad* (to speak) is conjugated in the *parasmaipada* when used without a prefix...
Or, "tikle" means dissatisfaction. || 9 ||
Thinking, "I shall converse with the king," he went toward him.
Because of its connection with the word "samiti," it is expressed as "by this. || 10 ||

He states another meaning of that very [term]: "saṃvadiṣye" (I shall agree). This is to be connected with the phrase "having bound the vow of conceptualization" (vikalpasya vrataṃ baddhvā). Anticipating the objection that the second explanation does not follow the syntax of the sentence, he says: "of this word 'sam'... The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "because of its connection with the verbal root. || 10 ||
Although he had no desire to speak, he replied to what was asked by Janaka.
In that regard, the Śruti proclaimed the granting of the boon for the purpose of stating the reason.

Now, one might object that in the first interpretation it is improper to say that the sage speaks whatever was asked by the king, because that would entail a breach of his vow. Anticipating this, [the author] states the purport of the passage beginning with "atha ha," starting with the words "avivakṣuḥ" (not wishing to speak). For once the sage has received the boon known as the "question at will" and the king has asked a question, silence on the part of the sage—who has been granted the boon—is impossible, as it would result in the charge of falsehood; therefore, even a breach of the vow must be accepted for the sake of truthfulness.
The meaning is that, according to the Vedic scripture, "He who is devoted to Truth does not count even a moment," he does not take account of time. || 11 ||
When it is explained as "I shall converse with him," [it refers to this].
In that case, a narrative is considered to be the cause for their dialogue. (12)

In the second explanation as well, he states the reason with the words "by this. [It means] by this [statement], such as Janaka's [instruction] to Śvetaketu regarding the Agnihotra, and so forth. [Variant readings: *ka* reads *iti sa*; *kha* reads *ucyate*.

Just as [the dialogue occurred] between the two of them, so too did a dialogue take place with Yājñavalkya, introduced by the narrative beginning, "Janaka, the King of Videha, came together with the Brahmins who were masters of the Dhāyyā verses.
In that context, the sage, having seen the excellence of the king's knowledge regarding the Agnihotra sacrifice, was pleased and granted him a boon.

And it has been stated that he chose precisely the boon of asking whatever question he desired; likewise, in the commentary on the dialogue with the king, it is explained that having resolved to go to him, the reason for doing so was the granting of the boon of asking whatever one desires. || 12 ||
It is understood from the statement "As the king formerly asked" that [the question] was auspicious.
The latter [explanation] of the *liṅga* is superior; the former is not correct because it lacks authoritative basis. || 13 ||

Which, then, of these two explanations is to be accepted? To this he says: "The King. From the passage beginning with "He [the sage] said to him," it is understood that the King obtained the boon of asking whatever he desired; for without that, the King—who was silent and did not know the sage's intention—would not have been able to ask.
By the force of this indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is understood that the second explanation is correct and not the first, because there is no evidence for the latter. This is the meaning. || 13 ||
No reason is observed for the vow "I shall not speak" in this context.
Therefore, out of dissatisfaction with that, this subsequent auspicious commentary has been composed.

He establishes that [point] with the words "No," and so forth. For it is not possible for one who has granted the power of fulfilling desires (*kāmaprabha*) to a king to form the intention, "I shall not converse with him," because that would result in his becoming untrustworthy. Therefore, since there is no evidence for the first interpretation and it is logically untenable, the second alone should be accepted; the meaning is that this is established by the analysis of the phrase as *saṃvādāvṛtteḥ* (of the repetition of the conversation) and *anena* (by this). || 14 ||
There, immediately after granting the boon, the king gave him a name.
The question [of the relationship] between knowledge and ritual acts is not stated [here], because they are mutually contradictory. (15)

[Objection: "But surely, since the question regarding desires was granted as a boon within the context of the Agnihotra, why were the question and answer concerning the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya*) not indicated right there? To this he replies: "He did not ask. This means that in that context of the Agnihotra, following the granting of the boon, the King did not ask about the true nature of the Self, nor did the Sage provide an answer; such is the non-utterance of the question and so forth, [which occurred] due to [the preoccupation with] ritual acts (*karmabhiḥ*).
The construction is: "because it is contrary to knowledge. || 19 ||
This knowledge requires another cause for its very own arising.
When the darkness regarding the inner self is destroyed, it requires nothing else. || 16 ||

[Objection: But surely, according to the principle of the *sarvāpekṣādhikaraṇa*, knowledge requires ritual actions; how then could it be contradicted by them? [Reply: One must choose between the alternatives: does it require them for its own origination, or for its own fruit? Having raised this doubt, he accepts the first alternative with the words, "In its own origination.
He refutes the second alternative with the principle, "And for that very reason, there is no requirement for firewood and the like," using the words, "The inner self... (16).
Because it destroys ignorance merely by the attainment of its own true nature.
Even the performance [of the rite] does not obstruct that which is to be enjoined, just as [the act of] giving [does not obstruct the gift]. || 17 ||

In this regard, the reason is stated: "Its own nature," etc. He concludes that knowledge is incompatible with action by saying "therefore. Regarding the point that once arisen, it does not follow after any worldly transaction, he provides a counter-example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta): "like an axe. For while an axe, even though produced, requires application for the purpose of cutting, knowledge is not like that—this is the meaning. || 17 ||

This body,
rendered powerless to engage with the great commentary on the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* composed by the best of gods,
is itself like a lump of clay.
The activity of being dependent on another arises from its own inherent nature, which is called "non-origination."

Having stated the unfitness for the inquiry and response regarding knowledge in the section on action (*karmaprakaraṇa*), he prepares the ground to state the question beginning with "O Yājñavalkya. [The phrase] "to engage in worldly activity" means that the body is not by itself capable of engaging in activity because it is insentient, like a lump of clay. Furthermore, he says [the body] possesses activity dependent on another because it is inert, like a chariot or similar objects: "dependent on another" (*parataḥ*). || 18 ||
Having determined [the nature of] earth and so forth through the grace of its own self-luminosity.
One performs actions such as sitting and so forth, and from that arises the connection with their fruit.
Anticipating the objection that the insentience of the body is unproven because it is observed to be an agent through the determination of earth and other elements, he says:
"Earth, etc. Anticipating the objection that its sentience is due to its possessing results such as pleasure, he says: "And from that," meaning: solely through the favor of self-luminosity. || 19 ||
Since this was so, the lord of men questioned Yājñavalkya.
"What is the light of this [self]?"—thus, with the desire to know the inner light (pratyag-jyotis).

Raising the question, [the author] states: "Since... (verse 20). He suggests that the King, having conceived the idea that the body and its actions, as well as their fruits, arise solely from the power of the inward light (*pratyagjyotis*), questioned him out of a desire to know that [truth].
Thus he introduces the inquiry. "Since... (verse 20).
The instruments, the body, and the person (puruṣa) are intended here [as the subject].
One who performs actions such as sitting and so forth, as well as rites concerning seats, sacred fields, and the like. || 21 ||

In this regard, he states the meaning of the word "person" (*puruṣa*): "the instruments. He explains the person's dependence upon light for the aggregate of body and instruments: "seating and so forth. Anticipating the objection that since each respective action is accomplished by depending on its own specific object, what is the need for light, he says: "the seat. The objects of actions such as sitting and walking—namely, seats, fields, and so on—are insentient; therefore, they depend upon light.
The meaning is that action does not arise from that alone. || 21 ||
What is the use of [a whole] that is distinct from its own collection of parts and belongs to a different genus?
This person is to be designated by means of the light that is not composite. || 22 ||
Or rather, let it be called "light" (jyotis) as that which is the opposite of those [qualities].
Furthermore, what follows from this if it is indeed so?

[The author] analyzes the interrogative statement beginning with "What" (kiṃ). That is to say, that light which is distinct from the aggregate of the body and its organs, from their individual parts, and from their collection—being uncomposite and untouched by such categories as "humanity" (manuṣyatva) and the like. By the uncomposite [light], [the composite... is [perceived].
The meaning of the alternative is that a person may or may not participate in worldly activity by means of the light. He asks: "If it is the first case, what indeed is the fruit?

If it is the second, what is lost? He says, "Furthermore," implying: "That which results from the first position and that which is forfeited from the other shall now be stated; listen with attention. || 22 || 23 ||

If there were an assistance by the light of those two in the manner previously described, [then... [Vol. 3, Page 248] 3 Brāhmaṇa: Commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri. 2381. If there were an assistance by the light of those two in the manner previously described...
Even though that [dharma] is imperceptible, it is known through the observation of its indicative mark, namely human action. || 24 ||
Then we shall infer that light to be exactly like that.
Now, its opposite, the conjunction with Jyotis, will be examined. || 25 ||
We shall then infer that light to be of such a nature.
Furthermore, if a dual nature is not perceived, then even in that case there would be uncertainty. (26)

In that regard, having restated the first [position], he states the result: "Of those two," etc. The meaning is this: if, between the two lights under discussion, it is ascertained at the time of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) that the person is assisted by a distinct light, then even in cases such as dreaming where the light is not perceptible and yet human activity is observed, a distinct light must be inferred there as well; thus, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is established. Having restated another alternative view, [he states] the loss—

The author says "māha" (he says). By the words beginning with "atha" (now), the meaning is as follows: if at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the favoring [of the self] by light is apprehended as non-different from the agent of worldly activity (*vyavahartṛ*), then in dreams and the like, that [light] must be inferred as non-different from the agent of activity on the basis of its mark (*liṅga*). Consequently, there would be a loss of the established doctrine (*siddhānta-hāni*), because the body and so forth would themselves result in being the self. He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "athāniyamaḥ" (now, if there is no rule) with the word "atha. He says: "aha—" (I say).

The word "ṣṭe" (in the commentary) is a [scribal] corruption for "ṣṭeti". The meaning is that if, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the positive concomitance (*vyatireka*) or negative concomitance (*avyatireka*) of the light is doubtful, then even through inference there is no establishment of its ascertainment. || 24 || 25 || 26 ||
With this intention in mind, Janaka questioned the sage.

And he, being questioned, gave a reply according to the inquiry. [Verse 27] He concludes the meaning of the question with the words "this is so" (ity etat). He introduces the passage beginning with "the light of the sun" (ādityajyotiḥ) with the words "and he" (sa ca).
The meaning is that he did not bypass the question out of a desire to know a light distinct [from the body]. || 27 ||
If this is so, for what purpose did the king question the sage regarding his skill?
Having inferred it for oneself, why does one not resort to such a light? || 28 ||
If, according to the manner stated, the king is capable of discerning merits and defects, he is likewise capable of inference; therefore, he would know the desired knowledge of the stars by himself.
Why then does he follow the sage? For who, being wise and acting with deliberation, would follow another when the matter is within his own power?
Thus he raises the objection with the word "nanu" (but/how then). || 28 ||
"True it is so; nevertheless, this king questioned that sage."
Because the relationship between the sign and the signified is difficult to discern due to its extreme subtlety. || 29 ||

Even though the king possesses skill, he concludes that a sage must be sought; thus he says, "It is true. To the question of why a sage must be sought, he replies, "By signs," for because the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is extremely subtle, it is difficult for a single person to discern.
The meaning is that the Sage is intended as the one who makes [the truth] known. || 29 ||
Confusion regarding gender and other such markers is observed even among many.
How much more so for one person? Therefore, the king questioned him.

Anticipating the objection as to how there can be such extreme subtlety in the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other factors, he says: "Of many" (*bahūnām*). The meaning is that even those who perceive only the appearance of smoke infer the possessor of smoke (fire) because they have not ascertained the distinction between them. He states the conclusion regarding the fact that the knowledge of the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is obtainable through effort: "He questioned" (*paryapṛcchat*). || 30 ||
For this very reason, Manu spoke thus for the sake of discerning subtle dharmas.
An assembly of at least ten members is required, and the wise look for such a gathering. || 31 ||

He cites the statement of Manu as an authority for their extreme subtlety, [beginning with] the word "subtle. The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that even for one who is skilled, there exists a dependence on other persons when it comes to determining subtle matters.
[As it is said: "Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*), has been understood through Dharma..."
Those Brahmins who have the Vedas as their direct authority should be known as the learned.
An assembly of at least ten members proclaims the Dharma, or even one of fewer than three who are established in virtuous conduct;
one should not disregard that Dharma.
One who has mastered the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the first three orders of life— this assembly consists of at least ten members.
"One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and one who knows the Sāmaveda—this assembly of at least three is to be known for the determination of doubts regarding Dharma.
This defines [the assembly]. By saying "ten," he illuminates that there is agreement among other authors of Dharmaśāstras as well on the matter thus stated.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for emphasis. Furthermore, even now, many people of subtle vision are seen to depend upon [the scriptures] for the determination of subtle matters, because signs (*liṅga*) and so forth are difficult to understand; thus he says: "And they depend... (31).
Or else, it is Śruti itself that [speaks] in the form of Yājñavalkya and others.
Through the path of inference, he has directly established light for us.
Having stated that even for one skilled in inference, it is appropriate to question the Sage for the sake of determining subtle matters, he states an alternative position: "O Yājñavalkya... (32).
Yājñavalkya, who understood the king's intention, spoke to that monarch as well.
When the aforementioned light is established, this [is expressed as] "the light of the sun. || 33 ||
Considering that the occurrence of a question necessitates the occurrence of an answer, he repeats the very same answer previously stated, beginning with the words "O King.

The meaning is that the King asks with the intention of referring to a light distinct [from the body], and the Sage likewise answers, taking the establishment of that [distinction] as his motive. || 33 ||

This person is indeed [known] by the light called the Sun alone— which is self-established, singular, and radiant, and which is utterly distinct from and of a different nature than the body, its limbs, their collection, the genus, the configuration, their actions, the location, and so forth.
It remains, it moves about, and having performed its action, it returns once more. || 34 || 35 ||

He explains the words of the response, which were raised as an illustration of the light intended to be discussed, beginning with "deha" (the body). And the body...

The meaning of the construction is as follows: that light characterized by the sun—which is entirely distinct from and dissimilar to their parts, their aggregate, the body, its birth, its location, its activity, and its space and time; which is abundant, independent, and does not depend on any other light—is "that" (tat). || 34 || 31 ||
In the midst of these two lights, this person exists, whose nature is insentient.
For everything from the intellect (buddhi) down to the objects of the senses is reflected within immediate consciousness. || 36 ||
Anticipating the objection that the light of the Self is unnecessary for the empirical functioning of the body and so forth, since the light of the sun and other sources is as stated, he says:

"In the middle. This distinguishes the person, whose nature is insentient, as being situated between the two lights—the insentient and the sentient. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that the establishment of the intellect and its adjuncts is impossible without their being colored by the reflection of consciousness. || 36 ||
The cause of delusion regarding that inward, unique, self-luminous, stable, uncomposite, and actionless [Self], which is the opposite of the sun, moon, and other lights, is as follows: || 37 ||
It consists of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; it possesses an agent, the instruments of action, and the result.
It consists of the departure from and arrival at the states of saṃsāra, such as hunger and the like. || 38 ||

Regarding what those luminaries are, he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*). The stability and immutability (*kauṭasthya*) of the inner self—which is internal to all, devoid of all distinctions, consisting of pure consciousness, unattached, and indifferent—is established there by the reason that it is "actionless" (*niṣkriya*); for that [actionlessness] is contrary to [change], and therefore, as stated:

The meaning is that [the world] is the opposite of that light: it is external, manifold, dependent on another for its manifestation, conjoined with what is to be manifested, and subject to transformation.

The phrase "it exists in between" is to be connected with the preceding [text]. In response to the inquiry as to what reason is stated here for the fact that the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties denoted by the term *puruṣa* do not depend on lights such as the sun, the text qualifies the *puruṣa* by saying "delusion," etc.; [this delusion] is born from ignorance of the Self.

The meaning is that the complex consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, the agent, the action, the effect, the enjoyer, the enjoyment, and the object of enjoyment—is subject to birth and destruction, and depends upon the non-material light [of consciousness], because it lacks self-luminosity (*svatobhāna*). || 37 || 38 ||
With his eyes illuminated by that very light which is of a nature contrary to it, [he beheld].
It always remains together with the sun; it goes out and comes back, and it performs its functions. || 39 ||

One might object: "Since the functioning of the intellect and so forth is established by non-inert light alone, there is no need for anything else. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "tadviruddha" (opposed to that), meaning: "The intellect and so forth, which are the opposite of the agent who functions as a composite of the intellect and other faculties, function as specific transformations produced by that light known as the sun. || 39 ||
The phrase "beyond the sun" does not serve to restrict the scope to the sun alone.

It favors that which arises from karma due to the cause of innate ignorance.
Even though the intellect possesses activities such as desire and so forth, how can the Self be devoid of activity while being its supporter? To this, he says: "The Self.

By the power of its own ignorance, the Self has emerged within the intellect and other faculties; accompanied by its own reflection, it illumines the intellect and the rest through its mere proximity—this is the meaning. || 86 ||
Just as the one sun illumines this entire world.
Thus, the traditional teaching states that he manifests the field, the knower of the field, and the entirety [of their relationship]. (87)
In this regard, he cites the word of the Blessed One as authoritative: "As it is said... (87)
That is indeed the ignorance of the inner self (pratyagajñāna) associated with various conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
It manifests in the form of memory regarding the intellect and so forth, by the power of karma. || 88 ||
One might object: "By asserting that the Self illumines the intellect (*dhi*), which consists of desire and so forth, you have stated that desire and the like are effects of the intellect;

this is incorrect, because ignorance (*ajñāna*) is accepted as the cause of everything. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not [so]... That very ignorance, accompanied by various latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, evolves (*vivartate*)—by virtue of the karma of living beings—into the form of the intellect and so on, as well as in the nature of its transformations such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*); thus, there is no abandonment of our fundamental tenet.
This is the meaning. || 88 ||
Therefore, like the sun and other luminaries, the intellect possesses its own manifestation as its sole companion.
The immutable one bestows grace in accordance with the ignorance inherent in his own self. || 89 ||

Since it has been stated that because ignorance is the cause of everything, the Self’s role as the sustainer of the intellect and other faculties occurs through its influence, the author states the resulting conclusion: "Like the sun and so forth. (89)
The connection with those to be favored [arises] from the continuity of a single genus.
The attainment of the sun and other [deities] here occurs for the self through the path of ignorance. (90)

1192 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

Because form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as the sense organs such as the eye (*mān*), belong to the same genus of being material (*bhautikatva*), it is logical that they stand in the relationship of the assisted (*anugrāhya*) and the assister (*anugrāhaka*), as do the intellect (*buddhi*) and the Self (*ātman*).

Anticipating the objection that this is not so because of the dissimilarity between the two, he says: "anugrāhya" (the object to be favored). Here, in the intellect and so forth, there is a connection of identity with the Self through the medium of ignorance; therefore, even in the absence of homogeneity (*sājātya*), there is the status of being a favorer (*anugrāhakatva*) characterized by witnesshood (*sākṣitva*). This is the meaning. || 90 ||
By the very ignorance of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa-avidyā), the Self, though immutable, attains the state of being a witness.
He stands alone amidst the many forms that come and go. || 91 ||

To the question of how that which is immutable (kūṭastha) can possess the nature of a witness, he says: "The light of consciousness" (cidābhā). This establishes the witnessing nature of consciousness by its non-deviation amidst things that deviate. He says: "Scriptural authority" (āgama). || 91 ||
Like the object of sight, this witness of the seer and the seeing is also non-different [from them].
Even though there is a distinction between the seer and the seeing, there is not even the slightest difference in this [consciousness].

It might be objected that unity among many is untenable, because—just as there is a distinction of sense organs due to the distinction of objects such as form and so forth—there would necessarily follow a distinction of the witness (sākṣin) due to the distinction of the witnessed (sākṣya). Anticipating this objection, he says: "As the seer" (dṛśyā). The meaning is: just as the sun, the illuminator, is not divided despite the diversity of things to be illuminated, or just as the eye remains one despite the distinction between white, black, and other colors, so too the witness ought not to be divided despite the diversity of the witnessed. [This is] the application of the analogy.
He elaborates: "The seer," [verse 92].
The reflection of consciousness within the intellect is also always accompanied by the causal connection.
Apart from the manifestation of consciousness, the transformation of the intellect is in vain. || 93 ||

Anticipating the objection that since witnesshood (*sākṣitva*) exists at all times, its cause—ignorance (*avidyā*)—would also exist at all times, and thus how could there be liberation, [the author], intending to show that one is a witness only when the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is present, establishes the persistence of the reflection within the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties. He states: "By the cause," etc. He provides the reasoning for the non-deviation of the reflection of consciousness from the existence of the intellect and so forth: "By the reflection of consciousness," etc., because of its insentience (*jaḍatā*).
The meaning is that it is because self-establishment is impossible. || 93 ||
The object and the inner self enter the intellect by means of their own manifestation.
Just as space and jars and so forth are perceived directly by themselves, appearing as their own forms.

Raising the objection that even though the Self is pervaded by that [intellect], it cannot be its witness because of the lack of a connection with the object, he says: "The object. Since both the jar and so forth, as well as the Self, reside within the intellect by means of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) bearing their respective forms, they are connected; therefore, the meaning is that the Self is the witness of those two. Just as the external jar and so forth have only a figurative entry into the intellect, why would the Self's [entry] not also be figurative, given the absence of a primary connection? [To this he replies: Because...

Anticipating the objection that [the Self] might be a witness [only indirectly], he says: "By its own reflection" (*svābhāsa*). Just as space directly pervades a jar and so forth, or just as the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) pervades the intellect because ignorance—which is its cause—is not an intervening factor (according to the maxim: "that which is one's own limb is not an intervention"), in this way the Self is directly pervaded within the intellect and other faculties due to their being its very self (*pratyaktva*). Therefore, it is appropriate that it is the witness of ignorance and the rest.
This is the meaning. || 94 ||

Even that connection with ignorance and the like is itself imagined by ignorance.
For there is no real connection of the self with the other [world]. || 95 ||

Fearing that the connection of the Self with ignorance and so forth might be real because it would otherwise lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if it were merely illusory (*āvidyaka*), he says: "Even this... The sense is that the infinite regress may be resolved just as in the case of the *samavāya* (inherence) and other categories accepted by others. By the two particles (*api*), it is indicated that this [connection] has already been resolved. He states the reason for the connection being imagined (*kalpita*): "But [it is not] real," because [the Self] is unattached (*asaṅga*).
The logical proof consists in [the Lord's] being without a second and so forth. || 99 ||
"Just as [the self is perceived] through knowledge and illumination, and not otherwise."
In this way, just as jars and other such objects possess suitability for action, so too do intellect and the rest.
It has been stated that the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses a connection with both the form of consciousness (*cit*) and external forms; this is now established by means of an illustration.

[The verse says] "Just as" (*yathā*). The meaning is: just as it is observed that objects such as a jar possess the capacity for activity only when there is a connection between the knowledge consisting of a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) and the light of the sun and so forth, so too, the capacity for activity in the case of the intellect and other things would exist only when there is a connection with these two forms. || 96 ||
When there is a connection with an external form, the mind may be sufficient for the performance of action.
But if the two had different substrata, the thought "I am suffering" would not be established. (97)

He explains the application to the case at hand with the word "cid" (consciousness). He states the defect that would arise if consciousness and the objective form did not reside in a single cognition, using the words "tayor" (of those two). || 97 ||
— Gwyllfígg: Ruanta a Kuus — London.
Because of its immutability, it is devoid of transformation, being certain [in its nature] while that which undergoes change is uncertain.
To the self, this entire universe would be like a darkness in which no one dances. || 98 ||

The reason for this is stated: "because of immutability" (*kauṭasthyāt*). This means because the Self is immutable. He states that in the absence of cognitions such as "I am suffering," there would be a loss of all worldly transactional activity (*vyavahāra*), saying: "it would be so" (*syāt*). || 98 ||
Therefore, one should accept that [the world] arises from delusion and so forth, just like the appearance of a jar and other such things.
Even the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) everywhere [is known] from the experience "I do not know. || 99 ||

He states the conclusion: that through the medium of the external form’s manifestation, there is a pervasion by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—as if it were transferred—into all states such as delusion (*moha*) and the like. He says "the jar, etc. This means that because the reflection of consciousness and the objective form necessarily share a single substratum.

[Objection: Since there is the experience "the jar shines," even though that [jar] is pervaded by the reflection of consciousness, how can ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the intellect (*buddhi*), etc., be pervaded by it?
To this, he says: "In all cases. (99)
This favor toward the internal self is what is intended here by the Śruti.
Just as the sun's favor leads to the attainment of a seat and other such things for a person, [so too does the grace of the Guru]. || 100 ||

Even though the light of consciousness (cidābhāsa) pervades both the intellect and its modifications, how is it established by scripture that the light of the Self (ātmajyotis) acts as their illuminator?
To this, he says: "This [is] his," etc. This means: "By the scripture beginning with 'by the Self alone' and so forth. Here, the meaning is "in the intellect and so on.
An illustration for the illumination of the inner self (pratyagātman) is given: "as the sun," etc. (100).

1394 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
"Self" [is designated] with respect to the aggregate of the vital breaths, the physical body, and so forth, which are its constituent parts.
It is distinct from genus, configuration, relation, quality, and action. (101)
Having established that the self-luminous [consciousness] acts as a favorer toward the person in the form of the arising of its reflection, he elaborates upon the meaning of the term "self" (ātman).

Regarding the phrase "it is the self": the meaning is that the element of consciousness (cid-dhātu), which is distinct from the vital breath, the body, the senses and their parts, and the collection thereof—being distinct from the connection of that body with genus and configuration, and from the qualities and actions residing therein—is what is meant here by "self. || 101 ||
Because it has that as its essence, that reality manifests ignorance and the like.
It consists solely of light, is eternal, and is known through its own unique means of cognition.
How can that which is distinct from the body, the organs, their aggregate, and their attributes be the Self? To this he says: "That thou art.
That reality is the actual nature of the body and so forth, because it is the innermost self (pratyaktva) of that—this is the meaning. How does it possess the quality of being that light?
To this he says: "From ignorance, etc. He states the distinction from the sun and other luminaries: "One," etc. || 102 ||
And because anything other than that is insentient, direct perception is not admitted for others.
Likewise, because there is no superiority [in that cognition], it would not be an object for another person. || 103 ||

Anticipating the objection that it is incorrect to say [the Self] is "accessible only to uncommon means of knowledge" because it is the object of perception and other such means, he says: "Of that which is other than that.

The meaning is that the light of the Self is not accessible through the perception and so forth belonging to another, because anything other than the Self is insentient (jaḍa), and because there is no other entity that is non-insentient (ajaḍa). Even if there were another non-insentient entity, it could not be known by it, because—as with two lamps—there would be no distinction between them; thus he says: "Likewise" (tathā). || 103 ||
Because it is devoid of qualities such as sound, and because it is inward-facing and non-composite.
And because its nature consists solely of being seen, the self does not deserve to be an object of vision. || 104 ||
He states another argument for its being inaccessible to perception and the other means of knowledge: "Sound, etc. (verse 104).
Because there is no connection with another location and so forth, and because there is no intervention by delusion and the like.
And it cannot be perceived as being of the nature of the inner self, in the same way that delusion and other such states are perceived. || 105 ||

He states another reason for [the Self] being inaccessible to inference: "deśāntarādi" (due to [being located in] another place, etc.). Furthermore, since the Self is untouched by ignorance, doubt, and error, no means of knowledge (*māna*) operates upon it; however, its status as being known through the Upanishads (*aupaniṣadatva*) is understood to be by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). With this in mind, he says: "mohādi" (delusion, etc.).

Anticipating the objection that even though there is no intervention between that [delusion] and it, the Self might still be an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*) just like the [delusion], he says: "na ca" (and not).
He says "so too" [in verse 105] to show that because the Inner Self (pratīc) is the witness of all, it has no similarity with ignorance and the like.
Let it not be maintained that the light of the Self is of the same nature as the sun and other such luminaries.
Because that [measure] cannot be understood through measurement, and because the sun and other such objects lack it. || 106 ||

Now, one might argue that this [self] is material because it is illuminating, like the sun; thus, its self-luminosity is not established. To this, he replies: "Not the sun, etc. The word "that" (tat) in the phrase "the light of the Self" (ātmajyotiḥ) is connected to that [subject]. The sense is as follows: the subject under dispute is non-material because it is not an object of cognition;
for whatever is material is an object of cognition, as is the case with the sun and so forth—this being an argument based on negative concomitance (vyatireka). || 106 ||
1 gha. *kāraṃ* | 2 gha. *ṇasaṃghā* | 3 ka. ga. *nyatpraty* | 4 kha *paryāsāspṛ* | [Vol.
3, page 262] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1395.
And that light which is desired as being of the nature of alliteration.
That [object] is perceived by means of the group of instruments such as the eye, just like a jar and so forth. || 107 ||

Having raised the objection that the light which is to be assisted is of the same class [as the eye] because it is light (*jyotiṣṭva*), like the sun, he refutes this by means of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*). [He says:
"That which is to be assisted... (Verse 107).
Nor is it considered to be "immeasurable" in the same way as a rabbit's horn or similar non-entities.
It is non-different from that, because of its pervasiveness and its nature as the inner self, just like the sun.

Anticipating the objection that the probans (the state of being an object of knowledge) is over-pervasive (*sādhanavyāpti*) because even the self-luminous Self would likewise be an object of knowledge—otherwise it would follow that it is non-existent like a rabbit's horn—the author says: "And not... He states, "That is not different from it," considering that the cause of non-existence is not being an object of knowledge, but rather insentience (*jāḍya*). The meaning is that the existence of the Self is pervaded by its own non-different luminosity. This also applies to the proof of insentience.

Fearing that there might be a pervasion [of the probans], he refutes it by means of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of "non-selfhood" (*anātmatva*). He states, "Because of being interior" (*pratyaktvāt*). Regarding its nature as luminosity (*prakāśarūpatva*), he provides the example: "The sun" (*dinakṛt*). || 108 ||
It has been determined that the possession of horns is cognizable through the means of direct perception.
Apart from that intrinsic nature, the horn transcends intrinsic nature. || 109 ||

If the self-luminous [self] were an object of cognition, why would even a rabbit's horn not exist? To this he replies: "Perceptual," etc. The sense is that it is logical for something that is fit to be an object of knowledge to be non-existent if it is not the object of that [knowledge]. || 109 ||
The nature of the entity that is not-self is to subsist by depending on the feet of pride.
This [power] bestows success such as that of the Mātrās and so forth; however, because it is self-established, it does not exist at all times.

[The opponent] objects: "The very nature of the self is its fitness for being an object of knowledge (*māna-yogyatva*), because it is a real entity (*vastu*), just like a horn; in its absence, however, there would be non-existence. [The author] replies with the word "māna" (knowledge). The intention is that even in that case, "non-selfhood" (*anātmatva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). [The opponent] objects: "In your view, it is the self itself, when unknown, that is fit for all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not any other thing; so how can you state it otherwise? To this, he says "mātrādi" (the knower, etc.). [This refers to] all...

This is not the inherent nature of the Self—that it should be an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatva*)—because it is always manifest by its own independence. Therefore, even the means of knowledge that operate by presupposing limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) do not take that [Self] as their object. This is because of such scriptural texts as "That indeed is beyond the known" (*anyadeva tad viditāt*).

The sense is that even the statement regarding its being an object of valid cognition is intended to illuminate its difference from other entities (*vastu*), not to indicate that it is actually an object of those cognitions. || 110 ||
When all the previously mentioned luminaries have set, the latent impressions [remain].
The light, being inwardly perceived by oneself, illuminates the seat and the other [limbs]. || 111 ||

Having stated that the self-luminosity of the light of the Self is conveyed by the word "light," he concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "by the Self alone this... with the words "when [all lights] have set. The construction is as follows: when all the aforementioned lights have set, the inner light (pratyag-jyotis), which is perceived by itself, illuminates the impressions (vāsanās) such as sitting and so forth. This is because, in states such as sleep, impressions and the like appear merely as mental impressions (vāsanāmātra).
Having intended "you" (tvam), [he uses] the word "vāsanā. || 111 ||
16. Also, *taki* [Vol.
3, page 263] 1396 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter—]
This Self is self-luminous, which [shines] in the sun, the moon, fire, and the eyes.
When they have set, he remains, illuminating the activity of the mind with his very gaze.

It might be argued that the statement "the light of the Self is perceived by itself" is untenable, because, like a lamp, it possesses the quality of illuminating [objects], which entails the consequence that it must itself be illuminated by something else. To this, he says: "This... When all other lights have ceased, that which remains—illuminating the mind, its activities, and the perception of one's own nature—is the Self, the self-luminous light; it has no requirement for another illuminator, as it is distinct from the insentient.
This is the meaning. || 112 ||
Immeasurable, he is the source of self-realization for all embodied beings.
Therefore, its lack of connection with a self is not established by means of valid cognition.

Now, it may be argued that the self’s distinctness from the body and so forth, as well as its self-luminosity, are for the sake of its non-difference from Brahman; yet that non-difference cannot exist because of the self’s association with agency and other such attributes. To this, he says: "The Self. Precisely because of its self-luminosity, the self has no connection with non-self attributes such as agency; for since there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for [proving] agency in the self-luminous, that [agency] is unestablished, as the self is not an object (*viṣaya*) of such a means of knowledge, and that [means of knowledge] likewise...
This is the meaning. || 113 ||
If the Self were not self-established,
then no object other than the inward-facing [Self] would be perceived by one who possesses the cognition "I am."
That which is established as the "Self" is so only insofar as it is not contradicted by other means of valid cognition. || 114 ||

Furthermore, he states that the scriptural passage beginning with "The Self which is free from evil" (*ya ātmā'pahatapāpmā*) serves as a supporting authority for the fact that agency and other such qualities are not connected to the Self. He says: "If not. If, through both the cognition of the form of the Self and its linguistic usage, agency and the like are not perceived as distinct from the Self, then because the perception "I am the agent" and so forth would be an error, there is no contradiction [with scripture]; thus, the passage "The Self which is free from evil" is appropriate, as is the passage "The Self which is the innermost of all" (*ya ātmā sarvāntara*).
And thus, the meaning is that this statement, which is intent upon oneness, is consistent and coherent. || 114 ||
If it is so, this is understood from such statements as "The Self is Brahman."
Oneness (aikātmya), which is not grasped by perception and other means of knowledge and is free from sublation, [is established];

thus he says that even sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) are appropriate regarding the self's lack of connection with agency and so forth, based on the previously stated reasoning and authority.

He says: "The Self... The connection is: "This oneness. He rejects the notion that [the scripture] is merely a restatement of what is already known through perception, etc., by saying: "By perception and so forth."
He shows its exclusion from doubt and error with the word "bādhā" (sublation). || 115 ||
But surely, since the self is non-different from the body and so forth, how can there be liberation?
Furthermore, oneness is not established by scripture, because it contradicts direct perception. (116)

Regarding the statement, "The Self alone is its light," it is said that the Self is distinct from the body, is self-luminous, and is devoid of all agency and so forth; this being the case, the proponent of the doctrine that the body is the Self (dehātmavādī) objects: "But surely... The meaning is that since the Self consists merely of the body and so forth—as will be shown by the forthcoming perception—and since agency and the like are possible for that [body], there can be no establishment of liberation for one who possesses such a nature. As for the claim that "this Self is Brahman"...

Regarding that, he states [the reason] for why the Śruti does not establish its status as Brahman: "By perception," etc. For there is a contradiction with perception—such as the thought "I am the agent"—which undermines the Śruti you favor.

Since the purport [of the scripture] regarding its own literal meaning is not established, the Self does not thereby attain the nature of Brahman; nor is the scripture a valid means of knowledge, because perception alone possesses that status.
Thus, the sense is that there would be a failure to establish either the destruction of bondage or the intended liberation consisting in the nature of Brahman. || 116 ||
For it is held that [sound] is produced by the conjunction of earth, water, fire, and air.
Even though consciousness is absent in each [element] individually, it [emerges] like the power of intoxication. || 117 ||
Since consciousness belongs only to that which is the Self, and since it is absent in the body and so forth, how can they possess the nature of the Self? To this he says: "For thus...

Since it is established that earth, water, fire, and air are the fundamental elements (*tattvas*), although each one of them individually lacks the power of consciousness, the consciousness that arises from their conjunction—that is, from the body as a composite—is its property. This is just as the power of intoxication, though absent in yeast and other ingredients individually, emerges from their combination.
The meaning is that, being associated with that [notion], the body is regarded as the self. || 117 ||
"I am a human"—thus [the self is known] through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
A direct perception arises regarding this body as being like a black serpent. (118)

He establishes perception as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the relationship of attribute and substratum (*dharma-dharmitva*) between consciousness and the body. [The text says] "I am. Just as there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the black snake," whereby blackness and the snake stand in the relation of attribute and substratum, so too, due to the coreferentiality in "I am a human," there arises a cognition in the form of perception whose object is that the "I" is an attribute of the body which possesses the genus of humanity; this is the meaning. || 118 ||
Furthermore, no object that is accessible to the notion of "I" has ever been observed as being distinct from the body.
O Goddess, blackness and other such qualities are attributes of the body; therefore, consciousness is distinct from them. (119)

Having stated the perception [of the self] as being the body qualified by consciousness, he states the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the self as postulated by others. With the words "And not...
(*na ca*), he states the result: that there is no proof for the body itself being the self, and likewise no proof for a self distinct from it, as in the case of snakes and so forth. || 119 ||
Is it not indeed appropriate [to speak of difference] in the case of an external object, because of its separation from the knower?
The connection with the property [of being a snake] in the case of a snake and so forth is due to non-difference from the self. (120)

The phrase "and like a black snake" implies that consciousness and the body stand in the relation of attribute and substrate (*dharma-dharmitva*). [The opponent objects: "But surely... The meaning is as follows: it is logical that there is a valid cognition (*pramā*) of the connection between blackness and so forth with the non-self, such as the snake, because for the perceiver—the cognizer—there exists a state of being distinct from both the snake and its attributes; however, there can be no valid cognition of the relation of attribute and substrate regarding the self, which is consciousness, because there is no cognizer existing apart from it. || 120 ||
Furthermore, the nature of phenomena such as the body is held to be insentient by its very essence.
Because it consists of nothing more than self-awareness, consciousness does not possess such a form [as an external object]. || 121 ||

He states another reason for the absence of the relationship between property and its possessor (*dharma-dharmitva*) between consciousness (*cit*) and the body: "Inert," etc. Such a nature constitutes the state of being a property (*dharmatā*). 121.
Just as in this world a qualification of a substance is apprehended by a single cognition.
In this way, the establishment of consciousness and the body is not possible, because consciousness is not an object of the power of consciousness.
Anticipating the objection—"Even if consciousness is non-inert, why should its status as a quality (dharma) not belong to the body, which is inert?"—the author says: "Just as...

Just as between two things cognizable by a single cognition there exists the relation of quality and qualified—for example, color, which is grasped by the same cognition as the possessor of form (rūpin), is a qualifier of it by virtue of being its quality—it is not so [in the case of the body and consciousness].
(Note: Variant readings indicate 'gu' for 'uktaṃ' and 'paṃ' for 'dharma'.)

The meaning is that since consciousness and the body appear within a single cognition, and because consciousness is not an object [of that cognition], there can be no relationship of attribute and substrate between the two. || 122 ||
It is not so; for by that very means through which the existence of consciousness is perceived, [it is established].
By that very [means], its true nature (dharmatā) is measured, just as [the nature] of an effect and so forth is measured. || 123 ||

The proponent of the doctrine that the body is the self (dehātmavādī) objects: "It is not so. For by means of reasoning, you reject the relationship of attribute and substrate between consciousness and the body;

yet that [rejection] is perceived as a fallacy because it contradicts direct perception. Furthermore, the existence of consciousness, which is established through experience and other means, also proves that it possesses the body as its substrate.
The meaning is: because its dependence on that [other] is well-established. || 123 ||
Is it not the case that the notion "this" arises with respect to the body, just as it does with respect to a jar and other objects?
But the inward-turning intellect resides in the "I" aspect; between these two, there is no relationship of attribute and substrate.

"Indeed, for these two—the body and consciousness—there is no relationship of property and property-possessor because of their contradiction"; thus he raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but surely). || 124 ||
Just as a bracelet or similar ornament is composed of the single substance of gold.
That which has not attained selfhood elsewhere appears as if it had attained selfhood.
In the same way, by the very nature of things, the power of consciousness is established in the elements.
It serves for the purpose of linguistic convention regarding cognitions such as "I" and so forth. || 126 ||

The proponent refutes this with an example: "Just as... Just as objects such as bracelets (*rucaka*) and swastikas, being modifications of gold, are observed to be the basis for practical usage and cognition as if they were distinct from it—even though their existence is not obtained elsewhere than in that [gold]—so too, consciousness, by virtue of its nature as an effect of the aggregate of the elements and its status as a property of the body, although its selfhood is not obtained elsewhere, serves as the basis for words and cognitions such as "I" and "self" through its own power.

The meaning is: although the object of hearing is not [the ultimate reality] itself, its nature as a phenomenon (dharma) is not thereby excluded, because there is no contradiction in its being a phenomenon—just as the nature of gold is not contradicted by [its presence in] bracelets and other ornaments. || 125 || 126 ||
If consciousness were a property of the body, then it would remain unimpaired even at the time of death.
Why is it not perceived directly, as is the case with that which resides within a living body? || 127 ||
Anticipating the objection that "even there, since the body vibrates, consciousness itself appears as belonging to it," he says: "Directly" (sākṣāt). || 127 ||
This is not a fault, for the body is indeed a composite of the four great elements.
Then, when the vital air has departed, consciousness also perishes. || 128 ||

The opponent replies with "No" (*na*) and so forth, stating that this is not the case because the status of being a property (*dharmatva*) is established for that [consciousness], even though it arises from a substratum such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

The meaning is as follows: the body is a composite of the four elements beginning with earth; at the time of death, due to the departure of air, the complete composite no longer exists, and thus its effect—consciousness—also perishes. Therefore, its being a property of the body is not contradictory, just like conjunction and other such qualities. [This is because] the effect of a collection...
The word "hi" is used to state that it has been understood in the assembly that even if any one of these [conditions] is absent, there is no existence. || 128 ||
Is it not indeed by the force of recognition related to one's own body and so forth?
Therefore, the distinction of consciousness from the elements is established even for one who is awake. || 129 ||
16. *yala* | 2 *gha* ‘avadā’ | 3 *kha* ‘tā cāvi’. [Vol.
3, page 266] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1399.

Relying on recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), he raises an objection: "In a dream... [etc. Although the dream-body in the form of a tiger and so forth is distinct from the waking body in human form, nevertheless—because there is a recognition of the consciousness residing in both bodies in the form "I am he who was asleep," and because there is no recognition of the attributes of one body as being associated with another body—the consciousness [is distinct] from the elements that originate the two bodies and from the two bodies originated by them.
Therefore, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is established; the meaning is that the body is not the self. || 129 ||
The creation of another body is as certain as the consciousness of the waking state.
The aggregate of elements produces [the body], just as one perceives oneself as a child, a youth, and so forth in a dream. || 130 ||

The proponent says: "In another body," etc. Just as the collection of elements initiates the youthful body endowed with the very same consciousness that remained in the infant body, and initiates the old man's body qualified by that same specific consciousness—such that there is no difference in consciousness despite the difference in states—likewise, he (the self) produces another body in the dream state endowed with the very consciousness residing in the waking body; therefore, even if consciousness were a property of the body [there would be no contradiction].
The meaning is that recognition is not contradictory because of the identity [of the object] in both cases. || 130 ||
And there is no recognition here [of the object] for you, because of the falsity of transformation.
For, unlike [the body of] childhood and so forth, the body is not perceived as such within the dream state. (131)

Having accepted the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding the consciousness residing in the body during dreams and so forth, and having stated that such [recognition] is possible even in the doctrine that the body is the self (*dehātmavāda*), he says "And not" (*na ca*) to show that its validity does not exist at all. Here, "herein" (*atra*) refers to the mention of the consciousness residing in the dream-body. He states the reason for this:
