"It is false" (*mithyā*). This is because, according to the doctrine of Māyā, the dream is false by the principle stated in such passages as "But [the world] is mere Māyā in its entirety."

The meaning is that recognition is an error because the consciousness residing therein [in the dream] is likewise [illusory]. Regarding his own position as well, he states the reason for the falsity of the dream:
"Not at all," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "therefore it is false. || 131 ||
If it is argued that the self is considered eternal on the basis of the example of recollecting past births;
Having seen a wound previously inflicted, why is the body not declared to be impermanent? (132)

[The opponent] objects: "Surely someone remembers a previous birth, thinking, 'Previously I was a Śūdra, but now I am a Brāhmaṇa. This [memory] would not be possible unless there were a single rememberer existing through both bodies; thus, when the Self is established as distinct from those two bodies, by that very example, the Self must be of this same nature everywhere. Thus he raises the doubt with the word *jāti*. [The author] replies that even in the view of the opponent, the memory of past births is indeed logical.

Regarding the term "wound": in a previous birth, in whatever part of the body a wound caused by a weapon or the like existed, it is that very same body, complete with that [wound], which is now experienced by him. Thus, the meaning is that our position—that the body itself is the eternal self—is established. || 132 ||
If it is held that the self possesses permanence there because of recognition;
That [cognition] which recognizes its own self is also false in its object, just as before;
for living beings lying with their bodies pierced by arrows are likewise [unaware].
They will produce another body, if recognition is admitted.

Furthermore, as for the recollection of past births—whether it be memory (*smṛti*) or recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—it cannot be the former, because that would not establish its eternity, since memory lacks intrinsic validity (*aprāmāṇya*).

Intending to show that this is due to the nature of the Self, Sureśvarācārya raises a second objection based on recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). The phrase "in that regard" refers to the two bodies, the previous and the subsequent.
Just as the recognition "I am he who slept," this recognition too is merely an error; therefore, it is not a recollection of a past birth (*jātismṛti*).

He refutes the proof of a self distinct from the three bodies with the words "In a dream... Anticipating the objection that this is not an error because there is an absence of defects in the cause and a lack of sublation, he says "As before. If it is recognized according to the aforementioned reasoning, then, as in the previous case, the elements initiate another body characterized by consciousness residing in one's own waking body; thus, recognition belongs to the other [the opponent] as well.

The meaning is as follows: since the elements residing therein originate that very body along with its wounds because they initiate a body possessed of wounds, the existence of a self distinct from the body and so forth cannot be established through recognition. || 133 || 134 ||
Just as these very elements are born in such a manner, so it is.
Why should there not be recognition in the form, "I am that very same person"? (135)
Fearing that the previous body, being scarred and reduced to ashes, might not be an object of recognition at present, he says:

"Those very [elements]. Just as you have recognition regarding the elements that constitute the scarred body, so too for me, there is the establishment of that [recognition] regarding the body produced by them.

For it is not the case that a body which was previously non-existent comes into being now, as that would lead to an over-extension; therefore, the body itself, characterized by consciousness, is the self.
The meaning is [as follows]. || 135 ||
And this quality of being the light of the self which has been described as distinct [from the body].
Through the dissolution of the sun and other elements here, that indeed becomes merely material.

Anticipating the objection—“How can the body be the self? For, by the mark of being a conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), just like the usage [based on] the sun and other [lights], it is inferred that the usage in dreams and so forth is caused by a distinct light”—he says: “And that which... This means the state of being the light of the self (*ātmajyotiṣṭva*), that is, the existence of that light which is its form. The phrase “as distinct from the aggregate” implies “from the agent of the usage. [This is known] through the dissolution of the sun and others.

The meaning is: [this is known] by the mark of the empirical usage of dreams and so forth, which is observed even when all other lights have set. Although the light of the Self is distinct from the body and its constituents, it argues that it is nonetheless material because it is a light, like the sun; thus he says: "It is material. (136)
That which is of the same class as the object to be assisted is the assistant.
For in this world, he is seen as clearly as the sun is to the eyes. || 137 ||

In that context, he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in order to set forth another inference: "The benefactor," etc. For this reason, there is a connection between the word [in the verse] and the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) located in the subsequent commentary (*vārtika*). || 137 ||
For no benefit to the olfactory organ and the others by means of sound and the rest is observed.
Therefore, light should be accepted as being of the same genus as that which has become [the object]. || 138 ||

Having stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—that whatever is an auxiliary (*upakāraka*) belongs to the same genus as that which it assists—he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "by sound and so forth. The word "hi" (for) is used to indicate that both the positive and negative concomitances are agreed upon by both parties. He states the resulting conclusion: "The subject of dispute belongs to the same genus as the body and so forth, because it is an auxiliary, like the sun. || 138 ||
1. Kha. And that is the state of having passed beyond; 2. Ka. Kha. [The opponent] suspects it is the self; 3. Ya. The vital breaths;
4. Katvam i; 5. Kha. Indeed.
An earthen pot and the like are perceived only by means of other earthen things. [Vol. 3, Page 268] 6 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā. 1401.
Just as the sun and other celestial bodies provide benefit in this world, so too does he. || 139 ||
Since the light of the Self (ātmajyotis) shares the same nature as the body and so forth, how can it be said to be material? To this he says: "Of that which is material.
The remainder of the sense is: likewise, it must be stated that the benefit of the material body and so forth is provided by the light of the Self, which is itself material. || 139 ||
If this light is indeed considered to be something other than the body and so forth;
Nevertheless, it does not manifest that which is of a different class, because it is a manifestor, like a lamp.

He states another inference: "The subject of dispute [the body, etc. is of the same nature as [other] bodies and so forth, because it is a manifestor, like a lamp. This refers to the phrase "of the body, etc. (dehādeḥ). || 140 ||
Is it not the case that [the self] is of a different class from the body, because it resides within and is beyond the senses?
Whatever light is perceived by the senses that is of the same nature as the body, [that is the object]. || 141 ||

The opponent raises an objection: "The subject under discussion [the Self] is distinct from the body and so forth, because it resides within and because it is beyond the senses, like the sun; this is established by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka). To this, the author replies with the words "nanu" (but surely). He states the impossibility of the reason in the contrary case (vipakṣe) with the words "yadyad" (whatever...). The phrase "and if it were not residing within" is to be supplied as the remainder. Therefore, the meaning is: if the light of the Self were of the same nature as the body and so forth, it would necessarily be perceptible by the senses and would not reside within. || 141 ||
Do not say so; for it is clear that the reason [adduced] by means of the sense organs such as the eye is not conclusive.
For the sense organs are internal, whereas they are not directly perceived as the Self is.
He refutes the two reasons by way of their being contradictory, saying: "Not so. He clarifies the contradiction, saying: "Residing within.

Just as your Self is distinct from the body and its constituents, residing within, and beyond the senses, so too the sense organs—since you accept them as distinct from the physical globes (golaka)—are held by you to reside within the body and to be beyond the senses; nevertheless, they are of the same nature as the body. Thus, the contradiction is evident.
This is the meaning. || 142 ||
The self-luminosity [of the soul] is of the same genus as the sun and other luminaries, yet it is beyond the reach of the senses.
Just as the sense organs such as the eye [are established] by virtue of being internal and beyond the senses. || 143 ||

Furthermore, he states a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*): "The subject of dispute is of the same class as the body, because it resides within and because it is beyond the senses, like the eye and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the sun and so forth": the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is that the subject of dispute is of the same class as the body which is of the same class as the sun and so forth. || 143 ||
If [the reason is applied] to a particular, there is no concomitance; if it is applied to a universal, it is a case of proving what is already established.
Because it is vitiated by such defects as these, our inference is not a valid cognition (*pramā*). 144.

Furthermore, he states that while it was spoken assuming the validity of inference, in reality it is not a means of valid cognition: "The particular" (*viśeṣa*). If the particular fire located on the slope of the mountain is the probandum (*sādhya*), then because of its absence in the kitchen, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the probandum.

If mere fire is the probandum, then since that is established somewhere or other, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*); and if the smoke-particular is the logical reason (*hetu*), there is the lack of a means of proof (*sādhanavaikalya*) regarding the locus.

The meaning is that inference is not a valid means of knowledge because it is vitiated by defects such as the unestablished nature of the subject (*asiddhi*). Is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two individuals, or between two universals (*jāti*), or between two particulars subsumed under those [universals], or between the states of possessing smoke and possessing fire? It is not the first, because pervasion involving a universalization over all instances (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) is unestablished; nor is it the second, because of those two...
1. "Therefore, there would be sight from you.
[Vol. 3, page 269] 1402 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]—

The meaning of the words [in the verse] is as follows: the third [alternative] is not [tenable] because of the difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the difference in the substratum (*dharmin*); the fourth is not [tenable] due to the aforementioned defects; and so forth, because an adventitious attribute (*aupādhikadharma*) that is distinct from the essential nature cannot be defined. || 144 ||
By the power of inference alone, [the self is established] as distinct from the body and so forth.
The inner self is established as self-luminous, and that is not [known] through inference.

One might object: "For one who establishes the self as distinct from the body and so forth, it is not undesirable that inference lacks authority, since that [self] is established through another means of knowledge. Anticipating this, he says: "anumāna... (inference...). That is to say, such an inference is not truly an inference. || 141 ||
By means of perception alone as the sole instrument of knowledge, [one realizes] directly that the body has consciousness as its attribute.
When it is apprehended by means of inference, it cannot be sublated. || 146 ||

Regarding the statement in the book, "But the body is not the self because it is composed of the elements, like a jar," he replies with the words "pratyakṣa" (perception). The meaning is that, just as in the case of the inference of non-heat [in fire], the inference of the body's non-selfhood does not arise due to its contradiction by direct perception. || 146 ||
Performing actions such as seeing and so forth at all times without deviation.
This body alone is perceived by direct perception; there is nothing other than this.

Anticipating the objection that "the body has a seer distinct from itself because it is an object of sight, like a jar," he says, "Because of seeing, etc.," [stating] that this is not so, as the previously mentioned defects apply equally. || 147 ||
The performer of actions such as seeing and so forth is accepted as being distinct from the body.
Why is it that vision and the other [faculties] of one who is unimpaired are not perceived in that same way? || 148 ||

He raises the objection: "The body is not the self, because it is subject to the absence of consciousness, like a jar. [The author replies: "Regarding the activity of seeing and so forth," meaning that even in states such as sleep or fainting, the same [argument] applies as before. || 148 ||
This fault would not arise here, because [the object] is established by direct perception.
For nothing else is considered more powerful than that which is directly perceived.

The proponent of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavādin) says, "No," and so forth. Here, "here" refers to the body. The words "of occasional appearance and non-appearance" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Anticipating the objection that even what is observed must be abandoned if it contradicts logic, he says, "For not... (149).
And the state of being luminous or non-luminous is perceived by direct perception itself.
Based on the inference from a firefly, there is no postulation of another cause. || 150 ||

How can you fear that something which is occasional, such as luminosity, could be an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), given that it is impossible for a real entity to possess an intrinsic nature and yet lose it? Regarding the term "luminous" (*bhāsvara*): one might object, "But even the glowworm's luminosity and so forth are produced by other causes, because they are occasional, like a jar.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By inference. The meaning is that [the opponent's view] contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). || 110 ||
When there is another reason and a subject of inference, [the fallacy arises] from even a slight scent of a commonality.
Everything would then be the indicator of everything, and that undesirable consequence follows. || 151 ||
Since the occurrence of a thing is occasional, if one were to infer a cause other than its own nature, one could even argue: "Fire is not hot, because it is a real entity, like water. [Note: 1. *ka*.
reads *gātmasva*; 2. *ka*. reads *stataḥ paṃ*].

He states another defect, namely the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), on the grounds that the contradiction with perception would be equal [in both cases], saying: "In the case of another reason" (*hetvantare*). And he says:

"For that [would not be so]," because it is not logical that fire be non-hot, as that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of the established order of cognized objects. || 111 ||
And yet, there is no object whatsoever in the world that lacks its own unique characteristic.
For the intrinsic nature of fire and other such things does not arise from any cause other than their own heat and so forth. (152)

There is no such thing as an "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) for entities; how then can there be an intrinsic nature based on the observation of occasional occurrence? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... The word *asādhāraṇa* (uncommon) is to be understood as a separate term. He provides an illustration, in accordance with experience, of the existence of such an intrinsic nature: "Of fire and so forth. || 152 ||
If it is argued that heat and other qualities of fire depend upon fuel, air, and so forth;
It is not so, because even in that case, the occurrence of the fault remains unremoved.

One might object that even heat and so forth are not intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) because they are produced by merit (*dharma*) and the like. [The author] raises this doubt with the verse beginning "prāṇi... (living beings). Is the causality of merit and so forth for heat and the like an intrinsic nature or not? If it is an intrinsic nature, then let that belong to fire alone, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*). If it is not an intrinsic nature, he says in response: "Not so. The meaning is that the doctrine of non-intrinsic nature is untenable, because it would be impossible to avoid the consequence that merit and the like would themselves depend on further instances of merit and so forth. || 113 ||
If it is argued that "let that also be so," we say: "By no means," because [entities such as] dharma and the like are not established.
If one accepts [the existence of] phenomena, the fault of infinite regress follows. (154)

He raises an objection, suggesting that there is no harm even if merit (*dharma*) and so forth grant their fruit by means of producing heat and the like in fire and other elements, provided they depend on another merit and so forth. [The author] replies: "Not so. For merit and the like are not perceptible, since you do not accept them as such; nor are they accessible through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because in our view they do not exist at all. Therefore, since they themselves are non-existent, the dependence upon another merit and so forth is utterly discarded. Thus he refutes it: "Not so."

[The author] states another fault regarding the fact that dharma and so forth depend upon another dharma and so forth: "dharma... etc. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that even in the case of another dharma, there is an equality of dependence, just as in the case of the first dharma and so on. || 114 ||
Nor can there be the establishment of the intended object through an infinite regress.

Therefore, enough of this painful conceptualization regarding that which is produced from the transformation of earth, water, fire, and air, and which is cognized by the senses as possessing consciousness. (155)

Anticipating the objection that an infinite regress is not a fault because it does not entail the destruction of the root, he says: "And not... This means that the intended point—that pleasure and so forth are produced by merit (*dharma*) and the like through the medium of fire, heat, and so on—is not established. He concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with: "Enough of this.
Since the body—which is a transformation of the aggregate of the four elements—qualified by consciousness is perceived directly, there is no need to postulate a self distinct from it.
The meaning is that it possesses the fruit of pride. || 155 ||
The accomplishment of one's desired object is achieved through the vision of all sacred sites.
Since its establishment is prevented precisely by the very admission [of it], how could it be established? || 156 ||
Even by all disputants who desire some degree of proof, a self-luminous, changeless entity distinct from the body and so forth must be admitted;
yet even that is a flaw.

1404 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopani�ṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]: He establishes the conclusion that it belongs to the Knower (*viddhatuḥ*). Regarding the phrase "by all the Tīrthas": since the nature of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) and so forth is accepted by all authors of the scriptures on the strength of eternal experience, the meaning is that such a non-dual experience must be admitted by them as well. || 116 ||
First of all, contradiction with direct perception is not tenable.
Since its object does not exist, its validity is difficult to establish. || 157 ||

As for the objection that non-duality (aikātmya) cannot be established because it contradicts perception, he replies with the words "by perception. The meaning is that there is no contradiction of the Śruti by perception, because perception lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) since it has no object other than the experience of non-duality. || 117 ||
For all those who hold the view of the various philosophical systems (tīrtha), the definition of valid cognition (māna) is common [to them all].
However, the apprehension of an unknown object is not tenable in what you have stated. || 158 ||

Anticipating the objection that there is no absence of an object distinct from that [cognition] because pillars and the like are its objects, he states the general definition of a means of knowledge (*māna*) in order to explain the non-existence of an external object: "All... etc. He says: "In the perception [accepted] by you," because that definition does not apply;
for since there is no proof for the existence of an unknown object, an unknown object is not established. || 198 ||
Prior to the arising of the means of valid cognition, for you, the object—such as the body and so forth—[does not exist].
It must be stated by whom the state of being unknown could exist for the cause that is the means of valid cognition. (159)

Anticipating the objection that the absence of a means of proof for that [object] is untenable because the means of proof itself is the prover, he says: "Priorly," etc. For one who denies eternal experience, there can be no cognition of the object's being unknown prior to the arising of the means of proof—since the body and so forth, which are the objects of that means, serve as its objective (karman) cause;
and in the absence of such an object, the operation of the means of proof does not occur. This is the meaning. || 119 ||
Furthermore, for you, this body and so forth must exist either as established by itself or as unestablished.
The validity of the means of valid cognition is not found in either case. || 160 ||
Having stated that perception lacks authority because its object is not something previously unknown (*ajñāta*), he now subjects its authority to analysis in order to reject it by another method.

He begins with the word "svataḥ" (inherently). By the phrase "the coming into being of the body and so forth," he indicates his dissatisfaction with the notion that such arising—whether of an existent or a non-existent—is logical.
With the word "bhavan" (while coming into being), he declares that there are defects inherent in both positions. [He refers to] "of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānām*). || 160 ||
If the body and so forth were established even without means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), [then what need would there be for them?]
Tell me, what purpose could there be in means of valid cognition? For there is no establishing of that which is already established. (161)

Clarifying that, he introduces the first [point] with the words "the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāni*). Therein, he states the fault of the uselessness of the means of valid cognition with the word "says.

Anticipating the objection that the illumination of the body and so forth is its function, he says "not indeed" (*na hi*). The meaning is: because it would not result in the completion of the means of proof (*sādhana*). || 161 ||
Since the object of cognition is not established by itself and is non-existent, there can be no means of valid cognition that manifests it.
Savitar does not manifest a sharp horn, even though it is throbbing.

Regarding the second [point], he says that because that which is unestablished in itself—such as a rabbit’s horn—is non-existent, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have no authority with respect to it. [Guṇaratna: "Therefore" (tataḥ). [Gaṅgeśa: "Those [cognitions]," etc.

"From itself" (*svataḥ*). The phrase "and in the case of the immeasurable" (*aprameye ca*) is the division [of the compound]. Anticipating the objection that a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), by virtue of being illuminative, might manifest even that which is non-existent, he says:
"No," and so forth. || 162 ||
Nor is non-existence established apart from the means of valid cognition.
Moreover, even if there is no difference [between the means and the object], the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge are established as possessing reality. || 163 ||

If it is argued that since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not manifest what is non-existent, it must therefore be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), he says "no," beginning with the words "pramāṇa... [and so on].

[Objection: In that case, the existence of non-existence (*asattva*) is also established through valid cognition alone; for that [cognition] indeed manifests even non-existence in its own form. Why is that?

In the final analysis, is the means of knowledge (*māna*) not the manifester? In that regard, is there non-difference or difference between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge (*meya*)? He refutes the first [position] with the words:
"Nor... (verse 163).
If it is possible that "amita" has a meaning beyond its conventional measure, then—
One may awaken him, but one should not desire to act with pride toward him. || 164 ||

He takes up the second [alternative], beginning with "yadi" (if). The meaning of the phrase "yadi... amitaḥ" (if... unmeasured) is a restatement of the possibility that the object of knowledge (*meyo*)—which is unknown prior to the arising of the means of knowledge (*māna*) and distinct from the means of knowledge—is [the object]. The word "amitaḥ" is to be split [as *a-mitaḥ*]. Even in that case, he first addresses the first [view], namely that the means of knowledge is either the indicator of the object (*meyabodhaka*) or the efficient cause (*kāraka*). He says "tadā" (then). However, the remainder [of the argument] is that in your view, it cannot be an indicator because there is no unknown object [for it to indicate]. [He then addresses] the second [view].
He refutes [the objection], saying "But not... (164).
For there is no other task anywhere except for awakening those who have not yet awakened.
Whether it be existence or non-existence, there is nothing here that is established by means of a valid cognition regarding the object of knowledge. || 165 ||

In this regard, the reason is: "because it is not a cognition. This concludes the demonstration that [the word] is unfit to be the producer of a mental state. Or, as for the term "existence" (*sattvam*):
because its inherent nature is to make known what was previously unknown, such is the meaning of the word. || 169 ||
It makes one understand that [the object] was already established prior to human activity.
Mother-of-pearl attains the status of being an object of valid cognition, whereas silver and the like do not when they are unestablished [as appearing]. || 166 ||

To the question of how even those [cognitions] constitute valid means of knowledge (*māna*) in that regard, he says: "Valid means of knowledge" (*māna*). The meaning is: in our system, a cognition is a valid means of knowledge when it makes known a shell and so forth—which are established by constant experience as being unknown—*prior to the arising of the valid means of knowledge itself*; it is not a valid means of knowledge when it makes known non-existent things such as silver in a shell, because in the absence of such a thing, there can be no state of being unknown and so forth. || 166 ||
Because, from the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the shell is not cognized as it truly is.
Some silver exists, yet it is perceived as if it were the reality of the self.

One might object that even the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell exists unknown prior to its own cognition, and thus the operation of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is easily established there as well; anticipating this, he says: "In the case of the mother-of-pearl. Just as the mother-of-pearl exists previously unknown before the operation of the means of knowledge, it is not the case that the silver remains unknown in the mother-of-pearl prior to the cognition of that [silver]; for in that case, the cognition of silver is an error (*bhrama*), being a cognition of something as what it is not, and thus it does not establish the unknown.
And because it is sublatable, that [object] is not known like the Self; therefore, the meaning is that it exists neither as known nor as unknown. || 167 ||
1 Kha, 'yanbhaveṃ | [Vol.
3, page 273] 1406 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya— ]
How can a thing be conceived through neither excess nor concomitance?
In that case, its status as a valid means of cognition would be like that of silver perceived in a mother-of-pearl shell. (168)

Lest it be argued that while silver may not exist in either case, the mother-of-pearl (śukti) is unknown prior to cognition and known afterwards—thereby implying that you, who desire a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) for an insentient object, abandon your own tenet—the author says: "Not by excess," and so forth. For the validity of a means of knowledge does not apply to silver superimposed upon the mother-of-pearl, because [in that case] the states of being unknown and being known are impossible; likewise, since an insentient object is imagined (kalpita), it is unfit for a means of valid knowledge.
The meaning is that experience must be admitted as having two objects. || 168 ||
Is this state of awakening produced for the sake of association with the mind?
Or rather, was the object [of cognition] not established as "Buddha" through a relationship with the word "mā," but rather from the word "māna"? || 169 ||

He states another reason for its being the object to be attained (*upeya*), preceded by an inquiry: "What [is it]? The meaning is as follows: in the first case, since the object is already known through the connection with a means of knowledge (*māna*), one must admit an experience that establishes its state of being unknown (*ajñātatā*), because there is no other establishing factor; in the second case, the means of knowledge would be useless. The phrase "from the connection" implies "from the connection whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the means of knowledge. || 169 ||
And how could the nature of cognition as consisting of awakening arise from its connection with the object of knowledge?
Or rather, prior to the connection with the object of knowledge, the nature of consciousness would exist as the self. || 170 ||

He states that experience must therefore be accepted here, saying "bodha" (cognition). In the first case, experience must be considered the means of establishing the cognizing nature residing in the instrument of knowledge (*māna*), which depends upon its connection with the object (*meyasaṃbandha*); for its own nature as a cognizer is not established by the object and so forth, since those are insentient (*jaḍa*) and thus incapable of being establishing factors.
In the second case, the meaning is that the connection with the object would be purposeless. || 170 ||
Nor is the fact that objects have not been previously cognized established by means of valid cognition.
For us, it is not the case that form is not apprehended by means of valid cognition through the ear and other senses. || 171 ||

Having stated that experience (*anubhava*) must be accepted as the means of establishing both the "knownness" (*jñātatva*) of objects such as jars and the fact that the means of knowledge (*māna*) makes them known, he states that it must also be accepted as the means of establishing their "unknownness" (*ajñātatva*). [He says: "Not the object... He provides an example for the case where the unknownness residing in the object would not be cognizable:
"Form... It is not the case that the unknownness residing in form is known by the eye, because the eye is the cause of the cognition of that [form's] knownness, and not...
The meaning is that it makes known its own state of being unknown prior to its own activity, because it grasps only the present. || 171 ||
If the apprehension of the object of knowledge were to arise from human activity, then—
Prior to that operation, the object of cognition would already exist as something whose nature is self-apprehended. || 172 ||

Having restated the objection that "the means of knowledge (māna) does not make known the object's state of being unknown, but rather produces it," he refutes it with the verse beginning "māna" (verse 172).
Since this is so, therefore, necessarily prior to the operation of the means of valid cognition, [the object must exist].
For that which is unperceived is established as something to be accepted, just like that which has been understood. (173)

He states the conclusion resulting from the fact that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) lacks the capacity to make known the state of being unknown or to produce it, beginning with the words "yataḥ" (since). The phrase "after [the object] has been cognized as if by a means of valid cognition" is the ellipsis to be supplied. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that it is experience alone that establishes the states of being unknown and being known prior to and subsequent to the means of valid cognition, respectively. || 173 ||
And it is not that its true honor has not been established, for its very nature is the embodiment of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
[Vol. 3, Page 274] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1407.
And it is not that its true honor has not been established, for its very nature is the embodiment of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
One should bear the aforementioned burden elsewhere, provided there is identity with the cognizer (matṛgaikātmya).
Let it be that an object is unknown prior to valid cognition (*māna*) and known thereafter; nevertheless, how is the establishment of experience (*anubhava*) possible as the means of proving both?
To this he says: "Not [if]... Where [the object] is not "unimposed"—that is, where the faultless valid cognition has not been set in motion to take it as its object—[it is] self-evident (*svataḥ*).

The meaning is that, apart from that innermost identity which is of the nature of pure consciousness, ignorance and so forth cannot be established by the force of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that apart from that innermost identity—which is unconditioned, beginningless and endless, eternally uniform, the accomplisher of all, whose very body is inherently pure consciousness—ignorance and so forth are not established by any means of valid cognition. || 174 ||
Just as there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified when [the object] is unknown, so it is not when it is known.
Consequently, this [notion] that ignorance and so forth exist would not be established through valid cognition.

Regarding the statement "that [unknownness] is not an object of knowledge," he states another argument: "For indeed... When a jar is unknown, there can be no cognition of the qualifier-qualified relationship (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatā) such that "the jar is known," because without the apprehension of the qualifier, there is no apprehension of the qualified. Likewise, even when a jar is known, it is not logical to say "the jar is unknown," because once the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) has operated upon it, its state of being unknown has ceased. Therefore, unknownness is not an object of knowledge; nor is knownness, because that would lead to an infinite regress.
The meaning is that both are unauthoritative and are merely accessible through direct experience. || 175 ||
And if [the object] has not been apprehended through a means of valid cognition, how could there be a cessation of that [ignorance]?
A physician should not employ fire for the purpose of curing a fever characterized by burning sensations.

He states another defect regarding the fact that "unknownness" (ajñātatva) is established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). [The text says: "And from a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇāt ca). He says "no" to the claim that the very same proof which establishes unknownness would also be its remover; for it is not so. The meaning is that it is undesirable because the removal of that [unknownness] by its own cause is never observed. || 176 ||
Just as a means of knowledge is observed on the plane of measurement to have the nature of both direct perception and valid cognition.
When these [cognitions] are not known through experience, no other [means of knowledge] is observed to exist in that manner. || 177 ||
One might then object: "In that case, [the existence of] ignorance and so forth cannot be known through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); even so, how is it established by experience?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the witness" (sākṣi). Just as in the domain of the means of valid cognition, the nature of the witness and others is experienced through experience—otherwise there would be an infinite regress—likewise, in the domain of ignorance, even though the nature of these [factors] such as the knower (mātr) and so forth is unmanifest, there is no establisher other than experience, since the aforementioned fault applies equally. Therefore—
The meaning is that fear depends upon one's own experience. || 177 ||
After the operation of the means of valid cognition, the states of being known and unknown are mutually [contradictory].
It is joined together by experience alone, and not by anything else whatsoever.

He states that both of these depend upon that [cognition] with the words "pramāṇa" (the means of knowledge). The meaning is this: by means of experience itself, immediately following the operation of the means of knowledge, one synthesizes the two—the known and the unknown—into a single unity, thinking, "That object which was unknown for so long, I now know.
Therefore, both of those are established solely by experience. || 178 ||
Even if the means of valid cognition are not intermixed, this is because they have been definitively ascertained.
Even so, there can be no denial of this experience, unlike [the case of] objects such as a jar. (179)
1. *ka*. *ga*. "For him, there is no pot that has not been experienced.
[Vol. 3, p. 275] 1408 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]

Now, does a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) operate upon that experience which establishes [the fact of] being known and so forth, or not? In the first case, there would follow the consequence that it is itself an object of experience; in the second case, however, there would follow the consequence of its non-existence. To this, he says: "If... Even for objects such as jars, which lack contact with the sphere of a means of knowledge, and for experience itself, since they are ascertained prior to any operation of a means of knowledge directed toward them, their denial is not tenable, as they are established by themselves.
The meaning is "from accomplishment. || 179 ||
Thus, even though the experience is established by its own power prior to any measurement, [it remains unestablished for the opponent].
The arising of valid cognition must be investigated for the sake of dispelling the darkness within.

If it is argued that experience is established even without a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), and thus there is a deficiency of pramāṇa in that regard, he says "evam" (thus). This means: by way of establishing [the object] as being unknown and so forth. He states the fruit to be sought and produced: "pratyak" (the inner self). Although this pramāṇa is the establisher of experience, nevertheless, it becomes purposeful for that [experience] by virtue of removing the ignorance residing therein—this is the meaning. || 180 ||
Although its true nature is already awakened, it nevertheless endures the state of being unawakened.
Because it is a real entity, it does not destroy darkness; nevertheless, [it cannot do so] without valid cognition.

[The opponent objects: "Since ignorance is contradictory to the nature of experience (*anubhava*), how can a means of knowledge (*māna*) be sought for its destruction? To this, he replies: "[Experience] does not [destroy it] when unawakened. Then, fearing that experience might destroy ignorance—which is of a non-substantial nature—by itself simply because it is a reality (*vastu*), he says:
When mounted upon the fruit of the means of valid cognition, one's own darkness is destroyed; not otherwise.
The object is that which is connected with the means of knowledge; the means of knowledge is that which dispels the darkness regarding it. (182)

Then, one might object: "Let cognition alone remove ignorance; what is the need for the object? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*). Neither the object nor the means of knowledge has the power to remove ignorance by itself, because that would entail the consequence of its removal being eternal and because [the object] is insentient (*jaḍa*). Therefore, it is only when consciousness is impelled by the intellect, or the intellect is impelled by consciousness, that they destroy ignorance; thus, both are purposeful. This is the meaning. || 182 ||
Therefore, for the sake of establishing perception as a means of valid cognition, by one who maintains the authority of perception:
The object that must be accepted as "mine" is that which effects the establishment of its being unknown and so forth. (183)

He concludes that since the validity of perception depends on an object being unknown, and that state of being unknown depends upon eternal experience, one who desires the validity of perception must accept an immutable experience: "Perception... (verse 183).
He is the agent of the activities of speech and the other organs, and is characterized by the qualities of sound and the rest.
It is perceived directly by the subject because of its absolute difference from the internal self. || 184 ||

Even if experience is accepted as the means of establishing [the self's] being unknown and so forth, one might suspect that something other than that is the Self. Anticipating this, the author raises the alternative—whether it is the gross body or the subtle—and refutes the first. "Speech and so forth": the gross body, performing speech, grasping, and so on, and characterized by sound and other qualities, is perceived by the knower as distinct from the inner witness through the cognition "this is mine. That [cannot be the Self].
The meaning is that its being the Self cannot be accepted because it contradicts direct perception; for the cognition "I am a human" is like the statement "the mountain is burning. || 184 ||
The mother, engaged in hearing and other [sensory functions], is surrounded by qualities such as suffering and the like.
The agent is directly understood through internal experience alone. || 185 ||
1 kha. rāk || kaṃ | 2 ka. ga. pratīco | [vol 3, page 276] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramakaranda* composed by Ānandagiri: 1409.

He states the second [point]: "By the ear, eye, etc. Just as the agent—characterized by hearing, seeing, and so forth regarding sound, form, and the like—is grasped by the knower through internal experience as external to himself, and just as that which ends with the body is grasped by the knower as external to the internal self (pratyak), so too is he (the agent) understood as external to that [internal self] in its own nature. Therefore, it does not belong to him.
The meaning is "the Self. || 185 ||
The inner self is not experienced by anything other than itself and is not an object for the knower and so forth;
therefore, such qualifiers as "free from evil" and the like are appropriate for it. (186)

Anticipating the objection that experience (*anubhava*) also cannot be the Self because it has objects such as the "measurer" (*mātr̥*) and so forth—just like the body—the author says: "Ananya... (not other). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the Witness (*sākṣin*) is included. He concludes what was begun—that the scriptural teaching of non-dual unity (*aikātmya*) is not contradicted by perception—with the words: "Since...
Since all particularities, such as sin and the rest, are attributes of the two bodies, and since the Self is distinct from them, therefore [the Self] is untouched...

The meaning is that it is appropriate for [the scripture] to qualify the Self with "sin" and so forth; thus, a statement that makes that [Self] known as Brahman does not contradict perception, because perception does not function with respect to such an object. || 186 ||
Of the Lokāyata, the Buddhist, Kaṇāda, and Akṣapāda.
By means of direct perception itself, the turning away [of the opponent] has been accomplished. || 187 ||

Now, one might object: the Lokāyatikas and the Vaināśikas do not accept eternal experience; furthermore, although the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas do accept it, they declare it to be non-self because it is a quality of God. How then can that experience be the Self? To this, he says:
"Of the Lokāyata," [it is said]. || 187 ||
There is a distinction between the means of valid cognition and its result, as well as between the instrument of knowledge and the object of knowledge.
The establishment of the self as the immutable consciousness and its identity [with Brahman] are proven through direct experience. || 188 ||

Anticipating the objection, "How can they be turned away by means of perception?", he replies to the first two [objections] with the words "pramāṇa" (means of knowledge), etc. The fact that the appearance of distinctions such as the means of knowledge and their objects establishes the eternal experience (*nityānubhava*)—by way of *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability)—is the reason for turning away the Cārvākas and others. For that appearance is not established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*); this is the meaning. He replies to the second two [objections] with the words "aikātmya" (oneness of self), etc., based on the experience of the wise (*vidvad-anubhava*).

The meaning is that because the self, when favored by me, is established as being nothing but eternal consciousness, there is a turning away from the Vaiśeṣikas and others. Furthermore, it means that once such a nature of the self is established, there is also a turning away from the Mīmāṃsakas and so forth. || 188 ||
For this very reason, it is established that this [cognition] is indeed a means of valid direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Therefore, let it be accepted that the Self is the seer of direct perception and is self-luminous. || 189 ||

He states another reason for that aversion [to the external world] in the verse beginning with "pratyakṣam" (perception). There is no dispute among anyone that perception is indeed a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

yet, it is not self-cognizable because it is undesirable [as such] and because it is illogical. Therefore, the meaning is that the eternal light of the Self (*ātmajyotis*), which establishes that perception, must necessarily be accepted. || 189 ||
One should [know] the means and so forth, as well as their absence, and doubt, falsehood, and certainty.
He who, having discerned them, favors the insentient objects such as sound and the rest individually. || 190 ||
1. ‘Sva’ | 177 [vol 3, page 277]

1410 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]: The body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect, as well as pleasure and so forth, and objects such as a jar, [are all distinct from the Self].
O sir, behold that one inner self which is beyond direct perception! (191)
Fearing that the qualification "one who sees directly" (pratyakṣadṛk) might imply a loss of the acceptance of the self-luminosity (ātmajyotis) as being the seer of all things, he says:
"the objects of knowledge and so forth. He states the reason why, although it is the illuminator of all these [objects], they nevertheless depend on another illumination due to their insentience:
"insentient" (jaḍān). Regarding the objection that no self other than the body has been perceived, he says: "that" (tam).
He who perceives within a dream the seer, the seeing, and the seen;
And since that [consciousness] is absent in deep sleep, let it be accepted that the Self is that which remains. (192)

Having raised the objection that because the phrase "perceive" (*prapaśya*) implies being an object of perception, it is inconsistent with the attribute of being non-perceptible, he says: "The seer" (*draṣṭṛ*). By the word "dream," the waking state is also included, since the word "dream" is seen used for both in the Śruti. The meaning is that the Self, which is self-luminous and establishes the existence or non-existence of seeing and so forth, is not an object of seeing and the like, as it is established by its own experience. || 992 ||
Furthermore, the sense faculties such as the eye do not have any existence in a dream.
In dreams and so forth, as well as in deep sleep, experience is the non-deviating [criterion] for those two. || 193 ||

One might object that the desired proof of the Self is not established because the experience of the existence and non-existence of objects such as the visible world arises solely through the influence of the senses and other factors.

To this, the author says: "The eye and so forth... [referring to the verse]. In the states of dreaming and deep sleep, since the senses and other such instruments are absent, and since one does not admit the existence of any residual impression (*vāsanā*) in deep sleep that is distinct from its cause, the manifestation of existence and non-existence therein occurs solely by virtue of the Self, which is termed eternal experience.

The meaning is that otherwise, the distinction between states would be untenable. Anticipating the objection that even direct experience (*anubhava*) does not exist there—just as the eyes and other senses do not—he says:

"But direct experience... The point is that if it were otherwise, such experience would not be established, and consequently, the subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) would also fail to be established. || 193 ||
The means of valid cognition has the object of knowledge as its domain, while its fruit resides in the cognizer.
That by whose witness the duality is established—let that be accepted as the Self. (194)
And for this reason, he states that the Self must be accepted as being of the nature of eternal experience: "The means of knowledge," etc. (194).
For that which is the fruit of pride is not within the sphere of pride itself.
"Since that [means of knowledge] has as its sole object the cognizable (meyam), the result must reside in the knower (pramātṛ).
Anticipating the objection—"The duality will be established by the means of knowledge; what need is there for your desired experience?"—he says: "Of the means of knowledge" (mānasya).
The word *hi* indicates that the result depends upon a substratum (āśraya). Even though that [means of knowledge] has only the cognizable as its object, the result does not reside in the cognizable.
Anticipating the objection that the status of being an object of human cognition is appropriate for that which serves as its substratum, he says: "But the fruit... (199).
Where the action is directly perceived, its fruit is not seen there.
Where that fruit exists, there no measure exists.

"In that case, let it be that the knower (mātṛ) is also an object of knowledge; what is the necessity of the restriction that [knowledge] must have an object of cognition (meyaviṣayatva)? To this he replies: "Perception... (pratyakṣam iti).

For consciousness (saṃvedana) does not reside in the object, because that would entail the consequence of the object being conscious; nor is the knower within the scope of the means of knowledge (māna), because that would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā). This is the meaning. || 196 ||
[Volume 3,
Page 278] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1411
This being so, for you, the self-natures of the knower, the fruit, and the object of knowledge [would all be identical].
How can the establishment of direct perception be possible if the self is not admitted? (197)

He states the conclusion: "This being so," [verse 197], meaning that since the mother and others are not objects of measurement, the self-luminosity known as eternal experience must be accepted as the means of proving them.
Among all the transitory mental states, the inner self alone is the witness.
The internal cognition alone is that which is non-deviant in all cases. (198)

Anticipating the objection that the desired conclusion is not established through inference—namely, "the object of dispute is not eternal because it is an experience, like the experience of a jar"—he says:

"In the case of those [experiences] which are variable. The meaning is that the impossibility of establishing a variable [experience] proves the existence of an invariable experience, and thus serves as a sublation of your inference. || 198 ||
Thus, first of all, through direct perception, [the self] is established as distinct from the body and so forth.
Thus, for one who experiences it directly, this Self is established. || 199 ||

He summarizes what has been stated concisely with the word "evam" (thus). The meaning is that, by the power of the Self known as eternal experience (*nityānubhava*), its state of being unknown is established; and since perception (*pratyakṣa*) is authoritative regarding an object that is [otherwise] unknown, by virtue of that, the Self—distinct from the body and so forth—is directly demonstrated for all philosophical systems (*sarvatīrthadṛśām*) according to the logic previously stated, such as "it is established through the experience of the wise. || 199 ||
And as for this which has been stated by you, based on the analogy of the black snake and so forth;
To that, [the following] is provided as a rebuttal: "I am a human being," and so forth. (200)

Under the guise of the Lokāyata [materialist] doctrine, the immutable, non-dual, self-luminous experience has already been refuted against all disputants; now, having restated what was said by the opponent in the passage beginning with "I am a human being," he declares the existence of a fault therein: "And that which... (verse 200).
If consciousness were a property of the body, then the cognition "this is a human being" would be valid.
Then, due to its non-commonality [with other cognitions], it would not exist, just like the notion "I am a speaker. || 201 ||

He points out the very same fault: "Consciousness," etc. If consciousness in the form of the "I" were an attribute of the body, then, just as the notion of "I" occurs in one's own body—which possesses the attribute of "I"—in the thought "I know the jar," it would likewise occur in the bodies of others; for the "I" and consciousness would be common attributes in all bodies.

The valid cognition that "this person is that [same] person" would not exist even in another body, just as there is the cognition of "white" everywhere in white cloths; likewise, since all bodies possess the attribute of consciousness (*caitanya*), it is logical that the notion of "I" (*ahambuddhi*) should occur in all of them. Even if consciousness were distinct from the "I," if it were an attribute of the body, that cognition would arise in others just as it does in one's own body; but this is not the case. Therefore, the meaning is that consciousness is not an attribute of the body. || 201 ||
For if consciousness were inherent within the body itself, it would indeed be present wherever [the body] is assembled.
That [result] belongs directly to him alone, and not to one residing in another body.

Just as one has the notion of "I" with respect to one's own body, because that same state exists in the bodies of others, the notion of "I" with respect to all bodies is not contradictory; this is called *mātṛtva* (the state of being a mother).

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four, verse 1412: [The author] says: "For it is inherent" (*samavetam hi*). Wherever consciousness is inherent in a body, for that very body qualified by consciousness, that qualification—namely, the "I"—is directly perceived. However, the consciousness residing in another body is not perceived directly as belonging to one who is not its substrate.

Consequently, there would be many bodies characterized by consciousness; however, since these cannot be perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for one who maintains that direct perception is the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the non-duality of consciousness (*caitanyādvaita*) cannot be established. Thus, the meaning is that the specific determination of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃbuddhi*) in this or that [body] would not be possible. || 202 ||
Apart from the activity of the instruments, the notion "I am a human being" would not arise.
But in the previous case, consciousness is distinct from that body which is the object of the "that-ness" (tattā). || 203 ||
If consciousness, even when residing in another, were to directly perceive that which resides in another body, then [the author] says: "By means of the instruments" (*karaṇa*).

Just as previously, in one's own body grasped as the self, the cognition "I am a man" arises without the operation of the instruments, so too in other bodies there would arise for that very same single [consciousness] the cognitions "I am Caitra" or "I am Maitra" without the operation of the instruments; but it is not so there.
The meaning is that since he possesses such a cognition regarding other bodies as well, consciousness is not a property of the body. || 203 ||
And this object of the intellect's grasp is not within the scope of that which is apprehended by the notion of "I."
For, due to contradiction, coldness cannot be a qualifier of fire, which is hot. (204)

In this regard, he states another reason: "And not... The meaning is that consciousness, which is apprehended by the notion of "I" (ahaṃdhī), cannot be a qualifying attribute of the body, which is apprehended by the notion of "this" (idaṃdhī), because there is a mutual contradiction between that which is apprehended as "I" and that which is apprehended as "this," and thus they cannot stand in the relationship of attribute and substratum. He provides an illustration for this: "For not... (204).
In the same way, consciousness does not belong to the body; such is the specific qualification.
Since it is pervaded by insentience, which is its opposite, how much more so must that be the case for another?
1.1 He states the application [of the example]: "Of the body," etc. Therein, he recalls the very reason already stated: "By that which is contradictory," etc. [The mental factors...]

The meaning is that because the body is pervaded by an insentience (*jāḍya*) that is not contradictory [to its nature], it cannot possess those specific attributes [of consciousness]. Furthermore, since the notion of "I" arises with respect to the body, one might suspect that consciousness is an attribute of it;
however, he says "but what... to show that such a suspicion does not even arise regarding sound and other objects, because consciousness is absent there. || 209 ||
Nor does it reach the qualificand as qualified by another property.
Since it resides solely in the qualified object itself, how indeed could it exist elsewhere? (206)

He elucidates that very point: "The substantive" (*viśeṣyam*). Although the body is reached as the substantive of consciousness—because of the perception of the cognition "I am a human"—it does not pervade it as its qualifier, since the body is itself qualified by insentience (*jāḍya*), which is opposed to [consciousness]. Therefore, in things such as stones, which lack the cognition of "I," [the sense of self] could not arise in any way. Thus, the substantive is the form of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) which is primary in itself; in that [consciousness], by its own majesty...
The meaning is that because it is eternally established, its true nature (dharmatā) does not reside anywhere. || 206 ||
If there were a connection between those two in the relation of qualifier and qualified, [it would be possible].
In that case, it would be cognizable by a single means of knowledge, like a black snake. || 207 ||

He states another argument for consciousness and the body being the attribute and the substratum respectively: "viśeṣaṇa... etc. And it is not the case that [the body] is cognizable by the same cognition as consciousness, because consciousness is itself uncognizable; this is the remainder of the sense. || 207 ||

Since this cognition of the body and so forth arises as distinct [from consciousness], like a jar, how could it be characterized by consciousness? (208)

Furthermore, since it is well-established that the body is not the self, consciousness cannot be its attribute; thus he says: "Until one is learned" (*āvidvat*). Indeed, the body—which is commonly recognized by both the learned and the unlearned as "my body"—is incapable of being the self, for if it were, the same would follow for jars and other objects. As for the notion of "I" [with respect to the body], it is merely...
The sense is that she was already led away long ago. || 208 ||
It does not even reach its mother, being fixed solely upon the object of cognition.
What power does that perception have to function within its own object, consciousness? || 209 ||

Furthermore, it is observed that only that which is an object of cognition, such as form and so forth, possesses the attributes of the body; since consciousness lacks that [objectivity], it does not possess those attributes. He states this with the words "the mother" (mātaram). He provides the reason why perception cannot have the cognizer as its object with the words "the object of knowledge" (prameya) || 209 ||
It is cognized precisely by means of knowledge arising from its own uncommon form.
Just as a jar, so too is the self; it is not the object of the notion of "not-self. 210.
He establishes this meaning—that consciousness manifests as its own object through independence—by means of a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), [stating]: "Asādhāraṇā" [etc.]. || 210 ||
A term ending in a kṛt suffix denoting its own object may serve as a qualifier of another word because of its independence.
Nor is any consciousness whatsoever obtained as something separate from consciousness itself.

Furthermore, since consciousness has itself as its object, it cannot be a subordinate qualifier for something else; for that which is independent cannot logically be a qualifier with respect to that which is dependent.
Thus he says: "It has itself as its object. One might raise the objection: how can consciousness be independent, given that it is dependent upon the grāhaka (the subject)? To this, he replies:
And not so. || 211 ||
For consciousness belongs only to the grasper, the Self; it does not likewise belong to that which is not the Self.
In the world, it is not logically tenable for the grasper to be the grasped object. || 212 ||

Since it is the grasper, it is not dependent upon that [object]; having stated this point, he provides the reason: "grahītṛ" (as the grasper). For this very reason, there is no state of being grasped, otherwise there would be an infinite regress; thus he says: "grahituḥ" (of the grasper). || 212 ||
It is the qualification of consciousness as it appears as divided through its inwardness.
Nor could the body exist [as a separate entity] due to its being turned away [from consciousness], just as coldness cannot exist in fire. (213)

Anticipating the objection that consciousness, due to its independence, might not qualify the body as its attribute even if it does, whereas the body, due to its dependence, would indeed be its attribute, he says: "By way of being the inner self" (pratyaktayā). He provides an illustration for the absence of the body qualifying consciousness: "Cold," etc. (śīta) || 293 ||
The gold in the bracelets and other ornaments is established as the measure of the object to be measured.
How could that [cognition] exist within one's own consciousness for the sake of establishing an object contrary to it? || 214 ||

It has been stated that because of the mutual opposition between consciousness (*cit*) and the body, there can be no relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmi*). Now, it is explained how poison and so forth— referred to in the passage beginning with "just as bracelets and so on"—
[behave].

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Chapter Four. [The author] explains: "Such as bracelets and so forth. An effect, such as a swastika, resides within its cause, gold; the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) directed toward that [effect] therefore possesses a distinct application and conceptualization (*prayoga-pratyaya*) from that [cause]. However, with respect to the Self, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), there is no means of valid cognition for the purpose of realizing a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*).
The meaning is that since consciousness (caitanya) pertains solely to the object of knowledge (meyamātra), it does not share the same nature as bracelets and other such objects. || 214 ||
Furthermore, the arising of consciousness from material elements is not established by the means of valid cognition known as direct perception.
Furthermore, even though it is impermanent, the existence of the lineage of beings is established through inference. || 215 ||

To this, he replies with the words "And from the elements," countering what was stated in the verse beginning with "earth, water, etc. Is the production of consciousness (cit) perceptible or inferable? It cannot be the first, because there is no such perception; nor can it be the second, because that is not admitted [by the opponent] and no logical mark (liṅga) proving its production is perceived.
Furthermore, the conjunction of the elements, termed "aggregation" (saṃghāta), is impossible; for such a thing cannot be established through either difference or non-difference from the elements.
The meaning is "in order to speak. || 219 ||
When consciousness has departed, how can there even be the perception, "I am dead"?
Nor can there be an absence of consciousness due to the dullness of the body; for how could there be an absence of consciousness? (216)

Anticipating the objection that consciousness might arise like a jar because it possesses existence and perishability, he says, "The dead. The question is: is the experienced destruction of consciousness [the destruction] of consciousness itself or of the body? It cannot be the first, because [consciousness] does not resort to its own destruction; for it does not know its own destruction by itself. Nor can it be the second, because the body is insentient (jaḍa). He clarifies the meaning of the second quarter [of the verse].
"Consciousness," thus [it is said]. || 216 ||
Nor is it held that one's own experience is false, as in the case of a dream.
For no sublater of that [cognition] is observed, since it possesses the experience of awakening. || 217 ||

Having refuted the claim that consciousness arises from the combined elements and dissolves back into them—stating therein that "there is no recognition [of it]" and so forth—he now refutes that by saying "nor even... He provides the reason for why the falsity of that experience is not accepted as being like a dream, by saying "awakening... Since waking cognition sublates the dream, its falsity is established; however, there is no such sublater for the dream-experience, due to a lack of evidence.
And since that body is thus illusory, the consciousness residing within it is likewise so; therefore, the meaning is that it is incorrect to claim that the recognition of it is an error. || 217 ||
The departure of even the vital air is known through the absence of direct perception.
Or rather, let the air itself be the conscious entity, because consciousness arises through its presence.
128. As for the claim that consciousness perishes when it has departed into the wind (*vāyu*), he says in response: "Of the wind" (*vāyoḥ*). Because that [wind] is imperceptible, its...

The meaning is that even upon the departure [of the self], its existence is impossible, nor can it be apprehended through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), because such is not admitted. He states that even if one were somehow certain of its departure, the identity of the body—which is a composite of the four elements—with the self remains unestablished: "Of consciousness" (*citeḥ*). ||218||
If consciousness were the product of the elements, then awareness would persist as long as the body remains.
Or rather, this body perishes like a painting on a wall due to the destruction of its causes.

Furthermore, since consciousness and the body are alike in being effects of the elements, their staying and moving would be identical upon the departure of the air; to this he says:
"Consciousness... (219).
If the dream-body were also real in substance, it would be like the waking body.
Since it has truth as its sole cause, how could falsity belong to it? (220)

In the phrase "nor even from the experience of a dream," the falsity of that experience was stated by accepting the falsity of the body; now, he says [the following] to show that even according to the opponent's view, that [dream experience] is not false: "jāgrad... (waking...). 220.
Whether it be real or false, the dream-body is thus accepted.
Nevertheless, because it is cited as being non-deviant, the desired [conclusion] is established. || 221 ||

Furthermore, let it be as it may whether the dream-body is real or not; nevertheless, the existence of my desired Self is established. For even though there is mutual deviation between the waking body and the dream body, consciousness (caitanya) is non-deviant, and thus its status as a distinct Self is logically proven. Thus he says: "Or [it is] real. (221)
Therefore, within the bodies of householders and others, and in the stages of waking, dreaming, and so forth—
The perfected subject is established as distinct from the body through recognition.
He states the conclusion regarding the impossibility of the recognition "I who was asleep am now awake" being an error: "Therefore," etc.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "dreams, etc.," the inclusion of memory and meditative absorption is intended. || 222 ||
Due to differences in place, time, age, caste, form, power, and so forth.
There would be no recognition of the body if it were produced anew; [recognition] is appropriate only when there is a rememberer. || 223 ||

Regarding the objection that since even another [person] can possess the recollection of past births (*jātismaraṇa*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—as suggested by the verse beginning "one whose body possesses a thorn" (*saśalyadehaśālinī*)—the self is not established as something distinct from those, he replies with the word "deśa" (place). The meaning is that when a body is produced with differences of place and so forth, there is no recognition because of the difference between individual instances (*vyakti*), and because there is no single synthesizer for the genus (*jāti*) residing in both. He states the justification for this in his own position with the words "in the rememberer" (*smartari*).
In short, recognition is logical when one accepts a self distinct from the body that remembers past births. || 223 ||
And for those who consider perception to be the sole means of knowledge, there is nothing of the same class as that which is to be assisted [by inference].
It is appropriate for one who is hostile to inference to establish [the existence of] light. || 224 ||

Regarding the claim that "the light of the self (ātma-jyotis) belongs to the same class as the object of perception," as stated in the passage beginning with "that which assists [is of the same class]," he replies: "anugrāhyeti" (it is of the same class as the assisted). The meaning is this: for the Lokāyatika, who holds that perception alone is the means of valid knowledge and who hates inference, it is impossible to infer that the light whose nature is the self is of the same class as the object to be assisted, because no such inference can arise in his view. || 224 ||
And what do you intend to say here by this expression of similar kind?
Whether it be the universal or the individual, if the universal is what is being spoken of, [it is untenable]. || 225 ||
There would be no universal of the same class; if that were the case, there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, those who maintain the doctrine [of universals] say that universals are devoid of further commonalities.

Having stated the non-arising of the aforementioned inference, he analyzes the probandum (*sādhya*) with the words "of the same class" (*sajātīya*). Here, the phrase "in this case" refers to the statement of the opponent's inference.
Having restated the first [alternative], he refutes it with the words "if. That which is called "of the same class" is that which is pervaded by an identical genus.

If it were a universal (*sāmānya*), then it would be incorrect to say "the universal possesses universality," because there is nowhere a universal that possesses a further genus (*jāti*). By accepting a universal that possesses a genus, he states the fault of non-termination (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, he states that for one who asserts that a universal possesses a genus, there is a contradiction with what is established by the consensus of disputants (*vādiprasiddhi*): "Universals are devoid of universals" (*niḥsāmānyāni*). Therefore—

This means that it would lead to an infinite regress. For it has been stated: "Since there is no further universal or particularity within universals and particulars, cognition arises from those [original entities] themselves. (229, 226)
If it is held that the luminous body is a benefactor [to the self] by virtue of being material;
Since that [power] also exists within the body, there would be no need for it in the sun.

He takes up the second [point]: "by being composed of the elements" (*bhautikatvena*). The meaning is this: since the manifest light residing as such within the manifest elemental body acts as a supportive factor, if an individual instance (*vyakti*) pervaded by a common genus (*tulyajāti*) is the referent of a word denoting a class (*sajātīya*), then that manifest light—such as the eye and so forth—exists even in the body; thus, it would be observed in the light that is not distinct from it, such as the sun and so forth.
He refutes [the opponent's view] by pointing out its contradiction with experience, stating that "there would be no dependence on pride even regarding the body," as in verse 227.
If a distinction were to be required, it is one that does not exist in this body.
It does not possess the same genus as that which is to be assisted, because it is the assister itself. || 228 ||

He raises an objection: even though the manifestation of the illuminating light in the form of the eyes and other organs situated within the body to be assisted is possible, one might expect that a distinct external light such as the sun would be required as the assister; thus he says, "If there were a distinction. Nevertheless, he states that even so, the requisite homogeneity is not established: "Not by the assisted," etc. Indeed, the light of the sun and so forth, when being depended upon, is not of the same genus as the body.

The meaning is as follows: because one [element] is the benefactor and the other is the beneficiary, and because both forms are absent in both cases, their distinctness is clear; thus, even though they share a commonality by being composed of material elements (*bhautika*), this is equally true for the subject under discussion, since both are excluded from what is insubstantial (*tuccha*). || 228 ||
Whatever object appears as the body must be of a different nature from the body itself.
It has entered the scope of dispute because of its luminosity, like the sun and the moon. || 229 ||

Having stated that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*) by pointing out the difference between the body—the object of favor—and the Sun and others who are the favorers, he states a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*). [The verse begins with] "From the body... The sense is this: there is no lack of the property to be proven, because even though the Sun and others belong to the same genus as the body in being composed of the elements (*bhautika*), they are shown to be distinct from the body as its favorers (*anugrāhaka*). || 229 ||
A thing of the same genus as that which is to be assisted is not the assister, nor is it the case otherwise; a jar never assists another jar, nor does the sun assist the moon. (230)

Furthermore, having raised the alternative as to whether the pervasion (vyāpti) between the relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary (anugrāhyānugrāhakatva) and homogeneity (sājātya) is uniform or non-uniform, he refutes the first [position] with the words beginning "No" (na). The meaning is that there is no such rule that wherever there is the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, there must be homogeneity, nor that wherever there is homogeneity, there must be the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary; for this is contradicted by the case of jars and other such objects. || 230 ||
