The benefit to the body is held to be provided by both homogeneous and heterogeneous factors.
Therefore, no such restriction is desired by the Earth, Fire, and Wind themselves. || 231 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "of the same class" (*sajātīya*). The body is an aggregate of the elements; it is sometimes seen that earth is assisted by water and so forth. In that case, the earth—which is the earthly portion residing in the body—is both of the same class (*sajātīya*) and of a different class (*vijātīya*) relative to other portions:
water and so forth are of the same class for the bodily portion belonging to their own kind, yet they are of a different class for other portions. Therefore...

The meaning is that there is no universal pervasion (vyāpti) such that wherever there is a relationship of mutual benefit between a body and its benefactors—whether through those of the same class (sajātīya) or different classes (asajātīya)—there must be sameness of class; nor is it the case that where there is difference of class, there must be the non-existence of the other. || 131 ||
It is not accepted that [a thing] arises from the assistance of something of a different class.
How can it be said that the body consists of the four elements? || 232 ||

One might raise the objection: "Since earth benefits only its own constituent parts residing within the body, and the same applies to water and the other elements, the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by this rule. Anticipating this, he says: "Of a different genus" (*vijātīya*). Earth and the other elements benefit the body alone; for we perceive the specific assistance rendered therein by each of them.

Furthermore, there is no homogeneity (*sājātya*) between the aggregate (*samudāya*) and its constituents (*samudāyin*), because a disparity is observed through their being both collective and individual.
This is the meaning. || 232 ||
For even non-existence, like existence, provides assistance in this world.
Therefore, this restriction regarding [the soul] being a benefactor and so forth is not tenable. || 233 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished: "Even non-existence... According to the maxim, "How can a foot be placed without first ascertaining the absence of thorns?", since the absence of thorns and the like is auxiliary to walking and so forth—just like light and the like—wherever there is such assistance, there is similarity of kind (*sājātya*); thus, there is no pervasion. This is the meaning. || 233 ||
Just as fire is assisted by various kinds of fuel, so is a king assisted by various kings.
In the same way, the assistance of water is observed for lightning. || 234 ||
He states another reason for the absence of the pervasion [of the desired property] by others: "By the earthly ones," etc. (234).
The benefit of water and fuel is seen only in relation to fire.
Furthermore, the pacification of fire itself is seen to be achieved by means of water and fire.

Although it is observed that the divine power of Bhīma’s fire was assisted by wood and water, [the opponent asks: "Even so, how is it that there is no rule of homogeneity (*sājātya*) between the benefactor and the beneficiary? To this, he says: "By water. Having set aside the restriction of homogeneity for the beneficiary and the benefactor, he now sets aside the restriction of heterogeneity (*vaijātya*) even for the victim and the victimizer. He says: "Fire... [and] "Lightning... [etc. *Note: The provided text fragment ends with "vaidyu-". Based on the context of the argument regarding the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, the intended completion is likely "vaidyutena" (by lightning), referring to the instance where lightning destroys fire.*
It is well known that fire is extinguished through contact with earthly fire; and it is observed that earthly fire reaches extinction when met by water. || 235 ||
Therefore, the restriction regarding what is of the same class and what is not of the same class is not tenable.
Regarding benefit and harm, it is by the very path previously described. || 236 ||
He concludes the refutation of pervasion (vyāpti) with the words "sajātīya" (of the same class). Even when assistance exists, there is no necessary restriction to being of the same class.

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the fourth chapter], regarding the point that there is a restriction of dissimilarity (*vaijātyaniyama*) when a cause of deviation exists, he states the very reason expressed by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). [He does so] by means of the phrase "pūrva... (the preceding...), which means by demonstrating the violation of the rule. || 236 ||
Furthermore, as for the inconclusiveness of the reason that was previously asserted on account of the sense organs;
And that too was stated by you [to be non-existent], because it was accepted as the locus (dharmin). || 237 ||
Because this body, endowed with sense-faculties, is accepted through the designation "person" (puruṣa).
For a single part of that which is to be proven is not fit to serve as an example. || 238 ||

Having now stated that the internal nature of the self-luminous light (ātmajyotis)—which was previously refuted on the grounds that it must be of the same class as that which is to be assisted—is due to its being beyond the senses (atīndriyatva), [the author] restates what was said regarding the two reasons for its non-material nature—namely, its internal location (antasthatva) and its being beyond the senses—which are not invariably concomitant (anaikāntika) with the eyes and other organs.

This is expressed in the words "And that which... First of all, when "being internal" is the property to be proven (sādhya), "being beyond the senses" is not an inconclusive reason in relation to the eyes and other organs.

Regarding the question, "What is the light of this person?"—here, by taking the word "person" (*puruṣa*) to refer to the aggregate of the body and its instruments, he states that when the self-light is said to reside within that [aggregate], the body together with its senses is intended as the locus (*dharmin*), since it is included within the category of the qualified probandum (*sādhyakoṭi*) consisting of the state of residing within it. He says, "And that... Even if it is included in the category of the probandum, how could there not be a contradiction if the reason (*hetu*) exists while the possession of the probandum (*sādhyavattva*) is absent?

Anticipating the objection that [the reason] might be contradictory (*viruddha*), he says: "Not so" (*na hi*). A part of the probandum (*sādhyaikadeśa*) cannot be an example of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because it is included within the subject (*pakṣa*) and thus its status as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is impossible.

Nor does the flaw of contradiction persist with respect to supersensible things like atoms (*paramāṇu*) which are internal, because the reason is qualified by the term "being light" (*jyotiṣtva*). Alternatively, the meaning is that [the self] is non-material (*abhautika*) due to the two reasons of being internal and being supersensible, as in the case of the light of the self (*ātmajyotis*).

If it is argued that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of the eyes and so forth, [the author] says "And that" (*tacceti*), meaning that even there, the state of being located within (*antasthatva*) is not inconclusive. For the reason (*hetu*) is indeed "being located within that which is to be benefited" (*anugrāhyāntasthatva*); and since the eyes and so forth are accepted as having the property of being the objects to be benefited (*anugrāhyatva-dharmitva*), they lack the state of being located within [the Self], and thus there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case. He says "As the subject" (*dharmitvena*). How is it that the eyes and so forth are grasped as having the property of being the objects to be benefited by the Person?

Anticipating the objection that this is because the scripture speaks of the Self as being of such a nature, he says: "Of that which possesses the senses. He removes the charge of fallibility (*vyabhicāra*) against the reason—that it is distinct from the supersensible—by saying: "For not... When the goal is to prove a distinction from the aggregate of the body and the instruments, the eye and other organs, which are parts of that aggregate, cannot serve as examples of fallibility;
for it has been stated that the subject (*pakṣa*) cannot be its own counter-example (*vipakṣa*), nor can it be maintained that a part of an aggregate is contained within that very aggregate.

The point is that there is no contradiction because what is intended [by the reason] is the state of being ungraspable due to being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*). Alternatively, he says that if "being internal" (*antasthatva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), then "being beyond the senses" is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the senses, because they are accepted as having the status of subjects (*dharmin*) that are graspable, whereas "ungraspability" is synonymous with "being beyond the senses. He says "as the subject" (*dharmitvena*). To the question, "How do they have the status of being graspable? he replies, "of that which possesses the sense organ" (*sendriyasya*). For the person (*puruṣa*) is [the subject] by virtue of being that which is to be manifested.

The meaning is that since the senses and so forth are included within that [subject], they are likewise [non-material]; therefore, there is no contradiction [of the reason] with respect to them. By this, the contradiction of "imperceptibility" (atīndriyatva) has also been removed when "non-materiality" (abhautikatva) is the probandum. As for the objection that "being located within" (antasthatva) is contradictory when that [non-materiality] is the probandum, he says: "Not so. The meaning of the word "probandum" (sādhya) here is the thesis: "The inner light (pratyagjyotis) is non-material. Its being "located within" refers to its occupying a particular location.

The meaning is that its inwardness consists in its being the witness of the body and the instruments [of action]; and such a reason is not fit to serve as an example of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the sense organs (*akṣa*), because they lack the status of being that witness. || 237 || 238 ||
If the gender were established as having the suffix *mātr*, then the refutation would indeed be a refutation.
As for what was stated, beginning with "there is no concomitance in the case of a specific [instance]," etc. (239).

Having restated the claim that inference is not indeed a valid means of knowledge, he refutes it with the words "of the mark" (liṅgasya). The absence of pervasion (vyāptyabhāva) [is due to] the fact that the probandum is already established.

The meaning of the refutation beginning with "tat" and so forth is as follows: that refutation would apply to the validity of inference (*anumāna*) itself; for, by the force of reasons such as the failure of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the invalidity of inference is being established.

Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) must be a valid means of knowledge (*māna*) in the form of an inference, because otherwise it could not function as a prover, and because it is not included within perception (*pratyakṣa*). || 239 ||
Because the probandum, consisting of fire and so forth, possesses both a general and a specific form.
Furthermore, there would not even be two faults, for [the opponent] suspects only that which is of a single form. || 240 ||

To this he replies, beginning with "sāmānya" (the universal), as to how there is no lack of pervasion (*ananugama*) and so forth in that case. For if the probandum (*sādhya*) were intended to be of a single form, then two defects would be suspected; however, it is not intended to be of a single form, since its dual nature is admitted.

Thus, because the probandum has the nature of a universal, there is no lack of pervasion, and because it has the nature of a particular, there is no proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). This is the meaning. || 240 ||
And you do not possess the sense organs, you who hold perception alone to be the sole means of valid cognition.
For their establishment is not possible without inference. || 241 ||

Anticipating the objection—"How can inference be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), given that it is impossible for a single thing to have two forms and that [the argument for] pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been refuted?"—the author says "And not... with the intention that even if its validity is not ultimate (*tāttvika*), it possesses conventional validity (*vyāvahārika*). The meaning of this is: for one who does not accept the validity of inference, even perception (*adhyakṣa*) would not be established, because the sense organs (*indriya*) cannot be established without inference; nor are they identical to the physical orbs (*golaka*).
Which [cognitions] do not depend on inference? Since the object is not perceived even when those [causes] are present, one must postulate another sense organ as the instrument for that cognition;
thus, for one who maintains that it is directly perceived, the validity of inference must be accepted as being useful for that purpose. || 241 ||
He is the knower of the distinctions between the grasper, the grasping, the grasped, existence, and non-existence.
Consciousness that exists independently of others and for its own sake is not perceived by the senses.

He states that there is a means of knowledge other than perception here, beginning with the words "grāhaka" (the grasper). For perception is not capable of making the aforementioned consciousness its object;
therefore, the scriptural statement must be understood as having that [consciousness] as its referent. This is the meaning. || 242 ||
Nor can it be said that [the effect] exists only when that [cause] exists, because the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not established.
For if there were no body, how could this consciousness exist? What would be its basis? (243)

Furthermore, he states that one who asserts that consciousness (*caitanya*) is a property of the body—on the grounds that it exists when the body exists and is absent when the body is absent—is forced to accept the validity of inference (*anumāna*). He says: "And not... The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the body. The fact that consciousness is non-existent when the body is absent is also indicated here. He establishes the lack of proof for the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by saying: "The body... For there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the absence of [consciousness] upon the absence of that [body].
The meaning is that because it penetrates the true object, there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it, since [such another] is not admitted. || 243 ||
The invalidity of inference as a means of valid cognition is not established by perception.
Moreover, if that [non-existence] were established even by a logical mark (liṅga), there would be a contradiction precisely with what you have stated.

Furthermore, if inference were not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), would perception or inference be the valid means? It is said that it is not the first [option]: "anumāna... [etc.]. [The text continues: "...is not seen in form," etc.
(ga); "even so, not indeed" (kha).

The meaning is that because it has as its object something possessing a beginning [in time]. He says "not the second" by means of the word *liṅgena* (by an inferential mark). For if that were the case, the authority of the inferential mark (*liṅga*)—
The meaning is that it is because [this] is necessary. || 244 ||
Furthermore, it would follow that all your activities without exception would be brought to cessation.
If the *liṅga* were not a means of valid cognition in this world, the universe would likewise be motionless.

He states another reason for the validity of inference (*anumāna*) with the word "tvat" (from you). For it has been said: "If inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) were invalid, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cessation of all worldly activity, such as eating and drinking. The word "iha" (here) refers to the state of worldly activity. Not only would there be a cessation of your own activities if inference were invalid, but the entire universe would be devoid of both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).
He says: "devoid of activity. The meaning is that engagement and withdrawal depend upon the inference of something being a means to what is desired or undesired. || 245 ||
Even this utterance of speech would not be established for you.
The word "bhārati" is not uttered by you for the purpose of establishing a self.
Furthermore, because we observe you uttering speech for the sake of communication with others, the validity of inference must be accepted; thus he says:

"Speech," etc. The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that if that [inference] were invalid, the utterance by another would likewise be untenable. Immediately after hearing a word employed by another, one perceives a cognition within oneself; then, based on one's own experience as an example, one infers that in the case of another person—their own listener—there is likewise [a cognition] upon hearing the word uttered by themselves.

Having inferred the knowledge of the meaning from the sound, one employs the word oneself; that inference is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), otherwise the employment of the sentence would be purposeless, for it is not uttered for the sake of one's own comprehension. By this, the validity of the sentence itself is to be understood—this is the intended meaning. (246)
Let that which has entered the scope of dispute be accepted as a means of valid cognition.
Just as the inference of a refutation is derived from a logical mark (liṅga) by virtue of its being an inference (anumāna). || 247 ||

He states the proof for its being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*): "In the dispute... etc. The first qualification is introduced to remove the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*) regarding the body.
He says that it is like the inference: "The self is distinct from the body, because it is not perceived apart from it, like a donkey's horn. [He addresses] the objection:

"And there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*)," for if the opponent’s position were not defective, one’s own position could not be established; since in a real entity (*vastu*), conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) are impossible.
The self is not an existent entity. || 247 ||
And as for that impermanence which is asserted of the light of fireflies and the like;
Because of the intervention of the fortnight and so forth, that [fault] does not apply to us with respect to them. || 248 ||

Having established the validity of inference (*anumāna-prāmāṇya*) and, by its power, stated the distinction of the self-luminous (*ātma-jyotis*) from the body, [the author] now refutes the illustrative example mentioned previously—namely, that luminosity and non-luminosity are the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the body even though they occur only occasionally—by stating "khadyotādi" (fireflies, etc.). That impermanence of light does not apply to fireflies and the like; rather, it applies only to us.

That [object] appears because its manifestation is obstructed for us by intervening parts such as the subject (pakṣa) and so forth; therefore, the meaning is that since the substratum exists, there is no example for something being an occasional nature. || 248 ||
Furthermore, the grasping at existence and non-existence cannot be established through direct perception as a means of valid cognition.
Because perception here is connected with an existing object in every respect. (249)
1 on the path 1

One cannot say that what is merely occasional constitutes an essential nature (svabhāva). Having thus raised the dilemma as to whether perception (*pratyakṣa*) or some other means of knowledge (*māna*) is the authority regarding non-existence (*abhāva*), he refutes the first alternative with the word "bhāva" [in the verse]. By the word "api," other means of knowledge are also excluded from non-existence, since the opponent does not admit them for that purpose. He states the reason why non-existence is not apprehended by perception with the phrase "vidyamāna... (of that which exists). And it has been said: "Apprehension belongs to that which exists, through consciousness; not to that which does not exist. Regarding the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*)—
Nor indeed is there a connection [between the object and the cognition], because the sense organ possesses [only] the capacity [for contact]. // 249 //
Now, if it is argued that even non-existence (abhāva) is what is apprehended by that [cognition], it is replied:
It must be stated: what is the means of valid cognition for the establishment of the non-existence of perception? || 250 ||

He raises an objection based on the perception [of the ground] such as "the ground is devoid of a jar" with the words "Now" (*atha*). He refutes this by accepting that the absence of an object is indeed perceptible, with the words "Perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*).
For perception does not establish its own absence, because they do not exist at the same time; nor does any other means of knowledge [do so].
The meaning is that it is possible for [the cognition] to penetrate that [object], because there is no admission [of such a penetration]. || 250 ||
Even the absence of the knower and the means of knowledge is being asserted by you.
If something is not a means of valid cognition even when [the object] exists, how could it be so when that [object] is absent? (251)

Furthermore, since the non-existence of the knower (*mātr*) and so forth is not established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) must be accepted to apprehend it; thus he says: "The knower... etc. In that regard, he states by way of a *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument that perception is not a valid means [for this]: "Even when [the knower] exists," etc. For perception is not a means of knowledge with respect to the knower or the means of knowledge itself, because if it were to operate upon its own locus or its own self, it would lead to the absurdity of it operating upon itself; nor is there an absence of that [perception] when it is not apprehended.

The meaning is that, according to your own view, the two cognitions must be apprehended by the same cognition; otherwise, it would follow that there is a separate means of valid cognition (mānāntara). || 211 ||
If it were to turn back from its own nature, this would be utterly impossible.
The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of a thing is its reality (tattva); because it is reality, it does not deviate from reality. || 252 ||

Having stated that non-perception and so forth cannot be the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) because they are not established within the doctrine of intrinsic nature—since that which is occasional cannot be an intrinsic nature—he states another reason for why intrinsic nature is not occasional, beginning with "it would cease. If [non-perception] were the intrinsic nature, it would be illogical for it to cease while the entity exists; for the intrinsic nature is the very essence (*svarūpa*) of the entity, and that does not perish as long as the entity exists, because that would involve a contradiction.
Such is the meaning. || 252 ||
The nature of dharma and so forth is necessarily such that they bestow their results.
Listen to me as to how that too must be accepted by you here. || 253 ||

He restates what was said [in the Siddhānta]—that even according to our own doctrine, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of dharma and so forth consists in their being the givers of results—in order to establish the theory of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*). The phrase "of dharma and so forth" connects with "the state of being the giver of that result. Now, one might object: "I do not accept an inherent nature called 'the state of being the giver of results' in dharma and so forth, because it is not established that subsequent dharma and so forth have those as their cause by virtue of preceding dharma and so forth. To this, he replies: "It must be accepted."
The statement expressing the mode is its meaning; "here" refers to the mention of dharma and so forth. || 213 ||
1 kha. *tasyānauṃ* | 2 gha. *saṃbodho* | 3 ga. *atha bhā* | 4 ga. *’pi na prāya* | 5. ga. *’ve tu ta* | 6 na. gha. *svavṛ ṃ* | 7 kha. *’dapi du* [vol 3, page 289]
1422 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
From action arise praise and blame, characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth.
The fruit of dharma and adharma is directly experienced through perception. || 254 ||
He demonstrates that it must indeed be heard: "from action," etc. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), inclusion of honor and contempt is intended.

By the second "etcetera," their respective subdivisions are grasped. For there is no dispute regarding what is established by perception; nor is the attainment of pleasure and so forth due solely to actions such as praise, since it is observed to occur otherwise as well. Therefore, in consideration of that, dharma and the like alone are the cause of those [pleasures], and not [praise].

In view of its dependence on [auxiliary] factors (dharma), its capacity to yield a fruit is not permanent; and thus, just as its capacity to yield a fruit is your inherent nature (svabhāva), so too is consciousness my body—this is the intended meaning. || 294 ||
Since scripture is the sole means of valid cognition, how can there be an illustration of dharma and so forth?
Just as [the existence of the self] is established through acceptance, so too is the acceptance of the Vedas.

He offers a rebuttal, stating that this example does not apply to one who does not accept scripture (*āgama*), by saying "scripture" (*āgama*). For it has been stated: "Dharma is a matter characterized by injunction (*codanā*). He then raises an objection, suggesting: "I have cited this while provisionally accepting Dharma and so forth as you desire. To this he replies: "In that case, the authority of the Veda must also be accepted in accordance with my position; for perception does not take Dharma and the like as its object, nor is it a means [of knowing them]."

The elders maintain that inference, comparison, and presumptive testimony lack independent authority because they are preceded by perception and because they contradict the logical principle that "one perceives only what is already present. Furthermore, he states "the Veda" because the *Autpattika-sūtra* declares that its [the Veda's] knowledge consists in instruction. || 259 ||
And since you accept other means of valid cognition, that being the case, [your position is untenable].
This contradiction with one's own established doctrine follows by force, even though it is undesired. || 256 ||

He states [the following] regarding what loss there would be in accepting that [self] as the object of cognition and that [cognition] as its means of valid knowledge: "By another means of knowledge," etc. (256).
If you claim that the nature of fire is its power, such as its capacity to burn;
Since that [object] is not established by perception, there is a contradiction for those who rely on inference.

By the passage beginning with "nor is it that there is no [nature] of things," it was stated that burning and so forth constitute the nature (*svabhāva*) of fire. Regarding this, one might consider whether that nature is its effect or its power (*śakti*). It cannot be the first, because since an effect perishes even while the fire exists, it cannot logically be the nature [of the fire]. With this in mind, [the author] restates and refutes the second alternative, beginning with "burning and so forth. For power is not perceivable by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); rather, it is to be inferred from its effect.
The meaning is that because you accept inference in this manner, there would be a deviation from your own established tenet (apasiddhānta). || 297 ||
If it were so for you as well, just as it is my own admission.
Since we accept all [theories of] pride, nothing of ours is ill-established. (258)

"By you alone, I too have accepted the validity of inference; therefore, there is no contradiction. Thus, seeing no other way out, [the author] restates and refutes the doubt with the words "my" (*mad*): "The meaning is that by following my path, since all means of knowledge that serve as instruments for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) are accepted, the proof of the self’s transcendence over the body and so forth is established. (298)
1 ga. *kriyate* | 2 gha. *kriyata* | [Vol.
3, page 290] 3 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1423
This effort is made by me for the sake of establishing your position.
If you accept what I have said, our purpose will be accomplished. || 259 ||
He clarifies what has already been stated with the words "tvad" (by you). The meaning is: I am striving to prove that even inference and the other means of knowledge must be accepted by you as valid;

if you yourself accept inference and so forth, then our desired conclusion—that there is a light of the self distinct from the body and such—will be established on the basis of that inference. || 259 ||
The objection that was raised regarding the lack of a firm foundation has also been refuted.
Because all [cognitions] are admitted [as valid], there is no infinite regress; therefore, it follows by force of logic.

He refutes the objection that "there would be an infinite regress" (anavasthā) when a dharma or the like ceases to bestow its fruit due to the influence of another subsequent dharma or the like. The meaning is that once the authority of the Vedas and so forth is accepted, [the problem] can be resolved by [positing] beginninglessness (anāditva) and other such factors. || 260 ||
Therefore, the Self is established as distinct from the body and so forth, as previously described;
it is of a different genus from the sun and other such objects, according to the aforementioned inference. (261)

Relying on the *Śābarabhāṣya*, which states that "the body is not the self; the self is other than the body," he concludes by means of the negation of the body itself: "dehādi" (the body, etc.). The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is the established validity of [the self's] being known through inference. That is to say, it refers to the previously mentioned reasons such as its being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*). || 261 ||
And it is the body alone that is accepted as possessing actions such as seeing and so forth.
If memory were [the cause] of what is seen, there would be no perception of an object in a dream. (262)

Having stated that the self is distinct from [the body] through inference, he states another reason for that very point: "Because of seeing, etc. If the body were the seer, there would be no seeing of an object already seen during recollection; for a jar seen by one with eyes is not remembered by one who is blind. Furthermore, there is no difference between the seer and the rememberer, because it is never observed that what was seen by one is remembered by another, as it has been said: "One does not remember what was seen by another. Therefore...

The meaning is as follows: according to the *Akṣapāda-sūtra*, "Because memory of what has been seen is impossible [if the body were the seer], the status of being a seer and so forth belongs only to that which is distinct from the body; since these qualities exist as attributes of the Self (ātman), there is no refutation [of the Self]. He states, "And in a dream," because if one were to accept that the body itself possesses the capacity for seeing and so forth, then the impossibility of seeing what was previously seen in a dream would necessitate the postulation of a seer and so forth that is distinct [from the body]. || 262 ||
In the absence of external factors such as the sun and so forth, and without the operation of the sense organs, [the cognition arises].
A man who is awake perceives that which he has previously seen while in the state of restraint.

In this regard, one might object: "Since the perception of that which is already perceived is unestablished, how can the existence of the Self as described be proven by its non-perception? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "External... (verse 263). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, the body is not the seer."
By that same collection of conditions through which he had previously seen the mountain peak.
Even without her, he then perceives his own self as it was before.

How is it that there is a perception in a dream of things such as the sun which are not present? For indeed, an effect is not possible without its causal complex (*sāmagrī*); to this, [the author] replies with the verse beginning "ādityādi" (the sun, etc.). [Variant readings: 1. ka. kha. 'riktaṃ dra']
[Vol. 3, page 291] 1424 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

"By means of the totality" (sāmagryā). Now, if it is argued that the mind in a dream—having transformed into the form of what was previously seen—is directly perceived by the Witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), then [the question arises: how could that [mind] have the form of what was not previously seen?

To the question of why even that which has been transformed [in a dream] is not an object for the witness, he says: "As before. Therefore, because there is a rule that what was seen [in waking] or something of the same class as it is seen in a dream, there is a seer who persists through both waking and dreaming, distinct from the body; he is neither the self (kha) nor anything other than the self (khanyah)—the sense being that "he sleeps" [only when this seer is withdrawn]. || 264 ||
This man, though his eyes have been plucked out, remains like a jar whose eyes have not been removed.
One perceives it within oneself; therefore, nothing other than the Self is seen.
He states another reason for the fact that only the *atirikta* is the seer: "utkhātā... (verse 261).
And from this, it would follow as established that whoever sees a jar in a dream [sees it there].
Even before [regaining] his sight, he recognized that very jar by means of his eye.

Even though the self is the dream-seer, one might suspect a difference between the seers by thinking that in the waking state there is another seer; anticipating this, he says: "And therefore" (*tataśca*). The meaning of the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) is that waking and dreaming have a single substratum. For in that case, there is no difference between the seers, because that would contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and so forth—this is the meaning. || 266 ||
And because, at the time of death, perception and so forth are impossible for one who is indeed unimpaired.
Furthermore, that [seeing] would not belong to the body if the body were the seer. (267)

He states another reason for the body not being the seer: "And in death," etc. The construction is as follows: if the body were the seer, then even when death has occurred, the activities such as seeing would continue for that very same intact body; since they do not occur, its status as a seer cannot exist either. || 267 ||
If the eyes, the intellect, and so forth were not the perceivers, recognition would not be possible.
For a synthesis cannot occur between things perceived by different perceivers. || 268 ||

Lest it be argued that while the body cannot be the self, the sense organs might be so because the notion of "I" is observed in relation to them, [the author], following the Nyāya-sūtra which states that "what is seen by the left eye is recognized by the other," replies with the words beginning "No" (na). 268.
The very Kumbha whom I saw before, that same one I touch today.
This reintegration must not involve different perceivers. || 269 ||

Having seen an object with the left eye, one recognizes it by seeing it with the other eye as well, thinking, "That which I saw, that very same thing I see now. And if consciousness belonged to the sense organ, another could not recognize what was seen by another; thus, recognition would be impossible. Relying on this *Nyāyabhāṣya*, he applies the meaning of the *bhāṣya* passage beginning with "that which I saw" to the point under discussion. That which I saw...
Thus [it is said]. || 269 ||
Therefore, the mind is the agent of reconnection because it relies upon formative forces (saṃskāra).
It is not so, because that [mind] is also seen as an object of the mind. || 270 ||

He raises an objection in accordance with the sūtra of Akṣapāda: "Because the causes for the cognition of a self are possible in the mind. He states the reason for the mind's being the synthesizer (pratisaṃdhātṛ) as follows: "Due to its unity and its latent impressions (saṃskāra) arising from prior experiences...
[vol 3, page 292]

The meaning is that [the mind] is the self because recognition is possible due to its latent impressions (saṃskāra), and because the grasping of a single object through both seeing and touching is possible therein.

He refutes this with the Nyāya-sūtra: "It is not so; it is merely a difference in designation, since the instrument of knowledge is established as belonging to the knower. [He says: "Not thus," [referring to] the mind—
He states the refutation as expressed in the Bhāṣya beginning with "so 'pi" (even that): "tasyāpi" (of that too). || 270 ||
The mind, directly filled with sound and other objects, has entered into the state of memory and dream.
Since it is perceived as being like a jar, therefore, for us, neither the Self nor even the mind [is the perceiver].
To the question of how it lacks selfhood because it is an object, he says: "Sound and so forth... (279).
Existence and non-existence belong to the subject and so forth, while [the reality] possesses a nature distinct from those.
It perceives directly and eternally; therefore, the mind cannot be the seer.
Anticipating the objection that "the mind is non-self because it is an object of sight, like a jar," he says: "bhāva... (verse 272). This is because there is no one who hates [it].
And the fact that this body is an object of enjoyment is established by perception alone as the sole means of valid cognition.
Why is its state of being an enjoyer postulated as something unperceived and immeasurable? || 273 ||

He states another reason for the non-selfhood of the two bodies: "Because they are objects of enjoyment. The meaning is that the subject under dispute is not the self because it is an object of enjoyment, like a jar. Some who maintain that the two bodies possess the status of an enjoyer do not consider the perception of being an object of enjoyment to be a valid means of knowledge; to them, he says: "Perception... Nor should it be argued that the perception "I am enjoying" is a valid authority regarding that [body], and therefore the claim that it is not perceived [as such] is unproven.
The meaning is that since that [cognition] has as its object a self that is distinct [from the body], no other means of knowledge is accepted as apprehending its status as an enjoyer. || 273 ||
"For this object is to be enjoyed through form, while the enjoyer is indeed formless."
The eater and the eaten are understood through perception to be of contradictory natures. (274)
Furthermore, he states: "The body and the self are mutually distinct because they possess contradictory properties, like two things commonly agreed upon. [Verse 274]
Thus, enough with these refutations consisting of mere verbal attacks arising from dry logic.
That which was commenced for the sake of accomplishing the goals of men is now being explained. || 275 ||

He concludes the refutation of that [opposing] view with the words "enough of this. By means of the refutations of those objections— which consist of mere verbal assertions arising from baseless reasoning, such as "the body alone is the self and there is no other, because the notion of 'I' arises in relation to the body and nothing else is perceived"— [the opponent's position is rejected].

The construction is as follows: "Enough with what has been said beginning from 'of those who hold all [other] views as sacred sites' (*sarvatīrthadṛśām*). This is the intended meaning: the body is a transformation of the food that has been eaten; if that [body] were the Self, why is its gross portion not called the Self? If it is argued that it is not so because the notion of "I" (*ahaṃbuddhi*) is absent, then the same applies to the other [the subtle body].

For the discerning, the absence of that [notion] is seen even in the other, due to its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), its insentience (*jaḍatva*), and so forth. Therefore, that [subtle body] is the non-Self; in it, there is the cognition of "I."

The notion "I am stout" should be understood as belonging to those lacking discrimination, like that of a dog; since the self exists prior to and after the body, this [body] is not the self. And it has been said:

"Because of the continuity of memories practiced in previous lives, a newborn infant experiences joy, fear, and grief. Thus, there are many refutations of the doctrine that the body is the self; therefore, the self is an entity distinct from the aggregate [of the body and senses]. He introduces the subsequent section with the words "Of men," etc., for those seeking liberation...
The meaning is that, for the sake of correctly understanding what has been omitted, one must simply follow the explanation of the scriptures. || 279 ||
1 ka. draṣṭṛbhā | 2 ga. 'taḥ || pra | 3 kha. gha. pā ye kṣe | 4 kha. gha. hi | 179
1426 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika, Chapter Four [Volume 3, Page 293]
Having accepted the statement "the self alone is his [object]," one perceives the contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Suspecting this, Janaka asked: "Which one, pray, is this self? (276)
Showing what is relevant, he raises the question: "The Self. || 276 ||
In this collection of the body and so forth, there arise the designation and the cognition "self."
In this world, which is well-known to everyone—from women and children to the learned—[this is so]. (277)

Anticipating the doubt as to how there can be a suspicion of contradiction between what precedes and what follows—the very root from which this inquiry proceeds—the author first demonstrates its established status with the words "dehādi" (the body, etc.). The particle *hi* (for) is used to indicate that the aforementioned established status is free from dispute. || 277 ||
There is a connection between the activity of the person and that which is distinct from the body and so forth.
He was previously established by means of the light, which is non-self, as the inferential mark. || 278 ||
Nevertheless, raising the doubt as to how there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows, he restates what was said previously: "Of the human activity... (verse 278).
Because of the statement "the self alone is his," there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Having conceived a doubt, the king questioned Yājñavalkya.

Now, raising an objection, he states the justification for the question: "The Self," etc. Having abandoned the body—which is commonly known as the "Self"—the human activity would have to proceed by means of a non-self, namely another light; thus, in passages such as "The sun is the light, O Emperor," a connection [of the self] with that [external light] was stated.

Now, however, by the statement "The Self alone is his light," etc., the connection of that [self] with the Self is stated. Therefore, [there is a contradiction between] the preceding and subsequent statements—
The meaning is that the king, having conceived a doubt within himself due to this contradiction between the two views, asks with the desire to resolve it. || 279 ||
If it is intended that the light of the self is something other than the body and so forth;
In that case, this contradiction between what precedes and what follows does not arise here at all.

He raises an objection to the question stated out of doubt due to the apprehension of contradiction, saying: "It is another meaning. In passages such as "the Self alone is his," if the word *ātman* were taken to mean the body, a contradiction between what precedes and what follows would have to be suspected—since previously the person's activity was said to be by means of a light distinct from the body, whereas now it is spoken of in connection with the body. However, if the word *ātman* is taken to signify something else [than the body], there is no contradiction; therefore, this [explanation] is rooted in a doubt born from the suspicion of contradiction.
The meaning is that there is no lack of proof. || 280 ||
And in this world, the word "ātman" is well-known to denote many different things.
Because the notion of "self" persists even with respect to witnesses, the intellect, and the body. (281)

He provides the commentary: "And the word 'self'... The particle *ca* (and) serves to dispel the doubt that the question would not arise. He clarifies the well-known usage with the word "witness" (*sākṣin*). || 281 ||
The suffix *ḍatamach* is used here because a plurality of meanings is possible in this context.
Which self is intended by you to be characterized as light? || 282 ||

Since the word *ātman* can have multiple meanings, when it is necessary to distinguish one from among many, the suffix *-tamap* is employed in the form *katama* (which one?). Having stated this meaning, the author provides the formal indicator (*liṅga*) by saying "*ḍatamañ*. This is because he observes the use of the word *ātman* in reference to many things.
He states the conclusion: "Being in doubt, he asks. The construction is: "Which one is that Self which you intend to designate as light? [282]
Thus questioned, he established [the point] through inference in a manner that was not contradictory.
Therefore, one [should perceive] this very king as the self-luminous light, perfectly manifest as "this. || 283 ||

He states the answer: "Thus questioned," etc. The construction is as follows: having been asked thus, the sage clearly spoke to the king with the words beginning with "This light which is the Self" (*ātma-jyotiḥ*), which is not contradicted by the previously mentioned inference. || 283 ||
First, there is the favor shown to the agent of worldly activity by means of luminaries such as the sun.
Consequently, there is grace for the inner self in regions such as Kṛṣṇasāra and others. || 284 ||

Having introduced the subsequent section, and in order to support the argument for the existence of the supreme self-luminosity (*ātma-jyotis*), the author recalls the manner in which both the insentient and sentient lights are favored;

he then restates the manner in which the insentient light is favored, beginning with the words "The sun and so forth. This means: in locations such as the *kṛṣṇasāra* (the black pupil), that is to say, in specific regions of the eye-socket and so on.
He states that through the mediation of the external senses, the mind becomes possessed of discrimination due to the favoring influence of the sun and other luminaries.
"Of one's own mind," [it is said]. || 284 ||
The aggregate, dominated by the mind, is reflected with the consciousness of the self.
Then, with his memory fully restored, he resumes external activity.

Having spoken of the favor bestowed by the light of the insentient (jaḍajyotis), he now proclaims the favor of the other light (the sentient). He says, "The mind" (manaḥ). He states that when it is pervaded by the reflection of the self’s consciousness (ātmacaitanyābhāsa), it acquires the power to contemplate objects such as sound and so forth; thus he says, "Manifested" (abhivyakta). He further states that the contemplation of objects that has arisen is the cause for engagement with those objects; thus he says, "Now" (atha). As they have said: "And all living beings have memory as their support."
These are the conventional usages. || 285 ||
In this context, the piṇḍa is first the single Self, and the second is designated as the liṅga.
And there is another, the fourth, which is the limit of what is reflected in consciousness, described as "not this, not this" (neti neti). || 286 ||

Anticipating the objection that the doctrine of two lights is incompatible with the doctrine of non-duality (advayavāda), [the author], intending to show its logical consistency through conceptualization (*kalpanā*), elaborates upon the verse beginning with "The word 'Self' in this world" by taking up the distinctions superimposed upon the Self. Regarding the term "body" (*piṇḍa*):
the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) and the Witness (*sākṣī*) are so called because they have as their limit that which is marked by [the body]. || 286 ||
Between the external and internal lights, the body is a composite of the intellect and other faculties.
One who possesses pleasure and so forth performs actions of speech, mind, and body. || 287 ||

He says "bāhya... [verse 287], meaning that once the two lights are established through conceptual distinction, it is logical to state that the aggregate—which partakes in the action and its fruit—subsists between them.
With his eyes perfectly illuminated by the light of the sun and other luminaries, he—this very one—[perceives].
Remembering that, with a trembling mind, he undergoes external activity. || 288 ||
1. By the word "light" (jyotis). 2. "Piṇḍa," etc.
[Vol. 3, page 295] 1428 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]...

How do these two support the aggregate? Regarding that, he says, referring to external light: "The sun, etc. Here, the term "this" refers to the aggregate as the one who engages in worldly discourse (*vyavahartā*). Referring to internal light, he says: "Through that, etc.

Having perceived objects by means of the senses supported by the sun and other sources of light, the person—pervaded by the manifestation of consciousness within the mind that has arisen through the doors of the senses—is [engaged] with them.
The meaning is that one performs the appropriate activity. || 288 ||
The assistance of external light for this [consciousness] arises from both dharma and adharma.
But the favor of the inner light is independent of any other cause. || 289 ||

Having recalled the statement that "a person proceeds when favored by two lights," the author restates—in order to express further—what was said regarding the connection with external light: that one is produced by dharma and so forth, while the other is innate. [Verse 289] "Dharma... etc.
Therefore, the grace of the deity occurs only in a single part of his body.
In the entirety of the internal, the divine, and so forth, there is the favor of the self-luminous light.

He states the intended further point: "deha" (the body). The meaning is that, according to the previously stated distinction, the favor of the sun and other luminaries toward this person occurs only in locations such as the physical orbs, whereas the favor of the self-luminosity (*ātma-jyotis*) occurs everywhere. || 290 ||
"The sun does not shine there"—thus is the statement in the Atharva Veda.
And as it is said in the Īśvara-smṛti: "Just as one [sun] illuminates... (291).

Considering that the light of the Self (ātmajyotis) is the sustainer of all and the illuminator of all, he cites scripture and tradition as authority for this: "Not there," etc. The locative case here has been explained in the section concerning the "imitation" (anukṛti-adhikaraṇa). || 299 ||
And because phenomena such as dharma are non-abiding, that which is to be employed must include its presiding deity.
Therefore, that which pertains to the self and that which pertains to the elements is unstable, yet it is personally realized by him.

Anticipating the objection that the body and so forth—which are the objects of illumination—must also be eternal because they are in a constant relationship with the illuminating light of the Self, he says: "Because of its instability. The meaning is that since the motivating factors such as merit (dharma) are non-eternal, and since the motivated body and so forth are effects, all of them are indeed non-eternal. Then, fearing the doubt that the light of the Self might likewise be non-eternal for that same reason, he says: "By that [it is not]."
Because everything is impermanent, as can be personally witnessed,
up to [the point mentioned]. (292)
Therefore, because it is the means of establishing that [consciousness],
the light of the Self is eternal;
hence, in the absence of external light, it is caused by speech, mind, and body.
In this worldly discourse concerning "self" and so forth, the light of consciousness alone is the reality, and nothing else.

If it is argued that the activity of a person occurs only when assisted by the two lights [the internal and external], then how can there be such activity in dreams and the like, given the absence of the assisting external light?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "External... The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is that the assistance of the two lights occurs only during the waking state. ||293||
For the purpose of establishing the distinctness [of the Self] from the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect.
That which is called "this" is the speech regarding the inner light, like the sun.
