3, page 296] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1429

Having recalled everything along with its supplementary details that had been obscured by the investigations and conventions of the Lokāyata school, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "This which... as it was introduced. He says: "The body. The construction is as follows: just as there is a distinction from the objects of the sun's favor, so too, for the sake of establishing the distinction of the light of the Self from the body and so forth, the statement beginning with "This which... is uttered by the Śruti. || 294 ||
First of all, an object established by direct perception is itself the means of valid cognition.
Existence and non-existence of the knower and so forth are established through his grace. || 295 ||

He first speaks of *sattva* (existence) for the purpose of demonstrating the superiority of the light of the Self, beginning with the word "itself" (*svayam*). Indeed, the Witness (*sākṣin*), up to the final manifestation, is self-luminous; because He is the establisher of everything, or alternatively, because the entire range of subjects and so forth, ending with the Witness, has the Self as its own self-evident authority—according to the etymology "that which has the Self itself as its authority"—therefore there is no suspicion of His non-existence. To the question "In what way is He the establisher of everything?", he says:
He cultivates it. || 299 ||
Then, by the cognizer who assumes the form of "I" and is permeated by the appearance of that [object].
The establishment of the means of valid cognition and so forth would likewise depend upon the object of cognition through those very means of valid cognition. (296)

He explains the sequence of the attainment of the mother and so forth through the grace of consciousness with the words "tadābhāsa" (appearing as that). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the mention of ignorance and the rest. || 296 ||
And the establishment of the operation of the means of valid cognition and its result occurs in the cognizer.
It would culminate in realization within the inner self of the knower. || 297 ||

He explains the manner in which the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is established: "By the means of knowledge," etc. Because the operation called "means of knowledge" (*māna*) occurs with respect to the knower (*mātṛ*), the establishment of the fruit is terminated in that very self-realization which constitutes the inner self (*pratyagātman*) of the knower; for a reflection is always terminated in its original object (*bimba*).
Thus, the meaning is that the knower, as well as the means of knowledge and so forth, are all established solely through experience (*anubhava*). || 297 ||
For in this case, it is cognition itself that is qualified by the knower and so forth.
The direct fruit of one's own self is logically established, having the inner self alone as its witness.

Anticipating the objection that the fruit of a means of knowledge (*mānaphala*) is self-luminous and thus not cognizable through experience, he says: "Since... In the world, it is precisely the apprehension of the object's own nature (*svarūpa*), when conjoined with the knower and other factors, that is conventionally designated as the "fruit. Therefore, it is logical that the fruit of the means of knowledge, as conditioned by these factors, is accessible to experience.
This is the meaning. The connection is with the phrase "direct comprehension. || 298 ||
"The form of the object of cognition exists in the intellect as the form of the perceived object."
The intellect, while residing solely within its cause, is capable of all worldly transactions. || 299 ||

[The author] establishes that the fruit of the means of knowledge (*māna*) is conditioned (*upahitatva*). [He says: "the internal" (*pratyak*), etc. First, the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) resides in the intellect (*buddhi*), because a reflection of consciousness is possible due to the clarity of that [intellect]. Thereafter, it is correctly apprehended as residing within the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which has transformed into the form of a jar or other object; otherwise, that [apprehension] would not be established. Therefore, it is called the fruit of the means of knowledge. The meaning is that [consciousness] is conditioned by that [fruit]. Alternatively, the object of cognition (*meyārtha*) is the jar and so forth.

Just as the form of an object becomes present to the intellect through the doors of the eyes and other senses, so too should it be understood that the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) likewise occurs; the meaning is that the fruit is conditioned by that [intellect]. Anticipating the objection that the intellect in which the reflection of consciousness appears might be independent, he says: "The intellect.
For an effect is not sufficient for empirical transaction if it were independent, because that would contradict its very nature as an effect. || 299 ||
1410 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
He who was questioned has transcended that which is to be measured by the outward-turned activity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This very thing is designated as "this" by means of perception alone. || 300 ||

Having stated the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "He who..."—which is to establish that the light of the Self, the accomplisher of all, is distinct from the body and so forth—the author explains the meaning of the two words [in the verse] starting with "He who was asked. That which is called "this" (ayam) refers to that which has been established through the direct realization of its own nature, transcending the status of being an object of knowledge for any cognition whose function is directed toward external objects; it is that very thing about which you asked, "Which one is it? (katamaḥ).
The meaning is that he has been asked this very thing. || 300 ||
The mantra declares it to be the "far-reaching," and the Śruti states that it is the Self manifest.
He awakened [the disciple] to the immeasurability of the Self, which is beyond all objects of cognition. || 309 ||

Regarding what was stated—that the inner self (pratīc) is not an object of perception and the other means of knowledge—he states the proof for that: "parā" [etc.]. He states the proof for its being perceptible through its own essential consciousness (svarūpacaitanya): "sākṣāt" [etc.]. He states the intended meaning of the Vedic mantra: "parāṅ" [etc. || 301 ||
Just as the purpose of a pot is perceived directly by the potter.
In the same way, it is apprehended by consciousness in the form of the internal self. || 302 ||

Raising the objection as to how the Self can be designated by the word "this" (ayam) even though its own nature as consciousness is directly perceived, the author establishes that point through an illustration. Regarding the verse beginning with "kumbha": the connection is with the phrase "by means of the cognition in the form of the Self. || 302 ||
It has as its sole means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) the perception arising from the universal form of "jar-ness."
The object "jar" [is established] because of the non-deviation between those two: the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge. || 303 ||

He explains the illustration with the word "ghaṭa" (pot). He states the reason for the pot being accessible through the aforementioned perception: "because it is non-deviant" (avyabhicāritvāt) || 303 ||
By means of that which consists of luminous consciousness, arising from the self and unique to the self.
The self, acting as its own agent, is eternally perceived by itself through direct perception.
He elaborates upon the illustrative application (*dāṣṭantika*). Regarding the word "Self" (*ātman*): the connection is with "by means of the Self through direct perception.

Anticipating the objection that if the Self were perceived by itself, it would follow that it possesses the status of agent, object, and instrument, he says: "It is not an agent" (*akārakaḥ*). || 304 ||
In the cognitions of the aspect of non-self, which do not deviate from one another.
• Only direct cognition itself is everywhere non-deviating. || 305 ||

Since the Self’s own nature as consciousness is established, its self-luminosity cannot be subject to deviation; yet, one might object that it is deviant because it does not appear during states such as deep sleep, just like the illusory snake in a rope. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The non-Self" (*anātma*). The meaning is that even in states such as deep sleep, the consciousness of one's own nature persists as the witness (*sādhaka*), and thus it is not deviant. This persistence of consciousness in those states will be explained in the passage beginning with "For there is no seer" (*na hi draṣṭuḥ*).
The word "hi" has the sense of indicating "māṇa. || 305 ||
1 ka. gha. nyasthi | [vol 3, page 298] 1 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1431
Since this is so, it is therefore taught by means of inward-cognizing awareness.
Therefore, it would be grasped by another, because the self lacks selfhood.

Having restated that the self’s own nature is established by consciousness (*caitanya*), he states the resulting conclusion with the words "Since... (*yataḥ*). The meaning is: because it is established by the inward-facing cognition (*pratyak-pratyaya*), which is the self's own nature-consciousness, this [self] is called "this" (*ayam*); that is, because of its fitness for such [immediate] apprehension. To those who, however, do not accept that the self’s own nature is established by consciousness and instead assert that it is an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*), he replies with the words "Other than that" (*tad-anyā*). Therefore, it is not an object of knowledge.
The remainder. || 306 ||
If it is perceived through the vision of the Self as devoid of dependence on anything else, [then it is truly seen].
The entire world would be the Self alone; nothing remains that is not known through wisdom.

Fearing that by one who denies that the intellect (*dhī*) is graspable as something distinct from the Self (*ātman*), the intellect and its objects would nonetheless be admitted as distinct from the Self, he says: "Excluded" (*apāsta*). If the entire world is seen in the form of the vision of the whole Self—such that it is independent of anything else for its existence (*sattā*) and manifestation (*sphūrti*)—then both the intellect and the object of cognition would be nothing but the Self; for once the Self is known, nothing remains unknown. Therefore, [ignorance...]
The meaning is that even though the intellect and other faculties exist during the state of dreaming, they do not exist after [the cessation of] cognition. || 307 ||
The proximity of a manifold object capable of being designated by the term "this."
The statement "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya) is for the purpose of delimiting that [Self], because of this. || 318 ||

He introduces the next phrase with "This [is]... (*ayam iti*). Since the word "this" would imply that the directly perceived object is its referent, there would be the undesirable consequence of it referring to multiple things such as a pot and so forth. Therefore, the qualification "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) is used to exclude those meanings from the referent of the word "this. Consequently, the literal meaning is that a pot or similar object is not what is denoted here by the word "this. || 308 ||
From this designation "consisting of consciousness," [the Self] is distinguished.
The self whose nature is light [is distinct] from the inert body, because of its nature as consciousness. || 309 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the exclusion of [the body as] the light of the self follows from the context, and since that [exclusion] is already obtained, what is the purpose of the qualification, he states its intended meaning: "Vijñāna... etc. He says that the body is insentient because it is composed of the elements, like a jar: "tasya" (of that). || 309 ||
By the term "consciousness" (vijñāna), it is precisely the intellect (buddhi) that is denoted here.
And that which is undifferentiated from the adjuncts of the intellect is called "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya). || 310 ||

By the word "anena" (by this), having taken for granted—as will be explained—that the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of "mostly," he states the meaning of the whole [compound] as "buddhi... (verse 310).
For this [object] is cognized because it is conjoined with the consciousness of the intellect (buddhi).
Therefore, it is composed of the knowledge of the Self, like the moon joined with Rāhu. || 311 ||

Anticipating the objection that the inner self (*pratyak*), being unattached and indifferent, cannot be "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) due to its lack of connection with the intellect (*buddhi*), he says: "By means of the intellect and consciousness," etc. For Rāhu is not perceived as an object of direct perception by his own nature; however, the moon and the sun are within the range of direct perception. Likewise, since this Self is perceived only through its connection with the intellect and so forth, the construction is: "Therefore, it consists of consciousness. In reality, however—
Even in the absence of a [real] connection, the conceptual cognition arises precisely from contact with that; thus, the meaning is "consisting of that. || 311 ||
1. Not so, because of proximity. (Ma. In proximity. 2. Ka. From that. 3. Kha. Is turned. [Vol.
3, page 299]
1432 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
"The connection with being the seer and so forth belongs to one who is at all times devoid of agency."
Therefore, because it is produced by the application of the intellect (*buddhi-yoga*), this [self] is called "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*).
He states another reason for its being composed of that [consciousness] in the verse beginning with *draṣṭṛtvāt* (492).
For it is the intellect alone that is the cause for the realization of the Self and the non-Self.
It accomplishes all purposes; it is like a lamp in the darkness. || 313 ||

[Objection: But surely the Self, like the intellect (*buddhi*), attains the status of a seer and so forth even when conjoined with the eyes and other organs; and thus, why is it distinguished by consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone, setting aside the eyes and the rest? To this, he says: "The Self. Just as a lamp, when darkness—the veil of objects—is present, becomes the cause for the apprehension of objects by way of removing that [veil], so too, because the intellect possesses primacy in grasping all objects—
The meaning is that the Self likewise deserves to be designated in that very same way. || 313 ||
For all objects of knowledge are entirely permeated by the light of consciousness.
Because one perceives it as "this is an illusion," the meaning of "illusion" is determined here.

Nevertheless, how can there be the application of the suffix *maya* [in the sense of "consisting of"] to the Self, which is eternally established, since it has not been proven that the Self is a modification of the intellect? To this, he says:

"vijñāna... (Vijñānamaya). The word "Self" is to be supplied as the subject of "knows" (*vijānāti*). The meaning of the suffix *maya* in this term is that the Self is similar to the intellect, resembling it, or having its form; such is the sense of the word. || 314 ||
To whatever extent it serves as a cause for that [cognition], this [object] is so [a cause] by virtue of being a single cause of that same kind.
Because it is considered non-distinct by way of having that single appearance as its path. (315)
Therefore, the Self is designated as "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya).
Because it is the witness of all intellectual modifications (buddhi-vṛtti) and because of its identity with that which is not the Self (anātman). || 316 ||

Fearing that this might not be so because a similarity between the non-inert Self and inert cognition is unestablished, he says: "To whatever extent" (*yāvān*). The meaning of the suffix *lyuṭ* here is "cognition" (*vijñāna*). Because this Self, by virtue of its own ignorance, resides within cognition and is considered "identical" (*samāna*) through the medium of its own reflection, it is therefore designated by the term "consisting of cognition" (*vijñānamaya*), even though in reality it is dissimilar. There is another reason for its being composed of that [cognition].

He says: "All. Not only is being composed of intellect (*buddhimayatva*) intended here, but rather being composed of everything (*sarvamayatva*); thus he says: "And because of identity" (*tādātmyāt*). || 315 || 316 ||
Therefore, the apprehension of all objects is like that of a lamp placed in front of one.
Pradhāna is the instrument; the intellect (buddhi) is merely its gateway, and everything else is subordinate to it. || 317 ||

Having established that the Self consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), he concludes what was stated in the passage beginning with "for the sake of awakening to the Self and the non-Self" with the words "sarvārtha...

(all objects). Anticipating the objection that other instruments would then be useless, he says "pradhānam" (the primary one), meaning that this is not so because they serve as gateways for the activity of the intellect (*buddhi*).
Therefore, the implication is that setting aside the ears and other organs, the Self is distinguished by the intellect alone. || 317 ||
But those of great intelligence have explained that the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).
There would be a contradiction with their own explanations, and there would be a connection to what is meaningless for them. || 318 ||
1. *kha* reads *kāraṃ*. 2. *ka* and *ga* read *vṛttasāṃ*. 3. *ga* reads *ātmanā* || 316 || 4. *ka* reads *haṇāttasmāṃ*. 5. *kha* reads *rārthama*. [Vol. 3, page 300] 3.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1433.

Bhartṛprapañca has stated that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the supreme Brahman, and that the individual soul (*jīva*), having that as its material cause, is "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*); thus, he raises the doubt that the suffix *mayaṭ* here has the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). To this, [the author] says: "They have explained... In passages such as "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) and "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), those very same [authorities] state that the suffix *mayaṭ* does not have the sense of a modification; for there, due to its co-occurrence with "mind," "consciousness" refers to the intellect (*buddhi*), and not to a modification of the Self.

Therefore, he states that for those who claim the suffix *mayaṭ* in this usage has the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*), there would be a contradiction with their own statement, by saying: "In his own commentary... Furthermore, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were a modification of the Supreme, then the transmigratory existence residing in it would extend into Him due to their identity; thus he says: "The calamity... The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate further defects. || 318 ||
And also because of the negation of all modifications whatsoever in the self.
"It is not born" is clearly established by relying on the statements of the Śruti. || 319 ||

Raising the objection that, even in your view, since the identity [of the self with Brahman] is no different [in both cases], why does the bondage residing in the individual soul (jīva) not extend to the Supreme?—he says, "And of the Self," etc., to show that in our view there is nothing faulty, because in reality the changeless pure consciousness is free from saṃsāra.
The two particles *ca* and *api* serve to include the Smṛti passage beginning with "It is neither born nor does it die. (319)
Furthermore, if the supreme self were subject to modification, it would follow that liberation is impossible.
It might be considered a modification [of the suffix], but here it is more appropriate to take it in the sense of "mostly" (prāyaḥ). || 320 ||

Having stated the contradiction with scripture and other authorities regarding the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Supreme (*para*), he states another defect: "anirmokṣa" (no liberation). The meaning is: if the individual soul were a modification of the Supreme, then liberation would consist in its returning to the cause; and since it is logically possible for that which has attained such a state to be produced again at the beginning of creation, the consequence would be the impossibility of liberation. Having concluded the refutation of the opponent's position, he states his own position: "mayaṭ" (the suffix *mayaṭ*). || 320 ||
Or, if it is maintained that the world is a transformation of that [Brahman] due to ignorance;
Just as a snake or the like [is imagined] upon a rope, so too is the defect [of the world] held to be [imagined]. (321)

Furthermore, having raised the alternative—whether the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of "modification" is used for the individual soul (*jīva*) by taking its modification from the Supreme [Brahman] as being merely due to nescience (*avidyā*), or whether it is real—one restates the first option and accepts it with boldness (prauḍhi), beginning with the words "If...". The word "or" (*vā*) indicates the aforementioned alternative. The word "world" (*jagat*) refers to the expansion of sentient beings. || 329 ||
In this sentence, "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya), the sense of "mostly" (prāya) is intended.
For it will be explained hereafter that the Self consists of earth and the other elements. || 322 ||

He refutes the second [position] by way of contradiction with the context, beginning with "vijñāna" (consciousness). The sense is that it is not logical for the Self to be a modification of earth and so forth, because its material nature (*bhautikatva*) has already been refuted. || 322 ||
An object that is everywhere doubted, except where it is certain.
It is to be well-ascertained either through practical application or through an absolutely certain logical inference. || 323 ||

He states [the following] regarding how another application is resorted to for the purpose of determining the meaning of the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*): "When there is doubt," and so forth.

Just as the sentence, "Having divided the *puroḍāśa* cake into four parts, he places it on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣadaṃ karoti*), is a single statement concerning the division into four of the *puroḍāśa* in general; so too is this [case].
180 [Vol. 3, page 301] 1434 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]

The meaning is as follows: just as in the case of the injunction "one divides the *āgneya* cake into four parts," where the connection with the purpose is determined by a specific reference to another branch (*śākhāntara*) stating that very fact, and thus it is restricted to the *āgneya* sacrificial cake alone; and just as in the case of "one places the smeared pebbles" (*aktāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*), where there is a doubt as to what they are smeared with, the resolution comes from the supplementary statement (*śeṣa*) "clarified butter is indeed light" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*); so it is here as well. Furthermore, if the Self were a modification (*vikāra*), liberation (*mokṣa*) would be impossible.

Alternatively, the determination of the meaning of the term *vijñānamaya* follows from such an uncontradicted principle. As it is stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*: "Or [the application is determined] by the purpose, because it is a part of the conceptual construction. For instance, in the case of the injunctions, "He cuts with the *sruva* ladle," "He cuts with the *svadhiti* knife," and "He cuts with the hand," since the *sruva* and the others are enjoined for all types of cutting, there would otherwise be no restriction; however, upon considering their functional capacities (*sāmarthya*), the *sruva*, *svadhiti*, and hand are applied respectively to liquids, meat, and solid substances.

Regarding the doubt as to whether there is a restriction among the various substances [to be offered], since no specific application (*viniyoga*) is indicated, the initial position is that there is no restriction. However, it is established that because application is for the purpose of performance, and because that application depends upon capacity (*sāmarthya*), the authority of the scripture is determined by conformity to that capacity. The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the absence of restriction. Thus, by virtue of the purpose, capacity, and suitability, each single implement such as the *sruva* ladle is restricted to each single substance such as the clarified butter (*dravya*).

The literal meaning of the words is that there is a restriction because, in a particular context, something is fit to be related [to another]. Likewise, here too, with the intention of establishing the distinction that non-self (anātman) is a modification of Brahman while the Self (ātman) is its very essence based on the authority of the scriptures, he says: "Or, by logic" (nyāyāt). || 323 ||
Desiring to cause [the mind] to emerge even from the senses such as the body, the Śruti says "in the vital breaths" (prāṇeṣu); fifteen vital breaths have been declared. (324)

Having explained the section consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), he states what is intended by the phrase "in the vital breaths" (*prāṇeṣu*). [He says] "from the body. Therein, he states the meaning of the portion concerning the source (*prakṛtibhāga*): "the vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*). || 324 ||
The locative case is employed here for the purpose of specifying a selection from among them.
Let it be understood that the object which persists through all the vital breaths is the Self. || 325 ||

Since it will be stated later that "of the mind, in the heart," [the author] mentions the number fifteen for the sake of the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*), namely: the ten organs of action (*karmendriya*) and the five vital airs (*vāyu*). Regarding the word "from them" (*tebhyaḥ*): it signifies selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), extraction (*niṣkarṣaḥ*), and differentiation (*vibhajanaḥ*). Filling out the required sense of the word consisting of both base and suffix, he says: "among the vital breaths" (*prāṇeṣu*). || 325 ||
That which shines as the inner self within the vital breaths, which are its own forms; |||
That alone is to be known as the Self among all those things which are not the Self.

Since the possibility of their being the Self has been raised, he states—beginning with the words "In the vital breaths" (prāṇeṣu)—why the Selfhood belongs to that which persists through them as a witness; for the meaning is that the possibility of the Selfhood of the instruments [the senses] is not like that of a lamp. || 326 ||
If it is argued that the intellect (dhī), which is of the same nature as the vital breath (prāṇa), is the self, that is not so.
For this reason, the Śruti has declared "in the heart" (hṛdi) in order to distinguish [the Self] from the intellect.
He takes up the word "in the heart" as a response to an objection, stating: "This is the view. || 327 ||
And by the word "heart" (hṛd), it is intellect alone that is denoted here, because [intellect] resides therein.
The self-nature that appears therein is the Self, which perceives the modifications of the intellect.
Having stated "in the heart" (*hṛdi*), he anticipates the objection: "If it were a different entity, even though it appears [there], how could it be distinct from the intellect?

and thus says: "By the word 'heart' (*hṛcchabdena*). For that [word] is well-known to refer to a specific piece of flesh, according to the Vedic text: "The heart resembles the interior of a lotus bud.

Anticipating the objection as to how [the Self] can be an object of cognition, he says "by metaphor" (upacārāt). He states "because of its being located therein" (tātsthyāt), completing the required sense of the locative case by saying "in its own meaning" (svārthe) || 328 ||
Because of the specification of the "heart" as the locus, it might be suspected that the self resides within the intellect.
Therefore, for the purpose of withdrawing from these mental modifications, the intermediate state is taught. || 329 ||
He states the intended meaning of the other qualification: "In the heart" (hṛdi). || 329 ||
It is beyond the deity, the object, the vital breath, the intellect, and its modifications.
Let that Self which shines as light be perceived as the innermost reality.

Having observed that the word "self" (ātman) is used in many senses, he asks out of doubt; regarding what kind of determination was stated for him in response, [the author] says: "The deity," etc. Virāj, the jar, and so forth are words whose objects are deities;
when asked, "Which one is the self?", that which is distinct from the intellect and the rest must be known as self-luminous, and it is seen as such through its own inwardness.
This is the meaning. || 330 ||
The selfless [stream of consciousness], possessing the nature of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, flows on in succession.
The object, beginning with the intellect and ending with the sense-objects, is perceived as if it were witnessed by that [Self]. (331)

If the Self were distinct from cognition and the rest, then a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) must be admitted; otherwise, its distinctness would not be established. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says "grāhaka" (the grasper), taking that [counter-correlate] to be merely imagined. The meaning is: since that [imagined grasper] is non-self and insentient, it requires a witness (sākṣin) in whom it is imagined to be established; therefore, the witness is other than that. Anticipating the objection that the non-self is finite because it possesses birth and so forth, he says "pravāha" (stream).

"Indeed, it is so. For there is no prior temporal limit devoid of any one of the individual manifestations such as the perceiver; therefore, the meaning is that it is beginningless by way of its continuous flow (pravāha). || 331 ||
Having been, they have ceased to be; and having not been, they come to be through this unreal nature.
That which is unknown and whose vision is never lost is called the Self, the Light. || 332 ||

Anticipating the objection that if birth and so forth are perceived even in the Self, how can it be the witness of the intellect and other faculties, [the author] speaks—relying on the principle beginning with "The Self is not [born], because there is no scriptural statement" (*nātmāśruteḥ*)—with the words "Having been... (*bhūtvā*). Here, in the state of ignorance (*avidyā*), because the Self appears to possess birth and destruction through forms imagined as being other than its true nature, that conscious Self whose essence is knowledge that neither rises nor sets is self-luminous and the establisher of the intellect and other faculties; thus, the wise one [knows this].
The meaning is "desired by the wise. || 332 ||
The proof of the coming and going [of states] regarding intellect and the rest is established because they depend upon that [substratum].
Behold that as the manifest Self within the self by means of inward vision alone.

He concludes the definitive conclusion with the words "āgamena" (by scripture). The instrumental case here denotes a state of being; by it, the agency of seeing and so forth—which would otherwise be attributed to one who sees through the act of saying "see"—is negated. || 333 ||
Since the fluctuations of the intellect follow after external objects, therefore...
By means of the qualification "internal," those that are external are excluded. || 334 ||
1 ka. kha. *ajāto* | 2 ka. ga. *vartante* | [Vol.
3, page 303] 1436 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Chapter]— [The text continues with the commentary on the fourth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.]

Having summarized and concluded the meaning of the passage for the sake of resolving the question, and desiring to explain the section beginning with "jyotiḥ" (light), the author states the reason for the exclusion of the internal modifications (*vṛtti*)—which were previously qualified as being external—in the phrase "parāk" (outward). To the question, "How does this much [description] effect their exclusion from the inward-facing Self (*pratīc*)," he replies:
"Because of their outwardness" (*parāktvataḥ*). The word "of the inward-facing Self" (*pratīcaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. || 334 ||
In that case, it would follow that the self is the cause of cognition and so forth.
Because the effect is observed to be internal [to it], the cause is seen everywhere.
He states what is excluded by the qualification "light" (jyotis): "the cause. Here, the word "everywhere" (sarvatra) is to be connected [to this]. || 339 ||
And those who subsist on the teachings of Kaṇāda maintain that insentience belongs to the self.
To prevent such misconceptions, it is designated as "light" (jyotis). || 336 ||

Since the intellect and so forth are born, it might be questioned how the Self—which is insentient—could be their cause; anticipating this doubt, he says, "And insentience," and introduces the qualification with the words, "Of these. || 336 ||
Or rather, [the verse beginning] with "yo'yam" [is intended] for the sake of the reality of the Self as previously described.
The connection with the previously mentioned light is designated as "light. || 337 ||

Now, one might object: "Since dullness (*jāḍya*) has already been excluded from the Self by the author while explaining the determination [of the Self] earlier, how can this qualification of 'light' (*jyotis*) be meaningful?
Anticipating this doubt, he states its further purport with the words beginning "This which... and so forth. This refers to the sentence under discussion.

The meaning is that the connection of the self whose nature has been determined with the light mentioned in the context—specifically in the passage beginning with "by this very light"—must be stated; therefore, it serves as a qualifier. || 337 ||
For the grasping of the intellect and so forth is called the ignorance of the self.
Pure consciousness, which is eternally manifest, is taught to be the light.

As for the claim that the qualification [“Self”] is intended to negate the idea that the material cause of the intellect and so forth is a non-conscious (jaḍa) entity, the author, while refuting this, states the true nature of the cause of the intellect and so forth: “the material cause” (upādāna). The word “for” (hi) is used to indicate that, because the intellect and so forth as well as ignorance (avidyā) share the common characteristic of being non-conscious, it is appropriate for them to stand in the relation of material cause and its effect. In this regard, he provides the consensus of the learned as proof, saying: “it is thus said.”
Thus, he states the capacity of the word "light" (jyotis) applied to the Self to exclude these [other meanings] with the words: "Once... (sakṛt). || 338 ||
In reality, one's own ignorance has been entirely destroyed.
This luminous form is radiant, whose true essence consists solely of the inward-facing [consciousness].

If it is argued that the inner self (pratyagātman), which is known as "I am ignorant," possesses the nature of the light as taught [in scripture], the author replies to that with the words "by the actual state of things" (vastuvṛttena). Fearing that a distinction might be suspected when it is said "the form of the Self," he says "luminous" (bhāsvat). || 339 ||
It is designated as light, consciousness, the inward-facing self.
That which always shines forth in its own nature during waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; || 340 ||
For among the intellect and other faculties, which exist for the sake of another and are subject to appearance and disappearance, [it is not perceived].
That which shines by its own form and is stable is called the self-object (svārtha). || 341 ||
1. Thus he says. 2. *Gha*: "the difference of the manifestation.

Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1437.
The word "light" (jyotis) refers to that which establishes the coming and going of the intellect and other faculties.
This [Self] is indeed self-originated, precisely because of its nature as the Self.

Fearing that the word "light" (*jyotis*) does not refer to the Self because it is conventionally established in other senses, he says "light" (*jyotiḥ*) by means of the principle [of the sūtra] "because light is seen. The intention is that, due to the context supported by words such as "Person" (*puruṣa*), this term is withdrawn from the previously mentioned light and restricted to the Self alone. He states another argument for the Self being light: "for its own sake" (*svārtham*).
The meaning is that that which shines eternally, independent of birth and destruction, throughout all three states and in all inert things—that is the Light (jyotis).

The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that because it is the Self, the light of the Self has its own purpose (svārthatva), whereas the non-Self, by virtue of being non-Self, has the purpose of another (parārthatva). To the objection—"How can the Self have its own purpose when we see it existing for the sake of sons and others?"—he says: "Itself" (svayam). Itself...

The construction is as follows: that which shines by its own nature, having been established as "light" (jyotis), is the stable and self-referential [subject]. The sense is that being for the sake of another belongs to the qualified [entity] and not to anything else. He establishes the aforementioned self-luminosity [with the words]: "of this" (asya). || 340 ||
By this very light as described, the entire world [is illuminated].
It undergoes the sixfold modification by means of that which is changeless and luminous.
Having established the first position, he supports the second with the words "by this. || 343 ||
Even though intellect and the like are insentient, they are regarded as if they possessed sentience.
The aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect, together with the vital airs. || 344 ||

He states the proof for the claim that "everything is illumined by the light of the Self" with the words, "Even though insentient. He clarifies the meaning of terms such as "intellect" (buddhi) and so forth with the word "body" (deha). The connection with the preceding [verse] is: "By this very light, it is seen. || 244 ||
Just as the one sun illumines this entire world.
"The Field-knower likewise illumines the entire Field"—such is the statement of the Smṛti. (345)
He cites the word of the Blessed One as proof for the self-luminous [ātman] being the illuminator of all things: "Just as... (349).
Just as a sapphire reflects its own shadow in all the water without exception.
A coin dropped for the purpose of testing would likewise produce a sound exactly as such. || 346 ||
Everything from the intellect (buddhi) down to the body has ignorance as its cause with respect to the inner self (pratyak).
It itself illuminates that which is eternal and insentient by nature.

He clarifies its quality of illuminating everything by means of an illustration: "the shadow of itself. He states the reason why the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties require an illuminator: "insentient" (*jaḍa*). || 346 || 347 ||
"Even among subtle things such as the intellect and so forth, that which is called the most subtle,"
The eternal cause of the intellect and other faculties is called the ignorance of the Self (ātma-avidyā). || 348 ||
1 gha. ṇātprākṛ | [vol 3, page 305] 1438 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]

It has been stated that the meaning of "insentience" (jaḍatva) is having ignorance of the inner self (pratyagajñāna) as its cause. When it is asked what that ignorance of the inner self is, he describes its nature as that which causes distraction (vikṣepaka): "In the intellect and so forth" (buddhyādiṣu). He qualifies it with "intellect and so forth" (buddhyādi) in order to exclude the light of the Self (ātmajyotis). Its eternity is mentioned in the phrase "it is eternal" (tannityam) for the purpose of establishing its status as the cause. || 348 ||
Even for the Self, whose nature is immutable, there exists that which causes attachment.
And they know that which is to be sublated by the knowledge arising from such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi). || 349 ||

He states the form that conceals that very [Self] with the word "api" (even). He provides the proof for the impossibility of the meaningfulness of scriptural knowledge regarding that which possesses both forms with the words "tattvam" (That Thou Art). || 349 ||
And for what reason does the Self possess the nature of being a witness as well as that of being a cause?
Even when all effects have perished, that which remains as the seed [is the cause]. || 350 ||

He states that the impossibility of the self being a witness and so forth also implies its existence: "That for which [it is] the cause. He further states that the impossibility of the re-emergence of effects that were dissolved at the time of cosmic dissolution also necessitates its postulation: "All... The connection is: "that which is the seed of arising, subsistence, and destruction. (350)
Then, kindled by that light of the Self, it remains eternally established.
And from the perspective of witnessing, one does not know [the nature] of arising, persistence, and destruction. || 351 ||

It precludes its independence by stating "that is its self. He says "no" because, being established through direct experience, it does not depend on any other means of proof; the ellipsis is that it shines forth from the witness, that is, from one's own experience. || 351 ||
The immutable Self alone is the witness here, by virtue of being the cause of the appearance of its own delusion.
[The witness-consciousness] is established without deliberation because it relies upon the experience of darkness (ignorance).
As for how it is said that the state of being a witness is due to its being a real entity (*vastu*), he says: "It is immutable" (*kūṭastha*).

Alternatively, raising the objection that since a transforming entity (*pariṇāmin*) cannot be a witness, there would be no need for ignorance (*ajñāna*) in that case, he says: "It is immutable. Here...

The phrase "in the case of the transforming intellect (buddhi) and so forth" means precisely that. He states the reason for its being the witness (*sākṣitva*) in the words "by its own delusion" (*svamoha*). Anticipating the objection that since delusion is a real entity (*vastu*), even that which is produced by it cannot be such [i.e., not a witness], he says "unexamined" (*avicārita*). To the question of how that which is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) can be unexamined, he replies with "experience" (*anubhava*). || 392 ||
In a case without witnesses, one does not proceed; it cannot be established by any means whatsoever.
Likewise, for one whose consciousness is immutable, this is not accepted at all. (353)

It is from experience alone that the establishment of darkness is proven. Regarding the phrase "without a witness": in the case of darkness, which does not require a witness, one does not say "I do not know [it]," for there is no such manifestation of it; the meaning is that it is not through a means of knowledge (*māna*) that such a manifestation occurs, because a means of knowledge cannot establish its own negation. Then, raising the objection that the Self is the witness of the knowledge of the Veda and thus, just as it is a witness to that by its very nature, it should be so in other cases as well, he says:
1 kha. *raṇam* | 2 dha. *’ttistadā* | 3 gha. *’tvāttatkṛ* | [vol 3, page 306] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1439.

"So be it. Just as darkness cannot be established in the absence of a witness (*sākṣin*), so too this darkness is all the more unestablished in the witness who is of the nature of changeless consciousness and independent of darkness.
This is because [darkness] lacks the capacity to establish itself and because any other establishing agent is excluded.
And because there exists that which sublates [ignorance], consciousness possesses the nature of a witness with respect to darkness.
The sense is that its capacity to establish both itself and others has been stated. || 393 ||
The self possesses both the causality of sovereignty and the state of being a witness.
Because it is connected with this [scripture] for the purpose of teaching, for the purpose of action, for the purpose of meaning, and for the purpose of testimony. || 354 ||

He concludes that being a witness and so forth are products of ignorance (*avidyā*) with the words "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*). For the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not dependent [on anything else]; it is either innate or non-innate, and whatever is non-innate is a product of ignorance, like silver [superimposed on mother-of-pearl]. As for those who maintain that sovereignty is not superimposed, they simply fail to reflect upon the meaning of the *Vārttika*, which states that sovereignty and causality and so forth [are superimpositions]. || 354 ||
Therefore, ignorance of the Self is always like a reflection in the inward-facing consciousness.
In this context, the causality of the self and so forth is accepted as the motivating factor.

He restates one’s own ignorance as that which sustains the status of being a witness and so forth: "The Self," etc. The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is the Self’s state of non-attachment and so on. "In this world" (iha) indicates the emergence of effects and the like. || 395 ||
From the inner self (pratyagātman), which is the limit of the ignorance that veils the innermost consciousness, [arises] that which possesses the appearance of consciousness.
Therefore, the establishment of everything from the intellect (buddhi) down to the objects of perception must depend upon the Witness (sākṣin).

Having stated that the state of being a witness exists as long as ignorance persists, he concludes by stating that from this, the establishment of all cognitions and so forth follows: "Caitanya... etc.

That which possesses the reflection of consciousness (caitanya-ābhāsa) is the inner Self (pratyak), and within that is the Witness; therefore, the meaning is that the establishment of the intellect and so forth proceeds from that inner Self.
The intellect's appearance as consciousness arises from its connection with its own cause.
Consequently, pride arises toward this [body], even among the great. (357)

If everything is accomplished depending on the light of the Self (*ātma-jyotis*), then—given that there is no distinction in its relationship [to all beings]—one might ask why the cognition of the Self arises first in the intellect (*buddhi*) alone of all beings. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By its own cause," etc. Because of the connection with the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya-ābhāsa*) in ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the cause of the intellect, the state of being a reflection of consciousness arises in that [intellect] immediately and without interval; therefore, the cognition of the Self occurs in it first. For it has been said: "I..."
Thus, this is the first superimposition (adhyāsa); therein, even the conviction of the learned (vidvān) serves as a means—this is the meaning. || 357 ||
And because it follows immediately upon its cause, as well as by virtue of its own transparent nature.
This cognition, possessing a reflection of consciousness, arises first. || 358 ||
He explains the commentary beginning with "In regard to the stated matter, the intellect... and so forth, as follows: "By the cause," etc. (358).
Therefore, the conceit of a self always exists within the intellect of all living beings.
It arises here for all beings, even for those who know everything. || 359 ||

He establishes the error regarding its being a reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) by means of the following proof: "Therefore," etc. Regarding such a conceit, there is universal non-discrepancy—[variant *gha*: "from this perception"; variant *ga*: "everything arises"].
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of illumination. Anticipating the objection that such a conceit belongs to the ignorant and not to the wise, he says: "api" (even).
Then the reflection of consciousness appears in the mind due to its being the immediate cause for the intellect.
And thus, through its connection with the mind, [consciousness] arises within the sense organs.
In response to the doubt, "How then can there be the notion of a self (ātma-buddhi) regarding the mind? he says: "Consciousness" (cid). The reason for this is given as: "intellect" (buddhi).

To the question, "How is that notion [of self] applied to the sense organs? he replies: "mind" (manaḥ). Thus, the meaning is that the notion of "I" arises by means of the reflection of consciousness [in the mind]. || 360 ||
Due to the connection with the instrument of the mind, this [consciousness] arises even in the body.
In this way, the Self causes the entire effect, together with its cause, to appear.
He establishes that misconception regarding the body with the words "by means of the mind and the instruments.

The meaning is that because of the connection of this Self with the mind and the instruments, there arises the notion of it [the Self] within the gross body due to the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). He concludes what has been stated with the word "evam" (thus). || 361 ||
It exists as a gradation of subtlety, extending up to the limit of objects.
From that, the notion of self-conceit arises inevitably in men. (362)

In this regard, the reason is given: "of subtlety. This means by way of the cause consisting in the degrees of subtlety (taratama) belonging to that subtlety which resides in the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, ending with the objects; therefore, [it refers] to the aforementioned sequence among the intellect and the rest. || 362 ||
And by that [knowledge] which says, "The eternal among the non-eternal," the Sun as well as the Supreme [is known].
Regarding this, there are indeed numerous scriptural citations such as, "The sun does not shine there. (363)

He cites the *Kaṭha Śruti* as authority for the fact that the light of the Self (*ātma-jyotis*) illuminates everything, beginning with the word "eternal" (*nitya*). The meaning is this: among those things that perish, this [Self] is imperishable;

and among the conscious beings (*cetana*), such as Brahmā and others who are themselves conscious, it is this very one who is the conscious principle. Just as the power to burn in water and other substances that lack fire is caused by fire, so too the capacity to cause consciousness in others is due solely to the causal factor of consciousness (caitanya). In that same context, by which the sun...

He recites the mantra beginning with "patiḥ tejasā eddhaḥ" (the Lord kindled by splendor). The connection with the subsequent passage is: "By which [means] one who does not know the Veda does not perceive that Great One. On that very point, he cites another scriptural text: "Not there... Here, the locative case in "tatra" (there) refers to the object; it establishes that the Brahman under discussion is the light of lights. Regarding the fact that the light of the Self is the illuminator of all, there is the Smṛti text beginning with "prakāśayati" (it illuminates).
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that it has been shown right at the beginning. || 363 ||
When this light within the self has thus awakened, through the destruction of darkness,
the self is called "Puruṣa" because it is the true nature of everything. || 364 ||

Having explained the word *jyotis* (light), he states the meaning of the word *puruṣa*: "In the Self," which means by the aforementioned scriptural passages (*śruti*), traditional texts (*smṛti*), and logical reasoning (*nyāya*). || 364 ||
"For when ignorance of the Self is completely destroyed, there is indeed no entity born from it."
A form distinct from the original form can be conceived by someone, somewhere.

Anticipating the objection that even though ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, the world is not destroyed and therefore the Person is not complete, he says: "The Self...
When the garland and the cognition are both annihilated, that [cognition] produced from it does not arise from another garland.
For form is indeed manifested from primordial matter (ādi) and so forth, just as it is from the nature of the Self (ātman). || 366 ||
Neither in the effect, nor in the cause, nor in their absence, nor from anything else.
Because its true nature consists solely of the inward-facing [consciousness], even a minute form is possible.
Then, he clarifies this by means of that illustration: "The garland," etc. The connection [of the words] is "other than the nature of the Self.
He states the reason why not even an atom of anything else in the form of an effect and so forth is possible: "the inner self," etc. || 366 || 367 ||
Because it remains as the mere inner self (pratyagātman), free from both exclusion and inclusion.
Because of its fullness, the Person (puruṣa) is declared to be the one light-essence itself. || 368 ||
He concludes the meaning of the word "puruṣa" with the words "avyāvṛtta" (unrestricted). The connection is: "[it is] such a light.

The reason for its being the *puruṣa* is given as "consisting solely of the inward-facing [consciousness]. Even though the light has the aforementioned nature, he states what that implies for the Self:
"the Self. || 368 ||
Moreover, even though the sun and other luminaries exist, they are like a body because they exist for the sake of another;
yet, in the absence of their own light, they are not even capable of being perceived as existing. (369)

Having explained the passage beginning with "He who [thinks] 'this... and so forth, he restates the favor of the light of the Self (*ātmajyotis*) in order to introduce the passage beginning with "Being the same... (*sa samānaḥ san*):
"Even in its existence" (*sadbhāve’pi*). Even though the sun and other luminaries exist during the waking state, because they are insentient (*jāḍyāt*), they lack the nature of a sentient light;
therefore, even while existing, they are not capable of illuminating at a distance—indeed, the gross, insentient body cannot maintain its own existence in the absence of a light distinct from itself.

Just as the sun and other luminaries likewise lose their manifestation in the absence of the light of their own worshipper, so too must a supreme light that bestows that [manifestation] upon it be admitted; this is the meaning. || 369 ||
If it is argued that the activity of the body and so forth arises from causes such as insentient matter (jaḍa) and the like;
This [world] would become as if without witnesses, like a dance in the darkness. || 370 ||

He states another reason for this: "of the body, etc. The meaning is that in the absence of non-inert light, there would be the consequence of non-establishment because there would be no means of proof for the activity of the body and so forth, which is impelled by the sun and other sources; therefore, non-inert light must be admitted. || 370 ||
Therefore, by means of the light of its own self-interest, the world perceives the nature of existence and non-existence.
Because one does not attain that [liberation] without him, nor even the mere possibility of attaining it. || 371 ||

He states the established conclusion: "svārtha" (one's own purpose). Therefore, he clarifies the meaning of the word: "tam" (that). The meaning is: one's own purpose, which is the light of the Self. || 371 ||
"That which is called the heart"—thus also is the teaching of the Āgamas.
All the worldly activities of living beings arise from the conceit of identifying with the inner self (pratyagātman).

1442 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]: Regarding the fact that the aforementioned light illumines everything without exception, he cites another scriptural passage, beginning with "That which... Both the heart and the mind follow this principle of being the illuminator of all.
Furthermore, since it is impossible for insentient instruments to achieve the status of being sentient, it must be accepted that they are always pervaded by the conscious Self;
thus he says, "The living being," etc. For it has been said: "Indeed, the conventional usage of all living beings is based on self-identification [with the body]. (372)

Because it is illumined by consciousness (saṃvit), it is "nothing but consciousness" (saṃvinmātra); thus I have previously stated that the Aitareyaka passage [describes] the light of the Self (ātmajyotis) and the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) which is the cause of all identification.
By means of the illustration of the perfect slayer, [the nature] of the reality of the self is shown. || 373 ||
How is it that there is the conceit of "I" everywhere, even in the intellect and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "All...

The connection is as follows: previously, by means of demonstrating specific examples, he has correctly understood that the reflection of consciousness within the reality of the Self is the cause of the conceit (abhimāna) everywhere. || 373 ||
Even though this supreme reality possesses such greatness as has been described, it is as follows:
Nevertheless, that [state] cannot be demonstrated while one is awake. || 374 ||

Having restated what has been said above, he introduces the subsequent sentence with the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*). For although this supreme reality is established by Śruti and Smṛti as being endowed with a majesty explained through its quality of illuminating all things, nevertheless, it cannot be shown in the waking state.
The meaning is that the Śruti introduces its own dream. || 374 ||
[Cognition arises] from the conjunction of the self, the intellect, the mind, the eye, the object, and light.
Therefore, that light cannot be shown while one is in the waking state.
When one's own intellect and other faculties have ceased, there remains only the latent impression (vāsanā).
It is capable of revealing light; therefore, it is called "the common" (samāna). || 376 ||

In order to show why [the Self] cannot be pointed out while one is awake—since all worldly activity is dependent upon it—he says: "The Self. Anticipating the objection that it likewise cannot be pointed out even in a dream due to the same logic, he says: "From that. This connects with the fourth quarter [of the verse]. The subsequent portion is intended to describe the light of the Self by extracting it from the intellect and other faculties, which are like the muñja grass and the iṣīkā stalk in a dream.
The meaning is "a statement. || 375 || 376 ||
And how can that which has such a nature [exist] within the stages born of ignorance regarding it?
This conventional usage regarding this internal [self] arises because speech is similar [to it]. (377)

He states another connection for the preceding sentence: "And how? The meaning is that the subsequent portion of the text is intended to explain how the eternally liberated Self possesses the state of being a transmigrator through ignorance (avidyā). || 377 ||
Because of the lights, because of the body, because of the subtle body (liṅga), and because of that which transcends them.
In response to his provocation, he spoke these words solely out of purity. || 378 ||
* Here, the application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is to be considered.

3, page 310] 3 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1443

He states another connection for that very same [topic]: "From the lights," etc. The meaning is that the subsequent text is intended to establish the purity of the Self, which is distinct from the body and so forth; [the term] *liṅga* refers to the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*). || 378 ||
The self-luminous [nature] is established through inference from everything beginning with the body and ending with the intellect.
That which has been extracted and described here is the *samāna* [vital breath], due to its own delusion.
Having first stated the word and its meaning, he takes up the identical term: "himself" (*svayam*). This means "by means of inference from the signs of worldly activity.
Here, the phrase "in this [world]" refers either to the immediately preceding text or to the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsārāvasthā*). He states the reason for their identity:
"due to his own delusion" (*svamohataḥ*). || 379 ||
The one Self, being identical, [appears as many] through its own self-knowledge and the products arising therefrom.
Because the reality of the self is characterized by ignorance and false cognition regarding its own nature. (380)

Having supplied the required meaning of the word "samāna" (common), he shows it: "samāna" means being one, the connection being that it moves along. He states the reason for the identity of the Self with its own ignorance and its effects: "ajñāna... (through ignorance). || 380 ||
When the question arises as to "by what [is it offered]?", it is said: "by the heart."
Because of the Vedic text "in the heart" (sadhīḥ) and because of the context here [of the word] "in the heart" (hṛdi). || 381 ||
Anticipating the objection—“How is this to be explained, since the term *samāna* (identical) is dependent [on another] and has not been explicitly stated?”—he says: “By what?

The words “it is said” are to be supplied as the subject, referring to the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*). He cites the Mādhyandina recension of the Śruti as the authority for the identity of the self with the intellect: “With the intellect” (*sadhīḥ*). He states the proximity [of this passage] to that very point: “In this regard” (*atra*). || 381 ||
That which is established without investigation is the cause of the intellect and so forth.
Reflected in the single consciousness of the immutable Self, it is real due to its own faultlessness.
This very one, who has the knowledge of his own self as his limit, is called the supreme cause.
"He is the witness, the cognizer, the seed of the universe, and the inner controller," so it is said in the Śruti.
When the identity of the Self with the intellect is being stated in both the scriptures and the commentary, why is that identity said to be due to one's own ignorance (*avidyā*)?
To this, he says: "Unexamined," etc. That indefinable ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the cause of the intellect and so forth, has the quality of *sattva* as its predominant factor;

when it is permeated by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) due to its own inherent clarity, it becomes an adjunct (*upādhi*). This very [ignorance] is the Supreme Person (*paraḥ puruṣaḥ*), who is heard of in the scriptures in the form of the causal agent and so forth.

Therefore, their identity is denied; the meaning is that the statement regarding its being the cause and so forth was made for the sake of establishing [the nature of] ignorance (avidyā). "Due to its own defect" means, as it were, because of the aforementioned obscuration. He qualifies [the subject] with the word "conscious" (cetana) in order to refute [the notion of] being the agent of seeing.
By saying "the cause," he first states the status of the Supreme as the efficient cause (nimitta), and then declares it to be the material cause (upādāna) by saying "the world. || 382 || 383 ||
Of that which abides as the effect of the intellect and so forth, whose nature is like a chariot in a dream or a castle in the air.
The status of being a cause and so forth for everything [is established] solely through the path of its semblance.
If it is argued that ignorance is its cause and thus nothing else need be expected, he says "buddhyādi" (intellect, etc. to address this doubt.
[Vol. 3, page 311]
1444 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

"In that [ignorance] which has its effect, [meaning] in that which persists through the practice of identifying with it. In this regard, he promises to address the requirement for its manifestation: "Its manifestation," etc. (384).
Through the form of the reflection of consciousness, the identity with the immutable (kūṭastha) is maintained.
Because the cause is connected with its own effects through that [very] non-cognition. || 385 ||

Anticipating the question "How so?", he establishes the dependence of causality upon that [reflection] in the verse beginning with "caitanya" (consciousness). The meaning is that the causality of ignorance (*ajñāna*) is accepted on the basis of its identity with the immutable (*kūṭastha*) Self through the medium of its reflection (*ābhāsa*), because it is impossible for it to be so [a cause] by itself. He demonstrates that the conscious Self also requires a reflection for its connection with its own effects, such as the intellect (*buddhi*), by way of ignorance, in the phrase "and with its own effects. For the Supreme...
The meaning is that there is a connection between the Knower and the intellect and so forth born of ignorance, either because they are unawakened or because he is connected to them. || 385 ||
The connection between cause and effect occurs through the remainder of the reflection.
But between those two, this is the connection with the remaining [aspect] of the response.

The mutual connection between the effect, the cause, and the Self has been stated; to the question of what kind of connection that [Self] has with those two, he says: "of the inner witness" (*pratīcaḥ*).

Just as the effect and the cause do not exist separately, such is its connection with them. To the objection that the connection of those two is likewise [non-existent], he says: "but of those two..."—just as the Self exists separately.

The meaning is that, in that way, they are not connected with anything else. The first word *tu* (but) serves as a qualifier, while the second *tu* has the sense of restriction and is to be connected with the phrase "with remainder" (*sāvaśeṣeṇa*). || 386 ||
There is no transcendence of its nature as a self and so forth, because it exists on the ground of cause and effect.
Therefore, neither the universal nor the particular can be the self of the body.
In that case, he states [the reason] why there is no difference between those two and the Self: "Because it is the Self" (nātmattvāt).

Having established that because there is no difference from the cause, the Self is the persisting cause and thus possesses the nature of a universal (sāmānya), and because there is no difference from the effect, it possesses the nature of a particular (viśeṣa) as that which is excluded from it—anticipating this objection, he says "no," and so forth. The word "tataḥ" (therefore/from that) is connected with the word "kārtsnyāt" (in its entirety).
But whatever establishment there is of the non-self, all that occurs through non-distinction [from it].
Therefore, because it arises from dullness and dependence, that establishment is declared to be false.
Anticipating the objection that, although the non-dual Self lacks a dual nature, it might possess one insofar as it is associated with duality, he says:
"But of the non-Self... The word *avyatirekataḥ* (due to non-separation) is the division [of the compound]. The words "from the Consciousness" (*citaḥ sakāśāt*) are to be supplied. Of that...

Since self-establishment is possible [for the Self], why then is there non-difference from the Self? To this he says: "Because of insentience" (jāḍyāt). How then can there be a separate manifestation? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therefore, that [manifestation]" (sātaḥ). The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is the impossibility of a separate manifestation due to insentience. || 388 ||
Furthermore, how could there be equality between the self and entities such as cognition?
Due to their separation, there is no experience of the two, like that of Varāha and the serpent.

3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 1445.

Thinking that it is incorrect to claim the identity of the self with its cause and effect on the grounds of similarity, because there is a contradiction between those two and the self due to their respective natures of insentience and sentience, he says: "Why? He provides the answer with the commentary beginning with "Like a horse and a buffalo," etc., stating: "Through discrimination. (389)
That which is considered the identity between those two is like that of the rope and the serpent.
Ignorance of the self alone is the connection; therefore, it is held to belong to the self. || 390 ||

He states the falsity of that which was described as being equal [to the Self] with the words "That which... He states the consequence of its falsity with the words "The Self..."; the word "by the non-Self" is to be supplied. || 390 ||
Of that ultimate reality, the self-entity, which is by nature devoid of agency.
The conjunction [of the self with objects] would be merely imagined through ignorance, like the blackness perceived in the sky. (391)
He establishes that their conjunction is imagined by means of this illustration: "akāraka" (verse 391).
For when the darkness of the inner self is dispelled by the light of the consciousness of the immutable Self, [the world] arises from that.
Error arises from the co-referentiality [of the word] with external objects. || 392 ||
Even though that [self] is such [in its true nature], how is the identity of the inner witness with the intellect and so forth imagined? To this he says: "Kūṭastha" (the immutable).

When ignorance regarding the Self is the cause, there arises the delusion of identity through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with its effects, such as "I am a man"; thus, the falsity of that identity is established. This is the meaning. || 392 ||
Because light, being subject to modification, comes into contact with blue, red, and other colors.
The transformation into blue and other colors is appropriate for a modification, but this [transformation] is not [of that nature]. (393)

Anticipating the objection that—just as the light of the sun and other luminaries undergo modifications such as assuming the form of blue and so on when in contact with those objects—the self-luminosity (ātma-jyotis) must likewise be subject to modification when in contact with the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties due to the non-distinction of their nature as light—he says: "Of the modifying [objects]" (vikāriṇaḥ). || 393 ||
For it is held that the transformation of delusion and the like consists in the appearance of consciousness.
It is not tenable that even for that [entity], there is the attainment of another transformation. || 394 ||
How can it be said that the Self, which is non-different from the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, is immutable? To this he replies: "For transformation...

Since the transformation of ignorance and the intellect is always illumined by the consciousness of the Self, it is illogical for that [Self] to undergo a particular modification; for it is impossible for the Witness to become an object witnessed. Therefore, the meaning is that He is indeed eternally unchanging (kūṭastha). || 394 ||
If that were the case, the states of being happy, being miserable, and being a witness would be untenable.
Because it is followed by pleasure and so forth, its exclusion [from those states] is extremely difficult to establish. || 395 ||
[The opponent] raises the objection: "Just as the sun, though it illuminates form, is itself possessed of form, so too the witness of transformation must itself be subject to transformation.

[The author replies: "He who is happy," etc. This is the reason for his wretched state. "In that way," etc.: when there is suffering and so forth, because of their commingling with it, the distinction between the Self and suffering and the like is difficult to discern due to the subtlety of the Self; yet, if they were one, that distinction could not exist because of contradiction. As for the example, it is not contradictory because it is a matter of direct perception.
And there is no proof here for its being subject to modification; therefore, the meaning is that it is indeed changeless. || 399 ||

If there were no modification, one would not be a sufferer; for how can there be witnesshood in that which is subject to change?
Because I am the witness of thousands of mental transformations, I am changeless.

Regarding the question, "Even if it is changeless (*avikriyatva*), why does it not possess suffering and so forth? he says: "No. He states the fault in being subject to modification (*vikriyāvattva*).
Relying on such scriptural passages as "The Witness is consciousness" (*sākṣī cetā*), he states the resulting conclusion: "The modification of the intellect" (*dhīvikriyā*) [is the cause]. || 396 ||
In this way, even for one who undergoes transformation, it is like the cognition of the immutable Self.
This transformation is not logical; it is not even accepted by worldly people.

Fearing that the self might be active like a mother, he says: "It undergoes transformation. To the objection—"Since it is a substance, like water, it follows by inference that the mother undergoes transformation; therefore, how can there be a deficiency in the probandum (sādhyavaikalya)?"—he replies: "Of the worldly [mother]. For there is no transformation of one who remains exactly as they were, because that would contradict their state of being; nor is there transformation of one who becomes something else entirely, because that would lead to instability. Thus, even the transformation of milk and the like is [only] authoritative...
The meaning is that it does not become a suffix (ṇika). || 397 ||
The intellect, along with the collection of the mind and the senses, exists within the singular path of the reflection of consciousness.
Therefore, by the power of ignorance, the Self has attained the state of being the essence of all things.

He concludes the discussion on their equality with the verse beginning "dhīsvānta" (intellect and mind). The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is that, in reality, the lack of equality [between them] is untenable. || 398 ||
Or it is the common causal self (kāraṇātman), wherein there is the withdrawal of all things.
For the causal self, having undergone transformation, attains the state of being the effect-self. || 399 ||
1.3 Having stated the meaning of the word *samāna* as explained in the Bhāṣya, he states another meaning: "The intermediate cause... [is what is meant by] *samāna*.

In order to exclude [other possibilities], he specifies the causal self (kāraṇātman) belonging to the fifth [chapter] with the words "wherein" (yatra). As for the remainder of the passage beginning with "both worlds," how is its application justified here? For it is not possible for the root cause, being all-pervasive, to move about. To this he replies: "the causal self. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the identity of effect and cause is well-established. || 399 ||
Because it arises solely from the cause of being produced by the cognition of dependence alone.
The true nature of reality is not perceived either in the effect or in the cause. || 400 ||

Anticipating the objection that the inner self (pratīc) would be impure if it possessed both natures, he says: "In dependence" (*apekṣā*). Knowledge of a cause depends upon its effect, and knowledge of one thing depends upon another; since ignorance is the single nature of that [duality] alone, and because [the world] has arisen from that as its cause, the reality of the effect and so forth is not established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). Therefore, the purity of the Self, which is the substratum for that conceptualization, is not contradicted—this is the meaning. || 400 ||
Therefore, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence does not arise from positive and negative concomitance alone.
Because the determination of the reality of things arises from the sentence itself as a means of valid cognition. 401.

If it is argued that even the pure reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is known only through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and not from a sentence, and therefore reflection upon that [sentence] is useless—the author says "no," beginning with the word *anvaya*. The meaning of the words [of the objection] is this: since effects and the like are unreal, and because the Self is non-dual (*advaya*), there can be no application of positive or negative concomitance; therefore, [the knowledge of the Self] arises from the meaning of the words [of the scripture]. If so, since a sentence likewise does not function in that same manner [as perception], the cognition of the sentence-meaning cannot arise from it; to this he replies with the word *vastu*. [The sentence functions] regarding the imagined...
