Therefore, the meaning of the word is the possibility of the cognition of a real entity (*vastu*). [The opponent asks: Why could that cognition not be of the imagined [universal] such as "concomitance" (*anvaya*) and so forth?

To this he replies: "By means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*). The sense is that even though there is no difference in their being imagined, the sentence possesses the capacity to cognize a real entity by virtue of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas the other [the conceptual construction] lacks that capacity because it is not a valid means of knowledge. || 401 ||
Therefore, because all conceptual constructions have ignorance alone as their cause.
Even though it is free from conceptual construction, the supreme [consciousness] spontaneously attained the status of being an object.

He concludes the meaning of the verse "being the same" with the word *ataḥ*. The meaning of the word *ataḥ* is that [the Self] is not inherently connected to being an object of conceptual constructions such as causality and so forth. The phrase should be read as "even though it is non-conceptual" (*avikalpo 'pi*). || 402 ||
They are indeed equal, sharing the same world, characterized by that which has been attained and that which is yet to be attained.
In due order, the Lord, possessed of ignorance, constantly wanders.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "both" as follows: "equal. He says that for the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*), there is in reality no difference from the Supreme. "The Lord. || 403 ||
It is characterized by the continuity of the appropriation and abandonment of the body, sense-faculties, and so forth.
This [consciousness] moves about through the convergence of hundreds of continuities, not by itself.
He elaborates upon the transition [of the self] with the words "the body" (deha). || 404 ||
For this [universe], its sole abode is the effect, because its sole cause is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa).
Since transmigratory existence does not arise from this [source], the Self does not possess transmigratory existence by its own nature.

He supports the statement "not by itself" with the verse beginning "kārya... (The effect...). The meaning is that the state of being a transmigrator belonging to the intellect and so forth is superimposed upon the inner self (pratīc) through the medium of its own reflection; therefore, it is not a transmigrator by its own nature. || 405 ||
Although the Self does not perform actions, it is dependent upon causes such as the intellect and the vital breath.
Through ignorance, the reflection of consciousness appears as the phenomenal world of saṃsāra. || 406 ||

The effect is to be conceived within its cause; however, how can the state of being a transmigrator (saṃsāritva), which resides in the intellect and so forth, be superimposed upon that non-dual Self through the medium of its reflection? To this, he says: "akārya... etc. Although the Self is in reality non-dual, it stands—in its own ignorance—within the intellect and so forth, which are the causes of transmigration; thus, by means of its own reflection, it experiences the appearance of being a transmigrator. This is the meaning. || 406 ||
Because there is no arising from itself, and because there is arising from the non-understanding of that [reality].
Therefore, that which consists of the form of action and its agent is denoted by the verbal root (śruti). || 107 ||
The falsity of the nature of action and agent resides in the inner self.
By the statement beginning with "he meditates" (dhyāyati), for the sake of knowing the direct immutability [of the Self]. (408)
He takes up the passage beginning with "as it were meditating" (dhyāyatīva). Regarding the phrase "impossibility," he states the utility of saying that [the self] is false: "pratyag... (407, 408).
1 kha. gha. *saṃcaraṇam* | [vol 3, page 315] 1448 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]—
Though it is immutable, it appears as if it were meditating; likewise, it appears as if it were moving about.
Because the Self is the witness of the agent who performs meditation and so forth, the Self does not possess the effects such as meditation.

He explains the syllables contained in the introductory statement: "as if meditating" (dhyāyatīva). To the question, "Why should it not be that [the Self] actually possesses meditation and so forth?", he replies: "Because of its immutability" (kauṭasthyāt). He states another reason for that very point: "Meditation and so forth... (dhyānādi) || 409 ||
Meditation would be the defining characteristic of all mental modifications without exception.
And "lelāyana" is the characteristic mark of all actions whatsoever.

[Objection: Let it be that meditation (*dhyāna*) is conditioned (*aupādhika*) in the Self; nevertheless, seeing and so forth are natural (*svābhāvika*), because in the fifth [chapter] the nature of seeing and so forth is taught [to belong to the Self]. To this, he says: "Without remainder" (*niḥśeṣa*). The meaning is that it was stated there that the nature [of the Self] consists solely of pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*).

Anticipating the objection that while movement is conditioned (*aupādhika*), speech and other functions are unconditioned (*anaupādhika*) because of scriptural statements such as "Speech [is the first]," he says: "The flickering" (*lelāyanam*). The sense is that it is not intended there that speech and the rest possess the inherent nature (*svābhāvya*) of those respective actions; rather, they are designated as speech and so forth through metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) by virtue of being the witness (*sākṣin*) of those actions. || 410 ||
The meditator, the meditation, and likewise the object of meditation—this triad has only one's own self as its witness.
The instrument, the action, and the agent do not exist apart from this witness of the journey and so forth. || 411 ||

Nevertheless, suspecting that the state of being a meditator and so forth exists in reality, he says: "The meditator. By the word "and" (ca), the phrase "witnessed solely by one's own self" is drawn forward. Because it is the witness of that [meditation], there is neutrality; this is the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ). || 411 ||
The relationship between the knower and the agent is like that between knowledge and action.
Likewise, there is the connection with the immutable witness, as well as with the cognizer and the agent. (112)

Anticipating the objection that the meditator and so forth cannot be objects of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) because they lack a relationship with it—and likewise that self-established existence is not proven—he says:
"Of the knower" (*boddhuḥ*). The meaning is that those two, being insentient, are known by the witness through a relationship superimposed [upon them] by that witness. || 412 ||
Because the self-effulgent Self, which is the immutable, singular consciousness, is the innermost essence of all.
Therefore, this [Self] has no connection [with objects], because it is the cause of the interiority of all things. || 413 ||

Anticipating the objection that if the journey and so forth are related to the witness (sākṣin), then he too would possess that [relation] through it—and that this cannot be the reason for his being imagined—the author says: "of all. Although the immutable, non-dual conscious self (cidātman) is the inner self (pratyagātman) of all, why is it that he has no relation [to them]? To this he replies: "of all," because a relation must reside in two things and is therefore impossible in one alone.
The state of being. || 413 ||
The inconsistency of witnesses arises from their testimony being based on the same origin or source.
But delusion is not at all dependent on the occurrence of a cause for an external reflection. || 414 ||

To the question of how there can be witnesshood (*sākṣitva*) in the absence of a real relationship, he says: "In one," etc. There exists a state of abiding in one—the immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthacaitanya*)—both for the witness of ignorance and so forth, and for the reflection (*ābhāsa*); and within that [consciousness] resides the Witness. Therefore, because they share a single locus, their connection is logical. (Variant readings: *...disvabhāvasyo*; *...rvasya pra*; *...dityarthaḥ || 413 ||*)
The meaning is "as a witness. He refutes the connection by another method with the words "But not... The cause of that is the reflection of consciousness produced by ignorance.

The meaning is that consciousness does not possess the status of a witness (sākṣitva) with respect to its own essential nature; rather, it possesses that status through the persistence of the reflection of consciousness upon ignorance and its products. || 414 ||
That which is the reflection of consciousness arising solely from the immutable Self is the devourer of delusion.
Because it conforms to its own material cause, it has no connection with anything else. || 415 ||

Furthermore, since even the appearance (ābhāsa) is in reality not connected with anything, how much less so is consciousness (caitanya)? Therefore, he says "kūṭastha" etc., [meaning] that it is the witness precisely because of its connection arising from ignorance (avidyā). This is because the self-substance (ātmavastu), which is its own material cause, is immutable (kūṭastha) and unattached (asaṅga); [the witness-nature] follows from that very fact. || 419 ||
Because it is the cause of the connection with the effects of ignorance based on the reflection of consciousness.
"Even though the supreme Self is beyond [all things], it is perceived as if it were meditating, appearing as its own internal reflection. (416)

Having stated that the state of being a meditator and so forth does not exist in reality within the Witness (sākṣin), he restates the meaning of the scriptural passage concerning meditation (*dhyāyati-vākya*): "The reflection of consciousness" (*cidābhāsa*), etc.

The meaning is that, due to its connection with the objective world (*sākṣya*)—the phenomenal expansion which is the effect of ignorance residing in that [Witness]—the Supreme Self also appears to be perceived as if meditating and as if moving about, as if qualified by its own reflection. || 416 ||
We indeed acknowledge that [the movement] arising from a single measure, such as the flickering of meditation and so forth, is [a form of] pratyāhāra.
It is designated as such, as if for the sake of practicing that which is false. || 417 ||
He states the meaning of the word *iva*: "It is perceived directly" (pratyakṣeti). || 417 ||
Just as one might, out of ignorance, falsely perceive a cloud-vehicle upon the moon.
In that same way, the Witness perceives the cognition that possesses the notions of action and its factors.
He clarifies that falsity, indicated by the word *iva*, through an illustration: "abhrety" etc. The word should be split as "ajñānāt" (due to ignorance). || 418 ||
Because of the reliance on a delusive [cognition], the relationship between the property and the substratum appears otherwise.
Just as one might conceive that the sky is blue even without touching it, so too [should one understand this]. || 419 ||
In a matter that is to be realized through one's own direct experience—devoid of action, devoid of agency, and devoid of fruit—
That dull-witted person conceives of an entity as possessing action and its factors, just like [the concepts of] action and its factors themselves. 420.

Thinking that while motion is possible for the moon even by its own nature, it is not so for the one facing westward (the observer), he states another illustration: "Dharma... He states the application to the subject of the illustration: "In the same way... 419 || 420 ||
Therefore, transmigratory existence is merely a conceptual construction within the inner self.
If there should be doubt regarding the matter thus stated, let it be examined through the vision of the inner self. || 421 ||
He concludes the meaning of the word "as if" (iva) with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). The meaning of that word [therefore] is that, in reality, contact with transmigratory existence is impossible.
In this regard, he provides the experience of the wise as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), stating: "It has been said. || 421 ||

1450 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Because it culminates in the Self alone, it is seen as not touching upon the objects of the non-Self.
The cognition of a self and the connection with a self are not observed in that which is non-self.

[Objection: But surely the inward-looking vision (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*) also perceives transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) within the inner self (*pratīc*), since there is the experience "I am happy" or "I am miserable. Therefore, how can there be non-transmigratoriness therein? To this, he says: "The Self" (*ātma*). [Objection: But even while apprehending the mere Self, that vision necessarily apprehends the happiness and so forth residing in it, just as the vision of a jar necessarily apprehends the color situated therein. To this, he says: "Relation to the Self" (*ātmasambandha*).

For an intellect that does not touch itself alone cannot possibly touch another object, as that would contradict its very nature as an intellect; nor can liberation (kaivalya) exist while the self is joined with suffering and so forth.
Furthermore, the perception of a jar takes on only a qualified [object] as its domain; such is the sense of the disparity [between the two cases]. || 422 ||
Others, however, formulate the connection with the statement of the similar instance in a different manner.
The eyes and other faculties of the wise are entirely distinct in form.
Likewise, various perfected lights are gathered together in mutual conjunction.
Even for those things that possess distinct characteristics, there exists a commonality when they exist in a combined state.

Having stated the explanation of the passage beginning with "Being the same" (*sa samānaḥ san*) as given in the *Bhāṣya*, [the author], while asserting that the interpretation of Bhartṛprapañca is to be accepted, first introduces the relevant context. In the verse beginning with "sasamāna," when it is asked how there can be a difference in the relationship, he states that opponent’s prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to explain that. In the verse beginning with "dhīmataḥ," [it is said that] the eleven organs are sustained by the lights such as the sun.

The meaning is that although they are established as being distinct from one another, they are nevertheless accepted as acting in concert. To the question of how those that are distinct can act in concert, he says: "of those that are distinct.

According to the manner stated, even though the eyes and other organs are mutually distinct, they possess a commonality by virtue of residing in a single body; therefore, it is in their combined state that they perform purposeful action.
And even though there is similarity of characteristics, it is the cognition itself that is distinct.
The property called "being an enjoyer" would be like the seeing of the eye. || 425 ||

Raising the objection as to how there can be a determination of the state of being a recipient of results for those very [atoms] which, despite having identical characteristics, act collectively to produce purposeful activity, he says: "Even though they have identical characteristics. For it has been stated that even when there is identity of characteristics, the distinct property of the intellect alone—namely, its being the experiencer—belongs to this [Self]. (429)
This distinction from cognition and the other [mental factors] would not be tenable if this were so.
But that which has arisen dependently is said to be "identical. || 426 ||
In that regard, he states the meaning of the commentary on the concluding statement—"How is distinctness established?"—by saying "buddhyādi" (intellect, etc.).

He states their own established conclusion by saying "upapannastu" (but it is established). This sentence is intended to refute the doubt that the Self is non-distinct from the intellect and other faculties.
This is the meaning. || 426 ||
Being the same, it pervades both worlds designated as waking and dreaming.
This [self] wanders through this birth and the next, yet not of its own accord.
He explains the words of that [verse]: "Being the same" (*samānaḥ san*). The particle *eva* is connected immediately after the word *san*.
If this Self were not distinct from the intellect and the other faculties, then— [Vol.

If this Self were not distinct from the intellect and the other faculties, then—
Because there is no distinction between the elements alone in both worlds. || 428 ||
In both cases, there would have to be simultaneous enjoyment, but it is not observed.
Therefore, let it be observed that light is something other than that, because [the latter] exists only when that [light] exists. || 429 ||

How is the distinction of the self from the intellect and so forth established? To this he says: "The intellect and so forth... And it has been said: "If this [self] were not distinct, then because there would be no difference between the two worlds in terms of being a mere aggregate of elements, both—"

"Even where enjoyment might arise, it does not occur. From this, the conclusion is drawn by the commentary: "There exists something distinct, because [enjoyment] occurs when that exists and does not occur when that is absent. He states the result of this as "tadbhāve" (when that exists). The meaning is that since enjoyment occurs when the distinct light of the Self exists, and otherwise does not, there is a distinct light of the Self. This is because [the light] is like that of a lamp and so forth.
It does not wander through those two worlds in succession; therefore, it is said to be distinct from them. || 428 || 429 ||
Because he goes to the same worlds as others by means of successive turns.
Therefore, let it be understood that the self is distinct from the intellect and the other [faculties]. || 430 ||
In the case of a difference [between the two], he states another reason: "by way of succession" (paryāyeṇa). || 430 ||
And there is no suspicion whatsoever here regarding the enjoyment of deities.
At the times of death and sleep, they depart just as they came.

Having refuted the agency of the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties as enjoyers, and having raised the doubt that the deities who preside over the instruments might be the enjoyers within this body, the author refutes this by means of the very passage under discussion. Regarding the word "deity" (*devatā*): in the view that those deities are the enjoyers, there would be an absence of an enjoyer during states such as dreaming; for at that time, they abandon their internal (psychophysical) limitations and abide in their celestial (cosmic) nature. Therefore, the meaning is that the enjoyer must be someone other than them. || 431 ||
Furthermore, it is not right for lords to enjoy that which is inferior.
It should be understood that the light which is the Self is indeed distinct from the deities. || 432 ||
In that very context, he states another reason: "Of the lords," etc. (432).
And due to the sovereign power of the deities, their enjoyment would be simultaneous.
And since that [external object] does not exist, let the self-luminosity of the Self be recognized as something distinct from it. || 433 ||

He states another argument: "Because of omnipresence" (*vibhutvāt*). Even though the self (*ātman*) is omnipresent, the regulation of experience (*bhoga-vyavasthā*) occurs by virtue of auxiliary factors;

this is not the case for deities (*devatā*) because of their independence. Furthermore, if [the self] were subject to the power of karma (*karma-pāravaśya*), there would be a contradiction with the [established] principles of reality (*tattva-vyāghāta*). Nor is the Lord (*īśvara*) an experiencer (*bhoktṛ*); the deities are cited as examples of those who are experiencers, and it is not necessarily the case that being an experiencer entails subjection to karma. Nevertheless, due to the consequence of there being multiple experiencers, [this cannot apply] to this body.
The intended meaning is that it possesses the quality of being an enjoyer. || 433 ||

Since the enjoyer who consists of pure consciousness for its own sake is directly perceived, there can be no suspicion—lacking any basis in valid cognition—that it lacks the nature of an enjoyer, for such a suspicion would contradict that perception. (434)

The objection that "the aggregate of the instruments (karaṇas) or the aggregate of the deities (devatās) possesses the status of the enjoyer here, because there is no evidence for an entity beyond them" does not hold; for [the text] says, "Thou art That."

Or likewise, the manifesting properties consist of the nature of vibration.
These do not belong to this Self by its own nature; rather, because it is their witness, they are illusory.
Having stated the explanation offered by others for the passage concerning *sa-samāna*, he states the intended purport of the passage concerning *dhyāyati* (he meditates) as follows:

"By means of the manifestor... etc. The meaning is that seeing, speaking, and so forth—characterized by the movement of meditation (*dhyāna*)—do not exist in the Self by its own nature, because [the Self], as their witness, is absolutely distinct from them; therefore, the cycle of transmigratory existence consisting of meditation and so forth, which appears in it, is indeed false. || 435 ||
The Self is imagined as if it were moving about in the field of the buddhi, and as if it were meditating.
Just as trees [appear to a person] who has entered a boat, so too is the delusion of saṃsāra. || 436 ||

He explains the words of the verse "dhyāyati" [he meditates]. Regarding the phrase "situated in the intellect," he states the meaning of the word *iva* (as if) along with an illustration: "of one situated on a boat.

Just as to a person on a boat, trees standing on the bank appear to be moving when the boat is moving, so too, for one situated in the intellect, there is the perception of movement and so forth due to the movement of that [intellect]; however, the delusion regarding the Self is such that in reality there is no movement and so forth. This is the meaning. ||436||
Just as a person standing on the bank does not perceive the movement of a boat, so too one situated on the boat does not perceive its motion.
Because he was occupied solely with the boat, even though his gaze was fixed on the single point [of the shore], he did not see it.

But surely, one standing on a boat, even while perceiving the movement of the trees on the riverbank, does not perceive it in oneself; how then can there be a perception of the saṃsāra residing in that [body] by the Self, which is the witness of the intellect? To this he says: "As one standing on the bank," etc. Just as a man standing on the bank observes the movement of the boat, so too one who is on the boat—even with eyes fixed upon the boat—does not perceive the movement as belonging to the boat itself, but rather [perceives] the movement of that [boat].
The meaning is that, having superposed that [movement] upon one's own self through reasoning, one determines, "I am going. || 437 ||
Just so, when the intellect is unified, the movement of the mind occurs within the sphere of meditation.
The witness does not perceive anything as separate from its own self, like one standing on a boat [does not see the boat as other than itself]. 438.

Having restated the illustration, he states the application to the subject: "Just as" (*yathā*). The meaning is that when there is the practice of identifying with the witness of the intellect (*buddhisākṣī*), one does not perceive meditation and so forth—which reside in that intellect—as being distinct from the Self, but rather as residing in the Self alone, existing solely within the intellect. In this regard, he recalls the aforementioned illustration: "Like one on a boat" (*nausthavat*). Just as a person standing on a boat does not perceive the motion [of the shore] as separate from himself, but only as belonging to those on the boat...
"He sees it in that same way"—this is the meaning. || 428 ||
Because of the fear of blame from people standing on the shore, he maintained a steadfastness regarding the tremors of meditation and other such matters.
Therefore, one who is free from internal meditation and the like perceives the intellect as the witness. || 139 ||
Then, fearing that the Self might likewise possess its own meditation and other such qualities, he says: "As a bystander.

Just as a man standing on the bank, observing a boat or similar object in a river which possesses the attributes of motion and so forth, does not himself possess those attributes; so too the Witness, while perceiving the intellect which possesses the attributes of being a meditator and so forth, is in reality not possessed of those attributes. || 439 ||

Because the Self is the witness of all modifications of the intellect without exception.

He concludes by summarizing the acceptable points of the opposing position: "Without remainder," etc. (443).
Because the state of being witnessed is not fully understood, there arises the conceptualization of a meaning contrary to that [witnessing].

How much less, then, can this [sensory] cognition [be considered direct perception], since it shares the same basis as the intellect?
The wandering of the world and so forth belongs to that [world] because He is its witness, but not by Himself. || 445 ||

He raises an objection in order to introduce the verse beginning with "sahī" (for he...). He asks, "From what? By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "wandering and so forth," activities such as meditating, seeing, speaking, and so on are included. || 449 ||
For that [reason] is intended as a statement of the cause of fear for the purpose of establishing what has been asserted.

Through the knowledge of the inner self, whatever state one conceives of, [that very state one attains].

In the witnessing of the mass of latent impressions arising from causes such as dharmas and so forth.

Ignorance of the Self alone is death; therefore, even for that which is eternal, there is death [from it].

He states the conclusion: since death cannot be apprehended through a means of knowledge, the presentation of its forms is intended to make it known. Thus, "the forms... || 498 ||
Therefore, the self transcends those states which are based on the waking condition.
Since these [elements] are the substrata for the fruits of action, he is therefore pure and eternal. || 459 ||

He concludes the subject matter under discussion with the words "it transcends. The word *ataḥ* has the sense of "because. Since it transcends those [states] during the entry into sleep from the waking state, the meaning is that the innermost essence (*pratyag-dhātu*) is immutable (*kūṭastha*) and stainless (*nirmala*). || 459 ||
1. Completed.
[Vol. 3, page 323] 1456 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya—]
It is established that the Self exists, and it is pure, eternal, and one.
In order to establish this very point, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is set forth. || 460 ||

One might raise the objection: "If the Self is already established as having the nature of being immutable (*kūṭastha*) and so forth, what is the purpose of the subsequent text? Anticipating this, he says: "It exists.

Having formulated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), its refutation serves to strengthen the aforementioned meaning; for according to the maxim that "only when purified by the prima facie view [is the conclusion firm]," the subsequent text is meaningful. || 460 ||
But surely, apart from cognition, no witness of cognition is apprehended?
"He who was previously established as the Self by means of the [Vedic] statement, 'identical with the intellect' (dhiyā samānaḥ)" || 461 ||
He explains the prima facie position [pūrvapakṣa]: "Now, however... (nanu). || 461 ||
There is no means of valid cognition for us regarding its existence, since it is neither perceived nor inferred.
If there were even the slightest [existence], its establishment would consequently be without any means of valid cognition.

He states the reason for this: "Because of its non-existence. Having stated that there are only two means of valid cognition—namely, perception and inference—and that the knowledge which does not contradict the meaning of the words of an omniscient being is a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he further states that it is of two kinds: perception and inference.
Since the view of a self (*ātman*) favored by others is not established by either of these two, the meaning is that such a self does not exist. || 462 ||
Just as there is another cognition at that time which is distinct from the preceding cognition.
In this way, cognition is not accessible through perception alone, nor is the self an object of perception.

In this regard, he clarifies the absence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): "As before," etc. The meaning is that just as within a single continuum (*saṃtāna*), another cognition simultaneous with the preceding cognition is not perceived apart from that [preceding] cognition, so too the self, being distinct from the intellect (*dhī*), is not perceived through direct perception. || 463 ||
Nor can its existence even be ascertained through inference.
"When the substratum exists, this consideration of its attributes is possible. (464)

Anticipating the objection that its existence is established by the inference—"Whatever is an object of perception is an object of perception distinct from itself, just as a pot; and this intellect (dhī) is an object of perception"—the author says "na ca" (not so), intending to point out the deficiency of the probandum (sādhyavaikalya). The word "api" (also) implies "just as [established] through direct perception. He states "satī" (being existent) to show that if the Self is not established as distinct from the means of knowledge, then its purity and other such qualities are cast far away. || 464 ||
As for that which [occurs] between the suggested and the suggester, it is due to the cause of an error regarding their similarity.
Because the distinction between them is not fully understood, that [error] is logical, and it is indeed accepted. || 465 ||

Anticipating the objection that there is a difference between the two—the manifested and the manifestor—based on the inference that "those which are the manifested and the manifestor are mutually distinct, like a jar and light; and the intellect and the Self are the manifested and the manifestor," he says: "The manifested... etc. The point is this: although there is a cognition of non-difference between a jar and light when they are in contact, this is due to a delusion of identity caused by their similarity and the failure to perceive their distinction; in reality, however, there is a difference. The same applies to the intellect and the Self. This is what has been stated.
The meaning is that an example has been provided there within a sentence containing a *samāna* [particle]. || 469 ||
Since, previously, there was a distinction between the suggested and the suggester due to their relationship.
Therefore, let there be as much distinction between those two as you wish, since one is apprehended by another means of valid cognition.
1 gha. *pakṣe*vi | 2 ka. ga. *dṛśyaṃ bhrā* | [vol 3, page 324] 1457

The reason for this is stated as "vyaṅgya" (that which is manifested). This means: on account of that connection, that is to say, due to their mutual interpenetration. "Another means of knowledge" refers to perception that contradicts the cognition of identity [between the two]. || 466 ||
However, because of their similarity, this notion that "this is non-different" is considered an error.
Because its distinction is perceived through valid cognition prior to its connection with that [property]. (467)

Then, as to how there can be a perception of non-difference between the jar and the light when they are in contact, he says: "But due to similarity" (*sādṛśyatastu*). Regarding their being an illusion, he states the very reason mentioned previously: "Because of the difference between them" (*tadbhedasya*). This means: because of their conjunction, that is, the mutual contact of the jar and the light.

Since the difference between them is perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*), the [perceived] non-difference is an illusion; for there is no inference for you to establish a difference between the intellect and the self, and thus that [non-difference] alone is an illusion.
The meaning is that difference, however, is the ultimate reality. || 467 ||
This very intellect, whose nature is consciousness, manifests itself in the form of the subject.
In that way, that very same [consciousness], though one, manifests in two ways through the form of objects. (468)
Anticipating the objection as to how difference can be considered illusory when inference is established as valid, [the author], considering that [inference] would contradict direct perception, says:
"Cognition" (dhīḥ) || 468 ||
Therefore, the inner self is not perceived apart from the intellect.
That which is called the witness of the intellect (dhīsākṣī) is known either through direct perception or through inference. || 469 ||
He states the result of the twofold division of *buddhi* itself: "Not from this," etc. (469).
And as for the example previously adduced for the sake of establishing difference:
The distinction between the witness and the object witnessed is like that between the manifest and the manifester. || 470 ||

Having accepted the distinction between the manifested (vyaṅgya) and the manifestor (vyañjaka), he previously stated "it is not so" regarding the intellect (buddhi) and the self (ātman). Now, in order to state that even between those two such a distinction does not exist—and thus to point out the deficiency of the probandum (sādhyavaikalya)—he repeats what was said: "And that which... The construction is as follows: just as there is a distinction between a jar and light, so too is there one between the intellect and the self; this is the example previously adduced for the purpose of establishing that distinction. || 470 ||
Precisely because you have accepted it, I too have accepted it.
In the ultimate sense, even there, no distinction whatsoever exists.

He shows the position of a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*) regarding that illustration by the word "tvad" (your). The example is for the sake of that [point]. Anticipating the objection that because difference is perceived in the illustration, it is not a mere concession, he says "paramārthena" (in the ultimate sense). The word "api" (also) is used to indicate that the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) is likewise being illustrated. || 471 ||
For the jar consists of luminosity and lasts for only a moment.
And because it also arises there through a continuous succession of mutual [dependence]. || 472 ||

He states the conclusion regarding the absence of actual difference between the jar and the light: "It appears... He asks: how can the jar, even when conjoined with light, have that [light] as its nature? To this he replies: "For a moment... Since the jar together with the light exists for only a single moment... [kha. ...states the obstruction; gha. ...by the absence of...; ga. ...and ours; ka. kha.]
It is so.
183 [vol 3, page 325]

1458 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]: The meaning is that because the difference between those two is difficult to perceive, there is indeed non-difference. If it is argued that a pot illuminated by light exists for only a moment, and yet there is a cognition of its permanence therein, he replies: "And they are distinct. The word "therein" (*tatra*) expresses an illustrative example. Therefore, the probandum is incomplete.
"Thus," is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 472 ||
Alternatively, the ultimate reality would be a mere consciousness or an object.
The appearance of a jar is momentary, yet it is constructed with numerous qualifiers.

Having refuted inference by means of the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*), he adopts the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*). He says "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); he states the distinction from the [previous] established position (*siddhānta*) with the word "momentary" (*kṣaṇa*). He qualifies it as "for the sake of conventional usage" (*vyavahārārtha*) with the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*). To the question, "How then is there conventional usage regarding cloth and so forth?", he replies with the word "assumed" (*kḷpta*). || 473 ||
And this being the case, your illustrative example is not tenable.
Because everything consists of nothing but cognition, and because anything other than that is impossible. (474)

He states the refutation of the aforementioned inference regarding this position: "If it is thus," and so forth. This means: when consciousness alone is the reality (*vijñānamātre tattve sati*). The underlying sense is that [the reason] would be devoid of a substratum (*āśrayahīnatvāt*). He clarifies the logical inconsistency: "of everything," and so forth. Alternatively, he supports the statement that whatever is merely a cognition of an object—such as a jar and the like—is indeed graspable by cognition: "that too," and so forth. (Verse 474)
Of that very same cognition-only, there is the characteristic of the grasped and the grasper.
Others, having postulated "impurity" (mala), explain that its absence is purity (śuddhi).
Anticipating the objection that the aforementioned inference contradicts perception because the distinction between the grasped and the grasper is perceived, he says:

"Of that" means its natural state; that is to say, the fact that it consists of mere consciousness (*vijñānamātratva*), which is by nature fragile and subject to dissolution. "The other" refers to the statement of the Vijñānavādins themselves. || 479 ||
For even the self of the Buddha is [misconceived] by those whose cognitions are subject to error.
It appears as if possessing a distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the consciousness itself. || 476 ||

The state of being the grasped and the grasper is merely imagined; it is not the established doctrine of the Buddhists, for they indeed maintain that this state exists as real within a single cognition.

Anticipating this objection, he cites a statement by Kīrti regarding its imagined nature: "Even [the Blessed One]... [and so forth]. The remainder of the sense is: therefore, in reality, there is no distinction between the grasped and the grasper. || 476 ||
Others declare that even for that pure form, there is peace.
Since form is likewise covered by impurity, it too is merely imagined.

Having stated the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*), he demonstrates the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). [The phrase] "of that too" refers to the reason for this. The meaning of "like a stain" is as follows:
in the absence of an object, how can cognition be known? This is because of the etymological derivation: "that by which an object is known. [As it is said:
"By which intellect the form of another is concealed by its own form..."
Based on entities that appear as distinct, [the mind] manifests as a single object.
By that [concealment], they are themselves concealed from their diversity; through conventional reality, they appear as distinct.
1. gha. ‘Knowledge here’ | [Vol. 3, page 326] 1 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1459

If it is argued that there is no contradiction with knowledge on account of the objects constructed by conventional reality—which are like the stains of passion and so forth—according to the maxim "they appear as if they were non-existent," then let that very [conventional] knowledge itself be what is constructed; for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), since every verbal object is conceptual in nature. As it has been said:
"It is fashioned by conceptual construction arising from beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)."
"The meaning of a word is to be known as threefold: that which is based on existence, non-existence, or both. || 477 ||
Furthermore, because there is an absence of corroboration regarding the existence of a self and such, the [truth] of the sentence is not accepted.
Its status as a means of valid cognition is not like that of perception, nor is it apprehended through perception. || 478 ||

It has been stated that in all three positions, there is no self (ātman) distinct [from the body], due to a lack of evidence. Now, having raised the objection that the self is established by scripture (*āgama*) and so forth, he says: "The self, etc. By the word "etc.," dharma and other such categories are included.

Perception is not your means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the self and so on, nor is inference, because it is neither accepted [by you] nor has it already been refuted; therefore, the scripture which you intend to be the authority for that—

The meaning is that because there is an absence of corroboration (*saṃvāda*) for this [scripture], and because its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) lacks any proof, it does not constitute a means of valid knowledge (*māna*). In this regard, he states an accepted example: "like perception" (*pratyakṣavat*). For that [perception] is not a means of knowledge regarding the Self (*ātman*) and so forth, since it is admitted that the Self is cognizable solely through scripture (*āgama*); likewise, that [scripture] too is not a means of knowledge for those things, because validity depends upon corroboration, and such corroboration is absent.

Some maintain that since the self is already established by the perception "I" and so forth, no other means of knowledge is required; to them, he replies: "Nor [is it established by inference]," etc. The point is that the cognition "I" requires only its own objective support, not the distinctness of that [self] from the intellect (*buddhi*) and so on, nor its permanence. || 478 ||
Furthermore, due to contradiction with inference, there is no possibility of an eternal self or similar entities.
There is no object of knowledge whatsoever that exists in contradiction with another means of valid cognition. (479)

He states that the desired proof of a self is not established because it contradicts the inference of momentariness to be explained later, by saying "by inference" (*anumāna*). He says that momentariness is not negated because the permanence of either the self or the non-self is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), by saying "by another means of knowledge" (*pramāntara*). Recognition is not a valid means of knowledge when it contradicts inference, because it is erroneous—just as in the case of [mistaking] hair and so forth. As he said:
Memory pertains to an object previously experienced, while perception pertains to a present one;
since these two are absolutely distinct, of what could non-difference be perceived?
The two words are distinct by their very nature, and the denoted object is likewise highly differentiated.
The word *sa* (he/that) refers to an object that is not present to the senses, while *pāyayam* (let him drink) refers to an object that is directly perceived.

"Therefore, this conceptual construction which apprehends a single object in things that are distinct is false. Nor does the invalidity of inference follow from its being erroneous; for in your own system, validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), while in our system, its validity is established by corroboration through perception—such as in the case of the momentariness of a flame. Therefore, because it contradicts that [inference], recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not a means of valid knowledge. This is the meaning. || 479 ||
Because perception accords with the object and because it is not contradicted by inference.
The Buddhist doctrine is wholesome, whereas other doctrines are full of defects.
1 gha.
What is this? [Vol. 3, page 327] 1460 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Chapter—]

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it was stated that there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*mānābhāva*) and a contradiction with such means; now he says that in his own system (*svamata*), neither of these two exists, beginning with the words "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*).

The meaning of this is as follows: there is a correspondence between perception and the statements of the Omniscient One regarding objects such as momentariness (*kṣaṇika*) and so forth. As it has been said:

"Regarding the objects of the Omniscient One’s words—such as momentariness, selflessness (*nairātmya*), and the like—that cognition which, by being free from doubt and error, causes one to attain the object as it was presented..."

Therefore, it is said that [perception] is non-contradictory because it seeks the object of the words of the Omniscient One. For that [perception], while apprehending the present, apprehends it precisely as excluded from what is not present. Indeed, it has been stated that its object is the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic). Furthermore, its non-contradiction is established by the inference of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) which will be explained later;
therefore, the doctrine of moments (*kṣaṇavāda*) is superior, and other doctrines should be abandoned. || 480 ||
Everything is either conceptual or otherwise, and is correctly or falsely so, according to its mode of cognition.
Since universal emptiness is liberation, non-return will also be established. || 481 ||

How is it that there is a conventional usage of "stability" (sthāyitva) when everything is momentary? To this he says: "By conceptual construction" (kalpanā). Through the terms "correct" and "false," stability and instability are expressed. In that regard, the conventional usage of "everything is correct" is due to conceptual construction, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for stability. For neither perception nor inference is a means of valid cognition in that case, since their object-hood belongs only to the momentary and so forth, due to the distinction between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the attained (*prāpya*).

Because it has been said: "Of the four kinds of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), by virtue of its connection with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the object to be grasped (*grāhya-viṣaya*) is the fourfold reality called the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), since there is no purpose in grasping anything other than that; however, among the truths, that which is to be attained (*prāpya*) is selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so forth.

But for inference (*anumāna*), the object is precisely the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) such as selflessness as previously described, and that alone is what is to be attained. All [this is established].

The meaning is that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) proceeds through the non-conceptualization of "falsity," because all things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*). How, then, is liberation (*mokṣa*) established, given the absence of a persisting entity to which both bondage and liberation could attach? Anticipating this objection, he says: "All... Because all worldly moments (*saṃsārika-kṣaṇa*) perish without leaving a trace (*niranvaya*), and non-worldly moments arise, liberation—designated by the term "non-return" (*anāvṛtti*)—is logical; for all of that is momentary.

The meaning is that, because the distinction between the subject and the object is false, the contradiction with direct perception previously mentioned regarding the inference is unestablished (asiddha). || 481 ||
Surely there is a distinction between the grasped and the grasper, because of the experience of that distinction.
And thus, the falsity of difference itself contradicts direct perception. || 482 ||

He raises the objection that the non-existence of the distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject is contradicted by perception; for the distinction between the grasped and the grasper is directly perceived in such cognitions as "I know the jar. Thus, he questions whether the contradiction with perception remains as it was. [Verse 482] "The grasped... etc.
Perception, which possesses a form characterized by distinctions such as the grasped object and so forth, is accepted as a valid logical mark (liṅga).
The learned have thoroughly refuted the dual nature of a single entity. (483)

Fearing the objection that perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding difference because it lacks corroboration, he states inference as the corroborating factor: "The object of apprehension," and so forth. The meaning is that even by inference—namely, "whatever is an object of apprehension is apprehended by another [cognition], just like a jar; and this cognition is an object of apprehension"—the form known through perception is correctly understood to be distinct. Since difference is cognizable by two means of knowledge, its existence is established; for it is the cognition itself that is the object of apprehension.

Anticipating the objection that— since it has been stated in passages such as "the very appearance [of an object] in the form of a grāhaka (subject) is itself consciousness" (*dhīreva citsvarūpā*)— the illustrative example lacks the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), and furthermore, there is no corroboration from perception— he says: "Of the one," meaning "by the learned ones, headed by Śabarasvāmin and others."
