As they have said: "If there is nothing other than consciousness, then how is it said that 'one knows'? The expression 'one knows' is perceived by the word as a designation for the agent of knowing; therefore, the word must be understood as having meaning in that very [context]. (483)
But its establishment [as real] follows from the non-difference of cognition; and likewise, the other [worldly activity] follows from the superimposition of that [cognition].
Knowledge accompanied by differentiation does not manifest anywhere as being based on a real entity. (484)
The proponent refutes [the opponent] by stating, "We postulate a self distinct from cognition," and so forth. The meaning of this is as follows:

perception is fourfold—sensory perception, mental perception, self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), and yogic perception. Among these, the fivefold cognition that arises as the direct realization of objects is produced by depending upon the five previously arisen and abiding sense-faculties, such as the eye, and by taking as its objective support the five previously arisen and abiding objects, such as form.

Sensory direct perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*), mental direct perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) produced by the gateway of the mind which directly realizes the six objects—including those beyond the senses pertaining to the three times that arise as the fruits of karma—and self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), which is the self-awareness of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arising at the ultimate limit of the cultivation of meditative concentration and wisdom, and the knowledge that directly realizes the true nature of reality (*bhūtārtha-sākṣātkāri-jñāna*), which is yogic direct perception (*yogi-pratyakṣa*). All of these are of two kinds: non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

And so it is. Among these, in the first case, the apprehended object—such as blue or yellow—is established through its non-difference from the apprehending cognition, because it is superimposed upon that very cognition.

Furthermore, another form, called the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender, which is determinable (*adhyavaseya*), appears as conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Yet, nothing ever arises having a conceptual entity as its objective support. Thus, since difference appears in that semblance of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*), whereas non-difference flashes forth in the other, the [true] means of knowledge... [the distinction between them is established].
The non-existence of the thief. || 484 ||
For it does not manifest at all as "the grasped" and "the grasper."
For the cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth, arises precisely as "this is blue."

To the question of how there can be a perception of blue and so forth within non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) by way of non-difference from the cognition itself, he says: "The object... and so on. For that non-conceptual cognition, which is the consciousness of blue and so forth, does not manifest as "this is the grasper of the object blue," but rather simply as "blue. Since it appears in that way, the meaning is that the object is established in non-conceptual cognition precisely through its non-difference from the cognition. The second "yataḥ" (since) is used in the sense of "ataḥ" (therefore).
Because of grasping that which is not as being that, everything involving conceptual construction would be false.
The perfection of that which is unattached manifests by its own nature. || 486 ||

One might object: "In cognition, the distinction between the grasped and the grasper appears through superimposition (*adhyāsa*) in conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*); therefore, how can it be said that this [distinction] does not touch the reality? For since that [conceptual cognition] is also a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) like the others, the reality of the distinction within its object is established. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Atasmin" (in what is not that).
That by which the self of all minds (*citta*) and mental objects (*caitya*) is known in its own nature—that is self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), which is perception (*pratyakṣa*). Conceptual...

The meaning is as follows: since it is established that cognition—which is of the single essence of luminosity (*prakāśa*), momentary (*kṣaṇabhaṅgura*), and devoid of all differentiation—is "unremoved" (*nāpoḍha*) and "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), yet because differentiation is grasped by conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), it is pervaded by the definition of false knowledge; thus, there is no reality to its object. [Objection: In that case, since there is no difference in their being direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*), even non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) would be erroneous. [Reply: No, he says: "of that which is unassociated" (*asaṃpṛktasya*).

For cognition that does not touch upon the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender, its true nature—known as being fragile by its own essence—is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) in its own form, while it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*) in relation to [other objects].

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [Chapter Four]: In a metaphorical representation, it does not appear; nor, in the case of self-cognition, does there exist a distinction between the object and the subject within the self-cognition of the Self. Since the distinction between the grasped and the grasper exists within the Self itself, there is no contradiction regarding modification in the Self. This is because [the Self] possesses a distinction from insentient matter (jaḍa) obtained through the power of its own beginningless material cause (upādāna), and thus [is distinct from] form...
This is because it is established that knowledge, which has the nature of illuminating its own object, possesses self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) precisely when it is not conjoined with anything else.
As it has been said:
"Consciousness arises as something distinct from insentient forms."
"This very self-awareness is its non-inert nature.
Thus, because it is not an object, it cannot be an error; the meaning is that the doctrine of the Vijñānavādins is to be accepted as true. || 486 ||
But surely, within this mere cognition, there occurs the apprehension of its being either correct or false?
Tell me, how could there be any distinction for you in that which is free from conceptual construction? What, then, is the cause of such a distinction here?

In that view, he challenges the distinction between the real and the false with the words "But surely" (nanu). The meaning is this: if one accepts only cognition in general—whether indeterminate (nirvikalpaka) or determinate (savikalpaka)—then it is not logical to establish a distinction such that correctness belongs to the indeterminate cognition and falsity to the other, because the grounds for such a distinction do not exist within cognition as such. || 487 ||
Just as the nature of knowledge appears pure and momentary.
In that case, it would likewise be conceptual; therefore, a distinction [between them] is difficult to establish. || 488 ||

It establishes the reason: "by cognition. Just as the nature of cognition—devoid of the affliction of objects, fragile by its own inherent nature, and ultimate—is experienced in non-conceptual [perception], so too it is logical that the object of apprehension, such as a jar, which appears in conceptual [perception] as distinct from cognition, is likewise ultimately real, because it is perceived and not sublated. Therefore, the aforementioned distinction between conceptual and non-conceptual [perceptions] is unestablished.
This is the meaning. || 488 ||
If this [cognition] itself is false, how can there be a grasping of falsity through it?
If it is a conceptual construction, it is false; and for you, there is no other alternative.
Furthermore, for the Vijñānavādin, the cognition that "the jar and so forth are false" is not tenable; for in this case, there must be either truth (*samyaktva*) or falsity (*mithyātva*).
In the first case, there would be no falsity in anything merely conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because of its truth. In the second case, however, one must apprehend the falsity of this [cognition].

Because of the absence of another [object], there is no apprehension; nor is there apprehension by itself, due to the contradiction of self-action; nor is there another apprehender, because that would lead to an infinite regress. With this in mind, he says: "This... Since the aforementioned cognition is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one might raise the objection that the faults regarding its being either true or false find no footing. To this, he asks: "If it is a conceptual construction... He refutes this, saying: "No," [for it is] "that which follows upon verbal cognition."

He states the reason—“because of its falsity”—for the consequence that if the cognition “this is false” were itself a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) based on the premise that “conceptual construction is empty of a real object,” then the cognition “the jar and so forth are false” would necessarily be established as existent. If it is argued: “Just as for you [the Yogācāra], the object of apprehension is neither absolutely non-existent because it appears, nor is it existent because it is sublated (*bādhā*), so it is for me as well,” he says: “No. For there is no [such thing] for you regarding the existence or non-existence of the object of apprehension...
The meaning is that there is no other possible state [for the object] than these two [truths], because an indefinability [of the object] is not accepted. || 489 ||
1. ‘Śava’ | 2. kha. *svayam* | 3. gha. *vikalpe* | [Vol. 3, page 330] 3.
Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1461
For false conceptualization would indeed exist only if a thing were permanent.
In the doctrine of momentariness, since all things have perished, what is grasped by whom, and through what means? || 490 ||

Furthermore, he states that if everything were subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the distinction between correct and false cognition would be unestablished, because the relationship between the grasped object and the grasping subject would be impossible.

He says: "It is false. The word *hi* (for/indeed) indicates the reason already stated. The genitive case in *vinaṣṭānām* (of those that have perished) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). || 490 ||
Let it not be so; for from sublation, the establishment of falsity would follow, as in the case of a mirage.
Even the external [object] is not apprehended; however, this is not considered to be due to its stability. || 499 ||

The proponent says: "Not so. Sublation (*bādha*) is the cause for [establishing] falsity, not stability; for it is observed that in cases such as a mirage, the external object—such as a pillar—is sublated because it is difficult to maintain [its existence] through either identity with or difference from its own parts. Therefore, the meaning is that it is false. He states that even for the opponent, the role of sublation in establishing falsity is accepted in the case of the example: "Of the external," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: since objects such as water, which are accepted as being distinct from cognition, are sublated, they are not apprehended; this is the view even of the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*). However, because the subject (*grāhaka*) and so forth are stable, they do not possess that falsity.
Therefore, even in the case of a pillar and the like—which are difficult to define as anything other than momentary cognition—there is sublation due to their falsity. || 491 ||
But surely, how can the establishment of falsity be accepted here for that which has already been destroyed?
This is not so, because it is established through direct perception; for that which is perceived cannot be untenable. (492)

He takes up the objection stated in the passage "in the theory of momentariness, of those that have perished," beginning with "nanu" (but). [The question is: At the time of the subverting cognition (*bādhadhī*), is the grasper of the erroneous object destroyed or not destroyed? It cannot be the first, because if it has ceased to exist, the cognition of its falsity (*mithyātva*) cannot be established; nor can it be the second, because such a cognition is never observed in the case of silver and the like when another person remains indifferent toward it. Furthermore, the second alternative would result in the collapse of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). Thus, the meaning is that the falsity of water and so forth is established through subversion.

"Because it has been seen, it must be accepted; for there is indeed nothing that is impossible when it has been seen, since even impossibility is dispelled by what is actually perceived. Thus he provides the resolution: "Not so"—verse 492.
Even in the case of external objects, falsity arises through the sublation of cognition.
For falsity belongs only to that which is stable; this, however, is not a royal edict. (493)

He says [in the verse], "bāhya... (external), because even for you [the opponent], falsity is accepted on account of sublation (*bādhāt*), and thus no logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*) can be raised.

Anticipating the objection that there is a distinction—namely, that falsity belongs only to a stable entity (*sthirasya*) due to sublation—he replies with the words "sthirasya" (of the stable). Since it is admitted that the cognitions falling within a single continuum possess a conceptualized unity (*kalpitaikatva*), the falsity of illusory water and the like is established at the time of their sublation by means of a cognition whose nature is the destruction of that conceptualized unity.

Furthermore, the absence of the cognition of falsity is not caused by the lack of stability while possessing such a nature of knowledge; therefore, the meaning is that even if [the cognition] is momentary, the falsity of the jar and so forth with respect to the apprehender and so on is not contradictory. || 493 ||
Such conceptual constructions as these arise from the cause of ignorance regarding the identity of the inner self.
All these are mere terrors for those who follow the path of the Vedas.

He concludes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "and so forth" (*ityādi*). The word "iti" has the sense of referring back to the aforementioned conceptual construction. For everything [is established] in its non-stability; [the variants] "bādhako" (in *ka* and *kha*) and "astasminmi" (in *ka* and *gha*), as well as "syaiveha mi" (in *kha*), are [readings of the manuscript].
5 ka. sna. 'svabhāgināṃ | 6 gha. nemiṃ | [vol 3, page 331] 1464 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya—]

The conditioned is composed of the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and is momentary. The aggregates are form, consciousness, feeling, perception, and mental formations. There is no persisting entity whatsoever, because its momentariness is established through both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). First, direct perception grasps the present and excludes what precedes and follows it. As it has been said:
"For the cognition of a real entity proceeds by delimiting reality, excluding non-reality, and proclaiming the impossibility of anything external to it."
Inference, too, is a means of ascertaining that [momentariness]. For it has been said:
"The pervasion—that whatever exists is momentary—is apprehended;
because existence is sublated in the non-momentary, it is therefore restricted to the momentary."

The power to illuminate both the self and the non-self is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the resulting comprehension of the object is its fruit (*phala*). Between these two, there is no real distinction, nor is the action (*kriyā*) anything other than the instrument (*karaṇa*). As it has been said:
"All conditioned phenomena are momentary; how can there be action for things that are unstable?"
"Existence itself is their action; that very same thing is called the agent."

Inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). Knowledge of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) from a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) is inference for oneself; the communication of the mark possessing the three characteristics is inference for others. There are four types of marks—namely, those called effect (*kārya*), cause (*kāraṇa*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)—which possess the three characteristics known as positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); such conceptual constructions are expressed by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). He states the root of these [constructions]:

"Pratyak" (the inward-facing). Furthermore, the Vedas are not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because their meanings are mutually contradictory; nor is there any relation between word and meaning other than convention (*saṃketa*).
As it has been said:
"Words express that which is conventionalized; this [convention] is remembered for the sake of worldly transaction."

Nor is the form (ākṛti) the meaning of the word, because in its absence, that [form] cannot exist—whether through difference or non-difference from the individual (vyakti); rather, exclusion (apoha) is its meaning.
For it has been said:
"The cognition whose seed is merely the distinctness of things is devoid of an external object."
Then, it produces [the result] by virtue of being a constituent part of the avoidance of that which is to be performed.
"And because it is based on a distinction between real entities, it is considered non-erroneous with respect to the object;
therefore, its object is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), since its existence depends upon that which performs [the exclusion]."

Nor does he imagine a fault in the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) by assuming that its eternity and lack of human authorship are incompatible with its being a sentence, nor does he intend any distinction based on contrary conceptualizations; [he calls these] "frightening threats. || 494 ||
A terrifying threat is here employed as a means of prohibition.
First, the critique of the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) is stated here as follows: || 495 ||

He promises to expose the faults that have been imputed [to his position] with the words "Vibhīṣikā" (a source of terror). Among the Sautrāntikas, Vaibhāṣikas, Yogācāras, and Mādhyamikas, he first addresses the faults against those two who are proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), stating in the Bhāṣya:
"Because a jar and so forth do not illuminate themselves," and so on. Thus he says: "External... (verse 499).
Objects such as a jar, as well as lamps and the like, are illuminated by one's own self; they are not [illuminated] by anything else.
How its externality [in relation] to such [a cognition] is established, that is now explained. (496)

As for the claim that there is no self distinct from the intellect due to a lack of evidence, he proposes the following to refute it: [the statement] "one's own self" (*svātma*). Even things such as lamps or the sun, which are manifested by cognition, are manifested by their own nature. Likewise, objects such as jars, though they are manifested along with light and are themselves manifested by that [cognition], are manifested by their own nature and do not require another light; in the same way, the intellect (*buddhi*) also [is manifested by itself].

The meaning is that the proof of an additional self (*ātman*) as being "of this very [person]" is established; first, the lack of logical foundation for the position that perception and inference are the only means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while verbal testimony and so forth are not, is demonstrated. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is intended to refer to the subject matter of the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*). || 496 ||
The view that an external object is illuminated by its own self-nature is inconsistent.
For an object such as a jar and the like would not possess the property of being manifested by nothing else. || 497 ||
Anticipating the objection, "How is this position devoid of logic?", he states the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) found in the Bhāṣya: "illuminating its own self.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the external object is pervaded by light. He states the reason for that: "No" (verse 497).
A jar situated in darkness does not manifest by itself.
But when conjoined with another lamp, it necessarily shines forth. || 498 ||

He demonstrates the pervasion—that whatever is manifest must be manifest by something other than itself—by means of the example of a jar. Regarding the phrase "in darkness": if it is argued that its nature is non-manifestness, he says "other than that" [to refute this]. || 498 ||
Even though those two are joined together, there is the certainty that they are distinct.
And because one observes a distinction between conjunction and disjunction. (499)

Anticipating the objection that "the jar is illuminated" implies no object of illumination distinct from it because their contact is observed, he says: "Of the two conjoined. He states the reason for ascertaining their difference: "And in the case of conjunction," etc. (499).
Therefore, one must understand that there is indeed a difference between light and a jar.
There is no identity [between the universal and the particular], because the particular is observed [as distinct], like a rope, a water-pot, and so forth. || 500 ||
He concludes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "otherness" (*anyatvam*). The connection is: "because of the observation of a distinction from that.

Here, "that" refers to the conjunction and disjunction of light with the jar; these are the meanings of the word "tataḥ. He intends to state the following inference: "Whatever is an object of illumination is illuminated by something distinct from itself, just as a jar is; and this cognition is an object of illumination. Regarding the rope: there is no identity between the cognition and its illuminator.

The remainder [is as follows]: the meaning is that it pertains to the cognition residing in the intellect, whether there is a connection with the illuminator of the particularity or no such connection. || 100 ||
But surely, does not a lamp illuminate itself by means of its own self?
For when the purpose of a lamp's light has been seen, there is indeed no bringing of another lamp. || 501 ||

He raises a doubt regarding deviation [of the reason] with the words "Now, however" (nanu). He clarifies the quality of being the illuminator of its own self with the words "By a lamp" (dīpa) etc. || 101 ||
Because of the lack of similarity in being illuminated, the lamp is also not [the illuminator] of jars and other objects.
A lamp does not illuminate itself by means of itself, just as a jar [does not illuminate itself]. || 502 ||
1 kha. ga. will be explained | 2 kha. ga. will be explained | 3 kha. ga. in the division | [vol 3, page 333] 1466 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya—]
He prevents the charge of fallacy with the words beginning "No," etc. (102).
First of all, there is a relationship between the manifest and the manifester in the case of the jar and the lamp.
That which is to be restrained by the self alone, other than that [external object], is experienced through direct perception. || 503 ||

When it is stated, "That which is an object of illumination is an object of illumination for something other than itself, just as a pot," [the author], anticipating an objection regarding the example, recalls what was previously said: "The pot... (Verse 103).
It is not manifested by a cognition of a self distinct [from the body], just like a jar.
In this case, the lamp deviates [from its function], and that too is due to its dependence on experience.

Having established the example through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he states the application to the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*): "Distinct," etc. Here, the word "here" refers to the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Just as it is directly perceived that a jar or the like is illuminated by light other than itself, so too it is ascertained from that [perception] that this [consciousness] is also illuminated by a cognition other than itself; thus he says: "And that," etc. (104).
And this being the case, let it be understood that, like a jar, a lamp and so forth must necessarily be manifested by a consciousness of a different genus. || 505 ||
He states the conclusion: that inference is logical once pervasion (vyāpti) has been established, by saying "And thus" (evañca). || 105 ||
But is it not observed that there is a dissimilarity between a lamp and objects such as a jar?
A lamp does not depend on anything else for its own manifestation as a self.

He raises an objection, saying "But surely," [arguing] that even though a lamp illuminates things other than itself, there is no rule that it must be illuminated by that very same thing; thus, the state of deviation remains as it was. He analyzes the dissimilarity, saying "Not the self," etc. The connection is with the words "other than itself. The meaning of the word "for" (hi) is: for illumination does not depend on another illumination, because they are equal. || 106 ||
A lamp never manifests itself by itself, just as it does not manifest a jar.
Because there is no distinction in this [entity], whether from itself or from another.
Since there is no distinction, this statement uttered by you is incorrect. (507)

He provides the answer with the commentary beginning with "not from itself" (*na svataḥ*). [The word] "manifests" (*vyanakti*) means: if a particular quality (*viśeṣa*), which was non-existent prior to the lamp’s own illumination, were to exist at a later time, then it would be logical that the lamp illuminates its own self. However, no such particular quality—whether inherent in the lamp or derived from something other than itself—is observed to be conducive to its being illuminated by itself; and in the absence of such a quality, the claim that the lamp illuminates its own self is untenable.
The meaning is that it is false for you. || 107 ||
Because, like a jar, the lamp is cognizable by a distinct cognition.
But as for that which is stated here, it is indeed not distinct from objects such as jars and the like. || 508 ||
That this lamp reveals itself by means of itself is not correct.
Because before and after its manifestation, no particularity is perceived. (509)
He states another reason for the lamp not being self-illuminated: "of the lamp," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "therefore, it is not self-illuminated. [Vol.
3, page 334] 2 Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary named *Śāstramakaranda* by Ānandagiri. 1467.

He concludes that, since a lamp lacks self-luminosity, the opponent's statement is indeed untenable: "As for what [was said]," etc. He states the very reason mentioned therein: "Prior," etc. (vv. 108–109).
Just as the form of a jar is perceived when a lamp is present, [but not otherwise].
And no such distinction is observed in the case of a lamp, as it is in the case of proximity. || 510 ||

He clarifies the non-perception of a specific difference by means of a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), beginning with "pradīpa" [lamp]. The meaning is as follows: when a lamp is absent, there is no jar; when it is present, there is the specific difference consisting in the destruction of darkness. However, there is no such specific difference in the lamp itself, because there is a lack of evidence for it. || 110 ||
For a lamp does not possess selfhood in the same way that a jar or similar object does its presence.
Or rather, this non-proximity is logical, because there is a distinction between these two substances. || 511 ||
Anticipating the objection that proximity and non-proximity might be distinct attributes of a lamp even in the absence of any other difference, he says: "Because it is its own self" (*ātmatvāt*).

To the question, "Where then would proximity or non-proximity reside?", he replies: "In difference" (*bhede*). This means: in the two substances, namely the lamp and the jar. Therefore, the implication is that these two do not exist in one and the same place. || 111 ||
Just as there is no inconsistency in the state of being a burner for a single manifestation.
Since both are equal, the relationship of the manifested and the manifestor is likewise [reciprocal].

One might object that, just as one lamp is illuminated by another lamp, it is possible for cognition itself to be illuminated by something of its own kind; therefore, the desired self is not established.
To this, [the author] replies: "By a single fire... The word "also" (api) is intended to draw in the negative particle (na). || 112 ||
Since this is so, what you have stated is incorrect.
This lamp reveals itself by means of itself, like a sword [revealing its own edge].

He concludes the result, given that there is no distinction in the lamp whether by itself or by another, with the words "yataḥ" (since). The meaning is: because it would be like other things such as jars, which lack self-nature. || 113 ||
Consciousness, too, should be held to be perceivable by a distinct class [of cognition].
Because there is no difference in their being manifestors, like the sun, the moon, and a lamp. || 514 ||

Having set aside the charge of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) and established the inference based on being an object of manifestation (*bhāsyatva*), he states another inference: "Cognition," etc. The meaning is:
whatever is manifold is manifested by something of its own dissimilar class, just as the sun and so forth are manifestors; and this [cognition] is such a manifestor. || 114 ||
Just as a lamp is perceived, so too is consciousness.
This [distinction] between doubt and certainty is known through direct experience.

He states another inference to show that "whatever is an object of cognition must be cognizable by another cognition, just as a lamp [is cognized by another cognition]," using the phrase "it is perceived" (*saṃcetyate*).

Nor is this a redundant statement because "being manifest" (*bhāsyatva*) is the reason here for its being made known by cognition; the point is that it is "manifested" (*bhāsyate*) simply by virtue of being manifest. He establishes its state of being perceived by saying "doubt" (*saṃśaya*). || 115 ||
And when consciousness has been directly and definitively ascertained, [the following occurs].
Is it a distinctness from the object of cognition, or rather, is it the state of being cognized by the subject? 516.
[Vol. 3, page 335] 1468 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Raising the objection, "Even if that [object] is graspable, how can the existence of the grasper as you desire be established? he reflects upon it with the word "cid" (consciousness).
The knowledge under discussion is the meaning of the word "bodha" (awakening). || 116 ||
In that case, when the matter is subject to doubt, the determination is according to worldly convention.
Moreover, it is established in the world that lamps and such things are perceived by a cognizer distinct from themselves. (517)

How, then, is there a definitive conclusion in that regard? He says: "In that case. Anticipating the objection, "Granted that the determination follows worldly convention, but how does the world [itself] proceed?", he says: "The world. (117)
He is the knower of the distinctions between the grasper, the grasping, the grasped, existence, and non-existence.
Let it be understood that the Self is that which is distinct from the act of grasping and so forth. || 518 ||
Even if consciousness were perceivable by another consciousness, how would the desired conclusion be established? To this, he says: "The perceiver... (verse 118).
But surely, if it were accessible through knowledge and so forth, there would be a reliance on another beginningless knowledge.
"Non-termination is unavoidable"—this fault does not arise, for what reason? || 519 ||

He raises the suspicion of a fourfold infinite regress with the words "But surely" (nanu). He refutes it with "No" (na). He asks for the reason there with "Why? (kutaḥ). He says that it does not exist because of the reason which will be stated, using the words "Because" (yataḥ). || 119 ||
For the status of being a grasper and so forth is established for the grasper and the rest through their own nature.
There would be no dependence on internal factors such as a grasper, because there would be no distinction [between them]. || 520 ||

He clarifies the reason with the words "from itself" (*svataḥ*). This means that the manifestation of the essential nature of the subject (*mātrādi*) and others arises from the Self, which is the immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthabodha*); it is not established by the subject and so forth themselves. Because there is no further excellence [in the process], as in the case of light, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*), since the Witness (*sākṣin*), being self-luminous, does not depend on any other means of proof. || 120 ||
If it were not [established] by its own majesty alone, then the grasper and so forth would have to come from something else.
It could not [be so], because there would be no excellence [in it] even over other perceivers and so forth.

It is stated that the establishment of the knower (mātṛ) and so forth occurs solely by virtue of immutable consciousness (kūṭasthacaitanya), and not from another knower and so forth, because there would be no distinction; this is now clarified:

"By its own majesty" (svamahimnā). The meaning is: if the knower and so forth were not established by the majesty of the self—the Self (pratīc)—which is its [consciousness's] reflection, then they could not be established even by another knower and so forth, since they would be identical and thus lack any excellence (atiśaya). || 121 ||
But surely, when there is the apprehension of a cognition by an apprehender distinct from it, [the following occurs].
If there were a dependence on another instrument, an infinite regress would result. || 522 ||
Having avoided the two types of infinite regress concerning the subject and the act of grasping, he now raises the infinite regress concerning the instrument:

"But surely," etc. If knowledge, which has the eye and other organs as its instruments, is itself an object of cognition, then another instrument must be stated for that [knowledge], and for that too, a knowledge...

If it were something other [than consciousness], then another instrument (karaṇa) for that [instrument] would have to be stated, because an instrument distinct from the grasped and the grasper is necessarily required.

Furthermore, the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) cannot be independent of that [instrument], for if it were not its very nature, its dependence on it would be inevitable; thus, there would be an infinite regress—this is the meaning. || 122 ||
1. *Kavasi*. 2. *Gha. ṇaṃ va*. [Vol.
3, page 336] 3. *Brāhmaṇam*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1469.
Because there is no such restrictive rule, this infinite regress does not follow.
Indeed, no fixed rule is observed regarding the relationship between the grasped object and the grasping subject. || 523 ||
He avoids [the objection] and restricts [the scope]. He states the reason for the absence of a means of knowledge in the absence of restriction: "grāhya" (as the object to be grasped).
The remainder of the sentence is that restriction belongs to the additional instrument. || 123 ||
The internal instrument, like a lamp, is undivided from the grasped and the grasper.
So that, in all cases, there would not be such a connection between the grasped and the grasper. (524)

He clarifies what was stated by means of a counter-example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*): "grāhyagrāhaka... etc. The meaning is this: just as a distinct instrument called "light" is observed when there is a connection between a jar and the eye—which are of different natures—it is not possible to restrict another such instrument in every case of the connection between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*), because of the diversity of entities (*padārthavaicitryāt*). The suffix *-vat* here refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*). || 924 ||
First of all, the perception of a jar is preceded by [the presence of] a lamp and so forth.
Just as when one observes a lamp, there is no need to seek another lamp.
Anticipating the objection as to how the diversity of objects leads to the breaking of the rule, he says: "Of the jar," etc. (125).
Therefore, an infinite regress cannot be established here in any way whatsoever.
Nor is it through the medium of the instruments, nor likewise through the medium of the grasper. || 526 ||

He concludes the state of infinite regress with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the statement that the intellect and so forth are objects known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedya*). He clarifies what was said with the phrase "in any way whatsoever" (*kathaṃcid api*). The word "also" (*api*) is used to include the infinite regress that occurs through the medium of the effects. [The result...]
"So be it," he said, in order to gather that Dvārikā. || 926 ||
Apart from the subject and so forth, there exists a real entity whose nature is contrary to them.
We have previously stated that its existence is established solely through the means of direct perception.

Anticipating the objection that the witness of those [entities] does not exist because there is no means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for its existence—since it would be distinct from the fourfold group beginning with the knower—the author says: "grāhakādi... ("The grāhaka, etc.").
The word "before" (prāk) refers to the statements in the *Saṃbandhagrantha* and other sections. "Direct perception" (pratyakṣa) means one's own experience (svānubhava). || 127 ||
From direct perception, from inference, and likewise from scripture as well.
Distinct from the subject and so forth, consciousness is established; it is supreme because it is their witness.

Regarding this, he says in reply to the disputant: "From perception" (*pratyakṣāt*). The meaning is that because of the experience of the wise, the inference stated regarding the Brāhmaṇa and others, and the scripture being explained here and there, the supreme witness who is distinct from the knower and so forth and whose nature is consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*) is established; therefore, one should not dispute concerning him. || 528 ||
Even in the investigation of Lokāyata, by means of perception as the sole authority, [the following is established].
The existence of that which possesses unimpaired vision by its own nature was previously established through direct perception. (529)

He speaks to one who is in disagreement even regarding inference and so forth, beginning with the words "Lokāyata. [This refers to] the view that perception alone is the desired means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[Vol. 3, page 337]

The meaning is that it has been established in passages such as "For the sake of establishing the existence of the Self, the eternal experience which proves the unknownness of its object must be admitted" that this is accepted by all philosophical schools (*sarvatīrthadṛśām*).
The second particle *api* is used to state that the dispute regarding inference and other means of knowledge has also been refuted in that very same place. || 129 ||
Even in the absence of the means of knowledge, [the Self is established] through its witness-nature as the knower and so forth.
The existence of the immutable witness-consciousness has been established even previously. || 530 ||
Anticipating the objection that [the Self] cannot be a witness because it is accessible through a means of knowledge (*māna*), like a jar or other objects, he says: "Even without...

The meaning is that the existence of the immutable Seer (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭi*) is established by itself as the witness of the knower (*mātrādi*), even without a means of knowledge; this has been stated in the investigation into the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and will be stated again later. || 130 ||
When the proponent of external objects has been refuted, the proponent of consciousness likewise [is refuted].
Now, an objection is raised: "But surely there is no external object at all. (531)

Having established that the self is distinct from the intellect by means of refuting the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*), he now introduces the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*). [The word] "external" [is used]. The phrase "just like that" (*tadvat*) is stated to indicate that the objection raised by the Yogācāra is equally subject to refutation as the objection raised by the Sautrāntika and others. Furthermore, in the *Śārīraka*, once the doctrine of external objects has been refuted, the doctrine of consciousness-only—
The word "atha" (now/then) is for the purpose of understanding the sequence, since the establishment of the order of the counter-arguments follows from their refutation. || 131 ||
Is it not the case that there is no external object at all, characterized by such things as jars and lamps?
Because no means of valid cognition is observed for it apart from consciousness. || 532 ||
He reveals the counter-argument with the word "nanu" (but surely). The reason for this is stated in the phrase "tasya" (of that). || 132 ||
For whatever object is not perceived here apart from something else, [that thing is not distinct from it].
Let that object be exactly as it is, like an object belonging to its own level. (533)

Having raised the doubt that there might be a lack of evidence for non-distinction just as there is for distinction, he says: "For whatever... Here, the word "here" refers to the empirical discourse of the waking state. The meaning is: whatever is not perceived apart from something else is not in reality different from it, just as an object in a dream [is not different] from the cognition;
and the external object is not perceived apart from cognition. || 133 ||
One's own [nature] is to be realized through non-cognition, because it does not exceed one's own ignorance.
Just as that [dream-object] does not exist as a real entity, so too the external object exists not.

Anticipating the objection that the probandum is deficient, he says: "svamā" (it is itself). He concludes the inference with: "tadvat" (in the same way). The remainder of the sense is: because it is not perceived apart from the arising cognition, there is nothing other than that. || 134 ||
An object such as a pot perceived while awake is [known] through its excess over waking-consciousness.
It is not real by virtue of being graspable, like a pot or other objects graspable through ignorance. (535)

He states another inference based on the reason of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatva*): "In the waking state," etc. The meaning is that whatever is an object of apprehension is not, in reality, distinct from cognition, just like an object of apprehension in a dream; and since this [waking world] is an object of apprehension, there is no such thing as a jar or other entity existing as a substance distinct from waking cognition.
1 ka. kha. ‘vāini’ | 2 ka. kha. tulyani | [vol 3, page 338] 3 Brāhmaṇa: Accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1471
And this being so, [the self] would be distinct from consciousness, like a jar.
"Could there even be a friend of the western light, which is stationary and luminous in form? || 536 ||
Fearing the objection that "while objects such as jars may not exist apart from cognition, the self might still exist as something distinct," he says: "If this is so.

The meaning is that since it is established that everything is mere cognition, there exists no permanent self distinct from momentary cognition, just as there is no jar or the like [apart from it]. || 936 ||
And thus, when external objects have been refuted, [cognition] cannot arise from lamps and the like.
What example could you have for the successful establishment of your desired point? (537)

[Objection: But surely, since the inference has been stated that "the intellect (dhī) must have an object of manifestation external to itself because it is an object of manifestation, like a lamp," how can the Self be denied as being external [to the intellect] while that inference remains valid? To this, he says: "External... That is to say, the desired object is distinct from the intellect, for the purpose of being perceived by the inner Self (pratyagātman). || 137 ||
Because you admit another entity [as the object], knowledge possesses the state of being knowledge [only] through that [object].
We certainly have many more examples; if you do not, then neither do you.

He establishes the conclusion: "As another entity," etc. Just as you accept cognition to be distinct from external objects, so too do we accept that jars, lamps, and the like are distinct from cognition; therefore, an example for our proof of a distinct self is indeed easily available.
If, however, you do not accept any object other than cognition, then for you as well, everything would be mere cognition, like a dream.
The meaning is that [the argument] is not established because of the absence of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta). || 538 ||
Having accepted that this very [world] is knowledge born of the intellect, and nothing other than that;
The reality of waking, dreaming, and so forth is negated as being false.

How is it that the Vijñānavādin accepts another entity? To this he says: "Because of the cognition" (*dhīmānāt*). Having accepted that the waking state and so forth, which appear as something other than that cognition, exist according to their appearance, you establish—by means of the authority consisting of the nature of cognition—that "this object is indeed cognition," and thus you negate the external object by asserting that what appears externally is false. For it has been said:

"In that [cognition], whatever form appears as if it were external, unitary, distinct from others, and as if excluded [from others], is devoid of reality because it does not withstand critical examination.

For it is not the case that its being merely cognition or its falsity is what is being proven, since that would involve proving what is already established or would result in contradiction. To which [subject] does that [property] belong?
The meaning is that false belief (mithyātva) exists as something distinct from those [other factors]. || 139 ||
Whether it be existence or non-existence, it is determined by a means of valid cognition through the medium of knowledge.
For one who says "it does not exist," shame does not arise except out of sheer audacity.

Anticipating the objection that external objects are false and non-existent, and therefore do not exist at all, he says: "Or [it may be] an entity. Whether it be an entity—such as a jar or a lamp—which appears as an object of cognition like cognition itself, or whether it be a non-entity, one who asserts that such a thing does not exist in perception reveals his own shamelessness, because it would follow that cognition itself must also be non-existent. As he has said:

"The establishment of properties and their substrata, as well as their difference and non-difference, is of such a nature that it is perceived in the world by those who have not investigated the true reality.
This means that there is no denial of external objects. || 140 ||
Furthermore, is an external object admitted to exist over and above cognition?
The lamp, the water-jar, and so forth were designated by the Buddhas for the sake of establishing conventional usage.
For this reason as well, there is no denial of that; thus he says "api" (even). The connection is with the words "even by the Buddhas. || 141 ||
Is it not the case that [the existence of] everything is not accepted because it is merely cognition?
Because that [measure] is impossible here due to the preeminence of my knowledge. (542)
It challenges the accepted position with the words "of all. Here, "here" refers to the domain of valid cognition (*mānabhūmi*). For it has been said:
"And how could that which is non-different from cognition itself become another object?
Therefore, this apprehension of a single nature in objects is a false conceptual construction (*mithyāvikalpa*). (942)
Knowledge, the jar, and the lamp—for the sake of establishing the basis of words, objects, and cognitions.
In this case, a distinction between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge must necessarily be admitted. || 543 ||

He objects: "Knowledge [is not the object]. Here, the phrase "in this regard" refers to the state of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Otherwise, since there would be no distinction between word and object, there would follow a confusion of mutual usage;
the implication is that in the case of citing words such as "fire" (*dahana*), there would result the burning of one's own body and so forth. || 143 ||
You must state the means of valid cognition for the sake of establishing both difference and non-difference.
For a wise person understands that what is stated by these two is not without authority.

He provides the introductory context to state that there is a difference between the two for the following reason: "The means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇam*). The meaning is this: since the proponent who asserts the difference between knowledge and its object must state the proof for that position, you too, as one who asserts their non-difference, must likewise do so in that regard. The reason for this is stated:
"Not [established] by either of these" (*nāssvayoḥ*). || 144 ||
You have accepted that the fruit of association with me is non-existent.
Because their activity is unified in its effect, their conventional usage is not established [as distinct]. || 545 ||

Considering that there is no evidence for non-difference, he states the case for difference as follows: "I am the knower" (*māmeyeti*). You must accept the mutual difference between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyya*), as well as between the result produced by their respective relations of being the object and the subject, and the knower (*mātṛ*). For if these were identical, undifferentiated practical discourse (*asaṃkīrṇa-vyavahāra*) would be impossible; therefore, the impossibility of such [non-distinction] serves as the proof for their difference. As it has been said:
“Relying precisely upon that [conventional reality], the establishment of the means and the goal is devised by the wise for the sake of entering into the ultimate truth.
The meaning is that the distinction between those [means and goals] is what is to be attained. || 545 ||
They seek to assume various forms for the sake of perceiving the objects of their knowledge.
Therefore, an object that is unknown must be accepted for the sake of establishing the nature of valid cognition.
16. And [the portion] exceeding that is from Kauṣītaki.

3, page 340] 3. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1473.

In that context, he states the accepted meaning in order to state another reason: "desiring to acquire" (*upāditsanti*). The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that this has been demonstrated many times. Having stated the accepted view, he forcibly leads [the opponent] to accept the disputed view: "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning of the word "therefore" is: because the operation of a means of knowledge (*māna*) occurs with respect to an object not yet known. The word should be split as *ajñāte*. 146.
Furthermore, it is not possible to establish the state of being unknown through a means of valid cognition.
For in this case, the fault of mutual dependence would necessarily follow. || 547 ||

Anticipating the objection that this [ignorance] might itself be an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), he says: "And not... If ignorance were an object of knowledge, then for the sake of the operation of a means of knowledge (*māna*), its ignorance must first be known; yet the knowledge of that [ignorance] would have to come from a means of knowledge. Thus, he states that there is an unavoidable circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*)—expressed as "mutually..."—[since each depends on the other]. || 147 ||
Nor can it be established by means of valid cognition, because that would contradict authoritative knowledge.
If there were no contradiction with perception, how could there be a denial of its being unknown? (548)
He states another reason for its immeasurability: "From the means of knowledge" (pramāṇāt). He establishes the contradiction with the means of knowledge by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"By the means of knowledge" (mānaiḥ) || 148 ||
Nor is the status of being both the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge possible either in its own nature or with respect to its own part.
Because there is no excellence at any time, and because [the nature] is non-different from awakening. || 549 ||

It has been stated that one who seeks to establish the distinction between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyabheda*) must accept an immutable experience (*kūṭasthānubhava*) as the prover of [the existence of] ignorance and so forth.

Regarding this, the proponent of the denial of external objects (*bāhyārthāpalāpavādī*) maintains that there is no distinction between the means and the object of knowledge, because both are applicable to a single cognition or even to a part thereof.

In response to him, [the author] says "No," and so forth. He states the reason for the first proposition with the words "at all times" (*sarvadā*). For the second [proposition], he provides the reasoning—

He says: "And because of [the distinction between] awakening. The meaning is: there can be neither identity nor difference between the two parts based on their cognition; not the first, because the established distinction between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyavyavasthā*) would not be possible;
nor the second, because that would entail a split in that [awakening] itself. || 149 ||
If cognition is the means of valid cognition, then the objects of cognition are forms such as blue and the like.
What mutual dependence could there be between those two, such that one is established by means of the other? || 550 ||

He raises an objection regarding the established distinction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*). [The opponent says: "If it is so, then because there is no desire for non-difference between those two, and because there exists a desire for their difference, the unity you have asserted is not established. To this, he replies: "Mutually... (verse 110).
Even if a distinction between the two forms is indeed admitted;
Granted that there may be such a connection with the object of knowledge, from what is it understood? || 551 ||

He raises the objection regarding the admission of a difference between the form such as blue and the cognition possessing that form during the state of conventional usage (*vyavahārāvasthā*), by saying "the form" (*ākāra*). He grants this, saying "let it be," acknowledging: "We too accept that difference there [in the conventional state], but not in the state of ultimate reality (*paramārthāvasthā*); since those two do not exist then, let the admission stand. To the question, "Once a conventional difference is accepted, how is the desired nature [of non-duality] established? he replies:

Regarding the term "pramā" (valid cognition): there exists a relation of the nature of the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyatva*) between the blue object and the cognition thereof; however, that [relation] is not self-cognizable (*svavedya*), because it lacks the status of being mere cognition (*jñānamātratva*). Nor is it suspected [to be so].
(185) 1. ka, ga: *śaṅkayate*; 2. gha: *na sa pa*.
[Vol. 3, Page 341] 1474 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

Its establishment is not through knowledge of its own parts, because it has only itself as its object; nor is it established by another cognition, since [that other cognition] would also function merely as a qualifier.

If that [cognition] were an object [of another], its status as self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) would be lost, because it is accepted that the self-cognition of all minds and mental factors (*caitta*) consists in their being cognized by themselves;
therefore, the intended meaning is that one must accept an immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthabodha*) as the establisher of that [self-cognition]. || 151 ||
The connection between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge arises from their relation as the effect and its constituent parts, and so forth.
But the nature of the object and the means of cognition is indeed distinct and different from one another. (552)

One might object: "The relationship between the blue object and the cognition of it consists in their being the form and that which is formed, or being cause and effect, or part and whole; this is what constitutes their connection. And since this will be established through the non-difference of cognition [from its object], there is no need for a witness (*sākṣin*) to establish it. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The effect... etc. Since we observe that clay and a pot, as well as threads and a cloth, stand in the relation of the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyatva*), their connection must be something distinct [from mere identity]; therefore, a witness who establishes that [connection] must exist.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, since there is a connection with being an object of knowledge (*mānameyatva*), even if it were one of those [categories], it must be established by something other than itself; for its establishment does not occur through identity with cognition, because that [connection] lacks the nature of being merely that [cognition]. Thus he says: "distinct" (*vibhinna*). The connection is with the words "the connection is indeed another" (*saṃgatiranyaiva*). ||152||
If that which possesses the aspect of the knower were the object of knowledge, or if that which possesses the aspect of the object of knowledge were the means of valid cognition;
Due to the absence of a relationship, both the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge are not established for it. || 553 ||

By establishing the witness (*sākṣin*) who effects the connection between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyasaṃgati*), it was stated that there is a cognizer and an object of cognition distinct from cognition itself. Now, he states another reason for the distinction between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge, beginning with the word "māna. If there were no distinction between those two, it would follow that the very part belonging to the means of knowledge is the object of knowledge, and the very part belonging to the object of knowledge is the means of knowledge. In that case, the status of being a means of knowledge and an object of knowledge could not be established, because they would not be related within a single entity, as the part and the whole would be identical. Therefore, there is a distinction between the two.
This is the meaning. || 553 ||
For the nature of both the means of cognition and the object of cognition is not apprehended here at all.
Therefore, the establishment of the nature of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge is not tenable in that case. || 554 ||

Anticipating the objection—"How can there be difference for that which is non-different from them, since it is impossible for existence and non-existence to reside in one and the same thing?"—the author clarifies this by stating:
"Of the state of being the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge. Here, the two locative endings denote cognition (*jñāna*). || 154 ||
If even in a single [entity] there were the conceptualization of being an instrument of knowledge, an object of knowledge, and so forth, [then...]
Because the means of proof is one with the things to be proven, the nature of the means of proof is itself not something to be proven. (555)

He states another reason for the distinction between knowledge and its object: "In one [thing]," etc. By the word "etcetera," the conceptualizations of cause and effect, part and whole, are included. The meaning is that if the goal (sādhya) and the means (sādhana) were identical, then neither the status of being a goal for the goal nor the status of being a means for the means would be established, because they would be mutually non-different. || 155 ||
Otherwise, it would follow that there is no distinction between the fruits and their means of accomplishment.
The instruction of the treatise would be useless, and its author as well would be a fool. (556)

He states another defect [arising] from the non-difference between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*): "Of the fruits," and so forth. The instruction regarding difference—namely, that "this is the means for this" and "this is the fruit"—would be without an object if there were no such difference; and thus, having introduced the subject as "the direct perception of the yogin," all of this follows: [it is] rooted in cessation, the attainment of another state, knowledge, self-awareness, and the realization of the Self.

The meaning is that [the opponent's claim] is mere idle chatter; for since one who has directly realized the dharmas that contradict all states of existence would be an *anāpta* (unreliable person) if he were a teacher of false matters—as [the opponent suggests by calling it] "the song of a negligent person"—therefore, the claim that "valid cognition is the knowledge that does not contradict the meaning of the words of an omniscient being" is nothing but empty talk. || 116 ||
Apart from consciousness, there is no such thing as an opponent or any other entity.
"From your own admission, there would be a distinction between the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the object of valid cognition (prameya).
[Verse 557] Having established the distinction between the means and the object of cognition, he states another reason why it is untenable to deny external objects: "vijñāna... [Verse 117].
Even you do not maintain that this [world] is merely consciousness alone.
The opponent and other such entities [are mentioned] because they are the objects to be refuted. || 558 ||

Fearing that his own approach might be unestablished because it exceeds that [position], he says: "No. The word "api" (also/even) is used for the purpose of including his own example as well. || 158 ||
In the case of the opponent and other objects of refutation, there is no occurrence of the relationship between part and whole.
Even in one who is utterly deluded, the intention to reject [the truth] arises. || 559 ||
Even though it is subject to sublation (*dūpyatva*), he raises the doubt that it might be non-different from cognition and says: "The opponent, etc. By the word "self" (*sva*), the Ātman is meant.

"Being a part" (*aṃśatva*) means being one's own; "being the whole" (*aṃśitva*) means being the essential nature (*svarūpa*). The phrase "even for one who is utterly deluded" is intended to illustrate the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic. || 559 ||
Objects such as jars and lamps, which are perceived by a distinct grasper, are indeed real and constant.
Thus, among his kinsmen, he remains awake like one who has overcome all disputants.

Having stated the impossibility of being an object of perception (dṛśyatva) in relation to either its own nature (svarūpa) or its belonging to itself (svīyatva), he states the resulting inference: "bhinna" etc. The thesis (pratijñā) should be understood as: "Even though it is an object of a grasper distinct from itself, it possesses permanence. || 160 ||
Or rather, it is like another continuum, or like another consciousness.
In this manner, such examples are intended here to demonstrate accessibility. || 561 ||

Furthermore, the continuum of Maitra is inferred from the continuum of Caitra through conventional usage, and the cognitions of non-omniscient beings are known by the cognition of an omniscient being;
since they too establish difference in those cases, it can be inferred—by means of those examples—that there is a difference between blue and the cognition thereof.
Thus he says: "continuum" (*saṃtati*). By the word "iti," the two aforementioned examples are referred to. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the previously mentioned [examples] are included.

This is the statement regarding the manner of citing examples such as those of the opponent. Therefore, the construction is that when the difference between the cognition and the object of the examples is to be proven, they are easily available according to the method already described. || 561 ||
Therefore, for the Vijñānavādin, there is nothing apart from consciousness.
The one Self, whose nature is unchanging perception, can be negated as something other.

He states the result of the inference: "vijñāna... etc. The meaning is that since the distinction between cognition and its object is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the self (*ātman*) as we maintain it—which is distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*)—cannot be refuted. || 132 ||
But surely, in a dream, no object exists apart from consciousness.
It cannot be like an object perceived while awake, because its nature consists solely of cognition.
1476 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:

By stating the distinction between knowledge and its object, it was implied that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is also distinct from knowledge; now, it is argued that the subject of dispute is non-different from knowledge.

He restates what was said—that [the dream object] is like a dream-object because it is an object of apprehension (*grāhyatva*)—with the words "Now, [it might be objected]" (*nanu*). Anticipating the objection that the example is not accepted, he says "No" (*na*).

For even for one who maintains the reality of enduring things (*sthāyivādin*), a dream-object does not exist in the same way as a waking object; thus, since in that case it is merely cognition (*jñānamātratva*), there is nothing else that exceeds [the scope of] that example, because it too is an object of apprehension. This is the meaning. || 963 ||
If that which is not a real entity were to obtain distinction through knowledge, like one who possesses knowledge, then [it would follow that it is real].
Since that [result] is established by its own inherent power alone, how can it be said that it does not exist? || 564 ||
Having raised the dilemma as to whether one's own object is perceived as distinct from cognition or not, he refutes the first alternative with the words "vibhāgam" (division).

The meaning is: if, like the distinction of cognition from the object of knowledge, the distinction of the object from cognition were seen in a dream, then by that very perception the dream-object would be established as something over and above cognition; consequently, its denial would be impossible, and thus the illustrative example would be devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). || 164 ||
If it is postulated that the form of the object belongs to cognition itself, just like its awareness;
Tell me, what is the proof for the non-existence of that which exists in the ultimate sense? || 565 ||

Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*). The meaning is as follows: an object is not perceived as distinct from knowledge, but rather as being that alone; however, this does not constitute its denial, because since it is non-different from knowledge, like knowledge itself, there is likewise no denial of the essential nature of waking objects. || 165 ||
If the object, such as blue and so forth, were distinct from consciousness, [it would not be perceived].
Whether it be an existent or a non-existent, there is the certainty that "it exists. || 566 ||

One might object: "We do not deny the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the waking object and the dream object themselves; rather, we deny that there is any excess of cognition regarding them. Therefore, this is a false accusation. Anticipating this, he says: "Vijñāna... (Verse 966). The meaning is that in both states, the external object must be accepted as the apprehended (*grāhya*) exactly as it is perceived; otherwise, the very manifestation [of experience] would be contradicted. || 966 ||
At the beginning, this waking state is experienced by you yourself as being your own.
Why is that [self] not accepted by you as the object of the cognition of a jar and so forth? (567)

Anticipating the objection that although there is a distinction between knowledge and its object in the waking state, such a distinction does not exist in a dream because of the absence of the eyes and other sense organs that grasp them, he says: "In dreams and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the mention of memory, meditative absorption (samādhi), and the like is intended. The point is that even though the eyes and other organs are absent there, the mind exists;
and whether that [mind] is the immediately preceding cognition (samanantara-pratyaya) or something else is a further matter for consideration. || 967 ||
“If that object which has been reached through experience is said not to exist, [then what can be said]?”
Even regarding knowledge, there would be a lack of confidence, because that [knowledge] is established through experience. || 568 ||
Having stated the existence of external objects based on the experience of two states, he points out the flaw in the opposing view with the verse beginning "yadvastu" (whatever object...). 168.
Just as there is no excellence beyond knowledge, so it truly exists here.
How can it be said that the pot, being other than the experience [of it], does not exist? || 569 ||

Regarding the distinction between knowledge (*jñāna*) and its object (*artha*), he states another argument: "From knowledge" (*jñānāt*). Just as in the state of conventional usage there is no object other than knowledge, so too the object exists because it is being experienced; therefore, it is difficult to maintain that the object is something other [than knowledge]. The word "distinction" (*atiśaya*) refers to the other [i.e., the object]. || 969 ||
If it is argued that this is because it is not observed at any other time, that is said to be incorrect.
Otherwise, because it is not seen in another moment, the consequence follows for you that it is non-existent. (570)

He raises the objection that because an object such as a jar is perceived only at the time of its cognition and is not perceived at another time, its difference [from the cognition] is not established; this is expressed by the words "tadanyeti" (as for that which is other than that). He refutes this by way of an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) with the words "kṣaṇāntara iti" (at another moment). [The opponent might argue: "The non-existence of the additional entity [the jar] may occur either at another time or at its own time. To this he replies: "Not the first, because it is accepted [that the jar exists then]; nor the second, because that which was seen as existing in its own moment..."

The meaning is that because they are not perceived at another moment, they would also be non-existent at their own moment; for since even a single cognition denoted by the term "moment" is not seen at the moment of another cognition, it would follow that it too is non-existent at its own moment, resulting in the voidness of all things. || 170 ||
Because it is not perceived in the winter season, there is a denial of the existence of Bhīṣma’s dharma.
It would be impossible to maintain such a proposition, and thus emptiness (śūnyatva) would follow.

Since a thing that exists at its own time is not perceived at another time, the proposition that it is non-existent even then cannot be sustained; herein lies another reason [for the opponent's position].

Rāmakaṇṭha says: "In winter. [The meaning is as follows: If things such as heat, which were perceived through their existence during the summer, were not seen in winter, then their non-existence during the summer would follow; and that is impossible to assert because it contradicts direct perception (*dṛṣṭi-virodha*). This being the case, the sense is that everything exists exactly as it is perceived at its own time. The word should be split as *aśūnyatvam* (non-emptiness). Alternatively, if one disregards perception and asserts non-existence, then everything would be empty.
He states the fault in the opposing position—that it would be something else—by saying "tathā" (so). || 171 ||
Since everything [is determined] solely by the differences in place, time, and so forth, as well as the state of the cow.
How can that which is established as a reality in this world be denied?

For this reason as well, he states that there is an absence of external objects: "deśa... etc. The meaning is that in the case of the contrary position, the cognition of spatial distinction would be contradicted. || 172 ||
For one who asserts that "the jar does not exist apart from consciousness," [this is the consequence].
If even the object does not exist, how could one live here, being devoid of the object that exists?

And because it would lead to a contradiction for one who denies external objects, he states that such a denial is unestablished: "In consciousness... [Verse 173]. It is said here that this is the ground for the conventional usage of existence and non-existence.
Non-existence does not exist by its own nature alone, without existing being.
Just as your consciousness exists, so too should jars and other such things be accepted [as existing]. || 574 ||

Anticipating the objection that "just as the meaning of 'is' (astyartha) is established independently of the meaning of 'is not' (nāstyartha), so too that [meaning of 'is not'] will be established independently of the meaning of 'is'," he says: "like the meaning of 'is'. He states the result of this contradiction with the word "just as.

If the meaning of "is" is not accepted, the meaning of "is not"—being devoid of a counter-correlate—cannot be established; yet if it is accepted, there is no proof for the denial of all external objects.
The meaning is that, just like cognition, the object of cognition also possesses existence. || 974 ||
