For if there were an exclusion of the meaning of "is," nothing at all would be established. || 575 ||
If consciousness and so forth are held to exist apart from the object that possesses existence, [then...]
Just as in the case of "non-Brahmins" and so forth, it would follow that [the object] is non-existent; this is the certain conclusion. || 576 ||

Anticipating the objection that "we do not desire an object that exists or one that does not exist, but rather we respect consciousness itself—which is self-destructive by its own nature and arises incessantly; therefore, nothing is untenable"—the author says: "The object that exists... Anticipating the further objection, "How can there be the failure of everything in the absence of that [object], since things like momentariness are established as being distinct from the object that exists?", he says: "Apart from the object that exists... For indeed, [it is not the case that] Brahman...

The meaning is that, just as the state of being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth does not belong to anything other than sound (nāda), likewise existence does not belong to anything other than that which exists. || 179 || 176 ||
Let it be understood that substances perish at every moment.
Because they are subject to destruction at their end, like the extinction of a lamp and so forth. (577)

It has been stated that the external object must be accepted as existing just like consciousness, and that it is enduring. Now, the proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādī*), unable to tolerate its endurance, objects with the words "at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇa*). The meaning of the inference is as follows: substances—namely, the entities consisting of cognition and the cognized—are momentary because they perish at the end, just as a lamp perishes at the end; and all things [perish at the end]. This is the sense of the inference. [The opponent objects: "The example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*)."...
The word "without a lord" (vinauśi) is used there in order to indicate that [the self] possesses the means of accomplishment (sādhana).
And the example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is for the sake of establishing the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā).
In this case, there is cessation through deliberation; therefore, everything becomes perfectly stable. || 578 ||

Anticipating the objection that a homogeneous example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is untenable because momentariness—characterized by spontaneous perishability—is not admitted in the case of lamps and the like, he says: "By way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇa*). The meaning is: whatever is subject to destruction at every moment is not subject to destruction only at its end, just as *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) is not destroyed only at the end;

whereas things such as jars are not destroyed only at the end [but are perishable at every moment]. Here, regarding the jar and so forth, the intended object of the proposition (*pratijñāta-artha*) is [momentary] destruction at every moment.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: for the sake of establishing the property of being momentary (*śitva*), there is the dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*); and since that is a destruction preceded by cognition (*buddhi*) resulting from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), our position—that everything is momentary—is well-established. || 178 ||
In this formulation of inference, the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā) is extremely difficult to establish.
Because of the existence of repetition and distributive iteration, and because momentariness is established by valid means of knowledge. || 579 ||

He refutes [the opponent’s position] with the words "by inference" (*anumāna*). He states the reason for the failure to establish the intended object of the thesis—that "the subject of dispute perishes at every moment"—with the words "repetition" (*āvṛtti*). The meaning is that, according to your own view, since repetition and distributive iteration (*vīpsā*)—which are understood from the prefix *prati*—do not exist as established by any means of valid cognition (*māna*), it follows that everything is momentary. || 179 ||
For the manifestation of the world is observed to be manifold and characterized by diverse activities.
And that [cognition] regarding a single entity such as Devadatta is not accepted by the Buddhist.

Anticipating the objection as to how these two [repetition and memory] could be impossible in the case of momentary entities, he states their essential nature in order to show that repetition is not possible [therein]: "Aneka... (multiple). First of all, repetition is well-known in the world as a series of multiple operations performed by a single agent of the same kind, such as when a single person like Maitra [performs the same action repeatedly]. (Note: 1. kha, gha: due to momentariness; 2. kha: destruction; 3. gha: destruction; 4. kha: unknown meaning.)
The meaning is that, just as in the case of eating many meals of the same kind, the repetition is understood from the expression "he eats" at every moment; it is not so for the Buddhist.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), it is not possible to accept the repetition of the act of destruction, because one [entity] is not admitted to possess multiple acts of destruction; thus he says:
"And that... (verse 180).
Because it is certain that all entities are devoid of activity and are momentary.
That which is called "gone" and "returned" would be a repetition that is extremely difficult to obtain.
He establishes this as follows: "They are devoid of activity. As it has been said: "All conditioned phenomena are momentary; how can there be action for those that are unstable? (181)
In this world, among words denoting various objects, there exists here [a relationship] between the locus and that which is located within it.
That pervasion which occurs through an action or a quality is designated as "vīpsā" (repetition for distribution). || 582 ||
Furthermore, that [simultaneity] is in no way tenable for the Buddhist.
If it is argued that [the cognition] occurs despite the difference [between objects] due to the similarity of the agent, the action, and so forth; || 583 ||

Having stated that repetition (*āvṛtti*) is untenable as a property of action (*kriyādharma*) according to the opponent's view, he states its nature in order to show that distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is also untenable as a property of words (*śabdadharma*). He says: "Not manifold" (*nānā*), etc. Here, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of either action or quality belongs to those objects—such as trees, villages, and their locations—which are the denotata of words possessing the habit of expressing manifold properties and substrates, and which exist in the relationship of locus and located.

The meaning is that repetition (*vīpsā*) is well-known, as in the example "the rain-cloud waters tree after tree," where there is a simultaneous pervasion of all trees and their respective locations by the act of watering; and as in "every village is beautiful," where there is a simultaneous pervasion of all villages and their respective locations by the quality of beauty. The point is that repetition should be understood in this same way in other instances as well. [Objection: Let it be so; what does it matter in the present context?

To this, he says: "That too. The meaning is that the aforementioned form of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is not established in the opponent's view, because they do not admit the simultaneous pervasion of multiple substances by the act of destruction, since such simultaneity is never observed; and furthermore, because the status of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) is rejected by statements such as "the determination of property and property-bearer [is impossible]... Even in the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the establishment of recurrence and distributive repetition regarding agent and action, quality and quality-bearer, similarity, and so forth, remains unproven.
Thus he raises an objection. [Verse 982] 183.
Furthermore, it is seen from the statement: "The Brahmins eat again at home."
And this would be untenable because of the adoption of metaphorical usage.

He says, "Even again," [addressing the objection]: "Just as in the expression 'the Brahmins eat repeatedly,' even though there is a difference between the eaters, it is not the case that those who stood up after eating at a previous time are the very same eaters at a subsequent time; likewise, even though there is a moment-by-moment difference in entities, the use of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) and so forth is possible. He says, "And this," [to show] that such is not the case because in the illustrative example that usage is merely figurative. || 184 ||
Because, in the absence of the primary [meaning], the application [of a secondary meaning] is not tenable.
Furthermore, by accepting that [position], there would be the abandonment of what has already been accepted. || 585 ||

Anticipating the objection that, even in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the repetition and so forth are merely figurative and thus consistent with the illustration, he says: "Of the primary [meaning]," etc. [Ga.
reads *syād anyaṃ*; Ma. reads *khyasya saṃ*].
[Vol. 3, page 347]

Just as a boy who has been metaphorically designated as "fire" cannot exist apart from actual fire, so too a metaphorical usage of repetition (*vīpsā*) and the like is not tenable in the absence of actual repetition; therefore, the meaning is that such primary [repetition] must be accepted. Let it then be accepted that this is the primary sense.
To this, he replies: "By what has been accepted. (189)
It is accepted that all conditioned phenomena are momentary, and so forth.
This [is established] by such statements as "all conditioned phenomena are momentary."
Consequently, the distributive repetition [of the term] is contradicted, and thus the assertion that [things] are momentary is not tenable. || 586 ||

He demonstrates the point already accepted: "momentary" (*kṣaṇikāḥ*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the following is included: how can there be activity for things that are unstable? For those for whom there is arising (*bhūti*), that very arising is called both the action and the agent. Furthermore, everything conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which is momentary, produced by causes and conditions coming together and combining—that entire collection of conditioned entities is momentary.

It is understood that [the term "momentary"] refers to existence at the very moment of origination alone. Considering that if the aforementioned admission is not abandoned, then since repetition (*vīpsā*) and so forth would be impossible in their primary sense, even a figurative sense (*upacāra*) would not be established, he says: "They are momentary. This means that the *saṃskāras*—which have another synonym, "latent impressions" (*vāsanā*), and consist of the nature of cognition—are entities. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has the meaning already stated.
To whatever extent this entity is perceived by direct perception, to that extent it belongs to the present time and is not qualified by any other time.
"And this time exists established as a single moment;
therefore, all that is perceived is, in my view, momentary."

Such statements as these constitute the meaning of the plural number. "Vīpsā" (repetition) is an elliptical expression for *āvṛtti* (reiteration). He concludes that, since those two—whether primary or figurative—are impossible in the case of momentary things, the object of the thesis is unattainable; this is expressed by the words "ataśca" (and therefore). The mention of "momentariness" serves to prove that [point], meaning the thesis that substances perish at every moment. || 986 ||
Moreover, if it is intended here that the suffix expresses possession in the sense that "they are momentary," [then the following applies].
In this way, there would be the proving of what is already established; thus, the conjunction of moments is indeed accepted [as a fact]. || 587 ||

He states that even though repetition (*āvṛtti*) and distributive sense (*vīpsā*) are impossible according to the manner already described, there is no fault in the proposition (*pratijñā*) that "the objects under dispute are momentary" (*vimatāni kṣaṇikāni*). He says: "Even so" (*athāpi*). Is momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) the state of being connected with a moment, or is it disappearance within a moment, or is it perishability, or is it being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of a destruction occurring in the moment immediately following its own production? Among these, he first restates and then refutes the first alternative.
The sense of possession (matvartha) is present here. || 187 ||
A stable entity necessarily [undergoes change] through moments characterized by the closing and opening of the eyes.
That conjunction would occur through partial portions; thus, for us, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established.
It establishes that [the reason] is already proven; [this is shown by the words] "of the stable," etc. (188).
If it is argued that disappearance is merely a momentary effect, [we reply: so be it.
There would be an abandonment of what has been accepted; even so, that which is desired is not established. || 589 ||
1. From the Yakṣa, all the Kṣatriyas. 2. Ka: "Nevertheless. 3. Ka: "Ha! Likewise. [Vol.
3, page 348] — 1. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1481.
The second [alternative] does not arise. Regarding the term "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*): in that case, does disappearance occur at the very moment of existence or at another moment?

It is not the first, because there would be a contradiction regarding the attainment of manifestation by entities whose nature is consciousness, which would result in the blindness of the world; thus he says, "Even if admitted. It is not the second either; thus he says, "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The meaning is: even if there is disappearance at another moment. || 189 ||
The cessation of manifest phenomena, which is held to be their existence in the form of a cause, [is the unmanifest].
In this context, the term "disappearance" (tirobhāva) refers to that of a stable substratum (dharmin). || 590 ||
To clarify the failure of his desired conclusion, he explains *tirobhāva* (concealment/disappearance). He says "manifest" (*vyakta*), etc. By the word *dharma*, the effect (*kārya*) is indicated.
The sense is that if *tirobhāva* is established as described, there would be no damage to the momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*) required by [the opponent] himself. || 190 ||
If those things that have arisen were to perish, then it would be a case of proving what is already established.

Since the destruction of all things that have a beginning is accepted by everyone, [the author] considers the first alternative among the three options—whether destructibility belongs to what has already arisen, to what has not yet arisen, or to what is currently arising—and adopts the first: "If... Even there, he further considers whether the destruction of what has arisen occurs at some time or other, or at the very moment of its production—the second [alternative].
He states the fault regarding either the [final] moment or the first moment: "It would be... (verse 591).
Since that which possesses birth must necessarily perish in the end.
In that case, there would undoubtedly be a loss of the very point you have accepted. (592)

He states the reasoning for why all things that have a beginning must resort to destruction: "Since" (yataḥ). This means that because there is a necessary rule that every entity possessing a beginning must ultimately end. Anticipating the objection that if momentariness is thus established, you too would have to accept it and thereby my position would be proven, he says: "In that case" (tathā). This refers to the fact that the very point you have accepted—namely, the state of being subject to momentary destruction—is exactly what I maintain. || 992 ||
Furthermore, you accept that destruction occurs at the very moment of origination.
In that case, creation and destruction would necessarily occur at one and the same time. || 593 ||

He states another alternative with the words "Now" (*atha*). He refutes [the opponent's view] by means of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) with the words "At the time of creation" (*sarge*) and so forth. || 593 ||
Consequently, there would either be no production of effects, or else their existence would be eternal.
Through opposition or non-opposition to that, one certainly encounters what is undesired.
He states that the consequence results in a logical fault: "And therefore," etc. Between existence and non-existence, there must be either contradiction or non-contradiction.
In the first case, there could never be the arising of that [existence], nor the persistence of it, because when existence and non-existence have arrived simultaneously, they are contradictory;

thus, existence cannot arise from non-existence, nor can the other (non-existence) arise from it. In the second case as well, the same fault remains, because those two, being non-contradictory, would necessarily coexist together.
This is the meaning. || 594 ||
And because two contradictory actions are intended for a single agent.
Because they are contradictory at the same time, the entire world is contradicted. || 595 ||

He states another fault regarding contradiction: "of two contradictory [things]," etc. The meaning is that, because the simultaneous production and destruction of two contradictory things in a single object would have to be accepted, the established worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) would not be possible anywhere, since the referents of contradictory words would cease to exist. || 599 ||
186 1 gha. Always.
[Vol. 3, page 349]
1482 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Now, if it is argued that things which are unknown perish, or else they are born;
Nevertheless, the meaning of the proposition is untenable; there is no perishability of an existing entity. (596)

Having rejected the two alternatives—that destruction occurs either at some time after arising or at the very moment of birth—he restates the second and third [positions] with the words "Now" (*atha*). Therein, he refutes the destruction of that which has not yet arisen with the words "Even so" (*tathāpi*). The meaning is that the thesis "unborn things are destroyed" is untenable; because that which is unborn is non-existent, and there is no destruction of what is non-existent, just as there is none for a continuum (*saṃtāna*) [that has not begun]. || 196 ||
What extreme cold could there be for one who is unborn when destruction has arrived?
Furthermore, there would be a mutual contradiction between the two terms of the proposition here.

He states another reason for its non-destruction with the word "What" (*ka*). Destruction is a modification (*vikāra*) caused by the non-existence of an object; however, since that which is unborn is non-existent for you, there is no destruction, and because there is no excellence [in it], that [destruction] does not belong to it—this is the meaning. Considering that destruction occurring at the moment of birth is already refuted by the refutation of birth itself due to the absence of difference (*bhedābhāva*), he states another fault with the words "The proposition" (*pratijñā*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the contradiction that will be stated.
The meaning is "liberation. || 197 ||
"To say that an object perishes while it is being produced" is the speech of a fool.
It is contrary to all the world and is also contradicted by one's own inferences. || 598 ||
He reveals the contradiction with the words "it perishes. For the state of being produced is its connection with existence (*sattā*), whereas the state of perishing is the absence thereof;
thus, there is a clear contradiction between the two terms of the proposition—this is the meaning. He states another contradiction with the words "all," etc.

You maintain that even what is contrary to worldly experience, such as the non-duality of Brahman, is accepted [by you]; I likewise accept this—regarding that, he says: "by means of valid cognitions" (*mānaiḥ*).
And so [ends the section]. || 198 ||
Now, if this destruction of what has arisen were to occur in the second moment, [then...]
Without the nectar of recognition (pratyabhijñā), this meaning of the proposition is not established. || 599 ||

Regarding the position that [the cognition] perishes as soon as it has arisen, he adopts the third alternative with the word "atha. Therein, he prepares the ground to state the defect by saying "pratyabhijñām" (recognition). || 199 ||
He alone who is born as the agent is this very one who perishes.
Just as it remains stable during two moments, let it likewise remain so in the subsequent moment. (600)

He states its essential nature with the words "ya eva" (he who...). [The opponent asks: "What loss is there if the aforementioned recognition lasts for two moments? To this he replies: "kṣaṇa... (moment...). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "[the self] would be a permanent entity that is the agent of birth and destruction. || 100 ||
That cognition does not arise, nor does it perish directly.
Or rather, it is free from conceptual constructions arising from causes at the beginning, middle, and end.

He raises the objection that since the connection between two moments—namely, the moment of origination and the moment of destruction—is not established, it does not follow that there is existence in another moment. This is expressed by the word "mata" (the view). He states that cognition is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), being devoid of the beginning, the end, the middle, and all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) produced by them, because it is apprehended as being free from all conceptualization. This is expressed by the word "ādau" (in the beginning). For it has been said: [The verse follows: ...devoid of the beginning, the end, the middle, and all conceptual constructions produced by them; such is non-conceptual cognition, for it is apprehended as being free from all conceptualization. Thus he says: "ādau... For it has been stated:
1. ka. kha. gha. *mānaṃ hi* | 2. gha. *sattāyāṃ* | 3. gha. *tathedamapī* | [Vol.
3, page 350] 3. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1483.
Ultimate objects are neither conjoined nor divided in themselves;
that they appear as both one and many is a cognitive distortion regarding them.
The word "vā" (or) serves to indicate that the meaning already stated is the reason for the meaning previously stated. || 601 ||
In that case, there would be a clear contradiction between the reason and the thesis. (602)
If destruction occurs at the end, what is this "end" that you speak of?
Whether [the object] is inside or outside the moment, it is not tenable in that way either. || 603 ||

He then refutes [the opponent's position] by stating that the previously mentioned inference cannot arise, using the words "hetu" (reason), etc. The meaning is this: since there is a contradiction between your statement—that the reason "because of perishability" applies to the ultimate reality (*satyanta*) which is devoid of all conceptual construction (*sarva-vikalpa-śūnya*)—and your own proposition of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), the inference does not arise; furthermore, if that [reality] is indeed free from all conceptual construction, it implies agreement with our own view. He raises the fourth [objection] with the words "mata" (view), etc., beginning with "ādima-".

Thinking that [the argument] results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) and a lack of distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*) because the destruction of that [non-existence] is established at the end, he sets forth another alternative at the conclusion in order to state a further fault: "What is this? He declares the untenability of both positions with "No" (*na*).
If destruction were to occur at another moment, its momentariness would be destroyed.
Even at another moment, this destruction is not tenable because of the prior absence [of the entity]. (604)
In response to the inquiry, "How is it untenable?", he states [the argument] regarding the word *anta* (end) meaning the middle of a moment (*kṣaṇa*). He says: "In a moment...

The meaning is that the existence of a momentary thing is desired within one completed moment; however, that existence is not established if destruction occurs in the middle of the moment. Regarding the second [alternative], he says: "In another moment. "Another moment" means outside of the moment; destruction therein is not logical for the moment itself.

The meaning is that because a cognition existing in a preceding moment cannot be admitted to have a connection with a subsequent moment, the entire collection of entities is momentary, since they possess existence only at the very moment of their arising; such is the established position. || 604 ||
Since it is destroyed at the moment of its utterance, the preceding [sound] cannot be joined [with the following].
Since its non-existence follows later, it would likewise be something that must be offered as an oblation.

It establishes the reason. Regarding the word "subsequent" (*uttara*): in the act of destruction occurring at that very moment, the preceding entity is not appointed as the agent, because the preceding entity lacks existence in the subsequent moment, and that which is non-existent cannot function as an agent. As it has been said:
"Because the manifestation of the non-existent is impossible, and because there would be the loss of the state of arising..."

"By whom can the substantiality of cause and effect in this manner be denied?"—this is the meaning: that the reason [for the argument] is established. He states the fault in the prior moment existing at the time of the subsequent moment: "And [there would be] permanence," etc. (609).
If it possesses the divisions of beginning, middle, and end, its partlessness is difficult to maintain.
Furthermore, regarding the continuity of moments, it is said that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established. || 606 ||

Furthermore, if there is destruction at the end, then because that end depends upon a beginning and a middle, cognition would possess three temporal parts; thus, its momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) would be undermined. Nor is it logical [to claim otherwise]. [Page 351, Vol.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four, verse 1484:

He says "partless" (*niraṃśatā*) and so forth. "At the beginning" (*ādau*) refers to the momentary cognition (*kṣaṇasya jñānasya*). Having raised the doubt that within the flow of that [cognition] there might be parts such as beginning, middle, and end—[a doubt] regarding that which is devoid of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—[the author states that] although conceptual constructions exist elsewhere than in cognition, in cognition itself they do not.

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "And in the case of a continuum," stating: "Our established doctrine is that knowledge is beginningless and endless due to its existence. The construction is as follows:

if conceptual constructions (vikalpas), while following a continuum, do not follow knowledge, then you are merely proving what is already established for us—namely, that consciousness is devoid of all conceptual constructions—since we too maintain that conceptual constructions exist apart from knowledge. 606 ||
And because that which is non-existent arises, and because it is joined with destruction at the end.
There would follow the consequence of a twofold destruction, and momentariness would be lost. || 607 ||

Regarding the fourth alternative as well: is the production [of an object] from that which exists or from that which does not exist? Not the first; for production is indeed the relation with existence (*sattā*), and that relation cannot belong to what already exists, since it has already acquired its form prior [to such a relation]. Considering this, he refutes the second alternative with the words "and from the non-existent. When the cognition of a non-existent thing arises, does that non-existence perish or not?

There would be the undesirable consequence of the destruction of even that cognition, because there is no difference between [the cognition] and its non-existence; if there were a difference, it would follow that it must have existed previously as the substratum (dharmin) of that [non-existence]. In the second case, its production would be useless, since its state of non-existence remains unchanged. Therefore, when non-existence is destroyed at the time of production, the cognition—which is non-different from it—is also destroyed. Furthermore, if a non-existent cognition arises in the form of existence, you maintain that it is subsequently destroyed; thus, for a single cognition...

The meaning is that there would be the consequence of two destructions, as well as non-momentariness; furthermore, if there were a destruction of what has already been destroyed, it would entail the absurdity of its remaining in that very same state. || 607 ||
If there is no arising of the non-existent, likewise there is no destruction of the existent.
An attachment to the doctrine of the immutable (kūṭastha) would arise from their false association.

Since that which is non-existent does not arise and that which is existent does not perish, cognition—which is of a single flavor and thus a groundless locus for the conceptual constructions of arising, perishing, existence, and non-existence—is [the reality]. Seeing no other way out, he raises an objection with the words "If not... He replies, "Then you have come to my own path," with the words "As immutable... Although there is an imagined connection between those two—existence and non-existence—and arising and perishing within cognition, in reality such a connection does not exist.

He says: "It is false. Regarding the reading "mitho'saṃgatis tayor" (there is a mutual non-connection between those two), the phrase "between those two" refers to cognition and conceptual construction. || 608 ||
The final destruction would be great, since non-destruction is accompanied by excellence.
Because there is no distinction, it is not so, since that [cognition] lacks any excellence.

It was previously stated that because momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is difficult to define, the probandum (*sādhya*) is impossible. Now, the opponent speaks of a distinction to the proponent (*siddhāntin*), who argues: "If a jar were momentary, then even before being struck by a mallet, it would have to be perceived as destroyed, since its destruction would be no different [from what it is after the blow]. To this, the opponent says: "In the final [moment]," meaning that although it is destroyed by itself prior to the blow of the mallet...

In a jar, that stream [of destruction] is not destroyed; however, subsequently, both the jar and its stream perish. Thus, the later destruction is greater while the earlier is smaller; consequently, there is no conventional usage of "destroyed" in the former case, whereas in the latter case, such usage certainly exists. Since destruction is thus characterized by degrees of intensity, there is no such thing as "momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). This is the meaning. He refutes this with the words "viśeṣa... (by way of distinction), according to the method stated above.
1 kha. beginning with *rasa*; 2 gha. *...gandhaḥ karaṇam*; 3 gha. *’stavadhvaṃse*; 4 ka. ga. *...nmitho’sauṃ*;
5. kha. *saṃhati*. [Vol. 3, page 352]

What does he say? "Of that" (tasya). Although the prior flow has not been destroyed and will not be destroyed later, nevertheless, because there is no distinction in the case of the destruction of the jar, the conventional usage of "destroyed" would apply to both [the prior and the subsequent states]. Thus, the meaning is that this position is refuted by a counter-argument (*bādhaka*). || 609 ||
Furthermore, because the sense of possession is untenable, momentariness and the like are impossible.
For in this world, there is no simultaneity between the existence of a substance and its destruction. || 610 ||
For this reason as well, he states that the proposition does not hold, saying: "matvartha" (possessive suffix). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), perishability and other such qualities are included.

He provides the reason why the possessive sense—characterized by expressions such as "this has a moment"—is untenable in the opponent’s position, saying: "dravya" (substance). If the substance and its destruction were simultaneous, the possessive suffix would be established; however, there is no simultaneity because of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), and a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) is a specific point of time.
The meaning is that because simultaneity with another [moment] is not admitted, and because there is no other time (*kālāntara*), that claim of momentariness is untenable.
And there is no time for destruction, neither within a moment nor outside it.
Because [destruction] exists outside the moment, since it is constant within the moment;

having thus refuted the simultaneity with the substance by means of its connection with time, he now states that, according to the opponent's view, there is no connection with time at all for that [destruction].
"And not," etc. First of all, there is no destruction of the substance within its own moment, because it exists while its own moment is complete.

Nor does its destruction occur outside of that [moment], because the substance is not perceived in the subsequent moment; therefore, the meaning is that there is no connection with time for its destruction. || 611 ||
"She was fortunate," he thought, seeing that her appearance contradicted [her previous state].
For there is the hearing of time as it exists in its defining characteristic.

He raises an objection regarding the previously stated impossibility of the possessive suffix (*matup*). [The opponent says: "As for 'wealthy' (*dhanī*)," etc. The meaning is that even though wealth and so forth do not exist at the same time as Devadatta, the use of the possessive suffix is observed in such cases as "wealthy" (*dhanī*) or "possessing cows" (*gomān*); likewise, even though the destruction of a substance and so forth occur at different times, that suffix will still apply. He refutes this with the words beginning with "No" (*na*). He establishes the contradiction with the definition with the words beginning with "In the definition" (*lakṣaṇe*), etc. That—

Regarding the rule that the suffix *matup* occurs in the sense of "that which exists in this," because the word "exists" (*asti*) is heard in the present tense, the meaning is that its application does not occur in the past or the future. || 612 ||
If it is said that "it exists" for the purpose of defining the three times, [then...]
Because there is no cause for that purpose, this also is not tenable. || 613 ||
He raises the objection that the hearing of the word "exists" (*asti*) in the definition serves as an indicator for the three times (*trikāla*). [The author] says "the three times.

The word *cet* has the sense of certainty. He refutes this, saying "it is not so," because there is no reason for "existence" (*astitva*) to be an indicator. He states the reason: "because it has that as its purpose" (*tādarthye*).

The point is that expressions such as "you were fortunate" (*dhanyāsīt*) are established by assuming that the time of the wealth and the time of the mantra are identical, even though they belong to the past.
The meaning of the word *api* (even) is that there is never, at any time, a simultaneity between the destroyer and the destroyed. || 613 ||

Furthermore, because it contradicts direct perception, the moment does not possess perishability.
Nor can there be a case of non-erroneous contradiction between perception and inference. (614)
If it is thought that [the reason] will perish because its probandum is already established, then there would be a loss of momentariness; what is lost by that being the case? (615)

Having stated that inference does not arise because its proposition (*pratijñā*) is difficult to establish, he says "by perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*) to show that it also does not arise because it contradicts recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). As for the claim that "this is a false conceptual construction (*mithyā-vikalpa*), a grasping of oneness in things that are distinct"—does this intend to preclude recognition from being a factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), or does it intend to preclude its capacity to reveal reality (*tattvāvedakatva*)? It is not the first, because that would contradict worldly transaction; nor is it the second, as [the opponent] accepts it.

And the meaning is that there is no contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*). Perception establishes the persistence of a substance, whereas inference (*anumāna*) establishes its momentariness; thus, one might suspect that since they do not deviate from contradictory meanings regarding a single substratum (*dharmin*), their status as valid or invalid is equal. Anticipating this, he says: "Perception... [and so on]. Because perception is stronger due to its being the basis upon which inference depends, inference is rendered invalid when sublated by it, even though...

The inference under discussion does not arise by depending upon recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); nevertheless, the sense is that because it depends on a member of the same class [of cognitions], recognition—which belongs to that class—is stronger. Anticipating the objection that the inference of momentariness, supported by perception grasping the destruction of jars and the like, is stronger than recognition, he offers an alternative analysis with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*). Is that perception [the one grasping the jar's destruction] of something already born...?
The meaning of the alternative is that [perception] sometimes grasps destruction or [sometimes grasps] its own existence. He restates the first [alternative]:
"it will perish. The meaning is: if it is desired that perception [grasps] an object such as a pot that has been produced in the sense that it will perish at some time or other.
Likewise, he states that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*), because even for a persisting produced thing, destruction occurs at some time or other.

Regarding the term *siddhe*: he addresses the position that perception grasps the destruction of jars and the like within their own existence. [He says: "of momentariness. The meaning is that if this were so, it would result in the consequence of total emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Anticipating the objection that because perception grasps existence only in the present moment and does not function at a non-present time, it never grasps destruction anywhere, he asks: "What? (vv. 614–611).
And because it is contradicted by such signs as causal efficiency (arthakriyā), it is not accepted [as real].
As for what was previously stated, that "all things must be momentary," [that is now addressed].

Having refuted the inference of momentariness by way of its contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he now refutes it by way of its contradiction with presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Regarding the word "artha":
by the word "ādi," birth and so forth are included; by the word "liṅga," logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*) is meant. (616)
There may be the carrying away of rice and other grains, or likewise the birth of a daughter.
Causal efficiency is not a means of valid cognition, because it is contradictory with [the nature of] a real entity. || 617 ||

What is that logical mark (liṅga) consisting of purposeful action and so forth, or how does it contradict [the opponent's position]? To this he says: "Śāli... etc. The fetching of rice, barley, and so on, as well as the going and so forth for that purpose, the birth of that which is about to be born, and the destruction and so forth of that which has already been born—these constitute the logical mark in the form of purposeful action. Since these are otherwise inexplicable, they contradict the inference of momentariness desired by you; therefore, [that inference] lacks validity. This is the meaning. || 617 ||
Momentariness is not in any way tenable for entities.
Nor can there be the act of fetching rice and other grains by means of that which is lost or perishing.

He states the conclusion regarding its lack of validity: "momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatvam*). The phrase "in any way whatsoever" (*kathaṃcid api*) means either by virtue of being naturally fragile or by persisting for two or three moments. Anticipating the objection that even for a momentary thing, such as a Buddhist entity, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is possible because agency can occur, and thus the aforementioned refutation does not apply—he raises the following alternatives: is that effect produced by what has already perished, by what is currently perishing, or by what is arising through a continuum (*saṃtati*)?
He refutes [the view] beginning with "pyāssdhau" by saying "naṣṭhena. The ellipsis to be supplied is "because of the non-existence of those two. || 118 ||
If [the result] were to arise through a continuum by means of those things which consist of the cause and the result, [then it would be so].
All purposeful activity is performed by entities, just as it is by lamps and the like. || 619 ||

He raises the third [objection]: "By way of continuity" (*saṃtatyā*). Just as by means of lamps, lightning, and the like—which perish by their own nature—illumination of objects and other functions are performed through uninterrupted succession, so too all purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), such as the fetching of water and so forth, is accomplished by momentary entities consisting of cause and effect that arise in a continuous stream. Therefore, there is no contradiction of inference by *arthāpatti* (presumption); this is the meaning. || 619 ||
It is accepted as being either about to arise, already arisen, or not yet lost.
How could that which is perishing or already lost be recognized without recognition (pratyabhijñā)? 620.

He establishes the contradiction of inference by means of *arthāpatti* (presumption) based on the impossibility of [the object] desiring to arise and so forth. Regarding the phrase "desiring to arise" (*utpitsu*):

the state of existing for eight moments is indeed necessary for entities, because through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) one perceives the very same single thing across those eight moments; and this has been stated in the investigation of the jar.
Therefore, the meaning is that the impossibility of [the object] desiring to arise otherwise than [as a momentary entity] serves as a sublater of that inference, just like recognition. ||620||
The flames exist as a continuous series within the fire, which is the substratum possessing those properties.
Those things existing in the present would perform causal efficiency, just like the attainment of a village and so forth. (621)

He refutes the example cited by the opponent in order to establish the contradiction consisting in the impossibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). [The phrase] "by means of a continuous series" (*prabandhena*) means as follows:
just as movement and so forth, existing as a continuous series while Maitra is present, perform actions such as reaching a village, so too do the flames of a lamp.

The meaning is that it is logical to hold that phenomena called "flames," though they are accepted as being momentary, would nonetheless perform purposeful actions such as burning while remaining supported by a persisting fire, existing in the form of a continuous stream. || 621 ||
For, like a lamp and so forth, the performance of a purposeful function (arthakriyā) by you is impossible.
If things were momentary, that [continuity] would not be possible, because its cause would be perpetually absent.

He states the discrepancy regarding the subject of the argument (*dāntika*) with the words "like a lamp, etc. According to the principle stated, the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of a lamp and so forth occurs in a manner that is not possible under the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). This is because the causal efficiency of bringing rice and so forth cannot be conceived [in that way], since its substratum does not persist, because the continuum (*saṃtati*) is not a real entity, and because causal efficiency lacks independence; thus, by implication, it contradicts the observed causal efficiency, and therefore what was stated [previously] is not [the case].

"Conceit" (māna) means pride. To the question "How is it impossible?", he replies: "Because of momentariness. The meaning is that if friendliness and so forth were inherently subject to destruction, then the performance of purposeful action—such as the bringing of rice—would never be possible, because the agent of that action would no longer exist. || 622 ||
That which has not yet arisen cannot function as a cause for the fetching of water and so forth.
Because it is non-existent in both that which is about to arise and that which is currently arising, it is likewise [non-existent].

How can there be an absence of its cause in that case? Is the state of being a cause [belonging] to that which has not yet arisen, or to that which is about to arise, or to that which is currently arising, or to that which has perished, or to that which is perishing, or to that which remains in its own moment? Having thus proposed these alternatives, he refutes the first with "No. He addresses the second and third with "About to arise," etc.; the connection is that there is no bringing forth of water and so on. The reason "because of non-existence" applies equally to the preceding cases as well.
"The cause is likewise" thus provides an example of that which has not yet arisen. || 123 ||
Just like the hair of a tortoise and so forth, likewise, there could be no such thing as its state of perishing.
No one, while dying, is able to procreate a son. || 624 ||

He refutes the fourth [position] with the word "action" (*karma*). Just as things that have not yet arisen and so forth lack causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) because they have not attained self-nature, so too, like the milk of a tortoise or similar [non-existent things], there is no such efficiency for that which has perished either, because it is absolutely non-existent—this is the meaning. He rejects the fifth [position] with "nor...
(*nāpi*). In this regard, the example is "dying" (*mriyamāṇa*). || 624 ||
Nor does it attain the status of being a cause while remaining in that very same state anywhere.
In that case, your established doctrine perishes at the very moment the task is completed. || 625 ||

He refutes the sixth [position] with the words "the state of being a cause" (*hetutvam*). Does a substance that has arisen perform its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) while remaining in its own moment, or in another moment? Not the first, because—just like something unarisen—it is not admitted that it performs an effect in its own moment; otherwise, the relationship of cause and effect would be unestablished, as it would be like two horns [existing simultaneously]. Nor the second, for does it remain until the effect is produced or not? If it does not remain, then due to its non-existence, it cannot be a cause. If it does remain...
If [it exists] by way of its own nature, as a continuum, or as a self, then in the first case, the meaning is that momentariness would be undermined. || 625 ||
If that which has arisen is pervaded by the activity of destruction, then it perishes.
Thus, by means of the continuity of cause and fruit, this [system] becomes well-established. || 626 ||

It assumes another eon. Regarding "destruction": if one accepts that a substance persists until the end of its causal process through a continuum—being born by way of a stream of cause and effect and then perishing as it is pervaded by the activity of destruction—then momentariness remains entirely unimpaired, because there is an absence of such [endurance] in the individual manifestation of the substance.
Such is the meaning. || 626 ||
And because a continuum is untenable, this [position] is not tenable even in this way.
If it is said that the "continuum" (saṃtāna) is so called because it "continues," then it would be designated as the agent.
And because that [self] is unitary and imperishable, a continuum is not tenable.
Nor can it be established as an ablative, nor from the locus of the substratum. (628)

1. Refuting the [notion of] continuity (*saṃtati*), he states the following reply: "In the continuity" (*saṃtāne*). The meaning is that because the members of the continuity (*saṃtānin*) are momentary, there is no connection between preceding and succeeding moments;

and since continuity itself is not a real entity (*avastu*), there can be no relation of cause and effect. How is that untenable? For that [continuity] belongs to the members of the continuity which possess a gross nature (*sthūlātman*).

Regarding the claim that there is an appearance of continuity (*nairantarya-pratibhāsa*), they ask: does the word "series" (*saṃtāna*) here denote an agent (*kāraka*) or a state of being (*bhāva*)? Even in the first case, having raised the alternatives—whether it denotes the agent, the source (*apādāna*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the object (*karman*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), or the recipient (*saṃpradāna*)—he states the untenability of the first by citing the etymology: "it continues" (*saṃtanoti*). He refutes the second and third [alternatives] with the words: "Nor indeed... [and so on]. From this it continues...
Alternatively, the two positions—that [the self] exists "in this" or that it is the "continuum"—are untenable; such is the meaning. || 627 || 628 ||

He refutes the remaining three positions with the words "not [so]," etc. The meaning is that the word *saṃtāna* (continuum) cannot apply—whether in the sense of the object (*karman*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), or the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) as expressed by case endings, or even in any other sense such as the agent (*kartṛ*)—to anything other than a continuum itself, whether it be understood as "that which continues," "that by which something continues," or "that from which something continues. He states the reason for the impossibility of these five positions with the phrase "by what has been stated," namely, by its being a single entity and its being subject to destruction.
Up to this point [it has been explained]. Now he states another alternative: "the continuum" (*saṃtāna*). The word *cet* (if) is used in the sense of certainty. || 629 ||
An entity is established only in dependence upon a bringer-into-being; it cannot be otherwise.
And such a thing cannot be found, for that which comes to be is subject to destruction.

Regarding the position that "continuity" (*saṃtati*) means "series" (*saṃtāna*), he first analyzes whether [the agent] will exist or not, and then addresses the view that it does not exist, saying: "The one who will exist" (*bhavitā*). This means that the independence of the action is not admitted. Regarding the view that it does exist, [the agent] must be either permanent or momentary; he refutes the first [option], saying: "And not... Here, "such" (*tādṛk*) refers to the permanent [agent]. The reason for this is stated: "For the one who will exist... (*bhavitā hi*).
Otherwise, there would be an abandonment of the thesis that "all conditioned phenomena are momentary"; such is the intended meaning. || 630 ||
Because that which undergoes becoming is eternal, the continuum itself is also impermanent.
Furthermore, in your position, the meaning of the root and the prefix is not obtained.

He states the second [objection]: "It is eternal. The meaning is as follows: if that which is momentary were the possessor of existence (*bhavitṛ*), then because an entity is necessarily dependent upon its possessor, that [possessor] too would have to be momentary. Consequently, the claim that the appearance of continuity is merely the appearance of uninterruptedness among the members of a continuum (*saṃtānin*) in their gross form is nothing but idle chatter.
Having stated the logical impossibility by relying on the term "continuum" (*saṃtāna*) as an undivided whole, he [now addresses] that...
He refutes [the opponent's position] by means of analysis: "The realm," etc. (631).
Neither contraction nor expansion is logically possible if things are momentary.
And because the past and the future do not coincide with one another in time. || 632 ||
And because the present moment is a single unit, a continuum is not logically possible.
Furthermore, the continuum [of consciousness] in relation to its constituent moments is either non-different or different; thus it is twofold. (633)

This demonstrates that there is no establishment of meaning for the verbal root *tan* and the prefix *sam* in the context of momentary destruction, by means of the words beginning with "no" (*na*). If everything were momentary, the meaning of the verbal root—extension (*vistāra*)—would not be tenable, because in your position, extension, which consists of one thing pervading many, is impossible. Furthermore, the meaning of the prefix *sam*, which is synonymous with "completeness" (*samyaktva*) and consists of a state of unification through contiguity, would also not exist if everything were momentary.

The meaning is that it is established. Now, one might object: "Since the production of moments occurring in a temporal sequence—through the relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*)—is what is designated as a 'continuum' (*saṃtāna*), the aforementioned logical inconsistency does not apply. To this, he replies: "Past... For that [continuum] is not independent, since it is perceived only as residing in the members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*); nor do those members abide in the same place and time, because they are by nature subject to spontaneous disintegration. Therefore, there can be no continuum based upon them.

The meaning is that [the continuum] is not established. To refute the continuum by another method, he analyzes it into three alternatives, beginning with "from the members of the continuum" (saṃtānibhyaḥ). || 632 || 633 ||
In the case of non-difference, there is the consequence of impermanence; in the case of difference, the status of being stable is compromised.
Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect would not be established for you as you intend it to be. || 634 ||

He states the fault in the position of non-difference: "If there were non-difference. The meaning is that if there were non-difference between the momentary [entities] and the continuum (*saṃtati*), the continuum itself would be momentary;

and if there were non-difference between the persisting [entities] and the continuum, the members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*) themselves would be persistent. He refutes the second [position]: "It would be enduring.
Like the members of the continuum, the continuum itself would be independent and ultimately real; and the continuum of a transmigrating being would be a momentary continuum.

The meaning of "non-release" (*amukti*) is that [the self] would exist as something fixed by way of being distinct [from its states]. He states another fault common to both positions with the words "kārya... and so on.
You maintain that there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect among the members of a continuum (*saṃtānin*) that are situated within a single continuum. As it has been said:
"And a continuum is merely the arising of preceding and succeeding moments in the form of a direct relationship between material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*). This...

The meaning is that [the continuity] would not be established if there were a difference between the members of a continuum (*saṃtānin*) and other continua, because it would then be impossible for them to ascend into a single continuum; nor would it be established even if there were no difference, because in that case the continuum and its members would simply not exist at all. || 634 ||
Furthermore, even for one whose nature is both different and non-different, this is not tenable due to contradiction.
Furthermore, for the Jaina, the destruction of his own established doctrine is not tenable.

He states the third [objection]: "bhinnetyādi. Having raised the doubt that there is no proof for the contradiction between difference and non-difference in a single locus, he states another defect indicated by the word "ca" (and): "svasiddhāntasyeti. Furthermore, if that which is different from something else were non-different from it, then—given the identity of the causal factors (*prayojaka*)—difference and non-difference would result in identity; if they were different, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of further difference and non-difference in that case as well. Thus he says.
And not [so]. || 639 ||
If one conceives of the possessors of the continuum as being distinct from their own continuum, [then...]
The faults to be expressed should be applied accordingly, in accordance with the meaning of the continuum.

Having refuted the difference and other [attributes] of the continuum from the members of the continuum, he now refutes the difference and other [attributes] of the members of the continuum from that [continuum]. Regarding the phrase "of the members of the continuum": following the faults stated for the positions of difference and so forth regarding the referent of the word "continuum" as distinct from the members of the continuum, the faults must likewise be stated as applicable to the positions of difference and so forth regarding the members of the continuum as distinct from the continuum; for if there were difference, it would entail the consequence of the continuum's independence, and if there were non-difference...
The meaning is that if there were both difference and non-difference, there would be a loss of momentariness and so forth, which would contradict the established tenet. || 636 ||
If the position is that it is inexpressible, do not say so; for even that is impossible.
For if one imagines it to have the nature of being other, not other, or both, it is indeed non-existent.
He raises an objection, suggesting that since the nature of the continuum (*saṃtāna*) is inexpressible, the aforementioned fault does not apply: "It is inexpressible.

He analyzes this inexpressibility of the continuum as being either a property (*dharma*) or its very essence (*svarūpa*). Even regarding the first case, he offers two alternatives: is it the unfitness to be spoken, or the mere absence of expressibility? Refuting the first, he says: "Not so. For you do not accept that the continuum is inexpressible [in the sense of being] neither different nor non-different.
The meaning is that, even for that [continuum], it is untenable according to your own position. He refutes the second alternative by stating "anyeti" (as something else).

That is to say, among the three possibilities—that the continuum is to be described as distinct from its constituent moments, non-distinct, or both distinct and non-distinct—not one is tenable. || 6.37 ||

Whether it is expressible or inexpressible, let it be told why this is so.

Furthermore, when it is asked whether the nature of the continuum (*saṃtāna*) is expressible or inexpressible, and for what purpose it is postulated, he says "it is expressible" (*vācyam*). If it is argued that the continuum (saṃtāna) is what is being explained, then it would be a real entity (vastu), like the members of the continuum; for that which is not a real entity cannot be the object of cognition—this is the meaning. || 640 ||
Furthermore, in your position, no entity whatsoever is admitted to be inexpressible.
If you assert non-existence regarding that matter, what further discussion can there be? (641)

If you accept that such inexpressibility is its very nature, [then...]

Having set aside the position on the side of *dharma*, he states another position: "that form" (*tadrūpam*). He refutes that with: "not so" (*naivam*).

He provides the reason for its being common [to both sides] with: "of the person (*pudgala*) and so forth. The meaning is: because you yourself accept the inexpressibility of external objects such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like. || 642 ||

Anticipating the objection that the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of chariots and other such things is observed and thus difficult to deny, he says: "momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatvam*). This means: by that [nature] which consists in being causally efficient. For causal efficiency does not belong to the continuum (*saṃtāna*), since that has been refuted; nor does it belong to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), because that [efficiency] belongs to the conventional itself.

If [the continuum] exists as a real entity (*sattva*), it would contradict its being a continuum (*saṃtānin*) because it would possess the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*); if it does not exist, it is impossible for it to possess that [nature] just like a continuum. Furthermore, no other mode [of existence] is accepted, and it has already been stated that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) does not reside in continua.

Therefore, the point is that if [things] were to perform causal efficiency, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*) would not apply to things such as chariots. By the phrase "momentariness and so forth" (*kṣaṇikatvādi*), the arising [of things] through a continuum is expressed. (651)
Furthermore, destruction and arising are considered to be simultaneous, like the two ends of a balance scale.
Because of the attachment to the absence of cause and effect, this is not tenable. || 652 ||

It was stated that the inference of momentariness is contradicted by the impossibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for things such as chariots—which are [alleged to be] momentary—based on the analogy of lamps and the like; now, he restates the favorable argument (*tarka*) put forward by the opponent regarding the inference of momentariness, namely, "because [something] arises without having destroyed [its predecessor]. [He says: "One... Since we observe the emergence of a sprout from a seed that has been destroyed, there is the destruction of the preceding moment and the arising of the subsequent moment.

The meaning is that some hold the view that because cause and effect are seen to exist at the same time, they must be momentary; for a sprout does not arise while the seed remains, but rather from the seed once it has perished—this is what is meant by "because of that observation. He refutes this with the phrase "like the ends of a balance. Just as when one end of a balance rises, the other falls simultaneously. Why is that? || 654 ||
Furthermore, there could be no relationship of cause and effect between those two if they existed at the same time.
Because both of those have been accepted by you, who are a nihilist.

Furthermore, he says "na ca" (nor indeed), meaning that the absence of the relation of cause and effect between two things existing at the same time is not something we need to prove, as it is already accepted by you as well.

The construction is as follows: there can be no relation of cause and effect between those two—the seed and the sprout—if they exist at one and the same time; for you, a nihilist (*vaināśika*), accept their existence in a single moment, and thus the absence of causal efficiency is as much your own position as it is ours, just like the case of [simultaneous] horns. || 655 ||
The activity of a Buddha is neither a transformation nor something to be undertaken, because it is impossible [to produce such a result].
In the Sāṃkhya doctrine, there is absolute difference between the modification and the material cause; in the theory of new production (ārambha), it is likewise. || 656 ||

Furthermore, having raised the alternatives as to whether [the effect] is something to be produced (*kārya*) or a transformation (*pariṇāma*), he declares the untenability of both positions with the words beginning "No" (*na*).

The term "Buddhist" (*bauddha*) is used to address the opponent; or else, it refers to the "effect" (*kārya*) favored by the Buddhist. He establishes its impossibility with the word "transformation" (*vikāra*). || 696 ||
Having accomplished his purpose through the existence of sentient beings, he has reached the finality within another stream of existence.
Nor does it transform itself like clay [into] a jar, a pillar, or the like. (657)

If it is argued that the absolute difference between cause and effect is indeed accepted, he says in response: "Because of existence" (*sattvāt*). For a jar, having emerged from the jar-series denoted by the word "existence," would certainly remain as something absolutely distinct from its own preceding cause—the jar belonging to that same series—just like a cloth or other objects; consequently, it would abide in another series denotable by the word "existent. And therefore, [there would be] an absolute [difference] between cause and effect.

The meaning is that if there were difference, the very existence of that [identity] would be untenable. Let it be, then, the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*); to that he says: "Nor even... It is not tenable.

For while clay may undergo transformation because it possesses parts, consciousness cannot undergo transformation in that same way as it is partless; furthermore, there is a disparity due to the momentariness [of the former], whereas Brahman is not momentary—this is the meaning. || 65.7 ||
Nor does it undertake an action before it, like a potter.
Because of the non-existence [of such entities], duality does not exist for you, just like the positions of the Sāṃkhya and the Kāṇāda.

"In that case," [the opponent might argue], "there will be a theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*), and because there is no absolute difference [between cause and effect], the impossibility of the relation of cause and effect does not follow—as it is established in the case of the potter and the jar. To this he says: "Nor even... Just as a potter, by virtue of the causal complex consisting of clay and so forth, initiates the production of a jar and the like due to his own persistence, a momentary entity cannot initiate an effect even through the power of auxiliary causes, because of the impossibility of its connection with them at the moment of the effect.

The sense is that because the effect itself is non-existent (*asat*), it is admitted to be likewise [non-existent] as its material cause; thus, the status of being an "originated" entity (*ārabhyatva*) is not established. He states a common *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of one's own tenets) regarding both positions: "Not both. || 658 ||
Thus, thousands of such refutations should be stated here.
Nor is there the existence of valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), since everything is merely consciousness.
Concluding the collection of faults stated regarding the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*), he indicates the existence of further defects with the words "and so forth" (*ityādi*).

As for what is said—that "whatever exists is momentary"—that is incorrect, because existence (*sattva*) as a universal (*sāmānya*) is not admitted; because the apprehension of a single referent among distinct things is accepted as being an error (*bhrama*);

and because, since individual essences (*svarūpa*) are excluded [from one another], there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) that could be inclusive (*anugama*). Furthermore, an inclusive entity is undesirable for the same reasons stated previously. Nor is there an object...

Existence (*sattva*) consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). Since existence is not established even in the absence of such causal efficiency, and since the attainment of causal efficiency is impossible apart from the relation of cause and effect—a relation which has already been refuted—furthermore, if existence were distinct from the momentary nature of things, it would entail permanence; if it were non-distinct, there could be no relationship of pervader and pervaded between momentariness and existence. And if momentariness were the very essence of being, then everything would be momentary.

The term "existence" (*bhāva*) is a synonym for "dharma," whether there be difference or non-difference; thus, the non-establishment of its existence constitutes such refutations as are indicated by the word "etcetera.

As for the claim that the Vedas are not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nor are they authorless or eternal, and that the relationship [between word and meaning] is merely a convention (*saṃketa*), that is not so, because it has been countered in the definition of valid knowledge—this is what is intended when he says, "refutations. Furthermore, existence is momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

Regarding whether a thing is capable or incapable of performing its own effect at its own moment: in the first case, because delay is impossible, there would have to be a succession of effects at that very moment. In the second case, the effect could never arise, because the thing itself is non-existent at the second moment. Furthermore, a momentary entity does not begin its effect at the time of the presence of auxiliary causes (sahakārin) as a stable entity might; for it does not persist until the time of their presence. Moreover, regarding the auxiliary causes—

In that case, do they assist [the cause] or not? If it is the former, is the assistance rendered by them distinct from the cause or not? If it is distinct, then its momentariness is lost upon its connection [with the cause]; if there is no connection, the auxiliary causes are rendered useless. By this, the argument that they provide no assistance is refuted. If there is non-distinction, then since the assistance would be produced by the cause itself, the status of being an auxiliary cause becomes untenable. Although many such objections could be raised here, they have not been set forth.

"And not," because in the Yogācāra view, since everything is nothing but cognition, there is an absence of any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) distinct from it, nor [is there any distinction] within a single [cognition].
The meaning is that because there is a contradiction regarding the status of being both the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge, that doctrine is untenable. || 619 ||

The meaning is that since those two [the self and the cognition] are established as distinct, and because there is no difference in their nature, the aforementioned contradiction would arise even when only one of them exists; therefore, the position of the Mīmāṃsakas is not proven. He refutes the claim that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is an error caused by similarity by means of refuting its cause: "This is not..."
Thus it is said. || 664 ||
Furthermore, similarity is impossible because everything is momentary.
Nor is there anyone who perceives multiple objects simultaneously; thus, similarity would not exist before you.

In that view, he establishes the impossibility of similarity. Regarding the word "sādṛśya" (similarity): for similarity consists in the connection with a plurality of common parts; however, if everything were momentary, its establishment would not be possible, because moments, being momentary, are absolutely distinct from one another—this is the meaning. Having stated its impossibility, he states the impossibility of its cognition: "Nor... (nāpi). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "similarity would have to be perceptible. || 665 ||
And because of similarity, there is no perception such as "this is that very same thing" with respect to hair and so forth.
Because the genus "hair" and so forth is unitary, this cognition is based upon that [genus].
He refutes the example with the words "due to similarity" (sādṛśyāt). To the question, "How then is there recognition (pratyabhijñā) in that case?", he replies: "hair, etc. (keśādi). || 666 ||
For when these [words] have arisen after being elided, there can be no [application of grammatical rules] without relying upon their genus (*jāti*).
The notion that "these are indeed those" arises from a cause of manifestation for someone.
"Why should this cognition not have the individual (vyakti) as its cause rather than the genus (jāti) as its cause? To this he says: "Not indeed" (na hi).

Since the multiplicity of individual instances such as hairs is established by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika), recognition cannot be produced by the individual, as that would contradict [the evidence]; such is the meaning. || 667 ||
For when there is no error regarding hair and so forth, that which is similar [to it] is then [the object].
The thought arises that "these hairs are similar to those hairs in front. || 668 ||

Furthermore, is recognition [of identity] due to similarity for one who is mistaken, or for one who is not mistaken? It is not the first, because it is not accepted; nor is it the second, as he says: "For one who is not mistaken. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that there is no disagreement among all authorities regarding the point stated. || 668 ||
The thought "these are those very same ones" arises, but it does not arise for anyone [regarding the self].
Therefore, recognition is held to have the mark of being of a single birth.

Now, [the author] says "ta eva" (those very same) because, due to similarity, even one who is not mistaken sometimes has the cognition of identity. To the question, "How can the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) observed even in the case of non-mistaken [perception] regarding hair and so forth be refuted?", he replies with "eketyādi" (beginning with 'one').
Therefore, the meaning of the word is the impossibility of [recognition] being based on the individual (*vyakti*). || 669 ||
And that [cognition] which is direct perception has "this very thing" as its object.
On the following day, that which was unrighteous arises manifestly as it is being scraped away.

He states the disparity with the illustrative example: "And [it is] perception" (*pratyakṣaṃ ca*). The meaning is that this very perception—namely, "this is that same [thing]"—arises by directly taking as its object things such as a jar, which serve as the substratum for the action and are characterized by the properties of being perceptible and imperceptible; this constitutes the disparity. || 670 ||
"This is that very same thing"—this experience is firm.
This direct perception is not sublated by any inference.

Anticipating the objection that perception is erroneous because it is sublated by the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), he says: "This very... [referring to] the fire...

The point is that, just as in the case of the inference of [the absence of] coldness, an inference of momentariness does not arise when it contradicts perception. He states the opposite—that which sublates and that which is sublated—in the verse beginning with "perception. || 671 ||
For when there is a contradiction with direct perception, the inferential mark (liṅga) becomes a fallacy.
Therefore, there is no sublation of perception by means of inference.

For the experience of heat is not sublated by the inference of coldness in the case of fire; the same applies here as well. He states the reason for this with the words "by perception. The sense is that having a subject matter not contradicted [by a stronger means of knowledge] is also a constituent factor of inference. Having taken up what was stated, he declares the final conclusion with the words "since... (672).
Furthermore, for one who has previously recognized a jar, when looking at another jar [of the same kind], [there occurs]...
A cognition of similarity is logical, but such a cognition does not occur with respect to momentary entities.

While explaining the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "And because the cognition of similarity is untenable," he restates what was said under the section "Nor is there one who perceives multiple objects," with the intention of adding further detail: "vijñāteti" (673).
Even if one has seen it previously, one should remain [in that state] until the next vision occurs.
And even if it is accepted [by you] that this is for the purpose of establishing the cognition of similarity, || 674 ||
Thus, the cognition of similarity is established, but momentariness is destroyed.
For the Self, which is the awakening to its own essential nature alone, there is neither destruction nor arising.
One recognizes knowledge, but not another [knowledge], because it has been destroyed.
The two [properties] you desire—similarity and momentariness—are not established. || 676 ||

He shows what is intended as being additional [to the previous argument], starting with the words "Previously" (*pūrvam*). Having restated the opponent's position, he states the fault of the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*).

Regarding the phrase "even if this is accepted" (*ityabhyupagame 'pi*): the meaning is that even if there were a persistence [of the self] from the time of perceiving a prior object up until the time of perceiving a future object.

Therefore, the memory-cognition (*smārtajñāna*) is exhausted by the thought "that very thing," and the present cognition is exhausted by the thought "this very thing"; consequently, the single cognition [would have to grasp both] "that" and "this similarity."

If it is argued that there is no cognition [of these], then the similarity and momentariness [of things] would remain unestablished; thus he says: "In its own nature" (*svarūpa*). Because cognition is self-luminous, it cannot establish even its own birth and destruction, nor can it establish similarity, since that pertains to other objects and is itself seized by destruction. Therefore, the meaning is that its similarity and so forth remain unestablished. || 674 || 679 || 676 ||
And memory is not [the same as] experience, in the form "this is that very thing."
For experience indeed delineates an object, like [the perception of] a blue or red lotus and so forth. (677)

In the view of the opponent (*paramata*), since similarity and so forth are unestablished, it is impossible for the perception "this is that very same thing" to be an error caused by similarity; therefore, it is established by the force of that [perception] that the object is stable. Now, [the opponent might argue]: the cognition "this is that very same thing" is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), but rather a memory (*smṛti*) because its object has been previously experienced; therefore, stability is not established from it. To this, he says: "And not... The reason for this is stated as: "Because of experience" (*anubhūtitah*). He establishes this reason as follows:
