Regarding the word "vastu" (the object): alternatively, since "from experience" (*anubhūtitah*) was made the reason for its being immediate (*aparokṣatva*), he now states the resulting conclusion—that this very immediacy of experience establishes its permanence. He says "vastu. He clarifies that this [cognition] is an experience by saying "nīla" (blue). Just as the perceptual cognition (*abhijñāna*) "this is a blue lotus" is an experience, so too is the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) "this is that very same thing" an experience, because there is no difference in their essential nature.
The meaning is that it indeed becomes an establisher of the objective reality. || 677 ||
The perception "this is that very same thing" is like the experience of a blue lotus.
Because it determines an object not previously known, this [cognition] cannot be memory. || 678 ||

Experience is not a doubtful cognition because its object is not already known, unlike [the case of] "that" and "this," for identity characterized by "that-ness" and "this-ness" is not known even when "that-ness" is known;
thus, the cognition "this is that very same thing" is established as accomplishing the desired goal. He confirms this stated point through inference: "The blue lotus...
Having established that the aforementioned cognition is a proof by virtue of being an experience, he states the conclusion: "Memory... (678)
Because their forms are mutually distinct, similarity is difficult to establish here.
In the cognition "this is that very same thing," it is like the case of the sky and the peacock.
As for the argument that this [cognition] is not a means of valid knowledge because it is false due to its dependence on similarity (*sādṛśya*), he replies with the word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*).
The meaning is that there is absolute dissimilarity due to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). The connection is as follows: it is difficult to maintain that similarity is the cause in this cognition.
For indeed, there is no similarity whatsoever between the sky and a mongoose; likewise, in the cognition "this is that very same thing," [there is no such basis].

The meaning is that it is impossible to establish a similarity that serves as a basis for identification between two objects characterized by "that-ness" and "this-ness," because they are distinct due to their inherent transience. || 679 ||
Of those things which are distinct from one another by way of their uncommon forms.
By what cause could there be similarity among you moments, which are themselves momentary? (680)
He elaborates upon the impossibility of similarity among momentary entities: "asādhāraṇa" (unique), etc. [Verse 680].
Therefore, the claim that "this object is similar to that" is also not logically tenable.
The designation of entities [occurs] because they are by their very nature momentary. || 681 ||
He states another fault in the opponent's position with the words "by that" (*tena*). The reason for this is given by "of the categories of things" (*padārthānām*).
The meaning is that, because things are by their very nature momentary and thus distinct from one another, they cannot serve as the basis for similarity. || 681 ||
"It was seen" or "I saw it"—neither of these is tenable.
Designation [occurs] by way of intrinsic nature, because the designator has perished.
In that very context, he states the impossibility of any other designation: "This," [etc. (682).
Because there is no moment of designation and because it is completely exhausted by the very act of prior perception.
Since there is no subsequent connection, how could there be a designator? || 683 ||
Designation occurs even without direct contact with objects that are past or future.
If one accepts its persistence in that state, its momentariness is destroyed. (684) [Note: Variant readings: 1. *rāṃkṣānu*; 2. *kṣitasyaikyaṃ*]

He clarifies what was stated based on the commentary beginning with "of one who has seen" (*dṛṣṭavataḥ*). [The verse begins with] "vyapadeśa" (designation). The reason for this is [stated in] "pūrva" (prior).
If it is argued that the seer situated there may be connected to the moment of designation by means of the prior moment, he says "no," [beginning with] "uttara" (subsequent).

The word "of the preceding moment" is to be understood as the ellipsis. To the question, "What would happen even if the designator were not connected to the moment of designation? he says: "Of the designator. [Objection:
"Then let the designator be permanent. [Reply: He says "that," meaning it is not so. || 683 || 684 ||
And just as one born blind cannot describe anything here without having seen it, so it is with this.
And no one here is capable of producing the cognition of similarity. (685)

Anticipating the objection that a single consciousness belonging to a continuum (*saṃtati*) is capable of designating [an object] even though it has not itself seen it—and thus, since the designator is simply the seer, there is no fault in the designation because of this lack of restriction—the author says: "The genus" (*jāti*). If it is argued that even for one who is not a seer, there might be a designation accompanied by a cognition of similarity (*sādṛśya-pratyaya*), he says: "Similarity" (*sādṛśya*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) in both cases.
By the word "anyone" (kaścit), one who is devoid of both types of prior observation is intended. || 685 ||
This tradition of the blind is established due to the absence of any valid means of cognition.
The tenet of the Red-robed ones [Sautrāntikas] is likewise established through their own admission.

He concludes the result [of the argument] with the words "pramāṇa" (valid means of knowledge). Furthermore, he states that even the Buddha himself considers his own doctrine to be rejectable because it lacks validity, using the word "tathā" (thus). The meaning of this is as follows: for the Buddha, due to his adherence to contradictory doctrines, [the Veda is accepted].

Having turned his back on the world and thrown it into confusion, he created this path in order to cast it down into the lower realms: the doctrine of external objects, the doctrine of pure consciousness as the seed of all sounds, and the doctrine of universal emptiness. Because these mutually contradictory meanings are thus established, and because he himself has admitted that his own system lacks authoritative validity and is intended merely for the delusion of those to be discarded, its status as a blind tradition is beyond dispute. As he himself said:
“Alas, by whom have these treacherous demons of dogmatic tenets been bestowed upon a person born empty and unable to discern virtue from vice? (686)
At the time of cessation, it is not logical for the mind to possess the quality of being perfumed.
Because of momentariness and because of the lack of connection, it is like the cognition belonging to another continuum. || 687 ||

Having already discussed the possibility of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) under the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), he now refutes the opponent’s claim that a perishing cognition, having infused a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of its own form and so forth into a subsequent cognition, then perishes. [The verse begins with] "nirodha" (cessation). The phrase "the state of being an infuser" (*vāsakatva*) implies "into a subsequent cognition. The example for the absence of a connection between a preceding cognition and a succeeding cognition is given as "in another continuum" (*saṃtānāntara*). This refers to a different mental stream.
The meaning is that there is an absence of mutual connection between the two cognitions, just as there is between two horns. || 687 ||
For you, there would be the fault of encountering what was not done, as well as the destruction of what was done.
Therefore, he who is the doer of actions experiences the fruit of those actions.

Having explained the commentary beginning with "And not... (*na ca*) for the purpose of showing that it is untenable to maintain that the preceding cognition perishes while the succeeding cognition perishes having been conditioned by it, he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "The acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*). [He says: "Not done... (*akṛta*...). [This refers to] the proponent of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*).

The meaning is that it is improper to assert that the agent alone is the enjoyer for those [who hold such views]. In order to eliminate these two defects, our desired [position of] a stable [self]—[is established]. To refute these two faults, our desired stable... [text continues].

He states the conclusion: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that when a permanent self (*ātman*)—who is both the agent of action and the enjoyer of its fruit—is established, there is no arrival of what was not earned (*akṛtābhyāgama*), no inconsistency in designations (*vyapadeśa*), and no lack of connection with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth; thus, everything is faultless. || 688 ||
But in whichever consciousness the latent impression of karma has been deposited, [in that very one it ripens].
The fruit arises in that very same continuum, just as redness [arises] in cotton. || 689 ||

One raises the objection that even in the absence of a permanent self (*sthāyyātman*), there is no such thing as "the arrival of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and so forth, by means of the verse beginning with *yasmin*. Just as when a cotton seed is sprinkled with the juice of lac and the like, redness persists in the sprout and other products arising from it— even though they are entirely different [from the seed]— so too,

according to the rule that the fruit of an action occurs in that very stream of consciousness (*vijñānasaṃtāna*) where the impression (*vāsanā*) produced by the performance of acts such as worshipping a shrine has been deposited.
The meaning is: from what [source] could there be the arrival of what was not done, and so forth? || 689 ||
Thus, even under this established doctrine, the undesirable consequence does not cease.
Because it does not exist at all apart from the possessor of the continuum. || 690 ||
He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "In this case... The phrase "of the acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and so forth is to be supplied as the remainder.

If one asks "How?", then he who asserts agency and enjoyership within that continuum (*saṃtāna*) must be questioned: is that [continuum] real or false? Regarding the first alternative, one must further analyze whether it is distinct from the members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*) or non-distinct from them. He refutes the first [possibility] with the words "The member of the continuum... In the case of distinction, there would be independence (*svātantrya*) and so forth.
The meaning is that the fault has already been stated. Therefore, the conclusion is that the position of exclusion (vyatireka) is not tenable. || 690 ||
However, the conditioned phenomena that constitute the continuum do exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Because they have mutual attachment, they are therefore not freed from these defects. || 691 ||

He states the second [objection]: "But as for the members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*). Although the members of the continuum exist in reality, they are nevertheless admitted to be of the nature of mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and to be fragile by their own nature. Thus, because there is no mutual connection among them and because there is no identity between them, agency and so forth cannot be established for the continuum as a single entity; consequently, the problem of "reaping what one has not sown" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and other such issues remains unresolved. This is the meaning. || 691 ||
If it is argued that a continuum is not accepted here because there is a lack of proof, [we reply: no.
In that case, a thesis is not established merely by the statement of defects.

He addresses the second [position] with the words "māna" (proof). Here, among those possessing a continuum (*saṃtānin*), a real continuum—whether as distinct or non-distinct—is not accepted, because there is a lack of proof for its existence; rather, it is accepted as conceptual (*kalpita*). The meaning is that by relying upon that [conceptual continuum], agency and enjoyership are established among the momentary members of the continuum. He refutes this with the words "doṣa" (fault): if the continuum is conceptual, then it is neither an agent nor an enjoyer.

Furthermore, because [the elements] are momentary, their production does not occur through a continuum; nor can their establishment be achieved in them by way of a continuum, since an imagined continuum is a non-entity.
Therefore, the meaning is that his own position is unestablished, because the Buddha himself has stated the faults of his own position and failed to state its virtues. || 692 ||
The perfuming by red and other colors is said to reside precisely within the cotton seed.
That very [cause] which performs its own form's function is not considered to be a "function-performer" with respect to that function. (693)

Regarding the statement, "Just as there is redness in the cotton," he says: "In the case of the cotton. That latent impression (*vāsanā*) of redness and so forth, which resides in the cotton seed and was cited as an example, is indeed stable; it produces its own form as an effect, such as the sprout and so on, and is not momentary.

The meaning is that since its status as a cause has been refuted, that which is seen to produce an effect cannot serve as an example for the relationship of cause and effect among momentary continua. || 693 ||
The mutual connection between moments is like that of the links of a chain or the rings of a bracelet.
Consequently, all [phenomena] such as the designation of similarity would be well-established. || 694 ||
If this is not the case, then that is not tenable, because it would entail the loss of momentariness.
Because the three moments are pervasively connected, like the links of a chain or the segments of a bracelet. (695)

Having established [the faults] such as the arrival of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), he raises an objection in order to avoid the previously mentioned impossibility of similarity (*sādṛśya*) and so forth: "Mutually" (*mithaḥ*).

Just as a connection is observed between the links called "bracelets" situated on a chain, and between the threads and so forth situated within a cloth and the like—even though they are mutually distinct—so too, despite the momentariness of entities, there exists a mutual relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) among those that exist in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior.

The meaning is that since [the continuity] is possible, the establishment of designations, similarity, recognition, and so forth is achieved, and thus the two faults— namely, the arrival of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and so on— are easily avoided. He refutes this by means of a *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of one's own tenets), saying "not that," thereby proving the loss of momentariness.

Regarding the term "moment" (*kṣaṇa*): the meaning is that just as a ring situated in the middle of a chain is connected to the preceding and succeeding rings, so too, when a central moment is connected to the preceding and succeeding moments, there is a pervasion of three moments, which results in the destruction of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). || 694 || 695 ||
Furthermore, the conventional usage of delimitation such as "mine" and "yours" would be undermined.
Because there is no mutual relationship between those moments. (696)

Anticipating the objection that there might then be no mutual relationship between them, he says: "My... (mameti). By the word "and" (ca), the previously mentioned conventional usage such as similarity and so forth is included. || 696 ||
And of pure knowledge, which consists solely of self-awareness.
Since no other [self] exists that is such, how could there be the experience of suffering and so forth? (697)

Regarding the claim that consciousness possesses the qualities of pleasure, pain, and so forth, he replies with the words "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*). Because of its purity and because there is no perceiver of its association [with such qualities], there is no influx of pain and the like into knowledge; furthermore, since self-cognition is admitted, it cannot establish those [qualities] within itself—this is the meaning. || 697 ||
Furthermore, it is not logical for cognition to possess a manifold nature.
Because its nature is purely transparent, it is like the fruit of a pomegranate or other such fruits. || 698 ||

One might object: "Is it not the case that the purity and singular nature of consciousness (*jñāna*) is unproven, since it is accepted as being the locus of various parts such as suffering, just like a pomegranate tree?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... Just as a fruit such as a pomegranate is experienced as possessing many flavors, so too, you do not admit that consciousness possesses various natures or parts such as suffering; for you accept its nature as being purely transparent, and [you hold that] in reality it does not possess parts such as suffering.
The meaning is "because of its occurrence. || 698 ||

And likewise, because it is an object of cognition and because it is experienced, it cannot be a mere part of consciousness.
Just as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth [are not perceived] in the same way that largeness, roundness, and other forms [are perceived]. (699)

In that very context, he states another reason: "By being an object of cognition" (*prameyatvena*). Whatever is an object of cognition is not a part of the cognition itself, just as a jar or the like [is not].

And suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth are objects of cognition; yet, even though they are objects of cognition, they do not consist of nothing but that [cognition] simply because they are parts of it—just as [the jar is not nothing but the cognition]. Thus it is.

The meaning is that when cognition exists, it is incapable of being overwhelmed by suffering and so forth; nor is there a deficiency in the probandum, because if [cognition] were a part of itself, its self-luminosity would be untenable. || 699 ||
All this is mere cognition; no object of cognition exists separately.
[This is established] through the example of cognitions such as those of one's own [dreaming state], and by means of reasons such as "being a cognition" (pratyayatva). || 700 ||

He challenges the example with the words "mere cognition" (*jñānamātra*). The meaning is that [the opponent's position] is untenable because it is established through inference as follows: whatever is cognition is devoid of an object distinct from itself, just like dream-cognition; and this [waking] cognition is likewise [cognition]; or, whatever is an external object is non-different from cognition, just like the object grasped in a dream; and this [waking] object is likewise [an object].
Thus, the claim that [the world] consists of forms such as "broad-chested" [Pṛthu] and so on, due to the absence of external objects, is incorrect. || 700 ||
First, there is a mutual distinction between the thesis, the reason, and the example.
Because it has the nature of mere cognition, it is not accepted by you. || 701 ||

Recalling what was stated previously—that if everything were merely cognition (*jñānamātra*), there would be no distinction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and other members of an inference, and thus no inference could arise—he refutes that view with the verse beginning "The proposition... (701).
Moreover, this position is contradicted by the means of valid cognition, namely direct perception.
Objects such as jars appear according to the differences of body and location. (702)
He states another defect: "And the thesis," etc. He clarifies the contradiction: "From the body," etc. (702).
And sensory cognition arises with respect to those very objects without error.
And your own perception is not admitted to be subject to the conceptualization of being either different or non-different. || 703 ||

If it is argued that perception does not contradict inference because it is erroneous, [the author] says "no," adding "and it is non-erroneous. The meaning is as follows: sensory cognition is non-erroneous due to its freedom from defects in its causes and sublation; furthermore, such cognition arises only with respect to objects distinct from the cognition itself, and thus it contradicts an inferential means of knowledge that is opposed to it. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that indeterminate perception, by grasping the non-difference between cognition and its object, supports the aforementioned inference? [The author continues: "Savi... [The sentence is incomplete in the source].

"Even though it grasps that distinction (*bheda*) which is conceptual (*kalpaka*), inference does not sublate perception because [the conceptual cognition] lacks validity; therefore, there is no contradiction of inference by perception.

To this, he says: "Distinct," etc. The meaning of this is as follows: First of all, that intended non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) [perception] does not exist for anyone—from cowherds, shepherds, to scholars—since every cognition arises as being colored by some word. Even if such [non-conceptual perception] were admitted, it [does not grasp] the distinction or non-distinction of its object.

Or, if it does apprehend [the object], it would result in the destruction of its non-conceptual nature; yet you do not accept that it is conceptual. Therefore, since the state of being "mere cognition" (vijñaptimātratā) is not established on the strength of that [apprehension], it cannot be a corroborator for that inference. || 703 ||
I see that which was not seen before, even though it stands at a distance;
such direct perception, being self-evident, is not sublated.

As for the claim that determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*), even though it apprehends difference, does not sublate inference because it is invalid, he says in response: "At a distance," etc. For there is no invalidity in determinate cognition, since there is no sublation of its validity; furthermore, perception itself is fourfold.

By asserting that [the scripture] possesses authority, one accepts it; therefore, the meaning is that because of its contradiction [with scripture], the non-arising of inference is established. || 704 ||
If it is argued that this consciousness is indeed of the nature of suffering alone;
How can it be your conceptualization that "it is pure because of separation from that"? (705)
Having established the example and restated the thesis, he states the fault: "duḥkhādi" (beginning with suffering), etc. || 709 ||
For it is held here that an object is pure when it is released from its conjunctions.
But when the intrinsic nature itself is liberated, what else remains? (706)

Anticipating the objection that "the establishment of purity is valid because it results from the separation from intrinsic nature (svabhāva)," he says: "Since... The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, there is no separation from intrinsic nature. He states the fault in the contrary case [of separation]: "Of the essential form (svarūpa)... The meaning is: if the intrinsic nature were destroyed, the entity itself would not exist; so how could the establishment of purity occur? || 706 ||
When its inherent qualities are destroyed, there remains only the adventitious nature of passion and the like.
And as for the statement that was uttered: "She was seen among the flowers. (707)

He restates the position that even though whiteness and other qualities are inherent in a flower, they disappear when the substance that is the cause of the flower is processed by another substance, and redness and so forth arise; likewise, through the power of the fourfold cultivation, suffering and other such things which are inherent in knowledge itself are separated from it, and purity arises. [The author] says "inherent," referring to the example cited of cotton and so forth.
The meaning is that this has been indicated here by the phrase "just as there is redness. || 707 ||
That was previously refuted correctly, both by way of disjunction and by way of the logical mark (liṅga).
Its state of having been preceded by conjunction is inferred, as in the case of two rams.

If it is argued that the Self exists in the form of an agent and so forth, [the author] says "it is not so," because the separation from its own nature has already been refuted while its essential nature remains established. Anticipating the objection as to why such a perception is untenable, he provides a counter-example to refute it: "separation..."

Diti [replies]: Just as the separation of two rams is preceded by their conjunction, so too the fact that the separation of the flower and its quality is preceded by a connection is understood from that very separation. For the quality is not the inherent nature (svabhāva) of the flower, because even while the flower exists, the quality is seen to depart; thus, in the case of the departure of an inherent nature, this is not a valid example. This is the meaning. || 708 ||
Or, due to being covered by another substance, even that which is innate may not be seen.
Because, upon the exhaustion of that substance, there is simultaneous vision as before. || 709 ||
Or, even if the flower possesses an inherent quality of whiteness, that is not an example for the case where there is a departure from its own nature;

thus he says: "By another substance" (*dravyāntara*). Although the whiteness of the flower is inherent, its non-perception is due to its being covered by another substance, not because of its non-existence; here he states the reason: "By that substance" (*taddravya*). For it is observed that when the dye of turmeric or other substances on cloth and such things is removed, [the original color reappears].
The sense is that it was previously white. || 709 ||

1506 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:
Such a reality has already been established through inference.
Nor is any fault whatsoever perceived therein in the case of inference. (716)

Anticipating the objection that the immutable, unattached, non-dual Self is unestablished because there is no means of knowledge (māna) for it, and that it cannot be established through scripture (āgama) due to disputes regarding its authority, he says:

"By inference" (anumānena). The meaning is that the aforementioned reality has been established in the *Brāhmaṇas* and other texts by the following inference: "The subject of dispute, namely worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), is caused by an uncomposite light, because it is a transaction, like transactions performed by the sun and so forth. Thus, the reality is proven.

Anticipating the objection as to how the stated inference establishes the stated reality, he says "na ca" (and not), meaning that it is because [the inference] is free from defects. The meaning of the rest is that defects of inference such as the sword [of contradiction] and so forth, as well as non-concomitance (*ananugama*) and the like, cannot even be suspected, since they have been refuted in the examination of the Lokāyata. The word "tatra" refers to the inference under discussion. || 716 ||
Furthermore, because they are perceived together, and because there is the impression [of them being so], the cognition perceives them as one.
In that case, there is no possibility of inference, for there would be no deviation [of the reason from the probandum]. || 717 ||

Anticipating the objection that the faultlessness of this inference might not be discernible—since it is possible for a fault to exist even when it is not perceived—the author states its definition in order to show that it is indeed faultless because it conforms to the characteristics of inference. He says: "Together" (*saha*). From the perception of the conjunction between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises; and subsequently, from the sight of one of those two, namely the pervaded, at a later time, [the memory] is awakened.

When the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*) is unknown, the cognition that arises [regarding it] is inference (*anumā*). And that is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) provided there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) from the pervader. For it has been said:
"In this context, the relationship intended as 'pervasion' (*vyāpti*) is that of the property of the mark (*liṅga*) with the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*)."
The pervaded is held to be the indicator, and the pervader is held to be the indicated.
Whatever may be equal to or even inferior to another in terms of space and time, that is the pervaded (vyāpya);
the other is its pervader (vyāpaka), whether it be equal to or superior to it.
"Therefore, when the pervaded object is apprehended, its pervader is also apprehended.

And this is the case even in the aforementioned inference: for one who possesses the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the simultaneous perception of the pervaded and the pervader, there arises at another time a cognition of the non-proximate pervader from the sight of the pervaded; and yet, there is no presence of obstacles such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
The meaning is that pride arises from that [attainment] due to its being a fault. || 717 ||
But surely, only an invariable relation can be a means of cognition?
It is not [established] merely by simultaneous perception, as in the case of a father and his son. (718)

If it is argued that there is the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case, [the author] replies, "No. By saying this, he has stated that the capacity to indicate (*gamakatva*) belongs to non-deviation; the Śākyan, unable to tolerate this and wishing to assert that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth possess the capacity to indicate, raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). Therein, first, he restates the intention of the proponent (*siddhāntin*): "Non-deviating" (*avyabhicārī*). This refers to the non-deviation of the pervaded (*vyāpya*), such as smoke, together with the pervader (*vyāpaka*), such as fire.

The non-deviant concomitant relation (*sāhacarya-sambandha*) is the indicator; for it has been stated that "among the properties observed in a pervasion (*vyāpti*), some property is the determinant (*prayojaka*). And that non-deviation is not established by mere simultaneous perception once (*sakṛt-sahopalambha-mātra*), as in the case of father and son, or the eye and form.

For one who has seen [the two] together once, whether with a disciple or a teacher, the cognition of one does not arise upon seeing the other; for there is also the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Because [the relationship] arises thus elsewhere as well, since non-deviation is not established by mere co-perception alone, the meaning is that the negative concomitance (vyatireka)—namely, the absence of smoke when fire is absent—must also be known, just like the positive concomitance (anvaya). || 718 ||
Let it be so; however, it is not possible [to establish certainty], for there is deviation within its own domain.
For when suspicion has arisen regarding the object of perception, deviation is indeed invoked.

Anticipating the objection that "the subject under dispute is perceptible to someone because it is an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), like a jar"—since in this case the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone is accepted as the means of proof and thus the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is rendered superfluous—the author says: "Let it be so. If it is argued that no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) from the pervader (*vyāpaka*) can be suspected within the scope of inference, then, according to your own view, in the case of a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*), the positive concomitance alone would indeed possess the power of proof.

Nevertheless, in other types of inference, mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone does not suffice as such; for those persons who harbor doubts regarding the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) within the pervader (*vyāpaka*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) must also be sought in order to dispel those doubts. Thus, both positive and negative concomitances must be required.

This is because the Buddhists have stated that in order to ascertain the very existence of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), one must ascertain its presence only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its absolute absence in the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*).
This is the meaning. By the word "hi" (for/indeed), the statement of another regarding the point already stated is illuminated. || 719 ||
But that [certainty] arises everywhere merely from simultaneous perception. Our doubt regarding the object of cognition follows from the observation of deviation. (720)

One might object: "For one who possesses the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) from observing positive concomitance (*anvaya*), even the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) does not arise; therefore, the search for negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is useless. Anticipating this, he says: "Together" (*saha*). The meaning is that even when positive concomitance is perceived between a teacher and a disciple, etc., deviation is still observed.

By the word "only" (*mātra*), the observation of negative concomitance is excluded. This refers to all cases of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Let it be granted that there is deviation—

"What is the loss [incurred] by the suspicion of deviation (*cāraśaṅkā*)? To this he says: *dhiyaḥ*. This is its meaning: regarding the pervader (*vyāpaka*) within the domain of inference, the suspicion that arises in us—following upon the possibility of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) deviating—is an obstacle to [the pervader’s] being a prover (*gamakatva*). "As long as the absence of deviation (*avyatirekitva*) is suspected even to the extent of a hundredth part..."
This is according to the principle: "How can there be any power of movement for a cause that belongs to the opposing side? ||720||
Therefore, one should exert effort to remove that apprehension.
The investigation into the absence of that cause by means of the absence of the probandum. || 721 ||

He states the resulting conclusion: "If the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is a defect, then for its removal, the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) must be known through the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Regarding the phrase "that suspicion" (*tadāśaṅkā*), he says "with effort" (*prayatnataḥ*) in order to express that even when the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has been ascertained in some instances, one must remain diligent in order to determine it within the general class (*sāmānya-upādhi*) across all individual instances (*vyakti*). || 721 ||
Explain how there can be an absence of the reason when there is an absence of the probandum.

Regarding the statement "the *svedanī* [is] in the feminine": in that case, when a nearby clod of earth or similar object is not perceived despite being perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*), one would—according to your view—cognize the absence of fire (the probandum) and thereby cognize the absence of smoke. However, this is not accepted by you, because the absence of smoke is just as easily known as the absence of fire in the clod of earth and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning is that the absence of fire, established through the non-perception of a perceptible object, cannot serve as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the absence of smoke. || 723 ||
If the absence of the probandum is asserted regarding that which falls within the scope of direct perception, [then there is a contradiction].
Since it is established by perception itself, inference would thus be in vain. || 724 ||

The proponent of the view that absence is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāvavādin*) raises an objection: "In the case of a nearby clod of earth and so forth, the absence of the pervader, fire, is not known through non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*), but rather through direct perception.

[The author] refutes this, stating "because it is already established": since at that time the absence of smoke in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (fire) is also directly perceived, the inference of the absence of smoke by means of the mark (liṅga) of the absence of the probandum is redundant. || 724 ||
For it is impossible to perceive [the object] in a location such as a mountain plateau.
Let it not be that smoke could ever arise even in the absence of fire and so forth.

[The author] sets aside another objection [regarding] "on the plateau, etc. If one were to know the absence of fire merely through non-perception and thereby cognize the absence of smoke, then—since it is impossible to perceive the pervading fire on a remote mountain slope—the certainty of its absence would have to arise from that mere non-perception;
yet the absence of smoke could not be inferred by that means, because smoke is directly perceived in the upper region.

The meaning is this: since the presence of smoke and other such pervaded (vyāpya) phenomena might occasionally occur even in the absence of fire and other such pervaders (vyāpaka), one should not conclude that there is knowledge of the absence of the pervader based on mere non-perception (anupalabdhi). Because it is stated that the ground near the base of a mountain is the "upatyakā" and the ground above is the "adhityakā," it should be understood that "adhityakā" refers to the upper terrain of the mountain. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the "upatyakā" is included. Indeed, it is not from mere non-perception...
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that [the absence of fear] would follow as a consequence because there is no distinction in the cognition [of the object]. || 725 ||
If this is so, then positive concomitance (anvaya) would also not be established here; how then [is it possible]?
Otherwise, if indeed there were the presence of fire in the absence of smoke, [it would follow that everything could be proven from anything].

This means that in a remote location where the concomitance of smoke and fire is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—

The meaning is that it is not possible to ascertain with certainty that "fire must exist there" because the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has not been grasped. Now, if one sees smoke in the space above and thereby achieves the certainty that "there is fire here," he says: "Smoke... For this perception of smoke deviates from fire, because it is a perception of a specific kind of smoke, like the sight of smoke resting on a clod of earth or similar objects; therefore, [the conclusion] cannot be reached through what is merely perceived.

The meaning is that it is not possible to infer the existence of fire by means of smoke, because the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are difficult to ascertain. || 727 || 728 ||
First, let him who knows the true nature of the characteristics of the *liṅga* speak on this matter.
What object is inferred by you here through such signs as smoke? (729)

Having refuted the means of cognition known as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he now analyzes [the object] in order to refute the object of cognition itself. "First of all," etc. Here, "here" refers to the domain of inference; "in this place" refers to the locus (*dharmin*), such as a mountain and so forth. The meaning of the alternative options is: is fire the object to be inferred, or is it a specific location such as a mountain, or is it the relationship between the two, or is it merely that [relationship] alone? || 729 ||
Neither fire [is the cause], because it is already established; nor is location, because it too is already established.
Nor can there be a mere relationship [between them], for the very reason already stated.

"It is not the first," he says: "not fire. "It is not the second," he says: "nor even. Intending that the third [option] is untenable because a relation cannot be easily described as being either different from or non-different from its two relata, he replies regarding the fourth: "nor is it. The ellipsis is "it would be inferable. As has been stated, since the cause is already established, there is the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatva*). || 730 ||
Therefore, that which is called inference is not at all accepted as a valid means of knowledge when subjected to logical scrutiny.
Since [the objection] "because of the absence of a means" has been reached, the following response is provided here. || 731 ||

He concludes by summarizing the result regarding the difficulty of defining the signified (*gamyaka*) and the signifier (*gamaka*). "Therefore" (*tasmāt*): the absence of the object of cognition (*meyābhāva*) is an indicator for the absence of the signifier (*gamakābhāva*). Since the validity of inference is untenable due to the absence of the signified and signifier as intended by the proponent, [inference] does not possess the nature of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

He concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, that the capacity for making known (*gamakatva*) and being made known (*gamyatva*) of effects occurs through a three-featured reason (*trirūpa-hetu*), whether that [object] be something inherently perishable, or an exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), or the possessor of that [exclusion]—with the words "Thus, this being the case" (*iti prāpte*). He introduces the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "here" (*atra*). ||731||
The form "avasitum" is a Vedic usage (chāndasa) for "avasātum. [Note: 1.
gha reads "dideśa"; 2. ka and kha read "makabhā"].
[Vol. 3, page 377]
1510 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
"By virtue of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from simultaneous perception, upon seeing smoke and so forth..."
A certain cognition arises regarding a remote object, such as fire and the like. || 732 ||

As for the claim that the validity of inference (*anumāna*) is difficult to establish, its invalidity therein must be due to one of five reasons: because it is doubtful, or because it is erroneous, or because it has not arisen, or because of the absence of a suitable causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or because it is fruitless. It is not the first case, because [inference] does not touch upon both alternatives (the presence and absence of the probandum).
Thinking this, he says: "Together" (*saha*). Because the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) are perceived together, an impression (*saṃskāra*) arises; and from that, at a later time...

The meaning is that, by virtue of perceiving the pervaded (vyāpya), a cognition arises regarding the unperceived pervader (vyāpaka) which is awakened [from its latent state] and is non-doubtful; thus, because it is not characterized by doubt, there is no lack of validity for that cognition. || 732 ||
First of all, this knowledge has arisen from a valid inferential mark (liṅga) and is free from sublation.
Because it has arisen, that which has arisen is not in any way unarisen. (733)

He states the second [reason]: "Because of the mark" (*liṅgāt*). He refutes the third: "Because it has arisen" (*utpannatvāt*). The meaning of the reason is that the cognition of the signified (*liṅgin*) from the sign (*liṅga*) is perceived as having arisen. || 733 ||
How can this [effect] be produced through a relationship of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) with such [a cause]?
Or whether it does not exist—this investigation would be pointless because [the object] has already arisen. (734)

The fourth [alternative] is set aside by the phrase "it has arisen. This means: this pervasive cognition—being of such a nature as to arise from the cognition of the pervaded—is it produced by an invariable relation between those two, or rather from a variable relation? Such an inquiry is indeed fruitless, because since the pervasive cognition has already arisen, its specific cause cannot be determined; for while its arising has been observed, one must merely postulate a suitable causal complex (*sāmagrī*) based on that fact of its birth, and that [complex] is difficult to define in its particulars.
The meaning is that because it is desired by you, conventional usage proceeds on the basis of what is well-known; thus, it is established that such usage has no ultimate foundation. || 734 ||
In every respect, the cognition of the result has arisen and cannot be otherwise;
therefore, like direct perception, it does not immediately produce any error.
As long as we do not perceive it, so long it is not considered immeasurable.
Because it is absolutely impossible for you to deny that [existence]. || 736 ||

He states the fifth [objection]: "In every way" (*sarvathā*). The meaning is this: if a cognition of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) has arisen—whether from a mere relation or from a non-deviating relation (*avyabhicāri-sambandha*)—then, because it has arisen as something neither doubtful nor erroneous, it possesses the very fruit of the manifestation of its object; thus, it is not fruitless. Furthermore, is the actual (*tāttvika*) validity of inference being denied, or its conventional (*vyāvahārika*) validity? Not the first, for that is accepted.

Thinking "it is not so," he states the second [point] with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). The meaning of the word "tat" (that) is the observation that inference is a constituent factor of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
The example for its having empirical validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*) is "like perception. The phrase "kiñcit" (something) refers to the statement of conditions (*upādhi*) and so forth.
The remainder [of the sense] is "by the pervader of the pervaded which causes deviation. The terms "yāvat" and "tāvat" refer to the self-validity (*svatastva*) of validity.
It is indicated:
"Others are dependent upon inferences employed by others;
even through those [inferences], the determination of the pervading factor (*vyāpaka*) is not desired."
1. Kha. ga. is sharpened.

If it is argued that inference proceeds only from the ascertainment of an unconditional pervasion (*anaupādhika-vyāpti*) according to this principle, we say no, because the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is difficult to apprehend.

If it is argued that "it is not non-pervasive, for it is pervasive of the probandum (*sādhya*)," we say no; because the cognition of pervasion and the cognition of the condition (*upādhi*) are mutually dependent.

If it is further argued that "pervasion is not non-conditional merely because no deviation from the probandum is perceived in the case of the condition," then by that same measure, the probans (*hetu*) would also be a means of proof (*gamaka*) merely through such perception. This being the case, there would be no distinction between a valid probans and a fallacious one (*hetvābhāsa*), since their distinction is established only through the recognition of whether they conform to their respective definitions.
The meaning is "because of this" (taddhetoḥ). As for the claim that inference lacks validity because the probandum (*sādhya*) is difficult to define, he says [in response]:

"Because of that. For one like you—who possesses the conceit (*abhimāna*) of denying the validity of inference—since it would be impossible for you to engage in activities such as eating if you were utterly denying the validity of inference, your very survival would be difficult to achieve. Furthermore, the probandum is not difficult to state, for it is that which is doubted.

The meaning is that because that [property] exists in what is perceived, the subject (dharmin) as qualified by that property would be the object of cognition (prameya), according to what has been stated. || 735 ||
If, in this case, you maintain that the self is established merely from the arising of consciousness, [then...]
If [the probandum] were established by the mere statement of the thesis, the citation of a reason would be useless. (737)

He raises an objection regarding the validity of inference being like that of perception, saying "here he says. To state that very point, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta), beginning with "if. The word "validity" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He states the intended objection, beginning with "the proposition" (pratijñā). The phrase "of the cognition of what is already established" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 737 ||
"Certainly, this would indeed be a cause for such a doubt, were it not so."
For something might indeed be perceived there, and thus the statement would be faultless.

Since it is established that inference is the cognition of an unperceived pervader (*vyāpaka*) arising from the perception of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) in one who possesses the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of their simultaneous apprehension, the statement of the reason (*hetu*) is necessary in inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), because the thesis alone would not establish [the conclusion] in such an inference; however, its mention is not required in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), because it is accepted that inference for oneself is the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) derived from a three-featured mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), whereas inference for others is the communication of that three-featured mark.

Thinking thus, he offers a rebuttal by way of another approach: "Certainly. This means that since this very knowledge of the pervader arises from the mere statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), there is no contradiction here; this is the sense of his acceptance. He explains that very point: "Suspicion," etc. If, when the meaning of the propositional statement has been understood, no cause for doubt—such as the non-perception of specific qualities—is observed, then the propositional statement is faultless, and [the reason] is...

The meaning is that it brings about certainty just like valid cognition (*kṣama*). The sense of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the capacity of faultless speech to bring about certainty must be accepted precisely because of its faultlessness. || 738 ||
But where doubt arises as to whether [the object] is a man or something else, [it is so].
In that case, certainty regarding the logical reason (hetu) would arise through both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). || 739 ||

To the question of where that reason (*hetu*) is employed, he says: "In the case of the person, etc. Where there is doubt regarding the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) due to factors such as the speaker, the listener, the instrument, or the object, it is in that case that certainty arises through the power of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth of the reason; and there is no lack of positive concomitance and so forth where [the reason applies], because in the case of "where there is smoke, there is fire," the positive concomitance is clearly established in a kitchen (*mahānasa*). Furthermore, since there is an absence of the specific kind of smoke in a clod of earth (*loṣṭa*) and the like, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) where [the reason would otherwise fail].

"There is neither fire nor smoke there," because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established in the case of a cold lake due to the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalambha*) on mountain plateaus and the like.
[Vol. 3, p. 379] (Note: *tatrā* in manuscript *ka* and *kha*).

1512 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]: Because the absence of fire is not ascertained from the mere existence [of smoke], this is not a ground for negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, since the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is considered the locus of negative concomitance, there can be no ascertainment of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth for the reason (*hetu*). Thus, there are four types of logical marks (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics known as positive concomitance, negative concomitance, and being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
The meaning is that these are intended by others as being called "non-perception of the effect," "non-perception of the cause," and "non-perception of the essential nature. || 739 ||
Therefore, as soon as knowledge has arisen, it is for the sake of removing doubt regarding that [knowledge].
Positive and negative concomitance exist, yet there is no cognition of the object to be inferred by means of them.

One might raise the objection: "If the ascertainment of the meaning of the thesis-statement depends upon a reason possessing positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, then because the thesis-statement would ascertain its own object by depending on positive concomitance and the like, it would follow that its validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*). This would contradict the established principle that 'the validity of all means of knowledge is intrinsic' (*svataḥ*). Anticipating this, he says: "Once arisen" (*utpanne*). This refers to when the cognition pervading the thesis-statement has already been produced.

The point is this: even when [the pervasion] exists, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) serve to destroy doubt regarding it—which arises from causes such as human error—and do not directly constitute the cause for the cognition of the pervader;

for the knowledge of that which is to be inferred is established from the very statement of the proposition (pratijñā), and since anvaya and so forth are useful therein by way of dispelling doubt, there is nothing objectionable. || 740 ||
Whatever else is stated, such as intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and so forth, is other than the resolution of doubt.
Since that [inference] is not a constituent part of inferential cognition, its threshing is obtained [as a futile effort]. (741)

Having stated the established conclusion—that fire and other such things are objects of cognition because a logical reason (hetu) possessing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) functions as a means of knowledge by way of destroying doubt, according to the principle that it consists of both general and particular forms—the author restates the opponent’s preferred definition of a means of knowledge: "Doubt," etc.

When a cognition of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) has arisen from the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), there is a doubt caused by factors such as human agency; the reason possessing positive and negative concomitance produces a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) that destroys that doubt.

The meaning is that the threefold [reason]—consisting of the non-apprehension of the nature, the effect, and the incompatible—is the indicator (*gamaka*), because the Buddha has stated that there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) precisely therein, and because that which possesses such a connection is an indicator.

Regarding this, he states the reason for the refutation: "of that" (*tasya*). Since doubt and so forth are destroyed by the cognition of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) as asserted in the thesis, and by a reason possessing positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so on, your desired nature and the like are established through inference, either directly or indirectly.
The meaning is that because there is no going away, it does not possess that [going] as its object. || 741 ||
Is it not this triad that is described for the purpose of establishing invariable concomitance?
However, because of the necessary connection (avinābhāva) with those three alone, the auspicious [result] has been proclaimed by them as well. || 742 ||

He raises the objection that this [definition] is redundant: "avinābhāva... (regarding inseparable connection). The meaning is that what is inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) is indeed the indicator (*gamaka*), and since the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth are accepted for the sake of establishing that inseparable connection, they are not redundant. He states that the Buddhists themselves have explained how the essential nature and other factors establish inseparable connection:
"triṣveva... (only in three cases). Where the essential nature and so forth exist, there is inseparable connection, as in the case of the *śiṃśapā* tree and others; therefore—

They have stated that [the reason] is meaningful because it serves as a factor for inference by way of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth. As Kīrti said:

"The reason is of only three kinds: the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), that which is pervaded by a part of it (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*), and [that which is established by] the rule of inseparable connection;
anything other than these is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)."
The meaning is that it is acceptable by its very nature. || 742 ||
- 1 kha. gha.
1 [Vol.
3, Page 380] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1513.
If there were an inseparable connection by way of intrinsic nature, heat would not be a logical mark for fire.
Alternatively, because of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), the nature of the effect (*kārya*) is established as being its own nature (*svabhāvatā*). (743)

How can "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) mean "inseparable connection"? Does it mean that the essential nature is inseparably connected, or that what is inseparably connected is the essential nature? Regarding the first [option], he states the fault: "Because of the essential nature. Just as one might say, "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*," one could also say, "This is fire because it is hot. However, this does not lead to comprehension; for in the absence of a relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), there is no relationship between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*). Thus...

The meaning is that, according to the principle that "the pervader is accepted as the signified (gamyam) and the signifier (gamakam) is the pervaded," [the second alternative] is stated and then refuted:

"If it were the essential nature (svabhāva). If being the essential nature belonged to that which is inseparably connected (avinābhūta), then even in the case of "there is fire here because of smoke," there would be essential nature due to inseparable connection;
consequently, the established rule—that there are two types of reasons for establishing a positive entity (vastu-sādhana) and one for negation (pratiṣedha-hetu)—would be destroyed. || 743 ||
Fire is observed to have heat as its intrinsic nature, because it is seen elsewhere as well.
The nature of earth, water, fire, and wind has been observed to consist of touch.

Regarding the objection that since it was stated previously that heat possesses the nature of fire (*agniliṅgatva*), this is indeed accepted; yet, there is no inconsistency in the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamakatva*) in a single locus—because it has been explained that the entire conventional practice of inference and the object of inference (*anumāna-anumeya*) proceeds through a distinction between property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*) as constructed by the intellect—the author says: "As for heat... Even though fire is observed to have heat as its very nature, nevertheless, its state of being invariably concomitant (*avinābhūtatva*) with that [heat] does not [follow] from that alone... [as the sun does not possess heat].

Since both [the property and the locus] are observed, there is no inseparable connection (*avinābhūtatva*) for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); nor is the linguistic convention of inference and the object of inference established by means of a distinction between property and locus that has merely ascended into the intellect, because the relationship of the signifier and the signified—which culminates in the probandum and the probans—is uncontradicted. Furthermore, this is not a fault due to the restriction [of the distinction] as it ascends into the intellect, because the restrictor itself, having ascended into the intellect, is likewise restricted as something non-different from that [intellectual representation].

The meaning is: "because of the absence of your [proposed] connection. Furthermore, he says "on earth" (*kṣiti*) to show that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*). The meaning is that even though touch is the essential nature of air (*vāyu*), it is observed elsewhere [in objects like wind], and therefore it is not invariably concomitant with that [air]. || 744 ||
If it is held that this [entity] is devoid of intrinsic nature because it does not possess activity toward a single object.
For even though it exists in the *dhava* tree and others, the *śiṃśapā* is not of the nature of a tree. (745)

He raises an objection: "Heat and so forth are not the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) [of fire], because they reside in many things, like conjunction. He says, "It is held [that... [referring to the opponent's view]. [The author] refutes this: you state that "treeness" is the intrinsic nature of the *śiṃśapā*, based on the example of an intrinsic-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) such as "this is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*"; however, that treeness also exists in *dhava*, *khadira*, and other trees. Consequently, treeness would not be the intrinsic nature of the *śiṃśapā*. Thus he refutes it.
"In [the case of] running and so forth" || 745 ||
"A *śiṃśapā* is indeed a tree" [is established] because of the impossibility of their being separated.
If that were the case, momentariness would not be the intrinsic nature of entities. (746)

It is incorrect to claim that "occurring in many instances" (*anekavṛttitva*) is not a reason for [something] lacking intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*), because it deviates (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of "treeness," since in that case the probandum (*sādhya*) exists just as the reason does. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The *śiṃśapā*... You yourself accept that the *śiṃśapā* has the very same intrinsic nature as a tree; wherever there is a *śiṃśapā*...

The meaning is that because "being a tree" is accepted as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of "being a *śiṃśapā*" by virtue of being an inseparable cause (*avinābhāva-kāraṇa*), one who asserts that "being a tree" is not the essential nature of a *śiṃśapā* would be abandoning their own position. Regarding the statement "being a tree is the essential nature of a *śiṃśapā*," [this is] the refutation of the opponent's acceptance.

The word *hi* is used as a particle of emphasis. He states another instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) for the reason of "subsisting in many" (*anekavṛttitva*). [He says] "momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatva*). That being so, it means that if there were subsistence in many, there would be possession of multiple intrinsic natures (*anekasvabhāvatva*). || 746 ||
Because it would reside in multiple objects, it follows that it lacks causal efficacy. || 747 ||
When there is momentariness in one thing, then it possesses a unique nature.
When a reason is considered to have a common nature with respect to multiple [conclusions], that is regarded as such. (748)

He states the reason for its resulting in being devoid of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*) with the words "of that" (*tasya*). It should be noted that it is not the case that this very absence of intrinsic nature [leads to] the contradiction of the established tenet (*rāddhānta*), because it would entail that entities possess the nature of permanence. To the objection—"Since momentariness is accepted as an intrinsic nature, its subsistence in multiple [entities] is unproven; how then can there be a deviation [in the logical reason]?"—he replies: "the state of being causeless" (*ahetutva*). [This is said] in the absence of subsistence in multiple [entities].

He demonstrates the consequence that [pleasure] would be causeless by stating "momentariness. In the argument, "The subject of dispute is not pleasure because it is momentary, like pain," the reason "momentariness" applies either to a single entity or to multiple entities. It cannot be the first case, because if there exists a similar instance (sapakṣa), the reason does not enter into it, resulting in the fallacy of being an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) reason.
In the second case, the reason for the matter at hand is inconclusive (anaikāntika). This is the meaning. || 747 || 748 ||
And because the fact that smoke is an effect of fire is observed.
In this case, the inconclusiveness of the reason, namely "being an effect," becomes attached [to the argument]. || 749 ||

Having refuted the capacity of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to serve as a means of proof, he now refutes that of an effect (*kārya*). Regarding the phrase "of fire": the fact that smoke is an effect is observed to be produced by fire and also produced by preceding moments of smoke, since it is accepted that there is a causal relationship between preceding and succeeding moments. Therefore, one cannot infer "there is fire here" from smoke, because the reason—the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between smoke and fire—based on the status of being an effect, is fallible; for there is no [necessary] positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between smoke and fire.
The meaning is that [the existence] of another [person] is established even from smoke; thus it is said here that there is inference having smoke as its logical mark (liṅga). || 749 ||
Even if it were the case that touch always exists even in air and so forth.
By this much alone, there would not exist in the world that which has the nature of the touch of white.
For in this world, the possession of tangibility by the earth is well-established. || 751 ||

Having refuted the capacity of both [the cause and the effect] to indicate [the other], he repeats what was stated in order to state another defect in the position that [the indicator is] the essential nature (*svabhāva*). [He says: "If...

The meaning is that the state of being invariably concomitant (*avinābhūtatva*) is not restricted to the essential nature, because even the touch which is the essential nature of the earth is observed in wind, water, and fire.
He states the reason for the claim that "the cow is the earth; its touch is natural" with the words: "For of the earth..."
Furthermore, even though one intends to examine the nature [of things] through non-deviation, [the following applies].
The non-deviation of an entity from its intrinsic nature could never be established.

Having restated the fault already mentioned regarding the fact that an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is inseparable (*avinābhūta*), [the author] says "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*) to show that this is not the only objection—that if what is inseparable were the intrinsic nature, then even an effect (*kārya*) would result in being an intrinsic nature—but that there is yet another as well. He clarifies this further objection with the words "From the intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvāt*). If being an intrinsic nature follows from inseparability, then a thing’s inseparability would not follow from its intrinsic nature either.
It is accomplished; such is the meaning. || 752 ||
1 kha. ga. *sajyate* | 2 ka. kha. ga. *vakṣitaḥ* | [Vol.
3, page 382] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1515.
"But because non-existence is absent in those three alone," as Dharmakīrti stated.
This promise that was pledged would undoubtedly be lost. || 753 ||

"Let there be no inseparable relation (avinābhāva) dependent on essential nature (svabhāva); what loss is there in that? To this he replies: "In the three alone. The meaning is that if one does not accept an inseparable relation dependent on those [three], then the proposition that "the reason is of three kinds because the inseparable relation is of three kinds" would be abandoned. || 753 ||
In the same way, for one who intends to express the nature of a thing as being non-deviant.
Since the non-deviation [of the reason] has already been fully established, what else remains from that?
State the probandum you intend to express by means of a reason that is an essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

He states another fault regarding the claim that "being a nature (svabhāvatva) depends upon invariable concomitance (avinābhūtatva). He says: "In the same way. This means that it would be like the fallacy of abandoning one's thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) if invariable concomitance were not established by the nature itself. For, if one attempts to establish "being a nature" by means of a reason consisting of a nature (*svabhāvahetu*), since invariable concomitance would already be established prior to that [establishment of being a nature], there would be nothing at all to be proven by the reason consisting of a nature.
The meaning is that its nature is dependent upon the state of being inseparably connected [with that cause]. || 754 ||
Because it is invariably concomitant with fire, the effect is also considered a nature (svabhāva).
Either the distinction "this is smoke" disappears, or [the distinction] between the two types of reasons ceases. || 755 ||
Having first restated the fault already mentioned in the passage "because it is inseparable, it is the essential nature" (*svabhāva*), he states another resulting fault: "Not so," etc. (*aneva*).

If an essential nature (*svabhāva*) were established through non-deviation (invariable concomitance), as in "this is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*," then even smoke, which is an effect of fire, would possess that same essential nature, since non-deviation exists [between them]. As it has been said: "Even for an effect, when there is a necessary connection based on essential nature, it is because that [effect] possesses that [cause's] essential nature and arises from it. Consequently, the distinction between the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) and the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*) would be destroyed; thus, the proposition that there are "three" [types of reasons] would be untenable.
The meaning is that the statement "these three reasons are characterized as effect, essential nature, and non-perception" is futile; the word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and).
And even though smoke and the like are effects, that aspect [of being an effect] is not considered to be the object of inference.
Because of deviation, the production of an arrow from the *śrā* and *śraṅga* [is] observed. || 756 ||

Having specifically demonstrated that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not a means of cognition, he states another reason why an effect (*kārya*) is not a means of cognition: "Even though it is an effect" (*kāryatve 'pi*).

The meaning is that even though smoke and the like are effects of fire and the like, the aspect of being an effect (*kāryatvākāra*) is not useful for the inference of fire and so forth, because that aspect lacks a necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*) with a specific causal aspect. He introduces this point by means of an example: "As in the case of an arrow," etc.

Because it is accepted that preceding and succeeding momentary arrows stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect, and because it is observed—and indeed accepted—that [the arrow] arises from the horns of a cow or other animals fallen in the forest, aided by earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth, there is no necessity of the form of the effect being determined by the form of the cause; and thus, the latter cannot serve as a means of inferring the former. This is the meaning. || 716 ||
And because it is an effect, smoke and the like serve as the cause for certain knowledge [of fire].
Because the reason for deviation is absent, this [smoke] attains the status of a valid reason for fire. (757)
If the effect were not indicative [of its cause], how could there be an inference of fire and so forth from smoke and so forth? To this he says: "Because it is an effect" (kāryatvāt).
Why? [As follows: *Note: The bracketed portion indicates the source reference provided in the original text.*
[In the phrase "of fire and so forth," the word "of fire" is the ellipsis. How, then, does smoke lead one to infer fire? To this he says: "Because of non-deviation.
The meaning is that smoke is the indicator of fire solely because of a relationship of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), and not because it is an effect (*kārya*). || 797 ||
Since it is observed that an effect, such as an arrow and so forth, has multiple causes.
Therefore, by virtue of its non-deviation, even an effect attains the status of a cause. (758)

Since smoke possesses both the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), how is there certainty regarding the specific causal factor (*prayojaka*)? To this, he says: "Aneka... [etc.].

Because an effect indicates only its cause in general, it does not indicate its specific cause; however, the cognition of a specific cause from a specific effect is not produced by the mere fact of being an effect.
However, the point is that the cognition of that [effect] from that [cause] alone is likewise dependent upon non-deviation (avyabhicāra). || 798 ||
Furthermore, in this case, no dependence arises with respect to the effect and so forth, because the indicative mark has already been stated.
The rising of the Kṛttikās is neither an effect, nor does it possess the same nature [as the moon], and thus it is not a logical mark.
He states another reason for the fact that neither essential nature (*svabhāva*) nor effect (*kārya*) is indicative [of the probandum], beginning with "dependence" (*apekṣā*). In the inference:

"This rising of Kṛttikā is proximate to the rising of Rohiṇī, because it is a rising of Kṛttikā, like a previously experienced rising of Kṛttikā," he provides the reason for why there is no dependence on essential nature and so forth by saying "and not an effect" (*akāryaśca*). The phrase "proximity to the rising of Rohiṇī" is to be supplied as the remainder of the thought; for even in the absence of being an effect and so forth, that [rising]...
The meaning is: because it is observed to be indicative [of the probandum]. || 759 ||
For it has already been stated that by the very mention of "because of being Kṛttikā," the [invariable concomitance] of both effect and essential nature is established.
However, dependence arises merely from positive and negative concomitance.

Since there is no dependence on intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth for the reason already stated, he asks: "In what, then, is there dependence? To this he replies: "Because of being Kṛttikā," and so on. The suffix *-tasi* here has the sense of the locative case. The two occurrences of the word *hi* (for/indeed) serve to establish the consensus of both common people and investigators regarding the point thus stated. || 760 ||
Because it is not an effect and lacks an inherent nature, [the probans] exists merely through inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
The rising of Kārtika must certainly be the *liṅga* (the indicative mark) due to its proximity;
therefore, it does not depend on the nature of the rising of Rauhiṇa.
Therefore, it is not tenable for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the like to function as causes. (762)

The reason for the absence of dependence regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth is stated as "because it is not an effect. Regarding how the rising of Kṛttikā can be an indicator (*gamaka*) for the rising of Rohiṇī in the absence of an intrinsic nature and so forth, he says: "due to invariable concomitance" (*avinābhāva*). He states the resulting conclusion—that the rising of Kṛttikā is a mark (*liṅga*) for the proximity of the rising of Rohiṇī precisely because of its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*): "therefore," [by] the rising of Kṛttikā, [the rising of Rohiṇī...].

[Objection: Let it be that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth lack the capacity to indicate [the probandum] in an inference based on proximity to the subject (*pakṣapratyāsatti*), such as in the inference of "treeness" from "śiṃśapā-ness"; however, they will possess that capacity in the inference of "treeness" and so forth from "śiṃśapā-ness" and so forth.

To this, he says: "Since... (yataḥ). The meaning is: if the capacity of intrinsic nature and so forth to indicate [the probandum] were to deviate in some cases, then that would not be the reason for postulating it elsewhere; for even there, the probandum is established precisely because of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). || 761 || 762 ||
In this context, the word "self" cannot refer to itself; for an action directed toward oneself is a contradiction.
Even the effect would possess the nature of being its own designator. (763)
1. Kha. gha. omit *tadviśeṣaṇam*. 2. gha. reads *daye ro*.
