Furthermore, regarding the capacity of *svabhāva* (essential nature) to indicate [its own object], there is a dilemma as to whether the word *sva* denotes the self (*ātman*) or that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). Regarding the first alternative, he states the fault: "Not in the self" (*nātmāni*). In the statement "the essential nature is the indicator," the word *sva* is not appropriate when applied to the self—that is, to the very form of what is to be indicated—because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself. For it has been said: [The following verse is cited: "One does not cut oneself with one's own blade; One does not illuminate oneself with one's own light. Thus, since the relationship between agent and object is impossible within a single entity, the word *sva* cannot refer to the self.
"And this very [reason], being of a dual nature, is both the object to be known and the means of knowledge;
it is the object to be known through its unestablished part, and the communicator through its established part."

Furthermore, it is not possible for both the state of being established (*siddhatva*) and the state of being to-be-proved (*sādhyatva*) to coexist within a single partless entity such as cognition; therefore, the first [alternative] is untenable—this is the meaning. Having restated the second [alternative], he refutes it with the words "of the effect" (*kāryasya*). If the word *sva* (self) were used in its own primary sense [to mean "one's own"], then even smoke would possess the nature of being "self," because it is related to the pervading fire. As they have said:
"For otherwise, this relationship of pervader and pervaded between those two would not exist.
Thus, the meaning is that it is precisely that which constitutes the abandonment of one's own thesis (*pratijñāhāni*). || 763 ||
Does the word "own" here refer to the self itself, or does it denote what belongs to the self?
If it is your view that the self's nature is its existence, [then... || 764 ||

He restates the two alternatives that were mentioned in order to state further defects regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Is it the self?"—the meaning of the word *iha* here is the sentence "the intrinsic nature is the indicator. He clarifies the second [alternative]: "The intrinsic nature... That is to say, if it is your view that the intrinsic nature is one's own pervaded state (*vyāpya-bhāva*) belonging to the self which is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). || 764 ||
If one's own self were one's very nature, then, because another would be impossible, [there could be no liberation].
For an object of cognition that is distinct [from the self], the self itself would be the inference of the self.
And thus, it would follow that the subject, the reason, and so forth are non-different from one another. (765)

He clarifies the first point with the words "in its own [form] alone. He recalls the fault stated in the context that "the indicator (*gamaka*) is nothing other than the nature of the indicated (*gamya*") with the word "then" (*tadā*). The particle *hi* is used to reveal that this has already been mentioned previously. He states another fault in that very same context with the words "and likewise" (*tathā ca*). If the indicator were merely the indicated, then since the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth—which are included within the indicator—would be non-different from the indicated, there would be no inference (*anumāna*).

The meaning is that, consequently, the occurrence [of the reason] in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its being pervaded by a part of that [subject] would be the reason; thus, [the definition of the reason as "that which is known through valid cognition"] would be redundant. || 769 ||
Now, if one intends to express "one's own nature" as meaning "that which belongs to oneself," [then the following applies].
Smoke belonging to fire would likewise possess the nature of that [fire]. (766)

He restates another alternative interpretation with the words "Now" (*atha*). This means: if, by the etymological derivation *svasya bhāvaḥ svabhāvaḥ* ("the state of one's own is its own-nature"), it is intended that the word *sva-* refers to a signifying factor (*gamaka*) that is connected to what is to be known (*gamyasaṃbandhī*); then he states the very same fault mentioned there: "one's own" (*ātmīya*).

And thus, since the distinction between essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*) is not established, the threefold classification of signifying factors is not established—this is the remainder of the argument. || 766 ||
Just as there is a distinction between consciousness and existence, so too is there one between their absences.
There is neither difference nor non-perception; therefore, there is no inferential mark (liṅga) whatsoever. 767 ||

Having refuted the capacity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*) to serve as means of proof, he now refutes that of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). He says: "In cognition... Just as in your own system... [vol 3, page 385] he restates; ...is intended to be expressed in the versions *kha* and *ga*.
1518 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:

No distinction is perceived between consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the object of consciousness (*saṃvedya*), because it is established that existence (*sattva*) is nothing but apprehension (*upalabdhi*), characterized by the fitness of the thing itself; likewise, no distinction is established between their respective absences (*tad-abhāva*), since there can be no difference in absences without a difference in their counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*). Therefore, in your position, the absence of consciousness—

The meaning is that there can be no inferential mark (*liṅga*) in the absence of something to be perceived, because it is impossible for the same single thing to be both the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*); thus, the claim that "there is no jar in a particular location because of the non-perception of what has reached the conditions for perception" is merely the prattle of the careless. || 767 ||
Thus, worldly identity and causality have been explained.
Now, intrinsic nature and the rest, as postulated by their own systems, are examined. (768)

Having established that the three [other] indicators lack authoritative status, he states "thus" (*evam*) to proclaim what has already been discussed and what is yet to be discussed, so as to avoid redundancy.
Identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) are established through worldly consensus as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*). As it has been said:

"For when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), one thing does not deviate from another, because that [connection] consists in identity. The essential nature is also the connection for the effect.

Regarding the phrases "of the nature of the thing" (*svabhāvasya*) and "because it arises from that" (*tadutpatteḥ*): by the method already explained, it has been established—that is to say, proven—that those two [reasons] do not possess the capacity to convey [the probandum] when accompanied by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). He states the purport of the subsequent section with the word "Now" (*atha*). [In this context,] "nature" (*svabhāva*) is identity (*tādātmya*), such as the tree-ness of a *śiṃśapā*; "effect" (*kārya*) is the moment of smoke arising from the moment of fire; and "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) is the absence of apprehension according to the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇa*).

The non-existence of that which has been attained is said to be eightfold or threefold. Thus, the meaning is that even the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth established by the Buddhist system are shown to be non-probative by the following textual sequence. For their system is twofold: first, the theory that exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is both the object of cognition and the means of cognition;
as it has been said:
"Therefore, the logical mark (liṅga) is proclaimed to have exclusion (apoha) as its object;
otherwise, if the subject (dharmin) were already established, what could remain unestablished beyond that?"
Another [view] holds that it is the state of being qualified by that [exclusion]; for it has been said:
"That which is established as having that [exclusion] as its object is distinct from the other [the thing itself]."
"And even there, 'this is another exclusion' and 'this is another excluded thing'—
both words and determinate cognitions follow convention. (768)
Even in the theory of exclusion of others (anyāpoha), [the distinction is made] through the differentiation of the exclusions of words.
The cause would not possess intrinsic nature, nor would activity exist. || 769 ||

Therein, he restates the first [position] in brief: "The other," etc. The meaning is that, according to your view, the exclusion of non-śiṃśapās—which constitutes the referent of the word *śiṃśapā*—is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), while the exclusion of non-trees—which is the denotation of the word *vṛkṣa*—is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Regarding that as well, he states that there is no capacity for logical proof (*gamakatva*) based on essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth: "The word," etc. [This refers to] the exclusion of non-śiṃśapās, which is the referent of the word *śiṃśapā*, [from] the referent of the word *vṛkṣa*.

Furthermore, because the exclusion of "tree" and the exclusion designated as "non-aśiṃśapā" are mutually distinct, the latter—intended as the probans—is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor the effect (*kārya*) of the former—intended as the possessor of the probans (*hetumat*). For two things that are mutually distinct, such as a jar and a cloth, there exists neither the relation of intrinsic nature nor the relation of cause and effect; therefore, since it is accepted that these two exclusions, being absolutely distinct, stand in the relation of the signified and the signifier (*gamya-gamaka*) despite the absence of the relations of intrinsic nature and so forth, [the objection of] non-perception...
The meaning is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because [the reason] such as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is not desired in that context as a prover. || 769 ||
1 gha. it is said; 2 kha. ‘caivaṃ saṃ’; 3 gha. ‘kavavya’. [Vol.
3, page 386] 1–Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1519.
In the statement "This tree is a śiṃśapā," [the śiṃśapā] is distinct from the meaning of the word "tree."
It is said that in all individual trees, such a form exists everywhere.
And likewise, that which is distinct from the non-śiṃśapā is also expressed in the same manner.
Regarding the phrase "even in the case of the theory of exclusion (anyāpohana)," he first states an undisputed point in order to elaborate upon the brief position [of the opponent]: "This is a tree.

The meaning is that when one employs such expressions as "The dhava is a tree," "The khadira is a tree," or "The śiṃśapā is a tree," there is no dispute between us two that in all these intended individual trees, there exists a nature consisting of the exclusion of non-trees—such as jars and the like—which is characterized by the exclusion of others (anyāpoha). What is this [exclusion] in its own right?

The term *niṣṭhā* refers to the state of being established. The word *kila* is used for the purpose of indicating acceptance (*saṃpratipatti*). He states another point that is accepted: "not-a-śiṃśapā.

In the usage "the tree is a śiṃśapā," it is accepted that the form consisting of the exclusion (*apoha*) of non-śiṃśapās is expressed by the word "śiṃśapā" with respect to individual śiṃśapās, just as the expression of the exclusion of non-trees is expressed by the word "tree" with respect to individual trees. This is the meaning. *Niṣṭhā* [refers to] the prior—
Thus it is said. || 770 ||
In that case, there is a convention regarding an object that is devoid of trees by means of the designation "tree."
And there is a convention that "śiṃśapā" refers to what is distinct from non-śiṃśapā. (771)

Having stated what is not contradicted (*avigīta*), he states the result with the word "therein" (*tatra*). Among these two—the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣavyāvṛtti*) and the exclusion of non-śiṃśapās (*aśiṃśapāvyāvṛtti*)—the convention (*saṃketa*) is grasped by the name "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) in respect to the exclusion of non-trees; and the grasping of that [exclusion] by the name "śiṃśapā" occurs in respect to the exclusion of non-śiṃśapās. The meaning is that the difference in the application of the words is due to convention, as it has been stated. The single *ca* (and) is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
In the case of *caya*, the second [syllable] is restricted. || 771 ||
From that, there would arise the conventional usage: "This is a tree" and "This is a śiṃśapā."
The arising of conceptual cognition occurs precisely through the superimposition of word and meaning. (772)

He states the result of grasping the convention (*saṃketagraha*): "This is a tree. This means: from that grasping of the convention. As he has said: "In whatever manner they [the words] are intended to be employed—whether as distinct or non-distinct—they, being so applied, manifest that object without obstruction. If it is argued that this linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) arises from conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) itself, even without the grasping of a relation (*saṃbandhagraha*)—

[The opponent] objects: "There is the word. [The reply is: The superimposition of word and object is the knowledge of their relation; by that alone does conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) arise everywhere.
For one who has not grasped the relation, there can be no conceptual cognition such as "this is a tree"; therefore, the knowledge of the relation is purposeful. This is the meaning. ||772||
The relationship of the signifier and the signified should be understood as existing between the exclusion of the word and the exclusion of the object within the indicative mark (liṅga).
The two types of logical marks are essential nature and effect; and essential nature and so forth are themselves that which is indicated by a mark. || 773 ||
Nevertheless, how can there be a relationship of indicator and indicated between the two exclusions (*apoha*) under discussion? To this he says: "Of the word-meanings," etc.

Between the two exclusions that constitute the meanings of the words *śiṃśapā* and *vṛkṣa*, when the inference designated by the term "mark" (*liṅga*)—in which the meaning of the word *śiṃśapā*, namely the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapā*, is intended to establish the meaning of the word *vṛkṣa*, namely the exclusion of non-trees—is being considered, then the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapā* functions as the indicator (*gamaka*), and the exclusion of non-trees functions as the indicated (*gamya*).

This is the meaning: [it] is to be known. Nevertheless, how can intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth possess the capacity to indicate [the probandum]? To this he says: "Intrinsic nature," etc. For in the case of an individual *śiṃśapā* tree, the exclusion from non-trees does not exceed the exclusion from non-*śiṃśapās*; and the exclusion from non-smoke arises from the exclusion from non-fire.

Therefore, intrinsic nature and effect are suitable as logical marks (*liṅga*), while the essential nature and the cause are what is to be indicated; such is the established position of our doctrine. ||773||
In that case,
there is no cognition whatsoever regarding that object which exists here as a real entity.
For this conceptual construction is considered to be either an intrinsic nature or an effect. || 774 ||

He begins to elaborate upon the established doctrine starting with the words "due to the difference in the exclusion of words" (*śabdavyāvṛttibhedataḥ*). Regarding the phrase "not there" (*na tatra*): the meaning is that since those two—essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*)—are intended as the objects of apprehension in that case, namely in the entity [such as] essential nature and so forth, cognition does not arise from them; therefore, in this context, the capacity of essential nature and the rest to function as indicators (*gamakatva*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). To the question, "How is it that cognition does not arise regarding essential nature and the rest in that case? he replies:

Or "its own nature" (svabhāva). The meaning is that if those two were of the nature of exclusion (apoha), they would not be indicative [of the object], because as mere conceptual constructions (vikalpamātra), they lack substantial reality (avastutva). || 774 ||
It is not so, because it is a conceptualization that touches upon a real entity, rather than being a mere objective support consisting of words.
How could those words, being [mere] sounds, ever possibly be fit to be those very objects? (775)

To the objection that even though the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapā* (aśiṃśapāpoha) and so forth are conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), they possess the capacity to indicate [the object] because they touch upon a real entity (*vastu*), he says "no" with the words "not a real entity. First of all, the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapā* is not itself a real entity, nor does it touch upon a real entity; for, being a conceptual construction, it has as its objective support merely the word. Therefore, since the meaning of words such as *śiṃśapā*—namely, the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapā* and so forth—is non-existent, the exclusions of non-*śiṃśapā* and so forth [cannot be the objects of words such as *śiṃśapā*].
The meaning is that, existing as mere words, they cannot be the actual objects [they denote]; therefore, how could there be the relationship of signifier and signified among them?

The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies that it is well known even from the *Yoga Sūtra*—in the sūtra beginning with "It follows the cognition of the word"—that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) lacks contact with the real object (*vastu*). || 779 ||
The establishment of essential nature and causal efficacy is based upon inference.
And from those two, inference is established; thus there is a mutual dependence.

Furthermore, is this exclusion (*apoha*) of non-*aśiṃśapā* and so forth perceived or inferable? It cannot be the first, because the exclusion of non-trees and so forth would also be established by that same perception, rendering inference useless. Nor can it be the second; as he says: "By its own nature" (*svabhāva*). If the establishment of the essential nature (*svabhāvatā*) and the effect-nature (*kāryatā*)—which consist of the exclusion of non-*aśiṃśapā* and so forth—is from inference, then there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*): the establishment of the essential nature and so forth is from inference, and from that [establishment], inference [is established].
The meaning is that "cognition" (buddhi) is that which is inferable through the exclusion (apoha) of non-śiṃśapā and so forth. || 776 ||
For the exclusion of what is not a *śiṃśapā* would not be its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Because the form of the exclusion of non-trees is absolutely distinct from those two. || 777 ||

He states another reason for the fact that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the other [types of evidence] are not indicative [of the probandum], beginning with the words "not a *śiṃśapā*. The term "intrinsic nature" is intended to include the effect (*kārya*) by implication.

Therefore, the remainder of the argument is that intrinsic nature and the others lack the capacity to indicate [the probandum], because even in their absence, the relationship between the indicated and the indicator would be lost. He states the reason—introduced by the word "for" (*hi*)—for why those two [exclusion and non-exclusion] are neither effects nor intrinsic natures, beginning with the words "of those two" (*tayoḥ*). || 777 ||
Furthermore, the cessation of smoke would also be of the nature of the exclusion of non-fire.
There could be neither an effect nor an intrinsic nature [in them], because of their absolute difference.
Since that manifestation is an effect of fire, it cannot therefore be the [primary] effect itself. || 778 ||

He states that [the reason] is not a prover by virtue of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and so forth, beginning with the word "api" (also). The particle *ca* (and) is used here for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and is joined with the negative particle *nañ*.

In that context, he recalls the very reason previously mentioned with the words "of those two" (*tayoḥ*). This is because, in the absence of the non-occurrence of the exclusion of non-fire being the effect of the exclusion of non-smoke, [the relationship would be impossible].

1521 He states another reason: "Because of the manifestation of that" (*tadvyakteḥ*). Since the manifestation of smoke is the effect of the manifestation of fire, there is the exclusion of non-smoke and the exclusion of non-fire.

The effect does not [arise] from that, for it is not the case that those two [non-smoke and non-fire] themselves possess the nature of being excluded from what is other than that, because that would entail the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) and the consequence of the redundancy of the term "exclusion of the other" (*atad-vyāvṛtti*).

Therefore, since one must admit the relationship of signifier and signified (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) between the exclusion of non-smoke and the exclusion of non-fire despite their not being cause and effect, the meaning is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the signifying capacity of the effect. || 778 ||
Now, the entity that possesses the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is both the object to be understood and the means of understanding.
In that case, it must be asked: what is the proof that the three-fold nature [of the reason] does not exist when [the object] is not perceived? (779)

Having refuted the theory that the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) possesses both the status of being the object of comprehension (*gamya*) and the status of being the means of comprehension (*gamaka*), he states another theory—that it is the possessor of that [exclusion] (*tadvat*) which possesses these properties—beginning with the word "Now" (*atha*). He rejects that as well, beginning with the words "It must be stated" (*vaktavyam*). When asked what the proof is for the fact that the entity consisting of the exclusion is the means of comprehension, you must state it; for if the means of comprehension is not perceived through a means of valid cognition (*māna*), its presence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its existence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) cannot be established.

Existence [of the reason] consists in its exclusion from the counter-instances; thus, the establishment of the three-fold nature [of the reason] constitutes inference, for it is established that inference is for the sake of knowing an object through a mark possessing these three characteristics.
Indeed, there can be no cognition of a property (*dharma*) when the substratum (*dharmin*) has not been cognized. And so it is said:
"Therefore, he described the ascertainment of the reason in all three of its aspects."
"Because of the opposition to the unestablished, the contrary in meaning, and the deviant."
The meaning is that it has been overlooked. || 779 ||
If it is held that the entity itself has as its nature the exclusion of what is not a śiṃśapā;
And the form of the exclusion (apoha) of non-trees constitutes the relationship of indicator and indicated between those two.
Expanding upon the position that [the sign] possesses the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), he first states the nature of the signifier and the signified: "Not-a-śiṃśapā.

It is intended that the very entity which is a *śiṃśapā*—as qualified by the form of the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās*—is the signifier; and the very entity which is a tree—as qualified by the form of the exclusion of non-trees—is the signified.

Thus, it is held that between these two, the *śiṃśapā* and the tree, both of which possess exclusion (*apohavat*), there exists respectively the status of being the signifier and the status of being the signified.
The meaning is "if. || 780 ||
The nature of the non-exclusion of the non-śiṃśapā would be the indicator [of the absence of the tree].
But that very [reality] is to be realized by oneself through the cessation of the self that consists of non-trees. || 781 ||

How can these two [the tree and the *śiṃśapā*] be accepted as indicators (*gamaka*) and so forth in the absence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the like? Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the intended probans. To this, he says: "In the exclusion of the non-*śiṃśapā*.

Because the tree-nature is characterized by the exclusion from what is not a *śiṃśapā*, the entity that is a *śiṃśapā*—being qualified by apoha—is the indicator of the tree, insofar as it is the tree-nature qualified by the exclusion from the form of a non-tree.

That very object consisting of a *śiṃśapā* tree is both the object to be understood (*gamya*) and [the means of understanding] because of its own nature; since the objects "tree" and "*śiṃśapā*" stand in a relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakatva*), there is no deviation of the causal factor—this is the meaning. || 789 ||
Even for one who exerts such effort to establish their own position, it is not established.
This position of one devoted to the Buddha is now explained accordingly. (782)
The phrase "it must be stated there," etc., reveals the established tenet (*siddhānta*). Regarding the words "one's own position" (*svapakṣa*):

the Buddhist tenet is that the meaning of the word *śiṃśapā*, which possesses the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapā*, is the signifier (*gamaka*), while the meaning of the word *vṛkṣa*, which possesses the exclusion of non-trees, is the signified (*gamya*).
1522 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Just as this position of yours does not succeed— even though you, who are affectionate toward the Buddha, strive for its accomplishment according to the method already stated— so it is.
The construction is: "all that is stated by us. || 782 ||
From what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) was the exclusion of non-śiṃśapā trees known by you? (783)
First of all, that [non-existence] is not [known] by direct perception, because the latter has only existent things as its object.
And because there is no other indicative mark, it is not established even through an indicative mark. || 784 ||

He analyzes [the argument] in order to clarify what was asserted: "It is not a *śiṃśapā*. Indeed, that [negation] must be seen as residing within the category of the indicator (*gamaka*) in the theory of exclusion (*apoha*). From what means of valid cognition (*māna*) is it known? Is it from perception (*pratyakṣa*), or from an inferential mark (*liṅga*), or from verbal testimony (*śabda*), or from non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)?
Such is the meaning of the analysis. He refutes the first [alternative]: "By perception... That is, the exclusion of the *śiṃśapā* under discussion is known...

The word "iti" (thus) is the remainder [of the sentence]. Thinking that the fact that perception (*pratyakṣa*) apprehends only what is presently existing is established in the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra*, he says: "of that" (*tasya*). He refutes the second [position] with: "of another mark" (*liṅgāntarasya*). Since you accept that the real entity which is a *śiṃśapā* tree qualified by the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās* is the signifier (*gamaka*), the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās* is also included within the category of signifiers; therefore, that which is intended as its mark (*liṅga*)— [...is not a mark because it is not perceived. The meaning is that since the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās* is not perceived, it cannot be a mark. Furthermore, even if it were perceived, it would not be a mark because it is not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). This is because the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās* does not reside in the subject, namely the *śiṃśapā*. For the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās* resides only in the *śiṃśapā* itself, and not in other things such as jars. Thus, the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās* is not a property of the subject. Consequently, it is not a mark. Therefore, the statement that "the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās* is the mark" is incorrect. The meaning is that it cannot be established even from that [other branch], because there is no other branch of it that is pervaded by the exclusion of non-śiṃśapās, and thus inference is impossible.
If it is thought that we shall apprehend this [object] from the word alone;
Because the conventional usage [of words] is beginningless, and because the relationship [between word and object] is established. || 785 ||
Why is it not stated that its connection with the meaning is preceded by a specific measure?
In this way, your position is indeed established; however, there would also be an undesired fault. || 786 ||

He restates the third [position]: "We shall apprehend. This means from the word "śiṃśapā"; that is to say, from the word "śiṃśapā," one apprehends this exclusion of non-śiṃśapās. If the exclusion of non-śiṃśapās is known from the word "śiṃśapā," then its connection with the object must be grasped;

for a word whose connection has not been grasped is not expressive. Furthermore, there can be no cognition of a connection when the related term is unknown; therefore, that [exclusion] is the basis [of the word's meaning].

Anticipating the objection that, in the absence of such a means of knowledge (*māna*), there can be no cognition of the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapā* from the word [“*śiṃśapā*”] itself, he says: “beginningless” (*anādimat*).

Since the relationship between word and meaning is understood through its basis in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), no separate means of knowledge need be sought for that purpose; for the usage of elders is the root of children’s acquisition of linguistic competence, and thus they too [the elders] are established in it—this is the meaning. From the word “*śiṃśapā*,” the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapā*...

He refutes [the opponent] by stating that even if the proponent of Apoha were to claim that [the word] is a means of comprehension through the establishment of its function (vṛtti), there would still be a contradiction with his own tenets;
thus he says: "It is established" (sidhyati). || 789 || 786 ||
Thus, since [the object] is accepted from that [word], the indicative mark (liṅga) would indeed be the word itself.
Neither the intrinsic nature nor the effect [would exist], and the thesis would be false. (787)

To address how the consequence of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) follows there, he says: "In this way" (*evam*). The meaning is that if one accepts that from the word "śiṃśapā" there arises a cognition of the exclusion of non-śiṃśapās, then the word "śiṃśapā" itself would be the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the exclusion of non-śiṃśapās; consequently, the logical mark you desire—such as essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth—would not exist. He states the fault in that [word] not being a logical mark: "The proposition" (*pratijñā*). || 787 ||

However, it was stated with effort that [the reason] exists only in the three [types of cases] because of its inseparable connection (avinābhāva).
It is not proper for the Śākya monks to abandon the meaning of their own proposition. || 788 ||

He states its nature: "In the three alone. The effort [of proof] consists in establishing that the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) exists only in these three and not elsewhere. Anticipating the objection that this might be intended as merely false, and intending to show the resulting over-extension (atiprasaṅga), he says: "Of the meaning of the proposition" (pratijñārthasya). || 788 ||
But surely, an object distinct from non-śiṃśapā and so forth is perceived?
But from that very knowledge derived from the word, there arises an understanding of an object that is beyond the senses.

He raises an objection regarding the contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhāntavirodha*) by saying: "But surely... [The opponent argues: An object in the form of a *śiṃśapā* tree, which is excluded from non-*śiṃśapās* such as *artha* (meaning) and so forth, is understood from that very word; from that cognition—characterized by the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās*—there arises a cognition of the object "tree," which is characterized by the exclusion of non-trees. Therefore, even though the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās* is apprehended from the word, there is no damage to our position.
This is the meaning. || 789 ||
Whatever exclusion of non-śiṃśapā is considered here by you [to be the definition of a tree], it is that which is intended.
This is not non-existence, because for you, non-existence is held to be due to non-apprehension.
He refutes [the opponent's position] by means of a dilemma: "Is it non-śiṃśapā? Here, "here" refers to the Buddhist position. The meaning of the dilemma is:

is the exclusion of the non-śiṃśapā a positive entity (bhāva) or a non-entity (abhāva)? First, it cannot be a positive entity; for if that were the case, the word *śiṃśapā* would have a positive referent and would consequently fail to have the function of excluding other things (*anyāpoha*), which would result in the conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) [of assuming two meanings]. With this intention, he addresses the second alternative: "Nor is it a non-entity. In that regard:

He states the reason: "Since," etc. In your own position, indeed, non-existence is to be understood through non-apprehension; as it has been said: "There is one cause for negation. However, the exclusion of what is not a *śiṃśapā* is desired [only] in the context of verbal cognition (*śābdī*). Thus, since that [exclusion] is not a separate non-existence, even for one who holds the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), [the word's] capacity to convey meaning is untenable; such is the sense. || 790 ||
If the non-perception of a *śiṃśapā* tree is [the reason], it is because it consists in the exclusion of other things.
Therefore, by that same principle of non-existence, the absence of a tree is also established as being eternal.

He formulates the fourth [reason]: "It is a *śiṃśapā*. There is the non-perception of non-*śiṃśapā* in a *śiṃśapā*, precisely because the *śiṃśapā* is excluded from all that is not a *śiṃśapā*. Thus, regarding the object that is a *śiṃśapā*—which consists in the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of non-*śiṃśapā*—the aforementioned non-perception constitutes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, through the absence consisting in the non-perception of non-*śiṃśapā* within the *śiṃśapā*, the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapā* (*aśiṃśapāpoha*) is known as the meaning of the word "śiṃśapā."

Therefore, since the meaning of "tree" as qualified by the absence of non-trees—which possesses the exclusion of others—is also always established, there is no fault in our position; such is the meaning. || 791 ||
Because there is no apprehension [of it], it is not as it is thus described.
Let it be explained how there could be a distinction between the non-existence of a jar and its non-perception. || 792 ||

He asserts that "just as the object of knowledge is absent due to the absence of knowledge," so too all of that is being stated by us; thus he makes his formal proposition (*pratijñā*). With the words "perception" (*upalabdhi*), he recalls what was stated in the passage "the distinction between consciousness and existence is as follows" (*saṃvittibhāvayorbhedo yathā*) in order to clarify that which was proposed.

The core philosophical content begins with the commentary on the Upaniṣadic passage concerning the "Self that is within all" (*sarvāntara*). **Translation of the Philosophical Content:** Regarding the Self that is within all: It is not possible for this Self to be perceived by means of the senses or the internal organ (*manas*), because it is devoid of form and other such qualities. Furthermore, since it is free from all attributes, it cannot be grasped through inference based on those characteristics. Nor can it be known through verbal testimony (*śabda*) alone, as there is no scriptural statement that establishes its existence independently of perception. Therefore, one might argue that the Self is unknowable. To this, the reply is given: The Self is indeed knowable. How so? Because it is the very essence of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). Just as the sun is known through its own light, the Self is known through its own self-luminosity. Moreover, the scriptures declare that the Self is the object of the highest knowledge; thus, it is established that the Self is not an unknown entity. The notion that the Self is unknowable arises only from a failure to understand the nature of the witness-consciousness itself. Once that is realized, the Self is immediately known, being non-different from the witness-consciousness. Thus, the Self is both the subject of knowledge and its own object, transcending the duality of knower and known. This is the meaning of the Upaniṣadic teaching. For it is not established that action is the cause of that [connection], since it is the latent impressions of experience (*bhoga-vāsanā*) that function as such. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Action" (*karma*). Action exists for the sake of the agent's experience; for there is no evidence for its existence if that [experience] does not commence, and otherwise, it would follow that such extremely subtle action is non-existent. Furthermore, there is no experience without a body. Therefore, for one who is bodiless, there is a connection with a body—[and this is due to action].
The cause is karma together with its latent impressions (vāsana) and ignorance (avidyā); this is the meaning. || 817 ||
This body is the product of evils, consisting as it does of both merit and demerit.
The conceit of "self" regarding that [body] is the attainment [of identity] through ignorance. || 818 ||

Having stated the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the word "pāpmabhiḥ," he explains the meaning of the case ending as being the agency of the aggregate, saying "the body. He states the meaning of the word "saṃsarga" (contact) with the words "in that... (818).
When the exhaustion of the body's karma occurs and his body falls away, at that time—
The immortal and immutable one abandons the effects of his past actions, which are rooted in evil. || 819 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "sa utkrāman" (as he departs) as follows: "deha" (the body). When the karma that initiated the present body has been exhausted through experience and the current body falls away, then the Self—being devoid of all modifications—abandons the effects and instruments (kāryakaraṇa), which are grasped by the term "pāpman" (evil) through secondary indication (lakṣitalakṣaṇā); this is the meaning. || 819 ||
One abandons the forms of death within the stages of death, sleep, and so forth.
But apart from knowledge, the self does not abandon its own darkness even through death.

An objection is raised: "If the body and so forth, which are the effects of death, abandon [the self] without knowledge, then death itself will likewise be abandoned; thus, since knowledge would be useless, the commencement of the scripture would be in vain. Anticipating this, he says: "He abandons" (jahāti). The meaning is that innate ignorance is "death," and its abandonment does not occur without knowledge, because there is no other contrary factor [to effect such abandonment]. || 820 ||
Just as [the self] is constantly [bound] by the taking up and casting off of its own nature, such as sin and so forth.
Being identical with the intellect (dhi), the self transmigrates until liberation.
1 ga. *mṛtyusva* | 2 kha. *diprākṛ* | [vol 3, page 397] 1530 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]

Having explained the literal meaning of the words in the passage beginning with "sa vai," he concludes by summarizing its purport and finalizing the illustration with the verse beginning "pāpmādī. This means: by means of the acceptance and abandonment of the body and so forth, which have "evil" (pāpman) and the like as their material cause. || 821 ||
And likewise, through ignorance, one perceives both the world beyond and this world.
It wanders through the continuous cycle of birth and death until liberation is attained.
He states the application of the analogy of the movement in dreams and so forth: "In the other world... (822).
Since this is so, it is therefore established that the self is distinct from the body and other such factors.
Through their conjunction and disjunction, like a garland, clothing, ornaments, and so forth. || 823 ||

He states the result of the transition between the two worlds in due order, beginning with the words "yataḥ" (since). The meaning is that the body and so forth are not the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the Self, nor are they its attribute (*dharma*), because they are subject to conjunction with and separation from it, like a garland or similar objects. || 823 ||
For one does not think "I possess it" regarding an ear that has been severed.
Just as it is thus, so it is with the remainder, by virtue of its being a qualification of that.

Anticipating the objection that although the gross body and so forth lack the nature of the Self, the subtle [body] might be it because of its non-deviation [from the Self], he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). For Caitra does not conceive of himself as "I am possessed of that" with respect to a hand or other limb that has been cut off and discarded; likewise, there is no connection of the Self even with what remains [of the body]. This is because there is no difference between a body that has been discarded and one that has not, insofar as both are equally qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the Self. Therefore...
Even the subtle body is neither the Self nor belongs to it, because it is its limiting adjunct (upādhi), just like the gross body; such is the meaning. || 824 ||
He is indeed characterized by overestimation (ābhimānika) by whatever specific quality he is distinguished.
Therefore, the self would be without qualification, like a garland, an ornament, or a garment.

How, then, is the appearance of the self’s connection with the body and so forth explained? To this he says: "Consisting of false identification" (ābhimānika). The meaning is that by whichever body or other [limiting adjunct] the self is qualified, its connection with that is of the nature of false identification and is not real. He concludes by summarizing the result of the self’s actual lack of connection with the body: "The self... [referring to] the two bodies.

Therefore, the meaning of the word [Ātman] is the impossibility of being that [body] or possessing its attributes. Just as there is an absence of selfhood and belonging-to-self in a garland and so forth, there is likewise an absence of those in the body and so forth;
thus, the Self is established as being without qualification, consisting solely of pure consciousness—this is the meaning. || 829 ||
But surely, these two worlds do not exist for him as long as this self continues to wander?
Through the continuous succession of birth and death, it is like the worlds known as waking and dreaming.
He states the doubt to be dispelled by the sentence beginning with "tasya" (of that), starting with "nanu" (but). || 826 ||
One's own two worlds, the waking and the dream, are [perceived] through direct perception as their means of knowledge.
But the next world and this world are not likewise within the scope of direct perception.
Anticipating the objection, "Why should this world and so forth not be accepted as being like a dream and the like? he says: "svapna...
(verse 827).
1 ga. mṛtija | [vol 3, page 398] 3 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1531
Because this world is perceptible, there is no doubt regarding it.
Nor is there any doubt regarding the next world, for its existence is always established through scripture.

Having restated the doubt expressed in the Bhāṣya, he raises an objection: "Because of perceptibility" (*prātyakṣyāt*). Since this world is perceptible, its existence is certain; and since the existence of the next world is established by such scriptural passages as "one who desires heaven," there is no doubt regarding its non-existence even there.
Therefore, the meaning is that the subsequent portion of the text need not be commenced for the purpose of refuting that [doubt]. || 828 ||
The validity of direct perception as a means of knowledge [is established] in both this world and the next.
The intended meaning of "existence" is that it is not measured by anything other than itself, as in the case of its own nature. || 829 ||
Anticipating this objection, the subsequent text states: "Or rather, of that."
Thus, this much has been said regarding the relationship; likewise, another [type] is also described. || 830 ||

He resolves [the objection] by first establishing the doubt: "The inward" (*pratyak*), etc. Just as the existence of both the dream state and the waking state is established by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) known as self-experience (*svānubhava*), so too must the existence of this world and the next be said to be established by the means of direct perception;
it is intended that their existence is not to be known through other means of knowledge such as scripture (*āgama*). However, the existence of the next world is not [actually] perceived directly.

Therefore, the meaning is that the subsequent section of the text is intended to establish the existence of the next world through direct perception itself, having raised the doubt that "the next world does not exist. He concludes the connection stated in the Bhāṣya with the words, "Thus this... He then introduces the connection stated by Bhartṛprapañca with the word, "Likewise...
'The self is light,' and another says, 'It is the same [as the breath].'"
He abandons evil"—thus are the three subject matters (padārtha) stated in the aphorism. || 831 ||

He recounts that narrative in order to explain it: "The Self," etc. The word "hi" (for) indeed illuminates his own commentary as it was cited, showing how those three subjects were thus introduced. || 831 ||
Therefore, the determination of these [categories] by means of their own nature shall now be stated.
Now, listen to this description of how that [state] is attained according to the prescribed rule. || 832 ||

He states the intended connection for the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) by saying "by means of sound" (*svanena*). The meaning is that because the determination of the three—beginning with the light of the Self (*ātmajyotis*)—must be stated by means of the analogy of the dreamer, the sentence "of that" has been introduced for that reason. To the question, "How is there a determination of these three here?", he replies:
"It is described. The word "now" (*atha*) is used to indicate the aforementioned objection. By which [means] this triad...

The construction is: "Listen to that procedure being described, which is detailed in the statement 'by the prescribed rule' (vidhinā tasya). The intention is that through this explanation of the sentence, the determination of the three [points] becomes clear. || 832 ||
This connection is described, and another as well, in the same manner.
Of that Self which has been described as self-luminous, [the notions] arise from ignorance and activity. (833)
Now, the stages (bhūmis) are described for the purpose of establishing the experience of karma.
This birth, the next one, and likewise that which is situated between them, are my own.
1 Kha. Thus it is said. As follows [Vol. 3, page 399]: 1532 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Chapter—]
1 He approves of the aforementioned connection with the words "And this. The word "also" (*api*) is used to provide an illustration of the connection stated in the Bhāṣya.

He states another relationship desired by himself: "And thus" (*tathāca*). He clarifies that very point: "By oneself" (*svayam*). Taking up the sentence beginning with "And this," he shows the very grounds for experience (*bhogabhūmi*). Regarding "this" (*idam*), he states the meaning indicated by the word "and" (*ca*): "In one's own [state]" (*svama*). || 833 || 834 ||
That which is yet to be born, and that which is currently being experienced through direct perception.
Because it is determined that these two alone are the stations of the All-pervading Lord. || 835 ||
Having restated what was said, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "tasya" (of that) and so forth, starting with "bhāvī" (that which is to be) and so on. || 831 ||
But surely, since the world exists even in a dream, how can there be such a definitive restriction?
"There are only two" because dream is not an intermediate state between the two locations. (836)

By showing the doubt regarding the word "saṃdhyam" (pertaining to the junction), he challenges the restrictive determination with the words "nanu" (but surely). He refutes the objection—that the restrictive determination is untenable because there exists for a person even a dream-body distinct from the two bodies—by means of the passage beginning with "na" (no).

A dream occurs at the junction (*saṃdhi*) between the body of this world and the body of the next; in relation to those two, it is not a third, for the junction between two villages is not [itself] those two.
The meaning is that, by depending on [the other two], it becomes the third; therefore, the establishment of the restriction [is achieved]. || 836 ||
The statement "the third is the twilight" is based on the hearing of the ordinal suffix.
The restriction that was stated is not for the purpose of negating other locations. (837)
This is for the purpose of excluding non-connection with that, and not with a view toward excluding connection with anything else.
And this [statement] "at that juncture" is likewise appropriate when that is the case. (838)

Having stated the meaning as explained in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*), he states another meaning: "The intermediate state" (*saṃdhyam*). Regarding the expression "the third, which is the intermediate state" (*saṃdhyaṃ tṛtīyam*), the term "intermediate state" (*saṃdhyam*) is used not to exclude any other location besides this world and the next, because the suffix denoting ordinal number is heard in the word "third," which signifies completion among three. Anticipating the objection that the hearing of the ordinal suffix itself must be discarded due to its contradiction with the restrictive particle *eva*, he says: "As for that... (*yattu*).

By the word "only" (eva), the non-connection of the self with two locations is excluded, but not its connection with another location; therefore, the meaning is that the direct scriptural statement (*avadhāraṇa-śruti*)—which is otherwise established—is outweighed by the scriptural statement of the suffix "pūraṇa," which is not otherwise established. He says, "In that [state]," because even the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) would be supported if the dream were a different location. || 837 || 838 ||
The existence of sentient beings in both dreams and this world is, for its part, within the range of direct perception.
Let it be stated: what is the means of valid cognition for the existence of the next world? (839)
In order to introduce the subsequent statement, he restates the objection previously raised: "In a dream... (839).
But while remaining in that very place of his own dream, he perceives it.
The Self, refined by action, knowledge, and other means, [migrates] to this world and the next.

Introducing the statement in order to say that dream-perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of the next world, he explains it [with the verse beginning] "In this... The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is intended to include latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 840 ||
1 [Vol.
3, Page 400] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1533.
Whatever karma was experienced during the birth of the elements, that is brought forth by the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Therefore, in the first stage of life, one perceives only that which pertains to previous births.

Anticipating the objection as to how a dream-perception can have the next world as its object, [the author] states that the aggregate (saṃghāta) has three stages according to the distinctions of childhood, youth, and old age; therein, a dream concerning the next world is possible during the stage of childhood. He says: "Having become... For in that state, there is no dream concerning objects of this world such as sons and so forth, because even now those desires are not yet fulfilled; nor is it the case that he has no dreams at all.

Since the dream of that sleeping person—though inferred from observed signs such as crying—is not to be denied, the meaning is that there exists for the child a connection with the world beyond. || 841 ||
In middle age, these were acquired here through the harshness of causes.
Generally, one perceives latent impressions in a dream by the power of karma.

"In that case, let it be that even for a youth there is a dream concerning the next world. To this he says, "In the middle," etc. "Roughness" (*kārkaśyam*) refers to the capacity for perceiving gross objects. "Here" (*iha*) is a statement regarding the present birth. The connection is: "obtained through the power of past actions" (*karmaṇo vaśād ārjitāḥ*). He uses the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*) because one may occasionally see, even in a dream, something impossible in this world due to the force of unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*). || 842 ||
But one who desires to go to the next world is enveloped by karma, ignorance, and the like.
One generally sees the form of the person from whom one is to receive teachings in a dream. || 843 ||

In his final stage of life, [the author] states that his own vision pertains to the other world, using the word "yiyāsuḥ" (desirous of departing). The word "prāyeṇa" (mostly) is used to indicate that there is no fixed rule regarding such visions. Thus, the seeing of an object conceived in one's mind within a dream serves as proof for the existence of the other world.
The meaning of the whole [is as follows]. || 843 ||
Because it has already been experienced, the past birth is not intended to be expressed here.
However, the other world and this world are mentioned for the sake of establishing the intermediate state.

Let it be that one's own dream is not perceived [by others]; nevertheless, how can the dream-state be established as being "intermediate" (*saṃdhya*)? For even when the present body is perceived, if there is an expectation for a second [body], one might ask: "In order to establish its intermediate nature, which body—past or future—is to be grasped? In response to this inquiry, he says: "Because it has been experienced," etc. The word "here" (*iha*) means "in the establishment of the dream-state as being intermediate. || 844 ||
First, there is the easy perception of that which pertains to this life, namely this present birth.
But just as it is with the next world, so too is it expressed by the word "atha. || 845 ||

Anticipating the objection—"Since there is no difference in the fact that both worlds are objects of apprehension, why is the world beyond taught by setting aside this world?"—the author states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "atha" (now), saying: "With ease," etc. (849).
Relying upon the state of dream, one perceives the next world;
by what method and relying upon what does the self perceive it? (846)
Now, this which is being stated clearly should be understood exactly as it is.
That by which one ascends to that world is called his "ascent" (āskrama) here. || 847 ||
1. *ga* reads: *vīkṣyate*. 2. *kha* reads: *nu*. [Vol. 3, page 401] 1534 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four.

He states the meaning of the word *atha* (now/then): "In a dream... and so forth. This means that this [awakening] is called *atha*. He introduces the phrase "This sequence... and so on with the word *etad* (this). The correctness of the perception (*pratīti*) consists in its independence from further questioning. He states the meaning of the word *ākrama* (sequence): "By which... The locative case (*śruti*) signifies the sense of the seventh case. || 846 || 847 ||
Whatever kind of means has been accumulated here for the sake of attaining the next world.
Just as the sequence belongs to someone, so this Self is according to its sequence.

Showing the compound [formation], he states the meaning of the word *yathākrama* (according to sequence) as follows: "Of such a kind" (*yādṛg*). The construction is as follows: whatever means, such as knowledge and so forth, have been acquired by this person in this life for the sake of the next world—that is his "sequence" (*ākrama*); he who possesses that is "according to sequence" (*yathākrama*).

Just as in the phrase "of whom [it is] thus" (*yathā yasya*), the word *yathā* has the sense of "of such a kind" (*tādṛg*), because it begins with *yādṛg*; and [in this context], the sequence consists of knowledge, action, and prior cognition.
The meaning is that there is another sequence. || 848 ||
The sequence and the means are characterized by knowledge, ritual action, and so forth.
Having taken recourse to him who has become oriented toward the other world, one should follow one's own sequential path. || 849 ||
Having established the station called Saṃdhyā, which consists of both fruition and non-fruition.
The self perceives suffering and bliss as resulting from unrighteousness and righteousness respectively. || 85 ||
He recites the preceding verse in order to explain "that method" (*tamākramam*) and so forth. With the word "yathā," he states the very meaning of "yathākrama.
With "yathopāya," he qualifies *māyā*. He explains "tam" and so forth with the words "paraloka...
(the connection being: "the ripenings of unrighteousness and righteousness"). He clarifies those very [ripenings] with the words "duḥkhānandān" (sufferings and joys). || 849 ||
[He perceives] the evil deeds arising from unrighteousness, as well as the joys born of righteousness.
The direct perception of sin and so forth does not arise from anything other than scripture.

He clarifies what has already been stated with the words "of evil" (*pāpmanaḥ*). The connection is with the preceding verb "he sees" (*prapaśyati*). To the question of why the word "evil," setting aside its well-known conventional meaning, is taken here to signify its effect, he replies: "On account of scripture" (*āgamāt*). The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) means "by means of perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*). || 891 ||
"Or likewise, one engaged in dharma or adharma through the grace of a deity."
In his own self, he beholds various joys and evils. || 852 ||
Regarding the question of what causes the perception of the fruits of merit and demerit—namely pleasure and pain—in a dream, he says: "Dharma... The word "vā" has the sense of "ca. || 852 ||
Because one perceives in a dream that which is impossible in this present life.
Therefore, such a dream-vision has the next world as its basis.
(853) Having raised the doubt—“Even if that [next world] is seen in a dream, how can the next world be directly perceived?”—he recalls what was stated previously with the word “iha” (here). (853)
[Volume 3,
Page 402] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
Thus has the procedure for twilight and sleep been fully described.
[This is] for the purpose of establishing the next world, or else [it follows] from the statement "or of that" (tasya vā). || 854 ||
He concludes what was stated with the words beginning "of that" (*tasya*). He states the result of that description with the words "in the next world" (*paraloka*).

The meaning is that the manner of dreaming is described by the passage beginning with "of that" for the purpose of establishing the existence of the next world through the direct perception of dreams. || 854 ||
As it has been said: "In the absence of all luminaries, beginning with the sun..."
The person acts by means of his own self-luminosity; this is known from the indicative mark (liṅga). || 855 ||

In order to introduce the passage beginning with "sa yatra," he recounts the interrupted narrative, stating "yad uktam" (as it has been said). Regarding the phrase "liṅgataḥ" and so forth—the meaning is:

even in the absence of the [external] light of the sun and other sources, by virtue of the activity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the like perceived in dreams and so on. And in that context, the word "manifests" (*unmiṣati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 899 ||
This person is distinct from all luminaries, such as the sun and others.
It must be stated who is the "accomplished one" (siddha) for the sake of accomplishing the purpose as described. || 856 ||

He states the meaning of the subsequent sentence in brief, preceded by the necessary inquiry: "The sun, etc. The construction is as follows: when it is asked where the conscious self (cidātman), untouched by the light of the sun and other luminaries, is established, since the desired location must be stated, the sentence beginning with "sa yatra" (when he... is intended to demonstrate that aforementioned location which is devoid of external light.
Or rather, the well-known fact of its being self-luminous was previously stated on the basis of inference.
Now, its establishment through directness and without mediation is being stated.

He states another connection with the words "by itself" (*svayam*). In passages such as "the Self alone belongs to this," the self-luminous conscious Self was described through inference based on the mark of empirical usage (*vyavahāra-liṅga*). Now, the meaning of the subsequent sentence is that its establishment must be stated by means of immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*) as the inward-facing aspect (*pratyagbhāva*). || 857 ||
He is the self-luminous Self alone, devoid of external light.
Just as it is directly perceived, so too is this described. || 858 ||
Having unified the two types of connection [previously] mentioned, he summarizes them for the sake of easy comprehension: "He" (sa).

Indeed, that Self, untouched by external lights, becomes light by itself; thus, this self-luminosity, which is directly capable of being experienced, is explained by means of the illustration of dreaming. For it has been stated: "Self-luminous"—this term 'self-luminous' was introduced as a designation for the light of the Self.

In order to determine that [Self] by means of an internal illustration, the example of a dream is introduced. The meaning is that, in every respect, the subsequent statement is intended for the purpose of determining the Self as self-luminous. || 858 ||
In whatever state one is said to be "asleep."
Then this person becomes absorbed into his own unborn Self.
Regarding the phrase "where he sleeps," he states its literal meaning: "where. || 999 ||
15.36 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Through the exhaustion of the karma of the waking state, the Self [is freed] from the identification with the external body.
Having emerged, being self-sovereign, he beholds his own māyā.

Having accepted that the word "sleeps" (svapiti) refers to deep sleep (suṣupti), it was stated [in the previous verse] that "he has merged into his own self, which is unborn. Now, in accordance with the present context, he states its meaning as "dreaming" (svapna): "jāgrad... etc. The gross body in the waking state is the external body; "having oneself as the primary object" means being free from dependence on that [body] due to being devoid of identification with it. || 860 ||
This birth which exists is set in motion for the purpose of yielding its fruit.
By the word "world" (loka), this very thing is denoted. 861.
Regarding the phrase "of this world" (*asya lokasya*), he explains "world" (*loka*) as follows: "that which is not surpassed" (*pranutta*). || 861 ||
Because he protects everything through the medium of sacrificial acts such as the *juhoti* offering.
Therefore, this self is said to be "all-pervading" until the end of the body.

He states the meaning of the term *sarvāvān*: "juhotyādi" and so forth. For this person (*puruṣa*), who is an aggregate consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the body, is the agent; since he protects everything from the gods downwards by means of sacrifices and other rites, he is called *sarvāvān* because he is perceived as such.
This is the meaning. || 862 ||
Taking the entire world as its basis, the action of each individual is accomplished.
Therefore, the entire collection beginning with the *juhoti* [offerings] is declared to be the cause of the universe.

Anticipating the question of how [the Self] possesses "all-inclusiveness" (sarvāvattva) through the medium of the oblation and so forth, he says: "The whole. It has been stated in the Madhu Brāhmaṇa that the operation of each individual aggregate does not occur without the material cause of the entire world; nor does the material cause of all exist without its fruit. Therefore, since the oblation and so forth are the cause of the entire world, the world—which is the locus of action—is all-inclusive.
The meaning is that it is so stated. || 863 ||
Or rather, all [these] belong to this Self, because they exist through the divisions of internal and so forth.
The elements and their derivatives would then be merely that; therefore, everything is said to be [unreal]. 864 ||
He states another meaning of the term *sarvāvata*: "internal and so forth" (*adhyātmādi*). || 864 ||
For the sake of establishing the enjoyment of one's own self within this entire body.
Taking up a mere residue of latent impressions, he expands his own illusory power.

He explains the passage beginning with "mātrām" (the measure). Regarding the phrase "of all": the connection is that this Puruṣa, having taken up the "measure" consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of this body which has been described as being composed of all things, extends the illusion called the dream state for the sake of its experience. || 865 ||
Just as in the waking state, the measure [of experience] occurs through the division of internal and other [states].
Through enjoyment they are diminished, and through actions they are accumulated. || 866 ||

Fearing that liberation might occur for one who has fallen asleep because the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through the enjoyment of dreams establishes their finitude, he provides an analogy:
"The internal self, etc. (verse 866).
1. ‘amarthāntaramā’ | [vol 3, page 404] 6 Brāhmaṇa] Together with the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1537
Likewise, these [consciousnesses] are also produced by karma within their own respective stages.
Through the continuity of decrease and increase, there would be measures consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā).
He states the example: "One's own [nature]," etc. (867).
And likewise, it has been established previously that [the cognition] is "by means of the intellect" (dhiyā dhiyā).
By means of the continuous increase of laughter, this world proceeds in such a manner. || 868 ||
By the word "dhiyā" (by means of the intellect), he causes one to remember what was stated by the Brāhmaṇa in the seventh chapter, as it serves to illustrate the meaning already explained. || 868 ||
"Having himself destroyed [it]" refers to one who negates the existence of deities.
The qualification "himself" is stated [in the text] with reference to his falling away from the body. 869.
Regarding the phrase "having himself destroyed," he states the purpose of the qualification "himself": "himself alone.
The meaning is that the qualification "himself" here serves to preclude the suspicion that the deities are the agents when this self's body falls away. || 869 ||
He who, by withdrawing from his own self, renders the body devoid of consciousness.
Desiring to sleep upon the destruction of karmas, he is then said to "having struck down" (vihatya). || 870 ||

He states the meaning of the word "having struck" (*vihatyā*) as follows: "one's own self" (*svātma*). The meaning is that he who, desiring to sleep, brings about a state of complete lack of movement due to the destruction of the karma that causes waking—and because of his withdrawal from his own body—is called the "striker" (*vihantṛ*) by virtue of being the agent of the cause for the body's lack of consciousness. || 870 ||
Cognition of the self occurs in the eyes and other senses through the favor of the sun and other factors.
Just as there is the activity of the body for the sake of worldly transaction, so too is the activity of the [Self] within the body.

Anticipating the objection—how can the self be the cause of the body's destruction even when it departs from the body upon the exhaustion of karma—the author says: "By the sun and so forth. For in the waking state, through the grace of the presiding deities (devatās) within the sense organs, the perception of form and other objects arises for the sake of the body's activity;
such being the case, the activity of the body is observed. || 871 ||
It is indeed impelled by its own karma for the sake of experiencing the fruits of dharma and so forth.
Because this body falls at the conclusion of the experience of the fruit of karma.
Anticipating the doubt as to by what the bodily activity is impelled and for what purpose it exists, he says: "The Self" (ātma).

Furthermore, anticipating the doubt as to how the Self can be the agent of its own destruction, he says: "By action" (karmanaḥ). Therefore, the remainder of the sense is that the Self is the cause of the body's fall through the supreme [knowledge]. || 872 ||
One should emanate [the deity] oneself, in accordance with one's own nature and karma.
Since the manifestation of one's own [nature] is non-proliferated, for that reason it is a qualification. || 873 ||
He states the meaning of the phrase "having himself created" as follows: "having created.

Just as there is the qualification "himself" in the expression "having himself destroyed," so too here, in order to dispel the suspicion that it might be [the work] of another deity, the meaning is that since the arising of the dream occurs in dependence upon one's own karma, the self’s status as the creator of the creation is likewise not contradictory. || 873 ||
193 1 gha. He! [vol 3, page 405]
1538 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Even for the Self, whose deities of all the sense organs have been discarded...
For the sake of establishing the action and its factors, creative contemplation alone is its cause.

Having stated that the arising of dreams is dependent upon one's own karma, he explains the intended meaning of the words from the *Bhāṣya*, "consisting of latent impressions" (*vāsanāmaya*), with the verse beginning "apāsta... (874). The particle *eva* is used for the purpose of emphasizing the predominance of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
That world which belonged to the Self here was to be created and then enjoyed.
Meditative cultivation is established in each of those respective forms. || 875 ||
In that case, let it be said that *bhāvanā* (creative mental effort) exists merely for the sake of establishing action and its factors; it is not the cause for the manifestation of all dreams.
To this he replies: "That which is to be manifested. The word *atha* is a synonym for the word *tathā*. The word *iha* refers to the waking state. || 879 ||
Although devoid of an agent, it is nevertheless a mental cultivation (bhāvanā) aroused by karma.
Because it is observed as the agent of cultivation, the single self acts as the agent. || 876 ||

Having refuted [the notion of] creation, it is not logical to attribute agency to the Self; for agency does not belong to that which is immutable and non-dual. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Having departed," etc. Because of the singular qualification, the word "also" (api) should be understood as applying to what follows as well. || 76 ||
That which was previously acquired by one while awake, characterized by its own cultivation, [is what arises].
Knowledge that rests upon the luminous intellect is expressed by the word "light" (bhās).
Regarding the phrase "by its own radiance, by its own light," a doubt is raised concerning tautology due to the identity of *bhās* and *jyotis*; therefore, he explains the meaning of the word *bhās*:

"Of the waking state," etc. The meaning is this: for a person in the waking state, that self-cognizing knowledge called *bhāvanā* which is acquired in that very state—consisting of a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) whose nature is luminosity—is what is denoted by the word *bhās*. || 877 ||
The qualification is for the purpose of excluding that which arises from instruments such as the intellect (buddhi).
The term "by itself" (svena) refers to the manifestation produced by direct perception (pratyakṣa). 878.

To the question "For what purpose is the qualification 'by itself' (svena) used?", he says: "buddhyādi... etc. The qualification "by itself," which takes the form of an expression, serves to exclude from the light under discussion—the light that is the cause for the manifestation of the inner consciousness (pratyak-caitanya) and proceeds through the medium of the intellect (buddhi) and so forth during the state of dream—the light consisting of mental impressions (bhāvanā-mayī bhāḥ) belonging to the dream state. For [that dream-light] is indeed the manifestation of the inner self.
The meaning is that the elephant serves as its witness, because it establishes its own self-luminosity. || 878 ||
In this context, the words "self" (sva) and "own" (sva) should be understood as denoting "belonging to the self" (ātmīya) and "the self" (ātman), respectively.
By the very force of the capacity [of the words], in accordance with the light of the vessel [in which they are placed]. || 879 ||

One might object: "How can there be an exclusion of the light of the immutable *jyotiṣ* by its own word [‘self’], since in the phrase ‘by his own light,’ even the word ‘light’ (*jyotiṣ*) is used as a qualifier? Anticipating this, he states that because the two words ‘self’ (*sva*) have different meanings depending on what they qualify, it is logical that the light of the Self (*ātmajyotiṣ*) is excluded by the qualifier ‘light. He says: “The two words ‘self’... Here, the word “here” refers to the present sentence. How, even while conforming to that [sentence]...
Anticipating the objection that the meaning of these two terms is established in this manner by their own verbal forms, he says: "By implication" (sāmarthyāt). || 879 ||
1. ka. ga. ‘vikāra | 2. kha. prakṛtāyāḥ | [Vol.
3, page 406] Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramañjarī* (The Illumination of the Treatise) composed by Ānandagiri. 1539.
Since the cultivation [of wisdom] for the sake of others is for one's own benefit, because the light of consciousness is one's very self.
Therefore, the two words "own" (sva) and "word" (śabda) have been cited as expressing the meaning already stated. || 880 ||
Regarding how those two possess efficacy in that regard, he says: "For the sake of others," etc. (880).
It is declared to be self-luminous, devoid of action, without an agent, and without fruit.
He who is that very self-luminous one is designated by the word "light. || 881 ||
Regarding the phrase "by his own light" (*svena jyotiṣā*), he states the meaning of the word "light" (*jyotis*): "himself" (*svayam*). || 881 ||
Of the unchanging witness alone to all the mental fluctuations of the entire world.
Such a state of the internal organ is designated as "he sleeps. || 882 ||
He states the meaning of the word "prasvapiti" (he sleeps) as follows: "niḥśeṣa... (without remainder). || 882 ||
The internal light and so forth are yellow, free from the states of waking, sound, and the rest.
The one Self, having the latent impressions (vāsanā) as its limiting adjunct, is itself declared to be self-luminous. || 883 ||

In order to distinguish it from sleep (svāpa) or deep sleep (suṣupti), he elaborates on the meaning of the phrase "by his own light" (svena jyotiṣā). [He says] "yellow," etc. Anticipating the objection—"In the absence of lights such as the sun, how can there be cognition of sound and so forth?"—he replies with "waking," etc. Anticipating the objection—"Even in the absence of gross objects, there is still cognition of them"—he specifies [the nature of that cognition] as "residual impression" (vāsanā). || 883 ||
Or rather, the totality consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth, is of the nature of latent predispositions (vāsanā).
In a dream, the light belonging to this self-luminous Self is denoted by the word "light."

Having raised the objection that the self is not self-luminous because the causal complex for pride (*māna*) and so forth operates within it, he elaborates upon the meaning of the phrase "it shines by itself" (*svena bhāsā*). He says:

"In the dream state... [The meaning is: because the manifestation (*bhāsa*) of the causal complex consisting of the measure (*mātra*) and so forth—which is of the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—has the inner self as its object, [the self is self-luminous].
The meaning is that there would be a loss of its self-luminosity. || 884 ||
All [states], such as being a cognizer and so forth, manifest in the form of objects.
Meditation [is for] the Self, whose nature is its own object and whose eye is unimpaired. || 885 ||

How can that [dream] be the object of the inward-looking [Self]? To this he says: "consisting of the state of being a knower, etc. He states the reason for its being of the nature of one's own experience:
"unimpaired," etc. || 885 ||
Just as one perceives one's mother connected with the object of measurement on the waking plane, so it is here.
Or, the mass of latent impressions, being devoid of activity, is perceived in that same way on the plane of a dream.
He states, by means of this illustration, that dream-cognition appears as having the inner self (pratyak) as its object: "The mother... (886).
This inner self is self-luminous and free from desire for all external means.
Immovable, this [Self] creates the appearances of consciousness as latent impressions within the dream state. || 887 ||
