Sarva | [Vol. 3, page 407] 1540 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]—

Anticipating the objection that if [the Self] perceives, it must depend on instruments, since one devoid of them cannot be an agent, he says: "By itself. To the question, "How then does the manifestation of chariots and so forth occur in a dream? he replies: "Unchanging" (kūṭastha). || 887 ||
In its proximity, the substance consisting of cause and effect possesses the nature of a reflection of consciousness.
That which is the state of this self being regarded as a non-seer due to delusion. || 888 ||

Fearing the objection that [the Self] would not possess immutability (*kauṭasthya*) if it were to act, he says: "In its proximity" (*tatsaṃnidhau*). "The state of being a seer" (*draṣṭṛtva*) means, in short, the agency of performing the acts of seeing with respect to various objects. || 888 ||
By means of light as its instrument, the Self exists without touching anything else.
Thus, there is no mutual conjunction between the reflection of consciousness and the latent impressions.
He establishes that the state of being a seer is produced by delusion. Regarding the phrase "by light": the word division is "not touching, though [it is] a non-agent.

Being established in immutable consciousness, the Self, while remaining unattached, is not even joined with latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the dream state; how much less so, then, could it be so in the waking state?

The meaning is that [the Self] possesses primary agency as the seer (*draṣṭṛ*). If it is argued that because the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are independent, that seership is not even primary, he says: "It is a reflection of consciousness" (*cidābhā*). For when latent impressions arise, they arise permeated by the reflection of consciousness; however, the Self is independent and is not connected with anything at all. Therefore, due to the absence of mutual contact between the Self and the latent impressions, [the seership] of the latent impressions [resides] in the Self through the medium of the intellect (*dhī*).
The meaning is that the Self's status as the seer of that [object] is merely superimposed, because it has been superimposed [upon the Self]. || 889 ||
Just as the pure, blazing, and steady flame of a gem of noble birth.
There is no modification of jars and other objects whether they are present or absent.

Because the Self is devoid of modification, its status as a "seer" is merely superimposed; to express this, he provides an illustration regarding its actionlessness with the word "yathā" (just as). It means:
of that pure gem which exists by birth—that is, which is naturally pure. || 890 ||
Thus, it is the witness of all cognition without exception, and the illuminator of the Supreme Self.
It remains changeless amidst the presence and absence of the fluctuations of the intellect.
He states the illustrative example: "Without remainder," etc. (891).
No activity of illumination whatsoever exists for it within its own self.
That proximity of the object to be manifested which constitutes its manifestation is [called] "action" (kriyā) by way of metaphorical designation. || 892 ||

If it is argued that even the witness (sākṣin) possesses a modification for the purpose of illumination, one must consider the alternatives: does that [modification] exist for its own illumination, or for the illumination of an object? He refutes the first alternative with "No," meaning that it is self-luminous by its very nature. He rejects the second with "Metaphorically" (upacārāt). || 892 ||
That very state of abiding which occurs through hearing is called "he sleeps."
In this sense, the third case ending is employed here [in Pāṇini’s rule] as "svena bhāsā" (by its own light). || 893 ||

Regarding how there can be the designation "he sleeps" for the Self, which is of the nature of unchanging, pure luminosity, the text says: "That which... It is that very state of abiding as the witness of the latent impressions (vāsanā) residing in the intellect that is described by the Śruti as "sleeping.

[Vol.
3, Page 408] 1 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary known as *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

1541. The meaning is that there is no loss of knowledge. He states the meaning of the fourth section of the third [chapter] with the word "thus" (*ittham*). It exists as the witness of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Since sleep belongs to the Self, therefore [the phrase] "by its own light, by its own radiance" uses the instrumental case; the meaning is that one should understand it as being thus: the immutable inner-light Self remains as the witness of its own mass of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 893 ||
Because of the absence of a causal complex, agency and so forth are not intended here at all.
And the non-agency of the self is what is primarily intended to be expressed. (894)

To the objection—“In an expression such as ‘by Rāma with an arrow’ (*rāmeṇa śareṇa*), why could that [agency] not belong to either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*)?”—he replies: “The causal complex” (*sāmagrī*). For that causal complex, characterized by cause and effect and so forth, does not exist apart from latent impressions (*vāsanā*). The word “here” (*iha*) refers to the context of dreams. Furthermore, he states that here agency and the like are not intended to be expressed: “of the Self” (*ātmanaḥ*). || 894 ||
In the past, this [inner light] was obscured by external lights such as the sun and others.
Because of the absence of any other light, this person is self-luminous. (895)

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "here" (atra) and so forth: "the sun and others," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "previously he perceived them while awake; now, however, during the state of dreaming. || 899 ||
For even in the waking state, there is no functioning of effects apart from the functioning of their causes.
And since the self is devoid of darkness (tamas), the mind does not abide [in it] during sleep. || 896 ||

One might raise the objection that there is no absence of light in the dream state because the light of the mind (*manas*) exists there; otherwise, it would follow that the dream state is indistinguishable from deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and thus self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣva*) does not belong to it. Anticipating this, he states the accepted point: "Not elsewhere. The word "also" (*api*) implies "even in other states. The particle "for" (*hi*) expresses the reason: because effects cannot be established as independent. Let it be so.
Regarding what has occurred in the present context, he says: "And the cause... For the inner self (pratyagātman), being unknown, is the cause of the world;

thus, since the mind—which is an effect—is dependent upon its own cause, it does not exist independently in a dream. Furthermore, that [mind] is the means of proving the Self, but it is not logical for it to be the means of proving the Self, because, being dependent on another, it is insentient like a snake. This is the meaning. || 896 ||
But is it not the case that only the waking body and so forth have been stated as the material cause?
While that [ignorance] exists, how can the self be designated as self-luminous? (897)

He raises an objection to what was stated with the words "In this regard" (*atretyādi*), beginning with "Now" (*nanu*). The meaning is that since the establishment of the self is possible solely through the force of impressions (*vāsanā*) from the waking state, its status as self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*) is not established. || 897 ||
This is true; nevertheless, this taking from another is [an act] directed toward one's own self.
It is always an object of perception, like a city of Gandharvas and the like. || 898 ||

[The opponent] objects: "It grasps only the mother. [The author] replies: "True. If that is so, since the self is established in accordance with the accepted latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it does not possess self-luminosity; therefore, he says: "Even so. For the collection of latent impressions does not contradict the self-luminosity of the self, because its manifestation occurs precisely as having the self as its object—this is the meaning. || 898 ||

In this adjunct of unreality, the Supreme can be shown.
In the nature of latent impressions (vāsanā), it is directly of the nature of self-luminosity. || 899 ||
Having stated that the mass of latent impressions (*vāsanārāśi*) does not contradict its own self-luminosity, he says "in this" (*etasmin*) to show that it actually establishes it.
The reason—that direct perception is possible because it serves as its establisher—is expressed by the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*). || 899 ||
When completely liberated from all limiting adjuncts, he cannot indeed be perceived.
Like one in deep sleep, he has thus taken this [world] from mere non-existence. || 900 ||

Anticipating the objection that the self-luminous (svayaṃjyotiḥ) Self can be shown even apart from the false limiting adjuncts known as latent impressions (vāsanā), he says: "All... For the Self cannot be shown to be self-luminous while gross adjuncts exist—as in the waking state—nor when all adjuncts are absent—as in deep sleep. Thus, in the dream state, the assumption of false latent impressions is made for the sake of the self-luminosity of the Self.
The meaning is that it is employed as a means for the attainment of light. The word "asat" (non-existent) has the sense of "false. || 900 ||
But surely, in the waking state, the grasper, the grasping, and so forth are perceived?
How can it be said that [the self] is self-luminous while those [elements] exist in the dream state? || 901 ||
He raises an objection against the self-luminosity of the self in dream through another method, beginning with "But surely" (nanu). || 909 ||
This is not so, because it consists in its being distinct from the waking state.
Because the body, the intellect, and so forth do not exist within the state of dreaming, they are merely a dream. || 902 ||

He states that the identity of the waking and dreaming states is unestablished: "Not this. Thinking that you yourself have accepted their identity, he asks for the reason: "Why? Having admitted a conventional distinction, he gives the answer: "The waking... He proves that very point: "The body... (902)
Characterized by the self, intellect, mind, the eye, light, objects, and so forth.
It is indeed waking, and not a dream, because it consists of nothing more than mental cultivation (bhāvanā). || 903 ||

He elaborates on the meaning already stated by means of the commentary beginning with "In the waking state, indeed" (jāgarite hi). [The word] "ātman" [is used]; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the diversity of the instruments and the diversity of the objects are included. || 903 ||
And the supreme Śruti, desiring to manifest this very meaning directly, [states as follows].
It does not exist there; this [tradition] has proceeded for the sake of purifying the inner self.

In this regard, he introduces the immediately following statement with the word "manifestly" (*āvis*). The construction is as follows: the scriptural passage beginning with "not there" (*na tatra*) has been set forth because it intends to manifest directly—by means of the characteristic of the dream's distinction from the waking state—the meaning for the purpose of purifying the inner self (*pratyagartha*). ||904||
He who performs actions, who is bound by the end of his debts, and who is possessed of desire and ignorance.
These two—sleep and waking—belong to that [mind], but not to the Witness, the Seer. || 905 ||

Anticipating the objection that "the purity of that [Self] is unestablished because it possesses states, like the intellect (buddhi) and so forth," he says: "Karma. [The objection is: Is the impurity of the qualified or the characterized [Self]? Not the first, because it is already established; for it is indeed accepted that the Self qualified by the intellect and possessed of defects such as ignorance (avidyā) and egoism (asmitā) [is impure].
[Volume 3,
Page 410] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri.

The meaning is that the agent of dharma and adharma is impure because it possesses various states, whereas the other [the Witness] is not, for the reason [of being an agent] is unestablished. Anticipating the objection that the Witness might be the agent of seeing, he says: "Of seeing" (dṛśeḥ). || 905 ||
By means of the immutable light alone, he remains in the state of dream, inactive and non-dual.
Through the latent impression (vāsanā) of the reflection of consciousness, its status as a witness is postulated. || 906 ||

He states the reason for its lack of possessing states [of consciousness] with the words "immutable" (kūṭastha). The meaning is: in dreamless sleep and other such states, the Self abides as mere changeless consciousness, characterized by the absence of duality and devoid of all activity; therefore, how could it possess states? Anticipating the objection that in the world, witnesshood is observed only in that which is active and dualistic, he says:

Regarding the phrase "as the reflection of consciousness" (cidābhāsa): the meaning is that the witnessing nature (sākṣitva) of the inner self (pratyañc) in the dream state—belonging to the immutable and non-dual consciousness—is based on the pervasion of the reflection of consciousness according to the impressions (vāsanā) of the waking state;
likewise, such a conceptual [witnessing] is not contradictory to the self-luminous nature even in other states. || 906 ||
Because of the absence of activity that would impel them, the lights such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth do not [function] here.
Therefore, there is no activity; it proceeds by means of its own inner light. || 907 ||
Having stated the purity of the Self by way of its being the witness of the various states, he concludes the purport of the present scriptural passage with the word "tat" (that).

Since the intellect and so forth, as well as the karmas that impel them, do not exceed their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the dream state, they consist of those impressions; and since these are illuminated by the Self, they do not function as illuminators toward it. Therefore, the meaning is that the Self itself is the light therein. || 907 ||
All objects perceived while awake are of the nature of mere mental construction.
When the karma of the waking state is exhausted and the karma of the dream state arises, they pass away [into that state]. || 908 ||
He clarifies the statement that in a dream, things such as cognition do not exist apart from their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) with the verse beginning "jāgrad" (908).
Those meditations, based on that [perception], were practiced part by part with a desire for pleasure in a dream.
He constructs chariots and other such objects for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyments experienced in dreams. (909)
The instrument, the object, and the agent—this action consists of these factors of action (kārakas).
Indeed, that which is most proximate and most subtle becomes manifest within the Self due to its nature as Being-Consciousness-Bliss.

Now, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "Then [he creates] chariots," etc., by saying: "Those... [The objection is raised: "If the Self creates chariots and so forth in a dream, it will likewise create [chariots] while awake; and thus, because it would be subject to the conditions of its own creation such as hunger and thirst, it would not be self-luminous. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the state of dreaming... All things consisting of the instruments and other factors of agency, which are of the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), manifest as objects for the sake of the inner self's experience in the dream state.

Therefore, the meaning is that it is not the illuminator of that [interior self]. How, then, is there the perception of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth as having the self as their object? To this he says: "The interior" (*pratyak*). For that intellect and so forth are superimposed upon ignorance accompanied by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*); because they possess the reflection of consciousness, they are superimposed upon the self together with ignorance. Therefore, the cognition of them as having the self as their object arises. || 909 || 990 ||
This world manifests as action in the form of cause and effect.
All this is superimposed upon the Self solely due to the cause of ignorance regarding the Self.
1 ka. is imagined; 2 kha. self-luminous; 3 ga. dream-enemy; 4 ka. ga. the non-dual nature of bliss;
5 kha. is conceived.

1544 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

Having restated what was said regarding "the instrument" and "the action," he establishes the meaning stated in the passage beginning with "pratyamoha" (delusion regarding the Self) and so forth. [Verse 911 begins: "The effect... That is to say, the action is that which has become the object. || 911 ||
The Self is absolutely the non-agent of all action and is distinct from it.
But the Self, being conjoined with that [aggregate], is itself unconjoined, devoid of qualities, and pure. || 912 ||

He states the conclusion regarding the point that the world is superimposed upon the Self by ignorance (*avidyā*). [The phrase] "of all" means "of the world," which is the object of action. The connection is with the word "absolutely distinct. The word "non-agent" (*akartṛ*) is to be read as a separate term. Anticipating the objection that the Self might be subject to pervasion (by the world) because it possesses qualities due to its connection with ignorance and its products, he says: "That... (verse 992).
When, through ignorance, one considers one's own self to be impure;
Then it enters into these states: waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. || 993 ||
If the Self is pure, how is its appearance as possessing states explained? To this he says: "By ignorance" (avidyayā). || 913 ||
Chariots do not exist in a dream-vision because of the non-existence of wood and other constituent parts.
In that same way, horses and so forth, as well as chariots together with their paths, do not exist.
Then, in this state, he creates chariots and other such things, which have waking activities and so forth as their causes.
Ignorance, desire, and action are this seed of creation for the vision [of the world].

Having explained the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "There [are] no... and ending with "...he is the agent," he states the literal meaning of the words beginning with "No" as follows: "Chariots, etc. Here, "here" refers to the dream state. To the question, "In the absence of causes such as wood, how can there be the creation of chariots and so forth? he says: "Now, etc. This is the answer therein.

Regarding the word "jāgrat" (waking): if the deity of action (*karmadeva*) is the cause of the creation of chariots and so forth, how is it that the Self (*ātman*) is called the creator? To this, he says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*).
Because of the absence of any means for the movement of karma here in this world.
Thus, the Śruti itself declares the falsity of going and so forth within a dream.

Anticipating the objection, "If chariots and such are created [in a dream], how can there be a statement regarding their non-existence?", he says: "Of action" (karmaṇaḥ). By negating the chariot and so forth—which are the causes for the action called "going"—the Śruti itself demonstrates that going and the like in a dream are false. Thus, the intended meaning here is that the entire dream is false, according to the principle of "it is mere illusion" (māyāmātraṃ tu). || 996 ||
Nor is there even the fruit of karma here in a dream, because its cause is impossible.
For this reason, the Śruti declared that even joys do not exist there.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "There are no joys" (na tatrānandāḥ) as follows: "Not by action" (na karma). He introduces a scriptural authority for the point that because there is an absence of action in a dream, there is an absence of its fruit, starting with "No" (na). The word "hi" (for/indeed) conveys the absence of the fruit when there is an absence of the cause; this he restates with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). || 997 ||
In this world, there are the Āiladas, as well as the Ānandas, the Harṣas, and the Mudas.
But the *pramuda*s are indeed just *muda*s characterized by an excellence of quality. (998)
[Vol.
3, Page 412] 1 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
"In this context, 'palvalas' are small ponds; the subsequent term has its meaning well-known."
Thus, by means of his own creative power (māyā), the Self is the creator of these very things that do not exist.

He states the non-repetitive meaning of the terms beginning with "ānanda": "There may be āhlādas. Here, the words *iha* and *atra* refer to the subject matter of the present passage. *Ānandas* are general forms of happiness. *Mudaḥ* are joys caused by such things as sons. *Pramudaḥ*, however, are the same joys distinguished by excellence; this is the distinction. *Palvalāḥ* are small ponds. [The section] preceding the word *sa hi* is the subsequent part.
The sentence: he concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "not there" with the words "in this way. || 918 || 919 ||
It has as its cause the karma of latent impressions (vāsanā) arising from the agent that is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa).
Having created it himself, he creates; thus, even though there is no [external] object, it is called "creation. || 920 ||
He states the reasoning for the Self’s status as a creator through its own *māyā*: "The manifestation of consciousness" (*cidābhā*), etc.

Because the Self—though in reality devoid of activity—is the cause of karma which, by means of ignorance (*avidyā*), serves as the motive for the experience of dreams manifested in the form of the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*) permeated by the reflection of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*);
it is therefore called the "agent" therein. The meaning is that the agency of the immutable (*kūṭastha*) Self is merely illusory (*māyika*). || 920 ||
The definition of action and its factors is established without critical investigation.
If this is held to be so even on the waking stage, how much more so when it is confined solely to the dream state?
He states the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so") regarding the illusory nature of the creation in a dream: "Unexamined... [Verse 921].

Because it is the cause of karma—the arising of mental fluctuations which are the nesting place for latent impressions (vāsanā) such as those of a chariot—the Self is designated as both "agent" and "non-agent. (922)

He states the meaning of the phrase "he is indeed the agent" as follows: "The chariot, etc. Since the Self is the cause of the action that manifests the transformation of consciousness—which resides in the mind and is the substratum for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the forms of chariots and so forth perceived during the waking state—it is called an "agent" in a figurative sense; however, in reality, it is not an agent, nor does it possess the status of a creator and so forth.
This is the meaning. || 922 ||
Even for one who is not an agent, the state of being an agent arises solely from the cause of ignorance regarding one's own self.
Since everything other than that is an effect in this world, the agent is the Self alone, which is the limit of darkness.

Fearing the objection that "if the self is a non-agent, it would contradict the fact that action is caused [by an agent]," he says: "of the non-agent. Fearing the objection that "if the agency of the self is produced by ignorance, then let there be another who is the agent in reality," he says: "of another than that. The meaning of the locative case is "scriptural convention" (śāstrīyo vyavahāraḥ). || 923 ||
In the occurrence of a dream, neither a material cause nor an instrumental cause exists.
Therefore, since the chariot and so forth are non-existent, the Self is only the seer, not the agent.

Anticipating the objection—“How can the Self, even in a dream, be the agent of the chariot and so forth, given that its material cause, such as wood, and its instruments, such as the axe, exist there?”—the author says: “In a dream... (924).
There exists even that wherein its appropriation or its means of accomplishment are present during the waking state.
Even there, by means of the causal factors such as the mind and intellect, which are the reflection of the self's consciousness;
1 kha. ṃtutaḥ || svaṃ | 2 ka. kha. gha. 'vyaktāvā | 3 ka. tmanaḥ ka 194 [vol 3, page 413]

1546 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Chapter]: The cause for the arising of mental modifications that serve as the nesting-place for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of chariots and other such things.
By that [agent], karma is brought to completion; therefore, he is called the "doer. || 926 ||

Raising the objection, "If the Self is the witness (sākṣin) of the chariot and so forth in a dream, how can it be called an agent (kartṛ)? he says [the following] because, through ignorance, it brings about the karma that causes the dream: "It exists," etc. The word "of this" (asya) refers to the chariot and so forth. || 929 || 926 ||
The agency [of the Self] is like that of the sun and other luminaries, because it causes the manifestation of objects such as the agent and so forth.
Because it is the witness of the agent of the intellect and so forth, the self would [otherwise] possess agency and other such qualities. (927)

If the Self is thus the agent, how is it said that "the seer alone is not an agent"? To this, [the text] says: "Of the sun and so forth. The meaning is that just as the sun and other luminaries are metaphorically designated as "agents of illumination" because their nature consists in the manifestation of objects such as agents, so too the agency and other attributes of the Self are metaphorical, since it is the witness of the instruments such as the intellect. || 927 ||
The very agency of action is the cause for its association with the intellect and the other faculties.
Therefore, the word "because" (*hi*) is used here in the sense of a reason: because of the failure to fully understand things as they truly are.

Regarding the word "hi" (for/indeed) in the verse beginning with "sahi," he states its meaning: "kriyā" (action). The sense is that the very agency of the Self—consisting of merit (*dharma*) and so forth—which arises during the waking state due to its connection with the ignorance of the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and other factors, is itself the cause for the creation of chariots and such things in the dream state; thus, the word "hi" is used in the sense of a reason.
Therefore, it is logical that the Self’s status as a creator in the dream state is illusory (*māyika*). || 928 ||
Having stated its self-luminosity and its transcendence over the intellect and other faculties, [the text proceeds].
Then, immediately after the statement of the Brāhmaṇa, he uttered mantras for this purpose.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore, these... as follows: "By himself," etc.; and the phrase "the meaning of the word *atha* itself is [stated] by the Brāhmaṇa," and so forth. || 929 ||
Having struck down this waking body by means of its own natural function through the exhaustion of activity, [he remains].
Remaining awake, he perceives the vital breaths (prāṇas) which have fallen asleep, in their forms as mental impressions (bhāvanā).

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "by means of a dream" (*svapnena*) as follows: "by his own power" (*svamavṛttyā*), which means having rendered [the body] motionless. Regarding the phrase "therein [he performs] action" (*tatra kriyā*): the meaning is that this occurs through the exhaustion of karma caused by the waking state and the emergence of karma caused by the dreaming state. He then states the meaning of the passage beginning with "unslumbering among those who slumber" (*asuptaḥ suptān*).
"Not asleep" (asupta). || 930 ||
It is not asleep because it is not the cause of activity; rather, it awakens the sleeping vital breaths (prāṇas) through the arising of action.
Due to the inherent nature of the immutable witness-consciousness, the self perceives its own dream.

To explain how the Self is not asleep, he says: "asleep" (asupta). Since the awakening of one's own Self is not caused by karma, even when the karma that causes [ordinary] awakening has perished, the Self remains awake; this is the meaning. To explain how the vital breaths (prāṇas) are asleep, he says: "asleep" (suptān). Because the activity of the vital breaths is caused by karma, one perceives these [breaths] as withdrawn once the karma has been exhausted; such is the sense of the statement "he sees. By the use of the word "sees,"...
Regarding the attainment of the status of being the agent of seeing, it has been said: "The immutable one... (931).
Having taken up the semen beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa), and having made it consist of that very contemplation (bhāvanā).
The self, inactive and established in its own nature, gazes upon the world as if it were space. || 932 ||
Showing the connection of the phrase "taking the semen" (śukramādāya) with the word "he gazes upon" (abhicākaśīti), he states the meaning: "prāṇa, etc.

3, page 414] 3 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā by Ānandagiri. 1547.

Since the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) is the subject under discussion among the senses, it is itself the "semen" (*śukra*); or rather, its "semen" is its luminous capacity for perceiving objects. Having raised the objection that it might be characterized by activity due to its being a grasper or a seer, he says: "It is inactive" (*akriya*). Nevertheless, fearing that suffering might still be attributed to it, he refutes this by declaring it to be a witness: "It is self-abiding" (*svastha*). || 932 ||
Having exhausted the enjoyment arising from sleep, he again takes recourse in the yoga of birth.
The eternal person, designated as the *haṃsa*, goes to the station of the intellect and the other faculties. || 933 ||
He explains the passage beginning with "again" and so forth: "kṣīṇa" (exhausted), etc. || 933 ||
For by turns, each one alone destroys both worlds by its own nature.
Therefore, that Lord was called Ekahaṃsa by those who know the Purāṇas. || 934 ||

Anticipating the question of how a person can be designated as a "swan" (haṃsa), he states the meaning of the term *ekahaṃsa*: "By way of succession. Here, the root *han* signifies "to go," according to the traditional rule that *hana* means both "to kill" and "to go. [It is so called] by those who know the Purāṇas—that is, by those who know the reality that is beginningless and endless—as is well known.
Alternatively, the word *purāṇa* has the sense of "ancient. For it is said:
"A swan rising from the water does not lift one foot;
if it were to lift that foot, there would be neither death nor immortality."
"Yogins behold that eternal Blessed One," and also: "Marīci, Damana, Haṃsa; the one, the non-one, the All."
"And they call Him the infinite, immovable Meru, the Swan, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Ordainer, the ageless and eternal, the supreme and immutable. (934)
Gold is light and consciousness; its true essence consists of that alone.
Therefore, the word "hiraṇmaya" refers to the God; here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of the thing itself (*svārthe*).

He explains the term *hiraṇmaya* [as "golden"]: "Hiraṇyam" [is used]. He sets aside the sense of *mayaṭ* as denoting a modification (*vikāra*) and states that it is used in its own primary sense (*svārthe*). || 939 ||
This belongs to another person, because it is a conceptual construction arising from a lack of understanding of that [other].
Therefore, because it consists merely of witnesses and so forth, this is called "harsh" (pāruṣya). || 936 ||

The Mādhyandinas [read] "The golden one, the Puruṣa, the single swan. Regarding that, he explains the meaning of the word *pauruṣa* [as follows]: "Of the Supreme," etc. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the division into the object of knowledge, the agent, the action, and so forth, is included. || 936 ||
The fulfillment of this entire complex of causes and effects.
This person (puruṣa) would be the Self (ātman), either because of its fullness or because it is non-dual in nature. || 937 ||

Regarding the statement "the Person is golden," the followers of the Kaṇva school explain the meaning of the word "Person" (puruṣa) as "because of filling" (pūraṇāt). The reason for being all-pervasive is stated as "the Self" (ātman); the reason for its fullness is stated as "non-dual" (advaya). || 937 ||
1 kha. 'Atijyotiṣma' | [Vol. 3, page 415] 1548 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Chapter—]
And by the accumulation of the nine conceptualizations of the factors of decline.
The sages, who perceive the further shore of existence, manifested themselves in the form of swans.
It has been explained that he is called the "Single Swan" (*ekahaṃsa*) because he goes alone. Now, he states another meaning: "By abandoning" (*hānena*).
This refers, that is to say, to the various limbs, which are specific forms of the body. And it has been said:
"By the abandonment of past times and by the accumulation of new ones..."
"Those who see the further shore say that the unborn one is the true essence of bodies. || 938 ||
For the higher self, by protecting the lower vital breath, guards the body from death.
Having wandered outside the body, it then returns again just as it came. || 939 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "by means of the vital breath" (*prāṇena*). Regarding the word "by means of the vital breath": the particle *hi* is used for the purpose of stating a well-known fact, namely that the protection of the body is brought about by the vital breath. The suffix *-ka* in the word *dehaka* is intended to clarify its inferiority. The meaning is that if the Supreme [Self] did not protect the body by means of the vital breath during sleep, there would be the delusion that it is dead. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "outside" (*bahiḥ*). Regarding the word "outside": although [the Self] resides within the body...
Although one sees a dream, it is said to be "external" because of the absence of false identification [with it]. He completes the required sense with the word "atha" (then). The meaning is:

immediately after the emergence from waking activity (*jāgrat-karma*). By the word "punaḥ" (again), the immediate succession following the exhaustion of the karma that caused the dream is expressed. || 939 ||
For, having abandoned the channels, the person [experiences] in the dream state those [channels] which bestow the enjoyments of the waking state.
Then, bestowing the enjoyment of dreams, she proceeds from the *iḍā* to the *vahni* [channel]. || 940 ||
This [verse] establishes that the seer is outside the body in a dream, beginning with the words "the channels" (nāḍīḥ). || 940 ||
Wherever the latent impression (vāsanā), manifested by karma and capable of assuming any form at will,
exists, there the immortal and immutable Hamsa— the Self— takes that [impression] and attains its own body.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "he goes" (*sa īyate*) by saying "by means of action" (*karmaṇā*). The meaning is that, depending upon the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—which consists of desire and resides in specific objects manifested by the karma that causes dreams—the Self (*ātman*) enters, in that dream, a body composed of that [desire] which is appropriate to its own karma. Anticipating the objection that if the Self were the *haṃsa* (the individual soul), then because it possesses the quality of going, it would be subject to destruction and decay, he reminds us of what was stated: "it is imperishable" (*avyayaḥ*), namely, "it is immortal" (*amṛtaḥ*).
In accordance with their karma and knowledge, they repeatedly assume forms that are high or low.
Abiding within the manifold world of dreams and illusion, the actionless Self appears as if it were acting.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "in the state of dream" (svapnānte) as follows: "karma... He states the reason for the use of the word "iva" (as if): "niṣkriyaḥ" (devoid of action). || 942 ||
The root *jakṣati* should be understood as having the sense of playfulness (*narma*), and likewise *modati* has the sense of joy (*harṣa*).
In this world, fear arises from ignorance; in a dream, it does not arise because its cause is absent.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "as if with women" (*uteva strībhiḥ*), saying: "for the sake of sport" (*narmārtha*). The word *narma* means jesting or derision. To the question of how fear caused by tigers and the like in a dream can be non-existent, he replies: "because of its cause," meaning that there is an absence of tigers and so forth other than [those produced by] ignorance (*avidyā*).
The meaning is that the fear in that case is produced solely by that [ignorance]. || 943 ||

The grove itself, which arises from *māyā* and is characterized by the construction of a dream. [Vol. 3, page 416] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1549.
Those who possess illusory power perceive him, but no one perceives him [in his true nature]. || 944 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "ārāmam" as follows: "ārāmam" || 944 ||
The self-luminosity [of the Self] is established through scripture as being distinct from the intellect and other such faculties.
Having thus established it through scripture, it is now further considered from the perspective of worldly experience as well. || 945 ||

He takes up [the passage] beginning with "not that" (*taṃ nā'yatam*) by way of restating what has already occurred. The word "then" (*atha*) is used here to establish that the world and the scriptures have a single meaning with respect to the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. || 949 ||
"One should not wake one who is sleeping deeply"—this indeed is a worldly proverb.
If it is asked "For what purpose?", in that case, the world is observed as the cause.

He explains that [saying] "deeply asleep" (*suptam*): therein, the word *hi* is for the purpose of attaining universal consensus among all people. He states the reason, preceded by a question, regarding why one should not suddenly awaken someone who is deeply asleep: "For what purpose? (946).
Having abandoned the channels of wakefulness, the self has entered these channels of sleep.
Thus, because it is well-known in the world, the world instructs him in that matter.

He clarifies that very reason: "prabodha" (awakening), etc. This means "while that person is asleep. If the reading is "tasmāt" (therefore), the meaning is explicit. The word "tat" refers to the statement of the authoritative teaching. || 947 ||
They instruct [the practitioner] out of fear that he might enter through the wrong channel.
"One should not wake one who is sleeping," they say emphatically, seeing the faults therein. (948)

Even though it is well known that [the soul] enters into another channel, why does common worldly experience instruct that one should not wake someone who is in deep sleep suddenly? To this, he says: "The channel," etc. (948).
Just as one who has been deeply asleep in these channels is awakened according to the circumstances.
If one does not resort to it, then this [treatment] will be a most painful medical procedure. || 949 ||

Showing the fault in the case of a reversal [of the order], he explains [the sūtra] with the words "difficult to cure" and so forth. "Just as" means: by way of the consequence of blindness, deafness, and so on. || 949 ||
For the purpose of entering and exiting the body, it is like a house or other such dwellings for the body.
Let it be determined that this self is distinct from cognition and the other [mental states]. || 950 ||

He summarizes the meaning established by the mantras, Brāhmaṇas, and worldly consensus: "The body" (deha). Just as Caitra is distinct from his house when entering or leaving it, so too the Self is distinct from the body due to its entry into and departure from it;
therefore, its difference from the intellect and other faculties, as well as its self-luminosity, are determined through worldly consensus and other means—this is the sense. || 990 ||
It is distinct from categories such as the internal self and so forth, and it abides within its own nature.
It is a pity that those of wicked mind do not perceive this misfortune and ill-fortune. || 951 ||

By asserting through the *Maṇtra* and *Brāhmaṇa* sections and other texts that the Self is self-luminous and transcendent, one does not contradict the statement in the *Mantra-bhāga*: "No one sees Him" (*na taṃ paśyati kaścana*).
[End of] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Chapter Four. [Page 417, Volume 3, Verse 1550].

Although it was introduced, it has not yet been explained; now he states its intended meaning (*tātparya*). With the words "adhyātmādi," he dispels the doubt that it is not seen because it is separated [from the main topic]. He says: "in one's own self" (*svātmani*). || 911 ||
The God whose sphere is direct perception, and the world which is exceedingly heedless.
Seeing him striking his head, Śruti, distressed, laments.

Anticipating the objection that because he is unfit to be seen, his non-appearance does not imply the misfortune of people due to his wicked-mindedness, he says: "Perceptible," etc. "Extreme negligence" (atipramāditva) means being inclined toward the non-self to the exclusion of the Self. || 992 ||
Although this [Self] is most directly perceived, free from darkness, and established by itself;
Alas, what a tragedy! We do not see anyone to whom we may go for refuge.

He explains his lamentation by raising the doubt that even though [the Self] is self-luminous, established in its own majesty, and directly accessible, it might not be seen due to an obstruction; thus he says:
"most directly perceived. Raising the doubt that it might not be seen because of being obscured, he says:
"itself. || 993 ||
That which has been stated here in the scripture regarding the Self, beginning with its nature as self-luminous;
This is stated as the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) regarding that which takes the form of the final conclusion (siddhānta). || 954 ||

Anticipating the objection that the sentence beginning with "atho khalu" is inconsistent with what precedes it, he says: "Self-luminosity. This refers to the scriptural passage beginning with "sa yatra prasvapiti. (994)
Wherever he has previously gone by virtue of being the prior position (pūrvapakṣa), [he remains there].
Then indeed, one should look at the passage beginning with "They say," and so forth, in due order. (955)

Having stated the self-luminosity [of the Self], he raises the objection, "If this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), how is it established here? and says: "In that case... Even though it is the prima facie view, why is this sequence? He states the meaning indicated by the word "for" (*hi*) as follows: "Thus... Since the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) occurs immediately after the prima facie view, the sequence is appropriate; thus, by the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*), the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) is set aside, as in the case of the *agnihotra* and the cooking of the barley-gruel (*yavāgū*).
The meaning is "from me. || 995 ||
Furthermore, its state of being the waking place [of the Self] is established by the statement beginning with "Now, indeed... (atho khalu).
The phrase "for those very [reasons]" is a statement of the reason for the sake of establishing the meaning of the proposition. || 956 ||

Having shown the sequence, he analyzes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "of this [self]" (*svamasya*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "is asserted on the basis of the statement" (*vākyataḥ pratijñāyate*). || 996 ||
In those channels within which the waking perception of a person occurs, this [state] exists.
One should understand it as being seen in a dream; there is no other way—this is the certain conclusion. || 957 ||
He explains the meaning of "cause" [with the verse]: "The waking state," etc. (997).
And while asleep, this person identifies with that very Self alone.
It abides in the awakening of the mind of restraint; it is never anything other than that. || 958 ||

Having stated that waking and dreaming share a single location, he provides the reason for the identity of the seer: "In a dream... (verse 998).
Characterized by waking relatives, cities, enemies, horses, gardens, and so forth.
In a dream, one recognizes those very same [objects] and not others than them. (959)
He states the identity of their object: "Waking," etc. (959).
If the dreamer were to see something entirely unprecedented while awake, [it would be so].
Another dream that has been described would be just as it was previously encountered.

Because the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the observer (*draṣṭṛ*) are identical, their identity has been stated; he now clarifies this by means of a negative argument (*vyatireka*). [The text says: "Something unprecedented" (*apūrva*).

Just as one who has traveled from one place to another sees something unprecedented, such as a camel, if the dreamer were to see something unprecedented compared to the waking state, then the dream would be distinct from that [waking state]. But since he does not see anything of the sort, the meaning is that the waking state itself is the dream. The prefix *sam-* [indicates]...
This is connected with the word "bhavet" (it would be). || 960 ||
Thus some have said, but that statement is not logical.
That this is illogical has already been demonstrated previously. || 961 ||

He concludes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "in this way. Their intention is that if, when the waking state itself is a dream, self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣya*) is difficult to maintain there, then it is equally difficult to maintain in the dream state as well. He declares that this is incorrect with the words "but not so" (*na tu*). He clarifies that very point with the words "it is illogical" (*ayuktimat*), meaning in passages such as "there are no chariots there" (*na tatra rathāḥ*). || 969 ||
In this context, by the phrase "this [is] here," the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is refuted.
By the previously stated and the about-to-be-stated reasoning, this is certainly so. || 962 ||

Having set aside the passage beginning with "atra" (here) as being outside the direct scope of the scripture (*śruti*), he states its intended meaning (*tātparya*) with the words "atreti. The construction is as follows:

the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) established in the immediately preceding scriptural passage is certainly refuted by this sentence, in accordance with the logic already stated and that which is yet to be stated.
Dream is not located in the same place as waking, because the causal conditions for waking are absent;
for one perceives dreams even in the absence of internal objects such as the body and so forth. (963)

He recalls, in brief, the principle already stated and to be stated further by means of the words beginning with "no" (na). He establishes the reason for that [negation] with the words beginning with "adhyātmādi. || 963 ||
Its self-luminosity has been stated, as well as its state of being devoid of agency during sleep.
And thus, from the preceding statement, there is the transcendence of the form of death for the inner Self.
In order to introduce the passage beginning with "Beyond this," he recounts what has preceded it, starting with the word "himself" (*svayam*).

The meaning is that, according to such scriptural statements as "In this case, this person is self-luminous" and "There, chariots do not pass; [there] the forms of death do not reach," [the Self is established as self-luminous]. || 964 ||
Its nature consists of desire and so forth; moreover, it may or may not be subject to death.
Suspecting this, the king questioned Yājñavalkya regarding the fault.

He takes up the subsequent statement: "Desires and so forth. Since it was stated that one transcends the forms of death, the King—wondering whether desire, action, and the like, which constitute death, are the very nature of the Self or not, and considering that liberation would be impossible in the former case—questioned the Sage with the words beginning with "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) in order to ascertain the non-duality [of the Self]. This is the meaning. || 969 ||
"From the statement made in the context, 'The matter asked about has been well-determined by me,'" [it is understood].
The king questioned the sage Nivītu again for the sake of liberation.

The Sage, having begun to determine for the King who asked "What is the Self?", does not desist until he has resolved that question; therefore, [the author] explains how the King was engaged in the midst of the assembly by saying: "Because it was asked. Perceiving that the Sage was intent on withdrawing after having answered with the thought that the very substance of the Self which was asked by the King had been determined exactly as it is through the words beginning with "This one who... and so forth.
The meaning is that the king questioned him once again for the sake of liberation. || 966 ||
He considered the state of self-luminosity mentioned [in the scripture] to be a constituent factor of liberation.
Nor does one consider the determination of the whole to be achieved solely by the statement of the determination of its parts.
Therefore, with liberation in mind, he questioned Yājñavalkya.

Anticipating the objection that liberation is already established simply by the statement that the Self is self-luminous (svayaṃjyotis) as distinct from the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties—and thus that a question for that purpose is not logical—he says: "By itself" (svayam). Then, anticipating the objection that since the determination of the self-luminosity—which is a constituent part (aṅga) of liberation—would suffice to establish the determination of liberation itself, which is the whole (aṅgin), there is no need for a question concerning it—he says: "And not... For when the constituent parts, such as the New Moon sacrifice (darśa), have been determined...

The meaning is that the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) are determined by their capacity to serve as instruments for the act of grasping [the primary], according to their specific purpose; however, the direct textual statement (*śruti*) and other means merely provide the door [to that capacity], for there is no logical necessity that the determination of the subsidiaries alone constitutes the final determination [of the relationship]. || 967 || 968 ||
"For the sake of detachment from attachment, he says 'or that' and so forth."
For it is through detachment from desire and the like that the self possesses the fitness for liberation. || 969 ||

Having stated the purport of the question, he states the purport of the reply: "Attachment," etc. Anticipating the objection—"Why is it that the discrimination of that [attachment] alone is required for liberation, and why should it be explained?"—he says: "Desire," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, the discrimination of that is appropriate. || 969 ||
If desire and the like were an inherent quality of the self, it would follow that liberation is impossible.
For indeed, there is no removal of a quality by the destruction of its substratum.

He clarifies the point already stated by means of a negative argument (*vyatireka*). [The verse begins with] "kāma... etc. One might ask: "How does this much [denial] establish liberation? For even if that [desire] is a quality of the self, its [mere] removal would not suffice. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "na hi... etc. The meaning is: as long as the self exists, the total destruction of its real quality is impossible; and if it were destroyed along with the self, there would be no subject for the result, and thus no liberation. ||970||
In this state, O Mṛtyu, this self transcends forms alone in its dream.
But death does not [occur], because even in a dream, joy, fear, and so forth are seen.
1. In the context of seeing and so forth.

3, page 420] 3. Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Anticipating the objection that—even though desire and the rest lack the nature of the Self—the subsequent statement does not go beyond the purpose of discerning them from it, since this is already established in the passage "the forms of death," he says: "The forms. || 971 ||
Death, characterized by joy, fear, and so forth, is not the inherent nature of the self.
Likewise, O Blessed One, explain to me that which is above for the sake of my liberation.

Having stated the purport of the question and the answer, he applies the question [with the words] "moda" etc. This means: because of the determination of self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣva*). || 972 ||
The "gift of a thousand" refers to the aforementioned reality that is self-luminous.
This is for the purpose of making known the limit of definitive conclusions, since there is no definitive conclusion for all questions without exception. || 973 ||

If a remainder of the question still remains, he explains why there is the gift of a thousand [cows] in that context with the words "sahasra" (thousand). The term "limit of the decision" (*nirṇayāghāṭa*) means the firmness of one's own conclusion regarding the matter indicated; that is to say, it is for the purpose of making that known. Anticipating the objection, "Why should the gift of a thousand not occur simply because there is no remainder of the question? he says, "Not due to the absence of a remainder," because a further question is observed [in the text]. || 973 ||
He who was previously explained is indeed this self-luminous one.
Unattached in its own ground, it becomes serene in the state of supreme clarity.

Having explained the words of the question, and desiring to explain the answer, he states the meaning by supplying the required sense of the words "he, this one, in that state of serene confidence" (*sa eṣa etasmin saṃprasāde*). He says: "He is self-luminous" (*svayaṃjyotiḥ*). The construction is as follows: that very Self who was previously established as self-luminous becomes unattached in the state of dreaming and becomes serene in the state of deep sleep (*saṃprasāda*).
By the term "serenity" (saṃprasāda), deep sleep is expressed. || 974 ||
Just as water attains extreme clarity through contact with the *kataka* nut, [so too does the mind attain purity].
Thus, for this Self, all conceptions of saṃsāra have been cast away.
Therefore, well-being and clarity exist within this state of deep sleep.
Those who know it call this state of perfect clarity "deep sleep. || 976 ||

Regarding that, he states the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the sign (*nimitta*): "of waters," and so forth. For it has been stated that "the state of perfect serenity" (*saṃprasāda*) refers to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), based on its etymological derivation as "that in which one becomes perfectly serene. || 979 || 976 ||
The theft of the mother which he committed out of a desire for sexual pleasure in a dream.
Upon the destruction of that [ignorance], he becomes free from attachment and finds serenity within his own self alone. || 977 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the term *saṃprasāda* has deep sleep (*suṣupti*) as its referent: "Mātrā... etc. The construction is to be understood as follows: when the Self, having taken up the *mātrās*—which are merely the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state—for the sake of experiencing dreams, ceases from that taking up of the *mātrās* which cause dreams, then that Self becomes serene once again in its own Self, which is devoid of desire and the like. || 977 ||
Compared to the waking state, [the mind] becomes somewhat clearer in the dream state.
For that [cognition] as well, there would be the qualification "having the nature of setting" in relation to the [preceding] cognition. || 978 ||
[Vol. 3, page 421] 1554 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

Anticipating the objection—“Why is the term ‘samiti’ (coming together) used as a qualification for deep sleep (*suṣupti*) when it is already indicated by the word ‘prasāda’ (serenity)?”—he says: “jāgrat” (waking).

The remaining residual impression (*saṃskāra*) also dissolves during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), whereby it becomes serene in its entirety; thus, the prefix [in *upasarga*] is meaningful—this is the sense. || 978 ||
Established here daily, he rests solely upon the foundation of absolute knowledge.
Because he is the causal self (*kāraṇātman*), he therefore performs the effects known as waking and dreaming.

Having explained the meaning of the term *saṃprasāda*, he shows the *prājña* (the wise one) who identifies with it by means of the word *kevala*. *Kaivalya* (aloneness) refers to the absence of gross effects; its meaning as *mātra* (merely) refers to the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). The word *iha* (here) refers to the state of *saṃprasāda*. He establishes [the soul's] nature as the causal self with the words *tasmāt* (therefore). This means "from ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is its own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). And it has been said: [Verse 1.26]... 1. 26. It is said: "The individual soul, being of the nature of the cause, is not perceived while in the body, because it is merged in the causal state, like fire covered by ashes. (Gaudapāda-kārikā 1.26) (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-verse; the translation reflects the available portion.)
"The darkness called deep sleep, which is ignorance, is the seed of both dreaming and waking. || 979 ||
How, and by what sequence, does the inward Self become serene in this regard?
Now, the Śruti declares this very point with the words beginning "having rejoiced" (ratvā).
Having explained the passage beginning with "all" (*savā*), he next introduces the subsequent sentence by way of a question: "How? (*katham*).

Having restated the word from the commentary, "how [is he] serene? (*saṃprasanna*), the statement of its meaning follows: "by what? (*kena*). Here, the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is being discussed. || 980 ||
Having enjoyed himself and played upon the plane of dream by means of his own creative power (māyā), he—
Having practiced and dwelt [in this way], the self is established through the means of latent impressions alone. 981.

Having stated the intended meaning—that the subsequent passage is intended to explain the clarity of the Self during deep sleep through the sequence of waking and dreaming—the author explains the meanings of the words. Regarding the phrase "in the state of dream" (*svapne*): the connection with what follows is that the Self, having sported and moved about in the realm of dreams by means of *māyā*, using nothing but latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as its instrument, becomes serene in the state of the *prājña* (the state of deep sleep). He refutes the notion that a dream is merely memory by stating "by the *māyā* of the Self"; it is a form of play (*krīḍā*).
The distinction is that *viharaṇa* consists of mental, vocal, and physical activities dependent on wife, children, and so forth, as well as wandering from one place to another. || 989 ||
By the word "only" (eva) in the phrase "only two," the status of being a causal factor (kārakatva) is excluded.
And here, the fruit of merit and demerit is expressed by the terms "merit" and "demerit."
He states the meaning of "having seen" and so forth: "Having seen," etc. (982).
Because in this waking state, there is the occurrence of the sense organs, their objects, and so forth.
Action is brought to completion, and it bestows upon the self results such as happiness and the like.

Anticipating the objection that the negation of agency is untenable because activity is accomplished even in a dream just as it is in the waking state, he refutes the supporting example with the verse beginning "asya" (983).
But in a dream, because of the absence of causal factors, there is no accomplishment of action for the self.
Therefore, from that which is changeless, there manifests as mere latent impression (vāsanā) the appearance of consciousness (cidābhā). || 984 ||

He states the disparity with the illustrative example (dāṣṭantika) in the words "But in a dream... He asks, "How then is there the perception of action there? and answers, "It is the reflection of consciousness (cidābha). The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is the absence of causal factors (kāraka). The word should be split as "of the changeless one" (avikāriṇaḥ). || 984 ||
1. Not internal. 2. *ka*. "Self-measure. 3. *ka*, *kha*. "Sufficient self-... 4. *ga*. "The state is attained. [Vol. 3, page 422] 1.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1555.
Since there is no action here, the Vedic revelation itself provides the restriction.
Having seen that "the Self has not done this," it is therefore inward-turned and not an agent. || 985 ||

He summarizes the meaning of the word "eva" (only/alone) with the words "yataḥ" (since). The locative case in "svapne" (in a dream) is the sense [of the locative]. The connection is: "having seen, he runs.
He states the immutability (*kauṭasthya*) which is the result of the absence of instruments [of action] with the word "pratyak" (turned inward). || 985 ||
And here, the fruit of merit and demerit is considered to be designated by the terms "merit" and "demerit."
Therefore, it is said that [the effect] possesses the cause only by way of metaphorical designation.

Having restated what was said here regarding the fruit of merit and demerit (*puṇyapāpaphala*), he states the logical justification: "Merit... Since every effect is observed to be pervaded by its cause, therefore the word for the cause—namely *puṇya* (merit) and *pāpa* (demerit)—is used figuratively to denote their fruit, as in the expression "he mixes with the cows."
This is the meaning of "it is said. || 989 ||
Then, upon the cessation of the activity of dreaming, the wise one becomes self-luminous.
The supreme deity becomes gracious, just as the western quarter [is serene] in the highest state.

He concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "having rejoiced" (*ratvā*) with the words "in dream" (*svapne*). The qualification "the supreme deity" (*paro devaḥ*) is for the purpose of making known that the cognitional self (*vijñānātman*) is not other than the Supreme;
and the phrase "only in the inward" (*pratīcyeva*) is used to state that in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the self abides in the Supreme Self. || 987 ||
In the past as well, this self has repeatedly gone from one place to another place.
Therefore, from this very point, by means of attaining the state of perfect serenity (*saṃprasāda*), there is a surpassing [of the previous stage]. (988)

He states the meaning of the word "again" (*punaḥ*): "Even previously" (*purāpi*). Since this Self has already gone many times in the past from the state of attaining serene bliss (*saṃprasāda*) to another state called dream, the expression "again" is employed in this way; such is the construction. || 988 ||
In this manner, through the path thus described, one attains the state of deep sleep by way of conformity.
Its emergence is the reverse process, consisting of the transition through the states beginning with dreaming. || 989 ||

He prepares the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) to explain the meaning of the word *prati*. Regarding the term *ānulomyam* ("in the direct order"): the phrase "by what has been stated" is an explanation of the word "thus" (*evam*);

it means by the sequence already described, namely, that one goes from the waking state to the dream state, and from there to deep sleep (*suṣupti*). He states the meaning of the word *prati*: "that" (*tat*).
From that which is under discussion, arising in the reverse manner is *prātilomyam* (the inverse order); that is the conventional meaning denoted by the word *prati*.
Such is the meaning. He states the meaning of the word *nyāya*: "In dreams, etc. (989).
Therefore, this word "prati" is intended here in the sense of "contrary" or "reverse."
The unborn one likewise establishes a contrary course in a dream.

Fearing that the word *prati* might mean "conformity," as in the expression *pratirūpaḥ babhūva* ("he became a counterpart"), he says: "prātilomya" (contrariety). He states the reason expressed by the word *ataḥ*: "viparītā" (contrary). For the arrival from sleep to the states of dreaming and waking is indeed contrary [to sleep];
therefore, the meaning here is that the word *prati* does not signify conformity. He summarizes the meaning of the phrase *pratiyonyādravati* (he runs back to his source): *prati-*...

Regarding the term "place" (sthāna): it means that just as [the self] goes to the state of serene repose (saṃprasāda), so too does the Supreme Person (paraḥ pumān) come toward the very place of enjoyment, such as the dream state, for the sake of experience. || 990 ||

This prefix *prati* is used in the sense of "according to," and this prefix *nir* is used in the sense of "certainty."
The root *iṇ* (to go) takes the suffix *gha*, resulting in *āya*, which signifies both "going" and "movement. (991)

He explains the meaning of the word *pratinyāyam* by its constituent parts: "yathārtha" means that when the arrival [of the breath] in the reverse order is intended, just as its attainment occurred in the forward order (*ānulomyena*). He analyzes the word *āya*: "ayanam. He indicates its derivation: from the verbal root *i*, which has the sense of "going," with the suffix *ghañ* added in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).

The meaning is that when the *ghakāra* and *nakāra* have been assigned the technical designation *it*, they are elided; and once the letter *a* remains, the formation of the word *āya* occurs through the substitution of *vṛddhi* for the preceding vowel. || 999 ||
In this context, the instruments such as the ear and so forth are the cause for the grasping of the objects of the senses.
It would be expressible by the word "source" (yoni) and would have as its basis the waking body. || 992 ||

Having begun with the passage, "He, indeed, having enjoyed himself in that state of dream," [the text] says, "he runs back to his source for the sake of the waking state" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15). Following this middle section, he explains the meaning of the word *yoni* (source): "The auditory organ, etc. The meaning is that the collection of instruments (*karaṇa-jāta*) residing in the waking body, which serves as the cause for the appropriation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the cognitions of objects such as form, is what is denoted by the word *yoni*. Here, there is either a reference to the waking state or to the sentence [of the Upaniṣad].
Whatever was the source of each [element] for the taking of its measure in the past, that is its own origin.
The self enters that very same womb again during sleep. || 993 ||
Having restated the meaning of the word *yoni*, he explains the meanings of the words *prati* and *ādravati* with the words "mātrā" etc.

That very *yoni*—characterized by the eyes and other senses—which belongs to that Self (*ātman*) and consists in the acceptance of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for the enjoyment of forms and so forth, and which persists during the waking state;

this same person, while situated in the dream state, [returns] to that very *yoni* residing in his own substrate upon the exhaustion of those [dream] actions and when the causes for waking arise again.
The meaning is that he practices; the person is situated therein. || 993 ||
Just as the grasping was previously performed by the Mothers in the creation of the dream.
Taking those constituent elements from the dream, he enters the womb of the dream-state.

The author explains the meaning of the Kaṇva recension, "He runs back to his own source, as it were, for the sake of sleep," with the words beginning "Just as. Previously, when the creation of dreams was introduced during the waking state, those *mātrās*—that is, the latent impressions (*vāsanās*)—were taken up according to their material cause; in exactly that same way, having accepted those *mātrās*, one who is in the dream state, upon the exhaustion of that [dream] karma, enters deep sleep. Then, when dream-karma arises again, because of the manifestation of the latent impressions existing in the form of the causal self, he [assumes] a body constructed from them.
The meaning is that one resorts to the sense-base consisting of that [dream-object], which is designated as having the dream as its source. || 994 ||
And by means of speech that follows the correct method, his true path is declared.
Each [element] is described here according to its place, by means of its own specific sound. || 995 ||

According to both readings, he states the meaning of the word *pratinyāya*: "Prati... This means that for one who goes from this deep sleep to dreaming, or from dreaming to the waking state. He follows the meaning of the word *pratiyoni* according to both readings: "Pratiyoni...
Just as previously, in a dream, his state consisted of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), so too, even when going from deep sleep to a dream, he encounters a state of that very same nature.
