2 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary known as *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

1557. It goes. Just as previously, while in the waking state, his body was the abode of the organs and the locus of the instruments such as the mother and others, so too, when going from sleep to the waking state, he goes to a body of that same kind; this is the meaning. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the sentence under discussion. || 999 ||
From whatever [cause] he took up the materials, he fashioned that dream.
In each and every instance, he maintains those measures together with the rays of his own self.

Following the Madhyandina recension, he concludes the meaning of the passage with the words "yasmāt" (because). Since, during the waking state, the Self has assumed dreams by taking up the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of forms and so forth—caused by the eyes and other senses—in this or that very place, namely within the eyes and other organs residing in the waking body; therefore, when moving from dream to waking, it deposits those powers of the latent impressions of forms and so forth, together with the reflections of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*), back into those very [organs].
This is the meaning. || 996 ||
By the very same path by which he went, he returned again by that same path.
Driven by the wind of karma, it departs, taking along its constituent parts (mātrās).

[The author] concludes the meaning of the passage from the Kāṇva recension with the words "by which": by that very path of desire, action, and so forth, through which one went from the waking state to the dream state, and upon the exhaustion of those actions to deep sleep; by that same path, when the actions of the dream state arise, being impelled by them, it takes up the latent impressions (vāsanās) residing in the cause.
The meaning is that he goes from sleep to dreaming. To reveal that the path for traveling through dreams consists of karma and so forth, he qualifies the traveler with the word "karma. || 997 ||
That self experiences the variously differentiated fruits arising from merit and demerit.
Abiding there in the state of dreaming, one sees and perceives here [in this world]. || 998 ||
Having explained the sentence ending with "as if for the sake of sleep," he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who there... as "That Self.
The word "there" is explained as "in the state of dreaming. By that same [principle], the word "here" is also connected [to the same context]. || 998 ||
One does not perceive it as having reached another location, just as one does not perceive a person who has gone from one village to another.
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious he has seen, that follows him directly.

He explains the passage beginning with "not followed by that" (*ananvāgatastena*) as follows: "Not this" (*nainam*). Just as merit and the like performed in one village follow the agent even when he is situated in another village, so too, the action which one has seen in a dream is not able to follow one who is awake.
The meaning is that the waking observer is not directly touched by the merits or defects of the dream state. || 999 ||
In this context, it is said that one perceives only the performance of auspicious and inauspicious actions.
But it is not that one who is inactive by nature sees what is an actual occurrence. || 1000 ||

Anticipating the objection that—because it is stated that the Self is the agent of knowing in the phrase "He sees," and because of the analogy with the merit resulting from the vision of a deity or the demerit caused by the perception of one's own birth at the end [of life]—there would be a connection between the seer and the auspicious or inauspicious things seen even in a dream, the author says: "Auspicious... etc. That is to say, in this passage, the Self is said to "see" solely because It is the witness (*sākṣin*) of whatever action, such as the auspicious and so forth, or its fruit; therefore, the qualities residing in the object of perception do not belong to the Self.
The meaning is that the two defects reside in the witness. He states what is excluded by the word "only" (eva): "But not... [when the self is...
[Note: The text fragment provided contains partial citations and references].
The meaning is that it is not described as the agent of seeing by saying "it sees that form," because such agency is incompatible with its immutable nature (*kūṭastha-svabhāva*).
Therefore, for the sake of establishing the meaning of the proposition "unfollowed," [the following is stated].
"Because it is unattached" may be stated as a reason, or it may serve as the meaning of the proposition. || 1001 ||

He states the distinction: "The statement of what has not yet been reached is the proposition (pratijñā), and its cause is the statement of non-attachment. By the word "tena" (by that), he states another mode: "the statement of non-attachment is the proposition," namely, "the meaning of the proposition. || 1001 ||
If it were thus already established beforehand, then the statement of the reason would be clearly redundant.
Therefore, he is "unfollowed" by ordinary karma alone. || 1002 ||

In that view, he states the status of the sentence concerning "not having followed" as the reason: "When... etc. "Prior" refers to the dream state as being prior in time relative to the waking state. The connection is that the sentence "not having followed by that action" is the statement of the reason, as has already been explained.
For this Śruti has proceeded from the apprehension that there might be danger.
For it is said that the phrase "not following after" functions as the reason. || 1003 ||

He states the proof for this position: "the state of being unattached" (*sāsaṅgatvam*). The meaning is that since the scriptural passage beginning with "He, indeed, in this state of serene clarity" (*sa vā eṣa etasmin saṃprasāde*) proceeded from the suspicion that the Self might be subject to attachment such as desire and the like, the proposition that it is "unattached" (*asaṅga*) is therefore logical.

For, while the word "hi" (indeed) indicates that the statement regarding non-attachment functions as a reason (*hetu*), he explains how it can simultaneously function as a proposition (*pratijñā*) there. Ana-... [text continues]

The meaning is as follows: because one who has reached the waking state and so forth is not touched by the auspicious or inauspicious [experiences] occurring in a dream, the word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that being unattached (*asaṅga*) is the reason for the state of being "not followed" (*ananvāgatatva*) even across the three states. || 1003 ||
One does not perform action in a dream, because of the non-existence of the factors of action.
There, he experiences that which consists solely of the fruit by way of his own manifestation.

Having stated the distinction between the two statements, he elaborates on the meaning of the statement regarding "not having followed" (ananvāgata). [He says: "Not action. What, then, does the seer do there? To that he replies: "The fruit. He shows that the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) residing in the intellect (buddhi) serves as the instrument for experience. [He says: "Its own reflection," etc. (104).
For an action accomplished in a dream is not like that which occurs in the waking state.
Therefore, that which is devoid of the nature of action does not enter into the place of the grammatical factors (kārakas) such as the agent.

He restates the absence of action in a dream by means of a dissimilar example, beginning with "For not... He states the reason for its absence there: "The locus of the agent and so forth... The waking state is the locus of the causal factors such as the agent; the dream activity does not follow the Self situated therein, meaning that for that immutable Self, there is no action there. || 1005 ||
If an action were to follow its own product once it has reached another location, [it would follow that the action itself had moved].
The undertaking of this treatise would be in vain; for who does not commit an offense in a dream? (1006)
Having restated the opposing view, he refutes it with the words "If... He states the reason for its futility with the words "In a dream...
[This concludes] the first Brāhmaṇa, together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri. (Volume 3, page 426) 1559.

For it is one who is awake that is qualified for the scripture; since various offenses such as the killing of a Brahmin can occur even in a dream, if those were to follow upon waking, there would be no qualification for the scripture, and thus the scripture could not be undertaken—this is the intended meaning. || 1006 ||
"Even for one whose means of cognition have departed, as he perceives the delusion of a dream..."
It is latent impression alone that assumes for this [consciousness] the form of action and its factors.
If the self does not act in a dream, how can there be the cognition of its being an agent and so forth? To this, he says: "Apeta... (verse 1007).
And because in a dream only the mere enjoyment of the fruit is observed.
Therefore, there can be no rule for the commencement of another effect from that which is devoid of activity.

He states the conclusion regarding the fact that the perception of agency and so forth in that state consists merely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*): "The result... The meaning is that pleasure and the like in a dream cannot be established as belonging to the inactive Self apart from [mere] cognition. || 1008 ||
For one does not perform [an action], since one perceives it as if it were an action in a dream.
Therefore, no connection with the fruit of the process is observed in this awakening.

Anticipating the objection that the perception of the fruit [of action] is as clear as the perception of the action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), he says: "He does not act. The meaning is: if action existed in reality even in a dream, then its connection with the fruit would be seen in the waking state as well; yet it is not so seen. Therefore, there is no real action there. || 1009 ||
Having been satisfied in a dream, he then wakes up feeling overcome by hunger.
For whatever is perceived here is indeed nothing but unreality.
Therefore, the one who acts inwardly is not smeared by the fruits of action.

He states another argument for the fact that actions and so forth in a dream are false, beginning with the word "tṛptaḥ" (satisfied). The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is the attainment of the body and its causes [the senses] by one who has awakened from sleep. The word "prakṛtaḥ" (present) refers to the dream, which is the sense of the locative case. He concludes by summarizing the result of that falsity, beginning with the word "pratyag" (the inward-facing Self). || 1010 || 1011 ||
However, as for the expiation that is prescribed on account of semen being discharged during a dream:
And because it is a modification of the sense-faculties by means of truth, that [modification] also cannot be without a substratum.
Objection: If the inner self (*ātman*) is not touched by dream-activities and the like, how is it that an expiation is prescribed for the emission of semen during a dream?
[It is said: "If, due to the weakness of the senses, one should see a woman in a dream and [the seed] should be emitted..."
"But the expiation prescribed for that is sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas)."

To this, he replies: "In a dream," etc. The meaning is that since the semen has emerged from the real Indra as its substratum, the injunction for expiation (prāyaścitta) based on that [emission] is not without a basis. || 1012 ||
Just as that which is discharged in a dream is seen in the dream, so too is it seen in the waking state.
Therefore, because it possesses the consciousness of the self, the expiation arises from that.
1. Sva. reads *mīkṣate*. 2. Na. reads *mīkṣyate*.
[Vol. 3, page 427] 1560 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya—]

He states that the injunction for this is also logical: "emitted in a dream" (*svapnaskannam*). The meaning is that the penance is prescribed by taking as its cause even semen emitted during the waking state that originated in a dream and was subsequently recognized. || 1013 ||
This is one explanation, which has been described according to what was stated.
And they explain this sentence, as it has been stated, in another way. (1014)
He concludes his own commentary on the passage beginning with "not followed" (*ananvāgata*) with the word "one" (*ekā*). The meaning is:

this is one interpretation of the passage concerning "not followed," which has been explained by us in detail, just as it was stated concisely in the Bhāṣya. He introduces the commentary of Maṭhara-Prapañca with the words "they explain" (*vyācakṣate*), indicating its worthiness of acceptance with the word "this" (*etat*).
The meaning is that this explanation should be accepted by him by following the explanation stated by us. || 1014 ||
By the statement "not followed by," the distinction from action has been established.
However, by means of his unattached speech, his liberation from desire is proclaimed. || 1015 ||

In that regard, he states the intended purport of the passage concerning "not having followed after" (*ananvāgata*): "Not having followed after," etc. He states the purport of the passage concerning "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*): "Non-attached," etc. || 1015 ||
But surely, it is not accepted that action directly brings about decrease or increase?
Moreover, desire is the cause of those two even in the waking state.

Having stated that there are two sentences for the purpose of distinguishing between desire (*kāma*) and action (*karman*), he raises an objection to be refuted by the passage concerning non-attachment (*asaṅga*):

"But surely" (*nanu*). Even in the waking state, with respect to the increase or decrease of the constituent parts of an action—which is the cause of its future fruit—desire is not the immediate cause of the action; rather, it is the cause of that [action]. Therefore, since desire is also the cause of activity in the dream state, the Self cannot be non-attached (*asaṅga*).
The meaning is "tumulam" (tumultuous). As they have said: "Even in the state of waking, it is not action alone that is the cause of increase and decrease;
rather, desire is the cause. || 1016 ||
For an action performed without desire is observed to be entirely fruitless.
"He acts according to his desire," and so forth; likewise, this will be explained further below.
To provide a refutation of this, it is said: "For [the Tathāgata] is unattached" (asaṅga). || 1017 ||

Anticipating the objection that since activity is observed even in one who is without desire, it is not necessarily rooted in that [desire], he says: "akāmasya" (of one without desire). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Therefore, fruitful action has desire as its cause. He provides scriptural evidence for the point that desire is the root of the accumulation of karma, and not mere action, with the remainder of the passage: "sa yathā... (Just as that...). And that unsevered desire is the root of its [karma's] accumulation in the dream state.

Therefore, since it has been stated that there must be an accumulation [of merit] even in a dream, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the soul's connection with desire is real; as a refutation of this, he cites the passage concerning non-attachment (asaṅga). [This refers to the phrase] "of this" (ityasya). || 1017 ||
Whatever attachment to Yama you perceive here in this dream at your will—
It is stated that for one who is sleeping, desire does not arise. || 1018 ||
1 kha. It is examined. 2 kha. Therefore, that desire does not exist.
[Vol.
3, page 428] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1561
For, by the statement "it is not so," its existence here [in this world] is impossible.
O lustful one, here the mind is devoured, leaving nothing but its latent impressions (vāsanā).

When it is asked, "In what way is there non-attachment? he states the purport of the passage with the words "yam" (whom). For it has been said: "He who sees that desire—which is rooted in accumulation and consists of mental activity—as attachment, is liberated from that at this time. He states the reason for the absence of desires in dream with the words "tadvataḥ" (of one possessing that). The meaning is that because the mind, which is the substratum of desires, does not exist in the state of dream, there is no existence of desire therein.

[Objection: Since the mind does not cease even when the external senses have ceased during sleep, how can it be said that the mind—the substratum of desire—is not present there? [The author] says in response: "It is swallowed. The word "by the cause" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. [Objection: If the mind is absent, how is there the cognition of dreams, as in deep sleep? [The author] replies: "By latent impressions (vāsanā). || 1018 || 1019 ||
Therefore, this person, when situated on the plane of dream, is indeed unattached.
It has been stated that "outside the nest" and that he "abandons evil. || 1020 ||

Regarding that, he states the result concerning the non-existence of the mind: "Since... Because desire, which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is possible even in a dream, he asks how there can be non-attachment there; to this, he replies: "Externally... (1020).
Desires exist depending upon the body; they do not exist anywhere else.
Indeed, the entire manifold of dreams consists of nothing but mental impressions alone.
To the question of how there can be an absence of desire for the self in the state of dream—even though it lacks connection with the body and its actions—the text says:
"The body... As they have said: "Desires belong to one connected with the body; they are the forms of death, and this [self] becomes divided by means of the body.
Furthermore, in order to state that there is no desire in dream, he declares its falsity: "In dream... (1021).
For, while explaining the dream, he declares it to be mere cognition. || 1022 ||
I know that ten thousand sons have been born; I know that my father has arrived.
In the same way, people explain their own words as being endowed with such speech. || 1023 ||

He states the reason for [the world] being mere latent impression (*vāsanāmātra*). He explains it by saying "expounding. He demonstrates its manner by saying "knowing. Having stated that a dream is false because it consists of mere appearance and lacks suitable objects and so forth, he provides the well-known consensus as proof for that very point, saying "And thus... [and] "I saw elephants today, made into jars, as if they were running"—thus, words joined with the particle *iva*...
The meaning is that those who explain dreams without having awakened from them for the sake of those seeking to see [the truth] have established their own falsity. || 1022 ||
"Just as the self-manifestation of a non-existent chariot or similar object is perceived,"
But in the same way, [the cognition] of the body, the senses, desires, and so forth, which are non-existent, [is likewise produced]. || 1024 ||

One infers the falsity of the creation of the dream-body and so forth by means of the following inference: "The object under dispute is false, because it is a creation like a dream, just like the creation of chariots and other things found therein. Regarding the phrase "of chariots and so forth," as they have said: "Just as there is the creation of external non-existent things such as chariots, so too is there the creation of internal things such as the body and the sense organs. (1024)
Therefore, let desire also be observed here as being like the chariot, the senses, and so forth. *Suresvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Chapter Four.
Therefore, one must accept that this person is unattached even in a dream. || 1025 ||

Nevertheless, how is there a separation from desire in a dream? To this he says: "The chariot," etc. That is to say, because there is no difference in their being products of a dream. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Let it be observed that [the chariot] is non-existent. For it has been stated: "Just as the creation and the perception of everything non-existent occurs, so too does the perception of attachment—which belongs to the side of the body and the senses—occur, even though it is non-existent. Of desire...
He concludes that [the result] has borne fruit in the sentient being with the words: "Therefore, this... (1025).
Or if the immutability of the person is expressed by the word "disconnected" (asaṅga).
For, without the connection to an action, there can be no correspondence with the result of direct perception. || 1026 ||

He states another meaning for the term *asaṅga* (unattached): "immovability" (*kauṭasthya*). And it has been said that "this Puruṣa is pure. One might ask: since there is no etymological derivation of the word *asaṅga* in the sense of immovability, how can it be used in this way? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "action" (*kriyā*). Without connection to action, there is no connection with its fruit for the witness thereof; therefore, because immovability and non-attachment are invariably concomitant, it is appropriate to use the word *asaṅga*.
The meaning is: "in order to state its immutability. || 1026 ||
But surely this person is the agent, for from the statement "he indeed is the agent," [it follows so].
It is not so in a dream, because in that case the agency of the person is produced by mental construction (bhāvanā).

It challenges [the opponent's] immutability (*kauṭasthya*). [The opponent objects: "But surely... [The author replies: Since agency in a dream arises from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is therefore unreal, there is no flaw in the doctrine of immutability; thus he says, "Not so. || 1027 ||
"And because the Self is manifested as both agent and object even during the waking state,"
Agency does not exist inherently; what more need be said regarding its existence in a dream? || 1028 ||
He states, by way of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) maxim, that agency in a dream is false: "katrī" (the agent). || 1028 ||
The agency and instrumentality of this self exist solely through the stream of ignorance.
By means of the reflection of consciousness residing therein, it experiences the fruit of karma. || 1029 ||

And because it follows the presence and absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), he states that it is false: "Ignorance" [is the word used]. Fearing that its reality might be like that of the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), he says: "Because it resides in that" (*tatsthatvāt*). By the word "that," ignorance is grasped. The meaning is that for this [Self], there is no dependence on action other than its being the witness of the fruit of action. || 1029 ||
That which was formerly the agency of this Self, the witness of the agent and so forth, has ceased to be.
For he alone would be the agent; thus, it would be a mere repetition of his own statement.
If agency and enjoyership do not exist in reality, how is it that he is said to be "the agent"? To this, he says: "kartrādi" (agent, etc.).
The word "pure" refers to the waking state. The meaning is that the repeated mention [of the agent] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and does not establish agency in the dream state. || 1030 ||
But surely all this very karma of his depends upon cultivation (bhāvanā).
How does [the notion of] its agency proceed, and how is it refuted? || 1031 ||

He raises an objection, saying "But surely," [suggesting] that the agency of the Self is not real based on the direct statement (*vākya*), but rather through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). For every action proceeds toward giving pleasure and so forth to the Self with a view toward desire; yet the fruit does not reside in one who is not the agent, since liberation is necessary for its accomplishment.

This is because of the maxim: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, for that is its defining characteristic. Therefore, it is illogical for action to proceed unless it is for the sake of bestowing the fruit upon the Self.
The meaning is that [ignorance] imagines a real agency where none exists. || 1031 ||
Let karma proceed; there is no fault whatsoever in this.
For this cultivation is always indeed a quality of karma.
It brings about its own witness, yet it is not a quality of the self.

Considering that the engagement in action is established through an imagined agency (*kalpitakartṛtva*), and thus the *arthāpatti* (presumption) can be accounted for otherwise, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "Kāmam" (Granted...). He provides the reason why there is no defect of agency in the Self even when it engages in action for the sake of yielding results, with the word "Bhāvanā" (Creative Contemplation). Since this [contemplation] is an auxiliary to action, being present therein, it constantly perfumes its own witness—the Self—by means of itself; therefore, in that regard...

The meaning is that the cognition of agency arises through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). He states what is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*) with the words "but not" (*na tu*). As they have said:
"For it is only when *bhāvanā* (the creative urge) exists as a quality of the action that it brings about the person. || 1032 ||
Just as the fragrance of a flower belongs to the flower itself even when it is situated elsewhere in front of it.
The mental cultivation (bhāvanā) residing in the causal factors such as the intellect is a subordinate element (guṇa) of the action (karman).
But [the quality] would belong to the self only figuratively; it could not be a quality in a direct sense. || 1033 ||

If it is argued that meditation (bhāvanā) would then qualify the Self, how could its quality not belong there? To this he says: "Like a flower" (*puṣpa*). For it has been said: just as the fragrance of a flower perfumes a casket, yet that [fragrance] is a quality of the flower alone and not a quality of the casket, so too meditation is a quality of the object alone and not a quality of the Self. How, then, does its manifestation occur in the inner self (*pratīci*)? To this he says: "Of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*). As they have said regarding that which is colored by meditation:
The designation of agency is applied metaphorically to consciousness with respect to its own cognition. || 1033 ||
At the time of birth and at the time of enjoyment, [the soul] takes up karma for the sake of cultivation.
For it attains its own self through that [means]; without it, that [self] would be purposeless. || 1034 ||

One might object: "Let it be that the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not a quality (*guṇa*) of the self; nevertheless, the action (*karman*) cannot be its quality, because [the action] is itself devoid of qualities. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In its production," and so forth. And it has been stated that one accepts that very same attachment (*anurañjanā*) as the agency during the times of the production and enjoyment of the action. Because the action is an instrument for its own production and for the granting of its fruit, the statement that the cultivation is dependent upon it is not like [the dependence of] color and other such qualities.
The meaning is that because it rests upon that, the internal organ (antahkarana) alone is its substratum. || 1034 ||
The same applies to action as well, because it relies exclusively upon repeated practice. || 1035 ||
It is determined that the very position of the connection with objects such as cognition (buddhi) and so forth is maintained.
But that action could never possess the quality of being a property of the self.
"Let it be that cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is a quality of action; it will become a quality of the self's true nature (*tattvātma-guṇa*). To this he says: "Even of action.

Just like cultivation, merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa-adṛṣṭa*), being invariably dependent upon activity, reside only in the causal factors such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, and not in the self (*ātman*). This is the meaning.

As it has been stated: "Since action (*karman*) is also entirely dependent upon its application, it never at any time becomes an attribute of the Self, because it falls within the category of contact with the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. (1035–1036)
Action remains dependent upon its application even when the intellect and other faculties have been dissolved.
For the sake of attaining its own self, it does not depend upon a self.
Therefore, the action of one who possesses meditative cultivation is distinguished from that of others. || 1038 ||

Anticipating the objection that at the time of death, because the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties dissolve, it is impossible for karma to reside in them, and therefore the unexhausted trans-worldly karma must reside in the Self itself, he says: "prayoga... The extremely subtle collection of instruments such as the intellect is the meaning of the word "prayoga" (application). For it has been stated that even upon the destruction of the intellect and other factors, karma remains dependent on application alone to obtain its own manifestation; it does not depend on the Self.

The meaning is that even when the gross form of the intellect and so forth perishes during states such as death, karma remains supported only by its subtle form and not by the Self. He states the conclusion regarding the absence of the status of being qualities of the Self for both mental impressions (bhāvanā) and karma: "sabhāvanam" [along with its impressions]. || 1037 ||
Therefore, [this applies] always only to one whose quality is action and who remains established in action.
The self as witness [abides] within its own abode for one whose desire takes the form of creative contemplation.

He concludes [the discussion on] the fruit of seclusion from desire and so forth with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). "Of the quality of action" (*karmaguṇasya*) means, in other words, of that which has become an instrument for action. "Residing in action" (*karmasthasya*) means, according to the sense, residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Thus they say: "Therefore, in this dream state, this self—which is the witness of the attachment belonging to the quality of action and residing in action—is the distinct one, free from attachment. (1039)
If attachment were an inherent quality of the self, like consciousness itself, it would be directly perceived.
One should not perceive desire as being situated within one's own action during both sleep and wakefulness, as if it were one's very self.
Furthermore, desire is not an attribute of the self because it is visible, like color; thus he says: "Attachment. (1040)
And this being the case regarding the position, the Vedic revelation has rendered it consistent.
The inclusion [of the term] "as it is well-known" is out of respect, for [the Buddha] is indeed free from attachment. (1041)
He says "And thus" (*evam ca*) because, when the self's liberation from all desires is established as if it were already accomplished, even the mention [of the means] serves as an indicator;
this indicates that repetition (*abhyāsa*) is a mark of the intended meaning (*tātparyaliṅga*), by saying "with respect" (*sādaram*). || 1041 ||
This accumulation of karma is not said to exist in a dream as it does for one who is awake.
Because of liberation from all attachments, with only the latent impressions remaining. || 1042 ||

To the question, "Even if there is an absence of desire in a dream, how can there be an absence of karma?", he says: "Not karma. He explains the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) itself: "All... It has been stated that because there is attachment [in the waking state], there is no accumulation of karma in the dream state. He shows the distinction from deep sleep: "Vāsanā... || 1042 ||
This [self] is not composed of karma, nor is it inherently composed of desire;
rather, due to ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyagajñāna), it appears as if it were composed of those. || 1043 ||

Having stated that there is an absence of desire and action within oneself during a dream, he describes the course of that perception with the words "This is not... [nāyam iti]. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "as if having attained identity with that" (tanmayatvaṃ prāpta iva). || 1043 ||
Agency is observed in the world due to the connection with various instruments.
But this non-attachment is that by which one neither acts nor is stained. || 1044 ||

Having stated that the self is, in reality, incapable of agency and so forth—as indicated by the word "as if" (iva)—he strengthens this point by means of the reason of its being unattached (*asaṅgatva*). [He says: "Not manifold... (1044).
For by negating the embodied, the unembodied, and so forth, he declared the true nature of the Self.
Therefore, there is no connection with a non-self, because of the cause that the self is eternally unchanging and one. || 1045 ||
He states another reason for its being unattached: "mūrta" (material), etc. The remainder of the sentence is that the Śruti says, "Not this, not this," "not gross," and so forth.
He completes what is required by the word "hi" (for/indeed): "nātaḥ" (not from this). Regarding the statement that there is no connection of the Self with the non-Self, he states two reasons:
"kūṭastha" (immutable), etc. || 1045 ||
But surely, since there is no consciousness in deep sleep, how can it be said that he has gone to the world of the gods and so forth?
But he will state that even the sentence "not, however," is likewise not external. || 1046 ||

Having established the opponent's view and concluded it, [the author] raises an objection based on the literal meaning of the passage beginning with "having rejoiced in the state of serene bliss" (*saṃprasāde ratvā*). He asks: "In deep sleep?"—that is to say, because of the lack of awareness, which means the non-perception of a second object such as a son and so forth. How is there a non-perception of a second thing there? To this he replies: "No.
For the non-perception of a second thing there is established by the two scriptural statements: "But there is no second thing there" and "He does not know anything external."
This is the meaning. || 104 6 ||
Just as it is considered that one does not experience pleasure and so forth while dreaming, this [position] is likewise untenable.
One whose speech is not followed by action may be angry, yet in a dream, that which was done is indeed experienced.

He raises the objection that there is no inconsistency, because it is accepted that one who wishes to enter from the state of dreaming into deep sleep (suṣupta) experiences pleasure and so forth while still in the dream state, and then becomes serene in the state of profound tranquility (saṃprasāda). [The opponent says: "In a dream... The proponent replies: "Not so. If pleasure and so forth are seen in a dream...
The meaning is that [the scriptural passage] beginning with "whatever is done there" would be contradicted, because what is performed there goes to the one who saw it [the performer]. || 1047 ||
Just as the action performed while awake follows after the agent.
In this way, one experiences the state of dreaming while remaining in the waking state.

Just as one does not follow that which is created in a dream while situated in another state, so too one would not follow the seer even when he is situated in a dream; such is your objection. [This concludes verse 1048.]
When this has been thus urged, some offer the following rebuttal.
Those who are skilled in the analysis of word-divisions [should understand it] by means of [the method beginning with] "not being [the case]," and so forth. || 1049 ||

Having restated the objection that was raised, he sets forth the resolution of his own school (svayūthya): "In this manner" means that there is no fault when the sentence is explained by breaking it down according to the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with each word, as in "having failed to find delight and having failed to practice in the state of serene clarity. || 1049 ||

Since it is stated there that "he is unattached," even this [objection] would not be a valid response.
And having superimposed that very view even upon that [objection], they set forth a refutation. || 1050 ||

He refutes [the opponent's view] by showing the inconsistency of the remainder of the passage, beginning with "sa yat" (as for that...). Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because the word "there" (*tatra*) refers back to the dream under discussion in the phrase "for the sake of a dream" (*svapnāyaiva*); for the pronoun "that" (*tat*) refers to something remote from the immediate context, otherwise the subsequent introduction of the dream would be redundant. Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that the introduction of the dream is intended to demonstrate the lack of attachment (*asaṅgatva*) while awake; for if that were the case, [the argument would fail].

The sense is that because introducing another Buddha would be purposeless, there can be no reference to the "serene being" (*saṃprasāda*) by means of the word *tat* (that), as the act of seeing (*paśyati*) is incompatible with that state; therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), there is a contradiction with the remainder of the sentence. Others, however—projecting the functions of seeing and so forth onto the state of deep sleep just as they do onto the dream state—interpret the passage by dividing the words even without connecting them to the negative particle (*nañ*). They maintain that since the word *sa* (he) refers back to the state of deep sleep, the remainder of the sentence is logically consistent, and thus they offer a rebuttal.
He says: "The view. || 1050 ||
There is experience even in deep sleep; likewise, there is the ground of bliss.
Or rather, there is sovereign enjoyment here, due to the conceit of being the master of all locations. || 1051 ||

He states that the perception of the fruit [of pleasure] is the cause for the superimposition of passion (*rati*) and so forth during sleep, saying: "It exists. Regarding the existence of enjoyment there, he states the proof: "And thus. The meaning is that there is an experience of pleasure in deep sleep, because it is accepted by the elders that "the *prājña* [self] is blissful" according to the *Mukta* [Upanishad]. He states another cause for the superimposition of passion and so forth there: "Or, [it is] divine. For indeed, the causal form exists there.

The meaning is that since the individual soul (jīva) exists as the very self of the Lord (īśvara), its experience belongs to that [Lord] alone, according to such scriptural texts as "of this bliss... and so forth; thus, there is a superimposition (āropa) of pleasure and the like. He establishes what has been stated [in the verse] with the words "sarva" and so on. Because he is the cause of all, the Lord considers the three states to be his own; therefore, the individual soul, existing in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) as that [Lord's] self, partakes in that experience. || 1051 ||
For when the self has entered the sphere of activity, it is observed to be in deep sleep.
Because the effect is pervaded by its cause, there is no lack of perceptibility in deep sleep.

Regarding this, having raised the objection that if there were the superimposition of [objects such as] visual perception and so forth, it would follow that there is no distinction from its other state [of deep sleep], he states another solution:

"The effect," etc. A person who has arisen from the causal state of deep sleep and is situated on the plane of effects—whether in dream or in the waking state—inferred the causal state of deep sleep as being indeed associated with that [state], because the cause pervades the effect and because of the observation of pleasure and so forth in that dream and so on, which serves as the mark (liṅga) for it.

The meaning is that, because of that [state], there is the figurative expression "having enjoyed" (*ratvā*) and so forth. Anticipating the objection that if deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is established through inference, it would be established as something remote (*parokṣa*), and thus the supplementary statement "whatever he sees there" would be untenable, he says: "No. Deep sleep is indeed the ignorance of the Self, which is the state of the intellect abiding in its causal form; and since that is the case, for one who has emerged from it, the recollection "I did not know anything" is the subsequent [awareness].
The meaning is that because it is directly perceived through reflection (*marśa*), there is no further inconsistency (*śeṣānupapatti*). || 102 ||
Or rather, let that which was mentioned, such as sexual union and so forth, be merely a dream.
Therefore, the state of not being followed by the two dreams [of pleasure and pain] is also due to the Prājña.

Fearing that even if deep sleep (*suṣupta*) were accepted as being characterized by pleasure (*rati*) and so forth—on the grounds of inference—it would result in no distinction from other states, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "Or rather" (*yadi vā*). If it is argued that pleasure and so forth are spoken of in the context of dreaming, then [the author replies] regarding the good deeds performed there and so on, for one situated therein...

1567 It was stated that there would be a contradiction with the sentence regarding non-connection due to the lack of connection; to that, he says: "In the two dreams," etc. The *prājña* (the conscious self) is the locus of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

Therefore, it is established that there is no connection between the two dreams—the one preceding and the one following [deep sleep]. Having gone from dream to deep sleep, one then goes from that to dream;

yet, having gone to a subsequent dream, one is not followed by the karma residing in the dream state prior to the deep sleep, nor is one situated in the prior dream stained by the karma residing in the subsequent dream. Likewise, there is no connection of the auspicious or inauspicious [experiences] occurring in the dream with the states of deep sleep or waking.

The meaning is that, because the reality (tattva) is not accompanied by ignorance even during the three states of existence, the statement that it is "unaccompanied" (ananvāgata) is not contradictory. || 1093 ||
Or, because each one is arranged in a threefold way, there is no fault.
Of the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states, [the distinctions arise] from waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
Regarding the question of how there can be "delighting and so forth" in the state of serene clarity (*saṃprasāda*), he states another solution: "In three ways.

The meaning is that since each of the states beginning with waking is conceived as being threefold through its own internal distinctions (waking-within-waking, etc.), there is no fault in the occurrence of delighting and so forth even while in deep sleep, provided one considers the waking and dreaming within that very deep sleep. || 1054 ||
That which is directly perceived through valid means of knowledge as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, and so forth.
Waking is that which is perceived as real; dreaming is the perception of what is false. || 1055 ||
Because of attachment to objects such as women and the like, it does not discern anything at all.
In that state, deep sleep would be identical to waking because of its nature of being devoid of discrimination. || 1056 ||

How is each [state] threefold? He demonstrates that regarding the waking state (*jāgara*) by saying "kārya" (effect) and so forth. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), things to be known (*ajñeya*), edible (*bhakṣya*), inedible (*abhakṣya*), and so on are included. By the word "tat" (that), the waking state is referred to. He states the reason for its being like deep sleep (*suṣupta*)—that is, its similarity to well-known deep sleep—by saying "nirviṣaya" (objectless). || 1055 || 1096 ||
Even while asleep, a man performs action in his dream as if he were awake.
The dream-waking state is of such a nature; herein, that which consists of the dream is itself the dream.
Even having seen it, one who has awakened would not be able to describe it at all.
Such a state would be dream-sleep; and sleep is said to be threefold.
One who is deluded while in the waking state is like one in deep sleep; such a person is said to be "peaceful" (śānta) in the dream state.
The lack of awakening to the reality of the single self is called deep sleep; it is known as the state of the Prājña. || 1059 ||

He divides dream into three types, beginning with "even when asleep. Here, the meaning is that the experience consisting of a dream which occurs while one is dreaming is the "dream-state dream. He then applies the threefold classification to deep sleep, beginning with "and deep sleep. || 1097 ||
Because deep sleep is of three kinds, all [states] such as being awake and so forth are logically possible.
The illustration is the state of serene clarity (saṃprasāda) in the two conditions of dreaming and waking. || 1060 ||

He states the application of that threefold nature to the subject at hand: "Because of its being threefold. This refers to the threefold nature of deep sleep according to the manner previously described.

The meaning is that, in relation to the dreams and so forth occurring therein, the occurrence of "rejoicing" (*ratvā*) and other such states is logically consistent. Deep sleep (*supti*) was previously mentioned for the purpose of distinguishing the Self—which is self-luminous and free from body and organs—from karma and the like; now, he states another intended purport (*tātparya*) for that mention: "As an illustration" (*dṛṣṭānta*). || 1060 ||
Just as it is possible to perceive [the self] during the state of deep sleep, so too is it possible during the state of serene clarity.
It should be understood that this applies elsewhere as well, because in those cases there is no observation of a real entity. || 1061 ||

He clarifies the correspondence between the illustration and the illustrated reality with the word "yathā" (just as). To the question, "How then is there the perception of sexual union and so forth in dreams and the like?

he replies with the word "tatra" (therein). However, according to the reading "tattva," the construction should be understood as follows: that very same object [is perceived] as sexual union and so forth in the two states because of its non-examination [as it truly is]. || 1061 ||
Therefore, since this is so, one should be free from the defects of ritual action and desire.
This person is established by himself through the very path already described.

He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "Since" (*yataḥ*). He shows the meaning of the word "thus" (*evam*) with the phrase "as has been stated. This means: by the path already described, namely that desire is a quality of action (*karmaguṇa*), and that it resides in the agent through the medium of its application (*prayoga*). Since this [desire] is free from all defects—
Therefore, the construction is: "the non-agent is established by itself. || 1062 ||
If it is argued that "because of being unattached, [the self] is not an agent," then this reason is said to be unestablished (asiddha).
Because one's own desire is seen [to be fulfilled], as stated in the scripture: "Wherever one desires. (1063)

The phrase "for [it] is unattached" states that non-attachment is the reason for its state of non-concomitance (*ananvāgatatva*); he raises the objection that this is unproven with the words "because of non-attachment. The word "this" refers to the statement of the reason. The reason for that is "in a dream," because according to the Vedic text, "He goes where he desires when dead," desire is observed in dreams; and since "desire" (*kāma*) and "attachment" (*saṅga*) are synonymous, the meaning is that it is not unattached. || 1063 ||
In order to refute this [objection], he [the Blessed One] spoke the words beginning with "sa vā" (that indeed).
Furthermore, why is it said that the undertaking of one's own dream has already passed?
Just as in the case of "buddha-anta" and so forth, there is no tautology here because of that [distinction]. || 1064 ||

He takes up the passage beginning with "He, indeed, having sported in this dream," as a subsequent [explanation]. Regarding the phrase "of this": he raises the objection of redundancy for this presentation of the dream state by means of the words "for that dream, having become... and so forth. By saying "again," he indicates a difference in meaning. If there is no other entity whatsoever apart from the entity that is the self, [then...]

Regarding the statement "whatever external action this [self] has," and so forth, one considers the alternative whether there exists a reality distinct from the self or not; having then restated the first position, the author refutes it with the word "ātma" (the self). 11905.
Whatever entity there is, such as objects, sense-faculties, and so forth, that is not distinct from ignorance.
Because the existence of another entity entails that their identity as one is sublated. || 1106 ||

Regarding the second [alternative] as well, he first addresses whether that [duality] is real or unreal by saying "viṣaya" (object). He states the reason why it is distinct from ignorance (avidyā) by saying "vastvantarasya" (of another entity). Nor is it merely sublatable [by knowledge], because that would contradict various Śruti, Smṛti, and logical principles;

therefore, there is no real entity other than the Self. In the second case, the previously mentioned conceptualization of the division between desire and action lacks any basis in valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
The sense is that, by means of ignorance (avidyā), everything born thereof accrues to the Self. || 1106 ||
Therefore, the non-coming of attachment occurs by way of the objects and the sense faculties.
Since there is no logical justification, it is indeed improper; nor can ignorance bring about that darkness. || 1107 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "But having come from that," etc., [the author] states that the attainment of desires in the Self could occur either through objects and the like, or through ignorance; [he then says] "not the first" and provides the reason: "of attachment. The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is the actual absence of objects and the like. Anticipating the objection that there might be an arrival of attachment in the Self due to the power of imagined objects and the like, he says: "by logic" (*nyāya*). [This refers to the fact that] by means of ignorance, objects and the like [are superimposed].

If it is argued that this imagined nature resides in the Self itself because that imagination occurs therein—and thus the attachment caused by it is also imagined in that very place—then it is not logical to imagine that desires come from outside; this is the meaning. He refutes another possible imagination with the words "nor also" (*nāpi*), meaning "nor also that attachment. || 1107 ||
Apart from false knowledge, no other effect whatsoever is admitted.
Because from ignorance there is no drawing in [of objects] through attachment and so forth by its own power. || 1108 ||

The reason for this is: "It is false. For it is not logical that the actual acquisition of desires and so forth occurs within the Self through ignorance, because that [acquisition] is merely an effect of delusion (*bhrama*), and since delusion is admitted to be unreal (*avastu*), there can be no acquisition of them within the Self. This is because it has already been stated that such a conceptualization (*kalpanā*) occurs only with respect to that [external object]. || 1108 ||
1. ka. ga. *yaiḥ samīkṣya* | 2. gha. *dyādivi* | 3. ga. *kalpate* | 4. kha. ga. *kaivaṃ nā* | 5. ka. gha. *’hiṣṭhaḥ kā*; kha. *’diṣṭhā kā* | 6. ka. kha. gha. *re* | [vol 3, page 444]
For since ignorance itself is established only through the non-establishment of the Self, [therefore] ignorance belongs to the Self.
Therefore, in reality, there is no [arising] of the inner self either from itself or from another. (1109)

Regarding the claim that "ignorance (avidyā) is dependent upon the knowledge of the Self," he says: "The Self. The sense is this: the connection of that ignorance [with the Self] is either merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*) or established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*); it cannot be the second, because no proof is established for a connection with ignorance that is established by valid means. The word "hi" (indeed) indicates the acceptance of an apparent connection with ignorance in the Self. In that—

The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that [the case] is like the acceptance of consciousness through the well-known establishment of [entities such as] motion and so forth. By the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), it is referred to that there is no evidence for a real connection with ignorance (*avidyā*) therein, whether by itself or by way of a cause; this is what is indicated. || 1109 ||
Likewise, because of the scriptural teaching that prohibits the entire class of modifications without exception.
And it is difficult to maintain that ignorance exists by transforming self-knowledge.

Regarding that which was stated, "that cognition which is one's own," and so forth, he replies with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). The meaning is: "tathā" (likewise) refers to the fact that, just as it is difficult to state the authoritative basis for the connection with self-ignorance, so it is here as well. || 1110 ||
Thus, ignorance, which appears as direct perception, has its establishment investigated.
This western direction becomes established as "east" until the arising of perfect knowledge.

[Objection: "In that case, how is it that ignorance (avidyā) is said to reside in the inner self (pratyak) even in your own position? To this, he says: "The inner self" (pratyak). The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is the changelessness of the Self. The meaning of the particle "hi" is that the indeterminability of ignorance, its being permeated by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), its appearance as false within the inner self prior to the knowledge of reality, and its immediacy are all established through experience and reasoning. || 1111 ||
For the sake of comprehending the meaning of the statement, there must be a discernment between the waking state and the dream state.
The destruction of ignorance regarding the inner self occurs precisely through the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence. || 1112 ||

Regarding the claim that the subsequent [section] is for the purpose of distinguishing [the self] from ignorance, he says: "In the waking state," etc. Because of moving through the three states in both sequential and non-sequential order, the meaning of the word *tvam* (the "you")—purified by the relinquishing of desire and karma in the waking state and so on—is intended for the realization of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), which is the identity of Brahman and the Self; for without knowledge of the word-meanings, knowledge of the sentence-meaning is impossible, and from that knowledge comes the destruction of ignorance. Therefore, the sentence [is dependent] upon the purification of the meaning of *tvam*.

Since ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge of reality (*arthajñāna*), no separate discernment of ignorance is required. Although the cognition of objects as distinct from ignorance and its products is useful for the perception of the meaning of a sentence, nevertheless, no such discernment of ignorance is performed in the *Śyena* injunction; the point is that there, one perceives the attainment of deep sleep, which has the form of the cause characterized by the unknown Brahman. || 1112 ||
This transition through the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep [is known] from another means of valid cognition.
Since it is already established, any statement regarding it would be merely reiterative.
Anticipating the objection that the narrative proceeding through the three states is not subsidiary to anything else because it concludes with its own purpose, he says: "Waking," etc.
One must infer another means of knowledge, consisting of a synthesis (pratisaṃdhāna), which has as its object the transition between the three states. || 1113 ||
Of that [self], which moves sequentially through the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
The state of being Brahman was not known from any other source; it is the Vedic statement that brings about its realization.
1 ga. Sequence!
[Vol. 3, page 445]
1578 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:

Anticipating the objection that even a "Great Sentence" (*mahāvākya*), like sentences concerning waking and so forth, does not have its own meaning as its primary purport because that meaning is already established and thus accessible through other means of knowledge, he says: "Krama... (verse 1114).
The state of Brahman is directly one's own self, and the state of the self is inherently that of Brahman.
This subject matter of the statement "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and others has been declared here. || 1115 ||

He establishes that the identity of Brahman and the Self is not established by any other means of knowledge. [The verse begins with] "of the Self" (ātmanaḥ). By the locative case, the scripture is referred to. The meaning is that since perception and other means do not function regarding the non-dual identity of Brahman and the Self which is devoid of distinctions, that identity is to be known solely through the sentence (of scripture). || 1111 ||
The analogy of the great fish illustrates the states of dream and waking.
Although it has been explained otherwise, others have explained the example differently. || 1116 ||

Having refuted the connection proposed by others for the textual passage beginning with the words of the "great fish" (*mahāmatsya*) and ending with the words of the woman, he sets forth that very [author’s] own commentary on the words of the great fish. Regarding the phrase "of the great fish": in the *Bhāṣya*, the example of the so-called "great fish" is explained as illustrating the discernment of desire and other states within oneself during dreams and so forth; however, Bhartṛprapañca has explained that same point in a different manner.
This is the meaning. || 1116 ||
Consciousness has been introduced; regarding it, doubt arises within us.
Is this knowledge material, derived from the elements, or does it belong to the Self, which is distinct from the elements?
He undertakes an investigation in order to show another method: "Consciousness," [he says]. || 1117 ||
Consciousness, for its part, is derivative, being born from the conjunction of the primary elements.
Just as [there is cognition] from the conjunction of the external eye, light, and the object. || 1118 ||
In this way, the arising of cognition regarding objects occurs for the self through its conjunction with the elements.
Manifestation is observed to occur through contact with the intellect, the sense organs, and so forth. || 1119 ||
If that were so, there would be no purpose whatsoever for a cognizer distinct from the specific cognition itself. (1120)
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Consciousness is material. He clarifies the stated reason by means of an illustration: "Just as...

The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "intellectual faculty (*buddhi*), sense-faculties (*indriya*), etc. is intended to include all related objects. "Of that" refers to consciousness itself, which is a specific kind of cognition, namely the apprehension of an object. For it has been said: "Just as from the contact of the external eye with light and an object there is the manifestation of a specific illumination, so too [is it] with the intellect (*buddhi*)."

"From the contact with the sense organs, there is the manifestation of perceptual consciousness. He states the consequence of its being composed of the elements (*bhautika*) with the word "tathā" (so it is).
When this has been thus urged by some, the following response is given here.
If a cognizer distinct from the elements is not admitted, [then the following ensues]. || 1121 ||

Having restated the doctrine that the body is the self, he refutes it with the words "Thus [it is]... Revealing the counter-argument, he reiterates the view that consciousness is material in nature with the words "If [consciousness] were distinct... (1121).
1 kha. ga. ṃnmataḥ || yauṃ | [vol 3, page 446] 3 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1579
Because the elements alone are equal in both one's own waking state and [the waking state of others].
In that case, it follows with certainty that cognitions would arise simultaneously for you. || 1122 ||

Regarding this, he states the defect: "Because of their equality. As they have said: "If there were no cognizer distinct [from the body], then at the time of dreaming, since the material light alone would be initiated without distinction, and because the elements (bhūtamātrās) exist without distinction in both the dream state and the waking state, there would be simultaneous perception in both places. || 1122 ||
Because consciousness arises sequentially, it is therefore not material;
for its awareness would belong to something else, [arising] from the nest of the waking state within the dream.
To make this meaning understood, an illustration is here set forth.
Moving gradually, like a powerful great fish in a river.

Anticipating the objection that the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) might be acceptable, he says: "Because of its sequential occurrence. He states the result of this consequence: "No," meaning "it does not happen. He states the conclusion regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*) not being material: "Of the other," as it has been said: "In both these nests—namely, the state of dream and the waking state—there is another, distinct witness. This explains the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca as previously described.

The word "hi" [indicates the reason]. Therein, he introduces the sentence with "asya" (of this). He states the meaning of the portion concerning the example: "krameṇa" (gradually); the ellipsis is "moving along, it exists. The absence of being shaken by the current of a river constitutes its strength. || 1123 ||
Just as fish come together with both banks here in turn.
In the same way, the connection with a knower occurs sequentially during both dream and waking states. (1125)

Having restated what was intended in the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states the point to be illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*): "matsya" [etc.]. The word "river" (*nadī*) has the sense of the locative case. || 1121 ||
If it is argued that, because the self is all-pervasive, there is likewise simultaneous cognition;
"Just as in the case of the elements alone"—thus the objection is the same for both of us. || 1126 ||

It has been stated that because cognition occurs simultaneously in both dreaming and waking states, the seer must be distinct from the body; now, the author raises a doubt regarding the parity of the undesirable consequences shown in the doctrine of the body being the self (dehātmavāda) even within the doctrine of a distinct self (atiriktātmavāda). [The opponent argues: "Because of its all-pervasiveness... [If] the body were the self, then in the state of dreaming...

The point being made is that what is asserted—namely, that there is a simultaneous attainment of experience in two bodies—is equally applicable here [in the case of the soul] despite its being distinct [from the body], because it is possible for the soul to be a knower simultaneously by virtue of pervading both bodies. For they say that if the soul were all-pervasive, there ought to be simultaneous perception and cognition due to its presence in both the dreaming and waking states. This is just as in the doctrine of the identity of the body and the soul (*dehātmavāda*).

He concludes that the objection is equal for both sides by stating: "bhūta... (1126). It is argued that because there is no distinction among the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) that initiate the two [bodies], there would be a simultaneity of experience in the two states; he shows that this same consequence would apply even in your own view according to the reasoning previously stated. Thus, he summarizes the parity of the challenge.
What, then, could be the cause for the sequence? Let it be caused by the deity.
Their activity occurs sequentially because of their nature as presiding deities. || 1127 ||

If it is maintained that the non-simultaneity of cognitions—whether produced by the body or produced by a self distinct from it—is not accepted in either of these two positions, then [the following applies] regarding the sequence of cognitions:
what was stated [is as follows]. (Note: Variants noted in the source text are *jñānāyī* for *ka. gha.*, and *jñānayau* for *kha.*)
[Vol. 3, page 447] 1580 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:
He asks, "What is the cause? He asks, "Who? The proponent of the view that the self is a deity says, "A deity," meaning one impelled by Āditya and the other deities.
Regarding how the sequence of cognition is asserted therein, he says: "In succession. To this they say: "The functioning of those presiding deities occurs by turns. || 1127 ||
In this case as well, it is just as in the two positions concerning simultaneous cognition and liberation.
Due to the pervasiveness of the deities, it occurs in both one's own waking state and [the waking state of others].
He refutes [the opponent's view] by showing that even on the side of the deities, the simultaneity of cognitions is unavoidable, with the words: "In this case also... (atrāpi).
Because it is impossible for the effort of a divine being to be simultaneous.
If it is argued that simultaneous cognition would not occur because of this, [we reply] that even so, that [simultaneity remains]. || 1129 ||

The proponent of the Deity (devatāvādī) says that the Deity is the cause of knowledge in dependence upon efforts such as [the performance of] dharma; however, since that [dependence] is not possible simultaneously, even though she is all-pervading, the knowledge produced by her occurs sequentially in both states. [The opponent] refutes this with the words "because it is impossible," meaning that even if the sequence of knowledge is caused by efforts such as ritual action (karman), the Deity is not the instigator therein. [The proponent replies: "No."
The proponent of our own position has stated here that which is established and desired by us.
If you ask "Whence is that?", listen from me as everything is being told. || 1130 ||

He establishes that very point by saying "he says. He asks: "If [the sense organs] were the cause for the non-simultaneity of the cognition of dharma and so forth, how could what you desire be established? He answers: "From me. || 1130 ||
There would be simultaneity everywhere, because the self of the deity is all-pervading.
And because of his sovereignty, there is no [need for] effort on the part of this Self regarding those effects that arise from exertion.

To demonstrate the establishment of his own position, he states the impossibility [of the opponent's view] regarding the side of the deity: "In all cases," etc. The ellipsis to be supplied is that simultaneity applies to the cognition produced by the deity. Even though the deity is omnipresent, it was stated that she acts sequentially depending on merit (*dharma*) and so forth; to this he replies: "On account of sovereignty. Because the deity possesses independence with respect to merit and the like, as well as the effects produced by them, there is no [dependence] on merit and so forth.

The meaning is "it is inferred. He states a specific distinction regarding the self (ātman) with the words "of this [self]. The meaning is that because the self lacks sovereignty over dharma and so forth, as well as their effects, its status as a cognizer of things in succession is established by virtue of its dependence on those [causes]. For it has been said: "Due to the omnipresence (vibhutva) of the deity, there is simultaneity in efforts toward their effects;
however, this is not the case for the individual soul (vijñānātman). || 1131 ||
For the sense organs, which are the objects to be presided over, are indeed impossible in the state of dream.
Therefore, there is not even the slightest activity of deities in a dream.

Furthermore, he states that in dreams and similar states, the deity is not the cause of the sequence of cognition, using the words "adhiṣṭheya" (that which is to be presided over) and so forth. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the well-known impossibility of the sense organs existing in the state of dreaming. The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is that the status of being a presider (adhiṣṭhātṛtva) is untenable in the absence of something to be presided over (adhiṣṭheya). || 1132 ||
1. k. ṃti | vra ṃ | 2. gha. 'padyāheṃ' | 3. kha. gha. bhave pra' | [Vol. 3, page 448] 3.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1581.
Therefore, the enjoyer is established by himself through the very reason already stated.
Because effort is not simultaneous, it is distinguished from the states of dreaming and waking.

He concludes the result regarding the impossibility of that [body] being the cause of the sequence of cognition with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is this: since the sequence of cognition is impossible in the case of the two positions—the body and the deity—and since such a sequence is possible for the Self in relation to qualities like dharma which arise in succession, the Self is established as the enjoyer distinct from the two bodies of dream and waking.
As they have said: by this reason of the manifestation of the state of being an enjoyer, and by the non-simultaneity of effort...
The establishment of the apprehension of a distinct perceiver. || 1133 ||
The soul's status as an enjoyer is established, and its nature as a knower is likewise proven.
Even though this self is all-pervading, effort must be exerted toward its agency.
That effort which occurs simultaneously in both nests is not possible.
Because it is observed through its maturation, it follows that [the soul] exists; thus it is established. || 1135 ||

Anticipating the objection that because the self (*ātman*) is all-pervasive, effort can occur simultaneously in both bodies, and thus the reason for their non-simultaneity is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "Of the self. Even though the self is all-pervasive, its status as an enjoyer and so forth is established sequentially;

for regarding the agency of experience and knowledge, there is no possibility of simultaneity in the effort consisting of merit (*dharma*) and other factors that serve as its causes, [due to the difference] in knowledge and so forth between the dreaming and waking bodies.

The meaning is that because the non-simultaneous production of effects from causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth is established by their sequential nature, it is proven that the status of being a knower and so forth resides in the self sequentially within the two bodies. As it has been stated: "For even though the self is pervasive during both dreaming and waking, that effort toward agency which exists in its capacity as a seer cannot occur simultaneously; therefore, it occurs in alternation."
Thus it is established that activity consists in being a seer. || 1134 || 7735 ||
The fact that [cognitions] are not observed to occur simultaneously is used as the inferential mark for the existence of the self.
Likewise, even if it were distinct from that, [it would be so] starting from the waking state, the dream state, and the family abode. || 1136 ||

Having resolved the objection raised by the proponent of the body as the self (*dehātmavādin*) in a manner similar to that raised against the proponent of the self (*ātmavādin*), [the author] addresses the inquiry: "What is intended here as the proof for the existence of a self distinct [from the body]? He says: "Because of non-simultaneity" (*ayaugapadya*). The meaning is: the subject under dispute is distinct from the body and so forth, because it is a sequential perceiver, like Devadatta who perceives smell, taste, and so on; for in the opposite case (if it were not distinct), the sequence of perception would be impossible. As it has been said: "Perception is non-simultaneous..."
The fact that [the self] is perceived is the mark for the existence of the self. || 1136 ||
And there would be no activity of a deity in the manifestation of a dream.
For they return to their respective abodes at the time of death and sleep.

In the view that the self is distinct [from the body], having established the sequence of cognitions, [the author] restates what was said in the passage "for the senses to be presided over" (*adhiṣṭheyendriyāṇām hi*)—namely, the absence of the deity's activity in a dream due to its lack of being the cause thereof: "And not... (*na ca*). He states another reason for this: "According to their own [nature]" (*yathāsvam*).
As it is said: "For at the time of dreaming, there is no activity of the deities on their own part toward one who wishes to depart for another world."
Setting aside their specific internal functions, they return to their own abodes, according to such scriptural passages as "Speech merges into fire";
likewise, the deities depart from one who desires to proceed toward his own task. || 1137 ||

Just as it is held that the gods depart at death, having relinquished their respective favors, so too do the gods perform their respective functions at the commencement of a new body. 1138.
Then, for one who desires to sleep, those deities depart from their respective offices.

Furthermore, in their own creation, they exercise their own authority. (1139) Since the accomplishment of the work of a dream does not belong to one who is not presided over by deities, it is not knowledge prompted by them; having been stated thus, he raises an objection by means of an example: "It is thought... (1138) (1139).
When this has been thus urged, the following reply is now stated.
Because the effects of the gender-signs are not manifested, the deities are not capable of producing an effect.
He introduces the resolution [of the objection] with the words "In this way. The meaning of the word *atha* (then/now) is that the objection serves as the occasion for the resolution.
He clarifies that very point with the words "By the subtle body (*liṅga*). Even in a dream, although deities do come together, they are not able to arrive in the same manner as when one is awake;

rather, they become partakers of the state of the subtle body through the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which has Hiraṇyagarbha as its self. And [it is not the case that] there is no subtle body in the form of deities during a dream.

Because [the subtle body] would otherwise face the undesirable consequence of being indistinguishable from its awakening through the manifestation of activity, the meaning is that in the dream state, the deities are not capable of performing specific functions.
As it has been said: "For a deity never abandons the subtle body (liṅga); however, when that subtle body is unmanifest, it is not capable of specific activity. || 1140 ||
Causes are ineffective, just as [the senses are] when the body has perished at death.
In the same way, the deities [assist] even in a dream for the accomplishment of one's own task. || 1141 ||
Without relying upon the instruments of action, one is not capable of exercising one's own authority.
And the absence of sense organs in dream has been established by the Śruti itself. || 1142 ||

He clarifies the stated point by means of an illustration: "The instruments," etc. Let it be granted that the deities carry out their respective offices in the dream state by depending solely on those [instruments]; to this he replies: "And in the dream," etc., meaning by the scriptural passage beginning with, "Then speech merges into breath. || 1141 || 1142 ||
Since this is so, there should be no apprehension regarding the deities in a dream.
For they have the authority over their own bodies.

Since it has been established that the deity has no activity in a dream, there is not even the suspicion that she could be the cause of the sequence of cognitions; thus he says, "Because... (yataḥ). Then, raising the objection that the deities would be useless within the body, he says, "The office" (adhikāraḥ). The remainder of the sense is: therefore, they are not useless here. || 1943 ||
This dream of the inner self occurs precisely by setting aside its connection with the body.
And this is determined from the statement regarding "outside the nest. || 1144 ||
Let it be granted, then, that even in a dream, when the self has a connection with a body, there is no activity of the deities; thus he says: "Having abandoned...
He provides the proof for the claim that a dream occurs without the self's connection to a gross body: "Outside... (1144).
16. By means of proofs. 2 kha. It is established. [Vol.
