Therefore, this cannot be composed of the elements, nor can it be created by a deity.
Consciousness, directed toward its own object, exists in the dream state due to the abandonment of the two bodies.

Having refuted the opposing view, he concludes his own position with the words "not from this" (nātaḥ). He states the reason for consciousness being for its own sake with the word "body" (śarīra). The sense is that although the subtle body exists during dream, because it lacks functional efficacy, it is held to be dissolved, just like other [bodies].
It is devoid of favor, devoid of motive, and consists merely of the limiting adjunct of latent impressions.
This must be a vision in a dream, based upon the reality of the inward-cognizing intellect.

He states that even the deities are dissolved there beyond their characteristic marks by saying "without support" (*niranugraham*). He states that even the organs are withdrawn there by saying "without instruments" (*niṣkaraṇam*). To distinguish this state from deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he specifies it as "impressions" (*vāsanā*).

He states that it is perceivable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) by saying "innermost" (*pratyak*). The very intellect (*dhī*), which takes on that form, is the reality situated therein; and by its power alone, the vision of dreams occurs.
The meaning is that it is established. For it has been stated: "Because [the self] is distinct from both times, the seer is distinct; he is neither material nor produced by a deity. || 9946 ||
Whether the deity-self is distinct from or non-distinct from the elements.
For what purpose is this suspicion regarding a deity entertained as being separate from the self?

Regarding the commentary on the statement of Mahāmatsya by Bhartṛprapañca, [the author] says that it is improper to refute the idea that the deity is the cause of the sequence of knowledge—having accepted its activity for the purpose of excluding the proponent of the identity of the body and the self—by raising the doubt that the deity is the cause of the sequence of knowledge. He says: "Or if there were separateness.
The meaning of this is as follows: Is the deity distinct from the elements or non-distinct? In the first case, [if it were distinct], its knowledge would be separate from the Self.
Having raised the objection that [the deity] might be the primary cause, it cannot be refuted on the grounds of its being non-different from the self, since its status as such a cause is accepted;
in the second case, because it is not distinct from the body, it is refuted by the very refutation of the doctrine of the body, and thus there is no separate objection or refutation.
Therefore, for an opponent, the raising of the doubt and the subsequent refutation of the deity’s status as the cause of the sequence of cognition are both untenable. || 1147 ||
This much fruit is intended from the words of the parable of the fish.
All this—the effects as well as the instruments—is of the nature of death.

Having restated the explanation of the "fish" statement (*matsyavākya*) by others, and having therein accepted what is reasonable and rejected what is unreasonable, [the author] now recites the preceding context in order to state the connection of the "hawk" statement (*śyenavākya*) as explained in the *Bhāṣya*. He says, "of the fish. What is that result? He states it: "in the form of death" (*mṛtyurūpa*).
The meaning is that the aggregate (*saṃghāta*), accompanied by desire and action, is of the nature of death and is not an attribute of the Self (*ātman*). || 1148 ||
But the Self, which has been explained here in its own nature, is distinct from those two.
The pure consciousness is devoid of activity when separated from both the gross and subtle bodies. || 1149 ||

Fearing that the Self might be included within those two because the notion of "Self" is well-established in relation to them, he says: "By those two. He qualifies the nature as being distinct from the two bodies for the purpose of making it an object of knowledge, stating: "pure" (kevala). || 1149 ||

In the very same way, it would be utterly distinct from desire and action.
In the same way, [the soul is the cause] of the body and likewise of the instruments by means of the two motivators. || 1150 ||

Anticipating the objection that one might again take up a body and its instruments even though they are distinct from the two types of bodies [the gross and subtle], because of the persistence of their causal conditions, he says: "And likewise," meaning: as if by the two bodies which are the objects of impulsion. 1150.
Therefore, the state of being in saṃsāra is produced solely by ignorance, and not by its own nature.
Therefore, upon the complete destruction of ignorance, liberation of the Supreme Self would occur. || 1151 ||

He states the conclusion regarding the lack of connection between the two bodies, along with their causal basis, and the real entity: "Ignorance" (avidyā). He asks what would follow if transmigratory existence were unreal due to its being rooted in ignorance, and answers: "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 1151 ||
Thus, by the preceding statement, the meaning of the whole is as follows.
Having examined the sequence of what precedes and follows, the Self is inactive, absolute, and non-dual. || 1152 ||
He concludes the restatement of what has been said with the words "Thus it was said. This refers to the preceding section, beginning from the sentence "Now this person, being born...
up to the sentence ending with the words regarding the fish. The meaning is that the inner self (pratyagātman) is distinct from the body and the organs along with their causal agents;
it is self-luminous and, by its very nature, not subject to transmigratory existence. He summarizes the collective meaning for the sake of clarity.

Regarding the phrase "the sequence of before and after" (*paurvāparya*): having observed the sequential order of the sentences explained previously, the meaning is that the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is distinct from action, desire, and the body, is realized as being of the nature of eternal purity and so forth. || 1112 ||
He has cast off attachment to the actions of the body and the senses, and is not attached to anything whatsoever.
The self is directly established with effort in one single statement. || 1153 ||

Having restated what has been said, the author provides an introductory preamble (*bhūmikā*) in order to introduce the subsequent text, beginning with the words "apāsta" (cast aside). Intending to show that when any one among desire and the other [afflictions] is liberated, the liberation from the others follows as a matter of course, he says "directly" (*sākṣāt*). An effort is made to present an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) regarding the Inner Self (*pratīc*), which is devoid of all specific attributes (*viśeṣa*). || 1153 ||
And it is accompanied by attachment, accompanied by death, and likewise possessed of effects and instruments.
Since this Self is perceived through ignorance as consciousness, || 1154 ||

He establishes this very point with the words "sāsaṅgaśca" (and it is associated). Therefore, the implication is that in the sentence concerning the waking state, the previously mentioned inner self (pratyagātman) has not been set forth. || 1194 ||
But in a dream, one is joined with the desires of latent impressions and is exempt from death.
In the state of perfect serenity, he is seen as both tranquil and likewise unattached. || 1155 ||

Anticipating the objection that its [the Self's] establishment might then occur in the passage concerning dreams, he says: "But in dream... If it is then argued that its establishment does not occur in the passage concerning deep sleep, he says: "In the state of serene composure (saṃprasāda)... Nor should it be said: "Let the Self, then, not be of the nature described";

for its establishment follows from the preceding passages through syntactic unity, and it is not right to say that since the Self has been established by those very passages, the subsequent portion is redundant; for it is not the case that [the Self is established] only in the preceding part.
1 kha. He was praised.

The meaning is as follows: the nature of the Self, which is free from the body (kārya), the organs (karaṇa), desires (kāma), actions (karman), and so forth, is gathered together in a single statement; nor is this gathering together in one place useless, because it serves the purpose of easy comprehension. || 1155 ||
"Or rather, this is his [form]," as has been stated here regarding the form of the Self.
Since this will be explained later, the following illustration is stated here.
Having provided this introductory transition (*pātanikā*), he takes up the passage concerning the hawk (*śyenavākya*): "That, indeed, is this...

This means that the passage concerning the hawk is cited here for the sake of providing an illustration of the nature of the Self—which will be described by gathering together [the descriptions] in one place starting from "That, indeed, is this, which is beyond meters, free from evil," and so forth. That very passage is what is referred to here as "this. || 1116 ||
And here, the form of the self is by its very nature enlightened, pure, and liberated.
It has not been shown by gathering [the points] together in the conclusion of a single sentence. || 1157 ||

In order to clarify the connection already stated, he restates the introductory context with the words "svataḥ" (by itself). This means that within the collection of words being subsumed as a single syntactical unit, the nature of the Self—characterized by eternal purity and so forth—has not yet been stated by way of synthesis.
For example, by saying "it is like a hawk," one demonstrates that illustration.
The form of the self, beginning with purity and awakening, is fully revealed. || 1158 ||

Now, he restates the connection that was mentioned: "tadyathā" (for example). Since the aforementioned nature of the Self (*ātman*) or its attributes is correctly demonstrated by means of such expressions as "that belongs to this," the sentence beginning with "tadyathā" has proceeded for the purpose of providing an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) of that matter; this is the meaning. || 1198 ||
In this context, the analogy between dreaming and waking has been fully demonstrated.
Now, an illustration for this state of serene confidence is being stated by means of the hawk. || 1159 ||
Having restated the relationship mentioned in the Bhāṣya, he states another relationship: "In a dream," etc. The word "example" implies the example known as the "great fish.
Having restated what was said in the passage concerning the great fish, he takes up the passage concerning the hawk: "Of the serene being," etc. (1199)
The Śyena is to be known as the Śaśāda, and the Rohita is of large body.
Swift is the falcon, the fair-winged bird, powerful yet small in body.
He avoids the charge of tautology by explaining the difference in meaning between the words *śyena* and *suparṇa*: "The hawk," [he says]. || 1160 ||
Just as a hawk, exhausted from circling in the sky for the sake of prey, [suddenly swoops down].
For, spreading its wings, it returns to its own nest in order to dispel its fatigue.

He applies the illustrative portion [of the simile]: "The hawk, being weary. Having spread out [its wings], having experienced exhaustion, and having folded them together, he brings about in those two the inclination to go to its own nest; this is the meaning. The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies that it is a world-renowned fact that a weary bird goes to its own nest for the sake of dispelling fatigue. || 1161 ||
The refutation of the example. 2 gha. [The word "śabda" etc.
[Vol. 3, page 453]
Just so,
this Self also, wandering through the states of waking and dreaming, remains as it is.
Being weary, for the sake of dispelling that weariness, he enters the nest of Brahman.

Having restated the illustration, he states the point to be illustrated with the word "yathā" (just as). He explains the meaning of the phrase "he runs toward the end" with the word "brahma" (Brahman).
It was said, "He runs toward the end"; this is a qualification of that end.
Where one who is asleep desires nothing, [that state] effects the cessation of waking and dreaming. || 1163 ||
Raising the doubt as to how the word "end" (anta) can signify Brahman, [the author] first restates what has been said and then adopts two qualifying attributes: "Endless... and so forth.
He demonstrates its function with the words: "Waking... and so forth. || 1163 ||
Because one is asleep in all three states, [the dream] is common to this or that [state].
Whereby, by the expression "asleep," one's own sleep is clearly distinguished [from that of others]. || 1164 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the waking state is already excluded by the very qualification "asleep," the passage beginning with "no desire whatsoever" is redundant, he says: "Asleep. Because each state is said to be threefold, the Self generally remains asleep even during all three states;
therefore, having stated "where [the Self] is asleep," he further qualifies this sleep of the Self by means of the words "no desire whatsoever" and so forth, making it explicit.
The interpretation: 1964.
"Nothing whatsoever" refers to that desire which exists in the states of dreaming and waking.
That [dream] which belongs to those two is likewise negated in deep sleep. || 1165 ||

"Let it be that this is a qualification of 'self-sleep' (*ātmasvāpa*); nevertheless, since by that [qualification] only desire (*kāma*) is prohibited, it is incorrect to say that it effects the prohibition of waking and dreaming. To this he says: "No," and so forth. Anticipating the objection that if, by prohibiting mere desire situated in the two states [of waking and dreaming] during sleep, those two states themselves are also prohibited therein, then other qualifications would be redundant, he says: "Likewise," [referring to] waking and dreaming.

Dreaming is negated by the second qualification in the state of deep sleep; therefore, like the first qualification, that [second one] is also meaningful. The sense is that in the former case there is a negation of two states with desire as the primary focus, while in the latter case it is with dreaming as the primary focus. || 1965 ||
Or in a dream, through the separation from one's beloved, by the very path already described.
Therefore, there is a prohibition of desire while awake, because desire and the like are possible in that state.
He states another meaning for the first qualification: "or in a dream. This means by the path already described in the passage beginning with "for [the Self] is unattached" (asaṅga hi).

Anticipating the objection that the absence of passion and so forth is equally present in the waking state according to the logic of non-attachment, he says: "In that case. The meaning is that while desire and the like exist in the waking state without being subject to sublation as long as the cognizer exists, this is not so in the case of a dream. || 1966 ||
In each individual state, there are the stages of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
Or else, there is some distinction [between them] by virtue of their gender. || 1167 ||
He states another meaning for the second qualification: "in each one. He provides the reason for this: "some... [ka. kha. gha.
reads "syāt"].

1587. The meaning is that the aforementioned distinction is established because of the qualifying word "anyone" (*kañcana*), which indicates difference in the statement, "No one at all sees a dream. || 1967 ||
"There are three dwellings," so indeed says the teaching of the Śruti.
This establishes the threefold nature of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
He states that there is another passage establishing the threefold nature of each state: "The three," [verse 1168].
In that regard, there is the negation of the three states: waking, dreaming, and [deep sleep].
By the phrase "not anyone," there is the grasping of those two alone, according to the Vedic revelation.

Once the threefold nature [of the states] has been established, what is established in the present context? To this he says: "Therein" (*tatra*). The meaning is that once the threefold nature of each of the three locations has been established, the negation of the first threefold waking state and of the second threefold dreaming state is established by the qualifying term [“dreamless”]. The reason for this is stated: “Of those two” (*tayos*). By the words “desire” (*kāma*) and “dream” (*svapna*), it is precisely those two waking states...
The meaning is that, because both dreaming and waking are mentioned by the scripture, what is intended here is the prohibition of those two in all their forms. || 1169 ||
By the statement "not any dream whatsoever," there is a negation of all dreams.
Thus, the state that is distinct from both waking and dreaming is described. || 1170 ||

He restates the meaning of the two qualifiers: "the dream," etc. By the statement "at will, not anything whatsoever," it should also be understood that there is a negation of all waking states. Nevertheless, he explains what is established in the present context: "thus, upon awakening," etc. (1170).
Spreading its two wings consisting of waking and dreaming, the Self, possessed of self-delusion, [flutters].
Having enjoyed pleasures and then becoming weary, he withdraws his two wings into himself.
Having stated the purpose of the qualification, he concludes the meaning of the phrase "he runs toward the end" with the verse beginning "jāgrat.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "he goes for the sake of the nest of Brahman," which is denoted by the word *anta*. The word *atha* is used to indicate that one who is weary requires a place of refuge.
Abiding in ignorance regarding the reality that has arisen from it.
This is established here by the Śruti through the analogy of the wings joined together. || 1172 ||
By means of the illustration of the hawk with its wings folded, he states the intended portion regarding the subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*). "In ignorance" (*avidyāyām*):

the meaning is that, according to the scriptural illustration—that the hawk remains in its own support after folding its two wings, thereby contracting its limbs within itself for the sake of destroying fatigue—the intended point is that the world abides within ignorance accompanied by the semblance of consciousness (*sābhāsāvidyā*). The connection here is with the phrase "in this ignorance."
"Into that which is called 'repose'—that which is the pure form of the inner self."
Having come to appear as the inner witness, it is sustained for the sake of the inner self (pratyagātman).

With the verse beginning "sam" [1173], he states what is intended to be illustrated by the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) in the case of the thing to be illustrated (dāṣṭantika). For a hawk, in order to settle properly, sustains itself in its own nest; thus, according to the scriptural illustration, that which is the nature of the inner self—pure, awakened, and so forth—is what is intended here.

To that inner Self (pratyagātman), the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī) appears as if it were the inner consciousness itself, due to its own limiting adjunct (upādhi) within the inner ignorance accompanied by its appearance.
[From Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four, page 455, verse 1588.]

The meaning is that when the intellect and other faculties are withdrawn, the conditioned self (upahita), being unable to remain separately, returns to its source which stands as the archetype (bimba) and sustains itself. || 1173 ||
"In the withdrawal of the primary and other effects, [the Lord] exists in the form of direct consciousness."
Even the withdrawal of the reflection of consciousness is like the dissolution of the sun in water. || 1174 ||

He clarifies the stated point by means of an illustration: "buddhyādi" (intellect, etc.). This refers to the reflection of consciousness (*cit-pratibimba*), that is, the *jīva*. Anticipating the objection that if the *jīva* were to undergo dissolution—that is, if it were a conditioned entity—it would be subject to destruction and thus also subject to birth, which would contradict the section of the Sūtras stating "The Self [is not so], on account of scripture" (*na ātmā śruter*), he says: "jala" (water). When the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) dissolves, that which was conditioned becomes the unconditioned.
The meaning is that the statement regarding dissolution (laya) is made because [the mind] abides in the state of mere [residual impressions], and not in reality. || 1174 ||
He who previously possessed ignorance and whose consciousness was subject to the effects of ignorance.
Through knowledge, a differentiation of this reflection of consciousness arises. || 1175 ||
Even though the self abides in Brahman during deep sleep, [the author] states "one possessed of ignorance" (avidyāvān) to address the doubt that there might be a difference from it in other states;
the word "in the city" (pure) refers to the mention of the two states. || 1175 ||
That ignorance, along with its effects, has indeed always been rejected by the Self.
But ignorance does not deny the conscious self, because that self is devoid of a [separate] self-nature. (1176)

Even so, if it is argued that its state of being Brahman occurs only when ignorance—the cause of differentiation—is destroyed, and not while it exists, [the author] says "no," beginning with the words "pratyākhyātā" (it is rejected). Why should the Self reject ignorance? Why might the opposite not be the case? To this he says: "pratyācaṣṭe tu" (but it denies). For ignorance does not discard itself independently, as it lacks its own essential nature; rather, the Self wards it off.

The meaning is that [ignorance] always stands in opposition by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness (*cidātmatva*). Alternatively, the meaning is that since ignorance has no self-nature (*nairātmya*) apart from the conscious self, it cannot possibly dispel that [consciousness]. || 1176 ||
The Self is entirely other than ignorance and its effects, without exception.
It is by its own nature unattached, for the very reason that it is the Self. || 1177 ||

Fearing that the Self might not dispel ignorance along with its effects because of its non-attachment and lack of connection to it, he says: "Ignorance... He states the reason for the connection [of the Self] with everything else without exception: "Because of being the Self. (1177)
Ignorance and its effect [present themselves] as a self for the sake of establishing their own existence.
Because it is not the self, one feels revulsion toward it; the self does not consent to that.

Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory for that which is unattached (*asaṅga*) to be connected, he says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). Ignorance and the like desire to connect with the Self for the sake of attaining its own nature, because such attainment is impossible through independence; however, the Self is unattached and consists solely of consciousness, and thus does not tolerate ignorance along with its effects. Therefore, even though there is a connection produced by ignorance, the Self's real unattachedness is not destroyed—this is the meaning.

Of the unattached with the attached, of the immutable with the selfless.
A real union of the self with the non-self is not logically possible. || 1179 ||
He reminds us that the illusory nature (*āvidyatva*) of the relationship has been established many times previously as well. Regarding the term "of the unattached" (*niḥsaṅgasya*):
it means [of that which is] devoid of a self (*nirātman*), that is to say, lacking a stable intrinsic nature (*niścalasvabhāva*). || 1179 ||
This [ignorance] has been rejected by the Self itself, which is the solitary inner Self.
Ignorance embraces the fire as a lump of ghee embraces a blazing flame. || 1180 ||
If ignorance along with its effects has been rejected by the Self, how can there be a relationship between the two, even if that relationship is unreal? To this he says:

"Rejected. The meaning is that ignorance, together with its effects, embraces the Self only in its negated form, because the Self—being non-attached, immutable, and of the single essence of consciousness—is incapable of sustaining a relationship. Regarding the relationship of the Self with the non-Self, which is to be removed:
The illustration: "fire," etc. || 1180 ||
The union with the Supreme Self is established without being investigated.
It should be understood that it is exactly so by means of ignorance and its effects. || 1181 ||
He states the example: "unexamined," etc. (1181).
In this way, there would be a sublation of reality, because it would depend upon the ultimate self.

He states the resulting conclusion: "Thus," [meaning] liberation occurs because of the sublation of this ignorance—which is the cause of the connection to the miseries of saṃsāra—through the support of the emergence of a cognition in the form of the unsublated Self, arising from the means of knowledge that is the Self (the Great Saying such as *tat tvam asi*), when there exists the aforementioned relationship between the Self and ignorance and so forth. || 1182 ||
By virtue of being mere inward consciousness, it is characterized as the inward, non-dual reality.
Because it lacks a relationship with a self, the non-self, though appearing like a self, is not actually so.

The remainder clarifies the nature of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Regarding the word "pratyak" (the inward-facing): one might suspect that if only that remains, the non-self (*anātman*) would also persist because it is non-different from it; anticipating this, he says "niḥsaṃbandha" (devoid of connection). || 1183 ||
Those who, under such circumstances, explain the state of being both collective and individual,
easily drag the root of the ear by means of the tip of the nose.

Since it is established that the non-self (anātman) is subject to affliction while the self (ātman) is not, the view of Bhartṛprapañca is also refuted; thus he says, "The aggregate... and so forth. Here, the word "here" refers to the self. He states the deluded nature of those who propound an impossible doctrine by means of an illustration: "karṣa... [1]
...so it is said. || 1184 ||
Apart from the entity that is the self, no other entity exists according to valid cognition.
If it is argued that "it is the measure of that," let it not be so, because prior to that awakening [it does not exist]. || 1185 ||

He clarifies the reason why the position that [the self] is both collective and distributive is untenable, indicated by the phrase "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*). He states: "The Self... [etc.]. He raises an objection:

it is improper to say that non-self-entities do not exist according to valid cognition (*māna*), because perception and other means of knowledge are well-known to apply to them. He refutes this: "Not so. Does that which establishes the non-self exist prior to the knowledge [of the Self], or even subsequent to it? In the first case...

That [world] is a manifestation of the ignorance regarding the Inner Self (pratyag-ajñāna); it perishes when that ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge of That. Therefore, how could there be any state of being both "as a whole" and "as parts"?

Since there is no second [reality], even after [the dawn of] knowledge, if the means of knowledge (māna) and the objects of knowledge (meyādi) were to exist, that knowledge would be futile; having considered this, he says: "yataḥ" (because). || 1981 ||
Let there be another distinct entity; yet even for that, there must be a connection with the self.

[The opponent] accepts that the non-self (*anātma*) entity is established by experience; [the author replies: "Let it be so. The meaning is that even from your [position], there is no factor other than ignorance (avidyā) to constitute a relationship. If it is argued that ignorance itself constitutes that [relationship], it is not so; for ignorance lacks the capacity to produce a real effect, and regarding an unreal relationship between the Self and the non-Self, neither the whole nor the parts can be real. Therefore, the explanation regarding their being both collective and individual is merely a blind tradition.
This is solely due to the boon granted by Vaiśvānara, and not according to logical reasoning. || 1187 ||

How then is it that Bhartṛprapañca explained the nature of the Self as being both collective and distributive, on the grounds that [the Upanishadic teaching] has both duality and non-duality as its objects? For his cognition regarding the realm of duality is like the rays of the sun.

As it has been said: "For its specific cognition regarding the realm of duality is scattered like the rays of the sun and manifests on all sides, as in the state of waking. The mental disposition of this inner self arises solely from its past actions.

"In that case" (tatra). When the knowledge of the self has duality as its object, karma accumulates; therefore, desire is brought about, and desire is the cause of all activity. For it has been said therein: "Desire is the fruit of action, and the latent impression (vāsanā) arises from action alone. (1189)

Action performed by oneself through cultivation according to its specific characteristics.

He states that when cultivation serves as the gateway for attaining a fruit corresponding to itself, the self's status as an enjoyer results; thus he says: "By that. For transformation follows consciousness, since it results from karma.

Since the experience of the fruit of action is impossible without the perception of the object, there is a modification [of consciousness].

It follows [the nature of] knowledge; therefore, it is logical that knowledge possesses the quality of discernment—this is the meaning. By the commentary stating, "Vijñāna is also ignorance when it perceives in a manner contrary to this," he describes its essential nature. Regarding the word "vijñāna": the term *iha* refers to one's own dream-object.
That ignorance is sufficient when an external object exists to be perceived, but it is not so when it does not exist.
That very desire is held to belong to this conscious self (*vijñānātman*) when it has attained awakening.

If it is argued that if false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) were consciousness (*vijñāna*), then if it were real, it could not be called "false," and if it were unreal, it would entail the denial of external objects—anticipating this objection, he says: "That [is]... The meaning is: even while the external object to be perceived exists, there is a consciousness called false cognition which is capable of producing the effect consisting of the determination of that [object]; therefore, that object does not deserve to be denied. "One should not entertain such a doubt," he says: "Desire. This refers to the desire of the individual soul (*jīva*) during the waking and dreaming states, which is accompanied by ignorance (*avidyā*) and other factors.

In that context, the productive imagination (bhāvanā) is the agent, while its object is that which undergoes transformation.

To show the distinction between the internal [faculties] such as desire (*kāma*) and the external ones, he states their difference in function: "The instigator" (*prayoktrī*), etc. The locative case in *tatra* is used for the purpose of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Desire (*kāma*) impels the person toward objects; action (*karma*) produces modifications such as pleasure and so forth in that person. Otherwise, "ascertainment" (*viniścitiḥ*) is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*); it is the cause for grasping what is contrary [to reality] and is not capable of determining things as they truly are.
The meaning is that there is a difference in their respective functions. As it has been stated therein: "The efficient force (bhāvanā) is the motivator; the object is that which is modified. (1199)
Of desire, striving, cultivation, knowledge, and the categories of meaning, respectively.
Precisely because of their mutual dependence, there would thus be syntactic unity (ekavākyatā). || 1196 ||
In that case, since desire (*kāma*) and the others are mutually independent, they would be like iron rods [standing alone]; therefore, he says: "Desire," etc.

The meaning of the word "thus" (*evam*) is "in due order. For it has been said: "Thus, because desire, action, mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and consciousness are mutually dependent, they have a single purpose. (1196)
In this regard, by means of mental cultivation alone, the self desires objects of desire; likewise,

by means of *vidyā* one perceives the object of duality. The locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The word "likewise" (*tathā*) serves as an illustration by means of *bhāvanā*.
The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the state of duality. || 1197 ||
But in the state of serene composure (saṃprasāda), because of the impossibility of any external object, this [is so].
Karma remains merely as its natural outflow, and even meditative cultivation subsides. || 1198 ||

Having spoken of waking and dreaming, he introduces deep sleep with the words "But in the state of serene clarity" (*saṃprasāde tu*). As it has been stated regarding the subject of non-duality, moreover, in the state of deep sleep, because of the absence of any external object to be acted upon, karma remains motionless; and even the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) residing in the conscious self subsides due to the absence of any effect to be produced. || 1198 ||
Likewise, because of the absence of an agent to be impelled, the effect of the action is impossible. || 1199 ||
Knowledge also [is required] for a differentiated object that has been misunderstood.
Due to the absence [of any other object], this knowledge of the self, being non-distinctive, remains established. || 1200 ||

Anticipating the objection that even in deep sleep, although desire (*kāma*) and action (*karman*) are absent, there might still be an effect produced by knowledge (*vidyā*), he says: "by the cessation of the object. The connection is: "knowledge also ceases. He clarifies the very absence of the object to be acted upon with the words: "of the contrary. The form of the self in deep sleep is liberated from desire, action, and so forth.

In this regard, he introduces the scriptural passage with the word "evam" (thus). The meaning is as follows: since, according to the manner explained, there is a destruction of desire and so forth in deep sleep, the scripture beginning with "na kañcana" (not anything) declares here, regarding the one who is asleep, that this form of the inner self (pratīcaḥ) is devoid of desire and the like, and is peaceful. || 1202 ||
Thus has the illustration of the hawk been explained by some with great reverence.
In that regard, whether it is logical or illogical, it should be determined in accordance with the statements of the scriptures.
Let this be investigated by oneself through reasonings well-established in the world.

By means of scholars who have fallen into no partiality, for the sake of establishing the reality [of the matter], he summarizes the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the hawk’s statement as expressed by others with the words "Thus indeed" (*ity evam*). He indicates the fault therein with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

He prevents [the notion] that the principles (*nyāya*) are supernatural (*alaukika*) with the word "in the world" (*jagati*). For the sake of achieving one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*), he himself—

Thus it has been said. Anticipating the objection—"The rationality of Bhartṛprapañca’s commentary has been determined through reasoning by his own disciples; why, then, should it be investigated?"—he says: "Without partiality," etc. Whichever person has a preference for a particular [commentary], he will accept that commentary; what is the use of investigation?

Anticipating the objection that this is not so, [the author] says "vastu" (the thing), because the diversity of human inclinations leads to various interpretations; if there were such a proliferation of alternatives regarding the nature of reality, the established reality would not be proven. This division—that the waking and dreaming states have duality as their object while the state of deep sleep has non-duality as its object—is untenable, whether the three states are considered real or unreal, for in the first case, it is only duality [that would persist].
The meaning is that because non-duality alone exists when existence is non-dual, the state of being both collective and individual has been refuted. || 1203 ||
This is its intrinsic nature, which has been illustrated here by means of a simile.
That which is reached in deep sleep is distinct from ignorance, desire, action, and so forth.

The nature of the Self in deep sleep has been described by means of the passage concerning the hawk; now, he recounts the preceding context for the purpose of connecting it with the section on the channels (nāḍī-khaṇḍa).
"This" refers to that which is the Self's own inherent nature. He states what that is: "That which...

Furthermore, he states what that nature is which was described as the inner self (pratyak) in the passage concerning the hawk: "Ignorance," etc. The word "etc. (ādi) is intended to include its effects.
This alone is the natural form of the Self, meaning that which is non-dualistic (aprapañca) and solely concentrated on Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). || 1209 ||

Therefore, this [suffering] should be understood as having solely the ignorance of the self as its cause.

Anticipating the objection—"How can there be such a restriction [that the Self is only the witness], when other forms characterized by agency and so forth also appear to this [Self] in states such as dreams?"—he says:
"Otherwise than this. He clarifies the meaning of the third quarter [of the verse]: "The Self... (1206).
That which is the cause of this form is ignorance, the bringer of misfortune.

Introducing the subsequent statement, he states the subject of the inquiry: "That which has as its cause... The meaning is that ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of misfortune, is the topic under discussion—that form consisting of agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth. Indeed, it must be investigated whether ignorance is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the Self, like consciousness (*caitanya*), or not its nature, like action (*karman*) and so forth. Thus it is said. || 1207 ||
But this ignorance is not adventitious, because that would lead to the consequence of no liberation.
It is now being investigated whether this ignorance has the nature of a self or not.

One might object: "It is not being deliberated here whether ignorance (avidyā) is the nature of the Self or non-nature; rather, it is being determined whether it has a beginning or is beginningless, since the Commentary mentions another alternative—namely, that it is adventitious like desire and action. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But not... [na tu...].

For if ignorance were adventitious, then in the absence of a cause for it, there would be the possibility of its re-emergence even in liberation, resulting in the impossibility of final release (anirmokṣa). Together with...

Even if [the self] were real, since there would be no cause for it other than the self, liberation from that [self] would still be impossible because ignorance could arise again as its cause; thus, that same defect remains.

Therefore, the meaning is that the investigation into whether ignorance is beginningless or has a beginning is not intended here, because [ignorance] cannot be characterized by adventitiousness and so forth. Now, even if ignorance were the very nature [of the self], the impossibility of the self’s liberation through its cessation would be equal [to our position]; thus, your desired [view] is also untenable.

Fearing that such an inquiry might be appropriate, [the author], intending to show that for those who maintain the self is non-inert (ajaḍa), liberation—which is the cessation of ignorance—is not [attained] in this way because it is something distinct, concludes the intended inquiry with the words "The Self" (ātma). Such an inquiry is also intended in the Commentary (bhāṣya);
by adopting the position of its being natural (svābhāvika) and stating its opposite as being adventitious (āgantuka), the word "that" (tat) refers to its lack of inherent nature (asvabhāvatva).
The meaning is that because this [view] is desired, otherwise the presentation of liberation therein would have no place, according to the logic already stated. || 1208 ||
In this world, the Self is entirely distinct from ignorance, desire, action, and so forth.
Form was presented first, with the intention of directly [demonstrating] it.

One might object: "Even on the view that ignorance (*avidyā*) is beginningless, liberation is something other than the destruction of ignorance; therefore, even when that [liberation] arises, there is no contingency of non-liberation, and thus our desired inquiry is established. Anticipating this objection, [the author states: since ignorance were beginningless, its cause would have to be sought; yet for the immutable Self (*ātman*), there can be no cause for it other than ignorance itself; and since a prior ignorance cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) of a subsequent ignorance, [it follows that ignorance must be beginningless].

Thinking that because the Self consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its products, the aforementioned inquiry is impossible, and thus the inquiry established previously must be maintained, [the author] states the motive for the inquiry: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*).

The meaning is this: the nature of the Self, free from ignorance and so forth, was described previously in the context of deep sleep; with the desire to establish that through direct perception by means of inquiry, the subsequent portion of the text is commenced. || 1209 ||

And whatever is the effect of ignorance must also be stated in its entirety; for this purpose, the subsequent section of the text is introduced in order to achieve complete manifestation [of the subject]. (1210)

He states another intention behind the passage concerning the channels (*nāḍī*): "And of ignorance" (*avidyāyāśca*). The meaning is that since whatever is an effect of ignorance must also be described in its entirety because it is useful for discrimination (*viveka*), the subsequent text is intended to reveal that. || 1210 ||
Since the perception of the effects of ignorance depends upon the nest, [it ceases] beyond that.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "The channel... The meaning is as follows: the notion of agency and so forth arising from ignorance is produced by the channels, for in their absence—such as during deep sleep—that notion would be untenable, just as it is then.
Therefore, the introduction of the channels is for the purpose of providing a basis for that perception, and that perception exists for the sake of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). || 1211 ||
Or rather, the mention of the channels (nāḍīs) is intended for the purpose of establishing their falsity.
For how could there be a perception of the interior of the Vindhya mountains and the like, which are exceedingly subtle?

He states another result of that presentation [of the channels] with the words "Or else" (*yadvā*). To the question, "Why is the presentation of the channels for the sake of showing the falsity of the two states?

he replies: "Because of the extreme... Because the channels are exceedingly subtle, the dream-perception of mountains such as the Vindhya—which possess a vast magnitude—within them is necessarily false due to the absence of a suitable location; by that example, the falsity of the waking state as well is established. || 1212 ||
If this, being the effect of ignorance, is held to be false like that which possesses ignorance;
Therefore, for the sake of establishing its falsity, there is the assumption of subtle channels. || 1213 ||

Thinking that [the opponent] has asked this, he suspects [the following objection]: "It is ignorance (*avidyā*). The meaning of the suspicion is this: according to the maxim that "ignorance makes the impossible possible," the perception of extremely large things like the Vindhya mountains within the subtle channels (*nāḍīs*) arises from ignorance. [The opponent then says: "In that case, my own position is established. To this, [the author] replies: "Like one possessed by ignorance" (*avidyāvat*). That is to say, because even when the effect is false, there is a necessary concomitance with its [the cause's] existence. || 1213 ||
Indeed, those subtle channels of his, called the hitā, are situated in the heart.
By means of which one perceives the nature of an effect as both diminished and otherwise.

Having explained the connection of the section on the channels (*nāḍī*), he explains its words, beginning with "Tā vā" (Those indeed...). The meaning is that those well-known channels—which were introduced in the fourth [chapter], are present in the sixth and following chapters, are related to the aggregate [of the body], bear the name "Hitā," and because they have spread out from the heart, are established therein—are extremely subtle and numerous. The phrase "his channels" refers to the man.

Anticipating the question of how the channels (nāḍīs) are connected, he says: "apakarṣa... etc. The meaning is that the genitive case is appropriate because these [channels] belong to him—the agent who experiences the increase and decrease of the fruits of karma and knowledge. || 1214 ||
In thickness, it is equal to one-thousandth part of a hair.

While those [channels] are filled with the essence of food, that Self, through ignorance of itself—
One situated in the midst of a dream considers [the objects] to have forms such as red or yellow.

The meaning is that while situated within those channels filled with the essence of food as the seer during sleep, the Self—having those channels as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—through ignorance (*avidyā*) imagines for itself also forms such as red and so forth. || 1216 ||
According to the requirements of the rasa and varṇa, [it assumes] the form of red, yellow, and so forth.

"By rasa... The essence (*rasa*) of the food consumed flows into the channels (*nāḍīs*), and through its connection with the constituent elements (*dhātus*), it becomes manifold in color.

In accordance with that, the deities residing in the channels—designated by terms such as "liṅga" and so on—assume the false nature of blood and other substances; and the Self, having those [deities] as its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), likewise assumes that same form.
The meaning is that he possesses a form liberated for the sake of his own enjoyment. || 1217 ||
But this is for the purpose of explaining the dispersal and withdrawal of the Buddhist consciousness.

"In the fourth [chapter], the introduction of the channels (nāḍī) is for the sake of purifying the nature of consciousness. And there is a further taking [of the offering] for the sake of knowing the subtle nature of the food of the deities.

The form of the conscious self is not held to be anything other than consciousness itself.
For its other form is essentially one with the knowledge of its own self. || 1221 ||

Fearing the objection that desire and the like are not distinct from the Self because they are of its very nature—just as consciousness is—the author recalls the non-establishment of that reason as stated in the passage beginning with "for [the Self] is unattached" (*asaṅgo hi*). This is done by the words beginning with "no" (*na*). Fearing the objection that desire and the like are inherent to the Self because of uncontradicted experience, and that the scriptural texts contradicting such a view must therefore have another meaning, he says: "one's own Self" (*svātma*). Desire and the like are produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) in the Self, as is evident from their positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
The meaning is that, because the perception of [the world] as possessing that [nature] is an error due to its non-reality, the Śruti should not be interpreted otherwise on account of it. || 1221 ||
For all conscious beings, indeed, possess a single uniform nature.
Because it has consciousness as its essence, it should be known that there is a distinction between that [consciousness] and the element of space.

If it is argued that, even in the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), the Self might possess forms such as desire and so forth just as it possesses difference, he says "no," beginning with the word *vijñāna*. The meaning is this:

individuals (*puruṣas*) who have the intellect (*buddhi*) as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) are the living beings (*jīvas*); they are of one uniform nature by virtue of being the conscious Self (*cidātman*). Any appearance of difference among them is produced by the power of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) caused by ignorance of that [Self].
Therefore, the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). || 1222 ||
This division into internal and so forth does not belong to the inner self (pratyagātman) by its own nature.
Because it is the sole cause for the non-understanding of that [reality], it does not attain the state of identity with the single reality. || 1223 ||

Anticipating the objection that difference [between things] is unestablished because of the lack of knowledge regarding that [reality], he says: "The internal self, etc. For the inner self—which is immutable, unattached, and non-dual—is not divided without its own ignorance; since this division arises from ignorance, it does not touch the reality.
This is the meaning. || 1223 ||
Therefore, the very form of the linga has ignorance of the Self as its sole cause.
And those meditative cultivations arising from karma, their form is also like that of the [inferential] mark.

In response to the objection that the form of difference must therefore remain [in the Self], he says: "The subtle body" (*liṅga*). The meaning is that the form called difference, which arises from one's own ignorance, depends solely upon the growth produced by that [subtle body]; therefore, there is no occasion for difference within the Self. Suspecting that desire and so forth might be innate—just like agency and the like—he says: "Karma. For those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of agency and so forth, which arise from karma, belong as attributes only to the subtle body.
The meaning is that form is like the various forms contained within it; furthermore, since desire and so forth are inherent, there is no illustration of agency and the like. || 1224 ||
And that liṅga is also extremely subtle, capable of moving within the center of the nāḍīs.
And by the power of its master's karma, that deity assumes that form.

If agency and so forth reside in the subtle body (*liṅga*), why is such a subtle body not perceived like the gross body? To this he replies: "And the subtle body. Having stated that it is unfit for direct perception due to its extreme subtlety, he establishes the reason [for its invisibility] with the words: "The channels... Now, is that [subtle body] conscious or unconscious? In the first case, it would be the Self itself under another name; in the second case, it must have enjoyment of objects.

If it is not the case that the internal self (*pratīc*) does not exist, then the experience of enjoyment would be unestablished; if it does exist, then since such experience is impossible for an insentient entity by itself, its cause must be stated.

To this, he says: "The Master" (*svāmī*). And that subtle body (*liṅga*), consisting of the deities, assumes the form of sound and so forth for the individual soul (*jīva*) through the power of its unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Such is the meaning. || 1229 ||
For the sake of accomplishing mere enjoyment, [it exists] solely as a reflection of consciousness.
This Self, which is not of a manifold nature, does not depend upon anything else whatsoever.
Having stated the cause for the subtle body’s (*liṅga*) assuming those forms, he states the result: "Enjoyment" (*bhoga*), etc.

The meaning is that there is no result other than the soul’s (*ātman*) enjoyment for the subtle body’s assumption of the form of objects. Anticipating the objection that the soul would possess activity during its enjoyment—just as Caitra does—he says: "Consciousness" (*caitanya*), etc. Since enjoyment resides merely as a reflection, there is no modification in the pure soul.

Lest it be suspected that the Self itself might assume a form for the sake of experience in the absence of a subtle body (liṅga) due to parsimony, he says "No. This means that which is treated as other than the Self, as something distinct from it. Here, the reason is its state of non-attachment (asaṅgatva). || 1226 ||
This very person of consciousness (vijñānapuruṣa) has the divine and other [levels] as its latent impressions (vāsanā).
In accordance with the subtle body (liṅgadeha), it [the mind] undergoes transformations such as being an agent and so forth within the manifest sign (salliṅga).
One whose self is afflicted by ignorance conceives of [the non-self] as the self. || 1227 ||

How, then, does enjoyment occur there? To this he says: "By consciousness," and so forth. This very Self, whose true nature is veiled by ignorance, having the intellect (*buddhi*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), following along with the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), and refined by various latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), [appropriates] the modifications such as agency residing within its own adjunct as its own.

The meaning is that when [the Self] imagines itself as such through the medium of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of ignorance, it assumes the form of objects; thus, experience (bhoga) occurs by way of its reflection.
Even that modification of the *liṅga* follows the sequence of the *rasas*.
For it is from this that the stability of the body—whether pertaining to the deities or otherwise—derives its cause of sustenance.
The Śruti states both "by these indeed" and likewise "these by that. || 1229 ||

Anticipating the objection that if the self possesses modification through the medium of the subtle body (*liṅga*), then that modification would belong to the subtle body itself by its own nature, he says: "of the subtle body.

He provides the reason for the statement that the modification follows the essence of food (*annarasa*) in the phrase: "with regard to the divine and so forth. The meaning is that since the essence of food is the cause of the subsistence of the subtle body—which consists of various specific elements—it is logical that its modification follows that [essence].
He states the authority for the claim that the essence of food is the cause of its maintenance with the words: "By these... (1228–1229).
Moreover, this rasa also depends upon the transformation of the food that has been eaten.
For that reason, he too conforms to the elements such as wind, bile, and so forth.

If it is argued that the maintenance of the body depends on rasa (nutritive essence), then how is its own production not self-sufficient? Lest this be thought to render eating useless, he says: "Rasa also...

As for how the transformation of the food consumed comes into being, he says: "From which... Since the transformation of food must be relied upon as the cause of rasa, therefore the meaning is that rasa, once produced from that [food], follows after the bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*). || 1230 ||

Then, in accordance with the nature of the elements, he spontaneously attains the red and other [colors].
The deity's body conforms to that color as previously described. || 1231 ||

In this regard, the reason is stated: "having the form of the constituent element (dhātu). The meaning is that the rasa produced by the digestion of food assumes the form of blood and so forth; it follows that constituent element, for otherwise its acquisition of that form would not occur. The word "atha" signifies the relationship of cause and effect between those two. He says [the following] because the subtle body (liṅga) follows the form of the blood and so forth residing in the rasa, since they share a common substratum by virtue of both being located within the channels (nāḍī): "that" (tam). || 1231 ||
Of the self, which is indeed changeless, [the appearance] occurs within the subtle body (liṅga) by way of its own manifestation.
The perception of white, yellow, and so forth arises through the power of karma.

Nevertheless, he explains what has arisen from the Self (pratīc): "From the Self" (ātmanaḥ). The meaning is that, although the Self is in reality devoid of action, through its own reflection (svābhāsa) in its own limiting adjunct—the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha)—the cognition of yellow and so forth arises by the power of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa); from that, the accomplishment of experience (bhoga) follows.
Since all this exists within the Self, it has ignorance alone as its cause.
For the manifold proliferation of the internal and so forth is like [the appearance of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like. (1233)

If the object of perception were to possess substantial reality because it is seen through action, he says [in response]: "In the Self. The remainder of the sense is that therefore it is false; and the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that its falsity is well-known from the Śruti and other sources. || 9233 ||
This is the distinction between truth and falsehood; nevertheless, regarding an unreal object, [the distinction remains].
Just as it is well-known to him in the waking state, so it is in the dream state.

Anticipating the objection that if everything were false, the distinction between things like a jar which are real and things like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell which are unreal would be untenable, he says:

"Satya" (real). Even though everything is unreal, just as there is a distinction between the real and the unreal in a dream, this same distinction exists even in the waking state within the realm of false objects;
therefore, because it is well-known in the world, that distinction is not contradicted. This is the meaning. || 1234 ||
Apart from the nature of consciousness, ignorance and the like cannot be established.
Just as reality is established by means of valid cognition, so too is the falsity of an object.

Even though the world is illusory, its Self must be either different from it or non-different; the first alternative is not tenable because it contradicts non-duality, and the second is not tenable because it would entail that the Self is also false.
Anticipating this objection regarding the contradiction of non-duality, [the author] says: "Of the nature of consciousness" (citsvabhāva). || 1239 ||
Therefore, this reality of cause and effect is nothing but pure consciousness alone.
This was proclaimed loudly by the Śruti in the form of "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and other such statements.

He addresses the objection regarding the consequence of the self being false by stating "cinmātra" (pure consciousness alone). Because the reality or unreality of entities such as ignorance cannot be established through any means of valid cognition as distinct from consciousness—this is what is referred to by the word "tena" (by that). The word "iha" (here) refers to the discourse of the scriptures on liberation.
Thus, the meaning is that since there is non-difference [of all things] in the residue of pure consciousness, the consequence of their falsity does not arise. || 1236 ||
In this world, for one whose mental modifications have been dispelled through the mere cultivation of the realization of falsity, [the state of liberation is attained].
The perception of the internal self in a dream is described by scripture as being false. || 1237 ||
1. It would not be established in the world. 2. Kha. *śrāderni* [vol 3, page 467] Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Chapter]—1600.
Having thus stated the falsity of the waking state, he now asserts the same for the dream state as well, by means of the scriptural support beginning with "yatrainam" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
The word "mithyā" (false) means that there is no disagreement regarding the established falsity of dreams that conform to experience. || 1237 ||
It would be white when there is an abundance of phlegm (kapha), and from the combination of wind (vāta) and bile (pitta).
They declare that blue and black are the transformation of wind.

The intended meaning of the passage beginning with "tā vā asya" has already been explained; now, he elaborates upon the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "śuklasya," which was previously summarized under the heading "in accordance with the form of the constituent elements (dhātu). Regarding the word "śuklam" (white): the meaning is that when phlegm (śleṣman) is in excess, because wind (vāta) and bile (pitta) are subordinate, the food consumed becomes white while residing within the channels (nāḍī). When wind is predominant, because the other two are subordinate, the transformation of the consumed food [becomes so] while residing within the channels.
He says, "They call it blue," meaning "blue"; its explanation is "black. || 1238 ||
Piṅgala is so called due to an abundance of bile (pitta), while Harita has little bile.
Thus, due to this imbalance, the complexion becomes excessively red when there is equilibrium of the bodily humors (dhātu). || 1239 ||

He says "piṅgala" (tawny) because, due to the predominance of *pitta* and the subordination of the other two [humors], they call the transformation of the food consumed that which resides in the channel *piṅgala*. He says "harita" (green) because, when there is an excess of *vāta* and *śleṣman* and a deficiency of *pitta*, the essence of the food residing in the channel becomes green. He concludes the description of the color of the food-essence as being caused by the imbalance in the relative predominance of the qualities of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Thus.
Regarding the phrase "due to imbalance": he states that when these [elements] are in a state of equal predominance, the food-essence residing in the channels becomes extremely red; thus he says:
"of the constituent elements" (dhātu). || 1239 ||
In this and other ways, they describe transformation in many forms.
Those who know the true principles of the science of medicine [know] that the food which has been eaten goes into the channels.

In this regard, he cites the medical treatises (*vaidyaśāstra*) as authority, saying "and so forth. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is intended that when there is a deficiency of wind (*vāta*) and the other humors, there is a corresponding deficiency of blue and other colors in the food-essence (*annarasa*). Furthermore, all the unmentioned varieties of the channels (*nāḍī*) and the distinctions of the food-essence contained within them are implied. For it has been stated: "According to their respective divisions into fourth parts, the wind and blood amount to one hundred and seventy-five [units]. This indeed is the division.

Even when the blood is purified of *pitta* and *śleṣman*, the *doṣas* sustain the body as long as they remain in their natural state; however, through their reversal, they cause affliction. In that regard, those [veins] which are dark-red, pulsating, subtle, and which in an instant flow with blood full and then empty, carrying wind (*vāta*), are characterized by a blue, yellow, or black color and heat to the touch, and they quickly discharge [blood]; whereas those carrying *pitta*-blood are white, unctuous, stable, and cold.

"Those with itching are due to *kapha* and blood; those arising from a combination of symptoms are due to *saṃnipāta* and blood; those that are knotty, firm, and red are *rohiṇī*; and pure blood [is the cause of others]. Suśruta also said:
"The vessels carrying wind (*vāta*) are reddish; the vessels carrying bile (*pitta*) are blue."
"The Rohiṇī veins carry blood, while the Gaurī veins carry phlegm."
And Yājñavalkya said:
"His rays are infinite, situated in the heart like a lamp—white, black, tawny, blue, brown, yellow, and red. (1240)

Now, regarding this aforementioned transformation of the essence of food:
Now that which is the effect of the delusion directed inward is being explained. || 1241 ||
He states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "atha" (now/then): "atha" [is used] in the locative case to denote an occasion. || 1241 ||
Having created the world within his own self, together with its constituent elements and presiding deities.
Through ignorance, the self perceives itself as residing within the channels that have the form of white and black.

Objection: Since there is no effect of ignorance (*avidyā*) in a dream, according to such scriptural passages as "There are no chariots there," how can this [scripture] be used to elaborate upon that?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The world. Through ignorance, the Self previously manifested the world consisting of various kinds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The connection is that one sees precisely because it is situated within the channels (nāḍī). || 1242 ||
Now, the ultimate limit of ignorance is clearly explained.
For that ignorance is differentiated according to the gradations of its effects. || 1243 ||
Now, one might ask: since the effects of ignorance (*avidyā*) have already been elaborated upon starting from the verse "Then [he goes] to another," what is the purpose of the subsequent statement?

To this he replies: "Of ignorance... The distinction here is that while the expansion of ignorance as the cause of the waking state was described there, here its effect as the cause of dreaming is being described. Furthermore, for one who accepts that ignorance is indeed one, how can its differentiation also be accepted? To this he says: "Its... [and so on].
Therefore, the understanding of their distinction is not contradictory; this is the remainder of the sentence. || 1243 ||
That ignorance is always differentiated by the distinctions among its effects, such as the subtle body (liṅga) and so forth.
But from its own nature, not even the slightest difference of ignorance exists here.

But those belonging to his own school (the Māyāvādins) assert that the difference in ignorance (*avidyā*) is inherent; to them he says: "liṅgādi" and so forth. Here, "ātman" is what is meant. For there is no difference in ignorance *per se*, because there is a lack of evidence; nor is such a difference experienced with respect to each individual self, since the very existence of such a difference is unestablished. Nor is its establishment achieved by the plural expression "by means of māyās," because that merely reiterates the difference already obtained from the diversity of effects; otherwise, [if it were not so, one would have to say] "māyām."

However, because this contradicts the singular number in the word *prakṛtim*, and because the identity of the genus cannot be the intended meaning when the identity of the individual is already established, the sense is that by this [argument], the passage beginning with "as many cognitions as there are" and so forth is explained. || 1244 ||
That subtle linga, which is the nest of latent impressions, is of a pure nature.
Due to contact with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the essence (rasa) residing in the channels, it is like a crystal or similar objects. || 1245 ||

Stating that the subtle body (*liṅga*), which arises from ignorance, exists in the form of the world, [the author] first declares its status as the locus of manifold mental impressions (*bhāvanā*), as it is necessary for the perception of various effects. He says "that" (*tat*). He states the reason why it is not perceived like a jar or other objects: "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).

He states the cause for its being the substratum of latent impressions (*vāsanā*): "transparent" (*svaccha*). Now, one might object: since the channels (*nāḍī*) themselves are filled with various fluids, [how can the subtle body be the locus of blue and other colors?]...

Anticipating the objection that it is appropriate for the latent impressions (vāsanā) of yellow and so forth to have [the Self] as their substratum, but not the subtle body (liṅga), he says: "situated in the channels" (nāḍīgatā).
He provides the example of crystal and the like to illustrate its transparency. He states the reason for its assumption of various colors with the words: "the channels" (nāḍī). || 1245 ||
Such is the meaning.

The Self, whose vision is never-failing, manifests as the various forms of chariots, women, and elephants produced by the impelling force of dharma and the other [qualities], and which consist of the various rasas and so forth.
That which is essentially nothing but ignorance and is perishable spreads before one.

Having restated the mark (*liṅga*) of the form already described, he establishes the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein with the words "dharma, etc. The meaning is that the mark—consisting of desire and so forth, endowed with various forms such as chariots produced by waking, dreaming, and burning, and assisted by the juices arising from the digestion of food—is manifested as an object to the Self. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that because it is insentient (*jaḍa*), it requires the witness-consciousness. Its mode [of manifestation]...
He wards off the expectation of peace by the word "unimpaired" (*alupta*). He avoids [the charge that] the gender-mark (*liṅga*) is a real entity (*vastutva*) by the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
The reason for this is given by the word "perishable" (*vinaśvara*). || 1246 ||

Thus, first, the rule for the accomplishment of meditative realizations (bhāvanā) has been declared for those whose sole abode is ignorance; now it is being stated regarding awakening, whether in the waking state or in a dream. || 1247 ||

Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) of the passage beginning with "atha," and having explained that the persistence of the subtle body (*liṅga*) in the form of the waking state is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), [the author] restates that and concludes the intended meaning by saying that this sentence is spoken in order to elaborate upon that [persistence] in the dream state: "Thus" (evam). || 1247 ||
Now, where there is that perception which, as it were, perceives [the self] as "I am," arising from delusion regarding the self;
And he falsely imagines that "I am indeed conquering him. || 1248 ||
Now, he explains the syllables beginning with "atha yatraiṇam. The word "atha" (now) means that the state of dreaming is being described immediately after the waking state.
That time at which the cognition arises, as it were, that some have come and are eating him—that is dreaming.

He clarifies the meaning of the word "iva" (as it were), namely that this cognition is merely an appearance, by saying "arising from the delusion of the self" (*ātmamohottham*). [The text continues: "Some, having approached, [say] 'me thus'..."

And he says that where there is a cognition as if [the objects] were being brought under control, that is a dream; [he explains this by saying] "they conquer. Regarding that, he states the meaning of the word *apa* as "false" (*mṛṣā*). || 1248 ||
In this there is neither a slayer nor a victor; rather, that [suffering] arises solely from ignorance.
One whose consciousness is permeated by latent impressions conceives of acts such as killing.
One might raise the objection: "Since the killer and so forth appear even in a dream just as they do in the waking state, why is the cognition of killing and so on considered false?

Anticipating this, he says: "It does not exist. Then, to the question of how there can be a cognition of its reality in that case, he says: "But rather... Anticipating the objection that this cannot be so because the conceit of killing and so on is extremely firm, he says: "Vāsanā... "Vijñāna" means the mind (manas). || 1249 ||
Falling into pits and the like arises from the intensity of unrighteousness and other such factors.
In this world, the perception of the opposite arises even in a deluded person during a dream.
The Śruti itself declares that very thing to be the cause of falsehood.

He says "the appearance" (bhāsam). He explains the purport of the passage beginning with "of the inward one" (pratīcaḥ) and "that which indeed" (yadeva) as follows: "regarding falsity" (midhyātva). The meaning is that since the Śruti itself declares the reason for the falsity of the dream state—which was sought to be known—we do not need to establish its falsity ourselves.
This is merely an object of the waking state, which was previously perceived as non-existent.
Therefore, in this matter, he considers his own self to be possible only through ignorance.
Neither ignorance nor its effect exists when there is the vision of the Self. || 1252 ||

Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he explains the words, beginning with "jāgrat" (waking). Whatever chariots and so forth a person has seen during the waking state, that too is indeed false, because the reality is non-dual (*advaya*). That very thing, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*), though impossible in the dream state, is imagined through one's own ignorance (*avidyā*) and is considered real; thus, the meaning is that the dream is false because it is characterized by ignorance. [The text continues: "In both the waking and the dream states, there is ignorance regarding the elephant and so forth..."

He addresses the impossibility that was previously stated by saying, "Not ignorance" (nāvidyā). The meaning is that since ignorance along with its effects is utterly destroyed through the direct realization of the Self produced by the Vedic statement, such [ignorance] is impossible. || 1252 ||
The wise, however, declare that fear is exclusively the effect of ignorance.
For those who have realized the true nature of reality, there is no fear from anything whatsoever.

Having stated that both states consist of ignorance and are composed of *māyā*, he cites the consensus of the learned regarding this matter: "But fear... He provides the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) for that very point:

"Since... The meaning is that fear exists only for those who do not know the Self, but not for those who do know it, because of the absence of a cause; therefore, it is produced by ignorance. || 1253 ||
This is what is meant here: regarding the karma previously acquired.
The remainder of that fruit which was experienced during awakening is called cultivation (bhāvanā). || 1254 ||

Raising the objection that—because of the qualification "whatever fear exists while waking"—fear may indeed be illusory (*āvidya*), yet agency and so forth in the dream state are not likewise illusory—the author states the intended meaning of the passage: "This... He explains that whatever karma was accumulated which yields enjoyment during the waking state, its fruit is experienced there; the remnant of that, namely the latent impression (*vāsanā*), is manifested in the dream. Thus he says: "The former... (1214).
If indeed cultivation, having accomplished its purpose, bestows its fruit here in this world;
At the time of male enjoyment, she employs a karma that is ever-new.

Anticipating the objection that—since the karma that grants waking experience has already been exhausted at that time, and since its latent impressions (*vāsanās*) have been spent through the experience of the dream—there would be no waking up, nor, for one who has woken, any engagement in activity due to the absence of a cause—he says: "If...

Even though, during a person's time of experiencing a dream, the waking impressions (*vāsanās*) become manifest and, having yielded their fruit, reach a state of exhaustion, nevertheless, upon waking again, another [set of impressions]...
Latent impressions (vāsanā) cause new karma to arise; for as long as ignorance (avidyā) exists, the emergence [of impressions] is not impossible.

Among these impressions, some provide experiences in dreams, while others serve as the cause for actions in the waking state; thus, "emergence" means the accomplishment of the performance of actions by one who has emerged [from sleep].

The very volition that acts is what makes the notions of self as agent and enjoyer false. (1256)
It concludes by stating that various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are the motivating factors in waking and dreaming, as well as in the arising of karma and the enjoyment of its fruits.
