The connection is with the word "prayoktrī" (the motivator). If one objects that if she (the *bhāvanā*) is the motivator there, it would result in the abandonment of the accepted doctrine of *avidyā* (ignorance), he replies:
"It is false. || 1296 ||
This being so, that which was previously experienced as the fruit of karma during the state of awakening—
The continuous dwelling of that [mind] upon the object of cognition is designated as "cultivation" (bhāvanā). || 1257 ||

To refute the view that the Self alone is the locus of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he says: "In this way. Since it is established that agency and so forth are accomplished through the activity of karma via the medium of ignorance (*avidyā*) and mental cultivation, the impression (*vāsanā*) known as *bhāvanā*—which arises subsequent to the enjoyment of the fruit of whatever karma was experienced during the waking state—is said to reside in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), not in the Self; such is the meaning. || 1217 ||
Just as the intellect is reflected by the reflection of the consciousness of the Self, so too [is it].
This cognition is always reflected by the image of the fruit arising from karma.

It has been stated that "the latent impression (vāsanā) resides in the intellect (dhī). He establishes this by means of an illustration: "The Self," etc. For the intellect never deviates from the manifestation of consciousness (caitanyābhāsa) in its own existence, because it is dependent upon the Witness (sākṣin); thus, it is always permeated by the latent impressions of the results [of actions].
Bound by ignorance, this very Supreme Self, though bodiless, [appears as such].
In its own states of non-waking, it appears as if it were both an agent and an enjoyer.

Anticipating the objection that even when residing in the intellect (*dhī*), it does not instigate agency and so forth because these are inherent to the Self (*ātman*) by its very nature, he says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). The meaning is that the Self is not inherently an agent or an enjoyer due to its bodilessness; rather, in both states, it appears as such when colored by ignorance (*avidyā*). || 1259 ||
And there is no [change] other than through ignorance, because the inner self is immutable.
We perceive another cause for the establishment of [the soul's] agency and so forth. || 1260 ||
He states the answer to the question: "What loss would there be even if one were to admit that the bodiless [Self] possesses natural agency?"—namely, "And not... (1260).
The sky is accompanied by dust, smoke, frost, clouds, mist, and so forth.
Just as the self is imagined by the deluded through such attributes as agency and so forth.

He clarifies this—that agency and so forth are ignorance (avidyā) with respect to the Self—by means of an illustration: "Dust," etc. Since frost has already been mentioned by the word *tuṣāra*, the word *nīhāra* here refers to darkness (*tamas*). || 1261 ||
Just as the relationship between a property and its substratum is not perceived through a means of valid cognition.
In this way, they are not perceived in the sky by means of direct perception, as has been stated.
1. ka. gha. vā | 2. ka. kha. 'tvādyeta | [vol 3, page 472] 3. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1605.
Having raised a doubt regarding the counter-example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he explains it in detail, beginning with the word "Dharma. For it has been said:
"Just as the single ether (*ākāśa*) appears distinct within jars and other vessels..."
"Thus, although the Self is one, it appears as many, like the sun in various receptacles of water.

Nor is it the case that space alone possesses the six qualities such as sound and conjunction; for if space were taken as the substratum (*dharmin*) from that perspective, there would be no corroborating example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because space is unattached and indifferent (*asaṅgodāsīna*), and because time and so forth are similar to it, and because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for those [qualities] has as its object only gross space. Thus, with respect to the Self—

It should be understood that even from the perspective of that [Self], agency and so forth are not cognized; for there can be no cognition of those [attributes] in that which is unattached and indifferent. || 1262 ||
This meditation relies upon the delusion produced by the appearance of consciousness.
It is said that [the qualities] are based on the immutable Self, which is Truth. || 1263 ||

If it is asked how *bhāvanā* can be said to be the instigator of that [agency] when agency and so forth in the self arise from ignorance (*ajñāna*), he says in response: "By consciousness" (*caitanya*). Because it rests upon the delusion (*moha*) of the self—which is permeated by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—*bhāvanā* is said to rest upon the true inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is devoid of all activity; thus, since delusion resides in the self and *bhāvanā* is established therein, it is composed of delusion (*mohamayī*).

The meaning is that since it is accepted that the internal organ (*pratīci*) is the instigator of agency and so forth, there is no contradiction in agency and the rest being produced by both [the Self and the internal organ]. From the passage beginning with "bhāvaneṣā" up to "āśritā," the extensive discussion should be understood as having grasped the difference and non-difference between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*).
For it is in the master alone that the fruit of all action converges.
The sense of "mine" and "I," as well as the state of ownership, arise from this cause and are born of ignorance.
Stating another reason for the fact that agency and so forth are products of ignorance (*avidyā*), he states a general principle: "The master" (*svāminī*). The reason for this is: "Mine" (*mama*).

In such cases as "I," there is the conceit of limitation; from that arises the thought "this is mine. Since all this action arises from these two [notions], and since the fruit of that action resides in the one who stands as the master, it is logical that ownership, agency, and enjoyership belong to the master alone.

The meaning is that [the Self] is the substratum. Even though the action and its fruit go to one's own self, he says [in response to the question] how agency and so forth are of the nature of ignorance:
"And ownership... (1264).
"For [the cognition] of an object that is not delimited by space, time, and so forth, and which is devoid of such [delimitations],"
Since the limitation of "I" and "mine" does not exist without the ignorance of the Self. (1265)

Regarding the question of how the conceit of "I" and "mine"—which implies a lack of true ownership—can be asserted as being born of ignorance, he says: "deśa... (the verse beginning with *deśa*). The word "hi" is used to indicate that its dependence [on ignorance] is well-known from such passages as "other than dharma" (*dharmād anyatra*) and so forth. Therefore, since both limitations (*avaccheda*) are products of nescience (*avidyā*), agency and the rest, which are produced by them, are likewise of that same nature; this is the remainder of the sense. || 1269 ||
The reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is said to have the same substratum as the latent impressions (vāsanā).
One whose knowledge is colored by meditative cultivation does not become free from duality. || 1266 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the Self does not possess agency and so forth in reality: "By latent impressions" (*vāsanā*), etc. It is colored by various types of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). [Note: *vaivikri* in manuscript *gha*; *te'nyataḥ* in manuscripts *kha* and *ga*; *notthaṃ svāṃ* in manuscript *gha*; *ṇacidā* in manuscripts *ka* and *ga*. [Vol. 3, p. 473]

1606 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]: Knowledge is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). He who possesses it is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). Because he abides in a single substrate together with the state of being an agent and so forth, which consists of the mind, he is said to be a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*); however, the non-dual Self (*advaya ātmā*) is not like that—this is the meaning. || 1266 ||
Because the reality of the self is witnessed by an intellect colored by meditative cultivation.
Therefore, it appears to those of dull intellect as if it were the basis for cultivation. || 1267 ||

One might object: "Since the transmigrating self, which is the substratum for latent impressions (vāsanā), appears [of its own accord], why resort to such a difficult conceptualization? To this, he says: "bhāvanā" (cultivation).
The word "ataḥ" (hence) is to be connected with the preceding ablative case. || 1267 ||
What is the use of saying much more here? Whatever this [yogi] perceives—
Just as an elephant and so forth appear in a dream within consciousness, so too does that very same thing appear within the self through ignorance.
It falsely perceives it as blue, just as one perceives the sky to be blue.

He summarizes the meaning of the passage beginning with "yadeva" (that very thing) with the words "bahunā" (by much). He demonstrates, by means of an illustration, the possibility through ignorance of that which does not exist by its own nature, with the word "nabhas" (the sky). || 1268 || 1269 ||
This has been demonstrated as the effect of ignorance that has arisen.
Now, the function of that which is being withdrawn from its function is stated: || 1270 ||

Now, by way of restating the preceding context, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "as if a god" (*atha yatra deva iva*): "The effect" (*kāryam*). The connection is with the phrase "of [the intellect] being drawn away from its effect" (*kāryataḥ apakṛṣyamāṇāyāḥ*). || 1270 ||
When his latent impressions (vāsanā) arising from objects such as gods and so forth [are present], then...
Whether in the waking state or in dream, that very same mental cultivation arises.
"Due to the power of his own past actions, he perceives himself as 'I am a god' or 'I am a king,' O Lord. (1271)

Having explained the meaning of the word *atha* through its intended purport (*tātparya*), he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "where" (*yatra*) as follows: "Of the gods," etc. When, during the waking state, knowledge regarding objects such as the gods has arisen for this seer, then a corresponding latent impression (*vāsanā*) is produced. Subsequently, by the force of karma which is the cause of dream-experience, that very previously arisen impression—taking the form of the vision "I am a god," and so forth—manifests in the dream; and that indeed is [the cause].

The meaning is that [the waking state] is false. The word "atha" (then) signifies the immediate succession following the exhaustion of the karma that causes the waking state. Sovereignty (*vibhutvam*) consists in being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtvam*) by virtue of mastery over the instruments [of perception]. || 1271 ||
When there is awakening to the Self, then one whose delusion regarding the Self and its effects has been destroyed becomes [liberated].
"In a dream, one conceives the thought: 'I alone am all this.'"
He states the meaning of "I alone am this" and so forth: "Dhvasta... (verse 1272).
In this context, it is determined that "I alone" refers to pure consciousness (cinmātra) as the self.
And by the word "this" (idam), the effect of ignorance is intended here.
He states the meaning of the three words in order to explain what has been summarized: "I," etc. The locative case expresses the subject matter of the current sentence. || 1273 ||
1 ka. ga. *nāśaya* | 2 ka. *’tyagja* | 3 ka. *’dirū* | [Vol.
3, page 474] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri: 1607.
This statement is sufficient for the complete eradication of ignorance.
"Therefore, it is fitting that one should think, 'I am the entire whole. (1274)

He states the meaning of the sentence, preceded by the mention of its fruit: "Of ignorance," etc. The meaning is that once the meanings of the words have been grasped in the manner described, the sentence—consisting of three co-referential terms—will be capable of destroying ignorance along with its effects by revealing pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). In this regard, he provides support from the remainder of the text: "All," etc. Upon accepting the stated meaning of the sentence, [one realizes] "I am all," which is the fullness.
The meaning is that it is logical for you to be described as "self" because there is no means of delimiting it. || 1274 ||
This is his supreme, full, and entire world, attained through knowledge.
But those worlds which are other than this are imagined by his ignorance.

He states the meaning of "so'sya" and so forth with the words "eṣo'sya. He states the meaning of the word "parama" (supreme) with the word "pūrṇa" (full). He excludes its being relative by saying "kṛtsna" (entire). The phrase "is obtained through knowledge" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Anticipating the objection—"Insofar as worlds such as heaven exist, how can this [Brahman] be full?"—he says "itaḥ" (from here). || 1271 ||
O King, such is the vision of the inner self that the god has revealed to you.
It is not logical that this should be the fruit of knowledge, because of its connection with the word "as it were" (iva). || 1276 ||
If it is argued that because knowledge of being a god and so forth is for the sake of human ends and is thus a fruit of knowledge, it is not complete, he says in response: "The god," etc. (1276).
Just as one who has not reached his own ground perceives himself through ignorance, so it is.
"Out of delusion alone, one thinks, 'I am like a god' or 'I am like a king'; such is the fruit of action. (1277)

Since it is established that the fruit of knowledge is precisely the full realization of the pure consciousness (cinmātra) of everything, the author explains the status of being seen as a deity and so forth within a dream.

[The verse says: "As if they were... Just as the dreamer experiences the fruit of actions such as killing through ignorance, so too he perceives the fruit of divinity and the like solely through delusion; therefore, that is not the fruit of knowledge—this is the meaning. || 1277 ||
The thought "I alone am this" is not a direct [realization] of the reality of the Self here.
In this context, however, it is the non-dual Self alone that possesses ignorance as its companion for the sake of awakening. || 1278 ||

In that case, one might object: "The fact that everything is pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*) is not the result [of waking experience], because it was seen in a dream, just like the killing and other acts seen therein. Anticipating this, he says: "I... The meaning is as follows: that which appears here in this dream as the pure consciousness of everything is not like other dreams; for, without the word "only" (*eva*), there is a direct hearing of the existence of all things, and because that [consciousness] is the Self, it is real. [This applies] in the waking state as well.

If it is argued that, just as the identity of the body with the Self is seen [to be false], so too the perception here of everything as the Self is false, he says "Bodha" (Consciousness) to refute this. In the waking state, the identification of the body with the Self exists accompanied by ignorance (*avidyā*), which serves as its cause; however, in the dream state, there exists only the Self as the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā*). Even though a semblance of ignorance in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) appears, gross ignorance does not appear as it does in the waking state. Therefore, there is no room for the suspicion of falsity here. Alternatively, in the waking state...

The meaning is that while the notion of the body being the self and so forth is accompanied by subverting cognition, in a dream the self alone remains devoid of such subversion; therefore, every state of existence in a dream is not false. || 1278 ||
1. Kha: *tadaitat* | 2. Kha, Ga: *yaḥ svapne* | 3. Ma: *akṣādevātmā* | [Vol. 3, page 475] 1608 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]
Whatever arises from ignorance is here restated as "this."
That which has been explained as the oneness of self is designated by the word "I. || 1279 ||

Having thus explained the passage beginning with "so'sya" (that is his), he now restates the meaning of the sentence beginning with "aham eva" (I alone am) along with its supplementary elements, with the intention of providing further detail; first, he restates the meaning of the two words [beginning with] "yāvat": "yāvat" means as it has been explained, that is, as stated in its fullness. || 1279 ||
This form, together with the elements and the presiding deities, ends with the body.
This "I," which is superimposed by beginningless ignorance, is qualified [by that]. || 1280 ||
Anticipating the objection as to how there can be a relationship of qualifier and qualified here, he states that "this" (*idam*) is the qualifier and "that" (*amo*) is the qualified, saying:
"up to the body" (verse 1280).
Through the two methods of positive and negative concomitance as previously described, [the relationship] between the two word-meanings [is established].
This statement, "I alone am this," is [spoken] by those who have realized it. || 1281 ||

To explain for what purpose the knowledge of the meanings of the qualifier and the qualified is required therein, he says: "By means of the connection," etc. The meaning is that since the operation of a sentence occurs when there is knowledge of the words through the connection [of their meanings] as taught in the fourth chapter [of the *Śābarabhāṣya*], that [knowledge of the meanings of the parts] is desired as being useful for the knowledge of its [the sentence's] meaning. || 1281 ||
When the object to be sublated and the sublater are thus known by the aforementioned method, [the sublation occurs].
Knowledge that destroys ignorance arises from the sentence directed toward the inner self.

Having restated the knowledge of the word-meanings (*padārtha-jñāna*) and its fruit, which is the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-jñāna*), he states the latter's fruit: "bādhyeti" [and so on]. The distinction is that this [world] is the object to be sublated (*bādhyatva*) and the "I" is the sublator (*bādhakatva*). He explains the meaning of the word "evam" (thus) with "ukteti. 1282.
For when darkness is destroyed by knowledge, duality along with its cause is likewise destroyed.
The entire Self in its totality is beyond the range of mind and speech.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that the destruction of the cause is the cause for the destruction of the effect; the word "hetu" (cause) functions here as a *nimitta* (efficient cause). || 1283 ||
Thus, this supreme excellence of knowledge has been fully demonstrated.
In this state of perfect serenity, all this remains as the Self alone.

Having restated the meaning of "I myself" (*ahameva*) and so forth, he now restates the meaning of "that is his" (*so 'sya*) and so forth. Regarding the word "that" (*sa*): having repeated what was stated with the intention of expressing something further, he states that further point. "The state of serene repose" (*saṃprasāda*); this is said to be the effect of ignorance (*avidyā*). || 1284 ||
In the same way, there is the cognition "the self is one" during both the states of dream and waking. (1285)
In the same way, the cognition of the non-self is also established without being subjected to critical inquiry.
Its nature is characterized by deviation, and it is witnessed solely by the inner self. || 1286 ||
Fearing that if the Self remains as the sole remainder through its nature as pure selfhood (*ātma-mātratva*), it would then be non-dual (*advaya*) whereas it was dual in its previous states, he says:
"One" (*eka*). The meaning is that just as the Self is non-dual in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), so it is [in this state]. The word "arises" (*udeti*) from scripture and so forth is to be supplied.
If it is argued that the Self is not truly non-dual because the non-Self (*anātman*) also appears there, he says in response: "Unexamined" (*avicārita*). From scripture...
1 kha. gha. *paskara* | 2 kha. *dviśiṣya* | 1 [vol 3, page 476]

Just as the cognition of the non-dual Self arises from the means of knowledge such as perception, so too the cognition of the non-Self (anātmadhī), though produced by perception and the other means, is established by its own experience as being of a nature subject to deviation; for the waking cognition of the non-Self does not persist in dreams and the like, nor does that [dream] cognition persist in the waking state. Therefore, the aforementioned cognition of the non-Self is [erroneous]. [This concludes] Brāhmaṇa 3, accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. [Page] 1609.
The meaning is that the non-duality of the Self is established in the sense that [the world] is merely an inexpressible ignorance (avidyā) that is to be experienced. || 1285 || 1286 ||
In this way, even amidst cognitions that are erroneous, there exists a non-erroneous cognition.
The establishment of the state of being deviant is based on the principle of identity. || 1287 ||

If it is argued that because the non-self (*anātman*) is false due to its variability (*vyabhicāritva*), the self (*ātman*) is non-dual (*advaya*), then one might suspect that since this conscious self (*cidātman*) is also variable during states such as deep sleep, it too would be false, and thus only the void (*śūnya*) would be non-dual. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The variable... The word "thus" (*evam*) is stated in accordance with experience. Since there is no other means of proving the variability of those cognitions (*dhi*) that are themselves variable, [the self] is non-variable (*avyabhicārin*).
The meaning is that they should remain established as nothing other than the non-dual nature of consciousness. || 1287 ||
However, even though ignorance exists, [the self] previously followed from the means of valid cognition.
For the actual occurrence sought here is established as being based on experience.

He states the conclusion regarding the proof of consciousness as previously described: "When [it exists]," etc. The word "previously" refers to the time of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). "The locus of experience" means that which is accessible through experience. The term "of such a kind" is used because it is non-deviating and non-dual. The particle "hi" is employed to indicate that such a reality is well-known from all the Upaniṣads. The non-dual reality of the Self must be accepted even throughout the three states; duality is false.
The meaning is: since it has been established by that [previous argument], what more need be said regarding the non-dual reality when ignorance is absent? || 1288 ||
In brief, the nature and the effect of both ignorance and knowledge are as follows.
Thus has the nature of the prides been explained, based on their prior manifestation and experience. || 1289 ||

Having concluded the discussion on the meaning of the passage beginning with "I alone am this," which arose as a secondary topic, [the author], continuing the explanation of the [main] passages, recites the preceding context in order to state the connection for the *Aticchandā* passage. He says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). The word "previously" (*prāk*) refers to the states of dream and deep sleep.
"Experience" (*anubhūti*) is an elliptical expression for the testimony of the Śruti. (1289)
For those who possess pride regarding things that are not the self, [this occurs] prior to their realization of non-self.
Only that form which arises from the object of cognition, whose self-nature is established by itself, is perceived.

Fearing that one who asserts "the perception of ignorance and so forth occurs prior to the arising of the means of valid cognition" might be admitting both a non-self entity and its corresponding means of cognition, [the author] says: "The non-self. In that regard, because the direct perception and other means intended as valid cognitions are related to that [non-self] even before their own establishment, they are perceived as having forms manifested by that object of measurement through their connection with the independent inner self (pratyagātman) which establishes them; therefore, their validity belongs to the Self alone.
This is the meaning. || 1290 ||
By those virtuous ones who possess such variegated [qualities], even that which is not for their own sake can be accomplished.
For when extended, the non-self cannot be measured, like darkness dancing.

Anticipating the objection—namely, that since the Self is not delimited [as an object] by perception and other means of knowledge in the same way that non-self-objects are, how can those means of knowledge have authority regarding it—he says: [The commentary continues: ...because of the arrival of the [scriptural] tradition... [and so on]. (Note: The provided text contains a series of manuscript variants indicated by letters such as *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *gha*, which refer to specific readings in different versions of the source text.)
200 [Vol. 3, page 477] 1610 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]—

Regarding the phrase "by means of those whose nature is consciousness" (*cidrūpaiḥ*): because they are insentient (*jaḍa*) like their own objects, they cannot by themselves establish [the object]; rather, it is only when they are pervaded by consciousness that the non-self object can be cognized by them. Apart from that [consciousness], since insentient means of knowledge (*māna*) are as difficult to know as a dance performed in darkness, they necessarily depend upon the conscious self (*cidātman*). Without being pervaded by consciousness, the insentient is ineffective, just like a jar; even a lamp is effective only when it is pervaded by that [consciousness].
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is "because it is accepted as being the means of accomplishment. || 1291 ||
Furthermore, even "non-self" does not become "non-self" without a self.
Because they are non-entities and devoid of self-nature, like the son of a barren woman or the horn of a human. || 1292 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if the non-self is not perceived by the cognizer and others who are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), the perception of it would still result in the loss of non-duality (*advaita-hāni*), he says: "Even the non-self.

The meaning is that, like the means of knowing the non-self, the non-self itself does not establish itself independently without depending upon the Self; therefore, there is no loss of non-duality. He states the reason for the non-self's lack of independent establishment: "Because of its being a non-entity (*avastutvāt*). [This is because] from a single entity...
Fearing that [the property] might exist as something other even for a non-entity, he says: "Because it is devoid of self-nature" (nirātmatvāt). || 1292 ||
In the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the ignorance regarding the Self remains false.
It has entered the path of conventional usage and is self-established, with the self as its witness.

To the objection that, since duality would then be non-existent, ignorance (avidyā) would be destroyed, he says: "In the waking state," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Ignorance regarding the Self manifests itself in the form of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and so forth. || 1293 ||
For this knowledge is "I am all"; ignorance is the perception of anything other than that.
Both [the object and its cognition] are dependent upon consciousness prior to the means of valid cognition.

Having set aside the objection regarding the destruction of non-duality (*advaita*) that arose as a consequence, he recalls the previously discussed topic by following the sequence of the narrative. The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies that the statement "the vision of all things is knowledge" was introduced in the *Brahmakaṇḍikā*. The meaning of "both" is the pair consisting of knowledge and ignorance, along with their respective effects. || 1294 ||
This is his supreme world, which has been shown as "I am all."
Hereafter, the supreme state (parāvasthā), which is free from ignorance (niravidyā), is demonstrated. || 1295 ||

Since the state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmabhāva*), which is the effect of knowledge, has been shown even in a dream, one might suspect it to be false—like the killing and so forth occurring therein—and thus [the text] recalls the refutation stated [previously]: "This is his... It states the reason for the truth of this state of being the Self of all, even though it was seen in a dream: "Therefore... This means immediately after the description of the dream; "free from ignorance" (*niravidyā*) means devoid of manifest ignorance (*vyaktāvidyā*). He who [was seen] in the dream...

That which is called "the state of all-being" (sarvabhāva) is also stated in the *Aticchanda* passage regarding deep sleep; therefore, the sense is that the reality of this state of all-being is established by its being non-sublatable. || 1295 ||
It has been stated that his desire for non-origination is caused solely by his knowledge of the Self.
Form was previously [described], but here it is said that its ignorance has been destroyed.

Anticipating the objection, "If all existence has already been shown previously, what is the purpose of the statement regarding *atiśaya* (excessiveness)? [the author] restates the preceding context and clarifies what was already said:
1. gha. ṃrapranṛ ṃ | 2. gha. 'tmākṣepakatva ṃ | 3. kha. 'kṣakatva ṃ | 4. gha 'stutve'vastuno' | 5. ka. kha. 'nātmakā ṃ | 6. ka. ga. 'midaṃ va' |
"Anāpta" means: in the previously mentioned scripture, "I alone was this," which occurred prior to that; it refers to that which is devoid of manifest ignorance and its products.

He states that although the state of being the self of all (*sarvātmatva*) was mentioned briefly in the passage concerning the dream state, it is made explicit in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*): "But here...
By the two genitive endings in the word *asya*, the Self (*ātman*) is indicated. || 1296 ||
Chandaḥ (desire) is kāma (lust), because of its governing role and because of its association with evil.
Because it transcends desire, it is therefore called "excessive desire" (aticchanda). || 1297 ||
Having stated the purport of the phrase *aticchanda*, he explains the meaning of the word *chandas* while commenting on its constituent parts. He says: "The word *chandas*.

Although the word *chandas* ending in a nasal (*sānta*) denotes meters such as *gāyatrī* and the like, this word *chandas* ending in the vowel *a* (*akārānta*) signifies desire (*kāma*), because "any desire whatsoever" (*kaṃcana kāmaṃ*) has been the subject under discussion, and it occurs here in conjunction with the word *pāpman* (evil), which denotes the action prompted by that [desire].
The meaning is "and because of the recitation. Stating the meaning of the prefix *ati*, he etymologically explains the word *aticchanda*: "it has transcended" (*atikrāntam*).
In this context, it should be understood that the etymological derivation is non-Vedic, because a secondary metaphorical sense (lakṣaṇā) is impossible here. || 1298 ||
And here, by the word "evil" (pāpman), there should be the inclusion of both merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma).
"He abandons evil," as has been stated previously. || 1299 ||
To the question, "In that case, why is length employed here?", he replies: "Expansion (*vivṛti*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the present application.

Anticipating the objection—"Why is Vedic length (*dairghya*) intended here? Why might it not be the primary [length] itself?"—he says: "Because the term *aticchandas* refers to the form [of the meter], there is no basis for applying length. Regarding the phrase "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*), he explains the meaning of the word *pāpman*.
"Of evil" (pāpman). Anticipating the objection, "How could one who is established in unrighteousness (adharma) speak even of righteousness (dharma)?", he says: "Of evil.
Because of the absence of causes such as an agent, and because of the destruction [of ignorance] through non-knowledge.
Evil deeds such as merit and demerit are said to be the form of the self.
Because he is eternally free from evil and because he transcends all causes of fear.
The nature of this Self is fearless, eternally risen and never-setting.

Nevertheless, one might raise the objection: "How can the Self be 'free from evil' (apahatapāpmā), given the common consensus that 'I am sinful,' 'I am a doer of evil deeds,' 'I am of a sinful nature,' and 'I am born of sin'?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Apeto" (gone away). Since ignorance—which is the cause of the distinction between action, agent, and fruit—has in reality departed from the Inner Self (pratyagātman), that Inner Self is said to have desires and so forth as its essential nature only because it is veiled by beginningless, phenomenal ignorance; [these are merely] its attributes [in appearance].

The meaning is that because duality (*dvaita*) is born of ignorance, its true nature is always devoid of it, according to such scriptural texts as "other than dharma [and adharma]" and so forth. He states the meaning of the phrase "the fearless form" (*abhayaṃ rūpam*) with the word "fear" (*bhaya*).
The meaning is that in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), due to the absence of the ignorance that causes distraction, the nature of the Self remains as the immovable, fearless state. || 1300 || 1301 ||
By means of the actual conduct itself, the task to be known is completed.
Therefore, all that is to be known has been accomplished; nothing else remains beyond this.
1. "Not the Self" (na ātmā). 2. *Gha*: "this" (idaṃ). 3. *Kha* and *Ca*: "thus" (evaṃ). 4. *Ka* and *Gha*: "the object of knowledge" (jñeyaṃ); *Kha*: "in the object of knowledge" (jñeye). [Vol.
3, page 479] 1612 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Chapter Four.

He states the fruit of knowing the meaning of the statement regarding excessive desire (*aticchanda*): "In reality," etc. The meaning is that because of such scriptural passages as "There is nothing whatsoever higher than Puruṣa," when that [Puruṣa] is known, there is the state of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatā*), since there remains nothing further to be known. || 1302 ||
Since this is so, therefore, whatever constitutes an obstacle to other duties [should be avoided].
Or that which was obtained while obstructed by delusion is [restored] through the awakening to Brahman. || 1303 ||

[Objection: Even effects and objects of knowledge appear as distinct from the Self; how then can they be non-existent, or how can there be an object of knowledge for the Self without it serving a human purpose? To this, he says: "Since... Since it is established that everything other than the Self is merely a modification of speech (*vācārambhaṇamātra*) and that the Self, being unsurpassed bliss, is the ultimate human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), therefore, whatever else there may be—whether another effect or another object of knowledge—[is likewise unreal].

The meaning is that one who knows the sense of the *aticchanda* verse has accomplished his purpose, because he has already attained that Brahman through the realization of it as the inner self (*pratyak*). || 1303 ||
The form of the self is free from the great delusion of desire and action.
It has been directly demonstrated by the Śruti, like a bilva fruit placed in the palm of the hand. || 1304 ||

He recounts the narrative in order to explain the connection with the woman's words: "Kāma... [etc. The greatness of delusion (*moha*) refers to its predominance over other factors with respect to *saṃsāra*. || 1304 ||
The self-luminosity of the Self was previously stated before the commencement of the inquiry.
Even that is suspected of belonging to the self in the future, just like desire and action. (1305)

Desiring to state the connection, he raises an objection with the words "by itself. The effort [of the author] consists in the refutation of the suspicion that [the self] is an object of cognition. || 1305 ||
Because this Self, in deep sleep, perceives neither itself nor non-selfs.
Therefore, its consciousness is like that of one who is awake, characterized by desire and action.
Fearing that the suspicion of being seedless might lead to an over-extension [of the argument], he says: "Because... (1306).
This is not so, because the cognition of difference arises solely from its dependence on a causal agent born of delusion; it is not admitted to exist when delusion is absent. || 1307 ||
He refutes this, saying: "This is not so. For one who asserts that consciousness is adventitious must admit its non-existence during deep sleep;

in that state, is it the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) that is denied, or is it specific knowledge (*viśeṣa-jñāna*)? It cannot be the first, because of the recognition upon waking: "I am he who was asleep."

The meaning is that because there is no contradiction with the Śruti which says, "Indeed, seeing, one does not see," the other [the agent] is not [perceived]; for [the perception of an agent] arises from delusion through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and because in deep sleep there is an absence of the manifest ignorance of "I am ignorant," and because the entire collection of causal factors has been cast far away, the negation of that [agent] therein is desired. || 1307 ||
Or rather, it is where he spoke of the cognition of difference, saying "this is other than that."
For as long as there is ignorance regarding the inner self, that [ignorance] persists through its connection with that very ignorance. || 1308 ||

He states the evidence for the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—that where there is ignorance, there is the cognition of difference—with the words "where" (*yatra*). That is to say, "therein" (*tatra*) refers to that cognition of difference (*bhedajñāna*). || 1308 ||
1. ga. *Samāśrayā* [vol.
3, page 480] 1. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
But where, through awakening, the ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by the realization "That thou art," [there is no such duality].
By the scriptural text "What should one see with what? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15), the perception of duality is negated.

Regarding the point that where there is no ignorance, there is no knowledge of distinctions, he states the proof for this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "But where... (referring to *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.12.4). The connection is with the Śruti passage beginning with "But when for him" (*yatra tv asya*) and continuing with "by what, whom? (*tat kena kam*). || 1309 ||
Therefore, in this case, oneness alone is the cause for the non-perception of difference.
This very point is established by means of the example of the woman and the man. || 1310 ||

He states another reason for the absence of specific cognition during deep sleep: "Oneness" (*ekatvam*). This means that the oneness of the individual soul (*jīva*) with that Supreme [Self] is the cause for the absence of specific cognition in sleep. He introduces the passage concerning the woman there: "The woman" (*strī*). The meaning is that this very oneness is the cause for the non-perception of distinctions. || 1310 ||
The qualification "by the beloved" is for the purpose of establishing the affection of the mind.
Even though she possesses womanhood, the mind does not become attached when she is disliked. || 1311 ||

Explaining the illustration, he states the function of the qualification: "The mind" (*cetaḥ*). Anticipating the objection that since she possesses womanhood, her mind would naturally be joined with passion through the sight of him, and thus the qualification would be redundant, he says: "In one who is hostile" (*dviṣṭāyām*). || 1311 ||
He was exceedingly under the sway of passion because of a woman endowed with all feminine charms.
In this world, a man is embraced by his beloved who desires him.

In that case, one might suspect that since the attachment of the mind is established by the mere existence of love for her, the feminine qualities such as "beautiful" (*subhū*) and so forth would be redundant; anticipating this, he connects the sentence with the word "exceedingly" (*atīva*). Nor is the attachment of the mind toward the aforementioned female body fruitful by means of one's own mere love alone—thus he specifies [the object] with the word "they desire" (*kāmayantya*). Here, the action whose fruit is embracing is designated as "unutterable" (*avācya*).
The connection is that "the person does not know. || 1312 ||
And here, by the word "embraced" (pariṣvakta), a state of intermingling is expressed.
Through the mutual affection of a man and a woman whose constituent parts are joined together. (1313)
The man who has produced the fruit of enjoyment in the act of sexual intercourse.
Overwhelmed by pleasure, he does not perceive what is external, nor what is internal.
He states the intended meaning of the word *pariṣvakta* (embraced): "Embraced," etc. Here, the term refers to the citation of the scriptural passage.

"Intermingling" (*vyāmiśrībhāva*) is the internal penetration of the male characteristic into the female characteristic. Now, as these two act in this manner, why does the male not perceive either the external or the internal [of the other]? To that he says: "Mingled," etc. When both have performed the action, they are dependent upon its fruit.
Even though ignorance is common to both, the designation "of the person" (puṃsaḥ) is used because of its predominance. || 1313–1314 ||
Just as before, through embracing, one clearly perceives the interior and exterior of the Veda.
But when embraced [by the Supreme], he knows neither what is external nor what is internal.
1 kha. 'tū | strīṃ' | 2 kha. ga. 'topahārasi | 3 kha. 'te || 9311 || Therein, in the *Dṛauṃ* [vol 3, page 481]:
1614 The *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya [Fourth Chapter—]
Since pleasure arises dependent upon a relationship, how can it be determined that this [pleasure] is ignorance? Why might it not be inherent?
To this, he says: "Because of embracing" (pariṣvaṅgāt). || 1315 ||
Thus, its singular self-nature is veiled by darkness, and it enters into the effects arising from ignorance.
He perceives the entire world as outside the Veda and himself as one enveloped in darkness.

He states the application of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "Darkness" (*tamaḥ*), meaning: for one who is not embraced [by the Self], there is the cognition of specific objects, just as there is the cognition of external and internal objects for one whose ignorance and its products have not ceased. || 1316 ||
Existing in the form of cause and effect, this person (puruṣa) is embraced by the Prājña Self through that very Self, which is of a single nature opposed to it. || 1317 ||

By stating that for one who is embraced [by the Supreme], there is no knowledge of particulars because of the manifestation of unmanifest ignorance and its products, the author applies the passage beginning with "evam eva" (just so). Regarding the word "kārya" (effect): the meaning is that the person, while possessing adjuncts (*sopādhika*), having attained unity with the Self of Brahman which is devoid of adjuncts (*nirupādhika*) in deep sleep, does not perceive particularity due to unmanifest ignorance and its products. || 1317 ||
When this [world] has ceased within the inner self at the end of the body, that [state] is bliss.
When the activity of one's own waking state has ceased through yoga with the self that is free from darkness (vitamaska), [one attains the state of deep sleep].
How is identity with Brahman, which is free from all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), established during deep sleep? To this, he says: "Tamasvinī" (the dark one).

When the karma that produces the experiences of waking and dreaming has been exhausted, that inner self (*pratyagātman*) which was characterized by darkness—upon the destruction of the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding objects ranging from the intellect (*buddhi*) to the body—attains union with the Self in the form of Brahman, which is free from darkness. When that state exists, [one] knows nothing; for it is said: "When [that] exists..."
The meaning is that this is based on such scriptural passages as, "Having attained [it], they do not know," and so forth. || 1318 ||
Ignorance follows its own effect, but it does not follow itself, because it is not an effect.
And the effect resides in its own cause, but not in itself, because it is not its own cause.

If it is argued that the state of being free from darkness for the wise one is unestablished because of the Śruti statement, "The wise one is bound by the cause," he says "ignorance" (avidyā) [to refute this]. He states the reason why ignorance does not follow the Self with the words "because it is not an effect" (akāryataḥ).

Anticipating the objection that ignorance, while following its effects, follows the Self as well through those effects—since the intellect and other faculties which are its effects reside in the Self—he says:

Regarding the phrase "it is an effect": he states the reason why the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth do not follow after the Self (*ātman*). He says, "because it is not the cause. The collective meaning is that the connection exists only between ignorance (*ajñāna*) and its product (*tajja*), and not with the Self. || 1319 ||
Even the appearance of a self manifests within cognition and in its effects.
This [consciousness] also transcends that which consists of the nature of cause and effect. || 1320 ||
With the intention that the Self might also have a connection with ignorance and its effects through the appearance [of those effects], you state: "The Self" (verse 1320).
Because it conforms to the immutable self, and because its nature consists of that alone.
Therefore, there is neither effect nor cause; he does not look even with a sidelong glance.
1 ka. na. 'vaddhvastājñā | [vol 3, page 482] 3 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1615

He states the reason for the lack of connection between the Self—existing as the cause in the form of the appearance of the cause, and existing as the effect in the form of the appearance of the effect—and the state of deep sleep, with the words "kūṭastha" (the immutable). Fearing that there might be a difference [between the Self and the intellect] based on its conformity to that [intellect], like the face's conformity to a mirror, he says "tāvanmātra" (only that much). That very conformity to it is what constitutes being "only that much"; the face's conformity to the mirror is [merely its reflection therein].

The meaning is that, because it is metaphorically so designated due to its connection with something else, even when one is in deep sleep, the Self does not possess that [state]. He states the point established by the lack of such connection: "No" (na). || 1321 ||
The conscious self is embraced by the supreme self, which is indeed the wise one.
When the causes of differentiation are destroyed, the cognition of difference ceases.

He concludes the statement regarding the identity with Brahman for the person in deep sleep, who is free from darkness, by saying "the cognizing self" (*vijñānātman*). He summarizes the probandum based on the reason of unity by saying "due to difference" (*bhedāt*). The meaning is that because its cause—manifest ignorance—is destroyed during sleep, the perception of distinctions is likewise destroyed therein. || 1322 ||
Since this is so, our scripture therefore declares: "It is not external."
Likewise, by one who has settled solely upon the unity of the Self, [the Vedas] are outside the Vedānta.

He brings forward a scriptural statement regarding the point already stated, beginning with "yasmāt" (because). He clarifies the meaning of "yasmād evam" (because it is so) with the words "aikātmya" (identity).
He states the meaning of the Śruti with the word "na" (not). || 1323 ||
In this manner, there is such a non-distinction between action and its factors, whether they be real or unreal.
The nature of the Self is at all times devoid of all distinctions whatsoever.

Fearing that the Self might be held to possess specific attributes because a cognition of distinction arises in other states—just as one who is asleep does not perceive distinctions—he says "action" (kriyā).
The cause of that [cognition] is manifested ignorance. This explains the phrase "of such a kind" (īdṛśam), namely, that it has been refuted. || 1324 ||
This is neither in consideration of one's own conduct, nor of external objects.
We do not perceive any entity whatsoever as possessing action and its factors, because it is beyond measurement.

One might raise the objection: "Does the distinction between activity and so forth appear during the waking state and others, or not? If it does appear, then because of its absence in deep sleep there would be a state of having distinctions; if it does not appear, that would contradict experience. Anticipating this, he says: "Not the Self. The nature of the Self is unattached, non-dual, immutable, and a single mass of consciousness. In relation to that, duality does not appear; nor does it appear in relation to the insentience and unreality of the non-Self. Therefore, since there is no cognition of duality, [the Self remains without distinctions].
The intended meaning is that the cognition of that [object] is desired. || 1325 ||
Everything, being independent of anything else, is perceived as nothing but one's own self.
Because of its single nature, not even an atom of a separate form is perceived as a real entity.
This demonstrates that duality is not authoritative when considered in light of the nature of the Self. Regarding the verse beginning with "all":

when everything is seen as nothing but the Self, such that it is independent of all else, then nothing whatsoever would be perceived as distinct from that single Self. Therefore, the meaning is that dualistic cognition is not authoritative because it does not conform to the nature of the Self. || 1326 ||

But it has been established that whatever form is relative is false.
That which does not exist by its own nature or as a real entity—how could it exist in dependence upon another? (1327)

He establishes that even with respect to the mode of non-self (anātma-vṛtti), that cognition is invalid. Regarding the phrase "but it is relative," he recalls the manner previously stated. Regarding the word "inherently" (svataḥ), the meaning is that the falsity of something adventitious—like silver and so forth—is necessarily required.
Therefore, that which is independent of everything else is established by its own majesty alone.

That alone would be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the unique essence and specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the entity. [Verse 1328] He explains what remains once duality is shown to be false, starting with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The reason for its independence from everything else is given by the phrase "by its own majesty" (*svamahimnā*).
The term "entity" (*vastu*) is a qualification intended to exclude the void (*śūnya*). He rejects the notion of it being a mere bystander by using the term "unique essence" (*aikātmya*). [1328]
Since this is so, our Śruti has therefore declared: "That indeed belongs to him."
The nature of the reality of the self has been described as being devoid of desire, ignorance, and the like.
Since the absence of specific cognition in deep sleep is established by the statement regarding women, he concludes that what is stated in the *Aticchanda* passage is logical:
Therefore, this [state] cannot be a property of death, just as desire, action, and so forth are not.
For consciousness is indeed the inner self, according to the reason already stated. || 1330 ||

Anticipating the objection that if there is an absence of specific cognition during deep sleep, then consciousness (caitanya) too would not exist because it is no different from [specific] cognition, he says: "Kāma... etc. Since consciousness is indeed the Self on account of the aforementioned reason of self-luminosity, it is therefore not adventitious as a property of ignorance (ajñāna), like desire and so forth; for what reason, then, would it not exist in deep sleep? This is the meaning. || 1330 ||
Because it is the Self, there is no division here characterized by the knower, the knowledge, and so forth.
Even one whose darkness has not been dispelled does not perceive differentiation within the Self. || 1331 ||

Fearing that if consciousness were identical with the Self, it would require a distinction of causal factors—just like the cognition of a jar or other objects—and thus the non-duality [of the Self] would be lost, he says:

"Because it is the Self. The point is that being occasional is the limiting condition (*upādhi*). Regarding the absence of distinctions such as knower and so forth within the Self, which is consciousness, he states an argument *a fortiori*: "Not discarded... The contradiction between the object and the agent must be established as the reason. [The word] "destroyed" (*dhvastā*)...
The remainder [of the thought] is: what need is there to say that cognition does not perceive itself? || 1331 ||
For it is only through the vision of the path of ignorance that one perceives the reality which is the effect of ignorance.
Duality appears in the void, like the appearance of circles of blue and other colors.

He states the resolution of the cognition of distinctions such as "knowership" and so forth with the words "Ignorance" (avidyā). The word "for" (hi) is used here to bring the scriptural passage beginning with "For where... into conformity with this context. "Its effect" refers to the object consisting of the intellect (buddhi) and so forth; that is to say, it is grounded in that [ignorance]. "Knowership" and so forth constitute duality. || 1332 ||
But that form which is independent of anything else for its establishment is indeed non-dual knowledge.
"That indeed is his this" is now described by means of that scriptural statement.

Having dispelled the doubt that the form described in the *Aticchanda* passage is adventitious consciousness by means of the passage concerning the woman, [the author] takes up the passage beginning with "whose desires are fulfilled" (*āptakāma*) in order to further elucidate the very meaning of the *Aticchanda* passage: "But [he] is free from ignorance" (*niravidyam tu*). || 1333 ||
Since this entire world is of one essence, such is the nature of the Self.
Therefore, it is manifested like a radish placed in the hand.

Anticipating the objection as to why the meaning of the statement regarding "excessive desire" (*aticchanda*) is clarified by the statement regarding "one whose desires are fulfilled" (*āptakāma*), he says:

"All... Since this nature of the Self is the non-metaphorical essential form of the entire imagined duality of cause and effect, and because it consists of the supreme human goal by virtue of being supreme bliss, it is therefore established by the scripture concerning one whose desires are fulfilled as being capable of direct perception.
This is the meaning. "Of such a kind" is a statement regarding the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). || 1334 ||
That form of the self which arises from ignorance and pertains to the plane of saṃsāra.
Having taken all that into account, where desire has not been fulfilled, this is stated here.
All [these states], beginning with the fulfillment of desires, depend upon the nature of the object and the mental modification.
Because the reality whose sole essence is bliss is devoid of anything to be attained and so forth. || 1336 ||
1.4 He introduces the qualifiers of the statement regarding one's own desire with the words "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*). Its form consists of cause and effect.

The meaning is that it has the characteristics of the *Kāmavyākṛta-sūtra* and others. The locative case in *śruti* expresses the sense of "in" (the locus). He states their purport with the words "vastu" (the reality):

the meaning is that because the reality, which is of the nature of pure bliss, is devoid of all difference in view of its actual essential nature, it is appropriate that it possesses such qualities as having all desires fulfilled (*āptakāmatva*).
The human goal is the meaning of the word "kāma," for no other object is desired.
Having attained all goals of human endeavor, he is free from desire for any means of achievement.

He states the meaning of the word *kāma* along with its reason: "the human goal" (*pumartha*). Fearing that if the word *kāma* has the stated meaning, then by the etymology *saḥ + anena + āpta* ("he who has obtained this"), it would belong to someone else [rather than the Self], he says: "attained" (*āpta*). The meaning is: because the Self is eternally attained by virtue of being the Self, and because it is not something to be desired as a human goal, it is independent of everything; thus, being both "attained" (*āpta*) and "desire" (*kāma*), it is called "one whose desires are attained" (*āptakāma*). || 1337 ||
Furthermore, that which has been stated elsewhere by means of terms such as "Satyakāma" and so forth;
In accordance with this statement, that too should be clearly explained. || 1338 ||

Anticipating the objection that—since in passages such as "whose desire is truth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.3) and "whose resolve is truth," the word *kāma* is heard in connection with the Self (*ātman*), the term does not have the meaning previously stated—he says: "Truth" (*satya*). Here, first of all, the meaning of the word *kāma* is the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpasukha*) from which all suffering has been wiped away, because of the qualifying attributes such as "desiring the Self" (*ātmakāma*). And therefore, in accordance with this, even what is stated in the Chāndogya must be interpreted accordingly.

The meaning is that because the two sentences have a single subject matter (*paraviṣayatva*), it is appropriate here for the word *kāma* to have the meaning already stated. He provides the reason: "It is clear," [meaning] that an explanation of one sentence in accordance with the other is proper, because a single sentence is evident when there is a single subject matter. || 1338 ||

[Volume 3, Page 485] 1618 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Chapter]
Having completely relinquished the mere notion of a self, for truth does not come from anything else.
In that very place it is determined, according to the scripture which states, "where there is nothing else. || 1339 ||

He states another reason for the fact that the word *kāma* in the passage concerning Satyakāma denotes the aforementioned bliss: "the mere Self" (*ātmamātram*). Therefore, the remainder [of the argument] is that the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is unsurpassed bliss, is what is to be known through the term "Satyakāma. Anticipating the question of how that very point is established, he says: "in that very [passage]," referring to the *Bhūman* section. Specifically, in the *Chāndogya* scripture itself, where one sees nothing else...

The meaning is that by the scriptural passage beginning with "Not this, not this" (neti neti), which prohibits [the perception of] seeing and so forth while describing the characteristic of the Infinite (bhūman), it is determined that the inner self, the Infinite, possesses both reality and bliss. || 1339 ||
For an object of desire is experienced as pleasure when it is accomplished through external means.
Since consciousness itself is bliss, therefore this [world] has its desires fulfilled.

Having uprooted the doubt regarding contradiction with other scriptural passages (*śruti*), and concluding the state of having all desires fulfilled (*āptakāmatva*), [the author] first states what is well-known in the world, beginning with the word "sukha" (bliss).

The meaning is that the direct realization of bliss—the object of desire for which external means such as the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) and so forth are the instruments—is well-established. Nevertheless, he asks what follows from this regarding the Self, and answers: "It is consciousness alone. This is based on the scriptural text: "Consciousness is bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam*).
Since there is no happiness or consciousness of it apart from the Self, its nature is that of a *karmadhāraya* compound, meaning "one whose desires are attained" (*āptakāma*). || 1340 ||
Through the distinction of those who desire objects of desire, this inner self possesses the state of having all desires fulfilled.
Or is it being described here as being without differentiation, like Hiraṇyagarbha? || 1341 ||
Taking up the phrase *ātmakāma* preceded by the desire [for it], he explains it: "kāma" means desire; "iha" refers to what was stated in the Śruti.
Desires are nothing but the self; they do not exist apart from the distinctions within the nature of the self.
"All this is indeed the Self," because nothing remains except the inward-facing Pure Consciousness alone.

He states the reason for the claim that desires do not exist through the distinction of the Self in the verse beginning with "ātma" (the Self). The meaning is this: the Self does not possess the state of having all desires fulfilled like Hiraṇyagarbha, because there are scriptural texts stating that everything is merely the Self due to the abandonment of succession and so forth; therefore, for that very non-dual Self, there is the absence of desire. || 1342 ||
And the subsequent statement is intended to eliminate the doubt regarding whether [the cause] is taken collectively or individually.
Because it is "undesired," its form—both collective and individual—is utterly destroyed. (1343)

He states the meaning of the term *akāmam* (without desire) with the words "samasta... etc. The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction with the position that will be stated later. He states the fruit of the qualification with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). The sense is as follows: the nature of the Self is devoid of all distinctions such as desire and the like; yet, even when that [Self] exists during sleep and so forth, those [distinctions] are absent. Furthermore, in the absence of the individual [parts], there can be no possibility of their collective totality which depends upon them. Therefore, because it is without desire (*akāmatvāt*), it is of a single flavor (*ekarasa*). || 1343 ||
These [objections] have already been refuted by the very statement that [the Self] has its desires fulfilled and is free from desire.
"Though it has been stated that all desires are undesirable, it is nevertheless stated again. (1344)

He anticipates the objection of redundancy with the word "āpta" (the authoritative one). The ellipsis is: "that [statement] is useless because of its tautology. Nor should it be said that this is intended to eliminate the doubt regarding whether [the terms] are used collectively or individually; for the meaning is that this is already established by the very words "one whose desires are fulfilled" (*āptakāma*) and so forth. || 1344 ||

[Brāhmaṇa] Some ignorant people explain that desires have the Self as their locus. This is accompanied by the commentary known as *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. [Page 486, Volume 3] 1619. Therefore, for the purpose of negating that [notion], there is the further statement: "without desire" (akāma). || 1345 ||

Having accepted the charge of redundancy, he states its meaningfulness with the words "The Self" (ātma). Anticipating the objection—namely, that since the distinction between the desire and the desirer has already been refuted, how can it be possible to suspect that the Self is the locus of desire—he says "the ignorant" (abudhāḥ). He concludes by stating the result: the qualification is purposeful for the sake of removing the misconception of those of dull intellect. || 1345 ||
Sorrow has desire and so forth as its cause; it has ignorance regarding desire and so forth as its cause.
Due to the absence of that [duality], the state of oneness is then described as the end of sorrow. || 1346 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "the interval of sorrow" as follows: "due to desire, etc. This means that in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because of the absence of those [desires], there is an absence of manifest ignorance (*vyaktājñāna*). || 1346 ||
Or perhaps an object associated with sorrow is expressed by the word "sorrow."
Because the word "śoka" functions as a quality (guṇa), the suffix matup must be elided. || 1347 ||

Anticipating the objection, "How can there be 'freedom from sorrow' (aśokatva) [in the Self] when it is connected with that which is its substrate?", he restates this by means of the word *atha* and, while stating another point, explains the meaning of the term *śoka*. He says, "Or rather... (*yadi vā*). Regarding the statement that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is denoted by the word *śoka*, he states the reason: "Because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*). This means, in effect, "because it denotes that [quality]. To the question, "Why then is it not said to be 'possessing sorrow' (*śokavat*)?", he replies: "Because of the suffix *matup*. (*matupaḥ*) [which implies possession].
The word "laptatā" (the state of being elided) is a Vedic usage; this is the remainder [of the explanation]. || 1347 ||
For this is of a different category from those things that serve as the basis for sorrow.
Because it does not have the nature of cause and effect, it is therefore considered to be a separate verse. || 1348 ||
Nevertheless, he states what that "otherness from sorrow" is: "it is the object of sorrow," and so forth.

The meaning is that the nature of the Self, because it is distinct from causes and effects and is therefore an object other than the intellect and other faculties which are subject to sorrow, has been realized by authoritative persons as being "other than sorrow. || 1348 ||
Or rather, the inner self (pratyagātman) is said to be the end of sorrow, being situated within sorrow.
Furthermore, how could the self, being the very opposite of the cause of sorrow, itself become possessed of sorrow? (1349)

Anticipating the objection that this might imply duality (*dvaita*), he states another meaning with the words "of grief" (*śokasya*). To the question, "In that case, how can it be free from grief? For the Self is not devoid of that [grief] when it is present," he replies with "of grief" (*śoka-*) and so on. The particle *api* serves to include grief. The sense is that just as a snake has no real existence apart from the rope, its possession of that [rope] does not exist in reality. || 1349 ||
Or rather, it is called "the interior of the Aśoka" based on the reliance upon another scriptural passage.
One Ashoka tree [is called] "another Ashoka" or "the interval between Ashoka trees. || 1350 ||
This introduces the Mādhyandina recension reading *aśokāntaram*. Regarding the word *aśoka*, he explains it as *aśokāt* (from the absence of sorrow). || 1350 ||
Unworthy of sorrow and devoid of grief, he is called by the word "Aśoka."
Or rather, it removes sorrow because its sole intrinsic nature is bliss.
Therefore, this state of sorrow would be like coolness in the midst of fire. || 1351 ||
[Vol. 3, page 487] 1620 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:
He states the meaning of the word "aśoka" (free from sorrow). Regarding the term "śoka": the Lord, distinguished by *māyā*, is the controller of all and is incapable of sorrow.

The meaning is that *tvādaśokaḥ* refers to the pure consciousness-element (*kevala-cid-dhātu*) which, because it is devoid of the sorrow consisting of ignorance and its products, is a different entity from sorrow; thus, it is "other than sorrow" (*aśokāntaram*). As for the reading in the Kāṇva recension, which says "other than sorrow" (*śokāntaram*) because sorrow is the inner self (*pratyak*), one might raise the objection that even if the inner self does not possess the nature of that [sorrow], it could still be identified with it. Anticipating this, he states another interpretation with the words "or else" (*yadvā*). In the phrase "it veils the sorrow that is the nature of the Self" (*ātmarūpaṃ śokaṃ tirayati*), [the following is meant].
The reason [is given]. "Ānanda" [is the subject]. "Coldness" is the illustration for its capacity to negate that [heat]. He concludes the application to the case at hand with "Therefore. || 1351 ||
Alternatively, that darkness which gives rise to sorrow and the like would itself be the end of sorrow.
Its hub would be a hole; this is a phonetic modification according to Vedic usage. || 1352 ||
Anticipating the objection that, even though it is a cause of sorrow, the Self does not entirely disregard its state of happiness when joined with it, he states another point:
"Of sorrow, etc. [Verse 1312]. If that were so, one might expect the form "śokāntāram"; he says "no," explaining that it is Vedic (chāndasī). || 1312 ||
Ignorance, desire, and action [are overcome] through the nature of non-attachment.
This self transcends [the world] in accordance with the nature of reality. || 1353 ||

Anticipating the objection that the self cannot be devoid of the cause of sorrow because of the perception of its being possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, he says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). To resolve the contradiction with such perception, he clarifies the meaning of the second quarter [of the verse]: "The reality" (*vastu*). || 1353 ||
Since a thing is enlightened by itself, it is therefore pure by itself and non-dual.
Therefore, it is established that [the Self] is liberated by its very nature, through the abandonment of ignorance and its products. || 1354 ||
Demonstrating the actual state of things, he concludes the meaning of the statement regarding one whose desires are fulfilled: "By itself," etc. (1354).
Since this entity is thus characterized by excessive desire and so forth.
Therefore, this [knowledge] has completely transcended all connection with darkness. || 1355 ||
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "atra" [here] as follows: "yataḥ" (because). || 1359 ||
From the connection between the producer and the cause, and from the union of the effect and the cause.
Because he has transcended the causes that produce [a son], even a father is therefore not a father in this context.

Explaining the passage word by word, he states here the meaning of the phrase "the father becomes a non-father": "By the son... and so forth. The meaning is as follows: because of the relationship with the son's causes—such as *dharma* and the like—the father and son are accepted as being in a cause-and-effect relationship; however, since that relationship ceases during deep sleep (*suṣupti*) due to the absence of such a connection, the causal relationship based upon it is also excluded.
Thus, in states such as waking (*jāgara*), the father is a father, but in deep sleep he becomes a non-father; this applies equally to the son as well.
For agency has ignorance alone as its cause, not reality.
When there is agency, actions belong to the self as the agent, and not otherwise.

He states the absence of agency and so forth in order to show that the Self lacks connection with merit (*dharma*) and the like during deep sleep. [He says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). Manifest ignorance is the cause of agency; it does not exist inherently [in the Self], because that would entail the impossibility of liberation (*mokṣa*). Furthermore, such ignorance does not exist in deep sleep, for it is destroyed then; therefore, [agency] does not belong to the Self at that time.
