3, page 488] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1621.

The meaning is "by way of being an agent. If it is argued that there would still be a connection with action even in the absence of that [agency], he says "no," [responding] with "in the state of non-agency. The word should be split as *akartuḥ*. The sense is that in the opposite case, however, there would be no liberation. || 1317 ||
Therefore, when ignorance does not exist, there can be no agency or object for the Self.
Therefore, no relationship such as that of father and son exists here for one who has entered the state of deep sleep.

He states the result when manifest ignorance (*avidyā*) is absent in deep sleep: "In ignorance... The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that agency is unreal and that there is an absence of action for one who is not an agent. He states the result regarding the non-connection with action: "The father... (1358).
Since this [self] is inherently unattached, it is therefore not [bound] to anything by its own nature.
Therefore, its connection [to the self] exists in all states; this is the connection resulting from delusion.
Fearing that because of the qualification "as in deep sleep" there might be no relationship such as father and son and so forth even in that state, he says: "This [Self] is unattached.
He explains the course of the notion of relationship with the words: "The relationship... The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is the impossibility of a real relationship.
The connection with purely virtuous karma is not at all prevented for him.
For even by means of a despicable action, yoga is prohibited.

Here, he states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "a thief" (stena) and so forth: "The auspicious," etc. The word "this" (asya) refers to the Self in deep sleep (sauṣuptātman). || 1360 ||
In this context, the word "thief" refers to one who has committed a great offense.
And because of his association with a killer of an embryo, the son of a Brāhmaṇī woman is a Caṇḍāla. || 1361 ||
One born by a Śūdra [man] is to be known as characterized by the reverse order (prātilomya).
And here, the slayer of a most excellent Brahmin is designated as a "bhrūṇahan" (feticide).

He explains the words beginning with "thief" (*stena*) and so forth by means of the passage starting with "vipra" and so forth. Anticipating the objection as to how the word "thief" can serve as a qualifier when it denotes any thief in general, he says "bhrūṇahan" (feticide). He further states that the term "Caṇḍāla" serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other *pratiloma* castes not explicitly mentioned, saying "prātilomya. As it has been said:
“The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Cāṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
these three base-born sons are born from a Śūdra woman in the reverse order.”
Another also says:
"From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
but from a Śūdra, a Cāṇḍāla is born, who is excluded from all religious duties."

[Objection: But since the thief (*stena*) is mentioned alongside the killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*), why is it restricted to "one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa"? To this he replies: "The most excellent... (1361–1362).
He who is born of a Kṣatriya woman by a Śūdra alone is called an Ugra.
A *paulkasa* should be known as a *pulkasa*; the suffix is used in its own primary sense. || 1363 ||
[Vol.
3, page 489] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
He explains the term *paulkasa*: "one who has arisen," and not...

"One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother becomes a Pulkasa by birth"—thus there is a contradiction. For a Niṣāda is indeed one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother. As it has been said:
"From a Brāhmaṇa, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born of a Kṣatriya woman; [from the same,] a Vaiśya woman [bears an Ambaṣṭha]; [and so forth].
"The Ambaṣṭha, Śūdra, Niṣāda, and Pāraśava are born [from such unions].

Thus, the sense is that since it is stated that a Niṣāda born from a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman is by birth a Śūdra, one born from him on a Kṣatriya woman is a Pukkaśa; therefore, a Paulkasa is one related to a Pukkaśa, but not a Pukkaśa himself.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "For its own sake. (1363)
Even by those karmas that bring about connection with an inferior body.
Unconnected [to objects], abiding in deep sleep, he is not subject to the causes of karma. || 1364 ||
He summarizes the purport of the statements regarding thieves and so forth with the words "nikṛṣṭa" (inferior), etc. The cause of karma is manifested ignorance and the like. || 1364 ||
In the same way, there is no connection with the duties designated by the names of the stages of life (āśramas).
The wandering mendicant is to be known as a *tāpasa* because of his proximity to ascetic toil. || 1365 ||

He states the intended meaning of the words "ascetic" (*śramaṇa*) and so forth with the word "thus" (*tathā*). This means: by means of karmas which are the cause for connection with an auspicious or inauspicious body.

Anticipating the suspicion that the word *śramaṇa* has a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) referring specifically to a Jaina mendicant (*kṣapaṇaka*), he says: "the wandering mendicant" (*parivrāj*). || 1361 ||
Of all actions whatsoever, including those based on caste, stage of life, and so forth.
It should be understood that the term "wandering mendicant" (parivrāj) serves as an illustration that includes the ascetic (tāpasa) as well. || 1366 ||

Because only two [states] are mentioned, one might suspect that even though the state of deep sleep (sauṣupta) is not connected with those actions, it might still be connected with the duties of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama). Anticipating this, he says:
"Caste," etc. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), age, condition, and so forth are included. || 1366 ||
Thus, these and other endless relations are the causes of delusion.
They cannot be fully enumerated by a person even in tens of millions of eons.

Anticipating the objection that even in the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), although there is an absence of the connection [to the waking state] mentioned in the scriptures, other connections will nonetheless exist because their varieties are infinite, he says: "In this way. The sense is that all of those [connections] cease in the person who is in deep sleep, because the manifest ignorance (*vidyā*) which is their cause is absent. He clarifies the point regarding their infinity with the words: "by the man" (verse 1367).
For merit and demerit are indeed the cause of every connection here in this world.
The wise one is not followed by those two, because of the non-connection with the cause of karma. || 1368 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "unattached" (*ananvāgatam*) by saying "by merit," etc. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the Self (*ātman*). The sense of the particle "hi" is that this has also been stated in the fifth [chapter]. He states the reason why a person is untouched by merit and demerit during deep sleep (*svāpa*) by saying "karma," etc.; that is to say, the agent arising from ignorance is the cause [of such contact], and that [agent] does not persist during deep sleep. || 1368 ||
1. *Putaḥ* || 1364 || 2. Kha: ‘...unable to explain’ | [Vol.
3, page 490] 3. Brāhmaṇam: Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1623.
Having entered into the supreme form, which has karma and ignorance as its cause.
In deep sleep, he transcends all relations such as those with father, mother, and others.

He states the reason for this: "The Supreme. Since Brahman—which is not bound by karma and the like—is what one attains during deep sleep, according to the Vedic scripture, "Then, my dear, he has become united with Being," therefore he says that the person, having entered into That, becomes free from connection with father and so forth: "Father...
How, moreover, can he live while remaining within this very body?
He is said to have transcended all attachments. || 1370 ||

The sentence beginning with "not having come" (*ananvāgata*), which has already been explained, is now introduced as a doubt in order to explain it by way of a response. [The text] says: "He lives indeed.
Then, as a reply to this, he introduces the following statement: "It is said. || 1370 ||
For, in deep sleep, this form of the Self is by its very nature unaccompanied.
If it is thought that even that [result] arises from both merit and demerit, how could that be? (1371)
He explains: "Since... The ellipsis is "therefore, [he is] beyond all attachment. He raises the objection that even the state of being unconnected with action is unestablished: "Why? || 1271 ||
Because it transcends the heart, it does not overstep those dharmas.
Therefore, the desires that impel action are well-established as previously described.

He takes up the passage beginning with "torṇo hi" as a subsequent reply. Regarding "hṛdaya": this means that, as previously stated, because there is no connection to karma during deep sleep, there is a total absence of all such connections. || 1372 ||
For grief, desire, and so forth are indeed properties of the heart alone.
"For one whose intellect has crossed over possesses those qualities; therefore, he transcends them.

(1373) Regarding the objection that it is incorrect to say "he transcends the sorrows of the heart" because desires and other such states denoted by the word *śoka* are attributes of the Self (*ātman-dharma*), some [commentators] respond with the words "of the heart" (*hṛdayasya*). [They argue that] the relationship in the phrase "sorrows of the heart" implies they are "resting in the heart," meaning they are supported by the heart (*hṛdayāśrita*).
Because of the scriptural teaching of identity in the passage, "All this is indeed his mind," these [qualities] do not belong to the Self, but rather are attributes of the mind;

therefore, the meaning is that while sleeping, by transcending that [mind], one transcends its attributes such as desire and so forth. The sense of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that when there is an absence of connection with the substratum (the mind), there is all the more an absence of connection with its attributes. || 1373 ||
The connection with merit and demerit occurs through association with the heart within a dream.
But here, even that [ignorance] ceases in the wise one through the mere residue of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 1374 ||
To the question, "Why should there not be an application of karma even during deep sleep, when there is no connection with desire and so forth, as in a dream? he says:
"Leaving aside the state of being an instrument here, there is only pure knowledge. (1374)
In a dream, one remains in the form of the mind, with a body composed of latent impressions (vāsanā).

Since the mind exists even in a dream, how can it be said that there is only latent impressions (vāsanā) there? To this, he states [the answer] regarding the connection with action: "The state of being an instrument" (karaṇatvam).
Therefore, it is only that which consists of latent impressions (vāsanāmaya) that experiences the fruit of action in a dream.
For indeed, there is no connection for the dreamer with anyone else within the dream.

If the mind does not remain in its own nature during sleep, how can there be experience therein? To this he says: "Vāsanā. The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is that because the mind, whose form is vāsanā, remains as nothing other than that—meaning it consists of or is dominated by vāsanā. Why should there not be gross experience in sleep just as in the waking state? To this he says: "Not indeed" (na hi). || 1376 ||
It abides by way of its own manifestation alone throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
It appears to sustain ignorance, desire, karma, and so forth, but not by its own nature.

Although in reality [the Self] is not joined with anything other than itself during dream and deep sleep, he states "svābhāsa" (self-manifesting) out of the suspicion that it might exist [as such] during the waking state.

The meaning is: the Self is always joined with ignorance and so forth only through the medium of the reflection of consciousness residing in the intellect and other faculties, and not by itself, because of the scriptural teaching of its non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are included. || 1377 ||
Consciousness itself would likewise not belong to the self, just like desire and action.
When he has been thus challenged: "The wise one [knows] phenomena through their subsequent nature," [1378]
And a refutation has been shown by means of the analogy of women and men.
Because of the absence of a cause for differentiation, it is not perceived during the waking state. || 1379 ||

He recounts the preceding context for the purpose of connecting the passage beginning with "That which indeed does not see" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23]: "Consciousness," etc. The meaning of the reason is that just as desire and other attributes are absent during deep sleep due to the absence of their causes, so too consciousness cannot exist [then] for the same reason. He restates the very solution already mentioned.

Regarding the term "division" (*vibhāga*): the external division consists of objects such as jars, and the internal division consists of states such as pleasure; the cause of this [division] is ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is manifest.
The meaning is that [consciousness] is free from that [ignorance]. The word "consciousness" (*caitanya*) is to be supplied as the subject. || 1378 || 1379 ||
It has attained a state of indivisible unity, and is no longer subject to desire and action as it was before.
And the self-luminosity of the Self has been established through diligent effort. || 1380 ||

He states another reason: "avibhāga" (non-distinction), meaning that it has become one with the non-dual Brahman. He says "na punar" (not, however) to show that non-existence is not the cause for its non-perception. To the question, "Why should that very [oneness] not be the cause for its being unseen there?", he replies: "And it has been established," referring to the fact that the self-luminosity of the Self is not merely figurative—as in the case of speech and other organs—because it cannot be illumined by anything else.
Because it illuminates everything, he says "not so" with the words "by effort. || 1380 ||
If this self is self-luminous, how [can it be affected] like desire, karma, and so forth?
Because consciousness would then be his very nature during deep sleep, he would [thereby] abandon it; therefore— || 1381 ||
This [quality] would not belong to his son, because that [quality] is not observed in him.
It is not a property of the self because it has perished; therefore, consciousness resides in that [body]. (1382)

1625. An objection is raised therein: "If [the text says] 'yadi' (if), [then it follows that] if the Self is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), it would not abandon its consciousness—just as desire and the like do not abandon their own nature."

Because of the impossibility of its abandonment, consciousness is not the inherent attribute of this [self]; for even while the self exists, it is absent during sleep. Even if it were adventitious—like conjunction and so forth—it would not be an attribute of the self by its own nature; and even if it were such an attribute, it would likewise perish upon falling asleep.
Therefore, the meaning is that the self is indeed insentient. || 1381 || 1382 ||
Moreover, that which is self-luminous by nature is even contradictory [to such a state].
It is stated here by the word *bhavati* that [the self] does not know the inward reality. || 1383 ||

Furthermore, he states that it is contradictory to say that the self-luminous [self] does not see, just as one might say "the sun is without light. He says "api" (also/even) and uses the word "iha" (here) to refer to the state of deep sleep. || 1383 ||
Likewise, due to identity, non-perception is not conclusive regarding cognition.
For it is observed here that even in the absence [of an object], there is no consciousness of consciousness itself.

He raises an objection regarding the meditative absorption (samādhi) described in the woman’s words, [beginning with] "Because of oneness" (*aikyāt*). He refutes this by stating that oneness with Brahman does not necessarily entail the non-perception of the existing consciousness;
thus he says, "Because of the inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntikatā*). The phrase "in that way" (*tathā*) means: if one accepts the non-perception [of consciousness] due to oneness.
He states the reason for this inconclusiveness: "Since," etc. [In the world, consciousness is not perceived] in stones and such things...
The meaning is that even in the absence of that [non-existence], the fact that non-apprehension is the cause of identity is subject to deviation (vyabhicārin). || 1384 ||
The subsequent section of the text is introduced for the purpose of refuting this [objection].
Having begun with "That which indeed is that," [the text proceeds] for the sake of purifying the inward reality.

"He takes up the answer" means: since that [Self] is self-luminous and not insentient (jaḍa), its purity is the purpose; thus, the objection must be resolved for that purpose, and for that same reason, the discourse beginning with "That which indeed... proceeds—this is the meaning. || 1385 ||
Likewise, another relationship is also stated here by some.
That which is called "the interior of the ashoka" is the true nature of the inner self.

Having stated the relationship as explained in the Bhāṣya, he raises the position set forth by Bhartṛprapañca with the words "tathā" (so it is). Here, the word "atra" (here) refers to the text under discussion.
He shows his own summary of that [author's] work as a supplement to it with the verse beginning "aśoka... (1386).
The Self remains in deep sleep as pure light alone.
But how, moreover, is this established—that there is a cessation of specific cognitions? (1387)
This reality, whose form is light, abides in the state of deep sleep.
The self-luminosity of the Self has already been stated by way of distinction [from other things]. (1388)

He explains the very nature [of the Self]: "Light. As it was said, "free from sorrow," so at this time He exists by His own Self as mere light. He raises an objection regarding the restatement of what has been said: "Why?
For it has indeed been stated that self-luminosity is established through contrast. He states the resolution as expressed in the Commentary: "It has been explained."
This means that because worldly transaction is observed even without [the existence of] the sun and so forth as distinct entities. ||1387||1388||
But has it not been stated that all this specific cognition of the self belongs to the living being? (1389)
204 [Vol. 3, page 493] 1626 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]
It would not exist by itself like consciousness, but would instead be partial toward ignorance.
This is not so, because this was previously perceived clearly by me.
Again, he raises an objection: "But has it not been said? You have stated that all specific cognition (*viśeṣajñāna*) is indeed nescience (*avidya*);

however, that [state] does not exist by itself like consciousness, for even the thought "I am all this" is nothing but specific cognition. And it is precisely this [absence of specific cognitions] that is called the self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*) of the Self and the absence of specific cognitions in deep sleep; therefore, it is established as a matter of fact that the Self is self-luminous therein.

The meaning is that there is no proof for the censure [of ignorance]. For it has been stated that the knowledge of its specific nature belongs exclusively to the side of avidyā. He refutes this with: "This is not so. (1389, 1390)
"Even though this [notion] 'I am indeed everything' possesses particularity,"
Consciousness is not like that either, for it belongs to the side of ignorance. || 1391 ||
It demonstrates exactly what has been shown: "All. Even the knowledge that "I am all," which is a specific cognition, does not fall on the side of ignorance;
such knowledge ceases in deep sleep, yet it is not merely that [knowledge] alone [that ceases]. Therefore, the self-luminous nature of the Self remains uncontradicted therein.
The meaning is that this is because it is established that such specific cognition is not ignorance. || 1391 ||
For it is held that the perception of diversity arises from fear born of ignorance.
Therefore, the counteragent to ignorance is the realization: "I alone am this. || 1392 ||

What is that knowledge which sides with ignorance? To this he says: "The perception of multiplicity," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "therefore, it ceases upon that deep sleep. For it has been stated that fear—which consists in the effect of perceiving multiplicity—is indeed ignorance. Anticipating the objection that the cognition "I alone am this" is equally partial toward ignorance, he says: "the opposite," etc. The cognition "I alone [am this]" is [the opposite] of ignorance.

It exists as an antidote; for it has been stated that knowledge (*vidyā*) is the antidote to the notion "I am all this. Therefore, since it is not born of ignorance (*avidyā*), its essential nature persists even during deep sleep—this is the meaning. || 1392 ||
This very [reality], when being churned, is characterized by the constant vision of oneness.
It becomes exceedingly purified, serene, and remains stable. || 1393 ||

Now, one might object: since this knowledge is a knowledge of distinctions, like the knowledge of a jar or similar objects, it arises from ignorance; therefore, it should not exist during deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

To this, [the author] says: "This very [knowledge]," etc. "Being meditated upon" (*madhyamānam*) means being discerned through the perception of difference. Regarding the word *bhavati* in the commentary—"this very perception of unity, while being meditated upon, becomes ever pure and serene"—[the author] explains its meaning as "it remains established" (*vyavatiṣṭhate*).

Thus, since it has been stated that even this specific knowledge does not fall on the side of ignorance because it is grounded in reality, the meaning is that it exists as one's own essential nature during deep sleep. || 1393 ||
At that time, there is no awakening to the Self because the perception of distinctions has not arisen.
The manifesting consciousness, shining brightly, abides as a specific nature. || 1394 ||

Anticipating the objection—"If the Self remains in deep sleep (suṣupti) as the self-luminous conscious essence (svaprakāśacidātman), how can the cognition 'I knew nothing' arise upon waking?"—he says: "viśeṣa... [etc.]. He further anticipates the doubt that, in that very same way, knowledge of one's own essential nature (svarūpajñāna) would also not exist at that time.
(Note: The footnotes provided in the source text indicate textual variants for the following terms: *meva sphuṭaṃ* [kha], *tvayaivoktaṃ* [gha], *vatvetaṃ* [ka, kha], and *tatsvarūpaṃ* [kha]).
"How should you sit? "As one who is intensely shining," he replied; for it has been said that one becomes intensely shining by means of one's own specific consciousness-as-self (*viśeṣavijñānātman*).

Thus: the non-arising of specific cognitions such as agency and so forth regarding the self during its state of sleep is precisely what is meant by "non-awakening" (*asaṃbodha*), because it has been stated that "non-awakening is the non-arising of specific cognition.
However, [the self] exists by means of a cognition of the form "I myself am this very thing"; such is the meaning of the whole passage. || 1394 ||
This very form residing in the state of deep sleep has been demonstrated previously. || 1395 ||
In this regard, the following doubt is raised: how can there be a lack of awakening regarding the Self within knowledge?
4.3 If there were existence, there would be no doubt, because of the determination [of the self] through the analogy of woman and man. || 1396 ||

Having refuted an incidental objection in the course of restating the argument, he concludes the restatement with the words "suṣupte" (in deep sleep). The meaning is that it has been stated that the Self remains in deep sleep by virtue of its self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣva*), which consists in the perception of unity. An objection is raised regarding the established self-luminosity of the Self with the word "tatra" (therein). The meaning is that since there is no ignorance when there is knowledge of one's own nature, it is therefore improper to claim that there is an absence of knowledge of one's own nature in deep sleep. [The text continues with] "strīvā-"...

He says "it might be" (*syāt*) because it has been determined that ignorance of even that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) is logical during sleep; thus, there is no room for doubt.

He states that the objection—"How can there be non-cognition when consciousness exists?"—is not to be raised, since it has already been answered by the illustration of the person embraced [by his wife].
Therefore, the meaning is that ignorance during sleep is indeed logical. || 1399 || 1396 ||
This is not so, because in that case, [the cognition arises] only when the causes of knowledge are present.
It has been demonstrated that [the universal] remains undivided among the particulars. || 1397 ||

He states the answer: "This is not so. In that regard, when a man and woman are joined together, even though the causes of cognition—the eyes and other senses—exist, and external and internal particulars are present, the person remains undivided, lacking the cognition of distinction because his mind is elsewhere; this is what was shown in the woman's statement.
Therefore, this objection does not apply there, for in that case, while the effects of specific cognitions are present, he remains undivided, and thus there is no such lack of awareness.
The meaning is: because of this statement. || 1397 ||
But here, moreover, it is not possible to discern the specific distinctions.
Because he abides here by means of his own undifferentiated consciousness. || 1398 ||

Then, raising the objection that even during deep sleep (*svāpa*), the causes of cognition are indeed present, yet there is no perception of distinctions because the mind is directed elsewhere, he says: "In this world" (*iha*). For in that state, distinctions are not capable of being known, because their causes are absent; otherwise, it would not be a state of sound sleep. Therefore, the meaning is that the Self remains there as mere consciousness of its own undivided nature. || 1398 ||
It is questioned how there could be non-awakening when knowledge exists.
If it is argued that it is merely darkness, it is not so, because the Self is self-luminous.
For this has been previously established here with great effort.
And because the established tenet is firmly situated through appropriate logical arguments. || 1400 ||

He states the consequence—that the aforementioned doubt remains as it was—in the words "lack of awakening" (*asaṃbodha*). Since it is accepted that the Self exists in deep sleep in the form of non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpaka-jñapti*), the absence of awakening is untenable; otherwise, the nature of the Self as consciousness would not be established, resulting in its being insentient (*jaḍa*). He concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the word "darkness" (*tamaḥ*). Regarding this, they say: "This form must be darkness itself, not light. He states the final position (*siddhānta*): "Not at all..."
1 1 1 No. || 1396 || 2 Ka. *nasāhityaṃ yu*; Kha. *narāhityaṃ yuṃ*. 3 Gha. *ṣāyaṃ*.
"Thus it is said. And it has been stated that the nature of being of the form of light (*jyotīrūpa*) has been demonstrated with great effort. The word 'here' (*iha*) is a statement of the Śruti."

The phrase "previously" refers to the commencement of the discussion on the Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, he states that the Self is not insentient (*jaḍa*). Regarding the words "of the established doctrine" (*siddhāntasya*): the self-luminosity of the Self is established here by the Vedic established doctrine in passages such as "This [Self] is its light. Since this is firmly established through uncontradicted reasonings—such as the argument that if the Self were insentient, it would not be the Self, just like a pot—the Self is not insentient. As it has been said: "And because the established doctrine is firmly established."
If it is argued that this [self] has perished like a lamp, [we reply: no.
It is not so from recognition, because of the object previously perceived. || 1401 ||

If the self were of the nature of light, then because it is not perceived during deep sleep, its destruction would follow—just like that of a lamp—since light is never dissociated from its own existence; and consequently, the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*) would result. Thus he raises this objection with the words "like a lamp. [The reply is:

Because recognition is observed upon waking regarding what was seen in the prior consciousness, if the previous seer had been destroyed during sleep and a different seer had arisen, [recognition would not occur].
He refutes the objection that there is no possibility of a momentary doctrine by stating, "Because of recognition" (pratyabhijñānataḥ). 1401.
For this reason, one who has arisen from deep sleep recognizes [the self] as before.
In all states, this self is eternal and never perishes.

He states another recognition regarding the non-destruction of the self during sleep: "Because... The meaning is that since there is the recognition by one who has awakened, "I am the same one who was asleep; I am awake," the self persists even through all three states; therefore, it does not perish during deep sleep.
Devoid of all sense-faculties, he is perfectly serene and undisturbed.
He who, while asleep, knows his own self is called the Ātman. || 1403 ||

He then states what that [self] is intended to be at that time: "By all [the powers]. When one who is asleep—with all the senses withdrawn—does not perceive dreams, which are various misapprehensions appearing in the forms of waking and dreaming, then, free from the agitation of gross and subtle [objects], he abides in Brahman by way of the channels and the pericardium. That which is asleep is said to be the Supreme Self; its absence [from the state of dream] occurs in the channels, according to the scriptural statement regarding them.
The meaning is "in such cases as 'tyādi' (and so forth). || 1403 ||
"I did not see it in my dream," says one who has awakened.
In waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, therefore, he alone is that Self.

Anticipating the objection that since recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is erroneous, how can the permanence of the self be established by it, [the author] considers that it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) because it is not sublated, and says "no" and so forth. Since one speaks thus while having arisen [from sleep], therefore the very same self that existed in each individual state is recognized across all three states; and since recognition is not sublated, it is not erroneous.
The interpretation: 1404.
From deep sleep one goes to the dream state, and from the dream state one goes to the waking state.
Thus it was stated even in ancient scripture; therefore, the Self does not perish. || 1405 ||
1 kha. ‘In a dream’ | [Vol.
3, page 496] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1629
In that very context, he shows the agreement with scripture (śruti): "The sound," etc.; the connection is "also by scripture. || 1401 ||
Therefore, the Self, abiding in its own nature as self-luminous, exists even in deep sleep.
By its very nature, it is untouched by the ignorance of the inner self and its effects.

He concludes the demonstration that the self is not destroyed even during sleep with the words "by itself" (*svayam*). Fearing the objection that because the term "deep sleep" (*suṣupta*) is used as a qualification, the self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) does not exist in other states, he says "the inner self" (*pratyak*). For it has been stated that [the self] exists by its own light alone. (1406)
As for that which is doubted: why does the Self not perceive [itself] while in the state of deep sleep (prājña)?
It is also of the nature of conscious self; listen now to that as well. || 1407 ||

Having restated the objection—"If the self has the nature [of consciousness] as described, why does it not know itself and others during deep sleep?"—the author adopts the passage beginning with "yadi" as the response: "yattu... (1407).
Desire, action, ignorance, and so forth, are not the inherent nature of the Self, just as they are not its consciousness.
Because of non-attachment and because of speech that lacks logical consistency, and because desire and the like are false. || 1408 ||

The connection with what is desired by others has been stated; therein, he will later refute the undesirable portion. Now, in accordance with the connection he himself has stated, he restates what was said in order to explain the words [of the verse], beginning with "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature). The meaning is that it is established through both scripture and reasoning that ignorance, together with its effects, is not the nature of the Self, whereas consciousness alone is so. || 1408 ||
Consciousness is the true nature of the self, which is immutable and not subject to desire.
Its connection with beginningless ignorance is considered to have a beginning through its effects. || 1409 ||

The phrase "like awakening" (bodhavat) illustrates a negative example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta). Regarding the term "consciousness" (caitanya): one might suspect that even this is not the nature of the Self because it possesses birth and so forth, like desire and the rest; therefore, he says "immutable" (kūṭastha). If ignorance (avidyā), like desire and the rest, were not the very nature of the Self, then its connection with the Self—just like the connection with desire and the rest—would also have a beginning. And if that [connection] had a beginning, then [ignorance] would be independent.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "beginningless" (*anādi*). Ignorance (*avidyā*) is beginningless; since no cause for it can be established, ignorance itself cannot be its own cause, because the relationship of cause and effect cannot exist in a single entity. Nor can there be another ignorance [as the cause], due to a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*). Nor can the Self (*ātman*) be the cause, because that which is free from ignorance cannot be a cause, and if that which possesses ignorance were the cause, then the beginninglessness of ignorance would be established; however, the distinction between such [ignorances] has been rejected due to a lack of evidence. Therefore, because it is beginningless, ignorance— [...is established. (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly.)
The meaning is that while their relationship is also beginningless, desire and the like, as well as their relationship, are not so. || 1409 ||
For this Self, which abides in ignorance and false cognition, where indeed [is its true nature]?
The connection with the instruction and so forth is what is stated here. || 1410 ||
It was stated that the passage beginning with "That which... is intended to establish that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is eternally liberated and immutable by way of restating what has been said;

now, he states another intended meaning [of the passage] with the words "Ignorance" (*ajñāna*). For one who exists under the sway of ignorance, thinking "I am ignorant," and who—mistaking the cessation of agency and other such attributes for false knowledge regarding the self—performs obligatory rites and so forth with the thought of dedicating them to the Lord, [his] non-...

In response to the inquiry as to what subject matter there could be for the connection with instruction—given that the seeker is one whose impurities have been destroyed, who desires liberation, and is dispassionate—the following is stated. [Vol.
3, page 497] (Note: The bracketed numbers refer to variant readings from different manuscript versions cited in the source text.)

The meaning is that the statement beginning with "That" (*yat*) and so forth is intended to declare that in deep sleep the reality of the Self, which is liberated from transmigratory existence, is established, and that the knowledge thereof leads to liberation. || 1410 ||
This self does not see here; it is self-luminous by its own nature.
Thus, that which is mutually contradictory does not incur fault due to the identity of the one Self. || 1411 ||
Desiring to explain three points,
he refutes the contradiction by restating it with the words "No," and so forth.

Since it is stated that through the two expressions "seeing" and "not seeing," the self of every person remains in the state of deep sleep as the nature of immutable consciousness, there is no contradiction, because one does not admit both existence and non-existence [of the same subject].
The meaning is "prohibition. || 1411 ||
This is a restatement of the challenged point, intended as a refutation.
Indeed, that which is expressed here by the Śruti with such effort as "yat" and "tat" is [the Brahman] directly.

Having resolved the contradiction that "the self-luminous does not see," he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "that which" (*yad*). [He says: "In the case of what has been enjoined. By the word *yat*, the introductory nature of the restatement (*anuvāda*) is intended. For this very reason, it was stated that there is no intention to provide a resolution [to a prior objection]. Because of its connection with the word *yat*, the restatement is clearly and directly expressed. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the sentence. (1412)
You should not think that it does not see in deep sleep; for that which is [perceived] there is not as you imagine.
For this Self exists as one who sees, with its faculty of sight unimpaired. || 1493 ||

He states the intended refutation with the words beginning "No" (na). Regarding the thought that this Self does not see while asleep, he says that it should not be so considered; here he provides the reason with the word "seeing" (paśyan). He precludes [the notion of] agency with the phrase "unimpaired" (avilupta).
Indeed, one does not see at all in this case, because the eye and other [faculties] are impossible.
In this world, one who is blind from birth and the like cannot see without the [visual] instruments.
The statement "seeing indeed" is challenged with the word "no. [The objection is: Why should there not be seeing even during deep sleep, when the eyes and other organs are absent?
To this he replies: "the instruments. The meaning is that it is the same for one who is in deep sleep as well. || 1414 ||
This is not so, because [it occurs] upon the observation of the agent who is the seer.
Instruments are required for the perception of an agent, but not for the perception of that which is not an agent.
He states that while the seer who possesses adventitious knowledge requires an instrument, the witness (sākṣin) does not, because of its nature as eternal knowledge: "Not this," etc. (1415).
Even in a dream, the dissolution of the eyes and other senses is heard of in the Śruti.
How could those [objects] exist in deep sleep, where even their latent impressions do not exist?

Furthermore, even for the knower (pramātṛ), there is no rule of necessity regarding dependence on the eyes and other organs, since scripture declares the withdrawal of the instruments (karaṇa) even during activities such as seeing in a dream. [Note: Variants indicate different readings for specific terms, such as *kāryān*, *tiṣiddham*, *śrutyaiva*, *yattacchaṃ*, *śabdoktasya*, *vīkṣyate*, *pīti śeṣaḥ*, and *vyapekṣante*.]
[Vol.
3, Page 498] 3 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

1631. He says this because [the Self exists] even in dream: "Even in dream... etc. The scripture states, "The Unsleeping among those who sleep," and so forth. This refers to the witness (*sākṣin*) of the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), such as the eyes and other senses...

He states the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic indicated by the particle "api" even in the context of the term *apekṣā*. [He asks] "Why? The word "tat" refers to the objects of the eyes and other senses.
The statement "it does not see" is due to the impossibility of [factors such as] an agent and so forth.
Indeed, it is said "seeing that" with reference to the actual occurrence. || 1417 ||
He concludes the absence of contradiction with the words beginning "no," etc. (1417).
If it is argued that "this [self] remains here even while seeing," from what source could this be known?
Thus, the statement "for there is no seer" is uttered for the purpose of establishing this reason. || 1418 ||

He introduces the sentence beginning with "na hi" (not indeed) preceded by a logical requirement, namely: "paśyan" (seeing). The meaning is that the required reason for the statement "the Self remains even in deep sleep as one who sees" is the non-destruction of the knowledge of its own nature; therefore, the sentence beginning with "na hi" is intended for the purpose of establishing that [point].
And even if there is a discrepancy among the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower, there is no such discrepancy for the Self.
Its establishment arises solely from the experience of something else, through its being the witness to that [other thing's] destruction. || 1419 ||

From where [does the self arise] if it is established through the very knowledge of its own nature, independent of the ego (māna) and so forth? To this he says: "meya" etc. The meaning is that because the Self is the witness of the absence of the objects of cognition (meya) and so forth, it is established even in their absence through the very knowledge of its own nature. || 1419 ||
For one must first perceive the object as it is, unpermeated by the knower and other such factors.
"I did not see," [he says], yet he sees as if seeing through his own self-awareness.

In that very context, he states another reason: "pramātrādi" (the knower, etc.). This means "prior to the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth," that is, in the previous state.

In the phrase "recollection preceded by prior experience," the word *hi* indicates what is well-known. The meaning is that because we observe the recollection of even that which was not seen [by the senses]—just as there is recollection of what was seen through a means of knowledge—it follows that [consciousness] is imperishable, since it has been apprehended by the consciousness of its own nature (*svarūpacit*).
For by whatever view a proponent is established, that very view belongs to the opponent.
Its destruction is not tenable, because of the absence of a cause. || 1421 ||

Having stated the purport (*tātparya*), he explains the words beginning with "na hi. [He says] "yasmāt" (because). He qualifies the vision (*dṛṣṭi*) with "yayā" (by which); the purpose of this qualification is to exclude a mental modification (*manovṛtti*). Therefore, the ellipsis is: "the Self remains in deep sleep while indeed seeing. The *hi* found in the scripture (*śrauta*) is echoed by the word *hi* [in the commentary]. The third case ending is used in the sense of manner (*itthaṃbhāve*). And this Self shines forth as the nature of vision; that [vision] belongs to it.

Because it is one's own essential nature and because there is no cause for its destruction, it is not lost; therefore, the construction of the meaning is that even during deep sleep, the Self is indeed seeing. || 1421 ||
Since properties such as destruction and origination belong to things that possess causes.
Those who lack a cause cannot be witnesses, because a witness must be subject to coming and going. || 1422 ||
1 kha. [He] saw dreams; 2 kha. [they were] seen; 3 ka. [he was] emaciated. || 1422 ||
1632 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya— 9] [Volume 3, Page 499]

Elaborating upon the absence of a logical reason (*hetvabhāva*), he states the meaning of the phrase "because of non-destruction" (*avināśitvāt*) with the words "destruction," etc. Therefore, regarding the point that destruction and so forth do not exist for a witness (*sākṣin*) who is devoid of causes, he provides another reason with the words "scriptural authority" (*āgama*), etc. || 1422 ||
Destruction and so forth cannot be established by themselves without a witness of destruction and so forth.
Therefore, there can never be any loss of the seer’s vision.

Anticipating the objection that its being accessible through perception is unestablished, he says: "Not [perceived] by destruction, etc. The implication is that otherwise, its insentience would be abandoned.
He states the result regarding the Self's status as the establisher of that [destruction]: "Therefore not... (1423).
That vision which is the very self of the seer is perceived through the inward-turned vision.
Its loss here is not possible in any way whatsoever. || 1424 ||

Having raised the objection that the existence of the Self is sufficiently established by the cognizer (pramātṛ) and thus there is no need for a witness (sākṣin), [the author] considers that this is not so because the existence or non-existence of that [cognizer] is itself established by it; thinking thus, he says: "Of the seer" (draṣṭuḥ). He provides experience as the proof for this: "The innermost" (pratyak). To the question of what follows from the fact that the vision of the Self is the establisher of everything, he replies:
"Of that" (tasyāḥ). The locative case in "sleep" (svāpe) signifies the locus. "In any way whatsoever" means either by itself or through another. || 1424 ||
The vision that the self alone is the imperishable reality of that which belongs to the self.
For that perishing seer, its non-annihilation is not logically possible.

Fearing that this [Self] too might be annihilated because it is a vision—just like the vision of a mother—he says: "The Self. The point is that the capacity for destruction is merely a limiting condition (upādhi). || 1425 ||
The vision that perceives [the mind] as coming and going is itself witnessed by that which is its witness.
Because it is the witness to the disappearance of the seer and the rest, its own disappearance is not logical. || 1426 ||
Anticipating the objection that the probans might be over-extensive (*sādhanavyāpti*), he says: "By scripture" (*āgama*). || 1426 ||
For it is only when a witness exists that both existence and non-existence are established.
Therefore, there can be no destruction of the world from any cause whatsoever, because the Self is perceived.

He states another reason for the permanence of the view of the Self (ātmadṛṣṭi): "Even when [the world exists]," etc. Since the existence and non-existence of the world are insentient and thus witnessed by the Self, the witnessing vision—which is the very nature of the Self—is indestructible; this is the meaning. The word "here" (iha) expresses the statement of the reason.
Is it not the case that a contradictory statement is being asserted by you here?
That this vision does not perish is an extreme act of rashness.
He raises an objection regarding the contradiction by means of another formulation: "But surely" (nanu). He clarifies that very statement [of the opponent] with: "No" (na). || 1428 ||
The connection between the agent and the action is said to be for the sake of the seer's perception.
Consequently, its non-destruction is not tenable, because it is something produced.
How is this such an act of extreme audacity? To that he says: "katra" (where?). || 1429 ||
1 gha. ‘ādityādyasyāṃ’ | 2 gha. ‘statsiddhe’ | 3. na hi na | [vol 3, page 500] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1633.
Surely, because of the statement "it is not lost," it will not be destroyed.
It is not so, because a statement established by valid cognition cannot be prevented from perishing.

He raises the objection that "there is no destruction even of the effect because of the scriptural statement," introducing it with "But surely" (nanu). He replies, "Not so," stating that the statement does not convey the eternality of the effect because it contradicts inference supported by the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is produced is impermanent. || 1430 ||
Since a means of valid cognition is the manifester of what is already established, it is not its producer.
Therefore, by this statement, the indestructibility of the seer’s vision is intended here.
Even though a statement does not cause one to understand an object that contradicts other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it nevertheless brings it about; anticipating this objection, he says:
"of the established" (*siddhasya*). Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers back to the first half-verse and has as its object the domain of the means of valid cognition. || 1431 ||
This is not a fault, because the Śruti provides a qualification for the seer.
Therefore, because it is the seer, the seer here is not an agent at all.
It is said that here the word "seer" (draṣṭṛ) refers only to the immutable witness-consciousness (kūṭasthadṛṣṭi), and not to the agent of seeing; therefore, there is no contradiction. He says: "No.

For the scriptural passage "of the seer" (draṣṭuḥ) does not denote the seer as the agent of the act of seeing, because the two genitives are in grammatical apposition (sāmānādhikaraṇya). Thus, the meaning is that the seer is the witness and not the agent, so there is no contradiction. || 1432 ||
The seer who brings about the end of the body is one who perceives and possesses the causes of phenomena and so forth.
In this case, the omission [of the witness] regarding what was seen by the horse is witnessed by each individual's own inner self.

Having accepted the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two genitives in the phrase "the seer whose vision is immutable is the Self" (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭirātmā*), [the author] has stated this; now, he says that it is likewise even if there is a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between them:

"The end of the body," etc. He who possesses attributes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, who is the agent of vision beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the body, is the seer (*draṣṭṛ*); of him, that—

Furthermore, the destruction of that [empirical] vision is established through mere inward vision during sleep and so forth; therefore, the meaning is that there is no destruction of that vision which is the witness of the seer, because it is of the nature of the inward-facing reality. || 1433 ||
But that vision which exists prior to the emergence of the subject and so forth is indeed devoid of an agent.
Because it is the witness to the destruction of the seer and so forth, that vision is imperishable.

He provides a justification for the statement that the Self is the immutable witness (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭi*). [The verse begins with] "Previously" (*prāk*). Anticipating the objection that such a vision is unestablished during sleep and so forth, he says: "The seer and so forth" (*draṣṭrādi*). || 1434 ||
But that very vision is the seer; it does not, however, possess the characteristics of an agent.
Because of the inclusion of the phrase "of the vision" as a qualification of the seer. || 1435 ||

Having abandoned the position of non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) and resorted to another position, he says: "The vision. He recalls the reason stated here—that that very vision is the seer and not its agent—by saying: "Of the seer" (draṣṭuḥ). || 1439 ||
For in the world, the destruction of effects is established as occurring within their own causes.
Therefore, [the self] is neither of the nature of a cause nor of a non-acting entity. || 1436 ||

In order to state another reason for the non-destruction of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), he states a general principle: "For there is no destruction... [etc.]. [The variants in the manuscripts are as follows: 1. *kha.* reads *maitraṃ*; 2. *kha.* and *gha.* read *ha*; *maivaṃ*; 3. *ka.* reads *'raṇam*; 4. *kha.* and *ga.* read *ṃgdṛṣṭathaikaṃ*. 205.
[Vol.
3, p. 501] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four:

He states that the destruction of what has been described is not established because the nature of the effect is dissimilar [to that of the cause], saying "Not from this" (*nātaḥ*). The words "there is no loss" (*parilopo na asti*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Fearing that [ignorance] might undergo absolute destruction like [the destruction of] ignorance itself, he says "Nor... (nāpi) [in verse 1436], stating that this is not so because of the difference in their causes.
"Because non-existence is itself a form of existence, and because existence is established through perception."
Therefore, there is no suspicion of non-existence regarding perception, because everything is established through its concomitance with that [perception]. || 1437 ||

He states another argument against its disappearance: "Of non-existence," and so forth. For it is not distinct from existence; for if difference were itself an existent, it could not reside within that [existence], and if it were a non-existent, the same fault would apply.

Thus, since there is no non-existence separate from existence, and because the establishment of that [non-existence] depends upon perception, there is no fear of its destruction. Even if non-existence were other than existence, [the point remains] because all perception depends upon the act of seeing.
He states that the Self is indeed the immutable witness (kūṭasthadṛṣṭi) with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 1437 ||
The well-known state of deep sleep would not be possible if there were a destruction of vision.
Therefore, this vision of the supreme Self is free from birth, destruction, and the like. || 1438 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the vision of the Self is indestructible, beginning with the words "Not [so]," and so forth. It is not correct to say, "Since that [Self] is established through inference alone, enough with the doctrine of the immutable vision," because such an inference cannot arise in the absence of a probans (liṅga) pervaded by it. Nor should it be argued: "I am devoid of the experience of pain and so forth during the interval between dreaming and waking, because I lack memory of those things belonging to that time, like a stone. For the absence of memory regarding those things is merely something to be disregarded.

Since the absence of experience in grass and such things does not prove [the non-existence of the Self], it is inconclusive; therefore, the meaning is that the immutable vision (*kūṭastha-dṛṣṭi*) alone is the means of proving it.
He concludes what has been stated—that the immutable vision is the Self—with the verse beginning "birth" (*janma*). || 1438 ||
If it is argued that perception must have an agent because of the hearing of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *tṛc*, [we reply: no.
"Beholding the seer"—for it is thus, and not otherwise, because of the impossibility of an agent and so forth. (1439)

He raises the objection that the vision is not immutable (kūṭastha), because we hear the forms of the verbal root and the agent in the words *paśyan* (present participle) and *draṣṭuḥ* (agentive noun ending in -tṛ). The word *hi* signifies that it is well known that both of these grammatical usages require an action. He replies that this is not so, because the meaning of the verbal root and the meaning of the suffix cannot be joined together as subordinate parts [of a single unified cognition], and thus the immutability of vision remains. || 1439 ||
Even then, there is no existence of the intellect and so forth here, because of the scriptural statement "it is not."
In deep sleep, neither the meaning of the verbal root nor the meaning of the suffix is admitted.

He establishes the reason [for his position]: "No. For there is the scriptural text beginning with, "Speech, then, merges into breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6). He states the result that follows from the absence of causal factors:
"In deep sleep," etc. (Verse 1440).
If the agent and other factors of action do not exist in deep sleep, how [could they exist]?
The statement "seeing the seer" is logically consistent only with respect to the immutable (kūṭastha).

An objection is raised here: "The occasional nature of perception and its agent do not exist during sleep because of the absence of causal factors," [expressed by the words] "by the agent," etc. (9441).
Just as space, though devoid of action, is called the "giver of room."
In the same way, the eternal Self is designated by words ending in the suffix -tṛc, as in "enemy" (śatru). || 1442 ||
1 gha. Because of being connected (*saṃhitatvāt*). 2 ga. Just like... 3 kha. ga. Do not say so. 4 gha. ‘Objection’ (*ākṣepaka*). 5 kha. Do not say so. — [Vol. 3, page 502]

He provides a resolution with an illustration: "Just as... (yathā). || 1442 || [This concludes] Brāhmaṇa 3, accompanied by the commentary known as the *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. || 1635 ||
And the intrinsic nature of the causal agents is that which they perform here without having previously acted.
Therefore, since the agent does not perform [the action], how can there be any excellence on the part of that which performs it? || 1443 ||

Furthermore, because the relationship of cause and effect is difficult to define, [the author] states that vision (*dṛṣṭi*) is immutable (*kūṭastha*). Having raised the dilemma as to whether an agent (*kāraka*) is a cause while acting or while not acting, he refutes the first alternative with the words "its own nature" (*svabhāva*). Here, the sphere of conventional usage regarding action and its factors has been described. The meaning is that an agent cannot be a cause while acting, because it would contradict the very nature of being an agent. He points out another fault in that same position with the words "of one who acts" (*kurvataḥ*). For indeed...
The meaning is that for one who performs [an action], there would be an excess of the nature of the effect, which leads to an infinite regress (anavasthiti). || 1443 ||
Prior to the completion of the action, that which has the nature of performing it is not perceived.
Therefore, that which does not act here would be an agent everywhere.
For this reason as well, he states that the position of one who acts [while already existing] is untenable: "Previously," etc. Here, "here" refers to the statement of action.
Likewise, in other cases as well, the cause is exactly the same because of the attainment of a state of unity; thus he says: "Everywhere. (1444)
If the causal agent were possessed of power, then the effect would always exist, just like that power.
For even the existence of potentialities is always like the potentiality itself. || 1445 ||

Having restated the position of the opponent who does not accept [the existence of] potentiality (*śakti*), he refutes it with the words "śaktimat" (that which possesses potentiality). He states the reason for the argument that if potentiality were eternal, then the effect would likewise have to be eternal, in the phrase "śakyānām" (of those things that are capable).
"Neither potentiality nor the possessor of potentiality are established as being distinct from one another."
Because the nature of the capacity and the object of capacity are mutually dependent. || 1446 ||
It establishes the reason. [The opponent says] "No. To that, he asks: "How so? and replies: "Mutually... (verse 1446).
The restriction of powers is according to what is possible, and also of possible things according to their power.
Furthermore, for the proponent of [inherent] power (śakti), there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence. || 1447 ||

He states another defect regarding the position that [the effect] exists as a potentiality (*śakti*): "Of the potencies," etc. The restriction—that the potency for curd and so forth resides only in milk and so forth—is to be accepted because curd and so forth are observed from that very [milk]. And that restriction—that the potency for producing it resides only in that [milk]—is to be desired on account of the restriction expressed as "from that very [milk] comes curd. Thus, the meaning is that there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*). || 1447 ||
Furthermore, if action were not something to be performed, the grammatical factor (kāraka) would not be established.
Moreover, if it were an effect, there would be an infinite regress, and even its production would be extremely difficult to achieve. (1448)
Furthermore, as to whether action (kriyā) is something to be performed or not to be performed, he refutes the position that it is not to be performed with the words "And of action" (kriyāyāś ca).

The meaning is that, according to the established principle that a causal factor (kāraka) is that which performs an action. He refutes the second [position]—that it is to be performed—with the words "And if it were to be performed" (kāryatve ca). He states that this [action], by destroying its very root, results in a fault, with the words "While performing" (kurvacceti). || 1448 ||
And because the sequence of priority and posteriority between the action and its fruit is well-established.
What is the goal to be accomplished and what is the means here? Certainty is not possible.

Furthermore, if action were not an effect, then—just as it would be beginningless—the result of that action would also be beginningless; consequently, there would be no evidence for a temporal sequence, and thus no relation of cause and effect.
Thus he says: "Action... The locative sense refers to the conventional usage of cause and effect. (1449)
But when ignorance alone is the cause, all of this is entirely consistent.
And because everything is the effect of that [Brahman], nothing at all is inconsistent.

Anticipating the objection that "the fault is equal for you as well, since you too accept the relation of cause and effect," he says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). The meaning is that in the case of a causal relationship based on ignorance (*āvidya*), because the aforementioned defects of conceptual alternatives do not apply, both the effect and the cause are consistent with how they are perceived. As for the argument beginning with "of the action and its fruit," etc., he states "that" (*tat*) to show that it also does not exist in our position, because the action and so forth are merely products of ignorance (*āvidyatva*).
The meaning is that even such a sequence [of cognition], as it arises from experience, is not contradictory. || 1450 ||
In this context, the connection of this mind with that which is not the Self is intended to be expressed.
In that regard, the connection with a cause, an agent, and so forth, arises from delusion due to ignorance.

One might raise the objection: "Does the Self have a connection with the non-Self, or not? In the first case, just as its agency is real, let that [connection] also be real elsewhere; what then is the use of ignorance (avidyā)? In the second case, its omnipresence is not established. Anticipating this, he says: "Where... This means: in the state of ignorance (avidyāvasthā). The phrase "born of delusion" (mohajā) is a restatement of the very same relationship already mentioned—that the conjunction of the agent and so forth is caused by ignorance.
The connection is with the word "thus" (tiriti). || 1451 ||
But where the notion "this is the self" arises for the wise man, it is like the notion of a non-self.
In that case, the cognition is exactly as it is; it does not depend here upon ignorance or other such factors.

If it is argued that in the cognition "all is the Self," agency is intended to be real, he says "no" with the words *yatra tu* ("but where"). Just as there is the notion of non-Self during the state of ignorance (*avidyā*), so too there is for a person the cognition "all is the Self" during the state of knowledge (*vidyā*). Because that [cognition] conforms to a reality free from phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), it does not depend upon ignorance or the agency produced by it within its own self; for even though it arises through the power of that [ignorance], it is the destroyer of it—this is the meaning. || 1452 ||
Even when waking and dreaming are abandoned, the nature of cognition is not lost.
Because that [transformation] is witnessed by the Self, the inward-facing one is devoid of birth and the like. || 1453 ||

Fearing the objection that the very reality of the self devoid of conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) does not exist—since in deep sleep the destruction of the self is accepted as being like [the disappearance of] duality—he says: "In waking... The reason for the non-deprivation of the inner witness (pratīc) is given by the words: "Because of its loss... He concludes that the inner witness is of the nature of immutable perception (kūṭasthadṛṣṭi) with the word: "The inner witness... (1453).
Just as the perception of a snake and so forth does not occur without first taking up the ignorance of the rope.
Without taking up the ignorance of the self, there is likewise no perception of the non-self.

Furthermore, because duality appears dependent upon ignorance like a snake [superimposed on a rope], it is false; therefore, he says that the reality is indeed the non-manifest, immutable Absolute: "Like a rope... (1454).
For, in the absence of the seed of conceptual construction, conceptual construction itself is not found.
The non-self is imagined within the inner self; it is found to be inconstant within the inner self. || 1455 ||
1 gha. ...tvāt tat pa | 2 ka. ...cārataḥ | [vol 3, page 504] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1637.

Anticipating the objection that even the internal organ (*pratīc*) might be as unreal as the non-self (*anātman*), he says: "It is a construction" (*kalpanā*). For there can be no construction in that [internal organ], because of the absence of a cause; otherwise, there would be an illusion without a substratum and a sublation without a limit—this is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that the non-self might be as unconstructed as the Self (*ātman*), he says: "It is constructed" (*kalpita*). || 1455 ||
The non-deviation of the self is everywhere witnessed by the self alone.
Therefore, for the sake of thoroughly understanding that [object], the self does not depend upon ignorance.
Fearing that even the internal (pratīcaḥ) might be imagined due to its variability, he says "of the Self" (ātmanaḥ).

He refers back to what was stated regarding the Self's self-established nature through its non-deviation across all states. With the word "since" (yataḥ), he states that therefore the Self does not require ignorance or its effects for the knowledge of itself; thus, because its existence and manifestation are independent, it is not imagined (akalpitaḥ).
"Therefore" || 1456 ||

Just as the sun possesses agency in relation to an object to be illuminated, it does not possess such agency in the illumination of itself, because it is not unilluminated [and thus requires no further illumination]. (1457)
Then, raising the objection as to how the Self could be immutable (kūṭastha) if it illuminates both itself and another, he states an illustration: "prakāśya" (having illuminated). || 1457 ||
Even when external objects appear, the sun and other such [factors] possess agency in this regard.
Because the sun is always of a single nature, it possesses no capacity for novel action.

One might object that this example is not applicable to the immutable Self’s illuminating both itself and others, since the sun, though immutable, possesses agency only in illuminating other things and not in illuminating itself. Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "External... [and so on]. If it is argued that the sun also possesses the agency of illumination regarding its own form and so forth, he says "No," and provides the reason: "Always... Just as the sun lacks any modification when illuminating things other than itself, so too is it with the Self.

It should be understood that while in the statement "the constant state of being changeless is the connection with the objects to be manifested," the sun's agency in illuminating other things is merely accepted as a concession, such agency has already been refuted in the context of the manifestation of external objects. || 1458 ||
Just like the bright, blazing, and steady flame of a gem of pure birth.
The luminous self undergoes no modification whether the objects to be illumined are present or absent.

Raising the objection that since the sun’s capacity to illuminate depends upon the removal of clouds and the like, how can it be said to be inactive, [the author] states another illustration, beginning with "Just as... (yathā). || 1459 ||
No act of illumination whatsoever exists for this [consciousness] within itself.
That proximity of the object to be manifested which constitutes its manifestation is [called] "action" (kriyā) by way of metaphorical designation. || 1460 ||

He states the refutation: "No. If it is argued that although there is an absence of the purposeful activity of manifestation within the inner self (pratīc) itself, such activity might exist with respect to another, he says "no," adding: "Because it is a metaphorical designation" (upacārāt). || 1460 ||
And this perception is not figurative, as in the case of "the boy is fire."
Because there is no perception of the inner self as having an understanding other than this. || 1461 ||

1 ka. *sarvānātmai* | 2 kha. gha. *pratīci* | 3 ga. *thā || atoṃ* | [vol 3, page 505] 1638 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]— [Note: The provided text fragment appears to contain scribal variants for the commentary on the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad*, specifically referencing the internal Self (*pratīci*) and the transition from the third to the fourth adhyāya.]
Fearing that the capacity to illuminate might be secondary rather than primary if it occurs without modification, he says: "And not...

The very fact that the entire world is perceived through the mere proximity of the inner self (pratyak), which is actionless consciousness, is what constitutes its "illuminating nature"; it is not so by way of undergoing modification, for there is no evidence for such a mode of illumination. This alone, therefore, is the primary [meaning]. || 1461 ||
But surely, the suffix -tṛc is used even in the world [of common parlance] for roots whose meaning implies transience?
How could there be an eternal vision of that which is expressed by the word "seer"? (1462)

Once it has been established that the inner self (pratyagātman) possesses an immutable vision (kūṭasthadṛṣṭi), one might raise an objection based on the hearing of the suffixes *tṛc* and *tṛn*. Anticipating this, the author first states what the ignorant person objects to:

"But surely... (*nanu*). Here, the particle *api* signifies pervasion (*abhivyāpti*). One might ask: even if the suffix *tṛc* is used in cases such as "the cutter" (*chettā*) or "the breaker" (*bhettā*), where there is agency in respect to occasional actions, what does that have to do with the present context? To this he replies: "The seer" (*draṣṭṛ*). (Verse 1462)
Because no solution has been stated, since [the phenomenon] is observed even in the case of the sun and so forth.
The illuminator is the sun, or likewise, it is the power that pervades.

He states the answer: "No. For there is no rule that the suffix *tṛc* must denote an agent of an occasional action; [for example], the sun (*savitṛ*) is seen as the "illuminator" or the "pervader" of space even in the absence of adventitious action. Thus, it is not contradictory to say that the Self is seen as the "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*). This is the meaning.
If it is argued that this may be so regarding illuminating entities, but not regarding the internal self;
It is not so, because the entity known as the inner self (pratyagātman) possesses the nature of being self-luminous. || 1464 ||

He raises an objection regarding the inequality [of the positions]: "Let it be so. The mention of the "illuminator" (*prakāśaka*) is intended as an illustration for the "pervader" (*vyāpaka*). This means that there would be both the state of being an illuminator and the state of being a pervader without undergoing modification (*vikāra*). The sense is that this is because they possess the nature of being illuminators and so forth. He says "No," because since the nature of illumination and so on is not established in the Self (*ātman*), it must necessarily undergo modification. [This refers to] the consciousness-illumination of the inner witness (*pratyak*).

And since its state of being unlimited is established by scripture and other means, he says "not so" [verse 1464], meaning that [the nature of Brahman] is not merely its quality of being a manifestor, which would be indistinguishable from agency.
In this world, it is directly perceived that there is the manifestation of objects such as the seer and so forth.
And because of the scriptural teaching on self-luminosity, the inner self is the illuminator.

To the question of how the luminosity of the inward-facing consciousness (*pratyak-cit*) is established by perception and other means of knowledge, he says: "Perception," etc. This means it is established by one's own experience. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to combine the logical argument that the seer and so forth are not self-evident due to their insentience (*jāḍya*). || 1461 ||
Moreover, it is the Self alone that is perceived here everywhere as self-luminous.
And according to the scripture, "He is the light even of lights; to Him alone [belong all luminaries]. (1466)

Regarding its being the illuminator of all things, he states another sentence preceded by a proposition: "Also the Self" (*apyātmā*). In this [verse], the object to be illuminated is understood through the locative case. The meaning of the particle *api* is that it is not only the illuminator, but also the object to be illuminated in the form of each respective thing.

1. ka. ga. *°lapyaḥ syān nityā* | 2. kha. *śayati sa* | 3. ka. ga. *yitriti sadā vyāpta vyāpi* | 4. kha. *yadyathā* | 5. ma. *ke'py evaṃ* | 6. kha. *tmano lo* | 7. ka. ga. *ke dṛṣṭā* | [vol 3, page 506]
"I directly perceive the jar," and "I do not perceive it"—this is how it appears to the world. (Brāhmaṇa 3) [From the *Śāstraprakāśikā* commentary by Ānandagiri, page 1639]
If it is thought that this cannot be so because non-existence is well-established, [we reply: 1467.
When it is stated that the Self is the immutable witness (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭi*), an objection is raised regarding contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*): "Directly," etc. (1467).
"I do not see the jar in this way," because of the perception [expressed as] "I do not see."
The state of being eternally imperishable is clearly understood as belonging to the inner self. || 1468 ||
He refutes [the objection], saying "not so. The meaning is that experience is of two kinds, and it supports its status as the immutable witness (kūṭasthadṛṣṭi).
Just as the witnesshood of the inner self (pratīc) is understood from the statement "I see."
And for him, the realization "I do not see" is likewise directly witnessed by his own self in this very life.

Having raised the objection—namely, that even if the aforementioned Self is established by the experience "I see" and so forth, how is it not also established by the cognition "I do not see"?—the word *sphuṭam* (clearly) was used to clarify this. Regarding the phrase "of 'I see'": since the absence of knowledge is established precisely because [knowledge] is not eternal, the meaning is that the Self is an unchanging witness (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭi*). In the same way, the witnessing nature of the inner self (*pratīcaḥ*) applies to the cognition "I do not see" as well.
The connection is that "it is understood. The word "here" refers to the sphere of worldly discourse. The ellipsis is "knowledge and ignorance, witnessed by oneself. || 1469 ||
Moreover, even those whose eyes have been plucked out experience vision in a dream.
Therefore, for me, vision is eternal, as it exists apart from the seer.

He states another reason for the permanence of the vision of the Self, beginning with the words "utkhātā" (uprooted). The meaning is that if it were a rule that vision is adventitious, there would be a contradiction regarding the vision of color and so forth by a blind person during the state of dream; furthermore, since mental impressions (*vāsanā*) are impossible in one born blind, and if one accepts [the existence of] other births, one must accept that vision is permanent because of the stability of the immutable vision (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭi*) which establishes those [impressions]. || 1470 ||
That is the light even of lights, because it illumines our intellect.
It appears as if of the nature of darkness, like the sun to those who see only by night.
If the view of the self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) were eternal, then why is it not experienced by everyone at all times? To this, he says: "By the lights," etc. (1471).
Since this is so, therefore let it be accepted that the vision of the Self is indeed eternal.
Because every instance of impermanence has its own individual direct witness. || 1472 ||

Having stated the absence of sublation and the presence of proof for the permanence of the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi), he concludes it with the words "yataḥ" (since). He clarifies the meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) with the phrase "anityatvasya. This means: of everything that is subject to coming and going. || 1472 ||
Having seen that [reality] which is without means of proof and whose nature is non-transformative.

This self remains as one who sees, because that [seeing] is its cause of perception. (1473) [Note: The provided text contains various manuscript variants indicated by letters such as ga., kha., gha., etc., which have been integrated into the translation for clarity.]
[Vol.
3, Page 507] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four:
He states the result of declaring that perception is eternal with the words "by that" (*tayā*). The word should be divided as "asādhanayā" (without means). He explains that very point:

He does not transform it. To provide another reason for its permanence, he says: "Because that is seen. The meaning is that if the Self were self-luminous, one might ask why it does not know itself and others during deep sleep; however, since the duality headed by such an objection is established through the perception of the Self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), there is no loss of that perception. || 1473 ||
"I see"—just as you saw [the dream] while awake through the very vision of the self.
Even when you say, "I do not see," you look in that same way with a permanent view.
