He establishes the non-destruction [of consciousness] during sleep by means of an illustration: "I see," etc. The ellipsis is "you perceive" in deep sleep. The intended meaning is that otherwise, the retrospective reflection (parāmarśa) of one who has awakened—namely, "I was not conscious"—would be impossible. || 1474 ||
Just as the perceiver, who ends with the body, perceives objects such as a jar.
The seer is connected with seeing because the state of being a seer has that [seeing] as its basis. (1475)
Because my self has the nature of being a non-agent, it has not acted in this way.
Therefore, the view of self should be understood as that which conforms to the nature of conditions.
Anticipating the objection that if the Self perceives during the waking state, it would have a connection with the act of seeing by virtue of being its agent, he says:

"Perceiving. Just as the perceiver—the grasper consisting of the intellect and so forth, ending with the body—is said to be a "seer" when perceiving a jar or similar object and is thereby connected with the act of seeing—since the status of being a seer residing in the knower is dependent upon its connection with the activity of seeing—the nature of the Self is not like that.

The seer exists in dependence upon bondage because of its nature as immutable perception (kūṭasthadṛṣṭitva). Therefore, although the seerhood of the subject (mātṛ) is occasioned by its connection with perception, the meaning is that the seerhood of consciousness (cit) is dependent upon its own essential nature (svarūpa). He summarizes the meaning of the passage beginning with "for the seer" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23] with the words "the vision of the Self. The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is the impossibility of destruction according to the principle stated. Its conformity to that [vision] is its eternity. ||1475||1476||
The word "vai" is employed here because the meaning as previously stated is well-established.
Therefore, by the word "does not see," the status of being an agent is negated. || 1477 ||

Having summarized the meaning of the statements regarding the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), and expanding upon the meaning of the proposition, he states the meaning of the word "vai" (indeed): "As has been said," etc.
That is to say, since the Self's state of being the immutable witness is well-known from all the Upaniṣads, the word "vai" is employed in this sentence for the purpose of recollecting that very fact.
He then states the meaning of the phrase "he does not see that": "He does not [see] that," etc. (1477).
Because the object of perception is impossible, one who sees does not see, even while seeing.
Just as [the existence] of an agent is not perceived from the perspective of the result, saying "I do not see," so it is here.
The non-perception of the self as a non-agent arises from the absence of engagement with the object to be seen.
That which was spoken of extensively by the word "view" (dṛṣṭi) is neither an action nor an agent.

Anticipating the objection that this [statement] might be taken literally, he refutes it by means of an illustration: "dṛśyārtha... (regarding the object of perception). Just as a mother, although seeing herself as "I," is said not to see objects such as a jar because they are absent, so too [the Self], being the agent with respect to cognition, [is said not to see objects]. Since the word "yathā" (just as) exists in this verse, the word "yadvat" (as if) is redundant.
1 gha. Thus it is for oneself. 2 kha. gha. According to the aforementioned method. 3 kha. "Always. [Vol.
3, page 508] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1641.

The meaning is as follows: just as one perceives the result of the cognition "I do not see" when the jar or other objects are absent, so too, for the Self whose nature is immutable vision (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭisvabhāva*), there is an absence of seeing during deep sleep due to the absence of anything to be seen, not because of the absence of the vision that is its own essential nature; for its permanence is certain through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Having explained the passage beginning with "That which indeed," he states the meaning of the word "seeing" (*paśyan*) with the words "the object" (*vastu*). By the word "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*), [he refers to] "seeing."
The meaning is "it is true. || 1478 || 1479 ||
Form is that which, for the self, is devoid of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped.
By the expression "that vision," it is directly established for us. || 1480 ||

He provides the remainder of the sentence as the reason for the meaning stated by the phrase "seeing a thing that is neither an action nor an agent" (akriyākārakaṃ vastu): "grāhake" [in the verse]. || 1480 ||
It is concluded as being just like the western direction, consisting of the nature of neither action nor agent.
It is said here that one does not perceive the form of the self through speech.

Considering that the word *vai* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), he states the meaning of the phrase "he does not see that" [in the verse]. He says: "The westward-facing [state]. Here, either sleep (*svāpa*), the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛtam*), or the sentence itself is understood by the locative case. By the words "he does not see that," the status of being an agent (*kārakatvam*) is negated;
thus, there is no tautology, because this [phrase] is employed to refute a potential objection regarding the contradiction with the words "seeing that. This is how it should be seen.
The end. || 1481 ||
But is this not a restatement of an objection, and not said by those who do not see?
From what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is a non-agent entity asserted here? || 1482 ||

He raises an objection: "Since it has been stated that this is a restatement of a previously enjoined meaning, the phrase 'he does not see' is merely reiterative; how then can it establish immutability? He begins with "But surely... [nanu]. To the suggestion that the intended meaning is established through another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he says "no," asking "Why?
The word "here" [atra] refers to a particular state. || 1482 ||
Prior to all measurement, the single nature of the Self alone was unknown everywhere.
And that which was unknown is indeed known; therefore, there is no possibility of an objection. || 1483 ||

He refutes the lack of evidence for a non-agent self with the words, "The oneness of the self" (*aikātmyam*). It is undisputed that in both common worldly experience and in scripture, in every place and at every time, what was previously unknown becomes known only after the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, it has been established that the oneness of the self alone is what is unknown;

therefore, since everything is a means of valid cognition only with respect to that [oneness], from what means of valid cognition could a non-agent entity be established? Thus, there is no possibility of such an objection.
Such is the meaning. || 1483 ||
And self-established experience is not distinct from ignorance.
Therefore, like the established doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas, this first [creation] was not made by me from anything other than myself.
If this oneness (*aikātmya*) is unknown, does it differ from ignorance (*ajñāna*) or not? In the first case, like the *prakṛti* of the Sāṃkhya school, ignorance would possess independence;

in the second case, even oneness itself would be insentient (*jaḍa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Self-established" (*svataḥ siddhā*). How then is the charge of insentiency resolved, given that if there is no difference from ignorance, self-establishment is contradicted? To this he replies: "Not from this" (*nātaḥ*).
206 1 ka. ga. yadvikīṇam | [vol 3, page 509]
1642 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:

The meaning is that since ignorance is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) as being either identical to or different from reality, the Self does not become insentient (*jaḍa*) due to its non-difference from that ignorance. To those who do not tolerate the non-dual nature of the Self, he says: "From Me" (*mattaḥ*). The objection you raised regarding the insentiency of the Self is [refuted by] that non-duality.

The point is that for one who maintains [the existence of] "you" (tva), since that which is delimited is invariably associated with insentience, it cannot be the Self, just like a jar or other such objects.
The proponent of monistic identity must necessarily accept a single object of cognition.
If another measure is admitted, then oneness of self is not established. || 1485 ||

Anticipating the objection that "how can it be that only the unity of the Self (aikātmya) is the unknown object of knowledge, since the same would apply to jars and other things as well," he says: "The unity of the Self... He states the reason for its necessity: "Because of [the contradiction with] other objects of knowledge. The sense is that its non-establishment cannot be maintained, for that would contradict all the Upaniṣads. || 1485 ||
In this world, agency arises from the completeness or incompleteness of the causal conditions for actions.
The statement that "one does not see" means "one sees," as it is expressed with a contradictory sense. || 1486 ||
In the case of "seeing while not seeing," such [a state] is not applicable to the Self.
Because its nature consists in the modification of the measure (mātrā), and because it does not produce unity. || 1487 ||

By restating the objection that "it does not see," the immutability (*kauṭasthya*) of the Self is established; it has been stated that all means of knowledge (*māna*) have such a Self as their object.

Now, fearing the doubt that—just as there are statements regarding seeing and non-seeing with respect to the knower (*mātṛ*)—the statement "seeing yet not seeing" might likewise not be for the purpose of [establishing] the immutability of the Self, he says: "Of the instruments" (*sādhanānām*), etc., [referring] to the Self in the passage beginning with "seeing."

He states the reason why the mention of seeing and not seeing is untenable: "It is mere vision" (*dṛṅmātra*). Anticipating the objection that if it were merely that, the Self would possess the nature of an action—since vision is of such a nature—he says: "Unchanging" (*avikriya*). Then, [anticipating] that it might therefore be a quality (*guṇatva*), he says "no," because it is not a quality, adding:
"Because it is the Self" (*ātmatva*). And this principle is the reason for what was stated; because of its oneness and its lack of agency, there is neither seeing nor not seeing in the Self.
He says "joined with the body" (tirayuktā), [beginning with] "oneness" (ekatva). || 1486 || 1487 ||
Since this is so, the subsequent statement is a reply specifically to the word "seeing."
The explanation "he does not see" is a negation of the factors of action and so forth. || 1488 ||
If the Self possesses the characteristics previously described, let it be that it "sees" eternally; why then is it said that it "does not see"? To this he replies with the words "yataḥ" (because).

According to the reasoning already stated, since the Self is of the nature of immutable vision (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭi*), the statement "it does not see" is intended to negate the sense of agency (*kartṛtva*) that would otherwise be implied by the expression "it sees. He states the result of this explanation as follows: "kārakādi... (verse 1488).
Therefore, in the statement "seeing, one does not see," a single meaning is expressed.
The light that is non-agent in nature is non-dual and of the nature of the inner self. || 1489 ||

He states what is obtained regarding the relationship between the commentary and the text to be commented upon: "Seeing," etc. He clarifies that very same single meaning with the words: "without a mark," etc. || 1489 ||
1. To be established (sādhya). 2. gha. Not that [it is] fraudulent (na tatkauṭa). 3. gha. "The state of being the Self" (yātmatvaṃ). 4. ga. It is accepted (iṣyate). [Vol.
3, page 510] 3rd Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1643.
The entity consisting of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped is said to be the object of vision.
Because the self-substance, consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth, is capable of being perceived by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 1490 ||

Having explained the Kāṇva recension beginning with "seeing," [the author] states the meaning of the word *draṣṭavya* (to be seen) in the Mādhyandina recension, beginning with "seeing indeed that which is to be seen.

[He says] "the grasper" (*grahītṛ*). Anticipating the objection that the meaning of the word *draṣṭavya* refers only to objects of perception such as jars and not to the subject (*mātrā*) and so forth, he says "pramāṇa... (the means of knowledge). The ellipsis to be supplied is "is the meaning of the word *draṣṭavya*. (1490)
And how these possess direct perceptibility, I have already explained previously.
Furthermore, the distinction between the Self and the seer and so forth was stated previously in that same manner. (1491)

Fearing that the cognition of both the knower (*mātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*māna*) might likewise be dependent on another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), he says "And perceptibility" (*prātyakṣyaṃ ca*) to show that this is not so, because their establishment is possible by relying on the view of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*). The meaning is that there is no infinite regress, since it is stated here and there—beginning from the *Saṃbandha-grantha*—that the knower and the rest are objects of cognition for the Witness (*sākṣivedyatva*). Furthermore, while the knower and the rest are fit to be designated by the term "object of sight" (*draṣṭavya*) due to their fitness for being seen, they are no different in that same fitness [for being the Witness].

Fearing that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the Self itself becoming an object fit for such [perception], he says: "Of the seer, etc. The word "in the city" means in the unmanifested state (*avyākṛta*) and so forth.
This being so, he says: "In that case," because the Self, being self-luminous, is not dependent on anything else, it cannot be an object of sight. || 1491 ||
Through the expressions "seeing" and "not seeing," the seer is established as being of an undivided nature.
Here it is stated that the light [of the Self] is different [from the body], whereas elsewhere it is like a division.

Having explained the meaning of the word *draṣṭavya* (to be seen), he says "darśana... etc., stating that the two readings, *paśyan* and so forth, have the same meaning. He states the purpose of referring to sleep with the word "here" (*iha*). With the word "elsewhere" (*anyatra*), he refers to the light of the Self as being differentiated in the two states of waking and so forth.
That is to say, "he is ashamed. || 1492 ||
And because it is the cause of manifestation, and because it is the innermost of all.
Even though seeing it in its entirety, one does not see it because of the true nature of that which is other than it.
The wise person does not perceive [it], because the stated reason is non-distinctive.
In the same way, this should be understood regarding one's own states of dreaming and waking.

If it is asked, "In that case, has it not been admitted that the light of the Self (*ātma-jyotis*) functions as an agent (*kāraka*) in certain specific states?", he says: "Of consciousness" (*citeḥ*). The meaning is that although it functions as an agent through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), there is no loss of the established doctrine (*siddhānta-hāni*) because, in reality, such agency is absent. He says: "All... to show that even in the waking state and so forth, the absence of real agency is the same. Nevertheless, since it was stated [previously] that it is "like a division," how can there be limitation (*pariccheda*)?

Therefore, he states its immutability (*kauṭasthya*) by saying "in its entirety" (*kārtsnyāt*). He asserts that the self-luminosity of the Self is intended to be immutable and non-dual, based on the statements regarding seeing and not seeing even during the waking state and so forth, by saying "even while seeing. Now, one might object: in that context, it would be more appropriate to say simply "seeing," and not "not seeing," otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of its being indistinguishable from deep sleep (*suṣupti*). To this, he replies: "so too" (*tathā*). Just as in deep sleep, the Self is likewise without distinction elsewhere as well.

The meaning is that because reasons such as being the seer, being changeless, and being of the nature of the Self are equally applicable [to both the intellect and the Self], it is never possible for the Self to be identified with the intellect, since the Self has the inherent nature of immutable vision (kūṭastha-dṛṣṭi). || 1493 || 1494 ||
And just as there is consciousness and non-destruction in one's own waking state, [so it is here].
In the same way, this [state] in the serene composure (saṃprasāda) is established due to the presence of the aforementioned reasons. || 1495 ||
1644 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

Even though the seeing and non-seeing have been described in relation to the waking state and so forth, it is more appropriate to say that one does not see during deep sleep; why then is it said that "one sees"?

Regarding this, he says: "Of the consciousness (citiḥ)," and the word "indestructibility" (avināśa) is the division [of the compound]. "As stated" means because of the reasons stated in the passage beginning with "because consciousness has no agent," namely, because these reasons always exist in the Self. The sense is that the establishment of specific distinctions occurs through the perception or non-perception of gross and subtle particularities belonging to ignorance (avidyā) during its various states. || 1499 ||
The statement of the reason, beginning with "no," serves to establish the meaning of the proposition.
And destruction, which is of two kinds, is negated by stating two reasons. (1496)

Having explained the statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*) in both readings and having restated the statement of the reason (*hetuvākya*), he states its meaning with the words "For not... (*na hi*). The meaning is that the statement beginning with "For not" (*na hi*) serves as the proof for the matter proposed in the proposition, namely, that "the Self is the immutable witness" (*ātma kūṭasthadṛṣṭiḥ*). Anticipating the objection that since the meaning of the proposition is established by a single reason alone, a further reason would be redundant, he says: "It is of two kinds" (*dviprakāraḥ*). || 1496 ||
The statement "for it is not so" refutes the view that its destruction is without remainder.
And here, the statement "indestructible" is also intended to deny any modification. || 1497 ||

Anticipating the doubt as to what two kinds of destruction there are, and which of them is negated by what, [the author] analyzes [the term] by saying "niranvaya" (without residue). This means [it is distinguished] by virtue of the two prefixes being reversed. He states the intended meaning of the phrase "because of its indestructibility" (*avināśitvāt*) by saying "and because it is indestructible" (*avināśīti ca*). The concealment of modification (*vikāra*) is contact with the cause; that is destruction with a remainder (*sāvaśeṣanāśa*), and [the indestructibility refers to] that which is connected to such [destruction].

Because the word "permanence" (śitvāt) is employed in this statement, the meaning is that the Self is an immutable witness (kūṭasthadṛṣṭi), since, like destruction without remainder, destruction with remainder is also impossible [for it]. || 1497 ||
In the *Maitreyī* [Brahmaṇa], the phrase "indestructible" (avināśī) serves to negate two kinds of destruction.
That very statement previously set forth is also presented here as the reason.

And he says that both types of destruction are refuted in the fourth [chapter] with the words "indestructible" (*avināśī*). If it is asked, "Since both types of destruction have already been prohibited in the passage 'Verily, this Self, O Maitreyī, is indestructible and of an imperishable nature' (*avināśī vā are'yam ātmā'nucchittidharmā*), why are they prohibited here?", he replies: "That very same... This statement from the fourth chapter is intended to establish the reason—namely, the absence of both types of destruction—for the proposition that "the Self is the immutable witness" (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭir ātmā*).
The meaning is that it has been drawn out by the mother. || 1498 ||
Because of being the witness of the self even when all things are annihilated, and because annihilation itself is impossible.
Likewise, there is the state of being the witness, consisting solely of the inner self, for all modifications. || 1499 ||

He states the reason for the absence of the soul’s destruction without residue (*niranvaya-nāśa*): "All," etc. Destruction without residue is the total cessation of the self; since the self is the witness (*sākṣin*), it does not possess that [destruction]. He states the reason for the absence of the soul’s destruction with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa-nāśa*): "And of cessation," etc. Cessation with remainder is destruction accompanied by a causal substrate (*hetu-saṃsarga*); such [destruction] is not possible for the self, because of the absence of a cause.
Furthermore, because it is the witness even therein, the meaning is that it is indeed eternally perceived. He states another reason for the absence of destruction with a remainder:
"In the same way. Since the individual self is the witness of all modifications, and because it is unchanging, there is no destruction consisting in contact with a cause;
this is the meaning. || 1499 ||
1 kha. 'kṣikaḥ || 1499 ||
Perceiving both the related and the unrelated, he remains here eternally steadfast.
Since these two do not exist, it is therefore established that the Self is characterized by unchanging vision.
He states the result regarding the impossibility of the self being divided into two parts: "Seeing," etc. (Verse 1900).
"Seeing, one does not see"—this is an independent scriptural statement.
The statement "no" is indeed an assertion that follows the sequence of the inferential statement. || 1501 ||
The statement of the reason, "because of its indestructibility," is for the purpose of establishing the meaning already stated.
Since it is stated that there is an absence of the capacity for destruction, there is no fallacy of being a part of the thesis (*pratijñaikadeśatā*). || 1502 ||

He analyzes the statement in another way, beginning with the words "perceiving," etc. The meaning is that a word in the form of scripture (*āgama*) does not require a logical reason (*hetu*), because it is an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the passage beginning with "for not," he states the intended division: "No. Just as, having made the proposition (*pratijñā*) "it possesses fire," one states the reason (*hetu*) "because it possesses smoke" to establish it, in the same way, having made the proposition that what is perceived is eternal, [one would state] its very...

The statement of the reason, "because it is indestructible" (*avināśitvāt*), is employed to establish what is already known by following the path of inference; thus, its meaning is that it serves as a means of proof (*sādhaka*) just like an inference. Anticipating the objection that for one who asserts the non-destruction of the vision of the Self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and then states the reason "because it is indestructible," there is a lack of distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*), he says: "vināśa... [etc.]. The proposition (*pratijñā*) is "it does not perish," and the reason is its "unfitness to perish"; therefore, there is no such [fallacy] here.
The meaning is that they have the same referent (*ekārthatā*). || 1101 || 1902 ||
Or, seeing two [types of] statements of a thesis, as expressed by the words "eternal" and so forth.
"No" and "because"—these two would be the respective replies to those two [objections]. (1503)
He states another way of classifying [the members of a syllogism] with the words "The proposition" (pratijñā) [at verse 1903].
He remains seeing; this is stated as a proposition for the sake of establishing [the following].
The statement "it is not the cause" is also a rebuttal to the subsequent argument. (1504)

He clarifies that very division with the words "even while seeing. This means that [the phrase] "he does not see the subsequent" refers to the statement "the subsequent [is not seen] because of its indestructibility. || 1904 ||
What is intended here to be refuted is destruction without a causal continuity (niranvayavināśa).
In the first statement of the reason, there is transformation; likewise in the subsequent ones. (1505)
Anticipating the objection that the two reasons have the same meaning, he says: "niranvaya" (without persistence). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "transformation is negated.
Or there are two reasons for the meaning as stated in both propositions.
Since, this being the case, the object would be established through the combination of these two. || 1506 ||

He states another method [of interpretation], saying "Or two," in order to apply two reasons to the two propositions (*pratijñā*). The meaning is: when it is stated that there are two types of objects as previously described—namely, those with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*) and those without remainder (*niravaśeṣa*). "Of the two" means of these two: "seeing" and "not seeing. In this view, the advantage—
He said: "By these two. That is to say, by these two causes existing together, he intended to show his own state of being a vision and his lack of destruction, having departed from the scriptures.

Since the object sought is accomplished from this [source], therefore the two reasons are to be applied to both propositions; thus, when the two statements are established, the meaning is that the self’s nature as immutable perception (*kūṭastha-dṛṣṭitva*) is proven. || 1906 ||
If it is argued that he remains right here while seeing, how can it be said [that he has departed]?
Listen to that statement "he does not see," exactly as it is. || 1507 ||

He takes up the passage beginning with "But not... following the necessary inquiry. Regarding the word "seeing": here, deep sleep (*supti*) is being discussed. By the pronoun "that" (*tat*), the statement of the sentence "he does not see" is referred to. || 1507 ||
That which previously occurred through delusion in the states of dream and waking;
That form which consists of causal agency does not exist here for that which is inward-facing. || 1508 ||
He explains the words and phrases introduced [in the previous verse]: "In the city," etc. That is to say, the characteristic of the subject (*pramātṛ*) consists of the factors of action (*kāraka*).
The locative case is as before. (1908)
"That which is a second [to the self] to the non-dual reality of the Self through ignorance,"
In deep sleep, that which is employed by its own respective objects does not exist here.

To the objection that the nature of the object perceived might indeed be real, he says: "of the Self. Anticipating the doubt as to why the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*), though rooted in ignorance (*āvidya*), does not exist even during deep sleep, he says: "employed. The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), accompanied by its reflection and endowed with instruments such as the ear, is designated by the term "knower" (*pramātṛ*); it functions when impelled by its own objects, such as sound. However, the impelling objects, such as sound, do not exist during deep sleep; therefore—
The meaning is that even the form of a mother does not exist there, even in the state of ignorance. || 1909 ||
That form of the self which is employed by its own kind and ends with the intellect.
In the wise person, that [suffering] caused by dharma and so forth is destroyed through the exhaustion of karma. || 1510 ||

In that very context, he states another reason: "By being of the same class," etc. The meaning is that the self's state of being a mother—which is brought about by the ear and other organs and caused by merit (dharma) and so forth—ceases therein, because at that time both the instrument (karaṇa) and the object (karman) have ceased. || 1910 ||
For that [unmanifest] is the second [cause], being the cause from the perspective of dissolution and the effect from the perspective of its manifested form.
Consequently, there is no apprehension of anything other [than itself], nor is there any distinct object to be grasped. || 1511 ||

He states another reason for the absence of the form of the knower during deep sleep (svāpa) with the words "from the end of darkness" (*tamontāt*). That form of the knower, designated as the second [state], being an effect, requires a cause; thus, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it arises from darkness accompanied by light (*sābhāsa*). However, in deep sleep, darkness is not manifest; therefore, the state of being a knower is not capable of manifestation there. This is the meaning. The phrase "other than that" (*tato'nyat*) is connected with the word "not" (*na tu*).
He states the combined meaning [of the verse] with the words "tataḥ" (therefore). This means that during deep sleep, there is no cognition of sound and so forth that is distinct from the Self.

He states the meaning of the individual words with the word "vibhaktam" (distinct/separated). The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that the collection of objects such as sound, which constitutes the "distinct," is also absent there. Therefore, because of the absence of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, the statement "he does not see" is applied in that context; this is the sense. || 1111 ||
Even in a dream, these three did not exist, since nothing remained but their mere names.
How much more so in deep sleep, wherein all duality has been utterly destroyed?
1 sva. ‘paṃ tatkāṃ | 2 gha. ‘yajñānaṃ triṃ | 3 ga. hetoḥ su | [vol 3, page 514] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1647.
Regarding the point that the triad beginning with the knower does not exist in deep sleep, he states the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument: "Even in dream... (1112).
That which remains here in deep sleep cannot be perceived as anything else, because of its immutability.
Even one who perceives something else does not exist here, because its cause is impossible.

If it is argued that even though such a self lacks the triad beginning with the *mātrā*, it is still the agent because it perceives their absence, [the author] says "no," beginning with the words "in deep sleep" (*suṣupte*).

The word "other" (*anya*) refers to the absence of the *mātrā*s and so forth. Anticipating the objection that although the self is not an agent due to its immutability (*kauṭasthya*), there exists another agent during sleep, he says "even that which... (*yo 'pi*). This means that the perceiver of the other—the non-self—is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Its cause—
The meaning is that because a cognizer is impossible [in that state], the cause is unmanifest ignorance, since it does not exist for him during deep sleep. || 1913 ||
The form of his own self was such that it was sufficient for a second viewing.
"That does not exist, nor does that second [entity] divided from it; therefore, one does not perceive [it].

(1514) He summarizes the meaning of the passage beginning with "But not... by means of the word "second" (*dvitīya*). That which is the form of the knower (*mātṛ-rūpa*) capable of perceiving non-self during the waking state and so forth—that does not exist in deep sleep. Therefore, the second—the collection of words and their referents in the form of the knower, as well as the knowledge thereof—does not exist at that time. Consequently...
The meaning is that one does not perceive a self. || 1514 ||
Or rather, that which is devoid of ignorance and without a second is intended by the term "eternal."
For one whose self is the single vision of the sun that has not yet risen, [the world] is devoid of burning heat. || 1515 ||

He states another meaning for the word "second" (*dvitīya*): "possessing ignorance" (*avidyāvat*). He provides the reason why it is intended that the second thing is the ignorance accompanied by appearance (*sābhāsa-ajñāna*) belonging to the Self, which is of the nature of immutable perception: "always" (*sadā*). The meaning is that because the Self consists of the single essence of immutable, self-luminous consciousness, the ignorance accompanied by appearance—which is distinct from that [Self]—is the "second. || 1919 ||
Neither darkness nor that which is born from it belongs to the Self, because of the absence of identity and non-existence [in relation to it].
Because of the contradiction regarding location, the supreme Self lacks the nature of cause and effect. || 1596 ||

Furthermore, let the "second" (dvitīya) be understood as ignorance or its effect; however, he states that the Self is never connected with it by saying, "tādātmya... (identity). He provides the reason why the second cannot be defined in relation to the Self through either difference or non-difference by saying, "virodha... (contradiction). Because there is a contradiction between the insentient and the sentient, and because we maintain that the Supreme is devoid of attributes, it is free from cause and effect.
The meaning is that, having done so, there is no second conjunction. || 1916 ||

That which is differentiated appears as if it were darkness, yet there is not even the slightest undifferentiated portion; because it is permeated by darkness, they perceive it as such, whereas in the wise, darkness is not perceived due to its absence.

If it is argued that "the second [state] is ignorance with appearance (*sābhāsamajñānam*)," [the author] replies with "But not... and so forth. How can there be a negation? For one might suspect that ignorance does not exist during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), as that would contradict the fact of waking up again; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Distinguished" (*vibhaktam*). That ignorance which appears through the distinction "I am ignorant"—though ultimately unreal—exists from the perspective of empirical cognition (*pratīti*) and is thus dealt with in two states. And in deep sleep, it is not known through such a distinction.

The meaning is that, for this reason, it is said that "this or that does not exist at that time. Furthermore, ignorance appears as belonging to one's own side (the subject), not as belonging to the other side (the object). [Note: Variants indicate *tu* for *na*, and *dhāddeśa* for *dhādeśa*.]
"And since there is no mother during sleep, it is appropriate to speak of her absence at that time"— thus he says "Darkness," relying on the perspective of those with a gross vision. (1117)
In that single, undivided, and immutably stable witness, [the world] appears in a thousand ways.
That which is divided from the vision [of the seer] by means of the distinctions of name-and-form and so forth—[is darkness]. (1518)
But that second [cause] does not exist here; darkness is the cause of misfortune.
Just as one might perceive [objects] during the waking state through the distinctions of forms such as the seer and so forth.
With reference to the word "second" (*dvitīya*) as denoting a cause, he states the meaning of the sentence: "The immutable," etc. Here, the term "here" refers to deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

The construction is as follows: just as in the waking state one perceives a second [object] by relying on the distinctions of the seer and so forth, so too in sleep; if one were to see a second [object] there by relying on those [distinctions], that [second object] does not exist here [in this state]. 1118 || 1119 ||
By the statement of the non-existence of ignorance and so forth, the immutable Self alone is being described.
For the cause is the non-existence of that entity here which is designated as the effect.
Fearing that, in the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects therein, the Self might thereby become possessed of duality (*sadvaya*), he says: "Of ignorance and so forth.

The reason for this is stated as: "Because of the cause. Since the appearance of nescience (*ajñāna*) is occasional and since it is sublated by knowledge, the reality known as its effect is non-existent;
its cause is nothing other than the immutable witness-consciousness (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭi*). For the immutable witness-consciousness does not [itself] possess existence or manifestation [as an object].

The meaning is that because there is something else [beyond this], there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*); the word "here" (*iha*) expresses one's own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*). || 1520 ||
"Just as there is no existence for anything that is not the Self other than through ignorance,"
In that same way, there is no cessation of the cause of that [bondage] other than through the realization of the Self.
To the question, "If the absence of ignorance and so forth is non-different from the Self, how can it possess the nature of a positive entity (bhāvatva)? he replies with the verse beginning "ajñānāt.
The meaning is: "of that cause," namely, of ignorance, which is the second cause [of bondage]. || 1121 ||
But that second thing, born of the cause of delusion, does not exist here as a reality at all.
It has become the object of the witness and is differentiated by way of its functional form. || 1522 ||
Furthermore, regarding deep sleep, [the author] states that there is no second entity, whether real or unreal; "not the first," he says, beginning with the word *tattviti*.
The reason for this is given as *moheti*: because the second [entity] arises from delusion (*moha*), it lacks substantial reality, according to the Śruti text, "Indra by means of his māyās.
He establishes its origin in delusion with the words *sākṣiṇa iti*: because it is an object of perception, because it is distinct, and because it is an effect—just like the rope-snake and so forth.
The meaning is that it arises from delusion, like [the fear of] a snake. || 1922 ||
Because [the world] is fully accomplished through consciousness alone, prior to the arising of the city of darkness (the objective world).
Darkness does not attain a second state, because the existence of anything other than itself is impossible.

He states another reason for the absence of a second entity during deep sleep (svāpa) with the words "by consciousness" (saṃvidā). The meaning is that because darkness and its products are resolved into pure consciousness alone, there is no second thing in deep sleep. Furthermore, regarding the second [alternative], one may choose between the option that this ignorance belongs to that [consciousness] or is produced by it; the first of these is refuted... [text fragment]. 1. In the case of the alternative (vapakṣe vā); 2. ka. kha. ...from that (dhāttatkā).
[Volume 3,
Page 516] [The Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the Commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
He concludes: "One obtains [the goal]. For there is no otherness for that indefinable darkness, nor is there a second thing in its absence; such is the meaning.
And because the effect, such as cognition and so forth, is not distinct from its cause.
That state of duality does not exist, because everything is fully encompassed by consciousness alone.
He states another alternative: "of the effect" (*kāryasya*). Furthermore, because a non-entity (*avastu*) is precisely a non-entity, it cannot have a second;

nor can an entity (*vastu*) have a second because it is precisely an entity. Therefore, one must state that neither the non-entity of ignorance (*ajñāna*), nor that which is produced from it, possesses a second, but rather that something else does.
And he says that this is not because of the absence of that [object], [but] "by consciousness" (saṃvidā). || 1924 ||
Therefore, for this reason, he said: "That entity does not exist here."
Whatever object that has come within the range of perception one might see, characterized by pleasure, sound, and so forth; || 1525 ||
Since the statement "that which one might see" refers to an object of action (karman), it is therefore the seer (draṣṭṛ) who is suspected [of being that object].
Therefore, there is no cause here for a perception that delineates an object.

He states the purport of the sentence regarding the meaning already expressed, beginning with the word "yataḥ" (since). According to the manner described, since in deep sleep only the immutable, non-dual consciousness alone remains, therefore the Śruti text beginning with "na tu" (but not) says that whatever external or internal object one might perceive does not exist here in the form of something to be seen. He provides the reason for referring to the subject as "yat paśyet" (whatever one might see) by stating "draṣṭā" (the seer). Regarding that...
By the word "tvit," he shows the connection. Regarding the phrase "tanna": in both instances, the meaning of the two locative endings (*saptamī*) is simply "sleep" (*supti*). || 1125 ||
For the internal organ is endowed with the instruments of hearing and so forth for the sake of perception.
The cause for perceiving external objects is not that imperishable [Self], because of its immutability.

If it is argued that the seer is denied in deep sleep, then the Self itself would be what is denied; for there is the Śruti text: "There is no other seer but this. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "The ear, etc. That [Self], together with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and equipped with the instruments of perception such as the ear, is the seer of sounds and so forth for the conscious Self (dṛgātman).

Since the cause [of perception] is transformed by way of being perceived, that imperishable [Self] is not accepted as the seer; for, by virtue of its immutable vision (*kūṭastha-dṛṣṭi*), it is not the agent of seeing.

The meaning is that the Śruti intends to show that this very [Self] is the witness (*sākṣitā*) with respect to the modifications of the mind—such as form and so forth—which occur through the doors of the eyes and other senses and are designated by terms like "seeing. || 1527 ||
The Seer, whose limit is the internal organ, is the cause of that internal organ up to its very end.
One is happy or miserable within the body due to the cause of ignorance regarding the innermost Self. || 1528 ||

To the objection that this would constitute an abandonment of the established tenet (*apasiddhānta*) because it accepts distinctions such as those between the mother and so forth, he says: "The end of darkness. The meaning is this: the inner self (*pratyagātman*), being the limit of ignorance, becomes the seer bounded by the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is the root cause of the intellect and so on—and the agent bounded by the body; thus, through beginningless ignorance, the Self itself remains as the cause and so forth. For one who maintains this position, there is no suspicion of abandoning the established tenet.

1 gha. The two points are pure consciousness (cinmātra). 2 gha. [The reading] "mānta". 3 kha. There is nothing else. 4 kha. That which is to be negated. 5 gha. Negated. 6 gha. Appearing within. 7 gha. And not further. 207
In the production of the intellect and the rest, dharma and so forth alone are the cause here.
Therefore, when the cause is destroyed, that which consists of cognition and so forth ceases, because it has the self as its cause. (1529)

He states another reason for the absence of the subtle body (mātra) and so forth during deep sleep: "And because of the intellect, etc. Here, the word "here" refers to the Self. That which arises from ignorance—namely, merit (dharma) and so forth—is the instrumental cause for the production of the intellect and its derivatives within the Self. He explains how, by that much alone, there is an absence of the subtle body and so forth during sleep: "Since," and so on. Because merit and the rest, born of ignorance, are the cause of the intellect and its derivatives, therefore [there is an absence of them] when those [merits] are not manifest.
The meaning is that when those two have been destroyed there, the intellect and so forth—which are incapable of existing separately—go toward the Self, which was previously unknown. 1929.
The sequence of darkness is logically applicable only to the effects of darkness, such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth.
But not so in this case, where there is no effect without a cause, regarding the Supreme Self who is perceived as eternal.

Fearing that if the self were not associated with ignorance, then ignorance would only be associated with the pure self—just as [ignorance] is associated with the intellect (buddhi) and so forth—he says: "The association with darkness.
He states the meaning of the particle *eva* (only): "But not... In that regard, he states the reason for the non-association with darkness: "Eternal... (113).
And it acquires its activity in its effect, not from anything other than its own cause.
In view of the inward-turned state [of consciousness], there exists neither effect nor cause. || 1531 ||

Anticipating the objection that "even though darkness does not inhere in the other [the Self], it might nevertheless inhere there through its connection with the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth," he says: "And the function (*vṛtti*)," etc. First of all, ignorance cannot reside in the unknown Self, because that would entail the absurdity of [ignorance] having itself as its own locus; nor can an effect exist elsewhere than in its cause. Thus, the intellect and the rest also do not possess that [inherence]. Consequently, if you do not admit ignorance and so on even in the isolated Self, how [could they exist]?

Anticipating the objection that [ignorance] must therefore be dependent on that [Self], he says: "No. The meaning is that although ignorance and so forth do not actually arise there [in the Self] following the behavior of the internal organ (*pratīcaḥ*), independence is impossible [for ignorance]; and since no other substratum is observed, just as a lump of ghee [rests upon] fire, ignorance and so forth would have to rest upon the Self itself.
Of this deluded person, who perceives pleasure, sound, and so forth as the end of his intellect.
When [the cognition] is destroyed due to the exhaustion of its own causes, the self does not perceive, even though it is capable of seeing. || 1532 ||
He states what follows from this in the present context, even though the absence of the senses and so forth [is common] during sleep: "Of that which ends with the intellect" (*buddhyantasya*).

Since the manifest ignorance (*vyaktājñāna*)—which is the cause of the senses and so forth—is destroyed in sleep, the Self, although self-luminous by virtue of its nature as consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is said not to see because that [ignorance] has also been extinguished at that time. This is the meaning. || 1532 ||
That which is divided by ignorance through the distinctions of being a seer and so forth;
It has been swallowed by the immutable Self, just as a snake is [swallowed] by a rope. || 1533 ||

[Objection: Is the destruction of the subtle body (mātrā) and so forth at that time with a remainder or without a remainder? In the first case, it is incorrect to say "due to the exhaustion of its own cause"; in the second case, a re-emergence would be impossible. To this, he says: "Because [the Self] is the seer," and so on. The statement regarding the absence of causes during deep sleep is intended to mean the absence of manifest ignorance; therefore, because the division into the subtle body and so forth is withdrawn into the Self which is [then] unmanifested, the destruction is with a remainder.

This is the meaning. He states an illustration for how the dissolution of the objects of measurement (mātrādi) occurs within one's own self by means of that cause which has the immutable Brahman as its Self: "As with a rope," etc. || 1533 ||
1 Kha cāsti | [Vol.
3, page 518] 3 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1651
Therefore, no relationship between the seer, the seeing, and the seen is perceived.
Because it has dissolved into darkness, one who is possessed by darkness does not perceive the effect of ignorance. || 1534 ||

To the question, "Since the self is in deep sleep due to its connection with the *mātrās* (subtle elements) and so forth, why is that connection denied there? he replies with the word "dṛṣṭi" (perception). He states the reason expressed by the word "ataḥ" (therefore): "tamasvinaḥ" (of one enveloped in darkness). The meaning is that because there are no *mātrās* and so forth distinct from the cause [the Self], and because that [cause] is not manifested at that time. He states the conclusion regarding the non-existence of the *mātrās* and their connection with it during deep sleep: "nāvidyā" (not ignorance).
That is to say, at that time one does not perceive ignorance and its effects. || 1534 ||
The distinction between the seer, the seeing, and the seen is imagined through ignorance.
Therefore, being destroyed by delusion, the seer and so forth are not perceived within the self. || 1535 ||

He concludes the explanation of the passage beginning with "That which it does not see," etc., with the words "the seer. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "the seen, etc.," [the categories] such as "the slayer" and "the slain" are included. || 1535 ||
One should establish what has been stated in the subsequent statements as well.
This alone is the explanation; nothing else remains beyond this.

He extends by analogy what was stated in the passage beginning with "that which one does not smell" (*yadvai tanna jighrati*). He says, "In the subsequent [passages]. He states the reason for this extension:
"The explanation [is the same]. || 1536 ||
Others, however, interpret this text in a manner entirely different from what has been stated.
For they explain it through their commentaries, and that too is being analyzed here. || 1537 ||

Having stated his own explanation of the passage beginning with "That which indeed," he introduces the explanation of Bhartṛprapañca with the words "Others, however. He explains how that well-known interpretation is otherwise by saying "And that... (1937).
Having set aside the statements of the prima facie position by means of the statements of the refutation in due order.
The wise one declared that the state of the Seer exists as pure light within the Prājña. || 1538 ||

In order to demonstrate the process of elimination (*vibhāvana*), he recounts the narrative: "Having cast aside," etc. Having sequentially rejected the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) by means of the refutations beginning with self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣva*), the Sage has stated that the Self, which is vision (*dṛgātman*), abides in the state of deep sleep as pure light (*jyotirmātra*).
The meaning is "or. || 1138 ||
Having clearly established by means of logical arguments that the self-luminous [Self] exists in deep sleep, |||
Now, why does even a wise person not perceive such an intrinsic nature? || 1539 ||
The subsequent passage is introduced for the purpose of dispelling this doubt.
And its explanation is clearly discerned by the lords of the yakṣas exactly as it is. || 1540 ||

To explain how [the Self] exists as pure light, he says: "Having established... The construction is as follows: having clearly established by means of the previously stated arguments that the Self is self-luminous in the dream state, the Sage declared its existence as pure light in deep sleep. Having recapitulated what has occurred, he speaks of the manner in which the passage beginning with "That which indeed" was introduced, starting with the word "Now" (*atha*), in order to fulfill the expectation [of the inquiry].
Having reminded the opponent of the relationship already restated previously, he promises an explanation of the words of the passage. By means of that—
[vol 3, page 519] 1652 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Chapter]...

Regarding the word "khyānam" (explanation): the particle *ca* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The meaning of the word *hi* is that this explanation is well-known among his disciples.
That you do not see [it]—thus you have excessive doubt regarding the Self.
Therefore, do not be afraid; for here, O wise one, the Self is seen abiding.

He clarifies that very point with the words, "For indeed, not... If it is argued that the Self does not see during deep sleep, [the reply is: no, for if its nature were light, it would be insentient; thus, you should not entertain the doubt that you suspect regarding the Self, because the meaning is that the Self remains there even while seeing. For it has been stated: "At that time, this one exists even while seeing. || 141 ||
Thus, for now, that which exists in reality should be perceived through scripture and reasoning.
Because it does not see, it cannot be seen again, due to the impossibility of a cause. || 1542 ||

He says "it is so" (ittham) to show that the Self exists in both ways during sleep—both seeing and not seeing—in accordance with scripture. "Jyotirmātrasvabhāvaḥ" means having the nature of pure light. "Paśyan" is the scriptural statement; "the consequence of insentience being non-self," etc., is the reasoning. He states the exclusion with "no" (na). 1542.
And furthermore, a distinguished knowledge regarding this arises here for him.
"Seeing, one does not see"—thus two meanings of the term have been stated. (1543)
To reveal that [truth], the supreme treatise is now commenced in its proper sequence.
For it is understood with ease that "the seer is not [the agent]," and so forth. || 1544 ||

If it is argued that the scriptural statement "he does not see" itself is the reason, to that he says: "as having a distinction" (*viśeṣavat*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "therefore, the scriptural statement 'he does not see' [is qualified]. As they have said: "And no specific cognition of this [Self] manifests. Having restated what has preceded, he introduces the subsequent sentence with the words "seeing" (*paśyan*). The passage beginning with "for not" (*na hi*) is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the term "seeing" as it was stated; it is not [the case that] "he does not see," as previously stated.

The meaning is that [the phrase] beginning with "na tu" was stated for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the word "artha. Alternatively, in the view that the explanation of the word "paśyan" begins with "na hi," he states that the meaning of the words of the sentence appears clearly. He says "na hi.
Furthermore, the meaning is that the natural clarity of those words is equal even in the case where the explanation of "na paśyati" begins with "na tu. || 143 || 144 ||
The seer, the agent of the act of seeing, the conscious self, is the person here.
And after that, there is the consciousness of form and so forth, which have been grasped by the intellect. || 1545 ||

He states the meaning of the term "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*): "The seer," he says. In common worldly usage, the individual soul (*jīva*)—the agent of the action consisting of seeing forms and so forth which are objects of the intellect—is called the "seer.

This person is the agent of the act of seeing; the meaning of the statement "he is the knower" is that he is the cognizer of the form manifested by the act of seeing and presented by the intellect. When his status as the agent of seeing occurs due to the completeness of its causes, then, in the immediately following moment, [the result] obtains its locus.
He says, "And consciousness," [meaning] that consciousness arises with respect to objects such as form through the doors of the eye and so forth. || 1941 ||
And even there, because the activity of cognition takes the form of the grasped and the grasper.
[This arises] from the object of cognition such as a jar, which consists of an action produced prior [to the cognition]. || 1546 ||
Even in the accomplishment of another action, the person remains the observer therein.
In that case, the power of cognition in the person is that which conforms to [the object's] form and other qualities.

He states that it is not only the self that is the agent of cognition, but also the agent of its fruit, which is experience (*saṃvedana*). To this effect he says: "In that case also. When the self is the agent of seeing and the knowledge of the object has arisen, because the mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*)—which is the knowledge having the self as its agent—is of the nature of a grasper with respect to the object of grasp such as sound and so forth, there arises from that first-occurring knowledge in the form of an action, directed toward an object such as a jar, another action which is experience.

In the arising of that fruit as well, the living self (jīva) is understood to be the agent. For it has been stated there too that, because of the relationship between the cognition (buddhi-pratyaya) and the jar or other object by way of the grasped and the grasper, when another action is accomplished, it is the seer alone [who acts]. The meaning is that the self is the agent of both that knowledge and its experience. To the question, "How can the self be the seer if the power of seeing belongs to the intellect (buddhi) alone? he says: "The power of vision... (dṛk-śakti).

The meaning is that the capacity for being the agent of the cognition and experience of sound and so forth resides in the Self, because such [agency] is impossible for that which is insentient (*jaḍa*). As it has been stated there: "In that Person (*puruṣa*), the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) is connected with the apprehension of form and so forth. (1946–1547)
The state of action, residing in the knower, has the self of consciousness as its sole agent.
For that vision and its activity always belong to the nature of the seer. (1548)
In this state, not even the slightest loss of the seer is found.
Because the qualities (guṇas) conform to the persistence of the possessor of qualities, like fire and its burning [they do not exist apart from him].

(1549) He states the result regarding the Self’s status as the seer: "The action" (kriyā). The meaning is that the state consisting of the action called the "cognition of knowledge" has the individual soul (jīva) as its agent and is dependent upon it. As they say: "That state of the act of seeing which is subordinate to the conscious self (vijñānātman) resides in the agent."

Having explained the two words "of the seer" (*draṣṭuḥ*) and "of seeing" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*), he explains the remainder [of the verse] with the words "of that" (*tasyāḥ*). The particle *hi* indicates the reasoning that will be stated hereafter. To the objection—"If seeing were a property of the seer, then even though the seer is imperishable, why would seeing not perish?"—he replies with the word "the possessor of qualities" (*guṇī*). Just as the burning of fire lasts as long as the fire exists, so too do the qualities persist in accordance with the duration of the possessor of those qualities.

The meaning is "as long as it exists in the possessor of the quality" (*yāvadguṇibhāvitva*). And it has been said: "For qualities exist as long as the possessor of the quality exists; as long as there is fire, so long is there heat. (1948 || 1949)
Since this is so, therefore, as long as the self— the seer— does not perish.
There would not yet be total annihilation, because the seer is seen based on that [basis]. (1550)

He applies the general principle to the present case with the words "yataḥ" (since). As it has been stated: "As long as there is a seer, so long is there seeing"—this constitutes non-extinction. || 1550 ||
It is held that by the destruction of one possessing virtues, even his virtue is destroyed.
If it is argued that [the self] is like the heat of fire and so forth, we say no, because this seer is indestructible. || 1551 ||

He raises the objection that, in that case, vision must perish along with the self, using the phrase "it is held" (*matam*). The meaning is that just as heat and other qualities perish when their substratum, such as fire, perishes, so too vision—which is a quality of the self—perishes through the destruction of the self. He refutes this with the commentary's statement, "For the seer is eternal," and the scriptural citation, "There is no seer other than him. (1551)
1 ga. One hundred and fifty-one.
Therefore, he says: "Because of its imperishability, the seer is always unconditioned by seeing. (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika, Caturthādhyāya, 1654)
It is not fitting for the self to perish, as is the case with a jar or similar objects. || 1552 ||

He introduces a scriptural passage as the reason for the indestructibility of the seer (*draṣṭṛ*). [The word] "therefore" (*ataḥ*) means: since the indestructibility of the seer is intended, the scripture states the reason, "because of its being indestructible. And because there is no destruction of the seer, vision (*dṛṣṭi*) always exists for the Self (*ātman*), since it is impossible to even suspect its destruction along with the seer—this is the meaning. [Objection: If the Self is indestructible, how can it be said to be "indestructible"? (This refers to the redundancy of the term.)
Anticipating the objection that "the reason is not distinct from the probandum," he says: "to perish. As they have said: "For its nature is not found to be such that it can perish. (1112)
Why does it not perish? Let the reason for this be stated here.
Because it is the self of all and because it is one, no destruction of the seer exists. || 1553 ||
He states the meaning of the question "Why? with the word "No. He provides the answer with the commentary: "Because of being the self of all, because of non-duality. [1953]
Because its destruction is suspected on account of that [non-perception], it follows that there is no distinction between them.
Its destruction is not possible, because there is no distinction between the destroyer and the destroyed.
Furthermore, as for the destruction of the Self—whether by something other than itself or by itself—it cannot be the former; thus he says: "By which...

He clarifies the very reason already stated—that there is no difference between the Self, which is intended as the destroyer, and that which is intended as the instrument of destruction: "Of the destroyer...
Here, the word "destruction" (*nāśa*) refers to the destroyer. As they say: "For by what second thing other than this [Self] could its destruction be suspected?"
That does not exist, because it is non-different from that. || 1554 ||
Furthermore, it is not logically possible for that very thing to be destroyed by that very same thing.
Regarding the subject of the non-duality of the single self, it is just as [the distinction between] fire and fuel. || 1555 ||
He says "not the second" [in response], stating "and not. He clarifies the impossibility by means of a dissimilar example: "In duality," etc.
When there is a distinction between fire and fuel, as the relationship of the destroyer and the destroyed is observed, so it is not possible in the case of identity; for in the case of identity—

The meaning is that the state of being an object depends upon a distinction [between subject and object]. As it has been said: "And there can be no destruction of something by that very same thing. (1155)
Therefore, because the seer is indestructible, the eternal subject is eternal.
Like a ray of the sun, even the vision is imperishable.

He states the result regarding the non-destruction of the self, both from its own nature and from another: "of the seer" (*draṣṭuḥ*). This means: "the seer being thus eternal. As it has been said: "Because of its indestructibility, it is eternal; for that eternal seer, the eternal quality of vision remains ever-abiding. (1556)
Always established, he perceives with an eternal vision that is never lost.
The one intended here is the witness who remains even while this [world] is blazing in deep sleep. || 1557 ||

In accordance with this commentary (*ṭīkā*), it is inferred that in the root text, the phrase "because of its imperishability" (*tato'vināśitvāt*) should be read as "thus, because of its imperishability" (*tathā'vināśitvāt*).
1. ka, ga: "is said" (*ucyate*); saṃ; 2. kha: "establishes" (*sādhayati*); 3. gha: "is suspected" (*āśaṅkyate*).
[Vol. 3, page 522]
If it is argued that nothing follows from the eternity of the vision, he says in response: "It is eternal. As it has been stated: "He remains seeing with that vision which is ever-present. || 1557 ||
Thus, for now, it remains as previously stated: "perceiving [the object] while remaining [in that state]."
That which was well-stated as "it does not see" is now being further elaborated. || 1558 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "thus it stands" with the word "evam" (thus). He states the meaning of the *bhāṣya* passage beginning with "na" etc., which takes up [the discussion] in order to determine the second category (*padārtha*). || 1558 ||
"One does not see this which is to be seen"—this is what was previously set forth in the aphorism.
If one remains while actually seeing, how could that be possible? || 1559 ||

Anticipating the objection that there is no weakness in the initial proposition beginning with "no" (na), so what is the purpose of elaborating upon it, [the author] states the meaning of the commentary—"He does not see"—in response to the question: "If he remains while indeed seeing, why does he not see? || 1119 ||
Listen also to how all this occurs; it shall now be explained.
Behold, this very person sits here due to the reliance upon prior causes. || 1560 ||

He introduces the passage beginning with "But not... while explaining the meaning of how one sees and yet does not see. The construction is as follows: "Listen; all that is being told so that it may be understood how it is possible that 'one who sees does not see'—listen to that reality. By restating what was previously established, he states the meaning of the phrase "first of all, this [Self] sees": "One who sees," etc. [This refers to] its state of being eternal vision.
The cause. || 1560 ||
That second thing, by depending upon which [the world] is to be seen, does not exist here.
The manifestation of specific cognition is intended [to occur] on the waking stage. || 1561 ||

Anticipating the objection as to how, then, one does not see, he states the meaning of the Bhāṣya: "In that [state], there is no second thing, through connection with which specific cognition might arise. The word "here" refers to the state of deep sleep. || 1961 ||
But surely there is indeed something to be seen, because [the object] consists of both duality and non-duality.
Please explain how there is nothing to be seen for this Brahman.
That which is divided should be seen as such; it is not undivided as previously described. || 1562 ||

Now, one might object: "If the subject matter were both dualistic and non-dualistic, then the objection that 'the divided [world] must indeed be seen' would certainly hold. Anticipating this, the author refutes it by stating that because seeing is impossible, one does not see. He introduces this with "nanu" (now). The response is given in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) with the words "syād vibhaktam na tv anyatvataḥ" (it may be divided, but not by way of otherness), followed by "draṣṭavyam" (that which is to be seen).
That is to say, the world can only be "that which is to be seen" if it is distinct from the seer; it cannot be so if it is merely that [seer] itself. However, in deep sleep, it is as has been stated.

The meaning is that by this [verse], it has been explained that Brahman alone, which consists of both difference and non-difference, is to be seen as the world; thus, statements such as "existence is other than that" and so forth are accounted for. || 1962 ||
If the object of sight were different from the seer, then it would exist as something distinct [from him].
Then one might see it as divided, but in this case, it does not exist that way at all. || 1563 ||
1 gha. Therefore, he says: 2 kha. It is said: [Vol. 3, page 523] 1656 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya—]

For if there were something else distinct from that, one would perceive it; however, [the Bhāṣya] states, "there is no second. Explaining this while elaborating on what was said, he says: "yadi" (if). Here, the word "iha" (here) refers either to his own established doctrine or to deep sleep. || 1963 ||
He remains here as if seeing, because of the perpetual non-existence of anything to be seen.
One is called a "seer" because one does not see, and not because of the destruction of vision. (1564)

Therefore, because the power of seeing exists, one remains as if seeing, yet does not reach the object of sight; for this reason, one does not perceive it—stating the meaning of the commentary in this way, he concludes the two propositions with the words "paśyan" (seeing). 1964.
Just as a blazing fire does not consume fuel that has not been placed within it.
In the same way, the seer here burns; he perceives the visible object as something not truly attained. || 1565 ||

Just as fire, even while blazing, does not burn what is not placed upon it, so too—relying on this statement from the *Bhāṣya*—he establishes the point by means of an example. "While blazing" (*jvalan*): the locative case here signifies the sphere of conventional activity (*vyavahārabhūmi*). || 1165 ||
Those of keen intellect who possess faith attend upon this exposition.
Because it stands outside of both reason and scripture, the wise do not worship it.
Having presented the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca, [the author] indicates its flawed nature while showing how it might be held in esteem by those of dull intellect.
He states that its flaw consists in its being something to be disregarded by the wise, saying: "The reasoning... (verse 1166).
And just as this [view] is incoherent and does not rely on logical reasoning or scriptural authority, so too is it untenable.
Thus it has been stated many times before, and it is being stated now as well.

To the question, "How can this be disregarded as being outside the scope of reason and scripture? he says: "Just as... The meaning is that this [view] has been taught by those who assert that the Self is the immutable witness (*kūṭasthadṛṣṭi*) as being defective, and it will be demonstrated as such. If so, for what purpose is this restated now?
To this he says: "Even now... The statement regarding its defectiveness in that explanation is for the purpose of dispelling the delusion that it is correct.
Such is the meaning. || 1967 ||
This very Self remains here in this state of deep sleep as if seeing.
Thus, the reason "this belongs to you alone" has been stated here. || 1568 ||

What, then, is the refutation being stated? To express that, he restates the opponent's position with the words "paśyan" (seeing). The meaning is as follows: since the Self indeed remains seeing even during deep sleep, and thus its vision is not destroyed—here, by the phrase beginning with "na hi" (for not), the reason is stated that because there is no destruction of the seer, there is likewise no destruction of the vision. || 1568 ||
And no other distinct knowledge arises for him.
This is stated to be the explanation of the sentence "he does not see. || 1569 ||
He restates the explanation of the alternative proposition: "And not," etc. (1969).
If it is argued that "it is while seeing indeed," this refers to the true nature of the object.
By the statement "the reality is thus," how can a dualistic activity be expressed? || 1570 ||
1 gha. because of that; 2 na. to say; 3 kha. what for the seer?
[Vol.
3, page 524] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri: 1657.

Regarding the explanation of the phrase "seeing" (*paśyan*): does this state that the Self has vision as its nature (*dṛṣṭirūpatā*), or does it state that it is the agent of that [vision]? To refute the first position, he says: "seeing" (*paśyan*). If the essential nature of the inner self (*pratyak*) were stated by the term "seeing" to have the characteristic of vision, then the inner self would be of such a reality—having vision as its very essence—and not the agent of it; therefore, by the statement "of vision" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*) in the passage beginning with "for not" (*na hi*), etc.,...
The meaning is that the action, which consists of the form of seeing, cannot be said to belong to a self that is the agent of seeing. || 1970 ||
If it is argued by you that the perception of an action is dependent upon the perceiver;
How can its destruction be prevented when it possesses the nature of an action? || 1571 ||
Having restated the second [position], he replies with the word "draṣṭṛ" (the seer). For action would indeed be sublated because it possesses the nature of action, just like motion;
thus, there would be a contradiction with prohibitions such as "for [the Self] does not... (na hi...). This is the intended meaning. || 1171 ||
If the status of being a seer is attributed to the agent of false views, then the seer is asserted to be the seer.
Likewise, when there is manifestation, there is the nature of action belonging to that which is non-existent as an action.
Furthermore, does the Self produce a vision that already exists or one that does not? Regarding this, he refutes the first position with the words "abhūtā" (as non-existent).

If it were the agent with respect to a vision that is non-existent—that is, one that has not come into being—it would be possible for the seer to possess the status of a seer; however, the Self is not able to produce that which already exists, because a vision that already exists, by virtue of its very existence, cannot be an object of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). Therefore, the first alternative is not established. He states another reason for that same point:

Regarding the term "manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*): just as a seer possesses the status of a seer by being the agent with respect to a non-existent act of seeing, so too the status of an act is established for a manifestation that is itself non-existent; therefore, the meaning is that the seer does not produce an existent vision. Furthermore, the second alternative is not tenable, because it is impossible to produce a non-existent vision—such as a hare's horn—as there is no means of accomplishing it. || 1172 ||
Vision is produced by the seer, yet it is not destroyed.
Thus, by one's own words alone, this is stated in contradiction [to itself]. (1573)

The view that the self is the agent of seeing and that seeing is its activity has been refuted. As for the argument that because the agent of seeing is imperishable, its quality—seeing—does not perish, to that he says: "And by the seer," etc. (1173).
And if the eternality of the effect were established on the basis of scriptural statement, [then what of it?]
It follows that the word lacks the status of a means of valid cognition because it is a causal agent. || 1574 ||

He raises an objection regarding the resolution of the contradiction based on the passage beginning with "na hi draṣṭuḥ" (For there is no seer...). Regarding the phrase "kāryasya" (of the effect): having proposed the alternatives that the sentence either produces or makes known the eternality of what is produced, he states the fault in the first case: "vacanasya" (of the word). || 1174 ||
All means of valid cognition are illuminators, and they [illuminate] only an already established entity.
"Because of the previous connection with the means of valid cognition, there is a relationship between the manifested and the manifestor. (1575)

To the objection, "Even if it is a causal factor (*kāraka*), why could it not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?", he says: "The means of valid cognition... To the question, "Even if it is a revealer (*bodhaka*), why could it not be a causal factor?", he says: "And that... He states the reason for the principle that "a means of valid cognition is that which reveals what is already established prior to its connection with the instrument of knowledge": "Because it is to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*)," and so on; the remainder of the argument is that it depends upon an existing object, as is observed in the case of a lamp and a jar.
208 [Vol. 3, page 525] 1658 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Chapter]
It follows that this statement contradicts inference.
Because there is an inseparable connection between impermanence and being produced. || 1576 ||

He states the second [objection]: "By inference," etc. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to combine this with the contradiction of such scriptural passages as "Just as here, by the performance of action... He states the reason for the contradiction with inference: "Because of the inseparable connection," etc. (1976).
The claim that "two categories have been presented" is altogether untenable.
Since this [statement] "because one does not see" is restated, something else is being conceptualized.

It has already been refuted that the vision, even when being performed by the self, does not perish. As for the statement that two distinct entities are described—namely, "seeing" and "not seeing"—he rejects that with the word "dvau" (two). The reason for this difficulty is stated with the word "yataḥ" (since). || 1177 ||
Because it has already been attained, the statement "he does not see" does not bring about the understanding of a previously unknown fact.
Having restated "he does not see," it is therefore enjoined that "he sees. || 1578 ||

Regarding how the aforementioned relationship between the restated (anuvāda) and the enjoined (vidheya) applies there, he says: "No," and so forth. Since the absence of seeing is already established during deep sleep, the statement "he does not see" does not inform us of an unknown fact; rather, having restated the non-seeing ("he does not see"), the seeing—which was not previously established—is enjoined by "he sees.
Thus, the meaning is that there is no possibility of two distinct referents [in the same sentence]. || 1178 ||
Or rather, this is an explanation of the word "paśyan" (seeing) for the purpose of negating its status as a causal agent.
The statement "he does not see" is not intended to express a different meaning [than the mere absence of seeing]. || 1579 ||

For this reason as well, he states that there are not two distinct entities: "of the word 'paśyan' (seeing)," etc. The word *vā* has the sense of an alternative, [indicating] the relationship between the explanation and the explained through the status of the restated (*anūdya*) and the predicated (*vidheya*). When "seeing" is mentioned, the state of being the agent of cognition is implied; in order to negate that, it is said "he does not see.
