The meaning is that there is no independent second entity there; thus, there are not two entities. || 1179 ||
Is this person called a "seer" because of the activity of seeing?
Or rather, what kind of entity consisting of vision is intended here as "the seer"? || 1580 ||
However, in order to refute the claim that "the seer is the agent of the act of seeing," he reflects as follows: "What [is it]? (1180).
First of all, the self-entity cannot be the agent of seeing because of its immutability.
And I have already stated numerous times the reasons that establish [the soul's] immutability. (1581)

He states the fault in the first [position] with the words "not, firstly. Anticipating the objection that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*), he says "by immutability" (*kauṭasthya*). The reason consists of being partless (*asaṅgatva*) and so forth. || 1981 ||
Because the nature of action and its agent exists only as dependent upon conditions.
Therefore, it cannot be an agent, because it is a witness to those things that possess activity.
And because there is no entity other than the Self, it does not possess the status of being the agent of seeing; thus he says, "Action" (*kriyā*). The two ablative cases are in apposition.

He states another reason for that very point: "And because of its being a witness" (*sākṣitvāt*). For one who is a witness of an agent is not capable of becoming an agent himself—this is the meaning. || 1982 ||
1 1 ka. na. cita | 2 ga. dapi du | [vol 3, page 526]
The self is not the cognizer of form and other objects apprehended by the intellect.
Its state of being an enjoyer here also occurs by way of the manifestation of consciousness. (1583)

If it is claimed that the object consisting of vision is intended by the word "seer," then it would not be acceptable that the self of form and other objects apprehended by the intellect is the agent of the act of seeing; thus, he refutes the second [position] with the word "buddhi" (intellect). The particle "ca" (and) is used for emphasis and follows immediately after the negation. The agency of the intellect has already been rejected regarding the self. As for the claim that the self is the seer in the accomplishment of another action, there too, it is merely the person (puruṣa).

Regarding this, he says: "The state of being an enjoyer. The meaning is that the Self's status as an enjoyer is intended with respect to objects such as sound, which are pervaded by the modifications of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) and thus permeated by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa); likewise, just as the Self is not the agent of the intellect's activity, it is also not the agent of the results thereof.
"This state of having a form similar to lac-dye and so forth is a modification of the gem itself;
it is not considered a modification of the lac-dye and such, because they are devoid of activity. (1584)
Regarding the question of how the conscious self (cidātman) does not undergo modification when objects such as sound take on the form of consciousness, he says: "Of the gem...
The reason for the negation [of modification] is that the gem’s assumption of that form is independent of any action [on its part]. || 1984 ||
It does not undergo modification for the sake of establishing [qualities] such as redness.
Just as lac-dye and the like [pervade] everywhere, so indeed does the reality of the self.

Having restated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states the point to be illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*): "Because of being red," and so forth. The meaning is that just as lac-dye and the like do not undergo any modification in order to establish the redness of a gem and so on in all cases, so too the reality of the Self (*ātmavastu*), when pervaded by the mental mode (*dhīvṛtti*) [of cognition], does not undergo modification even when it takes on the form of consciousness (*cidākāra*) through words and other objects. || 1585 ||
Furthermore, conformity to the persistence of qualities is not observed everywhere.
The quality of blackness in the hair disappears even though the hair itself remains present.

Having refuted the self's agency regarding knowledge and its fruits, [the author] now refutes the claim that the qualities (guṇas) conform to the persistence of the possessor of qualities (guṇin), stating: "The possessor of qualities... (verse 1186).
Even you do not accept the absolute destruction of fire.
Nor is heat perceived in wood and the like, even though fire exists there. (1587)

Regarding the argument that it is "like the burning of fire," he says: "Of fire. The meaning is that since fire exists in such things as fire-sticks and gems, its production [from those alone] would otherwise be impossible. Nevertheless, what follows from this in the present case? He says: "And not... The implication is that, therefore, this is not an appropriate illustration for the principle that qualities must follow the existence of their substratum. || 1987 ||
Let it be granted that the nature of the qualities conforms to their persistence.
What comes to the seer from seeing? Seeing is an action, not a quality. (1588)

In this regard, one might suspect that fire is not perceived precisely because its qualities, such as burning, are not perceived; however, when that [fire] is perceived, those [qualities] would also be perceived, and thus it would follow as a certainty that qualities must conform to the existence of the possessor of qualities (the *guṇin*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "The possessor of qualities... [and so on]. If it is argued that the existence of that [possessor of qualities] will necessarily persist as long as there is a perceiver, he says: "Action... || 1988 ||
1660 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
This is the inherent nature of causal factors— that they proceed without having performed [their prior functions].
The reality of action is said to be existence in such a way as it was not previously. || 1589 ||

If it is argued that action (*kriyā*) also exists only as long as there is a perceiver, he says "no," [introducing the verse] beginning with "of the causal factors" (*kārakāṇām*). Having stated the non-eternality of action by examining the nature of the causal factors, he states its lack of eternality by defining the very essence of action itself.
As for the phrase "just as": just as coming into being after not having been, so too is passing out of being after having been the essential nature of action; how, then, could it be eternal?
This is the meaning. || 1989 ||
The quality and the action do not necessarily conform to the duration of the substance.
Because even when a substance exists in this world, deviation [from its expected properties] is observed. || 1590 ||

He concludes that seeing, whether it be a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*), does not exist as long as the seer exists. [The word] "as long as" [is used]. Therefore, even if seeing is a quality or an action, it does not exist as long as the seer exists; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 1990 ||
Because of the negation of birth, action, qualities, and so forth, the reality of the self [is established].
"That which is not gross," "not this, not this"—by these [negations], everything other than the inward Self is denied. (1591)
As for the claim that the indestructibility of the seer is the reason for the indestructibility of its attribute, vision—therein, is the seer without attributes or with attributes?

In the first case, since it is devoid of attributes, it is incorrect to say that the attribute, vision, is indestructible; thus he says, "Born... He states the authority for that negation: "Not gross... (1591).
There is no permanence [of the soul], because it arises from the production of action.
The form of the action and the agent is mutually caused by one another. || 1592 ||

He states the second [point] with the words "of the seer" (*draṣṭuśca*). The word "also" (*api*) has the sense of "just like the seeing" (*dṛṣṭivat*). He states the reason for the absence of permanence in the seer who possesses attributes: "action" (*kriyā*). To the question, "Why might the seer, even in its form as an agent (*kāraka*), not be permanent? he replies: "Of action and the agent" (*kriyākārayoḥ*). And thus, the implication is that in the absence of action, there is also the absence of the agent. || 1992 ||
How can that which is not established by itself be established through something else?
And for that which is established by its own nature alone, how could there be dependence on anything else? (1593)

In the passage beginning with "na hi," the apprehension of action and its factors through the words "seer" (draṣṭṛ) and "seeing" (dṛṣṭi) was refuted; now he says that there is no such apprehension here because those two are dependent and therefore merely imagined. He states, "by its own nature alone" (svamātreṇa). The meaning is: "The subject of dispute is imagined, because it is dependent, like that which is commonly agreed upon. Anticipating the objection of a deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the Self (ātman), he says, "and by its own nature alone. || 1593 ||
There is no mutual dependence between two things already established, nor is there such dependence between two things that are not yet established in themselves.
Since this and more has already been stated previously, no further effort is made here. || 1594 ||

Furthermore, since it has already been stated in the discussion on the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and elsewhere that whatever is dependent is imagined (*kalpita*), there is no need to state it here; thus he says "No.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that there is no dependence even between the established (*siddha*) and the unestablished (*asiddha*). Therefore, it is said that everything which is dependent is imagined. ||1194||
1. ‘Speech.
[Vol.
3, page 528] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1661
Dependence does not exist for that which is non-existent, nor for an immutable reality.
For, depending upon the cause of the entity, it undergoes transformation while remaining in the state of potentiality.

He summarizes what was stated regarding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and so forth for the sake of ease of understanding: "Not from the non-existent" (*nāsataḥ*). Since there would be no dependence on either the existent or the non-existent, he asks whose dependence it would be; to that he replies: "By power" (*śaktyā*). The world, existing in the form of the power of the Self’s ignorance (*avidyā*), is unimagined (*akalpita*).

The meaning is that because birth and so forth occur in dependence upon a real entity (*vastu*), that which consists of illusion (*māyāmaya*) is dependent; the analysis of the compound is: "that world whose cause is a real entity that is immutable (*kūṭastha*). (1599)
That which has no origination is eternal, or that which is eternally existent is eternal.
It cannot be something that is being produced, just like a sky-flower or space. || 1596 ||

He states another reason for the fact that the manifold of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) is imagined (*kalpita*): "eternal," etc. The meaning is: "The subject under dispute is imagined because it has a beginning and an end, like a [temporary] conjunction. (1596)
"But that hundred which exists at the beginning of creation in the form of mere potentiality,"
But that very [entity], being dependent, undergoes arising and so forth. || 1597 ||
And because there is no existence of the effect apart from the cause, it is said to be imagined; thus he says: "In [the case of] origination and so forth.
If it is argued that being imagined would follow even for Consciousness (caitanya) because it possesses origination and so forth, he says: "That very [Consciousness]... || 1997 ||
Because the reality of the self is immutable, it lacks the capacity for arising and so forth.
And because of its non-duality, its arising and so forth are not established. || 1598 ||

One might object that consciousness (caitanya) too would undergo birth and so forth by virtue of its fitness [for such states], and thus it would likewise be merely imagined; anticipating this, he says:

"In birth... The reason for this is: "Because of its immutability" (kauṭasthyāt). He states another reason for its absence of birth and so forth: "And because of its non-duality" (advitīyatvataśca). || 1598 ||
Entities exist in a state of potentiality because a suitable cause is not present.
Seasonal flowers do not bloom, nor do they arise even when the appropriate causes are present.

One might raise the objection: "Let there be no birth and so forth for that [Brahman], but since the world always exists in the form of its cause, how can it be imagined as an effect? Anticipating this, he says: "By its power" (*śakti*). The meaning is that even though the world exists in the form of its cause, it does not undergo birth and so forth at all times, because it is dependent upon auxiliary causes (*sahakāri*). [The phrase] "the non-production of seasonal flowers, fruits, and so forth" refers to their failure to arise due to a lack of suitability.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The capable," etc. Time and so forth are the causal factors for capability. || 1199 ||
An effect does not exist while it is being produced, nor does a cause exist while it is not producing.
Cause and effect are not established as distinct from one another.

He summarizes what was stated briefly regarding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and so forth with the word "the effect" (*kāryam*). First, the effect is not that which is pervaded by an action (*kriyā*), because it would still be an effect even in the absence of that action; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor is it that which lacks such pervasion, for then even the visible world would [erroneously] follow as being an effect. Furthermore, the effect is not pre-existent (*sat*), because the operation of causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*) would be rendered useless; nor is it non-existent (*asat*), because then even things like fire-lotuses would [erroneously] follow as effects. Nor is a cause something that does not act.
1 ga. ca | [Vol.
3, page 529] 1662 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya—]

Because its status as a cause would be contradicted; for if it were acting [as a cause] while being eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence of the effect being eternal; if it were non-eternal, there would be an infinite regress. Furthermore, cause and effect are not established as either distinct or non-distinct from one another, because that would destroy their very nature, and because distinction and non-distinction are mutually contradictory.
Therefore, the meaning is that causality and so forth are merely superimposed. || 1600 ||
In this context, it is the object itself that is the vision; therefore, there is neither an action nor an agent.
Therefore, for this very reason of indestructibility, the logical reason (hetu) has been stated here. || 1601 ||

Even though that [action] is superimposed, he states what happens in the present context: "The reality alone" (*vastveva*). The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that action, its factors, and so forth are superimposed.
The sentence beginning with "For not... is stated here [in this regard]. The mention of "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the seer (*draṣṭṛ*).
The distinction is that vision is not the action and the seer is not the factor (*kāraka*). For this reason as well, the words "seer" and "vision" do not denote action and factor here.

Thus he says: "Therefore," meaning because there is no apprehension here of either the action (*kriyā*) or the agent (*kāraka*). The word "here" (*iha*) expresses that the perception is not sublated. The point is that if the action and so forth were apprehended, the reason of "indestructibility" (*avināśitva*) would be untenable, as has already been stated. || 1601 ||
It has been stated that one sees the first object as something already determined.
Now the explanation of that which was stated as "he does not see" is being given. (1602)

Having refuted the claim that the phrase "seeing" (*paśyan*) is explained by the words "for not" (*na hi*) and so forth, he now restates what was said regarding the explanation of the phrase "he does not see" (*na paśyati*), namely that it is explained by the words "but not" (*na tu*) and so forth. He introduces the passage beginning with "not" (*na*) after restating the meaning of the sentence beginning with "for not" (*na hi*). [Verse 1602]
If there were no destruction of vision, then why does one not see?

Regarding the objection, "In this state of deep sleep which is [supposedly] awakened," the following response is given. He raises that very point as a rejoinder to the doubt with the words "of perception" (dṛṣṭeḥ). The meaning of the word "then" (atha) is the inseparable connection between the non-cessation of perception and one's own seeing. || 1603 ||
One should perceive that "this very self is [the witness]," by relying on the reasoning already stated.
But the self, having entered deep sleep, does not perceive a second [object] as it does while awake. (1604)
He follows up with the statement "paśyann eva" (even while seeing) in order to explain the preceding sentence. After the word "iti," the word "siddham" (established) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

Having restated the established principle stated in the passage beginning with "because of its indestructibility," he states the meaning of the sentence beginning with "na tu" (but not). Thus: "na tu" || 1604 ||
Why one does not perceive a second [object] is explained right here.
One should see that the cause exists, but not the object itself, just as in the case of cognition.
Regarding that, he states the reason preceded by an inquiry: "The second," [verse 160].
The manifestation of the perception of specific qualities is established by depending upon that [substratum].
There is nothing from which, because of that, one does not see even while seeing. || 1606 ||
He concludes the meaning of the sentence with the words "viśeṣa" (particularity), etc. The word "yat" (that which) should be understood as referring to that which is to be perceived. || 1606 ||
1 gha. *rakatva* | 2 kha. ga. *nekṣyate* | [Vol.
3, page 530] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1663.
Thus, this explanation should not be regarded as correct, because [the object] is impossible.
There would be no perception of the seer and the act of seeing, just as in the well-known state of deep sleep.

The commentary beginning with "It has been determined by the words 'firstly,' etc. and ending with "he does not see" has elaborated upon the explanatory passage stating that "his knowledge does not manifest"; now, this [interpretation] is being refuted. As for the explanation: "Because of the absence of objects to be seen, such as sound and so forth, the seer, even though seeing, does not see during deep sleep"—this explanation is not tenable, because in the absence of an object to be seen, both the seer and the act of seeing depend upon it.

The meaning is this: since those two [the seer and the seen] are impossible, even if they were present in the absence of the other, there would have to be perceptibility of the seer and the seeing during deep sleep; yet one cannot argue that just as there is no perceptibility for the sleeper at that time, so too there is none for the seer and the rest. For while it may be true that [the cognition] is of the nature of light, it is impossible for the seer and the rest—which are themselves of the nature of light—to be non-perceptible. Therefore, the assertion that the seeing and the rest exist when the object of sight is absent is illogical. || 1907 ||
Remaining in darkness, one indeed does not perceive the knower, the knowledge, or the darkness itself.
One resorts to discernment just as one does in the observation of a jar or similar objects. || 1608 ||
But for a wise person, it is therefore illogical to deny the mere appearance of what is perceived.
Because it negates the existence or non-existence of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, and so forth. || 1609 ||

Having accepted that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is imperceptible, he says "In darkness" (*tamasī*) to show that even that [imperceptibility] does not exist. Just as when the perception of a jar or similar object is intended, a seer situated in dense darkness, though not perceiving those objects, nevertheless distinguishes the knower, the knowledge, and the darkness;
in the same way, the Self, even while sleeping and despite the non-perception of sound and other objects, remains within that very [state]—[distinguishing] the sleep, the vision, and the seer.

The meaning is that one should discern [the Self] within the locus, yet there is no cognition of such discernment. The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies that, in the illustrative example, the cognition of the discernment of the knower and so forth follows from experience.
He states the result when the vision of discernment is absent: "tataḥ" (therefore). The word should be divided as "ayuktam" (it is improper).
He clarifies the meaning of the word "tataḥ": "grāhaka... (by the perceiver...). For non-perception is the reason for the negation of the object to be seen, and that [non-perception]...

The meaning is that this [principle of non-perception] applies equally to the seer and so forth as it does to external objects; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the seer and other subjects also being negated during deep sleep, and thus not only the visible object would be absent there.
"Existence and non-existence" refers to birth and destruction. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), transformation and other such changes are included. || 1608 || 1609 ||
But surely that object of perception does exist, both in its collective and its individual forms.
It is not so with respect to the entity as it has been described, because that [entity] is not absolutely distinct [from its properties].

Having refuted the statement of another—that "one does not see during sleep because there is nothing to be seen even while seeing"—he restates the objection and the rebuttal put forward by that other regarding the point that "one does not see because there is nothing to be seen," beginning with the words "But surely... (nanu ca) and so forth. 1610.
"Certainly, that object of perception does exist, but it does not possess an absolute distinction [from consciousness]."
If that [object] were something other [than consciousness], it would be perceived as distinct, just as one perceives upon awakening. (1611)
He divides the section on the refutation [of the objection]: "Certainly. To the question, "How then is the statement that there is no object to be seen [to be understood]?
he replies: "But not... Even so, because the possibility of seeing that [object] exists, it is improper to say "he does not see"; therefore he says: "It might be... [the object to be seen].

If that [object] were absolutely distinct from the seer and other than himself, the seer would surely perceive it even while asleep, just as he does while awake; however, because there is an absolute absence of such distinction, he does not perceive it in sleep. Therefore, the meaning is that its existence is not like that of consciousness. || 1611 ||

1 ka. *pratyakṣam* | 2 ka. ga. *sthitaḥ paṃ* | 3 kha. *'syānātyaṃ* | 4 kha. *'santaṃ vi* | [vol 3, page 531] 1664 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]— [The text continues with the commentary on the fourth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad.]
This distinction is not observed to be absolute in every respect.
Therefore, it is said that any further qualification is utterly improper. || 1612 ||

He refutes [the opponent's view] by saying "not absolutely. In the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*), even during states such as waking, there is no absolute difference because the means of knowledge for such [difference] are absent;
thus, the qualification "absolutely" applied to sleep is improper. Therefore, the meaning is that the presence and absence of specific cognition would be identical across all three states. || 1612 ||
An object, whether distinct or non-distinct, [is so designated] by virtue of its dependence upon another object.
If everything were one, neither distinction nor non-distinction would be possible. || 1613 ||

Having accepted the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) and refuted its qualification, he explains why that very doctrine cannot even arise. Regarding the phrase "divided" (*vibhaktam*):

since, according to such scriptural passages as "All this is what this Self is," everything is nothing but the non-dual Self, there is an absence of any second entity; therefore, how could there be any occasion for the emergence of difference and non-difference? This is the meaning. || 1613 ||
For that which is divided from something must be distinct from it; how then could it be that very same thing?
Because it is contradictory, that which was stated is therefore not beautiful. || 1614 ||
Anticipating the objection that "since you admit that the one itself is both different and non-different, what is the use of a second entity? he says: "yaddhi" (for that which...).

The word "hi" clarifies the reason indicated by the phrase "because of contradiction. "Tasmāt" (therefore) means: "that which was stated by you—that the one alone is both different and non-different. || 1614 ||
For Apahnuti (concealment) is said to be the expression of a distinction as something non-distinct.
There is no entity other than differentiation; therefore, it is by means of the word "differentiated" [that we speak of it]. || 1615 ||

Now, [the opponent argues that] non-distinction (*avibhāga*) is a different entity from distinction (*vibhāga*), and thus, just as with color and taste, there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference in a single locus; to this, he replies: "Apahnuti" (Concealment). For the nature of the negative particle (*nañ*) is such that it makes known the non-existence of that which is connected to it—this is the *Bhāṣya* cited here as authority. The first word "hi" (for/indeed) [indicates this], while the second [indicates] that which is other than that or opposed to that, being invariably concomitant with its absence.

This is for the purpose of illustrating the maxim that "between the primary and the secondary, the primary is understood," since the negative particle (*nañ*) is secondary by virtue of that [non-existence]. For non-existence is the primary meaning of the negative particle; when that is possible, another meaning is not appropriate. Thus, the meaning is that by means of the indivisible word (*avibhaktagirā*), no meaning other than the [indivisible] distinction (*vibhāga*) is expressed. || 1619 ||
And it should likewise be seen that "the other is differentiated" and "it must be so viewed."
By virtue of its inherent capacity, a single meaning alone is expressed again and again. || 1616 ||

Furthermore, regarding the second [term], he states another defect in the opponent's view: that because it is "another" (*anyat*), the distinction between the meanings of the words is difficult to maintain, resulting in tautology.

He says: "Another" (*anyat*). The word "to be seen" (*draṣṭavyam*) expresses the accusative case. Although there might be synonymy by taking the aspect of non-difference due to the acceptance of both difference and non-difference, even if synonymy is avoided through difference, synonymy remains unavoidable due to non-difference; consequently, their simultaneous employment cannot be established.
This is the meaning. Alternatively, it means that because the unity of meaning is observed despite the distinct powers of the words, tautology is unavoidable. || 1616 ||
*It is inferred that the introduction to this [section] is missing.
16. The Meaning of Giving.* [Vol.
In our position, however, not even the slightest fault exists here.
An object fit to be seen is appropriately considered either distinct or non-distinct from the observer. || 1617 ||

Anticipating the objection that this is equally true for your own position as well, he says "asmad" (our). Here, there is the mention of three words. To explain the absence of redundancy, he states the meaning of the second word: "draṣṭavya" (to be seen). The meaning is that the object fit for seeing—the so-called ignorance and its effects—is the referent of the word "second. It is well known that the visible object is "second" in relation to the seer.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of explanation. He states the non-redundancy of that [word] with respect to the word "anya" (other): "anya" means that which is both other than and not other than the Self (*ātman*), because the term "object" (*artha*) is employed in both senses due to its suitability for being perceived. || 1617 ||
Likewise, from the perspective of the ultimate self, it is characterized by imagined ignorance.
"Even though it is not divided, it may be other [than that] due to mutual distinction.

(1618) He states the meaning of the word "other": "In the ultimate sense," etc. Although the object consisting of imagined ignorance and its effects is not divided from the non-imagined Self—since the imagined has no existence apart from the non-imagined—it may nevertheless be other than that [Self] because of avidyā.

The meaning is this: because there is a mutual disparity in the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of the self and [the other], just as the word "second" is applied to ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth by taking their fitness for being perceived as the cause, so too the word "other" is applied to that very same thing by taking the disparity in intrinsic nature as the cause. || 1618 ||
The distinctness of properties such as dharma and so forth exists even though the substratum (dharmin) is itself undivided.
In this way, the charge of redundancy does not apply to the "object of perception" and the other [categories]. || 1619 ||

He states the meaning of the word "vibhakta" (divided): "of dharma and so forth. Although the substratum—the self—is in reality devoid of division, the word "vibhakta" is used because of the mutual distinctness of the non-spiritual principles such as mahat, ahaṃkāra, and the rest, which serve as the locus for conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). "Dharma" refers to the sustaining of mahat and the others; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), mahat, ahaṃkāra, and the rest are included. There is no tautology of the terms...
He concludes the objection with the words "Thus" (evam). 1619.
The object of perception should be visible; otherwise, it would be something else, such as the mother of the self.
The seer, the seeing, and the object seen would be mutually distinct from one another. || 1620 ||

He summarizes what was stated for the sake of ease of understanding with the words "sādhyeti" (beginning with "the object to be accomplished"). The mother and so forth—consisting of the body and the organs, being the object of the Witness and fit for perception—is designated by the term "that which is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*);

it is the referent of the word "second. And because it is imagined, it is distinct from the unimagined Self; therefore, taking that very [Self] as the cause, another [entity] is intended. Since there is mutual difference among the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and the others, they are expressed by the word "divided" (*vibhakta*).
The meaning is that there is no tautology therein. || 1620 ||
Furthermore, the nature of being both dual and non-dual is not possible for the vital breath and food.
Just as [the nature] of an object is here directly perceived, so I have previously explained.
Anticipating the objection that even for another [author], there may be no tautology by virtue of the aforementioned causes, he recalls what was stated regarding the connection and so forth:
"dvaita... etc. "Here" refers to the statement of the scripture; the meaning is: directly, without conceptual construction. || 1621 ||
Just as the entire explanation was provided in the preceding verse, so too is it here.
Therefore, scholars should apply this same reasoning to the subsequent statements as well. || 1622 ||
1666 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:
Having restated the interpretation of the passage beginning with "When indeed he does not see" as provided by Bhartṛprapañca, [Sureśvara] proceeds to set forth his own interpretation.

In passages such as "When he does not smell that," [the text] merely restates what was already extended by analogy in the first sentence. By the word "pūrva" (previous), the meaning is that since the method of explanation is identical, there is no specific difference in meaning to be stated. || 1622 ||
The existence of actions such as seeing and so forth is not real.
Because the entity of the self is empty of any distinction such as existence or non-existence. || 1623 ||

If the reality whose single essence is consciousness is intended in all these alternative explanations, then how is it that there arises the cognition of distinctions such as the acts of seeing, hearing, and so forth?
To this he says: "Seeing, etc. He provides the reason why the cognition of distinction therein is an error: "Being," etc. (1623).
This is indeed other than the known, and likewise it is above the unknown.
"Brahman is the reality of the Self"—this scriptural statement is clear. || 1624 ||
Regarding the statement "the reality of the Self as described above," he cites the *Talavakāra Śruti* for its authority, paraphrasing it as: "From that which is known...
By the word "draṣṭuḥ" (of the seer), which ends in the suffix -tṛ, agency is expressed.
When there arises the expectation, "Of what is he the seer?", it is designated as "the vision. || 1625 ||
Having stated his own view—that the cognition of distinctions such as the acts of seeing and so forth in each successive turn is false—he states the view of Bhartṛprapañca: "Of the seer... etc.

For it has been said that the suffix *-tṛ* (in *draṣṭṛ*) expresses agency alone. He explains the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage, "Of whom is the seer the seer of seeing? with the words: "The seer... (verse 1629).

Even "vision" (dṛṣṭi) would be a state of being (bhāva), which is the completion of the nature of the action; that state, which here rests upon the fruit [of the action], is designated by the word "vision. (1626)

He states the meaning of the word *dṛṣṭi*: "‘Dṛṣṭi’ also [means]... He explains the state (*bhāva*) itself: "...is completion (*samāpti*). He states that the state has a fruit as its culmination: "...fruit (*phala*). Here, "here" refers to the sentence under discussion. As it has been stated: "The state called *dṛṣṭi* is indicated as having the sense of the completion of an action and as being dependent upon a fruit. (1626)
The fruit is the manifestation and knowledge of the object, as well as the agency of that [manifestation].
In these various statements, this very point regarding the nature of reality is expressed individually.

Furthermore, he states the meaning of the commentary’s question, "What, then, is the fruit of this manifestation? by saying, "The fruit. The word "and" (ca) serves to combine the self's agency in that fruit with its previously mentioned agency in the act of seeing. Having restated what was said, he shows that it applies to other synonyms as well, individually.

[The word] "thus" [indicates] the connection: that this [Self] is the agent of the object in respect to cognition and so forth. Regarding this, they say: "This twofold attribute—namely, illumination and being the agent of cognition—is taught individually. (1627)
Whatever refutation is to be stated here has already been stated; therefore, it is not mentioned again.
Because, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the agent and other such factors do not exist during deep sleep. || 1628 ||
1 gha. *kasyā*; 2 gha. *phalapra*'; 3 kaḥ kha. *'katva*'. [Vol.
3, page 534] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri: 1667.

He states that this interpretation has been refuted in the fifth [chapter] with the word "here" (iha). Furthermore, this statement concerns the self in deep sleep, and since the body and so forth do not exist there, how could it be the agent of seeing and so on? To this he says: "Because of the absence of causal factors and the like" (kārakādeḥ) || 1628 ||
Even though it is devoid of the properties of the factors of action (kāraka) and so forth, [the Self] appears as such due to the causes born of ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyag-ajñāna).
In that same way, the self is perceived through the forms of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped. || 1629 ||

Nevertheless, since those [states] exist during waking and so forth, the Self possesses distinctions such as seeing and the like; otherwise, how could there be the cognition of agency and so on even in those states? Anticipating this objection, he says: "kārakādi... (1629).
Because it manifests as both agent and action, this [Self] is the witness of the agent, the action, and so forth.
Though it is immutable, the Self appears as an agent, an object of action, and so forth, due to self-delusion.

He elucidates what was stated as "it is seen thus. [The word] "katrī" (the agent) [is used]; or there is a division [of the text] as "atathā" (not so). The meaning is: by those that are non-existent in reality, i.e., by those that do not exist. To the question, "How can there be an appearance of that [agency] in the immutable one, who is the witness of the agent and so forth? he replies: "katrī" (the agent). || 1630 ||
Therefore, this view alone is free from birth, destruction, and so forth.
The appearance of multiplicity, birth, destruction, and so forth, arises from association born of ignorance. || 1631 ||

Since it is established that the notion of agency and so forth in the Self arises from the greatness of delusion (*moha*), he states the conclusion: "One" (*ekā*). He demonstrates the very meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) with the words "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Since the vision associated with ignorance and its products obtains manifoldness and modification, therefore, by its own nature, it is the inward-facing, immutable, and single-flavored [Self]; this is the meaning. || 1631 ||
Regarding the phrase "it causes [the soul] to experience," it is stated that this occurs through discernment.
How can that which is deformed—that is, unjust—be said to be different from the form under discussion? || 1632 ||

It has been stated that in all the various passages, the intended meaning is the teaching of the non-dual, immutable vision by way of restating the distinctions such as the "vision" (dṛṣṭi) established in common worldly experience.
Now, regarding the passage "what indeed one does not taste," [the text] omits "tasting" (*rasayan*) and so forth, and instead says, "verily, knowing it, one does not taste it."
The reading of the Mādhyandina school refutes that [interpretation], stating: "That which is not... (1632).
This is not a fault here, for in this supreme self whose nature is representation-only (vijñaptimātra),
it is taught that "this differentiation of powers such as seeing and so forth must not be perceived. (1633)

He states the intended meaning of that statement: "This is not [the case]. The meaning is that, in order to exclude the distinction between the powers of seeing and so forth within the inner self (pratīc), which is of the single essence of consciousness, the Mādhyandina Śruti employs the term "vijānan" (knowing) where [the Kāṇva recension has] "rasayan" (tasting). || 1633 ||
Since this is so, therefore it is designated as mere-cognition-only.
Therefore, expressions such as "water" and so forth are meaningful when used with words like "vision" and the rest. (1634)

He states that, in accordance with the cited scripture, it must also be accepted that the Kāṇva recension has as its object the vision of the immutable, single-flavored [Brahman]. He says "yataḥ" (since).
And he says "tasmācca" (and therefore), indicating that based on the remainder of the passage, it is precisely the aforementioned vision that is intended in all the successive sections. || 1634 ||
1 kha. From connection, [there arises] vision.
[Vol. 3, page 535] 1668 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter—]
She has the supreme Self as her sole defining characteristic, having abandoned all objective supports.
In this context, "view" (dṛṣṭi) refers to that which is expressed by terms such as "view" and so forth, because of the negation of [the concepts of] destruction and the like. || 1635 ||

For this reason as well, he states that it is precisely that [Self] which is designated here by words such as "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*), etc., in the passage beginning with "external" (*bāhya*). The meaning is as follows: the inward vision (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*), abiding as the witness (*sākṣin*) within the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of vision and so forth—which are themselves modifications of the intellect—is what is expressed by these synonymous terms like "vision," etc.; it is not the act of seeing or other such functions, because that would contradict [scriptural statements] such as "due to its imperishability" (*avināśitvāt*). || 1631 ||

Even though they are included within "view" and the others, mental cognition (*mati*) and sensory consciousness (*vijñāna*) are mentioned separately here because their functioning is established as being independent as well. || 1636 ||

Although it has been stated that the aforementioned vision [of Brahman] applies to all modalities, one might raise the objection that since *manas* and *buddhi* are common to the eye and other senses, and since there is no function (*vṛtti*) distinct from those produced by them, the separate mention of them in the passage "That which it does not think" and "That which it does not cognize" is not logical.

Anticipating this, he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "Of thinking and cognition," etc., starting with the words "Even though they are included. Knowledge of the past and so forth is [due to] passion—
The meaning is that the term *divṛtti* is mentioned separately because it exists independently. || 1636 ||
Like burning and heat, they would be mutually distinct from fire.
The dharmas such as the seer and seeing exist with a nature that is both distinct and non-distinct. || 1637 ||
This is due to the differentiation arising from the non-realization of that very same reality.
This differentiation is perceived through delusion, like the waves arising from the waters of the sun.

Having refuted the interpretation of others regarding the passage beginning with "that which it does not see," and having stated his own position, he introduces an inquiry to determine that [position], starting with the words "dahaneti" (like fire). Just as the properties of burning, illumination, heat, and so forth are both different and non-different from fire, and are mutually different from one another, are the properties of seeing, hearing, and so forth—both different and non-different from their substrate, the *pratyagātman* (the inner self), and mutually different? Or are they...?

The meaning of the reflection is this: just as there is a memory that rain arises from the sun, yet due to delusion one perceives a distinction between that [sun] and the waters residing in various vessels, so too, although the Self is inherently non-dual, a manifold distinction appears due to the differences in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) imagined by its own ignorance. Because the Self is the substratum of all, the word "attribute" (dharma) is used with reference to it. 1637–1638.
In this regard, some explain that there is a nature consisting of both multiplicity and unity.
It is always to be apprehended by itself alone, just like consciousness.

He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "here" (*iha*). Regarding the claim that the nature consisting of both difference and non-difference is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), there is the following illustration: "consciousness" (*caitanya*). || 1639 ||
Since every object is observed to consist of both difference and non-difference, therefore...
Not even a single example can be found in the opposing position.

Regarding the question of what constitutes proof for the soul's being both different and non-different [from the body], he says: "bhedeti" (regarding difference). The meaning is that since the body is a real entity (*vastu*), the soul is likewise inferred to be so. Anticipating the counter-inference that "the soul's being of a single essence can be inferred from its being the soul," he states: "pareti. 1640.
1 gha. by the day; 2 ka. *manya*; 3 gha. not seen; 4 ka. kha. gha. *mātha*; 5 kha. *tatrā'cha*. [Vol.
3, page 536] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1669.
The single universal "cowness" follows the meaning of the dewlap and other such features in the individual cow.
The dewlap and other such features are mutually distinct, yet they are not mutually contradictory.

Regarding the argument that "the self is both different and non-different because it is a real entity," the same lack of an illustrative example applies here as well. Anticipating the objection that "we do not accept anything whatsoever as being both different and non-different," he says: "One... By the word "hump" (*sāsnā*) and so forth, the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of the possessor of those qualities are understood. In the case of the broken-horned (*khaṇḍa*) and the hornless (*muṇḍa*) [cows], there is only one "cowness" (*gotva*); and that [cowness] is both different and non-different from the objects possessing the hump and so forth, which are its own specific qualities. Those...

And [these individuals] are mutually distinct yet non-distinct by virtue of their "cowness. Nor is there a contradiction regarding the relationship of universal and particular, or the state of being both distinct and non-distinct, in a single locus;
for these do not possess mutual contradiction—this is the meaning. || 1641 ||
And here, the cognition of difference is not sublated by the cognition of a universal.
Nor is it accepted that a cognition of a universal sublates a cognition arising from a particular.

It establishes non-contradiction: "And not... Since there is no mutual relationship of sublated and sublator between the cognitions of generality and particularity, nor between the cognitions of difference and non-difference, there is no mutual contradiction among their respective objects; for contradiction does not exist regarding an object established by valid cognition, since such contradiction is abandoned when that [validity] is reversed. This is the meaning. || 1642 ||
Just as gross objects possess the nature of being both general and particular, so it is [with the subtle elements].
Such [a capacity] is to be expected even regarding all subtle objects without exception. (1643)

One might ask: "Even though gross objects such as cows and the like possess both difference and non-difference, how can this be established in the case of extremely subtle things like the self and space? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In gross [objects]," etc. The meaning is that such a nature of being both general and particular—that is, being both different and non-different—is present there as well. || 1643 ||
Just as a gross object is perceived as possessing both multiplicity and unity, so too is it [the self].
Let it be understood that the self and other supersensible entities exist because they possess the nature of real entities. || 1644 ||
He explains the commentary beginning with "yathā" regarding the stated meaning: "nānātva... (1644).
Thus do those who consider themselves wise [act] here by the power of inference.
They establish that an entity consists of both distinct and non-distinct natures without making any distinction. || 1645 ||

He concludes the prima facie position with the words "in this manner. Here, the word "here" refers to the state of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). The phrase "without distinction" means without any distinction between self and non-self. (9645)
Thus, the futility of what has been said is stated for the sake of [further] clarification.
May there be no confusion regarding the subject matter of Vedānta for those who seek the highest good through right reasoning.

He begins the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "Thus it has been said. He states the purpose of demonstrating, through reasoning, that the aforementioned position is utterly insignificant:

"The highest good" (*śreyaḥ*). This means that regarding the reality which is the subject matter of the Veda, there is no delusion; rather, the notion of its having manifold flavors is what constitutes error. || 1646 ||
Not even in the entire world is our cognition observed to grasp at difference.
Apart from the intrinsic nature of the object, there is no other object of cognition for the act of cognizing.

Anticipating the objection—"What is the reasoning by which the doctrines of difference and non-difference are rendered futile?"—the author refutes the first alternative of the opponent's inference by considering whether difference is a property (*dharma*) or the essential nature (*svarūpa*). He refutes the first [possibility] with the verse beginning "Difference" (*bheda*). The meaning is: a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not have the power to operate upon anything other than the essential nature itself, because that which is other than the essential nature lacks its own nature and is thus unfit for cognition. || 1647 ||
And there is no difference in the intrinsic nature of any entity whatsoever, anywhere.
And difference from its own nature as well as from anything else is the object of fallacious means of knowledge. || 1648 ||
He states another alternative: "And not... If difference were its own nature (*svarūpa*), would it exist in relation to itself or in relation to something else?

It cannot be the first, because that would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-existence of the entity, as has already been stated. Regarding the second [alternative], he says: "And from its own nature...

The meaning is that if the other were the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), then since that other would lack its own nature, difference from it could not be established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). || 1648 ||
They exclude one another by way of their unique forms.
Just as the particulars [do not exist apart from] the universal, so too does it (the universal) turn away from them. || 1649 ||

Having refuted the doctrine of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda-vāda*) on the grounds that difference lacks epistemic warrant, the author considers the proponent’s alternative—that the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are either mutually distinct or non-distinct—and refutes the first option with the words "asādhāraṇa... (etc.). The phrase "from those" (*tataḥ*) means "from the particulars. Thus, the implication is that the doctrine of mere difference (*bhedavāda*) alone would result. || 1649 ||
If, in your view, even those [particulars] are considered to be mere universals, then what would be the particulars?
In that case, because it is devoid of particularity, the universal as well is in a precarious state.
It adopts another alternative: "those too" (*te 'pi*). The meaning of "too" (*api*) is that [the universal] is merely the particular.

If those two were non-different from one another, then because there would be no particular distinct from the universal, the latter (the universal) would not exist in relation to it; and because there would be no universal distinct from the particular, the former (the particular) would not exist in relation to it.
And since those [particulars] would not exist, how could there be difference or non-difference? To this he says: "viśeṣa... (verse 1650).
The universal would either be distinct from the particular or not distinct from it.
In the case of difference, there would be only a particularity, like [the distinction between] a "hornless" and a "humped" [cow], as opposed to a universal. || 1651 ||

Having conceptualized and refuted both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), he now conceptualizes by relying on the universal alone, [asking] "or is it different? Having restated the first position, he refutes it with the word "difference" (*bheda*). If it were non-different (*abheda*), then that same fault would apply;
for it is impossible for a universal that is non-different from its particulars to possess the nature of a universal—this is to be understood from the word "if" (*cet*). || 9651 ||
If there were a distinction between that which possesses difference and that which possesses non-difference, an infinite regress would result.
Furthermore, the establishment of the property and the substratum would be undermined even if they were non-different. || 1652 ||
4. Furthermore, is difference distinct from the object or non-distinct? Regarding this, he states the first [position] with the words "bhedeti" (difference, etc.). By that very difference...

The meaning is as follows: if there is difference [between the whole and its parts], then by the second [part] there is the fault of self-dependence (*svāśrayatva*), and by the third, mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*) or a circular argument (*cakraka*); furthermore, if an infinite number of differences is admitted, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He states the defect in the second case with the words "dharme" (in the property). In every instance where there is both difference and non-difference, one should understand that the previously mentioned refutation applies, depending on whether one relies on the aspect of difference or the aspect of non-difference. || 1652 ||

If the Self alone were the specific attributes characterized as the properties of the substrate...
Otherwise, negative concomitance would not be established, and in that case, the self would possess the nature of a self. (1653)

As for the claim that seeing and the other faculties are both different from and non-different from the seer, and are mutually different—like fire and its burning—the author restates the aspect of non-difference therein and refutes it with the words "The Self" (*ātma*). If those specific attributes, which are of the nature of qualities belonging to the Self as their substrate, are indeed the Self itself, then since there is no difference between those [faculties] such as seeing and the Self, their mutual difference cannot be established; for how could there be a distinction from the very nature of the Self?
The meaning is that there is no distinction [between them] even further. || 1613 ||
Because it is of its own nature, the self is not indeed distinct from the self.
For this exclusion of the self would indeed have as its origin that which is non-self. (1654)
Anticipating the objection as to why there is no difference in the nature of the Self from anything whatsoever—given that it differs from the non-Self—the author says: "Itself.

For the Self, being the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of everything, does not differ from itself, because there is no counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). This is because it has already been stated that [if it did differ], it would follow that its own nature is non-existent. Furthermore, there is no non-Self other than that [Self], since anything else would necessarily lack the status of being an essential nature. How so?

To this, he says: "The notion of difference therein [is] non-self. The meaning is that the exclusion of the Self—caused by ignorance and its resulting limiting adjuncts—is an illusion. The word *hi* (for/indeed) is used to state that the illusory nature of difference is well-known in cases such as the distinction between a snake and a rope. || 1654 ||
And there are no other subjects (dharmin) that exceed the inner self (pratyagātman).
Dharmas obtain their own nature because they consist of dependence upon others. || 1655 ||

Having refuted the aspect of non-difference regarding the claim that "seeing and so forth are both different and non-different from the seer," he now undermines the aspect of difference with the words "na ca" (and not).

If it is accepted that seeing and so forth are different from the seer, then they must be either independent or dependent; [it cannot be] the first, because they possess the nature of being attributes (*dharma*).

Regarding the second alternative, [the question arises] whether there is the non-existence or the existence of another substratum (*dharmyantara*). In the first case, they would not obtain their own nature;
for the meaning is that since they are distinct from themselves, in the absence of another substratum, dependence (*pāratantrya*) is impossible. || 1659 ||
And if another property exists, the meaning of the proposition is not established.
The Self alone is declared to be one, in the form of both the collective and the individual. || 1656 ||
He states another alternative: "of another property-bearer" (*dharmyantarasya*). He demonstrates the very meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) with the words: "entirely" (*samasta*).
If those properties, though separate, were of that same nature as when they are combined.
Let the distinction here between the collective and the distributive forms be stated. (1657)

Furthermore, regarding the relationship between the whole and the parts and the Self, is there difference or non-difference? It is not the first [option], because it would fail to establish one's own position;

thus, considering this, he refutes the second [option] with the words "the parts" (*vyastā*). The meaning is that if there were non-difference between the whole and the parts and the Self, then the distinction that "this is the whole" and "that is the part" could not be established. The word "here" (*atra*) refers to the statement of the position of non-difference. (16.17)
A substratum is not qualified by properties that depend upon other [substrata].
Because there is no connection [of the probans] with the nature of being a property of the subject (dharmin). || 1658 ||
1 ka. 'tvaṃ tasaṃ | 2 ga. 'sathā''tma | 3 kha. 'ritam || 1656 ||
Furthermore,
because the state of being a whole is a property of the whole, and the state of being divided is a property of the divided, the Self does not possess these two forms.
He says: "In another locus (*dharmyantara*). The meaning is that the properties of a jar, such as broadness and so forth, do not exclude the cart.

He states the reason for this: "The locus" (*dharmī*). The meaning is that there is no connection between the properties of the jar and the cart by way of their being the property-possessor (*dharmin*) of those [respective] properties. || 1698 ||
Furthermore, the futility of statements such as "not this, not this" (neti neti) would result.
If Brahman were to possess both a collective and an individual form according to the Śruti, [then this would be the case]. (1659)

Anticipating the objection that the aforementioned qualifications are established because of the admission that Brahman alone is both the whole and the parts, he says "No," and so forth. The connection is with the words "of the Śruti" and "of the sentences. (1699)
Having set forth the duality of Brahman and having subsequently repeated it, the Śruti [proceeds] again.
"It is the Self alone," he said directly; how could there be the possibility of difference? (1660)

Furthermore, because it contradicts such scriptural passages as "All this is indeed the Self" (ātmaivedaṃ sarvam) and "All this is indeed Brahman" (brahmaivedam), he states that there is neither identity nor difference [between the world and Brahman] by saying "having raised [an objection]" (vyutthāpya).

Since the scripture, after describing the manifestation of duality from Brahman through the medium of Māyā in passages such as "He created that light" (tattejo 'sṛjat), subsequently declares the direct non-difference in the passage "This is indeed the Self, this is indeed Brahman" (tad idam ātmaiva tad idam brahmaiva), there is no possibility of both difference and non-difference, given that difference is impossible.
The application [of the method]. || 1660 ||
If an entity were to turn away from its own nature by means of valid cognition, it would no longer be that very entity.
An existent entity whose own nature has not been attained would be like the horn of a hare. || 1661 ||

Furthermore, in that view, one must consider whether the difference of an object is from its own nature (*svarūpa*) or from what is not its own nature (*asvarūpa*). He restates the first alternative with the words "it is excluded" (*vyāvartate*). If an object is differentiated from its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) by the force of a means of knowledge (*māna*), it would [then] be non-nature; for a cloth excluded from a jar does not possess the nature of a jar. The word *asvarūpam* is to be read as a separate term. For that which is not excluded from its own nature, there is a lack of nature (*niḥsvarūpatvam*).

It establishes [the point]. By the phrase "not yet attained," the second [case] is explained; for that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot function as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and since no difference exists in the intrinsic nature of anything, this is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that [point], and thus there is no tautology. || 1661 ||
Apart from the method of affirmation, there is no other single path by which it can be explained.
One obtains a connection with the object of cognition through the apprehension of that real entity. || 1662 ||

[Objection: Surely, difference established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be denied by reasoning (*yukti*). In that regard, is that [difference] mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), or is it separateness (*pṛthaktva*)?

In the first case, does the means of knowledge grasp only difference, or does it also grasp the entity itself? It is not the first; thus he says: "The means of knowledge" (*mānam*). The connection is "that means of knowledge. He states the reason for this: "Being" (*sat*). (Verse 1662)
There is no connection with objects such as a jar by means of the exclusion of non-jars and the like.
Since cognition has the nature of being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no operation of cognition with respect to non-existence.

Even in the second case [the alternative], is the apprehension of the object preceded by the apprehension of difference, or is the apprehension of difference preceded by that [apprehension of the object], or is there a simultaneous apprehension of both? In the first [sub-case], [the opponent] says: "It is the self alone. (1663)

Page 540] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
He states the fault: "not a jar, etc. The reason for this is: "not being thus. For the function of valid cognition is not the negation of other things;
the meaning is that, without its being a cognizer of a positive entity, it cannot be a cognizer of a negation. || 1663 ||
The exclusion of meanings such as "non-pot" with respect to an object such as a pot that is not yet established [in cognition].
How could one employ a means of valid cognition here, given that it would result in a mutual dependence?

To the question, "Whence does pride (māna) have such a nature?", he says: "Unestablished" (*aprasiddha*). The phrase is to be divided as "the removal of objects such as non-pots" (*aghaṭādyarthāpanodanam*).

The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the path of worldly discourse (*vyavahāramārga*). The sense is that there can be no cognition of absence (*abhāvadhī*) without the cognition of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogijñāna*).

Let it be, then, that the apprehension of difference is preceded by the apprehension of the real entity; to this he replies: "Mutually" (*anyonya*). When there is cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) and so forth, difference—

The meaning is that since the cognition of that [universal] depends on knowledge, and that knowledge depends on it, there is a circular dependency; thus, the cognition of difference is not preceded by the cognition of the real entity. || 1664 ||
This cooking of what is not a jar is joined with the destruction of the jar.

"Because the cognition of the object 'pot' occurs through the exclusion of the object 'non-pot,' the same mutual dependence applies even in the position that affirmation is preceded by negation"; thus he says: "The pot... (verse 1665).
Even for that which is both a pot and a non-pot, [the determination occurs] without the exclusion of anything other than that.
If there were no realization at all, then an infinite regress would result. || 1666 ||
Regarding the point that "an injunction is preceded by a prohibition," he states another defect in this very context: "like a jar" (ghaṭavat). || 1666 ||
And there would be no establishment of the measure of the mother without the exclusion of what is other than that.
Without those two, the object of cognition is by no means established.

He states another objection regarding the proof of the jar through the negation of the non-jar: "mātr... (the knower, etc.). He says "tābhyām... (by those two) to explain what would happen if those two were not established. He says "nitarām... (extremely), meaning: where even when the knower and so forth are manifest, the object of knowledge is not established without the witness who is the prover of all, then what need is there to say that it is not established when the knower and so forth themselves are not manifest?

By this, the simultaneous apprehension of both is refuted; for the cognition of difference, which is the effect of the cognition of the substratum (dharmin) and so forth, does not coexist with it, because there is a necessary rule of temporal sequence between cause and effect. || 1667 ||
And for those disputants for whom both difference and non-difference are qualities;
Even according to that very process, there is no cognition of difference here at all. || 1668 ||

Having refuted its being established by that [perception] in the view that difference consists in mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), he states that it is not established by it even in the view that it is a distinct quality (*pṛthaktva*):
"And as for distinctness... (1668).
It has distinct qualities from others, or it is distinct because of its distinct qualities.
Or they may be non-distinct from one another; nevertheless, a distinction will still be observed. || 1669 ||

Indeed, he offers this analysis to demonstrate that even according to the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, there is no valid cognition of difference (*bhedapramā*) in the world. He says "separately" (*pṛthak*):

therefore, when there is separateness from the substratum (*dharmin*), from other objects, and from itself, the quality of separateness—known as difference—resides either in that substratum or in the substratum possessing the quality of separateness from other objects. [He continues: from other objects, [it resides] in the substratum possessing the quality of separateness...

1674 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopani�sadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four:

The meaning is that, whether in that [entity] possessing distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) or in the substratum (*dharmin*) itself, the quality of distinctness called "difference" (*bheda*) subsists. Likewise, the quality of non-distinctness called "non-difference" (*abheda*) [subsists] in relation to the substratum from which other objects are not distinct, and from the substratum which possesses the quality of non-distinctness.

He raises a dilemma concerning non-distinctness (*apṛthaktva*) with respect to that [property] which exists either in distinctness itself, or in the substratum (*dharmin*), or in other categories (*padārtha*) that are not distinct from the substratum. He asks: "Or is it non-distinct? If distinctness were to reside in that substratum which is itself distinct, then the various types of distinctness would themselves be either mutually distinct or non-distinct; and likewise, if non-distinctness...

He formulates the dilemma: "If difference resides in a substratum (*dharmin*), do the differences from difference [itself] stand mutually non-distinct or distinct? He refutes this by stating that in the case of "mutually," the validity of difference is nowhere established. He says, "It is not so. If difference were to reside in a substratum of difference, and the differences from difference were themselves mutually distinct, then there would be no valid cognition of difference due to infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If the distinctions of separateness are not admitted to be mutually non-separate, then, because they are identical, for one who asserts that "separateness exists in the substratum when there is separateness," it is impossible to cognize separateness in the substratum when there is non-separateness, due to the contradiction between the two in a single locus. Or,

if non-separateness exists in the substratum when there is non-separateness, then because there would be no end to the mutual separateness of those distinctions, there can be no cognition of non-difference.

If there is non-distinctness, then because of that identity, when non-distinctness exists, the claim that "there is non-distinctness in the substratum" results in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatā*).

On the other hand, the persistence of non-distinctness in the substratum while distinctness exists is contradictory. Therefore, the meaning is that neither difference nor non-difference possesses any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). || 1669 ||
How could a substance that is non-distinct from its qualities ever resort to distinctness?
Because they are mutually contradictory, just as coolness [is incompatible] with fire (vibhāvasu).

Alternatively, even if there is separateness (pṛthaktva) in the substratum (dharmin), both separateness and non-separateness may reside therein; and since those differences are each respectively different and non-different [from one another], the aforementioned fault does not apply. To this, he says: "In non-separateness... (apṛthaktva). 1670.
And because its nature is one of dependence, it does not obtain a basis [for itself].
Just as a certain quality-giver (guṇin) acquires the status of being a quality (guṇatva) in the world, so too does he [attain it]. || 1671 ||

If the substratum (*āśraya*) is neither distinct, nor non-distinct, nor both distinct and non-distinct, then one might suspect that separateness (*pṛthaktva*) and non-separateness (*apṛthaktva*) possess independence (*svātantrya*) themselves; anticipating this objection, he says: "By way of dependence" (*pāratantryeṇa*). For in the world, a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) never becomes a quality (*guṇa*), and likewise, a quality that has not attained a substratum does not become a quality, because its very nature is one of dependence (*pāratantrya*). This is the meaning. || 1671 ||
Consequently, it follows that there would be no distinction from other things.
If another distinctness is not admitted for [the property of] distinctness itself, [then it follows that it is self-distinct]. (1672)

Furthermore, does separateness possess another separateness or not? Anticipating that the first alternative would lead to the same infinite regress (*anavasthā*), he restates the second position and refutes it with the words: "asaṃbhittiḥ" (non-connection). || 1672 ||
And separateness is dependent on another; yet the jar itself is non-separate.
The stronger [rule] subverts the weaker because it is internal (antaraṅga), while the other is external (bahiraṅga). || 1673 ||
