Section 3. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1675.
Having stated that separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is merely imagined because it is difficult to define, he states another reason for that very point: "dependent on another" (*anyāpekṣam*).

The meaning is that because it is dependent, separateness is imagined like a snake [in a rope]. Anticipating the objection that if non-separateness (*apṛthaktva*) were also imagined in the same way as separateness, then nothing at all would be unimagined, he says: "by itself" (*svayam*). Because it is independent, the single-flavored reality (*ekarasa vastu*) is unimagined.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, since non-difference (*apṛthaktva*) is its very nature (*svarūpa*), it is internal and thus powerful; whereas difference (*pṛthaktva*), being a property (*dharma*), is external and weak.
Because [non-difference] sublates that [difference], he says "it is more powerful" (*balīyān*), stating that [the latter] is merely imagined by the former. || 1673 ||
And having abstracted from qualities such as substance and so forth, what is the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) [of the substance]?
Since everything is non-different from itself, even difference is difficult to find.

Anticipating the objection—"How can it be said that the jar is itself non-different [from its qualities], since you accept its emergence from both difference and non-difference?"—he says: "Different. By the word "and" (ca), the quality of being non-different is also implied. This refers to that which, having been excluded from both [categories], is accepted as being different.

When the question arises as to what the natural form of substance, generality, and so forth is, [the answer is that] because everything is of a single flavor (*ekarasa*) by its own nature, there is no separateness (*pṛthaktva*). For that which is excluded from separateness is not also excluded from non-separateness, as that would entail the consequence of being devoid of any essential nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*). Therefore, the meaning is that the entity is of a single flavor and is the unimagined (*akalpita*); the other is imagined (*kalpita*). || 1674 ||
"Furthermore, it is your view that distinctness exists because of experience."
Not so; because it is a false experience, like [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like. || 1675 ||

Unable to tolerate the difficulty of establishing distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), he raises an objection with the words "Now" (*atha*). Does mere experience establish the distinctness of the pot, or is it uncontradicted experience? To [the first], he says: "Not so. The meaning is that since mere experience can even occur as an illusion, it does not establish a real entity. || 1679 ||

The distinction between entities is not obtained through the force of a single experience, nor is it obtained through distinct experiences, because those [experiences] are themselves not mutually connected. (1676)

In the second case as well, either the experience of the jar itself would establish its distinctness, or another experience [would do so]. In the latter case, there is the undesirable consequence that even the experience of a cloth would result in the manifestation of the distinctness of the jar. Regarding the first alternative—that the experience of the jar alone establishes its distinctness—he says: "Not by one," meaning that [the experience] terminates in the mere object [and not in its relation to another]. Nor [is it established] by another experience...
He says [in verse 1676]: "A cognition of a jar devoid of flavor establishes the distinctness of the jar, because separate cognitions cannot collectively establish a single object.
Thus he states: "Distinct... (verse 1676).
If no distinction is admitted for the Self within a single experience, [then it cannot be manifold].
In that very case, it would certainly be false because of mutual deviation. || 1677 ||

If it is argued that because it has been stated that "there is no connection between them," there would be an abandonment of one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*) due to the acceptance of a difference in experience, [the author] says "no" with the words "in a single [experience]. The meaning of this is as follows: Is the difference in experience relative to itself, or relative to something else? It cannot be the first, because it would entail the consequence of being devoid of its own nature; nor can it be the second, because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Thus, when examined in this way, if there is no possibility of difference within experience, then how could it appear in that [experience]?
1 kha. It is seen.
[Vol. 3, page 543] 1676 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Chapter]—

That [notion of] "I" would be entirely false; for if there were a difference between them, they would mutually deviate from one another—like a snake, a stream, and so forth—and thus the consequence of falsity would follow, whereby the non-dual reality (*advaya*) would necessarily be established. || 1677 ||
This internal experience does not perceive any difference, because there is no difference.
Furthermore, because it is not distinct from its own nature, one does not perceive [the self] in what is non-self. || 1678 ||

Furthermore, does experience itself apprehend its own internal difference, or does it do so through another experience? Regarding the first alternative, does it apprehend its own difference in relation to itself or in relation to something else? It says "no" to the first: [it cannot apprehend its own difference in relation to itself]. Regarding the position that another experience is the grasper of the difference of the [first] experience, he says "its own nature," etc. Indeed, another experience [cannot grasp it], because the difference [of the first experience] is as yet unestablished; therefore, it does not perceive that difference—this is the meaning.

He refutes the position that experience apprehends its own difference in dependence upon something else with the words "Nor indeed" (nāpi). The meaning is that experience cannot manifest its own difference by taking a non-self as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin), because that would involve the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya). || 1678 ||
Nor does the cognition of [the object] as a triad and so forth arise merely through the sublation by a single cognition.
Because it is the cause of that cognition, just as clay is the cause of the production of a jar. || 1679 ||
[Objection: Surely, first of all, the cognition "one" arises with respect to an object; therefore, by its sublation, the cognitions "two" or "three" arise.

For, according to the maxim that "the arising of a subsequent [cognition] is established only through the sublation of the prior," the cognition of oneness is an error because it is sublated by the cognition of duality and so forth.
Thus, the non-difference which is its object is indeed false, whereas difference—the object of the unsublated cognition—is not false. To this, he replies:
"Not so," he says. He provides an illustration for the fact that [the cognition of "one"] is to be relied upon as the cause for the cognition of "clay" and so forth:
"Just as clay... (1679).
The cognition of two, three, and so forth in a single object is false, because that object does not possess such a nature.
Even though the collection [of causes] possesses both [aspects], the Smṛti is nonetheless not a valid means of knowledge.

In that case, since the cognitions of "one" and "two or more"—just like the cognitions of clay and pot—are mutually non-sublating, the pot and so forth would have to possess both unity and plurality in accordance with both types of cognition.
Regarding this, is the object of the cognition of "two or more" the individual pot and so forth, or their collection? To refute the first alternative, he says: "Two, three, etc.

Since the pot is established as one by the cognition of "one," the cognition of "two or more" arising with respect to it must be admitted to be false, for [the pot] is inherently devoid of the nature of being two or more.

The meaning is that because an entity is accepted as a real thing (*vastu*), it does not depend upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for its cognition as having that nature; therefore, an entity is neither of a single nor a multiple nature. He states the fault in the second [alternative] with the words "of the aggregate" (*samūhasya*). Even if that aggregate is both different and non-different from its constituents, it cannot be the object of the cognition of "two" and so forth, because such [an aggregate] lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). Nor can that very cognition itself serve as the proof for it, since its status as a valid means of knowledge (*mānatva*) remains unestablished even now. This is the meaning.

Anticipating the objection that "the memory produced by the power of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) formed from the experience of each individual jar apprehends the collection of jars; so how can it be considered invalid? he says: "Of memory... (verse 1680).
If the aggregate does not exist as a real entity, because the members of the aggregate are each unitary.
Even if it were real, because it is likewise a single unity, there would still be no multiplicity; and yet, it remains so.

Furthermore, having raised the alternative as to whether a collection (*samūha*) is a real entity (*vastu*) or not, he refutes the latter [possibility] with the words "na cet" (if it is not). The meaning is:

if there is no such thing as a collection that is a real entity, then because each of the members of the collection is individually one, a single [collection] could not possess multiple natures (*anekarasa*). [Notes on variants: 1. *gha*: *stattadvā*; 1. *ga*: *asti tvekai*.

Or, having supplied the word "hi" (for), one may construe it as follows: for the purpose of showing that the collection and its constituents are difficult to define in terms of either difference or non-difference.

[The author] restates the position that [the aggregate] is a real entity (*vastu*) and then refutes it with the words "Even if it were real" (*satyatve’pi*). The meaning is that, because there is oneness among the members of the aggregate, as before, a single real entity cannot possess multiple natures (*anekarasa*). Furthermore, even if the aggregate were a real entity, since no difference from its members is observed and since it has already been stated that each member is individually one, a single thing cannot possess multiple natures; thus he says "No" (*na*). Nevertheless, regarding the aggregate...
"Even if it were a real entity," that is to say. || 1681 ||
This cognition that "there are two" or "there are three" has as its object non-duality itself.
Because the collection is a single entity, there is no distinction [of means] with respect to the valid cognition. || 1682 ||

He concludes the present topic—that because difference is not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), a single entity cannot be both different and non-different—by stating "non-duality" (*advaita*).

As for the cognition of those who maintain both difference and non-difference, such as "two," "three," or "four," that cognition, whether it refers to a collection (*samūha*) or to the members of the collection (*samūhin*), has as its object only a non-different entity, since each of those [members] and the collection itself is individually one. Therefore, due to the absence of a suitable object for difference, [difference is not real].
The meaning is: since it is neither that very means of valid cognition (*pramā*) nor another means of valid cognition, how could there be identity or difference? || 1682 ||
If the object is accessible through perception because it is distinct from its exclusion, then...
There can be no perception of the connection [between word and object] through the perception of a jar. (1683)

Having established that valid cognition (*pramā*) consists in the distinction between the experience (*anubhūti*) and the object of experience (*anubhāvya*), he states another reason for the lack of evidentiary status (*aprāmāṇikatva*) regarding the distinction between the object of experience: "If... (verse 1683). Even though objects such as a jar (*kumbha*) are perceptible, the distinction (*bheda*) is not likewise [perceptible]; for the meaning is that while the jar and so forth are experienced as the very objects of that [cognition], the distinction is something other than them.
If dharma were accessible through direct perception, then its exclusion would be asserted by you.
There would be only the cognition of the dharma, and even that would have a single object here.

He raises the objection: "The perception of a jar and so forth, being a property (*dharma*) residing in it—just like its color and other qualities—should also perceive its difference. [This is expressed by] the word *pratyakṣa*. [The author replies: Is this exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which is accepted as a property, non-different or different from its locus (*dharmin*)? In the first case, considering that the relation of property and property-bearer would be untenable, he states another fault with the word *dharmī*. If the property were merely the property-bearer itself, then the cognition of the property-bearer would be identical to the cognition of the property; and that [cognition] is what constitutes linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

The meaning is that if, on the level of ultimate reality (*paramārthabhūmi*), one were to take a single substratum (*dharmī*) as the object of action, then since its differentiation would be nothing more than the substratum itself, the entity would become of a single flavor (*ekarasa*). || 1684 ||
From cognitions of the substratum, a differentiation of cognition regarding the properties arises.
Because consciousness is undivided by place, time, and so forth, and because it possesses a single nature. (1685)

This demonstrates that if the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) were one, then their differences would also be one. [The author says: "The substratum. Furthermore, in the view of non-difference, since there is no distinction between the property and the substratum in terms of space, time, or substance, no further cognition regarding the properties can arise from the cognition of the substratum; thus he says: "Space," etc. Moreover, neither the property nor the substratum exists separately from consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is the fruit of knowledge, for that which apprehends them...

Because there is no other consciousness [apart from it], and because of its identity with that, he says that difference is merely a conceptual construction (vikalpamātra), on account of its being of a single nature (ekātmatvāt). ||1689||

Since all entities are momentary, there can first of all be no cognition of difference therein.
And that which is the object of the cognition of difference is excluded from the cognition of existence. || 1686 ||
He states another reason for the fact that difference is merely conceptual: "It is existent" (sad iti). Let it be granted that all entities have existence as their single reality;

how then, he asks, can difference be an error? To this he replies: "In that regard" (tatra iti). Since everything is nothing but existence and since that [existence] is one, difference is false; regarding this, he states another argument: "Difference... (bhedeti) || 1686 ||
By means of Being alone, all things maintain themselves through themselves.
Because it is imagined and because it is manifold, like a rope-snake or a double moon. || 1687 ||

How can there be a cessation of the cognition of difference from the object of the cognition of existence? For it is not the case that jars and other such things do not exist as objects of that [cognition]. To this, he says: "Because they are real. He states the reason for the fact that all things maintain themselves through their very nature as existence: "Because they are imagined" (*kalpitatvāt*). Just as a snake or similar object imagined upon the "this-aspect" (*idamaṃśa*) of a rope lacks any existence apart from its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), [so too do all things].
The meaning is that for the world, which is imagined upon pure Being (sanmātra), there is no essential nature apart from Being. He establishes its imagined status [with the reason]:
"because of its manifoldness. The meaning is: "The subject under dispute is imagined, because it is limited, like that which is commonly accepted [as imagined]. || 1687 ||
The meaning of the suffix is not understood as something distinct from the meaning of the base.
Therefore, in this case, the taddhita suffix in the word "sattā" would have its own primary meaning [as the referent]. || 1688 ||

Anticipating the objection that because "existence" (*sattā*) is etymologically defined as "the state of being existent" (*sato bhāvaḥ*), there is a distinction between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), and thus even in that case there is a lack of pervasion (*anaikāntikatva*) due to the presence of delimitedness (*paricchinnatva*), he says: "The meaning of the base... [and so on]. He then states the solution regarding the derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in that context: "From that... (verse 1688).
While that [consciousness] remains, any other object born of delusion necessarily undergoes change.
Therefore, like the object of a snake [in a rope], that which exists is true, while the other is false.

Having stated that the world is imagined because it is finite, he states another reason for that very point. "Satī" (in the presence of the real) means that everything other than that [real substrate] is imagined, being apprehended through delusion; this is the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
He states the reason (*hetu*) as "being subject to deviation" (*vyabhicāritva*). Regarding that, the example is "the snake and so forth. The object of dispute is imagined because it deviates—
He states the result of the inference, "like a snake and so forth due to its being a season," with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 1689 ||
For the distinctions [of objects] are perceived by one who has emerged [from meditative absorption] through direct perception, scripture, and inference.
Having attained the nature of non-existence, they are not perceived even by the lords.

[Objection: But surely, by the two reasons already stated, it is established that from the one [Being], there is only the non-exclusion (anuvṛtti) and exclusion (vyāvṛtti) of jars and so forth; it is not their imagined nature (kalpitatva). To this, he says: "For they are excluded... Jars and the like are excluded from Being; by that very exclusion, they have attained the state of being insubstantial (tucchatā). Indeed, Being itself does not exclude Being, because the relationship between a substratum (dharmin) and a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) depends upon difference (bheda). Therefore, because they are not accessible through perception and other means of knowledge...
The meaning is that [the self] and so forth are merely conceptual constructs. || 1690 ||
For oneness indeed exists without exception among all things, being non-deviating.
Whatever other entity exists apart from that is variable; therefore, only non-duality is real.
Regarding those many deviating [reasons], since they are both imagined and possess two causes, if it is argued that they deviate when these two exist, he says "no.
[Vol. 3, Page 546] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1679.
If it is argued that those many deviating [reasons] deviate when the two causes exist because they are imagined, he says "no."

"‘Sat’ [is the word]. The remainder of the sense is that, therefore, there is no suspicion of deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the existent (sat). Then, raising the objection that—since there is non-difference from the existent (sad-abheda)—both of those [existence and non-deviation] would be unestablished even in the case of jars and the like, he says: "Deviant" (vyabhicārī). He states the conclusion once it is established through one's own experience that the existence of the existent is characterized by non-deviation and unity, while jars and the like are characterized by deviation and multiplicity: "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 1691 ||
Because, having emerged from [meditative absorption], there is not even the possibility of an existing entity.
One does not even reach non-existence; what hope is there for prosperity without the self?

He states the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so") regarding the imagined nature of duality: "Having emerged" (*vyutthāya*). Since an object that exists as something distinct from Being (*sat*) neither attains existence nor non-existence once it has emerged [from it], therefore, even a mere mental wish for the prosperity of an object—that is, for its actual existence—cannot possibly occur without the Self, which is Being. This is the meaning. || 1692 ||
Anticipating the very attainment of perfection, the perfected ones think, "We have attained it."
All phenomena arise together with the yogi; they are accomplished through something else.
How, then, is the existence of jars and other objects—which are excluded from Being—established? To this he says: "The establishment of Being.

Since all entities such as jars exist as if possessing the conceit, "We are existent and we are manifest," in dependence upon the existence and manifestation that constitute the very nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it follows that because their difference [from the substrate] cannot be perceived, their exclusion from it is not established. This is the intention.

What does it say? It says "creation" (sṛṣṭi). The meaning is that just as a snake, though established by the existence of the rope as its substratum, appears as if established as something other than that, so too all entities, though having Being as their essence, appear as if emerged from it. || 1693 ||
Even by means of direct perception, non-existence is not cognized anywhere in the world.
Because that [cognition] has a real entity as its object of measurement, non-existence itself is impossible. || 1694 ||

One might object that it is incorrect to say that one who is mindful does not even reach non-existence upon emerging [from meditation], because that [non-existence] is established through the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) known as non-apprehension (abhāva). Anticipating this, he says: "By perception" (pratyakṣeṇa). The word "even" (api) is intended to include other means of valid cognition. The meaning of the reason is that all means of valid cognition have existence (sat) as their object, and there is no such thing as non-existence independent of that [existence]. || 1694 ||
Granted, this absence of a jar and so forth may be determined through direct perception.
1711. It must be stated: what is the means of valid cognition for the establishment of the absence of perception? || 1695 ||

Even while conceding that the absence of a means of knowledge (*mānābhāva*) is accessible through a means of knowledge (*māna*), he refutes it [as a proof for the non-existence of the object] with the words "Granted" (*kāmam*). || 1699 ||
Due to the distinctions of function, form, and designation, as in the case of things past and future.
The oneness of all entities exists by itself, despite their having diverse names and other attributes. (1696)

Since existence and non-existence are established as being merely conceptual constructs (*kalpita*), it has been stated that "pure Being" (*sanmātra*) alone is non-conceptual (*akalpita*). Now, an objection is raised: since existence appears to be diverse due to the difference in names such as "pot" and so forth, the difference in effects such as the fetching of water, and the difference in forms such as broadness and so on, how can that [existence] be non-dual and non-conceptual? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "kārya... (beginning with "effect," etc.). Just as in the case of Caitra and others who are related to past and other times, [the term] "child" [is applied].

Even though there is a difference in name, form, and function—such as "the old man," "the youth," "the father," or "the brother"—they do not differ; for Caitra never becomes non-Caitra. Likewise, even when jars and other objects possess different names and so forth, there is no difference in their essence; rather, it is only these [names and forms] that differ.
"Pure existence alone" means that it is non-dual and unconstructed. || 1696 ||
Now, if you say that there must be a difference here between the two, namely the property and the substratum;
Exclusion possesses the nature of both property and subject, for those two are not like heat and cold.

Since the cognition of the property (*dharma*) would be identical to the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) if there were no difference between them, the refutation has already been stated above; now, having restated the position of their difference, he refutes it with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*). || 1697 ||
The relationship of property and property-bearer is not accepted between two entities that are not distinct.
It could not exist between two absolute non-entities, nor between things that are both contradictory and non-contradictory.

Furthermore, having raised the alternatives that the relationship of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) must consist of either two existents, two non-existents, or an existent and a non-existent, he refutes them in succession beginning with "No" (*na*).
He emphasizes the point by saying "utterly" (*nitaram*), meaning that because two non-existents are themselves non-existent, their status as property and property-bearer is cast far away.
This refers to the case of an existent and a non-existent which are either contradictory or non-contradictory; the meaning is that these two are mutually contradictory.
Tell me, by what means can there be a breaking of a jar that is already without fissures?
If [the object] exists by its own nature, then you are proving my own position.
Furthermore, regarding the thought "this is one," first, a single jar appears; then one analyzes whether its difference [from others] consists in a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*).
Regarding the phrase "of that which is without difference": having restated the first alternative, he refutes it with the word "entity" (*vastu*).

The meaning is that if the difference were in the form of a real entity, then because the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) would be a real entity, the non-dual thing would become merely a substratum (*dharmin*); and in the absence of attributes (*dharma*), there can be no status as a substratum.

Since the operation of valid cognition does not function elsewhere apart from abandoning the intrinsic nature of the object, therefore non-duality (advaita) exists at all times within the object. 1700.
It refutes another alternative: [the view that] "it is the nature of the thing.

If there were a difference between the locus (dharmin) and its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) by way of the latter being of the nature of a non-entity (avastu), then that entity alone would be established by valid cognition (prāmāṇika), because it is impossible for a means of knowledge to operate upon a locus that is of the nature of a non-entity.

Therefore, since difference lacks validity, non-duality (advaita) is always the reality, and it is precisely therein that all means of knowledge possess their status as valid authorities. This is the meaning. || 1700 ||
Exclusion or inclusion applies to this entire reality.
This non-dualist position of mine is being established by you.

Furthermore, would exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and persistence (*anuvṛtti*) belong to a real entity (*vastu*) or to a non-entity (*avastu*)? In the second case [if they belonged to a non-entity], since the real entity would not be touched by them, it would result in its being a single, uniform unity;

regarding the first case, he says: "Exclusion... If those two are intended to belong to the real entity, then by the use of the genitive case, their extraction from that [entity] would imply their non-reality;
consequently, there would be non-duality of the real entity (*vastvadvaita*). This is the meaning. || 1701 ||
1. *vāSStma* [Vol.
3, page 548] 3 Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary named *Śāstramañjarī* composed by Ānandagiri. 1681.
Is the cognition "this is excluded" directed toward the jar, or toward something other than it?
Because its own nature is not excluded [from other things], this cognition does not [apply] to the jar alone. (1702)

Furthermore, is the cognition of exclusion (vyāvṛtti) without an object or with an object? Not the first, because that would entail the consequence of the Sugata’s doctrine [of non-referentiality]. In the second case, he asks: "Is the jar or something else its object? He refutes the jar being the object by saying "not the excluded," meaning that since the jar is experienced as a single entity in its own nature, a cognition of exclusion regarding it is contradictory.
Nor can there be a qualification of "jar" by means of the exclusion of "non-jar."
The coldness inherent in fire cannot serve as its distinguishing characteristic. || 1703 ||

To one who maintains that a jar (*kumbha*)—as distinguished from other things such as cloth—is the object of a cognition of exclusion, he replies: "Nor... It is not possible for a non-jar, such as a pillar, to serve as a qualifier of the jar by way of its own exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), because this would entail the absurd consequence that the pillar and other such things would also be qualifiers by virtue of being the locus of exclusion. Therefore, since everything is included within that which is excluded, the non-dual reality is what is accessible through the cognition of exclusion.
The meaning is "it would be so. The example for the point that exclusion (vyāvṛtti) qualified by a pillar or the like is not a qualifier of a jar is expressed as "for it is not... (na hi). || 1703 ||
The meaning of the genitive case, namely "this belongs to that," is understood through direct perception.
Why is there no absence of a jar in a cloth, or why does this [absence] not exist in the jar? (1704)

One might object: "Although coldness, which resides in water, lacks the status of being a qualifier of fire because it does not reside in fire, nevertheless, since the exclusion of pillars and the like resides in the jar, its status as a qualifier of the jar is established. Anticipating this, he says: *asya* ("of this"). By the genitive case in the phrase "the absence of the pillar" (*stambhasyābhāvaḥ*), the relationship between those two is made perceptible; thus, the meaning is that the absence of the pillar exists in the pillar, not in the jar. [Objection: But the jar...

One might object: "Since there is the cognition 'the cloth is not [here],' why is it not accepted that the absence of the jar is in the cloth and the absence of the cloth is in the jar? In that case, why is it restricted that the absence of the jar is in the jar and the absence of the cloth is in the cloth, given that there is no difference in the cognitions? Thus he raises the doubt with the words beginning "ghaṭa... (1704).
Existence and non-existence do not belong to that which exists; and since it does not exist, how could they belong to that which is non-existent?
"There can be no relationship of property and property-bearer between these two because of their mutual contradiction" (1705).

He offers a rebuttal, stating "existence and non-existence," etc., on the grounds that it is impossible to perceive through direct perception that non-existence resides either in the locus (*dharmin*) or in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), since such a view is fallacious as it contradicts reason. To begin with, birth and destruction are not properties of an existent thing.

The meaning is that because [the existent] always exists, it cannot be touched by those two [non-existence and existence]; nor can they belong to the non-existent, for that which lacks its own nature (niḥsvarūpa) cannot function as a substratum (dharmin). Therefore, those two are merely conceptual constructs (kalpita). One might object: "Let it be that non-existence and [the non-existent] such as a jar do not possess the status of attribute (dharma) and substratum; nevertheless, non-existence must be accepted as an attribute of the existent, since it is not independent. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not of these two... (verse 1701).
If all entities are inherently existent, upon what could their exclusion depend?
Just as darkness in the sky is itself rejected by the wise.

Having stated that because the conceptualization of distinctions and non-distinctions is itself conceptualized, there is only the unconstructed Pure Being (*sanmātra*), he provides another argument for that very point—
He says: "All. All entities, such as jars and the like, are experienced as existing by their own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*).

Thus, if everything were merely existence (*sanmātra*), then differentiation—known as exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—would not be established due to the absence of a substratum; this is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that existent entities will serve as the substrata for exclusion, he says: "Refuted," etc. Just as in the case of the ether, which is formless by its own nature...

The meaning is that just as blueness is not excluded [from the sky] by its very nature, so too is the exclusion [of the world] from pure existence (sanmātra) rejected; for such exclusion is impossible within pure existence. || 1706 ||
All this is like the sky; therein, that which exists by way of its own essence is the True Self.
The state of being a probandum is not observed otherwise, whether [the object] be non-existent or existent. (1707)

He establishes that everything consists of pure Being (sanmātratva) by means of an illustration: "like space" (nabhovat). The meaning is that just as the space within a well, a jar, and so forth is all merely space, so too the entire universe appears as nothing but pure Being. [Objection: How then is there the empirical usage of birth and so forth, for such usage does not exist in Being? To this he replies: "Therein" (tatra). That is to say, while everything consists of pure Being; [for example], a jar and the like...

That which is perceived does not attain the state of being an effect through the operation of causal factors by abandoning its nature as existence; rather, it does so through ignorance (*avidyā*) while not abandoning that nature.

This is because, since it is non-existent [in itself], it is impossible for it to be the object of the operation of causal factors. Therefore, there is no production or other modification of the existent or the non-existent; the meaning is that this [perceived world] is merely illusory (*āvidya*). || 1707 ||
For the exclusion of one thing from another object is indeed desired in the case of a different entity.
Since it is a real entity, let that [non-existence] be a real entity; if it were not, how could there be a distinction? (1708)
Furthermore, is non-existence (*abhāva*) a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*)? Regarding the first alternative, he states the defect: "From another entity" (*vastvantarāt*).

If it is maintained that the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of one entity occurs from the perspective of another entity, then since all four kinds of non-existence would likewise be real entities, there would be no obstacle to the exclusion of a jar and so forth [from them]. Consequently, because the jar and so forth would not be touched by the four kinds of non-existence, they would be non-dual (*advaya*).

Even upon contact with it, there is no injury [to space], for the sky touched by a jar does not perish. If it is argued that destruction would occur through contact with a contrary entity, we say no; for since existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) are indistinguishable in their status as real entities (*vastutva*), a contradiction between them is unestablished, just as in the case of the rat and the mongoose. If it is argued that even there, because they are both positive entities (*bhāvatva*), there is no contradiction and thus a contradiction would arise in our cognition, we say no; the meaning is that there is no contradiction when they are presented respectively as existence and non-existence.

He refutes the position that non-existence (abhāva) is not a real entity by stating, "It is a real entity" (vastu). The meaning is that if non-existence were non-existent, then difference—which depends upon it—would also be non-existent, and thus only a non-dual reality would remain. || 1708 ||
If your intended probandum is that "the jar exists as a positive entity" in its entirety, [then it is not established].
This entire duality has become like a pot; what is your opinion regarding its measure?

Furthermore, by the proponent of difference-and-non-difference (bhedābhedavādin), the non-difference of a jar from a cloth or other objects is admitted, whether in the form of a positive entity (bhāvarūpa) or a negative one (abhāvarūpa). Referring to the first case, he refutes it with the verse beginning "ghaṭa" [verse 1709]. The meaning is: if all that has been established by you through the nature of being both different and non-different is pervaded by the jar as a positive entity, then it follows that there is only the jar; thus, there is no such thing as difference, because there is a lack of evidence for it. || 1709 ||

That which makes known the object of cognition is accepted as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And since such non-existence of the means of valid cognition does not exist, it is therefore not tenable.

In the second [case], there is no non-difference; nor can the absence of a jar be established without a means of knowledge (*māna*). Nor is the non-arising of the five means of knowledge the means of knowledge for the absence of a jar; thus he says: "That which makes known" (*bodhaka*). Having raised the doubt that the same might apply to the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), he says: "And not... Since the absence of a means of knowledge lacks the capacity to make something known, it is not logical for it to be a means of knowledge regarding the absence of an object of knowledge (*meyābhāva*); thus he says: "Therefore..."
Thus it is said. || 1710 ||
If the absence of these means of valid cognition is itself understood through another absence, [then what of it?]
In the year 1695 [Bengali era], what will be the indicator for the non-existence of the five hundred and eighty means of valid cognition? || 1711 ||

Even while conceding that the absence of a means of knowledge (mānābhāva) brings about the cognition of the absence of an object of knowledge (meyābhāvabodhitva), he states the fault: "The object of knowledge," etc. The meaning is this: the absence of the object of knowledge does not lead to the cognition of the absence of the means of knowledge, because of mutual dependence (parasparāśraya); nor can that cognition arise from the absence of the means of knowledge alone, because that would involve self-dependence (ātmāśraya); nor can it arise from the presence of a means of knowledge alone, because that would result in the total abolition of the means of knowledge of non-existence (abhāvamāna). || 1711 ||
A single entity is said to be graspable by a single cognition.
Or even by the force of recognition, [the object] does not exist as a non-entity; for both of those [properties] reside in it. || 1712 ||

"Non-existence of the object of cognition (*meyābhāva*) and non-existence of the means of cognition (*mānābhāva*): there is no mutual distinction between these two types of non-existence, because it is not established that one is a property of the other. Therefore, if there is a means of cognition regarding the non-existence of the object, then there must likewise be one regarding the non-existence of the means of cognition. Anticipating this objection, he says: "One" (*eka*). By "one," a single entity is meant, which is grasped by a single cognition;

or its unity is grasped through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such as "this is that very same thing. However, neither of these two [conditions] exists in the case of non-existence. Therefore, there is no unity [between the two].
The meaning is that, because it is a positive entity (bhāvatva), it cannot be the locus of non-existence (abhāva). || 1712 ||
Just as there is the apprehension of a single object through both seeing and touching, so it is here.
For us here, there is no experience [of the self] through either perception or the means of knowledge consisting in the absence [of cognition]. (1713)

Anticipating the objection that the non-existence of the object of cognition (*meyābhāva*) is established by the absence of any means of knowledge (*māna*) that establishes it perceptually, and that the identity of the two absences is thereby established, he says: "darśana... etc. Here, "here" (*iha*) expresses the locus of the absence. The experience (*anubhūti*) does not have that identity as its object; for the identity of the two absences is not cognized by the two [cognitions] acting together, because they are mutually unaware of each other’s content. This is the meaning. || 1713 ||
Neither the means of valid cognition nor the object of cognition can be a qualification of that non-existence.
Then, because neither of the two is established, there is also an inconsistency due to contradiction. || 1714 ||

Just as you accept that there is a cognition of difference due to the distinction between limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as blue and yellow, even though consciousness is one, so too, although non-existence is non-different by its very nature, one might suspect that a difference exists therein due to the difference in counter-correlates (pratiyogin), such that one speaks of "absence of the means of knowledge" (mānābhāva) and "absence of the object of knowledge" (meyābhāva). Anticipating this, he says: "No. The reason for this is stated: "Because at one and the same moment... Since existence and non-existence cannot coexist in a single moment and because they are contradictory, there can be no distinction between them based on their qualifiers.
The meaning is: how can it be said that there is a difference in absences based on a difference in their counter-correlates? || 1714 ||
If even a non-existent phenomenon were to somehow exist through your skillfulness.
Why is it not established by those who trust [in logic] that the sky is material and the jar is immaterial? || 1715 ||
1684 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Even if existence and non-existence do not occur at the same time, why could there not be the relationship of qualifier and qualified? To this, he says: "If... (yadīti).
The meaning is that if even two things existing at different times could stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified, then everything would be easily established. || 1719 ||
The relationship of property and property-bearer is not accepted [in this case], because the two entities would be non-different.
The supreme [reality] at 924 would not exist in the absolute absence [of anything], nor would it be far removed from existence and non-existence. || 1716 ||

If it is argued that "the absence, being related to that very locus (dharmin) where the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is related, would be the qualifier of the counter-positive," [the author] says "No," because the relationship between property and property-possessor (dharmadharmibhāva) is difficult to define. || 1716 ||
There is no difference of a thing from itself, because difference depends upon another.
Even that which belongs to another could not be distinct from something else without conceptual construction.

Having refuted the relationship of qualifier and qualified, as well as the relationship of attribute and substrate, between existence and non-existence, and continuing the refutation of difference and non-difference, he recalls what was stated previously with the words "not by itself. First of all, there is no difference in a thing with respect to itself, because difference depends upon another;

nor is it logical for that difference to exist in relation to another without conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), because that would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, due to the absence of difference, a thing must be one.
This is the meaning. || 1717 ||
Because they are by nature non-different from themselves, there is no distinction, nor is there any mutual dependence.
How could that which is itself non-differentiated in both cases differentiate a contradictory object? (1718)

Furthermore, since everything is non-different in its own nature (*svarūpa*), there is no difference in essential nature; however, such a difference is not obtained in relation to a counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*).

This is because of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): a difference between the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlative cannot exist in a way that, while already present, could then differentiate the locus from its contradictory counter-correlative by depending upon it.
Therefore, he says "by itself" (*svataḥ*) [in verse 1718], meaning that difference does not have real existence.
Even when there is non-difference [between the qualifier and the qualified], the object that is the qualified does not become differentiated.
For even when there are distinctions such as white or black, the cow-substance itself is not divided. || 1719 ||

Having stated that the reality is of a single flavor by means of the elimination of the non-existence of difference, he says [the following] to show that even when differences such as pots and so forth are admitted, existence must be accepted as non-dual: "By the qualification... (verse 1719).
If the qualifier were separate from the qualified, it would be distinct [from it] like another qualified object.
Because they would be distinct, there could be no connection between the qualifier and the qualified. || 1720 ||

Now, fearing that by accepting the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*), the non-dualist’s established doctrine (*siddhānta*) would be undermined—since that relationship is inherently based on difference—the author refutes this accepted notion of qualifier and qualified with the words "The qualifier... and so forth. Is that [qualifier] different from the qualified, or non-different?

Not the first, because, like the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains, they would be absolutely distinct, and thus no connection could be established between them as such; nor the second, because of the impossibility of its very nature [if it were non-different].
The meaning is that it is superior. || 1720 ||
Furthermore, there would be no possibility of being apprehended by multiple cognitions, because cognition does not arise simultaneously.
For consciousness does not arise simultaneously with respect to both a jar and a post. (1721)

Furthermore, are those two apprehended by a single cognition or by distinct cognitions? It is not the first case; thus he says: "Not one.

For it is never observed that the Malaya and Himalaya mountains, which are absolutely distinct from each other, become objects of a single perception through mutual conjunction. As for the second case...

Regarding whether [the object] is cognizable by multiple cognitions arising simultaneously or by multiple cognitions occurring in succession, he says "of cognition" to show that the first case is not possible.
He provides an illustration for the impossibility of multiple cognitions arising simultaneously with the words "simultaneously. || 1721 ||
Even before there is a connection with a non-self, it has already acquired its nature at the very moment of its arising.
For one whose object of knowledge is the inward reality, the goal is accomplished by that alone. || 1722 ||
Therefore, that which is other than the means of valid cognition cannot possess the status of being a means of valid cognition.
Because it is subject to contradiction and because other things are subject to deviation [from their nature]. (1723)

And considering that if [the object] were to be cognized by multiple successive cognitions, it would be like a jar or a cloth— resembling a bundle of iron rods— and thus there would be no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*),

he states a defect common to both the theories of succession and simultaneity, beginning with the words "prāk" (before). This means that prior to the connection of a single or multiple cognition— whether functioning simultaneously or non-simultaneously— with its object, which is not the Self, the reality of the inner witness (*pratīc*)...

Because the object is apprehended through its imparting its own form [to the cognition], and because the means of knowledge (māna) is independent of anything other than the mere attainment of the object of measurement (meyalābha), the Self cannot have the status of being a means of knowledge (*mānatva*) with respect to any other object. Therefore, the meaning is that [attributes] such as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) are not the Self, are unestablished by valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*), and are merely imagined. Furthermore, since anything other than the Self is insentient (*jaḍa*), it is opposed to the fruit of the non-insentient means of knowledge; thus, due to the absence of any connection with it, the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is unestablished, and moreover, [such attributes] are subject to deviation (*vyabhicāritva*).
He states that what is so imagined is mutually inconsistent, like [the simultaneous perception of] a snake and a stream of water, etc., in the verse beginning with "virodhī" (1722–1723).
All [these] being mutually independent, they exist solely with the intention of expressing their own respective natures.
No entity beyond its manifest form is perceived by valid cognition.

He states another reason for the imagined nature of the non-self: "All," etc. According to the mere nature of its own essence, everything exists as independent of one another; and thus, because that [Self] is the sole essence, everything else is imagined—this is the meaning. To the question, "How is everything the sole essence of the Self? he replies: "The innermost," etc. (Verse 1724).
Whatever entity exists by its own nature does not exist for the sake of another, just as consciousness [does not exist for another].
And that which, by virtue of being for the sake of another, is distinct from that other; || 1725 ||
If it is suspected that the world is imagined as being merely the Self, then that [Self] too would likewise be so; anticipating this, he says "no," because of its lack of insentience (*ajāḍya*).

He says "that which" (*yat*) [in the verse]. Then, suspecting that the world is also unimagined because it is non-different from the Self, he says "not so," because of its insentience, adding "by way of being for the sake of another" (*pārārthyena*). || 1725 ||
Because the reality of pure consciousness is unique and non-common to anything else.
The knower and so forth, coming into being, must indeed conform to that very reality. || 1726 ||

Then, suspecting that the world and the Self are distinct because they are contradictory, he says: "Asādhāraṇa" (uncommon). Because the inner Self (*pratīc*), whose essence is pure consciousness, is neither a universal nor a particular, it is unconstructed (*akalpita*); whereas the non-Self, beginning with the "measurer" (*mātrādi*), consists of universals and particulars.

Because it is characterized by indifference (*upekṣā*), that which is imagined (*kalpita*) follows the true nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-tattva*); since there is no form of the imagined apart from that [substratum], it is logical that the world consists of nothing but the Self (*ātma-mātratā*). This is the meaning. || 1796 ||

[This arises] from the production of individual ignorance (pratyag-moha) following upon such objects as that which is to be seen.
How can there be a perception of one facing west by means of a vision directed toward an opposite direction? || 1727 ||

By stating that the non-dual reality is pure existence-consciousness (*saccinmātra*), the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-vāda*) has been refuted. Now, he says that in that [dualistic] position, the Self would be graspable by the cognition of objects, and that is untenable: "It is to be seen," etc. The word "etc. is used for the purpose of including what is to be touched, heard, and so forth. If the Self were both different and non-different [from the qualities], then because of its non-difference from form and other qualities, it would be perceived through the perception of those forms; yet it is not.

The meaning is that the vision of the inward-facing [Self], which exists internally in relation to external forms and so forth, is conjoined with the perception of those [objects]; and because it is an error born of ignorance regarding the inward-facing [Self], it cannot have the Self as its object. || 1727 ||
This, which is established by the authority of the scriptures, should not be disregarded by a wise person.
Likewise, the scripture clearly states, "It is turned away," and "Not from sight. (1728)
Having raised [the inquiry] beyond both the known and the unknown, he declared Brahman:
"There is no other reality to be known beyond this, because everything else is negated. (1729)

He states the proof for the fact that the Self is not an object of sensory perception: "By scripture," etc. This refers to the scriptural statement, "That is indeed other than the known. One might then raise the objection: "In that case, the world must be an object of cognition, otherwise the reference to 'the known' would be inconsistent. Anticipating this, he says: "Not from that," etc.
The reason for this is that no entity other than Brahman can be grasped by the means of valid cognition. [The text continues: "Other than that," etc. [It is] "not gross," etc.

The meaning is that, because the non-Self is negated by statements such as "not this, not that" (neti neti), one who has heard the Śruti understands that [the world] is merely seen through delusion. || 1728 || 1729 ||
That by which one thinks with the mind is called the "thought" (manas) of the mind.
Know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship.
From which words turn back, along with the further [instruction] "not this, not this."
Why, for what reason, is this clear statement disregarded as authoritative? || 1731 ||
Regarding the fact that the inward-facing [Self] cannot be grasped by the cognition of objects, he cites another scriptural passage beginning with "He thinks," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that this statement—like the passages concerning the sacrificer and the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*)—is not to be taken seriously, he says: "This is clear.

The sense is that there is no contradiction with the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the present context, because the meaning of the cited Śruti is unsuitable [for such a literal interpretation]. (1730, 1731)
That which is directly perceived by the inward vision within the Self of the seer;
It is, by its very nature, the undivided witness of the arising and destruction of views and other mental states.

If that were so, since the scriptural negation would be intent upon the non-existence of the world, it would result in the fallacy of the Mādhyamika view; [the author] says "no," stating "of the seer" (draṣṭuḥ). Even for the mother, within the conscious Self—the substratum—which exists as the innermost subject (pratyak), there is that collection of specific phenomena such as seeing, hearing, and so forth, which exist as objects of perception like birth and death; all that is directly perceived is what is being negated by the scriptural negation, while [the Self] remains inherently the innermost immutable...
The meaning is that since it is determined as being merely a vision of one's own mind, it does not result in the non-existence of the world. || 1732 ||
This very [Self] is thus [realized] through the means of knowledge, such as the "Tat tvam asi" (That thou art) and other [great sayings].
It is directly awakened to as Brahman by means of the path that destroys ignorance.

Prior to birth from the mother and so forth, there is no experience beyond [what is already established].

In that very context, he states another reason: "The mother and so forth," [verse 1736].
Because the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth, mutually deviate from one another.
Direct perception is non-erroneous because its nature consists in an experience that is not other [than itself]. || 1737 ||

If an object were established as existing independently of consciousness, [it would follow that it is non-existent].
Like a rope-snake and so forth, it does not even admit the possibility that "this is this."

If an object is established by means other than through the distinctions of cognition, place, and so forth;
Nor is there a connection between the cognition "the jar does not exist" and anything else; for these two do not arise from valid cognition.

He supports the statement that [the world] does not exist apart from the consciousness that has the knower and so forth as its substrate—just like a snake [superimposed] on a rope—by means of the word "consciousness" (*saṃvit*).

If it is argued that the knower and so forth are established as distinct from consciousness by way of differences in space, time, and so on, then their existence or non-existence cannot be established *per se*, because they are insentient (*jaḍa*).

A jar with its lid on has been found, possessing thick lips and existing in both space and time.

"Prior to the activity of the ears and other senses, consciousness exists as pure consciousness alone."

"Even though it is devoid of activity. The word *hi* (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of establishing the well-known fact that in the absence of space, no modification whatsoever of the world could occur. || 1742 ||
Having cast aside the meaning of the negative particle (nañ) through the mere presence of the true nature of consciousness.
Having realized its existence through the self, it does not consider itself to be something that cannot be the meaning of a sentence. || 1743 ||
Anticipating the objection that, like space, the inner self (pratīc) would then be insentient because it serves as the substratum for conceptual construction, he says: "Not so.

For consciousness, having withdrawn both existence and non-existence into its own nature as pure Being, and having further withdrawn even that into its nature as pure awareness alone, remains as nothing but the experience of the partless, single essence. This is the meaning. || 1743 ||
Just as the division of directions is conceptually constructed within space, even though space itself is undivided.
Even though all distinctions have been utterly destroyed within me, those of divided intellect perceive me in that same way.
Nevertheless, suspecting that if it were the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), it would be limited like a rope or similar objects, he says: "Direction" (dig). || 1744 ||
Even when the dream has vanished, the cognition of its own nature shines forth in the waking state.
Just as this duality born of delusion [persists], so too it remains even now, though delusion has been destroyed.

Anticipating the objection that "if all superimposition (adhyāsa) of ignorance upon consciousness is destroyed for the knower whose ignorance has been dispelled, then the appearance of duality cannot be established," he says: "In a dream... The sense is that it has been stated more than once that the knower's perception of duality arises from a remnant of ignorance. || 1749 ||
The self's state of being both different and non-different [from the body] is established through scripture and other means of valid cognition.
In the manner described, it is not apprehended even in the slightest degree. || 1746 ||
1. Therefore, do not [speak thus]. 2. Kha:
immeasurable. 3.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1689.
He concludes the demonstration that the inference of difference and non-difference is untenable with the words: "From scripture" (āgamāt). || 1746 ||
And regarding that validity which has been established by another means of knowledge, the Śruti [is authoritative] therein.
It cannot be conceived in any way as being a restatement, because it possesses the character of an explanatory reference (anuvāda). || 1747 ||

Anticipating the objection that "then let the identity and difference of the Self be understood from scripture," [the author] considers the alternatives—whether this is the object of another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) or of scripture alone—and refutes the first with the words "from another means of knowledge" (*mānāntarāt*).

The meaning of the first *ca* (and) in the phrase "from scripture and so forth" is the first alternative; the meaning of the second *ca* is "just as in the case of another means of knowledge. || 1747 ||
The status of being a means of valid cognition is attributed to cognitions only when their object has not been apprehended by another means of valid cognition.
And the statement, "Fire is the remedy for cold," would otherwise be rendered false.

Furthermore, because it would contradict the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as that which makes known an object not already known, the Veda has no authority regarding an object already perceived; thus he says: "The end of valid cognition...
He states the flaw in the opposing view: "Fire... || 1748 ||
Furthermore, the Śruti is not capable of authorizing that which is contradicted by another means of valid cognition.
Pride has as its object its own specific domain, not the domain of another form of pride.

Regarding the second [alternative], there is a dilemma: either the scriptural passages concerning creation and so forth, or the scriptural passage beginning with "That which... (Chāndogya 6.2.1), teaches what has been stated [i.e., the identity of Brahman and the individual soul]. He refutes the first position with the words "by another means of knowledge" (*pramāntara*). The meaning is that the scriptural passage on creation and so forth is unable to establish that the Self is both different and non-different from Brahman, as this would contradict statements such as "neither coarse nor fine" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.8); for a subordinate sentence cannot establish a meaning that contradicts the primary [context].
He states the reason why [a cognition] does not establish what is contradicted by another means of knowledge: "In its own domain... (1749).
Just like the sense organs such as the ear, there is therefore no confusion of their respective objects.
Nor is this scripture intended for the purpose of establishing both difference and non-difference.
For that which is expressed by the word "tat" (that) is directed toward an object other than this [immediate one]. || 1750 ||
He provides an illustration for the fact that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are "heroic" regarding their own respective objects. [The verse says: "The ear, etc.

The conclusion is stated as follows: because the means of knowledge possess sovereignty over their own objects, and because those objects are fixed, scripture (*śruti*) does not have as its domain anything that contradicts other means of knowledge. Having raised another alternative view, he replies: "Whether different or non-different. (1790)
This statement is not intended for the purpose of establishing distinctions such as those between views and so forth.
Since difference is established by other means, the scripture does not strive to establish it there. || 1751 ||

Anticipating the objection that, even though it is a different object from the distinct and non-distinct objects, it is itself a separate category of entity consisting of the differentiation of seeing and so forth, he says:
"Seeing and so forth... (Verse 1751).
But consciousness, too, would belong to it just like desire, karma, and so forth.
It has been stated [in this verse] because of the doubt that one who does not perceive by himself is not ignorant.
If the sentence does not establish either difference-and-non-difference or mere difference, then what does it establish? To this, he says:
[1] *ka* (in the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, and *gha*); [2] *sya bhaiṣajyam* (in manuscript *gha*: *ditiprakṛtaśru*).

"But what? [The author] states the meaning conveyed by the sentence: "Consciousness. The meaning is that this sentence establishes the non-destruction of vision during deep sleep by way of restating the distinctions of vision and so forth as they are well-known in the world. || 1752 ||

Just as the vision of this Self is self-evident during both dream and waking states, so too is that witness of the entire collection of modifications such as the objects of perception inherently indestructible.
In that regard, he provides an illustration for the non-destruction of perception: "In a dream," etc. The word should be divided as "avinaśvarī" (indestructible). || 1793 ||
In me, too, this [nature] remains exactly as it is, characterized by the identity of the immutable.
However, in this context, the distinction regarding ignorance and so forth consists solely in their existence or non-existence. (1754)

He states the answer to the objection: "Even in the case of the wise person. Anticipating the doubt—"If vision is desired there as well, what is the distinction between that [state] and waking, etc.?"—he says: "bhāva... (the word *bhāva*). The particle *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). The second [particle *ca*] is for the purpose of excluding any other distinction.
The word *kevala* is for the purpose of making manifest the meaning of the emphasis. The word *iha* refers to the three states. || 1754 ||
When all adventitious conditions, beginning with desire, have ceased, it does not cease.
Because it serves as the witness for that cessation, just as there is a witness for the existence of desire and so forth. || 1755 ||
To the question of how the doubt—that even consciousness perishes during sleep, just like desire and so forth—is resolved, he says:

"kāmādi" (desire, etc.). The meaning is that in all cases, as far as possible, one must accept the vision of the Self as indestructible, by virtue of being the witness of both the existence and non-existence of those [states such as desire].
Because it is the witness of both existence and non-existence, it is itself of the nature of both existence and non-existence.
Just as a pure gem is perceived by the ignorant through its settings, so too is it grasped by the deluded through ignorance. || 1756 ||

Anticipating the question, "How then can there be a perception of birth and so forth in that [Brahman]?", he says: "bhāva... (existence...). He provides an illustration for the point that the perception of birth and so forth is adventitious (*aupādhikī*), saying: "maṇi... (the gem...). || 1716 ||
It is truth, knowledge, and infinite; it is also a mass of pure consciousness.
"Brahman is consciousness"—thus, the self consists of nothing but knowledge. (1757)
He states the corroboration from another scriptural passage regarding the indestructibility of vision: "It is true," [verse 1797].
And we do not lack an illustrative example, for gems and the like are possible in this world.
The distinction of the inner self from seeing and so forth is like that of [the difference between] a dark-blue object and others. || 1758 ||

Since every entity is both different and non-different, the Self also, being an entity, must be so; this [argument] has been refuted, as has its claim to be based on the Vedas (*śrautatva*). As for the objection that there is no illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in the opponent's position, we consider the following alternatives: is the appearance of a single thing in multiple forms an illusion (and thus lacks an example), or is it that a real entity possesses only a single form (and thus lacks an example)? Refuting the first alternative, he says: "And the illustrative example... and so forth.
The word "here" (iha) means in the perception of one thing as many. He elaborates on the meaning of the second quarter [of the verse] with the words "of the gem" (maṇeḥ). || 1798 ||
Those who assert that the thesis, the reason, and the example are both different and non-different.
There are no things here that are mutually distinct, because they consist merely of identity-in-difference.
1. Not so; because of the oneness of the Self that is neither this nor that. 2. In those consisting of the Self.
