The non-arising of the inference of "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) due to the impossibility of the probandum (*sādhya*) and other reasons was stated previously; now, he states its non-arising by way of another method.

[He says] "the proposition" (*pratijñā*). The locative sense here refers to the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*). Therefore, for you alone, there is an absence of an example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*). ||1759||
In this case, the objection raised against us is merely that there is no supporting example.
We certainly have a clear example right before our eyes, namely your own face, because of its very greatness.

He replies to the second [objection] with the words "dṛṣṭānta" (example). Here, the word "iha" (here) refers to an entity of a single form. By the suffix "-mātra," it is indicated that even the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth do not exist in your position; this is the excellence [of our position]. If it is argued that the absence of an example is also a defect, he says in response: "the example exists. If it is asked how that [example] is understood, he says: "through your own mouth. || 1760 ||
In this doctrine of difference-and-non-difference, that which is said by you to be distinct—
Let that very thing be our example; I do not seek anything other than this.
Regarding the question of what example has been seen based on the statements of those who advocate both difference and non-difference, he says: "bhinnetyādi" (beginning with 'different', etc.). 1761.
These two, "distinct" (bhinna) and "non-distinct" (abhina), necessarily have distinct meanings.
Both [the universal and the particular] must be accepted by you yourself for the sake of establishing their being both different and non-different. || 1762 ||

To the objection—"How can the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) be established there, since by one who asserts that 'everything is both different and non-different,' a confusion between difference and non-difference is admitted, and thus a non-confused non-difference does not exist?"—he replies: "Necessarily" (avaśyam). || 1762 ||
If it is indeed intended that there is identity between the two designations, whether they are distinct or non-distinct.
For you, there would be no example at all, because everything would possess a single, identical nature.
He states the fault in the opposing view: "It would result in identity of meaning" (aikārthyam). || 1763 ||
Nor is even a single object denoted by the statement of being both different and non-different.
Because you negate distinct objects, your speech is non-differentiated.

Furthermore, he states that even the suspicion that the words "different" (bhinnā) and "non-different" (abhinnā) have the same meaning has no basis: "Different," etc. The phrase "of you" (tava) is an elliptical expression;
it should also be understood as "of me" (mama). || 1764 ||
Just as here the word "horse" (aśva) is used to express the meaning denoted by the name "go" (cow).
An object distinct from the meaning of the word "difference" is not [produced] by the word "difference" in that manner. || 1765 ||

Even though the two [terms] have different meanings, the negation of difference does not mean identity; rather, it is something other than difference. Anticipating the objection that such a thing is possible in one case, he says: "In the case of the word 'cow' (*gobhidhāna*)," etc. Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). The meaning is that, in the absence of the negative particle (*nañ*), [the term] is primary (*mukhya*). (1761)
Upon the attainment of the state of being the self of all, there is no longer any unique, particular entity.
You have relied upon the absence of valid cognition (pramābhāva) for the purpose of negating the state of being the self of all.

By stating that the words "difference" and "non-difference" have the meanings of existence and non-existence respectively, and thus lack a single common object, he has provided an example for his own position. Now, he states another fault regarding the claim that "everything is both different and non-different," beginning with the word "sarva. Since it is accepted that a unique entity such as a jar is both different and non-different from everything else—such as a cloth—it would follow that the jar possesses the nature of all things; consequently, the intended means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) known as non-apprehension (*abhāva*) would be destroyed.
[Vol.

3, page 559] 1692 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]—this is the meaning. One might raise the objection: "How does it perish by this much, since it has scope as long as it relies upon difference? Anticipating this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "being the self of all": 1766.
This discussion regarding difference and non-difference is like digging a hole and then filling it in.
Furthermore, because everything would be non-different from everything else, even linguistic convention would perish. || 1767 ||

For in the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*), it is impossible to deny that everything has everything as its essence; otherwise, the statement that things are both different and non-different would be untenable.

Therefore, [the author] says: "By you yourself, having cast the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāva*)—which is of the nature of the absence of valid cognition—into a pit, it has been covered over. He states this with the word "different" (*bhinnaiḥ*). He points out another defect in the opponent's view with the words "by all" (*sarvaiḥ*). (Verse 1767)
Each individual entity is distinct and mutually unconnected.
But if there were no difference [between the universal and the particular], there would be only one thing, like that which possesses neither generality nor particularity.

[The opponent asks: "How is it that all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) become untenable? To this, he states that transactions based on difference are absent therein: "Each one... [He replies: "No; for it is only one," meaning that there would be only a single entity. The implication is that, consequently, the entire world would be devoid of both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).
For in the world, the usage of words such as "view" (dṛṣṭi) and so forth applies only to cognition.
From the perception [of objects], there would be mere cognition, because those [objects] are established as being [nothing more than] that. || 1769 ||

By stating that the intent of the passage beginning with "that which is indeed this" does not concern whether vision and the other [faculties] are different or non-different, he has presented an illustrative example for his own position and the absence of such an example for the opponent's position. Now, he states another reason for their lack of difference: "vision and so forth.
He summarizes the aforementioned reason, saying: "because of common renown" (prasiddhitaḥ). || 1769 ||
It is observed that one thinks, "I know directly through the five [senses], such as the ear."
Therefore, in the world, sound and so forth are designated by the term "cognition" because they are perceived through seeing and other such means. (1770)

This [verse] clarifies that it is well known for words such as "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth to denote mere cognition (*jñāna*). [The commentary says: "paceti" (and so on). This means "of that word, namely vision" (*dṛṣṭyādeḥ tat-padasya*). The analysis of the compound is: the state (*tattā*) of that which has cognition alone as its object (*vāryya*). || 1770 ||
By which one [perceives] form, taste, smell, sounds, and touches, as well as sexual union.
"By this very [means] one knows," such also is the teaching of the Śruti. || 1771 ||

He cites the *Kāṭhaka-śruti* as authority for the view that seeing and the other functions are mere knowledge, using the phrase "by which": "By which"—that is, by this witnessing consciousness—people perceive forms and so forth;
when that [consciousness] is known, nothing remains of that which is to be known. This statement regarding seeing and the rest [establishes their nature].
The meaning is that [the scripture] makes known its state of being mere cognition, because the verb "to know" (jānāti) is employed in all instances. || 1771 ||
Whether it be a cutter or a piercer, because of the agent's connection with the bridge.
This differentiation would arise through actions; it is not, however, endowed with the status of a grammatical factor (*kāraka*).

Even the distinction between the various actions such as seeing, which depend upon instruments such as the eye, does not deserve to be rejected because it is established in common experience; thus says Pāṭhaka (variant: Pāvaka): "Not from this...
[Vol. 3, page 560].

Anticipating the objection that there might be a difference [in the case of a compound] because the denoted meaning of "seeing" and so forth— which resides in the cognition of the compound— is distinct, [the author] says, "The cutter (lāvaka)," intending that there is no difference in the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha), since it consists solely of the Self (ātman-mātra). || 1772 ||
The sun [is the witness] of those who go, those who study, those who eat, and those who perform various actions.
Just as it illuminates while remaining of a single nature, so too is it with cognitions.

Anticipating the objection that the Self's lack of agency is unproven because it is the seer of seeing and so forth, he says: "Of those who go... The connection is: "[the Self] beholds the cognitions. (1773)
Those [actions] characterized by different locations and so forth have distinct activities such as seeing and the like.
The intellect perceives that single, supreme light as having a single form.

He elaborates upon the illustrative example: "View and so forth. By the word "place" (deśa), the eye and other [senses] are expressed; the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to time; and the word "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the causal sign (nimitta). || 1774 ||
Having begun with the question "What is its light?", [the Lord] spoke with great effort and reverence.
This very meaning has been determined; what is said that contradicts it? || 1775 ||

Furthermore, having established that the Self is the immutable, single-flavored light, he states that there would be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows if one were to ascribe to it such activities as seeing and so forth. He asks: "Why? [The answer is: the greatness of the effort involved in establishing one's own position by means of refuting the opposing view consists in the clarity of both the proof and the refutation, the demonstration of due regard, and the citation of an illustrative example. || 1775 ||
Although the Seer is by its own nature non-different [from the Self], it appears so due to its connection with limiting adjuncts arising from delusion.
Just as lac-dye [colors what it touches], so do the notions of "seer" and "hearer" undergo diversification.

Anticipating the objection—“If the Self is the immutable witness (kūṭasthadṛṣṭi), how can it have the perception of multiplicity such as being the ‘seer’ or the ‘hearer’?”—the author says: “Through delusion,” etc. Just as a crystal gem, which is pure by nature, assumes various forms such as redness depending on the proximity of an external adjunct like lac-dye or something else, so too [is the Self]; thus he says: “Just as,” etc. (Verse 1776).
The differentiation of the light [of consciousness] arises from that which is illuminated, through distinctions such as red and so forth.
Just as there is a distinction among lights due to the distinction among the objects illuminated, so too is there a distinction of the self. || 1777 ||

Raising the objection: "Even if a non-luminous object such as crystal appears otherwise due to an adjunct (*upādhi*), how can the luminous Self appear otherwise through dependence on another? he says: "Red, etc.

Just as the light of a lamp or similar source appears differentiated according to the differences among the objects to be illuminated—such as red things—and so forth, so too, because the luminosity of the Self is without distinction, it appears as the "seer" and so on due to the differences among the objects to be manifested, such as that which is to be seen.
The meaning is that diversity is established. || 1777 ||
Nor does this apply to partless entities, as it does to things that possess parts.
The state of being both different and non-different cannot be brought about even by the Lords themselves, let alone directly.

The [notion] that seeing and the other faculties are neither different nor non-different from the seer, and are mutually different, has now been refuted; he now refutes what was stated [in the verse] beginning with "just as in the case of gross objects" (sthūleṣu yadvat) by saying "in partless [entities]" (niraṃśeṣu). || 1778 ||
Nor,
moreover,
is it possible here to conceive of the relation of difference and non-difference in things that are partless.
There is not even a single example to be found in this world, whether among the animate or the inanimate.

In this regard, he states the reason for the absence of an example with the words "And not... (na ca). The meaning is also that [the property of] being a cow and so forth is equivalent to the probandum (*sādhya*). || 1779 ||
The distinctions among the capacities of the sense organs, such as the eye, arise from the distinctions among their objects, such as visible form.
By this same reasoning, the postulation of modification has been refuted with respect to the Self.

By the very same reasoning that refutes the identity or difference of vision and the other [faculties] with respect to the Self, the conceptualization that the power of vision and so forth transforms itself into the eye and so forth, as well as into form and so forth, is also refuted; thus he says: "Vision and so forth... (1780).
For the existence of the potencies is established through their effects, by virtue of their being causes.
Since it is understood from this that [the self] does not exist, there is no causal capacity in the self. || 1781 ||

Furthermore, he states that there is no power (śakti) in the Self at all because there is a lack of evidence. [He says] "kārya... etc. He provides the reason for the claim that their existence is known through the effect as its mark (liṅga): "because of being a cause" (kāraṇatvataḥ). The meaning is this: a cause is that which possesses power, and since that [cause] is known through the effect as its mark, it follows that by virtue of being a qualifying attribute, the possession of power is also marked by that [effect]. || 1781 ||
The identity of power and the possessor of power is not tenable through reasoning, because of their difference.
It may be possible for someone to understand [the distinction] between the meanings of the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya).

If it is argued that because the Self is not an agent, it lacks the capacity [for action], and therefore the power to produce the world and so forth must reside in the Pradhāna and other such causes because they are agents—having raised this doubt, one should consider the alternatives: whether there is non-difference or difference between the power and the possessor of power in the case of the base and the suffix. Regarding the first [alternative]:

He states the fault: "śakti... and so forth. Furthermore, it should be understood that even if their difference were perceived, that [distinction] cannot be established, because of the impossibility of the relation between power and its possessor, just as in the case of the Himalaya and Vindhya mountains. || 1782 ||
Or this [suffix] may be used in the sense of the base itself (prakṛtyartha), or as the possessive suffix *matup*, or else in some other sense.
"In the former case, there is non-establishment of the thesis because of difference; likewise, in the latter, there is no identity.

(1783) To clarify the meaning stated [in the previous verse], he analyzes the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*) in the word "possessing power" (*śaktimat*). He says: "In the base... (*prakṛti*).

If the meaning of the base is power itself and this is the meaning of the possessive suffix, then the thesis—"the cause is that which possesses power"—is unestablished. Thus, he refutes the first position with the words: "In the thesis... (*pakṣa*). Of the power...
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is as follows: because it would follow that [the suffix] alone is the cause, and because that [suffix] cannot exist apart from its substratum and its object.

He refutes another alternative view with the words "bhedāt" (due to difference): if the suffix were to denote an object other than the meaning of the base—that is, the possessive sense—then, since there is a difference between the power (*śakti*) and the possessor of the power (*śaktimad*), their intended identity would not be established; nor could there be a mere difference between them, for that would preclude the relationship of power and possessor of power. || 1783 ||
The power of one capable of creating everything is indeed our own self-consciousness alone.
Therefore, the doctrine of potency is not established by any means of valid cognition in any other way.

One might object: "Surely the doctrine of power (śaktivāda) does not deserve refutation by means of the dilemmas of difference and non-difference, since you too have resorted to the concept of power. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The Self" (ātma). || 1784 ||

The powerless is empowered by power, and likewise, power is [empowered] by the possessor of power.
How can there be a mutual connection between these two, given that they are incapable [of such] due to the impossibility of a cause? (1785)

How is it that the theory of power (*śakti*) as something distinct from the self and ignorance lacks valid proof? To this, [the author] refutes the second alternative—that there is no power in either [the self or ignorance] individually regarding their mutual relationship—by stating: "It is powerless" (verse 1785).
If it is held that even those two possess numerous potencies,
then because the same objection applies there as well, an infinite regress would result.

Having restated the initial objection, he replies: "The powers" (*śaktayaḥ*). There too, the meaning is that it applies to both the respective powers and their possessors. The existence of an equal objection consists in the necessity of [admitting] the possession of power in each respective case. || 1786 ||
Therefore, the very Self, when unknown, is designated as "power" (śakti).
Therefore, the birth of space and the other elements is declared by the Śruti. || 1787 ||

Having refuted the opposing view, he concludes his own position with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He states the proof for this with the words "Of space, etc. (*ākāśāder iti*). For a cause is held to be possessed of power; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the Self is heard in scripture to be the cause of the universe while remaining unknown; therefore, the meaning is that the very ignorance of the Self is the power. || 1787 ||
If this is so, then its very nature is the state of undivided vision.
Now, let it be stated: what is the reason for the abandonment of intrinsic nature? || 1788 ||
The passage beginning with "Whatever one sees there" has been explained as referring to the immutable, undifferentiated inner Self (*pratyagātman*);

now, in order to introduce the passage beginning with "But where [one sees] another," he raises an objection: "Now, however... Having raised the alternative—whether the vision of the undifferentiated is the very nature of the Self or whether it is the knowledge of distinctions—he states the defect of the first position by pointing out the impossibility of the knowledge of distinctions during the waking state and so forth.
"If it were thus," [it would be as follows]. || 1788 ||
Or rather, its very nature is admitted to be specifically determinative cognition itself.
Why is it said that its abandonment occurs during deep sleep? || 1789 ||

Having restated the second [objection], he states the fault regarding the attainment of specific cognition even in deep sleep: "viśeṣa... etc. He introduces the subsequent sentence as a response to this: "abhidhīyate" (it is explained). || 1789 ||
In this phenomenal world of waking and dreaming, the Self is caused solely by ignorance.
Even that which is not other than itself is perceived as if it were other due to delusion. || 1790 ||
In that case, there would be one agent who is the seer, and he would be distinct from the eye itself.
One should see the other visible world as arising from ignorance, just as one sees objects in a dream.

He states its meaning: "In the waking state," etc. The sense is this: in that state of ignorance (*avidyā*), when the waking state and so forth produced by it exist, the Self—though inherently non-dual—is perceived as if it were dual due to delusion; therein, He becomes the possessor of the distinctions of agent and so forth.
(Variant reading: *bhāgabhogī*).
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four [Vol. 3, p. 563]. Verse 1790:
He clarifies, by means of an illustration, how that which is inherently non-dual appears as if it possessed duality due to ignorance, using the example of a dream. "In a dream... [etc.]
For, in the perception of distinction, ignorance alone is its cause.
Therefore, when that [ignorance] has ceased, all differentiation ceases. || 1792 ||
He states the result of accepting that "the perception of duality is ignorance" in the verse beginning with "viśeṣa... (verse 1792).
And thus, the statement of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad becomes logical.
Because it concludes with "where there is nothing else" and likewise "the Self alone," [it is established that the Self is the cause]. (1793)

He corroborates the point that the perception of duality is merely ignorance by citing another scriptural passage: "In the Chāndogya," etc. Since the Chāndogya Upaniṣad begins with "Being alone" (sadeva) in the sixth chapter and concludes with "the Self alone" (ātmaiva) at the end of the seventh, the non-duality of the Self is understood through the uniformity of its opening and closing statements; therefore, he states that the vision of duality is produced by ignorance. Thus it is said: "And so," etc. (1793).
And this statement has been explained with reverence in the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, no further explanation will be provided here at this point. || 1794 ||
He concludes the commentary on the passage beginning with "In which," having first stated the reason for its brief explanation, [saying] "Maitreyī.
That very reality which was introduced with the words "That indeed" has been explained at length.
By the words "water" and so forth, its conclusion is made here. || 1795 ||
He introduces the passage beginning with "salila" (water) by first stating its purport: "yad" (that which), etc. [1799]
For ignorance alone is the cause with respect to the relationship between cause and effect.
Because of right knowledge, when that [ignorance] has been destroyed, there remains only the Self.
He provides a transitional introduction for the purpose of explaining the category of water: "Ignorance" (avidyā). || 1796 ||
Indeed, without depending on ignorance, there can be no association with the non-self for the inward-looking [Self].
For upon its destruction, nothing other than the Self remains. || 1797 ||
He elaborates upon the fact that everything is nothing but the Self, beginning with the words "Not," and so forth. || 1797 ||
Since it is by its very nature pure self-awareness alone, how could there be any immersion in ignorance and the like?
Therefore, like water, it is pure through the abandonment of cause and effect. || 1798 ||

He states the reason why there is no connection with the non-self (anātman) for the Self (ātman), except through its own ignorance (avidyā): "By itself" (svataḥ). He states the meaning of the word "water" (salila) as the result when all that is characterized by ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge (vidyā) and only the Self remains: "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 1798 ||
Even without a [direct] connection between the entities of cause and effect.
Fearing that it might therefore consist of multiple natures by its own nature, [the author] states that it is one. (1799)
He raises the word "eka" (one) as a response to an objection, [saying] "without... || 1799 ||

The state of being a wood-apple and so forth is not, by its own nature, manifold in essence.
Having spoken thus, the Śruti declared that [the Self] is one, like water. || 1800 ||

He states its meaning with the words beginning "no" (neti). Or rather, the exclusion of similar things is expressed by the word "one" (eka).
For by the mention of "salila" (water), a connection with a different genus is indeed excluded. || 1801 ||

He states another meaning for the word *eka*: "of the same class" (*sajātīya*). The particle *hi* is used for the purpose of indicating that even in that case, the word *tat* (it) possesses the necessary logical force (*sāmarthya*). [The opponent objects: "Since the single term 'one' (*eka*) is capable of excluding all differences, what is the purpose of the qualification 'of the same class'?"

Anticipating the objection that the word "salila" might have another meaning, he says: "In water," etc. Since everything is designated as being nothing but the Self (ātman), and because any differentiation of the non-Self has been refuted, the single term is intended for the purpose of eliminating the notion of difference within the Self; this is the meaning. || 1801 ||
"The word 'one' here does not signify number, because a thing to be numbered is impossible in this context."
Therefore, it is precisely the state of being non-dual that follows from the negation of a second object.

Anticipating the objection that the word "one" (*eka*), when denoting a number, might instead intend a relationship between a quality and its possessor—and thus not convey the intended meaning—the author says: "One," etc.

Here, the word "here" refers to the Self. For oneness is not a quality in that [Self], because of the scriptural teaching of its being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*). [The word] "number," etc. [is used].
He states the established conclusion regarding the impossibility of accumulation: "without a second" (advitīya). || 1802 ||
And by the passage beginning with "together with the gods," its non-contradiction with reality is likewise established. (1803)
Since the inward-looking vision culminates in the realization of the inner Self alone, therefore...
Because its intrinsic nature is that of a non-agent, it is designated as "the non-seer. || 1804 ||

Raising the objection that the word *eka* (one) is well-known in the usage of the learned (*vṛddha*) as denoting a number and thus cannot mean "without a second," he says "It is so" (*sad iti*), meaning that this is indeed the case provided that the word *eka* has the sense of "non-dual" (*advaya*). He then explains the meaning of the term *adraṣṭṛ* (the non-seer), preceded by the statement of the reason for its being without an object (*akārakatva*): "The inner self" (*pratyag iti*). 1803 || 1804 ||
For it is because of the statement "where there is duality" and the teaching of the passage "but where [one sees] this."
The light that is inherently full is designated as the "non-seer. || 1805 ||
Anticipating the objection that "draṣṭā" (the seer) should be taken as a separate word, he refutes it with the verse beginning "yatra" (1809).
Since this is so, one is non-dual because of having transcended ignorance and its effects.
In the absence of knowledge and so forth, this cognition [of duality] is not possible. || 1806 ||

Since the Self is immutable (*kūṭastha*) and devoid of distinctions between its own kind (*sajātīya*) and other kinds (*vijātīya*), it follows that it is free from internal differentiation (*svagatabheda*); thus he states the meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Regarding the phrase "since": one might raise the objection, "Even in the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its products, why should the appearance of internal differentiation not occur? Anticipating this, he says: "Not indeed. The sense is that the non-existence of an effect is well-established when there is an absence of its cause. || 1806 ||
They say that "this is two" is *dvīta*; the state of being that is called *dvaita* (duality).
And by the negation of those [dualities], non-duality, the innermost reality, is denoted. || 1807 ||
[Vol. 3, page 565] 1698 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

Now, one might object: "Since there are three possible meanings for the negative particle (*nañ*), how can non-duality (*advaita*) be determined without first ascertaining one of them? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] addresses the word "non-duality" (*advaita*).

He states the meaning according to the [grammatical] case endings: "In two ways" (dvidhā). This excludes the possibility that non-duality (advaita) terminates in non-existence (abhāva). [The word] "pratyak" [indicates the opposite]. || 1807 ||
In this world, the existent cause may manifest in two ways, three ways, or in many ways.
Because that [duality] has been negated within the Self, the Self therefore becomes non-dual. || 1808 ||

He explains how the state of being characterized by the negation of duality is established there, beginning with the words "dvidhā" (in two ways): "If the cause of duality were not negated here in this Self, then there would be duality of many kinds in it; but since that cause is negated by the term 'absolute non-duality' (atyantādvaita), and because the negation of absolute duality is thus possible, the Self becomes non-dual"—this is the construction of the verse. (1808)
Even for the Śruti which thus exerts effort for the purpose of abandoning both difference and conjunction, [it remains as it is].
Disregarding this, they have spoken otherwise; oh, how great is this knowledge!

Having determined the uniformity of the Self from the passage beginning with "salila," he states the contradiction of that passage for those who maintain the doctrine of both difference and non-difference: "bhedā... (verse 1809).
The establishment of the mutual distinction between phenomena does not arise from their dependence on a self.
The relationship between a property and its substratum depends upon a perceiver, because it is an object of perception (dṛśyatva).
[Verse 1810] By mocking those who maintain that the Self is both different and non-different from the Veda by claiming "knowledge is great," their ignorance has been asserted;
now, he states the reasoning that establishes this [point], beginning with the word "mutually" (mithaḥ). If attributes such as seeing were to have the Self as their locus, then from that...

The meaning is that because difference is difficult to define, even the mutual difference between them is unestablished; therefore, they cannot be attributes of the Self. Anticipating the objection that seeing and the other functions are neither different from nor identical to the Self—since the relationship of attribute and substrate is untenable for either case—but rather are both different and non-different, as this is established, the author says: "Dharma... [etc.]. For in the case of form, a pot, and so forth, the relationship of attribute and substrate is observed precisely because they are objects of vision relative to a seer; however, such is not the case for the attributes of the Self.

If that [quality of being visible] were to belong to the Self as well, it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of the Self being an object]; yet the Self cannot be its own object of vision, nor can there be another seer. Therefore, the meaning is that seeing and the other [functions] are not attributes of the Self. || 1810 ||
The seer is pure like water, likewise unattached, solitary, and non-dual.
Therefore, those devoid of shame describe here a meaning for what is stated in the Śruti that is contradictory. || 1811 ||

Restating the meaning of the passage beginning with "salila" (like water), he summarizes the contradiction for those who maintain both difference and non-difference: "The Seer," etc. The word "artha" refers to the subject of difference and non-difference; the word "iha" (here) refers to the Self. || 1811 ||
Just as there is no portion of darkness in the sun, so too there is no non-existent portion in that which exists.
In this way, space itself would possess corporeality; thus, the self would be characterized by both difference and non-difference.

Having stated the contradiction with scripture and logic regarding the soul's being both different and non-different [from Brahman], he concludes that such a state is impossible by means of examples: "lama" (it is like a leaf), etc. || 1892 ||
Therefore, it was stated previously, again and again, that "beyond this, for the sake of liberation."
Because that liberation is fully accomplished, the Sage declared, "This [is it]. (1813)

He takes up the word "this" (eṣa) found in the sentence beginning with "This is the world of Brahman. The phrase "from this" means that which was previously mentioned and asked about.
Because of its proximity, the Self is denoted by the word "this. || 1813 ||
Because the reality of the Self is directly perceived, being unobstructed by the inward-looking vision.
"This" is the designation of the Self, as is the Vedic revelation: "That which is directly. (1814)
And fearing that this [Self], which does not have the form of "this" (anidamākāra) and is accessible only through scripture, might not be fit for the word *etad* ("this"), he says:

*pratyak* ("innermost"). The meaning is that because it is not separated from existence (*sat*) and is its very self (*tadātmatva*), the Self possesses the quality of being perceptible (*pratyakṣatva*) and is therefore fit for the word *eṣa*. He states the proof for the perceptibility of the Self: *yad*... || 1814 ||
It is neither excluded nor followed, being devoid of both generality and particularity.
The primary reality is designated as "Brahman" by the Śruti. || 1815 ||
He states the meaning of the word *brahman*: "unrestricted" (*avyāvṛtta*). The reason for this is: "without a universal" (*niḥsāmānya*).

If it is argued that Brahman exists even as a particularity such as the Lotus-Seated One (Viṣṇu) and others, he says in response: "primary" (*mukhya*). The term "here" (*iha*) is a reference to the word *brahmaloka*. The syntactical connection is:
"Brahman is designated by the Śruti as a reality that is neither excluded from nor followed by [other things]. || 1815 ||
Likewise, because the verbal root *lokayati* has the sense of "seeing" (*darśana*) as its cause.
Because it is the subject under discussion and because it is observed as such, the world is called "loka. || 1816 ||

By setting aside the conventional sense of the word *loka* as referring to the realm of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*) through the force of the context and other factors, he states what is intended: "In that way" (tathā).
Therefore, only a *karmadhāraya* compound is appropriate here.
But it is not a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa) here, because a division [of the object] is not established. || 1817 ||

Having explained the meaning of the individual members, he states the compound for the word *brahmaloka*. [He says: "The word *karman*. The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that the referent of the term *tat* is denoted by the word *brahma*, and the referent of the term *tvam* is denoted by the word *loka*, according to the manner previously described. Now, one might object: since other types of compounds are possible according to the logic of the *niṣādasthapati* section of the *Pūrvapakṣa*, how is the *karmadhāraya* determined? To this he replies: "But not... and so forth.
For in that case, having taken [the words] as distinct, another type of compound might be suspected; however, there is no proof for a distinction between the meanings of *tat* and *tvam*.
Thus, according to the logic of their own established doctrine, the meaning is that it is a *karmadhāraya* compound. || 1817 ||
In that very case, it is logical that the single case-ending is explicitly heard; there should be no assumption of what is not heard.
When there is no basis for conceptual construction, and when the word is heard as having no expectancy, [it is so]. (1818)

He states another argument: "And because it is heard [as such]. This is its meaning: First of all, the word *loka* is heard with the nominative case-ending (*prathamānta*). The word *brahma*, which is uttered in coordination with it and situated within a compound, has its case-ending elided and thus requires a case-ending.

Therefore, by virtue of the proximate word *loka*, it is logical to assume that this [word *brahma*] also ends in the nominative; this is supported by the existence of a basis for such an assumption and by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*).

However, one should not assume that this [word] ends in the genitive case, because there is no reason for it, because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), because it would require assuming an unspoken genitive, and because it would contradict the context.

1700 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]: In that context, since the reason is non-existent and the word "brahmaloka" is heard in the nominative case, the requirement for further information is satisfied by that very case; thus, the assumption of a genitive case is not required, and likewise, the assumption of a dative case and so forth is also not tenable. || 1818 ||
Therefore, it is said here that the conceptualization of a genitive case and so forth is incorrect.
And there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) as well as the relation of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatā). || 1819 ||
The relationship between the signified and the signifier exists between the Brahman-world and its designation.
And by the word "Brahman," the true nature of the Self is indicated, not denoted.

In this way, there would be a primary identity between the two referents of the terms "Brahma-world" and "world. || 1821 ||
He concludes that, by abandoning other types of compounds, the *karmadhāraya* alone must be accepted, stating: "The genitive and so forth. The construction here is as follows:
since it is not appropriate to assume a genitive, dative, or other case-ending for the two words *brahma* and *loka*, they are said to form a *karmadhāraya*.
Having established the compound, he explains its syntactical function, stating: "And there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words *brahma* and *loka*."

The meaning is that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two expressed meanings, which stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified; and between those very two—the indicated and the expressed—there is a relationship of the indicator and the indicated, as in the case of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Anticipating the objection that because the word "Brahman" indicates the non-self and the word "world" indicates the non-Brahman, the sentence lacks the nature of having an impartite meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*), since otherwise other words would be redundant, he says: "It is Brahman... and so forth. Nor [is it the case that] other words...

The sense is that [the two words] avoid redundancy because the objects to be excluded (*vyāvartya*) differ. Anticipating the objection—“Why should the two words not denote Brahman and the Self directly?”—he replies: “It is not denoted. This means that there is an absence of a ground for the application of a word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), such as a genitive relationship (*ṣaṣṭhyādi*).
He states the result of accepting the relationship between the indicated (*lakṣya*) and the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) according to the aforementioned method: “Primary” (*mukhya*). || 1899 || 1890 ||
For the state of being Brahman is not possible apart from the world.
The nature of being the inner self does not exist apart from Brahman, nor can it be found elsewhere.
He states the reasoning for the identity of the person with the following: "For not... (1822).
Due to the delusion of their identity, there arises the conceptualization of two forms of mediacy.
Therefore, this cyclic existence is [nothing but] delusion; when that is utterly destroyed, there is liberation. || 1823 ||

If there is identity between Brahman and the self, how can there be the perception of transmigratory existence? Or, if such perception exists, how can Brahman be eternally unliberated? To this, he replies: "Of these two" [verse 1823].
This has been heard for the sake of abandoning delusion, which is the cause of all misfortune without exception.
The statement beginning with "This" (eṣa) is spoken for the sake of producing right vision.
He summarizes the purport of the sentence with the word "therefore" (ataḥ). The meaning of the word "therefore" is that liberation occurs when delusion is destroyed.
The word *iti* serves to refer back to the meaning as it has been stated;
likewise, *samrāṭ* is used for addressing someone as "Your Majesty" based on traditional report (*aitihya*). (1825)
He states the meaning of the individual components of the word "samrāj" and so forth: "the word 'iti'. || 1821 ||
In the manner thus described, the sage addressed Janaka, who was desirous of liberation.
He instructed [them] for the sake of dispelling ignorance, which is the cause of all misfortunes.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "enam" by first restating the meaning of the word "iti": "by what has been said thus. || 1826 ||
Emerging from this narrative, the Śruti itself has spoken this to us.
If you ask how that wise man instructed the king, listen.

Anticipating the doubt that this statement in the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) appears inconsistent, he says "eṣa" and so forth to show that this statement belongs not to the sage or the king, but to the *Śruti* (the Veda). He introduces [the passage] beginning with "anvaśāt" after the phrase "vyutthāya," following the necessary inquiry: "Whose is this [instruction]? and so on. || 1827 ||
The consciousness of this person, as it has been described by the preceding statements.
This is his final destination, because all other possible destinies have been exhausted.

He states the meaning of the phrase "this is his supreme goal" with the words "vijñāna... and so on. The construction is as follows: that goal which belongs to the individual soul (jīva) conditioned by the intellect (buddhi)—as established from such scriptural passages as the *Aticchandā* hymn—is indeed its final, ultimate goal; for all other goals find their completion therein.
All other destinies than this result from relying on means that are subject to decay.
For this alone, and no other, is the supreme goal that is free from fruit.

It establishes its supremacy. Regarding the word "itaḥ" (from this): having raised the doubt of equality, he says "ato hi" (for from this), intending to express that because knowledge is inexhaustible in terms of its object, that which depends upon it—namely, merit—is also inexhaustible. The particle "hi" is used in the sense of "yataḥ" (since/because). || 1829 ||
Because their sole cause is ignorance, desire, action, and so forth serve as their means.
All these supreme states of existence are like the course of a dream.
He states that other states of existence are inferior by means of an illustration: "Ignorance," etc. (Verse 1830).
This alone is the supreme attainment; all other attainments arise from delusion.
Excellence beyond measure, as well as prosperity and majesty, is what is called *saṃpadvibhūti*. || 1831 ||

Having begun with "Of what light is he? and having stated in the preceding passages that his absolute oneness (*kaivalya*) is his supreme intelligence and not the fruit of action, [the text] now states the meaning of "this is his supreme wealth" (*paramā saṃpat*). He says: "And this is his wealth. He provides the reason for this restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

Regarding the word "moha": what, then, is this so-called *saṃpat* (attainment)? For it is not something different from the supreme goal (*paramagati*); and if that were so, its meaning would have been already covered by the preceding [section].
To this he replies: "Excellence" (*utkarṣa*). The meaning is that the supreme goal is an exalted support (*avaṣṭambha*), and thus there is no tautology. || 1831 ||
This world is supreme; other worlds are subject to decay.
However, because it arises from perishable means, this [knowledge] does not depend on what is not a means.

He states the meaning of the phrase "this is his supreme world" with the word "this. Anticipating the objection that liberation (mokṣa) might likewise be perishable because it is achieved through perishable means, he says: "But not... (na tu). || 1832 ||

Therefore, liberation occurs through the removal of that ignorance; it does not arise from any other means.

Since the primary meaning of the word "world" (loka) here is indeed the Self (ātman), for that reason...
In cases where [the world] is established by causes such as karma, its status as being for the sake of the world would be figurative. || 1834 ||

"Loka... [verse 1834]. If the word *loka* refers to the Self alone through both conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), then how can that term apply to fruits of action such as heaven?
Anticipating this, he says: "Karmādi... [verse 1834], according to the principle that "it is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings."
There is neither decrease nor increase of the inner self through even the slightest action.
Thus, as if raising up an arm, the proclamation has been made by the Vedāntas. || 1835 ||
[Objection:
Since it is well known that the world is accomplished through action, if the Self itself were the world, then it too would be something to be accomplished by action. [Reply: No;

This is the supreme bliss, because it is the culmination of the excellence of happiness.
Because it surpasses all forms of bliss, it will be described in this very manner.

He states the meaning of the passage, "This is his supreme bliss," with the word "bliss. The reason for the supremacy of the bliss of the Self is given by the word "happiness. To the question of how the culmination of this excellence of bliss occurs within the Self, he says, "all. He explains how that is so with the words, "and thus. Just as the excellence of bliss culminates in the Self, so too does the excellence of all bliss [culminate there].
The meaning is that this will be explained in the manner beginning with "He who [is] among men," and so forth, by way of [establishing] the selfhood within the self. || 1836 ||
The pleasures born from contact with sense objects are dependent upon their means of accomplishment.
Because they possess the nature of having a beginning and an end, they are indeed causes of suffering.
One might ask: since the bliss of objects belonging even to Hiraṇyagarbha and others is supreme, how can the bliss of the Self be distinguished by it? [The author] says: "Objects," etc. (1837).
Because his essential nature is that of the immutable Self, he is indifferent toward all means of accomplishment.
Because it transcends all forms of bliss, it is considered the supreme bliss. || 1838 ||
Anticipating the objection that, in the same way, the bliss of the Self (*ātman*) cannot be considered supreme because it is no different from [ordinary] happiness, he says: "The immutable," etc.
"Ānanda is the supreme of this"—this was stated for the purpose of establishing the meaning already expressed.
By the words "of this very [thing]," the capable reason is stated. || 1839 ||
1. And also the *Nyāya* and the *Ārṣeya*.

He states the subsequent passage—beginning with "Bliss" (ānanda)—in order to provide an unassailable reason for the claim that one's own happiness alone is superior while other happiness is inferior. || 1839 ||
Of this very [bliss] as described, which transcends all other joys.
Living beings subsist upon the poison of the bliss of Brahman. 1840.
He connects the statement with the words "of this very [state]," which is an explanation of the phrase "as previously described. This begins with "all-bliss," etc.
Since this very bliss is of such a nature, it is therefore supreme.
It surpasses all other joys in its entirety. || 1841 ||

Having restated the meaning of the reason, he concludes with the meaning of the thesis by saying "this. He explains the state of being supreme by saying "because of the attainment of bliss. The reason for that is given by "of this. || 1841 ||
And this entire bliss is produced solely from that single cause.
Due to the limitation imposed by adjuncts such as the intellect (buddhi), it is designated as the "knower" (mātṛ). || 1842 ||

To the question of how there can be the designation "merely" (mātra) when the bliss of the Self is complete, he says: "Even though it is complete. The meaning is that although bliss is full, it is fit for the designation "merely" due to its connection with ignorance, the intellect, and so forth. || 1842 ||
Desiring to awaken him with earnestness, he did so by means of the path of the subtle elements alone.
Just as the salt ocean [is formed] here by its constituent parts of salt, so it is in this case.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "That which belongs to humans" as follows: "Tanmātra" (merely that). Just as in the world one makes [the nature of] salt known by means of its constituent parts, so too the supreme Śruti proceeds, desiring to make known the possessor of the measure (the subject) by means of the measure (the object), namely, the mere bliss of Brahman. As for the emphasis, it consists in the successive adoption [of examples] as a means for awakening [the understanding]. || 1843 ||
From this human bliss, there is a progressive increase of bliss.
This supreme scripture has been set forth for the purpose of awakening the knowledge of supreme bliss.

But surely, a distinction among joys is described here as being characterized by gradation; how then can the subsequent scripture proceed with the desire to make known the unsurpassable bliss of Brahman? To this, he says: "The subsequent [scripture]," etc. The meaning is that the subsequent scripture proceeds by means of a hundredfold increase from human bliss up to the level of Brahmā, in order to demonstrate the unsurpassable bliss of Brahman. || 1844 ||
Among human beings, whoever has attained perfection through firm limbs [is such a one].
A person whose every limb is complete and beautiful is successful and capable of enjoying worldly pleasures.

Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he explains the words, beginning with "of men" (*manuṣyāṇām*). He clarifies the state of being perfectly formed through firm limbs with the word "complete" (*samagra*). He describes the beauty of the limbs as follows: "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) and so forth. || 1849 ||
One who is endowed with all means of accomplishment and is prosperous is here designated as "samṛddha" (prosperous).
Thus, a person endowed with these very internal means [attains success]. || 1846 ||
1 ga. *vipuṣa* | [Vol.
3, page 571] 1704 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]

He avoids the redundancy of the word *samṛddha* by means of the word *rāddha*. [The term] "entire" (*kṛtsna*) summarizes the meaning of the two words and concludes the section. [The phrase] "by external things" (*bāhyaiḥ*) [is explained as follows]. 1846.
Likewise, he who here becomes the sovereign lord over other men.
One who possesses self-mastery should be known as a lord; he is not overcome by human beings. || 1847 ||
He explains the phrase "of others" and so forth with the word "likewise. The connection with what follows is: "In this way, this is the supreme bliss of humans.
He asks, "What is that sovereignty? and answers, "It is independence. He further elucidates this very independence with the words, "by humans. (1847)
For men here who are endowed with human enjoyments, [this is the case].
Because he is endowed with excellence beyond measure, he is called the "most perfectly endowed" (saṃpannatama). || 1848 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "by all" as follows: "by means of human [birth]. || 1848 ||
He was endowed with all human enjoyments, but not with those of the gods.
Ānanda, this is declared here to be the supreme among humans. || 1849 ||

He states the purpose of the qualification "by human [means]" with the word "by all. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "of men" with the word "bliss. Indeed, the perfection of internal means is not fruitful when there is an absence of external means and a deficiency in enjoyment; nor is it meaningful without sovereignty, or without those two [internal and external means]. Therefore, he is one who enjoys the unsurpassed human enjoyment.
The meaning is that Yudhiṣṭhira and others represent the supreme bliss among humans, because of the absence of any distinction between the bliss and the one who experiences it. || 1849 ||
That joy of human beings which has been multiplied a hundredfold;
The bliss of the ancestors is one; it is equal in measure to that. || 1850 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "atha" (now) as follows: "śata" etc. "Pramāṇa" means measure. || 1850 ||
That happiness which is dependent upon means is said to be nothing but suffering.
Therefore, the supreme bliss, which does not depend on any other means, resides within one's own self.

Anticipating the objection that the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) spoken of in succession is not supreme—since it is possible for the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, which is of the same nature as what has been experienced, to be considered supreme—he says: "That which... (verse 1851).
Therefore, through the thorough knowledge of the self, there is the completion of all that is to be known and accomplished.
This is the definitive conclusion regarding the statement that one becomes bliss in which all excellence has been cast aside. || 1852 ||

Since sensual pleasure is of the nature of suffering—like milk mixed with poison—and since the bliss of the Self alone is supreme, the phrase "in succession" (paraṃparā) is stated as the conclusion for the purpose of determining that [bliss]. Therefore, [it is said]: "tasmāt" (therefore). || 1852 ||
Due to the gradation of the means, there is a corresponding gradation in the purity of the intellect.
And because of the degrees of purity, happiness likewise becomes graded. || 1853 ||
1. The suffering arising from connection with objects (*patrasaṃbandhaduḥkha*).
[Vol. 3, page 572] 3.
*Ākṣaṇam*. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1705.

Now, it may be objected: "Since all happiness is desired by the self, how can it possess degrees of intensity? For the self is non-superior (i.e., uniform). To this he replies: "Because of gradation. The meaning is that the perception of such gradation in that [happiness] arises from the disparity in the purity of the manifesting intellect (*buddhi*). || 1853 ||
To the extent that impurity departs from the intellect through the accumulation of merit and other virtues, [so far does it ascend].
To that same extent indeed is there stability of the intellect, and to that same extent is there the increase of happiness. || 1854 ||

He explains how the gradation of purity arises from the gradation of their practice with the words "yāvat" (as much as). He concludes that the cognition of gradation in bliss arises from the gradation in the purity of the intellect with the words "tāvat" (to that extent). || 1854 ||
To whatever extent there is an increase in the density of the intellect due to association with evil and the like, [to that same extent does it become obscured].
To that same extent, indeed, there is instability of the mind and likewise the arising of suffering. || 1855 ||

He states this by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), namely that the gradation of bliss is produced by the gradation of purification, which depends upon the gradation of skillful means (*upāya*): "As long as... (verse 1859).
The world of the ancestors is conquered by those through rites such as the ancestral sacrifices (pitṛyajña).
Those who have conquered the worlds are called the Pitṛs, the enjoyers of divine pleasures.

Having explained up to the point "that one [is the bliss] of the Pitṛs" by stating the cause for the gradation of blisses beginning from human bliss and ending with the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha, he now states the meaning of the phrase "of those who have conquered the worlds": "In the world of the Pitṛs. (1896)
That which is this southern path is called the world of the ancestors.
This [bliss] would be multiplied by more than a hundred times the bliss of humans. || 1857 ||
"What is this world of the ancestors? To this he replies with the word "ya" (which). The identity between the goal and the act of going is merely figurative.
He explains the connection of that [passage] with the statement "his bliss is onefold" by means of the words "manuṣya... (human...). || 1857 ||
In the subsequent statements as well, one should establish the point as previously explained.
"This bliss, Ānanda, is a hundredfold greater than the previous one, increasing in this sequence.

(1858) Now, he extends the aforementioned principle to the passages beginning with "those who are a hundred," etc., by saying "in the subsequent [ones]. He summarizes the established meaning across all the successive stages (paryāya) by stating "a hundredfold greater. (1818)
Those who were previously explained by the term "the world of the stars" (nakṣatraloka).
They are called *hastakarāḥ* (hand-makers), for they possess subtle forms. || 1859 ||

Having explained the purport of all the successive stages according to the Kāṇva recension, [the author] now explains the meaning of the term "world of the gods" (*devaloka*) in the Mādhyandina recension, which states: "Now, that which is a hundredfold bliss in the world of the Gandharvas is a single bliss in the world of the gods. He says, "In the stars," etc.; the phrase "previously" refers to the statement in the Gārgī-brāhmaṇa. || 1859 ||
Those who attained divinity at the beginning of creation through its production;
They would be born as gods here, possessing subtler forms than those of their predecessors.
1 ka. How? 2 gha. Of those who are to be protected... 3 ka. kha. indeed. [Vol. 3, page 573] 1706 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Chapter—]

In the passage, "He alone [is the god] among the *ājānadevas*," he explains the meaning of the term *ājānadeva*. Regarding the phrase "of creation" (*sargasya*): having accepted the initial accomplishment of the creation of humans and so forth as the limit (*maryādā*), the meaning is "prior even to that"; that is to say, prior to the previously mentioned *karmadevas*. || 1860 ||
The subtle bodies of those great-souled ones are all-pervading.
The bliss of these [beings] is considered greater than the previous blisses. (1861)

He states the reason for the superiority of bliss among the *ājāna-devas* with the words "pervasive" (*vyāpinī*). He states the reason for the perfection of their means of attainment given that their bodies possess the aforementioned nature with the words "of the great-souled ones" (*mahātmanām*). The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that the bodies described above are subtle and pervasive.
Because of the abundance of causes for the affliction of various pairs of opposites.
Therefore, Ājānadeva Ānanda shall be a hundred times superior to those who preceded him.

If it is argued that even among the *karmadevas* (deities by merit), the pervasiveness and subtlety of their bodies are equal [to those of the *sāṃsiddhika* deities], nevertheless, their happiness is inferior compared to that of the *ājānadevas* (deities by birth) and others; regarding this, he states the reason: "nānā" and so forth. This means: of those various causes of affliction—denoted by the term "pairs" (*dvandva*)—which consist of the objects characterized as suffering. Even among the *ājānadevas*, there is an equal abundance of such afflictions.

Anticipating the objection that there is no distinction in their state of being subject to saṃsāra, he says: "By birth" (ājāna). The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is that, in comparison with the former [state], there is a lesser degree of affliction for them. || 1862 ||
A Śrotriya is one who has studied the Veda and has indeed understood its meaning.
Because he performs all that is enjoined, he is free from all evil. || 1863 ||

In the passage beginning with "He who," etc., he explains the word *śrotriya*. Regarding the term *śrotriya*: it means that one who possesses the study of a single branch [of the Veda] culminating in the knowledge of its meaning is intended here as a *śrotriya*. He states the meaning of the word *avṛjina* (free from crookedness):
"entirely," etc. || 1863 ||
One whose disposition is unimpaired by desires that extend even to the gods born of the [Brahma-]egg.
Then, that man who has developed craving for further enjoyments, || 1864 ||

He states the meaning of the term *akāmahata* (one who is not struck by desire): "Ājāna... etc. The meaning is that one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) regarding all joys lower than the bliss of *ājāna* is here called *akāmahata*. Anticipating the objection that this implies an unrestrained state of dispassion (*vairāgya*), he says: "tataḥ" (from that). The meaning is that one who has turned away from desires for all higher joys starting from the bliss of the *ājānadeva*s is *akāmahata*. || 1864 ||
And whatever happiness he has is equal to the bliss of a god by birth.
Here, the excellence of his happiness is stated by virtue of his being unassailable by desire. || 1865 ||

He states the meaning of the word "ca" (and): "Ājānadeva" [etc.]. The point is that the happiness belonging to one who possesses the aforementioned qualifications while existing in a human body becomes equal to the bliss of the *ājānadevas*. [Note: The qualities such as being a *śrotriya* and so forth are not intended here as causes for a difference in the degree of bliss. 1 gha. yā na nyū; 2 gha. so'tra; 3 kha. ga. 'riheṣyate; 4 gha. 'tkarṣahe.
Anticipating the objection that this is because of the scripture's lack of distinction, he says: "of this. That is to say, of the qualified person who resides in a human body.
The locative case in *iha* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). || 1865 ||
The states of being a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) and a performer of sacrifices (yajin) are both equal, extending as far as Brahmā.
When the cause, which is being unhindered by desire, increases, delight increases accordingly. || 1866 ||

In this regard, the reason is given: "the Vedic scholar" (*śrotriya*). For, starting from human bliss up to the bliss of the hundred-fold [heavenly beings], when an equality is observed, the meaning is that the excellence of happiness arises from the excellence of being unafflicted by desire for those objects. To the objection—"Since that [bliss] is of a uniform nature everywhere, how can there be an increase in bliss due to an increase in that [freedom from desire]?"—he replies: "unafflicted by desire" (*akāma*). || 1866 ||
To the extent that one desists from each successive enjoyment, [one attains liberation].
As long as desire increases for a man, so long does pleasure flourish in his heart.
In that regard, he establishes experience as the means of valid cognition with the verse beginning "pūrva... (verse 1867).
For it is there that the sole destruction of desire occurs, whereby a man attains the height of happiness.
"Because it is not overcome by desire, this is the superior means compared to the two preceding ones.
(1868) He states the established conclusion regarding the superiority of freedom from being overcome by desire over the other two: "kāma... (1868).
Although the status of being a means may be common to all three here,
For here, the excellence of the destruction of desire is indeed the supreme means for the attainment of bliss.

To the question, "How can there be this distinction when the scriptural statement is common [to both]?", he says: "The state of being a means" (*sādhanatvam*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the bliss mentioned previously; the word "therein" (*atra*) refers to the person under discussion. The meaning is that a distinction established by one's own uncontradicted experience cannot be subverted by a common scriptural statement. The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to confirm the stated point through one's own experience. || 1869 ||
In this context, even the slightest intention to express a cumulative sense is not appropriate.
Because the knowledge that completely eradicates agency and so forth is relied upon here. || 1870 ||

Now, if it is argued that by the term "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahata*) the knowledge of Brahman is intended, and by the terms *śrotriya* and *avṛjin* ritual action is intended—thus the Śruti, by declaring the attainment of unsurpassed bliss for one possessing these three qualifications, intends the combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action—the author says "no," with the words "combination, etc. Here, in this passage, knowledge, action, and liberation are mentioned. The reason why [this interpretation] is untenable is stated as "agency, etc. (i.e., the attribution of agency and so forth to the Self).

The meaning here is that, since the aforementioned knowledge is intended by the term "unassailed by desire," a combination [of knowledge and action] is not what is intended regarding liberation. || 1870 ||
The logical principle previously stated is also intended to exclude the possibility of a cumulative collection [of causes].
Therefore, those who perceive with subtle insight should not entertain any doubt regarding the combination [of these means] here. || 1871 ||

By what reasoning, then, is the combination [of means] rejected? To this he says: "The combination... The meaning is: "previously," that is, in the section on the connection (*saṃbandhagrantha*) and so forth. He states the conclusion: "Not... The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is the contradiction with authority and reasoning. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to liberation. || 1871 ||

1 kha. ga. ˚riścataḥ| [vol 3, page 575] 1708 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]— [The text continues: "The Self, which is the witness of all, free from desire, devoid of attributes, and the one who has attained the state of being the Self of all, is the supreme Brahman.
