For the status of being a means [to the goal] is equal for both the learned Vedic scholar and the one free from evil.
Even among inferior enjoyments, there is no superior happiness beyond that. 1872 ||

Furthermore, he states that there is no combination [of the three] because the knowledge denoted by the term "unassailed by desire" is the means to supreme bliss, whereas that is absent in the other two; thus he says:
"The status of being a means. || 1872 ||
In this context, it is precisely the state of being unassailed by desire that [determines the distinction], because it possesses a nature characterized by degrees of intensity.
And because it brings about the highest happiness, it shall be the supreme means of accomplishment. || 1873 ||

Anticipating the objection that—just like being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) and so forth—being unassailed by desire (*akāmahatatva*) cannot be a cause for liberation because it is no different from other means to immediate happiness—he says: "Being unassailed by desire" (*akāma*). Since excellence and deficiency are possible regarding the degree of being unassailed by desire in relation to the currently discussed means, that which is deficient is a cause for occasional, immediate happiness, whereas that which is excellent is inseparable from knowledge and is the means to liberation; thus, liberation results from their combination.
This is the meaning. || 1873 ||
Because of the recitation of the Taittirīya Śruti: "The youth, the good youth."
Even in the subsequent statements, the terms such as "śrotriya" and so forth are intended to be significant.

One might raise the objection that, just as there is no mention of being "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahata*) in relation to the *ājānadevas*, there is likewise no mention of being a cause for enjoyment in the lower worlds in relation to being a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) and so forth, since the conditions of hearing and not hearing are equal; having raised this doubt, [the author] shows by means of scriptural authority that it is intended to be a cause for those [lower worlds]. He says: "Young.

Being "young and virtuous" implies freedom from wickedness (*avṛjinatva*), and "being a student of the Veda" implies being a learned scholar (*śrotriya*); thus both qualities are present even in the preceding stages, such that one should be "young and virtuous."

The meaning is that since this has been stated in the passage beginning with "or a reciter," it should also be understood to apply to those alternative cases where it was not explicitly mentioned. || 1874 ||
Virāṭ Prajāpati is to be known as the one who bears a body consisting of the three worlds.
Hiraṇyagarbha is Brahmā here, and likewise he is called Brahmagīr.

Fearing that there might be an apprehension of identity between these two—namely, "that is the one bliss of the world of Prajāpati" and "that is the one bliss of the world of Brahman"—he says: "Virāj. || 1879 ||
Beyond this, the calculation of infinity ceases.
Since this is so, therefore our scripture declares: "Now, this very one... (1876).

He takes up the passage beginning with "Now, this... with the words "Beyond this. Since it is impossible to count [the bliss] within the bliss of the Self, that alone is unsurpassed; such is the meaning. || 1876 ||
For by this one who possesses such excellence and who dwells within our own sphere of activity, [this is accomplished].
That bliss which has cast aside all excellence is here inferred through happiness. || 1877 ||
How is this established? Regarding that, he states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for those who lack knowledge [of it]: "By this," etc. The connection is with "by this pleasure.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that which has excellence by that which is unsurpassed. "The reality of the self" (*ātmatattva*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. The word "here" (*iha*) indicates the domain of inference (*anumāna*). || 1877 ||
1 ka. adhare ṃ | 2 ka. yottamā | ga. cottamaṃ | 3 ga. svāduṇi [vol 3, page 576] 3 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1709
Because in the world, that which possesses excellence is seen to abide in a state where its excellence has been surpassed.
Therefore, by means of that which possesses excellence, the unsurpassed bliss is reached. || 1878 ||

How does inference state the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in that case? [The verse says] "destroyed," etc.; the remainder is "the establishment of pervasion. Having restated that, he states the inference: "Since," etc. The meaning is: the gradation of the excellence of pleasure must terminate somewhere, because it is a matter of degree, like the gradation of magnitude. || 1878 ||
Wherein all these reach their final consummation in the Supreme Self.
This bliss, Ānanda, is supreme because it transcends all other blisses. (1879)

Fearing that there might be a suspicion of a difference in meaning because the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha is the ultimate rest for the gradations [of bliss], he says: "Where... Here, the word "these" refers to worldly pleasures, while "here" refers to the various types of bliss under discussion. || 1879 ||
This Ānanda, which was asserted as "this belongs to him," is established through inference.
It has been brought to its ultimate consummation within the inner self through a process of progressive intensification.

Now, you may ask: even if the Supreme Self as supreme bliss is established through inference, how can the inner self (pratyagātman) be expected to become that supreme bliss? To this, he replies: "This is his. (1880)
For those who have not realized supreme bliss, this is considered an inference based on intellectual understanding.
For those who have directly realized the true nature of the Self, that [Reality] is indeed most directly perceived.

Having stated the counter-inference regarding those who lack knowledge, he speaks regarding those who possess self-knowledge: "By one who has not known," and so forth. For it has been said: "This very supreme bliss is directly perceived by the śrotriya who is free from craving, and thus attained. || 1881 ||
Bliss within the inner self is accessible only to a mind that has not been struck by desire.
That very [reality] would be supreme compared to those previously mentioned, because it is infinite.
He establishes the supremacy of the bliss of the Self with the verse beginning "akāma" (1882).
And so it was that the blessed Vyāsa, who knew the true essence of the meaning of all the Vedas, [said this].
He himself has already stated this very point out of a desire to abandon what is harmful.

He introduces the authority for its being supreme with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). He explains the intention of one who says that the highest happiness is produced by freedom from the oppression of desires (*akāmahatatva*) with the words "Desire" (*kāma*).
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine happiness there is in heaven—
These [pleasures] do not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the destruction of craving for an Arhat. (1884)
He provides an illustration of that very point: "And that which... (1884).
From whatever one turns away, from that one is liberated.
For by turning away from everything, one does not experience even the slightest suffering.
He recites another statement from that same work: "Because... (verse 1885).
1. Thus indeed; 2. directly realized; 3. having been performed.
[Vol. 3, page 577] 1710 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Fourth Chapter.
The entire meaning that was previously promised by the words "water" and so forth—
Its conclusion would be reached by the statement ending with the world of Brahmā. || 1886 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "this" (eṣa) as follows: "Salilādīti. By the passage ending with "the world of Brahman" (brahmaloka), meaning that which has the word "Brahma-world" at its end or in its middle; [it is shown that] having begun with "In water, the one Seer," and ending with "subsisting on a mere measure," the inner Self—which is free from cause and effect, unsurpassed bliss, and perfectly full—is propounded.

Furthermore, the meaning is that the conclusion has now been made for that which was explained starting from "Now, he who among men... up to "...this very one," by means of the sentence beginning with "Of him, this... and so forth. || 1886 ||
Even when this question had been concluded, the king [addressed] that sage as before.
Having questioned me thus, you should speak hereafter of that which is supreme for the sake of liberation.

He explains the meaning of "So 'ham" (That I am) and so forth with the words "praśna" (question), etc. The meaning is as follows: although King Janaka had initiated his inquiry for the sake of attaining the fruit of liberation through perfect knowledge, and although that perfect knowledge has been determined according to the method already stated, the King—just as before its determination—asked, preceded by the offering of the payment for this knowledge, saying: "Tell me now what is the supreme means for my own liberation. This is the sense.
Yājñavalkya, having been thus questioned by the king, then remained silent as before;
it was not due to any other cause, but rather because of an inability [to respond].

Here, he states the meaning of the word "hetoḥ" (from fear) and so forth: "Yājñavalkya also... He thereby refutes the notion that the Sage’s fear arose from an inability to speak or from ignorance regarding the answer, by stating "from another [cause]. || 1888 ||
Because of his omniscience, the Sage had no fear arising from ignorance regarding the meaning of questions.
But the cause is indeed something else, since the Śruti has declared it thus.

He states the reason for the fact that neither incapacity nor ignorance constitutes a cause of fear for him: "Because he is omniscient" (*sarvajñatvāt*). The meaning is that Yājñavalkya, having become one with Brahman, is all-knowing and all-powerful; therefore, no fear can arise for him from ignorance regarding the subject matter of the questions and answers, nor from an inability to speak it. To clarify what the cause of such fear might be in his case, the phrase "from another cause" (*anyato hetoḥ*) is stated.
He raises [the objection] beginning with "medhāvī" (the wise one), stating: "But the cause... || 1889 ||
This king, by virtue of the power of his choice-question, will not wish to speak.
"What is its light?"—with these and other such questions, he questioned me again and again.
He prepares the introductory context for explaining that [point]: "one who does not wish to speak," etc. (1890).
For the goal of truth is indeed not to be rejected, because it must necessarily be protected.
Thus, the determination of self-luminosity has been established without exception. || 1891 ||

"Surely the king, seized by stubborn prejudice, will question you; however, you must not give an answer. For the vow of a cow, once undertaken by a traveler, is not to be abandoned all of a sudden. To this he replies: "For [the matter] is not to be rejected. He clarifies the very meaning of the word "for" (*hi*).
The reading "not being afraid" (*avibhyat*) found in all three manuscripts is merely a scribal error.
[Volume 3,
Page 578] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Regarding the phrase "of the truth": if that is so, let that which was asked and desired to be known be clarified in its entirety; therefore, he says "by himself. The word "therefore" (ataḥ) is intended to refer back to the reasons previously stated. || 1891 ||
Even though the matter had been decided, the king questioned me again and again.
"From this point forward," said the king, as if restraining me with those words. || 1892 ||
If that is so, from where has fear arisen for you who have reached this certainty? To this he replies: "Even when it is certain" (*nirṇīte'pi*).
The word *atha* is a synonym for the word *ataḥ* (therefore), and it is to be construed before the verb *niruṇaddhi* (it obstructs). || 1892 ||
Having brought me under his control by means of the hook of desire alone, he has made me devoted to him.
The exceedingly wise king desires to acquire knowledge in its entirety. || 1893 ||
Now, one might object: "Is not a king who imprisons his teacher a man lacking discrimination, and thus not a fit recipient for knowledge? To this he replies: "Kāma... (verse 1893).
Thus, this would be the cause of fear for Yājñavalkya, and not from any other source.
Because the cause of fear, which is ignorance, is impossible given his omniscience. || 1894 ||

He concludes that the seizure of all one's property is a cause of fear with the words, "Thus this... He states the reason why there is no cause of fear from anything else with the words, "Fear... (1894).
A definitive determination has been made more than once regarding the object in its entirety, once it has been questioned.
Nevertheless, this king obstructed me with the desire to seize my entire possession.

For a king worthy of knowledge desires to acquire the wisdom residing in the sage; and why would the teacher not fear to bestow it upon him? Anticipating the objection that "it does not mock itself when given to another," he says: "repeatedly" (asakṛt). || 1891 ||
Therefore, this wise and learned man [is here] because of the taking of the property of a Brahmin.
Since he does not fear anyone, one should therefore stand in great awe of Janaka.

This establishes the wisdom mentioned in the scripture. [The word] "medhāvī" (wise). Thus, he clarifies the very meaning of the word: "brahma. The meaning is: because of taking up the knowledge that belongs to *brahman*, i.e., the Brāhmaṇa. He states the conclusion: fear of Janaka must be maintained by one who desires to preserve the knowledge that has liberation as its fruit. [He says this] even though [Janaka] is a worthy recipient.
The meaning of the sentence is that knowledge which has liberation as its fruit must not be taught abruptly. || 1896 ||
Indeed, the questions as they were stated have already had their meanings determined by the preceding statements.
Not having reached a conclusion, what did the king ask the sage again? (1897)

He raises an objection beginning with "sa vā eṣa" and so forth, starting with "nanu. The sense is this: since the questions as previously stated—beginning with "What is the light of this?"—and the answers such as "The sun is its light," were already addressed, the subsequent questions are inappropriate; therefore, the corresponding answers are also not appropriate. || 1897 ||
The movement of the self through its own waking state has been previously described.
In this context, the king is intended by [the author] as an illustration for all [of them]. || 1898 ||
1712 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [in the Fourth Chapter]:

Demonstrating that which has not yet been determined, he supports the question and the reply with the words "He goes to his own self" (*svam eti*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the description of the movement between the two worlds.
An essential statement. || 1898 ||
The illustrative meaning of that [analogy] is not explicitly stated as long as it remains unexpressed.
The king did not yet desire to release him from the remainder of his questions.
Nevertheless, he states how there is scope for its efficacy: "Of that" (*tasya*).

Since the passage begins with "He who" (*yaḥ*), the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) is "him" (*tam*); this is the intended sense of the Teacher, because the subject to be explained—the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) consisting of bondage, which is the object of the question—remains to be stated. The transition between the two states serves as the illustration for the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) known as the transition between the two worlds.
The meaning is that the subsequent text is intended to explain the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*) of that very same point. || 1899 ||
He did not state the point of application for the example and for deep sleep.
The realization "I am Brahman" is held to arise from scripture, as illustrated by the example of deep sleep.
The meaning of the illustration is understood by the wise person through the complete analysis of the example. || 1900 ||

Having stated the purposefulness of the section concerning *saṃsāra*, he now states the purposefulness of the passage beginning with "one who does not desire" (*athākāmayamānaḥ*). [The phrase] "of the illustration" (*dṛṣṭāntasya*) implies that for this reason as well, the question has scope. He states what that illustrative point (*dārṣṭāntika-artha*) is: "Brahman. Since the illustrative point of the dream-example must necessarily be stated, the section on liberation (*mokṣa-prakaraṇa*) is commenced for that purpose.
He says, "It will not come," [referring to] "of the wise" (prājñasya). 1900.
Since this illustrative point has been stated and the purpose of the inquiry is thereby concluded.
Since everything has been explained, that subject is now being stated. || 1901 ||

Anticipating the objection that—even though two types of objects to be subdued (*dāntika*) have been specified—the question remains as it was because the expectation for further explanation has not been satisfied, he says: "It has been stated" (verse 1901).
One becomes unattached, like a fish, gradually through desires, actions, and so forth.
Just as one's own waking state and dream state coincide, so too does this [waking state] exist under its own power.
This cycle of existence in both this world and the next has its cause.
"That [teaching] must be explained in detail"—this is the supreme Vedic revelation regarding its meaning. || 1903 ||

Having introduced two sections, he first introduces the section on transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-prakaraṇa*) with the words "asaṅga" (unattached). Just as a great fish moves successively between the two banks of a river, so too this [Self], though in reality untouched by desire and the like, moves through the states of waking and dreaming as an independent entity; thus, its bondage—consisting of movement between the two worlds—is accompanied by causes and accompanied by details.
The meaning is that this section on cyclic existence (saṃsāra) has commenced in order to state [the defects of existence] for the sake of dispassion (vairāgya). || 1902 || 1903 ||
Bondage and the cause of bondage, as well as liberation and its very cause.
It should be explained in detail; for that purpose, there is another scriptural authority (śruti).
He summarizes the meaning of the two sections for the sake of ease of comprehension: "Bondage," etc. (1904).
1. ka. kha. rāya sa | 2. ka. kha. gha. vistāra | 3. kha. prakṛtami | [Vol.
3, page 580] 3. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1713.
Therefore, prior to that state of waking, the self has entered into the dream state.
He should be led to the waking state with the intention of providing an illustrative analogy.

Introducing the subsequent context, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "He, indeed, this one" (*sa vā eṣa*) and so forth: "In the waking state," etc. From the sentence "Having sported in the waking state" (*jāgraty ratvā*), the Self was led from the waking state to the dream state by the words "for the sake of the dream state" (*svapnāntāyaiva*).

Now, that [Self] must be brought back from there to the waking state for the purpose of demonstrating the manner of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); for bondage, as illustrated by the example, is not clearly manifest within the dream state alone.
Therefore, the meaning is that the subsequent sentence is intended to explain how one passes from the state of sleep into the waking state. || 1909 ||
But when the statement concerning "perfect serenity" ends with the determination of bliss, [it refers to Brahman].
Then, for the purpose of the conclusion, [the statement] has as its object the meaning of that which was previously proposed as the thesis.

He states another meaning for that very [passage] without contradicting the stated sense: "Ānanda" and so forth. When, in the passage beginning with "for the sake of reaching the end of dream" (*svapnāntāya*), "the end of dream" refers to deep sleep (*suṣupta*), and likewise the section beginning with the discourse on the great fish (*mahāmatsya*) up to "this indeed is the supreme bliss" (*eṣa eva parama ānandaḥ*) has that [deep sleep] as its subject, then the subsequent sentence serves as the conclusion (*nigamana*) regarding the matter proposed; even then, the transition from sleep to waking is the Self—
The meaning is that this is not intended here [in another way], because otherwise it would be impossible to demonstrate the various modes of cyclic existence (saṃsāra). || 1906 ||
This Self possesses unimpaired vision, as has been stated regarding the states of waking and dreaming.
And this is likewise the case even with regard to the wise person, according to the statement "that which is indeed so-and-so. (1907)

He states what that promised point is: "alupta" (unimpaired). The meaning is that it was stated in the examination of perception (*dṛṣṭiparīkṣā*) that just as the inner self (*pratyagātman*) does not perish in two other states, so too it does not perish in deep sleep (*svāpa*). || 1907 ||
And it is the cause of extreme benefit, just as this self is when in deep sleep.
Because it is merely the immutable witness, it remains so during both dream and waking states. || 1908 ||

He states another point that was previously promised: "Atikāraka" (beyond the factors of action). The meaning is that it has been stated in that very same place: "Just as the Self is devoid of duality such as the mother and so forth during deep sleep, so too it is in the two other states, because there is no difference in its being the immutable witness. || 1908 ||
Thus, this repetition is for the purpose of a concluding summary regarding a matter already established.
The passage beginning with "savā" and so forth is to be understood as such, and not out of any apprehension regarding destruction or the like. (1909)

Having reminded [the reader] of what was previously asserted, he presents the subsequent [passage] as the conclusion thereof: "In this way. Here, both the soul's state of being eternally perceived and its freedom from duality such as the "measures" (mātrā) and so forth, are concluded by the term *svapnānta*; for, by the word *svapna* (dream),...

The vision of distinction (*viśeṣadarśana*) is said to be his "deep sleep" (*supta*); when this is stated, it is established that the reality (*tattva*) is devoid of [the distinctions of] mother and so forth. And its cessation at that time depends upon the immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthabodha*), because there is no other agent [to cause it]. Therefore, the sentence, concluding both by means of the term "end of dream" (*svapnānta*), shows the attainment of waking by the Self from the state of dreaming—this is the meaning. Now, an objection is raised: one might suspect that the sleeper has perished like a dead man, or has gone to another place.
Since he [the opponent] is equal to a dead man because his mouth is agape and so forth, the subsequent statement is intended to refute that;
thus, he says "No" (na). He explains: "But not... Indeed, this statement was not made by suspecting either the destruction of the self or its migration to another place.

page 581] 1714 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya— ]

Since [the notion of agency] has never occurred in the eternally established, actionless inner self (pratīci), there is no room for such a suspicion; nor is he equal to one who is dead, because of the dissimilarity [of his state] with a corpse, such as the serenity of his facial expression and so forth—this is the meaning. || 1909 ||
From this point onward, the nature of the self within saṃsāra is now described.
And just as one attains self-awareness, so too, having departed from this world, one goes to another world. || 1910 ||
Thus, for the sake of understanding this meaning, an illustrative example is stated here.
For the sake of the listener’s intended meaning, and for the purpose of achieving easy comprehension. || 1911 ||

Having stated the purport of the section beginning with "sa vā eṣa" and ending with "buddhāntāya," he states the purport of the remainder of the Brāhmaṇa, beginning with "itaḥ. He takes up the illustrative sentence beginning with "tadyathānaḥ. Regarding the phrase "svapnāt," the word "atra" refers to the immediately following sentence. Anticipating the objection—"Let it simply be said that for the ignorant self there is the attainment of another body from this body; what is the use of an illustration here?"—he says: "sukham."

In this section, regarding the specific mode of saṃsāra intended to be discussed, the meaning is that an illustrative example is given for the transition from one body to another—just like the transition from sleep to waking—in order to facilitate easy understanding for the listener. || 1910 || 1911 ||
Just as a well-constructed carriage on a path is drawn by various means for accomplishing its purpose.
Producing various kinds of sounds due to the oppression of the heavy burden.
He explains the words of that [verse]: "nānārtha" (having various purposes), meaning by means of various instruments for attaining results, namely the mortar, pestle, cooking pot, and so forth.
He states the cause for the production of various kinds of sounds: "gurubhāra" (the weight of the heavy). || 1912 ||
One should travel here to another country under the guidance of a cart-driver.
And because of the meaning that has gone astray, she assumes a form that is distinct [from that meaning]. || 1913 ||
One should proceed on the path having taken that which was established for one's own sake by the cart-driver.
The connection with the meaning of the example is stated as "it is exactly thus. || 1914 ||

Fulfilling the required sense of the word "yāyāt" (he should go), he states the meaning as "vrajet" (he should go). The term "iha" (here) refers to the sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahārabhūmi*). Anticipating the objection—"But how can there be movement for one who is situated upon that which is mounted by a cart, when he has fallen into the middle of the cart?"—he elaborates on this with the words "anasaḥ" (of the cart).

He explains the meaning of "evameva" (just so) with the word "dṛṣṭānta" (example); the word "of the subject of the illustration" (*dāṣṭantikasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 1913 || 1914 ||
This subtle body (liṅga) has departed from the experienced physical body due to the exhaustion of its experiences.
In the same way, it goes to another body, which is prepared by karma, knowledge, and so forth.
He states the meaning of the phrase "this embodied self departs" with the word *bhukta* ("having experienced"). He states the cause for its departure with the word *bhoga* ("experience").
He indicates that the cause for attaining a specific subsequent body is *karman* ("karma"). The phrase *tadvat* means "like the aforementioned cart. || 1911 ||
It was devoid of deities, yet accumulated through the equipment of virtuous deeds.
This absence of gender-signs is for the sake of establishing the nature of the inner self.

Why is it that the *liṅga* (subtle body), having departed from the consumed body, proceeds to another body while being assisted by the sun and other [deities], and why does it not remain right here? [Variant readings:
kha. 'marge ya'; gha. 'sya tasya ku']

It remains, and there is neither cause nor fruit for its departure; regarding this, he says: "detached. This very point—that it is "accumulated through action, knowledge, and so forth"—is clarified by the words beginning with "action" (karma). 1916.
And here, by the terms "bodily" and "verbal," only the indicative mark (liṅga) is being denoted.
But because it is situated in a specific region of the body, it does not, however, reside in every single limb.

Anticipating the objection that because of the qualification "the Self" (ātman), it is improper to understand the word "embodied" (śārīra) here as referring to the subtle body (liṅga), he says: "The embodied...

The meaning is that since the word "Self" is used for the subtle body even in passages such as "the Self is the eleventh," it is precisely that [subtle body] which is intended here as the subject capable of traveling. || 1917 ||
It should proceed, presided over by the wise charioteer who has his own welfare as his form.
For the Self, like one who has mounted, is mounted upon the internal intellect (pratyagdhi). 1918.
Therefore, it is said that he is mounted by means of the wise self as his vehicle.
Just as the sun appears to rise over a vessel of water and the like, so too there is no actual rising of the Self by its own nature. 1919.

He states what is intended by the word "by the conscious one" (*prājñena*): "by the conscious one. He explains the meaning of the word "mounted upon" (*anvārūḍha*): "the inward" (*pratyak*). The "inward cognition" (*pratyagdhi*) is the reflection of consciousness; its "mounting" (*āroha*) is its pervasion within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Immediately thereafter, the Self (*ātman*) also remains there, having pervaded it. Therefore, [the individual self] is mounted upon the supreme Self, which is the conscious one, or upon the subtle body (*liṅgātman*), which consists of the intellect together with its reflection.

The meaning is that it is described in the sentence "smin. Having raised the objection—"Why should the self's pervasion of the intellect not occur by itself, rather than through the medium of a reflection?"—he says: "By the sun. Just as the pervasion of a specific limiting adjunct, such as a vessel of water, is said to occur by means of the sun through its own reflection, so too the pervasion of the conscious self (prājña) in the intellect occurs only through the medium of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), and not by itself.
The meaning is: because of being associated. || 1918 || 1919 ||
This statement beginning with "By himself as light," and so forth, was previously spoken by [the Lord] Himself.
"Know the self as the rider in the chariot"—such is the statement in another Vedic scripture.

Anticipating the objection that the subtle body (*liṅga*) might itself possess activities such as movement, being presided over by the conscious self (*prājña*), he reminds us of the statement that the activity of the intellect and so forth is dependent upon the Self. [He says: "Previously... Furthermore, he states that the *Kāṭhaka* scripture is also an authority for the fact that the aggregate of causes and effects is active only when presided over by the consciousness of the Self: "The Self..."
His mind was tormented by the pain arising from the cutting of his vital organs.
The sound characterized by hiccupping occurs when the time of death has arrived.
"That which emits is the *liṅga*"; this is within the range of direct perception.
This very thing is spoken by the Śruti for the sake of generating dispassion in men.

He clarifies the meaning of the word *utsarjan* (emerging) with the verse beginning "marmeti. The phrase "that sign" (*talliṅgam*) refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) together with its appearance (*sābhāsa*).
To the question, "Why does the Śruti restate a perceptible fact?", he replies with the verse beginning "tad idam. || 1921 || 1922 ||

While the vital points were being sliced open and the joints were being severed.
Let those seeking liberation remember that suffering which awaits one who is about to die.

If detachment does not arise when the true nature of *saṃsāra* is directly perceived, how can it be established by mere restatement? Anticipating this doubt, he states the intended meaning of the scriptural restatement: "In the vital spots," etc. The sense here is that while in a state of well-being, upon hearing of various sufferings, an effort toward the means for them becomes possible in order to achieve the correct knowledge that is their antidote. (1923)
At what time does this arise for a living being, and for what cause?
To provide a clear understanding of this point, the subsequent section of the text is introduced. || 1924 ||
He takes up [the verse] beginning with "where," preceded by the expectation [of the answer to] "in what? Here, "this" refers back to suffering. || 1924 ||
When the upward-moving wind (udāna-vāyu) is predominant, this occurs for one who is about to die.
There, at the time of death, that man is born with an upward breath, as previously described.

The answer to the first question is as follows: "By the *udāna*. When death has arrived for a living being about to die, if the vital air called *udāna* becomes predominant, the person is designated as one whose breath moves upward. Where this upward movement of breath occurs, there the departure of the *liṅga* (the subtle body), which is then under the power of another, takes place preceded by the aforementioned sounds such as "hā hā" and so forth; therefore, even before that death, one should be diligent.
The meaning is that it must come to be. || 1925 ||
When the physical body, afflicted by old age, attains a state of minuteness, then [it perishes].
Or, being afflicted by illness, one practices as previously described. || 1926 ||
He explains the answer to the second question, beginning with the words "sa yatrāyam," as follows: "piṇḍa" refers to that which was previously described as being "elevated upwards. || 1926 ||
When this body attains the state of minuteness, which is the nature of the atom, it becomes subject to the power of *aṇimā*.
Then, due to old age or the cause of disease, one becomes gasping for breath.
Having restated what was said, he clarifies the meaning of the fourth quarter [of the verse]: "aṇimānam" (the power of atomization). || 1927 ||
Due to old age or disease, a sense of unease arises within him.
Consequently, proper digestion of food does not occur for one with weak digestive fire. || 1928 ||
Therefore, because of the [absence of] nourishment by the bodily constituents such as the nutrient fluid (rasa) and so forth, this body [does not increase].
Being weak, he falls to the earth like an old, dilapidated house. || 1929 ||

Anticipating the question of how emaciation of the body occurs through fever and other ailments, he says: "By old age," which means by the bodily constituents (dhātus) such as the rasa, etc., when the skin and other parts are filled with digested nutritional essence (pakva-rasa). || 1928 || 1929 ||
Then, when the body has thus become emaciated, there arises within it [a transformation].
That mode of operation is explicitly stated with effort by means of an illustrative example.
1. Kha: *yāṃ yadduḥ*; Gha: *yāṃ tadduḥ*. 2. Gha: *ti sa puṃ*. [Vol.
3, page 584] 3. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

1717. He states the purport of the passage beginning with "tadyathā" (just as): "atha" (now). The meaning of the word "atha" is "immediately after" one has understood the time and cause of the suffering of upward exhalation and so forth. Within the gross body as previously described, that which is called the "internal movement" is the departure of the subtle body (*liṅga*); and of that...

The meaning is that by means of stating examples, a statement similar to direct perception (pratyakṣa) results in attentiveness toward the causes of knowledge through the gateway of detachment (vairāgya). Effort consists in the statement of numerous examples. || 1930 ||
Just as the mango fruit is released from its own skin once it has attained its flavor.
Likewise, in this case, when there is exhaustion from the essence of food, the sign is that it is released from the body. || 1931 ||
Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he connects the statement with the words "The mango" (*āmram*). || 1931 ||
By which juice it is held fast to the stalk until its full ripening.
That essence is to be known as the bond, or the stalk is considered the bond. (1932)

He explains the meaning of the word "bondage" (*bandhana*) as it occurs in the illustration: "the stalk" (*vṛnta*). That is to say, by an etymological derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇa*), "rasa" (sap) is the bondage; or, by an etymological derivation based on the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the "stalk" (*vṛnta*) is the bondage. || 1932 ||
The connection of the mango fruit with its stalk exists as long as the juice has not reached full maturity.
As firm as that [strength] was in childhood, it is not so in the case of the ripened grain.

Therefore, he states the cause for the falling of the mango and other fruits with the words "by the stalk. The word "thus" (evam) expresses the application of the analogy. The meaning is that this connection of the mango, whose sap has diminished, is not as firm as it was in its state of childhood according to the aforementioned illustration; consequently, it falls. || 1933 ||
Then, having entered the prison, when the time for cooking arrived, [he remained there].
The weak man is not at all able to hold a mango fruit. || 1934 ||

Anticipating the objection as to how the ripened juice can be the cause for the falling of the fruit, he establishes its causality with the words "moistening" (*klaidyam*). The word *abala* (weak) is to be understood as a separate term. It is stated that the moisture of the juice is the cause for the weakness of the fruit; the stem, which is the substratum for supporting the mango, is taken here by virtue of the locative case. || 1934 ||
Or else, it is released from its stalk due to its weight, its binding, or its sap. || 1935 ||
For the sake of understanding the fruit that falls from various causes.
In this context, there would be the statement of many examples possessing diverse forms. (1936)

Having stated the cause for the falling of the fruit, he now demonstrates that falling itself: "due to weight" (*gurutvāt*). Anticipating the objection—"If the desired point is established by even a single example, why are these diverse and multiple examples stated?"—he says: "not [limited to] one" (*nāneka-*) etc. The word "in the present context" (*prakṛte*) is understood as being governed by the locative case. || 1939 || 1936 ||
In this case, the falling of the mango occurs from its stalk; likewise, the udumbara fruit falls together with its stalk.
But the falling of the *aśvattha* tree occurs even when it is ripe, due to other causes.
1 gha. *ndho na pa | 2 ka. 'tuṃ na caivotsa' | kha. 'tuṃ na cehosa | [vol 3, page 585] 1718 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]

He states that the falling of the fruit has various causes according to experience, beginning with "from the stalk. The various types of fruits are included by the locative case. Other causes include contact with birds and so forth. || 1937 ||
The utterance of the syllable "vā" here is for the sake of accomplishing many kinds of attainments.
For death is observed in the world to have many causes for living beings. || 1938 ||

Having raised the doubt as to why three instances of the word "or" (*vā*) are mentioned in the example, he states [the reason]—namely, to establish that death, the subject of the analogy, has indeterminate causes—by saying, "in many ways. He clarifies that death has many indeterminate causes by relying on experience, stating, "having many causes. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Therefore, one should not dispute this point. || 1938 ||
Just as this illustration has been stated, so indeed is the person as well.
The person (puruṣa) should be known as having the nature of the linga, because its limbs are joined together here in this very way.

Having explained the illustration through both brief and detailed accounts, he elucidates the subject to which it applies, beginning with "yathā" (just as). The phrase "is completely liberated from the limbs" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that this complete liberation is not perceptible. He states the meaning of the term "puruṣa": "liṅga," etc. Here, the word "iha" (here) refers to the body. || 1939 ||
Furthermore, the ears, skin, and so forth are here designated by the term "limbs" (aṅga).
Among them, it is only through the subtle body (liṅga) that the self is fully capable of its own activity.

He states the meaning of the word *aṅga*: "The ear," etc. Now, why is the locus of the sense organs, such as the ear, grasped by the word *aṅga* in this sentence? To that he says: "In them," etc. The ellipsis is: "Therefore, they [the sense organs] possess the status of being denotable by the word *aṅga*. || 1940 ||
Of the black antelope, which is a part [of the sacrifice], and of the eye, which is an instrument.
In the relationship between the support and the supported, food-essence would be the cause. || 1941 ||

The unripened juice of the mango and other fruits remains as the cause for its persistence on the stalk; but what is it that causes the persistence of the *liṅga* (the subtle body) in the physical body? To this, he says: "Of the limb... (9941).
And it is also said that food is "tamed" through its transformation into the bodily constituents such as plasma and the rest.
As long as there is firmness in the body, so long shall the sign remain stable.

He states that it has been explained in the fourth [chapter] that the cause for the persistence of the *liṅga* (subtle body) in the body is the essence of food (*anna-rasa*), saying: "Food" (*anam*). If one objects that if that mere essence were the cause for the persistence of the *liṅga* in the body, then even when it is digested, it would remain so, and thus the fall of the body would be impossible—anticipating this doubt, he says: "From the essence, etc. (*rasādīti*). By the word "essence" (*rasa*), the subtlest transformation is understood; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the subsequent stages are included.
The middle transformation of mine has been grasped. || 1942 ||
But when it is ripened by causes such as old age, it falls down like a marvelous fruit from a tree.
By the phrase "from these limbs," this very point is expressed. || 1943 ||

Having stated that the solid food (*kaṭhina*), which is the essence of food (*annarasa*), serves as the cause for the maintenance of the *liṅga*, it is further explained that the same [essence], when digested, acts as the cause for the emission of the *liṅga*. [Variant readings:
ka. kha. ga. read *vyūhamaitra*] [Vol. 3, p. 586]
1 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Āmandagiri.

[The text] states that the cause for the fall of the body is old age and so forth. Here, "agency" (*kartṛtva*) is intended to refer to the body. Regarding the meaning thus stated, there is the triad of words.
It indicates their status as illuminators: "from these," [it says]. || 1943 ||
The prefix *sam* is used here to establish the sense of unification.
Likewise, the prefix *pra* is employed for the purpose of establishing excellence.
Regarding the term *saṃpramucya*, he explains the meaning of the two prefixes with the words: "the prefix. || 1944 ||
Since the instruments are distributed according to their respective locations, they are therefore [so named].
Withdrawn from their respective locations, they attain oneness at the time of death. || 1945 ||

To explain what this "unification" (*ekībhāva*) is, for the sake of which the prefix *sam-* is used there, he says: "separated. In their own state, the organs are separated due to their connection with different locations; therefore, at the time of death, having been withdrawn from their respective locations, they immediately attain oneness with the subtle body (*liṅga-ātman*). This is the connection [of the words]. || 1949 ||
In dream, [the soul's location is] within the body because the vital breaths remain there and because the sense organs have been withdrawn from their places.
And since death occurs together with this [attainment], excellence is observed here [in this state]. || 1946 ||

What is this excellence for the sake of which the prefix *pra-* is used? To this he says: "In sleep" (*svapne*). Even in sleep, there is a withdrawal of the organs from their own places, yet that withdrawal does not occur without residue, because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains. But at death, those organs are withdrawn from their own places along with that very breath; therefore, an excellence of the withdrawal of the organs is seen at death compared to sleep, and thus the prefix *pra-* is employed.
The meaning is that it illuminates that. || 1946 ||
Since this body previously came from another body, therefore [it is so].
With reference to that, moreover, the word is here denoted by the primary sense itself. || 1947 ||
He states the meaning of the word "again" (punar): "from another body. The connection is that [the birth] occurs precisely with reference to that [previous body]. || 1947 ||
From the beginning of one's own life up to the end of awakening is a dream; from the end of awakening, it is again [a dream].
In the same way, the self departs from its previous body and enters another body once again. || 1948 ||
He clarifies what has already been stated by means of an illustration: "From his own [state]"—that is, having departed from this [world]. || 1948 ||
In the same way, from the external body, one attains one's own internal liṅga.
Just as the *yathānyāya* and *atinyāya* [methods] were previously explained therein.
One should likewise declare that it is the same when passing from one body to another body.
In the phrase "to their respective wombs according to their place," it is exactly the same as there. || 1950 ||

This very point he summarizes with the words "from the external" (*bāhyāt*). Just as a person, when the karma that causes it arises, perceives the subtle body (*liṅga*) situated within—bound by its own merit—which was previously outside the waking body, and subsequently attains the waking body upon the activation of the karma that causes it;
in the same way, this Self goes from one body to another. He recalls the meaning of the term *pratinyāya* (returning in due order) with the words "as [it went] otherwise."

The meaning is that just as in the passage beginning with "He, having rejoiced in this state of serene composure" (*sa vā eṣa etasmin saṃprasāde ratvā*), the terms *pratinyāya* and *yathānyāya* were explained as being respectively the object of explanation and the explanation itself, so too here those two must be understood in the same way. This refers to the meaning of the term *pratiyoni*.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four. He says:

"Perception" (*pratīti*). Just as in the previous example the word *pratiyoni* was explained as meaning "according to its place," so too here in the case of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), that same explanation is to be understood; such is the meaning. || 1949 || 1910 ||
In accordance with the karma heard [in scripture], and in accordance with the eyes and other [senses].
It rushes toward its respective womb and proper place for the sake of birth. 1951.

Having explained the meaning of the two words, he states the meaning of the sentence: "śrutā" (having heard). He states the intended meaning of the explanation regarding each birth, namely the phrase "yathāsthānam" (according to their respective places): "cakṣurādi" (the eyes, etc.). The meaning of "prāṇāya" is "janmanaḥ" (of birth), because death leads to the assumption of another body for living beings. || 1911 ||
Then he says, "For the sake of life"; for where there is no birth, there is no death.

He elaborates upon that very same concise point: "In another body," etc. The meaning is that because death is pervaded by birth, one who has died necessarily takes up another body, according to such traditional teachings (*smṛti*) as, "For one who is born... and so forth. 1992.
And for the sake of the arrangement of the vital breaths, he hastens toward another body.
For one whose faculties are not concentrated upon the [proper] objects would not be capable of performing the task. || 1953 ||

Anticipating the objection—“Since the individual soul (jīva) departs together with the vital breath (prāṇa), as stated in the scripture beginning with ‘As he departs’ (*tam utkrāmantam*), why would the deceased assume another body for the sake of the vital breath?”—the author says: “The vital breath (*prāṇa*)... This means [the soul goes] toward another body from one body. Anticipating the further objection—“Since those [subtle elements] persist until liberation, the arrangement of them is of no consequence; so why would there be the assumption of another body for their sake?”—the author says: [the following].

Regarding the phrase "in the locations": it is true that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) continues until liberation; nevertheless, this self is not able to fashion karma in locations such as the solar orb (*tolaka*) and so forth without the placement of the instruments (*karaṇa*). Therefore, the meaning is that the assumption of another body is purposeful for the sake of the rearrangement of the vital breaths (*prāṇavyūha*). || 1993 ||
The doubt arises: "How is the complete accomplishment of this arrangement of the vital breaths (prāṇavyūha) achieved?"
Because of the inability to grasp a body, due to the organs not being fully developed. || 1954 ||

He states the objection that is to be set aside by the passage beginning with "just as [one suspects] a king," etc., in the words "prāṇa... (vital breath). The term "asya" (of this) refers to the enjoyer under discussion. To dispel the suspicion that [this objection] is groundless because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he states its basis in the words "śarīra... (body). || 1994 ||
Nor do they remain after creating another body, like the servants of a king.
For this person goes here alone, accompanied only by his karma.

Although one who has abandoned the body is unable to create another body due to being without assistance, nevertheless, some who stand in the place of servants will wait for him after having fashioned another body; therefore, he says "not" (na ca). "Here" (iha) means when death has occurred.
To provide a resolution to this, an illustrative example is here set forth.
The entire world has been acquired by a person through his own karma for the sake of his own enjoyment. || 1956 ||
1. Thus, with this... 2. To the King.
[The Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1721.
He accepts the subsequent statement as being the answer. Regarding the phrase "of this," the scripture (*śruti*) is cited here.
As for the objection that he has no servants standing in his place, he replies with the word "entire" (*kṛtsnam*). 1996.
Having fashioned a body for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of those actions, it awaits [the result].
Whether it be auspicious or even evil, according to the nature of the deeds one has heard. || 1957 ||
Anticipating the objection as to how there can be a state of waiting when Indra and the rest of the world are in the position of servants, he says:
"That karma. The construction is: having fashioned a body for the enjoyment of the Master, it waits for that world of Indra and others who are the enjoyers.

Anticipating the question of how Indra and the others were acquired through such karma, he analyzes the nature of that karma: "Whether auspicious," and so forth. [The remainder of the sentence refers to] prior knowledge...

The meaning is that, according to their karma—whether auspicious or inauspicious—they again accumulate karma, because of the traditional teaching (smṛti): "Conditioned by that, they proceed; therefore, that is what pleases them. || 1957 ||
The elements acquired through karma are employed by that [karma] for the embodied being.
Having assumed suitable other bodies, they stood there like those walking before the king. || 1958 ||
He says that the elements, acquired through accumulated karma, impelled by it, and directed toward its fruit, remain present.
Regarding the phrase "karma," he states the established fact that the elements are acquired through the karma of the embodied self. || 1918 ||
In this regard, an illustrative example is also stated for the meaning as it has been explained.
"How indeed might there be the successful communication of the intended meaning? (1959)

He introduces a scriptural illustration regarding the point already stated with the word "Therein" (tatra). The meaning is that the illustration beginning with "Just as" (tadyathā) is stated to show that there are companions for the embodied one when he takes on another body.

Anticipating the objection—"If it is intended to convey merely that the person possesses a wealth of companions when taking another body, let only that much be said; since scripture is beyond doubt, what is the use of an illustration?"—he says:

Regarding the phrase "vivakṣitā" (intended to be said): although the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is beyond doubt, the statement of an example is for the sake of facilitating comprehension; this is precisely the meaning of the particle *api* occurring in the first half-verse. || 1919 ||
Just as one welcomes a king who is approaching with offerings such as a dwelling, drink, and other requisites.
Having perceived this, the fierce people, such as the charioteers and others, waited with their preparations made. 1960.
He explains those words: "As follows" means that the connection is with the phrase "knowing [him] approaching. || 1960 ||
Those who are appointed by the king to perform harsh tasks against evildoers.
They are called "Ugras" here either by birth or by name. || 1961 ||
He explains the meaning of the word *ugra* in two ways: "Ugra... [verse 1961].
In this very manner, those who were thus appointed by the lords of men [were] sinless.
In this context, those who are debtors to you should be known as distinct according to their respective offices. 1962.

Fearing that there might be a redundancy in meaning between the two [terms] *ugrāḥ* and *pratyenasas*, he says: "Enas" (sin). The word "atra" (here) is used for the purpose of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*).
(Note: This is marked as *ga. paṃ kṛta*.)
[Vol.

3, page 589] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Chapter Four—Seventh Section]: Both are grasped by the word "that" (*tat*). "Entitlement" (*adhikāra*) refers to a specific injunction (*niyoga*) or a specific mode of engagement (*pravṛtti*).
The chariot-drawing horses and the charioteers should be experts in the management of chariots.
The village chiefs are considered to be the leaders of the villages and the commanders of the armies. 1963.
He explains the two terms beginning with "sūta" [as follows]: "ratha... || 1963 ||
These were acquired by the king through his own past actions even before he arrived.
Having provided food, drink, houses, and other necessities, they waited for the king.
Thinking, "This king of ours is approaching," they remain there, exerting every effort.
He summarizes what was intended in the illustration with the words: "Just as they... (1964).
Just as all beings are thus [governed] by the enjoyer through causes such as karma and so forth.
Thus, he acquired a body that was appropriate for the enjoyer and likewise capable of experiencing enjoyments.
Having done so, he first attained that state, just as Sūryodaya did toward the king.
They await him with great effort, out of a longing for Brahman to come.
He explains the passage beginning with "evam" (thus) and so forth. "Yathaivam" (just as thus) restates the example that was referred to. "Yathā" (as). || 1965 || 1966 ||
When that which has entered into the nature of consciousness is here called "Brahman," [it is so designated].
Although he is by nature Brahman, his state as a transmigrating being is due to ignorance.

Anticipating the objection—"What is the reason for employing the word *brahman* in the statement 'this *brahman* comes' with reference to that [self] which assumes another body after leaving one?"—he says: "Vijñāna... (Vijñānaghana). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the sentence [in question]. Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*), it should have been said "of that" (*tasya*). Anticipating the objection—"How can the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*) be the non-transmigrating *brahman*?"—he says: "Transmigration-ness... (1967).
How indeed could the thought "I am Brahman" arise in him here?
For the sake of awakening to those respective realities, the Śruti calls the person "Brahman. 1968.
He states another intended meaning of the word "Brahman" with respect to the individual soul (jīva). He asks, "How so? Here, the word "here" (iha) refers to the essential nature of the Self.
The construction is: "Since this is the intention of the Śruti, therefore [it is so]. || 1968 ||
This is a restatement (anuvāda) and not an injunction (vidhi); thus it is said: "one who is such. || 1969 ||
Because it is equally non-distinct with respect to all, there is this declaration: "one who knows thus."
For one who knows [the truth] as it has been explained, there is neither a mere restatement nor a mention of a result. // 1970 //

Thus, regarding the phrase "one who knows thus" (*evaṃvidam*), he explains the meaning of the word *evaṃvit*. He states: "It is a restatement (*anuvāda*). The reason for this is given: "All [beings]," etc.

Since death is common to all, the statement "one who knows thus should depart" (*utkrāntivid bhavet*) is not an injunction; rather, the meaning is that the departure, which is already established in the world, is merely restated for the purpose of announcing the assumption of another body. Having stated it as a restatement, he now presents the position that it is an injunction.
1. Thus he addressed the king. Pra. 1 ka. ga. Sārī sa svayi.
[Vol. 3, page 590]

"Thus" means: for one who, according to the scripture, contemplates the departure [of the vital breaths] and whose thirst for worldly existence has been destroyed, the statement of the result—"all beings wait upon him"—prescribes "one who knows thus" (*evaṃvit*) as such a knower; it is not merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), because there is no result in that alone.
The meaning is that it is also easily established because it is stated [in scripture] that [the soul] takes up another body. The word "vā" (or) is used for the purpose of emphasis.
And the elements that sustain the instruments of the one about to die.
Having prepared their bodies, they await [the end] just as men wait for the palace of a king. || 1971 ||
Regarding the phrase "all beings," he states the meaning of the word *bhūta* [as "the elements"]. Regarding the verb, he states its meaning as "having made. || 1971 ||
But who indeed follow that god as he desires thus to depart?
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in classical Indian script denote a section break or the end of a chapter. [End of Section] [End of Chapter]
Are they going by the motion of something else, or by their own independence? Or is it by [the motion] of the self? 1972.

It has been stated that for the ignorant self, who desires to leave its current body and go to another body, there is an acquisition of assistants for the construction of that new body. Now, [the author] raises an objection in order to introduce the passage beginning with "Just as when a king is about to depart" (*yathā rājānaṃ prayiyāsantam*): "In this way," [he asks], "who follow him as he goes? And even those who follow, by whose movement do they follow? Do they follow independently, or by the power of the Self?"
The meaning is that one desires to know whether [it] is unassociated. || 1972 ||
For this purpose as well, an illustration is stated again, as before.
For the embodied soul departing from this body due to the exhaustion of karma, [there is no return]. (1973)

He sets forth an illustration for the purpose of determining that speech and the other organs follow along, impelled by the self's own karma. The phrase "for this purpose" clarifies what was indicated by the word "also. The phrase "as before" indicates the point of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*). The connection is: "the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) come together from here. || 1973 ||
Just as in this world, people such as fierce charioteers and others [attend] one who is about to depart;
Just as the vital breaths follow a king, so do they depart from a man at death.
He explains the illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). He clarifies the point of application (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "prāṇāḥ" (the vital breaths). || 1974 ||
When there is only the upward exhalation for this person, then—
Then the vital breaths, bringing him happiness, depart from one who knows the time of death.
Thus ends the third section, the Jyotirbrāhmaṇa, of the fourth chapter in the *Śrībṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*.
The third Brāhmaṇa of the sixth chapter, according to the sequence of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "yatraitat" (where this occurs) as follows: "yadā" (when). Its meaning is this: for when, immediately after the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, a transmigrating being returns to that very state in which the upward breath (*ūrdhvocchvāsa*) has ceased, at that very stage, speech and the other organs follow the person—without causing him distress—who, in accordance with the scriptures, has previously practiced the knowledge of departure (*utkrānti-vidyā*) and is indifferent toward worldly existence; for it is at the moment of death [that this occurs].

He states the agreement with the supplementary portion of the scripture regarding the elemental nature of the instruments: "And it is clear. He explains the words of the sentence. Regarding the word *tasya* ("of that"): he clarifies this very point by saying "of what has been described. Regarding the word *kṛtsna* ("entirety"):

the analysis of the compound is "that heart in which there is the withdrawal (*upasaṃhṛti*) of all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*). The meaning of the word *atha* ("then") is the immediate sequence following the withdrawal of the instruments (*karaṇa*). This same meaning applies to the word *atha* found in the preceding commentary (*vārtika*) as well. || 74 ||
When all the sense organs, together with the vital breaths, have been thus withdrawn,
Then, for one who desires to depart from the heart, it flashes forth through the intellect. || 75 ||

He clarifies what has already been stated with the words "In all... The meaning is that at the time of death, when the withdrawal of all the instruments [of perception] occurs, the opening of the channel connected to the heart—that heart which belongs to the living being desiring to go to the next world—becomes manifest. The word "of the heart" (hṛdayasya) is explained as "of the intellect" (buddheḥ). The meaning of the word "then" (atha) is the immediate sequence following the person's orientation toward the next world. || 75 ||
This very radiance of the intellect, born of karma, arises at the time of death.
By which this self perceives the world as fashioned by its own karma. || 76 ||

He states the cause for that illumination at the tip of the heart: "That" (saḥ). The construction is as follows: that light which arises at the time of death from the intellect is born of karma. He describes its function: "By its own karma" (svakarma) || 76 ||
By action alone is his consciousness brought to identity with that [object].
Afterwards, having attained that state, he abandons this body.
If it is argued that knowledge of a future body arises by the power of karma, and that one might consequently conceive of "mine-ness" or "I-ness" toward it, [the author] says in response:
"By karma alone. For one who is about to depart [from the body], knowledge of a future body has indeed arisen by the power of karma; however, by that [knowledge], which has its own object...

The identity with the person is established solely by virtue of that [connection]; thus, the meaning is that the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) arises in the future body. He states the result for one who has become active in that sense of "I" with the word "afterwards" (paścāt). || 77 ||
That which consists of the future world is reflected within his immediate consciousness.
It is clearly stated in the words of Pradyota that the latent impression (vāsanā) alone is called the self (ātman).

At the time of death, for one whose aggregate of faculties has been withdrawn, how can there be the possibility of knowledge of a future body? For karma does not act without assistance. Nor is it its own [power]. It is manifest.

Anticipating the objection that this [light] must be the cause of that, he says: "The future," etc. The meaning is that the sense of "I am" which arises in a person even before death, starting from six months prior, is what is meant here by "the light. || 78 ||
In the past, he spoke by means of his own light in the form of the material cause consisting of the mother.
Just as it is by its own light, so too is it here.

Nevertheless, one might raise the objection that at the time of death, the manifestation of the aforementioned knowledge does not occur apart from the instruments (the senses), for in the absence of the mind, even latent impressions (*vāsanā*) would not manifest; anticipating this, he says: "Mātrā" and so on. Just as in the *Jyotirbrāhmaṇa*, the Śruti has declared that in a dream—wherein there is the taking up of waking impressions—the knowledge exists by itself through its own light, which is the light of consciousness, even apart from the instruments, so it is here as well.
Even during the state of death, the aforementioned illumination is indeed appropriate; for at that time, the intellect has not been withdrawn.
Even if it were withdrawn, the occurrence of illumination will become manifest—this is the meaning. || 79 ||
Then, having performed his duties along the path illuminated by the aforementioned light, he departs from the heart at his pleasure. (80)

He states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "tena" (by that) as follows: "By the light. The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is: when the time for the enjoyment of the fruit has arrived.
Alternatively, there is a word-break as "asukhaṃ sukham" (unhappiness, happiness). || 80 ||
Therefore, an action should indeed be performed with effort by a wise person.
Beholding thus this state of living beings, which is rooted in karma.
Now, one might ask: why is the external and internal conduct at the time of death being told, since it is of no use for the goals of man?
To this he says: "Well! He qualifies [the statement] in order to clarify the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ): "Behold! || 81 ||
The self [experiences] that which has been acquired through its own karma, according to what is appropriate for the light of knowledge.
Beholding the world, he emerges from his own heart according to the respective [path].
Regarding the manner in which the self departs from the heart, it is said: "The self.

The meaning is that the self, perceiving through the aforementioned light the world acquired by its karma, departs from the heart via the gates of the eyes and other senses, according to its karma and according to its learning. || 82 ||
Whether from the eye or from the head, whichever world he shall attain.
Emerging by that very door, one encounters no obstruction whatsoever. || 83 ||
The phrase "according to each" clarifies this very point: "in the eyes," etc. (83).
Upon reaching the world of Āditya, he departs through the eye.
Upon reaching the world of Brahmā, the self departs from the crown of the head. || 84 ||
He states the systematic arrangement of the aforementioned alternatives: "āditya... (verse 84).
One should perform the rite according to one's own ritual tradition or, as appropriate, according to others.
From here, the self departs by means of the channels extending from the heart. || 85 ||
