He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "or from others" as follows: "Action," etc.; that the departure from other regions is in accordance with experience.
This is the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed). He describes the path by which the self emerges from them with the words "hṛdaya" (the heart) etc. || 81 ||
And the *liṅga* (the subtle body), moving everywhere, is not obstructed anywhere.
Because its nature is exceedingly subtle, it enters even the ocean of iron.

Raising the objection that even though the *pratīca* (the inner self) has emerged from the body, its movement to another body is impossible because movement is untenable for something obstructed by various material objects, [the author] says "And the subtle body (*liṅga*)... to show that since the subtle body is unobstructed, the Self, which has it as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), is likewise not obstructed anywhere. Furthermore, since the subtle body emerges unhindered even through impenetrable substances such as iron, it is not obstructed by anything whatsoever.
He says "manifest" and so forth; [he uses] the word "also. || 86 ||
That Self, as it departs by the path described here;
The vital breath (prāṇa) departs first; then the other vital breaths and the remaining faculties follow after it.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "as he departs" (tamutkrāmantam) as follows: "As he departs" means by the path illuminated by the light [arising] from the heart's apex, as previously described. || 87 ||
Surely, because the self, the vital breath, speech, and so forth, are mutually intermingled;
Since there is no distinction of place, time, and so forth, how can there be a sequential or non-sequential progression? (88)
The word "śrutam" (the revealed scripture) sets aside the [presumed] sequence. [The author asks: "Is it not so? || 88 ||
This is not a fault, because here the time of sequence is not intended to be expressed.
For it is intended that these [factors] possess the relationship of the instigator and the instigated. || 89 ||

He says "this is not so" because that [sequence] was not intended to be expressed. By the word "here," the departure [of the breaths] is referred to. He states the reason for the non-intentionality of the sequence with the words "because of the motive. Since it is intended here that the Self is primary and the vital breath (prāṇa) is subordinate, or that the vital breath is primary and speech and the other organs are subordinate, therefore, due to the non-intentionality of the sequence, its absence does not constitute a fault.
The meaning is "it carries. || 89 ||
These [faculties], which have their sole refuge in his conscious self, are like the flesh of this [body].
She is the instigator of the departure of the vital breath (prāṇa) and of the departure of speech and the other [senses]. (90)
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of relationship exists between the self (*ātman*) and the others as the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*), he says: "In this world.

This means that whatever desire the people in the world have for the soul's (*jīva*) departure from its substrate (*utkrānti*), that [desire] instigates the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and that [in turn] instigates the departure of speech and the other organs. || 90 ||
The departure of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) alone is the cause of [the soul's] exit, and no other.
The primacy belongs to that meditative cultivation which has consciousness as its sole abode. || 91 ||

What, then, is the cause of the soul's departure? To this he says: "The principal [breath]," and so on. For that [principal breath], by being its own cause, implies the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and that [departure] produces the soul's departure, according to such scriptural texts as "In whom am I? and so forth; thus, its desire to depart is established.

The sense is that ritual action and so forth are the motivators. He provides an introductory transition (*pātanikā*) in order to introduce the passage beginning with "possessed of consciousness" (*savijñāna*).
Regarding "consciousness" (vijñāna): || 99 ||
For she indeed shows the path for the self when it attains another body.
Impelled by her, this vital breath (prāṇa) takes away the other vital breaths.

How is it that the cultivation known as "prior wisdom" (pūrvaprajñā) is predominant there? To this he says: "For that... The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, its predominance is logical. An objection is raised: since it has been stated that "it is the departure of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa)," etc., how can there be a predominance of cultivation? To this he replies: "By that... The connection is: "impelled by that, he departs from the body. || 92 ||
Being non-different from the Self, it appears externally like a vessel of water or the sun.
As he emerges, he becomes endowed with consciousness according to his karma. || 93 ||

He explains what happens to the individual soul (*jīva*) even when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departs due to the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). He says: "By means of the self" (*ātmanā*).

Just as the sun reflected in a vessel of water conforms to that vessel, so too the *jīva*, being non-different from it, follows the vital breath when it exits the body; the meaning is that it goes out following after it. He cites a scriptural passage on this point: "Just as... (*yathā*).

The meaning is that even before the aforementioned departure, he becomes endowed with the consciousness of his future body in accordance with the karma he has heard; and immediately after departing, he follows the destination illuminated by specific knowledge. || 93 ||
But surely, because all his faculties have been withdrawn, the person is without consciousness.
How can it be said that the vital breaths and so forth conform to that intention? (94)

Having explained the Kāṇva recension, and following the Mādhyandina reading which states that immediately after the passage on departure [the soul] "enters into consciousness itself," he raises the doubt that this reading excludes [the possibility of knowledge at death], beginning with the word "But" (nanu). For it is impossible for a person who is without organs to possess knowledge at the time of death.
The meaning is that it is illogical for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth to conform to that intention. He introduces the Mādhyandina passage as a response with the words:
"It is said. || 94 ||
Knowledge consisting of recognition is called "saṃjñāna."
That which was previously illuminated by the initial shining forth of the heart.
The cognition of a future object is called recognition (pratyabhijñāna).
With consciousness thus arisen, that self enters the body. || 96 ||

In that context, he states the meaning of the term *saṃjñāna*: it is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). What is this form of knowledge that constitutes recognition? Indeed, it is not logical for there to be a cognition arising from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding an object that is yet to exist, in the absence of a prior experience of that object. To this, he says: "That which was previously... and so forth. Regarding this:

The meaning is that what is intended here by "recognition" (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the knowledge of a future event belonging to a man about to die—designated as the "illumination of the heart"—which has been active for six months prior to death;

this recognition, consisting of the conceit "I am a god" and so forth, is present even in the state of dying just as it was in the state of living. Anticipating the objection that, according to the order of the text, this recognition occurs immediately after the departure of the soul (*utkrānti*), he says:

He said, “So be it. For that person on the verge of death, endowed with the knowledge called recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) produced in the manner described, departs from the body. Thus he says: [textual variants follow].
[Vol. 3, page 607]
The meaning is as follows:

since recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) has already occurred previously, the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is not intended to be significant; otherwise, there would follow an order for the departure (*utkrānti*) as well, and that [order] has already been refuted. || 95 || 96 ||
Even for one who has emerged from the body by means of the light at the tip of the heart, [the state of liberation is attained].
How can there be a transition to another body for one who is devoid of consciousness? (97)
He states the doubt to be excluded by the sentence beginning with "sa eṣa" (this is that), [starting] with the words "hṛdaya" (heart) etc. || 97 ||
To provide a resolution to this, there is the subsequent statement beginning with "sa" (he), and so forth.
This very knower, the divine person, becomes possessed of self-consciousness; then— || 98 ||
He takes up the subsequent statement: "of this," and recites that very [passage]: "he. The meaning of the word "atha" (now/then) is immediate succession to the departure [from the body]. || 98 ||
With all the sense organs withdrawn due to the causal influence of meditative cultivation.
Just as one possesses consciousness in a dream, so it is held to be even at the time of departure. || 99 ||

"He becomes endowed with knowledge and consciousness" (Chāndogya Up. 8.12.3)—this expresses the meaning of the Mādhyandina recension's statement, which he explains as follows: "When [the organs] have been withdrawn.

The meaning is that even though all the instruments [of perception] are destroyed at the time of departure just as in sleep, because he is conscious, he indeed remains possessed of knowledge regarding the path and so forth through his meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) and other means.
The connection with specific knowledge occurs through this very cause, which is action alone.
But it cannot be obtained through independence, because independence is impossible here.

Having also explained the *Mādhyandina* recension, and following both scriptural traditions, he says "viśeṣa... [in verse 100], raising the objection that because this [self] is conscious, its future knowledge of the body and so forth does not depend on karma but is inherent. Here, the word "iha" refers to the state of death. || 100 ||
Everyone would have accomplished their purpose through the attainment of specialized knowledge.
If it were obtainable here through independence, it would not be so unobtainable; and thus he has said. 101.
Whatever state of being one remembers when they finally leave the body at the end, [that state they attain].
To that very thing he goes, O son of Kuntī, being constantly permeated by the thought of it.

In that regard, he states the reason for this lack of independence: "having accomplished what was to be done. The word "here" (*iha*) is as before. He provides the statement of Vyāsa as proof for the point already stated: "so it is. He states the reason for the interval between the successful recollection: "always" (*sadā*). ||101||102||
Thus, the self, together with consciousness, must go to that which was previously acquired.
Then that very consciousness of one's own personal existence emerges from that [store-consciousness]. || 103 ||
He summarizes the meaning of the two statements from both branches with the word "evam" (thus). The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (hence) is "due to the power of karma. || 103 ||
Therefore, for this reason, men should strive with diligence for the sake of their own independence.
One should practice the means such as yoga and accumulate merit. || 104 ||

Reflecting upon the aforementioned course of karma, he clarifies the intended meaning of the two statements with the words "yataḥ" (since). Now, one might object: "If a person follows karma and is not independent, how can he be enjoined toward the accumulation of merit? To this, he replies: "with effort" (*prayatnataḥ*).

The sense is that even for one who follows the course of karma, there is no contradiction in exercising autonomy, as in the case of a king and others. Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind; its limbs are the restraints (yama) and so forth. He states [the following] to show that the practice of these means and the accumulation of distinguished merit must be performed with focused intent, in order to avoid dependence at the time of death: "Yoga and so forth... (104).
This great undertaking of all the scriptures here has that [liberation] as its sole purpose.
For the awakening of the means accomplished through speech, mind, and body. || 105 ||

Furthermore, it is observed in the sphere of worldly activity that the undertaking of every scripture is great, insofar as it prescribes auspicious actions and prohibits inauspicious ones; this too demonstrates that at the time of death, one must perform the accumulation of merit for the sake of independence.
He says "all," and he clarifies this very point with the word "speech" (vāk). || 105 ||
Likewise, there is the prohibition of means when it leads to what is disadvantageous.
This alone is the purpose of the scripture: that which depends upon the agent for the attainment of happiness. (106)

The prohibition of that which accomplishes the undesirable is also performed by the prohibitory scripture; and that [prohibition], like the injunction for merit, demonstrates at the time of death its function as the destruction of evil deeds for the sake of one's independence. Thus he says: "In the same way. Although dharma is enjoined by the scripture and adharma is censured, how is the attainment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) accomplished merely through the performance of dharma and the abandonment of adharma?

He said: "It is this much. For the sake of attaining happiness and abandoning suffering, only the accumulation of merit (*dharma*) and so forth prescribed in the scriptures should be performed, and nothing else that depends on a creator as the cause of human goals. Therefore, at the time of death, for the sake of independence, one should practice *dharma* and abandon *adharma*;
this is the meaning. || 106 ||
Having taken up the characteristic of measure, there is the creation of its own [nature].
Just as there is nothing here, so no appropriation whatsoever is observed.

Having explained the passage beginning with "possessed of consciousness" (*savijñāna*), he states what is being excluded by the sentence beginning with "that [is] knowledge" (*taṃ vidyā*): "merely" (*mātra*).

The meaning is that just as the creation of a dream is accepted as being caused by the impressions (*vāsanā*) and karma of the waking state, no such cause whatsoever is observed for the creation of another world. || 107 ||

Then, when the body has been thus abandoned by the deity and the *liṅga* has been drawn out from it;
Let it be explained regarding the transition to another world and the undertaking of causes and effects. || 108 ||
Anticipating the objection that the transition to another body and its commencement occur by the power of the organs, their instruments, and their presiding deities, he says: "Now" (atha).
He says "thus" (evam) according to the principle stated in such passages as "then one becomes a knower of forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5). || 108 ||
Whatever may be the cause for the self's departure to the next world.
And having gone there, he enjoys [the fruits], which is also the cause for the commencement of a body. || 109 ||

In that case, the soul’s transition to another body and so forth would occur without any cause; therefore, he says: "of the soul.
This is to be connected with the subsequent word "let it be told. The underlying sense is that an effect cannot arise without a cause. || 109 ||
As the subtle body (liṅgāna) departs from this body and enters another body, [it carries with it the impressions].
What is its equipment (saṃbhāra), and what is the purpose of its movement? Tell me also regarding the commencement of the body. || 110 ||

Anticipating the objection that the subtle body (*liṅga*) alone might then be the cause of movement and so forth, he says "the subtle body" (*liṅga*), etc., to show that this is not so because it is of no avail for one who is independent of the gross body. The connection is with the phrase "of this [being] whose vehicle is the subtle body. That is to say, "he whose vehicle (*anaḥ*) is the subtle body (*liṅga*) is 'this one whose vehicle is the subtle body' (*liṅgāna*); [the genitive] *tasya* means "of him. || 110 ||
For one who desires to depart from here, the knowledge and actions previously acquired [serve as the means].
These two, as well as whatever prior latent impression existed, seize hold of it.

Thinking that the statement beginning with "that [knowledge]" (*taṃ vidyā*) is intended to state the cause for the creation of the next world, for the transition to it, and for enjoyment therein, he takes up that [text] from here. || 111 ||
Consciousness may be either doubtful cognition or even false cognition.
Whether by means of valid cognition or invalid cognition, all is called "knowledge. (112)
He explains "knowledge" (vidyā): "consciousness" (vijñāna). The meaning here is that knowledge consists merely of cognition. || 112 ||
That knowledge which destroys the cause of saṃsāra and pertains to the supreme self—
Therefore, this [teaching] should not be accepted here, as it dispels all causes of calamity.

Anticipating the objection that knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*) should also be understood here by the term "knowledge" (*vidyā*), he says: "saṃsāra... (referring to verse 113). The reason for its not being included is given by "sarva...": here, the word "knowledge" refers to that which is a cause of bondage, because it occurs in association with karma and other such causes of bondage. The meaning is that the knowledge of Brahman, because it destroys those [causes], does not deserve to be called "knowledge" in this context. || 113 ||
Therefore, that which is not opposed to the ignorance of the self is the cause of saṃsāra.
Those who have not attained the ultimate reality seek to grasp mere cognition. 114.
Regarding this, he states the result [of the previous argument]: "the cause of saṃsāra. He provides the reason for its non-opposition [to liberation]: "because it has not been attained," etc. (114).
And that which is to be accomplished through speech, mind, and body, whether according to the scriptures or otherwise.
That which consists of visible and invisible purposes is understood to be action (karman). || 115 ||
He states the meaning of the word *karman*: "Speech," etc. The meaning here is that *karman* refers to mere activity (*vyāpāra*). || 115 ||
As he goes, knowledge and action, as previously described, follow him.
For [the elements] follow the departing person according to their respective natures.
Therefore, in this context, the word "anu" (after) is employed in the sense of "behind" or "following" one who is going. || 116 ||

Having first restated the previously mentioned knowledge and ritual action, he takes up the portion beginning with "they both take hold of him" (*taṃ samanvārabhete*). Regarding the phrase "they both take hold of him" (*anvārabhete*):
1. *sva*, *ga*: *yā vā'bhū*; 2. *ka*: *dātmajñānavi*; 3. *kha*: *namatra jiauṃ*. [Vol. 3, p. 610]

He states its meaning with the words "gacchantam" (while it is moving). The sense is that, by their very nature, knowledge and action possess a dependence on a substratum as their inherent character. || 116 ||
When a person engages in the performance of going and other such actions, they attain the status of being the means [to that action]. || 117 ||
The impression (saṃskāra) of an action being performed which rests in the heart—
And that which is called "prior wisdom" (pūrvaprajñā) is the memory of that fruit once it has been experienced. || 118 ||

Regarding the question "What is its equipment? and so forth, he says: "Going, etc. By the word "etc.," the commencement of another body by means of the [present] body is included. He explains "prior cognition" as being "of action. || 117 || 118 ||
It arises from the causes of formative predispositions accumulated in the past. || 119 ||
Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) has arisen in this embodied being during the remaining six months, [that alone remains].
They know that "prior wisdom" (pūrvaprajñā) is for the sake of another body for one who is about to die. || 120 ||

He states that *pūrvaprajñā* (prior cognition), which rests in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and is designated as the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of actions and their fruits, is the cause for its manifestation.

Regarding the word "prior" (*pūrva*), the meaning is that at the time of death, the aforementioned *pūrvaprajñā* manifests with a tendency toward its effects due to two causes known as "acquired action" (*upāttakarman*) and "prior [action]" (*pūrva*).
He states another meaning of the term *pūrvaprajñā*: "six months," etc. (verses 119–120).
For that very [discipline] alone is capable of uplifting both your knowledge and your action.
Therefore, because the person (puruṣa) is the principal [factor], it has been mentioned separately. || 121 ||

Regarding the reason for mentioning that [desire] separately from knowledge and action, he says: "capable," etc. For indeed, the knowledge and action of one who has died cannot exist in their own form, because of the absence of distinct causal agents (*kāraka*); therefore, they persist only in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Since those two are predominant [in that state], it is appropriate to mention desire separately—this is the meaning. || 121 ||
Since they have been indicated in brief precisely because there is no distinction in their status as causes.
And because knowledge and action are mutual causes of one another, they are mentioned here in the Śruti.

[Objection: Since there was previously a statement regarding the non-combination (*asamāsa*) of prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*), might there likewise be such for knowledge (*vidyā*) and action (*karman*)? [Reply: No; he says, "by way of combination" (*samāsena*).

For since knowledge and action are not different in their status as causes with respect to prior cognition, they are stated by the Śruti in combination as its cause. This is because it is logical that when there is a single effect, the causes should possess a uniform nature. Furthermore, there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect between prior cognition, knowledge, and action.

He states that a twofold division is logical because of the relationship between cause and effect regarding the two categories of cause and effect, saying "mutually" (*anyonya*). Here, knowledge and action—along with what is called prior wisdom (*pūrvaprajñā*)—are mutually related as cause and effect; therefore, knowledge and action are set apart by the scripture, and prior wisdom is likewise set apart from them.
This is the construction [of the verse]. || 122 ||
For from that [knowledge] comes the extraction of both knowledge and action as previously understood.
And from those two arises the cultivation; therefore, the instruction is as it has been described. || 123 ||
That very point is clarified: "The previous," etc. (123).

For when karma is being experienced, what remains is indeed the latent impression (bhāvanā).
And because it is the primary source of that which is being born, it is called the "Root" (mūla). || 124 ||
One might ask: since there is no distinction among these three in their mutual relationship as cause and effect, how can prior wisdom (pūrvaprajñā) be considered predominant?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of action" (*karmaṇaḥ*). The term "residue" (*pariśeṣa*) refers to the latent impression of the fruit (*phalavāsanā*). He states the result expected by the word "for" (*hi*):
"predominant" (*pradhānam*). || 124 ||
For this knowledge is indeed that which discerns and creates another world.
The vikartṛ and karmavadbhāva [operations] apply to the two preceding [suffixes], excluding those that follow. || 125 ||
Having first stated the specific functions of the three, he concludes the meaning of the sentence with the words "the delimiting [agent]," etc.

The sense of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that the fact of knowledge being the delimiting agent (*paricchettṛtva*) and action being the transformer (*vikartṛtva*) is well-established in the world. The locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). || 121 ||
Because various conceptual constructions exist, there is doubt regarding the act of going.
Does this [self] go forth as something limited, like a bird from a tree? (126)

Having stated that the attainment of another body belongs to one who possesses a collection [of factors] such as knowledge, he provides the introductory context for introducing the scriptural passage concerning the "caterpillar" (*tṛṇajalāyuka*) by saying, "Not manifold," etc. Explaining the doubt itself, which is rooted in the conflicting views of various disputants, he first states the position of the Digambaras:
"The bird," etc. (126).
Or rather, does he proceed toward another body by means of the subtle body?
The movement, expansion, and contraction [of consciousness] are like a lamp placed within a broken jar.
Or do you maintain that it is the mind alone that travels from one body to another? (127)

He states the view of those who maintain that [the soul's journey] is carried by a deity (*devatāvādin*): "The *ātivāhika*," etc. That is to say, it is by means of that subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) with which a deity leads the individual soul (*jīva*) to the other world. He states the view of the Sāṃkhya and others: "Expansion," etc.
He states the position of the Vaiśeṣikas and others: "What," etc. (Verse 127).
Or rather, what would be the purpose here for instruments that are all-pervading within the self?
In some cases, the loss or emergence of one's livelihood occurs in accordance with the actions heard [in scripture]. 128.
It demonstrates the Upaniṣadic view. "But what?"—this is the statement of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). "In some cases"—this refers to the states of death and life. || 128 ||
Thus, regarding this ground characterized by manifold conceptual constructions, the established conclusion is stated.
All these, characterized by speech, mind, and vital breath, are indeed infinite.

Having created doubt through the dispute of various disputants, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta) in order to remove it: "Thus, [they are] manifold" (iti bhūri). He elucidates that very point: "They are infinite" (anantāḥ). The meaning is that since the scripture proceeds by relying on the position of their omnipresence, other positions contrary to that must be abandoned. || 129 ||
[Volume 3, Page 612] 4 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā-vyākhyā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1715 1.
The size of the droplets and so forth is determined in accordance with the karma of living beings.
Thus, according to the statements of the Śruti, these [qualities] exist in each individual according to their respective intellect.
The destination, the location, the delimitation, and the extent are according to one's karma. || 130 ||

How, then, do the contraction and expansion of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) occur in bodies such as those of mosquitoes and those of elephants? To this he says: "The vital breath" (*prāṇīti*). He cites the scriptural authority here, beginning with the words "equal to a gnat" (*samaḥ pluṣiṇā*). Regarding the phrase "thus from the scripture" (*iti śrutīti*): the meaning is that, based on the aforementioned scriptural statement, it is certain that in all living beings the maintenance and movement of the vital breaths, as well as their limitation and expansion, occur in accordance with [the individual's] knowledge and action.
Whether it be independence, dependence, or even the sovereign powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
All this [world] of the instruments of action has knowledge, karma, and so forth as its cause.
Fearing that, like independence (*svātantrya*) and so forth, their movement (*gati*) and other qualities might also be independent of knowledge (*vidyā*) and the rest, he says: "Independence," etc.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the term *aṇimādi*, these [powers] are meant: *laghimā* (levity), *mahimā* (magnification), *garimā* (heaviness), *prākāmya* (irresistible will), *vaśitva* (mastery), *īśitva* (lordship), and *yatra-kāmāvasāyitā* (the power of determining the course of things according to one's desire). And it has been stated that these possess the nature of being attributes of the instrument (*karaṇa*), whereas determination (*adhyavasāya*) is an attribute of the intellect (*buddhi*), as are knowledge (*jñāna*) and dispassion (*virāga*).
This sovereignty is of the nature of sattva; that which is its opposite is of the nature of tamas. || 131 ||
Just as it is for those such as ourselves, so it is likewise according to the influence of knowledge and karma.
Furthermore, even for that which is non-self, infinity is not established by itself, just as it is not for the self.
If the limitation of Hiraṇyagarbha, whose nature is that of the instrument (the subtle body), is caused by karma and the like, then his infinity—like that of Brahman—is intrinsic;
for the Śruti says, "All these are indeed equal, all are infinite. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of those such as ourselves" [verse 132].
Relying upon this position, an illustrative example is stated by means of scripture. || 133 ||
Just as a leech, having left one blade of grass, moves on to another blade of grass; so it is here.
There, she gradually withdraws herself from her previous state by means of herself.

Having stated that the instruments (karaṇas) are infinite in their cosmic (ādhidevika) form and limited in their individual (ādhyātmika) form, he introduces the scriptural illustration with the words "Thus this... The meaning is that, having grasped the omnipresence of the instruments, the intention is to provide an illustration for the following point: the mental impression (bhāvanā) residing in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), while touching the future body, leaves the previous body. He explains that [illustration] with the words "As grass... and so forth.

The time when the leech exists is expressed by the locative case [saptamī]. "By itself" (ātmanā) is a reference to the whole; "itself" (ātmānam) is a statement regarding the subsequent part; "from the preceding blade of grass" refers to the first part; and "therein" (tatra) refers to the other blade of grass. || 133 || 134 ||
Just as this self [is freed] from this body upon the exhaustion of karma, so it is.
Having struck down [the opponent] and rendered him motionless, one withdraws the signs of one's own self. || 135 ||
Having thus caused this ignorance, dullness, and state of unconsciousness to pass away.
Then, having attained another body through a different process, he is anointed by meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
He withdraws the self, which resides in the previous body, by means of the self into the self.

1746 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Having restated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he explains the application (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words beginning "Just as" (*yathā*).

In this manner, according to the method described, just as the illustration has been explained, so too is this Self—once the commenced karma has been exhausted through experience—motionless and unconscious.

The construction is as follows: having obtained another body that is the object of its contemplation (*bhāvanā*), it abandons the previous body. He states the reason for the rendering of the gross body (*sthūladeha*) unconscious: "Its own self," etc.; that is to say, because of the withdrawal of the subtle body (*liṅga*), which is the self of its respective gross body.
This movement of the self has been explained as being like that of a leech.
In that regard, what is the material cause for the soul in the undertaking of another body? (137)
He recounts the preceding context in order to introduce the statement of the weaver: "Like a leech. He states the doubt regarding that [context]:
"In that case. The meaning is: when the commencement of another body is thus introduced for the self, what material cause (upādāna) exists, or does it not?
If it does not exist, then an effect in the form of a positive entity could not be established; if it does exist, then that must be explained. || 137 ||
Having repeatedly crushed it, what is this "perpetually appropriated" that you desire?
Again and again, or as something unprecedented, it serves to initiate a new body.

If it is argued that the five elements themselves are the material cause (*upādāna*) of that [body], he says in response: "Having destroyed" (*upamṛdya*). Does this eternal Self, having destroyed each preceding body, initiate another and another body by means of the five elements; or rather, does one set of five elements produce one body and another set of five elements produce another body? It cannot be the first case, because if the five elements were the material cause of each respective body, then the status of Māyā as the universal cause would be undermined.

The second [alternative] is not tenable due to contradiction, because even in the production of the five elements, another cause must be sought; the sense is that it is precisely that [other cause] whose status as the cause of another body is established. || 138 ||
Thus, the determination of this matter is described by means of the statement of an illustrative example. || 139 ||
Just as a goldsmith here takes up a measure of gold, so too [does the practitioner].
Having thoroughly crushed the previous arrangement, he creates another arrangement. || 140 ||
The form of fresh grain is indeed more auspicious.
"The example [is given] as 'from the auspicious' (kalyāṇāt)"; it is just like that here as well. (141)

He takes up the subsequent statement as a reply: "Thus, by way of an illustration. The meaning is that the determination of the point—that the five elements, which are eternally present, are indeed the originators [of the world]—is established through an illustration; nor is there any contradiction with the doctrine of Māyā, because the established position is that the world is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the five elements, which themselves are transformations of Māyā resting upon the consciousness of the Witness (*pratyak-caitanya*). He explains the illustration: "The goldsmith... [Sūtra...]
It is said that "here" refers to the sphere of conventional practice involving debtors and creditors. He states the application to the case at hand: "Thus is the illustration.
Here, "here" is the expression referring to the application to the case at hand. (139) (140) (141)
Depending upon the taking up of the new, that effect is called "new."
By means of the Śruti, he assumes a newer form that is indeed more auspicious.
Now, one might object that for a body being produced, it is only logical that it be "new" (*nava*), and not "newer" (*navatara*); to this, he says: "In relation to...

The effect of those five elements, in relation to the nine [elements], is the assumption of a new body from that [ninefold state]; this is here called "newer" and "more auspicious" than the previous one. Therefore, the meaning is that this present body and so forth are the effects of the elements perpetually assumed. || 142 ||
The elements and the sense organs are eternally appropriated by the embodied being.
I have previously stated that there are two forms of Brahman. || 143 ||

In this regard, he cites the *Mūrtāmūrta-brāhmaṇa* as authority: "The eternal," etc. Its meaning is as follows: that which is indicated by the phrase "the eye that shines" is the gross body; and [it is also indicated] by the phrases "this person who is in the right eye" and "this person who is in this orb."
A subtle body is assumed there; for it is said that "this is indeed its essence" and "this is its essence," thus stating that both [the gross and subtle bodies] are composed of the five elements.
Therefore, in this case as well, it is accepted that that which initiates their formation is precisely what has been eternally acquired. || 143 ||
Repeatedly destroying their former arrangement, once again...
According to their karma and according to their knowledge, they create another arrangement.

Anticipating the objection that while the aforementioned body and so forth may be the material cause (upādāna), the efficient cause (nimitta) must still be stated, he says: "Having destroyed" (upamṛdya).
The rites for the ancestors and others are suitable for the ancestors and so forth; they are classified as superior, inferior, and middling.
In the worlds of the ancestors and others, this self [dwells] according to its karma and according to its learning.
Through ignorance, it expands the many forms born of the body.

He explains the passage beginning with "pitryaṃ" (belonging to the ancestors) and so forth with the words "pitrādi" (ancestors, etc.). He states the internal subdivisions within that [category] with the word "uttama" (highest). The particle "hi" is used to indicate that the diversity of those [worlds] depends upon the diversity of the means of attainment (*upāyana*). Having stated the literal meaning of the words, he states the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) with the words "pitryādi" (belonging to the ancestors, etc.). || 149 || 146 ||
But transmigratory existence is not considered to belong to it directly by its own nature, as consciousness does.
Thus, for the sake of conveying this meaning, the subsequent speech was uttered.

Fearing that the aforementioned cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) might be as natural to the Self as consciousness itself, he introduces the passage beginning with "That indeed is this" (*sa vā ayam*), stating: "But not so" (*na tu*). || 147 ||
That which is the true nature of this self, and that which arises from ignorance regarding the self;
Now, its determination is being made by means of the words beginning with "sa vai" and so forth.
"How indeed could the entire meaning remain undetermined after the determination of that [word]? (148)

He states the purport of that [verse] with the words "And that which... He states the resulting conclusion: "If the two forms of the Self—real and unreal—are determined, then the entire meaning of the Veda would be determined," using the word "That" (tad). || 148 ||
The transmigrating being is that which has been established by the aforementioned text.
This sound is for the purpose of grasping, and likewise for the sake of recollecting that; so indeed it is.
9. ka. kha. 'thoktaṃ de'; 2. kha. 'trirṇītāvaśe'; 3. ka. ga. 'thaṃ tviti'. [Vol. 3, page 615] 1748 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]...
He states the meaning of the two words "sa" and "vai": "The transmigrating being... (149).
In this characteristic of cause and effect, there is no self-existent entity.
That object which is manifested in saṃsāra as being non-different from the Self; || 150 ||

This explains the meaning of the word "this" (ayam). Regarding the term "non-self" (anātman): the meaning here is that the self-luminous reality, which is free from ignorance and its effects, is what is referred to by the word "this. || 150 ||
That by which the existence and non-existence of what has been described are established as witnessed.
This very thing that constitutes cyclic existence is here designated as the "self. (151)
He states the meaning of the word "Self" (ātman) with the words "That which... The meaning here is that the Self is the changeless witness, the essence of consciousness (ciddhātu). || 151 ||
He who possesses no deviation among all things that are subject to deviation.

Because its accomplishment is always dependent upon that, it establishes its immutability (*kūṭasthatva*). [The word] "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*)—its connection with the preceding [verse] is: "that [which is non-deviating] is here the Self. He states the reason for its non-deviation: "upon that" (*tadavaṣṭambhataḥ*). || 152 || || 112 ||
Because it is directly manifest as the inner self (pratyak), and because it is neither an action nor a causal factor (kāraka).
Because it is the measure for the cognition of nothing else, it is therefore called "this" (ayam). || 153 ||

To the question of how the Self—which is devoid of the distinction between existence and non-existence and is the accomplisher of all—can be designated as "this" since it lacks the quality of being conjoined with what stands before one, he says: "By way of its own nature (*pratyaktayā*). The meaning is that because the Self is proximate and immediate, it is denotable by the word "this. He establishes its immediacy [by saying]: "Non-other" (*ananyā*). To explain how that is so, he says: "Actionless" (*akriyā*).
By means of the path that completely refutes both the self and its causes.
The selfhood of the self would be established as not being subordinate to anything else, unlike that which is non-self. (154)
If it be argued that the Self must be limited because it is denotable by a word, like a jar or other objects, he says "no," [concluding with] "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder).
The reality of the self would be established only through its own unique establishment.
Therefore, the very reality of the Self is the world, appearing as cause and effect.

Anticipating the objection—“How can the self be established by means of refuting non-self and its causes, given that there exist entities consisting of cause and effect distinct from the self?”—the author says: “Asādhāraṇa... (The uncommon...). The meaning is that because the world is superimposed upon the non-dual, self-luminous Self, its fullness is logical. || 155 ||
For this [self] does not hear its own location, nor does it hear anything other than that.
For it is only through non-distinction from the Self that the non-self is established. || 156 ||
He establishes that the world is superimposed upon the Self, beginning with the words "For not... (*na hi*). By the word "this" (*idam*), the world under discussion is indicated.
[Variant readings: 1. ka. kha. *ṃturātme*; 2. kha. *tmani sthā*]. [Vol. 3, page 616]
He states the reason for both cases with the words "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*). For the non-self (*anātman*) cannot be established either through difference or non-difference from the Self;

because if there were difference, it would lack its own nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*), and if there were non-difference, it would be impossible for the insentient and the sentient to be joined. Therefore, the meaning is that the non-self is superimposed (*adhyasta*). This is also the case here.
The negative particle (*nañ*) located in the first half [of the verse] is drawn forward [to apply to the subsequent terms]. || 196 ||
But the Self, because it is the inner witness of the non-Self, cannot admit of any distinction from it.
Just as [the perception of] a snake, a staff, and so forth [arises] from a rope, so does the object produced by ignorance [arise].
There is no accomplishment anywhere else apart from the reality of the corners (sraktattva). || 157 ||

If it is argued that just as the non-self (anātman) is distinct from the self (ātman), the self should likewise be distinct from the non-self, [the author] says "no," beginning with the words "But the self... Here, the illustration for the fact that the non-self is not established through either difference or non-difference from the self is given by the words "In a garland... For the snake and so forth, which are imagined by ignorance, do not exist elsewhere apart from the garland in which they appear; nor, on the other hand, are they established as being identical with the nature of that garland itself.
The meaning is that, in the same way as buddhi, the existence of multiple selves is not established through either their difference from or non-difference from the self. || 157 ||
Nor should this [non-existence] be determined as non-existent, for non-existence is [a reality] just like existence.
Because its true nature consists solely of the individual soul (pratyagātman), it is not heard [as such] either through scripture or by implication. || 158 ||

If it is argued that the world is unestablished through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) because its non-existence is determined, he says "no" with the words "And not... Furthermore, is the world's state of being grounded in non-existence inferred from scripture (*śruti*) or from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? It is not the first, as he says: "Because it is not heard [in scripture]. This is because scriptural passages such as "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*), unable to tolerate the existence of the world, declare its limit to be grounded in non-existence; thus, it is not the second [alternative].
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Not so" (na ca). || 158 ||
Having restated the entire universe for the sake of realizing its respective true nature.
Since it has been heard that "it is the Self alone," nothing other than this is admitted to exist. || 159 ||

He states the reason why the weaker presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) is sublated by the stronger direct scriptural statement (*śruti*): "Having restated... It is said that the emptiness of the world is something else [than what is perceived]. || 159 ||
And having rejected [the notion of] the Self, the non-Self is not found to exist apart from it.
Furthermore, because it is of the nature of exclusion (vyatireka), it is not established in relation to the self (ātman). || 160 ||

Having refuted the view that the world culminates in non-existence (*abhāva*), he restates the rejection of its inherence (*anvaya*) and so forth with the words "having rejected" (*pratyākhyāya*). The meaning is as follows: apart from the Self (*ātman*), the non-self (*anātman*) is not established independently, because it has already been stated that this would entail the consequence of it being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpa*); nor is it established as non-different from the Self, because, being insentient (*jaḍa*), it is distinct from that which is non-insentient (*ajaḍa*). || 160 ||
Therefore, the Śruti declares that everything exists within the Self.
And likewise, by stating "all is the Self," it negates any distinction [between them]. || 161 ||

He states the proof for the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the world with the words "he rejects. He states the proof for the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "all...
(verse 161).

The characteristic of Brahman is that it is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior.
Therefore, because the nature of the reality of the self has been explained, there is this statement: "The Self is Brahman. (162)

Having explained "This indeed is the Self," he states the meaning of the word *brahman*: "apūrva... [etc.]. He explains the intended sense of the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): "uktā... [etc.]. Brahman, which is devoid of generality, particularity, and so forth, has been described in various places; because that [Brahman] is the very nature of the Self, the statement "the Self is Brahman" expresses the Brahman-hood of the Self through the scriptural coordination. Thus, the meaning is that there is identity between the two. || 162 ||
The reality of Brahman is inwardness, and likewise, the reality of the Self is Brahmanhood.
For it is by the removal of the two aspects of remoteness that the Self is understood to be Brahman.
[Objection: How can there be identity between those two, given the contradiction arising from their being remote and non-dual? To this, he says: "Pratyaktvam" (the state of being the inner self).
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that identity through the abandonment of contradictory parts is well-known in cases such as "This is that very person. || 163 ||
The meaning of the word "Brahman" is held to be neither excluded nor followed.
This [Self] is not found apart from the Self, nor is the Self found apart from Brahman.

Having restated the meaning of the word "Brahman" as "the reality of Brahman is inwardness," [the author] clarifies it with the words "not excluded" (avyāvṛtta). He expresses that the reality of the Self is its being Brahman with the words "nor indeed" (nāpi). || 164 ||
Just as the self is hidden from itself due to ignorance regarding Brahman.
Just as my own self possesses a second, so too does Brahman possess one for me.

Nevertheless, raising the doubt as to how the abandonment of both remoteness (pārokṣya) and duality (sadvaya) occurs, he states that remoteness and so forth are products of nescience (āvidyaka) in order to explain that:
"Even of the Self... (verse 165).
Therefore, upon the complete destruction of ignorance through the realization of things as they truly are, [the cessation of suffering follows].
This self, being Brahman itself, attains Brahman, which is inherently non-dual.

He states the consequence of its being ignorance (*avidyā*) with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is this: although this very Self is by its own nature Brahman, it is perceived as if it were not Brahman due to ignorance; when that ignorance is destroyed through right knowledge, it attains Brahmanhood itself. || 166 ||
Due to the absence of the aforementioned awakening, there arises for him a succession of misfortunes.
The specific connection with consciousness and so forth is now explained accordingly. (167)

Having stated the actual nature of the self, he explains the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). He says: "As has been stated. He clarifies that very point: "Consciousness and so forth" (*vijñānādi*). || 167 ||
This self, being Brahman itself, is endowed with as many attributes as there are.
One wanders in saṃsāra here due to ignorance; that is now described in brief. (168)

He applies the Bhāṣya beginning with "of whom" (*yasya*) to the subject already stated. [The word] "ātman" refers here to the passage beginning with "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). || 168 ||
For it is through the succession of ignorance that the entire mass of miseries of saṃsāra comes into being.
Therefore, upon the destruction of that [ignorance], the purpose of the self is fully accomplished. || 169 ||
[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
1751. "Let this [Self] transmigrate through the gateway of association with cognition and so forth due to ignorance; what do you gain from that? To this he says: "Since..."
Thus [ends the section]. || 169 ||
For the connection of the self with misfortune arises solely from the cause of ignorance.
The subsequent section of the text is introduced for the purpose of explaining this point. || 170 ||

If it is argued that the bondage of the self is established by the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), [the author] says "ignorance" (*avidyā*) to address the doubt that this ignorance itself is not established due to a lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Here, the word "for" (*hi*) is used to provide the reasons through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). In that regard, he corroborates it with scripture using the words "of this" (*asya*). || 170 ||
If the state of being a transmigrating soul were caused by ignorance alone, then that would belong to the Self.
This undertaking is appropriate for the sake of knowledge; it would not be so otherwise. || 171 ||

He states the reasoning for bondage being rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*) with the words "If... etc. Since the commencement of the scripture has the purpose of producing knowledge (*vidyā*), and since that knowledge aims at the destruction of all rootless evils, it is logical that bondage is rooted in ignorance; for the opposition between knowledge and ignorance is well-established. Otherwise, the commencement of the scripture would be impossible—this is the meaning. || 171 ||
Being one who identifies with the self as the vital breath (prāṇa), from him the vital breath is produced.
Even though it is the life-force of the vital breaths, through delusion it undergoes the process of breathing and so forth.

Having stated the purport of the subsequent section (*uttaragrantha*) and disregarding the order of the text, he explains the meaning of the phrase "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*). Regarding the word "breath":

because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is born from the Inner Self (*pratīc*), as per such scriptural passages as "From this [Self] the breath is born" and "He created the breath," and because of the Vedic hearing that "He is the breath of the breath" (*sa prāṇasya prāṇam*), even the "breath of the breath" (the *prāṇamaya-kośa*), through delusion, identifies with it, thinking "I am the breath."
The meaning is that, having come into being, it undergoes activities such as breathing and so forth. || 172 ||
Then, upon the arising of the intellect, there occurs the state of "I am consciousness."
"It attains the state of being composed of consciousness (vijñānamayatā), as if [attaining] the state of being composed of the stars" (173).

Since it is impossible to consist of consciousness and so forth without movement, he first demonstrates the state of being composed of vital breath (prāṇamayatva) and then explains the state of being composed of consciousness.
He states "tataḥ" (thereupon). He states the meaning of the term "manomaya" (composed of mind) as "buddhi... (173).
And here, the mention of the mind (manas) is an indication for the functions of the intellect (buddhi).
For this reason, there is no cognition of all the sense-faculties and the self. || 174 ||

The term "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "mind" (*manas*) here serve as indicators for the functions of the intellect—the unmentioned organs of perception—as well as the functions of the vital breaths and the organs of action. Therefore, it is stated that the Self should be seen as consisting of the skin and so forth, and as consisting of speech and so forth. [Objection:
How can the senses possess the functions of the intellect and the vital breath, given that those functions have been attributed to the Self? To this, he says: "the vital breaths and the intellect."
Therefore, because they are effects of those [elements] and thus reside within them, they do not constitute attributes of the Self; this is the remainder of the sense. || 174 ||
Prāṇa is said to be the cause of the sense organs together with their objects.
That very excellence of cognition is also the cause for the auditory faculty and the others.
