He analyzes the subsequent sentence—which serves as the reason for the statement that, although a person consists of everything, being composed of action (*karmamayatva*) is the primary cause—by means of a question, beginning with "Why? (*kutaḥ*). Desire (*kāma*) is not the primary cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

He establishes this [point] regarding "action" (karman) by means of an illustration: "The instigator," etc. When it is examined whether knowledge and the rest—excluding desire—are the instigators (prayojaka) or the instigated (prayojya), it is determined that action alone is the instigator of those others, according to such scriptural statements as "Verily, by merit [one attains merit]," and so forth; this is the sense. To the question, "How is it determined that desire is the primary instigator?", he says: "That," etc. (210).
When ritual action and so forth function as the instigating cause, it is stated that desire is predominant.
When there is a state of completion for the instigators, however, the desire [of the agent] is not intended to be expressed. || 213 ||

With the intention that, since desire is the final ground that impels one toward saṃsāra, it would follow that the ignorance of the inner self (pratyagajñāna) is not its root—thereby abandoning the accepted position—he says: "In [the case of] being the impeller," etc. (213).
Lack of thorough knowledge regarding things as they truly are is also a cause of desire.
Because the reality of the self has attained all happiness and cast off suffering. (214)
There is no happiness whatsoever that has not been attained, and likewise, no unhappiness that has not been cast aside.
Indeed, by the statement "He who is Bhūman" and also by "He who is Aśanāya," [the Lord is established] in the Self.
1 kha. "Thus it is accepted.
[Vol. 3, page 625] 1758 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter—]

He states the reason for the fact that desire lacks both a motivating cause and a terminal point: "As it truly is" (*yathāvastu*). To demonstrate that, he first declares the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya*): "The one who has attained" (*āpta*). He provides the proof for its state of having all happiness attained: "Or whoever" (*yo vā*). He provides the proof for its state of having suffering cast off: "He who" (*yaḥ*). The grammatical connection is: "[This is known] from the statement regarding the Self. (214–215)
Since such an object exists by its very nature, it follows that [the world] arises from the non-cognition of that [nature].
The arising of desire, hatred, and so forth is due to the cause of false knowledge.

Having stated the nature of the object (*vastu*), he explains that desire and the like arise from ignorance regarding it. He says "from itself" (*svataḥ*). He states the cause for that: "false" (*mithyā*).

The meaning is that the birth of desire and so forth occurs due to that cause, which is the state of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) consisting of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of something as beautiful and so on. || 216 ||
Having pointed out an object that is unknown, for the sake of realizing its true nature.
Otherwise, the operation of the means of valid cognition would not be possible.

Now, one might object: "In the present sentence, ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not heard as the cause of desire; so how can birth arise from it? Anticipating this doubt, he states the general principle: "The unknown" (*ajñātam*). Having stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) depends upon an unknown object, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—that in its absence, there is no such operation—with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). || 217 ||
Even if this ignorance (avidyā) is not explicitly mentioned here as the motivating cause (prayojaka), [it must still be understood].
Nevertheless, because it is the cause for the occurrence of cognition, that [non-existence] is likewise indeed resorted to here.
Let it be so; what follows from self-ignorance being the cause of desire and the rest? To this he says: "In its capacity as the motivator.

Since the operation of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is necessarily restricted to that which is unknown, and since the authority of the Śruti applies to the Self, self-ignorance—even though not explicitly stated there—is accepted as the cause for the operation of that [Śruti]. Thus, when desire and the like are observed in the inner self (*pratīc*), and in the absence of any other cause, one accepts ignorance itself as their true nature.
Such is the meaning. || 218 ||
Of all means of knowledge, the Śruti is the supreme authority.
This is due to the awakening to the true nature of the Self, which transcends all objects of knowledge. || 219 ||

Anticipating the objection that, since the authority of the Vedas is the cause for their application [to the Self], the existence of ignorance regarding the Self is established, yet the authority of those Vedas itself is doubtful due to the disputes among disputants, he says: "Of all... The sense is that there is no doubt regarding the authority of the Veda, as that was already refuted in the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā*; however, the Upaniṣads are authoritative as revealers of reality (*tattva*). Regarding their being revealers of reality...
He states the reason for its being the knower: "All," etc. (219).
Therefore, it is the very Self, while remaining unknown, that must be the motivator of desire and the rest.
When these two are destroyed for a person, there shall be the state of having accomplished all that was to be done.

Anticipating the objection that—since ignorance (ajñāna) resides in the Self as the cause for the activity [of the mind] based on the authority of the scriptures, and since it is accepted that the Self is the cause of everything—it cannot be the cause of desire and the like—he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt). The meaning of the word "that" (tat) refers to the fact that ignorance is established in the Self. He states the conclusion regarding the fact that the unknown Self is the motivator of desire and so forth: "Since" (yataḥ) || 220 ||
1. Na. Gha. *tatra nimittam* | 2. Kha. Gha. *na pra* | 3. Ga. *yojikā tv avi* | 4. Kha. Ga. *to 'to*—bo | 5.
Kha. Ga. *dha vi* | [Vol.
3, page 626]
The activity accomplished through speech, mind, and body has its root in desire.
In order to explain that [point], the subsequent scriptural passage begins with "as" (yathā). || 221 ||
Having explained the passage beginning with "consisting of desire" (*kāmamaya eva*), he states the purport of the passage beginning with "as that" (*sa yathā*) as follows: "Speech," etc. (verse 221).
Merit and demerit are declared to be the causes of the entire world.
Even though desire is indeed the primary cause here for those two as well.

Anticipating the objection—namely, that it is stated how the threefold activity has desire as its root because the statement "Verily, by merit one becomes meritorious," etc., implies that action is the root of the entire world—he says: "Of all. The sentence beginning with "Verily, by merit one becomes meritorious" is what is referred to here. || 222 ||
No action whatsoever is seen here belonging to anyone who is devoid of desire.
For whatever a living being does, all that is the activity of desire.
Regarding the fact that desire is primarily the motivator for activity of every kind, he states the proof: "Of one who is without desire...
Every action would be fruitless if it were not preceded by desire.
And it is observed that even for a man, the lightness of an offense is seen when committed unintentionally. || 224 ||

Now, since activity is observed even in one who lacks desire—given the Smṛti passage beginning with "for no one [remains inactive] even for a moment"—the statement that there is no perception [of results] contradicts experience; therefore, he says: "It is fruitless. He states the reason why an action performed even without desire is fruitless: "Because of the fault," etc. According to the Dharmaśāstra, even when a sin occurs through negligence in the absence of passion, it is not a fault for the person.
This is seen in the Smṛtis; as it has been said:
"If a twice-born man should eat the food of a Caṇḍāla through negligence, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and observe the vow for one month."
The meaning is that such action, being preceded by the absence of desire, is without fruit. || 224 ||
For a man impelled by desire accumulates both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
This was already declared previously by the Vedic statement, "The Self alone was this.

[Verse 225]—regarding the point that "the threefold activity impelled by desire is fruitful," he establishes this by first stating the proposition and then citing the Vedic text beginning with, "In the beginning, this was the Self alone; He was one; He desired... and so forth. [The word] "desire" [indicates] the favorability of both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) in that regard.
The word "hi" is used for the purpose of explanation. || 229 ||
*Kāma*, *gardha*, *abhilāṣa*, and *tṛṣṇā* are synonyms expressing the same meaning.
Desire is preceded by attachment; it does not exist in the absence of attachment. (226)

Having stated that all activity has its root in desire (*kāma*), he explains the meaning of the word *kāma*. Regarding the phrase "desire" (*kāma*): attachment (*āsanga*) is also a synonym for desire;
why then is it not included here as it is in cases such as longing (*abhilāṣa*)? To this he replies: "Attachment," etc. Attachment is indeed [included] here.
[Vol. 3, Page 627] 1760 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:
"The settling [of the mind] is false superimposition (*mithyādhyāsa*); from that cause desire arises. Indeed, those who are devoid of superimposition do not become desirous."
And thus, because they are distinct by virtue of being the cause (*nimitta*), there is no co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*); this is the meaning. || 226 ||
In a person who dwells upon sense-objects, attachment to them arises.
"From attachment, desire is born"—this is from the scripture of the Omniscient One.
He states the authoritative proof for the point that attachment is the cause of desire in the verse beginning with "dhyāyataḥ" (227).
That desire of a person to obtain an object is called *kāma*.
Through the practice of recollecting his virtues and so forth, a person's desire increases. || 228 ||

Having stated the purport of the passage beginning with "Just as," and while explaining the words, he restates the meaning of the term *kāma* (desire). Regarding the phrase "of the person" (*puṃsaḥ*):

intending to declare that "whatever kind of desire that person is joined with, such becomes his resolve" (*kratu*), he provides the introductory transition to explain how desire constitutes a resolve. In the phrase "by its quality" (*tadguṇena*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the objects of sense. || 228 ||
At that time, nothing other than the desired object is pleasing to him here in this world.
And it cannot be refuted by anyone whatsoever. || 229 ||

He states the fruit of the increase of desire: "from that which is desired. This means: at the stage of the repeated practice of recollecting the qualities of the object. "Of that" refers to the person whose nature consists of desire (*kāmapraya*). "In this world" refers to the state of ignorance (*avidyā*). Anticipating the objection that there might be aversion toward the desired object due to the contemplation of its defects, he says: "in order to dispel [that]. Even if there is aversion toward the object due to the contemplation of defects, if there is an absence of such contemplation—
The meaning is that dependence on sense objects is impossible to eliminate. || 229 ||
Thus increasing in this manner, it attains the state of a *kratu*.
That which follows immediately after this is called the sacrifice (kratu) of desire (kāma). || 230 ||
Having provided the introductory transition (*pātanikā*), he explains the sentence "that becomes the *kratu*. [He says] "in this manner":
from the context, the agent is desire (*kāma*). He clarifies the meaning of the word *kratu*: "immediately after which" (verse 230).
By whatever kind of resolve this man here may possess, such shall be his resolve.
One performs such action by means of speech, mind, and body. || 231 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "yat kratuḥ" as follows: "By means of the ritual season. Here, "here" refers to the land of action (karmabhūmi). || 231 ||
Whatever action this person performs, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
Then this person truly becomes that very Self.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "yatkarma" (whatever action). Regarding the word "yat": the meaning of the word "atha" (then) is that the action which has been performed is conducive to the fruit. He explains this very attainment directly as being "by way of the Self. || 232 ||
And this [apūrva] would be what is called the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
It has been previously described that [the body] consists of merit and demerit. || 233 ||

Anticipating the objection that it is illogical to claim that the agent obtains the fruit through the power of karma alone—since it is accepted that the *apūrva* (the unseen) is the cause of the fruit—the author says: [Note: The provided text contains two variant readings for the commentary portion:
1. *ga.* reads: "it could be [effected] by another. 2. *kha.* reads: "that which is the sacrifice (*sakratuḥ*)."

Regarding the phrase "and as something unprecedented": he states that the attainment of the fruit through the power of action was already explained in the passage beginning with "consisting of dharma" and "consisting of adharma."
"Merit," [it is said]. || 233 ||
A person, consisting solely of desire, would be the motivator of action and so forth.
Just as that has been stated here by the Śruti, so too is a mantra recited here.
Having restated what was said by the Brāhmaṇa—that for the ignorant one, desire is the cause of transmigratory existence—he cites a mantra on that very point: "The person...
The word "here" (iha) refers to the context immediately preceding. || 234 ||
The person goes to that very place to which his mind may be attached.
The self is attached to this subtle body (liṅga) along with its karma at all times.

He explains the first half [of the verse] with the words "tadeva" (that very thing). When the mind of this ignorant person becomes fixed through determination upon a certain object such that desire arises for it, then at that very object—this "liṅga" (the subtle body) being attached to it and unified with it—the person goes along with that very [object] and its action.
Thus, the meaning is that the self, dependent on objects due to desire and action, transmigrates. || 235 ||
In this context, the subtle body is the *liṅga*, because it serves as the mark (*liṅgana*) of the inner self.
Though detached by means of the reflection of his own conscious self, he becomes attached through the [limited] self. || 236 ||

He states the meaning of the word *liṅga*: "subtle" (*sūkṣma*). The reason for its being a *liṅga* is given as "because it indicates" (*liṅganāt*). For by means of that [subtle body], a very clear knowledge arises regarding the inner self (*pratyagātman*); thus, since it is by this [body] that the self is indicated—that is, known—the subtle body is called the *liṅga*. Anticipating the objection—"How can there be a connection with a *liṅga* for the Self, which is unattached?"—he says: "one's own self" (*svātma*), etc. Regarding the Self—

The meaning is that even in the state of association, a conceptual attachment with the Self through the mark (liṅga) by means of the reflection of one's own consciousness is not contradictory. || 236 ||
The movement of the self is like the movement of the sun reflected in a vessel of water.
And likewise, in the passage "It meditates, as it were," its own movement is indeed negated.

Nevertheless, one might object: "It is illogical that the Self, having attained identity with the subtle body (*liṅga*), goes wherever the mind is attached, because such movement is impossible for the immutable and all-pervading Self. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As in the case of water... Just as the movement of the water-vessel is superimposed upon the sun situated within it, so too, although the Self is devoid of motion, its movement is superimposed upon itself by means of the movement of the subtle body; thus, movement is attributed to it.

This is the meaning. He states the proof for the position that the self’s movement is adventitious (*aupādhika*) with the words "dhyāyati" (it meditates). Just as movement here is adventitious, so too—in accordance with that—is the point. || 237 ||
Either that very thing goes, or else it is the destination that is being denoted.
And thus, the predominance of desire conforms to the subject matter at hand. || 238 ||
Having stated that the portion beginning with "tadeva" (that very [thing]) has a meaning external to the Bhāṣya, he states the meaning as expressed in the Bhāṣya: "tadeva" (that very).

When a person's mind becomes fixed with certainty upon a fruit such as heaven, and his desire for it arises, then by the word "tat" (that), the object to be reached is grasped. And as to how he goes—when there is this expectation—the answer is: being attached to the fruit, he goes together with whatever karma he performed.
16. Therein also: 2 gha va gaṃ | 221 [vol 3, page 629]
The meaning is that it appears as though one attains that fruit. This [second] interpretation is more appropriate than the previous one, as it is directly useful for the subject at hand.
He states the degree [of intensity] with the words beginning "kāma" (desire). || 238 ||
For it is taught here that the phenomena such as desire pertain solely to one's own mind.
Therefore, those who consider themselves to be that [Self] would [regard] those as their Self, but not by virtue of their own nature.
Regarding the objection that it is incorrect to say "where the mind is attached with arisen desire," because desire and so forth are attributes of the self (ātman), he says:
"Desire and so forth. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "desire, volition, doubt," and so on. (239)
Due to attachment to the subtle body (liṅga), the Self is said to be attached.
Being attached, the self, together with its action, attains the fruit of that action.

Fearing that the qualification "attached" (sakta) might imply that the Self inherently possesses desire and so forth, he states [the following] to show that this qualification—being otherwise established due to its contradiction with numerous scriptural passages—does not prove inherent attachment in the Self. He says: "By a mark" (liṅga). Having explained that attachment is adventitious (aupādhika), he states its result: "Being attached" (saktaḥ san). || 240 ||
For one who is under the sway of mental attachment goes along with his karma.
Therefore, desire possesses primacy, because it is that which impels the cycle of transmigration for the self. (241)

He states the intended meaning of the mantra which says, "The self, possessing the limiting adjuncts (liṅga-upādhi) and attached to results, goes with that very karma which it has performed, along with its fruit," by saying "the mind" (manaḥ). He clarifies the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) by saying "impelled by that" (tat-prayukta). || 249 ||
The mind is called the "liṅga" because it is predominant; thus, the mind is here referred to as the liṅga.
Or rather, the mind is here the "liṅga" (indicator) of the self, because it is by means of it that [the self] is indicated.

Anticipating the objection—“The group-of-seventeen is the *liṅga* (the subtle body); it is not merely the mind (*manas*). How then can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between ‘the *liṅga*’ and ‘the mind’?”—he says: “The *liṅga*. The construction is as follows: in the phrase “the *liṅga* is the mind,” the term “*liṅga*” refers to the mind, because even for the group-of-seventeen which constitutes the *liṅga*, the mind is the primary element. Alternatively, he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with “or else”: “Or if... (verse 242).
With certainty, one is attached to that very object toward which the self is inclined.
The "conjunction" (saṃgati) is that it goes to that very same object together with its action. || 243 ||

He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "That mind [goes] where... as follows: "By means of certainty. The meaning is that the mind—the subtle body (*liṅga*)—together with the self conditioned by adjuncts (*upahita*), goes to that very object—such as heaven—in which it was previously attached, under the influence of a desire that has arisen there due to the performance of action; thus, the self and the mind go to that object because of the cause of attachment. || 243 ||
Thus concludes the summary of the doctrine that desire is predominant.
Having reached the end of his karma and having experienced its fruit without remainder, || 244 ||

He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "tena" (by that) as follows: "iti kāma" (thus, according to desire). By the word "iti," there is a reference to the portion of the mantra under discussion. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "prāpyāntam" (having reached the end) as follows: "karmaṇaḥ" (of action). The connection with what follows is: "imaṃ lokaṃ punaraiti" (he returns again to this world). || 244 ||
16. Kṛtaḥ | [Vol.
3, page 630] 4 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1763
When it was asked, "Of what action? the reply was: "Whatever [it may be]. (245)
Then, at the conclusion of the enjoyment of the fruit, what does he attain?
From that world he returns again to this world for the sake of action.

He states that the action is qualified by the phrase "whatever [is done]" and so forth, preceded by a desire [for results]. He asks, "Of what? and then, following the question, he takes up the passage beginning with "therefore," etc., [concluding with] the word "fruit. || 245 || 246 ||
And for this world, for this body, there is the conjunction with a body for the sake of action.
Thus, without weariness, he wanders again and again.
He distributes the portion [of the sacrifice] with the words, "For this world, for the sake of action. Regarding the phrase "for this," one might wonder for what purpose the action is performed;
therefore, he says that it is for the purpose of attaining the fruit. Thus it is. || 247 ||
Not having realized the true nature of the self, one is bound by the fetters of desire.
Like a water-wheel, a person wanders incessantly and without rest.

He states the cause for wandering excessively and repeatedly between this world and the next with the words "anirjñātā" (unascertained). He clarifies this incessant delusion by means of an illustration: "like a water-wheel" (ghaṭīyaśravat) || 248 ||
The word *iti* is used for referring back to what has been said; *nu* is used for both dejection and compassion.
Thus, the ignorant one, under the power of desire, enters various wombs again and again. || 249 ||
He states the meaning of the two prefixes: "itītyukteti" (thus it has been said). When it is asked, "What was that which was said?", he shows it by saying "evam" (thus).
From this world to that world, and from that world back to this very one.
The ignorant man, dragged by the hook of desire, is born and dies again and again. || 250 ||

It clarifies [the Buddha's] weariness and compassion with the words "from this. The connection is with the phrase "he enters. It reveals the attainment of the two worlds with the word "ignorant" (ajña). || 250 ||
Thus [ends the description] of the sequence of the misfortunes of cyclic existence for one whose primary concern is sensual desire.
Having spoken thus, he concluded that [discourse] with the words "iti" (thus).
He states another meaning of the word *iti*: "Thus [saying] 'kāma'. Here, the word *iti* is connected with the verb "having spoken" (*uktvā*). || 211 ||
Desiring in this manner, this man is like one in his own waking state.
Being unawakened, he wanders through transmigration, moving between this world and the next.

He shows that it has indeed been withdrawn by the word "thus" (evam). The meaning is that such is the state of the Self—which is by nature eternally pure, awakened, and liberated—due to ignorance and other factors; therefore, one who desires the highest good (śreya) should strive for its removal. || 252 ||
Then he spoke to her, just as [he had spoken] previously regarding the embrace of a woman.
The form of one who has attained the [thirty-six] locations is free from desire and the like. || 253 ||
1. And not anything else. 2. Kha. Ga. *marśo nvi* 53. Ka. Ga. *gatiḥ*.
It has been stated [in the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika composed by Sureśvarācārya, Fourth Adhyāya, page 631].
This very point has been established previously by the statement, "That indeed is his."
Liberation is the subject of the illustration; its corresponding example is described here. || 254 ||

Now, in order to introduce the passage beginning with "Then, one who does not desire," [the author] recounts the preceding narrative. The word "atha" (then) serves to mark a transition in the subject matter. Just as the Śruti described the form of a man in the embrace of a woman by means of the words of the woman, so too [it describes] the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-sthāna*).

The meaning is as follows: for one who has attained [liberation], the form devoid of desire and so forth—which serves as an illustration of liberation—was described immediately after by the passage beginning with "excessive desire" (*aticchanda*); and subsequently, the bondage, which is the illustrative counterpart (*dārṣṭāntika*) to the illustration of the movement in dreams and so forth, was described. Now, he introduces the subsequent section, beginning with the word "liberation. (253) (294)
The word "atha" (then) here has the sense of a reason, since that which has been stated depends upon it.
For it is through desire alone that the undiscerning one wanders incessantly in saṃsāra. || 255 ||
With the commentary beginning with "Because" (*yasmāt*), he states the meaning of the word *atha*. Regarding the phrase "the word *atha*," the reason is given: "of what has been stated.

The meaning is that it was intended [in the previous passage] that "bondage arises because it depends upon desire; since one who possesses desire transmigrates, therefore one who is free from desire is liberated. He establishes the dependence of transmigration on desire with the words "only when there is desire. [He further explains] the fact that desire is the root of misfortune—

The word "hi" (for) has the sense of "bhavānusārī" (following worldly existence). This is because the word "yataḥ" (since) is connected with the subsequent word "ataḥ" (therefore). The reason for [his] desirous state is that he is "avicakṣaṇaḥ" (unwise). || 295 ||
Because liberation occurs through the cause of being present when that [desire] is absent, one who is free from desire is therefore liberated.
A person should be free from desire, because the cause of desire has been eliminated.

He states the reason why the transmigrating being is indeed characterized by desire (*kāmin*). [The phrase] "tadbhāva... means that since bondage exists when that desire exists, and does not exist when it is absent, its status as the cause of that [bondage] is established. Once it is established that "the one with desire is the transmigrator," he states the resulting conclusion with "ataḥ" (therefore). It is true that one who is free from desire is liberated; however, how does one become free from desire? To this he says: "naraḥ" (man), or rather, "not one who is free from desire."
Anticipating the objection that one might be released even while asleep and without desire because of rising again, he says: "The man. (296)
All happiness is attained by oneself alone within one's own self, which is free from all suffering; yet, due to delusion, there is a misconception regarding that very state. (257)
What, then, is the cause of desire? To this he says: "Inherently" (svataḥ). || 297 ||
Not having attained it, one mistakenly imagines this supreme pleasure to be like suffering due to delusion.
"The ignorant man always desires, 'May I have happiness. (258)
In the inner self, which is unsurpassed bliss, he manifests a misconception produced by delusion, thinking, "It has not been attained. || 298 ||
Likewise, even though he has himself abandoned all causes of suffering, [he remains].
"May I have no suffering"—thus, out of sheer dullness, he desires this incessantly. (259)
In that state where all suffering has been cast away, he points out the misconception arising from ignorance with the words "Thus."
1. ka. kha. *samāraṃ* | 2. ka. *ptatā ca stra* | 3. kha. *te'ndhadhīḥ* || 258 ||
There is the non-attainment of complete bliss and the attainment of unhappiness.
It does not arise in accordance with the reality of the self, because that [self] is not cognized; therefore, it is non-existent.
The non-attainment of happiness and the attainment of suffering—both of these are rooted in ignorance; he elaborates upon this in the verse beginning with "entirely" (kṛtsna). || 260 ||
In reality, knowledge exists, and within that very [knowledge] resides agency and action.
Therefore, the state of being a desirer arises from the cognition of agency and effort. (261)

It has been stated that one's own ignorance is the cause of desire; in that same context, in order to state another reason, he states the general principle: "The object," etc. He asks: "Let that be so, but what happens in the case at hand? To this he replies: "Therefore," etc. Since desire, being of the nature of an action, is dependent upon an agent, and since the agent is born of ignorance, it follows that desire is also produced by that [ignorance]; such is the meaning. || 261 ||
Knowledge destroys the factors of action, just as salt soil destroys a seed.
Because it destroys its own cause, it is not a causal agent by virtue of its very birth. // 262 //
U.S.

Anticipating the objection that knowledge (*vidyā*), like action, is dependent upon an agent, he says: "The causal factors" (*kārakāṇi*). To the question of how it is established that knowledge sublates the causal factors, he says: "That" (*tat*). The meaning is that knowledge does not depend on a causal factor merely by its birth; rather, by its own mere arising, it sublates the ignorance (*avidyā*) which is the cause of those factors. || 262 ||
Since this is so, therefore the wise man, by crushing desire, [attains liberation].
One might be free from desire here, but never so the ignorant person.

Since it is established that one's own ignorance is the cause of desire, he states the resulting conclusion with the words "yataḥ" (since). Here, the locative case in "atra" is used for the purpose of specifying the qualified person. || 263 ||
When it is thus urged: "From what could one be free from desire?"
The statement "a desire for cold" is called the response to the preceding [question]. || 264 ||

While explaining the passage beginning with "atha" (now), it was stated that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the root cause of desire (*kāma*); now, in order to state its intermediate cause, the author introduces the subsequent statement preceded by an objection: "From what? The construction is as follows: the answer to the preceding objection is the statement, "He who is without desire. || 264 ||
For him who possesses no desires for external things, whether perceived through sight or heard through tradition.
"He is to be understood as being without desire, because of his complete rejection of all ritual action. (265)

He states the meaning of the word *akāma*: "Desires" (*kāmāḥ*). The meaning is that one who has no varieties of craving preceded by seeing or hearing regarding external objects such as sound and the rest is called *akāma*. He states the reason for the absence of desires of the aforementioned kind:
"Entirety" (*kṛtsna*). By the word *karman*, both activity and its object are expressed. For there is no external object for the knower.
Or rather, there is no activity [of the Self], because its sole nature is non-dual consciousness that has directly realized its own changeless character; such is the meaning. || 265 ||
1 ka. ... as if on a barren rock; ta. ... as if on a barren rock; kha. ... as if on a barren rock; ga. ... as if on a barren rock.
Thus, 2 gha. yam itya | [vol 3,
page 633] 1766 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Chapter]—
Just as desire, when being acted upon, gives rise to ritual acts and the like.
Even while thus renouncing, he remains established in actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).

He establishes the absence of desire in the wise by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "being performed. Just as desire, when performed by an ignorant person through the superimposition of beauty, brings about [the cycle of] seasons and so forth, so too, even though being sublated by discernment (*viveka*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and the like, it remains in a state of isolation (*kaivalya*); therefore, the meaning is that the wise man is one who does not desire. || 266 ||
When asked "Who is this one who is without desire?", he is called "one free from desire" (niṣkāma). || 267 ||
He from whose intellect desires, which consist of motivation, have departed.
He who is free from desire regarding these objects of grasping is called "wise" by the learned. || 268 ||

He raises another qualification by means of a question: "Even one who is desireless" (*akāmo 'pi*). Fearing that this might be redundant with what preceded, he explains it: "The instigator," etc. Here, "desires" (*kāmāḥ*) refers to the latent impressions (*vāsanāḥ*) of sound and other objects, which are termed "excessive graspings" (*atigrahāḥ*), which have ascended into the intellect together with its appearances (*sābhāsabuddhi*), and which are the causes of gross desires. One from whom these have departed is "desireless" (*niṣkāma*); therefore, by the term "desireless" (*akāma*), [gross] desires are excluded.
The meaning is that there is no tautology, because external [desires] are being cast out, whereas internal ones are excluded by the term "free from desire" (niṣkāma). || 267 || 268 ||
There is a mutual relationship of cause and effect between external and internal things.
Ignorance regarding the inner self would be its cause; therefore, that [knowledge] does not exist once it has been destroyed.
[The text provided consists solely of vertical bars (||) and does not contain any content to translate.]

By stating that desires consist of motivators (*prayojaka*), he has shown the mutual relationship of cause and effect among desires situated both externally and internally. He states what the motivator for that [relationship] is: "Of the external... When it is said that there is a mutual causality among desires produced by the ignorance of the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*), he states the established conclusion: "Upon their cessation... (269)
Therefore, the knowledge of the true nature of the inner self is said to be that which brings about its cessation.
By the words beginning with "one whose desires are fulfilled," which bring about an understanding of things as they truly are. || 270 ||

Anticipating the question, "What is the cause for the destruction of one's own ignorance? he employs two qualifying attributes. Regarding the word "that" (tat): the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is that, upon the destruction of ignorance, there is no possibility of any cause other than knowledge. || 270 ||
All his desires that require external means are already attained by himself.
As a result, he has attained his desire, by virtue of having the nature of supreme bliss.

Anticipating the objection that "the state of having all desires fulfilled" (āptakāmatva) is untenable because it is not established that even a wise man who does not perform rituals can obtain results such as heaven, he says:

"They are attained" (āptāḥ). The meaning is this: although things such as heaven depend upon sacrifices and other means, for the wise man they are all attained by his very nature; thus, he becomes one whose desires are fulfilled. Furthermore, [the opponent might argue] that happiness alone is dependent on means, and that there is something else to be obtained beyond that—[this is the view of the] Vipra...

Anticipating the objection that this is prohibited, he says: "As a result. The meaning is as follows: Brahman is of the nature of supreme bliss (*parānanda*), and the knower has that as his own essential nature; because of the principle that "one becomes what one intends" (*tad-kratu-tvāt*), he has consequently attained all desires, since all forms of bliss are included within supreme bliss. || 271 ||
Starting from human bliss, indeed, by way of progressive increase in each subsequent stage.
By the statement regarding the tenth part of a thousand, supreme bliss (parānanda) is defined.
[Volume 3, Page 634] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1767.
To those, however, who dispute even regarding supreme bliss (*parānanda*), he says: "Mānuṣa... This has not been established merely here.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that this is so not only here, but also in another scriptural passage. || 272 ||
This is stated because it is relevant to the *Kāmikāgama* and its various divisions.
According to the Veda, "one who desires the Self"—thus these [objects] are indeed the Self and not separate from it.
Having explained the state of having all desires fulfilled (*āptakāmatva*), he explains the state of desiring the Self (*ātmakāmatva*): "one who has desires" (*kāmī*). || 273 ||
When there arises the realization that "the Self alone is everything," one attains the state of having all desires fulfilled.
Without exterior or interior, the whole consists solely of a mass of pure consciousness.
Thus, for one whose knowledge regarding the Self has arisen from the statements of the Vedānta; || 275 ||
Because all darkness has been destroyed, it arises from perfect knowledge.
Tell me, from what cause—such as desire and so forth—would its origination arise? || 276 ||

He states that the state of desiring the Self (*ātmakāmatva*) is the cause for the state of having attained all desires (*āptakāmatva*): "The Self alone... etc. When it is realized that the entire phenomenal expansion of sound and so forth is nothing but the Self through knowledge, one is devoid of any object of desire other than oneself; this is "desiring the Self. Consequently, even the pleasure to be accomplished through sound and so forth is nothing but the Self; this is "having attained all desires. From desiring the Self comes the attainment of all desires, and from that, freedom [from desire].

Having considered that there is "I-ness" (the sense of self), and from that, desirelessness, and from that, liberation for one who is free from desire—intending this, he says: "He does not desire," and so forth.
For it is said that even when there is something else, it is indeed while ignorance exists that one says "this is so."
Since darkness has been destroyed, that duality consisting of the knower, the knowable, and so forth, no longer exists. || 277 ||
Fearing that even when ignorance has been destroyed by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), desire and the like might still arise due to the distinction between the knower and so forth, he says:

"Where... Since it was stated that the distinction between the knower and so forth exists only in the state of ignorance, the meaning is that once ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, desire and the like are not caused by the distinction between the knower and so forth. || 277 ||
But regarding that [state] where the darkness of the self has been destroyed, the Śruti says "But when for him... and so forth.
"That by what, and whom? and so forth—this statement is itself accompanied by an objection. (278)

He states the proof for the absence of distinctions such as the knower (*jñātṛ*) in the state of knowledge with the words "But where... (*yatra tu*). Beginning from the passage "But when for him all this [has become the Self]" (*yatra tv asya sarvam*), the Śruti itself, including the challenging statement "then by what and whom should one see? (*tat kena kaṃ paśyet*), declares that for a person in whom the darkness of the self has been destroyed, there is no occurrence of desire and so forth, because distinctions such as the knower have vanished through knowledge once ignorance has been destroyed. This is the meaning. (278)
Since [reality] culminates in the awakening to the immutably fixed state of pure oneness, how [could there be any duality]?
The possibility of the conventional usage of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower [is established]. || 279 ||
Manifesting an objection, he clarifies the meaning of the Vedic text as stated in the Bhāṣya: "Aikātmya... (279).
For how can one who does not understand that which is to be known desire sensual pleasures?
For everyone desires objects only after having first known them. || 280 ||
1 ka. "The Non-Existence of the Object.
[Vol. 3, page 635] 1768 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]—

Anticipating the objection that desire might still arise even in the absence of the conventional usage of "knowledge" and so forth regarding knowledge, he says: "Not knowing" (*avijānan*). For one who desires has an object of knowledge, according to such Smṛti texts as, "Meditating on objects... (Gītā 2.62). And the knower of the Self does not perceive objects distinct from himself; therefore, how could there be desire for him? He explains what is indicated by the word "hi" (for/indeed): "Having known... (*jñātvā*)...
Daughter! || 280 ||
Thus, because he has this nature of desiring the Self, he who would be one whose desires are fulfilled in this state— || 281 ||
Through the fulfillment of all desires, one attains desirelessness with respect to that very thing.
And by being free from desire, he who is desireless—that knower of the Self—is liberated. || 282 ||
He concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "atha," which was stated by way of cause and effect, with the words "ity evam" (thus). || 281 || 282 ||
Through the awakening of the self, there is the total destruction of the seed of the misfortune of saṃsāra.
Therefore, when the Self is known, the cause of desire becomes impossible. || 283 ||
Due to the presence of desire, action, and so forth, the Self remains full.
This aforementioned point is supported by the subsequent statement, "Not for him" (na tasya). || 284 ||

Anticipating the objection that "What is this liberation? For it has not been definitively established due to the conflicting views of disputants," he says: "saṃsāra... [and so on]. The meaning is that liberation is the abiding in one's full form, resulting from the destruction of ignorance and its effects through knowledge, because the cause of incompleteness has ceased to exist. Therein, he introduces the two statements beginning with "na tasya... for the purpose of dispelling those conflicting views. "No" (neti). || 283 || 284 ||
It has been stated that the inner self (pratyagātman) is the cause for the removal of what is undesirable.
He who, by means of the words beginning with "yo kāmaḥ," knows the Self from the scripture; || 285 ||
Out of conviction in the scriptures, the teacher, and oneself, one desires to grasp even heated iron.
His vital breaths do not depart, nor do they remain there.

He clarifies the very meaning as it was stated [in the previous verse] with the words "apāsta" (cast aside). He supports the two subsequent statements—which describe liberation (*mokṣa*) characterized by abiding in the form of the indivisible Brahman-Self—as taught in the preceding statement; the meaning is that there is no dispute among the Vedists regarding this Vedic sense, whereas others have been refuted.
He explains the words of the passage with the words "yo veda" (he who knows). Here, the non-departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) from the body is the point of the statement.

The meaning is this: it is not a knower of Brahman who is spoken of here, but rather one who possesses a firm conviction that "I am Brahman"—just as one might say "I am a human"—who is committed to truth and is capable of performing oaths such as grasping a heated axe. || 285 || 286 ||
For the cause of both persistence and departure is the self, characterized by ignorance and so forth.
Because all of that has been destroyed through the vision of the true nature of the inner self. || 287 ||

"Why is it that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not depart from one who knows Brahman? For indeed, even in his case, departure is seen just as in others. To this, he says: "Because of the non-existence [of ignorance, etc.]. The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that the fact that ignorance and so forth are the cause of departure and the like is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because of the non-existence of its effects. (287)
1 ga. Or, "without desire. 2 ka. That has been said.
