3, page 636] 4 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1769.
Since this is so, therefore the vital breaths [are subordinate] to the arising of right knowledge.
They do not depart, they do not remain, nor do they perish without a cause. || 288 ||
He concludes the meaning of the passage regarding the absence of causes for departure and staying with the words "yataḥ" (since). || 288 ||
Just as in the world a rope-snake exists for one who does not know the true nature of the rope.
It does not depart from the rope, nor does it remain [as something separate], nor does it perish. || 289 ||

He provides an illustration for the point that, upon the destruction of ignorance and the like through the knowledge of the true nature of the Self, the departure, persistence, and dissolution of the vital breaths (prāṇas) are not established: "As in the case of a rope... The word should be split as *ajñātā* (unknown). || 289 ||
Therefore, the rope is the essence of persistence, departure, and destruction.
When the knowledge of the rope arises, nothing other than the rope remains. || 290 ||

It is stated that the rope alone is the reality of the imagined snake; he elaborates on the reason for this with the verse beginning "sthitau" (in its persistence). The implication is that when the knowledge of the Self arises in this manner, since nothing else remains, the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇotkrānti*) and so forth cannot be established. || 290 ||
It is said that the reality liberated from ignorance and its products is right here.
The stability of the vital breaths is said to consist merely in their state of union as a single identity. || 291 ||

"In this very [place] they are completely merged," thus [the text] states the meaning of "in this very [place]" according to the Mādhyandina recension. He explains the meaning of the prefix by saying "avidyā" (ignorance).
He explains the meaning of the prefix "sam-" by saying "samiti" (coming together). || 291 ||
By the statement "they are led away," there is no going elsewhere than toward destruction and so forth.
Because it is solely intent upon the internal measure alone, there is no abiding in either existence or non-existence. || 292 ||

He states the meaning of the verbal root: "they are caused to descend" (*avanīyante*). He establishes that "causing to descend" is the abiding of the vital breaths as nothing but the Self, by way of removing [the objection] regarding the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "the inward-facing" (*pratyak*)—thus [he says]. 292.
There is indeed identity between all things that stand in the relation of cause and effect.
And because of the departure [of the self] and so forth, as well as the scriptural teaching that "the Self is everything," [it follows that the soul is all-pervading]. || 293 ||
He states the proof for the fact that there is no existence of breath and so forth in the form of either presence or absence without being opposed [to consciousness]: "Identity" (tādātmyam) || 293 ||
Thus, the object is known by itself, and ignorance is known through experience;
for, because it consists solely of the true nature of the inner self, that delusion and the rest are entirely [dispelled].
That "it ceases" and "it has ceased"—this too is established through direct experience.

[Objection: "But if everything were merely the Self (ātman), the Self would remain unestablished due to the absence of a means of proof; nor can its establishment come from scripture, because scripture functions only toward that which is unknown.

Furthermore, if everything is the Self, there can be no ignorance other than it, and yet the linguistic usage of 'ignorance,' 'its cessation,' and 'having ceased' is possible. To this, he says: 'Thus, the thing... [The commentary continues: "First of all, the Self has no requirement for a means of proof, as it is self-luminous..."

Nor does the lack of authority for the scripture arise there [in that context], because ignorance is established there by direct experience; and since there is an absence of any form other than the inner self (pratyagātman), the cessation of nescience (avidyā) and so forth at all three times is established by the experience of the wise and is not contradictory—this is the meaning. || 294 || 299 ||
222 [Vol. 3, page 637] 1770 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]
Since this is so, therefore that which is already liberated is what is liberated.
And it is also said in the Kaṭhavallīs: "The one who is already liberated is liberated [again]. (296)
Having explained the *Mādhyandina* recension and introduced the passage beginning with "Brahman alone," he provides the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) for its explanation:

"Since... The meaning is as follows: because the reality of the Self is understood to be, in its true nature, eternally pure, enlightened, and free, yet otherwise [appearing] due to ignorance (*avidyā*), it is therefore established that, though naturally liberated, it appears as if bound by ignorance; thus, upon the destruction of ignorance through knowledge (*vidyā*), it becomes designated as "liberated."
In this regard, he cites another scriptural passage in corroboration: "Kaṭha... (296).
Here too, [the teaching] is surrounded by serpents, yet it is consistent with the logic of the Vedas and established through reasoning.
And the Śruti declares that very reality: "Being indeed Brahman. (297)

Having provided this introductory transition, he introduces the statement for the purpose of showing that liberation belongs only to one who is already liberated. "In this world," etc. This scriptural passage—"Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman"—declares that very reality established by other scriptures, which has been made the object of study through hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) accompanied by the retinue of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, and designated as being supported by the logic of scripture. Therefore, here too, as in other scriptural passages, liberation belongs only to one who is already liberated.
The meaning is "accomplished. || 297 ||
That very reality which was previously aphorized as "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman."
Having explained that clearly through scriptural citation, it is now concluded.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the passage "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman," the knowledge of Brahman along with its fruit was aphoristically stated, and that same Brahman was explained by the words "I shall tell you of that Brahman" and so forth?

Therefore, the statement "Being Brahman itself... and so on is redundant. To this he replies: "Brahman. The word *hi* (indeed) is used to show the occasion for the conclusion of that which was introduced and referred to [at the beginning]. || 298 ||
This one who abides on the planes of saṃsāra has been described as one whose true nature is unknown.
This [distinction] consists of cause and effect, following from the operation of delusion. || 299 ||
In order to elucidate that which is being concluded along with its supplementary details, he restates the nature of the transmigrating self: "He who is this... The construction is as follows:

that very inner essence (*pratyag-dhātu*), whose true nature was previously unknown in passages such as "But from Him, verily, this [arose]" (*tad dha idaṃ*), and which has entered the plane of transmigratory existence, is "this one" who has been explained by the passage beginning "Where this Self... He elaborates upon the inner self situated on the plane of transmigratory existence: "The effect... (verse 299).
For this [Self], being Brahman itself, expands through delusion as something other than that.
Being Brahman itself, it attains Brahman here; therefore, for the sake of dispelling delusion, [one should practice]. (300)

Now, concluding [the discussion], he connects the statement with the word "yataḥ" (since). Here, the word "iha" (here) refers to either of the two states: that of knowledge (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*). || 300 ||
The existence of a second self is not other than ignorance, just as [the appearance of a second moon is not other than a visual defect].
In the same way, its cessation is not something other than the realization of the Self.
Fearing that one might suspect the Self to be something other than itself due to the destruction of delusion, he causes [the reader] to remember what has been stated repeatedly: "No. || 301 ||
1. Chapter 12, Section 'ga'. "'Po' then 'mo'.
At that time, the branches increased through the Vedas; thus the attainment of Brahman.
Since this is by nature enlightened and by nature pure, it is therefore non-dual.
Because the cognizer and so forth cease once that ignorance has been removed. || 302 ||

Having understood the nature of the Self, he demonstrates it with the words "because" (*yasmāt*). [The opponent asks: "How can there be non-duality, given that the subject (*mātṛ*) and so forth exist? To this, he replies: "[It is] of the subject and so forth" (*pramātrādeḥ*). 302.
And because reality is inherently liberated from this [duality], it is metaphorically designated as "liberated."
Therefore, through the destruction of ignorance and the rest, I swear this oath to you. (303)

[The opponent] objects: "How can there be a statement regarding the liberation of that which is eternally pure and non-dual? For in the absence of impurity, liberation—which consists in the removal of that [impurity]—is untenable. To this, he replies: "It is liberated. He states the basis for this metaphorical designation: "That... He speaks thus to those who are in doubt regarding the nature of the Self as previously described: "Three times... (303).
He who is directly devoid of action and agency, whose very nature is the absence of action and agency.
The Self directly knows itself by means of itself, as in deep sleep.
It is devoid of all differentiation, pure vision alone, and stainless.
He who knows the Self is free from darkness; others than him have deluded minds.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to say "liberation belongs only to the knower of Brahman who is already liberated," because proponents maintain that even for such a person there must be the performance of rituals to avoid transgression, [the author] says: "He who... To state that for one who knows the immutable Self, such a state is unimpeded by virtue of the principle of "as is one's intention (tatkratu)," the word "directly" (sākṣāt) is used. By the words "the Self" (ātmānam), it is meant that the ritual action itself is the Self; and by "by the Self alone" (ātmanaiva), it is meant that the instrument itself is the Self.

And [the objection] is refuted immediately thereafter. The second word, *sākṣāt* (directly), is consistent with its literal meaning, and thus there is no tautology. Just as the sleeping state was described as the nature of the Self serving as an illustration for liberation, so too one who directly realizes the Self in its form as liberation is called a "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*), according to the scripture: "He is a knower of Brahman. Those, however, who conceive of the Self as being in reality a transmigrator or subject to transgression do not know.
The meaning is that this is according to the Vedic scripture (śruti) which says, "Those people who are destroyers of the Self... [304-305].
For him, there is no distinction whatsoever between being alive and being dead.
For ignorance alone is the cause of all particularities.

It is incorrect to say that the wise man is liberated while still living; for liberation is contradictory to being alive, as it is not possible for the possession of vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the like to coexist simultaneously with their absence. Therefore, one might suspect that even for the wise man, liberation occurs only upon death. Anticipating this objection, the text says: "Not of him" (*na tasya*). That ignorance (*avidyā*) is removed from the wise man while he is yet alive; therefore, those who maintain that liberation occurs only after death are deluded.
The remainder. || 306 ||
Because there is an absence of even a mere obstruction characterized by the delusion of the senses and so forth, which are established without investigation, one is said to "attain Brahman. || 307 ||
Since there is no distinction for the knower between the state of being alive and otherwise, how can it be said that "he attains Brahman"? To this, he says: "Not having investigated... (307).
1 ka. self-established; 2 kha. destroyed by you three times; 3 sva. of the self; ā; 4 ga. and; 5 kha. of this "a"; 6 ga. established. [Vol. 3, page 639]
1772 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]: If liberation were to occur otherwise than this, the undertaking of the Śruti would be purposeless.
Furthermore, because liberation would have karma as its cause, it would follow that it is impermanent. || 308 ||
Why is the word *apyeti* explained as being figurative with the intention of signifying the absence of the veil of ignorance and its products?

One might ask: "Why could it not be that the individual soul (*jīva*), which is distinct from the Supreme, attains Brahman through knowledge and action that are unsurpassed? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "From this [it follows]. Liberation is the abiding of the Self in its own essential nature; and that liberation requires knowledge for the purpose of removing the veil of ignorance.

In that case, the scriptural text concerning identity with the Self would be purposeful. The meaning is that if liberation were the attainment of Brahman as a distinct state of being for a self that is inherently different [from Brahman], then the introductory portion of the texts on identity would be contradicted. He states another defect if liberation were something to be accomplished: "And if liberation... || 308 ||
The scriptural statement, "This greatness is eternal," would be contradicted.
And from the essential nature, there exists nothing whatsoever that is eternal and distinct. || 309 ||

Anticipating the objection that this might be an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says: "This" (*eṣa*). Anticipating the objection that even the state of being Brahman (*brahmabhāva*), though produced, might be eternal like cessation (*dhvaṃsa*), he says: "From its own nature" (*svābhāvikāt*). The word "inherent" (*svābhāvika*) is used for the purpose of excluding an artificial nature; for the Śruti states, "Whatever is other than this is perishable. However, since cessation is merely a conceptual construct (*vikalpamātra*), its eternity is not accepted; so how could it be?
The meaning is that this serves as an illustration. || 309 ||
If liberation were the intrinsic nature of the self, it would be eternal, like the vacuity of space.
And like fire and heat, it is impossible to say that [the self] arises from karma. || 310 ||
Fearing that liberation, though its nature is unconditioned, might nonetheless arise from karma, he says: "The Self" (verse 310).
If it is argued that light, heat, and so forth are the effects of fire due to its activity of burning;
Because it does not depend on the obstruction of perception, the destruction of the object, or manifestation. || 311 ||

One who disputes this by means of the following analogy objects: "The excellent heat and light residing in the fire-drills (*araṇi*) are not perceived while the fire is absent, yet they are seen when the fire is present; therefore, those two are adventitious (*āgantuka*) because their perception occurs only occasionally. [The author replies with] the words beginning with "jvalana": Indeed, it is not logical for these [heat and light] to be occasional by their own nature, because we observe that their concealment is due to external factors such as the forest fire and the like, whereas their manifestation occurs through friction, ignition, and so forth.

Nor [is it the case that heat and so forth] depend upon the manifestation of fire, because it is admitted that their own nature, such as heat, is manifested; thus he refutes [the objection] with: "Not by perception... (311).
From fire, which is inseparable from its blazing, there arises light, heat, and so forth.
But it is not so in the case of heat and the like, which possess a manifested nature in dependence upon fire. || 312 ||

He elaborates upon that [point] with the words "jvalana" (blazing), etc. Since it is admitted that fire arises from activities such as friction (*mathana*) as something characterized by heat and so forth, there is no manifestation (*vyakti*) of its luminosity and other qualities in relation to the fire that has already acquired its own nature (*labdhātmaka*). This is because those qualities do not possess a nature different from that [fire]. Therefore, the manifestation of heat and so forth cannot be established as something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in relation to the fire itself; however, in relation to the person (*puruṣa*), this is indeed accepted, because the person is distinct from the fire and because an obscuration (*vyavadhi*) is possible.
This is the meaning. || 312 ||
1 gha. *vyasvabhāṃ* | [Vol.
3, page 640] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1773.
Nor is the Self to be brought about by a manifestor, as is the case with a jar or similar objects.
Manifestation [occurs] because its sole nature is pure consciousness, which is self-luminous.

Anticipating the objection that—just as the manifestation of heat in fire and so forth depends on a person and is accomplished by means such as kindling—the manifestation of the Self’s state of being Brahman and liberation must likewise be accomplished by means such as ritual action (karman)—the author replies: "No. He provides the reason for why the manifestation of the Self's Brahman-nature is not something to be accomplished, just as the manifestation of a jar and so forth is accomplished by means such as a lamp: "By itself" (svataḥ). || 313 ||
[This occurs] for another person, such as fire, by means of causes such as the blazing of fire.
The manifestation of heat and light is possible because of their being obstructed.

[Objection: One might suspect that even the manifestation of fire’s heat and so forth is not something to be established, since it is of the nature of luminosity, just like the manifestation of the Self; anticipating this, he says: "Of fire... [314] / [394].
Even in this liberation, which consists of manifestation, there is no state of being an effect.
A jar or similar object is not at all an effect that is manifested by a lamp or the like. (115)

Because fire and the person are distinct, the person possesses heat and other qualities that are the very nature of fire; and just as there is a distinction [between them], it might be suspected that for the self and liberation (*ātma-mukti*) as well, a distinction could be conceptually constructed, such that their manifestation would be something to be accomplished through karma and the like. Anticipating this objection, he says "even" (*api*), while conceding the point: even if one accepts this position—that the nature of manifestation is produced by karma and so forth—the liberation is nonetheless not something to be accomplished. This is the sense. Liberation—
Anticipating the objection as to how that which is manifested by white karma could not be produced by it, he says: "Of the lamp, etc. || 319 ||
Furthermore, there is no manifestation whatsoever of a thing whose nature consists of heat and so forth.
Because of the non-existence of obstacles therein, it is real and not born of delusion.

It was stated that in the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta), having accepted that the manifestation of heat and so forth—which possess the nature of fire—is produced by combustion and the like, yet in the case of the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika), liberation is not a manifestation produced by karma and the like; for even if it were of such a nature, liberation would still not be something produced by those [causes]. Now, one might raise the objection: why could that manifestation of heat and so forth in the example not also be produced by combustion and the like with respect to the fire itself, just as it is with respect to the person?
[It] must have been so; and [there is] manifestation (*abhivyakti*). For the entity called fire (*vahni*) consists of heat and light;

there is no obstruction between it and its light and so forth, because there can be no obstruction of a thing by itself. Therefore, the meaning is that, with respect to fire, the manifestation of its heat and so on is not something to be accomplished by burning and the like. How then is there the conventional usage of the manifestation of fire’s heat and so on through friction and the like?

He says: "It is real. This means that the conventional usage of the manifestation of heat and so forth in that [fire] does not follow the actual nature of fire; rather, it is born of delusion. || 316 ||
Because fire is perceived through the favor of its flames, as seen in its illumination and other qualities.
This is an error: the conceptualization that heat and so forth arise from the activity of fire.

Anticipating the objection that the birth [of heat] from fire and so forth is merely the production of heat and the like, and not a manifestation—since there is no restrictive factor—he says: "The flame," etc.

The meaning is: because of the influence of that flame, through the perception of its own superior heat and so forth, there arises the illusion that it is born by way of that [flame]; in reality, however, it is only a manifestation, not a birth. || 317 ||
If the nature of fire as consisting of light and so forth were not admitted— [Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four, Verse 1774]
Whatever belongs to something by its very nature, that shall serve as its illustration. || 318 ||

He raises an objection, suggesting that since the heat of fire and so forth are not inherent, they do not serve as an illustration for liberation: "If [it be argued]... He considers the two alternatives—whether an entity possesses an inherent property or not—and refutes the first: "That which...
(the word "example" refers to liberation, as is understood from the context). || 318 ||
And there is no entity whatsoever that lacks an intrinsic nature.
For, in your own view, there is a conjunction of one thing with another entity. (319)

He refutes the second [position] with the words "na ca" (and not). The reason for this is given by "svayaṃ tu" (but itself). For an entity that has acquired its own nature is connected with another entity; otherwise, all entities would be confounded. And indeed, there is the cognition of bitterness in the *nimba* tree—this is the meaning. || 319 ||
Furthermore, liberation for the person here does not consist in the destruction of fetters, as it does for the self.
The mere cessation of bondage is somehow possible. || 320 ||

It has been stated that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the state of Brahman and is not achievable through ritual action (*karman*). However, others, unable to accept this and asserting that liberation is the destruction of bondage (*bandha*), claim that it is achievable through action. In response to them, he says: "Not by a shackle... For the destruction of bondage as it exists [in its current state] is impossible due to contradiction; nor is it possible for it to exist otherwise, because it would then not be bondage at all. Nor is there a contradiction with common experience, since the destruction of something whose nature is difficult to define is itself difficult to establish.
He says "because it is an object" [in response to the objection], [stating] "in cessation," etc. (320).
"That which is truly one and without a second appears as having a second due to a lack of understanding."
And there is no other bound being apart from that [self] for whom bondage could perish. (321)

Furthermore, the destruction of that bondage—which is rooted in ignorance—is not something distinct from the Self, because such bondage lacks independence. For the existence and non-existence of the serpent imagined through the ignorance regarding a rope do not exist apart from the rope itself; likewise, liberation is simply the abiding in one's own true nature. To this he says: "One" (ekam).
Anticipating the objection that even if Brahman is non-dual, liberation might still be the destruction of one's own bondage for some other bound soul, he says: [the following].
And not [so]. || 321 ||
Likewise, [it is established] through both the distinction from and the non-distinction from the internal self.
One should diligently [ascertain] the existence and non-existence of other entities. || 322 ||
Through well-reasoned arguments, you have refuted [this view]; therefore, liberation is the destruction of ignorance.
Just as the absence of a snake and so forth [occurs] through the mere cessation of delusion regarding a rope. || 323 ||
He recalls what was stated previously regarding the indeterminate (avyākṛta) and other matters—that there is no one who is bound or unbound—by saying "of the Inner Self" (pratīcaḥ).

Effort (*prayatna*) is the intense pressure of inquiry; sound reasoning (*suyukti*) is logic that follows scripture. Anticipating the objection—"In the absence of any entity distinct from the Inner Self and Brahman, what kind of liberation could there be?"—he says "liberation" (*mokṣa*). [This occurs] upon the destruction of the ignorance that obstructs it.
1. ga. That which is that very thing.
[vol 3, page 642]

Regarding the phrase "the empirical usage of that," he provides an illustration: "like a snake and so forth. Just as the destruction of a snake and the like produced by a rope occurs through the mere destruction of the delusion concerning the rope, so too, through the knowledge of the Self, there is the destruction of the bondage arising from the ignorance of that [Self] due to the destruction of that ignorance; thus, when the rope's own ignorance and what is born from it are destroyed...

The meaning is that, just as the state of being a rope [is attributed to what was previously a snake], the nature of Brahman is figuratively attributed to the Self once its own ignorance and the products thereof have been destroyed. || 322 || 323 ||
But those who explain that in liberation there is a single object consisting of eternal bliss—
Thus, by relying on our own established doctrine, it is the manifestation of knowledge [that occurs]. (324)

It has been stated that liberation is the self’s state of being Brahman. Now, [the author] presents the view that liberation is not merely the state of being Brahman, but rather that bliss and knowledge—which are distinct from worldly pleasure and cognition—are manifested in liberation, and these two stand in a mutual relationship of object and subject; this he introduces with the words "But those who... (ye tu). In doing so, he indicates the lack of both scriptural authority and logical reasoning [in that position] by saying "according to their own tenets" (svasiddhānta). || 324 ||
By those [proponents of manifestation], it must be stated what kind of thing is intended as the meaning of a word that is manifested.
If the object is already established, then it would follow that it is attained as the objective support of consciousness. (325)

Is this manifestation (abhivyakti) production (utpatti) or illumination (prakāśa)? It cannot be the first, because if pleasure and so forth were produced in liberation (mokṣa), their impermanence would follow; having considered this, he says: "by them" (taih). The second [alternative] is accepted. He says: "well-known" (prasiddha). The meaning is that the manifestation of pleasure and so forth consists in their being objects of cognition, just like a jar or other such things. || 325 ||
Does the attainment of the object of consciousness pertain to that which exists or to that which does not exist?
If manifestation were [the nature] of that which already exists, then that happiness would belong to one who is liberated. (326)
Since its very nature is that [non-existence], the qualification is redundant.
If it is asserted that in liberation both knowledge and bliss are manifested; || 327 ||

He formulates the alternative: "Is pleasure and so forth manifested by the self while it exists or while it does not exist? [The author] states "vijñāna" and, having restated the first position, refutes it with "abhivyakti. If pleasure and so forth, which already exist in the self, are manifested at liberation, then the nature of the liberated one would be nothing other than that [pleasure]; for there is no evidence for its remaining as something distinct from it. Therefore, since it is eternally manifested...

The meaning is that the specific statement that "pleasure and so forth are manifested in liberation" is purposeless. The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of "even," implying "even though [pleasure] was unmanifest during saṃsāra.
For that which has become one's own self is never obstructed by anything.
Because the self has that as its intrinsic nature, it is certain that [this] exists at all times. || 328 ||

Anticipating the objection that although [the Self] is always existent as its own nature (*svarūpa*), it is unmanifest because it was previously obstructed prior to liberation, he says: "One's own Self" (*svātman*).

The meaning is this: for the bliss of one's own nature and so forth, there is no real obstruction, because that would contradict its being one's own nature and because there is a lack of evidence [for such an obstruction]. However, if that obstruction were unreal, then there would be no establishment of a difference of opinion regarding it. If something is the very nature of a thing, it cannot be obstructed from it—just as light is not obstructed from a lamp.
The word "hi" has the sense of pervasion (vyāpti). || 328 ||
Whether they are unliberated or liberated, there is no difference whatsoever between them.
Therefore, because pleasure and cognition have the nature of the inward-facing self (pratyagātman), [they are not distinct from it]. || 329 ||
1. Nor even...
[vol 3, page 643] 1
In the case of liberation, the specific statement that "it is abandoned" is false. *Suresvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Chapter Four.
There is also a contradiction with one's own tenets for the proponent of its manifestation.
For those who maintain the theory of the pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda), manifestation is highly praised.
All this is manifested from the essence (sattva) of every entity. || 331 ||

He concludes by stating that the specific assertion—that there is a manifestation of pleasure and so forth in liberation because there is no excess [of it] in bondage—is purposeless. He says, "In the state of non-liberation. Furthermore, having raised the alternative as to whether this view belongs to the proponents of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) or the proponents of the theory of the existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), he addresses the first position, saying, "According to their own tenets. Anticipating the objection, "Even in their own system, how could they praise that? he restates their doctrine.
It is given; it is manifested. || 329 || 330 || 331 ||
But in the theory of origination (ārambhavāda), desire and so forth, being effects, possess the nature of non-existence.
Furthermore, the manifestation of that which is non-existent is not logical, just like the horn of a donkey. (332)

Even in the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*), why does it not simply become manifest? To this he says: "The theory of new production" (*ārambha*). Nor is the second [alternative] possible, because the futility of the qualification has already been stated; such is the meaning of the word "but" (*tu*). Having refuted the position that pleasure and so forth which already exist are merely manifested, he refutes another position: "And of that which is non-existent" (*asataśca*) || 332 ||
The relationship between the suggested and the suggester is like that between a lamp and a jar.
When both [cause and effect] are already established, a causal relationship between them is not desired. (333)

Anticipating the objection that even for him there might be an indeterminacy regarding that term, he says "tad-viśeṣo nāsti" (there is no distinction from that). He then says "vyaṅgya" (manifested) and so forth.

Furthermore, whether manifestation is existent or non-existent, in either case it cannot be an effect produced by a cause, because neither the existent nor the non-existent is observed to be something that can be accomplished [by a cause].
Thus he says "neṣṭā" (it is not accepted). || 333 ||
Furthermore, is there non-difference or rather difference between pleasure and consciousness?
The meaning of the word "manifestation" is never obtained in the case of identity.
To state another defect in the view that [the universal] resides in the individual, he offers an alternative analysis, beginning with "sukha" (pleasure).

Regarding the first [alternative], he says "no," because it is impossible for a single thing to simultaneously function as both the object and the subject, which would otherwise result in the non-establishment of the individual known as the objective support (*ālambana*) of cognition. || 334 ||
Furthermore, if there were a difference between those two, it would follow that there must be an intervening space.
Furthermore, you possess no means of valid cognition here for establishing either their difference or their non-difference. || 335 ||

He refutes another [opponent's] position by restating it, beginning with "Now" (*atha*). If there were a difference between pleasure and knowledge, it would follow that they are separated by space and so forth; consequently, like a jar or other objects, a subsequent cognition distinct from eternal knowledge would have to apprehend pleasure. In that case, since the relationship of cause and effect would persist even in liberation (*mukti*), there would be cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

The meaning is "no difference. One might suspect that between knowledge (jñāna) and bliss (ānanda), there is neither mere difference nor mere non-difference, but rather both difference and non-difference;
[the author] intends this by saying "that" (tat). Here, "this" (iha) refers either to the Self (ātman) or to liberation (mukti). || 331 ||
A means of valid cognition that apprehends difference is not found by us anywhere other than this [case].
For all means of knowledge always determine only the object of measurement.
1 ga. naḥ | [vol 3, page 644] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1777

He establishes that difference lacks any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇikatva*) in order to show that there is no evidence for either difference or non-difference between the two. Regarding the phrase "difference," he provides the reason why there is no means of knowledge (*māna*) that apprehends difference even in the case of two jars, stating: "because of the notion of 'I'. (336)
Apart from its own object of cognition, it does not depend upon any other object of cognition.
There is no operation such as exclusion or inclusion belonging to a means of valid cognition anywhere.

Anticipating the objection that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while manifesting its own object, simultaneously manifests the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) of that object from others, he says:

"Its own nature... (verse 337). The meaning is this: means of valid cognition, whose function is restricted to their own respective objects, do not apprehend the difference, non-difference, or both of an object from something else;
for those which are "heroes" regarding their own objects remain indifferent toward other things.
Let there be the manifestation of pleasure at will through its conjunction with knowledge.
But what is the proof for the manifestation of cognition, on account of which this term "manifestation" is used? (338)
Or, let it be granted that the manifestation of pleasure occurs through some kind of conjunction with cognition; however, the manifestation of that [pleasure] itself is not established.

Therefore, he asks: "How can there be a manifestation in the liberation of both? He says: "Manifestation. The meaning of the question is: is there a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for this [manifestation] within cognition itself, or is it something else? || 338 ||
The validity of the means of valid cognition does not consist in their being objects of knowledge by their own nature.
Nor can it be established by another means of valid cognition, because those two possess an identical nature.

Therein, he refutes the first [position] with the words "of the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇānām*). The meaning is: because the distinction between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge is well-established. He rejects the second [position] with the words "not," and the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "the status of being an object of knowledge for the means of knowledge is not desired. (339)
Furthermore, manifestation is considered to be occasional, not constant.
Due to the existence of obstacles to that [attainment], there would certainly always be a lack of manifestation. || 340 ||

Furthermore, having raised the dilemma as to whether the manifestation of bliss through knowledge is impermanent or permanent, he adopts the first alternative [the impermanent view] with the words "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*). He states that if the manifestation of bliss were impermanent, then in liberation there would be only the non-manifestation of that [bliss], because at that time its cause would be absent; this is expressed by the phrase "in the interval between those" (*tadantarāle*). Having taken for granted that the non-manifestation of bliss during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is accepted—*sade-*... [text continues]
Thus it has been stated. || 340 ||
Furthermore, it would follow that you must depend upon the removal of obstacles.
Other means of accomplishment have that [object] as their domain, because they are distinct from the cognition thereof. || 341 ||

Anticipating the objection that bliss might become manifest at the time of liberation (muktidaśā) due to the destruction of the veil (vyavadhi), he says: "Because of the intervening [obstacle]" (antarāya). Since the veil is a real entity and knowledge does not destroy it, another cause must be cultivated for its removal; in the absence of such a cause, the veil remains unbroken at liberation, and thus there is no manifestation of bliss. This is the meaning. || 341 ||
If they share a single locus of apprehension, the postulation of an obstruction [is required].
And it is not tenable [that they are distinct] on account of pride, because those two are of a single nature. || 342 ||

If that which is called ignorance—the obstacle—is not a real entity, then its destruction must depend on either eternal or adventitious knowledge; [this is the dilemma]. No; for [it is not so], because [the obstacle] is constant. 223.
[Vol. 3, page 645] 1778 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:

He refutes the first [position], that it consists of silver, with the words "upalabdhi" (perception). Since knowledge and pleasure have the same locus—namely, that wherever there is knowledge, there is also pleasure—in their having a single substratum...

The meaning is that their separation is unproven because both [ignorance and eternal knowledge] always exist within a single self; thus, ignorance is eternally obstructed by eternal knowledge. || 342 ||
And this being so, there would always be the manifestation of pleasure and cognition.
If manifestation does not exist in this way, then there would never be manifestation at all.
He states the conclusion resulting from the impossibility of intervention with the words "If this is so. He states the penalty for the contrary position with the words "Manifestation.
If one conceives of it otherwise than this, no means of valid cognition is observed.
In this world, the decay of phenomena is observed nowhere.
Likewise, the relationship between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge exists due to their mutual suitability.
If it is argued that in liberation, adventitious knowledge—termed "ignorance"—dispels the veil, to that he says: "Otherwise than this" (*ito 'nyathā*).

The meaning is that if one postulates adventitious knowledge in liberation in the absence of eternal knowledge, then a measure (*mātra*) and so forth would have to be postulated there; and that is improper, because it would result in no distinction from bondage and because there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, he states that the manifestation of knowledge and so forth in liberation is also untenable: "Nor... (*nāpi*).

The meaning is that two things under dispute do not have each other as their respective objects of cognition, because they share a single substratum, just like [the simultaneous perception of] such forms and tastes. || 344 || 349 ||
That which is considered to be in a state of transmigratory existence prior to the manifestation of pleasure and so forth.
He is indeed distinct from that which is eternally unmanifest and whose nature is constant knowledge and bliss.
Because of their mutual distinction from one another, like cold and heat.

He provides the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) in order to state another defect in the theory of manifestation (*abhivyaktivāda*). [The verse begins with] "Sukha... He states the reason for the difference between the higher and the lower by means of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in [the verse beginning with] "śīta... (346).
Furthermore, in the postulation of a distinction between the self and the other, the abandonment [of your own position] follows for you.
Therefore, on the basis of the Vedic position, no distinction of the self should be postulated here.

Anticipating the objection that "bringing about such a distinction is precisely what we desire," he says: "The other [view]," etc. The Vedic position is that "the one God is in all beings, one alone, without a second," and so forth. || 347 ||
Because the single reality that is the inner self consists merely of the cognition and the conceit of a self.
Furthermore, there would be an impossibility of any means of valid cognition if one were to postulate a plurality of selves.
Anticipating the objection that even the Vedic position is abandoned because its internal distinctions are established by perception and other means, he says: "The Self.

Since a means of knowledge capable of grasping difference is impossible with respect to that which is self-luminous, the meaning is that liberation is the state of being Brahman, which is without attributes and eternally established.
The word "and" (ca) serves to combine this with the contradiction of the aforementioned proofs. || 348 ||
But surely, if there were no distinction [between the two states], then liberation would now be exactly as it was then.
Excessive effort on the part of men would be unnecessary, and the scriptures themselves would become useless. || 349 ||
1 ga. °saṃbodho miṃ | 2 ka. ’kṣaṇyaṃ paraṃ | 3 ka. ga. gātmātmava | [vol 3, page 646] 4 Brāhmaṇa [accompanied by the commentary named Śāstramakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri | 1779]

Unable to tolerate the liberation thus described, he raises an objection with the word "nanu. Beyond ordinary worldly effort lies the supreme effort consisting of scriptural tranquility (*śama*) and so forth;
the scripture here concerns the subject of liberation. || 349 ||
This is not so, because the scripture, by its very nature, functions solely to eliminate ignorance regarding the Self.
Therefore, the effort is fruitful, and the undertaking of this treatise is also purposeful. (350)
He provides a rebuttal, stating that although liberation is devoid of distinctions, the scriptures and other means are purposeful because they destroy one's own ignorance and its products.
He says, "Not the Self," etc. As they have said: "Because the scripture has as its primary aim the cessation of the distinctions imagined by ignorance. (350)
This distinction consisting of being bound or liberated does not exist in the ultimate reality.
That very ignorance is the producer of all particularities without exception.

Now, one might ask: "Why should there not be scriptural effort for the sake of a particular state of liberation for the Self that is not yet liberated? To this he replies with the word "liberated. He states the reason why, in reality, there is an absence of particularity therein: "that ignorance" (tadavidyā).
The wisdom born of the scriptures [destroys] that ignorance which is the cause of all misfortune without exception.
Since it destroys [the afflictions], there shall be success for both one's effort and the scripture. || 152 ||
He concludes that the treatise and the effort [to study it] are purposeful with the verse beginning "aśeṣa" (352).
Now, for one possessed of ignorance, [the state of being] would depend on the removal or non-removal of that ignorance.
If it is argued that there is some specific quality of the self, we do not accept this. || 353 ||
Because it has as its basis the state of being an object that arises solely from the cause of ignorance.
Just like the cessation of a snake or similar [misconceptions] arising from ignorance regarding a rope-segment and so forth. || 394 ||

I.1 He raises an objection regarding the non-establishment of the Self as being devoid of distinctions with the words "Now" (atha). He answers that objection with the words "That too is due to ignorance" (āvidyaḥ so'pi).

"Not so," [it is said]. The meaning is that, just as there is no real distinction in the rope—whether its snake and so forth, which arise from ignorance regarding the rope, are destroyed or not destroyed by knowledge of it—so too, even though the Self possesses distinctions arising solely from its own ignorance, there is no real distinction between the destruction and non-destruction of those [distinctions]. || 353 || 354 ||
If it is maintained that the self is both the agent of delusion and the non-agent;
There would be no such distinction, because of the prohibition [in the scripture] that "it meditates, as it were. (355)

Nevertheless, he states that the existence of specific qualities in the Self is difficult to avoid, beginning with the words "of the Self. Having raised the alternatives—whether the agency of delusion consists in its production by the Self or its being the locus of that [delusion]—he refutes the first with the words "not so" (naivam). || 395 ||
"Unborn, he is not born," and "He meditates, as it were"—thus by means of the scriptures.
Here, a negation is made of all modifications and so forth belonging to the Self. (356)

He elucidates that very point with the words "unborn" (aja). By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "of modifications, etc.," the inclusion of the modified is intended. The word "here" refers to the statement of the scriptures on liberation. || 356 ||
1 kha. [The section on] ropes, saline soil, and so forth; 2 kha. [the section on] the maker of the bitter; 3 kha. [the section on] the self. || 356 ||
And because it is logically established that both the direct perception and the cognition arising from it have the same object.
Therefore, the self would neither possess ignorance nor possess its effects.

He states another argument against [the opponent's position]: "Insofar as it is an object," and so forth. Since ignorance and the like are visible to the Self, they cannot have the Self as their substrate;
for that which resides in something cannot be perceived by that very thing, as this would entail the fallacy of partial self-perception. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of restriction.
The word "ataḥ" (therefore), however, is connected with the preceding ablative case. || 357 ||
The establishment of the non-existence of the state of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped.
Just as it is witnessed by oneself, so too do I know that forest; thus it is witnessed by oneself.

He elaborates upon its being visible to the self: "The grāhaka... etc. The meaning is that, just as that which arises from ignorance is visible to the self, so too is this [object] visible to it; this is witnessed by one's own direct experience (svasākṣika). || 358 ||
Because the establishment of both non-cognition and erroneous cognition occurs through the single witness that is the Self.
Therefore, for one who has the Self as their witness, there is neither ignorance nor erroneous knowledge. || 359 ||
Although everything is witnessed by the Self, he says "of you" (tava) to indicate that; thus he says: "because of its being unknown," etc. (399).
For indeed, one who is a witness to something here is not said to be ignorant of it.
Because that [consciousness] is established through its non-commonality with the categories of the witness and the witnessed. || 360 ||
Fearing that the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) might also have that [ignorance] as its substrate—on the grounds of the intuition "I am deluded"—he says: "Not indeed" (na hi).

The word "here" (iha) refers to the state of empirical transaction (vyavahāra). He states the reason for the absence of the relationship of substrate and superstrate between those two: "By way of non-commonality" (asāmānyena). This means by way of mutually exclusive, specific forms; that is to say, "of those two" (tattayoḥ). || 360 ||
In that case, it is utterly contradictory that there should be both a witness and a deluded object of cognition.
Therefore, one who possesses self-respect should not speak such words to another in private.
He states another reason for the fact that the Self is not the locus of ignorance: "In that [Self]... The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Therefore, the Self is not the locus of ignorance. (361)
"I do not know even a fraction of what you have said; I am truly deluded."
If you view it thus, then [the self] is deluded and ignorant, like a jar. (362)

Thinking that the opponent's argument regarding the self (praticin) being the locus of ignorance has been refuted by logic and that such a view is contradicted by experience, he says: "No. [The opponent] asserts that the mother [the individual soul] is its locus based on experience; [the author] replies to this by asking: "Do you perceive?
It should be known.
"You are indeed a fool; be as you wish, O Kāma."
But he who is the witness of the two deluded ones is neither deluded, my dear, nor indeed a limb.

In accordance with this, it would follow that the word "bowed" (*vānata*) should appear in the root text, or else, in accordance with the root text, the word "thence" (*tataḥ*) should appear in the commentary.
He applies the commentary beginning with "bhava" (be) to the point already stated: "But you... He states another alternative: "O fool...
In the world as well, whoever is the witness for someone is indeed his true seer.
Just as in the world, so here too the witness perceives correctly. || 364 ||

He establishes worldly consensus as the authority for the absence of delusion and other defects in the witness of the Mother (mātṛsākṣin), stating "In the world also. Having raised the doubt that there might be a distinction between the witness in this context and the worldly witness, he says "Just as" (yathā), according to the maxim: "But the meaning of the sentence is not different [in both cases]. || 364 ||
And he declared that everything from the great elements up to the sustaining power is indeed the field (kṣetra).
The Self-existent One himself, whose nature is the Veda, [appears] for the sake of pacifying the miseries of saṃsāra.

He states that the words of the Lord also serve as proof for the self's freedom from delusion and other such defects: "The great elements, egoism, intellect, and the unmanifest; the ten senses and the one [mind], and the five objects of the senses... (Mahābhārata).
"Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude—
this is declared to be the field, together with its modifications, in brief."

The meaning is this: since the great elements and so forth, which arise from ignorance, are distinguished as the "field" (kṣetra) from the Witness (sākṣin), it is established that even their cause—ignorance—is untouched by Him. Nor is this [teaching] without authority, because it was spoken by a reliable person (āpta); thus he says: "Directly" (sākṣāt).

And he says that this [teaching] is not equal to the word of the Sugata because it is rooted in the Vedas, stating "the Veda... He then explains for what purpose the Blessed One spoke in this manner: "transmigration... (365).
Just as the one sun illuminates this entire world.
Thus, O Bhārata, he illuminates the entire field as well as the knower of the field.
He provides supporting evidence for the point that, because delusion and the like are seen by the self, they do not reside within the self, stating: "Just as... (366).
It is the light even of lights; it is self-luminous, according to the Vedic revelation.
For there is the Vedic revelation: "The sun does not shine there," and "There is nothing else besides this. || 367 ||
In that very context, he corroborates [the point] with scripture: "Of the luminaries" (jyotiṣām). Anticipating the objection that the Self might also be an object of perception, he says:
"Itself" (svayam). Furthermore, because there is no other seer, the Self is not an object of perception; thus he says: "No other" (nānyaḥ) || 367 ||
Since this is so, there is not even the slightest distinction here.
The firm conviction is that this [process] consisting of bondage, liberation, and so forth, pertains to the self (ātman). || 368 ||
Having established that the Self is devoid of distinctions, he concludes his own position with the words "yataḥ" (since). || 368 ||
But those of great intelligence who conceive of this otherwise than thus—
And they likewise explain the Arthavāda as well as the Śāstras on bondage and so forth.

[The opponent] objects: "If there is a scripture stating that 'fear arises for him' and so forth, implying that bondage results from ignorance and liberation from knowledge, how can the Self be essentially possessed of distinctions? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "And [it is] a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda). Thus, he asserts that even if that were so, the distinction between the bondage and liberation of the Self exists as a reality. He says: "In that way. (Verse 369)
Having been told this repeatedly previously, the refutation has also already been described. || 370 ||
Even when it has been refuted in this way, opponents still voice their criticisms as they please.
Therefore, such people should be disregarded by the wise, for they are equal to children and the insane. || 371 ||

Having restated this very assertion of the dualists (*dvaitins*), he says, "Thus stated," because [the truth] has been established in various ways in several places; therefore, one need not strive further for that purpose. The particle *api* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇārthe*) and follows immediately after the term *niṣṭhā*. Having reminded [the reader] of the defect in the opponent's position even outside the commentary (*bhāṣya*), he states the purport of the commentary beginning with "They venture even in the sky" (*ta utsahante khe api*). Thus [ends the section]. || 370 ||
The statement "Brahmā also goes" is based on figurative usage.
Because it is the cause for severing the continuity of the body and so forth, which arise from beginningless ignorance. || 372 ||

He concludes the meaning of the statement by refuting the opposing view with the words "Brahman. He summarizes the grounds for the metaphorical designation with the words "that ignorance" (tadavidyā). || 372 ||
Depending solely upon the destruction of ignorance through the mere arising of right knowledge.
Being Brahman itself, the Self directly attains Brahman; thus it is said. || 373 ||
He states the cause for the cessation of the continuity of future bodies and so forth with the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*). He states the cause for its destruction with the word "right" (*samyak*).

He concludes the interpretation of the stated sentence by resorting to figurative usage with the word "Self" (*ātman*). Having relied upon the destruction of ignorance through right knowledge, and taking as the instrumental cause the destruction of the body and so forth produced by that [ignorance], the Self—being none other than Brahman itself—attains Brahman.
Therefore, the application of the Vārttika is that this sentence is so called by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra). || 373 ||
Thus, this entire essence of all the Vedāntas has been declared by the Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture is for the purpose of strengthening the meaning declared by the Brahmana. || 374 ||
Having restated the subject matter that has been discussed, he declares the purport of the Vedic scripture beginning with the word "tat" (that), saying: "This, namely... (374).
He recited two verses from the *Yathākāmamaya* [section].
Through the thorough realization "I am Brahman," there arises the abandonment of ignorance regarding the inner self. || 375 ||

When all desires, together with the objects of desire, [are stilled].
They are liberated from [bondage] and perish due to the cause of their ignorance.
The operation of effects is observed to reside in their cause, and nowhere else in the world. || 376 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the meaning stated in the Brāhmaṇa is already established with firmness by that very [Brāhmaṇa], there is no need for the citation of the mantra, he says: "Just as... (yathā).

The intention is that even though the matter is firm by what was stated in the Brāhmaṇa, the citation of the mantra is for the sake of strengthening the inclination of the listener. He explains the words beginning with "when" (yadā): "Brahman... (brahma...). The connection is: "then one becomes immortal. Even when ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge, desires...

If it is argued that [the effects] will persist, he says "no," [referring to] "of those. Anticipating the objection that desire and so forth are observed even in one whose ignorance has been destroyed, he says "of the effects. When the cause is destroyed, the effect cannot remain, because it is impossible for it to exist elsewhere; thus, the observation of passion and so forth in one whose ignorance is destroyed is merely a persistence of what was sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*), arising from a trace of ignorance (*ajñānaleśa*). This is the meaning. || 375 || 376 ||
By the very statement, "When desires are relinquished," one's purpose is fulfilled.
For what purpose is the qualification "all" stated? || 377 ||

He raises the objection that the qualification "desire" (kāma) is redundant with the words "yadā" [when]. "Kṛtārthatā" (the state of having accomplished one's purpose) means being free from further expectation because the mere destruction of desire has been established. || 377 ||
Upon the cessation of waking and dreaming, all desires of men are completely liberated.
With only their residual impressions remaining, they go to complete dissolution in deep sleep.
Therefore, for the purpose of excluding that [undesired consequence], every qualification must be applied. (378)

He explains: "While awake. This means that for the sake of including those [impressions], even the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of desire are to be subsumed because they too can be turned back through the power of knowledge. The term "all" is a qualifier; that is to say, it qualifies all desires. (378)
For when the cause of desire is destroyed, nothing whatsoever remains.
Whether it be a mental formation (saṃskāra) or anything else, everything has its root in ignorance. || 379 ||
Anticipating the question of how the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of desire are destroyed by means of knowledge, he says: "Desire... Here, the word "other" refers to desire.
The particle *hi* is used to establish the well-known principle that in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the effect. To the question of what that cause is, he replies:
Regarding the word "of all": the remainder is that for desire as well, that very thing is the root. || 379 ||
The mind spoke these words to Kāmadharmī: "They have taken refuge in my heart."
"Desire, volition," and so forth; likewise, there is the citation from the Māṇḍūkya Śruti.

It has been stated that all the desires of this person pertaining to the two worlds perish through knowledge; now, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "in the heart" (hṛdi). [He says] "in the heart. Therein, he corroborates the section concerning the three foods (tryanna). [He says] "desire" (kāma). || 380 ||
And this is the statement of the reason for the matter that has been proposed as a thesis.
Since all desires are rooted in the heart, they are thereby completely liberated.
1 kha. ga. 'pyanyatsarvam | [vol 3, page 651] 1784 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter—]

Anticipating the objection that this [statement] is redundant because its meaning is already established by that [previous statement], he says: "And this... He clarifies this very distinction: that "the desires are liberated" is the proposition (*pratijñā*), while "they are seated in the heart" is the statement of the reason (*hetu*).
Thus he says: "In the heart. (381)
For the effect of ignorance is that which is characterized by the internal [self] and so forth.
Or rather, this has been stated as a triad, distinguished as speech, mind, and breath.
Therefore, upon the complete destruction of ignorance, that which is caused by it [is destroyed] without remainder.
There shall also be the destruction of desires, which take the form of the seizing and the further seizing.

[Objection: But surely, for those who know Brahman, desire is destroyed by knowledge; how then can their state of being "within the heart" (*hārdatva*) be the cause [of the world]? For it is not the case that when ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl is destroyed by the knowledge of it, the fact that [the silver] resided in the person is made out to be the cause of that [silver]. To this, he says: "Of ignorance... Since it was stated in the passage "This world is indeed [Brahman]" that the threefold world consisting of speech and so forth is born of ignorance, therefore, upon the destruction of ignorance, that which is born of it—namely the internal... [is destroyed].

The meaning is this: since the instruments [of action] are destroyed, the desires that depend upon them—the entire host of objects—are likewise utterly destroyed; thus, for the wise person, the statement that desire is "situated in the heart" serves as the reason for the destruction of desire through knowledge. || 382 || 383 ||
Desire alone has been determined to be the cause of complete destruction.
The excessive graspings, which are desires, are dependent [on them] and are the activators of the senses.
"The words 'resting in the heart' were spoken by them with the desire to conceal [the truth]. (384)

[Objection: But surely, when ignorance (*avidyā*) is destroyed, its effects are destroyed; and when desire (*kāma*), which is dependent upon that [ignorance], is destroyed, another effect will still remain. How, then, is there liberation? To this he says: "Without remainder" (*niḥśeṣa*). [The sense is: "This person consists of desire alone," and "this is indeed the bondage of desire"—such is the remainder [of the scriptural passage]. Since dharma and so forth have desire as their cause, when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge (*vidyā*), action (*karman*) is also destroyed; and thus...

The meaning is that its establishment [as the cause] follows from the absence of any obstacle to liberation. Since the word *kāma* has multiple meanings, he states which ones serve as the cause for the birth [of the world]: "resorted to" (*śritāḥ*). Desires known as the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and so forth, residing in the intellect, impel the two kinds of organs;
thus, producing various activities, they generate the world. As it is said: "Action generates [the world] through each successive thought."

The meaning is "because of the Vedic revelation" (*bhiriti śruteḥ*). He states the reason why the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and so forth are included here under the term "desire" (*kāma*): "in the heart" (*hṛdi*).

This qualification is for the purpose of including passion and the rest within the word "desire"; for being situated in the mind is not primarily [the defining characteristic] of anything other than passion and the like—this is the meaning. || 384 ||
And the sage Vedavyāsa also spoke this exactly as it has been related.
Having accepted the meaning of the sacred revelation, and out of a desire to favor the world. || 385 ||

It has been stated through both proposition and reason that for those who know Brahman, there is the destruction of all desires by means of knowledge; in this regard, he cites Smṛti as authoritative evidence:
"Vedavyāsa also [says]... (385).
The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food.
With the exception of taste; even this sense of taste ceases upon seeing the Supreme.

O mighty-armed one, slay the enemy who can assume any form at will and is difficult to overcome.
He states another sentence of his [the opponent's] as follows: "In this way," etc. (387).
And this word "atha" (then) has the sense of a cause (hetu), because its meaning follows from what has been previously stated.
Because a mortal is [so called] due to ignorance, he becomes immortal through the destruction of that ignorance. || 388 ||

Having explained the first half of the mantra, he explains the second half. Regarding the phrase "and for the sake of the cause" (*hetvarthe ca*): among the various other possible meanings, what is the restrictive factor here? To that he says, "for the sake of the cause. This means that because the sense of "cause" (*hetvartha*) is the subject under discussion, as in the expression "residing in the heart" (*hṛdi śritāḥ*).
Clarifying the meaning in the form of a cause, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "mortal" (*martya*), starting with the words "because" (*yasmāt*). || 388 ||
That which is designated here as "pratyagyāthātmyavijñānam" (the direct realization of the true nature of the inner self).
Upon the arising of right knowledge, he attains Brahman right here.

He states the meaning of the word "here" (atra) with the words "the inner self" (pratyak). Having restated what was previously mentioned, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Brahman" (brahma) with the words "perfectly" (samyak).
For when the knowledge of Brahman arises, the bondage of birth is cast off.
Death consists in the notion of a self; its cause is the destruction of that which is similar to a cause. || 390 ||

He states the reason for the claim that the attainment of Brahman occurs at the very same time as knowledge: "Brahman," etc. Since ignorance regarding one's own self (*svājñāna*) is the cause of the bondage called birth—consisting of *dharma* and so forth—and since the knowledge of Brahman is the remover of that [ignorance], it is said that the knowledge of Brahman is the death of the bondage of birth and so on.
Therefore, because bondage departs simultaneously with knowledge, the liberation of the knower is logical; this is the meaning. || 390 ||
Therefore, the wise should strive to explain this [text] in a manner entirely different from what has been stated [by others].
They explain the verse [as follows]: "By means of improper reasoning, through reliance on the best of those who offer oblations into the fire. (391)

The mantra has been explained according to our own school with the aim that liberation belongs to the wise man when all desires have been utterly destroyed. Now, he introduces the interpretation of the mantra by Bhartṛprapañca. With the words "yathoktāt" (from what was said), he mocks [the opponent] for the effort involved in abandoning the syllables of the verse as they are heard in scripture and imagining what is not heard; he mocks him because the cause of such an alternative explanation is an abundance of intellectual artifice. He says: "budhāḥ" (the wise).
"This explanation is not produced by reasoning, but rather depends upon the grace of the deity"—with this, he states another point of ridicule: "Not by reasoning" (ayuktyā).
Just as cyclic existence was previously described as having its root in desire.
By this verse, even the liberation of one who is free from desire is described.

How else could there be such an interpretation? To this he says: "Just as... It has been stated that, just as in the previous verse beginning with "by desires [there is] bondage," [the point] was already suggested, so too here in this verse beginning with "even one free from desire is liberated," he intends to suggest the same. ||392||
1 gha. Therefore, he says. 2 ka. kha. In the mantra.

"What are these sensual pleasures?"—to this question, their specific definition is stated: || 393 ||
Having introduced [the following] into the opponent’s position, he states its meaning: "From the wise one" (*prājñāt*). The connection is: "then the mortal becomes immortal.

Having raised the expectation—"Whose destruction of desires occurs there, both those residing in the self (*svasthāḥ*) and those residing in the intellect (*dhīsthāḥ*)?"—he introduces the passage beginning with "those which... with the word "ta" (those). || 393 ||
But those very desires that have taken refuge in his heart are utterly liberated.
But those [qualities] which are dependent upon the self are not permanently released from it. || 394 ||
Demonstrating the very qualification, he joins the sentence [with the word] "in the heart. He states the meaning of the particle "eva" (only/itself) as "the Self" (ātman). || 394 ||
That which is called the heart is said to be both consciousness and a mass of flesh.
By conventional usage, the term "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the aggregate of consciousness because it resides therein. (395)

He states the meaning of the word *hṛdaya*: "The heart," he says. To the objection that it is illogical for a single word to have multiple meanings—since one thing cannot possess multiple meanings—he replies: "By conventional usage (*rūḍhyā*). The meaning is that it is not contradictory for a single word to have multiple meanings through both direct denotation (*śruti*) and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). || 399 ||
Furthermore, the desires mentioned here are those which consist of latent impressions (vāsanā).
By means of the passage beginning with "māhārajanam," [the author] [teaches] for the sake of the purification of the self. (396)

He states the meaning of the word "kāma" (desires): "Kāmāḥ" (desires). The word "iha" (here) refers to what was spoken in the mantra. To the question, "Why were the desires residing in the mind explained in the Mūrtāmūrta Brāhmaṇa?", he replies: "Ātmā" (the Self). As it has been said: these desires take the form of food, progeny, and so forth. || 396 ||
The internal form of the wise one consists of those [subtle elements], such as saffron and the like.
But those [deities] who reside in the heart become external by virtue of having an external locus. || 397 ||

He states that this form, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is the internal nature of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) by saying "of the Prājña. Anticipating the objection that all desires might be identical with the self because they are non-distinct from it, he says "in the heart. To be external means to have a nature other than the Self.
As it has been said: "Those specific desires characterized by saffron dye and so forth are located outside the heart. (397)
For [the qualities] residing in the self arise from those residing in the heart and the objects of desire.
Therefore, the fulfillment of desires here arises from relying upon many [conditions]. (398)
The taking of refuge in the heart is here stated to be their distinguishing characteristic.
For that is indeed the fruit: the cessation of desires based on the self. || 399 ||

He states that gross desires residing in the mind serve as the cause for subtle desires residing within the self, by the words "having the heart as its locus. The word "here" (iha) refers to the state of bondage. He states the resulting conclusion regarding the causal relationship between desires situated in the self and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) with the word "therefore" (ataḥ). He explains the purpose of the qualification "resting in the heart" with the word "self" (ātma). Just as [the thumb is the measure], from that indeed their production occurs.
"It becomes non-existent. The word "hi" (for/indeed) illuminates the aforementioned commentary. || 398 || 399 ||
1. *Sva.*: *guhyā* (secret) *māṃsam* (flesh). 2. *Ka.* and *Kha.*: *narmadā*. 3. *Ka.* and *Kha.*: *tanmahā*. 4. *Ka.*, *Kha.*, and *Gha.*: *ye mahā*. [Vol. 3, page 654] 4.
