The cultivation that has entered through the door of the mind remains established within the self.
That [ignorance] is the seed of birth for the embodied soul; through its destruction, one is liberated. || 400 ||

If desires, which are rooted in the self, do not cease, then liberation would not be established, because of the contradiction that one who possesses desire is liberated; anticipating this objection, he says: "By means of the mind" (verse 400).
Just as one relies upon the earth for the birth of a sprout residing within a seed, so too [is it here].
Thus, birth arises from its very basis, as desires arise from their basis in the heart.

By means of this illustration, he establishes that the production of desire based on the self occurs through the power of desire based on the intellect. [He does so] by the words "of that which resides in the seed."

Regarding the statement that the birth of a sprout residing within a seed occurs on the plane of empirical usage by depending upon the earth, he states the reason for perceiving it as such through its dependence on that [earth]:
"From the support" (*āśrayāt*). Some, however, explain the phrase "from the support itself" (*āśrayādeva*) as "from the support of the heart" (*hṛdayāśrayāt*). For it has been said:
"Just as the production of a sprout residing within a seed occurs by depending upon the earth, so too the heart is the womb (*yoni*) for those things dependent upon the *prājña*."
Thus [it is said]. || 401 ||
And because of their connection with the heart, all of them are perceived by him.
Therefore, they are distinguished by the heart itself through their specific functions. 402.

If desires arise in the self through the door of the mind (*manas*), why then are they said to "reside in the heart"? They are specified by that very [organ] in this context: "by the heart. This means that because the specific manifestation of desire is observed in the heart due to its specific function. (402)
When the desires dwelling in the heart are cast off by this embodied soul,
Then the mortal becomes immortal and wise; this is the certain conclusion.
Having restated the meaning already expressed in the first half-verse, he explains the second half-verse: "In the heart," etc. (403).
By which [means] this [world] [is produced] from the Supreme Self through the aggregate of knowledge and action.
When he has completely severed his state of being subject to saṃsāra and attained [liberation], he is made whole.
Then, by the abandonment of that, one is liberated; being pure, one attains Brahman. || 404 ||

If it be argued that even when bondage is destroyed through the destruction of desire and the like by means of knowledge (*vidyā*), another cause must still be sought for the sake of attaining the state of Brahman (*brahmabhāva*), [the author] says "no," beginning with the word *vidyā*. When all those desires and so forth— which, rooted in ignorance, have caused this conscious self (*vijñānātman*) to be separated from the Supreme Self and led to transmigratory existence— are completely liberated through the combination of knowledge and action (*vidyā-karma-samuccaya*), then...
The meaning is that, through the removal of bondage by means of the absence of causes, the self becomes completely pure and, being unimpeded, becomes Brahman. || 404 ||
And because of the statement regarding one who desires the Self, this has been determined even previously.
The desires belong to this very Self; they are not distinct from it, unlike the desires within the heart.
Desires rooted in the intellect, through it in the self, and residing in the heart, cease; thereafter, the liberation of the living being is seen, and no longer bondage.
[vol 3, page 655]

1788 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]: It has been stated that there is the destruction of the desires for truth (*satyakāma*) and so forth, which are co-natural to one's own self (*svātman*). Now, in order to show that there is no destruction of the innate desire within the Self, he cites the scriptural passage concerning the "Self-desire" (*ātmakāma*) as authority. He says: "The Self-desire," etc., and shows it to be certain: "In the Self," etc.
In that regard, those which are non-different from the Self [are so] because of the reason of their non-otherness.
There is no liberation for the self because of its constant non-association with them.

1.1 | He states the result when there is no distinction between desires and the self: "In that regard" (*tatra*). The locative case here is used for the purpose of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), meaning "among those desires. Regarding desires—
He states the reason: "Because there is always an absence of contact with those [objects] that are non-different from the self," using the word "by them" (*taiḥ*). || 406 ||
For association or separation occurs only between two distinct entities.
Therefore, because there is no difference among those who abide in the Self, one who is liberated is not distinct from them. || 407 ||

One might object: "Why should conjunction (*saṃsarga*) and separation (*vyāvṛtti*) not occur for that [liberated soul] even with respect to desires that are non-different from its own self, just as they occur between a substance and its qualities, since such [conjunction and separation] are possible? Anticipating this, he says: "Conjunction... [and so forth]. It has been stated that in the case of a liberated person, because the desires residing within it are non-different [from it], there can be neither conjunction nor separation with them; for these two are observed only in the case of two distinct things, such as milk and water, and they do not exist there [in the case of the soul and its desires].
The meaning is that there exists a relationship of quality and qualified (guṇaguṇibhāva) capable of conjunction (saṃsarga). || 407 ||
But those [colors] beginning with saffron, which arise from false views, [are not so].
They remain distinct [from the soul] and always serve as the cause of bondage. (408)
For that reason, they always maintain both association with and seclusion from themselves.
It is with reference to those very [beings] that this qualification has been stated here by him.

Anticipating the question, "With whom, then, are association and solitude attributed to the Self?", he says: "It is false. The phrase "in this way" expresses the lack of equal strength [between the two]. The phrase "by the path already stated" refers to the manner in which one sublates the other. Now, an objection: since in the *dahara* passage, which concerns the reality (*vastu*), there is heard the connection of the Self with desires in the words, "These are His true desires," the *aticchandas* passage and the *satyakāma* passage must also concern the reality.

Because they are equal in this respect, there would either be an option between them or both would lack authority; to that he says: "Asatya... (In truth). That sentence concerning the small ether (*dahara-vākya*) does not have the ultimate reality as its primary object, because it is intended for meditation (*upāsti*), according to the scriptural passage: "That which is within it is to be sought" and so forth. Even if it were intended to convey the ultimate reality, it does not establish that this Self possesses desires, because its purpose is to negate unreal desires within that [ether]; or else, it is intended to enjoin the meditation on Brahman.

Here, a hymn of praise to Brahman is introduced; for Brahman is indeed praiseworthy because within it desires are truly realized. Therefore—[variant readings in manuscripts kha and ga: "pecikiṃ"]—[vol 3, page 663].

The meaning is that because the statement of Hara is not equal to the *aticchandas* statement, there is indeed sublation (*bādha*). This refers to that which is situated in the eighth [chapter] of the eighth *prapāṭhaka*. 492 || 413 ||
If desires do not exist within the self, then that statement is indeed fruitful.
"Aticchandā" is auspicious, as it effects the cessation of desire and grief. || 454 ||

Even in the passage concerning the sacrificial materials (*vastu*), where the statement of Prajāpati says "Satyakāma," there is heard a connection with desire; fearing that this might result in either an option (*vikalpa*) or a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*), he says: "They exist. This is its meaning: because the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpasukha*) is without beginning or end, it is not false;
thus, the Self’s state of being non-false bliss is the meaning of the word *satyakāma*. Alternatively, Brahman—the object to be known—is praised by that term in every respect.

There is no connection with desire for the Self; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *Aticchanda* passage. Furthermore, an option (*vikalpa*) regarding a real entity (*vastu*) has been refuted, nor is that [Self] non-existent because of the absence of any cause for its non-existence. || 414 ||
If the desires as described are not negated within the inner self, [then...]
Furthermore, if this [self] consists of desire, even cyclic existence cannot be prevented.

Furthermore, having raised the doubt as to whether desires consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within the self are or are not the cause of *saṃsāra*, he addresses the first alternative by saying, "They are prohibited. The meaning is that if the desires which are the cause of bondage within the self were not prohibited, then there would never be liberation for it, according to the scriptural text: "As is one's desire, so is one's nature" (*sa yathākāmo bhavati*). The word "atha" (then) is used in the sense of purpose. [This implies] the presence of the result when there is the presence of the cause.
The word "also" (api) has the sense of cultivation (bhāvanā). || 455 ||
Those desires which exist within the inner self are considered not capable of sprouting again.
For what purpose, then, do you postulate their continued existence there?

He addresses the second [objection] with the words "of those who hold such a view. He raises an objection: if it is argued that those [defilements] do not serve as a cause for bondage within the Self, then their persistence there cannot be postulated due to the absence of any result; thus he asks, "For what purpose? (496)
There is no utility whatsoever for sensual desires here in the state of abiding [in truth].
Just like the fleshy protuberance on the neck of a goat, [there is no purpose] in the authority for bondage and liberation. || 457 ||

Fearing the objection that their persistence there, even if not a cause for bondage, might produce some other result, he says: "Not any... Here, "here" refers to the Self. For that [persistence] cannot be a cause of liberation because it is contradictory to it; nor can it be a cause of bondage, in which case it would be fruitless, since no other result is established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). This is the meaning. || 497 ||
That which has its existence established by valid means of cognition is not to be rejected, even if it is fruitless.
The connection with desire in the case of the internal [self] is not like that; thus it is negated. || 458 ||
Not only is there no connection with desire in the self because of its fruitlessness, but also because of the absence of proof; thus he says: "By means of valid cognition...
In the Śruti, hundreds of undesirable things such as desire and the like are [declared] with respect to the Inner Self.
Furthermore, there are prohibitive statements even within the teachings of the Smṛtis.
1 gha. ‘The statement regarding desire residing in the body’ | 2 ka. ga. ‘O Deva, phauṃ’ | 3 gandā ati | [Vol.
3, page 664] 4 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri | 1797

And because it is opposed to that [knowledge], he says that there is no connection with desire in the Self: "Of desire and so forth. That is to say, due to the contradiction with Vedic statements such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) and Smṛti statements such as "this is unchangeable" (*avikārya*), there is no association with those [qualities] in the Self. || 459 ||
Therefore, the fabrication of desire is not applicable here to the inner self (pratyagātman).
Therefore, because no means of valid cognition is possible, that [self] should not be postulated by a wise person.
He concludes the result [of the discussion] regarding the absence of pride and its fruit, as well as their contradiction, with the verse beginning "kāma" (verse 460).
Even if they are very numerous, unseen things that possess valid means of cognition must be postulated.
Not even a hundredth part of what has not been perceived should be postulated, as it lacks any means of valid cognition.

Regarding the point that because pride and other such states do not exist, there can be no postulation of desire and so forth within the Self, he cites the consensus of the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda: "Those [means of knowledge] which possess valid evidence...
And in the phrase "one who desires the Self," the Self is not the locus of desire.
Because it is established by another means of knowledge, the authority of the Veda is obtained. || 462 ||

An objection is raised: since it was stated that because of the phrase "one who desires the Self" (*ātmakāma*), the Self itself is his desire and not distinct from it—just as in the case of the desires within the heart (*hārdakāma*)—how can it then be said that there is a lack of authoritative evidence? Anticipating this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*). In the expression *ātmakāma*, "desire" (*kāma*) may mean either happiness or a variety of longings. In the first case, if your intended meaning is accepted, the scripture lacks authority regarding the object [of the Self], because it culminates merely in the fact that the Self is happiness. In the second case as well, even if the Self is the substratum of those [longings], the scripture [remains] without authority.
The meaning is that its status as a means of knowledge (*mānatva*) lacks novelty (*apūrvatva*), because its being based upon that [other means] is already established in the world. || 462 ||
Nor is this object to be meditated upon, because of the scriptural statement regarding "all desires" and so forth.
Because it is devoted to illuminating the true nature of the reality of the single self. || 463 ||

Furthermore, is the Self’s connection with desire stated as something to be known or as something to be meditated upon? It is not the first, because that would be undesirable; nor is it the latter, as he says: "And not... In this regard, he provides a negative example: "All... The reason for this is: "Because of scripture" (śruteḥ).
The meaning is that the passage concerning "one whose desire is the Self" (ātmakāma) has as its purport the reality itself. || 463 ||
If the self's status as the locus of desire and so forth were established by the logic of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika), [then...]
Since scripture is independent of that [logic], it does not depend upon Kaṇāda.
Having established that the opponent's position is contrary to scripture (*āgama*), he raises an objection in order to demonstrate that it is also contrary to logic (*nyāya*).

He says, "Kaṇabhuj" (the follower of Kaṇāda). The intention is as follows: since desire and the rest must reside in something because they are qualities (*guṇatva*), like color (*rūpa*), the substratum (*dharmin*) is established in a general sense;

then, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the Self (*ātman*) will be established as their substratum. [This is countered by the fact] that there are scriptural statements regarding them being attributes of the mind (*manas*), and scriptural statements regarding the Self being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*).
He refutes that view by stating that it should be disregarded because it does not follow the tenets of logic, [concluding with] "Because of scripture" (śruteḥ). || 464 ||
Furthermore, because there are scriptural passages prohibiting those [objects], they are not to be relied upon, as that would contradict [the scriptures].
Therefore, like the reasoning of the Sugatas, the self does not have the senses as its basis.
Is it because, by such passages as "When all are completely liberated" and "neither gross nor subtle," desires and the like are negated in the Self, there is a contradiction with that?
[End of section 1798 from the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, Fourth Chapter]

He states that such a view must be abandoned with the words "tanniṣedha" (the refutation of that). He states the conclusion regarding the fallacious nature of the arguments of the logicians with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). || 461 ||
And no other evidence whatsoever is observed for their having desire as their basis.
Because it transcends both the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge, and because the reality is established by itself. || 466 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if there is no scriptural authority or logical reasoning for the self’s dependence on desire, there might still be another means of knowledge (pramāṇa), [the author] elaborates on the statement that there is no other means of knowledge for the self being the abode of desire, beginning with "na ca" (nor). Anticipating the further objection that, in that case, the reality of the object would not be established, he says: "svataḥ" (by itself). || 466 ||
The knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge are always subject to appearance and disappearance.
He who perceives with unblinking eyes is the Self, free from the conceit of "otherness."

Anticipating the objection as to how [the Self] is established by itself, he demonstrates that this has been stated repeatedly with the verse beginning "mātṛmāna... (The knower, the means of knowledge...). The word "ca" (and) is used for the purpose of emphasis and is connected with the word "sadā" (always). || 467 ||
That which, by its very nature, neither comes nor goes, and which is always opposed to those things that do so;
In that very [self], this notion of "I" arises for the wise, but not in things that come and go.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to attribute "selfhood" (ātmatva) to the Witness because that [notion] is well-known only with respect to the body and so forth, he says: "He who [is known] by himself.
The sense is that the attribution of selfhood to the body and so forth is merely an error. || 468 ||
He who, with unblinking eyes, beholds the one who is lustful, suffering, and deluded;
Neither is that desire, nor the desirer, nor indeed its connection itself [the cause]. // 469 //

Even though [the Self] is the witness of the mother and others, what happens in the present case? He says: "The lover. Since the conscious principle (cid-dhātu), which is the witness of the mother who is the locus of desire and so forth, is the Self, it has no connection with that [desire]; this is the meaning. || 469 ||
In this way, it should be understood that [the nature of] suffering and so forth has been explained by relying upon direct perception.
Since desire and so forth are properties of the mind, their status as residing in the object is well-established. || 470 ||

He extends the same reasoning regarding desire and so forth to suffering and the rest by saying "in the same way. The ellipsis to be supplied is "the previously mentioned [qualities] such as non-selfhood. "Direct perception" means immediate experience by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). He states another reason for the absence of desire and so forth being attributes of the Self: "of desire and the like. || 470 ||
He who always directly perceives the mind, which possesses qualities such as desire and so forth.
By what means of valid cognition is its connection with desire and so forth understood? || 471 ||
Anticipating the objection—“Just as heat resides in water [as a substratum], why could desire and so forth not reside in the mind which is itself situated in the Self?”—he says:

“Desire, etc. The point is that while the cognition of heat in water is an error, the cognition of desire and so forth in the Self would likewise be an error, and thus there is no contradiction. || 471 ||
1. He refutes [the objection] by means of a comparison.
[Vol.
3, page 666] 4. Brāhmaṇa, together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
How could the inward reality [be known] by desire and other qualities, which are accessible only to the outward intellect?
Because of their mutual contradiction, the qualified object would be [negated], just as the sun is by darkness. || 472 ||
For this reason as well, he states that desire and so forth are not attributes of the self: "The inner," etc. (472).
The qualifier and the qualified are apprehended by a single cognition.

It is not observed [to coexist] like a blue lotus and so forth; that is not observed because two contradictory things cannot be grasped by a single cognition. Furthermore, because desire and the like are mutually contradictory, they cannot be attributes of the Self (ātman); thus he says: "A single...
(verse 473).
Nor is any grasper determined to exist as something other than the self.
And since desire and the like reside in the subject, how could they become objects of apprehension? || 474 ||
Furthermore, if that [cognition] were a property of the self (ātman), one must consider whether the apprehender is distinct or non-distinct from the substratum (dharmin).

He refutes the first alternative with the words "Nor also" (nāpi). He rejects the second with the words "The apprehender" (grāhaka). The meaning is that it would follow that [the cognition] would partially apprehend itself. || 474 ||
Since it is seen by the eye, one should observe that blackness and so forth do not reside in the eye.
Desire and the like, which reside in the knower, would likewise attain the status of being objects of knowledge.
He states, by means of an illustration, the impossibility of [a cognition] grasping its own inherent property: "The eye," etc. (479).
Or else, it is because of the perception of selfhood even in this insentient object.
Let there be desire for objects and so forth for that [person], but not for one whose self consists of mere perception.

Furthermore, regarding whether the self that serves as the locus for desire and so forth is insentient or sentient, he accepts the first alternative [the insentient], stating "ātmatva... (the state of being the self). The word "vā" (or) indicates a dilemma. The word "iha" (here) refers to the statement of the opponent's position. He rejects the second alternative with the words "dṛṣṭi... (perception...). The meaning is: because it would contradict the state of absolute homogeneity (*aikarasya*). || 476 ||
The state of having a single non-conscious locus is also established here by me. || 477 ||
And in a dream, one shines by oneself, free from all desires and the like.
The phrase "by its own light" was stated for the purpose of establishing its self-luminosity.
He explains the acceptance of the insentient as the locus of desire and so forth with the words "acetanā" (insentient). The word "iha" (here) refers to desire and the rest.

The meaning of "api" (also) is that if you too establish that very same point, then there is no disagreement. Furthermore, having begun with "by himself he shines," the scripture states "he dreams by his own light"; thus, for the purpose of establishing self-luminosity, [the text describes] the Self in the dream state as devoid of all specific attributes such as desire and the like.
Because it is considered liberated from form, and because of its opposition [to desire], it does not serve as a basis for desire and so forth; thus he says: "By itself... (477, 478).
And the establishment of its self-luminosity is preceded by scripture and reasoning.
By the mention of the spheres beginning with the desire realm, that [objection] would be refuted by you through implication. || 479 ||

In that very context, he provides an introductory transition (*pātanikā*) to state another reason, beginning with the word "himself" (*svayam*). According to the Vedic scripture, "This person here is self-luminous," and according to the logical principle that insentience would entail non-selfhood, although the Self is indeed self-manifesting, [desires and so forth]—
[as indicated by the commentary variants *āśrayitaḥ* and *anvayāḥ*].
1800 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika, Chapter Four [Volume 3, Page 667]

To the question of why [the self] might not be the substratum in that case, he says: "Because of desire, etc. For that well-known self-luminosity of the self—whether based on scripture (śrautī) or based on logic (naiyāyikī)—would be sublated by your assertion that desire and so forth have the self as their substratum;

for, as in the Vaiśeṣika school and others, the perception of the self as their substratum is possible precisely through a specific modification occurring within its own locus. This is the meaning. || 479 ||
In the same way, when the Self is seen, everything becomes seen.
If desire and so forth were other than the self, then that [self] too would be subject to sublation.

Furthermore, he states that by one who asserts that desire and so forth have the Self as their locus, the scriptural teaching that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" would be contradicted, because of the admission of their difference [from the Self]. He says: "In the same way. The meaning is: just as [the Self's] self-luminosity is contradicted because it is not well-known [in that sense]. || 480 ||
Furthermore, if it were the locus of desire and so forth, there would be a contradiction with all the Vedānta texts.
The self would be admitted [as existing] by those who deny it. || 481 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the Self is not the substratum of desire and so forth, beginning with the words "all. The reason for this is given by the words "of those [desires]. The meaning is that [the scripture] culminates in the reality indicated by them. || 481 ||
Because the oneness of the Self is the meaning of scripture, and because the Veda is independent of anything else.
Therefore, we do not take those words of the logicians into account at all. || 482 ||
He concludes what has been stated—that the Self is not the substratum of desire and so forth—by means of both scripture and reasoning, with the words "of the oneness of the Self" (*aikātmyasya*).

Since the meaning of scripture is a single-flavored reality (*ekarasa*), the status of the Self as the substratum of desire and so forth cannot be established by scripture; nor can it be established by the reasonings of logicians, because such reasonings do not depend upon the scripture that establishes the Self. Therefore, reasonings that contradict it have no force regarding a matter established by valid authority (*prāmāṇika*).
Therefore, the arguments of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, which show the self to be the substratum [of cognition], are to be disregarded because they contradict the Śruti;
this is the meaning. || 482 ||
Surely, the qualification "residing in the heart" has been stated here with respect to desires.
And that [reason] would be fruitful only when there is both presence [of the probandum] and deviation [from it]. (483)
Having raised and refuted the objection beginning with "because of the hearing of a qualification" (*viśeṣaṇasya śravaṇāt*), he raises it again with the intention of explaining further:
"In the heart" (*hṛdi*). The meaning is that, by the force of that [qualification], desires exist as residing in the Self. || 483 ||
For those whose desires are not rooted in the heart, that very [attainment] is indeed desirable, such as birth and so forth.
And I have already stated previously that this [cognition] does not exist apart from its own substratum.
He recalls what was stated in the passage beginning with "for the sake of [showing] the division of the Anāśrita" and so forth: "The Anāśrita in the heart. || 484 ||
This [universe], which is embodied, mortal, and existent, consists of earth, water, and fire.
From the statement "it is not a qualifier," there follows the conceptualization [of it] as being formless and so forth. // 485 //

Now he states that which he intended to say further, having already provided the objection and its resolution within the very statement itself: "The embodied," etc. For there is no restrictive rule that only that which differentiates is a qualifier; otherwise, the qualifiers of the three elements—such as "embodiedness" and so on—would also [erroneously] apply to the Self, which is unembodied. The meaning is that, because it is logically possible for [the term] to exclude desires residing in something else, the existence of desire and so forth in the Self is not established by virtue of the qualification. || 485 ||
It is said that fire is mobile by nature, mortal, eternal, and a burner.
Because of the hearing of these qualifiers, there can be no determination of these two, which are contradictory to them. (486)

Furthermore, he states that it is impossible to restrict [the definition] by saying that a qualifier is that which excludes [others], because [the self] is of the nature of motion: "calanātmeti" (it is of the nature of motion). || 486 ||
Since all latent impressions (vāsanās) reside in an object that is of the same nature as themselves.
How could those [qualities] exist in the inner self, which is unattached and distinct from all classes [of things]? (487)

It has been stated that because "residing in the heart" is a qualification of the essential nature—just as in the expression "the luminous, radiant form is fiery"—it does not follow from that [qualification] that the self (ātman) is established as the locus of desire and so forth. As for the claim that the latent impressions (vāsanā) of desire and so forth reside in the self, one must consider the alternative whether this refers to the Supreme Self or to the individual soul (jīva). He refutes the first position with the words "vāsya" (to be perfumed), anticipating the opponent's view that even the Supreme Self could be the object of perfuming.

"Also in the case of what is of the same class. If it is argued that "sameness of class" might also apply to that [mind] by virtue of its basis in desire and so forth, as well as the heart, he says "no": "It is unattached. || 487 ||
If it is intended to be stated that the wise one (prājña) is other than the inner self (pratyagātman), [then there would be a contradiction].
Because of the negations stated as "not this, not this," there is no possibility of its existence here.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "pratyak" (the inward-facing). "Prājña" refers to the individual soul (jīva). The word "iha" (here) denotes the sphere of scriptural discourse.
Having raised himself up from all desires, karmic actions, and the like without exception, he spoke to himself:
By the statement "That indeed is his this," desires and the like do not exist here [in that state]. (489)
He states that desires and the like do not exist in the Self even by considering such passages as "That indeed is his state where all desires have been attained," etc., with the words:
"Without remainder" (niḥśeṣa). || 489 ||
This refers to the passage beginning with "That indeed is his," which describes the inner form of the Prājña (the conscious self).
How can latent impressions, desire, karma, and so forth possess an internal nature? || 490 ||
Regarding the claim that the internal form of the Prājña consists of [the states] such as "dyed with saffron" (māhārajana) and so forth, he replies: "That indeed...
Since it is accepted that the internal form of the Prājña is a nature free from desire, karma, and the like, the meaning is that desire and the rest do not constitute its internal form. || 490 ||
It is engaged with forms such as yellow and red, which are the effects of karma.
Therefore, although it is indeed inexpressible, it can nevertheless be pointed out.

To state that the Self cannot be the substratum of desire and so forth because it would contradict its own statements, [the author] restates the system of Bhartṛprapañca found in the Mūrtāmūrta Brāhmaṇa, beginning with the words "pīta" (drunk). Regarding the connection with form consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which are the effects of karma, he states the result: "nirdeṣṭum" (to point out). || 499 ||
226 1. By his statement, O Nidhi; 2. ka. kha. gha. tanmahā. [Vol.
3, page 669]
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, chapter four:
"It is mental ideation (*bhāvanā*) itself, expanding, that attains the state of grossness."
By way of being unmanifest and so forth, it is designated as space, wind, and the sun.

Anticipating the objection as to how that which is inexpressible can be made expressible through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he first describes its gross form: "Meditative cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). That is to say, meditative cultivation, manifesting itself through the relationship of material cause and effect, attains a state of grossness consisting of the elements and their derivatives. || 492 ||
For it is that very [nature] which indeed wanes through states such as the formed and the formless.
Having colored the Self, which is devoid of qualities, it remains [therein]. || 493 ||

He says that this very [consciousness] also attains subtlety: "mūrtā" (embodied). The ellipsis to be supplied is "attains subtlety. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that there is a lack of evidence for the existence of any gross or subtle object of perception apart from mental cultivation (bhāvanā). Anticipating the objection—how can both types [of objects] bring about empirical usage within the Self—he says: "nirguṇam" (devoid of qualities). || 493 ||
This cultivation is multiform; it is the multiformity of the self.
It provides a covering for that which is without name or form, just as one covers a gem with a cloth. || 494 ||
He states the result regarding its connection with the conscious self: "The cultivation... (verse 494).
All this has been stated by you yourself in the context of discussing latent impressions (vāsanā).
Because this statement contradicts that [previous one], there is mutual inconsistency. (495)

He concludes the system of others with the words "ityādi" ("and so forth"). By the word "ādi," the postulation of the three heaps, the inclusion of the self under the term "heap of karma," and so on, are understood. Although this was stated in the context of mentioning specific details regarding the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the passage beginning with "tasya haitasya puruṣasya," he says "iha" ("here") to address what fault there is in the present case. Here, in this mantra, [he speaks of] desire and the rest—

The meaning is that the Self is not the substratum of desire and so forth, because your statement that "the Self exists as such by its own nature" contradicts your own previous statement asserting that the connection of desire with the Self is adventitious (aupādhika); thus, due to this mutual contradiction within your own explanation, the Self cannot be the locus of desire and the like.
If the self were also intended there as part of the mass of karma, [it would be included].
Because of the negation "not this, not that," it follows that there is only emptiness. || 496 ||

Furthermore, since the author of the *Mūrtāmūrta-brāhmaṇa*, while postulating three heaps, includes the Self within the term "heap of karma," he states that for that [Self], which is the object of negation, there can be no existence as the substratum of desire and so forth. Thus: "Karma... (Verse 496).
Or else, something other than the ultimate self is called "the self."
Let it be as you wish; it is not denied that he is the substratum for desire and the like. || 497 ||

The self is indeed twofold: the ultimate (paramārtha) and the non-ultimate (aparamārtha). An objection is raised that even if the non-ultimate self—which serves as the basis for desire and so forth—is negated because it is included within the aggregate of karma, emptiness does not follow, since the other [the ultimate self] remains. [The author] responds by accepting this consequence: "If it exists... (verse 497).
Even its subsistence in the form of potentiality within the causal self is logical.
This is due to its connection with a capacity, and not because the self is without a cause.

Desires are of two kinds: gross and subtle. Among these, one might object: "In this classification, where the non-ultimate self (*aparamārthātman*) is the substratum for the gross and the ultimate self (*paramārthātman*) for the subtle, how can your desired conclusion be established? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By power" (*śakti*). This means: "by way of that self in its subtle form. (498)

Nor is it accepted that the nature of the Supreme Self is merely being a cause; for [otherwise] there would follow the consequence of no liberation, and the commencement of the Śruti scriptures would be rendered purposeless. (499)
Anticipating the objection that it is improper to designate the Self as "without cause" since you yourself accept its causality, he says:

"And not... The meaning is this: even though [the Self] is a cause through ignorance (avidyā), such causality is not possible in reality; otherwise, liberation would be impossible, and consequently, the Upanishads intended for that purpose would never have been composed. || 499 ||
And because [the scripture] negates all things, such as grossness and so forth, within the inner self (pratyak).
Therefore, there can be no connection of qualifiers with the inner self.
Not only is there an impossibility of desire and the like in the Self, but rather an impossibility of the entire class of qualifiers; thus he says: "of the gross and so forth. (900)
That desires have the self as their locus is established neither by reasoning nor by scripture.
Due to their false interpretation, they hold that desires have the self as their locus. || 501 ||
He concludes the refutation of the opposing position: "It would entail the fallacy of self-dependence" (ātmāśrayatvam). || 101 ||
Thus, when the vital breaths have been withdrawn into the self for one who knows that [reality], [the state of liberation occurs].
Why, then, does a connection with a previous body not arise here in this same way? || 502 ||

Having stated the meaning of the mantra beginning with *yadā* as explained in the Bhāṣya, the interpretation of another [author] has been refuted. Now, he states the doubt to be removed by the passage beginning with *tadyathā*: "In this way" (*evam*). The sense of the objection is: even though the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) have been sublated within the self through knowledge for the knower, if he still exists in the body as before, there would be a continued connection with it; consequently, knowledge would be rendered useless. This is the point of the challenge.
By "here," the state of knowledge (vidyā-daśā) is understood. || 102 ||
Like the slough of a serpent, it is entirely born from the single cause of ignorance regarding the self.
Having abandoned [the sense of "mine"] through a cognition that accords with reality, one is free from possessiveness and free from egoism. || 503 ||

Demonstrating his disconnection from the body as before, he establishes the purposefulness of knowledge with the words "like a snake" (*sarpa*). Just as a snake remains after shedding its skin, devoid of the sense of "I" and so forth regarding it, so too this [knower], having abandoned the body and other such things—which arose from his own ignorance—by means of the knowledge of reality, remains free from the sense of "mine" and the like; this is the meaning. || 503 ||
Even while existing within the body and so forth, [he does so] with regard to worldly perception.
He does not regard the body and other such things with the notion that they are the self or belong to the self.
"How can one who exists within the body and so forth become free from the sense of 'mine-ness' (mamatva) and the like toward them? To this, he says: "Even while existing... (vartamāno'pi).
Because of the destruction of the cause of the genitive case-meaning through the realization of things as they truly are.
The complete reality abides as neither excluded nor followed along. || 505 ||

He states the reason why one who, through the perspective of ignorance, is established in the body and so forth, does not yet partake in notions such as "mine-ness" regarding them from his own [enlightened] perspective: "The sixth case-ending," etc.
The meaning is that because ignorance—the cause of the connection with the body and so forth—has been removed by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). Then, in what form does the knower abide?
To this he says: "Unrestricted," etc. (Verse 105).
Speech is said to be like the slough of a snake that has cast it off.
Having died, she was cast by a serpent into a hole within an anthill.
Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he begins the word-by-word commentary with the words "ahī" etc. The connection is with the verb "śayīta" (he should lie down). || 106 ||
In this context, the term "dead" (mṛta) denotes the separation from the physical body.
Because it rests upon an anthill, its [the earth's] reflection is said to be "pratyasta" (reverted). || 507 ||
He states the distinct meaning of the two words "mṛtā" (dead) and "pratyastā" (cast down) in the phrase "ahideha" (like a snake's slough). || 107 ||
The activity concerning the sloughed skin of a snake has thus been described.
But the state of being free from possessiveness and egoism is based on the analogy of the snake.
Two similes are intended here: the serpent and its slough. Among these, the simile of the serpent’s slough for the body of the knower has already been explained;
he restates this with the word *ahi* ("serpent"). The activity consisting of the separation from the serpent's body and its lying within an anthill, and so forth, is the illustration.

He states that the serpent is the illustration for the knower and proceeds to explain it with the words *nirmama* ("free from 'mine-ness'"). The word "of the knower" (*viduṣaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 108 ||
Just as when its own slough has been cast off by a snake, it is no longer as it was before.
A snake, whether going out or entering, follows its own slough.
He states the method of explanation: "In the cavity," etc. (109).
Neither the notion "I" nor the notion "mine" arises there in the formless realm.
Just as it is for that very [Self], so it is for the inner Self existing right there. || 510 ||
Because the cause of connection has been eradicated, it is devoid of any relation to a self.
The body, both subtle and gross, lies [there], its sense of oneness with the Self destroyed. || 511 ||

The phrase "I am not" clearly demonstrates the snake's disregard for its discarded slough. Having explained the two analogies, he restates the analogy of the slough with the words "Just as... He then explains the application of that analogy to the subject at hand with the words "In this way...
This is stated as the illustration of the snake's slough and its corresponding application.
Now, the meaning corresponding to the illustration—the snake—is being stated. || 512 ||
1. "It is called *vatī*. 2. Ga. reads "*yatā va*. [Vol. 3, page 672] 4.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1805.

Having restated what was previously said, he introduces the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth. He says "ahīti. The use of the hiatus (*visandhi*) is for the purpose of taking up the opening words of the sentence. || 112 ||
In this case, the connection between the snake and the slough is mutual, as previously described.
Its persistence is here emphatically denied; it is not intended to be asserted. || 513 ||

One might object: "In the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), since the snake and its slough exist as distinct entities, should it not be the same in the case of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*)—the wise man and his body? Otherwise, their [respective] states would not be established. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] shows the intended point in both cases with the words: "Of the snake and its slough. Here, the phrase "in this [example]" refers to the statement of the illustrative example. "As before" means as in the prior state, due to their mutual separation; however, effort involves many specific...

The mention of "ṇa" [in the rule] implies that, likewise in the case of the illustrative application (dāṣṭantika), what is intended to be expressed is the negation of the connection termed false conceit (mithyābhimāna); however, its continued existence as a distinct entity is not intended to be expressed—this is the remainder [of the meaning]. || 113 ||
The doctrine of primordial matter (pradhānavāda) holds that [the self] would attain [liberation] if there were a distinction between the body and the self.
Stability is what is intended to be expressed here, and that has been refuted many times.

He states the fault in the opposing view: "pradhāna... and so on. The word "iha" (here) refers to the state of knowledge (*vidyāvasthā*). Anticipating the objection that this might be an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says:
"nyaṣedhi... (it was prohibited). || 114 ||
However, this word "atha" has the sense of a reason, because the statement of a reason is the subject under discussion.
The intended meaning of the cause is the abandonment of the body along with its causes. || 515 ||

Having set aside the incidental matter, he now states the meaning of the word *atha* (then). In the phrase "but in the sense of a reason" (*hetvarthe tu*), he provides the reason for the restriction (*niyama*) among the other possible meanings. Regarding the expression "because of the statement of a reason," the words "in this case" (*atre*)—referring to the passage "then the mortal becomes immortal"—are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. He clarifies the meaning in the form of a reason with the words "of that which has a cause" (*sakāraṇasya*). By the word *atha*, it is indicated that the reason for [attaining] "bodilessness" (*aśarīratva*) and so forth is the destruction of the body together with ignorance (*ajñāna*).
This is the meaning. || 515 ||
Just as there can be no connection with a garland without first taking up the knowledge of the garland.
Likewise, the connection of the inward Self with the body does not exist apart from ignorance of the Self.
Anticipating the objection that ignorance is not the cause of the body because the Self is by nature unattached, he says: "A garland," etc.
The meaning is that a natural connection with the body and so forth is indeed impossible for that which is unattached. || 116 ||
When false knowledge, along with its cause, has been destroyed by the fire-brand of inward-facing gnosis, [the Self remains].
Because its nature is "not this, not this" (neti neti), it is therefore bodiless.
Having restated the meaning of the word "atha," he takes up the qualification "bodiless" with the word "pratyak. || 117 ||

"For that reality which is pure consciousness, devoid of darkness, and inherently lacking direction, space, time, and so forth, there can be no connection with a body possessing space and other such attributes, except through ignorance (tamas).

He explains its meaning [with the verse beginning] "svataḥ" (inherently). The analysis of the compound is "adigdeśakālādeḥ" (lacking direction, space, time, etc.). This is for the purpose of [explaining] the union with and separation from the body.
It distinguishes [it] by saying "it dispels darkness. || 118 ||

A connection with a conceptualized [entity] does not belong to a conceptualized thing.
If it exists even during the time of ignorance, how much more so when that ignorance has been dispelled? || 519 ||
He establishes by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument that there is no connection with a body for the wise, stating: "by that which is imagined. || 119 ||
By the word "boneless," the gross body is here negated.
Likewise, by the word "bodiless" (aśarīra), the subtle body is negated. || 520 ||
Now, regarding the Mādhyandina recension which reads "this is boneless and bodiless" (*anasthiko 'śarīraḥ*), he explains the meaning of the word *anasthika*. [He says: "As for *anasthika*...
Anticipating the objection that the word *aśarīra* would then be redundant, he says: "Likewise" (*tathā*). || 120 ||
By the statement negating the subtle body, the gross body is also negated.
Therefore, an effort to refute them is not mentioned by the Kaṇva Śruti.
In that case, since there is no mention of the removal of the gross body in the Kāṇva recension, he says: "Subtle... (verse 121).
Or rather, by the word "bodiless" (aśarīra) in that scriptural passage, there is the negation of the subtle body (liṅga).
Because the gross [form] is prohibited by the statement "it is not the nectar," there is no negation [of the subtle form]. || 522 ||

Anticipating the objection that—according to the principle that "that which is implied by the literal meaning [of a passage] is not the intended meaning of the injunction"—the negation of the gross body in the Kāṇva recension might not be what is intended, he says, "Or else... In the Mādhyandina recension, the meaning of the two qualifiers is stated collectively in the Śruti concerning the Immortal.
The witness is designated by the word "prāṇa" as that which is to be qualified.
But by the word "Brahman" itself, its specific qualification is expressed. || 523 ||
Anticipating the objection that it is not appropriate for the aforementioned liberated sage to be designated by the word "prāṇa" because his vital breaths have been removed, [the author] says:
"of the witness. He states the meaning of the word "brahman": "Brahman. || 123 ||
The witness possesses a second, and Brahman is beyond perception.
By negating its cause, this statement negates it. || 524 ||

He states the intended meaning of the two terms in apposition: "of the witness," etc. The cause of that [ignorance] is the ignorance of the Self, which is the cause of its being accompanied by a second and so forth. || 924 ||
It begins with names, ends with peace, and rests upon the cause of the vital breath.
By the statement "Brahman is the vital breath," that [notion] is negated within the Self.

It is not only through the knowledge arising from the statement "Prāṇa is Brahman"—which [negates] duality and so forth—that negation occurs; rather, he says "Name," etc., to show that by that [knowledge], everything else, along with its cause, is also negated. || 125 ||
And let there be no association between Brahman and the self, like that of a black snake.
Thus, the Vedic scripture, which wards off the notion of association, states "it is indeed light.

Having declared that "breath is Brahman itself," the statement "it is indeed light" is inappropriate, for the word "light" (tejas), which is conventionally established in reference to the sun and so forth, cannot apply to the Witness. (Variant reading: "which wards off [association]").

Anticipating the objection that [the term] "Brahman" cannot be applied [to the individual self], he says: "Brahman. The scripture states that the vital breath (prāṇa), the witness (sākṣin), and light (tejas) are indeed Brahman and the Self.

The connection is with the word "concealing" (*saṃvoriṇī*). Demonstrating the possibility of their conjunction through an illustration, he indicates the method of exclusion by means of another verse: "Nor is there an inapplicability of the word 'light' (*tejas*) to that [Brahman], because of the scriptural statement 'of its light,' etc., since it is the illuminator of all and is the referent of the word 'light'. This is the intended meaning. || 126 ||
The difference between the words "Brahman" and "Ātman" appears only due to the difference in what they exclude.
In reality, however, the Self is one alone, just as the qualities such as humility (amānitva) and so forth are one.

Since Brahman and the Self are non-different, how can there be an appearance of their difference? To this, he says: "By excluding... (vyāvartya). The meaning is that the two words "that" (tat) refer to the possessors of those [qualities]. || 927 ||
For in both cases there is the restrictive emphasis: "Brahman alone" and "splendor alone."
This is for the purpose of negating association, so that it does not become like [the case of] "blue lotus" and so forth. (528)

Having stated "Brahman alone," when it is further said "only light," [the author] states there [the following] to negate the conjunction of Brahman and the Self: "Brahman alone. The meaning is that the two occurrences of the particle *eva* (alone) serve to exclude conjunction. The sense of the word *hi* (for) is that the capacity of Śruti to establish a meaning through its own power is well-known elsewhere as well. He demonstrates the manner of that negation by means of a gesture: "Let it not be so" (mā bhūt). || 528 ||
Of the one who is all things, whose nature is the ignorance of the inner self.
In the case of an effect, only sublation by verbal testimony is accepted, and no other. || 529 ||

Now, one might object that even due to ignorance regarding the Self, agency and so forth cannot possibly exist, because the Self is non-different from Brahman, which is beyond saṃsāra; and thus, there can be no distinction between action and its factors within the inner self (pratīc) arising from one's own ignorance. To this, he says: "Of Brahman and the Self" (brahmātmanoḥ). || 973 ||
And likewise, even if it were indeed preceded by the aforementioned knowledge, as has been stated.
The cognition of an external object conforms to the actual state of the thing itself. || 574 ||

[Objection: Surely, the manifestation of every insentient thing is preceded by the manifestation of the conscious Self (*cidātman*), and that [Self] always possesses manifestation through knowledge of its own nature; so how can there be the attainment of evil due to ignorance of it? To this, he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). This means: while there is non-difference between Brahman and the Self. Because, in accordance with the actual state of reality, the Self—whose nature is an indivisible, ever-shining essence—possesses the inherent quality of being the illuminator of all, whereas the non-Self...
The meaning is that, due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*), it is impossible for it to manifest without depending on a conscious self (*ajaḍātman*). || 974 ||
Nevertheless, one who does not know Brahman does not attain that state of absolute liberation;
therefore, the knower of Brahman attains it, for the Śruti declares: "There is no other path. (575)

If it is claimed that the manifestation of the self's own nature (*svarūpa-sphūrti*) is desired as being existent, then, since liberation would be established without effort by depending on knowledge, there would be no connection with evil;
thus he says, "Even so" (*tathāpi*). [This means] without the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the nature of non-dual, indivisible Brahman arising from the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).

1815. The meaning is that liberation does not result from mere knowledge. Having explained the passage beginning with "This," he explains the passage beginning with "By that" (*tena*). Regarding "by that":

By means of the path of knowledge already described, the knower of Brahman goes to liberation; for it is established by scripture that no other path leads there. Therefore, the meaning is that one who is not a knower of Brahman does not partake in liberation. || 175 ||
And regarding the question "What is the cause of Brahmā and Viśva?", our Śruti says:
One who has performed meritorious deeds and is radiant with splendor shall become the most excellent among those who know the delight of Brahman.
He takes up the two words beginning with "puṇyakṛt" in accordance with the requirement of syntactic expectancy, [stating]: "Brahman. || 176 ||
For it is because of this that a person of pure intellect is born here as a doer of merit.
Then, with a purified being, he perceives that Brahman directly within himself.

Having stated that both [the knower of Brahman and the performer of merit] are causes for the knowledge of Brahman, he establishes that the former is the cause for that [knowledge]. [The verse begins with] "puṇya... The locative case in "iha" is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) from among those under discussion. Therefore, the meaning of the word "atha" (therefore) is that the state of being a performer of merit is the cause for the knowledge of Brahman. || 177 ||
By the word "splendor" (tejas), it is precisely the completely purified sattva that is denoted.
In that state, existence would be luminous, characterized by a nature inclined toward the inner self.

To state that "being composed of *tejas*" (*taijasatva*) is also a reason in that context, he explains the meaning of the word *taijasa*: "By the word *tejas*... [verse 578]: "In this context, the person of pure intellect who is inclined toward the Self is *taijasa*."
Knowledge arises in people through the destruction of sinful karma.
Just as one sees one's own self within oneself, as if in the surface of a mirror.

Regarding the phrase "the arising of knowledge therein," he states the authority for it: "Knowledge. To the question of why knowledge depends upon the purity of the intellect (*buddhi-śuddhi*), he says: "Just as... (979).
By means of the fire-oblations pertaining to the womb, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle;
By means of the great sacrifices and the ritual offerings, this body is made fit for Brahman.
Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification.

When it is asked, "How does the destruction of evil lead to the birth of knowledge for those of pure intellect, and how, in turn, does that [knowledge] destroy [evil]?", he states another verse: "By means of the womb... and so forth.
In that very context, he cites the agreement of the Blessed One: "The yogi... || 180 ||
Or the yogi may here be of the nature of light (taijasa), by virtue of his capacity for inward vision.
For one whose intellect is drawn away by sense objects is incapable of perceiving the inner self. || 581 ||

Anticipating the objection that the state of being "luminous" (*taijasatva*) is irrelevant since the purity of intellect is established by the very fact of performing meritorious deeds (*puṇyakṛttva*), he states another point: "Or the yogi. He provides the reason for the luminosity of the yogi whose intellect is concentrated: "The inner self... [and so on]. To the question, "How is the capacity for seeing the Self attributed to one-pointed intellect, when everyone is already able to see their own self as 'I'? he replies: "Regarding objects... [and so on]. The inner...

Because of the Vedic scripture stating, "No wise man whose intellect is not concentrated on the nature of the Self has attained success; [only he] beheld the inner Self," the meaning is that concentration of the intellect is the cause for knowledge, since the practice of *nididhyāsana* (repeated contemplation) is enjoined. || 181 ||

When the being is thus purified, there arises steady mindfulness.

It has been stated that there are scriptural texts (*śruti*); he now cites them, beginning with the words "In which. By the word "which" (*yat*), the mind (*citta*) is meant;

for it is the subject under discussion in the passage, "This subtle Self is [grasped] by the mind," and thus the phrase "this Self" (*eṣa ātmā*) is understood as the remainder of the sentence. In that very context, he quotes another scriptural text: "In purity... (*satva-eva*).

He says that [the text] enjoins for the arising of knowledge with the word "that" (*tam*). He concludes the aforementioned scriptural passages with the words "those based on scripture" (*śrautāni*).

In this world, some great-souled ones, together with the severing of their own delusion, [attain liberation].
They say there is a combination [of the two] by virtue of merit and spiritual luster, as well as through knowledge. (586)

Having stated his own intended interpretation of the passage beginning with "tena" (by that), he restates another interpretation, beginning with "iha" (here). The connection is: "by means of knowledge, there is the cutting away of delusion. || 986 ||
The yogi who performs meritorious deeds and possesses meritorious karma is called taijasa.
Being solely devoted to the knowledge of Brahman, and being a performer of meritorious deeds characterized by radiance.
One who is capable is able to perceive through yoga the identity taught in the scriptures.

To demonstrate the manner of their combination, he states the meaning of the two words [in the verse] as "the performer of merit" (puṇyakṛt). A "yogī" is one who worships the Sūtras and so forth, or one who has attained perfection through the Yoga-śāstra.

When merit and demerit have ceased, those who are fearless of rebirth [attain that state].
The peaceful renunciants go [to him]; salutation to that Self which is liberation. || 592 ||

There, clarifying what was stated—that pride arises [from such a view]—he states the authoritative proof for the fact that actions cannot be directly combined with knowledge for the sake of liberation: "Not by merit... (592).
Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.
Even though there is no combination of knowledge and action, he says "abandon" [in verse 993] out of the apprehension that such a combination might exist through discriminative knowledge.
Free from longing, free from undertaking, free from salutation, and free from praise.
The gods know him to be a Brahmin who, though his karma is exhausted, remains undecayed.

Anticipating the objection that even for those who know Brahman there might be a combination of knowledge with rituals such as praise because they still perceive them, he says: "To one free from desire" (*nirāśiṣam*).

"Non-commencement" (*anārambha*) means the non-performance of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*). "Untaintedness" (*akṣīṇatvam*) means the non-practice of forbidden acts (*niṣiddha-karma*). There is no wealth for a brahmin such as this: namely, singleness, equanimity, and truthfulness.
Virtue, steadfastness, laying aside the rod of punishment, uprightness, and then withdrawal from all worldly activities. ||595||
Regarding the non-combination of knowledge and action, he states another passage beginning with "No" (na), etc. Unity (*ekatā*) means independence; [it refers to] indifference toward all [else].
[The phrase] "the great medicine for both" [is used]. [The word] "does" (*karoti*) is from manuscript *gha*.

The laying down of the rod and devotion to non-violence. || 995 ||
Deceit is the root of wealth; patience, beauty, youth, and physical form are the roots of desire.

Any other philosophical view different from the one previously stated arises from the perception of a single self (aikātmya).

Tamas has many individual characteristics through its divisions such as tamas, moha, and so forth.

Anticipating the question, "For what purpose is 'blind darkness' (andhaṃ tamaḥ) used as a qualification?", he says: "Tamas... By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and utter darkness (andhatamasa). || 199 ||

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is a mention of the remaining sovereign powers (aiśvarya). || 602 ||
That which, through the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, has consciousness alone as its cause.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that by the word 'knowledge' (vidyā) here, the higher knowledge (paravidyā) is intended, since that is the subject under discussion? How then can they enter into blind darkness when attached to that?

In this context, "knowledge" (vidyā) is also defined as that which illuminates the meaning of karma.
Those who take delight in that [world] are indifferent to the meaning of the Vedāntas. || 604 ||
But those virtuous ones enter your limbs, and from there they proceed further into the supreme darkness.
Due to the predominance of false knowledge, there would be an abundance of darkness.

Having explained the meaning of the word "knowledge," he states the meaning of the sentence: "In that... Now, one might object: "Darkness (tamas) is indeed ignorance (ajñāna), and since that is the absence of knowledge, it does not become more; for increase and non-increase are not possible as dimensions (parimāṇa) within it. To this, he says: "Falsehood (mithyā)."

Those who delight in ignorance take refuge in Īśvara and acknowledge the authority of the Upaniṣads as having Him as their subject; thus, they possess a great lack of discrimination (*aviveka*). The Mīmāṃsakas, however, who are devoted to ritual action, hate Īśvara and declare that the Upaniṣads lack authority because they are subordinate to injunctions and have only "what is to be done" (*kārya*) as their purpose. Therefore, due to their excess of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), their lack of discrimination—which is the cause of that [false knowledge]—is also abundant; yet this is not a mere absence of knowledge.
The meaning is that knowledge [is the cause] because it is the primary cause of the world. || 604 || 605 ||
