Desiring what, or for whose sake, would one then cause this body to suffer?

Having introduced the passage beginning with "this" (*ayam*) by first addressing the expectancy [of the reader], he explains it with the words beginning with "how" (*katham*). The meaning is that one should know, through such statements as "This Self is Brahman," "I am Brahman," and "That thou art," that "I am this Person known as the Supreme Self.
He takes up the latter part of the verse: "Desiring what? (*kim icchan*). The word "then" (*tadā*) refers to the state of knowledge. || 610 ||
Because all desires have been fulfilled through the awakening of one's own innate wish.
Therefore, desire is implied here by the statement, "desiring what? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
He states that the word "what" (kiṃ) has the sense of a challenge: "of all desires. The word "here" (iha) refers to the speech of the wise. || 611 ||
And because one perceives nothing other than the inner self (pratyagātman).
For whose sake, then, is this entire non-self drawn forth from that [Self]? (6.12)
He states the meaning of the phrase "for whose sake" as follows: "the inner self," etc.; the connection is that "all that is non-self. ||612||
How could a Brahmin suffer from the fever of worldly existence while seeking the fever of the body?
For one who is free from attachment, there is no connection whatsoever with this body.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "the body" by saying "the body. He clarifies the aforementioned logical inconsistency by saying "of the one who is unattached.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies the mutual contradiction between being unattached and being attached. || 613 ||
Therefore, the inner self does not suffer through the suffering of the body and so forth.
Through awakening, there is the destruction of the cause for connection with all suffering without exception. || 614 ||

He states the conclusion resulting from the absence of such a relationship: "No. Furthermore, he says that for this reason as well, the Self is not subject to suffering: "In its entirety... [Verse 1138]. "Not in any way whatsoever."
Furthermore, the entry into a body that is a nest of unbearable and great suffering— [from *Ānandagiri’s* commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā*, Chapter 4, Brāhmaṇa 4, p. 1821].

"How could one enter a body through the total integration of the cause, which is ignorance? (615). He explains the meaning of the Mādhyandina recension’s reading, "he would follow along with the body," by means of the word *bhūyaḥ*. The particle *ca* serves to exclude the possibility of the knower's association with another body. The word *bhūyaḥ*, however, denotes immediate succession to the falling away of the current body; it is connected either with that [particle *ca*] or taken as a whole, as follows:
May it be heard. || 619 ||
But by the grace of the Teacher and the Preceptor, all their sins have been utterly destroyed.
Thus, the Lord, the witness of the intellect and other faculties, is awakened and likewise solitary.

He explains the meaning of the portion of the mantra beginning with "yasya" (of whom): "Śāstrā" etc. The connection is as follows: he by whom the Supreme Self has been attained and directly realized is the creator of all. || 616 ||
Because the body is excessively consumed by the fiery energies of food.
Because of that, this body is called *saṃdeha*; the form *saṃdegha* occurs due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). || 617 ||

He states the meaning of the word *saṃdeha*: "In this [context]," etc. That which is thoroughly accumulated (*saṃdihyate*) is what is meant; that is to say, it is piled up. To the question, "How then is the letter *gh* used in the Vedic scripture?", he replies: "*Saṃdegha*," etc. (617)
Because of the extreme confusion of internal, elemental, and divine objects.
Therefore, this [system] is considered profound because of the relationship between the subordinate and the primary qualities.
It establishes the impenetrability of the body: "ādhyātmika... etc.

The meaning is that because the internal and other objects—being subordinate to the [guṇas]—are incapable of being separated from one another, they are fused within this body; therefore, it is impenetrable. || 618 ||
In this profound doubt, the self has entered like the sun reflected in water.
He by whom [this] has been known through discernment shall be the Lord of the Universe. || 619 ||
He explains the word "entered" [in the verse] as "doubt. He states the meaning of the phrase "he is the creator of the universe" as "having discerned.
Through the realization of the true nature of the inner self, everything has been accomplished by him.
Since all goals of human endeavor have been attained without remainder, no further task remains.
Fearing the objection that the knower of Brahman cannot be the creator of the universe because the universe does not exist [for him], he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*).

He states the reason for the knower’s status as the creator of all: "Without remainder" (*niḥśeṣa*). The meaning is that since everything is included within the fruit of knowledge, it is said that everything has been created by the knower. || 620 ||
For he is indeed the creator of all; therefore, he is designated by that very name.
Because he has accomplished all that was to be done, this world belongs to that world-transcender.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "sa hi" (for he). Regarding the word "sa" (he), he clarifies what is referred to by that pronoun. He says: "kṛta" (having performed). [This refers to] by means of knowledge.
[Vol. 3, page 689] 1822 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

The meaning is that the wise man is called "the doer of all" because he assimilates everything to his own self. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "of him" (*tasya*) as follows: "In the world," etc.
This supreme Self is the very nature of that wise one, because no other nature is possible for him; such is the meaning. || 621 ||
Or, because he knows the cause of all produced effects without exception.
"In this way, he would indeed be the creator of the universe, because of his grasping [the cause] through the knowledge of *itihāsa*.

(622) He states another meaning for the passage beginning with "he is the creator of the universe" (*sa viśvakṛt*), etc., [starting with the word] "niśeṣa" (remainderless). Even though the ignorant person (*ajña*) does not possess the nature of the universe, the realization of that [nature] is not established for the knower of the Self (*ātmajña*). Thus, from where could there be the designation "he is the creator of the universe," given that the word "he" (*sa*) refers to the wise man? This is the objection.

What does he say? "Thus. For since he is the cause of everything—meaning that it is the Knower himself who, while in the state of ignorance, is the creator of the universe by means of that [ignorance]—this is the sense. || 622 ||
This world is his direct manifestation, I who have been awakened to the realization that "I am Brahman."
In order to dispel the suspicion of difference, it is said: "That indeed is the world. (623)

He explains the passage beginning with "of him" (*tasya*). Regarding "of him": he who is the immutable conscious Self (*cidātmā*), the creator of the universe due to his own ignorance (*ajñāna*), is that by which—through knowledge—the ignorant state and so forth are cast off and directly realized; for such a knower, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the direct Self (*ātman*).
Alternatively, it means that this knower is the direct Self of that Supreme One. He states the meaning of the phrase "he indeed is the world" (*sa u loka eva*).

Regarding the word "bhedeti": when "of that" (*tasya*) is stated, a doubt regarding difference (*bheda*) arises; in order to dispel that, the sentence beginning with "sa" (*he*) is provided. The meaning is: for he is the supreme nature of the knower, or he is [the nature] of the Supreme; therefore, there is no suspicion of difference. || 623 ||
If only we were virtuous, we would have accomplished our purpose right here and now.
We know Brahman as the inner self (pratyak) somehow through the destruction of impurities. || 624 ||

Explaining the passage beginning with "right here" (*ihaiva*), he states the fruit of the aforementioned knowledge of non-difference: "Right here" (*iha*). If, by the power of infinite merit accumulated over many births, we come to know the Supreme Brahman as our own inner self (*pratyak*) through the removal of the sins that obstruct the knowledge of reality, then—even while remaining in this body which is beset by manifold misfortunes—we become that very Brahman itself by virtue of having attained the supreme human goal through knowledge; therefore, [we are] great—
The meaning is that the knowledge of Brahman is the rightful inheritance. || 624 ||
If we do not know what lies beyond this, it is because we follow the scriptures and the teachings of our masters.
If that ignorant child is not protected, great ruin will ensue.
Explaining the passage beginning with "na cet" (if not), he states that one incurs sin (*pratyavāya*) through ignorance. Regarding "na cet":

by beginning with the plural and then indicating [the subject] again in the singular, he suggests that plurality is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Regarding "avedinam" (one who does not know):

the meaning of the word "atha" is drawn forward as "tadā" (then). If, according to the scriptures and other authorities, we do not experience the Supreme Brahman as our own inner self (*pratyaktayā*), [then...]
The meaning is that at such a time, that great ruin which awaits me—who am devoid of discernment and like a child—might suddenly seize and overwhelm me. || 129 ||
And he who is unwise regarding the unknowable Self incurs great ruin.
Furthermore, there is great ruin here, arising from destruction and its consequences.
1 ka. kha. 'isyavi | 2 gha. to'sya vyaṃ | 3 gha. ṣaḥ sa pa | [vol 3, page 690] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 1823.
The non-discrimination of the self alone is thus indicated by way of grammatical coreferentiality. || 627 ||

Having stated that one who lacks knowledge possesses the state of being an object (*karmatva*) and that one whose [knowledge] has perished possesses the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), he states another method [of explanation] with the words "the great destruction" (*vinaṣṭim*). He explains the lack of knowledge with the word "Self" (*ātma*). The meaning is: he who is devoid of self-knowledge remains under the sway of that which is called "great destruction," relying upon it. What is this "great destruction"? For there is no such thing as "greatness" in annihilation (*dhvaṃsa*); to this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "the great destruction" (*vināṣṭari*): the connection is that because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "great destruction," it is indicated that it is indeed the ignorance of the Self (*ātmāvidyā*).

To the question, "Since the ignorance of the Self is of the nature of an undivided, unborn reality, how can it be 'destruction' even if it is 'great'? he says: "Because of its being destruction, etc. (verses 626–627).
The latter half is spoken for the purpose of illuminating the meaning already stated.
By means of the scriptural passage "Those who know that," for the sake of clearly understanding the meaning. || 628 ||

Fearing that the second half of the verse beginning with "ye tad" might be redundant with the first half, he says: "of the matter already stated. The construction is as follows: the meaning of the first half is restated by the second half in the form of the scriptural text "ye tad viduḥ" for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*), and this elaboration is for the purpose of ensuring a clear comprehension of the matter already stated. In this regard, the meaning of the first quarter-verse is elaborated by the third quarter-verse, and the meaning of the second quarter-verse [is elaborated] by the fourth quarter-verse.
The division is as follows: "dena" [is the first part]. || 628 ||
Being Brahman indeed even before realization, one becomes so through the awakening to Brahman.
O Brahmā, we have become unattainable by others, like the tenth [digit] of ten.

He concludes the meaning of the mantra with the words "Brahman indeed. For we are in reality Brahman even prior to knowledge; therefore, having appeared as non-Brahman due to ignorance of that [Brahman], we become Brahman once ignorance has departed through the knowledge arising from the sentence. We do not obtain Brahman through knowledge as something previously unobtained, like heaven and so forth; rather, it is like the tenth boy who, by means of the knowledge arising from the sentence "You are the tenth," shakes off his ignorance.
The meaning is that one attains the tenth self in that same manner. || 629 ||
When one truly realizes this divine Self as "I am Brahman," then...
He beholds that Lord of the past and the future directly before his eyes.
Because of the attainment of the Lord as one's own inner self, there is then the destruction of the distinction between them.
Because he has attained mastery over what is to be ruled, he does not feel aversion toward it. || 631 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "yadā" (when) as follows: "Brahman," etc. The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is an explanation of the word "face-to-face" (*ābhimukhyena*). When one perceives—that is, realizes—"I am" that very Self, the Lord of all, the Supreme Self, which was previously described as self-luminous, in accordance with the instruction of a teacher, then, because of the attainment of the Supreme as one's own inner subject (*pratyaktvena*), the delusion of difference is destroyed; and consequently, even that which was previously apprehended as undesirable, namely the state of being an object of rule (*īśitavyatva*), [ceases].
The construction is: "Because of the power of knowledge alone, he does not feel aversion toward the cessation of this [world]. || 630 || 631 ||
Everyone desires protection because they are afflicted by fear of the Lord.
But this [person], because of being non-different from that, desires protection from it. || 632 ||
1. Kha, Ga: *vainamā*; 2. Gha: *menamā*.
[Vol. 3, page 691] 1824 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]—
He analyzes the fourth quarter that has been introduced: "guptim" (protection). The ellipsis is "because there is an absence of fear due to its non-differentiation from that.
From which words turn back, together with the mind, unable to reach it.
"The knower of Brahman as bliss does not fear"—such is the declaration of the scripture. (633)

He states the authority for the absence of fear in the wise: "Since... Here, the section on non-composition (*asaṃdhi*) is introduced in order to provide a justification according to the literal wording of the text.
Nor does he criticize [others], because he has completely destroyed all causes for discord.
Through the vision of the single self, the wise one [realizes this] from the scripture which says, "But where there is [oneness]," and so forth.

He states a different meaning for the passage beginning with "not from that" (*na tataḥ*) with the words "or not" (*na vā*). He provides the proof for the destruction of all duality, together with its cause, through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) with the verse beginning "where" (*yatra*). || 634 ||
Because it is the cause for the transcendence of time, which is the cause of all transformations without exception.
The occurrence of the sixfold modifications, such as birth and so forth, is not admitted for that [Self]. || 635 ||
Having shown that knowledge has an immediate fruit, he states the purport of the mantra beginning with "yasmāt" (from which): "niḥśeṣa... [verse 11.82911].
Since this time, being subject to transformation, has produced the world of births from that which is prior.
The year revolves by means of its own constituent parts, the days.
That is the light even of lights; the gods worship it as the source of life.

Having stated that this sentence is intended to establish the immutability (*kūṭasthatva*) of the true nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is the object of knowledge, he explains its words, beginning with "Arvāk" (Before). This time known as the year, by means of its own parts—days and nights—continually transforms the aggregate of effects;
yet, even before that [time], they meditate upon that immutable Self as the light of lights and as Life itself. Therefore, by Him—
The meaning is that you, sirs, are luminous and renowned. || 636 ||
It is immortal light because of its immutability, due to its transcending the realm of death.
Because he causes time to age, the Self is considered "Kālañjara" in the Śruti.
In that regard, he establishes its immortality [by the word] "because of immutability" (*kauṭasthyāt*). Immutability is the reason for the absence of being within the sphere of death;
therefore, the meaning is that light is immortal. Furthermore, he states [the following] by the words "of time" (*kālasya*) to show that there is no alteration in the Supreme caused by time.

The meaning is as follows: from the Vedic texts stating "Jhaḥ is Kālaka, the possessor of qualities, the knower of all" and "he who would cause all things to be digested," it is certain that the transformation of Time is caused by the Supreme Self; therefore, its transformation is not caused by anything else. Alternatively, the construction is: "That which is considered in various Vedic passages as this Self becomes 'Kālajara' (the devourer of time) because of its swallowing of time."

For it is said in the *Śvetāśvataropaniṣadbhāṣya*: having taken the root text "kālakāra" (the maker of time), [it] is explained as follows: 1. ... and his course; 2. ... [of] people. saṃ. Ga. tiścāsya | Kha. Ga. 'jjanān || saṃ.
"Time cooks all beings indeed, by means of the existent Self. — [Brāhmaṇa 4, with the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri]. 1825.
Time ripens and follows that which is ripe; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.
In that place where he is cooked, Time is indeed not the master—
not of Time itself, nor of Death, nor of anything moving or stationary.
"The Blessed Lord alone rules; I tell you this as the truth. And in the Mokṣadharma:
"Having struck down all volitions, one should establish the mind in pure being (sattva)."
"Having caused the mind to enter into the *sattva* [quality], one then becomes Kālañjara. || 637 ||
Of this entity consisting of cause and effect, which is of the nature of both existence and non-existence.
The Supreme Self is established by its own nature; his lifespan exists for the sake of others.

One might raise the objection that even if there is no alteration in the conditions of time for another [entity], it does not follow that it is immutable, because its lifespan exists, and because that lifespan varies from one living being to another; anticipating this, he says: "bhāva" (existence). How is it that, although self-established, it is the life-force of the phenomenal world? To this he replies: "asya" (of this). Since the phenomenal world of cause and effect is insentient, it lacks both existence and manifestation per se; therefore, [it depends on] the Supreme—
The meaning is that the self itself is its own essential nature. || 638 ||
The Gandharvas, the Pitṛs, the Devas, along with the Rākṣasas and the Asuras.
In which all people, ending with the five elements up to the sky, are established.

Having explained the immutability (*kūṭasthatva*), self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), and the state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmatva*), and having demonstrated that the Self is the substratum of all mental constructions by means of the mantra beginning with "In whom" (*yasmin...*), [the author] accepts that the intended meaning is the identity of the knower with Brahman, and states the meaning of the first half-verse:
"The Gandharvas... The connection is: "I consider him alone to be [that]. (639)
Or rather, they may be the five beginning with breath (prāṇa) and ending with food (anna), because that is what is heard in the scripture.
In the absence of food, these [names] are intended for the Kāṇvas together with Jyotis.
I consider that very one, the causal self, to be the immortal knower of the immortal.

Fearing that this might contradict the sūtra stating "The vital breaths and so forth [are the five], because of the supplementary passages," he states another position: "Or else. He raises the objection: "In the supplementary passage 'the breath of the breath' and so forth, the Mādhyandinas also recite 'food,' whereas the Kāṇvas do not; how then, in their view, is the number five completed? Anticipating this, he says "Food" according to the principle of "By means of light for some," and so on, [referring to] the Kāṇva Śruti.

In the absence of that reading, the meaning is that the five *pañcajana*s—beginning with *prāṇa*—are intended together with the genitive-form *jyotiṣām jyotiḥ*. He takes up the portion beginning with "Him" (*tam eva*), namely: "Him" (*tam*). || 640 ||
Because the reality of cause and effect is none other than the non-dual Self itself.
Therefore, I consider myself [to be] like this world, consisting of causes and effects.
1. ka. gha. *ātmanaḥ*; kā. 2. kha. *kālam*; gha. *kāle*. 3. ka. kha. gha. *pacate*. 4. *nsatye ca*. 5. kha. *satye*. 229.
1826 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopani�ddbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

Because it is stated that "the causal self" (*kāraṇātmānam*), there might appear to be a division of cause and effect within the Self; however, this is not so, because the Śruti speaks of it as being distinct from both.
Anticipating the objection that [the self] is "joined," he explains: "The effect... (641).
Because the causes of differentiation have been destroyed, and because [causes] such as a material cause are impossible.
"The Knower himself says, 'I am the immortal, the immortal,'" so says the Śruti.

Anticipating the objection that if the world, which consists of both [subject and object], is understood as being merely the Self, it would follow that the Self possesses distinctions, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "the wise one" (*vidvān*). He says: "Pradhvasta... etc. The construction is: the scripture beginning with "the wise one" declares, "The wise one is himself immortal; the immortal is Brahman. || 642 ||
For those who [perceive] that very [Self] as the cause of this state of being breath and so forth for the breaths and so forth;
Having perceived it, they know directly the supreme, eternal Brahman.

He states the purport of the verse beginning with "of the vital breath" (prāṇasya) as follows: "Since... The meaning is that, in response to the inquiry—"How can that [knowledge] be [attained], since the knower was previously called Brahman in the preceding mantra?"—the mantra beginning with "of the vital breath" demonstrates this point: how the knowledge consisting of the cognition of the meaning of the sentence arises for those who know the meaning of the term *tvam* (the "thou"). || 643 ||
For here, for every self-possessing being, [the activity] occurs solely through a self that is independent [of external causes].
The vital breath and so forth would possess selfhood, because [the scripture states] "the breath of the breath. (644)

One might ask: why is it that the nature of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth as being "vital breaths" and so on is not produced by the Self, but rather is simply inherent (*svābhāvika*), like consciousness (*caitanya*)? To this he says: "independent," etc. The construction is as follows: since, between the Self and the non-Self, every non-Self such as the vital breath possesses its own "Self-nature" (i.e., its existence) solely through the Self; therefore, the scriptural statement "the vital breath of the vital breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇam*) and so forth is logical.
For the selfless, not being established by itself, depends upon that which is established by itself.
But because the self is established by itself, there is no dependence upon that which is not-self.
Furthermore, because it is non-self (anātman), it does not manifest by itself; and because it is non-self, it does not exist by itself.

Therefore, it is established only in dependence upon the Self, which is both existent and manifesting. Thus, it is logical that the status of being "life-breath" (prāṇa) and so forth for the vital functions belongs to them by virtue of that [Self]. This is what he states with the words "anātma" (non-self).
The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to establish the two reasons already mentioned. || 645 ||
Association with others is a service whose establishment is unexamined.
Remaining right within the lap of ignorance, it perishes through the knowledge of reality.

The self, too, possesses an equal state of dependence, for it is established as the substratum for the cognition of objects; how then can the vital breaths and so forth possess the nature of a self by means of the self? To this he says: "From another. He states the result of the fact that the relationship between the self and the non-self is merely imagined: "In reality," etc. (646).
The very nature of the cause-and-effect entity is that it is devoid of both effect and cause.
The supreme imperishable reality of everything from earth up to space has thus been declared.
1 Kha. 'Therein, the meaning alone' | [Vol.
3, page 694] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1827
Then, fearing that if their conjunction were to perish, those two would become separated and independent, he recalls the [teaching] from the fifth chapter: "akārya... (Verse 647).
When it was asked, "What might be the means for the vision of this [reality]?"
Therefore, the Śruti says that the realization of Brahman occurs through the mind alone.
Having stated that the knowledge of the meaning of words is the means for the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence, he introduces another mantra preceded by a desire to know other means.
The phrase "of that" (tasya) means that the present scripture declares that the mind, refined by hearing and other disciplines, is the instrument for the realization of Brahman;
this is the sense of the word "therefore" (ataḥ), which indicates that an answer is appropriate immediately after the objection. || 648 ||
For it is stated in the Śruti: "And she was held fast by the mind alone."
Since there is no dependence on anything other than the mind itself, there is consequently no need for any other means of proof.

He explains the particle *eva* (only). [The first *eva*] means "you must grasp it," while the second *eva* is for the purpose of combining this with another scriptural passage, namely, "This is to be attained by the mind alone," and is intended to exclude the perception of any other means. || 649 ||
It is the means for the arising of discernment regarding the categories of self and non-self.
The mind is observed to be common [to all], because it is the sole cause of all cognitions.

Furthermore, the fact that the mind (*manas*) is an instrument for the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*) is not something we need to prove, because its status as a common instrument for all cognition is accepted by everyone; thus he says: "The Self... He states the reason why the mind’s status as a common instrument is accepted: "All..."—that is to say, because among all the causes of cognition, the mind is a cause as one of their members. || 610 ||
In that state, the forms of both the attribute and the substrate are always manifest to direct consciousness.
Because it does not depend on any other cause, because it is of the nature of the self, and because it is always present. || 651 ||

If the mind (*manas*) is a means for the knowledge of the Self just as it is for the knowledge of what is not the Self, then—given that the Self is accessible through it—it might be suspected that the Self would likewise become subject to birth; anticipating this objection, he says: "The inner" (*pratyak*). There is always a pervasion of the substrate (*dharmin*), such as the intellect (*buddhi*), and its attributes, such as knowledge, by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), because there is no dependence on any other cause for the pervasion of consciousness beyond the mere acquisition of their own nature; and thus, in that [intellect] and so forth...
The meaning is that the Self is not insentient because it is the agent of realization. He establishes the stated reason with the words "because of being the Self.
The meaning is that since the intellect and so forth constitute its very nature, the conscious Self is ever-present therein. || 651 ||
Therefore, the form of the self is eternal, because its cause always exists.

And because it is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), that [reflection] is not excluded from its true reality even by ignorance and the like. (652) He states that the eternal reflection of consciousness belongs not only to the intellect and its attributes, but to everything: "The Self," etc. The connection is: "because of the possibility thereof. The form of the Self is eternal for everything, because of the proximity of the Self everywhere.

The meaning is: because this entire [phenomenal world] exists as its own self-nature (*pratyaktva*). How can it be that the form of the Self (*ātmākṛti*) is eternal for everything, given that doubt and the like are absent?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "And because of ignorance, etc. This is because, by its very nature, that same conscious element (*ciddhātu*) has ignorance and so forth as its own essential form.

The meaning is that there is no existence apart [from it]. Since the existence and manifestation of everything arise solely from the clarity of the Self (*ātman*), the Self is not insentient (*jaḍa*).

As for the statement that the mind is the instrument for perceiving it, the intended meaning of the two *Vārtikas* is that because the mind always possesses the form of that [Self], it occasionally assumes a transformation into that form by depending on the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth. || 652 ||
Because it depends on dharma, adharma, and so forth, and because it is distinct from other entities.
Therefore, the assumption of the forms of sound and so forth must be occasional for the cognition. || 653 ||

One might ask: since the mind (*manas*), which is common to all cognitions, has the form of the Self (*ātman*) and is eternal, why is it specified as such? Anticipating the objection that its non-Self-form (*anātmākṛti*) is likewise [eternal], he says: "Dharma... etc. The mind's assumption of the forms of sound and so forth is not eternal, because that assumption of form depends upon unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors, and because sound and the rest—being non-subjective—do not have constant proximity to the mind. Therefore, its non-Self-form is not eternal.
Such is the meaning. || 653 ||
Although these two in this world are preceded by the knowledge of the self,
The existence and non-existence of the cognition of sound and so forth as being without self-nature exist by way of their own-being. || 654 ||
Nevertheless, it is precisely from experience that there arises the lack of recognition of the nature of the inner self.
Therefore, ignorance is established in the inner self (pratyagātman) just like the non-apprehension of the self.

One might object: "Even though the forms of sound and so forth are impermanent, if the form of the Self were eternal for everyone, then because the cognition of sound and other objects is preceded by the manifestation of the Self, the non-cognition of the Self would never be possible; for that [non-cognition] would be removed by a mental modification (manovṛtti) pervaded by the manifestation of the Self. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though... [The meaning is: even though there is the presence or absence of mental modifications (dhīvṛtti) bearing the forms of non-self (anātma), the consciousness of the Self (ātmacaitanya)— [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a verse beginning with "yadyapi," likely from a Vedāntic work such as the *Pañcadaśī*. The translation above reflects the philosophical argument being raised.]

Even though [the Self] is all-pervading, it is only the mental modification (buddhi-vṛtti) arising from sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), which takes the form of the realization of non-duality, that dispels that ignorance; another mental modification, even if it has the form of consciousness (cidākāra), cannot remove it because it grasps a different form. Therefore, the meaning is that the ignorance regarding the Inner Self (pratyak) is established by experience and is impossible to deny. He concludes the matter established by experience with the words "anātma... (not-self). The word "ataḥ" (therefore)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
The meaning is experience. || 654 || 655 ||
Furthermore, even for that which has already arisen, there is a further arising, just as in the case of compassion, space, and so forth.
Through the mastery of the knowledge of the true nature of the inward self, derived from the teacher and the scriptures.
Let it be granted that there is knowledge of the cessation; nevertheless, does that [cessation] itself cease or not? If it does not, there is no liberation.

If it does cease, is there an agent of its cessation or not? If there is not, then cessation exists eternally. If there is, is it action (*karman*) or knowledge (*jñāna*)? Not the first, because it is not admitted [by you].

As for the second, is it the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) or another knowledge (*jñānāntara*)? Not the first, because it would entail the consequence of either eternal cessation or non-cessation, which renders practices such as hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*) futile.

In this context, one might raise the following objection: Is the subsequent cognition that [is supposed to] remove ignorance also insentient (*jaḍa*) or sentient (*ajaḍa*)? In the first case, it could not remove ignorance because there is no opposition between them; in the second case, if it were something other than the Self (*ātman*), it would contradict your own tenets (*apāraddhānta*); if it were the Self itself, then it too would necessarily be occasional (*kādācitkatva*), and the defects already mentioned regarding the position that [the Self] is self-luminous knowledge would apply. Anticipating this, he says: "Of that which has arisen. Just as space, though eternally established, is delimited by wells and the like...
Likewise, although the realization of the true nature of the inner self is eternally attained, its manifestation occurs through the power of the scriptures and the teacher.

The meaning is as follows: immediately after the mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) "I am Brahman" arises, it is accepted that only that [Self] as conditioned by that modification arises. Consequently, there is no fault, because it is admitted that the sentence effects the destruction of ignorance precisely for the knowledge of one's own true nature as conditioned by such a mental modification. || 696 ||
Therefore, following faith in the scriptures and other means, it is by the mind alone [that one attains realization]; thus says the Śruti.
"One should perceive the true nature of the self," so says she who desires our welfare. (657)

He summarizes the meaning of the passage beginning with "manasā" (by the mind) as follows: "prasādāt" (through clarity). The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (hence) is that it is possible for the purified mind to be the cause of knowledge. The prefix "anu-" is to be connected with the word "draṣṭavyam" (is to be seen). || 657 ||
If this object of vision is perceived by the mind alone, through such distinctions as that of the seer and so forth.
Furthermore, the objection regarding multiplicity has been raised; let it not be so, because it is refuted [as follows]. || 658 ||

He states the doubt to be set aside by the passage beginning with "not here" (neha), namely: "If [the world] were visible... He says: "Not so," meaning that there is no plurality within the Self that is Brahman, because such plurality is being negated. || 658 ||
Here, there is no object of knowledge established by means of valid cognition, because nothing whatsoever exists as manifold.
Whether unknown or known, an object indeed appears as manifold.
Demonstrating precisely this negation, he applies the statement: "Not so" (neha). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, there is no possibility of duality.
He elaborates upon this negation: "The unknown" (ajñātam) || 699 ||
Since an infinite object is not sufficient for the cognition of diversity, therefore [it is not so].
That which is unknown, known through doubt, or known erroneously does not serve as a foundation.

This establishes that an unknown object does not, in reality, possess a state of difference from the object itself. Regarding the word "nānātva" (difference): the meaning is that the distinction of an object not apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established by authority (*prāmāṇika*). || 660 ||
Even when correctly known, an object is not held to produce the cognition of duality.
Because the state of perfect knowledge is established through the sublation of the cause of duality. || 661 ||

The statement that "an object known in its true nature does not partake of manifoldness" is clarified by the word "properly" (*samyak*). For the inner self (*pratyagartha*), when understood correctly through the influence of the scriptures and the teacher, does not produce the cognition of difference; this is because, by dispelling the ignorance that is the cause of manifoldness, it has been properly known—this is the meaning. || 661 ||
Furthermore,
the pervasion of means of knowledge is not established by way of the exclusion of others.
Even when objects are withdrawn, because of attachment to them, one does not attain the limit [of mastery]. // 662 //
If an object—whether known or unknown—is not characterized by manifoldness (*nānātva*), how can perception and the other means of knowledge delineate manifoldness?

Anticipating this objection, the author considers two alternatives—whether these means of knowledge apprehend manifoldness through a positive mode (*vidhimukhena*) or a negative mode (*niṣedhamukhena*)—and addresses the second alternative with the words "meyeti. The various means of knowledge do not pervade their objects by way of the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*), such as [the cognition] "a jar is not a cloth," in the case of cloths and so forth.

The meaning is that since there would be the consequence of an infinite regress of exclusions even among those things to be excluded, such exclusion could never find a final resting point; therefore, the operation of a means of valid cognition does not occur by way of negation. || 662 ||
1 kha. ‘Non-selfhood’ | [Vol. 3, page 697] 1830 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Adhyāya—]
Since it is completed by that very means, there is no further activity beyond it.
Therefore, valid cognition does not apprehend either the pervasion by another entity or its exclusion.

It sets aside the [objection regarding] another alternative: "by the means of knowledge" (*meyena*). This means "because [the means of knowledge] results in the cognition of the thing-in-itself. Since the means of knowledge are exhausted solely by the cognition of the mere thing (*vastumātra*), they do not have difference and non-difference as their object; this is the meaning. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) signifies the absence of any other function. || 663 ||
"And because exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is also a non-entity, it cannot be apprehended by the perceptions of real entities."
Furthermore, there is no connection whatsoever with the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest. 664.

Furthermore, is difference (*bheda*) merely the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), or is it a distinct entity (*arthāntara*)? Regarding the first case, he states that it is untenable for difference to be apprehended by perception and other means of knowledge, saying: "And because of exclusion" (*vyāvṛtteśca*). The meaning of the particle *api* is that, like the exclusion itself, the difference included within it is a non-entity (*avastu*). The phrase "in some cases" (*kvacit*) refers to the objects of space and time. || 664 ||
Because it cognizes mere non-existence, there is no cognition of difference even from non-existence.
One does not perceive [them] through the manifestation of existence and non-existence, as if by direct perception.

Anticipating the objection that even if the five means of knowledge beginning with perception do not bring about the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), the sixth means of knowledge will nevertheless cognize it—and thus difference (*bheda*) would also be established as having a basis in valid cognition—the author says: "abhāva... (and so on). Since non-apprehension of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*) only brings about the cognition of mere absence (*abhāva*), no cognition of difference—which is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*)—can arise from it. For difference is not merely the exclusion of others; if it were so, then because that [exclusion] would be a non-entity (*avastu*), the consequence of monism (*advaita*) would follow. By this, the [objection regarding] the conceptual construction... is refuted.

The meaning is that even the [objection] immediately following has been answered, because there is no evidence for a difference that is distinct from exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Having accepted that non-existence (*abhāva*) is both the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge, it was stated that difference is not established by valid cognition; now, he abandons that acceptance. [He says: "If [it is argued]... If non-existence is apprehended by means of non-existence, then existence (*bhāva*) must also be apprehended by that same means, because the two stand in the relation of property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*); for a means of knowledge that does not apprehend the substratum cannot [apprehend] its property.

One should not argue that sound and the like are apprehended even when space and so forth are not apprehended, for in that case too, the disagreement is equal; moreover, if one follows mere perception, it contradicts logical reasoning. Furthermore, no one determines either existence or non-existence by means of "non-existence" (abhāva) as a means of knowledge; just as when an existent thing is being grasped by perception, its non-existence is not grasped, so it is with non-existence as well.

Therefore, there is no grasping of both [subject and object] by itself, because it is impossible for it to be a grasper; thus, the meaning is that even non-existence cannot be external to it. || 661 ||
Furthermore, there may be some proponent who perceives non-existence through direct perception.
Because it terminates in that much alone, even he does not perceive non-duality.

[The author] says "even he" (yo 'pi) after suspecting that the example might be unestablished in the position of one who denies the existence of perception. He states "only that much" (tāvanmātra) to show that even in his view, since perception has as its object merely the absence consisting of the exclusion of others, it does not have difference as its object.
"He [perceives] the conformity of perception, its exclusion, and its differentiation."
How one might perceive [it] by means of direct perception itself—let this be explained. (667)

Anticipating the objection that "since non-existence (*abhāva*) is constituted by a substratum (*dharmin*) and a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), how is it that perception does not grasp difference?", he says:
"Of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*). The proponent of difference (*bhedavādī*) is referred to by the pronoun "all" (*sarva-*); however, the prefix *sam-* should be construed with the verbal root.
[Note: The variants provided are: 1. *rabhisaṃ* (ga); 2. *va tava ta* (gha).]
[Vol.
3, Page 698] 4 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by Ānandagiri’s sub-commentary, the Śāstraprakāśikā: 1831.
Its persistence toward objects, its withdrawal from them, and the distinction between these two are not within the scope of perception, because they are only partially grasped by it.

And because that [cognition] would require another means of knowledge (mānāntara) to perceive it, there would be an infinite regress; therefore, perception cannot establish even a difference in objects.
Thus, the meaning is that, like that [object], it [the cognition] does not establish a difference because its own difference has not been apprehended. || 667 ||
For there exists here no pride for the sake of perceiving multiplicity.
If it were said that space is black, that would be established without investigation.

Having stated that nothing whatsoever possesses plurality through direct perception, [the author] anticipates the objection that there might be another means of knowledge (*māna*) that makes plurality known. He says, "Since... Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the entity (*vastu*). || 668 ||
Since the cause is indeed the unknown reality, he therefore spoke of it as manifold.
He who perceives multiplicity here attains death after death.

Having explained the passage beginning with "not here" (*neha*), he takes up the statement beginning with "of death" (*mṛtyoḥ*) as a premise, [commenting on] the word "unperceived" (*ajñātā*). The locative case is as before. || 669 ||
Death would be Hiraṇyagarbha, because of the dissolution of its own effects.
His death, too, should be understood [to have occurred] from the moment he appeared.

[Objection: But death is one; how can it be said to be twofold? To this he says: "Death... The word "yataḥ" (from which) is a statement regarding the ignorance of the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*) along with its appearance (*sābhāsa*). || 670 ||
Because it is defiled by the fault of false view, it is the cause of false view.
He who perceives no diversity here goes from death to death.

Having explained the meaning of the words "mṛtyu" (death) and "śabda" (sound), he joins them in the sentence: "mithyā" (false). Here, "iha" (here) refers to the statement regarding Brahman as the Self. ||671||
For previously, before the arising of knowledge, there was indeed the thought that it is not manifold.
But when knowledge arises, because that [error] is sublated, the term "as it were" (iva) is employed. || 672 ||

He explains the meaning of the word "iva" (as if): "Previously," etc. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of establishing the common perception of multiplicity during the state of ignorance. The meaning is that he who considers what existed previously as if it were manifold to be indeed manifold even after the arising of knowledge—that ignorant person, perceiving through the intellect of ultimate reality that which is merely an appearance as if it were manifold, wanders in saṃsāra. || 672 ||
Since the actual state of things is non-dual, multiplicity arises from the cause of delusion.
"This Self is to be seen as one alone by those who follow the path of the Vedas.
[He] introduces the passage beginning with "ekadhā" (as one) along with its supporting reasoning: "vastu" (the reality).
In one single manner, it shines as the very form of pure consciousness.
"Brahman is to be perceived by the inner self through the scripture alone as its sole authority.
He states its meaning with the word "by one" (ekena); here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of "in this manner" (itthaṃbhāve).
1 Kha. Tukam | [Vol.
3, page 699] 1832 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]
The view that [the Self] is both collective and individual arises from the statement "as one alone."
It is understood that [this] is false, both because it is heard [in scripture] and because of the censure [of it as] death. (675)

Having stated the literal meaning (*śrautārtha*) of the sentence, he states its implied meaning (*ārthikārtha*): "samasta... etc. In that very context, he states the supportive nature of the negation of the perception of difference: "śrautāt... etc. (Verse 675).
This is the immortal Brahman, by virtue of its negation of the cause of death.
Death is indeed said to be darkness, and that is dispelled by awakening.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "this" (*etad*). Regarding the word "this": since ignorance—which is the cause of all bonds, foremost among which are birth and death—is negated by the knowledge arising from the [Vedic] sentence, and because that [ignorance] lacks the capacity to reveal the reality (*vastu*), it is logical that the reality is not an object of knowledge (*aprameya*); this is the meaning. He dispels the appearance of the objection: "Even if death itself, known as Hiraṇyagarbha, is negated, how can Brahman be beyond the scope of knowledge?"
"Death," [it is said]. || 676 ||
Since the reality of the entire world is indeed one, therefore [it is so].
It should be understood that the cognition which conflates action and its factors is false. || 677 ||

Having raised the objection—"Since Brahman is established as being cognizable by all means of knowledge (*pratyaya*), how can it be said to be 'immeasurable' (*aprameya*)?"—the author says: "In one way alone" (*ekadhaiva*).

Because the cognition of difference is false, that which is grasped by it is likewise of the same nature; furthermore, the pure [Brahman] is not cognizable by all means of knowledge, because it is known only through the Upanishads (*aupaniṣadatva*).
This is the meaning. || 677 ||
For where there is duality, as it is said, and "But where for him," so says the Śruti.
In the past, he himself declared that the view of manifoldness is false.
Or, regarding the falsity of the cognition of difference, he shows another statement that restates the positive and negative concomitance [of the reason] in the words: "For where... (678).
If the Supreme Brahman is to be seen as one, how can it be said [to be manifold]?
Because the state of being an object of vision is established only when there exists a distinction between the seer and so forth. || 679 ||

He raises the objection that there is a mutual contradiction between the two phrases "is to be seen as one" (*ekadhā draṣṭavyam*) by saying, "If [it were] as one" (*ekadhā cet*). He then states what the inconsistency therein is: "The seer and so forth" (*draṣṭrādi*). || 679 ||
How can an immeasurable object be measured by a means of valid cognition?
If it is measured by a means of valid cognition, then that is accepted as the object of cognition (prameya).
He states another contradiction, namely that "it must be seen" and "it is immeasurable" are mutually opposed. He clarifies this opposition by saying: "If it is measured... (680).
This is not a fault, because the refutation has already been stated directly.
If one were to state the refutation once again, it would be like grinding what has already been ground.

He resolves [the objection], saying: "This is not a fault. If it is argued that even though the two contradictions have been resolved, they must be resolved once more, he replies: "Furthermore... (681).
1 kha. Let it be understood. 2 ka. The object of knowledge (prameya). 3 sna. ga. ... from that. mṛ. [Vol.
3, page 700] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1833.
"The appropriation of the subject and so forth is an obstacle to the realization of oneness."
Therefore, for the awakening to that [reality], this [text] does not depend upon a knower or other such factors.
If [the Self] were one, how could it be seen? Thus, he recalls the resolution of this contradiction stated as being manifold: "of the knower and so forth.

The meaning is that since the acceptance of the knower and other factors constitutes an obstacle to unity, by their removal, there is no longer any requirement for a real knower and so forth in the knowledge of That; therefore, oneness and the state of being seen are not contradictory. || 682 ||
When there is a relationship between the object of cognition and the means of cognition, this term "prameya" (the object of cognition) is used.
But since the fruit of valid cognition has no object of cognition, there is therefore no contradiction.
Since, in this world, mental application toward an unknown object [is impossible], therefore—
And because that which is already known cannot be an object of measurement, there is no dependence [on another means] for its inclusion within the category of valid cognition.

Regarding the statement of contradiction that "that which is to be seen is immeasurable," he states the general principle while reminding us of the previously mentioned resolution, beginning with the words "of the measurable" (*meyasya*). He then asks what follows from this in the present context, answering with "since" (*yataḥ*). The locative case in *pramāṇabhūmau* signifies the sense of the seventh case (the locus). The particle *ca* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and is to be connected immediately after the fifth case ending. || 683 || 684 ||
That [cognition] is a means of valid cognition only by virtue of its nature as a result, and not by way of being a subject (mātrādi) or other such forms.
It does not manifest what is already known; therefore, it cannot be an object of cognition for this [consciousness]. || 685 ||

Anticipating the objection as to how, if [the Self] is immeasurable (*ameya*), its being measurable (*meyatā*) could depend on its being an object of vision (*draṣṭavyatva*), he says: "By way of the nature of the fruit" (*phalātmanā*). For that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), having proceeded toward the self-luminous inner Self (*pratīc*), makes it directly known to us precisely as the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*) which is not an object; it does not, however, make it an object by depending on the knower (*mātr*) and so forth. Therefore, while being pervaded by the mental modification (*vṛtti-vyāpyatva*) is imagined, being pervaded by the fruit (*phala-vyāpyatva*) is real.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction. || 685 ||
Just as cutting is not intended to result in a state of duality, so too is it here.
Likewise, knowability exists when [the object] is unknown, but not when it has become the nature of the result of cognition.

Anticipating the objection that even if [the object] is not pervaded by the expansion [of the mind], why could its being pervaded by the mental mode (*vṛtti*) not be real, he says: "But rather... (686).
One should [perceive] this self, which is like raw cow dung, by means of the path that destroys that darkness.
It is described in this way from the perspective of the reality of vision: "it causes awakening. || 687 ||

Anticipating the objection that, like other objects, the Self must also be considered as being "objectified by the fruit" (*phalavyāpyatva*) because it is the subject matter of the Upaniṣads, he says: "Even scripture... The meaning is that one should not postulate for the inner self (*pratīc*) an objectification by consciousness (*saṃvidvyāpyatva*) apart from its being objectified by a mental modification (*vṛttivyāpyatva*), because [the Self] is of the very nature of that [consciousness].
Since the self is established by itself, its establishment occurs even from that which is unknown.
Since the cognizer and so forth are established regardless of success or failure, what does [the means of knowledge] depend upon for its own establishment? (688)

For this reason as well, he states that the Self is not pervaded by that [object], beginning with the words "from its own self-established nature" (*svataḥ siddhāt*). This is because [the Self] is the cause of the existence or non-existence of the states of being a knower (*mātr*) and so forth. [Note:
*gha* reads *phalavyā*; *ka* reads *phalavyā*; *gha* reads *iti bhāvaḥ* || 687 ||].

By his grace, there is the attainment of that self-luminous reality which, though previously unknown, is treated as "attained" through its being pervaded by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by a means of valid cognition (*māna*).
The meaning is that it does not depend on another consciousness. || 688 ||
For the pervasion by knowledge would indeed exist in sound and so forth, because they share a single primordial nature.
How could there be a pervasion (vyāpti) between that which is not cause and effect and the inner self (pratyagātman)? [689]

Furthermore, he states that its being "pervaded by a mental modification" (*vṛttivyāpyatva*) is also difficult to define, beginning with the word *jñāna*. Therein, the particle *hi* is used for the sake of mutual agreement. He provides the reason for the claim that there is pervasion by knowledge (*jñānavyāpti*) in the case of sound and so forth, beginning with the word *eka*. The meaning is that both sound and the like, as well as the mental modifications (*buddhivṛtti*), have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their material cause (*upādāna*). However, he states that there is no pervasion by knowledge in the case of the Self (*ātman*), beginning with the word *akārya*. [The Self is] of the nature of the single primordial matter (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is this: although existence is common to both, it is observed that form and the eye stand in the relationship of the grasped and the grasper; however, the self does not share the same nature as knowledge because they are not related as cause and effect, and therefore there is no pervasion of knowledge—even in its mode of functioning—into the self. || 689 ||
Because the causes for the application of words are impossible in the inner self (pratyagātman).
Therefore, it is awakened [to reality] not through the connection of the designator and the designated. || 690 ||
He states another reason for the fact that the self is not an object of verbal knowledge: "By the word" [etc.]. The connection is: "Therefore, because of the impossibility.
Wherein the non-self is established through the cause of ignorance regarding the inner self.
In that case, there would be a distinction between the knower and the object of knowledge, as well as between the individual self and the non-self. || 691 ||
He establishes the preliminary context to state another reason for the fact that consciousness does not pervade the inner self (*pratyak*). [The verse begins with] "pratyak" (the inner).

In that state of ignorance (*avidyāvasthā*) wherein the non-self (*anātman*), born of the ignorance of the Self, is known, there occurs the appearance of difference between the inner self and the non-self by way of the relationship of knower and known, according to such scriptural texts as "for where... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14). Therefore, the meaning is that in that [state], there is no pervasion of knowledge within the Self. || 691 ||
But where the self alone would be the object of knowledge, there [knowledge] would exist apart from the object.
"Who is the knower or the means of knowledge? It is he alone," so says the Śruti. (692)

He introduces the state of knowledge (*vidyāvasthā*) with the words "But where... The meaning is as follows: in that state of knowledge where the non-dual Self alone is pervaded by the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) arising from the [great] sentence, there is no objectivity (*saṃvidyāpyatā*) because, due to the absence of anything other than the Self—such as the knower (*mātrā*) and so forth—in accordance with such scriptural passages as, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone" (*yatra tvasya sarvam ātmaivābhūt*). He corroborates this absence of the knower and so forth with another scriptural passage: "Whomever... (*yameva...*). Whomever this [Self]...

"By that [grace] he is obtained," according to the Śruti; thus there is an absence of division into the measures (mātrā) and so forth. For this is the Supreme who, thinking "May this seeker realize Me as his own inner self (pratyagātman)," bestows grace upon him; it is the meaning of the Śruti that he can be known in that way by him alone. Therefore, how could the distinction of the measures and so forth be established? This is the sense of the verse. || 692 ||
That entity which exists only in dependence upon pride does not exist at all when free from pride.
But why should that which is established independently of any means of knowledge depend upon a means of knowledge? || 693 ||

If it is argued that the object of knowledge (meyam) is implied by an excess of the means of knowledge (māna), then the objection is raised that the self (ātman) as the object of knowledge would be non-existent, because existence belongs only to that which is established by the means of knowledge.
He says: "Not [by means of] a means of knowledge" (māna). Since the Self is also a reality, one might think it requires a means of knowledge; therefore he says:
"independent of a means of knowledge" (mānānapekṣa). The meaning is that for that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), there is no dependence on a means of knowledge. || 693 ||
Because the reality of the Self is inwardness, it is distinct from the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
Therefore, that [consciousness], whose nature is self-cognition, does not have the status of being an object of knowledge.

For this reason as well, he states that the Self is not pervaded by knowledge; [he says] "mātra" (only). The connection is: "because of its nature as the inner witness (pratyaktva). He provides another reason for that very point: "and by itself" (svataśca). The meaning is that because the Self has the nature of shining forth by its own essence, it is not pervaded by a means of knowledge (māna); rather, the Vedāntas, by producing a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of that [Self], serve as the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding it through the removal of ignorance concerning it. || 694 ||
Because there is no difference between the means of valid cognition and its result, no such objection can arise here.
For when there is a distinction between two actions, it is asked: "Which one is prior? (695)

Anticipating the objection—“If the sequence between the destruction of ignorance and the arising of knowledge is not certain, how can that destruction be the fruit of valid cognition?”—he says: “Valid cognition” (*pramā*).

For no other fruit of valid cognition is conceivable in relation to the Self; since there is a fixed sequence between that valid cognition and its fruit, the destruction of ignorance, by virtue of their relationship as cause and effect, the question of which of these two comes first is not to be raised. This is the meaning.

To the question, "In what case, then, does that [simultaneity] find scope? he replies: "Of two actions. The meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is the non-determination of their sequence. That [sequence] is called priority and posteriority (*paurvāparyam*). || 695 ||
Just as a person who has entered deep sleep remains with the collection of sense organs unassimilated [into consciousness], so too is it here.
Then, having cast off sleep by means of sound, one awakens to reality as it truly is.

Now, one might object: "Verbal cognition indeed does not arise with respect to the Self, because that Self is devoid of genus (*jāti*) and other such categories; since a word cannot convey meaning when its conventional relation (*saṃgati*) has not been grasped, the sequence of the cognition and its fruit is far removed from that case. To this, he provides an example of a word conveying meaning even when its relation is unknown:
"Even when swallowed" (*apīta*). The word *atha* indicates that the experience of that [conveyance] is something directly perceived (*ānubhavika*). (Verse 696)
Without even grasping the relationship between the signifier and the signified.
Just as [beings] awaken from sleep in the Āsuri heaven (3/106), so too do they awaken within the Self in this world.
Having restated the intended aspect of the example, he states the corresponding point regarding the subject of the illustration: "Without having grasped," etc. (697).
Because the power of sound is inconceivable, and because it is the Self, whose nature is consciousness.
And because sleep is subtle, it is destroyed by knowledge through the removal of delusion.

He clarifies the example of the tamer (*dāntika*): "The word," and so forth. For its majesty is not to be understood as being of a mundane nature, because it remains equal with respect to the past, future, present, and so on. For it has been said: "The Vedic injunction (*codanā*) indeed [makes known] what has been, what is becoming," and so forth. That which is unknown—

The meaning is that it is impossible to determine [otherwise], thinking, "Does this not awaken? Furthermore, since awakening is of the nature of manifestation (*sphurad-rūpa*), there is no need for a separate awakener; thus he says, "Because it is the Self" (*ātmatvāt*). If it is accepted that the unknown reality of the Self is what is to be known through the Vedāntas, then how is that so? To this he replies: "Because it is the object of its own witnessing" (*tatsākṣyatvāt*). || 698 ||
1 kha. This is the meaning. || 694 || 2 ka. kha. ... by being a witness. 3 ka. kha. of that which is to be known. 4 kha. gha. ... by being a witness.
[Vol. 3, page 703]
1836 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:
Dharma and adharma are to be known as *rajas*, because, like *rajas*, they consist of impurity (*mala*).
"Brahman is free from passion (*viraja*) because it is not an agent; it is free from passion because it is not a cause.

(699) Having stated the meaning of the sentence regarding the "immeasurable" (*aprameya*), he states the meaning of the word *viraja* in order to explain the subsequent sentence. [He says: "Dharma... and so on. The reason for those two being "passion" (*rajas*) is given as: "like passion" (*rajovat*). He states the state of Brahman being free from passion along with its reason: "because it is not an agent" (*tadakartṛtvataḥ*).
He states the reason for Brahmā’s non-agency regarding dharma and adharma: "Because of being without a cause" (akāraṇatvataḥ). || 699 ||
One who does not possess the true nature of right knowledge [is subject to rebirth] because of being of the nature of that which is born.
The Self alone is what is taught here by the word "ether" according to the Śruti.
I explain the word "ākāśa" as "not correct. In the third [case], it is a coordinate construction (samānādhikaraṇa); the mantra under discussion has the sense of the locative case. || 700 ||
The Self, which is characterized by attributes such as grossness and so forth, arises from a cause that possesses birth.
He is to be known as beyond space, because his nature is without beginning or end.

He explains the meaning of the word "para" (the other): "that which possesses birth," etc. He states the reason for the Self's difference from the cause of the world—namely, from ether and the unmanifested (avyākṛta), which are characterized by such attributes as "not gross"—in the words: "of that," etc. (701).
Since it is thus, therefore He is unborn, because He is neither an effect nor a cause.
The removal of all modifications without exception occurs precisely because of being unborn (*ajatva*).

[Verse 702] He states the meaning of the term "unborn" (*aja*) with the words "because" (*yasmāt*). He clarifies the very reason already mentioned as that which is to be relied upon (*upajīvya*) with the words "not an effect" (*akārya*). He states the implicit meaning of the qualifier "unborn" with the words "because of being unborn" (*ajatvāt*). [702]
Because it is neither excluded nor followed by anything else, it is called the "Great Self."
And because it is immutable, it should be known as eternal, since the possibility of modification or cessation does not exist. (703)

He states the meaning of these two [terms], "the Self" and "great," with the words "unrestricted" (*avyāvṛtta*). He states the meaning of "constant" (*dhruva*) with the words "immovability" (*kauṭasthya*). Since neither modification nor destruction is possible, there is immovability; therefore, the meaning is that it is "constant. || 701 ||
Through the statement of the Śruti as the inner self, one realizes that very [Self] endowed with the aforementioned attributes.
Having first understood the Self through both positive and negative concomitance, || 704 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tameva" (that very [Self]... as follows: "as the inner self" (*pratyaktayā*). This means one who possesses the aforementioned qualifications, that is to say, the qualifications such as being free from passion (*viraja*) and so forth.

The meaning is that, having purified the categories of reality (*padārtha*) in accordance with the fourfold methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and by means of the foundational scripture (*śruti*), one should cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*). || 704 ||
Wisdom that destroys the desire to know by dispelling all ignorance.
And because all that is to be known has been fully accomplished, one should act through the realization of the meaning of the words. || 705 ||

He states the meaning of "one should cultivate wisdom" as follows: "one should desire to know. Because all that is to be known becomes known through the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, [the result is] the realization of the true nature (ātmatattva).
[Variant readings: 1. 'thātmya; 2. ka. ga. cchedanīm.]

And because knowledge has been established as having all [objections] refuted, there is the cessation of all desire; therefore, by means of sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), one should bring about that wisdom (*prajñā*) which consists in the cognition of the meaning of the sentence, which is the cause of the supreme human goal by virtue of destroying all desires. This is the meaning. || 709 ||
In this regard, some explain it differently from the explanation already stated.
When it is asked, "What kind of wisdom is this that performs what has already been done? (706)

In the passage "Having understood, one should exercise wisdom," the meaning of the sentence is stated as follows: having accomplished the knowledge of the two word-meanings (*padārtha*), one should produce the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Now, he states the view of Bhartṛprapañca. With the words "In this case" (*iha*), he introduces the objection raised by him in order to explain his own alternative interpretation. He begins with the words "Of that which has been performed" (*kṛtāyāḥ*). By means of the gerundive suffix *-lyap* in the word *vijñāya*, "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is expressed; and of that—
To state again that "one should exercise wisdom" is improper, for it would be like grinding what has already been ground; such is the meaning. || 706 ||
It is said that by means of speech, only the mere object is presented to the intellect.

The establishment of the identity with that which has been cognized as its true nature is called the "instrument of wisdom" (prajñākaraṇa) through the continuums of cultivation and knowledge. || 707 ||
At this time, however, that wisdom should be brought to its ultimate consummation and perfected. || 708 ||

He speaks of *samādhi*: "It is said" (*ucyate*). An object that has not yet ascended into direct experience is reached by the intellect through a word; this is called verbal, indirect knowledge (*śābdaparokṣajñāna*). Having understood [the Self] thus, the direct realization of identity with Brahman—which has been known indirectly—through one's own inner self (*pratyak*), arising from the accumulated practice of verbal knowledge, is *prajñā*. The intended meaning here is that this *prajñā* is to be accomplished through the effort of one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*). I...
Fearing the objection that "if Brahman is known through verbal testimony, what is the use of direct realization (sākṣātkāra)?", he says: "In this...

That wisdom indeed produced by the word, when brought to its culmination at the time of direct realization, becomes fruitful; therefore, even for one who possesses verbal knowledge, direct realization is required—this is the meaning. || 707 || 708 ||
Having accepted this, it was said with reverence, "having understood."
Having thus stated the operation of the means of valid cognition, [it is said] by the statement "by the mind alone" (manasā eva). || 709 ||

In order to demonstrate the intention of the Śruti regarding the matter already stated, he describes the manner in which that [realization] arises, beginning with the words "Thus this... Having accepted that verbal knowledge—which has not yet ascended to the level of direct experience—arises first, and that when practiced it leads to direct realization (sākṣātkāra) and thus becomes fruitful, he explains the manner in which the means of valid cognition (śabda-pramāṇa) brings about understanding through the statement "It is to be seen by the mind alone," and then [continues] with "Having known... and so forth.
The meaning is that the statement was introduced by the Śruti itself. || 706 ||
Brahman is eternal, non-dual, and truly existent, undivided from its causes and so forth.
"How is that which is to be seen to be perceived directly, given the impossibility of the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth?

How is it said that [it is known] 'by the mind alone' and so on?"—anticipating this objection, he sets forth the opponent's challenge in order to demonstrate that [point]. He says: "The knower, etc. The meaning is that Brahman—which is non-dual, beginningless and endless, and devoid of the knower and so forth—cannot be directly realized because of the absence of a cause [for such realization].
