This is to be perceived by the mind alone; no other path is desired.
If it is asked how that is so, the operation of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is stated here.

I.1 He connects the passage beginning with "by the mind" as a subsequent elaboration of this [point]. Regarding the word "to be seen": here, "here" refers to the statement concerning the vision of Brahman. The mind—

He raises an objection: "It is improper to say that 'that very [Self] is to be seen as Brahman,' because its status as being known through the Upaniṣads (aupaniṣadatva) is accepted precisely by the negation of its being an object [of the senses]. He asks: "How so? In response, he says: "In this context," meaning that while the point to be established is that even that which is known through the Upaniṣads must be seen by means of that [scripture], the manner in which the word brings about cognition is first demonstrated. || 711 ||
When the statements such as "That thou art" are uttered, there is the observation of mere sound.
But that [determination] of the sound which has been perceived by the ear is performed by the mind. || 712 ||
That which possesses sequential order through the utterance of vowels, consonants, and words is what constitutes differentiation.
It is conceived by his mind as having a distinct sequence. || 713 ||

He clarifies the manner of expression [with the words] "the reality" (*tattvam*). Its meaning is as follows: after the teacher has uttered the sentence beginning with "the reality," the seeker of liberation grasps that alone by means of the sense of hearing.

For him who has grasped the mere sound, there arises a sequence consisting of the flow of utterances composed of vowels, consonants, and words; this sequence is characterized by each individual vowel and exists in the form of both the initial and the subsequent.

That which is well-known as possessing a distinct sequence is mentally constructed from that sound manifested by the auditory organ; it is apprehended by means of that [mental construction] alone. || 712 || 713 ||
The connection of an established word with its own inherent meaning is eternal.
This is perceived by the mind alone; it is not perceived here by anything other than that.
Granted that sound in its mere form is perceivable by the sense of hearing alone, yet that sound as qualified [by its meaning] is accessible to the mind;

nevertheless, the connection between word and meaning is cognizable through inference and not through the mind. Therefore, how could the cognition arising from a word be mental, given that it too—like the connection itself—is established as being inferential? Anticipating this objection, he says: "By its own... That relationship between word and meaning which always...

By the established maxim, "The relationship between a word and its meaning is innate," it is settled that at the time of birth, usage understood through inference is indeed the root of a child's linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*). Furthermore, since that [relationship] is remembered by the mind alone at the time of cognizing the meaning from a word whose [meaning] has already been acquired, the meaning is that the cognition produced by a word known through that [relationship] is purely mental, because the relationship itself is mental. This is what is meant by "here."
The meaning is: at the time of learning [the language], and for one who has already learned it, at the time of linguistic usage. || 714 ||
In that regard, the cognition of the object is that which belongs to the cognizer and is mental in nature.
That which remains is [the object] because of its connection with the external object of measurement. || 715 ||

He states that the mental cognition arising from a word regarding an object possesses the form of that object, preceded by the recollection of the relationship between the word and its meaning. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*):
it means when there is the recollection of the relationship between the word and the object. "Undifferentiated" (*aviśiṣṭa*) means having that nature or that form.
He states the reason why this [cognition] has the form of the external object of knowledge: "by the object" (*arthena*). || 719 ||
1. *ka*. *kha*. ‘rāyaikai | 2. *ka*. *kha*. ‘tmani jñā’ | 3. *ka*. vetyarthaḥ | [Vol. 3, page 706] 4. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 1839.
And whatever kind of mental condition arises for him, it is according to its nature.
Through that identity, my own self also attains the state of being composed of that. || 716 ||

He states that not only is the cognition (*pratyaya*) composed of the object, but the self (*ātman*) as well, with the words "And the cognition... The meaning is that because it is identical with the mind (*manas*), and because there is no distinction between that which is to be known and [the mind], the cognition—which is of the nature of that [mind]—also possesses the state of being that [object]. "Consisting of that" means consisting of external objects; that is to say, having those as its primary constituent. || 716 ||
In this context, the usage [of the terms] "mind" (manas) and "intellect" (buddhi) is heard in scripture as being non-differentiated.
This being the case, even that conviction of his which pertains to a deity remains as a mental representation, just as it is in the sacred scripture.
In that very same manner, by means of that very sequence, that human being attains identification with it.

Anticipating the objection that "it is incorrect to say that the cognition of the meaning of a word is mental, because that [cognition] is admitted to be *bauddha* (intellectual)," he says: "By the mind.

This means in such passages as "by the mind alone," and so forth. Having stated generally that the Self consists of the knowable through the medium of knowledge, he states the specific point—that when there is knowledge of a particular deity or the like, one becomes identical with that through its worship—saying: "Therein. Therein...

The meaning is as follows: when the self, through the medium of the intellect (*dhī*), consists of external objects, even that cognition of this self directed toward a deity—which occurs when the scripture (*śruti*) serves as the instrumental cause—abides in the mind alone. Therefore, just as there is identification with those [external objects] due to the repeated practice of cognition regarding them, so too, through the repetition of the cognition of the deity, one gradually attains identification with the deity, in accordance with such scriptural passages as "having become a god" (*devo bhūtvā*).
The qualification "human" (mānava) is used for the purpose of indicating that only a human being has the entitlement (adhikāra) to all forms of worship. || 717 ||
When he perceives here, through the revealed word, the identity of duality and unity;
Then there would arise the Buddhist knowledge that the self is the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha). || 719 ||
Indeed, having produced that consciousness and being absorbed in it, he would proceed in that manner.
In that very form of the self, that consciousness should remain established. || 720 ||
Then, when he perceives the supreme reality within the Buddhist [teaching],
Then, having analytically distinguished the forms, he gradually [attains] the purity of the intellects.
He perceives only the pure reality, the eternal Brahman.

Having stated that the self consists of Indra and the other deities, he speaks of its consisting of the *sūtra* (the thread). Regarding the verse beginning with "dvaita": when the Self perceives the *sautra-tattva*—which consists of both the aggregate and the individual—as the word "Sūtra" taught in the scriptures used within the context of authoritative worldly discourse, then his cognition, which takes the form of a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*), becomes fit for repetition; and he, having thus produced that knowledge, [becomes] its master.

Being composed of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), it proceeds, by following that consciousness, toward the state of being composed of the thread of the object of knowledge (*vijñeya-sūtramayatva*). Then, when that very [state] is known through the grasping of "I" (*ahaṃgraha*)—that is, when it is realized as one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) designated by terms such as "Buddha"—the practitioner abides therein; this is the meaning. According to the commentary on the passage concerning the attainment of the state of the thread (*sūtrāvasthā*), it is inferred that in the root text, where it says "in sequence" (*krameṇaiva*), it should rather read "from that sequence" (*kramāt*).
1. Not so; it is not thus. 2. Gha: *tāvijñā*. 3. Ga: *dāpyasau*. [Vol. 3, page 707] 1840 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]

He states that [the Self] consists of reality (*tattvamayatva*). Regarding the word "then" (*atha*): after remaining in the form of the *sūtra* (the subtle thread), when that person, abiding thus, correctly perceives the supreme reality as "I am Brahman" through such statements as "Tat tvam asi," then—by means of that contemplation—he gradually abandons the forms of the deities and so forth which were the objects of his intellect. He becomes Brahman, which is liberated from all transmigratory existence, devoid of its causes, non-dual, real, and without beginning or end.
The meaning is that he who perceives [it] without interruption becomes that very thing, according to the principle of "as is one's intention (kratu), so is one's attainment. || 719 || 720 || 721 ||
Then, having attained the goal within your own self, you will find honor among others.
As one directly sketches these forms, Nirvana itself becomes fully absorbed.

An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that Brahman is not non-dual, because of the existence of a second entity, namely the mind, which is the cause for its realization? Anticipating this, he says: "That mind. The meaning is that the mind, together with its own effects, dissolves directly and completely into Brahman. The word "atha" (then) is used to state that the dissolution of the imagined occurs within the unimagined, like the dissolution of a snake imagined upon a rope. "Labdhalakṣyam" means having attained its scope or found its opportunity. || 722 ||
Having thus beheld the supreme reality, non-duality has dawned within the mind.
Consciousness alone, pure, abides in its own self. || 723 ||

In that regard, he explains what remains when the mind has dissolved into its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). He says "supreme" (*param*); by "alone" (*kevalam*) non-duality is expressed, and by "pure" (*śuddham*) it is stated that there is an absence of contact with cause and effect. || 723 ||
Just as fire, having consumed its fuel, becomes extinguished of its own accord, so too does the giver [attain peace] after the act of giving.
In that same way, this mind perishes, and duality likewise attains the state of non-duality.
Having properly reached its object, it dissolves by itself.

He establishes, by means of an illustration, the dissolution of the mind into Brahman within its own self. [The verse begins with] "the combustible" (dāhyam). The word "object" (viṣaya) is connected with the word "duality" (dvaita). || 724 ||
But when this mind has dissolved, that bliss which is witnessed by one's own self arises.
Those who know yoga call this the supreme state of yoga.

Following the dissolution of the mind (*manolaya*), the state of the Supreme Brahman, which consists of supreme bliss, is established through the experience of the wise. In this regard, he cites the consensus of the Yoga scriptures:

"In the mind... As it has been stated: "When all mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) are suppressed, however, there is the *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi* (the concentration without cognitive content)," known by the name *dharmamegha*.

Having thus described this meditative absorption (samādhi), it was further stated that from it follows the cessation of afflictions (kleśa) and karma; therefore, the afflictions such as ignorance (avidyā) and so forth are uprooted, and the latent impressions of wholesome and unwholesome karma are destroyed along with their roots. Due to this cessation of afflictions and karma, the wise one becomes liberated even while living. || 729 ||
In the example of fire,
iron that has been heated returns to the state of earth.
Likewise, when the mind is fixed on the Imperishable, one attains the state of non-becoming.

Anticipating the objection that—just as fire and the destruction of wood have different substrata—the mind and the destruction of duality likewise have different substrata, and thus there can be no dissolution of the mind in the Self—he says: "In the ground" (bhūmau). || 726 ||

And this is also seen in the world: by whatever things one is joined, [those very things one experiences].
The mind attains identity with that, being colored by its nature.

Raising the objection that—since iron is a modification of earth, that which is placed within it becomes identical with it, whereas the mind, being material, is not a modification of the Imperishable (akṣara) and thus the case is not the same—he states a general principle to resolve this: "And this... (verse 727).
In this way, when this supreme reality is being meditated upon by one seeking liberation,
One attains that state before long and achieves stability right here.

He applies the aforementioned reasoning to the present case with the word "evam" (thus). Just as the mind, though colored by and absorbed in sense objects, is sometimes seen to turn away from them, so too, one might suspect that the mind fixed upon the Self—even if it has taken that form—might at some point deviate from it. Anticipating this, he says: "And stability... [The meaning is: for a mind that has become one with the Self, there is no falling away from it, because that would entail the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa-prasaṅga*) and because there is no other object of contemplation remaining.
This is the meaning. || 728 ||
Following the destruction of the mind, this conscious self dissolves.
Just as the intended object [is realized] through both the path of knowledge and the path of yoga.

Anticipating the objection that even when the mind is dissolved into Brahman, there is no liberation for the transmigrating soul because of its continued existence [as a subtle body], he says: "The mind... The meaning is: "because it has that [the mind] as its limiting adjunct. Anticipating the question, "What is the proof for this?", he says: "Just as... [referring to] the combination [of means].

Just as the dissolution of the mind in the Self is shown, so too is the dissolution of the individual soul (jīva) in this [Supreme Self] presented; such is the construction [of the verse], meaning that knowledge and action are to be practiced in combination. || 729 ||
Intending this very point, it was said: "There is nothing whatsoever here."
"There is no diversity"—in this way, oneness is declared in this scripture. (730)

Having explained the meaning of the passage beginning with "by the mind alone" (*manasaiva*), he introduces the section beginning with "not here" (*neha*) and states its purport: "This" (*etad*). The meaning is that, having accepted the non-dual nature of the Self as existing in the state of fruition, the text proceeds with "not here" and so forth to declare the absence of manifoldness (*nānātva*) in that liberated Self. Anticipating the objection that this denial contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, he says: "In this way" (*ityevam*). This is because, although manifoldness exists during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), [it does not exist in liberation].

The meaning is that unity is intended by the scripture in this manner—that [the difference] is non-existent in the state of liberation; thus, there is no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, as they have as their object the manifoldness belonging to saṃsāra. || 730 ||
This is the means for entering liberation by following the path as it has been described here.
It has been stated that when there is a single cognition in the mind, it is therefore a mental [cognition]. || 731 ||

Having explained the purport of the sentence part by part, he states the intended meaning as a whole with the words "mukti" (liberation), etc. As for the question of what the cause is for a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) to enter into liberation through the dissolution of the mind and so forth—what is intended here regarding the connection with the mind—he says:
"In one," etc. That mental conviction which is extremely firm regarding the one Brahman, namely, "I am the non-dual Brahman"—that is [the cause].
The meaning is that it is the cause for entering liberation; the word *yataḥ* is used in the sense of the first case (nominative). || 731 ||
It should be understood that even the determination of oneness belongs to the mental [consciousness] alone.
That activity,
however,
being undissolved, would become this mental modification (*manovṛtti*).
This shall continue until all these particularities have come to an end.

How can the cognition of oneness be mental? [The author] states this because it must be one of two things: either the self-reality itself or a modification thereof. He says: "Oneness... and so forth. First, that cognition is not the self itself, because it possesses a beginning and an end; nor is it a modification, because the self is unchanging.
Therefore, since it establishes the self as Brahman, it is called a "determination" (vyavasthā); the conclusion is that it is merely a mental modification (mānasī vṛtti). This is the meaning.

The word "api" (also) has the sense of "like the cognition of diversity. He states the limit of its duration with the words "But that... The meaning is that it subsides because, like a fire without fuel, it lacks further utility. || 732 ||
Then, within its own self, knowledge is completely purified, having the nature of non-duality.
Having performed it in this way, it would become manifest; thus it is said.

When the objects have perished and that [consciousness] has also perished, what remains? To this he says: "In its own self. The word "then" (*atha*) is used to establish the absence of any obstacle to knowledge being established in its own majesty. The term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) expresses its very independence.
He states that the passage beginning with "at one time" (*ekadā*) proceeds by keeping in mind the previously described nature of the Self: "having done thus" (*evaṃ kṛtvā*). || 733 ||
Having entered into this by means of the mind, one gradually attains the supreme state of oneness.
That reality, which is immeasurable, should be perceived with effort by the wise man.
He states its meaning: "By the mind," etc.; the sense is that it occurs gradually by way of attaining the deity-sūtras. || 734 ||
I.1 Because it is immutable, it is eternal and imperishable, abiding within the inner self.
The meaning is that he is stainless and pure, abiding beyond the ether.
Because he is unborn and greater than all that is great, he is called Mahat.

He states the meaning of the word *dhruva* (constant) with the words "because of immutability" (*kauṭasthyāt*). He explains the phrase beginning with *viraja* (free from passion/dust) as follows: "free from passion" (*virajaḥ*).
Having thus known the Self to be of such a nature, one should make one's resolve firm.
Firmly rooted in the continuum of the knowledge born of cultivation, and unshakable. || 737 ||
At the time of meditation, one should not contemplate words that express duality.
These [words] cause this speech of yours, which expresses oneness, to grow weary.
He states the meaning of "tameva" and so forth: "tam" (that). || 737 || 738 ||
When she is ill, his mind is directed toward her for her sake, and does not dwell upon this [other object]. || 739 ||
Therefore, one should not contemplate these [distinctions], but rather that which expresses oneness.
Having first reflected upon that [truth] with speech, one should fix the mind upon its meaning.
[Objection: Let there be exhaustion of speech that expresses oneness; what loss is there in that? [The author] says: "In the case of exhaustion...
[The reading] *anādhyāna* is found in manuscripts *sva* and *ga*; *cālanī* in manuscript *ka*; *tu caika* in manuscripts *ka*, *kha*, and *ga*; and *nīm* or *vā* in manuscript *ka*.

1843 He concludes the meaning with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). What, then, ought to be done by one desiring liberation? To that he says: "But rather" (*kiṃtu*).
This commentary on the verses of the illustrious Bhartṛprapañca has thus been declared.
Having begun with the words "by the mind alone," that very point is now being investigated.
Or, with effort and through logical arguments, one should distinguish between what is right and what is wrong. || 742 ||

He concludes the opponent's position with the words "śrīmad" and so forth. He anticipates a fault therein with the words "sā tu" (but that). He states the fruit of the investigation: having investigated with intent and divided [the text], the portion accompanied by reasoning is accepted, while the other is rejected;
this is expressed by the words "yatnāt" (with effort). || 741 || 742 ||
"That which was stated by you, 'it is to be perceived by the mind alone'—"
This is true: apart from the mind, that [consciousness] has no other course.
Showing that what stands on the path of others is acceptable, he accepts the statement, "This is to be seen by the mind alone; there is no other way," with the words:
"By the mind alone. || 743 ||
Therefore, the view has been stated by us that [this] is indeed through the mind alone.
It can be perceived by the mind in that very same way, because it follows from valid cognition.
Anticipating the objection that "accepting what is propounded by another is indeed a state of having no other recourse," he says: "That [is not so].

The meaning is as follows: just as we have stated that the vision of the Self is by means of the mind alone, so too when you say that the reality of the Self can be seen by the mind alone, we do not refute that; for the fact established by such scriptural passages as "it is to be perceived by the mind alone" is beyond reproach.
Furthermore, the operation of the means of valid cognition which has been described here [is as follows].
That too may indeed be desire; no fault is said to exist therein. || 745 ||

Regarding the manner in which verbal cognition is produced, as shown by the passage beginning with "yattu tattvamasyādivākyoktau" (as for what was said regarding the statement of "That thou art" and so forth), he states that even this has been accepted by us: "pramāṇa... etc. The word "iha" (here) refers to the statement of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa). || 745 ||
In the initial activity of the cognizer, consciousness has sound as its primary object.
Thereafter, sound arises through the sequence of its own operation.
It attains the state of being predominant in knowledge by way of the convention of its own object.
1) He elaborates upon the manner of verbal cognition as stated by others and accepted by himself, along with its supplementary details. Regarding the word "śabda":
immediately after the utterance of a word by the teacher, for the cognizer—the listener—there arises [a cognition] whose instrument is the sense of hearing and whose object is the mere word.

The meaning is that when the activity known as cognition occurs, that cognition initially has sound as its primary object, because the object (karman) is predominant among the factors of action (kārakas). Immediately after that, by way of the sequence of cognizing its own object—dependent upon the recollection of the relationship between the word and its meaning—it [cognizes] that very object. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopani�ṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya (1844), [the author] states that knowledge is made primary, while action becomes subordinate to it as its instrument, because it brings about that [knowledge]. He says, "Immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*).
The word "atha" (*then*) serves to conclude the manner in which the aforementioned meaning has been explained through the words. || 746 ||
It is colored by the form of sentences, following the sequence of phonemes, vowels, and so forth.
But when there is the apprehension of an unknown object, knowledge is called valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 747 ||

He clarifies what was stated from the words "sound is primary" up to "is produced" with the verse beginning "varṇa... etc. Regarding "varṇa...": the cognition arising from the auditory organ which takes as its form a sentence qualified by the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*), vowels (*svara*), and words (*pada*)—that cognition is called a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the sentence, because it functions by taking as its cause the apprehension of the meaning of the sentence in its unapprehended form; thus, cognition [is established] in relation to the sentence.
The meaning is that its quality [is expressed] as the object (karman), because it is the primary element. || 747 ||
Previously, cognition was non-different from the word, being colored by the form of the word. (748)
"Just as it has been stated here that this is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to its own object of cognition (prameya)."
The same applies even to the object of cognition; previously, this [cognition] was primarily focused on the object. (749)

Expanding upon the passage beginning with "immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*), he restates the aforementioned point by means of an example: "Sound" (*śabda*). The meaning is as follows: just as at the time of the arising of the cognition of sound through the auditory organ, sound possesses primacy as the object (*karman*), whereas immediately after its arising, during the time of its existence, the cognition possesses the status of a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*) because it is the instrument for establishing that sound;
and since cognition is non-different from sound, it is established in the preceding [section] that cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*māna*) regarding its own object, namely, sound.

He states the very meaning of the phrase "non-different from the word" as "having the form of the word. He states the application to the case at hand (*dāṣṭantika*) with the words "even in the object of cognition" (*prameye 'pi*).

Following the aforementioned example, the meaning is that even regarding an object of cognition such as a jar, this cognition arising from the word, at the time of its production, has the jar and so forth as its primary [object], because the jar is primary by virtue of being the object (*karman*). || 748 || 749 ||
Subsequently, through the activity of the means of knowledge, there occurs the coloring [of the self] by the cognition that has been attained.
When there is knowledge, the object of cognition becomes a quality in the cognizer. (750)

He says [the following] regarding the phrase "it becomes the object" (*meyeti*): Following the arising of a cognition in which the object is predominant, by virtue of the operation consisting in the object's being pervaded by the means of knowledge (*māna*), that object to be measured (*meyo 'rthaḥ*) attains the state of being a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*) within that cognition—which is a transformation of the knower (*mātṛ-pariṇāma*)—because it is connected with its own object, the cognition; for it is rendered possessed of manifestation (*sphuraṇavat*) by the knower. Thus he says: "it becomes the object. (750)
Knowledge that follows immeasurable objects is colored by the objects of cognition.
By the aforementioned means of valid cognition, the object of knowledge is stated through its connection [to the means]. (751)

In this regard, he says: "The cognition of an object has the word as its source, takes on its form, and is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) because its object is an unknown thing. [He states] "unmeasured" [etc.].
He provides the reason for the pot and so forth being objects of knowledge: "by the previous," meaning by the cognition in the form already described. || 751 ||
The relationship between the object of measurement and the means of measurement is established here just as it has been explained.
In this very same way, it should be understood regarding other objects of knowledge and means of knowledge as well.
He extends the process described for verbal cognition and its object to other cases as well, stating: "The notion of 'mine'... (verse 752).
1 ga. That is their knowledge.

4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri:
"Because of the connection between the object of knowledge and the means of knowledge, there would be a confusion of the objects of knowledge and the means of knowledge."
That which was a qualifying attribute in the process of destruction attains the status of a means of knowledge within the nature of the result.

Having demonstrated the process culminating in knowledge and its object, he now describes the process connected with that knowledge and its fruit: "māyā" etc. The meaning is that, following the mutual relationship between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyya*), the momentary knowledge, as it perishes, becomes a qualifier within the fruit. || 753 ||
Because it has that much as its primary objective, it is called the fruit of the means of valid cognition.
Thus has this activity of Mānava been described exactly as it is. || 754 ||

He illustrates that manner [of cognition] with the words "merely that much" (*tāvanmātra*). The fruit alone is the primary [result] of the means of knowledge (*māna*), because without its determination, that [means] would be negligible;
therefore, since "this is the fruit of that," the means of knowledge also becomes subordinate (*viśeṣaṇatva*) to the fruit, which is called "manifestation.
Furthermore, the meaning is that this [fruit] is beginningless, endless, and non-dual. Having accepted the operation of the means of knowledge, he concludes by elaborating upon what has been refined.
"Thus is this," [it is said]. || 794 ||
Activity, which has the body, speech, and intellect as its instruments, must depend upon an agent.
In that regard, because the person is independent, it is the scripture of knowledge (*vidyāśāstra*) that sets him in motion. (755)

In the system of Bhartṛprapañca, the portion to be refuted has been shown as something to be accepted; now, with the words "only the thing-in-itself [is grasped] by speech in the intellect," etc., he prepares the ground to refute what was stated—that in passages such as "having understood," the act of making known (*prajñākaraṇa*) is the enjoined duty. He says: "an operation.
That which can be done, not done, or done otherwise by a person is what is enjoined, such as a sacrifice and so forth, which are accomplished by means of the body and other instruments.
The meaning is that the agent possesses independence with respect to the root-meaning. He shows that the scripture of injunctions has scope regarding the action already mentioned:
"one should know" (vidyāt). || 755 ||
But the reality of the matter is that wherever consciousness arises by force, that is the actual locus.
In that case, since it does not depend on a person, no injunction whatsoever is required. (756)

Having explained the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), he states that in the present case, an injunction for the production of knowledge is impossible due to the absence of such a subject matter. He says: "The thing" (*vastu*). Among the types of injunctions—restrictive (*niyama*), original (*apūrva*), or exclusive (*parisaṃkhyā*)—none is possible here. This is because knowledge arising from the power of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is dependent solely on the object itself; it is not contingent upon the person. Furthermore, since the realization of reality can arise from the Word alone, there can be no injunction regarding repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) directed toward that end.
The meaning is: because it is ineffective. || 796 ||
For activity depends upon the agent, according to the scriptural teaching that "one should meditate upon this very [Self]."
Or it may be eternal, consisting of meditation and so forth, for the sake of the purification of the intellect. || 757 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the sentence concerning the means of knowledge (*prajñākaraṇa*) does not have injunction (*vidhi*) as its primary purport: "The activity" (*vyāpāra*). For here, since knowledge is not fit for injunction, its cause must be enjoined; and that cause—namely, activities such as the recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*) and so forth, as well as tranquility (*śama*) and the like, which depend upon the person—is enjoined by the sentence concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) and by the sentence concerning tranquility and the rest. Therefore, the meaning is that this [sentence] does not have injunction as its primary purport. [This applies to] the injunction regarding the means to knowledge.

Anticipating the objection, "If it will be explained later, how can it be said that its production arises from the word alone?", he says: "That [result] would be... [referring to the injunction of the Veda].

Since it is well-established by Śruti and Smṛti that the means consisting of recitation and so forth, which cause the purification of the mind, possess the status of being causes for that [knowledge], and since one who is pure and enlightened— (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be an incomplete sentence or a section heading. The translation reflects the available portion.)

The meaning is that the word of one who acts [as an authority] generates knowledge for one who is qualified, according to the principle that "the Veda is a producer of valid cognition for those who possess the requisite qualification. ||717||
When the intellect becomes liberated from darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas) through the aforementioned practice, [it attains its true state].
Then, through tranquility and the other [qualities], one perceives reality as it truly is, and then the Self. || 758 ||

As for the objection that, if the knowledge of reality arises from the word alone, why does it not occur to all who have heard the words, that too is refuted by this very point; thus he says: "That [darkness]. Considering that tranquility (*śama*) and the other means are more proximate to knowledge than the recitation of the Vedas and so forth, he qualifies [the subject] as "one possessed of tranquility and the rest. Since the passage begins with "When" (*yadā*), the word "then" (*atha*) means "at that time" (*tadā*). || 798 ||
When that [Self] is seen, then, because everything consists solely of that as its single reality, [all else vanishes].
Likewise, from the total eradication of all ignorance, there arises omniscience. || 759 ||

If it is argued that self-investigation is neither enjoined nor fruitful, he says "no," beginning with the words "In that" (*tasmin*). The fruit of vision is the fruit seen [in this life], namely, the state of having accomplished all that was to be done; this is the meaning of the word *atha*. To demonstrate this, he states that everything to be known is already known by the knower of the Self, beginning with the words "all ignorance. He provides the reason why all things are known through the knowledge of the Self, beginning with the words "of all. Finally, he states the fruit of knowing all things.
The attainment of all human goals without exception, and the destruction of the flood of all suffering.
Therefore, because one has accomplished all that was to be done once the Self is known, [there is no further duty]. 760.
There would be an impossibility of activity accomplished by speech, mind, and body.
Because all means in this world have the fruit as their ultimate limit. (761)

When all ignorance has been destroyed, what is accomplished? To this he says: "Without remainder," etc. The meaning is that for the knower of the Self, the state of having fulfilled all duties (*kṛtakṛtyatva*) is thus established. If it be argued that even such a knower would remain subject to injunctions, he says "no," because [he states] "since," etc. Since it is impossible, there is no injunction for the knower; this is the ellipsis. He supports this impossibility of an injunction for one who has fulfilled all duties by means of worldly consensus.

"It bears fruit" (phalati). Even in the world, since all means culminate in their result, once the result has been attained, there is no further performance of the means by way of an injunction, because it would be fruitless; this is the meaning. || 760 || 761 ||
Granted, let this very cognizer indeed become identical with the object of cognition.
Because that very [consciousness] undergoes transformation and because it is connected with the object of cognition. || 762 ||

The method for making [the self] an object of cognition has been briefly refuted. As for the claim that the conscious Self also attains identity with that [object] due to its being of the same nature as it, the author analyzes this by posing the alternatives: does this "being of the same nature" belong to the mother or to the witness? He accepts the first alternative, stating "as the object of cognition. He states the reason for accepting it in the words "of that... (verse 762).
Because it is devoid of the six modifications of existence, and because it is unattached and without a self.
The nature of consisting of consciousness and so forth does not belong to the inner self (pratyagātman) by its own nature. 763 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the verse beginning "ṣaḍ" (six). [This concludes] Brāhmaṇa 4, from the *Śāstraprakāśikā* commentary by Ānandagiri. [Page/Line reference: 1847. 763.
Even though it has become thus, it remains unperceived in its nature as cause and effect.
Just as this rope, when not recognized, assumes the form of a snake. || 76 ||

If the Self is devoid of all modifications, unattached, and not by its own nature composed of consciousness and so forth, how then is there the scriptural teaching of its being the self of all? To this he says: "Even though it is such," [verse 764].
The entire [phenomenal world], beginning with the mind, arises from the cause of ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyag-ajñāna).
When the cause is destroyed, there is destruction; [this occurs] in the imperishable, which is neither an effect nor a cause.

Although it may be argued that this conscious self (vijñānātman) dissolves following the destruction of the mind, and that its dissolution therein consists of either sublation dependent on knowledge or destruction and so forth—having thus raised this alternative, the author accepts the first option with the words "The mind... [verse 769].
"From the awakening to reality, there would be no destruction, nor would there be negation and affirmation."
Because of the identity of each individual [cognition] with the reality [of the object], ignorance and so forth do not exist here within the Self. (766)
He refutes the second [alternative] with the words "tattve" (in reality). "Destruction" means non-existence; "separation" means distinctness from the entity;
"conjunction" means contact with the cause. He states the reason for the impossibility of all three types of dissolution with the word "pratyak" (the inner self):
the connection here is that within this Self, there is neither the destruction of ignorance and so forth, nor their conjunction or separation. || 766 ||
Wherever destruction is produced, whether it be through negative concomitance (vyatireka) or positive concomitance (anvaya).
Due to the relationship between cause and effect, liberation there is extremely difficult to attain.

He states the defect in the opposing view [the view that bondage is real] with the words "destruction" (*vināśa*). First of all, there can be no absolute destruction of ignorance and the like, because that which possesses a counter-correlate (*sapratyogika*) cannot be so [absolutely destroyed]. Furthermore, regarding non-absolute destruction, since it involves a connection with a cause, if there were an absence of such a connection, a temporary connection would be possible; and since such a connection is accepted in the case of its presence, there would follow a re-bondage—this is the meaning. The two pronouns *yat* and *tat* refer to the subject of the proposition (*pakṣārtha*). || 767 ||
If the mind, conditioned by meditative absorption and so forth, perishes at liberation, [then what remains?]
If [the object] were thus accompanied by conceptualization, then all meditative absorption would be entirely useless. || 768 ||

He states another defect in the position that [the mind] is destroyed: "Dhyānādi... etc. If liberation is desired when the mind is in its specialized state, then its destruction would be useless; for if it were to perish during the intended liberation, then since meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth would fail to establish themselves as its cause, statements such as "as he wills" and so on would be mere empty prattle. Nor is it said that the mind, having brought about liberation like knowledge, perishes; for [the scripture says], "By meditating upon that... and so forth.
The meaning is that there is an absence of proof for this point; such is the intention. || 768 ||
Then, upon liberation, it follows that [liberated soul], for it would have followed along with its cause.
When ignorance exists, tell me, by what can saṃsāra be warded off? (769)

He elaborates on the weakness of liberation in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*). Ignorance is the cause; and as long as it exists, there is a continuous connection with misfortune, so there is no liberation—this is the meaning. || 769 ||

The cause of iron and the like is the earth; it resides in the earth and is measured by the nature of the earth.
Due to contact with a contrary cause, iron and other such substances do not attain the state of air.

Having set aside the dissolution of the mind and other faculties as the point to be illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*), he refutes the example stated in the passage beginning with "just as iron placed on the earth," by saying "of iron and so forth.
Earth is the cause of the emergence of bronze, iron, and the like; however, their being composed of fire (*taijasatva*) is merely a theoretical construct (*prakriyāmātra*).

Furthermore, when there is non-natural fluidity (*asāṃsiddhikadravatva*) in a specific class (*jāti*) or limiting condition (*upādhi*), it does not constitute a uniform form that proves their being composed of fire. For non-natural fluidity indeed...

[The definition of light as] "being the substratum of fluidity produced by [external] causes" or "not being the substratum of natural fluidity" is not tenable. In the first case, there is a deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*) in the example of lamp-light. In the second case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to certain specific portions of earth; for even before and after heating, the color in those parts is not of a single kind.

This is because of the scriptural statement that "whatever is black belongs to food," which indicates that the color of earth is of a single kind, and that [color] exists in the earth by its own nature.

The meaning is as follows: when iron situated in the earth melts due to contact with another opposing substance, it returns to its own causal state, which is earth, and does not attain the state of air or other elements that are not its own causes; therefore, while the transformation of iron and the like into earth is possible, the transformation of the mind and so forth into Brahman—which is not their cause—is not established. || 770 ||
It is held that all this effect is eternal and resides within its own cause.
And that [entity] does not possess causality; therefore, what was stated is untenable.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "that which is seen," etc., [the author] intends to show that it is not possible for an effect to dissolve anywhere other than its cause; thus, he addresses the proponent who asserts that even Brahman is the cause by saying, "residing in its own cause. The view of the proponents of transformation (*pariṇāmavādin*) is that all this effect always exists within its own cause, Brahman, in the form of that [cause]; therefore, that effect [is never separate from its cause]. At times, it [appears as] the state of being the cause...
Thus it is stated; and in that case, the meaning is that the causality of Brahman would not be established in reality. || 771 ||
Through the destruction of the formative impressions arising from the potter and so forth, that [pot] perishes of its own accord.
It attains the status of cause and effect, but not because of the persistence of that [prior] cause. || 772 ||

Just as it is a worldly convention that an effect such as a jar, although always residing in its cause such as clay, reaches a state of destruction through the operation of a mallet or similar instrument, so too the world, though always situated in Brahman, perishes through meditation and other means.

Anticipating the objection that "it becomes this" is not contradictory, he says: "From the potter, etc. What is called *saṃskāra* (latent impression/disposition) is a specific configuration such as the shell-like neck [of a jar];

its concealment or destruction by the striking of a mallet and so forth causes its effect to perish. It is said that [the effect] "returns to the state of being the cause," but it is not the case that the effect itself perishes and attains causality; for it [already] exists eternally within the cause.

Therefore, because [Brahman] is eternally established and because there is no [external] example, meditation and the like have no utility for the world’s becoming that [Brahman] in the view that Brahman is the cause; such is the meaning. || 772 ||
Wherever there is work to be done, one's exertion must certainly be directed toward that very place.
The meaning of this scriptural passage is to be understood as [the culmination] of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), knowledge (jñāna), and ritual action (karman). || 773 ||

Where, then, is their utility? To this he says: "It is commenced" (ārabhyam). In that view where the effect known as the desire to know Brahman (*vividiṣā*) is commenced through meditation and the like, it is precisely there that their fruitful engagement is to be understood, according to the scriptural passage beginning with "him [one seeks to know] by the recitation of the Vedas" (*tametam vedānuvacanena*). Therefore, the meaning is that their utility lies in the desire to know. || 773 ||

Being Brahman itself while living, one reaches Brahman there through the destruction of darkness.
There is no activity of these [senses] therein, because it would contradict their production and so forth.

To the question, "Why is it not accepted that liberation follows for them directly? he replies: "Brahman itself. The meaning is this: according to the established doctrine that one who is Brahman by nature becomes Brahman upon the destruction of the darkness of obstacles, meditation and the like do not function there with the attainment of that state as their fruit, because they have fruits such as origination (*utpatti*) and so forth, and because that [attainment] is contrary to [the realization of] that [Brahman]. || 774 ||
Even the practice of knowledge that destroys the ignorance of the inner self is not accepted [as the means].
For, by the very fact of the self's single arising, ignorance is destroyed through awakening. || 775 ||

Anticipating the objection that meditation (*dhyāna*) and other practices might be useful for the destruction of the obstacles to the state of Brahmanhood, he says "pratyak" (the inner self). The word "api" (also) serves to include the recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*) and so forth. The reason for this is stated as "sakṛt" (once). || 779 ||
For there is nothing in this world that,
being pure existence, depends on repetition to destroy darkness regarding its own object of cognition, just as a means of proof destroys ignorance regarding its own objective.

For this reason as well, he states that there is no requirement for repetition when consciousness destroys darkness, by saying "na hi" (for not). He provides an illustration for that with "svasādhya" (in its own result).

The meaning is: just as the means such as sacrifice, when prescribed, do not require repeated practice toward their result—whether that be heaven or the supreme *apūrva*—so too is the knowledge of the Self arising from the [Vedic] sentence. || 776 ||
Whatever fruit may arise from cultivation, and whatever may be the fruit of karma;
"It should not be thought that [the self] resides therein, just as in the case of approaching a prostitute.
(777) Those, however, who—refusing to admit that [the self] is obscured by ignorance—proclaim that liberation is achieved directly through meditation and other such means, [should be refuted].
To this he says: "cultivation" (bhāvanā). The example for the instability of a result that depends upon cultivation is "a courtesan" (paṇyastrī) || 777 ||
If one thinks, "I am a transmigrator," that [ignorance] remains undestroyed, having been nourished for kalpas beyond measure.
In this regard, what proof is there that a cultivation born from even slight practice is stable? (778)
Anticipating the objection that because the contemplation "I am Brahman" (brahmāsmi) is stable, its fruit—liberation (kaivalya)—will also be stable, he says:
"The transmigrator" (saṃsārī). || 778 ||
Therefore, this is not correct for those who seek the accumulation of meditative cultivation.
The meditations and other practices that were set forth for the sake of liberation from all misfortune.
He concludes the demonstration that meditation and the like cannot be the means to liberation with the words: "Therefore... (779).
If that which has been communicated in its entirety by means of speech is directly realized within oneself;
Tell me, what does an object require from the operation of meditation for it to appear in the intellect? (780)
If it is argued that even though meditation does not have liberation as its purpose, it must still be practiced for the sake of knowledge, he says "no," [citing] the scriptural statement.

1850 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
The supreme cause of the attainment of absolute liberation and the complete cessation of all misfortune.
That which was intended to be done has been completed and brought to an end by that knowledge.

Anticipating the objection that although meditation (*dhyāna*) is required for the arising of knowledge (*jñāna*), it might still be required for its fruit, he says: "niḥśeṣa... (without remainder). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, meditation is not purposeful. || 781 ||
Everything that was intended to be done has been accomplished, and all that you desired to know has been understood.
Through the arising of right knowledge, everything that was intended to be abandoned has been relinquished.
And thus, having attained what was desired, there is the state of having accomplished all that was to be done.
From the awakening to the Self, which consists merely in the destruction of the delusion regarding the true nature of the inward-facing reality. || 783 ||

"Through knowledge, it manifests that which has indeed attained all desired objects. [The word] "accomplished" (*kṛtam*) clarifies what was stated as "from the arising of perfect knowledge" (*samyagjñānodayāt*).
[The word] "inner" (*pratyak*) is connected with the preceding phrase "the state of having accomplished all that was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtyatā*). || 782 || 783 ||
If the object, as it has been described, is presented to the intellect by means of a word;
It must be stated for what purpose there is the injunction, "One should cultivate wisdom. || 784 ||

Anticipating the objection—"Since there is the injunction 'one should cultivate wisdom when [the Self] exists,' why is meditation (dhyāna) dismissed as fruitless?"—he considers the alternatives of whether that injunction applies to Brahman known or unknown, and refutes the first by restating it: "If it has been presented," meaning, if it has been presented with the characteristics such as freedom from passion (virajastva) as previously described. || 784 ||
If the object as it was described by the scripture has not been directly presented [to the senses], then...
The Veda would incur invalidity because it does not convey its own meaning. (785)
Having restated the second [position], he refutes it: "If not," etc. (785).
A means of valid cognition, being operative toward its own object of cognition, [is established] by virtue of its own attainment.
Without the removal of ignorance and the like, there is nothing in the world that can bring about awakening.

Anticipating the objection that the authority of the Śruti is based on its capacity to convey its own meaning, whereas the injunction for meditation is useful for destroying ignorance and so forth regarding the object [of meditation], he says: "In its own object of knowledge" (svaprameye). The meaning is that since it is impossible to convey its own meaning without destroying ignorance and so forth, there is no need for an injunction regarding the destruction of ignorance and so forth in the Self beyond the verbal comprehension [arising from the Śruti]. || 786 ||
There is nothing other than ignorance, error, and doubt.
In the case of an object of knowledge that is its own counter-correlate, there is no further desire for a means of valid cognition whatsoever.

Raising the objection that since knowledge, by destroying ignorance and so forth which reside in the object of knowledge, might as well destroy the consciousness (caitanya) and other qualities inherent in that [object], he says "ajñāna... [verse 787] to show that even though it destroys its opposites, it does not destroy everything.
The triad beginning with ignorance is to be sublated, because it depends upon the true nature of the object of cognition.
In this case, pride alone is the sublater; for it is not sublated by that which is itself sublated. || 788 ||

Anticipating the objection that, since there is no difference in their being mutually opposed, knowledge itself might be what is removed by ignorance and so forth—thereby reversing the relationship—he says: [The text here indicates a lacuna or corruption in the manuscript tradition, as evidenced by the various readings: 1. *aṅgā-prāptiḥ* (the non-attainment of the auxiliary); 2. *kaiṃ* (an abbreviation or corruption); 3. *dadha dhva* (variant reading); 4. *prakaṭayati* (he makes manifest); 5. *na vihaṃ* (not here). "Is not [the case]" (*nādīti*) provides the reason for the sublation of the means of knowledge (*māna*). "It is mine" (*meyeti*) expresses the subject of sublation under discussion here. He states the restriction that eliminates [other possibilities] with the words "by the object of sublation" (*bādhyena*). || 788 ||
The validity of a means of knowledge arises precisely from its sublation of that which is to be sublated.
But for that which has always acquired its form through a connection with what is to be cognized by itself...
He supports the statement that pride is indeed an obstacle with the words: "Of that which is to be sublated... (789).
Fire is not considered to possess the nature of fire until it has burned the fuel placed upon it.
Just as a sublater cannot exist without first subverting that which is to be sublated, so it is not the case for the validity of cognition.

He clarifies this point—that the validity of a means of knowledge arises precisely through the sublation of any one of [the defects] such as ignorance—by means of an illustration: "No," [he says]. || 790 ||
And valid cognition is not employed for the sake of producing [an effect] and so forth.
Because it is manifested from its own object of cognition, no other effect is admitted for it. || 791 ||

If it is argued that even though meditation (*dhyāna*) is not enjoined in the statement concerning the "instrument of knowledge" (*prajñākaraṇa*), there must be an injunction regarding the knowledge denoted by the word *prajñā*, we reply: Is this [injunction] based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? In the first case, one must consider whether what is enjoined is any one of the causes for the arising of that [knowledge], or whether it is for the sake of some other fruit. Regarding the first alternative, he says: "Not so. The meaning is that the status of the arising of valid knowledge as a fruit is not supported by any means of valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*).
He states the second [point]: "In one's own self," etc. (791).
Nor is contradiction with other means of knowledge admitted in the case of what is to be known by a means of knowledge.
Because the objects of the means of knowledge are unique [to each], just like the eyes and other sense organs. || 792 ||

Regarding the claim that knowledge called *prajñā* must be cultivated even if it is invalid—whether that invalidity arises from non-corroboration by other means of knowledge (*māna*) or from contradiction with them—the author, considering that such [invalid] cognition does not lead to practical activity (*pravṛtti*), refutes the second alternative with the words "And not...

The reason for this is given as "asādhāraṇa" (uncommon). The meaning is that because the various means of knowledge are "heroic" (*śūra*) regarding their own respective objects, there is no mutual contradiction between them. || 792 ||
If it is admitted that there is a contradiction of this means of knowledge by other means of knowledge, [then...]
In that case, there would be no reason for their exclusion, because contradiction rests upon valid cognition.

Or, even if there were a contradiction between statements such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and perception and other means of knowledge, one must still consider whether that contradiction is merely apparent (prātibhāsika) or real (vāstava). Having accepted the first alternative, he states the defect in the second case: "By other means of knowledge" (mānāntaraiḥ). || 793 ||
Nor is knowledge in its general form denoted by the suffix -lyap;
for the internal reality is established as being devoid of both generality and particularity.

Having refuted the view that the phrase "having known" (*vijñāya*) refers to a verbal, indirect cognition (*parokṣa-jñāna*), and that the injunction "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kuryāt*) prescribes its repetition for the sake of direct realization (*aparokṣa-jñāna*);

and having also rejected the claim that while "having known" denotes general knowledge, the word "wisdom" (*prajñā*) in the phrase "one should cultivate wisdom" denotes specific knowledge because Brahman possesses a dual nature—he now refutes that [position] with the words: "And not... (794).
For one who perceives this object both through its general characteristics and its specific details, [there is no contradiction].
Previously, it was described that there is no denial [of his existence], for they do not perceive him. || 795 ||

In this regard, he cites scripture as authority with the words "in general. The sense is that it is incorrect to claim that the meaning of the sentence is an injunction for repeated practice (*abhyāsa-vidhi*)—having first referred to general knowledge by means of a word ending in the suffix *-lyap* (i.e., *sāmānyena*), and then intending to express specific knowledge by means of a word ending in the accusative case—in order to establish that [specific knowledge].
But others, who consider themselves wise, [act] according to their own tradition.
However, they explain this scriptural statement, "having understood," in another way.

In the view of Bhartṛprapañca, it was refuted that the relationship of cause and effect and the relationship of universal and particular exist in reality within Brahman; now, [the author] sets forth the interpretation of that statement by Maṇḍana and others, who maintain that the inner self (pratyagbrahma) is neither an effect nor a cause and possesses neither universality nor particularity. "But others," he says. || 796 ||
By means of the realized knowledge arising from such statements as "That thou art," as previously described.
Having understood that [the self] is not in contact with objects, one should apply oneself diligently to the cultivation of wisdom. || 797 ||
How else could there be such an explanation? He states that: "The reality... [and so forth]. It is indicated that the word "with effort" (*yatnataḥ*) is to be repeated. || 797 ||
But surely, even here, that [action] is already expressed by means of the suffix -lyap.
Why, moreover, is its instrument prescribed as being unknown? (798)

He raises a doubt in order to clarify what has already been stated, beginning with "Now, [an objection]... The meaning is as follows: just as in the position of Bhartṛprapañca, in this position as well, it is said that wisdom (*prajñā*) is already accomplished when one "knows" (*vijānāti*); thus, since wisdom has already been brought into being, its further production cannot be enjoined by the injunction "one should produce wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kuryāt*), for that would entail the fallacy of grinding what has already been ground (*piṣṭapeṣaṇa*). || 798 ||
Let it not be so; for that which consists of the relation between word-meanings is itself of a nature other than that [of the external object].
Or rather, because of the cause for the arising of the cognition produced from the sentence regarding oneness (aikātmya). || 799 ||
Because that [Brahman] is not associated with anything else, it possesses neither generic nor specific qualities.
Or rather, the knowledge arising from a sentence has the form of a relation, like [the cognition of] "a blue lotus" and so forth. (800)

He refutes [the objection], saying: "Not so. The meaning is that since verbal knowledge—which consists of a mediated (parokṣa) form involving a relation between things—cannot arise with respect to Brahman, which is unrelated (asaṃsṛṣṭa) and immediate (aparokṣa), it does not touch upon Him.
Therefore, because the intended goal is a direct realization (sākṣātkāra) that touches Brahman, there is no grinding of what has already been ground.
He establishes that verbal knowledge is non-related to Brahman by stating: "Not being a universal," etc.; for it is opposed to Brahman, which is unrelated and immediate.

The meaning is that verbal cognition which is associated with a composite [object] and is mediate does not touch upon Brahman. An illustration for the mediacy and compositeness of verbal cognition is given: "blue," etc. || 799 || 800 ||
By its very nature, every sentence indeed consists of a relation [between meanings].
And likewise, it makes known the object itself even when it is beyond the senses. || 801 ||

How is it asserted that verbal knowledge is a direct perception of a related object? To this he says: "By its very nature. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to provide the example of the sentence concerning one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*). || 801 ||

And not by overstepping its own nature through resorting to another nature.
And the word is directly capable of making known that which is not associated with Brahman. (802)

One might raise the objection: "Even though a word produces a cognition that is associated with something other than Brahman and is indirect (*parokṣa*), it will nevertheless produce such a cognition regarding Brahman—which is unassociated and immediate—because a means of knowledge conforms to its object. Anticipating this, he says: "its own nature" (*svasvabhāvam*).
Since the essential form (*svarūpa*) is more primary than the external object, the word does not cause understanding by overstepping its own nature; this is the meaning. || 802 ||
Since the knowledge arising from the [Vedic] statement has not yet attained the true nature of Brahman, one should therefore cultivate wisdom that has as its sole object Brahman itself. (803)
He states the consequence of verbal cognition not touching Brahman: "alabdha... (803).
By which, when all associations have been cast aside, Brahman is attained.
And when there is the expectation "by what?", it is understood that it is "by consciousness."
Because of the proximity [of the word] spoken by Lya-ban-to, nothing other than that is required. || 805 ||
It reveals the wisdom that is to be accomplished. Regarding the word "apāsta" (cast aside), he states the instrument for the production of wisdom preceded by an inquiry: "By what?
He states the reason for its being the instrument: "Because of its proximity. For even [factors] such as Brahminhood are instruments because of their proximity.
Anticipating the objection that this might be a transgression, he says: "No. || 804 || 805 ||
This [word] is observed to be appropriate, proximate, and expectant [of completion].
Consciousness has been described as possessing power; that very thing is the means of accomplishment here.
In that regard, he shows the distinction: "suitable" (yogya). || 806 ||
Therefore, through the constant practice of the means for producing the knowledge arising from the [Vedic] sentences, [one attains the goal].
One should cultivate wisdom that brings about the realization of the true nature of Brahman, which is beyond all association.
Anticipating the objection that because it is momentary, it cannot serve as a means for producing wisdom, he says: "Therefore... (807).
Brahman is realized precisely through that state in which all associations have departed.
Therefore, it is precisely that wisdom which destroys all darkness without exception that is intended here.

He clarifies what was stated [in the previous verse] regarding non-association and so forth with the words "apeta" (having departed). Anticipating the objection that Brahman is already eternally known as one's own inner self (*pratyak*), making it useless to produce wisdom (*prajñā*), he says "yataḥ" (since). By the term "prajñā," direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) produced through repeated practice is intended.
For the sake of accomplishing direct vision, it is prescribed even elsewhere.
By the term *nididhyāsana*, the means characterized as meditation (*dhyāna*) is indicated. || 809 ||
He states that knowledge is not enjoined solely with a view toward direct realization here [in this context], but also in the "draṣṭavya" (to-be-seen) passage as well: "Directly," etc. (809).

Such statements as these belong to those who know the profound principle.
Some explain that this is refuted here with effort.
He summarizes the opinion of certain [teachers] with the words "and so forth" (*ityevamādi*). By the word "etc.

(*ādi*), sentences such as "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*) and "it is to be sought to be known" (*sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ*) are included. The meaning is: "by its own power, without following the actual nature of the thing through effort. He establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "here" (*atra*). || 810 ||
"A clear valid cognition regarding an object of knowledge that is not already known through another means of cognition..."
By subverting the status of what is not known, it is called a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 811 ||

To reveal that [definition], he first states the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). The qualifiers [in the verse] "mānāntara... and so forth are intended to exclude the status of being a pseudo-cognition (*ābhāsatva*) by means of its agreement or disagreement with other means of knowledge, and by the absence of a result. || 811 ||
"And this Brahman is not apprehended by means other than the [Vedic] word."
Just as a statement that awakens [the mind], so should it be understood to be exactly so. || 812 ||
Regarding the definition "valid cognition is that which makes known what was not previously known," he states what follows when this is under discussion: "Brahman.

If Brahman is perceived by the Śruti as being associated with mediacy (*parokṣatva*), then it must be accepted exactly in that way; it cannot be grasped as being dissociated from mediacy and immediate (*aparokṣa*). The meaning is that an object established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika-artha*) cannot be otherwise. || 812 ||
How can that which is established by valid cognition itself be subject to doubt?
Whether it be in the form of Brahmā, Saṃsāra, or Garuḍa, or otherwise, according to the Śruti. || 813 ||

In order to establish what has already been stated, he declares the general principle: "From the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāt*). The meaning is that it is not proper to entertain doubt by overstepping the means of valid cognition, because that would contradict the means of valid cognition itself. He applies that result to the subject at hand: "Brahman. The ellipsis to be supplied is "is known exactly as it is. (813)
If a thing is suspected even after it has been established by means of valid cognition, [then what can be trusted]?
Then, for the sake of removing doubt, what other means of knowledge could be sought? (814)

Having restated the opposing view, he states the fault: "Even by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*). This means that one is excessively suspicious; that is to say, doubt is raised even beyond what is warranted by valid cognition. || 814 ||
Nor, moreover, do means of valid cognition exist with respect to their own objects of measurement, because they are the causes of cognition.

Just as there is a gradation among causal factors with respect to their effects because such a gradation is impossible [in the case of Brahman], so too, regarding Brahman—which is understood through words as something mixed and beyond direct perception—the injunction for meditation is intended to produce a non-mixed, immediate realization; thus, the contradiction with the authority of verbal testimony has been stated here. Now, [it may be argued that] just as the eye perceives a distant tree as "a building" or "a substance" in relation to it, [so too might verbal testimony function].

Having first awakened the intellect to Brahman in a general sense, and then—just as the cognition "this is a tree" serves as a cause for the knowledge of reality by depending on subsequent approaches and so forth—the word also, following its own nature, first makes known Brahman as something associated and indirect (*saṃsṛṣṭa-parokṣa*); through the practice of that [cognition], it subsequently brings about the knowledge of the unassociated and immediate (*asaṃsṛṣṭāparokṣa*). Anticipating the objection that there is no contradiction in this sequence of awakening, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

He states the reason for the claim that "this is the nature of a producer (*kāraka*), not of a manifester (*bodhaka*)," namely: "because of impossibility" (*asaṃbhavāt*). For it is impossible for producers, such as clay and the like, to produce multiple effects simultaneously, as this is never observed; however, manifesters may indeed manifest multiple objects at once, since this is observed in the case of lamps and similar things. This is the meaning. || 815 ||
And [this is so] because the reality of Brahman is not directly known through other means of valid cognition.
It is possible for a wise person to state that this is a cognition not corresponding to reality. (816)

One might raise the objection that even in the absence of a sequential process of awakening among those who cause awakening, non-conceptual immediate knowledge (*asaṃsṛṣṭāparokṣajñāna*) regarding Brahman arises through the repeated practice of verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*) which is its opposite; yet, because that [verbal knowledge] is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), it cannot by itself be the cause for the attainment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Anticipating this, the author considers the alternative—whether or not the non-conceptual immediate Brahman is known through other forms of knowledge—and in response to the second alternative, he says: "If not. [The text continues: *asaṃ-*...

The meaning is that it is impossible to assert that verbal knowledge—which concerns Brahman as associated with the manifest world and perceived indirectly—is invalid simply because Brahman, when manifested as immediate, is not within the scope of other means of knowledge; for there exists no means of knowledge that contradicts it. || 816 ||
Even when [an object] is known through another means of valid cognition, it possesses a nature that is contradictory to that [other cognition].
And it is not logical to say this, because both [the means and the result] are indeed cognitions.

He refutes another alternative with the word "api" (even). The meaning is that it is not proper to say that verbal knowledge is invalid even in the case of Brahman—which is unconditioned, immediate, and accessible through means of knowledge other than words—because, just as with other means of knowledge, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is likewise unavoidable. || 817 ||
If Brahman, whose nature is non-association, is known by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), [then it would be an object of that cognition].
In that case, since wisdom has already been produced, this further injunction is fruitless. (818)

Anticipating the objection that the validity of verbal knowledge—which apprehends Brahman as being associated [with attributes] and beyond the senses—might be precluded by the contradiction of another means of knowledge that apprehends it in the opposite manner, he states another defect, intending to show that this is not so because the contradiction is equal [in both cases]: "By another means of knowledge... (818).
And because wisdom has reached its fulfillment, ignorance is dispelled.
And since the goal of human endeavor has already been attained, for what purpose would there be an injunction? (819)
He elaborates upon the fruitlessness of ritual action [vidhi] with the words "and of wisdom" (prajñāyāśca). || 819 ||
Knowledge arising from verbal testimony is said to be non-conformable with reality.
The manifold activity of the Omniscient One arises from reality as it is and is free from conceptual construction. || 820 ||
Furthermore, he mocks the one who claims that verbal cognition is invalid while that which arises from practice is valid, saying:
"The phrase 'vākya' [refers to] the practice of what is invalid. (820)
Furthermore, right knowledge does not arise from the repeated practice of false cognition.
In that case, liberation would come to all embodied beings without any effort. (821)
1. ga. known by others; 2. kha. [the word] *vaka* is not present.
1856 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya, Section 1] [Vol. 3, Page 723]
Furthermore, he says "not" [in verse 821] to address the objection that if verbal knowledge were invalid, then through its repeated practice, right knowledge could not arise for one who is fearful.
He states the fault in the opposing view with the words "tathā" (so). || 821 ||
They constantly practice this very false consciousness regarding saṃsāra.
And for living beings, right understanding does not arise regarding Brahman.

Having stated the over-extension [of the argument] by accepting that the arising of right knowledge occurs from the practice of false knowledge, he says "saṃsāra... (verse 822) to show that such [arising] does not exist because it is unobserved.
And because it does not produce right knowledge, it arises solely as an obstacle.
The latent impression (saṃskāra) has false cognition as its cause for practice, but not for [the initial] birth.
He states that it is not only the practice of false knowledge that fails to produce right knowledge, but rather that it is its opposite as well: "Right... (verse 823).
And so the blessed Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, has declared.
Previously, the cognition was directed toward another object and has now passed into a different time. (824)

He states the proof for the claim that "the practice of false knowledge is opposed to right cognition" with the words "And so it is. He illustrates this very point with the verse beginning "Previously.
The meaning is: in the beginningless succession of births, the mind first functions naturally toward objects such as sound, which are distinct from the Self;
and having been repeatedly refined by the habituation to those objects, it persists in that very state. || 824 ||
Therefore, due to hatred, one does not accept another object even though it exists.
He who does not accept after having examined [the matter], and accepts through the opposite [of examination]. || 825 ||

He states the fruit of attachment with the words "by that. The meaning is this: by the cause of attachment to objects (*viṣayāsaṅga*), one—due to aversion—does not accept the Inner Self (*pratyak*), which in reality transcends objects and consists of unsurpassed bliss (*anatiśayānanda*), even though it exists; for acceptance of that [Self] would be contradictory to the experience of objects. Having stated that the practice of experiencing objects is an obstacle to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), [he now speaks of] the obstacles...

He states the intermediate [verses]: "Having examined... The ellipsis is "it does not grasp an existent object. He says "and it grasps" to show that, without examination, it grasps an object even when it is non-existent. || 829 ||
And because of the firmness of their previous learning, as well as due to worldly negligence.
By these four causes, one does not find reality as it truly is. || 826 ||

One who possesses firm prior learning and an uncontradicted tradition does not, therefore, know reality merely by speculating on his own while examining the scriptures; thus he says: "Firm... etc. Worldly negligence refers to being under the sway of sense objects and so forth. The word "api" (also) serves to include sleep and laziness. || 826 ||
Therefore, the practice of false cognition does not lead to the birth of right knowledge.
Even the practice of false cognition leads to the birth of right knowledge.
This might indeed be so if the scripture were the means of knowledge; it is not so, because [the scripture] merely manifests what is already known.
He concludes the point agreed upon by the elders—that the practice of false knowledge is opposed to right knowledge—with the words "Not from this" (*nātaḥ*). [Note: 1.
*kṛtā*; 2. *kha. dādapi*; 3. *kha. 'nirapekṣa'*] [Vol.
3, page 724]
4. Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page 1857] Considering that a Smṛti text lacks authority when it contradicts Śruti, he raises an objection based on Śruti: "Even if it be false. If the cognition expressed by the suffix *-lyap* in the word *vijñāya* were right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), then the injunction "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*) would be purposeless; therefore, what is denoted by that [word] is indeed false knowledge, and its repetition—
