And the meaning is that the arising of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) occurs because the scripture that brings about wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa-śruti*) is a means of valid cognition (*māna*). He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating, "Not from a means of cognition" (*na miteḥ*), on the grounds that since a means of cognition functions as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), it must conform to the object of cognition (*meyānusārin*); therefore, its production cannot arise from the repeated practice of false knowledge (*mithyājñānābhyāsa*). || 827 || 828 ||
The independence of the cause alone is certain regarding the production of the effect.
Because it is the manifestor of the object of cognition, the mind conforms to the true nature of the object of knowledge. || 829 ||

Anticipating the objection that even a means of valid cognition (*māna*) might be turned away from its object, he says: "The effect," etc. Independence is the turning away from the object; however, since that is absent in the case of a means of valid cognition, it does not arise from the practice of false knowledge. Thus he says: "Of the means of valid cognition. (829)
Moreover, the fruit of that which is being practiced is seen even in this world.
Therefore, by the power of that very practice, let it be determined in this case as well. || 830 ||
In that very context, he states another reason, beginning with "Moreover" (api ca). Whatever is practiced becomes strengthened; this is observed, for example, in the case of a long recitation.
Likewise, since there is the practice of false knowledge, it is that alone which gains firmness, and correct knowledge finds no opportunity—this is the meaning. || 230 ||
The meaning has indeed been explained by you, and there is certainly no other [meaning] for these words.
That [text] should be explained by another as well, provided it is not done at the command of kings. || 831 ||

If it is argued that false knowledge, when practiced repeatedly, does not produce right knowledge, and therefore the sentences that enjoin wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa*) would lack authority due to the absence of any other cause [for their invalidation], he says "bhavat" (it being so) to address this doubt. For there is no absence of a different object from what you have stated; rather, if one does not accept what has been stated by you, there is no invalidation because there is no preventer, since it could be applied elsewhere as well—this is the meaning. || 831 ||
We have thus described the succession of faults resulting from the explanation of existence.
That statement should be explained here according to how it applies; such is the word. || 832 ||

Anticipating the objection that "since our own explanation is faultless, one should accept it and desist from seeking another," he says: "Because of [the defects in] the other's explanation" (*bhavavyākhyānataḥ*). The suffix *-tas* has the sense of the locative case because it is applicable to all cases. Alternatively, it may be construed as "on account of that cause," meaning "by means of the passage beginning with 'And this Brahman is not apprehended... He then states how the sentence should be explained: "As that... (*sā yathā*).
The word "here" (iha) is an expression used to explain the meaning of the sentence. || 832 ||
Just as the meaning of a sentence is understood without contradicting all [other] forms of valid cognition.
That should be explained by a truly wise person either through the function of its qualities or otherwise. || 833 ||

He clarifies what has already been stated with the words "All [sentences]. The meaning is that the sentence concerning the instrument of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa*) must be explained by a discerning person through one of the modes of expression—primary, secondary (indicative), or metaphorical—in such a way that its meaning is understood without contradicting all those sentences, such as "not gross" (*asthūla*), which establish the immediate Brahman as non-composite. || 833 ||
Verbal cognition is said to be that which arises from the greatness of the sentence.
Wisdom is said here to be that which is born from the true nature of the object of knowledge. || 834 ||
1 kha. 'rakasyai | 2 ka. kha. gha. cedityāṃ | 233 [vol 3, page 725]

In 1858, Sureśvarācārya composed the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*. In the fourth chapter, following an interpretation that is not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he states the meaning of two words, beginning with "vākya" (sentence).

The term "vijñāya" (having known) refers to a superficial knowledge produced by the grace of the sentences studied; whereas [the term "viditvā"] refers to that which is accomplished in accordance with the true nature of the object of knowledge (*meyasvarūpa*), being the fruit of inquiry, free from all association [with duality].
The meaning is that, in the context of the sentence under discussion, the knowledge of cessation is stated to be wisdom (*prajñā*). || 834 ||
By means of the valid cognition consisting of verbal knowledge, one attains wisdom characterized by identity with the One Self.
One should cultivate the firm conviction "I am Brahman," which cuts through the desire for knowledge [of the world]. || 835 ||

He states the meaning of the sentence: "By verbal [knowledge]," etc. By means of the motivating knowledge arising from words, preceded by inquiry, a non-conceptual, immediate knowledge in the form "I am Brahman"—free from doubts regarding its possibility and so forth—must be brought about; for by that, all expectations are destroyed. This is the meaning. || 839 ||
By the form "vijñāya," which ends in a gerundive suffix (lyap), the pervasion by the means of valid cognition is expressed.
The non-pervasion of that [object] by the means of knowledge is designated as "ignorance" (prajñāmiti). || 836 ||

He states another explanation: "It should be understood as follows. The meaning is that there is no duality of knowledge here: the pervasion of the object of cognition (*meyavyāpti*) by the knowledge that destroys ignorance and its products is *vyānartha*, while the pervasion of the means of cognition (*māna*) by the object of cognition is *prajñā*. || 836 ||
Because of the operation of the means of valid cognition, and likewise because of the operation of the object to be cognized.
Then the fruit of wisdom arises, characterized by being unprecedented and so forth. || 837 ||

He states the utility of their mutual pervasion [between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge] with the words "pramāṇa" etc. Through the mutual pervasion of the means of knowledge (māna) and the object of knowledge (meyya), the fruit of the means of knowledge is that which is unprecedented (apūrva).

The meaning is that because liberation of such a nature is accomplished by it, she (the *vidyā*) is to be described. The word "atha" has the sense of "therefore," indicating the aforementioned result. || 837 ||
Through the division into the knower and so forth, the means of knowledge attains equality with the object of knowledge.
But that destruction of the object of cognition occurs through the mere true nature of the object itself.

Anticipating the objection that the object of knowledge is established merely by the pervasion of the measure (māna) by the measured (meyya), and thus the pervasion of the measure by the measured is redundant, he says:
"The knower, etc. He provides the reason for the statement that when the measure is pervaded by the measured, there is the destruction of the distinctions such as the knower (pramātṛ) and so forth:
"The measured," etc. (verse 838).
Because the mother and so forth, along with their causes, are excluded from the perspective of the inward-looking vision.
Since reality is nothing other than that, its realization occurs through that alone. || 839 ||

How can the subject (mātrā) and so forth possess that same nature [as the Self], given that their cessation is admitted when the means of knowledge (māna) pervades the object of knowledge (meya)? To this, he says: "Of that which has a cause.

Since the existence and non-existence of the subject and so forth do not exist apart from the Self, it is not contradictory for them to consist solely of its true nature (tadyāthātmya). This is the meaning. || 839 ||
Just as one who is blinded by sleep [perceives] in a dream through contact with tigers and the like, [though they do not exist].
By abandoning sleep and dreaming, one becomes a partaker of the object that is mere awakening.
Through the awakening that arises from the manifoldness produced by ignorance regarding the inner self.
Through the destruction of delusion regarding the self, one likewise attains the state of oneness. || 841 ||

1 ka. la. °cchedamī | 2 gha. 'vaikamasaṃ | 3 gha. 'rtho meyokta | 4 kha, "yeneti | 5 gha. ṇāsaṃ- [vol 3, page 726] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary known as Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri: 1859.

Anticipating the objection that since the objects of the senses (*mātrā*) and so forth appear as distinct from the inward-looking vision (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*), they must be false; and that because of this falsity, there would be an absence of the cause for the knowledge of reality (*tattvadhī*), resulting in the non-establishment of the previously mentioned liberation—the author says: "As in sleep" (*nidra*). The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is the well-known fact that one who has been awakened by a dream-object attains a result. Just as an awakening productive of a result arises through the power of a false tiger or similar object seen in a dream, so too [does it arise] through false objects of the senses.
The meaning is that knowledge accompanied by action is not contradictory to the attainment of the fruit, just as [the example] of the day [and its result]. || 840 || 841 ||
Or, in this context, it is said that "having understood" refers to the understanding of the teacher’s intention according to the scriptures.
For by means of speech that is directed toward oneself, self-conviction is expressed. || 842 ||
He states another meaning of the sentence: "The scripture," etc. The cognition resulting from hearing, reflection, and so forth is expressed by the word *vijñāya* (having known);

the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence is *prajñā*. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that one should perform the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence after having performed hearing and the other [steps]. The word *hi* (for/indeed) indicates that hearing and the rest are the causes for the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence. || 842 ||
Because it depends upon the scriptures and the teacher, that cognition is indeed dependent on others.
The independence of the inwardly awakened one is to be understood as being due to non-dependence on anything else. || 843 ||

He states the internal distinction between the cognition derived from the scriptures and teachers (*śāstrācāryamati*) and the self-validating cognition (*ātmapratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "from the scriptures and teachers": the cognition consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth is dependent upon them; because it relies on those [scriptures and teachers], it is designated as "dependent" (*paratantra*). However, the meaning is that the intellect directed toward the object itself—namely, the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthajñāna*)—is "independent" (*svatantra*), because even when the causal complex of hearing and so forth is present, it lacks dependence on anything else. || 843 ||
The self is one's own witness; the self alone is the second [witness] of the self.
I am that which has the realization of non-self; I have arisen as something entirely alone.

Furthermore, since the intellect (*buddhi*) takes on the form of the object to be known, and because the object of knowledge is independent, it is logical that the cognition of that object is also independent;

thus he says, "The Self" (*ātma*). Because it is self-luminous, the Self is non-dual and the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); whereas the non-Self (*anātman*), being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), is false (*mithyā*).
Since that [non-Self] is independent with respect to the inner witness (*pratīc*), the cognition of it is likewise so. The word "kevala" (alone) has the meaning of independence. || 844 ||
Or, if [the state] consisting of non-duality is [attained] precisely through the knowledge of the true nature of the self as it has been described;
One should perform the knowledge of Brahman by relying upon its specific attributes. || 845 ||

He states another meaning of the sentence with the words "Or else" (*yadi vā*). It is said that the Self’s state of being Brahman is realized (*vijñāya*), and Brahman’s state of being the inner self (*pratyaktva*) is designated as "wisdom" (*prajñā*); therefore, the meaning is that having realized the Self’s state of being Brahman, one should contemplate (*anusaṃdadhīta*) Brahman through that very form of the Self.

To the question—"How is the state of being Brahman known for the inner self, or the state of being the inner self for Brahman, since there is no evidence?"—he replies with the words "By the qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*). That [Self]...

By the force of the restrictive particle "vā," the self-nature (*pratyaktva*) of Brahman is understood. The meaning is that through the qualification "the great" (*mahān*) in the passage "the unborn Self is great," the status of the inner self (*pratīc*) as Brahman is established. || 841 ||
The meaning of Brahman is neither excluded from nor followed by anything other than the non-self.
Since it is obtained here from that very source, it is therefore designated as "that alone. || 846 ||
He elaborates on the meaning established by the force of the word *eva* (only/alone): "avyāvṛtta" (unturned away). The locative case ending in "adhyātmaśāstre" signifies the locus [of the teaching].
1178€ 11 1 gva. sva. svapnāsa.
[Vol. 3, page 727] 1860 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
Furthermore, even for those whose objects are Brahman—neither excluded from nor followed by anything else—from another source...
Therefore, the Great Self (mahānātman) is directly attained as the inner witness; hence, it is so described here.

He clarifies what is intended by relying on the qualification "greatness" (mahattva): "neither excluded nor inclusive. The mantra beginning with "virajaḥ" is taken [as the subject] by means of the locative case. || 847 ||
Apart from the objects being excluded, there is no difference between the referents of the words "ātman" and "brahman."
In its own nature, there is no distinction whatsoever, just as in the case of such entities as non-conceit (amānitva) and the rest. || 848 ||
Having stated the mutual non-difference between the inner self (pratyak) and Brahman, he describes the way in which the notion of difference is sublated: "By excluding... (verse 848).
That which is non-active in nature is contradicted by those things whose essence consists of actions such as pride and the like.
Just as it is here, so too should the reality of non-conceit and the other qualities be understood. || 849 ||
He elaborates upon the illustration with the words "is contradicted. The phrase "of the nature of non-action" (*akriyārūpam*) is the grammatical split.
Humility (*amānitva*) and so forth are contradicted by pride (*mānitva*) and its like; and because those opposites are distinct, humility and the rest appear as if they themselves were diverse.

In reality, however, the essential nature of the thing is one alone, characterized by the absence of each respective opposite. Similarly, non-duality and remoteness are contradicted in the case of Brahman as the Self.

Having restated the example—that the difference [of the world] is perceived only because of its difference from that [Brahman], while in reality there is only oneness—he states the point of application (the *dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "Just as" (yathā).
Although the inward reality is non-dual, there is nevertheless the destruction of ignorance regarding it.
It manifests falsely as differentiated forms, such as garlands and so forth.

If it is objected that the state of being dual for that which is non-dual, or the state of being remote for that which is immediate, is contradictory, then how can there be cessation [of duality]? And if it does not cease, the desired unity cannot be established.
Anticipating this doubt, he states that the state of being dual is merely due to ignorance (*avidyā*): "The inner self... (verse 810).
In the same way, the Self is also that Brahman, due to the single cause of ignorance regarding it.
It appears as if remote, like a moon produced by an optical illusion. || 851 ||
He states that, just as the self possesses duality, so too the remoteness (pārokṣya) of Brahman is produced by ignorance. Thus [he says]: "In the same way" (tathā). || 851 ||
For the state of being accompanied by a second [object] and the state of being imperceptible are both caused solely by ignorance.
Therefore, because it arises from a cognition produced by a means of valid knowledge, it does not touch the real entity. || 852 ||
Having restated that both [the self and the non-self] are characterized by ignorance, he states their result: "By being accompanied by a second," etc. (852).
Because they are connected to things as they truly are, those two [extremes] along with their causes cease.
For one who has realized the self as being without an agent, there is the destruction of darkness by the very fact of birth.
He states the reason for the fact that the cognition arising from authoritative means (prāmāṇika-bodha) is a remover [of ignorance]: "In accordance with reality" (yathāvastu).

Anticipating the objection that—since the cognition derived from the sentence removes ignorance because it conforms to reality—it might also remove both [ignorance] and its effects; yet, that which is unborn cannot be a remover because it does not exist, and that which is already born cannot be a remover because it has arisen in a state of non-opposition [to what is already there]—he says: "Not an agent" (akāraka). || 813 ||
1 gha. Two [types of knowledge] regarding that which is not perceptible.
[Vol.
3, page 728] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1861
Its existence is established neither by positive and negative concomitance nor by non-existence.
Because it is negated as being of one and the same nature with the referents of the terms "Self" and "Brahman. || 854 ||

He states the distinction from the well-known cessation [of ordinary darkness] by means of the phrase "the cessation of the darkness under discussion. He says "no," and the reason for that is "the Self" (ātman).
The existence of a second self does not exist apart from ignorance, just as [the appearance of a second moon does not exist apart from it].
Even the cessation of ignorance is not something other than the realization of the Self.

When it was stated that "the cessation of the primal nature (prakṛti) is the Self itself," this was demonstrated many times by means of examples; now, he reminds us of what has arisen in the context of the discussion with the words, "Nothing else. || 855 ||
Or rather, the cognition of word-meanings [serves] for the production of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning.
It is stated in the Śruti that "having known" (vijñāya) refers to the independence of the person therein.

He states another interpretation: "of the word-meanings," etc. The knowledge of the two word-meanings must be performed for the sake of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning by means of the Śruti "having known";
thus, the knowledge of the sentence-meaning is *prajñā*. Therefore, the meaning expressed is that one should know the sentence-meaning after having thoroughly purified the word-meanings.
The construction is as follows: because a person possesses independence regarding the knowledge of objects, he is capable of performing that [action]. (856)
Through positive and negative concomitance, [the relationship] between the sentence and its constituent word-meanings [is established].
A person is sufficient for discrimination, but not for the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence.

He establishes that a person’s independence regarding the discrimination of word-meanings (*padārthaviveka*) has been stated [in the previous verse]. [The commentary says: "By means of *anvaya*," etc. The meaning is: within the nest of the sentence—that is, within the two words *tat* and *tvam* which reside therein—the discrimination of their respective referents (*tadarthayoḥ*), which is their purification (*śodhana*) by means of *anvaya* and so forth, is for the sake of which the person becomes capable; he should perform that very purification.

Since independence is possible for a person even with respect to the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthajñāna*), he should be enjoined to that [purification] just as he is to the discrimination of word-meanings.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "But not... (857).
There is no injunction regarding that which has not arisen, because it is impossible for a person [to act] with respect to the actual state of things.
Even when it has arisen, because its purpose has been fulfilled, it would not [be capable] of bringing about the cognition of the sentence-meaning. (858)

He establishes that very point with the words beginning "no" (na). For there is no injunction regarding the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence; because that [knowledge] depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object itself, it does not depend on the person.
Furthermore, when that [knowledge] has not yet arisen, there can be no injunction, precisely because it does not exist and is thus unfit for an injunction.

Nor, once it has arisen, is there an injunction, because by the mere arising of that [knowledge], the person has achieved their purpose, and thus there is no further fruit of an injunction. This is the meaning. || 898 ||
Because the two word-meanings are worldly [conventional], they are established through positive and negative concomitance.
One is capable of producing knowledge regarding that [word-meaning] for the sake of understanding the meaning of the sentence.

This refutes what was stated regarding the "discrimination of word-meanings" (*padārthaviveka*). [The phrase] "by means of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatirekābhyām*) is to be construed as follows: since word-meanings are worldly, a person is capable of producing knowledge of them—through positive and negative concomitance—for the sake of attaining knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). This is the discrimination (*viveka*).
The meaning is that, because it is an action, just as in the case of sacrifice and so forth, the person possesses autonomy therein; therefore, an injunction is appropriate for it. || 859 ||
1. Or seclusion; 2. the Saṃgha.
[Vol. 3, page 729]

In the passage beginning with "The Self is to be seen," this very [Self] is enjoined as the object of the injunction. *Suresvarācāryakṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four, verse 1862.
The operation of a person, which consists of inference, has the categories (padārtha) as its object. || 860 ||

Furthermore, he states that it has been established even in the passage concerning "that which is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) that the injunction pertains to the subject matter of discrimination (*viveka*), not to the subject matter of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-jñāna*).

He says: "The Self," etc. This means that [the injunction] consists of inference, which is dependent on positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, and is of the nature of purification (*śodhana*). || 860 ||
However, for the awakening to the meaning of a sentence, it is precisely the lack of knowledge regarding the meanings of the individual words [that acts as an obstacle].
Therefore, because there is an obstacle, there is the teaching regarding the knowledge of the meaning of the words. (861)

Anticipating the objection that since the cognition of that meaning arises from the sentence itself, the knowledge of the meanings of those words for that purpose need not be enjoined, he says: "vākyārtha... (verse 861).
Having known that very Self as "I am That," [one is freed] from the non-Self arising from delusion regarding it.
This [investigation] has as its primary object the meaning of selflessness, for as long as the self is being examined.
The realization "I am Brahman" does not arise so long as there is an internal obstacle.

It establishes the injunction itself [by the words] "having known. Having distinguished the Self from the body and so forth arising from one's own delusion, and having known it, the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) knows the meaning of the sentence; therefore, the injunction regarding discrimination is purposeful, as indicated by the words "that very [Self]" and so on. It clarifies that ignorance of the meanings of the words is an obstacle to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence [with the words] "the non-Self" etc. || 862 || 863 ||
When one [discerns] the Self, which is not the self, from that which is imagined through the ignorance of the inner self;
When one discriminates [the parts] by means of inference, then the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises. || 864 ||

When, then, does the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence arise? To this he says: "of the non-self" (anātmanaḥ). This means by means of inference through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, as well as by the Śruti that follows it. || 864 ||
When a person, having withdrawn the self from non-self entities, [establishes] the self within the self alone...
Then one understands everything and perceives that it is indeed the Self alone. || 865 ||
He concludes the fruit of the method of discrimination with the words, "In the Self alone," etc. (861).
Alternatively, because the knowledge of the Self serves the human purpose, it is the instrument for men.
Having restated that which is already established by itself, it is here restricted by the words "that very [thing]. 866.

He states another explanation with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*). The direct realization of Brahman is called *prajñā*, and since that is well-known as the supreme human goal by virtue of having the nature of supreme bliss, the meaning is that one is restricted [by the scripture] to the knowledge of the Self alone, which is other than that [realization]. After the word *prāptam* (attained), the word *ataḥ* (therefore) must be supplied. || 866 ||
If one should make me here, let it be exactly that which has been described.
One should perform that [meditation] after realizing one's own self, and not that which is not the self.

He shows the method of interpretation according to that position: "prajñām" (wisdom). [The phrase] "one should practice that wisdom" refers to what is stated here in the sentence as "jñāṃ praku... (one should practice knowledge).

It is understood that one should act after having realized one's own Self exactly as described; it is not understood that one should act after knowing the non-Self. Therefore... [vol 3, page 730] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1863. It is seen that one should indeed realize that very Self as stated, and thus it is concluded that one should act; however, it is not [the case] by knowing the non-Self. Thus.
The construction is: "the making of wisdom. || 867 ||
The Self alone is the reality of all things, whether they be effects or causes.
Therefore, having understood the self itself as wisdom, one should act. || 868 ||
1.1 He states the reason for the aforementioned rule: "The reality" (tattvam). The word "iti" is used for the purpose of defining the rule. || 868 ||
In the cognition of an object other than that, one does not know anything in reality.
Nor is there the total destruction of darkness, nor the arising of omniscience.
Having stated the reason for the formulation of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa*) by knowing the self, he states the reason for [the formulation of wisdom] by not knowing the non-self:
"tadanyeti" (by that other...). Furthermore, he says that the formulation of wisdom is by not knowing the non-self: "na ceti" (and not). || 869 ||
But when the inner self is known by the very path declared in the Śruti, [then liberation follows].
Knowledge has never arisen anywhere, nor has darkness ever been destroyed here. // 870 //

He states the distinction regarding the knowledge of the Self: "The inward... and so forth. The path mentioned in the Śruti refers to hearing (śravaṇa) and the rest. The word "therefore" (ataḥ) is intended to signify the arising of all-knowledge. || 870 ||
Having understood this here, a virtuous twice-born man should therefore cultivate wisdom regarding that very [reality].
Likewise, ignorance and all else exist only when there is cognition of something other than the Self.
"Everything is indeed the Self"—such is the statement of the Śruti as well.

He concludes the position regarding the restrictive rule (*niyama*) with the words "having known" (*vijñāya*). Here, the locative case in *ihātmānātmanoḥ* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that the performance of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa*) has already been established. Anticipating the objection that it is improper to say that the performance of wisdom occurs only after knowing the Self alone—since the non-Self must also be known as something to be abandoned and avoided, just like the inquiry into unrighteousness (*adharmajijñāsā*)—he says: "due to ignorance, etc. (*ajñānādi*).

Even if one accepts that sensation (*vedana*) is other than the Self (*anātman*), the entire form of the non-Self must be known as the Self alone; for it is only with respect to the Self that states such as "being unknown" are possible. Therefore, the meaning is that when one knows the Self alone, the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa*) remains exactly as it is.
He states the authority for viewing everything as the Self alone: "Everything," etc. One sees everything as the Self, and the Self alone as the world.
The meaning is that even such statements as "pāsīta" (he should sit) follow the sense already demonstrated. || 871 ||
Or rather, it is said that wisdom is established here as being devoid of activity.
"Knowing that his karma belongs to that [very state]" is stated as a restatement (anuvāda). || 872 ||

He states another interpretation: "niṣkarmikā" (devoid of action). [The phrase] "one should practice wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*) prescribes a wisdom that is devoid of action; however, such [wisdom] alone is not tenable, because immediately thereafter, when there is a requirement for action, that very action is stated by the sentence "him alone" (*tameva*). Thus, the meaning is that the sentence is intent upon prescribing both wisdom and action. If this sentence were intended to convey that the self alone is the object of the act of wisdom (*prajñākarma*), then [the word] "having known" (*vijñāya*)— ...[would be unnecessary].
1 gha. Thus. Prajñāśa. 2 na. The meaning is that it is restricted by the rule that "it must be performed. 3 ka. ga. Known, etc. 4 ga. Just as.
[Vol. 3, page 731]
Fearing that [the statement] might be purposeless, he says: "vijñāya" (having known). The word "vijñāya" is restated as an *anuvāda* (reiteration) of "prajñā" (wisdom);

the meaning is that this is for the purpose of illuminating that when wisdom—which has the Self as its object—is present, there is the completion of all effects and objects of knowledge, and thus one’s purpose is fulfilled. || 872 ||
Or rather, wisdom (prajñā) is the supreme self here, according to the statement "consciousness" (prajñāna).
Having realized that Self here in this world, a virtuous twice-born man should cultivate wisdom.

He states another explanation: "Or wisdom. Having stated the meaning of the words, he joins them into a sentence: "Having known. The meaning is that one should extract the referent of "Thou" (tvam) situated in the body and so forth, know it, and then reconnect it with the nature of Brahman. "Of the twice-born" means possessing the fourfold means (sādhana-catuṣṭaya). || 873 ||
Having realized this Self residing within the body by means of the path described, [one should proceed].
"One should cultivate supreme wisdom"—this is the summary of the treatise. || 874 ||
He concludes the final explanation with the words "imam" (this). This means by way of the sequence [of reasoning] such as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) already mentioned.
"Supreme wisdom" (*parā prajñā*) is the realization of the meaning of the sentence. || 874 ||
In this regard, when a matter is possible in such a way that it is not contradicted by any means of valid cognition, [it is accepted].
Why is a sentence-meaning postulated that is contradicted by other means of valid cognition? || 875 ||

When the eightfold meaning of the sentence has been established as being consistent with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that reveal the non-manifest Brahman, he states the resulting conclusion: "In that case," [meaning] that the two previously mentioned positions are not to be accepted. Since the manifold meaning of the final section concerning the instrument of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa*) has been proven to be unopposed by valid cognition according to the method explained above, any sentence-meaning that contradicts valid cognition cannot be postulated.
The interpretation. || 879 ||
Therefore, others here point out many faults on account of this lack of contentment.
Those who had determined the meaning of the Vedas provided an interpretation different from that [original] explanation. || 876 ||

Having explained the sentence concerning the "instrument of wisdom" (*prajñākaraṇa*) in various ways by refuting both positions, he states another opinion held by those of his own school [the Vedāntins] with the words "out of dissatisfaction" (*asaṃtoṣāt*). Other [scholars], who possess a definitive determination of the meaning of the Veda, have provided an alternative explanation of this sentence; for even though there are three explanations presented here, they remain dissatisfied and perceive many defects therein.
Such is the meaning of the words. || 876 ||
The knowledge born from the Vedanta texts destroys delusion exactly as it accords with reality.
Since the word of the Veda is authoritative, how could that which arises from it be false? (877)

Anticipating the objection as to how faults are seen in all three positions, he states the defect in the two positions other than the established conclusion (siddhānta) [in the verse beginning with] "Vedānta":

Knowledge arising from the Vedic sentences, by conforming to the reality, brings about that realization and thereby removes ignorance, because the sentence possesses authority (prāmāṇya). Consequently, a word does not produce false knowledge; therefore, verbal knowledge is neither a composite (saṃsṛṣṭa) nor a mediate (parokṣa) cognition, since the Self is non-composite and immediate (aparokṣa).
Such is the meaning. || 877 ||
1 Kha. 'yehemā' | [Vol.
3, page 732] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1865
At the time of hearing those words, it dispelled the darkness from all his limbs.
Even though knowledge arises which has its basis in the entirety of the oneness of the self, || 878 ||
Immediately after birth, this entire world [is enveloped] by beginningless darkness.
Nevertheless, knowledge is sublated because one perceives the effects of ignorance. (879)

He states the defect in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "vākya... etc. Although, by virtue of destroying all ignorance and its products, true knowledge arises from the sentence at the outset, nevertheless, that [knowledge] is sublated by beginningless ignorance, because of the perception of attachment and other such effects [of that ignorance]; this is the meaning of the two *Vārtikas*. "Akhilam" means "not small," i.e., accompanied by objects. (878, 879)
Ignorance is the cause of attachment and the rest; [these are abandoned] immediately after right knowledge.
Therefore, we observe that from this [knowledge] comes the sublation of ignorance.
He explains what was stated as "because of seeing the effects of ignorance" with the verse beginning "Ignorance... (880).
Knowledge is traditionally held to be of two kinds: innate and adventitious.
In the case of an object, it would be adventitious; in the case of the self, it is held to be innate.

Raising the objection—how can ignorance (ajñāna) sublate knowledge (jñāna) when that lost ignorance has not arisen again and no other [ignorance] exists—the author states the twofold nature of ignorance for that purpose, beginning with the word *naisargī*. In this context, the particle *hi* is used to indicate what is well-known to others. To the question—"How can there be a distinction between two ignorances within a single Self without a difference in form?"—he replies with the word *āgantukī*. (Verse 881)
Whatever ignorance exists therein is removed by the single arising of knowledge.
Just as the notion "you are a Śabara" departs upon being told "you are the king. || 882 ||
But that ignorance which is innate [is destroyed] by the single arising of knowledge.
Even though it has been destroyed, it returns once again, as is seen from its aging and so forth. (883)
Nevertheless, suspecting that all ignorance might depart through the ignorance of the inner self (pratyagajñāna), he states a distinction with the words beginning "tatra" and so forth.
The phrase "even though destroyed" means even though [ignorance] has been suppressed. || 882 || 883 ||
Since this innate ignorance possesses such a nature, therefore—
Even after realizing the supreme reality, one should repeatedly cultivate wisdom.

Since it is established that innate ignorance is the sublater of wisdom, he states the resulting conclusion with the words "yasmāt" (because). Its having such a nature means its being the sublater of knowledge. || 884 ||
One should exercise wisdom until [the afflictions] have been destroyed without remainder.
The ignorance regarding the self [is removed] through diligent practice of the aforementioned knowledge of the self. || 885 ||
He states the limit for the cultivation of wisdom with the word "tāvat" (for so long). Effort consists in the practice being characterized by long duration, reverence, and continuity. || 885 ||
234 1. In manuscript *ga*, it reads "sarvā" instead of "'le tu". 2. In manuscript *kha*, it reads "hetūtrāgā". 3. In manuscript *kha*, it reads "ganta yauṃ".
[Vol. 3, page 733]
1866 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:
And the verses [of Gauḍapāda and others] are witnesses to the aforementioned meaning.
Those who know the tradition themselves study this with effort here. || 886 ||

He states the authoritative evidence for the fact that even one who has realized the truth must practice knowledge (*jñānābhyāsa*) for the sake of destroying ignorance: "And from the verses," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), Vyāsa and others are included. The meaning of the locative case is "in accordance with the aforementioned sense. Effort (*yatna*) refers to service to the teacher and so forth. (886)
"Having perceived the reality within, and having perceived the reality without,"
Having become one with reality, he finds delight therein and shall not fall away from that reality. || 887 ||

In this regard, he recites two verses from Gauḍapāda, beginning with "That which is the Reality" (tattvam). The meaning is as follows: having realized that everything—the body and so forth, as well as the earth and so forth—is merely the single reality of the absolute Self, and that apart from that [Self] it is unreal, being a mere modification of speech; and having thus remained established in that [Self] as its own basis for all conceptualization, one should be fixed upon that, free from attachment to sense objects, and intent on the perfect knowledge: "I am Brahman. || 887 ||
When the mind neither sinks into dullness nor is distracted again, [that is the state].
Then that Brahman is established as unmoving and without appearance.

Having stated the passage from the *Vaitathya-prakaraṇa*, he cites the passage from the *Advaita-prakaraṇa*: "When... and so forth. When the mind—restrained by the means described in the verse beginning with "the mind [is restrained] for the sake of awakening during dissolution"—neither dissolves as in deep sleep, nor is it again distracted by objects, but remains unshaken like a lamp in a windless place and does not appear in any imagined form of an object, then it is perfected in the form of Brahman.
The meaning is that it comes into being. || 888 ||
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings.
When it is attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage; when free from sense objects, it leads to liberation. || 889 ||

In that very context, he cites two statements of Vyāsa, beginning with "The mind," and so forth. To the question of how a single mind can possess such contradictory results, he replies: "For the sake of bondage. (889)
It should be restrained within the heart precisely until it has reached its exhaustion.
This is both knowledge and meditation; all else is merely an extensive proliferation of words. || 890 ||
He states the limit of that cessation with the word "tāvat" (so much). This means "in the heart, which is the nature of knowledge.
He praises self-knowledge or the restraint of the mind with the word "idam" (this). The construction is as follows: "any other extensive treatise is merely a supplement to this very [work].
Thus some explain the clear statement "having cognized"; here, the wise Great Mīmāṃsakas offer a rebuttal. (891)
He concludes the view of his own school with the words, "Thus they explain. He establishes the final position [siddhānta] with the word, "In this regard" (atra). || 891 ||
When uncommon ignorance has the inner self alone as its object.
If it were established as consisting of ignorance and so forth, then how could there be that twofold nature? (892)
1. gha.
So Mithovi [vol 3, page 734] 4 Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary titled Śākhaprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 1867.

Revealing this very point, he refutes the two-fold nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) asserted by others. [The verse begins with] "When": since ignorance indeed consists of non-cognition, doubt, and false cognition, and exists as a state residing within each individual self, it is held to be unique to that [self]. When this is accepted, then because the inner Self (*pratīc*), which is non-dual, is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), a distinction [within it] is impossible;
therefore, there is only one ignorance which is the cause of error and so forth, and not a two-fold nature of it—this is the meaning. || 892 ||
The object of all means of knowledge is said to be unknown [prior to their operation].
The Self alone is to be known and sought by one who maintains the doctrine of the absolute unity of the Self. (893)

To the question, "How is it that this [ignorance] is unique (asādhāraṇa) because its object is not within the range of our individual perception? he says: "Of the unknown" (*ajñāta*). Since the object of a means of valid knowledge (*māna*) must be something unknown, the Self alone—by virtue of being unknown—is accepted by everyone as its object; therefore, ignorance, which has that [Self] as its sole object, is unique to it and is not of two kinds. This applies everywhere, meaning in all scriptures. The phrase "by the proponent of non-dualism" (*aikātmyavādinā*) is an elliptical expression for "by everyone."
This is to be understood by investigators. || 893 ||
For an object unknown [to oneself] cannot be established through another, since it is not identical with that other. || 894 ||
Furthermore, there would be no establishment of "non-apprehension" by means of a valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And there is no sublation of this [cognition] because of its basis, due to the presence of extreme cold. || 895 ||

Having raised the objection as to how the Self alone can possess the status of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) when it is itself unknown, [the author] states what was indicated by the word "certainly" (*dhruvam*): "The unknown," etc. Since nothing else can be the cause of ignorance, the remainder of the sense is that the Self alone, being unknown, is the object of knowledge. Furthermore, is the unknowability of the non-Self established through a means of knowledge (*māna*) or by its own power? It is not the first; thus he says: "Nor... (vv. 894–899).
Furthermore, there is no establishment of an unknown object in this world by means of that which is not itself established.
Since that too is of the nature of ignorance, it is accepted as being insentient and non-self. || 896 ||

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; thus he says, "And not even... The reason why the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) inherent in the non-self (*anātman*) is not established by the power of the non-self itself is given by the word "of that" (*tasya*). The particle "api" (also/even) implies "like one possessed of ignorance" (*avidyāvat*). Furthermore, since it is not accepted that the non-self is an intrinsic prover (*sādhaka*) of itself, he states that the state of its being unknown cannot be established by virtue of that [non-self], saying "insentient" (*jaḍa*). || 896 ||
Therefore, even in the absence of a measure (mātrā), that which exists for the sake of establishing the state of being unknown—
In this context, that very ultimate object (alamartha) is intended as the cognized object when it is yet unknown. || 897 ||

He states the conclusion resulting from the fact that, due to the absence of a knower (sādhaka), it is impossible for the non-self (anātman) to be unknown: "Therefore" (ataḥ). Here, "here" (atra) refers to sleep and so forth, while "in this" (iha) is an expression for the domain of valid cognition (mānabhūmi). The syntactic connection is: "That very [self] is what is unknown; that is accepted as the object of knowledge (meyam). || 897 ||
Apart from mere consciousness, there is no other object that brings about the establishment of ignorance.
Therefore, the triad beginning with ignorance has as its sole refuge self-awakened consciousness.

Even if the object that establishes its own state of being unknown is itself an unknown object of cognition, what does that have to do with the inner self (pratīc)? To this he says: "Bodha" (Awakening).

He states that the inner self is not only the object of ignorance but also its locus: "ajñānādi" (ignorance, etc.). The meaning of the word "tat" (that) is the absence of the perception of any other locus. || 898 ||
1. sva. How is this? 2. kha. minds.
[Vol. 3, page 735] 1868 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Chapter]
In this world, it is possible that [this] is preceded by mere awakening alone. (899)
For a mother or other [relative] is not experienced when they are unknown.
Therefore, because it is like the movement of the unknown consciousness, experience is said to be unknown. || 900 ||

He provides experiential evidence for the statement that ignorance rests solely upon the Self (ātman) by saying, "It is possible. To the objection—"Why might these three [the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object] not also rest upon the *mātrā* (the measure/subjective factors) and so forth?"—he replies: "While it is not being known. Just as the conscious Self is seen to be their substratum, the *mātrā*s and the rest are not; for they are always swallowed up by experience. Therefore, the conscious Self alone is their substratum.
This is the meaning. || 899 || 900 ||
Just as there is a determination of an object such as silver with respect to a mother-of-pearl shell when it is not recognized [as such].
In the same way, there is certainty regarding the selflessness [of the object] when the experiencing self is not known. (901)

For this reason as well, he states that the Self alone is the unknown: "In the case of the unknown" (ajñātāyām). The meaning is that, just as the silver which is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl has no established state of being unknown, so too space and other such things, which are mere manifestations of the ignorance regarding the Self, cannot have their state of being unknown established. || 909 ||
Since silver and the like are not established as distinct from cognition, they lack the status of being objects of knowledge.
Just as with a pearl-oyster shell, the state of being known or unknown [is determined] by something other than that [shell itself]. || 902 ||

One might object: "In the case of a mother-of-pearl shell and the like, when it is not known [as such], the determination of it as silver and so forth is logical because that [determination] lacks validity; however, when the Self is not known, there can be no determination of the non-Self, because that [determination of the non-Self] possesses correctness and thus has validity. Anticipating this, he establishes its lack of validity—just like the determination of silver and so forth—for the purpose of showing that it is invalid. He says: "From knowledge" (*jñānāt*). The validity of the knowledge of silver and so forth [would require] its having that as its object, namely, having the mother-of-pearl shell and so forth as its object.

Nor can it be the first [alternative], because—just as the "cognizedness" (*jñātatva*) of an unperceived shell is established as something distinct from silver—its "unperceivedness" and "cognizedness" cannot be established through a cognition that is separate from them; thus, they would lack the status of being objects of knowledge (*meyatva*). This is the meaning. || 902 ||
Because this cognition of silver does not apprehend its object in the case of mother-of-pearl.
In this case, the cognition of silver would not be a valid means of knowledge, because the object of cognition (prameya) does not exist.

He states the consequence resulting from the fact that silver and so forth lack the status of being objects of knowledge (*meyatva*): "Since... The connection is with "here, in the mother-of-pearl" (*śukti*). || 903 ||
Just as one does not conceive of silver in mother-of-pearl, so too is that [nature of reality].
Because of the affliction caused by the non-awakening to that [nature], there is the [perception] of that [silver] as having the nature of mother-of-pearl. || 904 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "yathā" (just as). The meaning is that the cognition of silver and so forth possesses no validity (*mānatā*) with respect to mother-of-pearl and the like, just as it lacks it with respect to silver and the like, because it does not destroy ignorance regarding those [objects] and because it lacks their form (*tadākāratva*). || 904 ||
In this very way, all measures do not exceed their respective conditions.
The certainty is that only those things which have the nature of being non-self are to be known. || 905 ||

Having stated the invalidity of cognitions such as that of silver, he declares the invalidity of all cognitions of the non-self (anātman) by means of that same illustration, beginning with "yathā" (just as). Just as the cognition of silver and so forth is not a valid means of knowledge according to the method described, so too, setting aside the single cognition of the inner self (pratyag-jñāna), all cognitions of the non-self are to be understood as invalid. This is because, due to the absence of a real object, the states of being unknown or known are impossible in the case of the non-self; and because [the non-self] does not destroy ignorance, it lacks the form of that [reality].
And because of that, the notion of a non-self is indeed false; this is the meaning. || 909 ||
Just as the knower is not distinct from immediate consciousness, so too is it experienced here.
Even prior to the pervasion of the mind, as long as it is not produced, it does not exist.

He states the intended meaning of the qualification "as distinct from the inner self" (pratyasmāt) with the word "pratyak" (inner). The meaning is that because the state of being unknown in the inner self is established by experience, and because knowledge in the form of that [inner self] destroys that ignorance, there is valid cognition (mānatā) regarding it. Regarding the state of being unknown in the Self—

He clarifies the fact that [this] is established by existence (*bhavasiddhatva*). The word "even" (*api*) means that as long as it has not been demonstrated that this person is not a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*) but is rather the Existent alone (*sad eva*), so long there is a state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*), which is established by one's own experience even though it is self-luminous, prior to its connection with the means of knowledge (*māna*). ||906||
For it is precisely from that [experience] that the perfection of experience is established.
There would be no sublation of that which is unknown, just as in the case of the established sublation of mother-of-pearl. || 907 ||

Nevertheless, one might suspect that [the ignorance] is indeed sublated, just as darkness is by the sun; therefore, having raised this doubt, he considers the alternatives—whether it is through the knowledge arising from the sentence or through the knowledge of the true nature—and refutes the first with the words "vāstavī" (real). The meaning is: the manifestation of the true nature of the conscious Self (cidātman) exists eternally, not that which arises from the sentence; therefore, by its power, there is no eternal sublation of the state of being unknown within the Self. He refutes the second alternative with the word "na" (no).

The meaning is: just as there is no sublation of the mother-of-pearl's own state of being unknown by [the knowledge of its nature], so too there is no [sublation] by the knowledge of its true nature; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). || 907 ||
I am not connected with pride, just as the sixth sense-organ is not connected with its objects.
Nor [is it so] because of the experience of deep sleep and the like, for that too is an experience.
It is indifferent toward the attainment of valid cognition, like a *bilva* fruit held in the hand by one who possesses authority.

If it is argued that cognition arising from a statement does not exist at all times, then in that case, even the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) would not exist at all due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*māna*); anticipating this objection, he says: "By means of a means of valid cognition" (*mānena*). He states the reason why experience (*anubhūti*), though not an object of measurement (*ameyā*), is nonetheless not non-existent: "Because of experience" (*anubhūteḥ*).

This means that it is self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*) by virtue of being the very proof for states such as deep sleep. If that is so, then when it attains itself through a means of valid cognition, it would be independent and self-evident.

Anticipating the objection, "Since it is already established, how can it be 'pertaining to the Upaniṣads' (aupaniṣada)? he says, "And not... The meaning is this: A bilva fruit held in the palm, which is perceived directly, does not require further attainment through a means of knowledge; however, experience (*anubhūti*) is not like that. Even though its nature is self-shining, it has no need for a means of knowledge for its own attainment;
yet, because it destroys one's own ignorance, it is dependent on the cognition arising from the [Upaniṣadic] sentence. || 908 ||
Thus, prior even to the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the object of cognition (meyo) is obtained here.
This is not so in the teachings of systems other than the established doctrine of the Vedānta.
Since the object of cognition is established [by that very means], no other means of valid cognition exists therein. || 910 ||

He concludes by stating that the very self of consciousness (cidātman), when unknown, is the object of knowledge (meyam). He says "pramāṇa... [etc.]. The word "evam" (thus) expresses a statement in accordance with experience;

"atra" (here) expresses the statement of the established conclusion (siddhānta). Having explained the operation of the means of knowledge (māna-pravṛtti) in his own position, he states its impossibility in the opponent's position with "naivam" (not thus).
But here, the ignorant person is indeed the self, and it is likewise falsely known.
Because of its connection with the means of valid cognition, there is the abandonment of all ignorance. || 911 ||
1 kha. ga. *tayaiva* | 2 ga. *yādiva* | [Vol.
3, page 737] 1870 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, [Fourth Adhyāya—]

Thinking that even the fruit of pride does not exist there, he states its existence in his own position with the words "But here... (*iha tu*). The phrase "in that very way" (*tathaiva*) is a conjunction of doubt. The syntactical connection is: "What task remains to be done after the abandonment of all ignorance? (911)
From sentences such as "That thou art," there arises all-encompassing knowledge.
And because of the removal of all ignorance, and because of the completion of what is to be known and what is to be done. || 992 ||

[Objection: Since [the Self] is connected with the mind, how can there be the destruction of all ignorance? For when it is connected with the mind, it is only logical that its own ignorance be destroyed. To this, he says: "That" (tam). The meaning is as follows: when the Self is known through the power of the Great Saying (mahāvākya), because there is no other entity apart from It, knowledge arises regarding everything according to the principle of "by knowing one, all is known"; thus, there is the destruction of all ignorance. He states the result of that: "all... (sarva...).
This is because everything that is to be attained has been attained, and likewise, everything that is to be abandoned has been abandoned.
What task remains to be done once right understanding has been produced? || 913 ||

Having raised the doubt regarding what remains to be attained or avoided, he says: "Of that which is to be attained" (*prāpyasya*). He says "perfectly" (*samyak*) in response to those who maintain that even for the knower of Brahman there is further practice to be performed; the sense is that all the fruits previously mentioned are accomplished by the single birth [of realization]. || 913 ||
If ignorance were to persist as before even when the object has been correctly known, [then it would be permanent].
Furthermore, what proof is there that she will lead [him] beyond death? (994)

By stating that "the Self alone is both ignorant and unknown," the twofold nature of ignorance has been refuted. Now, having restated the claim that knowledge is sublated by ignorance that arises again after it had been destroyed, he refutes it: "Ignorance" (avidyā), etc. The meaning is that even after the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), ignorance could arise; since its emergence would be possible even after the attainment of disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya), there would be no final release (amukti). || 994 ||
Because there is a relationship of sublation and sublated between ignorance and knowledge.
Apart from this, there is no other relationship, just as between that which burns and that which is burned. || 915 ||

Lest one should suspect that ignorance (avidyā), though destroyed, arises again—on the grounds that it was not truly destroyed by the mere emergence of knowledge (vidyā) but merely became latent and will become manifest once more—the author says: "Ignorance... The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: therefore, ignorance is indeed destroyed by knowledge; it does not merely become latent. || 999 ||
Tell me, how can ignorance, which is itself sublated, sublate knowledge, which is the sublater?
For that which is burning, there is no burning by means of another burning object.

As for the claim that ignorance (avidyā) is the sublater of knowledge (vidyā), he refutes it with the word "bādhyā" (the sublated). The meaning is that it is illogical for ignorance to possess the quality of being a sublater, just as it is illogical for that which is to be burned (dāhya) to possess the quality of being a burner (dāhaka). || 996 ||
Although this ignorance exists, may it not destroy knowledge beforehand.
"Once destroyed, ignorance will obstruct knowledge"—what is the proof for this? (917)

Furthermore, does ignorance (avidyā) obstruct knowledge (vidyā) while it is present or while it is absent? It is not the first case, because if beginningless ignorance were an opposing obstacle, there would be the undesirable consequence that knowledge could never arise; with this in mind, he refutes the second alternative: "While [ignorance] is present" [verse 997].
If it is destroyed by ignorance, then that which is to be enjoined must be accomplished in its entirety.
How could a dull-witted person, having lost the self-knowledge of his own nature, ever exercise wisdom? (918)
As for the passage beginning with "Since it has such a nature," he refutes it with the words "by ignorance" (avidyayā). || 998 ||
Furthermore, if birth were caused by a specific reason, it would occur everywhere again and again.
But when ignorance, the cause of all, has been destroyed, from what could existence arise? (919)

For this reason as well, he says that once ignorance has been destroyed, it does not arise again, beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*). For if it were to arise again, it would either require a cause or not; if it does not, he says [the following] regarding that: "Of that which has a cause. If it does require a cause, he asks: "From all [of them]" (*sarva-*)?
The meaning of the question is whether [it arises] from something else or from Brahman. || 999 ||
If it were Brahman, its non-release [from bondage] would follow as a logical consequence.
It is eternally present within Brahman, like the rays of the sun.

Thinking that the first [alternative] is not tenable because there is no similarity between ignorance and its products, nor their absence, he takes up another hypothesis and refutes it with the words "of Brahman" (brahmaṇaḥ). He makes the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) explicit with the words "because of being stationary" (sthāsnutvāt). || 920 ||
Nor is there non-cessation for that which is beginningless, because cessation is observed everywhere.
For it is through the abandonment of ignorance regarding those objects that are most difficult to know from beginningless time. || 929 ||

He addresses the incidental doubt that if ignorance (*avidyā*) does not arise due to the absence of a cause, then its cessation would also be impossible because it is beginningless, like the self (*ātman*); he says: "Because it is beginningless" (*anādeḥ*). He clarifies the phrase "in all cases" and so forth with the words: "beginningless" (*anādi*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "among those [objects], there is the state of being unknown, and the destruction of that [state] occurs through experience. The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that the establishment of the cessation of beginningless ignorance is indeed possible.
Having here accepted that the object of knowledge is entirely enveloped by beginningless ignorance.
They cut away the means of valid cognition, which are directed toward the object of knowledge that consists in the nature of reality.

Raising the objection, "Even if the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) regarding objects is destroyed, how can beginningless ignorance (*anādyajñāna*) be destroyed?", he says: "Beginningless ignorance... (verse 922). The meaning is that as long as ignorance persists, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are not able to sublate the state of being unknown residing in the object of knowledge (*meya*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that if those [means of cognition] were to destroy that [ignorance], they would be rendered useless.
Nor is the destruction of ignorance admitted to occur through the conjunction of causes.
Because Brahmā is not the cause of living beings such as serpents and the like. || 923 ||
Nevertheless, fearing that because destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) consists in a reconnection with its cause, there might be a recurrence [of the effect], he says: "And not...

The meaning is this: the destruction of a snake or the like imagined upon a rope is not a reconnection with its cause, but rather its becoming the form of the rope; likewise, even the destruction of ignorance in Brahman does not consist in a reconnection with its cause, because Brahman is not its cause and because it (ignorance) is not an effect. || 923 ||
Apart from making known what was previously unknown, there is no other injunction here;
since the purpose is fulfilled by that alone, no further task remains.
1. ‘In knowledge. 2. gha, ‘...indefinite certainty... [Vol. 3, page 739] 1872 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Chapter]

As for the statement beginning with "one should first exercise wisdom" (prajñāṃ prakurvīta), he refutes it with the words "unknown" (ajñātā). The word "here" (iha) refers to what is stated in the treatises on liberation (mokṣaśāstra).
The reason for this is given by the word "first" (tāvatā). || 924 ||
The self alone is the cause of all knowledge, as inferred from its effects.
Since the self is established by its own nature through self-linking, no cognition of that [self] need be produced.

Furthermore, regarding the injunction for either worldly knowledge of the self or its continuity, or for Vedic knowledge of the self or its continuity— in the first case as well, one must choose between the Prābhākara system, the Bhāṭṭa view, the Sāṃkhya position, the Vedānta doctrine, the Vaiśeṣika terminology, or the Lokāyata method— and [the author] refutes the first alternative with the words "The Self alone... In the Guru's (Prābhākara) system, [it is held that] mere cognition...

The self alone is the substratum; and since knowledge is dependent upon it, the self is connected to that [knowledge] by virtue of being its substratum. Thus, because the self is established even without an injunction, there can be no injunction regarding the knowledge of the self or its continuity. This is because the self is perceived as the substratum even in the case of the cognition of jars and other objects. || 925 ||
Due to the connection between part and whole, even the Self is experienced through the notion of "I."
Furthermore, because it is eternally connected [to the self], this cognition of the self cannot be something that is to be enjoined.

He refutes the second [position] with the words "part" (*aṃśa*) and so on. For the Bhāṭṭa who holds the connection that the Self consists of both parts (*aṃśa*) and the whole (*aṃśin*) for the sake of cognizing the substance—since the Self is experienced by him through the cognition "I," therefore, because that [Self] and its knowledge are always connected even without an injunction, the cognition of the Self or its continuity cannot be something to be enjoined; this is the meaning. || 926 ||
For whom the thorough knowledge of self and non-self is considered common [to all].
In this context, the instrument is indeed the intellect; there is no injunction with respect to that [intellect] either. || 927 ||

He states the third [position]: "The self" (ātma). In the Sāṃkhya system, since the intellect (*buddhi*) is the common instrument for all cognition, the realization of the self is established through its modification; therefore, there is no injunction regarding the knowledge of the self or its continuity. This is the meaning. || 927 ||
Of everything other than the inward Self, beginning with the intellect and ending with the objects of the senses;
Therefore, because of [the absence of] self and what belongs to a self, this world has consciousness as its intrinsic nature.

He relaxes the fourth [objection]. Regarding the phrase "of intellect and so forth": according to the Vedānta view, because there is a relationship of identity between the *pratyagātman* (the inner self) and whatever entity appears as other than that—due to the notions of "self" and "belonging to the self"—the entire world is determined to have consciousness (*cit*) as its essential nature. Therefore, even in that system, there is no injunction regarding knowledge and the like. This is the meaning. || 928 ||
That [consciousness] would always have consciousness as its intrinsic nature, because it does not depend on any other cause.
Because it depends upon dharma, adharma, and so forth, [the cognition] possesses the aspect of selflessness. || 929 ||

He states another reason for the fact that everything has consciousness as its intrinsic nature (*cit-svabhāva*). [He says] "Consciousness" (*cid*). Indeed, in the Upaniṣadic view, the world does not require a cause distinct from consciousness; this follows from the reasoning beginning with the Sūtra on "Birth and so forth" (*janmādi-sūtra*) and continuing through the principle of "and the material cause" (*prakṛtiśca*), as well as the principle that the effect is not something separate from its cause, as stated in the Sūtra on "Mere mention" (*ārambhaṇa*).

Because it would contradict the locus of the argument, the meaning is that everything is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Since that [consciousness] does not depend on prior perception and so forth, it is independent of any other cause.
[Note: *ka* and *ga* do not have *na tatpratyakṣam*; *ga* has *tadā*; *gha* has *dṛṣṭāya*.]

Anticipating the objection that [the Self] is established [as an effect], he says: "Dharma... etc. The meaning is this: although the existence of the non-Self depends upon causes such as dharma and so forth arising from the ignorance (avidyā) of the individual self, it does not depend upon any other material cause (upādāna); therefore, it is logical that its nature is pure consciousness (cinmātra). || 929 ||
"A pot does not attain its various forms of existence without being filled by space."
Or one may undergo separation from material objects, and likewise, the intellect [is separated] from consciousness.

He establishes, by means of an illustration, that everything from the intellect (*buddhi*) down to objects is always pervaded by the conscious self (*cidātman*). [The verse says: "Like space" (*viyat*).

For just as a jar, pervaded by space, undergoes conjunction and disjunction with curds and other substances, so too the world, pervaded by consciousness, attains its purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*); this is the meaning. || 930 ||
They take on the form of sound and so forth, as well as the nature of doubt and the like.
Apart from the fullness of direct perception, those [states] are never emptiness.

He elaborates on the example of the tamer: "Sound and so forth. For, being insentient (*jaḍa*) and lacking inherent capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), objects do not themselves maintain a form—whether existent or non-existent—except by attaining consciousness through the intellect (*dhi*). Therefore, the meaning is that the world is always full within the conscious self (*cidātman*). || 931 ||
Therefore, one should not conceive of a self, nor likewise of its continuum.
For that [cognition] is established by its very nature even for all living beings. (932)
He states the result of that pervasion of everything at all times: "Since... He clarifies the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ): "By its own nature.
By the word "that" (tat), the self-cognition and its continuum are grasped. || 932 ||
And because all things, though distinct, likewise possess the nature of non-difference.
The cognition of a self cannot be an effect produced by persons, precisely because it is caused [by that very self]. (933)

Furthermore, he states that in our view, neither the knowledge of the Self nor its continuity is something to be enjoined, by saying "of all. Since the entire manifold of difference is non-different from the Self, the knowledge of that [manifold] is also the knowledge of the Self; therefore, since that [knowledge] is established without effort, there is no injunction regarding it. This means that, in some cases, it follows the rule of pervasion (*vyāpti*). || 933 ||
"Furthermore, for that proponent here for whom knowledge and the other qualities have the self as their substratum,"
For that [Self] as well, the notion "this is mine" (ātmīya) should not be formed, because it is eternally attained.

It rejects the fifth [alternative], namely "self. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), desire, effort, and so forth are included. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the state of conventional usage (*vyavahārāvasthā*). || 934 ||
This body, as long as it lives, is always by its very nature consciousness.
Even for the proponent of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavādin), this cognition of a self cannot be produced in that manner.

He discards the sixth [alternative]. Regarding the phrase "of the body": the word *api* (also) is used to provide another illustration. The word *tathā* (so) is used to state that the fact that the living body has consciousness as its essential nature (*cit-svabhāvatva*) is in accordance with experience. || 935 ||
16. He who is always mindful.
[Vol. 3, page 741] 1874 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]
In the case of a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) or an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), [the result follows] from not perceiving all things as the Self.
The futility of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) follows as a consequence, because it would be rendered rootless. || 936 ||

The injunction regarding worldly knowledge of the self and its continuity has been refuted through the distinctions among various disputants. Now, with respect to Vedic knowledge of the self and its continuity, he examines the alternatives—whether it be an *apūrva* (unprecedented result), a *niyama* (restriction), or a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification)—and, considering the first option untenable due to the absence of absolute non-attainment (*atyantāprāpti*), he refutes the other two. He says: "As for restriction (*niyama*)," etc. In that case, because there would be an absence of knowledge of the non-self, your ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) would be rootless and thus invalid.
Such is the meaning. || 936 ||
Nor, moreover, is there any possibility here of those two, because they are eternally attained.
For it is held that every ritual injunction always pertains to things not yet attained. || 937 ||

Having stated that two types of injunctions are accepted regarding the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), he states another reason for their impossibility [in that context] with the words "And not" (*na ca*). To the question, "Even though the knowledge of the Self is eternally attained, what inconsistency is there in those two [injunctions] being applied there? he replies: "Because it is unattained" (*aprāpta*). When both [injunctions] apply to a case already established, there is a restrictive injunction (*niyama*); when [the act] is eternally attained, there is an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*). However, since that very knowledge exists immediately after the knowledge arising from the sentence, neither of these two is possible here.
The meaning is "no. || 937 ||
The notion that "self-knowledge must be cultivated" has already been refuted right here.
Although the procedure is of every kind, it does not, however, consist in the awakening of an object that was not already known by the intellect.

Regarding the point that there is no injunction whatsoever for the knowledge of the Self, he recalls the reasoning stated in the *draṣṭavya* (to-be-seen) passage by saying, "it is to be performed. By this, the *draṣṭavya* passage is restated in terms of its meaning. Anticipating the objection that if every kind of injunction is rejected, then since even the making known of what was unknown is rejected, the statement that "there is no other injunction here apart from the making known of the unknown" would be self-contradictory, he says:
"But not... means that even when the injunction as an impeller is rejected, the other [factors] remain exactly as they are desired by others. || 938 ||
The state of being something to be done is not enjoined for that which is already known as an object to be accomplished.
And because sacrifice is itself suffering, it is not a means [to liberation]; therefore, it is not taught here. || 939 ||
Furthermore, intending to show that an impelling injunction (*pravartaka-vidhi*) is not possible even in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), let alone in the knowledge section (*jñānakāṇḍa*), he says:

"The state of being something to be done" (*kartavyatā*). When that [state] is to be enjoined, it must belong either to the fruit (*phala*) or to the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). It cannot be the first, because the fruit, having become the object of desire, is already attained through inclination (*rāga*) in that case and does not require an injunction; nor can it be the second, because that [meaning of the root], being of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*), cannot be performed...

The meaning is that, because [the nature of Brahman] cannot be established [by action], the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) of the Veda also does not possess the authority to enjoin it. How, then, is its validity established?

To this he says: "As a means" (upāya). The meaning is that its validity consists in its being the cause for the knowledge of the means to attain the desired end when that end is unknown. The absence of any other thing to be enjoined is indicated by the word "hi" (for/indeed), and is referred to by the word "ataḥ" (therefore). By the locative case, however, the ritual section of the Veda is grasped.
"Whether it be engagement or non-engagement, it conforms to the nature of the object of cognition."
Therefore, since the knower is nothing other than pure consciousness, there is no activity arising from a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

If it is not accepted that the injunction (*niyoga*) is the instigator, then the word itself must be so; thus, the proponent of *bhāvanā* addresses those [opponents] with the words "activity" (*pravṛtti*).

In the case of an object of knowledge, activity and cessation do not arise from the word itself through passion and aversion caused by the superimposition of "beautiful" or "ugly"; rather, the word merely makes known the means to what is desired or undesired; therefore, the meaning is that the word is not the direct motivator. || 940 ||
"And because the causes such as the ears have been destroyed, there is no possibility of activity."
Because the object of cognition does not function as a causal factor in the arising of correct knowledge. || 941 ||
