Having stated that an impelling injunction (*pravartaka-vidhi*) is impossible in the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), and having explained its incompatibility in the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*), he states another reason for its absence when knowledge exists: "The agent, etc. The meaning is that since the notions of the "measurer" (*mātra*) and so forth have been destroyed, and because the Self is immutable (*kauṭasthya*), activity is impossible once knowledge has arisen; therefore, there is no impelling injunction. || 941 ||
Knowledge destroys ignorance, yet it does not possess the nature of an agent.
Having grasped it here, one destroys darkness; in certain cases of division, it is like a sword.

Anticipating the objection that even when knowledge has arisen, there may still be no other [ordinary] activity, yet an activity called "repeated practice" (abhyāsa) is possible—therefore [the author] speaks of it as an injunction that impels action. He says: "In the absence of ignorance," etc. Here, "here" refers to the inner self (pratyagātman). The example of dissimilar nature is "cleaving in two"; the meaning is that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which makes known the instruments such as the axe does not require repetition to be fruitful. || 942 ||
The realized inward consciousness, free from the sense of "mine," is like the mother who undergoes birth and death.
Always as the fruit of the mere inward-turned [consciousness] and as the witness.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Self-knowledge merely awakens the Self; it does not destroy ignorance (*tamas*). Its destruction, however, depends on another practice [such as ritual injunction]. Anticipating this, he says: "The inner" (*pratyak*), etc. First of all, the establishment of the Self is not dependent upon a means of knowledge (*māna*), because the Self is self-luminous and because it is the witness of the senses and so forth.
Just as the mother’s own existence is not established by a means of knowledge since she is the witness of her own self, so it is with the Self. Therefore, self-knowledge...
The meaning is that it is exclusively a cause of cessation. || 943 ||
The self does not exist by means of a non-self entity, because it is not its producer, except in the case of darkness.
In that same way, even the non-self directly attains a connection with the Self. (944)

Having raised the doubt that there might be a relationship between the Self (ātman) and the non-Self (anātman) based on the status of being a witness, [the author] considers whether this relationship is real or unreal; since it cannot be the first [real], because that would contradict the scriptural texts concerning the Self’s lack of attachment (asaṅgatva), he says: "The non-Self... The word should be divided as "akārakatvāt" (because of being a non-agent). || 944 ||
Because cognition and the like are insentient in nature, they do not establish themselves by their own power.
Like the nature of awakening itself, it is established by its own inherent establishment alone. || 945 ||

He accepts the second [alternative], stating "intellect and so forth. The meaning is that intellect and the rest do not establish themselves independently like the Self because they are insentient (jaḍa); rather, they are superimposed upon the self-luminous, immediate consciousness (pratyak-caitanya), and thus their relationship is established through superimposition (ādhyāsika). || 949 ||
Indeed, every purpose for others is accomplished only through one's own purpose.
Just as one's own emanation is accomplished for the sake of those who perceive it as a dream. || 946 ||
16. Accomplishment of the Intellect (*adhīsiddhi*).
[Vol. 3, p. 743] 1876 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter—]

He establishes, by means of an illustration, that the perfection of the intellect and so forth—which have been practiced—results from the grace of the inward-facing reality that serves as their substrate: "For its own sake," etc. (946).
Whether it be distinct or non-distinct, its nature as falsehood does not exist at all.
Because its distinctness is established by its own power alone, just like that of another self. || 947 ||

Furthermore, having raised the dilemma as to whether the world superimposed upon the Self is different from it or non-different, he clarifies that the relationship is merely imagined. He asks: "Or if it were separate? Anticipating the objection—"How is falsity not established in either case?"—he demonstrates its non-establishment in the first instance by stating: "If there were separateness. For if there were difference, a relationship with the Self would be difficult to explain; thus, its establishment [of reality] is inherently unestablished.

Whether [the self] exists or does not exist as a non-self, in neither case can there be falsity; for the self is not established by itself and yet is seen to be false, nor is it unestablished like a sky-lotus and the like.
The meaning is that for that which is absolutely unperceived, specific attributes such as its true nature cannot be established. || 947 ||
And no proof is seen for its non-separateness from the self, nor for its destruction.
Without entering into the ultimate truth, it cannot be established as "not false. || 948 ||

In the second [verse], he demonstrates the non-establishment of falsity: "Because it has the nature of the Self" (*ātmatvāt*). The connection with the preceding [argument] is that the world does not have a false nature.

Nor can it be argued that the world must simply be non-false because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), like a rope-snake; such is the sense. [This is stated] regarding the world’s relation to the Self by way of difference or non-difference.

If it is argued that, upon proof, that [object] must necessarily terminate in non-existence, he says "no," providing the reason: "there is no means of knowledge (*māna*). For there is no perceived means of knowledge for the claim that "it has become non-existent"; furthermore, for one who asserts its non-existence, there would be a contradiction with specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and cognition. Nor will something that previously existed become non-existent after the act of cognition, because of the scriptural teaching: "The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being. This is the intended meaning regarding the self (*ātman*).

If it is argued that the world cannot be established as false because it possesses the nature of both difference and non-difference, then one might suspect that, being devoid of those two, it would likewise exist in its own right by its own nature; anticipating this, he says: "The ultimate reality" (paramārtham). || 948 ||
This absence of imagined snakes and the like is not distinct from the reality of the sacrificial ladle (sruk).
Since it is established through exclusion, one should not pursue the self either. || 949 ||

Regarding the point that for a conceptualized entity (kalpita), existence and non-existence do not occur apart from its substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), he provides an illustration with the word "lṛpta. Non-existence here serves as an indicator for existence; the remainder of the sense is that, likewise, for the world, existence and non-existence do not exist apart from the Self. He states another reason why difference and non-difference are impossible for the conceptualized world apart from its substratum with the words "vyatirekeṇa" (apart from). || 949 ||
Because one's own goal is the inner self, and because it is the true nature of that which is inward.
Just as a person intoxicated by drinking from various vessels such as broken or shaven ones perceives them as distinct, so too does the manifold self perceive division.
Anticipating the objection that "if the distinction is merely apparent, then let it be real, since it is not sublated," he says: "svārthe" (in its own object). || 990 ||
From this statement, "All is the Self," one attains the state of non-dual oneness.
By abandoning ignorance of that [reality], we perceive the Self of the world. || 959 ||

1877. By refuting the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the world—which is sublated by the cognition arising from the Vedic statement—is established as a mere mental construct (*pratyaya-mātra*) through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).
Thus he concludes: "All. || 991 ||
Except for the awakening of the entities consisting of cause and effect.
By means of words whose referents are unprecedented and so forth, no connection or the like is cognized. || 952 ||

Fearing that [the opponent might object]: "By such statements as 'All this is what this Self is—without prior, without posterior, without interior,' the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the world with Brahman are being stated, but it does not culminate in the realization of the pure inner Self (*pratyagātman*) by means of awakening to that reality," he says: "Tattva... (Verse 952).
For even consciousness, though it is not an agent, destroys ignorance here within the self.
Nor does it remove darkness by depending on its own recurrence, because it is merely a manifestor.

He concludes the impossibility of an injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self according to the Vedas with the words "bodho 'pi" (even cognition). The connection is "even though it is not an agent.
The ellipsis is "therefore, there is no injunction in this regard. He concludes that even in its repeated practice, such [an injunction] does not exist, with the word "na" (not).
And so forth. || 953 ||
Thus, when one's own self is known to be inactive, a non-agent, and devoid of fruit, tell me: what cause could there be for either engagement or withdrawal? (954)

Anticipating the objection that even in the absence of an injunction for engagement (*pravartaka-vidhi*), there might still be an injunction for desisting (*nivartaka-vidhi*) for the knower, he says: "In this way" (*evam iti*). || 994 ||
"Indeed, apart from that ignorance, there is no state of oneness with the individual soul."
The wise man should perceive another alternative, for such indeed is the sacred revelation (śruti). || 955 ||

Anticipating the objection that even for the wise man, the perception of duality is indeed caused by that [ignorance], he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*). The meaning is this: the wise man does not perceive any form other than the one inner self, because ignorance—which is the cause of the cognition of duality—has been sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*). He provides the proof for the statement that the cognition of duality is produced by ignorance with the words: "Where... Since the perception of duality in the wise man is merely a persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*), it does not lead to rebirth.
The meaning is that it is either the state of being produced or the state of being a negator. || 955 ||
Therefore, there is no cessation of ignorance through the knowledge of the true nature of Brahman.
There is no further possibility of the existence of ignorance within the inner self (pratīci), according to valid means of knowledge. || 956 ||

One might raise the objection that even if ignorance (*avidyā*) has been destroyed, it may arise again and thus manifest duality, whereby the performance of scriptural injunctions (*vaidhapravṛtti*) and so forth would be established; anticipating this, he says: "Not from this" (*nātaḥ*). The meaning of the word "from this" (*ataḥ*) is the sentence beginning with "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). || 996 ||
Furthermore, it is urged here that even for a person of knowledge, the appearance of passion and so forth may still occur.
Since that [cognition] arises precisely from what has been sublated, even that which was stated does not constitute a refutation. || 957 ||

He restates what was said—that ignorance exists even for the wise—on account of their observation of passion and so forth: "Passion and so forth... The locative case ending signifies the sphere of worldly activity (*vyavahārabhūmi*). Regarding the point that once destroyed, ignorance does not arise again, the observation of passion and so forth by the knower does not bring about any fault, because... [text fragment].
[Vol.
3, page 745] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four: He provides the following resolution:
that which has been sublated during the state of knowledge appears merely as a semblance, according to the analogy of a burnt cloth. Thus he says: "bādhi... [sublated...]
"Of that," [it is said]. || 957 ||
For the relationship between the sublated and the sublator occurs only once.
But at a time subsequent to the connection, there is indeed a conjunction of the two recollections of them. || 958 ||

He states the reason why passion and the like are indeed sublated for the knower: "bādhyeti" (as that which is to be sublated). Because the perception of duality and the perception of non-duality stand in a relationship of the sublated and the sublator, their connection occurs only once; therefore, the cognition of duality—which consists of the cognition of passion and so forth occurring after [the dawn of] knowledge—is [already] sublated.

The meaning is "mere continuity. Now, an objection is raised: for a knower (*jñānin*), that very knowledge does not persist as a single, uninterrupted state because it is momentary (*kṣaṇika*); furthermore, repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) is not required, and if his memory were admitted, then since the memory of duality would also be possible, the performance of Vedic rites and so forth would be established. To this, he says: "From the connection... Following the connection between the cognitions of duality and non-duality, the memory of non-duality is connected as the sublater (*bādhaka*), while the memory of duality is connected as the sublated (*bādhyā*).
Such is the classification. || 958 ||
Furthermore, the validity of memory as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not accepted in any established doctrine.
Furthermore, there is no sublation by means of what is not a valid cognition, because it lacks the characteristics of a valid means of knowledge.

In order to establish the aforementioned relationship between the sublated and the sublator regarding the two Smṛtis concerning duality and non-duality, he restates the lack of authority of both Smṛtis as established by both parties, beginning with "na ca" (nor...). [Objection: If that is so, since there is no distinction in the lack of authority for both, how can there be a relationship of the sublated and the sublator? To this he replies with "na ca" (nor...). The meaning is that the Smṛti concerning duality, being preceded by what is not authoritative, is the sublated, whereas the other, being preceded by what is authoritative, is the sublator; such is the established rule. || 919 ||
Because the causes such as the mother have been destroyed, and because there is no obstruction to the supreme departure.
Therefore, no contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition can be raised in any way whatsoever. 960 ||

Anticipating the objection that the cognition of non-duality (*advaitadhī*) is not authoritative because it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, and that therefore the Smṛti concerning non-duality cannot be preceded by such authority, he says: "mātrādi" (beginning with the measure).

Since perception and the rest are sublated after the destruction of ignorance along with its effects by the cognition of non-duality, no contradiction with them should be suspected for this [Smṛti]. Thus, by virtue of its own authority, the Smṛti preceded by it is more powerful and sublates the other. || 960 ||
And in the sequel, he will explain the means of practice, such as tranquility and the rest.
In order to establish the aforementioned wisdom, independence is asserted in those [cases]. || 961 ||

The claim that even for the wise, because ignorance—which is the cause of passion and other defects—persists when viewed through the lens of attachment, there must be an injunction for practice in order to destroy that ignorance, is now refuted. He refutes the position that "since wisdom depends upon means, one must perform practice as the means required by that [wisdom]" with the words beginning with "udarka. He states their fitness for injunction with the words "yeṣu" (in which). || 969 ||
Therefore, one should not dwell upon words that do not lead to the realization of the self and its true meaning.
The word "many" (bahūn) is a restatement, since that plurality is already established.

Having refuted the interpretation of others regarding the sentence concerning the instrument of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa*) and established his own interpretation, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "one should not meditate" (*nānudhyāyet*), etc., by saying "No. This is because tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities are to be enjoined as means, and thus there is no [injunction] for the mental recitation of words denoting the non-Self.
1. But as for the time; 2. ka. kha. ga. it is observed.
|| u || [vol 3, page 746]

The meaning of the word [in the text] is that [the Self] is opposed to that [non-self], because of its contradiction with it. He states that the employment of the word "many" (bahu) is for the purpose of restating the essential nature [of the non-self]:
"The word 'many'... The ellipsis to be supplied is: "of the quality of being many, in words denoting the non-self. || 962 ||
By the scriptural phrase "weariness of speech," censure is expressed.
This is for the purpose of establishing the negation of that [notion] through the contemplation of the word "bhūri" (abundant). || 963 ||
He states the intended meaning of the latter half [of the verse]: "Of speech" (*vācaḥ*). He states the fruit of its censure: "By its prohibition" (*tanniṣedhena*) || 963 ||
Meditation on abundant sounds is not sufficient for the accomplishment of the goal of liberation.
If it were not so, that fruit would merely be the parching of one's voice, palate, and throat.
He states the reason for the prohibition against meditating on words that express "non-self" with the word *prabhūta*. What, then, is the fruit of that?
He states it with the words *na cet* (if not). || 964 ||
Since any other interpretation than the one already explained has been refuted by the logic set forth above, we shall not exert ourselves to refute it here. || 965 ||

He refutes the statement of Bhartṛprapañca that one should not contemplate words denoting duality at the time of meditation. [The author says: "It has been stated. The logic set forth is applicable to the refutation of the injunction for meditation; however, there is no occasion for the contemplation of words expressing duality at the time of meditation such that it would need to be prohibited. Furthermore, if there were a prohibition of this for a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) at all times, the distinction between the two positions (pakṣabheda) could not be established.
The state of being. || 965 ||
One should always meditate thus on "Om" alone; abandon all other words.
And likewise, the statement "having understood those" is a clear expression regarding the abandonment of the three Vedas. || 966 ||

He cites another scriptural authority (*śruti*) to show that one desiring liberation (*mumukṣuṇā*) should not engage in the contemplation of words known as the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), which denote the non-Self (*anātman*). [The text says: "Om, thus indeed... He states another scriptural authority regarding their being established in the syllable *Oṃ*: "And they, having understood... Abandonment of the threefold [Veda] means the abandonment of the rituals enjoined by it; through that, [the text speaks of] being established in the *Praṇava* for those of qualified capacity. [The text says: "The gods, indeed, from death..."

The meaning is that the statement of the Chāndogas—that "beginning from the Ṛgveda, they followed them upwards and entered into the very *svara* of the Ṛc, the Sāman, and the Yajus"—is clear. || 966 ||
This word "iti" has the sense of "cause," intended to avoid the repetition of many words.
Or, for the sake of completing the traditional transmission (āmnāya), one should perform the "if indeed" (yadi vā) breath-exhalation. || 967 ||

He states the meaning of the word *iti*: "the meaning is 'because' (*hetvartha*). Since meditation on numerous words has as its fruit merely the drying up of the palate and other organs, many words should not be meditated upon by one seeking liberation; however, a few words whose object is the unity of the Self are permitted even for him. Otherwise, the qualification "many" (*bahūn*)—which merely restates their nature—would be redundant, and the qualification "other" in the phrase "abandon other speech" (*anyā vāco vimuñcatha*) would be meaningless.

And this is the intended meaning. Since the reason has already been stated by the word "hi" (for), he says "matrā" (in this [verse]), fearing that if the word "iti" were also for that same purpose, it would be a redundancy. || 967 ||
1. Therefore, indeed... 2ka. ...the subsequent connection.

Bondage and liberation have been explained with effort as being accompanied by their respective causes.
Through the recitation of mantras and the words of Brahmins, for men desiring their own welfare. || 968 ||

In order to state the connection between the preceding and following contexts, he recounts what has occurred [in the previous section] with the words "with their causes" (*sahetukau*). He clarifies that very effort [of the Self] with the word "mantra.

By the statement of the mantra beginning with "clinging to that very thing along with action" (*tadeva saktaḥ saha karmaṇā*) and by the statement of the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "where this Self reaches weakness" (*sa yatrāyam ātmābalyam*), bondage—accompanied by the causes such as desire—is declared as something to be abandoned by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). When all [desires] have been relinquished...

The meaning is that by means of the mantra beginning with "cyanti" and the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "athākāmayamānaḥ," liberation caused by perfect knowledge has been stated as being dependent on those very [means]; furthermore, its essential nature has been elaborated upon in verses. || 968 ||
Why is it said here that "one should not meditate on various sounds"?
Or rather, let it be explained why there is no abandonment of even the very fewest [of these]. || 969 ||

He raises an objection in order to introduce the passage beginning with "That indeed is this Great One" (sa vā eṣa mahān), starting with the words "No" (na) and so forth. The meaning of the seven [verses] is that the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) is the qualified candidate (adhikārī). || 969 ||
Since even a very small portion of the word has not been abandoned there, that much is stated here.
"Let there be the abandonment of these very causes; this is what will be stated as 'that very one'. (970)

By the qualification "many," it is shown that there is no abandonment of even the very few words such as *tat* and *tvam*; the reason for this which is sought to be understood is stated by the sentence preceding "that very one" (*etametaṃ*). He says: "of the word. This means: regarding the abandonment and non-abandonment therein.

In passages such as "That indeed is this" (*sa vā eṣa*), the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya*) is restated; therefore, that portion of the Upaniṣad must have that [Self] as its subject matter.

The meaning is that this was intended [by the author] prior to the passage "Therefore, one should not meditate on many words," because even upon abandoning that [Veda], the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) would not be established. He states that the sentence beginning with "that" (*tam*) is for the purpose of stating the reason for the abandonment of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), namely, "one should not meditate on many words. Regarding the phrase "of the Trayī," he explains: "In the abandonment of that extensive [Veda] consisting of the ritual section, the reason will be stated by means of the passage beginning with 'that' (*tam*); for by that..."

Ritual actions are enjoined for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); thus, when one who has produced that desire abandons ritual action because it no longer bears fruit, the abandonment of that entire section [of the Veda] is also accomplished—this is the meaning. || 970 ||
Or rather, because the sections on ritual action and the knowledge of reality constitute distinct sentences.
Because of the mutual contradiction between the Vedāntas and the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa). || 971 ||

He proposes another intended meaning for the *vividiṣā*-sentence with the words "Or rather" (*yadi vā*). He raises an objection to state that very point with the word "But" (*bhinnaiḥ*). The sense of the objection is that because the two sections have distinct purposes—one established and one to be accomplished—they constitute separate sentences, and due to their mutual contradiction, they cannot stand in the relationship of principal and subordinate (*śeṣa-śeṣitā*). Furthermore, just as there is a contradiction between the ritual section (*karma-kāṇḍa*) and the Vedāntas, there is also a contradiction between the Vedāntas themselves and that [ritual section], resulting in a mutual contradiction.
It is nine hundred and seventy-nine yojanas and a half.
Even actions serve as causes for liberation;
this is explained by their function as the formative factors (saṃskāra) of the intellect. || 972 ||

Just as ritual injunctions (*karmavākya*) serve as supplements to the statements concerning knowledge (*jñānavākya*) by means of purifying the intellect, so too does the subsequent section serve that purpose; thus he states the answer.
"Being the cause" means "just like cognition"; this is the sense of the word "also" (api). || 972 ||
The entire first part [of this work] is for the purpose of understanding the meaning of the Vedānta.
It is now explained in such a way that it accords with the Veda. || 973 ||
Having restated the meaning of the Vedānta exactly as it is, the Śruti speaks with reverence:
With the words beginning with "savā," he commenced to explain the meaning that had been stated.

He applies [the commentary] to the meaning stated in the Bhāṣya beginning with "Thus, in this... by means of the word "pūrva" (previously). Anticipating the objection that the status of the Karma-kāṇḍa as a supplement to the Jñāna-kāṇḍa is not being stated by the passage beginning with "sa vā" (that indeed... in the manner previously described—and thus the mention of the *kaṇḍikā* in the Bhāṣya would be inappropriate—he states the purport of the Bhāṣya beginning with "tacceti" (and that...). [The phrase] "vedānta... [is explained as follows]: the connection is that [the passage] beginning with "sa vā" restates the meaning of the Vedānta.

He states the reason for this restatement with the word "yathā" (as). This means not exceeding the form established by the Madhu-kāṇḍa, which emphasizes scripture (*āgama*), the Muni-kāṇḍa, which emphasizes logical reasoning (*upapatti*), and other Vedānta texts. The *Śruti* passage beginning with "tam etam" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1) refers to this. The stated point is that ritual actions are the cause for the arising of knowledge by way of purifying the intellect. 973 || 974 ||
That which is expressed by the word "sa" (that) is a reference (parāmarśa) to what was previously mentioned, because of its well-known status.
The word "vai" (indeed) serves for the purpose of recollecting that [Self] which possesses the attributes of death, birth, and so forth.

Having stated the purport of the section (*kaṇḍikā*), he explains the meaning of the two words while showing the purport of the portion of the text preceding the *vividiṣā* passage, part by part, beginning with the word "parāmarśa. The word "vai" (indeed) is the reason for its being intended as a reference to that very same [subject]. Regarding the phrase "on account of well-known usage" (*prasiddhitaḥ*), he says "mṛti" (death), anticipating the objection that since the referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadalakṣya*) was also mentioned previously, it might be suspected of being referred to by the pronoun "sa" (he). ||975||
This is designated as that which is declared in the sacred tradition (Āmnāya) to end with the syllable *dhruva*.
The word "great unborn" (mahānaja) is used for the purpose of establishing that qualification. || 976 ||

By the word "this" (*eṣa*), he also excludes the possibility that [the word] refers to anything other than that very [Self]. Regarding the word "constant" (*dhruva*): the meaning intended here is that the referent of the term *tvam*, which was previously described as "dustless, beyond the ether, unborn, the Self, great, and constant," is what is taught here by the word "this. He states that the word "unborn" (*aja*) is for the purpose of purifying the meaning of *tvam*.
He further states that the word "great" (*mahān*) is for the purpose of establishing the specific attributes of Brahman for that purified [Self]. Thus, he says: "Great."
The scripture beginning with "That which is this... has as its meaning positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
The statement "of all" is likewise intended to indicate the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified. || 977 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "He who is this... as follows: "By means of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvaya-vyatirekābhyām*), which means for the purpose of purifying the referent of the term *tvam* (the "you").

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "The controller of all" (*sarvasya vaśī*) as follows: "By means of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇaiḥ*). This is for the purpose of establishing that just as the inner self (*pratīc*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) by virtue of being qualified by Brahman, so too is Brahman the substantive by means of qualifiers such as "the controller of all."
The meaning is "a statement. || 977 ||

Whatever remains to be said regarding this matter has already been stated previously.
Since [the matter of] grammatical coreferentiality and so forth has already been addressed, it is not stated again here. || 978 ||

If it be argued that Brahman is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the inner self (*pratīc*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), then one must also state that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words, that their respective meanings stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified, and that the pure essential nature (*svarūpa-mātra*) is what is indicated (*lakṣya*). However, it cannot be maintained here that such coreferentiality and so forth exist, because of the mutual contradiction between Brahman and the inner self. Anticipating this objection, he recalls what was stated in the *Brahma-kāṇḍikā*.
Regarding the phrase "yadatra" (what is here): the words "iha" (here) and "atra" (in this) refer to the current section (*kaṇḍikā*) under discussion. || 978 ||
"It is not that one becomes more virtuous through action"—this is said to be the fruit of knowledge.
And by the statement "the Lord of All," there is a praise of that very same [reality] as it has been described. (979)

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Not by the good" (na sādhunā) as follows: "Abundant" (bhūyān). He states the purport of the passage beginning with "This is the Lord of all" (eṣa sarveśvaraḥ) as follows:
"This" (eṣaḥ). The phrase "of that which has been described" (yathoktasya) refers to the inner self (pratyagātman). || 979 ||
This is what is meant here by the passage beginning with "this which... and so forth.
It is described as being secluded from desire, action, and the like, and as self-luminous.
This very one is the Lord himself, as demonstrated by the Śruti.
In this context, the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified belongs to the Lord and the one who is to be ruled.

Anticipating the objection that this is a praise of something non-existent—like saying "You are Brahmā" or "You are Viṣṇu"—the author demonstrates the manner of the praise by using the word "this" (*etad*). The phrase "here" (*atra*) refers to the *Jyotir-brāhmaṇa*. The intention is that because identity is established through statements such as "That Thou Art," this is indeed a praise based on reality.
In that regard, he shows the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified by the words "qualifier," etc. By the word "here," the Śruti is indicated.
In relation to whom would there be the state of being a Lord? Thus [the scripture] refutes it.
Because it is contradictory to its own qualification, just as "greatness" residing in a jar [is contradictory to the qualification of being a jar]. || 982 ||

He states the result when the individual soul (*jīva*) is the substantive qualified by the attribute "Lord" (*īśvara*). Regarding the phrase "him": by the force of the attributes such as "being the Lord of all," the qualities residing in the substantive soul—such as being subject to rule (*īśitavyatva*)—depart; this is the meaning. He provides the reason why the relationship of qualifier and qualified functions as a negator: "by the attribute," etc. Because it is contradictory to the state of being the Lord, [the soul] is qualified by that [attribute].

The meaning is that there is a cessation of the state of being ruled by the individual soul (jīva). Just as when it is said, "the space within a jar is the great space," the limitedness residing in the space within the jar ceases, so too when it is said, "this is the Lord of all," the state of being ruled by the individual soul ceases; thus he says, "the Great.
And because, when that which is to be ruled over has ceased to exist, [the ruler] depends solely upon that [non-existence].
Even lordship over all things without exception ceases for the inward-looking Self.

He states the result when the state of being subject to rule has ceased: "The object of rule... and so forth. Thus, the sense is that the manifestation remains as the indeterminate (nirviśeṣa) reality. || 983 ||

1. *Ka.* and *Sva.* read *coktataḥ*. 2. *Pa* and *Tra* read *pra*. 3. *Gha* reads *brahmā*. 4. *Ka.* and *Kha.* read *yabhā*. 5. *Mbhakhaṃ yauṃ*. [Vol. 3, page 750] 4. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Just as there is nothing remaining but pure space here, so it is within the Self.

He elaborates upon the example stated in verse 1883 with the words "mahat" and so forth. He provides the application to the subject of the illustration with the word "ghaṭa. He states the application to the present case with the word "iha. || 984 ||
Just as there is no connection between two contradictory things, so too there is none between two non-contradictory things.
Upon the complete cessation of ignorance regarding that, the meaning beyond words remains. || 985 ||

He clarifies that very point with the words "of the two opposites. The non-duality residing in one category and the immediacy residing in the other do not have a connection with Brahman and the Self respectively, precisely because they are mutually contradictory.

Likewise, there is no mutual conjunction between immediacy and non-duality, because those two are one. Therefore, the meaning is that when ignorance regarding Brahman and the Self is destroyed, there remains a single-flavored reality. || 989 ||
This, first of all, is the intended meaning; now the meaning of the words is being stated.
Since the meaning of the phrase "sa vai" has already been explained, it is not further elaborated upon here.
For the purpose of explaining that [point], there is here once again a restatement of it. || 986 ||

Avoiding the charge of redundancy between what has already been said and what is about to be said, he restates what was previously stated and promises to explain what is to come, saying: "The purport of this [is as follows]. Anticipating the objection that since the meanings of the words were already established by implication, their repetition would still constitute tautology, he says: "That indeed... Even so, anticipating the objection that there is still redundancy with what was said starting from the question "Which one is the Self?", he addresses that very point...

He says that there is no tautology because this is a restatement for the purpose of stating the reason, without abandoning the portion that constitutes the *upaniṣad* (esoteric teaching): "Of that," [he says]. || 986 ||
And by a voice from the sky, the Supreme Teacher of the World was addressed, though he remained unaware.
The cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world is a specific attribute of the Self.

He recalls the meaning of the word "space" with the words "ākāśa. He manifests his status as the teacher of the world with the word "jagat. He excludes [the notion of] his being a mere bystander with the word "ātman. || 987 ||
This intrinsic nature of the field and the knower of the field has been previously described.
Being of the nature of the reality of the non-dual Buddha, he abides as the self of the cause. || 988 ||

He reminds us that the fruit of being the cause of the world—namely, the state of being the Self of all—is stated in such passages as "all this" and so forth; [he does so by saying] "the field," etc. (988).
Because everything is under his control, he is therefore the controller of all.
If it is argued that there might be mastery over the "da" [the letter 'd'] when it is neutral, then [this is] refuted. || 989 ||
This is not so, because of the connection with the state of mastery; for there is a further statement:
He is indeed the sovereign of all; he is always the lord over everything. (990)

He states the meaning of the phrase "the controller of all" with the words "all. Taking up the expression "the lord of all," he explains it by way of inquiry with the words "of the indifferent one. || 989 || 990 ||
Like the prince Kumāra, that sovereignty of the Supreme Self would likewise belong to him.
If this is argued, it is not so, because he is called the sovereign lord (adhipati). || 991 ||

1 gha. *dbhāgatyāṃ* | 2 ka. ga. *tvamapi ca* | 3 ga. *śivaṃ* | 4 ga. *saṃbhedānmai* | [vol 3, page 751] 1884 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]— [Fragmentary notes regarding textual variants for the commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad.]
Because it has itself as its object of action, it exercises its presiding influence over [the soul's] arising, subsistence, and destruction.
By means of a threefold sovereignty, he always protects the world.
He introduces and explains the qualification "the sovereign of all" by means of a preliminary objection: "O Youth!

Indeed, he possesses a threefold sovereignty consisting of the causes of origination, maintenance, and destruction; for, presiding over the world through the aforementioned sovereignty throughout its three states, he protects it eternally, since the world is his own effect and the accomplishment of presiding and protecting resides in him—this is the second [verse].
The application of the commentary. || 999 || 992 ||
The conjunction of dharma and adharma arises from the teaching of the Lord, just as it does for the world.
If it were attained, then there would be no attainment of that [Self], according to the scriptural statement: "He is not this" (na iti). || 993 ||
He raises the objection beginning with "not by what is good" and so forth, [starting] with the word "dharma. || 993 ||
It is held that the inherent nature of actions is to yield their fruit to their own agent.
Because he lacks both agency and ownership, the Lord has no connection with the fruit [of action]. (994)

He states the reasoning required for that [point], according to the principle "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because it is characterized by that," in the words: "In one's own... (994).
Because it is immutable, it possesses no agency, since it is neither an effect nor a cause.
Through the distinction between cause and effect, that very ignorance remains established.
Anticipating the objection that the Lord’s lack of agency is unproven because he is accepted as the creator of all things, [the author] says: "Because of his immutability" (*kauṭasthyāt*).
He explains this by saying: "Not an effect" (*akārya*). Then, he states how he can nevertheless be a cause: "The effect... (verse 995).
"It is not gross, 'not this, not this,' it is not born"— so says the Śruti.
And thus, the statement beginning with "neither prior nor posterior" becomes logically consistent. || 996 ||

He states the conformity of the Śrutis to the view that the inner self (pratīc) has no agency by itself, but rather through ignorance (avidyā), with the words: "asthūlam" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8].
Likewise, a relationship such as that between property and owner does not exist for this [Self], because it is non-dual.
For where there is duality—in this way indeed stands the teaching of the Śruti. || 997 ||

Having stated the absence of agency in the Lord, he states the absence of ownership: "svasvāmitvādi" (ownership of one's own self, etc.). By the word "etc. (ādi), he indicates that other relations as well are merely imagined; thus, the meaning is that they are like the relation between cause and effect. Regarding the fact that every relation of the Self is imagined, he cites scripture: "yatra hi... (For where...). 997.
Those modifications such as being produced, and those which are considered to be relations;
All these would belong only to one who is afflicted by ignorance, but not by their own nature. || 998 ||

He concludes by restating what was said—that agency and so forth do not belong to the self in reality: "The produced and so forth. Birth (*jani*) means origination; "and so forth" refers to modifications such as transformation and the like. || 998 ||
Since this is so, the Lord would not become greater by means of good action.
Even the younger [brother] is not [guilty] because of the sin, due to the reason of his non-agency therein. || 999 ||

Taking up what was stated regarding the self’s lack of inherent ownership and so forth, he connects the sentence by stating the non-connection with the fruits of action: "Since... He clarifies the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) as: "because of that [self's] lack of agency. || 999 ||
Just as there is a connection with merit and demerit for one who exists as a knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
Because of the conceit of being an agent and so forth, [this applies] to the non-Lord (anīśa), since that [conceit] is impossible for the Lord (īśa). || 1000 ||

He states another reason for the Lord’s lack of connection with action and its fruit: "Of the knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). The meaning is that the connection with action and its fruit belongs to the qualified [self] because of the conceit "I am the doer," and not so to that [self] as characterized [by such attributes], since that [conceit] is absent in it. || 1000 ||
Because this darkness of the inner self is always without cause.
Therefore, there is neither decrease nor increase for him, because he is not conjoined with merit or demerit.

For this reason as well, he states that the Lord has no connection with karma and the like: "Because of being without cause" (*nirhetutvāt*). The "darkness" (*tamasvitva*) of this individual soul (*pratīc*) consists in its lordship (*īśatva*) produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*). Since that [lordship] which has ignorance as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) exists eternally—being independent of adventitious causes—it has no association with merit (*dharma*) and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that for the Supreme Being (*para*), there is no increase or decrease caused by karma. || 1001 ||
Therefore,
there is neither its effect nor its cause— that which would be the cause of its agency and so forth.
Because its intrinsic nature is by itself unattached, and likewise because it is partless and one. || 1002 ||

Having accepted sovereignty and other attributes as belonging to the Self, and having stated that it is not connected with dharma and so forth, he says that those very [attributes] do not belong to it by means of the words beginning with "no. He states the reason for the absence of agency and the like, whether as cause or effect, with the word "intrinsically" (*svataḥ*).

Anticipating the objection that agency and non-attachment might exist through a distinction of parts, he says "partless" (*niraṃśa*). [The opponent asks: "What then is the agency of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)?"

Anticipating the objection that [the Self] might be non-connected with another, he says: "Because of oneness" (ekatvataḥ). The meaning is that, because the Self possesses the characteristics as previously described, it does not possess lordship (īśatva) and so forth. || 1002 ||
Even though its nature is thus self-existent, it exists by relying upon that ignorance.
This God is the Lord of all, [designated as such] in dependence upon that which is to be ruled.

Then, how is it that he is the Lord of All (sarveśvara), and so forth? To this, he says: "By himself" (svataḥ). This means that his very nature consists of such qualities as being unattached (asaṅga) and partless (anaṃśa). The connection [of the sentence] is: "due to the dependence upon his own ignorance (avidyā), [his lordship exists] relative to the objects to be ruled.
Why is it stated redundantly that "he is the Lord of all"?

He raises the objection regarding the redundancy of the phrase "the Lord of all" (*sarvasyeśāna*) for the purpose of establishing that the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) which is about to be described has [Brahman] as its object. He says, "This... and so on, demonstrating the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of that [phrase] in order to resolve the objection.
Rati says: "To be mentioned later. This is not a redundancy, for it is stated in order to declare that the inner self itself, when unknown, is the object of the desire to know (vividiṣā).
[Note: ka, kha, gha read 'bandhe ka'; ka, gha read 'tad'; ga reads 'cāsya'; kha reads 'cābhāve'; gha reads 'ti'].
So be it.
[Vol. 3, page 753] 1886 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]...

The meaning is this: since the reference is to the "inner one" (pratīcaḥ), its state of being unknown is indicated by the word "Lord of All" (sarveśvara); and since that very thing is intended as the object of the desire to know, there is no tautology here. || 1004 ||
As long as this very Self remains unknown, it is in reality merely that much.
Therefore, everything from Īśvara down to the objects of the senses must be considered as being merely imagined.

Since the status of being its object is possible even for Hari, Hara, and others by virtue of their being unknown, how is it that only the inner self (pratyagātman) is thus asserted? To this, he says: "Unknown" (*ajñāta*). This is the reason for the restriction. "Only that much" (*tāvanmātra*): how is it that the mere inner self [is the object] of everything?

Anticipating the objection that even Īśvara and others are established as real entities (*vastu*) in the world because they possess existence (*satattva*), he says: "Īśa, etc. The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is [their] insentience, finitude, and so forth. || 1005 ||
Or, if no connection with "good" and so forth is intended, then it is called a reason (*hetu*).
By such words as "this," the Self, who is the Lord of all, is clearly [revealed]. (1006)

Since it is observed in the world that connection with dharma and so forth through the favor bestowed by one who performs protection and other such acts is unavoidable, one might raise the objection: "How then can there be such a statement as 'it is not'? Anticipating this, he states another meaning for the repetition [of the word], beginning with "sādhvādi" (the virtuous, etc.). || 1006 ||
In this world, one who is dependent on dharma, adharma, and so forth, is tainted by their fruit.
The self consisting of consciousness is not so; rather, it must be the Supreme because of its sovereignty over all. || 1007 ||
This [result] belongs to every action as well as to its agent, being produced by that [action].
Since God is not self-existent, He cannot be the cause of dharma and so forth.

He states that very person who is the undisputed cause of the non-dependence: "Dharma... [and so on]. The individual soul (*jīva*) is subject to desire, action, and ignorance, and is therefore connected with their fruit;

but the other [the Self] is not like that, for it is not subject to action and the rest, owing to its being the Lord of all and because it is the controller even over that [soul]. Therefore, there is no connection with the fruit of that [action].

The meaning is that [the Lord] would be bound. Here, the word "iha" (in this case/here) serves to distinguish between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). To the question of how, despite being the Lord of all, He can remain unconnected to the fruits of karma, he says: "sarva... (all...). 1007 || 1008 ||
For this Lord protects all beings that possess birth.
Therefore, the god Bhūtapāla is so called because he is the cause of all effects.

Anticipating the doubt that "Paśupati" or "Śrīpati" might refer to the Lord of all (Sarveśvara) rather than the inner self (Pratyagātman), the text intends to address this by means of the qualification "this [is] the lord of beings. With this in mind, it explains the meaning of the term "protector of beings" (*bhūtapāla*) with the words "beings" (*bhūtāni*). The reason for this is given as "of effects" (*kāryāṇām*).
For effects are protected here from this or that by means of their causes;
and because beings are effects, the Self possesses the nature of a protector of beings. || 1010 ||

Although, starting from the Sūtra on "birth and so forth" (janmādi-sūtra), the Lord is the cause of all effects according to the reasoning stated here and there, [the author] asks: "In what way is He the protector of beings? To this he says: "By the cause," etc. The meaning is that for an effect neglected by Him, there would be no existence at all. (Note: This passage appears to be a commentary on a verse concerning the Lord's role as the sustainer of the world, clarifying that His causal agency is not merely a mechanical process but involves active oversight.)

The word *hi* (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of stating that the sphere of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra-bhūmi*) has been described here; therefore, the meaning is "everywhere. This general principle is now applied to the subject at hand.
He joins [the argument], saying: "Because it is its effect. || 1010 ||
By the term "Lord of Beings" (bhūtādhipati), Brahmā is intended here.
And here, Indra is likewise the Lord of the World (lokeśvara) through his nature as Varuṇa and others.
And this guardian of the world as well, because of seeing such an action.
And although he is also the ruler, this very point is now being stated. || 1012 ||

He states another meaning for the term *bhūtādhipati* (lord of beings): "The one called *bhūta*... etc. That Brahmā who is known in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas by names such as Sūtra and so forth, is designated here in this sentence by the term *bhūtādhipati*. This is because of the Vedic text: "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists. And the meaning is that he is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) here, because this is the context concerning Him. This...

The Mādhyandinas explain the term *lokeśvara* there as "this is the Lord of the World" (*lokeśvara*), and [the text] says "Indra," thereby stating the meaning of the term *lokapāla*. Regarding the phrase "Varuṇa and so forth," the reason given is that just as the Supreme Self alone is the Lord of the World (*lokeśvara*) in the form of Indra, so too is He the Guardian of the World (*lokapāla*) in the form of Varuṇa and the others; for such is the case regarding the tasks of governing and protecting the world performed by Indra and the rest.
The meaning is that because the non-Lord (anīśvara) cannot do so, He Himself, by abiding in various forms, performs those respective effects.

He introduces [the passage] beginning with "This is the bridge" (*eṣa setuḥ*) with the words "as the ruler" (*praśāsita*). That is to say, as the upholder of the boundaries (*maryādā*). The second *api* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). || 1011 || 1012 ||
This established arrangement of the worlds, beginning with the earth and so forth, [is the work of Him].
That [distinction] is also established here through his very teaching, without being confounded.
If it is argued that there might be some other ruler distinct from [the Self] because such a distinction is well-known, he says "no," with the words "of the worlds.
The meaning is that this has already been refuted by the passage beginning with "another ruler than this is distressed" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.2). || 1013 ||
The non-confusion of the established rules regarding the causes such as caste (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama).
It should be observed that this "bridge" could not be established at all without a cause. || 1014 ||
Even though it is the Supreme alone who is the ruler, he explains why the word "bridge" (setu) is applied to Him: "varṇa... (verse 1014).
He is the destroyer of enemies and likewise the bridge that maintains the world.
That Supreme Lord is the bridge for all the established orders of the world.
He explains the qualification "support" (*vidharaṇa*) in order to establish the state of being a bridge for others by means of an illustration: "Just as... (1015).
When there arises the inquiry, "For what purpose is it a bridge?", the subsequent statement [provides the answer].
"It is said [thus] for the sake of the non-confusion of these worlds. || 1016 ||
He takes up [the passage] beginning with "of these" (eṣām) and so forth. For what purpose? || 10196 ||
How indeed could those [entities] as described exist with their respective definitions unconfounded?
Therefore, the Lord shall become a bridge sufficient for each respective fruit.

He explains that supreme speech as being "for the sake of non-confusion" (*asaṃbhedāya*). This means that the aforementioned letters (*varṇa*), stages of life (*āśrama*), and worlds (*loka*) such as the earth and so forth—each has its own distinct fruit and its respective effect dependent upon those [factors]. || 1017 ||
Thus, first of all, that which was stated in the sixth chapter has been briefly presented with reverence.
Having restated every object through scripture, [the author] then [proceeds] for the sake of its realization.
In such a way that this entire Veda attains the status of being a means.
This very thing is expressed by the phrase "that which is this. || 1019 ||
1.1 Having restated what has been discussed, he states the purport of the *vividiṣā* passage: "In this way, first... [referring to] the reality, which is the identity of Brahman and the Self.

"Obtains" means by the Śruti beginning with "This [Self] is indeed great," and so forth. "Akhilam" (the whole) means full. "Tasya" (of that) is a statement of identity. The word "atha" (now/then) indicates the requirement for a means to realize that [identity]. The word "veda" refers to the meaning of the Karma-kāṇḍa.
It has been stated that they desire to know this [Self] through the study of the Vedas and other such means.

Having stated the purport of the *vividiṣā* passages—that the Lord, from whom all conceptual constructions have departed, is to be known directly through means—he now applies the words of those passages, beginning with "aitam. [He says: "directly" (*sākṣāt*)—the desire to know...

The connection is with the word "pantī" (they reach). The meaning is that this has been stated in such passages as "He who is stainless, higher than the ether," and so forth. By the word "Īśvaram" (the Lord), he indicates that the unknown inner self (pratīcaḥ) is the object of the desire to know (vividiṣā). He then describes its very nature as being free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika) and eternally liberated: "apeta... (1.20).
Even the independent desire to know the Lord as an object is extremely difficult to attain.
It is understood that the means for [attaining] that are prescribed with effort in the Śruti.

He states the distinction of the desire for knowledge regarding the Inner Self (*pratyak*) from worldly desire by means of the word "independently" (*svātantryeṇa*). Worldly desire is easily obtained, being produced by the cognition of an object as desirable; however, with respect to the Inner Self, even the mere desire to know (*bubhutsā*) is not attained by a person independently, let alone the knowledge of It. He provides the evidence for this rarity of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) by stating [the difficulty of its] means.
The presentation of many means is the effort. || 1021 ||
And because of the difference in application and effort between the sections on ritual action and knowledge.
It is understood that there is a difference between distinct sentences; there is no talk of application (viniyoga) within a single [sentence]. // 1022 //

He states the established meaning by examining the *vividiṣā* (desire to know) passage, beginning with the words "viniyoga" (application). As for the claim made by some that the two sections (*kāṇḍas*) constitute a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), that is incorrect; for it is understood that they are indeed distinct sentences, since their syntactic unity (*vākyatātparya*) is seen only in the application of ritual actions toward the desire to know. Furthermore, even if there were syntactic unity between the two sections, it would not be logical to speak of the application of those actions therein.

The meaning is that, since one who has attained the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) must abandon ritual action when that [desire] is applied [to its proper object], there is no possibility of [the two injunctions] forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). || 1022 ||

Even the desire to know [the truth] is difficult to attain; tell me, how then can there be an awakening to that reality?
Even more difficult to obtain than that, from where could it be acquired through any means? || 1023 ||
Regarding the phrase "the desire to know concerning the Lord," he states the meaning indicated by the word "also" (api) in verse 1023: "That which... etc.
These practices, such as the recitation of the Vedas and so forth, serve solely to produce the desire to know.
Since they have been assigned [to other purposes], therefore these are not for the sake of accomplishing the knowledge of that.

Having stated that there is no syntactical unity between the two sections (kāṇḍas) by following the statement regarding the application of ritual actions toward the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), he states another meaning obtained precisely from the force of that same statement regarding application: "The desire to know" (*bubhutsā*), etc. (Verse 1024).
For this very reason, the Śruti will specifically teach tranquility (śama) and the other qualities with great effort.
For the sake of knowing the true nature of the self through skillful means, [one should contemplate] those things whose nature is the self.

He states that the supplementary portion of the text supports the view that ritual actions are indeed means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) and not means for knowledge itself, by saying "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Following the *Yoga Sūtra*—which defines the restraints (*yama*) as non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession—he qualifies the [qualities] such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth as being "of the nature of restraints" (*yamātmakān*). (1025)
Among these means for the desire to know, such as the recitation of the Vedas and so forth.
For the entitlement [to this practice] belongs to all stages of life (āśramas) without distinction, according to their respective capacity.
"Let it be that ritual actions are indeed the means for the desire to know [Brahman]. But who has the qualification for them? To this he says: "The desire to know," etc.

The word *aviśeṣeṇa* (without distinction) is the required reading. The meaning of the particle *hi* is that they possess the fitness for those actions by virtue of being their masters. Anticipating the objection that the systematic arrangement of duties according to caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*) would then be undermined, he says: "According to their respective [duties]," etc. That is, whatever action belongs to whichever caste or stage of life...
The meaning is that, by virtue of the treatise, it is appropriate; not transgressing that conjunction, he has authority over that [subject] in that [context]. || 1026 ||
According to what is appropriate and according to one's faith, for the sake of accomplishing the desire to know that.
All the duties of the stages of life, such as the recitation of the Vedas and so forth, must be performed by her. || 1027 ||
He elaborates upon that with the words "as appropriate": the desire for that [knowledge] is the wish to know the inner self (*pratyagvividiṣā*). || 1027 ||
By the expression "recitation of the Vedas," the daily study of the Veda is intended here.
By means of scripture, the characteristic of the perpetual private study (svādhyāya) is here being told to us.
The meaning of the sentence has been summarized, and its purport has been stated in various ways; now he explains the meaning of the term *vedānuvacana*. He says: "Veda... and "In this...".
The mention of "in this" refers to the context of the *vividiṣā* passage within the sphere of Vedic usage. || 1028 ||
And here, the mention of "brāhmaṇas" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the twice-born (dvijas).
Because their qualification for the realization of the Self is not distinct [from that of others]. || 1029 ||

Fearing that—because of the qualification "brāhmaṇa"—only he has the entitlement to the study of the Vedas and other such means for the desire to know (vividiṣā), and thus it would be improper to say that these [acts] such as the study of the Vedas must be performed by all stages of life (āśramas)—he says: "brāhmaṇa... [1029].

And likewise, from the Vedic text regarding the refinement of the person: "This [body] is mine; by means of the mind [I shall purify it]. (Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Four, Verse 1892)
The statement of the Smṛti, "Sacrifice, charity, and austerity," is also clear on this point. || 1042 ||

He cites the Śruti and Smṛti as authorities for the fact that actions are the cause of purification. The phrase "this [is]" indicates that the authority [of these texts] is clearly established in demonstrating that actions are the cause of purification. || 1042 ||
And in that [state] where there is purity, there is constant mindfulness regarding the purity of sentient beings.
Vedic passages such as these have been cited to establish the point already stated. || 1043 ||

He states the authority for the claim that "knowledge belongs to one of purified intellect who desires to know through actions" in the verse beginning with "yasmin. The meaning already explained—that knowledge arises for one of pure mind by means of the desire to know and so forth—is indicated here. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), such scriptural passages as "Then, with a purified being, one sees Him who is partless" are included. || 1043 ||
Knowledge arises in people through the destruction of evil karma.
Just as one sees one's own self within oneself in that which resembles the surface of a mirror.
Regarding the statement "knowledge belongs to those of pure intellect," he cites a traditional authority (smṛti): "Knowledge... [1044]
Acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed.
Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are indeed the purifiers of the wise.
And there is the traditional teaching that there are forty-eight conditioned factors.
Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification.

Having restated the very same Smṛti that was mentioned in the passage "purity [is attained] through actions," he cites another Smṛti with the words beginning with "yajña" (sacrifice). Regarding that very point, he states another sentence: "yoginaḥ" (the yogins). The meaning is that, having abandoned desire for fruits, practitioners of action perform their duties with the intention of dedicating them to the Lord for the sake of purifying the intellect. || 1045 || 1046 ||
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, whose mind is conquered, and whose senses are mastered.
Having become the self that is the self of all beings, one is not tainted even while acting.

Regarding the fact that [certain] actions are causes for purification, he cites another scriptural passage: "By yoga... He states that from the purity of the intellect, the result is that the intellect—denoted by the word *ātman*—attains self-mastery and the other senses attain subjection to it: "Conquered... Nor does action [taint] him.
He says "sarva... [verse 1047] to explain that even for one who remains [in this state], there is a connection with that fruit, because Brahman—which is the self of all beings—is his very self.
By means of the fire-oblations for the womb, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle;
The taint arising from seed and the taint arising from the womb are cast off by the twice-born.

Regarding the statement that the destruction of sin results from the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), he cites another Smṛti text: "By the *gārbha* [rites]," etc. The meaning is that for members of the three higher castes, the sin potentially incurred through the connection with the seed and the connection with the womb is removed by the *puṃsavana* and other such rites. || 1048 ||
