[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
"By the study of one's own Veda, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the threefold knowledge, by sacrifice, and by sons..."
Through the great sacrifices and the ritual offerings, this body is made fit for Brahman.

He states that there is another scriptural passage as well regarding the purification of actions through [Vedic study], beginning with the words "svādhyāyena" (by Vedic study). The connection is with the phrase "by the threefold Vedic study" (*traividyena svādhyāyena*). Alternatively, there is a distinction: *svādhyāya* is mere recitation; *traividya* is the constant study of the Vedas;
or else, *svādhyāya* is the studied Veda itself, while *traividya* is the knowledge of its meaning. || 1049 ||
In this way, there are hundreds [of such examples] for the purpose of establishing the meaning as it has been stated.
The statements of the Smṛtis, which praise the purification of the intellect of men through ritual actions, [are authoritative]. 1050.

He states the purport of the aforementioned Smṛtis with the words "In this manner. He states the fruit of purification with the words "As stated," meaning for the sake of attaining knowledge by means of the desire to know (vividiṣā). || 1050 ||
And it is precisely for the sake of knowing that actions are the cause of the misfortune of saṃsāra.
The exposition of the optional rites here is for the purpose of establishing the desire to abandon them.

Having stated that obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) are connected to the supreme human goal because they serve as a means to the fruit of liberation through purification, he now describes the manner in which optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) are connected to it: "In saṃsāra... When it is understood in the Veda that optional rites prescribed therein are causes of misfortune such as dwelling in the womb, then a desire to abandon them arises; consequently, for one whose intellect has been purified by the performance of obligatory rites and so forth, [the connection occurs] through the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) and other stages.
The meaning is that liberation is logically applicable to them as well, because it is associated with a superior fruit. || 1051 ||
Or rather, even those rites performed for the sake of specific desires may serve the purpose of the desire to know.
By the statement "this very [one]," because of the distinctness of the conjunction. || 1052 ||

He recalls what was stated in the *Saṃbandhagrantha* regarding their connection with liberation through another method: "Or else" (*yadvā*). To the question of how those [actions], being enjoined for the sake of other fruits, can be utilized for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), he says: "Because of the connection" (*saṃyogasya*) || 1052 ||
Giving, preceded by faith and other virtues, [should be performed] with regard to the place, the time, and the recipient.
For a person whose intellect has been purified by the scriptures, even that which is outside the Vedic fold shall become pure.

By citing "by great sacrifices" (*mahāyajñaiḥ*) and so forth, [the author] has already explained the meaning of "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*). Now, he states the meaning of "by giving" (*dānena*). Regarding the word "place" (*deśa*): it refers to a location such as Kurukṣetra and the like. "Time" (*kāla*) refers to an occasion such as an eclipse of Rāhu and the like. "Receptacle" (*pātra*) refers to one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), a knower of the supreme self (*adhyātmavit*), and so forth. By the word "faith and so forth" (*śraddhādīti*), devotion (*bhakti*) is expressed. [An objection: But is it not the case that the gift known as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is included within the sacrifice? And thus...

He says that it is not a redundant repetition of "by giving" (*dānena*) because it has already been covered by the word "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*). He explains this with the word "externally" (*bahiḥ*). He provides the authoritative basis for the claim that even giving outside the sacrificial altar (*vedyāḥ*) brings about purification with the phrase "according to scripture" (*śāstrataḥ*). The meaning is that this is established by such scriptural statements as, "Everything is founded upon giving; therefore, they say giving is supreme. || 1053 ||
The endurance of the onset of calamities through self-restraint is called austerity.
Its status as a cause for the purification of the intellect is also established by scripture. || 1054 ||
He states the meaning of the word *tapas*: "from restraint" (*niyamāt*). This is for the purpose of excluding the endurance of afflictions caused by passion and the like.
[Vol. 3, page 759]
It was stated, "due to a rule" (*niyamāt*). This means by virtue of scriptural injunctions regarding rites for the sake of the next world, such as *japa*, fasting, and so forth. By that, how...
Regarding that, he states the accomplishment of the desire to know (vividiṣā): "Of that too," [verse 1014].
And the Śruti says: "Desire to know that Brahman through austerity alone."
Furthermore, the teaching of the Smṛti states: "One destroys impurity through austerity. ||1055||

He provides an illustration of that very point with the words, "Desire to know. Anticipating the objection that "penance" (tapas) intended here refers to the method of positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka), he introduces a Smṛti passage indicated by the word "and" (ca): "By penance," etc. || 1011 ||
That which is most difficult to cross, that which is hard to attain, that which is difficult to traverse, and that which is hard to perform.
Everything is to be accomplished through austerity, for austerity is indeed difficult to surpass.

In that very context, he cites another Smṛti passage, beginning with "yat" (that which). "Dustaram" means difficult to overcome or avoid, such as the suffering of Kumbhīpāka and other hells. "Durāpam" means difficult to attain, such as the happiness of heaven and the like. "Durgamam" means difficult to understand, such as the Self (Ātman) and so forth. "Duṣkaram" means difficult to perform, such as the Aśvamedha sacrifice and the like.

He states the reason why everything is accomplished through austerity (*tapas*) with the words "tapo hi" (for by austerity...). For indeed, by austerity, [even] the one born from a jar (Agastya) [attained his goal] from the waters...
The sense is that since the treasure was swallowed up in a single gulp there, his greatness is easy to describe. || 1096 ||
And fasting is the non-eating characterized by the non-enjoyment of desires.
For it has indeed been said: "Those who are free from passion and hatred [should enjoy] sense objects. (1057)
Even Vedavyāsa exerted himself with great effort for the sake of attaining enlightenment through the renunciation of desires.
Or even that which is restricted by a vow until death—that too brings about ultimate purification. (1058)

He states the meaning of the word *anāśaka*: "And *anāśaka*... He provides the authority for the definition that *anāśaka* is the practice of limited scriptural objects beyond the intensity of attachment, aversion, and dogmatic adherence: "Attachment... The effort regarding the statement of results such as serenity (*prasāda*) and so forth is the restraint of the senses and the mind. Following the conventional usage of the word *anāśaka*, he states another meaning: "until death..."
The meaning is that *anāśaka* refers to the avoidance of food until death, accompanied by a restrictive resolve (*niyama-saṃkalpa*). To the question "What is the result of that?", he says:
"Even that," etc. (verses 1097–1098).
Since it is the cause of the mere desire to know the inner Self, there is no fear of death.
And because of the Smṛti text: "Having attained perfection through many births, he then departs. (1059)

One might suspect that its status as a cause for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is not established by way of purification, since purity and the like are achieved only while one is alive; anticipating this, he says: "The inner self" (*pratyag*). Since fasting (*anāśaka*) is a cause solely for the desire to know the Self, there is no such rule regarding the desire to know in this present life; therefore, one should not suspect that fasting is fruitless because it results in death, for it serves as a cause for that [desire] in another birth.

This is the meaning. Regarding the point that even a means belonging to this life is a cause for liberation by way of the desire to know [Brahman] (*vividiṣā*) arising in another birth, he states the proof:
"aneka... (verse 1099).
And through these cultivated faculties, throughout many births in the cycle of existence, he—
The pure-souled one indeed attains liberation in the first stage of life.
[Vol.
3, Page 760] 4 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
1895. Refuting the restrictive rule that liberation occurs even in another birth for one who has practiced all the stages of life (*āśrama*s), he cites another scriptural passage.
"By those cultivated," [it is said]. || 1060 ||
Likewise, death at sacred fords such as Pṛthūdaka is recorded in the Smṛti.
It is heard that liberation is attained directly here; therefore, there shall be no fear of death.

Although sacrifices and the like performed in the present life are useful for attaining purity and other qualities in a future birth, one might still ask: how is it that death at a specific place is likewise so? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "At Pṛthūdaka and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), Prayāga and other such places are included. This refers to Smṛti texts such as: "They are liberated through the knowledge of Brahman or by dying at Prayāga," and so on. Thus, the lack of fruitfulness for one who does not fast until death is caused by the manner of dying.
He states the conclusion—that there is no fear for oneself—with the word "no" (na). || 1061 ||
But when a person is appointed by scripture as a witness for the cognition of a fact, [he must speak the truth].
A wise person should diligently avoid therein the cause of death.

One might raise the objection: "In that case, all seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should practice fasting unto death; why then do they engage in hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*) and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "Directly" (*sākṣāt*). Where a person is enjoined by scriptural injunctions such as "one should hear" (*śrotavya*) toward hearing and other means for the sake of knowledge, one who is capable and endowed with the fourfold qualifications (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*) should, from afar, abandon fasting—the cause of death—and [instead practice] hearing and so forth.

The meaning is that because of the qualification "one should heed the cause of death," one who is capable of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, yet practices fasting unto death for the sake of discerning the meaning of the *tvaṃ* (thou) word, would incur sin;
this is according to such Smṛti texts as those beginning with "for the sake of discerning the meaning of the *tvaṃ* word. || 1062 ||
Or [he may attain it] through the recitation of the Vedas and so forth among the four stages of life (āśrama).
In this context, the mention [of the word] "śruti" (scriptural revelation) should be understood as being for the purpose of establishing the desire to know that [revelation].

Having stated that words such as "the recitation of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacana*) refer primarily to ritual action (*karman*), he states that they have the stages of life (*āśrama*) as their subject matter by saying, "of the four. Anticipating the objection—"For what purpose are the stages of life mentioned in this sentence by means of the scriptural injunctions consisting of 'recitation of the Vedas' and so forth?"—he says, "That [is for the sake of... This is for the purpose of establishing the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of all stages of life, whether directly or indirectly, with respect to the desire to know the Inner Self (*pratyag-vividiṣā*).
The meaning is that there is the grasping of them. || 1063 ||
The inclusion of the religious student (brahmacārin) is effected by the statement at the end of the section on celibacy (brahmacarya).
By austerity for the ascetic, and likewise by sacrifice for the householder.
But it is understood that the statement regarding the destruction of faith applies to all objects.
"Having understood this very [truth]"—thus he will speak regarding the life of a wandering mendicant.

In response to the inquiry as to which word denotes which stage of life (*āśrama*), he states the division following the Mādhyandina recension: "Ending with studenthood" (*brahmacaryānta*). For they read: "Brahmins desire to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through studenthood, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting. Nevertheless, only three stages of life are intended here.
Anticipating the objection that there is an absence of a word indicating the fourth stage of life (turīyāśrama), he says: "This very [one]... || 1064 || 1061 ||
1. Kha. *kṣāca vaṃ* | 2. Ga. *thā || 1064 || addhā* | 3. Ka. Kha. *ṇa vi* | 4. Ka. Kha. Gha. *°banti iti* | 5. [Fragmentary] *°vantīti* |
1896 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:
All these, when practiced in their proper sequence according to the rules, [lead to the goal].
They lead the Brahmin who acts according to what has been taught to the supreme goal.
By means of these four stages of life (āśramas), when practiced according to the scriptures, [the goal is attained].
Āpastamba also declared that one attains ultimate security. || 1067 ||

By stating that words such as "recitation of the Vedas" (*bedānuvacana*) refer to the stages of life (*āśrama*), it has been asserted that the stages of life are means to liberation (*mokṣa*) by way of the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) and so forth;

he states the authority for this [in the verse beginning] with "all indeed. The term "extreme" (*atyanta*) is used as a qualification in order to understand liberation (*mokṣa*) by the word "security" (*kṣema*).
That Supreme Being whom they intensely desire to know through the aforementioned means—
one who has known this very Self indeed becomes a sage, as previously described.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Having known this very [Self]" (aitameva viditvā) by means of the word "yam" (whom). The word "atha" (then) is used to indicate the absence of any interval between the knowledge of the Self and the state of being a sage (*muni*). The word "prāk" (previously) refers to the statement concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*). The meaning is that he is one who possesses the desire to know the Inner Self as it has been described. The term "uccaiḥ" (loudly/highly) expresses the possession of the intended purport (*tātparya-vattva*). || 1068 ||
I have previously declared that the state of a sage culminates in the perfection of both wisdom and childhood.
Because it belongs to those liberated from all karma, it is therefore not common [to others]. || 1069 ||

It has been stated that one who desires to know that inward Self becomes a man of knowledge (*jñānī*) by knowing it alone. Now, having raised the objection that since the state of being a sage (*munitva*) resulting from the knowledge of the Self is common to all stages of life (*āśrama*), and that the desire to know (*vividiṣā*)—which is the cause of knowledge through the means of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—is likewise shown to be common to all stages of life, the author recalls what was stated in the fifth chapter: "By scholarship... (1069).
And for the sake of generating the inward-cognizing wisdom of the entire yoga.
Therefore, there is no application superior to the arising of self-knowledge.

Furthermore, since ritual actions assist from afar by way of generating the desire for knowledge (vividiṣā) and because they are no longer applicable after the attainment of knowledge, he states that the status of being a knower belongs only to those who have renounced action, saying:
"Of yoga... (verse 1070). This means "of action" (karmaṇaḥ); the phrase "the supreme yoga" (paro yogaḥ) is to be supplied as the remainder. || 1070 ||
Since tranquility and the other qualities are themselves the means for attaining knowledge, therefore—
How could that state of being a sage, which lacks any authoritative basis, belong to one who has not renounced? || 1071 ||

If it is accepted that action is a means for the arising of knowledge, then one might ask how even a performer of ritual actions (karmī) could possess the status of a sage (muni). To this he replies: "Peace [of mind] and so forth. Peace and the like are the internal means for knowledge, whereas action is the external means; therefore, the meaning is that only renunciants (saṃnyāsins) are truly knowers. || 1071 ||
Its function consists solely of reflection and nothing else; therefore, for that reason...
The state of a sage is appropriate for one who has renounced, and he should always maintain silence as well.

Anticipating the objection that even for them there is no status as a "knower" because their minds are occupied with the duties of their own stage of life (*āśrama*), he says: "By reflection" (*mananena*).

For a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), having ascertained the purport of the Vedāntas—which concerns the non-duality [of the Self]—to lie precisely in that very object of purport, [he realizes it] through the scriptural... [text fragment].
[Vol.
3, Page 762] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

1897. By means of the support of reasoning, there is indeed uninterrupted contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) alone; no other action opposed to that, such as ritual purity (*śauca*) and the like, persists as a mere residual trace once it has been sublated.

The meaning is that because he has practiced [restraint], his status as a sage (muni) is appropriate. Furthermore, he states "and because of his silence" to show that his status as a sage is also appropriate due to his constant and highly disciplined engagement in speech and other activities. || 1072 ||
For sagehood consists in being firmly established in the direct realization of one's own true nature.
Because that state of being a sage (munitā) is the fruit of the birth of that knowledge, it does not exist after [the attainment of] that knowledge has arisen.

Others, however, maintain that muniship does not arise from the mere knowledge of Brahman derived from words alone, because that [knowledge] is mixed with conceptualization and remains indirect; rather, they hold that it depends upon the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) arising from the repeated practice of that [knowledge]. To address them, he says: "Pratyak" (the inner). Knowledge derived from words concerning the nature of the Self arises as having direct realization as its very fruit; the attainment of such knowledge is muniship, because it is of the nature of the result itself. Therefore, regarding the knowledge derived from words—
The meaning is that, with respect to the direct realization produced by practice subsequent to knowledge, it is not possible [to attain] the state of a sage. || 1073 ||
"Only this," [is said] because of the restriction to this one single entity alone.

Because all non-self entities have that [ignorance] as their sole cause; (1074) he explains the use of the restrictive particle *eva* in order to state that this [state of being a sage] belongs only to renunciants. He provides the reason for this restriction in the phrase "because of that ignorance" (*tadajñāna*). (1074)
And by implication, therefore, for this very person who knows the true nature of the inward Self—
The state of being a sage [is attained] through the abandonment of even those karmas caused by innate ignorance. || 1075 ||

Let it be so; what happens in the context at hand? To this he says: "And by virtue of its capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*). Only the Self (*ātman*) is the reality, while the non-self (*anātman*) is produced by ignorance regarding that [Self].

Therefore, for one who knows the true nature of reality, the abandonment of action caused by ignorance is established through the power of knowledge; thus, the meaning is that only such a person is a sage (*muni*).
Furthermore, this very self is the sole cause of all misfortune.
Desiring to know [the Self] which is obscured only by delusion, they apply themselves with reverence. || 1076 ||

In that very context, he takes up the subsequent statement as another reason, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*). The connection is as follows: desiring the attainment of the Self under discussion through means such as purification, they renounce the world (*pravrajanti*). One might raise the objection: since the Self is eternally attained, how can there be a desire for its attainment? To this, he replies with the verse beginning "All" (*sarva*) [verse 1076].
"By the knowledge of the true nature of the Self, which destroys all ignorance..."
With the lamp of right knowledge, their intellects are directed inward. || 1077 ||

He states the means for attaining that [Self]: "The Self. Knowledge is precisely the true nature of the Self; since there is no other locus for the objects of ignorance in any of its forms within that [Self], it is called the lamp of right knowledge which destroys that [ignorance]. The construction is: "those who desire to attain the Self by means of that [lamp]. He states the intended meaning of the term "renunciants" (pravrājinaḥ): "the innermost," etc. (verse 1077).
They were dispassionate toward the entire cycle of worldly existence, from its very beginning, due to the purity of their intellect.
Having seen the defects [of worldly existence], they desire to abandon all arisen evils. || 1078 ||
1 kha. gha. *śakyam* | 2 ga. *śrutiraṃ* | 238 [vol 3, page 763]
How can there be an inward orientation for those whose nature is directed toward sense objects, given the scriptural statement, "The senses are turned outward"? To this, he says:

"Those who are dispassionate. This refers to one who has attained dispassion through the purification resulting from the successful performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), and who is aided by the cognition of the defects inherent in sense objects.
He states the result: "Having arisen," etc. (1078).
Therefore, those whose nature is to go forth from home are so called because of their actions of speech, mind, and body. || 1079 ||
Because of the restrictive emphasis "this very one," it is not [the case] for those who desire the three worlds.
The meaning that there is eligibility for the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya) is thus understood. || 1080 ||

He states the action resulting from the desire of those who have attained the wish to renounce all worldly existence, beginning with the word "vāk" (speech). Since such seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) are thus [oriented], the connection is that they go forth as renunciants (*pravrajanti*) with their intellects turned inward (*pratyak-pravaṇa-buddhi*). Demonstrating the meaning of the particle "eva" (only), he states the sense of the commentary passage beginning with "etam eva lokam" (this very world). He says: "etam" (this). || 1079 || 1080 ||
Just as sons and other such things have goals that are not shared [with others], so it is in this case.
Even the renunciation of desires for sons and the like would be extraordinary and purposeful. || 1081 ||

Having described the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) for one who is dispassionate, he states—by means of an illustration—that this very mendicancy is the cause of liberation through the gateway of knowledge:
"Asādhāraṇa... (Verse 1081).
And because there is mutual contradiction between those whose natures consist of external and internal fruits.
And [the means] for sons and so forth, as well as the path of renouncing them. || 1082 ||
Anticipating the objection as to why renunciation (*pāritrājya*), when combined with the means such as sons and so forth, is not a cause of liberation, he says: "Mutually... (1082).
The path that leads to the eastern ocean does not go to the western one.
"Indeed, Vyāsa also declared that there is but one path to liberation. (1083)

He states an example for their mutual contradiction with the words "In the former [case]. Regarding the view that renunciation alone (*pārivrājya*) is the cause of liberation (*kaivalya*), he cites the consensus of the elders with the word "One. The phrase "also" (*api ca*) is used to include the *Smṛti* texts in support of the meaning of the *Śruti*. The word "also" (*api*) serves to collect such statements as: "Indeed, for all [people], renunciation alone is the supreme means to liberation. || 1083 ||
Here, "wanderers" (patrājinaḥ) are understood as [the Jainas] due to their renown, or else as others.
They are well known as Tridaṇḍins because of their extreme renown among those very [sects]. || 1084 ||

Having explained [the term] with the intent that "those who have gone forth" (*pravrājinaḥ*) refers to those whose nature is to go forth (*pravrajanashīla*), namely those desiring liberation (*mumukṣavaḥ*), he now states another meaning for that very same term: "In this context, *pravrājinaḥ*... He clarifies the reason for this by stating "on account of common usage" (*prasiddheḥ*). By the phrase "on account of the designation" (*samākhyāyāḥ*), the intended meaning is that those desiring liberation, being tridaṇḍins, adopt the mode of life of the paramahaṃsa. || 1084 ||
And Vedic utterances such as "The openings [of the senses] are directed outward" are for us.
Having censured those [views] with the words "or rather," [he concludes] that the *nyāsa* is Brahman, according to the scriptural teaching. ||1085||
Thus it is said. 2. For the purpose of [avoiding] conflict.
Therefore,
renunciation alone is the means for the arising of the knowledge of the inner Self.

Because mental, vocal, and physical actions are opposed to the knowledge of the inner Self (pratyag-jñāna), one might raise the doubt: "Since those very performers of action obtain the intended knowledge, what is the use of the state of a Paramahaṃsa? Anticipating this, the author states the scriptural evidence (*māna*) that those outward-turned performers of action do not possess such knowledge, beginning with the word *parācī*. The scriptural indication (*liṅga*) for the fact that the state of a Paramahaṃsa alone is the cause of perfect wisdom is as follows: [The text continues: "The gods, having reached the height of heaven, did not find peace; they found it only when they reached the state of a Paramahaṃsa. This indicates that the state of a Paramahaṃsa is indeed the cause of right cognition.

The text says: "Those [austerities]," meaning "renunciation" (*nyāsa*). Having stated, "Brahmā is Brahman, for Brahman is the Supreme; the Supreme is indeed Brahman," and having censured those aforementioned lesser austerities beginning with truth, it says, "Renunciation alone excels them.

Thus, because the superiority of the *paramahaṃsa* renunciation is taught, its status as an internal means (*antaraṅga*) toward the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is certain. This is the meaning. [The text continues: "Speech... [is]... [omitted].
The connection is that there is indeed the renunciation of our bodily actions; the reason for this restriction is [the word] "pratyak" (innermost). || 1085 || 1086 ||
The effects and the instruments are indeed of the nature of sound and the other [tanmātras].
Therefore, because they are contradictory, those [means] are not at all sufficient for the knowledge of the inner self.

It establishes the contradiction: "Sound, etc. The meaning is that the body and the senses, being material and thus opposed [to the realization of the Self], are not capable of producing knowledge of That; and since actions are likewise effects of those [body and senses], they too are similarly incapable. || 1087 ||
Therefore, for the sake of attaining one's own welfare and the world, this is the supreme means.
For renunciation alone is to be understood as the relinquishing of actions of mind, speech, and body. || 1088 ||

He concludes what was stated—that the renunciation of action is the cause of knowledge—with the words "The Self," etc. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that its status as a means to knowledge is well-known from the Śruti and Smṛti. || 1088 ||
Just as sons and other such things are to be acquired by those who seek the three worlds.
In this world, they are likewise certain for those who desire to attain the inner world.
The renunciation of all actions is considered the supreme means of accomplishment.
For indeed, when [the primary means] are unavailable, rituals are prescribed for him in every respect.
He clarifies that very point by means of an illustration: "pratisādhyam" (to be accomplished individually). Here, "iha" refers to the attainment of the world of the *pratīc* (the individual self).

If the renunciation of action (*karmatyāga*) were the sole means to knowledge (*jñāna*), then—fearing the objection that this would render the injunctions for ritual action useless according to the maxim of "washing away mud"—he says:

"asaṃbhave hi" (for when it is impossible). This means that since renunciation is impossible for one who is not dispassionate, [ritual action serves] as a means of purification for the purpose of generating dispassion toward everything.
Since these actions are prescribed, the meaning is that this is not a case of the "washing away of mud" maxim. 1089 || 1090 ||
If, because his mind is drawn away by passion and other afflictions, he is unable [to practice] completely, [he should strive for the next best].
Let that man perform his duties according to the prescribed rule in order to renounce them.
Day and night, one should perform actions for the sake of attaining the capacity to renounce action.
Not by the non-commencement of actions [is liberation attained], for such is the teaching of the Smṛti.
He elaborates on that very point with the words "passion and so forth. The capacity for the renunciation of actions, by way of the purification of the intellect, is dispassion;
this is Brahman. [The author] states the reason for this.
[Vol. 3, page 765]

This refers to the purpose [of the preceding discussion], namely, that the performance of ritual action belongs to the ignorant person who lacks dispassion; regarding this, he states the authoritative source: "Not so" (na). 1091.
For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means.
For that very person who has ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means. || 1093 ||

If it be argued that, according to the Lord’s view, actions themselves are the direct means to *naiṣkarmya* (the state of actionlessness), then there would be the emergence of a *vetāla* (a ghost) from within the very ritual for its pacification;
to this he replies with the verse beginning "ārurukṣoḥ. By the word "yoga," either the purification of the mind or the arising of knowledge is meant. || 1093 ||
"What is the intention of those men who, seeking the world of the Self, renounce all action along with its means?"—to this question, the following meaning is stated: (1094)
The passage beginning with "etameva" has already been explained. Now, he introduces the section beginning with "idānīm etaddha sma," preceded by a question: "What is the intention?
This refers to the means, namely, the topknot (*śikhā*), the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth. || 1094 ||
By the words "etaddha sma," renunciation (pārivrājya) is designated.
The reason is stated with effort by means of direct scriptural statement (śruti) in the form of an explanatory praise (arthavāda).

He elucidates the intended meaning that was promised as being stated [in the following]: "This" (*etad*). The construction is as follows: by means of the statement beginning with "this," which has the nature of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), the reason for wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) is stated through the *śruti* with its underlying purport (*tātparya*). || 1099 ||
This very reason is clearly stated in favor of the life of a wandering mendicant.
The word "ha" signifies traditional authority (aitihya), and the word "smā" is used for the purpose of recollection. || 1096 ||
Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), while explaining the words and demonstrating the connection between the terms *tat* and *etat*, he completes what was required:
"That very thing" (*tadetad*). He explains the three particles [beginning with *iti*] as "thus it has been said" (*aitihya*). || 1096 ||
The wise men of former times, who had transcended past time, were those who had realized the true nature of reality.
The phrase "progeny" (prajā) should be understood as an illustration for the three types of seeking (eṣaṇā). || 1097 ||

He explains the two words [of the verse] with the word "pūrve" (the former). The syntactical connection is: "they do not desire offspring. Raising the objection—namely, since only "offspring" (*prajā*) is heard [in the text], how can the commentary state that they do not desire "action and the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman" (*karma parabrahmavidyā ca*)?—he says: "Of the three... (verse 1097).
They do not desire nor do they wish for things characterized by the birth of sons and so forth.
Why are all these called "seekings" (eṣaṇā)? This is now explained. || 1098 ||

He states the meaning of "no," etc., with the words beginning "no. Having stated the literal meaning (*vācya*), he states what is intended (*vivakṣita*) with the word "son," etc. The phrase "they do not desire" is to be connected with the preceding [sentence]. He asks for the reason why they do not practice the means for attaining the three worlds, beginning with sons, as explained in the commentary. He introduces the passage beginning with "why" as the reason, stating: "It is said," etc. (1098).
Listen to this intention of those who are renouncing their desires.
The objection as to why there are even three types of seeking is now stated. || 1099 ||
He states its purport: "Eṣaṇā" (desire). The meaning is that this sentence is intended to show their intention.
He excludes the meanings of interrogation, deliberation, or censure for the word *kim*, [interpreting it instead] as "eṣaṇā. || 1099 ||
"What shall we do with offspring, we who possess such a small fruit? [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22] — thus accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1901.

For those for whom the world is eternal and imperishable, the Self is indeed established by itself as one.

The verse provides a statement that expresses an objection (*ākṣepa*). Regarding the word "with offspring" (*prajayā*): the meaning is that for us, whose ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is the immutable conscious Self alone, we do not perceive anything to be accomplished by means of offspring and so forth, which are causes for the three worlds. The reason for this objection is stated in the second half of the verse. || 1100 ||
And precisely because it is the Self, it has already been attained, being free from desire for all means of attainment.
Because it depends upon means such as the production of the object and so forth. || 1101 ||

Even the human goal known as the Self is to be accomplished by means of instruments, just like heaven and so forth; how then can there be a refutation [of that]? To this he says: "Because it is the Self. He states another reason for the Self’s independence from instruments: "Because it is a reality. Therefore, the remainder of the sense is that the reality of the Self is devoid of origination and the like, and is independent. || 1101 ||
Whatever entity possesses origination and so forth is void, like the objects of one's own dream.
But in the knowledge of the Self, because all other fruits are included therein without exception. || 1102 ||

Now, is the entity characterized by origination and so forth other than the Self or non-other? In the first case, because another entity would be admitted, there is a deviation from one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).

In the second case, it is not established that the Self is independent of means of proof. To this, he says: "And that which... If that [entity] were insubstantial (*tucchatva*), the attainment of heaven and so forth would not constitute the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). If, on the other hand, it were something other than that [Self], then even the attainment of the Self would likewise be a different thing.

Anticipating the objection that this would lead to an infinite regress, he says: "But in the case of self-knowledge. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "its status as the supreme human goal is unavoidable.
No gain greater than the attainment of the self is seen anywhere in the entire world.
Because all objects to be attained have been fully attained, and because all bonds have been cast off. || 1103 ||
In that very context, he states the reason for the absence [of other fruits]: "No," and so forth. He provides the reason why the knowledge of the Self includes all other fruits without exception:
"All," and so forth. || 1103 ||
Having thus resolved in their minds, they indeed cast off their subjects and other such concerns.
All the fruits beginning with the world of men, as well as the three types of seeking, [are attained] through diligent [practice]. 1104.

He concludes the intention of those who have renounced all seeking with the words, "Thus in the mind. The meaning is that when self-knowledge has arisen, because everything to be attained has been attained and everything to be rejected has been rejected—and since all other fruits are included within that [knowledge]—the wise, realizing that there is no gain higher than the attainment of the Self, cast aside their children and so forth. When there is one who casts aside, the casting aside is logically established.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) has the sense of "because. || 1104 ||
The fruit of desire is that which is to be produced, obtained, refined, or transformed.
In such a situation as this, what satisfaction could there be even for the wise? (1105)

He states another reason for the objection: "that which is to be produced. This means that such a thing, being subject to excellence, is characterized by birth and destruction.
"The abandonment of the six is desired through conformity with the Self and Brahman."
The means for the birth of the knowledge of Brahman is indeed the science of Brahman itself. || 1106 ||
Since it has been stated that this applies even to the wise, it is indicated that for one who is ignorant yet dispassionate, the renunciation of desires such as for sons serves as a cause for wisdom.

Now, he establishes that such renunciation is a cause for that [wisdom] by means of an illustration: "The Self," etc. Just as the knowledge of Brahman is the cause for attaining That because it conforms to the Brahman that is the innermost Self, so too the renunciation of desires, being opposed to ritual action (*karman*), conforms to the knowledge of Brahman which is characterized by freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*).

Because that [knowledge] is desired as the means for its birth, therefore renunciation becomes fruitful even for one who is ignorant [of the scriptures] provided he is dispassionate; this is the meaning.
Of him who has attained all human goals and who has awakened to the true nature of the inner self.
For a person whose darkness regarding the self has been burnt away, no desire for what is sought after is admitted.
Having described the fruit of renunciation for the ignorant, he speaks of the ease of attaining renunciation for the wise: "Attained," etc. (1107).
For one who has become the self of all beings and perceives the single identity of all, [there is no distinction].
For one who has attained all human goals, abandoned all suffering,
and reached supreme composure— tell me, what would sons and the like avail?
Having thus resolved, those free from attachment indeed renounce everything and go forth into the homeless life. || 1109 ||

This demonstrates that for the wise, there is no dependence upon worldly pursuits (*eṣaṇā*). [The verse begins with] "sarvabhūta... [which] restates the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and then restates the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*). [The verse continues with] "sarva... [which] states the fruit of seeing that [truth]. [The verse says] "āpta... [which] states that for such a person, progeny and other such things are of no consequence. [The verse says] "vadet... [which] states, according to the aforementioned method, that for those possessing knowledge, the renunciation of pursuits is effortless. [The commentary concludes with] "iti niścitya" (having thus ascertained).
Having seen the ignorant man running, seeking water from a mirage.
For one who knows that very reality does not run about like a fool. || 1110 ||
He clarifies the abandonment of their pursuit by means of an illustration: "running," etc. The word division is *aviduṣaḥ* (of the ignorant). || 1110 ||

Just so, according to scripture, for those here who possess knowledge of the true nature of the inner self—which is the object of the engagement of all means of speech, mind, and body without exception—[there is no further duty]. || 1111 ||
Toward those lustful men whose intellects are shrouded by the veil of ignorance.
Having observed with effort those who are engaged in activities aimed at goals such as the birth of a son, etc., [he perceives them].
For us, there would be no further activity, because our purpose has been accomplished.

Following the analogy, he states the point of application (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). The body and so forth are the substratum for the three types of activity; yet the Self, abiding as the inner witness (*pratyak*), is the true nature of that [substratum]. The meaning is as follows: having seen those who possess the conceit of being human—whose intellects are shrouded by ignorance, who are subject to passion and other afflictions, and who strive for the birth of sons and so forth solely under the influence of scriptural injunctions—their engagement in the birth of sons and such acts does not occur, because it is opposed to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). He says, "Because their purpose has been fulfilled" (*kṛtārthatvāt*), to show that it is not only we who possess this knowledge and its fruit; for this reason as well, there is no [such] engagement. || 1111 || 1112 ||
That activity which arises from ignorance—how could it arise from the knowledge of that [reality]?
Therefore, through the awakening to the Self, there shall be the cessation of all worldly activities. || 1113 ||

For this reason as well, there is no further activity for the wise person; thus he says: "Because of ignorance of which... He applies the general principle previously stated to the present case: "Therefore... (1113).
Since it exists eternally, the self is likewise neither to be produced nor to be attained.
The Self is not to be conditioned by ritual action, because it is not an auxiliary to action and likewise because it is devoid of qualities.
Since this [Self] is immutable due to its immobility, tell me, what indeed could karma do to it? (1115)

And because the Self is independent of action, there is no engagement for the knower who abides in that [liberated] form; thus he says with the words beginning "always" (*sadaiva*), meaning "because it is non-existent at all times. || 1114 || 1115 ||
That which has no cause and so forth by itself, and that which exists by itself—[that is what is meant].
For him there is no dependence on karma; therefore, there is no dependence on karma from anything else.
Furthermore, since an existing or non-existing entity does not depend on action, and since the Self exists, it likewise does not depend on it; this he states with the words beginning "no" (na).
To the question, "Then what depends on action? he replies: "Action" (karman). || 1116 ||
Whatever is capable of arising and so forth depends solely upon its cause.
Action that bears fruit occurs in that very [moment]; otherwise, it would be fruitless. || 1117 ||

He elaborates upon that [point] with the words "at the time of origination, etc. The meaning is that there is a dependence on karma for that which is indeterminable (anirvācya), being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent.
However, he states that karma is useless in the case of the inner self (pratīci), which is determinable and of the nature of eternal existence, with the word "tataḥ" (therefore). || 1117 ||
Therefore, having understood the Self by means of the self through the power of the stated reasons, [one should realize it].
The wise should quickly go forth from all these worldly desires. || 1118 ||
Even though the nature of the Self is of such a character, what follows for the present context of renunciation? To this he says: "It has been stated," etc.

Having known the Self as being of the nature of eternal liberation and so forth, the wise should quickly renounce worldly desires because of the force of the aforementioned reason—namely, that the Self is distinct from the fruits of the four types of ritual action; therefore, the renunciation of the ignorant is a limb of knowledge, while the renunciation of the wise [is its fruit].
The meaning is that he is established as being the fruit of that state. || 1118 ||
Indeed, the taking of a wife is an aspiration directed toward the birth of a son.
This is called the desire for sons, or else it is the desire for something other than that. (1119)
16. Of the wise. 2ka. 'ṇā'tra ki | [vol 3, page 769] 1904 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]

Having explained the passage beginning with "this" (*etad*), [the author] explains the meaning of the term *putraiṣaṇā* in the section beginning with "those" (*te ha*). Regarding the word "son" (*putra*): the connection is that the well-known taking of a wife for the purpose of procreating a son is indeed what is called *putraiṣaṇā* in this scriptural text (*śruti*). He states an alternative view—that it might be an effort toward some other end than the aforementioned desire—by saying "or else" (*yadi vā*).
This seeking of his is directed toward attaining the human world.
The desire for a son is said to be that [desire] directed toward the birth of a son here [in this world], and toward the attainment of his [the father's] own state once he has been born. || 1120 ||

He reveals another interpretation with the words "manuṣya" (human). The construction of the sentence is as follows: the desire for a son (*putra-iṣaṇā*) in this passage refers to that desire of an ignorant person which is established by scripture—that this world is to be won only through a son, directed toward the attainment of the human world caused by the birth of a son. || 1120 ||
Both divine and human wealth are the motivators of action.
The thorough knowledge of deities and so forth consists of [knowing] a god, a beast, and a human.

He states the meaning of the term "desire for wealth" (*vittaiṣaṇā*) with the words "and that which is divine" (*daivaṃ ca*). He explains its application with the words "of action" (*karmaṇaḥ*). He divides the two kinds of wealth with the words "the deity and so forth" (*devatādīti*). || 1121 ||
That knowledge which destroys the causes of saṃsāra and bestows liberation—
It should not be accepted on the basis of its fame or reputation, because that would contradict its ritual function.
Some maintain that even the knowledge of Brahman is included within "wealth" (*vitta*) because it falls under the category of "divine wealth"; to them, he replies with the verse beginning *saṃsāra*.
For wealth is that which motivates action and is employed for that purpose, whereas this [knowledge of Brahman], being its opposite, is not worthy of that term; such is the meaning.
He who possesses the capacity as the means for the performance of all ritual actions.
Just as in the case of a plow and so forth, that knowledge possesses the nature of an instrument (vittatva) with respect to actions. // 1123 //

Raising the objection that knowledge of deities and so forth, like the knowledge of Brahman, should not be designated by that term [“wealth”], he states the distinction with the words “of whom... (*yasya*).

He provides the example of a pit and so forth, such as the form of the *āhavanīya* fire-altar. Alternatively, since worldly things like pits and thorns are unfit for ritual action, they do not constitute “wealth,” whereas the knowledge under discussion does; thus there is a contrast (*vyatireka*), as indicated by the alternative reading “like cattle and so forth. (*gartāderivetyāhavanīyarūpādi dṛṣṭāntyate | yadvā gartakaṇṭakādervyavahārikasya karmānarhatvānna vittatvaṃ naivaṃ prakṛtasya jñānasyeti vyatireko gavāderiveti pāṭhāntaram*)
However, knowledge is not held to be wealth that is contrary to the cause of karma. || 1124 ||
Knowledge that desires the details of action becomes a quality of action.
For that which belongs to a particular context is declared to be its respective limb (aṅga). || 1125 ||

1/63 He restates what was said—that the knowledge of Brahman cannot be acquired through wealth or scriptural study because it is opposed to ritual action—with the words "Karma... Anticipating the objection that the opposition between the knowledge of Brahman and ritual action and its causes is unproven, since such knowledge might be an auxiliary part of the rite—just like the "looking at the clarified butter" (ājyāvekṣaṇa)—he says: "Karma..."

The reason for this is stated as "yaddhi" (for that which...). The meaning is that because there is no authoritative means of application (*viniyojaka-pramāṇa*), this is not an auxiliary part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*). || 1124 ||
By the mere attainment of its own true nature, it destroys our ignorance.
In that case, there would never be any knowledge that is either a subordinate part or the primary factor of an action.

If it be argued that even in the absence of being a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), knowledge might still have a connection with ritual action by virtue of its primary importance, he says "no," [introducing the verse] beginning with "its own nature" (*svarūpa*).
"In some cases" means either in its own nature or in its fruit. || 1126 ||
By the strength of this [knowledge], this renunciation is determined as being [free] from desires.
It is understood that the very seeking [of knowledge] is the fruit of the world of the gods. || 1127 ||

Having stated that the knowledge of Brahman cannot be considered "wealth" because it is opposed to ritual action (*karman*), he states another reason for that very point: "This [is not wealth]," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Therefore, there is no renunciation of this on account of its being wealth. Anticipating the objection that—just like the cognition of Brahman—one might abandon even the meditative worship (*upāsti*) and instead grasp some other form of knowledge through the scriptural mention of "wealth," he says: "The world of the gods," etc. [This refers to the passage] where it is said, "for whom there would be the state of being a means," and so forth.

It has been stated here that the knowledge which impels action is indeed wealth (*vitta*); however, the distinction is that in this case there is also meditation (*upāsti*). For the reason is that the aforementioned fruit is not something other than the desire for knowledge, since it would otherwise follow that the fruits of the world of the fathers (*pitṛloka*) and so forth—which result from ritual action and the like—are also distinct from those desires. This is the intended meaning. || 1127 ||
For by the very grasping of the desire for worldly existence, the inclusion of wealth is established.
For any activity directed toward the attainment of a result is precisely what constitutes the worldly desire (lokaiṣaṇā). || 1128 ||

He raises the objection that the term *lokaiṣaṇā* (desire for the worlds) is redundant with the term *vittaiṣaṇā* (desire for wealth). [The author] says: "By that very [term], the desire for wealth is included," because wealth, being a means to the worlds, is established as being contained within the desire for the worlds; this is the construction. He establishes this inclusion by saying: "As a result. Therefore, since all types of action that are means to the worlds are grasped by the term *lokaiṣaṇā* itself, [there is no need for] the word *vitta*.
Nor is there a redundancy in that regard; such is the meaning. || 1128 ||
But as for that which is performed merely because it has been enjoined, such action is fruitless.
We call that "the quest for wealth" (vittaiṣaṇā) for the sake of turning away from kinship (jāmitva).
He offers a rebuttal by demonstrating a difference in meaning: "As for that which... The term "fruitless" means being devoid of a fruit situated in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*).
By the word "wealth" (*vitta*), both the obligatory rite (*nityakarma*) and its means are to be understood in order to avoid redundancy; this is the sense.
Whatever activity is undertaken for the sake of the world through the means of speech, mind, and body;
Those people who understand the meaning of "seeking" call that the "seeking of the world. || 1130 ||

He states the meaning of the term *loka-eṣaṇā*: "Regarding *loka*... The meaning is that there is no tautology here, because what is intended is both desirable action (*kāmya-karma*) and its means. || 1130 ||
From the awakening [to the truth] regarding these cravings, which consist of the forms of action and the agent...
They know that the state which proceeds in the reverse order is "emergence" (vyutthāna). || 1131 ||

Regarding the word "having emerged" (*vyutthāya*), he states the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*): "action" (*kriyā*). || 1131 ||
Passages such as these are to be explained in this manner; however, they have already been explained previously.
Since it has not been [discussed] in the Kolabrāhmaṇa, an effort is made here to explain it. || 1132 ||
He replies to the statement beginning with "atha" by saying "ityevamādi. To one who asks about the method of explanation, he replies:
"It has been explained. || 1132 ||
Therefore, wise Brahmins who desire the world [of liberation] should go forth into the religious life.
And "they go forth" is an injunction, because it is connected with an explanatory statement (arthavāda). || 1133 ||

Although the meaning of the word itself is not directly expressed, he states the sense of the context with the words "they should go forth. The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that the world of the Self cannot be accomplished through ritual action. Nor is it the case that Brahminhood alone is the cause for wandering mendicancy by way of the desire to know; rather, he says "the wise," implying that it is the dispassion produced by discrimination [that is the cause]. Furthermore, "they should go forth" is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because it is a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*).
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And 'they go forth'. (1133)
For it is not logical that an explanatory passage (arthavāda) should depend upon another explanatory passage.
It is logical that the explanatory passage (arthavāda) forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction (vidhi) alone. || 1134 ||
Even though this [passage] beginning with "etaddha sma" is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), why should the statement regarding wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) be considered an injunction?

To this he says: "Not so," and so forth. In that context, the word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to establish the reason of its being unobserved [in common practice]. He establishes its inconsistency by saying "by an injunction.

This is because it is seen that passages such as "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*) form a single syntactical unit with injunctions such as "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi rajataṃ na deyam*); thus, an *arthavāda* [is connected] to an injunction.
The meaning is that it has been established in the section concerning explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that dependence on another [source] is not logical. || 1134 ||
Therefore, by means of the indicative mark of the explanatory passage (arthavāda), this injunction is clear.
Since an explanatory passage (arthavāda) does not derive its meaning from anything else once it has abandoned its status as a supplement to an injunction (vidhiśeṣatva). || 1135 ||

He states the result of its connection with the injunction precisely through the rule: "by the explanatory passage" (*arthavāda*). He clarifies the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*): "the injunction," etc.
Because of the mention of a common agent, the mention of separation, and [the mention of] the result.
"They go forth"—this rule follows from the connection with the explanatory passage (arthavāda). || 1136 ||

For this reason as well, he states that renunciation is intended to be enjoined: "samāna... (identical). Just as it was stated that the injunction "they go forth" (*pravrajanti*) is established through its connection with an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), so too, because of the designation of a common agent for the renunciation called *pārivrājya* together with knowledge—through the phrase "having known, having risen above" (*viditvā vyutthāya*)—the renunciation accompanied by knowledge results in the fruit of the world called the Self (*ātmaloka*), after one has distinguished oneself from the three worlds which are the fruits of sons and other such [desires].
The meaning is that renunciation is indeed intended by the Lord of the World. || 1136 ||
It is heard that its status as a single agent is established by means of consciousness.
And he distinguishes their fruit as well, with the words beginning "of those who... (verse 1137).

[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

[page 1907]. He applies the commentary beginning with "vijñānasamāna" (equal to knowledge) to the meaning already stated. Regarding the phrase "by means of knowledge" (*vijñānena*), it is indicated that because of the word "api" (also/even) and its recitation alongside the study of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*) and so forth, this is not a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). || 1137 ||
Nor is it accepted here that they go forth [into homelessness] all at once.
Having attained its own strength, it is for the purpose of being praised by the world and is dependent upon explanatory passages (arthavāda).
For one who speaks as if [the self] were the primary cause, this would not be intended as praise for the world. || 1138 ||

For this reason as well, he says that this is intended to be enjoined: "They go forth" (*pravrajan*). It is not only in the present passage that this state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) is heard; rather, it is repeated here and there: "The wanderers go forth," "Having renounced, they lead the life of a mendicant," and "Having known [this], one becomes a sage. Therefore, the meaning is that this is something to be enjoined. Now, an objection is raised: just as in the case of "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest... [the text continues].

By means of such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) which state what is already established—such as "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu"—the action enjoined by that injunction is praised through the glorification of the deity and so forth.

Similarly, by means of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), the intended praise of the "world of the Self" (*ātmaloka*) is meant to be expressed, [the sense being]: "Exalted indeed is this world of the Self, since for its sake they practice even the difficult life of a wandering mendicant. And since there is no injunction in that regard, he says: "As if it were already established" (*prāptavat*).

The phrase located in the first half [of the verse] is to be supplied here as well. Furthermore, just as the primary rites such as the *darśa* sacrifice require an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) such as "for the sake of the heavenly world," so too this renunciation (*pārivrājya*) requires an explanatory passage such as "this indeed... Therefore, he states that the notion that this [text] is merely for the purpose of praising the world is nothing but an illusion: "by the explanatory passage" (*arthavādena*). || 1138 ||
Nor is there praise by means of the state of wandering mendicancy as something to be practiced.
Nor would there be a praise of the knowledge of that [self], for it would be appropriate only for one's own world. 1139 ||

The passage beginning with "studying his own sacred texts" (*svādhyāyam adhīyāna*) does not, however, negate the existence of other stages of life (*āśrama*); rather, it commends the householder’s state for the ignorant person who lacks dispassion. If it is held that the Smṛti-śāstra is independent of the Veda-śāstra, [then...]
It follows that your Smṛtis would be equivalent to the scriptures of the Nirgranthas. || 1151 ||
