He asks: "Let such a Brahman exist; what does this have to do with the inward-facing self (*pratīc*)? To which he replies: "The inward-facing one... (*pratyaṅ*). Having restated the Brahman mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa, he describes the application of the mantra there: "By the mantra... (*matreṇa*). The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the Brahman spoken of in the Brāhmaṇa; the word "this" (*etat*) refers to the form of the Self present here. By the word "thus" (*iti*), its perceptibility is intended.
is seen. || 1179 ||
The seer directly beheld him who had been previously described.
Having reached firm conviction in that very [reality], one should utter this mantra.

Having introduced the mantra, he takes up the *pratīka* (the opening words) in order to explain it. He says, "This," and indicates its status as the subject under discussion by saying, "which was mentioned.

An "ṛṣi" is one who is said to be the seer of a mantra. To the question, "How does a mantra seen by another enter the path of our vision?", he replies, "In that very [context]. The meaning of the word "that" (*tad*) is the meaning of the mantra. || 1180 ||
Those who have attained perfection up to the level of Brahmā, [have done so] through the causes of ignorance and karma.
All these manifestations of greatness are considered to perish in an instant. (1181)

He states that which is excluded by the constant qualification: "up to Brahmā. By the genitive case in the word *asya* ("of this"), Brahmā is referred to. By the word *mahiman* ("greatness"), a specific kind of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is designated. || 1181 ||
1. He caused it to be made of clay.
1 [vol 3, page 780]
This alone is the one eternal [Self], free from desire for external means.
The greatness of the Brahmin was previously declared through such arguments as "not this," and so forth.

Now he states the summarized meaning of the first quarter-verse: "This very [Self]," etc. He states the reason for its very permanence: "External," etc. Anticipating an objection regarding the difference [of this Self] from what was stated by the expression "the greatness of the Brāhmaṇa," he qualifies it: "As stated," etc. || 1182 ||
Since this one [Self] is established by its own nature, there is no increase through meritorious deeds.
Nor can there be a reduction in sin, because that [sin] is by its very nature incurable. || 1183 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "it does not increase through action" and so forth, [introducing it] with the words "of this. || 1183 ||
For the increase and decrease of an object to be accomplished through action are observed [only] when it is perceived.
Tell me, how can you [maintain] the perfect establishment of [the world] without depending on karma? (1184)

He provides a logical argument for the meaning stated by the words of the scripture, beginning with "vṛddhi" (increase). The meaning is that increase and so forth are observed only in the case of things like heaven, which are of a nature to be produced; this [increase] is not established for the reality of the Self, which is of a non-produced nature. || 1184 ||
He is the one designated as a "brāhmaṇa" by the word [brāhmaṇa] as established through sacred revelation (śruti).
"The grasping of a Brāhmaṇa" refers here to that very reality which is the Self.
Regarding the statement "the greatness of the Brāhmaṇa," fearing that the word "Brāhmaṇa" might be taken as referring to caste (jāti), he says: "He...
Although greatness exists, it is associated with increase, decrease, and so forth, for one who possesses a body born of that ignorance, such as birth and the like. || 1186 ||
Its greatness should be understood as non-existent due to the lack of realization.
Therefore, by the mention of the "brahmin," one who has accomplished all that was to be done is here intended.

If, as stated here in the mantra by Kahola and others, the knower of Brahman who abides in the form of the unconditioned Self is designated by the word "Brāhmaṇa," then why is the greatness (*mahiman*) of that Self—which is understood to be eternal as the very nature of Brahman—not perceived eternally? To this he replies: "The greatness. Although the greatness exists, it should be understood as if non-existent due to the lack of awakening to that greatness.

Such is the connection [of the words]. The reason for this is stated as "ignorance of that" (*tadavidyā*). The meaning is that because of the connection with birth, body, and so forth—which arise from ignorance regarding the Self—the true nature and majesty of the Self appear as if they were non-existent due to such associations as growth and the like. He states the conclusion regarding the fact that the knower of Brahman, whose essential nature is the unconditioned Brahman, is denoted by the word "Brāhmaṇa": "Brāhmaṇa... [referring to] the Brāhmaṇa spoken of by Kahola.
Therefore, in this mantra, the meaning of the word "graha" is [the act of] seizing. || 1186 || 1187 ||
Since such is the greatness of a brāhmaṇa, therefore one should treat him with reverence.
One who knows the path of this greatness shall obtain the great fruit that comes from such knowledge.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tasyaiva" (of that very one) as follows: "mahimā" (magnificence). That is to say, it is of such a nature as to be devoid of increase and decrease. [End of page 781, vol.
3]. *ka. kha. reads "gataḥ kiṃ".*

The meaning is that Brahman is the locus (*pada*) of the referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*); one who desires liberation should be a knower of that. He states the purport of the passage beginning with "having known him" (*taṃ viditvā*) as follows: "Great," etc. (Verse 1188).
The intention behind this mantra is that one should become a knower of reality through this greatness;
the subsequent statement regarding the fruit is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) for this very injunction.

He analyzes exactly what has been stated: "The knower of reality," etc. The construction is as follows: the passage beginning with "having known that" is an *arthavāda* (eulogistic statement) concerning the fruit of the injunction (*vidhi*). || 1189 ||
Or rather, [it serves] for the direct awakening to the meaning of the sentence of this very [text].
Through positive and negative concomitance, one becomes discerning regarding the meaning of words. || 1190 ||

If this [instruction] regarding the caravan leader (*sārthavāda*) were a formal injunction (*vidhi*), then there would be a contradiction with the desired conclusion regarding the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*); having raised this doubt, he states another meaning for the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*). Regarding the phrase "of greatness" (*mahimnaḥ*): the word "greatness" (*mahimnaḥ*) refers to the form of the referent "Thou" (*tvam-artha*); it is the knowledge of that which is enjoined here, in the sense that "one should be a knower of that very word. For what purpose is that enjoined? To that he replies: "directly" (*sākṣāt*). He thus expresses the injunction for the knowledge of the word-meaning itself.
It leads; it follows. || 1190 ||
For it is by means of this [knowledge] that one attains the realization of the true nature of things, characterized as "not this, not this" (neti neti), and so forth.
If one knows the greatness of the Veda and its fruit, what more could there be than that? (1191)

Anticipating the objection that knowledge of the meaning of words need not be enjoined for the sake of knowing the meaning of a sentence—since the knowledge of that meaning is established from the sentence itself—he says, "Since... The meaning is that because one who does not know the meanings of the constituent words cannot possibly know the meaning of the sentence, knowledge of the word-meanings is required for that purpose. He asks about the fruit of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning: "And if [it is] the fruit... (1191).
Having understood that, he stated the result arising from the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence.
Therefore, since knowledge has such a fruit, one should strive for it with effort as if it were Mount Meru. || 1192 ||
Having become one who accomplishes tranquility and the other [virtues], one becomes a knower of the steps of greatness.
Thus, the very meaning stated in the mantra is also described by the Brāhmaṇa. || 1193 ||

He states the answer by means of the portion of the mantra beginning with "him" (*tam*). He explains the purport of the passage beginning with "therefore" (*tasmāt*) with the words "since" (*yasmāt*). "Having such a fruit" means having as its fruit the state of abiding in one's own true nature, which is unconnected to ritual action (*karma*). "One who knows thus" (*evaṃvid*) means one who, through knowledge, knows that the aforementioned fruit belongs to him; this is the meaning. The word "with effort" (*yatnataḥ*) is used to show that tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities are to be accomplished through exertion. "This is his eternal greatness"—

Fearing that this might be a mere repetition, he says, "Thus it is said in the mantra," and so forth. The intention is that the meaning expressed by both the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa attains greater firmness when further embellished by the Brāhmaṇa. || 1192 || 1193 ||
Since the non-union of dharma and adharma is the fruit for one whose intellect is turned inward.
Therefore, through such reverence, a person whose intellect is inclined toward the inner self [should act]. (1194)

Having stated the purport of the sentence, he explains the meaning of the word *tat* (that): "Dharma... and so forth. Therefore, for the sake of generating the knowledge of the inner self (*pratyag-jñāna*), this [injunction] is enjoined; that is the meaning of the word *tat*. From such knowledge, [liberation] arises. This is known as the injunction (*vidhi*). This is the function of the injunction.
[Volume 3,
Page 782] Jw 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1917.
The connection is with the word "is born" (*jāyate*). He explains the meaning of the term "one who knows thus" (*evaṃvid*) as follows: "With reverence.

The meaning is that one who possesses self-knowledge—knowing that the fruit of action is the destruction of its results—should, through faith, always have a mind inclined toward the inward Self. || 1194 ||
Having developed the desire to know the Self, one [should proceed] by means of the recitation of the Vedas and other such practices.
Dispassionate toward the worlds of the elder brother [Brahmā], he remains within the stages leading down from liberation. || 1195 ||

He states the reason for the inclination toward the inward [Self] with the words "arisen" (*utpanna*). This connects with what preceded. By the phrase "desire to know" (*bubhutsā*), he indicates that the purification of the intellect, which depends upon the recitation of the Vedas and other such practices, is the cause for the arising of that desire. He says "Veda... [etc.]. Now, one might object: even when those practices are performed, that inclination does not turn away, because all people by their very nature have a tendency toward sense-objects; for it has been said that "the senses are by nature directed toward sense-objects. To this, he replies:
"Detached," thus [it is said]. || 1195 ||
His intellect was thoroughly purified by Vedic means alone.
He has been turned away from [worldly attachment] by means of those various worldly fruits through purification.
He states the cause for dispassion: "thoroughly purified" (saṃśuddha). He describes the fruit of purification: "turned away from" (parāṅ) [verse 1196].
Because all things are of the nature of suffering, like a hand placed upon a flame. (1197)
Thus, by means of these prior practices, all impurities have been entirely destroyed.
Having abandoned all possessions, he has developed the desire to know the self.

It is appropriate to turn one's back on the fruits of saṃsāra; thus he says: "Suffering," etc. It has been stated that for one whose intellect is purified by obligatory rites (*nityakarma*) and the like, dispassion (*vairāgya*) produced by discrimination is accomplished. Now, he describes mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) as another qualification for one who is dispassionate:
"In this manner," etc. (vv. 1197–1198).
One whose intellect is not distracted by defects such as passion, darkness, and greed.
Having thus attained the state of one desiring liberation through the previously mentioned means, || 1199 ||

He describes the perfection of tranquility and other qualities for one who has renounced all action. [The verse begins with] "Rajas... Having considered the three aforementioned means, he brings about the state of desiring liberation (*mumukṣutva*). Thus, [he speaks of] the stage of the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣv-avasthā*). || 1199 ||
Now, it is being applied [to its specific purpose] by means of that which consists of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas.
For the sake of generating the knowledge of the inner self, which completely destroys all darkness, by means of the Śruti; || 1200 ||

Having described the qualified seeker as distinguished by the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), he states his connection with the injunction (*vidhi*) in the words "In this [work]... The meaning is that the aforementioned qualified seeker—who has been enjoined by the Śruti, "He who knows the meaning of the word 'That' should see the Self in the Self alone"—is directed toward the means such as the discrimination of the meaning of the word "Thou" for the sake of attaining knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*vākya*). The meaning of the word *atha* (then/therefore) is that there is no possibility of engaging in this [inquiry] apart from those aforementioned means.
The word "now" (idānīm) expresses the state of expectancy for the knowledge of the sentence-meaning. || 1200 ||
1. Reṣā | [Vol. 3, page 783] 1918 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]—
Thus, the wise one who knows the meaning of the previously mentioned mantras and understands their fruits—
One should know that tranquility and the other means are the causes [of knowledge] through positive and negative concomitance.
Having emerged from the non-self, one should behold the Self by means of the self, having entered into it.

In response to the inquiry as to how the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*) is enjoined by the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* texts toward the aforementioned means of accomplishment, he states the manner of that injunction: "Thus" (*evam*). Having become a knower of the primary meaning of the mantra beginning with "This is the eternal greatness" (*eṣa nityo mahimā*) and its fruit—by means of the sequence starting with the purification through the performance of ritual acts (*karmānuṣṭhāna*)—and acting with full deliberation, he extracts the Self from the body and other [constituents] through the methods of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

The meaning is that what is stated—namely, "having entered into That very [Self] by means of one's own full Self and having attained identity with It, one should see"—is intended to mean that this person, possessing the means such as discrimination and tranquility (*viveka-śamādi*), should know [It]. || 1201 ||
Then, by the word alone, one perceives that the Self is all, being free from attachment.
This is what is prescribed here with great effort by the Brāhmaṇa. || 1202 ||

He states the result achieved through the application of the mantra with reference to the knowledge of the meanings of the words: "From the sentence" (*vākyāt*). The meaning is that after the knowledge of the word-meanings, the qualified seeker—being free from attachment to the body and so forth—indeed experiences the Self as an undivided, single essence through such sentences as "That Thou Art" (*tattvamasi*). To the question, "In that case, what is the purpose of this injunction by means of the Brāhmaṇa? he replies: "This [is]... (*ityetad*). By the word "this" (*iti*),...

If that [tranquility] is said to be for the sake of peace (*śama*), then this is enjoined with intent (*tātparya*) by the Brāhmaṇa passage toward the cognition of the sentence-meaning as the goal; yet it is not enjoined by the mantra, nor is there a cognition of the sentence-meaning without it.
Therefore, the meaning is that the Brāhmaṇa passage exists in order to enjoin tranquility and so forth for the purpose of attaining that knowledge. || 1202 ||
Having become self-controlled, one should then become tranquil, and thereafter one should become fully withdrawn.
The order of meaning should be more powerful than the order of the text, because of this [in the case] here. || 1203 ||

Having explained two words, and desiring to explain the remaining words, he first sets aside the order of recitation and states another sequence, beginning with the word "dāntaḥ. The reason for departing from the order of recitation is indicated by the word "artha" (meaning). By the word "iha" (here), he points to the scriptural path.
The application [of the term] is observed in the world with respect to the cessation of action.
Because the denotation [of words] such as "peaceful" and so forth is entirely perceived here through direct perception. || 1204 ||
Anticipating the objection, "What is this sequence of meaning whose superior force [is asserted]?", he states the common meaning of the five words, beginning with "action" (*kriyā*).

The connection here is "in this world. "Everywhere" means throughout the entire field of linguistic usage. "By perception" means by one's own experience produced through linguistic acquisition. || 1204 ||
When the activity of the external organs has ceased, one is said to be self-controlled.
Whether it be a tamed horse, a bull, or even an elephant, their application is observed therein. || 1205 ||

Now, he explains the term *dānta* according to the sequence of its meanings. [He says] "externally" (*bahiḥ*). In that regard, he provides the usage of the elders as proof, [saying] "tamed" (*dānta*). The meaning of the locative case is the cessation of the activity of the external organs and so forth. || 1205 ||
1 ka. ga. śāntyādeḥ | [vol 3, page 784] 4 brāhmaṇa ] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1919
When the activity of the internal organ has ceased, one is said to be "peaceful."
"A monk is peaceful and an ascetic" is [known] from observing his application [to those qualities]. || 1206 ||

He explains the word "tranquil" (*śānta*) as follows: "By the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The meaning is that because the usage of the word "tranquil" is observed in reference to a person characterized by the cessation of the activity of the internal organ, upon observing its application [in that sense]. This is the point: without the cessation of the external organs' attachment to objects, the internal organ's clinging to objects does not turn away; for indeed, [without that]—

It is logical that the intellect (*dhī*), being oriented toward objects, possesses an inclination toward external instruments; thus, even when those [external senses] are not withdrawn, their cessation is possible. This is supported by the traditional teaching: "He who remains restraining the organs of action, yet remembers with the mind. Therefore, following the sequence of meaning as stated above, there is a departure from the sequence of the recited text (*pāṭhakrama*). However, if one disregards the usage of the elders regarding the words *śānta* and *dānta*, the meaning explained in the Commentary [should be adopted].
If that were the case, then the order of recitation would also be [determined by the same principle]. || 1206 ||
Surely an injunction is appropriate for what has not been previously established; however, these qualities such as self-control and the rest are already established.
If it is asked, "Whence is its attainment?", it is explained in the same manner as its attainment [was previously described]. || 1207 ||

[The author] raises an objection regarding the status of tranquility (*śama*) and the other [means] as things to be enjoined, beginning with "Now, however" (*nanu*). Anticipating the doubt that tranquility and the rest are likewise unestablished, he says: "But they are established. He asks: "Why? [and answers: "Because there is no means of establishment, they are not established without an injunction. He then states that their establishment is demonstrated by pointing out the means of establishment: "Just as... (1207).
Likewise, one should always avoid prohibited actions, those performed for the sake of desire, and all forms of restlessness.
In this world, only this much activity of men is observed. || 1208 ||

To that end, he first states the fourfold nature of actions, beginning with "the prohibited. He defines the prohibited as an act of negligence requiring expiation (*prāyaścitta*). By saying "only this much," he excludes the existence of any other type of action. || 1208 ||
Because that which is prohibited is indeed prohibited, even in the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), [there is no performance] of such an act.
How could there be even the slightest attainment of the knowledge of Vedānta for him? || 1209 ||

Now, by means of [the discussion on] rebirth, he states that tranquility and so forth are attained even without an injunction, through the destruction of what is prohibited. He says, "Of the prohibited," etc.
The phrase "in the knowledge of Vedānta" is a reference to the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa). || 1209 ||
Because one desires liberation, one is detached from those rites performed for specific desires that fall short of liberation.
Therefore, even optional ritual action (kāmyakarman) is not possible here for one who seeks liberation.

He states that even optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) are destroyed through the expression of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), and that their attainment occurs without [further] injunction. Regarding the word "liberation" (*mukti*): he gives the reason for the dispassion (*viraktatva*) toward optional rites other than liberation, such as those concerning the attainment of a thread-bangle (*sūtra*) and so forth, by saying "because of the desire for liberation" (*mumukṣutvāt*). He states the fruit of dispassion with the words "optional" (*kāmya*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the knowledge of Vedānta. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is connected with the phrase "because of dispassion."
It is connected. || 1210 ||
Because it transcends rajas and tamas, and because it is the cause of the purification of sattva.
Furthermore, there are no actions of his that are even characterized by frivolity.
1920 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]:

It shows that the cessation of rebirth occurs through natural attainment, independent of any injunction. Regarding the phrase "passion" (*rajas*): when the seeker of liberation has transcended the two qualities (*guṇas*), [the cessation follows].
He states the reason: "sattva" [and so on]. Here, the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is also touched upon in this very context. || 1211 ||
Or because of the prohibition stated as "not fickle with hands or feet."
Therefore, no action whatsoever is possible for one who desires liberation, nor is there any instability.
"One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes; one should likewise not be fickle with speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others."
He states that even in accordance with the Smṛti prohibitions, there is the destruction of fickleness even without a formal injunction: "Not [with] the hands," etc.
The word "vā" has the sense of "and. || 1212 ||
For one who is eternal, there would be misfortune from non-performance, and likewise from performance.
If that [liberation] is obtained by means of the eternal [soul], then what is the use of obligatory rites?

To state that even the destruction of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) is established independently of scriptural injunctions, [the author] declares that performing or not performing them results in harmful consequences: "Of the obligatory," etc. Here, "this" refers to the harm consisting of dwelling in a womb and so forth. (1213)
Thus, for one who performs the obligatory rites with a purified mind, [the results follow].
A desire to renounce arises in a person even toward eternal ritual acts.

To show that it is not the case that there is absolute disregard for them, he says "thus" (evam). He uses the word "thus" to demonstrate that this is by virtue of the scriptural injunction [to perform rites] "as long as life lasts.
Furthermore, the phrase "and also" (api ca) is used to provide other ritual acts as examples. || 1214 ||
If constant ritual action is not sufficient for the swift liberation from saṃsāra, [then what is?]
What purpose would there be for a person here in this world through what is done or what is left undone? || 1215 ||

He demonstrates the manner of his desire for renunciation with the verse beginning "In this cycle of existence" (saṃsāra). "Swiftly" (āśu) means instantly; "directly" (sākṣāt) is the sense. "Here" (iha) refers to liberation (mokṣa). || 1215 ||
Thus, having conceived supreme dispassion toward his daily obligatory duties, he—
He indeed effects the abandonment of [the self] by itself; through that, tranquility and the other qualities are attained.

He states the fruit of the desire to abandon [the world] with the words, "Thus, having arisen... He concludes the statement regarding the attainment of tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities through natural occurrence, without formal injunction, with the words, "They have been attained. || 1216 ||
A wise person should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not necessarily the observances (niyamas) at all times.
One who fails to perform the restraints (yamas) but devotes oneself solely to the observances (niyamas) falls into the realm of Yama.

He states that its attainment occurs not only through rebirth, but also by means of the rules prescribed in the Smṛtis, beginning with the words "the restraints" (yamān). The *yamās* are celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth, which cause the purification of the intellect and are not restricted by place, time, or circumstance. For it has been said: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamās*. The *niyamās* are specific ritual acts that cause purification and do not depend on place, time, or circumstance.
The restraints (yama) begin with devotion to the Lord (īśvara-praṇidhāna). And it has been said: "Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyama).
He shows the explanatory praise (arthavāda) for the rule already stated: "the restraints" (yamān). || 1217 ||
[Vol.
3, Page 786] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
"True; since tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities have already been attained, no injunction is required for them."
However, it is precisely those [means] that have already been obtained which are enjoined as the instruments [of attainment].
For the arising of the direct knowledge of the true nature [of the Self] from the words of the Śruti. || 1218 ||

He accepts the alternative by means of a dilemma: whether the injunction regarding the nature of tranquility (*śama*) and the other [means] is being refuted on the grounds that they are already attained, or on the grounds that they are the cause for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). He says "True" [to the first], and then he addresses the second [alternative] with the words "Of those already attained. ||1218||
Their status as means of proof regarding the subject matter as previously described does not derive from [independent] authority.
Therefore, since it has been obtained through scripture, its status as a means is enjoined. || 1219 ||

Anticipating the objection that even the status of being a means to knowledge (*jñānasādhanatva*) need not be enjoined because it has already been attained, he says: "As stated" (*yathokta*). This means: at the time of the arising of the knowledge of the true nature of the inner self (*pratyagyāthātmyajñāna*); by the *śruti*, that is, by the passage concerning tranquility and so forth (*śamādivākya*). || 1219 ||
Or it may be merely a state of cessation attained by the path already described.
But since the cessation of duty has not been previously established, it is now enjoined. || 1220 ||

For this reason as well, he states that they are to be practiced, beginning with the words "nivṛtti" (cessation). It has been stated [in the previous verse] that the path of what is prohibited is [to be followed] because of its very prohibition, and so forth.
The word "vā" (or) is intended to indicate an alternative method. Alternatively, it concludes the status of tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities as being things to be practiced.
The word "vā" here serves the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). || 1220 ||
But surely, O Tamed One, by the very renunciation of all action here, [liberation is attained].
Since it has been prohibited by the cessation of hearing, what else could possibly be enjoined? || 1221 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the fact that tranquility (*śama*) and the other [requisites] are things to be practiced, by setting aside the [objection] refuted by the scriptural passage concerning cessation (*uparata*): "But surely... (1221).
Since no action exists other than external and internal action.
For, by the rule of general application, there is no sublation of the specific exception. || 1222 ||

Anticipating the objection that "cessation of hearing" (*uparata-śruti*) is intended for the purpose of preventing unimpeded activity through tranquility (*śānti*) and self-control (*dānti*), he says: "Externally" (*bahiḥ*). Therefore, since those two [tranquility and self-control] have already been enjoined, the remainder of the sense is that "cessation of hearing" would be purposeless. He refutes this with: "No. To state the subject matter of "cessation of hearing" so that it is not redundant, he states a general principle: "In the case of a general rule" (*utsarga*), etc. [of] one prohibitive injunction, its own...

The meaning is that because there is a contradiction in the application [of the rule] to both the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and because [the general prohibition] has scope regarding violence for the sake of the person, it cannot have as its object violence for the sake of the sacrifice; otherwise, it would follow that it is dependent upon entering into another qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, there is no sublation of the exception (*apavāda*) by the general rule (*utsarga*). || 1222 ||
Since the injunction for non-violence toward living beings has not been set aside regarding the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, the vital breaths of a young man depart upward when an elder approaches. (1223)
In this regard, he states a scriptural illustration: "bhūta... and so forth. For the prohibition "one shall not harm any living beings" depends upon that which is prohibited for its definition;

Since that [eating] would be impossible without it, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*)—stated in the passage "Or it is a modification of the sacrifice, because the purificatory act is for its sake"—is that by the phrasing "he should act as this [priest] does who eats the remnant," the connection with the *yoga* (the ritual application) itself is enjoined; thus, even though the eating of the remnant is already implied by the sense through its taking on the function of the Soma, it is merely restated.
In that context, although the eating of the remnant is directly enjoined by the rule "he should give him that portion to eat," it is subordinate to the primary [act].

When there arises a doubt as to whether the portions [of the *iḍā*] should be eaten by others or by those very same persons, the following is established: since the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are already included among all those entitled to eat based on their role as performers of the ritual, the re-mention of the *iḍā* in the text—"the five, including the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), eat the *iḍā*"—serves to exclude other types of eating. Thus, by way of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), it is determined that these [priests] eat only the *iḍā*. Consequently, regarding other portions, the rule "others [eat them]" would follow. However, this is countered by the fact that the sacrificer, not being a performer of the ritual action, was not previously entitled to eat; therefore, this text serves to establish his entitlement.

By accepting the scriptural statement beginning with "the sacrificer as the fifth," and because other [types of] consumption have not been specifically enumerated, it is established as the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) that even in those cases, only those already engaged in the primary ritual act serve as the agents, and no others; thus, just as the consumption of the remnants, though directly enjoined,

Just as, by virtue of being the performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one’s agency is certain even regarding the consumption of their remnants, so too in the present case, that which is prohibited but not opposed to the primary rite must be accepted; however, that which is opposed to it must be abandoned even if it is prescribed. Alternatively, because of the scriptural statement of common agency in "having pressed [the Soma] and having offered, they consume," the consumption of the remnant—though directly enjoined by terms such as "pressing" and so forth—is not [to be performed] in contradiction to the primary rite.

They perform [actions] in accordance with the requirements of their actual purpose; for no fruit whatsoever is declared to be contingent upon the consumption of remnants (*śeṣabhakṣa*), but rather they practice it as a rite of disposal (*pratipattikarma*). Likewise, even though those who are detached and seek liberation (*mumukṣu*) perform the renunciation of all actions—which has become a rite of disposal—they do not abandon begging for alms and so forth, precisely because of their adherence to the primary factor, which is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Having stated that because it is prohibited, one must follow what is non-conflicting, and thus argued that since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are means to knowledge, the distraction that arises as a matter of course during their performance does not oppose the arising of knowledge; he now says "In this way" (*evam*), anticipating the objection that since ritual action (*karman*) also serves that same purpose, the mental distraction occurring at the time of its performance does not oppose it either, and therefore seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should not abandon it.

Just as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are enjoined as the means to that [knowledge] by restating vision (*darśana*) as the goal, action is not directly a means to that [knowledge]; for the scripture speaks of a mediation in the phrase "those who desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*), since its purpose is the purification of the mind. Therefore, for one whose intellect is purified and who seeks liberation, action must indeed be abandoned, because it lacks a fruit [in that regard]. This is the meaning. || 1241 ||

Then, being fully engaged in their tasks, they proceeded day and night.
He cites a statement from another branch [of the Veda]: "Of liberation... The meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that this statement has been cited previously more than once. || 1290 ||
Since karma is the cause of darkness, for that very reason, by those seeking liberation...
Having pierced through delusion, which is the sole refuge of all misfortune, by means of knowledge.
He states the conclusion regarding the fact that actions are the product of non-discrimination (*aviveka*): "Since... The word *tamas* refers to non-discrimination;

that is to say, by means of knowledge, which is discrimination (*viveka*). "Delusion" (*saṃmoha*) means non-discrimination. The reason why it must be abandoned is given by the words "all... The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) must be performed by those alone who desire liberation. || 1291 ||
Having renounced all actions, the man whose intellect is inclined toward the inward Self—
One should take refuge in nothing other than the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self. || 1252 ||
He shows what is to be performed immediately thereafter: "having renounced" (saṃnyasya). || 1212 ||
For by that alone, from the very beginning, one is completely liberated from saṃsāra.
Thus he has clearly stated this in the words of the Bhāllavi Brāhmaṇa. || 1253 ||

To the question, "Why should one repeat only hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, depending solely on knowledge? he replies with the words "Therefore" (*tataḥ*). He concludes the *Bhāllavi* scriptural passage with the words "This very thing" (*ity etat*). The meaning is that what is intended by the *Bhāllavi* scripture is that hearing and so forth, preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), must be performed for the purpose of attaining the knowledge that is the means to liberation. || 1253 ||
When the five cognitions stand still together with the mind,
And when the intellect no longer functions, they call that the supreme goal.

Furthermore, he cites a passage from the Kaṭhavallī regarding that very same point, beginning with "When... and so forth. The meaning is that this indicates that for renunciants seeking knowledge, the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and other means must be performed preceded by meditative concentration (samādhi); for it is the cause of the supreme human goal to remain steady by abandoning the subjection of the external senses, as well as the mind and intellect, to their objects. || 1254 ||
They consider that steady holding of the senses to be yoga.
Then one becomes vigilant, for yoga is indeed both the source and the dissolution.

For yoga is that which must be practiced by renunciants who seek liberation and desire knowledge; those who know yoga say it is the state of all the senses being motionless—thus he says, "That [state]. Furthermore, what is obtained through the practice of yoga? To this he says, "The vigilant. What is this yoga, through the practice of which there is the destruction of the negligence called *saṃsāra* by means of knowledge? To this he says: "Yoga..."
1. Kha: ‘In the case of having a single meaning’; 2. Gha: ‘...of us, the means’; 3. Ka, Kha, Gha: “This is the Sūtra”; 4. Ga: ‘shines’; 5. Gha: ‘Therefore he says’. 1 [Vol. 3, page 794]

"Indeed" (hi): Yoga is the practice of the repetition of mental impressions (*pratyayāvṛtti*) consisting of the continuous contemplation of creation and dissolution. Even those learned in the Yoga-śāstra call this aforementioned yoga "cognitive absorption" (*saṃprajñāta-samādhi*), and its meaning is that it is the cause of the result already described. || 1295 ||
The wise man should restrain speech and mind; he should restrain those two within the self of knowledge.
One should place that knowledge within the Great Self, and that [Great Self] within the Peaceful Self.

He says "one should restrain" (yacchet) [in the verse] to indicate that one should withdraw the external senses by making them dependent upon the mind. The word "vāk" (speech) is used in the nominative case in the sense of the accusative. The lengthening in "manasi" is a Vedic archaism. He speaks of the withdrawal of the mind into the intellect (*buddhi*) with the words "one should restrain that" (tadyacchet). He speaks of the withdrawal of the individual intellect (*vyaṣṭi-buddhi*) into the universal intellect (*samaṣṭi-buddhi*) with the word "knowledge" (*jñānam*). Finally, he speaks of the dissolution of the intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha into the Supreme Self, which is neither an effect nor an instrument.
He says: "That," [as in] verse 1296.
Arise, awake, and having obtained the supreme [teaching], understand it.
This Self is indeed to be attained through truth, through austerity, through perfect knowledge, and through constant celibacy.
For within the body there is indeed a pure one consisting of light, whom ascetics whose defects have been destroyed behold. || 1257 ||

He prays for the awakening of those seeking liberation from the sleep of ignorance, saying, "Arise! He states the means for that: "Awakening. To the question of how one awakens, he says: "Having attained. This means that having approached preceptors who are superior and established in Brahman, one should attain the certain realization of reality through their grace. He shows two statements from the Atharva Veda regarding this very point, beginning with "By truth..."

The word "eternal" (*nitya*) is connected with each of the terms beginning with "truth" (*satya*). The meaning is that liberation is the attainment of the Self through right knowledge acquired by the power of the means consisting of eternal truth and so forth. Anticipating the objection that, like heaven and other such goals, it might be something external, he says:

"within" (*antar*). The reason for the identity of the higher and the lower is stated as: "for [the Self] consists of light. This is because the higher Self, being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), is the inner self (*pratyak*).

If it is argued that the state of being a transmigrating being would consequently attach to him, he says "no," [answering] with the word "pure" (*śubhra*). Therein, he provides the experience of the wise as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with the word "whom.

He excludes the status of being a seer for all others with the word "ascetics" (*yatayaḥ*). He states their primary characteristic with the words "whose [impurities] have perished" (*kṣīṇa*); thus ends verse 1297.
It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by other senses, nor by austerity, nor by ritual action.
Then, with his inner being purified through the clarity of knowledge, he beholds that partless [Self] while meditating. || 1258 ||

Having stated that "they see," [the author] anticipates the objection that [the Self] must be perceptible by the eyes and other senses, and says "No," etc. By the word *deva*, the shining senses are intended. To the question "In what way do they see?", he replies with "by knowledge" (*jñāna*), etc. The meaning is that, through the performance of obligatory duties and so forth, one whose intellect is purified performs hearing and other [means of knowledge] with an excellence of discrimination, and thereby realizes the Self directly.
Likewise, there are other [texts] for each branch, for the purpose of establishing the means of knowledge.
Likewise, there are millions of other Smṛti statements that have those as their source.
They indeed exist for the sake of establishing the means for the thorough knowledge of the Self.
The sage should be without fire, without a dwelling, without shelter, and without refuge.

1930 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Adhyāya]:

Like the aforementioned statement, all other statements in all the *śākhās* that establish tranquility (*śama*) and so forth— such as "one who is tranquil should meditate" (*śānta upāsīta*)— [are likewise intended].

He says "in every recension" (*pratiśākham*) because there exist such [passages] as "O Śīta, seek to know Brahman through austerity" (*tapasā brahma vijijñāsasva*). He indicates the existence of Smṛtis in that very context with the words "having them as their source" (*tanmūlāni*); the meaning is that they are like the Śruti. Regarding the phrase "having summarized" (*piṇḍīkṛtya*) and so forth, he states their purport (*tātparya*) in relation to the previously mentioned Smṛtis, by saying "the Self" (*ātma*). He introduces those very [Smṛtis] with the words "without fire" (*anagni*) and so forth.

By this [verse], being a "five-fire" practitioner (*pañcāgnitva*) or a "three-fire" practitioner (*tretānitva*), and so forth, are prohibited. By the word *aniketa* ("homeless"), the prohibition of association with a house implies the absence of a wife. By the word *aśarma* ("without comfort"), he expresses a lack of greed for even a slight fragment of pleasure produced by contact with sense objects. By the word *aśaraṇa* ("without refuge"), he expresses the absence of a fixed place such as a monastery (*maṭha*). By the word *muni*, he expresses dedication to hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*) and other practices.
Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.
He states another passage concerning renunciation: "Abandon," etc. (1261).
From whatever one turns away, from that one is liberated.
For by turning away from everything, one does not experience even the slightest suffering.
He states the fruit of total renunciation: "Because... (verse 1262).
Whose treasury is it, from where does it come, who might possess it, or how could it exist?
One who has the mind intent on the goal should always remain thus in the stage of life dedicated to liberation (mokṣāśramī).

Anticipating the objection that if the destruction of all suffering results from the total renunciation [of everything], then there would be nothing further for the renunciant (saṃnyāsin) to do, he says:
"Who am I?"—that is, among the body and so forth, who might I be? To whom am I related? From where have I come, or how was I born?

The meaning is that a renunciant, having investigated what he will become among gods, humans, and so forth upon the fall of his current body, and being endowed with an inquiry into the final result—asking "by what manner shall I exist?"—should always be skilled in [understanding] the underlying continuity (*anvaya*) and other such factors. || 1263 ||
There is no wealth for a brahmin such as this: namely, singleness, equanimity, and truthfulness.
Virtue is steadfastness, the laying aside of the rod, uprightness, and the gradual withdrawal from ritual actions. || 1264 ||
Since both types of wealth are useful for both worlds, they should not be abandoned by one seeking liberation; anticipating the objection as to how, then, there can be a "renouncer of all," he says:
"Not such as this. (1264)
Having withdrawn the tongue from tastes, the nose from smells, and the ear from sounds;
From touch, the body [is perceived], and from the quality of form, the eye; thereafter, one perceives one's own true nature.
Fearing the objection that there can be no cessation from all activities because the nose and other senses are naturally inclined toward odors and so forth, he says:

"having turned back. By the word *tanu*, the skin is understood here. Because of the qualification "from touch," he states the result of the withdrawal of the sense organs. "Thence" [refers to the following]. (1265)
1 kha. *nivarteta* | 2 ka ga. *'śāṃcaṃ ru* | [vol 3, page 796] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Together with the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1931.
In this same way, there are thousands [of such instances] even in the Dharmas of Manu, Vasiṣṭha, and others.
There are clear statements for the purpose of establishing the meaning as it has been described.

He states that there are likewise many passages in the scriptures of Manu and others for the purpose of establishing tranquility (*śama*) and other means of knowledge, just like the words of Vyāsa. Thus he says: "In this way," as Manu said—beginning with the *Vāsistha*...
“Let him be without fire and without a fixed dwelling; let him resort to a village only for the sake of food.
Let the sage, endowed with the true state of being, be indifferent and free from accumulation.”
"A skull, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated," and so forth.
"For one who dwells constantly in the forest, whose senses are conquered, and who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses..."
For one whose mind has reached inward reflection and who is equanimous, there is indeed certain non-returning.
"There is no liberation for one who delights in the science of grammar, nor for one who delights in worldly acquisition;
there is none for one proud of food and clothing, nor for one who is fond of beautiful dwellings.
And Yājñavalkya says:
“Restraint of the senses from their objects, the avoidance of drowsiness and laziness, a thorough examination of the body, and the perception of the defects in worldly activities.”
"Freedom from passion, equanimity, purity of being, desirelessness, and tranquility—by these means, one whose being is thoroughly purified becomes fit for immortality. || 1266 ||
Because the action to be accomplished is abandoned, it is established by its very capacity.
If one abandons the means for achieving that [liberation], what is the point here of speaking of "faith" and "wealth"? (1267)

Having explained the passage beginning with "Therefore" and ending with "composed in mind," he raises an objection in order to explain the Mādhyandina recension of the scripture, "having become one whose wealth is faith" (*śraddhāvitto bhūtvā*). He asks: "Of that which is to be accomplished"? By the etymological derivation "one for whom faith itself is wealth" (*śraddhaiva vittam asya*), the abandonment of other forms of wealth is intended; and since that [abandonment] occurs precisely through the renunciation of ritual action (*karman*), there would be a redundancy (*paunaruktya*) between the scriptural mention of "faith as wealth" and other passages such as "having renounced all this. Thus...
The meaning is that this is a reading from the Māda [recension]. || 1267 ||
"Do not say so; for regarding matters within the scope of perception, whatever action remains of his—"
For this reason, there is a statement intended to establish non-attachment toward the means for achieving that [liberation]. || 1268 ||

He refutes [the objection], saying "not so. The purpose of maintaining the body is seen [in the world]; regarding that matter, whatever action such as wandering for alms is not prohibited by the previous qualifications and remains prescribed for the renunciant—[it is taught] for this reason that one should not harbor a sense of "mine" even toward the implements used for those actions, such as the alms-bowl and so forth.
It is said that one is liberated by the wealth of faith. For it has been stated:
1. *ka* is not a portion; 2. *gha* is passion and darkness; 3. *kha* is delight; 4. *kha* 6. *’dam*. [Vol. 3, page 797]

1932 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Fourth Chapter]: "He who has no attachment to a wall, nor to water, nor to a cloth, nor to the three *puṣkaras*, nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food— he indeed possesses the knowledge of liberation."
Therefore, the meaning is that the Mādhyandina recension is logically consistent because it does not involve redundancy. || 1268 ||
Faith alone is his wealth, for he has nothing else whatsoever.
"He whose wealth is faith" is said to be the renunciant of all actions. (1269)
He explains that which was stated regarding the meaning: "Faith," etc. The word *iti* is to be connected with the word *yataḥ*. || 1269 ||
The word "having become" (bhūtvā) is connected with all the words beginning with "peaceful" (śānta).
And because it is also implied by the injunction, its dependence on the injunction is accepted.

In both readings, he dispels the doubt that the word *bhūtvā* ("having become") is connected only with what is immediately adjacent and not with *śānti* (tranquility) and so forth, which are separated by other words. His point is that proximity alone is not the cause of syntactic connection; rather, factors such as semantic fitness (*yogyatva*) are also required. He then raises the objection: if there is an injunction here such as "one should be tranquil" (*śāntaḥ syāt*), then because tranquility and the rest would be the objects of independent injunctions, they could not be subordinate to knowledge (*jñāna*). Anticipating this, [the author] says:

He says "not so" because of the proximity of the injunction "one should see. [The word] "by the injunction" refers to the injunction "one should see," which is the injunction present in both cases. || 1270 ||
This is the summary of that which was previously described, beginning with "erudition" (pāṇḍitya).
And as for what was previously stated, that "he knew only himself."
Now, the injunction whose specific duty is yet to be determined is stated as follows: || 1271 ||

Anticipating the objection that since qualities such as tranquility (*śama*) have already been enjoined in the *Kahola-brāhmaṇa* and other passages, what is the purpose of enjoining them here, he says:

"From scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), etc. He states the purport of the passage beginning with "In the Self alone" (*ātmany eva*), etc., by saying: "Previously," etc. In the third chapter, at the point where it says "He knew the Self alone as this" (*tad ātmānam evāveda*), the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence was taught; regarding the means to that—namely, the knowledge of the meaning of the term "Thou" (*tvam-pada*)—the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of tranquility and the rest is [here] prescribed.

The statement beginning with "The injunction is for the Self alone" (vidhirātmanyeva) expresses that one who is endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities becomes a knower of the meaning of "Thou" (*tvamartha*), and thereby, becoming a knower of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*vākyārtha*), is liberated. The word "now" (*atha*) is used to indicate the necessity of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning as the cause of liberation. || 1271 ||
Endowed with the aforementioned means of proof through both positive and negative concomitance. || 1272 ||
Having extracted that very Self from the mass of what is not-self, right within the self itself.
The connection is with "one should see," or it may be "he sees. || 1273 ||

In order to clarify that this is not an injunction regarding the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), [the author] restates the injunction regarding the knowledge of the word-meanings (*padārtha*) and explains the passage beginning with "in the self" (*ātmani*). Regarding the term "concomitance" (*anvaya*): the construction is as follows—the qualified seeker, endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities, having extracted the Self from the aggregate of non-Self through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), should perceive that Self in the Self alone. The locative case denotes the aggregate (*saṃghāta*). The second...
By this, the pointing out of that witness is stated; "he should see" is according to the Mādhyandina recension. || 1272 || 1273 ||
Because the meaning of the injunction was previously obtained from the restatement of the Kāṇvas.
Therefore, based on such reasoning regarding the object of vision and so forth, it is designated as "seeing.
4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Āmandagiri:

[Page 1933] Anticipating the objection—"Since it is stated in the Kāṇva recension as 'he sees' (*paśyati*), which is a statement in the present tense, how can there be an injunction regarding the knowledge of the meaning of the words?"—the author says: "An injunction... (*vidhi*). Although the knowledge of the meaning of the words is established for both the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas from the passage beginning with "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), nevertheless...

The Mādhyandinas maintain that the injunction for that [knowledge] is intended because it is superior and has not been previously attained; however, for the Kāṇvas, the injunction concerns the qualification after having restated the knowledge of the meaning of the words. Since this is a statement of an existing fact (*vartamānāpadeśa*), the point is that in reality there is no difference between the two schools. || 1274 ||
Because it is dominated by both self and non-self, it is not perceived in its true form as Brahman.
Even though its own meaning is a qualifier, it has entered into the effect as a cause.
Now, [one might object]: "In this case, since [the world] arises from ignorance regarding one's own self, it must have that very ignorance as its substratum. (1276)

The injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self has as its object merely the qualifications such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, because the notion "I" is always already present even without an injunction for self-knowledge; therefore, he says: "The Self. Although the Self is perceived as "I," it is nevertheless not attained in its ultimate nature, because one possesses the conceit of the Self in the body and other [objects]; thus, the meaning is that the purification of the referent "thou" (*tvam-artha*) is what must be enjoined. How [is this possible] for the unborn, immutable mass of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*) which is independent?
It might be argued that the self is primary there; to this he replies: "The state of being a qualifier. || 1275 || 1276 ||
For [the Self is distinct] from the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect, by virtue of positive and negative concomitance.
Having drawn back the arrow from the bow, one should behold the Self within the self.

He concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore" with the words "deha" (the body). The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used because the distinction between positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and the two causes [of bondage] are well-established in the fourth chapter. 1277.
When, having distinguished the Self from everything that is not-self, one [perceives] the Self within the very Self;
When one perceives thus, the non-self does not remain as something separate. || 1278 ||

Having distinguished [the Self] from the two bodies through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and other means, it is established that the fullness of the inner self (*pratīc*) is realized because the non-Self—which was superimposed upon the Self abiding in its own glory like a snake on a rope—is completely eliminated without remainder; thus he states the conclusion: "In the Self alone... (1278).
This very Self is "not this, not this"; now, from that which was previously described:
From this statement, one perceives the Self as entirely free from all association.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "all" (sarvam) as follows: "This very [Self]... The word "then" (atha) denotes the immediate succession to the perfection of the means [of knowledge]. The meaning is that the qualified aspirant perceives the entire world as the Self, which is of one essence, through the [instruction of the] sentence. || 1279 ||
Because ignorance and its effects are sublated by the realization of the inner self.
One perceives the Self as Brahman, which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else.
1.1 He states another meaning of the sentence: "Ignorance" (avidyā). By the word "all" (sarva), Brahman is understood. He states its definition.

Regarding the term "non-excluded" (*avyāvṛtta*): the first part [of the verse] is for the purpose of establishing this. The meaning of the sentence is that the qualified seeker—one whose nature as *tvaṃ* (the "thou") has been purified and who is endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues—realizes Brahman as the inner self (*pratyak*) through the sentence. || 1280 ||
Therefore, knowledge is not unarisen, nor is ignorance unrebutted.
Because all that is knowable has been fully encompassed, nothing whatsoever remains.

He states the fruit of the knowledge of the Self’s identity with Brahman: "It is not unarisen. He provides the reason why, when the Self is known, knowledge is not unarisen: "Entirely," etc. He provides the reasoning for why even uncontradicted ignorance does not exist: "Nothing," etc.
The word "ataḥ" (therefore) refers both to the object of the knowledge of the Self and to the meaning of the locative case [in the preceding verse]. || 1281 ||
This is that very knowledge of Brahman which was previously declared in the Madhu-kāṇḍa.
The fruit of that birth, which was previously mentioned in the Śruti, is now being stated.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "evil does not reach him" (*nainaṃ pāpma*) by first restating the context: "This is that. The meaning of the restatement is this: that very Brahma-knowledge which was previously indicated in the Madhu-kāṇḍa is here elaborated upon in the Muni-kāṇḍa. || 1282 ||
Because the cause of ignorance regarding the self has been destroyed through the realization of the self as being without an agent.
Evil does not overcome this knower of Brahman in the same way that it overcomes the ignorant man. || 1283 ||
He explains the syllables of the revealed scripture beginning with "Not this" (nainam), starting with the words "By its non-agency" (akartṛtva). || 1283 ||
By the word "evil" (pāpman), dharma is also [meant], because it is a cause for the acquisition of a body.
Because that is undesirable for one who seeks liberation, it is stated here to be entirely [absent].

Because of the qualification "evil" (*pāpman*), there might arise the suspicion that only evil does not touch the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), whereas merit (*puṇya*) does touch him; therefore, he says: "Evil. For in the present passage, the word "evil" encompasses merit (*dharma*) without exception, just as it does demerit (*adharma*), since both merit and demerit are causes for the assumption of a body, and the assumption of a body is undesirable for one who seeks liberation. Therefore, merit also does not touch the knower of Brahman.
Such is the meaning. || 1284 ||
The absence of suffering does not exist for one who possesses a body; such is the view of the Śruti.
Therefore, the body too is a source of misfortune, for it is subject to destruction at all times.

This demonstrates that the assumption of a body is undesirable for one who seeks liberation. Regarding the verse beginning with "duḥkha" (suffering): the connection is that for one possessing a body—that is, for one who identifies with the body—there is never an absence of suffering; this is the view of such scriptural passages as "Indeed, for one who possesses a body... The word "api" (even) is intended to indicate that the fact that human and other bodies are sources of harm is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*). Furthermore, there is another reason why even the mere body is undesirable...
Rāmānuja says: "And because of destruction" (nāśāt); this [word] is connected with the word "always" (sarvadā), which signifies "uselessness" (anartha). || 1285 ||
Why, then, does even that tormentor not burn him who knows the Self?
Now, the reason for that is stated by the scripture as "sinful" (pāpmā). || 1286 ||

Evil, consisting of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), does not touch the knower of Brahman; and since it does not touch him, it is incapable of inflicting suffering upon him—this has been stated. Now, he introduces the passage beginning with "all" (*sarvam*) by way of a necessary inquiry, starting with "no" (*na*).
Since the capacity of evil to cause suffering is established through perception, the meaning is that for one who knows the Self, action is not a source of suffering. (1286)
Because [it is consumed] by the fire of correct knowledge regarding the true nature of the self as being without an agent.
It consumes all evil and reduces it to ashes like fire. || 1287 ||

He recites a scriptural passage regarding the matter already stated: "This very [person]... This means "through diligent practice. Intending that the order of the text is not intended to be significant here, he restates the meaning of the phrase "evil does not overcome him": "him [evil does not overcome]... He qualifies this with "by himself" (*svataḥ*) in order to avoid contradicting common experience. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "all [evil]...": "one who knows Brahman... [referring to] the knower.

Fearing that if there were a transgression of action together with its cause, then that which is to be transcended would become a real entity (vastu) like a river or similar things, he says: "Serpents, etc. || 1291 || 1292 ||
He who knows the true nature of the self is, by his very nature, free from sin and free from passion.
He would be free from action, sinless, and even free from passion through the absence of desire. || 1293 ||
And because of the destruction of all causes of doubt and of delusion, which is their opposite.
Therefore, he would be free from doubt and devoid of all uncertainty. || 1294 ||

He explains the words beginning with "free from evil" (vipāpa) by means of the passage beginning with "the self" (ātman). The word "ataḥ" has the meaning of "right knowledge" (samyagjñāna). || 1293 || 1294 ||
When, through such thorough knowledge of the self, one's ignorance has been destroyed, [then...]
Then one attains that state of Brahminhood which is without beginning, middle, or end. || 1295 ||
He states the meaning of the phrase "he becomes a Brāhmaṇa" as follows: "In this way," [verse 1299].
1 ka. kha. ... it is eternal.
[Vol. 3, page 801] 1936 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]...
One who has attained this state is called a preeminent Brāhmaṇa.
But by virtue of his future state, he may be called a Brahmin even before that [attainment]. || 1296 ||

Anticipating the objection that "the status of a Brahmin is not the fruit of knowledge, because it was already obtained previously," he says: "this" (imām). He states the reason for employing the word *tat* (that) with reference to the prior state: "future" (bhāvī). The word *ataḥ* (therefore) refers to the state of knowledge. ||1296||
The Śruti [declares] this so that the word "Brāhmaṇa" might not apply to one born [merely by birth].
Therefore, he himself explains [this] with great effort by means of the term "the world of Brahman."
He states the intention of the Śruti, which, having referred back to the Brāhmaṇa under discussion by means of the word "eṣa" (this), applies the term "brahmaloka" to him.

[The commentary says: "In the case of the genus," etc. The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied after the word "iti. The word "tam" (him) is a reference to the one denoted by the word "Brāhmaṇa. The effort [of interpretation], however, is as before. || 1297 ||
It is stated here that Brahman is neither excluded nor followed.
The world, too, being a mere perception, is defined as consisting solely of causal conditions. || 1298 ||

He explains the word *brahman* [as] "non-excluded" (*avyāvṛtta*). Here, the expression "here" (*atra*) refers to an indivisible term. He explains the word *loka* [as] "the world also" (*loko 'pi*). || 1298 ||
But because their meanings are mutually completed, it is indeed a *karmadhāraya* compound.
In this case, a compound is to be accepted, just as in the term "niṣādasthapati. (1299)

Having stated the meaning of the words according to the maxim "the analysis of the words and the statement of their meanings," he explains the compound: "anyonya" (mutual). The meaning is that because the two words *brahma* and *loka* terminate in a single referent, the *karmadhāraya* compound "Brahman itself is the world" (*brahmaiva lokaḥ*) is evident in this term. Anticipating the objection that a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), namely "the world of Brahman" (*brahmaṇo lokaḥ*), is also possible, he says: "niṣāda," etc. Just as in the case of the *niṣādas*...

The genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa) "sthapati" [meaning "the chief of Niṣādas"] is not desired because it involves conceptual complexity (kalpanāgaurava); rather, based on parsimony (lāghava), it is a determinative compound (karmadhāraya) meaning "a Niṣāda who is a chief," as established in the *Niṣādasthapati* section; the meaning here is that it is exactly the same in this case as well. || 1299 ||
The fact that [the word] is heard with a single case-ending [is established] by the postulation of another case-ending.
Since it is more concise than that, it is indeed a karmadhāraya compound. || 1300 ||
He states another reason for accepting [the compound] as a *karmadhāraya*: "It is heard" (*śrutam*). It is heard that the word *loka* ends in the nominative case;

it is therefore appropriate to accept that very same [case-ending] for the word *brahma* occurring within the compound, due to proximity and parsimony (*lāghava*). Thus, since being in the nominative case is far more parsimonious than postulating an unscriptural genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), this is not a different type of compound here; rather, it is *eṣa brahma*.
The meaning is that this has been explained in detail in the passage: "He instructed him, saying, 'The world is the Sovereign (samrāj). (1200)
O Emperor, by means of the knowledge of Brahman, you have directly attained this world of Brahman.
I have previously granted you freedom from fear, as I had promised.

This shows the intention of the Sage who addresses him as "Emperor" (*samrāj*). Regarding the phrase "the world of Brahman" (*brahmalokam*): one might object that in the *Kūrca-brāhmaṇa*, the fruit of knowledge is stated to be fearlessness, as it says, "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness," whereas here it is said, "you have attained the world of Brahman. However, [it is not a contradiction].

Fearing that there might be an alternative regarding the fruit of that [knowledge], he says "fearless" (*abhayam*) to show that this is not so, because the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) is indeed fearlessness itself.
