"And there would be an option regarding its fruit..."—anticipating this doubt, he states "fearless" to show that it is not so, since the world of Brahman is nothing but fearlessness.The final answer is: "And there would be an option regarding its fruit..."—anticipating this doubt, he states "fearless" to show that it is not so, since the world of Brahman is nothing but fearlessness.I hope it is correct.
Thus did Yājñavalkya [instruct] that king by means of the path he had described.
"This is the statement of the Śruti: 'He instructed him directly. (1302)

Thus he states the meaning of "iti ha" and so forth. "Iti avam" means "thus. He explains the meaning of the word "evaṃ" (thus) as a gloss on the word "iti," stating: "by what has been said. The directness of the instruction refers to its being the cause for the non-arising of further doubt. Furthermore, he states that this is a statement of the Śruti and not of the King: "this utterance. || 1302 ||
Then the king was instructed for the purpose of obtaining the payment for his knowledge.
He, filled with haste, addressed the Guru with the words beginning "So, I am," and so forth.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "I am [your] self" (*māṃ tvam anuśāsiṣva*): "Being instructed. The meaning of the word *atha* (now) is the immediate succession to the attainment of knowledge, which is the fruit of the instruction.
He indicates that there is no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) commensurate with the knowledge of Brahman. Regarding the phrase "endowed with haste":
the meaning of the sentence is that the king offered his kingdom and himself as the sacrificial fee to the teacher. || 1303 ||
This non-dual Brahmavidyā, together with renunciation, is hereby completed.
This [Veda], along with its constituent parts and its prescribed duties, leads men to the supreme good. || 1304 ||

He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*). By the term "consisting of non-duality" (*advayātmikā*), he expresses that its form is that of an undivided reality.

The meaning is that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) has been stated along with its ancillaries and sub-ancillaries, as well as its fruit. The prefix *nir-* should be understood as having the sense of "certainty" (*niścita*) and not as being compounded [with a following noun]. || 1304 ||
Through the awakening to Brahman, this entire human goal is completely fulfilled.
And for the sake of eliminating all misfortunes, this much alone has been proclaimed by those who have attained [the goal]. (1305)
One should apply effort toward that which, once accomplished, results in the fulfillment of one's purpose.
One cannot achieve the fulfillment of one's purpose through anything other than the knowledge of what has been taught. || 1306 ||

Even upon the completion of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), [the author] speaks out of a concern that some further task might still be required for the attainment of supreme bliss: "niḥśeṣa... (without remainder). Furthermore, fearing that another duty might be necessary for the removal of all evils, he says: "sarvānartha... (all evils...). By the phrase "etāvān" (this much), the realization of Brahman already described is understood. The excellence of the virtues taught in the scriptures—beginning with "one who is not a hater of any being"—is the locus of effort.

He states the fruit of that performance: "done" (kṛtaḥ). Fearing the objection that one might achieve the state of having accomplished all duties (*kṛtakṛtyatā*) even through other means, and thus it could not be determined that [this alone] is sufficient, he says: "no" (na). || 1305 || 1306 ||
This self that has been explained here is [defined] in accordance with its consciousness.
It is now stated that [the cause] may be unperceived for the sake of the fruit. || 1307 ||
Having summarized the subject matter already discussed, he states the purport of the following two verses: "It has been explained," etc.

The meaning is that this very inner self (pratyagātman) previously mentioned is stated in the second sentence to lead to liberation when known, whereas it is stated in the subsequent sentence to lead to the fruit of sovereignty called worldly existence (saṃsāra) when unknown. || 1307 ||
1938 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [In the fourth chapter, up to the end of the fifth: "The supreme goal of the giver is established as *rāti* (the act of giving)."
And there is here a summary of the statement "for one who stands knowing that. || 1308 ||

Fearing that since the fruit of ritual action and knowledge has already been stated in the passage, "Night is the refuge of the giver, of him who stands firm, and of him who knows that," there would be a tautology if they were mentioned here as well, [the author] states that they have different meanings: "At the end of the fifth" and so on. The meaning is that the first sentence is intended to conclude the fruit of ritual action, while the second is intended to conclude the fruit of knowledge. || 1308 ||
By this statement ending with "ātmanā," its reality is here stated to be intrinsic.
But that which arises from ignorance is said to result from the giving of food and the giving of wealth. || 1309 ||
Raising the objection as to how it is possible for the immutable Self (*kūṭastha*) to be both an eater of food and a giver of wealth, he states the purport of the first sentence by dividing it:

"By the word 'Self'... The phrase "here" (*iha*) refers to the first section (*kaṇḍikā*). The remainder of the meaning is that the nature of the Self arising from ignorance (*avidyā*) is the root cause. || 1309 ||
Because he satisfies himself by eating food without remainder, he is called "Annada" (the Eater of Food).
Since this Self is the cause, therefore everything is its effect. 1310.

Anticipating the objection—"How is the primary cause denoted by the word 'eater of food' (annāda), for by that term only the state of being an eater appears?"—the author says: "Without remainder" (niḥśeṣa). The meaning is this: the Supreme, whose nature is Prāṇa, is intended as the causal self (kāraṇātman) because He is the devourer of all effects (sarvakārya-saṃhartṛ). To the question—"How does He possess the quality of being the devourer of all effects?"—he replies with the word "Self" (ātman): [He is] the root-cause of the world...
The meaning is that its status as the destroyer of the world is well-known from such passages as "that into which they enter when they depart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7). || 1310 ||
That effect which is not present within its cause does not exist here.
That which is not conducive even to the effect is not called its cause. || 1311 ||

In the context of explaining the nature of the objects of food and so forth, having arrived at the discussion of cause and effect, the author states their mutual dependence in order to show that they are both imagined like a rope and a snake. He says, "In the cause," etc.; "useless" means "independent"; "here" refers to the sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahārabhūmi*).
Because the entities of cause and effect are mutually dependent upon one another as noble [principles].
Cause and effect are not established as existing apart from their mutual relationship.
He states the result regarding their mutual dependence: "anyonyeti" (mutually...). 1312 ||
The "vasu" is said to be the means of enjoyment; he bestows that because of his lordship.
Therefore, this unborn Self is called the "Giver of Wealth" (Vasudāna) here.
He explains the term *vasudānapada*. "Vasu" means an implement, that is to say, a means of enjoyment. "Iha" is an expression used to indicate the sentence. || 1313 ||
He who regards [others] through the two qualities of providing food and granting wealth;
That man obtains from the Lord the fruit exactly as it was seen.
1. From breath comes food; from food, the earth.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "he finds" (vindate) and so forth: "The eater of food" (annāda), etc. || 1314 ||
Thus has been described the fruit for one who perceives things as they are not.
Even those who perceive things as they truly are are thus, like those who perceive a rope and so forth. || 1315 ||

Having stated that this is the fruit of right knowledge (*samyagdhī*), he dispels the doubt of those of dull intellect with the words "in this way. What, then, is the fruit of right knowledge? He states it with the word "just as" (*yathā*). This means that liberation follows from such a vision. An illustration for the attainment of a corresponding fruit by one who possesses right knowledge is given: "just as," for instance, when one perceives a rope and so forth as it truly is, fear and the like are destroyed.
Thus, the meaning is that the fruit for one who perceives the reality of the self is the destruction of bondage. || 1315 ||
In whatever way people approach Me, in that same way do I reward them.
And thus the Lord spoke these words for the sake of understanding the meaning already stated. (1316)
Regarding the phrase "the fruit that follows from practice," he states the Blessed One’s consensus: "Those who, in whatever way... (1316).
But he who directly realizes the reality of an object as it truly is, though previously unknown—
It is said that its fruit, too, must be exactly according to the reality of the object. || 1317 ||

He introduces the immediately following statement regarding the view that liberation results from the perception of the Self with the words "yathā" (as). The word "ajñātam" (unknown) is to be understood as a separate term [in the compound].
Or rather, the meaning of the two sections is stated here in brief.
Indeed, by means of the sentence beginning with "sa vai," [the author] desires to grasp the essential meaning. (1318)

He states another meaning of the sentence with the words "of the two sections. He states the fruit of the summary conclusion with the words "of the essential meaning. The meaning is that the statement is made in brief for the sake of facilitating the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self. || 1318 ||
It was previously stated that one who possesses ignorance undergoes the cycle of transmigration consisting of birth, death, and so forth.
By the word "all" (savāḥ), he is reminded here of his association with Brahman.

Having stated the purport of the sentence, he explains the meaning of the two words *saḥ* and *vā* with the phrase "the one possessed of ignorance" (*avidyāvān*). The expression "he who was mentioned before" (*ya uktaḥ*) refers to what was previously stated regarding the Brāhmaṇa and so forth; the usage of *uktaḥ* here is like [the usage of] *imām* in the verse *semām*. The analysis of the compound is: "one whose transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛtiḥ*) consists of death, birth, and so forth. He states the purpose of this reminder with the word "Brahman" (*brahma*); that is, the connection of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman, which is their identity (*tādātmya*).

The meaning is: "in that [state] which is to be indicated by wisdom. The word "here" (*atra*) refers to the statement in the final section (*kaṇḍikā*). The intention is that, since it is logical to enjoin what is not already established by restating what is well-known, the recollection of the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*) is fruitful. || 1319 ||
He, indeed, is this very one who has been revealed by the previously stated statement.
With ignorance and its products utterly destroyed, he has attained supreme bliss. || 1320 ||

He states the meaning of the word *eṣa* (this): "That which is yours" (*sa vaḥ*). For that which is denoted by the term *tvaṃ* (you) is what is referred to as "that" (*saḥ*). In the sentence concerning Brahman and the world (*brahma-loka-vākya*), it is revealed by the word *loka* (world) as being devoid of ignorance and its products, eternally liberated; that which is its indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) is intended here as "this" (*eṣaḥ*). This is the sense. || 1320 ||
1 gha. Yo’ham ra | [Vol 3, page 805] 1940 Sureśvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtikaṃ [Caturthādhyāye-]
By the designation "the Great," its characteristics such as truth, knowledge, and so forth [are indicated].
Brahman alone is directly declared to be the qualification of the inner self (pratyagātman). || 1321 ||

He states the meaning of the word "Great" (mahān): "It is 'Great'. He states that this, which is indicated by that term, functions as a qualifier with respect to the Self: "The innermost" (pratyak). The word "directly" (sākṣāt) expresses its non-mediacy (aparokṣatva). || 1321 ||
The Self is indeed Brahman by its very nature; yet, due to ignorance, it appears as if it were not Brahman.
Therefore, that which possesses properties such as old age and so forth is qualified by Brahman itself.

Regarding the phrase "the Great Self" (*mahān ātmā*), one might raise the objection that there can be no relationship of qualifier and qualified between Brahman and the Self, because the Self is subject to old age and other such conditions, and thus it is unfit to be qualified by Brahman. Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "Brahman alone. The meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) is that the possession of attributes such as old age is produced by ignorance (*abodha*) within the inward-facing consciousness (*pratīci*). || 1322 ||
The nature of Brahman in the inner self is not apprehended by any other means of valid cognition.
In the same way, the inwardness of Brahman is awakened by speech alone.

Having stated that two word-meanings stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*), he explains the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words with the verse beginning "pramāntara... (1323). By the phrase "tadvat" (like that), it is implied that which has not been apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This means that [the Great Self] is coreferential with the word "Great Self" through speech. || 1323 ||
From the realization arising from the statement "I am Brahman," [the identity] of the inner self [is known].
Now, that nature which remains when ignorance along with its effects has been destroyed is described here.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "aja" (unborn) and "prabodhaphalam" (the fruit of awakening) as follows: "Aham" (I). The immediately preceding sentence is referred to here by the word "iha" (here).

The word "atha" (then/therefore) is used to illuminate the fact that, upon the destruction of ignorance and its effects through the knowledge derived from the [great] sentence, there remains no differentiator; thus, the non-dual, attributeless, and uniform nature of the Self is established. || 1324 ||
Just as a rope does not appear as a snake and so forth without ignorance, the Self does not arise [as a world] without ignorance.
Since it exists as the nature of the effect, the Self is therefore called "unborn" (aja).
He explains the word "unborn" (aja) as "rope. 1325.
Since birth is the root of all modifications of existence, therefore...
There would be a negation of all [entities], because of the negation of the birth of the self.
It implies the qualifiers such as "undecaying" and so forth, [expressed by] the word "all. || 1326 ||
Nevertheless, scripture prohibits those [defects], such as old age and the like, with great effort.
In order to establish the negation of the suspicion that [the self] possesses intrinsic nature. || 1327 ||
Having accepted the negation of the other modifications by virtue of the negation of birth, he provides the resolution with the words "tathāpi" (nevertheless).

The meaning is that since the negation of old age and so forth is implied rather than directly stated, there might be a suspicion that they are ultimately real; therefore, their negation is stated explicitly to dispel that doubt.
Because it is delimited by time as its own nature, this [Self] is not subject to the limitations of time.
Like the body and other such things, it undergoes decay; therefore, the Self is traditionally held to be undecaying.

He explains the term "undecaying" (*ajara*). Regarding the phrase "by time": just as the body and so forth decay because they are delimited by time, the Self does not undergo old age; for precisely because it is beyond time, the inner self (*pratyak*) is not delimited by time.
Thus, it is said that this [Self] is remembered as "undecaying" (*ajara*) by the wise. This [verse] serves to illuminate that the state of being beyond time has already been predicated of the Self.
The word "hi" [is used here]. || 1328 ||
Because every transformation consists merely of relinquishment and acquisition.
Therefore, by the negation of old age and birth, everything here is negated.

If the qualification "free from old age" (*ajarādi*) is intended to negate the inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) of old age and so forth, then the suspicion that growth (*vṛddhi*) and the rest might likewise possess such a nature remains; for there is no qualifying term to negate them. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of all" (*sarvasya*). Here, the word "here" (*atra*) refers to the Self (*ātman*).
This means that because [the Self] exists within birth and old age merely by way of their abandonment and acquisition (*hānopādāna*). Thus, the word "ataḥ" is connected with the ablative case.
Its final transformation is what is prohibited here by scripture. || 1330 ||
The cessation of the body's existence is designated by the word "death."
The negation of those [attributes] here by means of the term "immortal" refers to the eternal self. || 1331 ||

He states the indicator (*gamaka*) for the meaning already mentioned: "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). The meaning is this: in this passage, immediately after the negation of birth and old age, the final modification of the self called destruction is negated by the scriptural statement regarding immortality (*amṛta*); by that very reason, the negation of all intermediate modifications such as growth and so forth is intended. Having raised the objection, "In that case, what is the purpose of the word 'immortal' (*amara*)?", [he replies: it is for the sake of negating death in the form of the abandonment of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
He states [the following] for the purpose of negation: "The body," etc. He states the reason for that negation: "Of the eternal," etc. (1330, 1331).
Death is not observed for that which is unborn and unchanging.
Because he was declared by him to be unborn and undecaying, he is therefore remembered as the Immortal (Amaraja).

It establishes immortality by relying on [the attributes of] being unborn and so forth. Regarding the phrase "not of the unborn": the construction is that since it is unborn, it is ageless; and since it is ageless, it is therefore immortal. || 1332 ||
Death consisting of transformation has been set aside by the statement that [the self] is immortal.
Furthermore, by the statement of immortality, that destruction which is without residue is prevented.

One might object: "Since the exclusion of the final modification (death) is already established by the word *amara* (immortal), the word *amṛta* (undecaying) is redundant; nor is it appropriate for that word to exclude destruction like that of a jar, because such destruction is already ruled out by the word *ajara* (ageless). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "pariṇāma... [etc.]. By the mention of *amara*, the death consisting in the abandonment of life is excluded; and by the mention of *ajara*, the death consisting in contact with a cause is excluded. Therefore, [the word *amṛta*] serves to exclude destruction without residue (*niranvaya-nāśa*).
The meaning is "the state of death. The word *atha* is used to indicate that the term "state of immortality" (*amṛtapada*) has not already been covered [by the previous discussion]. || 1333 ||
1 ga. *niṣedhya* | 2 kha. *'jarāmara* [vol 3, page 807] 1942 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fourth Adhyāya]
Likewise, even the statement "it is indestructible" implies a twofold destruction of the self.
The scripture directly negates [the agenthood] in order to establish the immutability of the witness-consciousness.

He states that even in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, two kinds of destruction are denied of the Self by the scriptural text: "Verily, this Self, O beloved, is indestructible and of an imperishable nature. This is expressed by the words "even as 'indestructible'" (avināśītyapi). The word "likewise" (tathā) is used to indicate that this is stated by the very same scriptural passage under discussion. He states the result of that denial: "the inner [Self]" (pratyag). || 1334 ||
Due to the states of passion, action, and darkness, one is neither immortal nor truly deathless.
Therefore, fearlessness arises from that very source, for fear indeed stems from a lack of awakening to it.
This is the negation of the cause, resulting from the negation of the effect that would otherwise produce fear. || 1335 ||

He introduces the state of being "unassailable" (abharyatva), which is based on immortality and other qualities, with the words "kāma" [etc.]. He analyzes that [state] with the words "bhayaṃ hi" [etc.].
The word "hi" is used for the purpose of conforming to experience. || 1339 ||
When it is questioned how the realization of fearlessness regarding the inner self (pratyak) is accomplished:
They say "Brahman" is the true nature of the Self, for Brahman is indeed the state of fearlessness.

He introduces another qualification preceded by a desire for further clarification. [The question] "Why? arises; and with the intention of explaining how, even so, there is fearlessness, he states the meaning of the phrase "Brahman is indeed fearlessness" (abhayaṃ vai brahma). He says "But Brahman... The word "hi" (indeed) is used to conform to the well-known usage in the Śruti. || 1336 ||
"Therefore, 'I am Brahman'—this is the direct realization, by the very path already described."
By the removal of the cause of fear, he attains the fearlessness of Brahman.
The passage beginning with "abhayaṃ hi" explains [the previous statement]. The word "aham" (I) is used; the particle "iti" has the sense of referring back to that knowledge (*jñāna*).

The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is its being the cause (*nimitta*). The term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is stated in order to show that it is precisely immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) that destroys immediate delusion along with its root. It indicates the means for the arising of the knowledge of identity (*aikyajñāna*) by saying "by what was stated," namely, through the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth regarding the meanings of the words.
The meaning is: by means of a statement consisting of what has been heard, preceded by purification. || 1337 ||
The essential meaning of all the Upaniṣads has been declared here in brief.
This conceptualization of arising and so forth is for the sake of understanding this very [reality]. || 1338 ||

He concludes the meaning of the final section with the words "of all the Upaniṣads. One might ask: if the meaning of the Vedāntas is the immutable, non-dual Brahman which is the inner self (pratyag-brahma), why does the Śruti speak of creation and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "creation and so forth" (utpattyādi). || 1338 ||
The countable [numbers] beginning with one are [determined] by means of the system of symbolic lines.
The practice of an incalculable number of entities may be in whatever manner it may be. || 1339 ||
The realization of a reality that transcends the domain of all means of valid cognition and is devoid of cause and effect may occur through the path of the destruction of birth and so forth. 1340.

Number (*saṃkhyā*) is the cause for the comprehension of infinite objects by means of superimposing them upon specific lines; this is because without knowledge of number, the knowledge of the numbered object is impossible. The meaning is that, just as there occurs a manifold comprehension of various objects through the superimposition of numbers—starting from one up to the highest unit (*parārdha*)—upon specific lines, so it is with the subject of the illustration. He states the application of the analogy: "In the same way," [referring to] the world superimposed upon the Supreme.
The meaning is that [it is established] by means of the word *tīr* and so forth. || 1339 || 1340 ||
"Neither the state of being numerable nor the state of being a number is attributed to a line."
Nevertheless, for the sake of such comprehension, it is done precisely by means of that superimposition.

Fearing the objection that neither the number nor the object to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) is superimposed upon the line, he establishes an illustration: "The state of being the object to be numbered" (*saṃkhyeyatvam*).

Although the number inherent in the line and its state of being the object to be numbered are not superimposed [upon it], nevertheless, that by means of which the line makes known the object to be numbered is superimposed upon it; for neither a jar nor a number actually exists there in reality.
Therefore, the meaning is that the probans is effective only by way of superimposition. || 1341 ||
Just as they thus understand it, with all conceptual constructions utterly destroyed.
The self [is established] merely through the conceptualization of its persistence, birth, and so forth. || 1342 ||
Having restated the example, he elaborates upon the point illustrated by it, beginning with "Just as" (yathā). || 1342 ||
Or as [one might do] with lines of collyrium on a leaf, by way of superimposition.
They recognize the phonemes, such as 'a' and so forth, as distinct from the leaves and other such objects.

Likewise, by way of superimposition consisting of origination and so forth, that which is distinct from it [is perceived].
Through the destruction of the causes of birth and so forth, Brahman is understood as "not this, not this" (neti neti).
He states the example: "In the same way. Its distinctness [from the intellect] is its immutability; the cause of that is non-discrimination. (1344)

Now begins the fifth Brāhmaṇa:
That Brahman which was previously determined through the scripture of the Madhu-kāṇḍa.
This has been established through reasoning by means of the section belonging to Yājñavalkya. || 1 ||

In the preceding Brāhmaṇa, having set forth the fourfold scheme consisting of the objects of human pursuit (puruṣārtha) and their causes—both beneficial and harmful—as well as the means thereto, through both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇa; and having explained the application of the entire Veda to the path of human goals as elaborated by the Mantras themselves; and having further described Brahman, the knowledge thereof, and its fruit, according to the distinction between Brahman with and without limiting adjuncts (sopādhika and nirupādhika), there now remains nothing further to be said, and thus the subsequent Brāhmaṇa would be of no purpose. To this [the author replies]:

Anticipating this objection, he recites the verse: "Without support," etc. He uses the word "atha" (now) to state that it is logical for the reasoning (*yukti*)—which remains after the scripture (*āgama*)—to follow immediately after the scripture, because it conforms to the sequence of the primary subject matter. || 1 ||
That was previously established in the fifth [chapter] by way of informal discussion (jalpanyāya).
This has been explained more fully and correctly in the sixth chapter by means of the Vādanyāya.
He recites [the following], having divided it according to its chapters as taught by the preeminent sage who prioritizes reasoning: "One should speak," etc. (2).
Now, that which corresponds to the conclusion is stated as follows:
Having heard the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa as well as the words of those learned in logic.
He states the connection with the subsequent Brāhmaṇa: "Now" (atha). He explains what this so-called conclusion (nigamana) is: "And thus" (tathāca) ||3||
That which is a reply to a proposition whose object is already established by the statement of a reason;
That which partakes of the expression of the members of a sentence is the conclusion (nigamana) of the speech.

The author of the *Nyāyasūtras*, an expert in inference, cites the sūtra: "The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the statement of the reason (*hetu*). By the phrase "from the statement of the reason," the great sentence consisting of five members in the form of an inference is understood.

Regarding the fact that the conclusion is the final member, the division of the members is indicated by the [sūtra]: "The proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion are the members."

This should be understood from the Sūtra. What is meant is this: whether the reason (hetu) is stated through similarity (sādharmya) or dissimilarity (vaidharmya), when it is applied according to the example—as in "therefore, because it possesses the property of being produced, sound is impermanent"—the conclusion (nigamana) follows. For by that [conclusion], the proposition (pratijñā) and the other members are indeed brought into harmony as having a single purpose; likewise, in the present case as well, the matter established by scripture and reasoning is summarized by this [conclusion]. || 4 ||
The knowledge of the Self, together with renunciation, which is proclaimed in the Madhu-kāṇḍa of the scripture.
Even though rebirth is the primary concern, that very same [discipline] is determined to lead to liberation. || 5 ||

The author states another purpose for the Brāhmaṇa: "Accompanied by renunciation" (sasaṃnyāsa). The meaning is this: in the Madhu-kāṇḍa, within the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, the knowledge of the Self—accompanied by renunciation—which was declared on the strength of scripture as the means to liberation, is now to be understood through reasoning (*nyāya*) as the cause of liberation even in the Munikāṇḍa, which primarily emphasizes reasoning; it is for this reason that the present Brāhmaṇa has been commenced. || 5 ||
Just as the scriptures state that self-knowledge, together with renunciation, leads to liberation.
And the conclusion is that it should also be understood as such through reasoning. || 6 ||
Having raised the objection that the aforementioned knowledge is already established through reasoning in the inquiry of Kahola and other passages, so what is the purpose of this Brāhmaṇa?

This Brāhmaṇa passage is intended for the purpose of summarizing the matter established by scripture and reasoning; nor is the conclusion (*nigamana*) useless, as it has been said: "When the relationship of probandum and probans between two properties residing in the example is established, the conclusion serves to negate the opposite of the probandum. Therefore, it is a summary.
The meaning is that it possesses a purpose. || 6 ||
For the meanings of the words have already been explained in the fourth chapter itself.

The birth of the Self as sound alone has been explained in the fourth [chapter].
In this context, it is also stated that [the fruit] arises from the complete withdrawal of all [actions], such as sacrifice and the like. || 8 ||

One might suspect that if the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) is not to be stated because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) has already been expressed, then the Brāhmaṇa would simply be concluded; therefore, he states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "is desired" (*iṣṭam*). Regarding the phrase "of the word" (*śabdasya*): even though [the performance of] sacrifice and so forth is already implied by the sense, birth is explicitly mentioned here because a comprehensive summary of everything is intended in this context. || 8 ||
This word, though divided in many ways, is indeed born from the Supreme Self alone.
Ritual acts such as sacrifice and giving have form and are preceded by the world.

He states the division [of the Vedas] based on such scriptural passages as "That which is the Ṛgveda," etc.: "This sound. This sound is divided in many ways through the distinction between mantra and brāhmaṇa;

that this is merely a name, and that it is born from the Supreme Self alone, is concluded by the passage beginning with "The Ṛgveda" and ending before the word "iṣṭam. By the passage beginning with "iṣṭam" and preceding "And this world," it is shown that rites such as sacrifice are born from the Supreme Self.

The conclusion is made with "this," and having begun with "and this," it is restricted by the subsequent [text] as being of such a form; this is the meaning of the division of the scripture concerning creation. || 9 ||
All this has emerged with effort from that very source.
Because it is non-different from that, reality is declared by them to be directly perceived. || 10 ||

How can the threefold world arise from the Supreme, given that He lacks effort and other such faculties? Otherwise, the Veda produced from Him would be included within the category of "named" things and would thus be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). To this he says: "Everything. The meaning is that even in the absence of effort and so forth on the part of the Supreme, a creation consisting of *māyā* is not contradictory, according to the principle: "Because all properties are possible [in *māyā*]. He states the conclusion: "ananyā" (not other). The meaning of the word is the non-existence of the effect apart from the cause; by that [cause], which is to say, by the Supreme Cause. The remainder [of the sense] is that this is the reality of every effect. || 10 ||
It is as solid within and without as a single block of rock salt.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Just as a lump of salt" and so forth: "Within," etc. || 11 ||

He states the meaning of the word "wandering" (*vijahāra*) with the words "it being said thus. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śāstraprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Sureśvaravārttika*, composed by the venerable Ānandajñāna, disciple of the venerable Śuddhānanda, the holy wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya*). 4.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 10,408.
[Vol. 3, page 814] Now begins the fifth chapter.
The section belonging to Yājñavalkya, which is established in the realization of the oneness of the Self, is completed.
Now, the section on the "Stumps" (Khilakāṇḍa) is described here according to its true nature.
In the preceding chapter, the knowledge of Brahman as the Self—along with its subject matter, its fruit, and its ancillaries and sub-ancillaries—was explained according to the method of debate.
Now, having recapitulated what has been discussed, the author states the connection [between chapters] and introduces the next section, saying: "It is completed. || 1 ||
That which was not previously conceived in the sections on karma and consciousness.
To this it is replied: because of its being the cause for the state of all the *khila* sections. (2)

[Objection: Is it not the case that what was not stated previously and remains to be stated is called "supplement" (*khila*), and thus it is improper to begin this section (*kāṇḍa*) with that as its subject matter, since all matters have already been stated in the two preceding sections and there is nothing remaining? To this, he says: "That which is possible. The meaning is that because a specific ritual action remains to be taught, and since that constitutes a supplement, the section is begun with that as its subject matter. Of that which remains—
He states the reason why that which was expected must be explained here: "In the *khila*," etc. (2).
Brahman, from which all darkness has been cast out by its splendor, has been thus described.
That which was taught by the four preceding chapters for the sake of attaining the perfection of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
He clarifies the connection already stated with the words "apāsta" (cast aside). He states the fruit of that statement with the words "yaddhī" (for that which...). || 3 ||
Of that very [Self], which is conditioned by limiting adjuncts and follows after worldly transaction.
Furthermore, those modes of worship which have not yet been mentioned shall now be described.

Having divided the section beginning with "It is finished" (samāptam), he divides the Khilakāṇḍa [as follows]: "Of that which possesses adjuncts" (sopādhikasya). The connection is: "Therefore, the remaining [sections] are to be explained hereafter. || 4 ||
They are for the sake of supreme worldly prosperity and lead to gradual liberation.
And that they should be expressed without contradicting ritual actions—this is the supreme Vedic revelation.

He divides them into three kinds: "excellent," etc. The construction is as follows: since there are three types of meditations—those having prosperity as their fruit, those having gradual liberation as their fruit, and those for the purpose of the success of ritual action—it is with reference to these that the subsequent Śruti is stated. || 1 ||
Likewise, [he taught] "so be it," self-control, generosity, compassion, and so forth.
An effort is made here to explain those things which constitute the constituent parts of all forms of worship.

He states another point to be expressed [by the word "tathā"]: "In the same way," meaning as in the case of meditation (*upāsti*). The connection with the action is with the verb "should learn" (*śikṣet*), which is to be mentioned later. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the movement (*gati*) and the fruit (*phala*) are included. The reason for their being expressible is stated: "All... (verse 6).
Relying on the pretext of the relationship between cause and effect, that [scripture] is supreme.
This has been explained with effort previously for the sake of establishing self-knowledge.

Having stated the commencement of the section and having restated the subject matter of the complete sentence, he declares its purport: "The effect... etc. He states the fruit of the exposition of Brahman, which is based upon the illusory relationship between cause and effect: "The Self... etc. (7)
Because that entity consisting of cause and effect has already fulfilled its purpose.
This statement, beginning with "it is full" and so forth, would be for the purpose of negation.

He states that the complete sentence is for the purpose of negating [the notion of] effects and so forth—which are imagined for the sake of the Self-knowledge of Truth—since they have already achieved their purpose and are therefore no longer required; thus he says: "Because its purpose has been fulfilled" (caritārthatvataḥ). || 8 ||
All this is not excluded, for it is known through external cognition.
It is not thus continuous, nor is it established solely in non-existence.

Now, one might object: "If it is argued that effects and the like are denied in Brahman here [in this context], just as a denied pot exists elsewhere, then Brahman would lack fullness; and even if it were held to be nothing but Brahman, that same defect would remain, because that which is non-different from a limited thing cannot be full. Furthermore, if that [effect] were unreal (tuccha), there would be a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge. Anticipating this, he first dispels the defect arising from its existence elsewhere, beginning with the words "No" (na). Indeed, this...

The meaning is that apart from Brahman, difference (*bheda*) cannot be defined; nor can it be established as something other than that [Brahman], whether by itself or through another, because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*) and lacks connection with consciousness (*cit*). He states the defect resulting from non-difference (*abheda*): "parāk" (the external). For this [world] is not non-different from the inner self (*pratyak*), since it appears as something external (*parāktvena*). Furthermore, he says "no," meaning that because a distinction between the insentient and the sentient is impossible, that [world] is not non-different from Brahman.
The meaning is that just as this [entity] is not excluded, so too it does not persist either. He refutes the fault based on its being a mere void (tucchatva) with the words "Nor...
(nāpi). The meaning is: because there is immediate cognition (aparokṣapratīti) and because purposeful action (arthakriyā) is observed. || 9 ||
It is said that self-cognition is neither excluded nor followed [by others].
Because this [universe] is full, identity with That is directly described by means of it. || 10 ||
He states the conclusion regarding the difficulty of defining the world through the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "avyāvṛtta" (unexcluded), etc.

Since this world is non-dual Brahman itself, self-luminous, by virtue of the abandonment of positive concomitance and so forth, therefore the identity that is clearly expressed by the statement beginning with "of the Full One" (*pūrṇasya*) is logical; such is the meaning. || 10 ||
It is established solely in the reality that consists merely of the unknown and the falsely known.
Because it is right knowledge, that object of knowledge is therefore called "complete. || 11 ||

Now, [an objection is raised]: "Is the inner Brahman known or not? If it is not known, then there is no certainty regarding its fullness; if it is known, then because of the separate existence of the knowledge, there is no fullness.
To this, he says: "Unknown," etc. Because it is the substratum of all conceptual constructions, that very nature of Brahman is perfectly...

The meaning is as follows: since the object of that knowledge—which consists of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) arising from the sentence—is Brahman itself, because it is included within its very nature (*kārya*), it is therefore logical that this [knowledge] is complete (*pūrṇatā*). || 11 ||
"That wherein [the universal] follows along like 'cowness' (gotva) and [the particular] is excluded like a broken horn (khaṇḍa)."
That which is free from pride and possesses bliss is called "Full" (Pūrṇa). || 12 ||

Having stated that the purport of the sentence "Pūrṇamadaḥ" is to make known the non-dual inner Brahman, he explains the word "pūrṇa" while commenting on the syllables:
"Like the nature of a cow," etc. (12).
That which is entirely beyond perception is the cause of every effect.
One should know that its true essence consists solely of the Fullness (pūrṇa), which is to be inferred from its effects.
He explains the word *adaḥ* (that). He states "ada" [as the subject] and provides the reason for its absolute transcendence (*ātyantikaparokṣatva*) by saying "sarva-".
Having restated the cause, he states the meaning of the sentence as follows: that which is the mere reality (*vastumātratva*) is the predicate (*vidheya*). Thus ends [the commentary on verse] 13.
This is whatever exists that possesses birth, characterized by name, form, and action.
That which is fully determined by perception and other means of knowledge is also, like the former, [to be understood as such]. || 14 ||

Having stated both the literal meaning (*vācya*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of the word *tat* (That) by means of the two phrases "Full is That" (*pūrṇam adaḥ*), he states the meaning of "Full is this" (*pūrṇam idam*) with the words beginning with "this.

He states the cause for the application of the word "this" (*idam*) there with the words beginning with "perception, etc. Just as the state of being the mere reality (*vastumātratvam*) was enjoined after restating the cause, so too, after restating the effect, its state of being that alone (*tanmātratvam*) is to be enjoined; thus he says, "as before."

By these two words, the denoted (vācya) and the indicated (lakṣya) meanings of the word "thou" (tvaṃpada) are expressed; thus, through the juxtaposition of the four words, the identity of the referents of "that" (tat) and "thou" (tvam) is intended. || 14 ||
The activity between cause and effect is understood as "from the full, the full."
This state of affairs regarding the object exists even prior to its connection with cognition.
[Verse 15.1] He states the intended meaning of the statement "of the full sun" as follows: "the production of the effect," which is of such a nature.

The meaning is that the function [of the mantra] is stated by the words "the full sun" (*pūrṇāditya*) and so forth. Here, the literal (vācya) meanings of the two words *tat* and *tvam* have been explained in detail. Now, one might object: In the passage beginning with "the full," the reality (*tattva*) is described as being devoid of cause and effect; yet, although it possesses such a nature only after the arising of knowledge, prior to that it must indeed consist of cause and effect, otherwise there would be a contradiction with the statement "the full sun" and so forth. To this, he says: "the actual state of things" (*vastuvṛtta*). Or rather, the aforementioned cause and effect—

Having raised the doubt that this negation might be a real entity (*vastu*), it is said: "the actual state of things" (*vastuvṛtta*). Since ignorance is possible prior to knowledge, there exists therein the functioning of a real entity consisting of effects and so forth;
nevertheless, the meaning is that this does not exist in reality. || 15 ||
Now follows the subsequent statement for the purpose of refuting the obsession with cause and effect.
Taking the fullness from the full, only the full remains. || 16 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "of the Full" (pūrṇasya) with the word "Now" (atha). The meaning is that this sentence is intended to state the fruit of knowing that [Fullness] by rejecting the relationship of cause and effect described in the verse beginning with "from the Full" (pūrṇāt), and by taking up the remaining reality. || 16 ||
That which was proclaimed in the Madhu-kāṇḍa, beginning with "This, indeed, is Brahman," and so forth;
That very [state] is summarized here by the passage beginning with "That indeed is full" (tadeva pūrṇam). || 17 ||

[Objection: "The knowledge of oneness as the fruit has already been stated in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*; why is it stated here? [Response: You say this because grinding what is already ground is useless. To this we reply: 'Brahman' refers to that [section], while 'here' (*iha*) is a reference to the *Khilakāṇḍa*. (17)
1952 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopani�ṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Fifth Adhyāya]: Having dissolved all effects, it remains as pure Being (sat) and pure Darkness (tamas).
This [reality], which is radiant, whose own nature is consciousness, and which is established as one, is here called "the full. || 18 ||

Anticipating the objection as to how the phrase "by the word *tāta* (dear one)" constitutes a single syntactical unit with the full sentence, he states that the two words beginning with "full" (*pūrṇam*) have the same meaning through the word "Brahman. [He says] "and merged" (*apīta*). He excludes the support for liberation [as the referent]. [He says] "mere darkness" (*tamomātra*). [He says] "shining" (*bhāsvat*).

The state of being a witness (*sākṣitva*) is said to mean independence from others, which is for one's own sake. The reason for this is given as "situated in the One Consciousness" (*cidekastham*). The meaning is that the Consciousness which is the witness of ignorance—that which is denoted by the word *tat* (That) and designated as *Brahman* in the third chapter—is here described by the statement "This [world] is full" (*pūrṇam adaḥ*). || 18 ||
And whatever action was performed in the darkness, which has come before witnesses as testimony;
One should know that this [world] is likewise full, yet it is perceptible and subject to appearance and disappearance.

By the word "this" (idam), he states the identity of meaning between the two phrases "full" (pūrṇam) and "this" (idam). Regarding the phrase "and associated with darkness," the qualifiers such as "of the witness" (sākṣiṇaḥ) are intended to establish that the intellect and so forth are effects. The meaning is this: the consciousness that is the witness of the intellect and so forth—which was previously denoted by the word "this"—is here described as "this full [Brahman]," and thus is the referent of the term "thou" (tvam). || 19 ||
Thus, between the Lord (Īśa) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), who abide as darkness and its offspring respectively.
The identity of the self is declared through such means as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) from the [Vedic] sentence. || 20 ||

By the passage beginning with "then [he realized] himself" (*tadātmānam*), he demonstrates the same meaning as that beginning with "of the full" (*pūrṇasya*). Regarding the word "Lord" (*īśa*): the illusory relationship of cause and effect between the referents of "That" (*tat*) and "Thou" (*tvam*) is stated by the passage beginning with "the full" (*pūrṇāt*). The knowledge of their identity arises from the sentence—just as in sentences such as "That thou art"—by means of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);

and that has liberation as its fruit. Therefore, what was previously stated in the passage "all that became That" (*tatsarvamabhavat*) is here [referred to] by the passage beginning with "of the full."
The meaning is that it was taken by day. The word "evam" (thus) is for the purpose of illustrating the aforementioned example. || 20 ||
The reality, divided by the distinction between the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara), is [actually] undivided due to ignorance (avidyā).
When duality is destroyed through awakening and darkness is dispelled, the Self remains as "not this, not this. || 21 ||

Anticipating the objection—“How can there be a cognition of identity between those two when it contradicts the cognition of difference?”—he says: “The Knower of the Field,” and so forth. Although in reality the entity is non-different, as is well-known from Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning, it nevertheless appears divided through ignorance (avidyā) into the distinctions of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and the world. Therefore, the meaning is that when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge (vidyā), the single, undifferentiated nature of the Self alone is established. || 21 ||
Neither difference, nor conjunction, nor even non-existence is perceived.
When that ignorance, which is the root [of bondage], is destroyed by means of the authority of the aforementioned scriptures, || 22 ||

Anticipating the objection that the meaning of a sentence must be established as either the non-distinct reality of the Self (ātmatattva) remaining alone, or as a relation (saṃsarga), or as a difference (bheda), or as the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), he says "No," and so forth. The reason for this is stated: "Because it has that as its root" (tanmūla). || 22 ||
Without taking up the knowledge of the garland, there is an association with that which arises from it, namely the garland itself.
Just as that [non-existence] is not at all conceivable, so too should it be observed here in the Self. || 23 ||
Even when the ignorance rooted in difference and so forth is destroyed by the knowledge arising from the Vedic statement, why would that association with the Self not remain innate?

Anticipating the objection that [this might] be so, he says: "The garland," etc. Let it be observed that the association with distinctions and the like arising from ignorance is caused solely by ignorance.
The remainder. || 23 ||
Through the understanding of the reasoning concerning the unprecedented [nature of reality], there is the destruction of both cause and effect.
Relying upon self-realization, one's own true purpose remains as the Self alone. || 24 ||
Anticipating the objection—namely, how there can be such uniformity (ekarasya) in the Self when, due to ignorance, there exists a relationship with distinctions and the like—he says: "kārya...
(verse 24).
In whatever manner its form in duality is understood by oneself alone.
At that very moment, for one whose blindness has been destroyed, everything other than that [knowledge] is eliminated without remainder. || 25 ||

If it is argued that when ignorance along with its effects is destroyed, the Self remains only in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then it must have been different before—that is, possessed of attributes (*saviśeṣa*)—and thus one might suspect it was not truly eternal. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In whatever manner" (*yādṛk*). Whatever form, characterized by being the witness (*sākṣitva*), was experienced as the very nature of this Self during the state of ignorance regarding the body and so forth, that same form is the nature of the Self once ignorance is destroyed upon the attainment of knowledge. Since nothing else remains once that ignorance is destroyed, [the Self is indeed eternal].
The meaning is that one should be joined in a state of non-duality. || 25 ||
And likewise, the mantra "yadeveha" proclaimed loudly to us.
And the Śruti text, "It is indeed other," prohibits that which is different from the effect.

In this regard, he cites scripture as authority: "Whatever [is here]... The meaning includes the supplementary portion of the text: "That which is there, that is here; and what is here, that is there. The word "thus" expresses their identity. Regarding the statement that reality is neither effect nor cause, he also cites scripture: "Other than... (26)
The status of being an object of cognition for the view "this is the self" is distinct from the comprehension of its own referent.
"I previously declared that nothing else is capable of bearing [this]. || 27 ||

Fearing that the scriptural statement negating [the existence of] that [non-self] would contradict other scriptures—given that it is accepted that everything becomes known when the Self is known, because through the knowledge of the Self everything becomes an object of knowledge—he says: "The Self... First of all, that vision of the Self does not take the non-Self as its object, for that would contradict its nature as a vision of the Self; nor is the non-Self its object, because that would contradict its true nature. As for the scriptural statement that through the knowledge of the Self there is the knowledge of everything, it refers to [everything] other than that...
The meaning is that, because everything is non-existent, the negation of both the effect and its opposite is established. || 27 ||
Thus, even when the object has remained at the magnitude as previously described, [the following occurs].
Otherwise, some have explained this statement with a lack of proficiency. (28)

The sentence regarding the Full (pūrṇavākya), which refers to the indivisible, non-dual, inner Brahman, has now been explained. Now, he introduces the interpretation of Bhartṛprapañca with the words "Thus" (evam). The means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is the sentence regarding the Full. || 28 ||
Together with the concluding statement of the sixth chapter, beginning with the word "Full" (pūrṇam).
For, desiring to speak, he thus carefully composed this connection.
Anticipating the objection as to how there could be another interpretation, he restates the connection [of the text] as stated by others for that purpose: "The Full," etc.

Desiring to state the connection of the sentence beginning with "pūrṇamadaḥ" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 5.1.1) with the sentence beginning with "yatra hi... (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.23), they explain its meaning in the manner that will be described.
The meaning is that they reflected and then fashioned [it]. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is intended to introduce the opening words of the passage at the end of the sixth chapter.
It is said that Brahman, whose nature consists of both duality and non-duality, was described to Maitreyī.
For it is by the statement "where there is duality" and with the emphasis on "but where [one sees] this," [that this is established]. (30)

He shows the constructed meaning of the sentence with the words "dvaita" (duality). The particle "kila" indicates a lack of agreement. If it is argued that there is no statement in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa regarding Brahman as both different and non-different, he replies with the words "yatra hi" (where indeed). Having stated that Brahman consists of duality in the passage "yatra hi dvaitam," it is then stated that it consists of non-duality in the passage "yatra tv asya. Thus, by these two statements, the establishment of Brahman as both different and non-different is achieved.
This is the meaning. || 30 ||
If non-duality is the supreme Brahman, then it must exist there from the perspective of ultimate reality.
The imagined non-duality is like the perception of water in saline soil.

Those wishing to state the relationship [between the two views] raise an objection in order to explain what that relationship is, assuming that the object has been conceptualized in this manner. He introduces the objection with the word "yadi" (if). The phrase "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa. It was stated that if non-duality (*advaita*) or duality (*dvaita*) were real, then the falsity of duality would necessarily follow; in that regard, he provides an example containing the underlying reason: "toyeti" (like water, etc.). On a mirage...
The meaning is that the cognition of non-duality is an error, like the cognition of water in a mirage. || 31 ||
Because the various categories of differentiation are false, there is no possibility of creation, maintenance, or dissolution.
But the subsequent description of creation, maintenance, and dissolution would be entirely false.

Anticipating the objection that its being imagined is indeed accepted, he states the fault that the scriptural passages concerning creation and so forth would consequently lack authority due to having no real object: "Because it is false" (mṛṣātvāt). || 32 ||
Furthermore, hearing and practice would both be rendered useless in such a non-dual [reality].
Now, if it is argued that duality exists by its very own nature, [then the following applies]. || 33 ||

In that very context, he states another defect: "Hearing," etc. The meaning is that if the non-dual reality were already established, then hearing accompanied by reflection and so forth, as well as the injunction for its fulfillment, would be fruitless—since no excellence can be imparted to a self that is incapable of receiving it—and thus the Upaniṣads would lack authority. He raises the second alternative with: "Now," etc. (33).
The subsequent description of the creation and other processes should likewise pertain only to those things that truly exist.
Nevertheless, there would be a contradiction, as the perception of non-duality would be false. || 34 ||

He states the consequence of the reality of duality in its own right: "The subsequent explanation" (*anvākhyānam*). Having provisionally accepted the authority of the scriptural texts concerning creation and so forth, he refutes it with: "Even so" (*tathāpi*). Suspecting that the perception of non-duality might possess validity just like the perception of duality, he says:
"Because of contradiction" (*virodhataḥ*). The meaning is: those two perceptions cannot both be valid authorities in one and the same place, just like the perceptions of darkness and light. || 34 ||

In this way, the fault of being merely imagined (parikalpitatā) would follow here.
The scripture beginning with "pūrṇam" [is taught] for the purpose of removing those defects. (35)

He concludes the fault shown in the two alternatives with the words "parikalpitatā" (the state of being imagined). Here, the phrase "atra" refers to the statement of the two alternatives. He introduces the mantra as a response to an objection with the words "taddoṣa" (that fault). The meaning is that this is a complete sentence intended to remove the undesirable consequence of the suspected fault. || 35 ||
There is no fault whatsoever here; how that is so shall now be explained.
Therefore, everything will be well according to one's own direct experience. || 36 ||

Anticipating the objection, "How is that [objection] refuted here?", he says: "No. Just as the defect resulting from the falsity of either duality or non-duality does not occur, so too the reality of both these states is declared in this mantra; therefore, [the defect of] the non-duality of one's own experience—
The meaning is that since duality is accepted on the basis of the Śruti, the authority of the Karma-kāṇḍa and so forth is possible. || 36 ||
That which is entirely beyond perception is called the full cause.
The existent Brahman is all-pervading like space, entirely undivided on every side.
Having stated the purport, he explains the meaning of "pūrṇamada" with the word "ada". || 37 ||
That very state of Brahmā has first been described here.
If Brahman is thus non-dual, the state of duality cannot be established. || 38 ||
Thus, for the purpose of negating defects, this is understood as "complete."
Let there not be falsity of Brahman at all times in the two aforementioned states. (39)

He concludes the meaning of the sentence with the words "of Brahman. He introduces the sentence "This is full" preceded by a doubt with the words "If it is so. Having stated that the reality of the two states is what is revealed by the mantra, he asks how this could be established and answers with the word "yathā" (as).
The reason for this is given by the word "sadā" (always); the meaning is: because those two states exist eternally. || 38 || 32 ||
Because of the reason that it is non-different from the complete and thorough knowledge of Brahman.
Therefore, let this task also be understood as being entirely fulfilled. || 40 ||

Although the state of non-duality (advaitāvasthā) is eternally real, one might suspect that the state of duality (dvaitāvasthā) is not so; therefore, he says "pūrṇa" (complete). The meaning is: Brahman alone is complete, being all-pervasive in the nature of consciousness; and because the effect is non-different from its cause, the effect as well is indeed complete.
Because of non-difference from the Full, the effect must be full; it cannot be false, according to the scripture.
Whatever is not distinct from something else is determined to be that very thing. (41)
Nevertheless, raising the doubt as to how this can be real, he says: "By the Full One" (pūrṇena). He states the proof for its non-difference from that [Fullness] with the words:
"From Śruti. The meaning is: because of the scriptural hearing that "this is the Full One" (pūrṇam idam). Even though the effect is not distinct from the Full One, how is it real?
Regarding this, he says: "If from that... Here, the examples are a jar, a bowl, and so forth. || 41 ||
1956 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fifth Adhyāya]—
Thus, when this reality, which is of the nature of *tat*, has been established as true;
Consequently, there would be an absence of creation and so forth, because [the cause] remains in a state of uniformity. (42)

He states the doubt to be excluded by the passage beginning with "pūrṇam adaḥ" (That is full): "If that were so... (evaṃ tarhi). The meaning is that if the two states were real, the established relationship between cause and effect would be untenable. Here, "uniformity" (ekarūpatva) is to be understood as having the nature of both duality and non-duality. || 42 ||
It is not so, because the Śruti declares: "From the Full, the Full is drawn forth."
From the full cause, this full duality is projected forth.
He introduces the statement as a response to that [objection] with the words "Not so. He explains it with the words "From the Full" (pūrṇāt). || 43 ||
For when duality is scrutinized, it does not at all exceed [the nature of] non-duality.
If it is held that this very [process] constitutes the vomiting out of non-duality; || 44 ||

When it has been stated that duality is an effect of non-duality, the proponent [of the opponent's view] raises an objection with the words "yasmāt" (since). For a snake arising from a rope is not distinct from it; thus, the doctrine of illusory transformation (*vivartavāda*) would result. This is the meaning. As for the example...
For such is the word "hi" (indeed). || 44 ||
This is not so; why? Because it would entail the abandonment of what has been perceived.

The partisan of a particular school (ekadeśin) refutes [the previous argument] with "Not so," on the grounds that the falsity of duality is untenable. Thus, it is established by direct perception and determined through scriptural injunction.

Having established, by relying on scripture, that duality is as ultimately real as non-duality, he now states another reason for that very point: "By way of fullness.

The waves have intense motion at their front, while in their middle they possess slight motion.

Just as these [waves] arise simultaneously from the self through its own movements.

The conduct of Devadatta would be unwavering through the Supreme Self.

And by virtue of being the Virāj, it was exceedingly like the surging waves of a fierce storm.

Therefore, for the sake of removing contradiction and for the realization of truth, [this is stated].

The meaning is that Brahman does not consist of both duality and non-duality, because there is no conjunction of the two due to their mutual contradiction; for in this case, neither an option (*vikalpa*) nor a conjunction (*samuccaya*) between a general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*) is possible. In this case, the non-dual state is not [attained] through such effort as by the abandonment of what is heard.
Having been brought to that specific [state], it partakes in negation because of its partless nature.

He states the refutation: "No. Here, "here" (*iha*) is the word for Brahman; its "particularity" (*tad-viśeṣaḥ*) is a single part (*ekadeśaḥ*) of Brahman. This refers to that state of non-duality (*advaitāvasthā*). The term "effort" (*yatnaḥ*), however, is connected to both [the attainment and the negation]. || 66 ||
And because conceptual construction is untenable, as in the case of the taking up of the sixteenth vessel and so forth.
For in reality, agency is not conceptualized as our own pride. || 67 ||

Having stated the impossibility of [the Brahman] being subject to emission (*utsarga*) and so forth, he establishes the impossibility of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Regarding the word "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*): the ellipsis is that the conceptualization of Brahman as consisting of both duality and non-duality is not tenable. As an illustrative example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) for the impossibility of conceptual construction in Brahman, he says: "The sixteenth," and so on.

He states the reason why conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is impossible with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), beginning with the word "entity" (*vastu*). Thus, once that [entity] has been cognized through valid means of knowledge (*pramita*), no conceptual construction exists regarding it.

Without before or after, without exteriority, and devoid of differentiation or conjunction.

Because of the possibility of doubt regarding the absence [of such a person], the determination of the noble ones as previously described is not established.
Those [teachings] would be considered spurious because they could not have originated from anyone other than an Ārya. || 72 ||

Anticipating the objection that these [texts] might be intent on injunctions because they impart objects for worship, he says: "Not so" (*amātvā*). The meaning is that if the unity of the Self were not accepted, these means of knowledge would become devoid of an object altogether. || 72 ||
Likewise, there is also a contradiction with logic regarding that which consists of action and its factors.

Furthermore, for one who asserts that [the self] is both different and non-different, there would follow a contradiction.

The meaning is that because it is partless (*niraṃśa*), if it were to possess multiple natures, it would necessarily follow that it has parts (*sāṃśatva*), is active (*sakriyatva*), and is non-eternal (*anityatva*).

Furthermore, because it is not to be studied, this construction of the meaning of the scripture has been made by you [in vain].

As for what was stated: "Because it is a portion of the Veda, it brings about the cognition of distinct entities... [Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika, Pañcamādhyāya, 1962]...

Having stated that there is no difference in flavor (*nānārasatā*) in either case, he restates the objection previously mentioned with the words "As for that which... (*yattu*). The meaning of the restatement is as follows:

if it is argued that the *karmakāṇḍa*—which teaches the cognition of distinct entities—is invalid because it lacks a [corresponding] object, then the *jñānakāṇḍa* would also be invalid since it too is part of the Veda; consequently, neither heaven nor liberation would be established. For the Veda possesses no authority regarding the establishment of distinctions such as birth and so forth.
For its status as the Self is established in that which is not grasped by perception and the other means of knowledge. || 83 ||

First, he replies: "No" (*na hi*). This is the meaning. || 83 ||

This distinction of a real entity is not observed to exist either from itself or from another.

Regarding the reading *anatiśayaikatvāt*: "distinction" (*bheda*) is what is meant by "excess" (*atiśaya*); that which is other than this, namely the relation that causes it, is "non-excess" (*anatiśaya*). He states another alternative: "Even in the case of division" (*vibhāge 'pi*). The meaning is that even when there is no relation between a jar and a cloth, there is no mutual difference [between them], because each exists with its own uniform nature. Anticipating the objection that "even a jar unrelated to a cloth makes known its own difference from the cloth," he raises the dilemma—whether that difference from the cloth is identical to the jar itself or something else—and refutes the first option with the words: "Even one belonging to another" (*anyadīyo 'pi*). This refers to the jar's lack of relation to the cloth.

Therefore, a jar does not reveal its own difference from itself; for in the absence of a relation, it is impossible for it to function as a subject (dharmin) or a counter-correlate (pratiyogin). This is the meaning of the phrase "because of the lack of relish" (*aruci*). || 87 ||
"O you who are absorbed in the true nature of the Self, pride attains the state of being mere pride."

In the second [alternative], this nature is either the property (*dharma*) or not; since the first leads to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-existence of the entity (*vastu*), he intends to refute the second by stating the general principle regarding universals (*sāmānya*). He says: "The means of knowledge" (*mānam*). Even so, what happens in the case at hand? To that he replies: "Difference" (*bhedam*). By making the object of knowledge (*meyam*) its own object, the means of knowledge does not take difference as its range (*gocara*), because difference is a property (*dharma*) of that [object] and is therefore distinct from it; nor [does it take difference as its range] from the object of knowledge—

Since a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) operates even in this case of difference because its object is solely the cognizable thing (meyaviṣaya), the meaning is that even the difference between properties (dharmabheda) is not established by valid cognition. || 88 ||
There is no difference apart from Being, nor is there [difference] through the persistence of Being.
Just as it is thus with the non-existent, so too no distinction whatsoever is perceived.

Furthermore, is difference (bheda) distinct from existence (sat) or non-distinct? Not the first, because it would lead to an infinite regress; and since that which is distinct is non-existent, it would result in the undesirable consequence of the non-duality of existence alone. Regarding the second case as well, with the intention of establishing the non-duality of existence, he says: "of existence" (sataḥ).

Just as it is difficult to define difference through either distinction or non-distinction from existence, he extends this [argument] to non-existence as well, stating that those two are equally indefinable for it: "as... (yathā).
He concludes the stated reasoning with the word "evam" (thus). || 89 ||
Whether this entire world, including the gods, is held by someone to be real or unreal;
What would be the locus of that difference? Because of contradiction, it cannot have both as its locus. (90)

Furthermore, he states that difference is not established within the systems of the Sāṃkhya, the Buddhist, and the Jain (Kṣapaṇaka): "All [is... etc. The meaning is that in both of the first two positions, difference is not established because there is an absence of specific subjects and counter-correlates, and because there is an absence of any form of difference; and in the third position, it is not established due to contradiction. ||90||
If separateness depends on something else, then the jar is inherently non-separate.
The stronger [rule] subverts the weaker because it is internal (antaraṅga), whereas the other is external (bahiraṅga). || 91 ||
He states that even in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), difference is not established: "dependent on another" (*anyāpekṣam*). || 99 ||
