If separateness were distinct from substance, then one who desires to avoid infinite regress would be in haste.
If distinctness were merely a substance, then this entire world would be non-distinct.

Furthermore, having raised the dilemma as to whether distinctness (pṛthaktva) is different from or non-different from substance (dravya), he refutes each in turn, beginning with "From substance. He indicates that infinite regress (anavasthā) constitutes a fault because it destroys the very root [of the argument], stating "satvara" [meaning "quickly"]. || 92 ||
If the difference of an entity were intrinsic, it would follow that the entity is empty.
[The text provided consists of two vertical bars (||), indicating a section break or the end of a chapter. [End of Section]
Even though it is relative, difference does not exist because it is merely imagined, like a snake in a rope. (93)
He concludes by stating that there is no difference either from itself or from another: "If [it were] from itself," etc. (93).
In this way, there are many such refutations regarding the nature of being both different and non-different.
That which was stated previously should also be applied here for the sake of establishing the reality of the matter. || 94 ||
Fearing that since difference (*bheda*) has been refuted more than once, its refutation here would be a mere repetition, he says: "and so forth" (*ityevamādi*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the impossibility of the established relationship between teacher and disciple and so on is included, because such distinctions do not exist when there is non-difference (*abheda*) in the state of [ultimate] differencelessness. The connection is with the word "previously" (*prāk*), meaning at the beginning of the treatise. Here too, in this commentary by Bhartṛprapañca, [the phrase is used] for the purpose of reflecting upon the logic already stated.

If it is argued, "Then for what purpose is that [refutation]? he says: "The reality," etc. The meaning is that the refutation of the views of others is for the purpose of clearly manifesting the oneness of Brahman and the Self. || 94 ||
Or, if the authority of even a single portion of the Veda is not accepted;
It would follow that this applies to the entire ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) of the Veda as well. || 95 ||
Thus, the refutation of that which was previously set forth is now stated.
In the connection between the probandum and the probans, that [scripture] is also accepted as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 96 ||

Having refuted the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, he restates—in order to elaborate upon what was briefly stated by the words "because it is a part of the Veda" and so forth—the refutation of the contradiction with the Śruti: "Even the Veda... [and so on]. The meaning is that the lack of authority would follow [for the entire Veda].

He says that it is improper to claim that the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) lacks authority because the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) lacks authority, since there is no such lack of authority for the latter.

Regarding the phrase "of that": how can the scriptural injunction for ritual action possess authority in the non-dualist (advaita) system, given the absence of objects? To this, he says: "The goal... [91] [96].
The distinction is established by other means of valid cognition, and not by relying on scripture.
For even animals perceive difference through the measurement of their senses and so forth. || 97 ||

Anticipating the objection, "Why should its authority not consist precisely in having difference as its object? he says: "Difference. Anticipating the objection that, like duality, non-duality might also not be accessible through scripture—or conversely—that it might be the opposite—he says: "Even animals [know this]. The sense is that non-duality, however, is scriptural because it is something previously unknown (*apūrva*). This very meaning is indicated by the particle *hi*. || 97 ||
And no one here possesses a cognition of falsity regarding difference by the very fact of birth.
Nor is there any lack of conviction regarding the distinction [of the self] even for those whose intellects have been awakened. (98)

If the scriptural statement regarding action is authoritative with respect to the relationship between the goal and the means, then duality must be accepted as real; otherwise, in the absence of a basis for reliance, the relationship itself would not exist.

Anticipating the objection that [the relationship] is established, he says: "Not so. The meaning is this: if that [relationship] were false, there could be no cognition of it without the knowledge of Brahman; and since that [knowledge] does not exist previously, the establishment of the relationship depends upon the prior acceptance of a falsely imagined difference. Therefore, the validity of the Vedic revelation regarding ritual action (*karman*) in that regard is not established.

Taking up the imagined distinction (*kalpita-bheda*), he states another reason for its validity with the word "even" (*api*). Just as the disciples of the Sugata and others, though they know through reasoning that difference is false, nevertheless accept the authority of their own scriptures only insofar as it depends upon difference;

so too, for those who—due to causes such as discernment (*viveka*)—are turned away from the duality of the body and so forth, yet remain devoid of the knowledge of Brahman, there arises a sense of improbability regarding difference.
And thus, prior to the arising of such [knowledge], the authority of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) exists by means of imagined duality; this is the meaning. || 98 ||
When action and its factors are completely integrated, let there be no [separate] hearing of the reality of things.
Because its sole object is the relationship between the probandum and the probans alone. || 99 ||

Fearing that, even if it were to convey a specific relation by accepting a difference established in common worldly experience (*loka-siddha*), the reality of the object to be known (*bodhya*) would still have to be admitted, he says: "Action" (*kriyā*). "Commixture" (*saṃbhitti*) means "commingling" (*saṃbheda*), that is to say, "relation. He states the reason for this as follows:
"Regarding the word *sādhyā*: the meaning of the single term is neutrality (*tāṭasthya*) with respect to its truth or untruth. (99)
Therefore, for the sake of establishing the desired object, one should accept the distinction as it is established in the world.
"This must be done, this must not be done"—thus the Vedic scripture proceeds.

He concludes the authority of the *karmakāṇḍa* with the verse beginning "loka... (verse 100). The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (hence) is that there is no dependence upon the previously mentioned reality of the non-difference of the eternal [Self] regarding the authority of the *karmakāṇḍa*.
But that man whose intellect is purified by his actions and who is detached from everything.
Desiring the fruit that is complete and distinct from birth and so forth. || 101 ||

As for the claim that the *jñānakāṇḍa* (the section on knowledge) is also non-authoritative because it is a part of the Veda, one must consider whether its lack of authority arises from the absence of a qualified person (*adhikārī*), the absence of a fruit (*phala*), or the absence of a subject matter (*viṣaya*). To refute the first alternative, he says: "But from all [of them]," etc. "Desiring" (*kāmayānaḥ*) means "one who desires. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "he is the qualified person endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). (101)
Because the inner self, which is of a full nature, has only the quality of darkness (tamas) as its obstacle.
Because it is established by itself, nothing other than its manifestor is perceived for it. || 102 ||
He states the second [view]: "mere darkness" (*tamomātra*). The sense is that here the fruit is the destruction of ignorance along with its manifestations (*savilāsāvidyādhvasti*).
He answers the third [view] with: "of the inner self" (*pratīcaḥ*). The meaning is that since the unknown [Self] is the object [of knowledge], it cannot be devoid of that [objectivity].
Regarding those who say that even when the fruit is the destruction of ignorance, there is a dependence on ritual action (*karma*), he says: "by itself" (*svataḥ*) || 102 ||
When that which is already attained by itself is fully realized through the sentence, there occurs the total destruction of delusion.
Thereafter, there should be no further regard for pride, because one has attained the fruit and thus achieved one's purpose through that.

He states the reason why a seeker of liberation requires only valid knowledge (*māna*)—and not ritual action (*karman*)—for the purpose of destroying the ignorance that veils the inwardly manifest Self:
"svataḥ" (inherently). Others maintain that even knowledge which has already arisen must be practiced repeatedly in order to destroy ignorance; he refutes them [with the following].
1 ka. *brahmājñā* | 2 kha. *api jñāna* | [vol 3, page 831] 1966 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Fifth Chapter—

"By knowledge alone": the meaning is that since ignorance is destroyed by knowledge arising even once, and because the person has thereby accomplished all that was to be done, there is no dependence on a repetition of knowledge. || 103 ||
For the requirement for a means of proof exists only when there is something to be proven; once that is established, such a requirement ceases.
Or rather, because the entire [deity] is completed through its perfection within the unspeakable (asādhya). || 104 ||

Others, however, maintain that the attainment of Brahman requires repeated practice (*abhyāsa*); he refutes them with the words "For in the case of what is to be accomplished" (*sādhye hi*). The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that dependence on such practice is observed in the case of things to be accomplished, like heaven and so forth, but its absence is observed in the case of what is already established (*siddha*). || 104 ||
When Brahman, which consists of both duality and non-duality, is accepted as being atomic in size;
Even then, this contradiction cannot be refuted by anyone. || 105 ||
Having refuted the contradiction with scripture regarding non-duality, he demonstrates that contradiction elsewhere: "Dvaita... and so forth.
For one whose self has come to rest in Brahman, whether as the aggregate of all beings or as each individual being.
"Tell me, what is the cause for action in those who perceive all things as non-different from one another? (106)

Anticipating the objection—namely, how it is possible for the *karmakāṇḍa* to possess authority with respect to duality in this state of freedom from disease (*viroga*), while other sections [of the Veda] possess authority with respect to non-duality—he says: "The entire... (verse 106).
And because there is mutual contradiction in [the claim that] all things possess birth and so forth.
There would be no engagement [with the injunction] due to contradiction, whether it be a prohibition or likewise a positive injunction.

Anticipating the objection that the very possession of specific caste and so forth is the cause [of the distinction], he says: "All," etc. For the wise one who abides in Brahman, which consists of both duality and non-duality, even while being endowed with all castes, stages of life (*āśrama*), and so on—because the qualifying attributes such as caste are mutually contradictory, there would be a mutual conflict between injunction and prohibition; for instance, due to his Brāhmaṇahood there would be engagement in the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, yet due to his Kṣatriyahood there would be desisting from it. Thus, there is a contradiction between the two.

In that case, there would be both engagement and withdrawal; thus, the entire universe would be without engagement. The sense is that, due to the lack of authority of the Śrutis regarding action, the same would apply to the Upaniṣads as well. || 107 ||
Furthermore, there is no sense of limitation for the wise one, because such a state belongs to the demonic nature.
Even for the learned, if they possess an asuric nature, the vision of Brahman would be fruitless. (108)

Furthermore, even though the wise man possesses all [the factors] such as birth and so forth, there is neither engagement nor withdrawal because of his lack of identification with them; thus he says, "And not... He states the fault in the opposite case: "Even for the wise man... It should be understood that the conceit of limitation is demonic, according to the Vedic scripture: "For this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Asuras. || 108 ||
Therefore, this song [of yours] is incorrect for the purpose of establishing both difference and non-difference.
However, that which is contrary to both scripture and logic is now being discussed. (109)

He concludes the refutation of the opposing view with the words, "Therefore. Regarding the claim made by Bhartṛprapañca that Brahman is both different and non-different, he states the reason for rejecting that position as being untenable with the word "śruti" (scripture). Having established that the entire passage cannot have the meaning desired by the opponents and must instead be devoted to the sense of a single, uniform essence, he now declares his intention to follow the actual interpretation of the scripture: "The subject at hand..."
Thus [it is said]. || 109 ||
[Brāhmaṇa 1] This mantra, "Oṃ Khaṃ Brahman," is prescribed here by the Śruti for the practice of meditation. *Ānandagiri’s Commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā, Volume 3, Page 832.* 1967.
Oṃ Khaṃ Brahman—this mantra is [prescribed] here by the Śruti for the act of meditation.

It is enjoined for the attainment of the fruit; this is now explained accordingly. Continuing with the very subject at hand, he introduces the mantra beginning with "Oṃ," namely "Oṃ Khaṃ. He shows its application by saying "by means of scripture" (*śrutyā*). When the attainment of the fruit of gradual liberation is intended, meditation upon the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahman*) is prescribed.

In this context, the meaning is that this mantra has been employed by this Brāhmaṇa because of its capacity to illuminate the object of meditation. To explain how it is employed in meditation by virtue of being an illuminator of the object of meditation, he says: "Just as... (verse 110).
Just as there is the direct realization of the true nature of the supreme Brahman.
Thus it has been directly proclaimed by the Śruti in the four preceding chapters. || 111 ||

Anticipating the objection that meditation is taught for what purpose, since the attainment of the desired goal follows from perfect knowledge alone, he restates the subject matter of the two sections [of the Vedas] with the words: "Of the Supreme," etc. (111).
Furthermore, for the purpose of practicing this very [teaching], there is meditation upon them.
"Oṃ Khaṃ Brahman"—with these words [one should worship] for men who desire their own highest good. (112)

Now, it is stated here that this very meditation (*upāsti*) is the means for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of reality; he says "of this very [meditation]. By this, he indicates that because right knowledge (*samyag-dhī*) does not arise instantaneously, there is a requirement for meditation. Then, with the word "now" (*atha*), he illuminates the qualification of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) for this practice.
He says "of men" (*puṃsām*). || 112 ||
In this context, "Brahman" is the object to be qualified, and "space" is likewise the qualifier.
Because of the statement of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), its function is like that of a black snake. || 113 ||

In this regard, he states the determination of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified: "Brahman," etc. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the statement in the mantra. By the particle *api*, the reverse order is also indicated. The intended meaning is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words;
that is to say, it is like "a black snake" or "a blue lotus. From this coreferentiality, there is a function toward a single referent. This is established.
This is the meaning. || 113 ||
The application of the word "Brahman" has as its sole object the vast reality.
In this context, he distinguishes that [object] by means of that which falls solely within the category of the universal aspect. || 114 ||

Anticipating the objection that because the word "Brahman" has been uttered, there is no further expectation for a qualifier and thus it cannot have a qualificand, he says: "The activity... For it has been stated:

"Indeed, when the word 'Brahman' is being etymologically derived, meanings such as eternal purity and so forth are understood, because they follow from the meaning of the root *bṛh*. Here, the word "here" refers to what was spoken in the mantra. A specific part of a general category is its particular; [the word denotes Brahman] by virtue of being that alone.
The connection is with the phrase "staying in the sky. || 114 ||
Brahman is excluded by space from those things whose intrinsic nature is not space.
Likewise, by implication, space [arises] from those things whose nature is not Brahman, and Brahman [arises] from space. 115.
1. *Sna*. Therein he says: 2. *Kha*. ‘*sya vyu*’.
[Vol. 3, page 833] 1968 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Fifth Adhyāya—]

By that [statement], he states the result of *brahman* being the qualificand: "not non-space" (*anākāśa*). He states the result of space being the qualificand by means of *brahman*: "in the same way" (*tathā*). This means that just as *brahman* is distinguished from non-spaces by means of space, so it is here;
the sense is that, by implication, it is impossible for *brahman*—which has been thus qualified—to be anything other than *brahman*. || 111 ||
Because the word *kha* denotes only a generality, it requires a qualifier.
He provides this etymological explanation of "purāṇa" for the sake of understanding its cause.

Thus, although the greatness of space (*kha*) is established by its being the qualificand, nevertheless, since there are two types of causes and effects, in response to the inquiry as to which one is to be understood here, he says: "The universal," etc. Since the word *kha* denotes both the effect and the cause as a universal—because it expresses that alone—there arises a doubt as to which is to be grasped. To resolve this, he provides a definition of space as a qualification for the sake of understanding the cause, stating: "the ancient" (*purāṇa*).
The meaning is that through hearing [the scripture], there is likewise the cessation of doubt. || 116 ||
That Brahman which has been called "space" (kha) is beyond the designation of words.
The wise one should constantly contemplate either the [deity] or the object of focus itself. || 117 ||

He shows the meaning of the sentence with the words "yat tad" (that which...). The meaning is that the meditation on the causal Brahman is directed toward the word "Om," which is its designator, or toward the effect [the universe], which is its symbol. || 117 ||
And the scriptural teaching is that this is the most excellent object of focus.
For the Atharvaṇas also recite: "By this very syllable. (118)

Regarding the second position, he states the proof with the words "this" (etad). Regarding the first [position] as well, he states the proof with the words "by this" (etena); the remainder of the sense is: "one should meditate upon the Supreme Person by means of the syllable. The word "hi" is used to indicate that this is also well-known from such passages as "Om is Brahman. || 118 ||
How could there even be worship of that which is beyond the senses?
He said, "Wind is space," for the sake of establishing that as an object of focus.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "vāyur am" [the wind is *am*] as follows: "Because it is beyond the senses. The word "api" (also) has the sense of "like that which is neither effect nor cause.
The intended meaning is that this sentence is for the purpose of establishing the vision of Brahman as delimited by space, which has the syllable *oṃ* as its support. || 119 ||
It is considered that the ancient void (kha) is not to be understood within this mantra.
The wise Kauravyāyaṇija is renowned as Vāyu. || 120 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "iti ha sma" as follows: "The ether" (kham). || 120 ||
The word "kha" functions by conventional usage (rūḍhi) to denote air, while it is indicated (lakṣyate) as referring to space.
And because its application is manifold, let the wind be understood as space. || 121 ||

It clarifies the established usage with the words "by conventional usage" (*rūḍhyā*). In that very context, it shows the frequent employment of the word *kha* in such passages as "space, wind, fire," and so forth, with the phrase "many times" (*bahuśaḥ*). It concludes the result of these two reasons with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 121 ||
1. This is also in the *Atharvaveda*.
Whether it be the Purāṇa of those two, or perhaps the Vāyavaṃ [Vāyu-purāṇa], may it be so. [Brāhmaṇa 1] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 1969.
That which is to be meditated upon as "Om" should always be contemplated during both fortnights.

Anticipating the doubt as to which is superior—the position that it is the causal Brahman (*kāraṇabrahman*) or the position that it is the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*)—the author says: "The ancient" (*purāṇam*).

Just as the causal Brahman, the elemental ether is likewise beyond the senses; and its frequent application [in scripture] is indistinguishable, since the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is used many times in the Śrutis even with respect to the causal Brahman. Therefore, because both positions are supported by the word, there is a twofold view regarding the letter 'A'.
The meaning is "a sneeze. || 122 ||
The syllable Oṃ, as the object of focus, becomes the sphere of meditation.
A wooden block marked with four arms appears like that of Viṣṇu. || 123 ||
Having stated that Brahman, which is of two kinds, is to be meditated upon with the syllable *oṃ* as its symbol (*pratīka*), he explains its nature as a symbol by means of an illustration:
"by way of being a support" (*ālambanatayā*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Viṣṇu is the object of meditation by way of being a support. || 123 ||
Let it be understood that "Om" is this very place nearest to Brahman.
Just as the Śālagrāma stone belongs to Hari, who removes all misfortunes; || 124 ||
Since there are other objects of perception, why is the vision of Brahman superimposed on this one alone? To that he says:
"The most proximate" (*nedīyaḥ*). This means it is the nearest, being exceedingly close and the object of supreme affection. An example of this is given: "the Śālagrāma. (124)
"Or rather, one should know that the designation 'Om' belongs to that very Supreme Self."
For one whose mind is fixed upon that, that Brahman quickly becomes gracious.

He begins to establish the position that [the syllable Om] is without parts (*apratīkatva*). Or rather, he states the distinction here: "In that... The meaning of this is as follows: in the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*) "That I am" (*so'ham*), the syllable Om arises; when the letters *sa* and *ha* are elided, it consists of three parts beginning with the letter *a*. Among these, the triad known as Virāj, the waking state, and Viśva is the letter *a*; the triad consisting of Sūtra, the dreaming state, and Taijasa is the letter *u*.

The letter *ka* is the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and the wise one (*prājña*); these three constitute the letter *m*. When each preceding one is withdrawn into each succeeding one, the letter *m* culminates in the Innermost (*pratīc*). That [Innermost], which is Brahman—whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated—is meditated upon as being denoted by the syllable *oṃ*;
thus, it bestows its fruit immediately. || 125 ||
The Brahmins indeed declare that the syllable Om is the Veda itself.
Since by means of this [knowledge] Brahman, which is to be known, is known, it is therefore considered "Veda."
When it has been stated that Brahman is to be meditated upon as being denoted by the syllable *oṃ*, he introduces the passage beginning with "This Veda" (*vedo'yam*) to explain that point.
He explains the phrase "This Veda" and so forth as the reason for that [meditation], stating: "Veda... (121).
They know this syllable *oṃ* directly as the very means of designation.
Through meditation upon that, the Brahmins know the fearless Brahman.
He summarizes the intended meaning of the thesis and the reason with the words: "by way of expression. || 127 ||

And there may be the statement "this is the Veda" with respect to the aforementioned meditation.
Since this is a praise, it is an explanatory passage (arthavāda); no other meaning is determined from it.

He states another meaning for the passage beginning with "This is the Veda" (vedo'yam). Regarding the word "Veda": the statement "This is the Veda," etc., is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) concerning the meditation on the syllable *Oṃ* as its representative symbol; since no other meaning is perceived from that praise, the meaning is that because this *Oṃkāra* is the Veda—since by means of it the Vedic reality (*vedārtha*), namely Brahman, is known—therefore one should perform the contemplation of Brahman upon it. || 128 ||
Or that which the twice-born know through the distinctions of the *udgītha* and other [limbs of the sacrifice].
"This is the Veda" is how it should be understood, because therein the threefold [Veda] reaches its completion. || 129 ||
He states another point: "The Udgītha, etc. By the word "etc.," the Prastāva and Pratihāra are included. The reason for this is given: "Of the threefold [Veda].

For the threefold Veda is indeed completed within the syllable Om; as stated in such scriptural passages as, "Just as by a pin... Therefore, the meaning is that it (the syllable Om) possesses the nature of the Veda. || 129 ||
Therefore, when that [Veda] is being applied, the entire Veda along with its compendia [is included].
Therefore, it should be understood that the Veda is applied [to the sacrifice] by means of the syllable Om. || 130 ||
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika. || 1 ||

In this context, demonstrating the fruit of its completion, he concludes the subject at hand with the words "In that" (*tasmin*). The meaning of the first *ataḥ* is that the threefold Veda (*trayī*) is completed therein. The meaning of the second *ataḥ* is that when that [Veda] is employed, the entirety of the Veda is thereby employed. ||130||
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Ṭīkā on the Vārttika to the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣya. 1.1.1.

Now begins the second Brāhmaṇa.
Thus far, the internal means for the meditation upon Brahman has been explained.
Now, the syllable Oṃ is prescribed as the means for self-restraint and the other [virtues]. || 1 ||
Having restated what has been said, he states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa: "It has been stated," etc. (1).
Self-controlled, generous, compassionate, and pure both internally and externally.
Such a person shall be qualified for all stages of meditative worship.

How is it that those [elements] serve as the means for meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), given that meditative absorption—consisting of mental activity—is accomplished even by one who lacks them? To this, he says:
[Page 836] 1. kha. 'ka upā' | 2. kha. 'vidate' |

"Self-controlled" (dānta): the sense is that meditation upon another [object] cannot be successfully accomplished regarding the supreme reality, which is exceedingly subtle. Considering that this qualification of the qualified candidate applies equally to other forms of worship as well, he uses the qualifying term "in all" (sarvāsu). || 2 ||
Let it be accepted that this is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to the injunction regarding self-restraint and the like.
The passage beginning with "yā" and so forth is clear in meaning; therefore, no effort is made [to explain it]. || 3 ||
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

Having stated the purport, he speaks of the non-explanatory nature of the syllables while analyzing them, beginning with the words "damādīti. The meaning is that this preceding section of the text—which forms a supplement to the injunction "one should learn these three"—is not to be explained because its meaning is already clear. || 3 ||

Now begins the third Brāhmaṇa. That Brahman which is free from limiting adjuncts has been explained with effort in the preceding section; now [it will be explained further].
For the meditation upon that very same [Self] when it is possessed of adjuncts will be clearly explained. || 1 ||

Having restated what has been discussed, he states the purport of the subsequent composition: "Brahman," etc. The meaning is as follows: in the two sections (*kāṇḍas*), Brahman without attributes (*nirupādhika*) was taught as the primary purport;

the syllable *Oṃ* and the triad beginning with self-restraint (*dama*) were sung in the preceding Brāhmaṇas as ancillaries to meditation (*upāsti*). Now, the subsequent body of text is intended to explain the various meditations upon that very same Brahman when it is with attributes (*sopādhika*). Immediately after the description of the attributeless [Brahman], there is the realization of it—
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that it is not appropriate to speak of one who lacks qualification as possessing limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*). || 1 ||
Prajāpati was heard of in the past; who he was is not understood.
To specify the particular meaning from the general statement, the words "this one" and so forth are spoken. || 2 ||

He states the intention of the immediately preceding Brāhmaṇa passage, preceded by the desire to know: "It is heard," etc. Since the general statement that Prajāpati instructs the gods and others could apply to Dakṣa and others as well, the phrase "This Prajāpati," etc., is intended to distinguish and show the specific Prajāpati who is meant to be discussed. This is the meaning. || 2 ||
The heart is a mass of flesh; however, by virtue of its location therein, the notion [of "heart"] is observed [to be applied] to the intellect.
In that [state], Śākalya declared the withdrawal of the Name and the rest into the heart.

Regarding the phrase "that which is the heart" (yaddhṛdayam), he states the meaning of the word *hṛdaya*: "hṛt. Then, as to what kind of meaning the word *hṛdaya* has here—whether it is the primary denoted sense (*vācya*) or the indicated sense (*lakṣya*)—he says: "in the heart" (*hṛdi*). The meaning is that the indicated sense is intended here, and that has been introduced in the fifth chapter.

Because of the origin of all beings and likewise because of being the Lord of all.
For that reason, the heart should be known as Prajāpati.
He establishes his status as Prajāpati with the words "All... How is there an identity between the heart and Prajāpati through their having a single characteristic?

To that he says: "By that... The meaning is that there is an identity between the two because they possess a single characteristic, by virtue of the reasons stated in the Śākalya Brāhmaṇa and in the section on the three foods (tryanna). || 4 ||
For one who has transcended all that is knowable, even Brahmā would become the heart.
Since this is so, one's own heart should always be venerated with effort.
And the meditative worship of the syllables known as the "Heart" is declared through the Śruti.
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.
He states the meaning of the phrase "This is Brahman" with the words beginning "All. His status as Prajāpati, according to the manner previously described, is the cause for his all-pervasiveness.
He states the resulting implication of the heart being Brahman with the words beginning "Since. There is no other fruit for the magnification of that [heart] by virtue of its being Brahman.

This is the meaning. By the word "with effort" (*yatnāt*), the three qualifiers—respect (*ādara*), continuity (*nairantarya*), and long duration (*dīrghakāla*)—are understood as belonging to the meditation (*upāste*).

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "these three syllables" (*tad etad tryakṣaram*) as follows: "The heart" (*hṛdaya*). That is to say, of the three syllables contained in the name "Heart.
Furthermore, the meaning is that this statement regarding the meditation on the syllables of its name is for the purpose of praising the Heart, which is the object of meditation. || 5 ||
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the *Śrībṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtikaṭīkā*.

This is another mode of worship of that very Brahman called the Heart.
That which is qualified by the adjunct of truth is called "that indeed is that. || 1 ||
He states the purport of another Brāhmaṇa passage: "tasyaiva" (of that very same). The reason for its being different from that is given by "satya" (truth). || 1 ||
The word "tat" (that) serves as a reference, and the word "vai" is for the purpose of recollection.
And when there is a description by another means, the expression "it was thus" (tad āseti) is used for that [past state]. (2)

He states the non-repetitive meaning of the words in the sentence with the phrase "by the word *tat*. By the first *tat*, there is a reference to the Brahman known as the Heart (*hṛdaya*). When it is asked "What is that?", the third statement—namely, "this very thing was that"—is expressed by the word *etat* (this), and thus it is co-referential with the [first] *tat*; such is the meaning.

"That which was spoken by the heart-self, 'Truth alone existed then,' is indeed so."
Brahman, whose nature consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, has been previously explained as the Truth.

Regarding "It is indeed truth": the connection is that the Brahman which was described as being of the nature of the heart is indeed truth. It is called *mahat* because of its magnitude, and a *yakṣa* because it is most worthy of worship.

Whoever meditates day and night upon this which has been thus explained, [attains the goal].

It has been stated that Truth is the first-born; how that is so is now explained.
By the statement "Water indeed was this," however, there is praise for the meaning as it has been explained.

He states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa, preceded by an inquiry: "It has been said. When it is asked how that Brahman which was described as Truth is the "first-born," the answer is given by the following passage; and the meaning is that this is for the purpose of praising the meditation upon Brahman as Truth. || 1 ||
Milk, Soma, and other waters [are used] in the rites of the Hotṛ and others.
In all oblations, it is mixed [with other substances]; because of its abundance, there is no grasping of water. || 2 ||

Having stated the purport, he explains the word "waters" (*āpaḥ*) with the word "milk" (*payaḥ*). The particle *hi* is used to indicate that their being mixed together in the *agnihotra* and other oblations is a point accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas. To the question—"Since the inclusion of the other elements is also intended here, why is there this specific mention of 'waters'?"—he replies: "Because of their predominance. (2)
Although other elements are also present, it is water alone that predominates.
And because of its predominance, it is grasped; however, nothing else is thereby excluded.
Anticipating the objection, "Why might the qualification not be intended solely for the purpose of excluding other things?", he says: "While [they] exist... (verse 3).
After the addition [of the correction], they transcend all measures.
They remained everywhere, assuming a subtle form and relying upon activity.

In ritual acts, because of the abundance of substances offered, water is the most prevalent; yet it is predominant among those waters consisting of oblations which have become the *apūrva* (unseen potential), since they are heard of in the context of the *agnihotra* as the cause of the transformation of the entire universe. Although the waters such as Soma being poured into the fire are inherent to the ritual act, how is it that they remain so in subsequent times? Regarding this [the text says]: "The ritual acts..."

Anticipating the objection that this is not so because they are non-abiding, he says: "By being cast in" (prakṣepa). The connection is that, having relied upon the action [of casting], they remained everywhere in a subtle form after the time of being cast. || 4 ||
Whatever little is required here in this world for the sake of the oblation, [all that is provided].
For that [water] is included within it, since it is said, "Water alone was this. || 5 ||

Having explained the literal meaning of the words, he connects the sentence with the phrase "as much as" (*yāvat*). Here, in the context of the Agnihotra and other rites, by means of the oblation (*āhuti*) which exists as the cause, whatever is required in this world as an effect is all included within water; for this is seen from such scriptural passages as "All this is indeed water" (*āpa eva*). This is the connection. The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to indicate that this is a matter of observed fact. The term "water" (*āpaḥ*) refers to the root cause.
This is what is intended to be expressed. || 9 ||
At the beginning, prior to creation, [the Lord] created the waters as the Truth (Satya) from the Progenitor (Prajāpati), who was born at the very outset; therefore, the waters are the causal source.
This summarizes the meaning of the sentence that "the world existed as *tanmātra* prior to the emergence of the Sūtra. [The word] "in the beginning" (*agre*) [is explained].

He states the meaning of "those" (*tāḥ*) and so forth: "the Real" (*satyam*). The reason for this is: "because of being the cause" (*kāraṇatvāt*). The meaning is that because water is the fundamental cause in the manner described, the possibility of being a creator of the Real exists. || 6 ||
This is the manifestation of Hiraṇyagarbha from Maheśvara.
By means of this statement of Āditya, it is described for the sake of attaining preeminence.

Having raised the doubt—"How can Brahman, which is heard in scripture as 'truth, knowledge, infinite,' be born from the unmanifest (avyākṛta)?"—the author explains the intended meaning of the passage, saying: "That this... This refers to the birth of that which was sought to be known—the individual soul (jīva) within the sun—as described in this Brāhmaṇa section beginning with "those [waters]," and so forth; for neither non-existence (asat) nor existence (sat) can possess the connection to birth unless it is already established in the form of its cause.

The meaning is that since it is accepted that birth (*janman*) is simply the manifestation (*vyaktībhāva*) of this very [entity], the mention of it is for the purpose of establishing that the Sūtra refers to what is not born (*ajāta*). || 7 ||
The manifestation of even the first-born [Mahat] occurs through the manifestation of the elements (bhūta) and so forth; it cannot be otherwise.
He said "That is the truth," for Brahman is called "Truth" (Satya) because of its extreme vastness.

Anticipating the objection that there would then be a contradiction with the *adhikaraṇa* [sūtra] "The Self is not [born], because it is not so heard" (B.S. 2.3.17), given the acceptance of birth for the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), he says: "Of the elements," etc. Like Brahman devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), its birth is not intrinsic (*svataḥ*), but rather due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*). And that... [Ga.
reads 'tābhivya'].

The limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the elements is the five gross elements in their unevolved state (*apañcīkṛta-mahābhūta*), because they constitute that body and because it arises from them; thus, its status as an adjunct is established. This is further supported by the section concerning the dependence on the moving and the non-moving (*carācara-vyapāśraya-adhika*).

The meaning is that it is established in debate. He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the claim that the birth of the *sūtra* is conditional (*aupādhika*). "Those" (*tāḥ*)—the sense is that since the birth of both the existent (*sat*) and the non-existent (*asat*) is impossible, manifestation alone is intended. Having restated the sentence "Brahman is truth," he states the reason for the *sūtra*'s being Brahman: "Truth" (*satyam*). || 8 ||
Brahmā created the god who is the teacher of the world and the maker of the sun and other celestial bodies.
It is understood that Virāj, as well as Brahmā, created the gods. || 9 ||
He explains the passage beginning with "Brahmā" and so forth as "the sun and so forth. || 9 ||
This being so, the world was produced from Brahman in this manner, arising from the beginning through a gradual process.
Therefore, Brahman is the Great Truth; however, its nature as a Yakṣa is described here.

He concludes that truthfulness, greatness, and being the first-born are established in the Sūtra with the words "Thus. He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Those gods" as follows: "The state of being a Yakṣa. || 10 ||
Having passed beyond their father, the gods worship the grandfather.
Therefore, they know Brahmā and Yakṣa to be Truth, the first-born.
He explains that [verse]: "Having passed beyond" (atītya). The construction is as follows: they know that Yakṣa to be that Brahman which was described as the first-born Truth. || 11 ||
Even that name of Brahman is said to consist of three syllables and is truth itself.
But in the first and the last [syllables], there is immortality due to their being endowed with sound. || 12 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tadetad" (that this...). Regarding the phrase "tasyāpi" (of that also), the word "api" (also) serves to include the illustrative example of the heart as Brahman.
He states the reason for the immortality of the letters *sa* and *ya*: "because they possess vowels" (*sasvaratvataḥ*). || 12 ||
Death is without form in the midst, existing like a body devoid of life.
Furthermore, that which was burnt by nectar is dead even by its own nature.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "from the middle" (*madhyataḥ*) as follows: "devoid of vowels" (*nirackam*). He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "that very thing" (*tadetad*) as follows: "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).

Although the syllable *takāra* is inherently dead (meaningless) due to the absence of a vowel, because it is grasped on both sides by the letters *sakāra* and *yakāra*, it is therefore rendered ineffective; this is the meaning. || 13 ||
Thus, a man who always attends upon [the Buddha] in this manner becomes one possessed of the superknowledges.
"It will surely become true; it cannot be otherwise"—such are the words of reasoning and scripture. (14)
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

Stating the connection between the aforementioned divisions and meditation, he declares its fruit: "In this manner," etc. For the knower, in the form of Truth—[variant: *from death, he is liberated*].

Now begins the sixth Brāhmaṇa. This [section] concerning the cosmic structure follows; now, moreover, [it concerns] the internal self (adhyātma) and the divine realm (adhidaivata).
Having conceptualized a form of the Truth, its worship is described. || 1 ||
Having stated that the qualified Truth is the object of meditation, he declares the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa with the words "like a structure" (*saṃsthānavat*).

The meaning is that immediately after the meditation on the qualified Truth, when the opportunity arises, the following Brāhmaṇa is intended for the purpose of meditating upon that very Truth by conceiving its forms as distinguished by different locations within the microcosm (*adhyātma*) and the macrocosm (*adhidaivata*). || 1 ||
These two, known as the Eye and the Sun, reside within their respective nests, distinguished merely by their locations.
Though appearing as if divided, that deity remains truly one.
Fearing that meditation might differ due to a difference in deities arising from the difference in the locations of the eyes and the sun, he says: "The eye...
Although the deity called Sūtra is indeed one, nevertheless, because of its connection with two such locations, it appears as if distinct merely on account of that difference in location.
Therefore, the meaning is that although the sun and the eye are seen as if they were distinct, there is no difference in their meditative worship (upāsti). || 2 ||
Through the relationship of mutual assistance and being assisted.
These two are established within the self, in the eye and in the sun respectively.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "those two" as follows: "The beneficiary," etc. He demonstrates their mutual establishment by saying, "with respect to the self.

The meaning is that the sun is established in the eye with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), and the one belonging to the eye is established in the sun with respect to the divine (*adhidaiva*). || 3 ||
How it is that those two are established in dependence upon one another is explained as follows:
The sun [is established] in him by means of its rays, and the visual faculty by means of the vital breaths.

Clarifying the relationship as it was stated, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "by means of rays," starting from the words "are established. For the sun, by assisting the eye through its light, is established [in the eye], and the visual organ likewise assists the solar orb by illuminating it. Alternatively, the sense organs such as the eyes lead the enjoyer—the master of the instruments—to their objects, and that [enjoyer], by way of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), leads to the sun.
The meaning is that it produces [the cognition] in such a way that there is a statement regarding the presence of the visual [cognition] therein. || 4 ||
And here, as a relevant digression, the observation of omens (ariṣṭa) is now being discussed.
How indeed can a man who has recognized the signs of his own end perform what is for his own welfare?

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "When he... as follows: "Ariṣṭa...". To the question, "How is this mentioned in the context of meditative worship (*upāsti*)?", he replies:

"Prāsaṅgikam" (incidental) means that this has come up in connection with the discussion of the person seen in the eye and the person in the sun. He states the purpose of mentioning that [person]: "jñātā" (the knower). ||1||
When the enjoyer is about to depart at the exhaustion of his lifespan in this world, he shall transcend.
He beholds the solar disc as pure as the lunar disc.

The rays do not converge upon the person of consciousness.
Through enjoyment, there is exhaustion for the enjoyer who has brought that karma under his control.

In that context, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "not this" (*nainaṃ*) for the purpose of establishing the reason: "the rays" (*raśmayaḥ*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the intellect (*buddhi*);
the person (*puruṣa*) conditioned by that is the individual soul (*jīva*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the rays are understood. || 7 ||
Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Ṭīkā on the Vārtika-commentary on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. The cumulative number of verses from the beginning is 10,572.
Now begins the seventh Brāhmaṇa:
The body is conceived as consisting of the Vyāhṛtis, corresponding to the two eyes and the sun.
Now, for the sake of accomplishing the meditation upon that very one whose name is Truth, [the following is said]. || 1 ||

He states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa: "The body," etc. He states the result of this conceptualization: "Of that," etc.; that is to say, for the sake of establishing its worship, the Vyāhṛtis are to be meditated upon as constituting the body. The word "atha" (now) serves to introduce the commencement of another Brāhmaṇa. || 1 ||
The secret name (upaniṣad) of that very Brahman is said to be twofold.
When these two chariots stand still, that which was obscured by the gods becomes clearly visible.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Its secret name (upaniṣad)" by saying "of that very [name]. He states the fruit of giving it a name by saying "Because one calls out to Brahman. The connection is: "it becomes directly propitious. || 2 ||
It is held that this [word] "ahan" is derived either from the root *han* (to strike) or from the root *hā* (to abandon).
By that [means], one destroys evil and abandons it; of this there is no doubt. || 3 ||
Thus ends the seventh Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

He indicates the manner of derivation for the two words *aharahaḥ* and *iti*. Regarding the word *hanter*: [it is derived] either from the root *han* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, or from the root *hā* (to abandon).

When the vowel shortening (*hrasvatva*) and the elision of the suffix (*ṭilopa*) have been applied to the prefix (*upasarga*), the word "ahar" is formed from those very two [roots] preceded by the prefix "āṅ."

The meaning is that when the suffix *ḍam* is applied to the two roots, and the preceding prefix undergoes shortening and so forth as before, the word *aham* (I) is produced. He states the fruit for one who meditates on Truth as qualified by these two names, beginning with the words "He slays," etc. The word "evil" (*pāpmānam*) refers to sin. Thus ends the seventh Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika-ṭīkā.

Now begins the eighth Brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "consisting of mind" (manomaya) refers to another aspect of that very same Brahman.
For now, the meditation upon [the Self] as qualified by the limiting adjunct of the internal organ (svānta) is being described. || 1 ||

He states another Brāhmaṇa passage: "Consisting of mind" (manomaya). The meaning of the word "then" (atha) is: "as in the case of the meditation on [the Self] as qualified by limiting adjuncts such as Truth (satya). || 1 ||
Due to mental conceit and ignorance, this person is composed of mind.
Or if it is perceived by the mind through the manifestation within the mind. || 2 ||
Luster is light, the stainless radiance; that is truth because of its indestructibility.
The statement beginning with "In that" (tasmin) and so forth is for the purpose of establishing the previously mentioned location. || 3 ||
He explains the words beginning with "the mind" (*manaḥ*) and so forth. The cause for that identification (*abhimāna*) with the Self is stated as "due to ignorance" (*ajñānāt*).

By the word "pure" (*amalam*), he excludes the illumination of inert matter (*jaḍaprakāśa*). He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "in that" (*tasmin*) and so forth. Regarding the passage beginning with "in that," this sentence is intended to include the distant location of the heart (*hṛdaya*), rather than abandoning the previously mentioned locations of the eye and the sun; nor is it [contradicted] by that.
The meaning is that the sense has already been conveyed here by the mention of a previously unmentioned quality. || 2 || 3 ||
The state of having the size of rice and other grains arises from the delimitation by the limiting adjuncts of the intellect.
By virtue of being infinite in itself and by its own authority, it possesses the nature of the primordial Lord of all.
Thus ends the eighth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.
How can there be subtlety in the full *pratīc* (the inner self), as in the statement "as subtle as a grain of rice," and so forth? To this he says: "Buddhi... [and so on].

That [subtlety] is not joined with being the Lord of all and so forth, for one equal to an atom cannot possess such a nature; to this he says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). How is there infinity? He says: "From scripture" (*mānāt*), based on such Vedic texts as "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *amānāt* (from non-measurement). Regarding its being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatve*)—
The meaning is: "not because of being devoid of measure. || 4 ||
Thus ends the eighth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Ṭīkā on the Bhāṣyavārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad.

Now begins the ninth Brāhmaṇa:
another mode of meditation upon that very same Brahman who has lightning as his body.
Furthermore, it is established by the Śruti for the sake of the total destruction of all sins. || 1 ||

He states the purport of another Brāhmaṇa passage: "Lightning," etc. The word "atha" (now) serves to introduce the subject matter of another Brāhmaṇa passage, and it should be construed first. || 1 ||
It is joined with lightning; indeed, it is called "lightning" because of its piercing nature.
This form [of the word] is derived from the root *dyati*, which signifies the act of breaking or splitting.

He states the literal meaning with the words beginning "Lightning" (*vidyut*). What the Brāhmaṇas say—that lightning is Brahman—is appropriate; for it is called "lightning" (*vidyut*) because of its "piercing" (*vidāna*), and Brahman also shatters the evil of the practitioner; therefore, the meaning is that it should be lightning. To explain how lightning is thus [Brahman], he indicates the etymological derivation of the word "lightning" with the words "from *dyati*. Therefore, the remainder of the sense is that it is fitting that lightning is of such a nature. ||2||
It destroys all the blinding darkness in an instant.
Just as lightning [flees], so shall evil depart from one who worships that [Self] from us. || 3 ||
Thus ends the ninth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.
He explains the statement regarding the fruit: "Tamas" (darkness). There is no tautology because the term refers to well-known darkness caused by clouds.

Alternatively, the word *tamas* is connected with the word *pāpman* (evil). The construction is as follows: that Brahman, being meditated upon, shatters for us—the meditator—the evil rooted in darkness which is the obstacle to attaining the gods. || 3 ||
Thus ends the ninth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Commentary on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Vārtika-Ṭīkā.

Now begins the tenth Brāhmaṇa.
Herein is stated another mode of meditation upon that very same Brahman.
Now, through the application of the cow of speech as a limiting adjunct, for the sake of great fruit. || 1 ||

He states the intended meaning of another Brāhmaṇa passage: "tasyaiva" (of that very same). The word "atha" (now/then), however, is as before. The word "iha" (here) is a statement by the Brāhmaṇa. "Consisting of speech" refers to the cow as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); that is to say, by means of its connection with that [speech]. || 1 ||
In this context, the word "speech" (vāk) should be understood as the three Vedas, not as the places of articulation, the organs of production, and so forth.
The utterance of "svāhā" and other such ritual elements are not found anywhere else outside of the three Vedas.

He explains the meanings of the words with the passage beginning "Speech," etc. By the word "etc.," the mention of deities is intended. The reason for this is given as "the utterance of *svāhā*," etc. The phrase "in certain cases" means in specific locations, instruments, and deities. || 2 ||
This triple Veda nourishes everything by means of its breasts, namely the utterances of *svāhā* and so forth.
One should always worship that Bhāratī as "the Cow" by means of that [mantra]. || 3 ||

He provides the scriptural passage that states the reason for meditating on the threefold speech as a cow: "The threefold... and so forth. It means that which nourishes (*dhayate*) or flows forth (*kṣarati*). || 3 ||
From what does that cow flow? This is now being explained.
By the statement "She has two breasts," the breasts are likewise described.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "To her two... by way of a question: "From whom? The word "this" refers to the mention of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "To her... as follows: "And they are told," meaning that they are like the recipients. || 4 ||
Its bull should likewise be known as Prāṇa; from that, it is produced.
For one who is without breath, speech does not exist; even speech is uttered by means of force.

He states the meaning of the phrase "her breath is the bull" with the word "bull. He says that it is like a worldly bull [is related] to a worldly cow. He says "likewise" (tathā). The reason for this is stated with "therefore" (tasmāt). He explains the dependence of the activity of speech upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the words "of one who is breathless" (*aprāṇasya*). The sense of the particle *api* is that it is just as other actions depend upon strength (*bala*). ||5||
Because it is the cause for the flow of speech, the mind becomes like a calf to the cow.
Whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that very thing one expresses with speech.
He states the meaning of the phrase "the mind is the calf" with the word "speech. He establishes the reason with the words "whatever... (verse 6).
The fruit of the aforementioned meditation is the state of having the nature of Brahman as one's own self.
This is understood even from the lack of specification in the statement "in whatever manner. || 7 ||
Thus ends the tenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.
Fearing that it would be improper to state that [meditation] leads to a great fruit if no fruit is heard of when meditation is not intended to be taught, he says: "As has been stated.
It should be understood that what is intended here is the passage beginning with "As one acts...," and not the mere form of the words or their euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*). || 7 ||
Thus ends the tenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

concerning another form of meditation upon this very Self, which assumes a body within the belly.
Then, by means of the scripture stating "This is fire," it is enjoined with effort.

He states the purport of another Brāhmaṇa passage: "Another meditation" means that effort [is made] toward the statement of the immediacy of the object of meditation. || 1 ||
Because she is designated by the term "Vaiśvānara" in a general sense.
That which is expressed by the statement "he who is within" is stated as its qualification. || 2 ||

One might ask: since the purpose of the meditation is accomplished by the mere statement "this is Agni Vaiśvānara," what is the point of adding "who is this" and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Vaiśvānara... The meaning is that the qualification is intended to specify the fire within the body (the gastric fire). || 2 ||
This must be the roar of that fire; cover your ears so as not to hear it.
The direct manifestation of the object of worship is described in the form of a sound. || 3 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*). Regarding "of that": it means "having covered," that is, having concealed [the ears] with both hands. "That which is heard" (*yacchruti*) means "that which is the hearing of that. For what purpose is this sound pointed out? Because the light within the belly (*kaukṣeyaṃ jyotiḥ*) is what must be made manifest here as Brahman.
Since that which is conditioned by those [attributes] is what is to be meditated upon, he says regarding that: "As the object of meditation" (upāsya). || 3 ||
And here, the observation of omens (ariṣṭadarśana) is now stated as a supplementary topic.
"The man who does not hear this sound has his death near at hand. || 4 ||
Thus ends the eleventh Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

[The author] explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "When he goes" (*sa yadaiti*) by saying "Ariṣṭa," etc. Here, the word "here" (*atra*) refers to the sentence under discussion. This is incidental, arising from the context of the "village" (*ghoṣa*).

"Passed away" is the meaning of *gatam*. The word *atha* signifies the immediate succession following the presentation of the object of worship (*upāsya*). Regarding how one who has recognized the signs of death (*ariṣṭa*) [should act], what was stated previously should be kept in mind. || 4 ||
Thus ends the eleventh Brāhmaṇa in the Commentary on the Vārttika to the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. 11.

Since it was not mentioned previously, the goal and the fruit must now be stated.
This is the supreme traditional teaching (āgama) regarding all forms of worship. || 1 ||

He states the purport of another Brāhmaṇa passage: "The destination," etc. The distinction is that while the destination is universal, the fruit pertains to the unmentioned subject. The reason for this is stated: "In the previous [passage]," etc. || 1 ||
When the wise man departs from the body due to the exhaustion of his lifespan, he transcends.
He, possessing great speed, approaches as swiftly as the wind that is difficult to pierce.
For one who has attained this for the sake of worldly enjoyments, the vital breath departs.
How large a hole could Marut give, according to the measurement of the space of a chariot wheel? (3)

One should know the bherī and the dundubhi; by means of these, the practitioner ascends upwards. || 4 ||
By the power of meditation, he perceives that world as Prajāpati, as Brahman.
And [he attained] the majesty of the Aśoka tree, which is free from suffering and its causes. || 5 ||
And he dwells in this world for eternal and perpetual years.
This is the fruit of those meditations whose specific results were not mentioned previously.

He explains the words beginning with "he steps out" (*utkrāmati*) and so forth. This means that it departs from him and creates an opening within his own self. Now begins the thirteenth Brāhmaṇa.
When one afflicted by a disease such as fever suffers, he is indeed tormented by that illness.
That supreme austerity should be contemplated by one who desires to attain the highest world.

Certain meditations on Brahman have been described as fruitful; now, desiring to point out certain meditations on what is not Brahman that are likewise fruitful, he introduces another Brāhmaṇa with the words: "Fever, etc. (1).
Possessed by diseases and seizing spirits, one experiences unbearable suffering.
Therefore, for one who does not perform medical treatment, austerity indeed becomes supreme. || 2 ||

The word *vyādhi* (disease) establishes that the suffering associated with disease constitutes austerity (*tapas*). Regarding the term *vyādhi*: the first [mention] refers to a connection, while the second is well-known;
this is the distinction. The particle *hi* indicates direct experience. The meaning of the word *ataḥ* (hence) is suffering in general.
He specifies the qualified practitioner (*adhikārin*) with the word *tat* (that). Here, one should understand non-censoriousness and non-despair as being included. || 2 ||
"The officiating priests or others shall carry me, dead, from the house to the forest."
That too is the supreme object of meditation, which is commensurate with the stage of the forest-dweller.
This indeed is the supreme austerity; he states the purport of the passage beginning with "him who is deceased" as follows: "they carry him out. || 3 ||

And whatever food my kinsmen place upon the fire for me as a deceased one, that too [is mine].
Even that [state] is to be meditated upon as supreme, because it is equal to the penetration of fire.
He states the meaning of another sentence: "placing [the fuel]" (*abhyādadhati*). The word "then" (*atha*) expresses the immediate sequence following the carrying of the firewood to the forest.
One instance of the word "that" (*tat*) is connected with the ablative case in the sense of "therefore. || 4 ||
Whatever is appropriate for anyone is called by that very name in the speech of the world.
Such is the fruit of austerity, of the ascetic, and of the immersion in the sacred fire.
Thus ends the thirteenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

One might object that since the scriptural texts everywhere declare the fruit to be the same—namely, "he indeed conquers the highest world"—the meditations must be identical. Anticipating this, the author says: "It is appropriate.

For whatever fruit belongs to each individual among austerity, asceticism, and entering the fire, that very same fruit is appropriate for each of these meditations mentioned here; therefore, because the word *loka* (world) is used here in its distinct senses, there is a difference between the meditations. || 5 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth Brāhmaṇa in the commentary on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Vārtika-Ṭīkā. || 13 ||
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning is 10,604. Now begins the fourteenth Brāhmaṇa.
It explains that "Food is Brahman," as another meditation similar to the previous one.
For the sake of accomplishing the noble fruit, its determination is made through reasoning. || 1 ||

Having described the meditations on [the Brahman] as food (*anna*) through three sections (*kaṇḍikā*), the author states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa while continuing the very same meditations on the Brahman under discussion. "Food" (*annam*): the meaning is that the subsequent text is intended to enjoin a meditation on the Brahman—conditioned by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of food and vital breath (*prāṇa*)—as characterized by two specific qualities (*guṇa*), namely *virat* and *mita*, which yields a specific fruit. How is it determined that the Brahman is to be meditated upon in such a manner?
Regarding this, he says: "Of that," [verse 1].
Some wise ones say that food alone is the supreme Brahman.
That should be understood accordingly: food decays without water. || 2 ||
Others say that Brahman is the vital breath (prāṇa), but that too is not to be accepted as before.
For without food, the vital breath quickly undergoes desiccation. || 3 ||

Demonstrating the very logic, he analyzes the words beginning with "food" (*anna*). Thinking that for Brahman, which is eternally established, neither moistening nor drying out is possible—based on such Smṛti texts as "This [Self] is not to be cut"—he says: "It is moistened. With the intention that there can be no drying up of Brahman, who is both the elements and their products, because it would contradict the Smṛti stating its indestructibility, he says: "From food."

Since the state of being Brahmā is not logically possible for either of these individually.
Because they manifest together, they both attain the state of Brahman.
He explains the passage beginning with "But they indeed," etc., as follows: "the office of the Brahman priest. || 4 ||
Having reflected upon this, Mātṛda indeed said to his father:
"Out of what cause? and so forth; he was thus delighted because he did not perceive that fault. (5)

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "taddha sma" (That indeed...). "Tadetad" means: having determined that Brahman, conditioned by the limiting adjuncts of food and vital breath, is the object of meditation; this indicates that the following is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). When it is asked, "What did he say?", he cites the subsequent sentence. Why? He states the reason for that: "taddoṣasya," meaning: because of the defect [arising] from meditating on Brahman as described when it is devoid of its qualities. || 1 ||
What indeed is beneficial for one who knows thus, since it is the cause for attaining all that is beneficial?
Or we might do what is unkind to him, since he has warded off all that is unkind.

He explains the statement: "What indeed... The sense is that one who has worshipped food, vital breath, and Brahman has accomplished all that was to be done; for him, there is nothing further to be attained nor anything to be abandoned. || 6 ||
With the words "Do not do so," the father restrained him with his hand.
Who, being inherently powerless, could attain supremacy by coming together with others?
He states the meaning of "sa ha sma" and so forth with the words "pāṇinā. He states the purport of "kaḥ svid... and so forth with the words "saṃbhūya.
The meaning is that since food and breath, individually, lack the fitness for being Brahman, no one is able to know them as such even when they are combined. || 7 ||
In this world, power is not observed even in a conjunction for those who lack it inherently.
Even when conjoined, two people born blind lack the power to perceive forms.

He provides an illustration for the point that even when joined with another thing that is itself incapable, there is no capacity in that which is inherently incapable, by saying "svataḥ" (inherently). ||8||
Therefore, in whatever manner, it is precisely the possessor of power and the portions of the object of consumption that [are unified].
The power of satisfaction would exist here as well, upon the union of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the nature of food.
It being established that there is no power even when those lacking power are joined together, he states the conclusion supported by an illustration: "Therefore," etc.

Just as morsels of food, which are themselves inherently capable, possess the power to produce satiety only when combined, so too the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and food (*anna*), being inherently capable, would possess the power of becoming Brahman through their mutual connection. This is the meaning. || 9 ||
If it has not attained the state of being supreme, how can it be called supreme?
The statement that each [of these] possesses power is expressed by the words beginning with "vī" (the suffix vi). || 10 ||
How then is it that these two possess causal capacity? He asks this with the words "If not... He introduces the response beginning with "Therefore... by stating "Each individually. || 10 ||

But for the sake of explanation, regarding the prefix *vi-*: food indeed is called *vīti*.
For indeed, by means of this, even those things that are impure attain the state of being a living being.
"All beings are pervaded by it," thus is food called.
"By that [breath], the vital force (prāṇa) is always satisfied; thus it is called 'ram' here.
He states the intended meaning of the word "vīti" as "food" (*anna*). To provide an explanation, he clarifies that very explanation with the words "In food" (*anne*).
All beings are dependent upon food; for whatever reason they attain the state of being living beings (*bhūtatva*), by that [reason] they [attain it] through food.

By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of "viṣṭāni" (entered), it is said that *vat* is food which has become the support of all beings; this is to be construed with the word "sadā" (always). The meaning of the particle "hi" is that the fact of the mind being the support of all beings is well-known in the world. He states the meaning of "ram" and so forth as "prāṇa" (the vital breath); the word "iha" refers to the statement of the sentence. || 11 || 12 ||
For when there is pride, people always find delight in the things seen in this world.
Because the elements are said to delight (ram) [in it], the wise therefore call the vital breath (prāṇa) "ra" as well. || 13 ||

Establishing that very point, he explains the passage beginning with "for in the vital breath" (*prāṇe hi*) and so forth. Regarding the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*): the meaning of the particle *api* is "just as it was stated that food is [the source of] strength. || 13 ||
In this way, there would be [a distinction] between food and breath, which are inherently possessed of qualities.
For that which is declared as the statement of the fruit is indeed the attainment of the supreme state through their coming together.

He states the fruit of describing the possession of qualities by those two [the sun and the moon] with the words "svataḥ" (by itself). The word "hi" (for) indicates the previously mentioned illustration. He introduces the scriptural statement regarding the fruit for one who meditates on Brahman as described, with the words "phala" (fruit). The construction is as follows: that very scripture which was cited beginning with "sarvāṇi ha vā asmin" (all indeed [enter] into him) is the statement of the fruit for the meditator under discussion. || 14 ||
All beings enter into that Prajāpati who has become the non-being.
They take delight even in living beings; this is the fruit for one who worships [them]. || 15 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

He clarifies the statement regarding the result with the words "entering," etc. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that it is extremely well known that the stability and departure of living beings depend upon food and vital breath. || 19 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad. 14.

For it is seen that for one who knows thus, there is no non-eating whatsoever.
The fruit shall be union with the vital breath (prāṇa-sāyujya), for indeed, everything is his food.

One might ask: why should the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) not also be the master of the instruments? To this he says: "For they consist of that. Since the instruments are dependent upon the individual soul (*jīva*) for their origin, subsistence, and dissolution, that soul alone is their master; this is the meaning based on such scriptural passages as, "As he departs... (*tamutkrāmantam*). He states the purport of the sentence concerning the fruit: "For one who knows thus... (*evamvide hi*). For when the knower possesses the nature of the self of the vital breath, it is possible for him to have all things as his food.

"One should surround him with water before eating," according to the Śruti.

He states the doubt to be refuted by the subsequent sentence: "With water," etc. Since it is heard in scripture that "one envelops the breath with water" both before eating and after having eaten, this constitutes a scriptural injunction for the drinking of water; and since that scriptural sipping (*ācamana*) is distinct from the Smṛti-based sipping and is not obtained from any other source, it must be enjoined.
Therefore, the meaning is that this sentence is an injunction for that [scriptural sipping]. || 36 ||
If it were postulated that the purpose of the injunction is [merely] for the sake of the ritual act, then the scripture would have only its primary meaning.
If the rule regarding the acquisition of clothing were indeed [to apply], then its connection with the fruit would be logical. (37)

Anticipating the objection—"Since it is stated in the present tense as 'he sips' (*ācāman*), how can there be an injunction?"—the author says: "The scripture" (*śāstram*). He says "it is proper" (*yukta*) to show that there is an injunction because [the act] possesses a result. If there is an injunction for the sipping of water, then [it serves as] a garment for the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The construction is as follows: "Gain is not connected with a fruitless result, because it is connected with the injunction. || 37 ||
Moreover, certain followers of specific Vedic branches clearly recite it as being of the nature of an injunction.
According to the view of some reciters of the Veda, the consumption of water [is performed] by means of the mother-mantra. || 38 ||

Furthermore, because of the scriptural injunction in the *Chāndogya*—"One should sip water before eating and one should sip water after eating"—this rule must also be accepted here, according to the principle that all Vedānta texts convey the same teaching (*sarvavedāntapratyayanyāya*). Thus he says: "And some [hold this]. Moreover, some maintain that the sipping of water (*ācamana*) prescribed by the mantras, "The immortal is the under-layer" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*) and "The immortal is the cover" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*), should be performed both before and after eating; others, however, hold that it should be done without the mantras, as an independent rite (*apūrva*).
They say that it is to be performed; he says that there is a treasure within it, by means of the mantra. || 38 ||
And some declare that the perception of clothing is like the perception of food.
Since drinking water for the sake of purification is observed here through the context and other indicators.
There would be the consequence of eating all things unfit for consumption, if ritual action were intended to be performed.
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika. || 1 ||

When it has been argued as a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the Vedic (*śrauta*) sipping of water (*ācamana*) must be enjoined here as something previously unestablished, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Just like the sight of food" (*annadarśanavat*). The meaning is "according to the principle of *miti*. He addresses one who disputes the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) by saying "all," etc. If the eating of all food were enjoined for the knower of the vital breath (*prāṇavid*), then even garlic and other such things that are not to be eaten would follow as being edible;

this would contradict prohibitions such as, "Those who eat what is not to be eaten become worms," and so forth. Nor is there a prohibition elsewhere for the knower of the vital breath, because there is no basis for him to consume everything.

The meaning is that, because there is no contradiction with the general prohibition [against eating all things] since the statement praising knowledge cannot be authoritative in its literal sense, no one may eat anything at will except in an emergency; for it is observed that such permission regarding all food applies only when life is in danger. || 39 ||
