The total number of verses from the beginning is 10,773.
Now begins the second Brāhmaṇa.
That which was not previously considered [as such] due to the predominance of the subject matter [is now treated].
I shall now state here that which is to be said, according to the section on the Khilakāṇḍa.

He restates the meaning of the *kāṇḍa* in order to explain its connection with the subsequent *Brāhmaṇa*. "That which... [etc.]—the meaning is this: whatever subject matter was not possible to state as the primary focus in either the *Karmakāṇḍa* or the *Jñānakāṇḍa*, that is to be stated in this *kāṇḍa*; for this is a *khilakāṇḍa* (supplementary section), commenced for the purpose of stating what has not been previously mentioned. Alternatively, that which was previously [intended] to be stated in the *Jñānakāṇḍa*...

It is not considered [as the primary subject] because the substance (vastu) is predominant; rather, it is the form of the action (kriyārūpa) that is to be expressed here, since this [work] was undertaken for the sake of that—this is the meaning. || 1 ||
In the seventh chapter, it was stated that there is a longing for the path arising from fire.
In that context, it is heard as "supatha" (the good path), which is a qualification of the path according to the sacred revelation.
Now, at the conclusion of the preceding chapter, he restates what was said regarding the Brahmin’s purpose, which had not yet been explicitly stated: "In the seventh," etc.

Having raised the doubt as to what would happen even if one on the verge of death were to pray for fire while performing a collective rite (samuccaya), he shows its status as a qualifying attribute: "By the good path," etc. (2).
When there is both possibility and deviation between the qualifier and the qualified, [the qualification is meaningful].
Just as a qualifier is observed in the world, let it be seen in this case as well. (3)

Nevertheless, one might ask: "What follows from this? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the case of possibility. In the expression "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), since the qualifier and the qualified are possible [together], and because the qualified could potentially deviate [from the qualifier] in the absence of the qualifier, the qualifier "blue" is seen to be purposeful; likewise, in the case of "lead me by a good path" (*supathā naya*), since deviation is possible, the qualifier is understood to be purposeful.
The meaning is "that which. || 3 ||
Therefore, "the good path" is appropriate, since many paths are possible.
Therefore, the paths, which have karma as their cause, must be described with their specific qualifications. || 4 ||
"In that case, let this too be a differentiator"; to this he replies with the words "supathā" (by a good path).

The meaning of the word "tataḥ" (thence) is the differentiating nature of the qualifier. He states the conclusion: "Therefore," [it is called] "Brāhmaṇa," in order to designate those many paths which appear by virtue of their respective qualifiers. || 4 ||
The paths to the south, the north, and downwards are prescribed for those [actions] that are enjoined and prohibited respectively.
The results of the two types of karma must be stated for the sake of establishing detachment from them.
To the question, "Who are those travelers whose description is intended? he says: "The southern [path]. He states their essential nature:
"Those for whom [rites] are prescribed. He states the purpose of mentioning them: "They are to be described. The word "tat" (that) refers to the fruit of ritual action. || 5 ||
Not for one who is not dispassionate toward all worldly goals of human life in their entirety.
Therefore, for the sake of liberation, that [truth] is taught with effort by the Śruti.

If it is argued that the statement regarding dispassion (*vairāgya*) is of no avail, he says "no," and so forth. When the various states of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-gati-bheda*), which abound in suffering, have been described, dispassion is established for the discerning person (*vivekin*);

and that [dispassion] is the cause of the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*). Therefore, the meaning is that the Śruti intends to convey dispassion through the discrimination of action (*karma-viveka*). || 6 ||
They are not able to accomplish actions that fulfill all desires.
Or rather, it is for the purpose of warding off all misfortunes, since the fruit [of such practice] is exceedingly meager.

Anticipating the objection that since all human goals arise solely through the power of karma, it is not appropriate to have detachment toward the objects of its fruition, he says: "They are able. (7)
Action is not the cause of liberation, nor is fire the remover of the fever of burning.
Birth is determined by karmas; if there is birth, how can there be liberation? (8)
Anticipating the objection that because those [meditations] have liberation as their fruit, the reason [of the argument] is unestablished, he says: "No. He proves that very point with the words:
"From actions" (karmabhyaḥ). || 8 ||
Neither by action does the inner self become lesser or greater.
Thus, as if raising up an arm, the proclamation has been made by the Vedāntas.
Regarding the statement that in liberation, which is of the nature of the Self, there is no fruit of action, he states the authoritative proof: "Not by action," etc. (9).
No sacrificial fees go there; it is attained by knowledge alone.
Thus it was proclaimed by the illustrious Yājñavalkya with an open throat. || 10 ||
In that very context, he cites a scriptural authority: "Not there," [it is said]. || 10 ||
Therefore, by those desiring liberation, [the path] which is opposed to arising and so forth [should be investigated].
Having abandoned all actions, one should then take refuge with one's whole being in the knowledge of the oneness of the Self.

But you do not know the specific characteristics of these two, such as their departure from the body and so forth.

Thus he uttered such words as "this question," "your reply," and so forth.

This is the unprecedented transformation resulting from the ritual known as the Agnihotra.

Taking that very [teaching] as the support here, for the sake of accomplishing the vision of its summit.

The meaning is that the word "fire" (agni) refers to the tastes. The particle "hi" signifies that the dependence of cooking upon fire and the dependence of transformation upon cooking are well-known in the world. || 19 ||
For the father, having performed the graduation ceremony for his son who had completed all branches of learning, [sent him forth].

Desiring to explain the words of the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*), he provides this introductory context (*bhūmikā*). Regarding the word "completed" (*samāptā*): by the word "entirely" (*aśeṣa*), there is a reference to the Vedic declarations along with the Purāṇas and Nyāya. The particle "hi" is used to reveal that Śvetaketu’s clarity of knowledge was understood by others as well. For the purpose of removing his doubt, the father’s speech beginning with "it is completed" constitutes the general rule (*utsarga*) for establishing his independence.

He shows Gautama's intention as he lets go [of his pride] with the words "on the touchstone. "Touchstone" refers to the effort—the application of the mind toward the stabilization of the awakening of intelligence—through persistent inquiry into those things which serve as the locus for testing gold. For the learning among the Brāhmaṇas of Pañcāla is indeed exceedingly renowned.
He returned to that very assembly from there, filled with haste. || 22 ||

Anticipating the objection—given that there were assemblies of learned men elsewhere, why did Śvetaketu come specifically to the assembly of the Pañcālas?—the author explains the words [of the text], beginning with "prasiddha" (well-known). The word "hi" (for) has the sense of "yasmāt" (because); it indicates an excess of desire for victory.
The word "tvareta" (he would hasten). || 22 ||

Such conduct as this is not observed in the world among one who has been properly instructed. || 27 ||
He explains the question: "Have you been instructed? The absence of sandhi (visandhi) is for the sake of clarifying the two alternatives.

"Certainly, I have been instructed by my father; do you not see my majesty?"
If you have any doubt, ask me regarding all those who are wise in your eyes.

He states the meaning of "Om" and so forth with the words "Certainly. Regarding the instruction, he states the sign that makes even a king fit for knowledge with the words "Is it not? Thinking, "My victory does not reside in them alone, but in you as well," he says, "Ask. || 28 ||
Thus, when the king has accepted the instruction according to what was said, [the teacher should act].
Then the king questioned Śvetaketu on five questions in succession.

The passage beginning with "Do you know? introduces a series of questions. The word "thus" (*evam*) refers to the manner in which the instruction was given by the father, as expressed by the King in the statement beginning with "I have been instructed," provided that this instruction was indeed received by Śvetaketu.
By the word "thus" (*evam*), he points to the assent (*om iti*). The reason for that assent is indicated by the fact that the instruction performed by the father had already taken place previously.

If you have been instructed, then speak to the subjects regarding death, even though it is common to all.
Just as they fall into error through the various divisions of divergent paths. || 30 ||

Just as by what means and by this cause the subjects have died.

Always by many great beings who are constantly moving forward.

By means of these two, all this proceeds according to one's karma and according to what has been heard.
In the midst of heaven and earth, he meets the world for the enjoyment of its activity.

He excludes any other path for those who are qualified [for this journey]. Regarding the phrase "by those two," he states there which path leads to which destination with the words "as follows. The connection is that the world moves between heaven and earth for the sake of experiencing the results of karma. || 42 ||
Not even a single point from the multitude of questions you have posed has been explained as something to be known.
Having said, "Do not ask me a question from this point forward," he indeed sat with his head hanging down.

He states the meaning of "I am not," and so forth: "from what you have said. He expresses what is indicated by the word *cana*: "Do not [look] at me. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) has the purpose of referring back to ignorance. The particle *hi* serves to illuminate that the state of having one's head cast down is governed by the shame produced by ignorance. ||43||
Having beheld him whose every impurity had been shaken off and whose pride was stilled, [he spoke].
The king invited him to stay, saying, "Please remain here."
1. "In that case, there is the cognition of extreme differentiation.
[Vol. 3, p.
884] 2. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 2019.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "atha enām" (now this) as follows: "nirdhūta" (shaken off). He states the reason for the absence of turbidity: "śānta" (tranquil). He provides experiential evidence for that: "samīkṣya" (having perceived). || 44 ||
Out of anger, he spoke those words for the purpose of making Vasati dwell there.
Disregarding [him], he fled to where his father Gautama was staying.
He explains the passage beginning with "anādṛtya" and so forth: "hrītaḥ" (being modest). || 45 ||
Then, having approached his father, he spoke with anger and malice,
uttering words that were inconsistent with what had preceded and followed.

He states the meaning of "taṃ hovāca" (he said to him) with the word "prāpya" (having reached). He gives the reason for the king's anger and his failure to understand the stated matter with the word "atha" (then).

What did he say accompanied by indignation? That is expressed by "iti vāva" (thus indeed). The meaning is that Śvetaketu spoke these words, beginning with "iti vāva," to his father due to the confusion arising from the perceived contradiction between the preceding and following statements. || 46 ||
The phrase "iti" is a reference to what has been stated; this dialogue was prompted by the king.
"Because it is not perceived, it is said 'indeed' (kila); for its comprehension arises from inference. (47)

He explains the meaning of the word *iti*: "itīty ukteti" (the word *iti* means "having been said"). By the word *ukta* (said), either the collection of questions or the father’s speech is denoted. He explains the meaning of the word *vāva*: "vākovākyam" (dialogue). For *vākovākya* refers to a treatise on logic (*tarkaśāstra*);
by that term here, the collection of questions spoken by the king is indicated. Taking that as a sign, the father’s speech—of the form "you have completed all branches of knowledge"—is [implied].

The meaning is that it is remembered as being contradictory. He states the sense of the word "kila" (it is said) with the phrase "because of the absence of direct perception. By the mark of not knowing the answer to the question asked by the king, it is understood that the instruction given by the father was incorrect; for its incorrectness is not directly perceived, but rather the cognition of it arises solely from the aforementioned mark. Therefore, the intention is that the use of the word "kila" is appropriate. The falsity of the father's instruction is not directly perceived—
He establishes this by means of inference: "From inference" (anumānāt). || 47 ||
From the mark of being overwhelmed by the king’s words, it is inferred that "I have been deceived."
For one who has been instructed according to reality, there is no overcoming by anything else.

[Objection: Surely a father instructs his son only for his benefit; how can it be suspected that such instruction is a mere semblance? To this he says: "O King," etc. The words "the father was deceived" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. One might suspect: "The instruction was given by the father, not a deception; rather, your subjugation by the king is due to your own fault. To this he says: "As it truly is. Therefore, it was not instructed as it truly is...
The word "establishment" (sthiti) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence]. || 48 ||
Why did you say that to me previously, without even having instructed me?
"I have been instructed as a son," he thought, "therefore I have been deceived. (49)

Although he did not provide instruction exactly as it should have been given, he nevertheless spoke thus—"That me"—out of the apprehension, "How have I deceived you, my son? The meaning is that by saying, "You have been instructed," even without having actually provided instruction, he has deceived me. || 49 ||

Tell me the reason why you have not been instructed.
"Therefore, he said to me, 'Five,' just as there was no instruction."

He states the meaning of "How so? and so forth: "How so? He states the purport of "Five" and so forth: "Five. The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is the immediate sequence following the father's question. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the son's speech indicates the absence of the father's instruction. || 10 ||
Which are those questions, my child, which you have not understood?
Being questioned by his father, he spoke briefly on the introductory points of the questions.

He states the meaning of another question posed by the father: "The questions," etc. He explains the meaning of "these," "hi," and so forth: "He asks," etc. The word "pratīka" refers to a partial quotation. The connection is: "He spoke briefly. || 51 ||
The king inquired about knowledge other than that of the Brahmins.
For indeed, there is nothing in the knowledge of a Brahmin that has been attained by you.

He [the author] states the meaning of the words "sa hovāca" (he said): "brāhmaṇa" etc. Now, one might suppose that the King’s question arose from ignorance because he thought, "Even though knowledge is to be attained by them, I still have something remaining"; to this he says: "na hi" (indeed not). || 52 ||
Keeping this in his heart, he replied, "It is not so."
Therefore, do not suspect me; for it was not said by me that "everything belongs to me."

He takes up the sentence beginning with "tathā" (so be it). Regarding the phrase "it etat" (this [is] that), he states its meaning: "mā śaṅkiṣṭhāḥ" (do not fear). The meaning of the word "tataḥ" (therefore) is: because all knowledge contained within the Brāhmaṇa has been entrusted to you. The particle "hi" is used to state another reason for the absence of fear, namely, the relationship between father and son. || 53 ||
Go there; we two shall go for the sake of attaining the mastery of that vidyā.
And having gone there to that king, we two shall dwell in celibacy (brahmacarya).
He states the meaning of "prehi" and so forth: "prehi. Therein, "tatra" refers to the royal capital. He states the fruit of going: "tadvidyā.

He shows the duty for that purpose: "and celibacy (brahmacarya). The connection is "we two in going. The locative case [in "pāṣāṇā vṛkṣeṣu"] is used in the sense of proximity, as in the expression "stones among the trees. || 54 ||
Let your honor go there yourself; I do not venture to go there.
Thus addressed by his son, he was overcome with grief and went to him himself.
Rising up in haste, he brought a seat for him.
He caused water to be brought for the purpose of providing the guest-offering (arghya) and the water for washing the feet (pādya).
Then the king, having honored him according to the scriptures, said to him:
"We grant you whatever boon or desire you wish for."
Then the seer spoke to the king for the sake of accomplishing his desired purpose.
Thus, a boon has been promised by you, even though it was not requested.
1. It is conceived.
[Vol.
3, page 886] 2. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 2021.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "bhavāneva" (you yourself) as follows: "yā tu" (as for that...). Fearing that the son might be suspected of being untrustworthy due to his transgression of his father’s command in speaking thus, he says: "hrītaḥ" (ashamed). The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is: whether it be after the honor [shown to him] or whether it be the sage's state of being a petitioner.
The king's fitness to speak is indicated by the indeclinable particle. The meaning of the second "atha" is: having obtained an opportunity by chance.

"Of the desired object," meaning the acquisition of knowledge; he qualifies the boon [by saying] "even though unasked," indicating that you should not follow the logic of the story where a Brahmin, having come himself to beg while being destitute, was granted a boon. || 59 || 56 ||
Let him be true to his promise here, regarding that which was promised by you in this place.
Give me the answer to the question which you spoke concerning my son.
Then the king also spoke these supreme words regarding the gods: "Thus it is among the gods."
"This boon has been granted among the gods; choose a boon from among humans."

He prepares the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) in order to introduce another statement: "Let it be so. The construction here is: "In this assembly, regarding that which has been promised by you—namely, 'let your honor be one whose promise is true' regarding this matter [already] promised"—[the opponent] says "Let it be so. Anticipating the king’s statement, "My promise is indeed unimpeded," he says: "Give! The word *atha* is used for the sake of emphasis. He explains the king’s statement.
"Regarding the divine [offerings]," thus [ends the section]. 19 || 60 ||
For one who possesses discernment, that which belongs to the divine realm should not be sought from the human.

But a human is fit to give and to receive; [one] superior to a human is not. Anticipating the objection that because such a being is difficult to find, he might be unobtainable even when requested, he says "Not indeed. Anticipating the further question of how, then, there can be a formal promise (pratijñā), he says "But a human," intending to speak of one who is superior to a human. || 61 ||
"I too possess all those human things that you wish to give."
It is understood by me alone, and also by you through another means of valid cognition.

Gautama, however, says: "Mine too. [The opponent] says: "It is known," meaning that although you possess wealth, it is not known by me; therefore, he speaks out of the apprehension that one might desire what belongs to another. [This is established] through other means of knowledge, such as the words of a reliable person (*āptavākya*). 62.
Nor do I desire that abundant wealth which already belongs to me.
Therefore, let the boon of the gods be granted to me; that [human boon] is not for me. || 63 ||

Fearing that he might think, "Even though wealth already exists, let more be requested for the sake of abundance," he says, "Not so. To the question, "What kind of boon, then, should be granted to you? he replies, "Therefore..."—meaning, because a human boon is not worthy of being requested.
He indicates that it is a divine boon that is worthy of being requested when he says, "There is none. (63)
Out of greed for abundant wealth obtained through limitless and boundless fate.
Do not become one who withholds gifts; having been a giver to us here, do not turn away.
Fearing that he might be unable to give it due to greed, he says: "Of much," etc. Even a vast amount of divine wealth, when being given—[variant:
*ka* and *kha* read *tīyo'tha*; *kha* reads *nuṣo varaḥ*].
[Vol. 3, page 887]

Raising the objection, "How can that which departs in due course be given away? Sureśvarācārya says, beginning with the word *ananta*: "Because it is infinite (*ananta*), it is boundless and devoid of end;
when given to another, it attains a preeminence that is exceedingly firm and distinct from human wealth. That indeed is true wealth."

The meaning of "tasya" (of him) is as follows: since you have become a donor to all these people seeking [your help], do not be miserly toward us alone; that is, even though you possess wealth, do not be a non-giver out of greed for the riches mentioned. This is the construction. || 64 ||
It is better for fate not to grant a boon at all than to refuse that twice-born man.
Having thus fallen into a state of misery, he spoke to him, saying, "I desire [initiation] at a sacred ford. || 65 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "sa vai gautama" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.9.3] as follows: "The divine" (daivam). The remainder [of the verse] means that [the teacher] is not able either to bestow or to refuse [the knowledge]. On one hand, the secrecy of the *vidyā* must be protected; on the other, since the twice-born is a petitioner and the king is the giver, [the knowledge should be imparted].
The reason for this is as follows: || 65 ||
"Knowledge is imparted through the proper channel (tīrtha), not through what is not the proper channel"—such is the traditional teaching (āgama).
Therefore, having gone to a sacred ford, you must receive knowledge from me.

To explain why the king spoke thus as if slighting the Brāhmaṇa, he says: "By the *tīrtha*. He shows the statement of Manu and others that knowledge should be given by a teacher to one who has approached him through any one of the six *tīrthas*, such as being a disciple; and that very same text states that even if requested, the teacher should not give it to one who is not a *tīrtha*.
The meaning is "he speaks. He states that the king’s speech is appropriate by relying on what has been said: "Since... (verse 66).
Then, reminded of the meaning of the scripture by the king, he replied, "I understand."
For it is by speech alone that those who are superior first approach those who are inferior; from that [speech] it proceeds.
Together with Upāyanakīya, he indeed lived the life of a religious student.
For he did nothing else, but repeatedly proclaimed, "I approach [the Lord]. || 68 ||

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "I approach" (*upaimi*) by saying, "the meaning of the scripture" (*śāstrārtham*). He establishes that the sage’s engagement in the practice of that [scripture] once he has been reminded of its meaning by the king is due to his being intent upon that purpose. Regarding the word "now" (*atha*): the second occurrence of the word *atha* has the sense of "likewise" (*tathā*). The construction is as follows: just as the one devoid of learning requested learning from the king, so too did he approach him. [Objection: But is this not contrary to the natural order?

Regarding the fact that a Brahmin approaches a king, he says there: "By means of speech. The meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that this approaching is well known among Uddālaka and others as being directed toward Aśvapati. The particle (*nipāta*) emphasizes the primacy of celibacy for the arising of knowledge. He explains that very point with the words: "I approach [you]. The word *hi* is used to establish the reason that there is no other duty to be performed. || 67 || 68 ||
Avoiding his own guilty self through prudent policy, the king—
He then sought forgiveness from that sage with the words, "It is not so."

He introduces the passage beginning with "He said," etc., [with the words] "sāparādham" (with fault). The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is immediate succession following such acts as approaching [a teacher]. ||69||
Your ancestors, the Grandfathers, were not arrogant toward those who had committed offenses.
They did not consider it so, just as you yourself [did not consider] those who were guilty.
1. ka. kha. 'tuṃ cāśaṃ | 2. ka. ga. tha || kṣām | [vol 3, page 888] 2.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 2023.

He explains the sentence: "mā na" (do not [slay] us). The meaning is: "Do not you destroy us who are innocent; just as your ancestors, our grandfathers, did not consider their own innocent ancestors to be at fault, so too may you not consider us, who are innocent, to be so. || 70 ||
Indeed, prior to being bestowed upon you, it must never at any time be subject to anyone else's command.
A virtuous woman does not dwell even with a Brahmin who is like Bṛhaspati himself. || 71 ||

One might object: "When Gautama approached the king among the Brāhmaṇas and requested this knowledge, how was he not at fault for not granting it? Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "Because of your gift. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used because this knowledge is well-known to belong only to the Kṣatriyas. Although previously this [knowledge] did not dwell in a Brāhmaṇa who lacked the requisite fitness, nevertheless—
Anticipating the doubt that she might be considered suitable in some respect, he says: "Directly" (sākṣāt). || 71 ||
Even though she is thus protected, I shall nevertheless speak to her directly.
O King, who would be able to refuse a Brahmin when he speaks thus? (72)

Having explained the concealment of the knowledge, he says "Thus" (evam), fearing that you might lose your promise by engaging in the rejection of me. He says "To reject" (pratyākhyātum) with the following doubt: "Even though I, seeking this knowledge, have come into your presence, if your mind does not become gracious toward giving it, then let there be a rejection. || 72 ||
It must be explained: for what reason was this sequence broken by saying "asau" (this one)?
Because the fourth question is predominant here, the sequence is altered.
He asks for the reason why the fourth question is determined first by the passage beginning with "That world, indeed, is the fire.
[The text says: "Asau" (that). He provides the answer: "Of the question," etc. The word "here" (iha) refers to the entire collection of questions. || 73 ||
Because origination is dependent upon that [cause], so too is stability dependent upon birth.
Because the departure [from the body] occurs upon the cessation of the state [of life], the sequence was distinguished by the Śruti. || 74 ||

By demonstrating its primacy through its importance, he establishes a departure from the sequential order [of the text]. Regarding the phrase "because of origination": since the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of human beings depend upon the resolution of the fourth question, that [question] is primary. Thus, while it holds the first place, the sequence of the reading (pāṭhakrama) is disregarded in favor of the sequence of meaning (arthakrama); this is the sense. || 74 ||
"This person shall belong to that world from afar"—such is this saying.
Even the worldly speech of people is perceived through forms such as smoke from a sacrificial fire.
The word "vai" (verily) serves for the purpose of recollection, and fire [arises] from its transformation.
For the Āhavanīya fire exists as the very self of the heavenly world. || 76 ||

He explains the words by breaking the sequence: "from afar" (dūrataḥ). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "for the sake of remembering the well-known heavenly world. Anticipating the doubt as to how that [heavenly world] can be a transformation of fire, he says: "since" (yataḥ). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "therefore, its being a transformation of the fire of the heavenly world is logical. || 79 || 76 ||
2024 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Sixth Chapter]:
This is the transformation of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) resulting from the ritual act known as the Agnihotra.
The onset of the world should be understood as extending as far as the origin of the Puruṣa. || 77 ||

To explain how the Āhavanīya fire exists as the nature of the heavenly world (dyuloka) and so forth, he says: "Not [produced] by prior action" (*apūrva*). For ritual action, being by its very nature solely that which is to be accomplished, does not exist independently of its causal factors (*kāraka*); thus, the *apūrva* of the Agnihotra and other rites originates the heavenly world only when accompanied by causal factors such as the Āhavanīya fire. This is because of the Vedic scripture: "They make the heaven itself the Āhavanīya. Therefore, it is logical that the Āhavanīya is the heavenly world.
The meaning is: abiding in the form of [the letters] beginning with *ka*. || 77 ||
The power of the two oblations of the Agnihotra that was previously described—
That very [knowledge] is explained directly by the Śruti here for the purpose of destroying false views.

Furthermore, even upon examining the context of the Agnihotra, he states that it is logical for the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) and so forth to possess the nature of fire (*agni*). He says: "Of the two oblations" (*āhutyoḥ*). In the preceding section on the Agnihotra, it was stated—for the sake of praising the two oblations—that the universe is a transformation of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of ritual action; that very same universe is here restated by the scriptural passage beginning with "this" (*asau*) for the purpose of enjoining a meditative visualization (*dṛṣṭi*). Therefore, it is appropriate that the heavenly world and so forth have the nature of fire; this is the meaning. || 78 ||
Regarding the internal self, the sacrifice, the worlds, and the divine.
The Śruti clearly explains the extensive dimensions of the Āhavanīya and other fires.

Raising the objection as to how the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) and so forth can be fire, even though the universe consists of unprecedented transformations (*apūrva-pariṇāma*), the text restates the manifestation of karma with the words "In the internal self" (*adhyātma*). It is heard in the *Ṣaṭprapāṭhika* that fire, in the form of the *āhavanīya* and other sacrificial fires, exists through the divisions of the internal self and so on; therefore, it is precisely that transformation of fire as the *āhavanīya* and others which is restated here for the purpose of prescribing the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*). Thus—
The meaning is that the world and so forth possess the nature of fire. || 79 ||
One should contemplate that the world is the Āhavanīya fire, and this [sun] is that very fire.
Likewise, among the Ādityas and others, there is the observation of the sacrificial fuel (samit) and so forth.

Having thus established the nature of fire in what is not fire, he states the intended mode of meditation in the passage beginning with "this" (*asau*) and so forth. Regarding the word "world" (*loka*):

the meaning is that the perception of fire should be applied to the world of heaven (*dyuloka*), even though it is not actually fire. He explains the purport of the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) as follows: "in the sun and so forth.
That is to say, just as the perception of fire is applied to the world [of heaven], so too [should it be applied] to the sun and other such objects. || 80 ||
Because they kindle [the fire], the sun's rays are called *samidh* (fuel), and they are also called *dhūma* (smoke).
Because of the commonality of their departure, the path of the rays and that of the day are likewise the same. || 81 ||

He states the reason for perceiving the fuel (*samit*) in the sun: "Because of kindling" (*samindhanāt*). Having restated the perception of smoke in the rays, he states the reason: "The rays" (*raśmayaḥ*).

The meaning is that the perception of the flame (*arcis*) during the day is the effect. He explains how the state of arising from the fuel (*samidutthatva*) serves as the reason for the statement "the day is the flame":
"In the same way" (*tathaiva*). || 81 ||
And because of their peacefulness, the quarters are like embers due to the transformation brought about by the kindling.
Just as the states of flame and embers are caused by the sun, so it is with these.
These rays and these directions have the sun as their common support.
