3, page 890] 2 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 2025.

He states the reason for the meditation on the firebrand (*aṅgāra*) in the day: "Because of its peacefulness" (*śāntatvāt*). He provides another reason why the meditations on smoke, flame, and the firebrand are to be performed upon the rays, the day, and the directions: "As fuel" (*samit*).

Just as smoke and the others have fuel as their substratum because they are transformations of fuel, so too, since the rays and the rest are modifications of the sun, they have that [sun] as their substratum; therefore, the meditation on smoke and the others should be performed upon them—this is the meaning. Of the directions...
The fact that the linguistic usage of that [object] has "being abandoned" as its object should be understood as being dependent upon that [state of abandonment]. || 82 ||
Likewise, the intermediate directions arise from the single cause of being dispersed.
They should be known as sparks within that aforementioned fire. (83)

He states the meaning of the phrase "the intermediate directions are the sparks" with the words beginning "avāntara... (intermediate). This means that the intermediate directions are like the embers of those [directions].
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tasmin" (in that) with the words beginning "tasmin. The words "the gods offer oblations" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 83 ||
And those who are the thirty-three gods, they abide on the planes of the internal self and so forth.
The Hotṛ priests should be stationed here and there according to their knowledge of the ritual procedures. || 84 ||

"Who are those gods who are the Hotṛ-priests there? To this he replies: "Thirty-three. These are the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, Indra, and Prajāpati. Those who are the gods, being divided by the distinctions of the internal self (adhyātma) and so forth, become the Hotṛ-priests in various fires according to the particular state of the sacrificer and in accordance with his respective rites; therefore, they are the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the sacrificer.
The meaning here is that speech and the other [senses] are the deities. || 84 ||
For they were present in the form of officiating priests, just as in an ordinary ritual.
Likewise, the Hotṛ priests [are present] at the ritual conclusions and in the higher stages. || 85 ||

He clarifies that very point by means of an illustration: "The officiating priest," and so forth. Just as in the Brāhma ritual such as the Jyotiṣṭoma there stand sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as *hotṛ*s, so too in the subsequent transformations of the ritual apūrva, such as the heavenly world and so on, those gods who are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the sacrificer become the *hotṛ* priests in the form of officiating priests; this is the meaning. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to establish the well-known status of the officiating priests upon the sacrificial ground. || 85 ||
This transformation of the two oblations is called "the potent essence" (ūrgrasa) and also "the unprecedented" (apūrva).
Because it has faith as its sole cause, it is celebrated by the name "faith. (86)

In this way, even though the *hotṛ* (the priest) has been established [as the agent], one might suspect that *śraddhā* (faith) cannot be the object of the oblation (*homya*) because it consists of a particular mental state (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*). Anticipating this objection, he states the meaning of the word *śraddhā*: "Of the two oblations" (*āhutyor iti*). The meaning is that the *apūrva* (unseen potentiality) resulting from rituals such as the *agnihotra* is figuratively designated by the word *śraddhā*, since it is the effect (*kārya*) of faith. || 86 ||
And from that oblation as well, King Soma comes into being.
Its growth is its manifestation, for there is no birth of what has not previously existed. || 87 ||

He takes up the subsequent statement: "And of that... The first two particles (*ca*) are used to state that once faith is established as the object of oblation (*homya*), its function as an oblation is also necessarily established. The second *ca* is for the purpose of providing an illustration, meaning "just like the function of the oblations of Soma and so forth which will be mentioned later.
The word *iti* is for the purpose of indicating meditation. To the question, "Of what nature is the origin of Soma?", he says: "Of that... The reason for this is as follows.

"But not so," it is said. Since Soma is already established beforehand, its birth is impossible for that which does not exist; therefore, "becoming" (*saṃbhūti*) is simply growth, and that occurs in the world of Soma.

2026 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopani�ṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Sixth Chapter]: The meaning is that the authorship of the commencement of another body for the sake of experience—therein, having entered the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), the agent initiates a body within the lunar orb; such is the sense of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*). || 87 ||
The sky is the fire, the sun is the fuel, and faith is that in which the oblation is offered.
When the sun has risen and is blazing, the deities offer faith as an oblation.

He summarizes the meaning of the initial sequence in brief: "The sky. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate the remainder of the passage, namely that from that oblation comes the increase of Soma. He clarifies this very point: "The sun. By taking the term *śraddhā* (faith) to refer to the unseen merit (*apūrva*) of ritual action, it is stated that from that oblation arises the production of Soma. || 88 ||
The wise say that *śraddhā* (faith) is derived either from the root *śri*, meaning "to resort to," or from *śrad-dhā*, meaning "to trust. || 89 ||
Because they flow and because they sustain, the waters are called *śraddhā*, being of the nature of their cause.
And because of the indicative mark "having become water," therefore water is designated by the term *śraddhā*.

Now, one might object: even for that which is called *śraddhā* (faith), which is indeed something unprecedented (*apūrva*), there can be no status as an oblation; for if the oblation were merely its entry into the heavenly world, then the primary meaning of the word *śraddhā* would have to be abandoned, since such an oblation is possible even for that specific desire [which is the primary sense]. Anticipating this objection, he explains the etymology of the word *śraddhā*. He says: "from the root *śrayati*. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*). He states the intended meaning of the derived word: "relying upon... (*śraya-*).

[The opponent objects: "No. [The author replies: Because they are the substratum and the nourisher of the material world (*bhautika-prapañca*), the waters, together with the other elements, are what is meant by the word *śraddhā*. How is it that they undergo the process of being offered (*śrayaṇa*) and so forth? To this he says: "Being of the nature of the cause" (*kāraṇātmikāḥ*). He provides another reason for why the waters alone are denoted here by the word *śraddhā*: "Having become... (*bhūtvā*). The sandhi has not been applied to the word division for the sake of explaining the commentary's meaning. Not... [end of fragment].

Considering that water alone is understood by the word "śraddhā" because of the introductory statement, "The waters alone, having assumed human speech, rose up and spoke," and also because of the scriptural text, "Śraddhā, indeed, is water," he says: "From that... (89) (90).
The water drawn up by the rays rests within the sun.
Therefore, the moon, having gone to the sun and become waned, is replenished once again.

Anticipating the question of how the statement that "the origin and growth of Soma arise from the oblation of faith" (śraddhā-huti) can be sustained, he says: "Drawn up" (ākṛṣṭam). The word *tat* refers to water. During the dark fortnight, the waning Soma enters into the sun at the new moon;
it is then gradually replenished during the bright fortnight by the water flowing from that [sun]. This is the growth and origin of Soma.
“O twice-born one, Vivasvat takes up the water of the world with his sharp rays and releases it into Soma; then the Moon, by means of channels consisting of wind, [releases it].”
The meaning is that this is based on such Smṛti passages as these. || 91 ||
Soma is a transformation of water; because he is the cool-rayed moon, he is composed of water.
For it is stated in the scripture that the origin of Soma arises from faith. || 92 ||

However, regarding those who assert that Soma possesses a fiery nature (*taijasatva*), [the author] states that there is a contradiction with the scriptural passage, "King Soma comes into being from that oblation. He says, "For it is a transformation," where the word "for" (*hi*) is used for the purpose of establishing what is well-known from scripture. Furthermore, he says, "It is the cool-rayed one (*śītāṃśu*)," because its watery nature is directly perceived. Moreover, the fact that Soma arises from the oblation of the waters called "faith" (*śraddhā*) is what is described in the scriptures.
In that world of Soma, there is indeed the commencement of another body for the sake of the agent's enjoyment; thus, even if it is of a fiery nature (*taijasa*), there is no contradiction.
Wishing to speak, he says: "Because of faith" (śraddhāteḥ). || 92 ||
The embers were the moon; when that fire was offered, it became the source of Soma.
Thus, the distinction between Soma and the Moon has been shown by the scripture. || 93 ||
Now, one might object: "If the production of Soma from faith and water occurs in the fire of the heavenly world, then how can it not be considered charcoal from the human world, given the Vedic text:

'The moon is charcoal'? Anticipating this doubt, he establishes the distinction between Soma and the moon: "Charcoal," etc. The phrase "in that" refers to the fire of the heavenly world. The distinction is that the moon is the instrumental cause (*kāraka*), whereas Soma is the result (*phala*).
This is the meaning. He reveals the authority for that [point] with the words "Soma" and so forth. Here, the scripture refers to the moon as the *aṅgāra* (the fire-ember);
[the authority is] such passages as "Soma the King is the offering for that [libation]," and so on. || 93 ||
The lunar disc is indeed clear, for it is measured by the moon-mark.
But Soma is white in the mandala, and he who increases and wanes [is the moon]. || 94 ||

He states that even upon the observation of the object, the establishment of difference [is achieved], beginning with the words "the moon" (*candramā*). He explains the ground for the application of the word *candramas* to the orb (*maṇḍala*) with the phrase "by the lunar spot" (*candrakeṇa*). This means it is compared to a speck of mica (*abhraka*). The word *sa-* refers to the orb. He explains the application of the word *soma* to the person residing within the orb with the words "but Soma... (*somastu*). He states the ground for this there as follows:

The word "it increases" (*vardhate*) refers to the observation of increase and decrease in the form of a creeper; since that state exists in this case as well due to the distinction of the two sides, the application of that term [“creeper”] occurs.

Nor is it the case that the increase and decrease belong to the orb alone, because there is no restrictive rule [to that effect]. Furthermore, the scriptural statement, “they eat them there,” does not refer to the orb, because that alone is not something to be enjoyed. This is the meaning. || 94 ||
The moon is beyond the sun, while Soma is considered to be below it according to the Vedic revelation.
He said, "From the sun to the moon—these [do not take] one year in that manner. (95)

He states another distinction [between them] with the words "the moon. If it is argued that there is a scriptural distinction between Soma and the Moon based on their being mentioned before and after the Sun, he asks, "What is that scripture? and answers with the words "from the Sun," referring to those traveling by the northern path to the year.

The Śruti states that "the doors go to the Sun, and from there they go to the Moon," thus declaring the Moon to be beyond the Sun. These travelers on the southern path do not reach the year; rather, from the months they go to the world of the fathers (pitṛloka), and from the world of the fathers to the Moon—this being the King Soma.
Such scriptural passages declare Soma to be on this side of the Sun. Furthermore, if the Moon were situated beyond the Sun, [there could be no] those residing within it.

The meaning is that it is not possible for Soma to be posterior [to the gods], because such a state is possible for a deity by virtue of its sovereignty, according to the principle of multiple manifestations (*aneka-pratipatti*). || 99 ||
Therefore, the distinction between Soma and the moon is clearly understood.

"Because of the Vedic revelation, 'This Soma is non-different from Deśaridu. (96) [The author] concludes the established distinction with the word "Soma. Anticipating the objection—"If there is absolute difference between those two, how can there be a statement of non-difference?"—he says: "Deśa... Even while there is a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*), due to the non-difference of location (*deśābheda*), [there is the statement of non-difference]: "This King Soma [is non-different] from the world of the ancestors."
The meaning is that there is no hearing [of the sound] because the soma resides in a sphere (maṇḍala) and thus lacks spatial location. || 96 ||
And because they are distinct due to the difference in their attributes, the Śruti is thus twofold.
Parjanya is to be known as Agni, and the year is remembered as the fuel. || 97 ||
For when the year is kindled, it is through the kindling of Parjanya.
"Smoke, clouds," and likewise "lightning, lightning"—[these are used] because of similarity. (98)
From Śāntivartula come embers; from Parjanya, fire and lightning.
Because they share the single common characteristic of being scattered, sparks and thunderclaps [are similar]. (99)
There, in that fire, they offered oblations of Soma; the gods had previously risen from there.
And because of the impossibility of vision, that [sight] is also offered as an oblation in this world. || 100 ||

How then is the scriptural statement regarding their difference to be understood? To this he says: "And they are different. This means that they are different in terms of their attributes (*dharma-bheda*) and in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*). He concludes: "Therefore," [meaning] the scriptural statement of non-difference is due to the non-difference of location, while the scriptural statement of difference is due to the difference of essential nature. He explains the second alternative with the passage beginning "Parjanya," etc. When the year is set ablaze by the seasons, the well-known blazing of Parjanya occurs.

The meaning of the word *hi* (for) is that otherwise it would be purposeless. In the phrase "smoke, clouds," the word *iti* serves to draw in [the previously mentioned] "knowability. The similarity of clouds to smoke is their smoky color (*dhūmratva*). In the phrase "lightning, radiance, vision," it establishes the similarity of color as the reason. And likewise...
Thus he introduces the third fire with the words "In this world... (vv. 97–100).
This world is difficult to comprehend; the earth is said to be the sacrificial fuel.
For this [fire] is kindled by the earth; therefore, the earth is considered its fuel. || 101 ||
Fire is smoke because it arises from that; likewise, night is so called because of its lack of light.
They say that night is the shadow of the earth, while the moon is like a coal,
due to its tranquility and roundness, and because it is equal to a spark.
The stars would be sparks in that [fire], and so forth, as previously described. || 103 ||
From that comes the production of food, and that [food] is offered into the fire of the person.
The Puruṣa is to be meditated upon as the fire; his wide-open mouth is remembered as the fuel.
For that radiance is in the opened mouth, and smoke is the breath arising from the mouth.
Or, because the illumination of the person has speech as its cause, it is called "lightning" (arcis) by means of that speech. || 105 ||
The eye is like glowing coals when fixed [on its object], and the ear is likewise.
It should be understood that these are like sparks, arising from its state of mental projection. || 106 ||
They offer oblations there into that fire; from that, the birth of semen occurs.
The woman is to be known as the fire, and the generative organ is likewise the fuel. || 107 ||
From its proximity, it is ignited; from its similarity, smoke arises from the body hairs.
Because it shares the same color as the flame, the womb thereafter becomes like a flame.
Whatever one who is full of desire does within [the body], that is like embers because of its similarity to them.
The fragments of pleasure are like sparks, for their sole cause is momentariness. || 109 ||
There, the gods, in the form of the senses, offer semen as an oblation into that fire.
From that fifth oblation, this person comes into being.

He explains the passage beginning with "This world, indeed, is fire" by means of the words "this world" and so forth. There is a distinction between this world and the earth in the sense of the relationship between the body and the embodied. The word "hi" (indeed) is used to provide the reason that the radiance of the body is well known through its possessor, the embodied one.

By the word "that" (tat), the earth is called the fuel (*samit*). "In the same way" means precisely because the earth is the source from which the fuel arises. But how is it that night is the source from which the aforementioned fuel arises? To this he says: "Night. For, according to the Vedic text, "These [worlds] carried across the moon, which was afraid of the night, of darkness, and of death," we understand that night is indeed darkness; and since "darkness is indeed death, the shadow," it is by that very [darkness] that [the fuel arises].

By means of that light, one crosses over death, darkness, and shadow; for there is a scriptural mention of "the shadow of the earth. Darkness is the station of Rāhu, and it is well known as the shadow of the earth—as it is said: "Having lifted up the shadow of the earth, it was fashioned in the form of a circle."
For there is a Smṛti text stating: "That third, vast abode of the Sun is composed of darkness."

He raises the fourth fire with the words, "In that fire... He explains [the passage] beginning with "The fire is indeed the person" by means of the words "The person," and so forth. The word *hi* (indeed) is used to state that the radiance (*dīpti*) of those possessing speech is manifest. Therefore, in speech—

The meaning is: "by means of the sentence. He explains [the passage] beginning with "Woman is indeed fire" (*yoṣā vā agniḥ*) by means of the words beginning with "Woman" (*yoṣit*). "In that manner" (*tathā*) means "like the blazing of a kindled fire. Regarding the perception of smoke in the body hair, he states the reason for the similarity of color as "because it is similar" (*sāmyataḥ*).
Indeed, just as embers are the cause of the subsiding of fire, so too is this act the cause of the destruction of the splendor, vigor, and so forth, of both the woman and the man.
Because it brings peace through its nature as a fire, one should have the perception of charcoal toward that ritual; thus he says: "on account of its similarity to that. || 101 ||
For, by the path already described, the waters have attained the state of transformation into the male.
This transformation born of digestion occurs in this manner through these five fires. (111)
He shows the relevance of the "five-fire" cognition (*pañcāgnivijñāna*) to the present topic by way of resolving the fourth question. Regarding the phrase "as stated":

the particle *hi* indicates that it is well known that water is the constituent material (*prakṛti*) in Vedic rituals such as the *agnihotra*. If milk, clarified butter, and so forth, when offered in the *agnihotra*, undergo a transformation into the form of a person, how is it that they become suitable for practical use in their gross state? [Regarding] those [waters...]
You may raise the objection that this is due to the subtlety of its intrinsic nature; [the author replies: "It is produced by ripening" (pākaja). || 111 ||
Therefore, the waters, being subtle in nature, attain grossness through the process of digestion.
Indeed, when ripened by the five fires, they come to be designated as "persons" (puruṣa).

He states the conclusion regarding the transformation called *puruṣa* being produced by maturation (*pākaja*) with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Water, characterized as the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*), [is meant]. (Note: Variant reading 'kha' omits 'nā').
The Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika composed by Sureśvarācārya, Volume 3, Page 895. 2030.
[In the sixth chapter—] Having abandoned subtlety, the aforementioned fires proceed from that state toward grossness; nevertheless, how is it that they are designated as "persons" (puruṣa)?
To this, he says: "By the fires. Because the transformation produced by cooking possesses hands, feet, and so forth, the designation "person" is appropriate.
This is the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed). || 112 ||
Therefore, by this improper means, the officiating priests carry away the deceased beloved kinsman.
Just as the fuel and other materials for the Āhavanīya fire are well known.
In the same way, all this should be understood as being like a cremation ground; it is not to be conceptualized.

Desiring to explain the destination of those who know the five fires (*pañcāgnividaḥ*), [the author] explains the passage concerning the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) in order to demonstrate the body that serves as the vehicle for the destination to be described. He says, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Alternatively, the sixth fire is mentioned as a supplement to the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) that "I am absorbed into the fire. The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the exhaustion of the karma that was the cause for the persistence of the current body. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) as follows: "Just as... (*yathā*). [This is] eternal... (*nityānu-*).
He states the result of the argument: "No," [as in verses] 113 and 114.
For the sake of accomplishing the final rites, [he should act] in that fire as it has been described.
The officiating priests offer the man as the final oblation according to the prescribed ritual.
From that oblation, a man bearing a radiant form is produced.

He states the meaning of the verse beginning with "tasmin" (in that) as follows: "antyeṣṭi" means the final oblation; "for the sake of that" means for the purpose of that [oblation], which is the dual injunction regarding the ancestors as previously stated; "by virtue of that" is the intended sense. || 115 ||
For the rājasika and tāmasika forms will be described elsewhere than this. || 116 ||
From these fires, he shall attain fire itself as his own source.
Thus, according to common worldly practice, his birth was from the fires. || 117 ||

He states the object to be excluded by the qualification "of radiant complexion" (*bhāsvaravarṇaviśeṣaṇa*): "rājasa" (passionate). "From this"—that is, from this [state] of the wise which is characterized by *sattva*.

"Elsewhere" means in action that has fallen away from both [paths]. He provides the consensus of the wise as proof for the fact that the person is born from fire and is dissolved therein: "from this. That is to say, he has come together. "The world" refers to the community of the wise who follow the path of the Vedas (*śrutimārga*).
Their origination is characterized by dissolution. || 116 || 117 ||
Thus, birth under a male name is proclaimed to occur at the fifth oblation.
Then its movement must be described according to the distinction between north and south. || 118 ||
He states the connection of the passage beginning with "They, thus... by first restating what has preceded it. Regarding the phrase "in the fifth":

it should be understood that "birth" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) intended to include the final oblation as well. The word "atha" (now/then) indicates the deceased's need for a path [to reach the next state]. The euphonic conjunction (*saṃdhi*) is not intended to be significant here, as it serves no purpose. || 118 ||
And they [attained] this knowledge, which rests upon the five fires, exactly as it was born.
The twice-born ones, whose splendor is like that of the fire, come together when many words are spoken.
1 kha. Let them go. 2 kha. Just as. [Vol.
3, page 896] 2 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 2031.

He applies that [to the following]: "those who... By the use of the plural number in the phrase "those who know them, they come into being," he states that here only the members of the three castes (*traivarṇika*) are included as those entitled to the qualification, because of the mention of plurality. || 119 ||
Arising, persistence, and dissolution have fire as their sole cause, as previously described.
Those who know thus become self-cultivated.
Fearing that for them the mere arising of the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*) might be the cause for attaining the path beginning with *arciḥ*, he says: "At birth," etc.

The meaning is that those who know, "My birth and so forth are produced by the oblations of faith and the rest in the heavenly world and other realms," being constantly possessed of such reflection, go to the world of Brahmā by way of the path beginning with *arciḥ*. || 120 ||
Those who have indeed performed sacrifices and charitable works, and those who are superior to the village-dwellers.
The term "forest" (araṇya) is understood [to include these], because the others are mentioned separately. || 121 ||

In the passage beginning with "And those who," he speaks of the intended qualified practitioners. Regarding the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*): the meaning is that these householders who perform the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis, as well as others who dwell in the forest (*vanastha*) and perform rites such as those of the Śrutis—they are intended as the qualified practitioners for the meditation on the True Brahman preceded by faith and so forth, according to the passage beginning with "and those in the forest. He anticipates the objection that even students (*brahmacārin*) might be included in the phrase "and those who," etc.

He says, "Of the others. The meaning is that since the lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins) proceed by the northern path to the world of Brahman based on Smṛti alone in the absence of Śruti, they have no place here [in this context]. || 121 ||
Sacrifices, gifts, and austerities here [are practiced] by the ascetic just as they are by the householder.
And because they dwell with a householder preceptor, there is no ritual seizure (graha) for those who are celibate students (brahmacārins). || 122 ||
Having raised the doubt—namely, that while householders perform sacrifices and other such rites, how can forest-dwellers be their performers—the author says: "yajña... (verse 122).

He states another reason for the non-inclusion of students (*brahmacārin*) in this passage: "gṛhastha... (verse 122). The meaning is that because they are dependent solely upon their teacher and reside within his family, they lack independence in matters such as meditation (*upāsana*). || 122 ||
Neither forest-dwellers nor village-dwellers have need for knowledge here.
Because it is apprehended by a general term, there is no inclusion of a specific instance. || 123 ||

Anticipating the objection that—as in the case of the knowledge of Truth (satyavidyā)—in the knowledge of the five fires (pañcāgnividyā) as well, only householders and forest-dwellers are entitled, and because it is stated [in other texts] that many [are so entitled], this [claim] is improper, he says, "No," and so forth. Here, "here" refers to the discussion regarding the eligibility for the knowledge of the five fires. He states the reason for the absence of a specific restriction: "Because of the general... Since the phrase "those who know this thus" employs a non-specific mention, the distinction of householder and so forth is not established.
This is the meaning. || 123 ||
Even though truthfulness accompanied by faith may be possible elsewhere;
Nevertheless, ascetics are to be accepted because of the qualification "in the forest. (124)

Regarding the passage beginning with "ye ca" and so forth, the mention of householders (*gṛhastha*) and forest-dwellers (*vanastha*) was stated as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*); now, however, he states that what is intended here as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the inclusion of forest-dwellers and renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) other than the Paramahaṃsas. He says: "of one possessed of faith" (*saśraddhasya*). Although—[note: the commentary continues with textual variants regarding the sequence of verses and the reading of certain terms].
• [Vol. 3, page 897] 2032 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Sixth Chapter]—

The meaning is this: although the practice of meditating on the Truth preceded by faith is possible even among householders, the mention of "those who" and so forth refers to forest-dwellers and non-primary ascetics, because the qualification "in the forest" is applicable only to them. || 124 ||
"Those who know thus"—this may refer either to householders or to those who have taken up the life of a forest-dweller.
It is logical [to maintain] a connection with the sacred fire, since it is possible even for one dwelling in the forest. || 125 ||

Fearing that, as in the passage beginning with "ye ca" and so forth, only the ascetic (*yati*) and the forest-dweller (*vanastha*) might be understood even in another sentence, [the author], setting aside the position stated in the phrase "because of the inclusion of the general term," states an alternative view: "te ya" (those who...). The connection is that because the possibility of a connection with fire exists, the forest-dweller is also included. || 125 ||
Nor is it accepted that the aforementioned perception is subordinate to the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Because it is grasped in a general sense, and because of the indicative mark "five fires," that [is the path]. || 126 ||

Some, however, argue that since the vision of the five fires (*pañcāgnidarśana*) is not intended as a praise of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, the path (*gati*) connected with it is also not intended; thus, their attempt to define the traveler [of that path] is a confusion out of place. To them, he replies: "And not... In this context, the vision of fire being presented does not have the status of a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) to the *agnihotra* by way of praising it; for, apart from such a connection, the statement "that world is fire" is a general [description].

The meaning is: because it is not stated [that he knows six fires], because of the hearing of the number five remaining from the accumulation in the case of the fires consisting of the sacrificial altar (*sāṃpādika*), and because of the observation of the connection with six fires as seen in the *agnihotra* remnant and in the six questions (*ṣaṭpraśna*). || 126 ||
Because he has abandoned the means of achieving the three worlds, there is no attachment even for a renunciant.
For divine knowledge is indeed true wealth, since renunciation proceeds from wealth. || 127 ||

Since liberation (*gati*) is not a subordinate element of any other [result] than vision (*dṛṣṭi*), even when the goer is defined by means of defining the going, one might suspect that in the passage beginning with "and those who," the term "ascetic" (*yati*) refers only to those other than the *paramahaṃsa*, because they too are included due to the qualification "in the forest. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The three worlds...

He further addresses the suspicion that although the two worlds [of men and ancestors] are abandoned through the renunciation of progeny and ritual action, knowledge—the means for attaining the world of the gods—is not renounced by the *paramahaṃsas* because it serves that purpose. To this, he says: [the following].

Regarding the word "devī": the meaning of the particle *hi* is the acceptance of the twofold nature of wealth (*vitta*). Therefore, the ellipsis is that by them, as previously stated, knowledge has been abandoned.
"What shall we do with progeny?"—this is the rejection [of worldly aims] due to the knowledge of Brahman. 128.
In this context, the state of one who possesses the five kinds of superknowledge is also always to be cultivated.
The state of being an enemy has also been described; otherwise, its manifestation would not occur. || 129 ||

He states the authority for their renunciation of the cause of the three worlds with the words "by progeny" (*prajayā*). The ellipsis is that the renunciation already mentioned is established by implication from the word "of them" (*teṣām*). Having explained the meaning of the passage beginning with "and those who...

(*ye ca*), he states the purport of the mention of the "going" (*gati*) in proximity to the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*): "the five fires. The locative case signifies the context. He says that because proximity would be purposeless if they were not objects of meditation, the "going" is an object of meditation by virtue of that proximity: "not another" (*nānya-*)... [text fragment].
Thus [ends the section]. 128 || 129 ||
Because the worship of deities is the subject under discussion here, and because it is understood accordingly.
By the word "flame" (arciḥ), it is the deity itself that is understood here. || 130 ||
[Volume 3,
Page 898] 2 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

In the passage beginning with "they [go] to the light" (*te 'rciṣam*), he sets aside the view that the word "light" (*arciḥ*) refers merely to a flame and states that it refers to a deity, saying "the deity. The word "here" (*iha*) indicates the context; the word "therein" (*atra*) states the specific sentence. Thus, the meaning is that because the "light" is heard of as a stage on the path (*gatiparvan*) in proximity to the knowledge under discussion (*prakṛtavidyā*). The second occurrence of the word "here" (*iha*) is for the purpose of indicating proximity to the knowledge. || 130 ||
Having attained oneness with the deity of light, one attains oneness with the deity of day.
The phrase "they arise" is to be understood as connected to everything here. || 131 ||
Having restated the meaning of the passage beginning with "they [attain] the light" (te 'rciḥ), he states the meaning of "from the light to the day" (arcir ahnaḥ). Regarding the word "light" (arciḥ):

he says that just as the connection "they attain" (saṃbhavanti) occurs in this sentence, it should be understood that this same connection applies everywhere in the subsequent passages as well. || 131 ||
If the deity were not grasped by the words "the short-lived ones" (arcis) and so forth, then [it would be so].
Since it is impossible [for them to exist] other than after death, the scriptural teaching regarding their destination is meaningless. (132)
He provides the reasoning for why the deity alone must be understood even by the words "day" and so forth, just as it is by the word "flame," stating: "It is grasped.

If the deity were not grasped by the words "flame" and so forth, then the attainment of the fruit by the worshiper would be impossible; for death could occur even during the dark fortnight and other such times, since those periods are not fixed. Consequently, the scriptural teaching regarding the path (gati) would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, [the words] denote the deities.
The meaning is that [this applies] to the words "light" (arciḥ) and so forth. || 132 ||
That which is heard in the Smṛti regarding Bhīṣma’s dependence on the northern solstice (udagayana).
Let that [story] of Śantanu also be considered for the purpose of establishing the truthfulness of his speech. || 133 ||

Indeed, it must be admitted that words such as "day" and so forth refer to specific points of time, since we observe that even the learned Bhīṣma awaited the northern solstice for the sake of his death;

regarding this, he says: "As for that which... Although the time for Bhīṣma's death in battle had arrived, the praise of the ancestors is intended here with the view that the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) constituting the beginning of his body remained until the end of the northern solstice—[he was] a person of great power.

The meaning is that because of those words, Śantanu’s son Bhīṣma attained death at his own will; however, in the attainment of the fruit [of the path], no specific time is intended by way of being a "mountain of transition" (gatiparvata). Therefore, due to the contradiction with the maxim "even during the southern course," in the passage "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight," etc., it is the deity alone that is intended, according to the logic of the "conveying deities" (ātivāhika); such is the meaning. || 133 ||
Otherwise, there would be the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done.
Therefore, because it is the grasping of the deity, it is called "deity" (devatā). || 134 ||

If a specific time were required for the Śruti and Smṛti rules because they constitute the path [to heaven], then, since there is no fixed rule regarding the time of death, one would have to wait for the day and so forth even when death occurs at night or other such times; otherwise, it would be impossible for that which lacks a means of departure to bear fruit. Consequently, there would be the destruction of what was performed—which brings about death at night—and the arrival of what was not performed—the cause for waiting for the day. Thus he says: "Otherwise... (anyathā).

He concludes the meaning of the word "flame" with the words "the deity. The construction is: "because by means of the words 'day' and so forth, there is an unambiguous apprehension of the deity, therefore [it is so]. || 134 ||
Therefore, the wise who know this [attain] the one who identifies with light (arciḥ) without delay.
Having reached the deity in due order, they go to that state of Viṣṇu.
He concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "They indeed," etc., with the words "Therefore. By the word "that" (tat), the mention of the deity-cup (devatā-graha) is intended. || 135 ||
255 [Vol. 3, Page 899] 2034 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Sixth Adhyāya]
Full of faith, practicing austerity, established in truth, and concentrated in Brahman.
They worship outside the village; from this, the fires arise. || 136 ||

Having concluded the discussion on the attainment of the northern path by those who maintain the five fires and keep the vigil at dawn, he summarizes the meaning of the passage beginning with "And those who... with the words: "The faithful ones.
They attain the station of Brahmā, or else [attain it] through the duties of their own stage of life (āśrama).
Through renunciation, one attains the station of Brahman; such also is the teaching of the Smṛtis.
Having stated that the word "truth" (*satya*) is the subject of the aphorism, and having understood it as referring to truthful speech, he states another meaning of the sentence:

"Of Brahman," etc. He provides the authority for the claim that those in the highest stage of life (*uttamāśramin*) go to the world of Brahman by performing the practice of truthful speech and so forth, prescribed for their own caste and stage of life, preceded by faith: "From renunciation," etc.; the meaning is "from [renunciation] alone, when performed correctly. (137)
From there they go to the deity of the day, and from there, in due order, to the bright fortnight.
And from there, they proceed for six months characterized by the northern course [of the sun].
And from there they go to the deity who presides over the world of the gods.
From there they go to the sun, and from the sun to the lightning.
Then, by Brahmā, a mental person (puruṣa) was created through his mind.
He leads them to the worlds of Brahmā; he too, having arrived, then proceeds to the worlds of Vaidyuta.
Shining in those worlds of Brahmā, they remain for supreme ages.
The years in the worlds of Brahmā are to be understood as being equal to those in the Brahma-world, according to that scriptural statement.

Having explained the passage beginning with "They [go] to the flame" (*te 'rciṣam*), he connects the subsequent section beginning with "From the flame to the day" (*arciṣo 'har*) by means of the words "Then" (*tataḥ*) and so forth.

The word "in due order" (*kramāt*) is stated for the purpose of grasping the process described by the terms "flame" and so on. The word "for" (*hi*) is stated for the purpose of establishing the traditional authority of the Smṛti text, "Six months [constitute] the northern course. The syntactical connection is: "From there, from the world of Brahman, they return. The term "belonging to lightning" (*vaidyutān*) refers to those who are under the control of the deity of lightning. "Of the knowers" (*viduṣaḥ*).

The word "atha" (then) indicates swiftness. The grammatical connection is: "they dwell in those. He states the reason for taking the year mentioned by the word "samā" (year) by saying "in the worlds of Brahman" (*brahmalokeṣu*). By the pronoun "tat" (that), the word "samā" is referred to. || 138 || 139 || 140 ||
This elaborate discourse is based on the expectation of attaining the eightfold states, including residence in the same world and union with the divine.
Or rather, this extensive discourse is made with reference to the distinction between the collective totality and its individual manifestations.

Anticipating the objection—how can there be a plural number in expressions such as "the worlds of Brahmā" (*brahmalokān*) when the world of truth (*satyaloka*) is one—he says: "sāṣṭha... (along with the eight). The meaning is that the plural expression is used by taking into account the gradations of results corresponding to the gradations of their respective means of attainment. He states another alternative: "samaṣṭi... (as a collective whole).

The meaning is that since the world of Brahmā, which is the body of the Thread (*sūtra-deha*), possesses many forms through its nature as both general and particular, the plural expression is used with reference to those. || 142 ||

In both manuscripts, the phrase "of the word 'satyopāsti'" (or "of the word 'satya-upāsti'") occurs; however, considering that something may have been omitted or some letters may have been erroneously added, I have established [the reading] as "of the word 'satya'," which is consistent with the intended meaning.
There is no return for them again until the dissolution of all beings.
For immortality is said to be that state which endures until the dissolution of all beings.

He explains the passage beginning with "of them" (teṣām) and so forth. Regarding the term "repetition" (āvṛtti), he says "until the dissolution of beings" (ābhūta-) to address the objection that the qualification "as long as" and so forth is inappropriate because of the scriptural hearing of immortality for the deities. || 143 ||
Or else, [liberation occurs] through the arising of the cognition of the identity of the self from the world of Brahman.
They are liberated and do not return, just like those who travel by the path of smoke and so forth. || 144 ||

He states another position, according to which the scriptural teaching of non-return (anāvṛtti) is to be taken in its primary sense, beginning with the words "aikātmya" (identity). In that regard, there is a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), introduced by the word "yathā" (just as).
Because of the qualification [of the mantra] beginning with "imaṃ mānavam āvartaṃ."
In this very kalpa there is no returning, but not so in others, because [the restriction] is not applied there.

In the passage beginning with "of them" (teṣām), it was stated that either gradual liberation (kramamukti) or non-return (anāvṛtti) is intended in a relative sense; regarding this, he provides the evidence for the second [interpretation] with the word "this" (imam). Because the meaning of the term "non-return" is qualified by the word "this," the non-return refers to the current kalpa; there is no such non-return in other kalpas, as there is no means of prevention therein—this is the meaning. || 149 ||
The path of the gods has been briefly explained with effort.
Now, the explanation of the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāṇa) is properly commenced.

Now, having restated the subject matter of the passage beginning with "Then those who [attain] by sacrifice," he states its purport: "The path of the gods" (devayāna). This means that it is done in brief, with little text. The effort is made to present each of the stages, such as light (arcis) and so forth, individually. The word "atha" (now/then) serves to indicate the proper occasion for the subsequent mention of the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) immediately after the description of the path of the gods. || 146 ||
O virtuous brahmins, those who [perform] sacrifice here while being devoid of knowledge of the gods and so forth—
Likewise, one should follow the Lokāyata system through giving that is accompanied by praise and so forth. || 147 ||
Or by one who lacks wisdom, through austerity that destroys all impurities without remainder.
Having died, they go to smoke; from smoke, they go to the dark night.
The latter half of the night and the deity of the southern solstice.
From the months [they go] indeed to the world of the ancestors, where the ancestors lie.
And from the world of the ancestors, they go to the moon; that is the food of the inhabitants of heaven. || 149 ||

Having stated the purport (*tātparya*), he connects the sentence [with the words] "devādīti. With the word "atha," he shows the consequence of winning the worlds immediately following the completion of mere meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*). He speaks of the one entitled to perform ritual action (*karmādhikārin*) with the words "sadvijā iti. Regarding the phrase "dātavyamiti," it refers to that which is a gift (*dāna*).
This indicates that it is a gift distinguished by its specific place, time, and recipient that is the cause for conquering the worlds. Regarding the phrase "in a good place, etc.":

the capacity of austerity (*tapas*) to destroy all impurities (*kalmaṣa*) should be understood from the traditional scripture (*smṛti*) stating, "One destroys impurity through austerity. The word *avipaścitaḥ* (the ignorant) should be read as a separate term. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "they [go] to smoke" (*te dhūmam*). Regarding the phrase "having died," since it has been stated that the deities of the southern path (*dakṣiṇāyana*) are intended, [it follows that] even in the case of smoke and so forth, there are deities.

1 ka. 'khyārthapa' | 2 ka. kha. ti | Why is "because of being a seeker" (*arthitvāt*) a qualification? 3 ka. kha. tā ityu | [Vol. 3, page 901] 2036 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Sixth Chapter—]
The mention of "that" (tad) excludes the deity of the world of the ancestors. [It says] "the ancestors" (pitaraḥ). The word "that" (tat) is for the purpose of referring back to the form of the moon.
And having reached the moon, they become food, because they remain there [in that state].
They consume these repeatedly, nourishing them again and again like the Soma juice.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "They [enter] the moon" as follows: "Into the moon. The connection is that they "attain the state of food. He explains the passage beginning with "Those [who... as follows: "Since... Just as the officiating priests at a sacrifice, having repeatedly replenished the Soma situated in the cups, consume it, so too do the gods residing in the world of the ancestors, having repeatedly replenished those performers of ritual action who have reached the moon, consume them; therefore, this is appropriate for them.
The meaning is "not so. || 150 ||
Having nourished him during the bright fortnight, they then consume him during the dark fortnight.
And their state as the means for enjoyment is what is meant by the term "they consume."
But it is not fit to be consumed by those who abide on the path of the Vedas. 152.

He explains the illustration by way of another method: "In the case of the [sacrificial] side" (*pakṣe*). The meaning of the word *atha* is the repetition of both nourishing and eating. Having raised the objection that if those performing ritual acts, having reached the moon, were to be eaten by the gods, then reaching it would lead only to misfortune and thus no one would undertake the practice, he says "enjoyment," etc., according to the principle of "or it is figurative because they are not knowers of the Self. One might ask: why should the scriptural mention of "eating" not be taken in its primary sense?

He says: "But not... The reason for this is: "Because of the Veda... That is to say, let alone those beings who are superior in goodness (*sattva*) and are inclined toward non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth. || 111 || 152 ||
But when accumulated karma reaches its culmination through experience, [it bears fruit].
Then they return along that same path by which they came. || 153 ||
Having followed after space, they enter the wind, being free from enjoyment.
Then, having obtained the vision of the wind, she beheld the earth as if it were before her eyes.
Therefore, those who dwell upon the earth come to have the nature of food from the earth. || 154 ||

He explains [the passage] beginning with "of them, when... with the words "But when... By the maxim that "one who possesses residual karma (*anuśaya*) returns after the completion of [their current state]," he indicates that residual karma is the cause for returning. With the word "then" (*atha*), he addresses the objection regarding the possibility of experience in various places such as space;

he says "those who do not experience. The word "then" (*atha*) is used to indicate the principle that there is not a very long time before reaching the state of rice and so forth from [staying in] space and so forth prior to that.

The particle *ca* (and) serves to aggregate the principle of attaining similarity (*sābhāvyāpatti*). The state of being food (*annabhāva*) consists merely in conjunction with rice and other grains, according to the principle that there is a description [of the self] as before when presided over by another. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*). For, having been transformed into the state of rice and so forth, the performers of action (*karmiṇaḥ*), along with that [food], subsequently become conjoined with it in the form of rain immediately after reaching it; and from that, [they obtain] a body through great hardship.
The meaning is that this is according to the Vedic scripture: "From here, indeed, it is truly more difficult to emerge. (113–114)
Just like a waterwheel, they proceed in this very manner again and again without ceasing.
Driven by the winds of karma, they revolve in saṃsāra. || 155 ||
1. Of those who exert effort.
[Vol. 3, p.
902] 2. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 2037.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "evam" (thus) as follows: "Like the sound of a water-pot. For indeed, those who follow the Vedas, who are the very embodiment of the Veda and who employ [the language] like the Veda itself, would not be censured by worldly people. || 155 ||
The explanation of the southern path has been described exactly as it is. || 156 ||
But those two paths, the higher and the lower, which have been described according to their characteristics—
Those who experience suffering here, such as insects and the like, do not know this. || 157 ||
Then, having introduced [the passage] beginning with "atha" by way of restating the preceding context, he explains it with the words beginning with "dakṣiṇasya. || 116 || 117 ||
They did not respect this knowledge, which is the means for attaining the path upward.
Or, upon reaching the path of the ancestors, they would go to the state of insects and the like due to their karma.

Raising the objection: "Even if there is ignorance regarding the two paths, since knowledge and action—which are the causes for attaining them—exist [in all beings], how can there be the attainment of the state of insects and the like? he answers with the words beginning with "No" (na), according to the maxim: "But because knowledge and action are the subjects under discussion. (198)
Insects born from cow dung and the like, as well as moths and locusts;
Deer, mosquitoes, biting insects, and serpents; || 159 ||
He states the non-repetitive meaning of the words "insects" (*kīṭa*) and so forth: "cow-dung, etc. (verse 119).
The question "On which occasion? has been addressed by the statement regarding the birth of a male.
Immediately after that, the exclusion from both paths has been stated.

Now, it may be objected: five questions were introduced here as subjects to be resolved, yet their resolution has not been provided; thus, what is this "unseasonable dance" (akāṇḍatāṇḍavam)? To this he replies: "In which [night]... He states that the first question has been resolved by means of the contradiction regarding whether some go by the path of light (*arcis*) and others by the path of smoke (*dhūma*) immediately after reaching the sixth fire. "Immediately after that... (160).
Through the complete manifestation of space and the other elements, one has undergone the cycle of returning again.
And having performed that by which the path of the gods and the path of the ancestors are attained. || 161 ||
That means of accomplishment (sādhana) has also been described here, characterized by knowledge and action.
The cause for the non-filling of the world has been clearly stated at the conclusion. || 162 ||

He answers the second question with the words "ākāśādīti" (beginning with space). He describes the manner in which the fifth question has been resolved with the words "devayānaṃ ca" (and the path of the gods). He provides the answer to the third question with the words "lokasya" (of the world). || 161 || 162 ||
Because insects and the like do not come from elsewhere, and likewise because those who have gone [to other worlds] do not return.
Thus, all five questions that were previously posed have been resolved.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.
[Vol. 3, page 903] 2038 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Sixth Chapter]:

He clarifies what has already been stated with the words "of worms and so forth. The meaning of the word "likewise" (*tathā*) refers to the principle beginning with "having experienced [the results] in the Saṃyamana [hell]," and so on.
He concludes the section on the Brāhmaṇa with the words: "Thus. || 163 ||
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
The cumulative number of verses from the beginning:
10,936. Now begins the third Brāhmaṇa.
Without wealth, there can be no success in actions aimed at visible or invisible results.
Therefore, the ritual action known as "Mandha" is designated by that name because it is for that purpose. || 1 ||
The course of knowledge and action has been explained; now he states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa. "Wealth," etc.;
that is to say, [the former was taught] for the sake of wealth. || 1 ||
Just as a son is born here through the father's karma, so too does he attain the world of his father.
The ritual for those desiring such a son is stated in the verse beginning with "tveṣām" (II.2).

He states the purport of the *Putramantha Brāhmaṇa* with the words "of the father" (*pitur iti*). The word "as" (*yathā*) has the sense of "in whatever manner. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the state of knowledge (*vidyā-daśā*). In the phrase "by means of action" (*karmaṇā*), the word "by which" (*yena*) is to be supplied. Furthermore, the pronoun "that" (*tat*) should be understood [to refer back] to "action" (*karman*) as well. || 2 ||
He who is seized by the demon of desire regarding wealth and offspring;
It should be understood that this rite is intended for him alone, and not for one who lacks desire.
Now, since the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) has the qualification for this scripture, these two rites are also appropriate for him; therefore, he says: "He who may...
The sense is that, because the passage begins with "He who may desire," and because the seeker of liberation lacks the desire for wealth and offspring. || 3 ||
He who should desire, "May there be a very great event," [should perform this].
By this statement, it is understood that for one who has acquired wealth [through other means], this ritual act is not required.

Having stated the purport of the two Brāhmaṇas, he explains the passage beginning with "sa yaḥ" (He who...). [The word] "prāpnuyām" (may I obtain) is a particle used for the purpose of indicating that such a desire is well-known in the world. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "this is the ritual action intended for him. He states the intention of the sentence spoken by one who tells the ritual to a seeker of wealth: "ityuktyā" (by saying this). || 4 ||
Or that householder who excessively desires greatness for himself.
Greatness does not exist without wealth; therefore, for the sake of accomplishing one's work, [one must seek] wealth.

Having grasped another meaning for the word *mahat*, he joins the sentence in a different manner: "The greatness... (the remainder being "this is its action"). If this action belongs to one who desires greatness, then it belongs to one who desires wealth; thus there would be a loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*). To that, he says: [vol 3, page 904]

"Greatness" (mahattā): Greatness is indeed sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and that cannot be obtained without wealth; thus, by implication, its accomplishment results here as a fruit, so there is no abandonment of the initial proposition (*pratijñāhāni*). This is the meaning. || 5 ||
And the time for this ritual act called "churning" is prescribed here.
According to the Vedic injunctions regarding the northern course of the sun, one should strive diligently for the successful accomplishment of ritual acts.
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "during the northern course of the sun" (udagayane) as follows: "Time. Here, the term refers to the householder who desires wealth.

Relying on the principle that "action is prescribed for the proper time, not for an improper time," he says "of action. He states the fruit of that injunction: "Action. By the word "with effort," he indicates the necessity of practice. || 6 ||
First, one should pray for the right time, and thereafter for the purification of the self.
Next, the substances, the medicinal herbs, and the location [are described]. || 7 ||

Anticipating the objection that [the result] might be accomplished at some point in time by performing the action and subsequently waiting for a specific occasion, he says: "is to be prayed for. Substances such as milk and ghee; medicinal herbs such as rice, barley, and so forth. ||7||
In this action, there is a combination of time and the other factors, as well as the qualities.
Neither doubt nor success would be appropriate for this action. || 8 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the undertaking of an action is possible even through the attainment of only one among place and the other factors, it is not necessary to examine all of them beforehand, he says:

"Of time and so forth. [The word] "qualities" refers to purity, faith, and the like. Anticipating the objection as to what loss there would be even in the case of an alternative (vikalpa), he states the result of accepting their combination (samuccaya): "Prosperity" (8).
And for the accomplishment of this action, even learnedness is relied upon.
Therefore, this which has been stated is not what was intended by the authors of the Sūtras.

Anticipating the objection—"If this is a Vedic rite like the Agnihotra and others, why was it not codified by the authors of the Kalpasūtras?"—he says: "And of the rite... The word "and" (api) has the sense of "just as in the case of the previously mentioned time. || 9 ||
Indeed, that which was previously described as "the state of being learned" by means of the expression "he who [knows] the eldest," [is this].
In that [context], this ritual action belongs to her, because of the indicative mark (liṅga) such as "to the eldest" (jyeṣṭhāyai) and so forth. || 10 ||

To the question, "What kind of learning is useful in this regard?", he says: "For he who... The meaning is that, through the power of the mantras inherent in the ritual action under discussion, the knower of the vital breath (prāṇa) has attained the aforementioned ritual action. || 10 ||
Sleeping on the ground, drinking water, celibacy, and restraint of speech.
This should be the Upasad vow, according to the indicative mark "on the new moon day. (11)
Regarding the phrase "having become one who performs the *upasad*," what is that vow (*vrata*) in the *upasad*s? To this he says: "On the ground. He provides the evidence for this:

"On the new moon day" (*amāvāsyā*). According to another scriptural passage stating, "Having been initiated on the new moon day during the northern course of the sun, [one should perform the rites] of the bright fortnight," and because practices such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) are well-known in the context of the fire-sacrifices (*sāgni*) as being performed on the new moon day, the meaning is that a fourfold set is intended here by the term "the vow of the *upasad*s. || 11 ||

Because of the singular form "Agni" and likewise because of the marking [of the ground] and so forth.
It is understood that there is no possibility here for the primary Upasads. || 12 ||
Fearing that, based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "the vow (*vrata*) is indeed the *upasad*," one might conclude that the four [acts] previously taught are not to be included, he says:

"Agnim iti. Because of the scriptural injunction, "Having established the fire" (*agnim upasamādhāya*), this ritual act is connected to a single fire; however, the *upasad*s, which are heard of in the context of the *pravargya* day in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, pertain to the three fires (*tretāgni*). Thus, this act—being connected to such things as the scraping and sweeping—is not possible for the *upasad*s.
The meaning is that, since those [etymologies] are impossible here, the derivation must be "the vow during the Upasads" (upasatsu vratam). || 12 ||
Copper or udumbara wood should be taken for the fuel, because of its opposition to that [iron].
Therefore, according to the Śruti, a sacrificial vessel made of udumbara wood should be taken from among the products of trees.

Regarding those who claim that in the alternative statement "audumbara" means copper (*tāmra*), he says: "It is copper. He states the reason for the contradiction with the supplementary text "the fuel-sticks are of *udumbara* wood" by saying: "By means of fuel-sticks. To the question of what kind of *audumbara* should then be taken, he says:
"That which belongs to the trees" (*vānaspatya*). || 13 ||
The ten types of cultivated grains and fruits and flowers are found everywhere.
And whatever impure foods there are here that cause one to lose the sense of "mine," [one should avoid them].

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "all herbs" (*sarvauṣadham*) by saying "those grown in villages" (*grāmyāṇi*). "From all" (*sarvataḥ*) means "all [of them]. He excludes intoxicating fruits by saying "without negligence" (*apramāda*). "In this case" (*iha*) means "when there is eating. He specifies what is to be excluded, such as garlic and the like, by saying "having eaten" (*bhakṣya*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "these [herbs] are to be taken in this ritual act. || 14 ||
The mention of "ten" would serve as a restrictive rule (niyama), not for the purpose of excluding anything other than that.
Because the restrictive injunction (parisaṃkhyā-vidhi) is vitiated by many defects. || 15 ||

He states the intended meaning of the qualification "ten" based on the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). Regarding the phrase "as ten": the purpose of the restriction is the taking of a counted number of substances, not the exclusion of others; the sense is that even when more than that [number] are taken, the qualification remains non-contradictory. To the question, "Why should the qualification not be for the sake of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) which excludes others?", he replies with the word "many" (*bhūri*). [For] there would be the abandonment of the scriptural (*śrauta*) qualification "all" (*sarva*).
The acceptance of the non-return [of grains] as heard in scripture:
"Rice, barley, wheat, millet, and sesame;..."
There were fragrant priyaṅgu flowers, excellent kora-dūṣa blossoms, and cīnaka grains.
Māṣas, mudgās, masūras, niṣpāvas, along with kulatthas,
āḍhakīs, caṇakas, and śyāmākas— these are recorded as the seventeen [types of pulses].
Thus, these are recorded as the species of cultivated plants;
including the medicinal herbs and the barley, there are fourteen types of village and forest plants.

The meaning is that because this [view] is corrupted by many defects, such as contradiction with Smṛti passages beginning with "ityādi," and because a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) is inapplicable here, there can only be a *niyama* (restrictive rule). The word "iti" serves the purpose of concluding the restrictive rule. || 15 ||
For the sake of establishing the forms of Kaṃsa and others, the account of Kaṃsa and his associates is related here.
Having ground rice, fruits, and flowers, one should place them in a vessel.
Having ground it with curd and honey, one should thoroughly stir it together in a vessel.
One should carefully place it in a pure location after performing the protective rite. || 17 ||

He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the alternative statement (*vikalpavākya*) beginning with "Kaṃsa, etc. Here, "here" refers to the vessel. The sense is that there is an option regarding the shape, whereas there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the *audumbara* wood which possesses that shape. He states the intended meaning of the phrase "having collected," beginning with "rice-grains. "Having stirred" means having churned it with a churning-stick (*khajaka*). The connection is: "having performed the protection with effort. [The word] "protection" (*rakṣā*)—
The instrument is the avoidance of injury by crows, dogs, and other such creatures. || 16 || 17 ||
And here, by the words "having circumambulated" and so forth, the consecration of the site is expressed.
Then, one should indeed establish the fire upon a consecrated plot of ground.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with *parisamuhya* (having swept around) as follows: "The word *pari*, etc. The purification of the site (*deśasaṃskāra*) consists of sweeping around, smearing, drawing lines, removing [impurities], and sprinkling water. The phrase "here" (*atra*) refers to the sentence under discussion. He explains the meaning of *agnim upasamādhāya* (having established the fire) as "purified" (*saṃskṛte*). This indicates that the purification of the ground is the cause for the installation of the fire. Then, the word "now" (*atha*)—and this...
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that what is well-known from the Gṛhya texts is what should be accepted. || 18 ||
And the application of ointments and so forth must be performed, because that procedure was prescribed even for one who has previously undergone it.
Thus says the statement of Kātyāyana, because [the rite] has an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha). || 19 ||

Now, one might object: since the ritual has already been commenced after ascertaining the purity of the location, a further consecration (*saṃskāra*) in that pure place is not required, as its purpose has already been accomplished; therefore, he says: "smearing and so forth. Even in a location that has been purified for a visible purpose, smearing and other rites must still be performed;

such is the statement composed by Kātyāyana, which is found [in the texts]: "having swept around, having smeared, having sprinkled [the ground], having removed [the dust], and having sprinkled [it with water]..."

And so forth. Thus, because the injunctions for sweeping and so on—like the injunctions for the Darśa and other sacrifices—are for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), they constitute a duty (*kāryatā*). For purification is of two kinds, distinguished as seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and unseen (*adṛṣṭa*); therein, the first is already accomplished prior to the performance [of the rite] even without an injunction, whereas the second is brought about by an injunction (*vaidhī*).
Therefore, the meaning is that sweeping and so on must be performed by means of the injunction for that purpose. || 19 ||
Having consecrated the clarified butter according to the rules of the *pākayajña* ritual, in the prescribed manner.
Having churned it with his hand and other non-perishing limbs for the sake of accomplishment, by the man. || 20 ||

Then, having unified the other substances with the *khājaka* ladle, one should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) at the place of insertion and thereafter perform the regular daily offerings (*nityāhuti*).
Beginning with the words "as many as," one should offer clarified butter with the mantras in due order.
[The text provided consists of two vertical bars, which function as a delimiter or section marker. ||
Having offered oblations repeatedly, he should frequently pour the remnants into the churning vessel.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "having strewn around" (*paristīrya*) and so forth with the words "the *pākayajña*," etc. Having performed the spreading of the seat for the Brahman priest, the placing of the *praṇītā* water, the strewing around, and so on, according to the instruction; having poured out the clarified butter and placed it over the fire; and having carried fire around it—this is the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* as stated.

The meaning is that one should offer the clarified butter (*ājya*) after having consecrated it by means of pouring, heating, and so forth. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "puṃsā" (by a male) as follows: "puṃseti" (regarding the word "male").

[The author] states the reason for the restriction regarding the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*): "Because of the accomplishments" (*siddhibhyaḥ*). For that [mansion] is useful for the attainment of wealth to be accomplished thereby; otherwise, it would contradict such scriptural texts as "by a man," and so forth—this is the meaning. "By the churning-stick" (*khajakena*) means by the first churning; [it refers to] another substance of the fire, which is the Self (*ātman*).

The remainder [of the sentence] is "he should place [them] to the south. He states the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) with the words "from this point forward. "The place of insertion" (*āvāpasthāna*) refers to the location for the specific pouring of the oblation. The connection is: "having sacrificed, he should pour the *saṃsrava* (residue). By the term "regular oblations" (*nityāhutīḥ*), those characterized as the two *āghāra* libations, the two *ājyabhāga* portions, the *mahāvyāhṛti*s, the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), and the *sviṣṭakṛt* are intended.
