He says "tataḥ" (therefore). O Jātavedas, whatever crooked-minded deities dependent upon you obstruct the goals of my person, to them I offer a portion of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) in you; and they, being satisfied by that, may satisfy this [person] with all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). "I am dependent on you, I am offered"—such is the meaning of the first mantra. He who knows what has been born, born again and again... (*jātaṃ jātaṃ vetti iti*... he is [Jātavedas].

Or, *jātavedāḥ* means "He who exists in every birth. That deity who, having become crooked-minded, exists depending upon you while thinking, "I alone shall sustain everything"—that all-accomplishing deity I worship with a stream of clarified butter; *svāhā*. As before, this is the meaning of the second mantra. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*), being connected with the *saṃsrava*, which is the clarified butter smeared on the *sruva* ladle. *Tikā* [is used] for connection.
The word "atha" (now) is used for the purpose of distinguishing the oblations to be described hereafter from the two preceding types of oblations. || 20 || 21 || 22 ||
All mantras as they have been described should end with the utterance of "svāhā. || 23 ||
A wise person should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the eldest brother and the others using two portions of my [mantra].
In the rite of establishing the sacred fires (agnyādheya) and others, it should be performed one by one, up until the stirring and touching of the fire-drill (mantha).

It makes known the measure of the mantra: "svāhā. It shows that which is intended by the word *atha* (now/then): "by one who knows thus" (*matrā iti vijānatā*), meaning by one who acts in the prescribed rite as if following an instruction. "In Agni and so forth" means in the mantra beginning with "to Agni, svāhā," starting from "to semen, svāhā"; as it is stated in the Bhāṣya, beginning with "of semen," each [offering] is a single oblation.
"Having offered," and so forth. || 23 || 24 ||
Then, at the conclusion of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, immediately after that oblation, he performed it.
2. Having stirred it with the second [hand], he touches it with his hand as prescribed. || 25 ||

Now, he explains the meaning of the word *atha* even here [in the phrase] "then him" (*athainaṃ*). He says: "Then" (*atha*). This means that when this oblation (*homa*) has been completed, the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation must be performed. He clarifies the meaning of the word *atha*, which was already stated, by saying: "oblation" (*homa*), etc. He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "by the other," etc.: "that," etc.; that is to say, another substance. When there is a stirring together with curds and honey by means of the first churning-stick...

The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that it is liberated in that same way. The word "atha" (then) excludes the immediate sequence of churning following the reflection, as in the expression "he sleeps having opened his mouth. || 25 ||
Reciting "bhramasi" and so forth, one should remember the churning-stick and its presiding deity with the heart-mantra.
You wander about as the very life-force of beings; indeed, you do not remain in one place.
He introduces that mantra with the words "bhramasi" and so forth; for the performance of a mantra whose deity is known is fruitful.
Having considered this, he says: "Remembering. How can the substance of the churning be addressed as "you are revolving," for it is not possible for that insentient thing to revolve by itself?
To this, he replies: "You are revolving. || 26 ||
Blazing and burning intensely, you perform the digestion of what resides within the stomach.
It is entirely full, all-pervading, and everywhere unbroken.

How, then, is it said that "it blazes," for there is no blazing in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is of the nature of movement? To this he says: "blazing. Whence, then, is the fullness of that which is limited? To this he says: "and full. He establishes its pervasiveness by means of its nature as Brahman: "everywhere. (27)
You are rendered motionless by your stability, O Forest of Space, and you do not tremble.
Because it is not an obstacle from any side and is entirely favorable to all.
It has been stated that "you alone are the single hoof," meaning that which is the single hoof is of your own nature.

Nevertheless, fearing the objection that even so, that which possesses activity through the nature of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth cannot be motionless, [the text] asserts that even that is indeed of the form of Brahman.

He said: "You are paralyzed. To the question, "How can it be called unconfined (*anavacchinna*), changeless (*avikriya*), and one-hoofed (*ekaśapha*)? For one who is devoid of feet and so forth cannot possess that meaning," he replied: "On all sides" (*sarvataḥ*). The meaning is this: since the vital substance in the form of breath (*prāṇa*) lacks any obstructing factor and is favorable to everything, the entire world remains included within the Self like a single hoof, existing in an unconfined state.

He summarizes what has been said with the word "śapha" (hoof). The meaning is: that which is indeed the single hoof consisting of the world exists as a mere portion of Your foot, and it is not even sufficient for the state of being a full foot; therefore, You are unlimited. || 28 || 29 ||
For the *hiṃ* was clearly uttered by the Udgātṛ priest while he was chanting the preceding *stotra*.
Then, at the commencement of the sacrifice, and while the Sāman was being sung in its middle portion, || 30 ||
For even when the *hiṃ* is being uttered, one should likewise designate it as the *udgītha*.
And you were made to hear [the mantra] by the Adhvaryu priest, and likewise by the Agnīdhra priest for the subsequent [rite]. || 31 ||

Nevertheless, one might ask: how can that which was previously *hiṃkṛtam* (already performed as *hiṃ*) be the very same thing being *hiṃkriyamāṇam* (currently being performed as *hiṃ*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says "by the difference in time," beginning with the words "udgātrā" (by the Udgātṛ). To indicate the consensus of ritual practitioners (*karmiṇām*) regarding the point that what was previously *hiṃkṛtam* is indeed the same thing being *hiṃkriyamāṇam* in the middle [of the rite], he uses the word "atha" (now/then). He extends the aforementioned meaning to the feet of the *udgītha* by saying "tathā" (so too). How [is it so] for the Udgātṛ, who is of the nature of the action to be accomplished?

Anticipating the objection that [the Self] consists of actions to be accomplished by the Adhvaryu and others, he says "because it is the self of all" (sarvātmakatvāt) in the verse beginning with "śrāvitaḥ" (30).
When lightning flashes within the womb of a cloud, it is said that you have been kindled.
Since you alone become manifold, you are therefore called the All-pervading (Vibhu).
Therefore, you, O Soma, prevail as the Lord through the states of vision and the rest.
Āditya exists as the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), and Soma as the nature of wealth (dhana).

He explains [the verse] beginning with "blazing in the moist" by means of the passage beginning with "in the moist. The connection is as follows: because you originate in the form of Soma and so forth, you are called "Lord" (*prabhu*). Now, one might object: how can that which has been described as all-pervasive (*vibhu*) be merely food and so forth, as stated in the passage beginning with "you are food"?
Regarding this, he says:

"The Sun. The division is as follows: the meaning of the first quarter, "Thou art light," and the second quarter, "Thou art food," has already been stated. For it is possible for that which is unlimited to assume the state of being food and so forth, because it is the Self of all—this is the sense of the word "hi" (for).
The meaning of the word [is as follows]: || 32 || 33 ||
O Lord, even that entire duality of the eater and the eaten is You alone.
You are the dissolution because you are the cause; for the effect merges back into the cause. || 34 ||

He states that very point in brief: "As food. Having raised the objection that it cannot be the *nidhana* because it is food, and that in its absence as food there would also be an absence of that [state], he says: "The *nidhana*. Even so, how can it be the *nidhana*?
To that he says: "Because it is the cause. || 34 ||
Because speech and the others merge into the Self, it is called "the absorber" (saṃvarga).
Thus ends this mantra for the rite of touching. || 35 ||

He states the meaning of the mantra "Thou art the absorber" (saṃvargo'si) with the word "Speech" (vāk). The meaning is that because speech and the other [senses] are withdrawn into the Self in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa) internally, and fire and the other [elements] are withdrawn in the form of air (vāyu) externally. He explains the meaning of the word "iti" with the word "iti. || 35 ||
Then he raises him up, purified by mantras, exactly as prescribed.
This [verse] beginning with "āma si" is the manifestation of that very meaning. || 36 ||
Having described the raising of the *mantha*, he introduces its mantra and promises an explanation of it with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*).
The meaning of the word "now" (*atha*) is immediate succession to the act of touching (*abhimarśana*). || 36 ||
The form *āmaṃsīt* would belong to the root *man*, which has the meaning of "knowing."
Because of the restrictive rule stating that [the suffix] *śap* is elided (*śabluk*) when preceded by *leṭ*, the form is established as *saṃsiddham*. || 37 ||

In order to explain the meaning of the word, he first states the manner in which the word is formed: "āmasītīti. The construction is as follows: from the verbal root *man*, meaning "to know," preceded by the prefix *ā*, when the suffix *leṭ* is applied and the *śap* affix is elided, this form is established. In this regard, he provides the authority of grammatical procedure: "because of the restriction [expressed] by 'iti'. (37)
You perceive everything throughout the entire world, from the most subtle to the coarsest.
Therefore, he always perceived whatever is knowable, as far as the world extends.

Now he states the meaning of the word: "on all sides" (āsamantāt). The meaning is that since you always know everything whatsoever—whether subtle or otherwise—that exists in this world from every direction, you are therefore designated by the conventional term "Jagadāma" (the Knower of the World). || 38 ||
Just as you know us, so do we always know you.
We consider him to be more excellent than those possessed of virtues, for he is superior in virtue. || 39 ||

Having stated that the *mantha* is omniscient by virtue of its being the self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he explains the meaning of the verse beginning with "āmaṃhi te" (RV 10.87.21) with the words "yathā... (as follows). The phrase "varīyāṃsam" is explained as "guṇavṛddhayaḥ" (for the increase of qualities). || 39 ||
O Lord, we know your greatness to be vast; you are indeed the Unborn.
Yet you do not suffer the destruction of your fruit-bearing forest through your association with fire.

He states the meaning of the word "mahī" (earth). Having taken the indivisible word "āmaṃhī" and explained its meaning, he then takes the two words...

He states the meaning of the mantra "tvām āmam" as "āmo 'si" (you are raw). This means, in accordance with the knowledge of its greatness. He establishes its state of being raw [or unmanifest] with the words "na tvam" (not you). || 40 ||
Even rawness that has reached you is called "greatness."
Because he is the king of all this, and that god is always mine as well. (41)
And likewise, may you make me the sovereign king and the lord.
Having raised it with this mantra, he then consumes it portion by portion.

He states the meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed): "Āma" [is the word]. The meaning is that the wise person, knowing that even the greatness established in you is, like you, *āma*—that is, indestructible—ascertains it as such. Having relied upon the indestructibility of that greatness, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "sa hi" (for he), starting with the words "yasmāt" (because). Since there are instances where, despite being born into royalty, one lacks the power of governance, he states a distinction from that case.

Regarding the word "Īśānam": since it is observed that even one who possesses the power of a ruler, such as a prince, may be subject to the control of ministers and others, he qualifies [the term] by saying "Adhipatim" (the Sovereign Lord). Then, having first restated the context, he explains the meaning of the phrase "Then he sips water" with the words "Having raised," etc. The word "atha" (then) is used to state that eating is the result of raising [the vessel]. || 41 || 42 ||
One should [recite] the Gāyatrī, the Madhumatī, and the Vyāhṛtis, each by its quarter-verse.
For he eats a morsel of the churned drink (mantha), and likewise in the subsequent [sections]. || 43 ||

Regarding how the consumption is to be performed portion by portion, he says: "With the Gāyatrī," and so forth. Having divided the substance of the *mantha* into four mouthfuls, one should consume one mouthful with the first foot of the Gāyatrī, the first *madhumatī*, and the first *vyāhṛti*; the rule for consuming the remaining mouthfuls is exactly the same. One should consume the second mouthful with the second foot of the Gāyatrī and the second *madhumatī*.

Eating the second morsel with the second *vyāhṛti*, he should eat the third morsel with the third foot of the *gāyatrī*, with the third *madhumatī* verse, and with the third *vyāhṛti*; and he should consume the fourth morsel with the entire *gāyatrī*, the whole *madhumatī* verse, and all the *vyāhṛtis*.
The meaning is that the consumption is to be performed in portions accompanied by these mantras in this manner. || 43 ||
That most excellent splendor of the Great-Souled Savitṛ is his food.
Likewise, the winds blow in accordance with the cosmic order, bringing about happiness like honey.

He states the meaning of the verse beginning with *tatsaviturvareṇyam*. Regarding the word *savitur*: the word "pada" (the state) is *vareṇya*, meaning it is to be chosen, to be worshipped; he states the meaning of the word *bharga* as the reason for this. Regarding *bhargam*: the connection is "of the great-souled Savitṛ. Great-souledness consists of being all-pervasive (*vyāpitva*), being the self of all (*sarvātmatva*), being the progenitor (*savitṛtva*)—that is, being the cause of the production of everything—and being the means of accomplishing that.
He explains the first [verse], "madhumatī": "ṛtāyantaḥ. He states the meaning of the word "tathā" as "sukhakāriṇaḥ" (those who cause happiness). || 44 ||
They cause no agitation, are pleasing to the heart, and carry one toward the truth.
Nectar, honey, and even rivers are always auspicious for my sake. || 45 ||

He explains that very point: "free from agitation. He states the object to be attained: "the immortal. The word "and" (*ca*)—[as found in Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Six, page 911].

The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a conjunction with "bearing the nectar that produces happiness. The connection is as follows: the rivers (*sindhavaḥ*), meaning streams, always flow (*kṣaranti*) with auspicious honey, which is to say, nectar. || 45 ||
"By which we, being satisfied, rejoice and flow"—this is the verbal action (*kriyāpada*).
And may our medicinal herbs possess exceedingly sweet flavors. || 46 ||
He states the fruit of the flow of honey: "Satisfied" (tṛptāḥ). Intending that the accusative case is used in the sense of the nominative, he says: "Exceedingly" (atyartham).
The word "hi" (for) is used to state that the sweetness of the juices of herbs is well-known in the world. || 46 ||
Having recited the *trikam*, one should cast an oblation into the mouth with the words "bhūḥ svāhā."
Having likewise uttered each triad, one should apply them to the others as well. || 47 ||
Having uttered the triad consisting of the two previously mentioned items together with "bhūḥ svāhā," he states that the consumption of the first morsel occurs at the end of the *vyāhṛtis*.

Regarding the word "trikam" (the triad): just as with the first oblation, one should perform the second and third oblations by uttering the triad each time; however, for the fourth, one should utter everything.
Thus, one should understand the procedure for the three morsels. The word "hi" (for) is used to indicate the equality of the underlying principle. || 47 ||
May we contemplate that which is dear to the heart of the radiant God.
The night is honey-sweet, and thus the night is sweet, destroying all suffering. (48)
May the sweetness of both the dawn and the day be ours forever.
And the world [consists of] the earthly dust, as well as Halāyudha, Madhu, and Mān.
The world is the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), for the father is indeed considered to be heaven.
One should offer the second oblation of the stirred drink with the mantra: "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā. || 50 ||

1.1 Since the word *bharga* has already been explained in the passage beginning with "the splendor (*bhargas*) of the god," he now explains what remains: "of the god" (*devasya*). [The remainder is: "excellent... (*vare-*)...
He restates what was said as "pleasing" (*hṛdyam*). The construction is: "May we meditate upon that foot of the God which is pleasing.
He explains the second [verse], the "Madhumatī" (Honeyed). Regarding "madhu": the word *atha* following the word *rātri* is connected in the sense of "also" (*api*).
"Lokas" are called "rajas" (worlds). Relying on the Vedic text, "He strode across these worlds," he says: "Rajas means world (*loka*)."

Thus [ends the passage]. The word "tathā" (likewise) serves as an illustration by means of the example of night and so forth. Regarding the statement that "the sky is the father," he states the reason: "For he is the father. The word "mataḥ" (is considered) implies "in the Śruti" as the ellipsis. The word "atha" (now/then) serves as an illustration by means of the motherhood of the earth, as in the phrase "this earth is indeed the mother.

Having recited the second quarter of the Gāyatrī verse concerning the aforementioned meaning, and having recited the second Madhumatī verse, and having said "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā," [he offers] the second [oblation].
"One should perform the oblation," he said. "Bhuvaḥ. (48) (49) (10)
May He who, rising, impels our intellects and our sense-faculties [grant us wisdom].
May the Divine impel us toward our own ultimate welfare at all times. 51.

Taking the third foot of the *gāyatrī*, he analyzes it: "Dhiyaḥ... The meaning is that Savitṛ, who exists as he rises, may at all times impel our thoughts—that is, the cognitions and the instruments thereof—as well as ourselves, toward our highest good. || 11 ||
May the lord of the forest, as well as the moon and the sun, be sweet for us.
May the rays be cows, or else may the quarters of the sky be full of sweetness.

He explains the third [verse], "madhumatī," as "vanaspati. According to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), "The Moon is the deity of the trees (*vanaspati*); Soma is the deity of the herbs (*oṣadhi*)," it follows that the word *tat* (in the compound *tanmadhu*) refers to those [trees and herbs]; this is the meaning. The word *tathā* is used for the purpose of connecting [the phrase] with "may it be sweet" (*madhuro'stu*). Anticipating the objection that there would be a redundancy because the rays (*dīdhiti*) are already included by the mention of the planets such as the Sun, he states another alternative: "diśa-" [etc.].
Thus [ends the section]. 12.
Then one should utter the entire formula "Svaḥ Svāhā" while casting the oblation.
As well as the Sāvitrī, the Madhumatī, and likewise the three Vyāhṛtis.
In this manner, one should offer the fourth oblation into the mouth as before.
Speaking thus: "May I alone become the entire world," (54)

Having stated the two previously mentioned meanings, he says, "Svaḥ svāhā," [prescribing that] one should offer the third oblation while uttering "Svaḥ svāhā. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "sarvāṃ ca" (and the whole) by saying "samastām" (the entire). Since it was stated "as before," there might be a doubt regarding the fourth oblation that it lacks a mantra other than the Gāyatrī and so forth; therefore, he says, "I myself... The connection with the preceding is: "one should cast the oblation. ||53||94||
However, the Smārta sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed here at the end for the sake of purification.
Then, at the end, he should lie down to the west of the fire with his head facing east. || 55 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "finally, having sipped water" as follows: "Smārta" (pertaining to the Smṛti). If this sipping of water is mentioned here at the end of the fourth mouthful, it is not something previously unestablished; rather, it is for the sake of purification—[as stated]:
"Having sipped water, being pure and composed, one should always perform both the twilight devotions."
"In a pure place, one should perform the recitation of that which is to be recited, attending to it according to the rule."
The meaning is that what is well-known from such Smṛti texts is merely being restated here. He explains the meaning of "having washed his hands" and so forth with the words "of the fire.

The word "atha" (then) signifies the sequence following the sipping of water (*ācamana*) and the subsequent washing of the hands. The word "ante" (at the end) means when the consumption of four mouthfuls has been completed.
Then he says "tataḥ" (thereafter), meaning that one should remain established in the vow until the morning twilight (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*) and sleep [only then]. || 55 ||
Then, at dawn, he worships the sun with devotion.
One should always worship the Sun with the mantra that is about to be recited.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "In the morning [one should worship] the Sun" by saying "At dawn. The meaning is that, having risen from bed and gone outside, one should perform the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*) and, with devotion and faith, perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) upon the Sun at the time of its rising. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that this twilight worship is well-established in the *Smṛtis*. Introducing that mantra, he describes the nature of the ritual attendance by saying "by what is about to be stated."
The word "sadā" (always) is understood to mean "at every rising"; the particle "hi" is used for the purpose of indicating that the worship of the Sun is also well-known. || 56 ||
The phrase "a single lotus" is intended to signify preeminence.
By the word "one" (eka), we do not mean numerical unity, as in the case of "the one Śvetavāhana. (57)

He explains the mantra. Regarding the word "one" (*eka*), he says [it is used] because there is a suspicion that it refers to a numerical category. He says [the following] having raised the doubt that the word "one" is not used in the sense of the primary [cause]: "Just as... (17).

Just as you are the foremost among the quarters, so indeed am I among human beings.
O Lord, by your grace, may I become prosperous through the means for human enjoyment. (58)

Having stated the meaning of the individual words (*padārtha*), he states the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). Regarding the word "of the directions" (*diśām*): the particle *hi* is used for the purpose of indicating that [the quarters] are capable of fully recognizing their own preeminence and excellence. He clarifies such self-preeminence with the word "abundant" (*sphīta*). || 18 ||
Having returned by the same way he came, he then sits down behind the fire with a concentrated mind.
One should recite this lineage with effort and devotion, saying "That indeed is this. (59)

He brings down the recitation of the *vaṃśa* (lineage). "In the same manner" means that immediately after the worship of the Sun, having returned from the outside by the way he came, sitting behind the fire, one should recite the *vaṃśa* with effort, concentration, and devotion; this is the meaning. || 19 ||
I consider that very same point which was stated there by the wise son of Uddālaka.
Having spoken thus, he, filled with wonder, then addressed that [instruction] to Yājñavalkya.

He explains the passage beginning with "taṃ ha" and so forth. Regarding "taṃ ha": the meaning of the first word "atha" (now) is immediate succession to the meditation on Prāṇa; the meaning of the second word "atha" is immediate succession to the performance of ritual action. The sense is that having performed both, Uddālaka, being struck with wonder, instructed Yājñavalkya in the Mantha and spoke again. || 60 ||
If one were to pour the aforementioned consecrated churned drink even upon a withered tree stump, [it would cause it to flourish].
Indeed, its branches would be born and its leaves would sprout. || 61 ||
In response to the expectation of what was said, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who [knows] this," etc., as follows: "The churning-stick" (mantham). || 61 ||
The meaning of this statement is the same even in the subsequent passages.
The meaning of the statement regarding the four udumbara fruits has already been explained previously.
And because it is easy to understand, let it be realized by oneself alone. || 62 ||
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

In the subsequent sentences beginning with "this" (*etam*), he extends by analogy what has been stated [previously]. Regarding the phrase "of such a kind" (*yādṛg*): this was stated when the explanation of the sentence beginning with "it consists of four *audumbara* [pieces]" (*caturaudumbaro bhavati*) was reached. Regarding the word "four" (*catur*): the meaning is that it refers to the very same [cup] previously mentioned as being either made of *udumbara* wood or a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*). Furthermore, he says "easily" (*sukha*) because there is no further expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) since the sentence concerning the four *audumbara* pieces and so forth has already been explained through its own recitation (*nigada*). [The text mentions] another substance...

Having placed [the oblation] in a vessel made of udumbara wood and having smeared it with the triad beginning with curd, one should perform the constant ājya oblations according to the previously stated procedure;

the meaning of the particle "eva" (only) is that one should effect the *saṃpāta* (pouring together of remnants) during the subsequent oblations, as has already been stated. Anticipating the objection—"In the passage concerning the four udumbara vessels and so forth, how can there be an understanding of its meaning in the absence of an explanatory commentary?"—he says: "By himself alone. || 62 ||
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtikaṭīkā.

Now begins the fourth Brāhmaṇa.
By the statement "of these," the praise of the seed of man is intended to be expressed.
"I shall fashion a foundation upon which masculinity is established. (1)

Having described the rite called *mantha* for one who worships the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and desires wealth, the text introduces another *brāhmaṇa* section in order to describe the *putramantha* (the rite for obtaining a distinguished son) for that same person desiring a son. The connection is with the passage beginning with "of these" (*eṣām*) and ending with "semen" (*retaḥ*).
He introduces the phrase beginning with "together" (*saha*) by saying "as a support" (*pratiṣṭhām*); [he refers to] such a support upon which the semen is established and attains virility.
The meaning is that Prajāpati reflected, "I shall fashion a foundation. || 1 ||
Wherever this semen is emitted, there it attains the state of manhood.
The Lord Prajāpati fashioned such a foundation for it. || 2 ||
He explains it thus: "The bright. || 2 ||
He created a woman suitable for that purpose, as described in the Madhukāṇḍa.
Having created her, he then worships her in the lower region according to the worldly way.

He explains the passage beginning with "He [beheld] a woman" (*sa striyam*). Regarding the word "woman": the pronoun "that" (*tat*) refers to the purpose of the emission of semen. He states that she is Śatarūpā, who was designated by the word "wife" (*patnī*) in the passage "Then he became both husband and wife" (*tataḥ patiśca patnī cābhavatām*). Regarding the phrase "in the Madhu-kāṇḍa": he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "For the sake of creation" (*sṛṣṭyai*). The meaning of the word "then" (*atha*) is the immediate succession to the fitness for the act of procreation. [He explains] the method of meditation according to the *Kāma-śāstra*...
This indicates what was stated previously: "vulgar," etc. || 3 ||
For the production of offspring, Prajāpati [created] the lower region of women.
Therefore, he previously worshipped that which was to be worshipped with great effort.

He explains the passage beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore) as follows: "apatya" means by that seeker of offspring, that is to say, by the lover; it refers to the effort involving the sequential and non-sequential order prescribed by the treatise. || 4 ||
Now, therefore, that which was previously mentioned is stated for the purpose of establishing the nature of the Soma-pressing.
He drew his own penis out, just as one draws a pressing-stone from water. || 5 ||
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "sa etam" as follows: "Soma... Here, a conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of the Vājapeya sacrifice is applied to the act of sexual intercourse;

therein, the perception of the pressing-stones used for crushing Soma is superimposed upon the generative organ, which is an ancillary part of that act. The meaning is that by means of that stone, the capacity of the fivefold sense-organ—namely its hardness—is expressed either by this [stone] or by another. The word "atha" (now) serves to introduce the conceptualization of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
He applies the sentence to the meaning already stated: "This... (1).
Then, having made that penis into a pressing-stone, just as it was.
One should carefully cause him to sit together with the woman in a state of union.

In response to the inquiry as to what Prajāpati did after making his own generative organ as hard as a stone, [Sureśvarācārya] says:
"Toward the east" (*prāñcam*). Here, the intended meaning is the making [of it] straight and long; "effort" (*yatnaḥ*) refers to the exertion applied toward the task at hand.
The word "woman" (nārī) refers to the object of her sense organ; "unification" (ekībhāva) is the mutual mingling of the two.
With such a stone, he repeatedly hurled it at this woman.
For the sake of one's own human goal, there should be meditation as previously described. || 7 ||

He explains the passage beginning with "In this [way]," etc. Regarding the phrase "in that manner" (*tathā*): for what purpose is the performance of the animal sacrifice (*paśukarma*) intended to accomplish the Vājapeya?

To this he says: "Of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*). That which constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) will be explained later in the passage beginning with "But as great as that [human goal] is," and so forth. || 7 ||
In which [womb] the procreative power of the man is internalized within the woman.
Her lap shall be the sacrificial altar, visible above her thighs.

Explaining the passage beginning with "its altar," he states the method of meditation. Regarding the phrase "in which": he states the intended meaning as "on the thighs. The sense is that one should perform the visualization of the altar in a location that is not explicitly mentioned [in the primary description]. || 8 ||
The hairs are the bladder, and likewise the skin is the two pressing-boards.
One should look upon the hide of a bull for the successful pressing of the Soma.

He explains the passage beginning with "the hairs" (*lomāni*) and so forth. Regarding the word "outside" (*bahis*): the meaning is that one should perform the visualization of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon the body hair of the private region, the visualization of the ox-hide (*ānaḍuhacarma*) upon the skin located there, and likewise the visualization of the two pressing-skins (*adhiṣavaṇa*) upon the two masses of flesh situated on both sides of the testicles.

He clarifies what was mentioned as "skin" by saying "skin": that well-known ox-hide used in the sacrifice for the purpose of pressing the Soma is here [to be visualized] as the second [pressing-skin].
The construction is: "one should perceive the skin arising from the region of the anus. || 9 ||
And one should designate the two pressing-boards according to their respective order. || 10 ||
Whatever region is situated within the womb, one should designate as the blazing armor.
The two testicles situated around that region are the *vṛṣaṇas*. || 11 ||

He clarifies what was stated as "likewise on the pressing-boards" (*adhiṣavaṇe tathā*) by saying "and on the two boards" (*phalake ca*). For on the two pressing-boards—the southern and northern boards used for pressing the Soma—one should superimpose the vision of the two *muṣka*s (testicles), the southern and northern *vṛṣaṇa*s, respectively, according to their numerical correspondence upon those two boards.

The meaning is that one should designate [them as] "form" (rūpa) and so forth. He states the meaning of the phrase "kindled in the middle" (*samiddho madhyataḥ*) as: "that which is in the womb" (*yo yoni*).
The meaning is that one should form the visualization of fire upon the region within the womb. He states the meaning of the phrase "those two testicles" (*tau muṣkau*) as: "the skin.

One should designate those two testicles (*muṣkau*) situated inside the skin that surrounds the region of the womb as the "testes" (*vṛṣaṇau*). The meaning is that the visualization of the two pressing-sieves (*adhiṣavaṇa*) has been stated for those two.
The world belongs to the one performing the Rājapeya sacrifice by virtue of his honor.
He attains as great a world as one does from the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having explained the manner of worship, he introduces the statement regarding the fruit with the words: "The world would be. It is prescribed by means of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
The meaning is that as great as the light may be for one who possesses knowledge, so great shall it be for the worshiper of this [Self] as well. He explains that very statement regarding the fruit:
"tāvantam" (to that extent). || 12 ||
For the foods are prepared in portions, seventeen in number.
That [rite] is prescribed for one who desires food in the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 13 ||

Having raised the objection—“Even if there is a superimposition of the subsidiary parts of the Vājapeya upon the limbs of the animal-sacrifice, how can that superimposition exist there given the lack of similarity?”—the author establishes the nature of the Vājapeya as food in order to demonstrate that similarity. He says: "Foods. According to the scriptural injunction, "He sacrifices seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati," foods are prepared in the Vājapeya for each respective deity without confusion; and this [Vājapeya] is for one who desires all kinds of food.
It is ordained as the object of enjoyment for one who desires self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), because that fruit is not distinct from food; therefore, the meaning is that he consists of food. || 13 ||
Where the oblation of food is observed, it is indeed of the seed, which is the essence of food.
Therefore, the sacrifice known as sexual union is intended to be the perfect attainment of the Vājapeya.
This should be understood as being due to similarity for those who desire the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 14 ||

He states that even the act of animal sacrifice (*paśukarma*) has that same nature. Regarding the phrase "of semen" (*retasaḥ*): in whatever sacrifice the oblation of the essence of food—namely, semen—is intended to be of the nature of food, since that [act] called sexual union is fit to be considered food, it follows by this very commonality that the attainment of the Vājapeya sacrifice occurs in this ritual. Alternatively, in whichever person the oblation of food is desired, in that very "fire" (the sacrificer), the gods...

The meaning is that because of the Vedic text, "They offer food," the semen of that man consists of the essence of the food he has eaten; since that [semen] is offered as an oblation in a particular rite, it possesses the nature of "food" (*anna*) as previously described, and thus the perception of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice is to be applied to it. Anticipating the objection that meditation (*upāsti*) might be open to all, he says:
"It is to be understood thus. This means that meditation in the manner described belongs to those who desire its fruit, even without the actual performance of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice.
...up to verse 14.
He enjoys the merit of women and wins all that is auspicious.
The wise man who indulges in derisive laughter as previously described, || 15 ||

He states that there is a superior fruit for this meditation: "And of women," etc. The connection is that one who knows the aforementioned excellence of the animal sacrifice as being identical with the Vājapeya [sacrifice] [attains the fruit]. || 15 ||
Women do not appropriate merit or well-performed deeds unless they are of such a nature.
This is indeed the reality of the secret doctrine of sexual union; so it was said by the Perfected One.

In the phrase "my son is Śukla," he explains the word *śukla* in two ways. Regarding the explanation of [the passage] beginning with "it is the Veda," it was stated [in the previous verse] that it is "easy to explain. The word *iti* marks the end of the supplementary portion. || 70 ||
Then the husband himself cooked that milk-rice with that same [milk],
and the couple ate that rice mixed with ghee.
May those two, independent and sovereign, be for the birth of a virtuous son.

He states the meaning of "rice cooked with milk" (*kṣīraudana*) and so forth: "Milk," etc. The meaning of the word *atha* (then) is the immediate succession to the aforementioned desires. He explains "abounding in ghee" (*sarpiṣmantam*) and so forth: "The couple" (*daṃpatī*). The meaning of the word *atha* is the immediate succession to the oblation (*homa*). He states the meaning of the word *īśvara*: "Independent" (*svatantrau*). || 71 || 72 ||
Either upon the birth of a son as previously described, or if they act with haste.
By means of this armor as previously described, those two shall indeed become husband and wife.

Anticipating the objection that there is no independence [of the agent] because of dependence on unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, he says: "As stated. By this, it is meant "by means of the *caru*-oblation and so forth. (73)
"The daughter is wise" refers here to women's appropriate duties.
That should be known as true scholarship here, and not that which has the meaning of the Vedas as its object. (74)

Regarding the statement, "My daughter is wise," one might raise the objection: how can wisdom concerning the meaning of the Vedas be desired for a daughter, since she lacks the qualification for Vedic study? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The daughter. The word "that" (tat) refers to the daughter; the word "here" (iha) is connected with the phrase "in the duties appropriate for women. || 74 ||
1.1 Not so.
[vol 3, page 925]
2060 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter Six:
He who has been proclaimed as the one who has utterly conquered this world.
An assembly of the learned is a *samiti*; one who is fit for such an assembly is a *samitingama*. || 75 ||
He explains "vijigīta" and so forth with the passage beginning "vijigīta," etc. (79).
Because the word "all" is employed in reference to the number three that is under discussion.
One should study the four Vedas for the sake of knowing the meaning of all words.

Anticipating the objection that since the word "all" (*sarva*) in the phrase "all the Vedas" has already fulfilled its purpose by referring to the three Vedas, the expression "the three Vedas" would be a mere repetition, he says: "In the context at hand... (verse 76).
Having cooked rice mixed with meat, they know it as *māṃsaudana* (rice with meat).
The bull (ukṣan) is a cow capable of sprinkling; he himself is the great bull (ṛṣabha). || 77 ||

Regarding the phrase "having cooked meat-rice" (*māṃsaudanaṃ pācayitvā*), he explains the meaning of the term *māṃsaudana* with the word "rice-grains" (*taṇḍulān*). Regarding the two-word compound in "or with [the meat of] a bull" (*aukṣeṇa vā*) and so forth, he states that there is no tautology between the two words with the word "bull" (*ukṣā*). || 77 ||
Since the [ancient] tradition is no longer possible today, it is appropriate regarding meat-rice that they prepare the meat from black deer and goats. (78)

Fearing that the consumption of beef might also follow as a consequence due to the force of qualifiers such as "with a bull" (*aukṣeṇa*), which contradicts common consensus, he says: "Common consensus" (*prasiddhi*). The word "for" (*hi*) is used for the purpose of indicating what is generally accepted in the world. If so, how then is there the scriptural mention of "meat-rice" (*māṃsaudana*)?
To this he says: "Meat" (*māṃsa*). If one then asks how it can be a qualifier, he replies that it is with reference to a specific time.
If he should bring meat that has been acquired through effort, or purchased;
Because violence is prohibited, one should not kill animals oneself. (79)

Then, one might object that one should personally kill black antelopes and the like to procure meat; this is raised with the words "by effort" (yatnena). He refutes this with the words "having purchased" (krītvā); the word "or" (vā) is for the purpose of removing the objection. He states the reason why meat should not be procured by killing it oneself with the words "because of violence" (hiṃsāyāḥ). || 79 ||
The word "atha" (then/now) has the sense of an alternative, according to one's preference among those [methods] already mentioned.
For it is said with reference to one or another of the optional positions. || 80 ||

Now, he explains the purpose of the frequent use of the word *atha* in the phrase "atha ya icchet" (if one should desire). He says: "atha. He reveals the meaning in the form of an alternative. The word *hi* is used for the sake of establishing the multiplicity of the aforementioned desires.
The ellipsis is: "it is said that this is the rule regarding food. (80)
From the moment the sun begins its ascent, all [acts] such as bathing and so forth must be performed in their entirety.
Then, having performed the purificatory rites with effort, he was proclaimed as Māghya. || 81 ||
He removes the restriction that the preparation of rice through threshing and so forth occurs on the previous day, while the eating of desired food occurs on the following day, by stating:

"beginning with. This means that starting from the time of sunrise, after having completed all the obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*), immediately thereafter [one may eat], as previously mentioned, that which is [the result of] threshing.
Having prepared such a consecrated offering with effort, one should perform the eating of the desired food; the meaning is that there is no distinction between these two days regarding this duty.
The word "atha" (now) is used to indicate that the performance of occasional rites follows immediately after the daily obligatory rites. || 81 ||
The ritual performed with the *sthālīpāka* is designated as the *āvṛt*.
And likewise, having consecrated the clarified butter according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* offering.

Regarding the phrase "with the procedure of the *sthālīpāka*," he explains the meaning of the word "procedure" (*āvṛt*). He says: "the *sthālīpāka*. Thus, the connection with what follows is: "he offers oblations with the very same procedure prescribed for the *sthālīpāka*. (82)
The mention of clarified butter (ājya) should be understood as an indicative mark for other substances as well.
Or, due to the elision of the word "ādi" (and so forth), it should be understood as "ājyādi" (clarified butter and the rest). || 83 ||

Having raised the objection that since only the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is heard in the injunction "having consecrated the *ājya*," there is no intention to include the consecration of the sacrificial cake (*caru*) and other materials, he says:

"It is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, he says that the phrase "having consecrated the *ājya* and so forth" does not suffer from the fault of the non-appearance of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), because the omission of what actually exists is possible due to the negligence of the reciter and other causes; thus, the word "and so forth" [is justified].
"Of him," [it is said]. || 83 ||
Then, having repeatedly offered portions of the *sthālīpāka*, it is so considered.
Having offered the daily oblations there with devotion at the place for insertion (āvāpasthāna), [he should proceed].

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "of the *sthālīpāka*," etc., by saying "having offered" (*upahatya*). The meaning is that after the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth, one should perform the *caru*-oblation by repeatedly offering oblations at the previously mentioned place of insertion (*āvāpasthāna*), according to the force of the *sthālīpāka* mantras such as "to Agni, svāhā," because the intent is for these to be obligatory (*nitya*). || 84 ||
There are three principal oblations which begin with Agni and the others.
Having offered the oblations and completed that [rite] as prescribed, ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, || 85 ||
Then, with a concentrated mind, he should take this sacrificial portion (karman) from the vessel as a caru offering.
Then, one should eat food accompanied by clarified butter, in accordance with the desired purpose. || 86 ||

He states the rule for the number of oblations to be performed immediately after the completion of the *āghāra* and other preliminary rites, beginning with the words "pradhāna" (the principal). He explains the meaning of the passage starting with "tvoddhṛtya" (having drawn out) with the word "hutvā" (having offered). Having performed the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) *homa* with clarified butter (*ājya*) and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and having completed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should then, with a concentrated mind, draw out the remaining *caru* from the vessel, drench it in ghee, and [offer it] for the birth of a desired son.
The meaning is that one should eat facing [the east]. He states the reason why eating the remnant of the oblation as described is beneficial for the son: "Now," [he says]. || 89 ||
Having himself partaken of the sacrificial oblation (caru), he gives the remainder to his wife.
The husband gives the sacrificial porridge (caru) to his wife as leavings (ucchiṣṭa).

He explains the passage beginning with "having eaten" (*prāśya*) and so forth. Regarding the word "caru": fearing that one might think the husband gives the remainder of the *caru* still situated in the cooking pot to his wife, he says: "the leavings" (*ucchiṣṭam*). || 87 ||
1 ka. kha. *jyādi saṃ* | [Vol.
3, page 927] 2062 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [Sixth Chapter]—
Having washed one's hands with care, it is understood by implication alone.
The Smārta rite of sipping water (ācamana) is for the sake of purification, as stated in the injunction regarding the washing of the hands.

He explains the passage beginning with "having washed," etc., as follows: "The hands. Effort consists in bringing a large quantity of water and washing repeatedly for the purpose of removing dirt. The connection is that one should sprinkle the wife. Since only the washing of the hands is mentioned in the scripture, and since there is no purity without *ācamana* (sipping water), how could the husband be authorized to perform the sprinkling and other rites? To this he replies: "By implication" (*sāmarthyāt*).

Then, since the object of the designation is pure, the sipping of water (ācamana) is established by implication; for the object of the designation cannot be established without it—such is the construction. || 88 ||
Then, taking a water-pot, he should sprinkle it three times with that water for the sake of obtaining a son.
One should repeatedly sprinkle the wife with the mantra that is about to be recited. || 89 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "udapātram" (a vessel of water). Regarding "udapātram": the word "atha" signifies the sequence immediately following the washing of the hands. By using the word "muhur" (repeatedly) after having said "tris" (thrice), he indicates that the repetition applies only to the sprinkling and not to the mantra. || 89 ||
Therefore, rising from this place of ours, come to us from elsewhere.
By the name Viśvāvasu, a Gandharva is awakened here. || 90 ||
He explains that mantra with the words "from this" (ataḥ). This means from one thing to another; "here" (atra) refers to the statement of the mantra. ||90||
The word "prapūrvyām" here refers to a woman; indeed, it denotes a young girl.
O Viśvāvasu, go quickly to another woman who is more abundant and more plump. || 91 ||
Explaining the word "anyām," he connects the sentence [as follows]: "prapūrvyām" means one who is firmly established, resolute, and capable—so it amounts to saying. || 91 ||
And from the indicative mark of the word "prapūrvyām," the husband of a virtuous wife is always [present] with a young woman.
One should perform the ritual as prescribed when the truth exists, for the sake of begetting a virtuous son.

He states the meaning established by the force of those words: "prapūrvyām" (in one who has reached [maturity]). This means, by virtue of the word indicating youth; the connection is "when there is a young woman. It is stated that "the time of the season is present. He states the fruit of performing the ritual acts as prescribed—such as the threshing and so forth—up to the end of the animal sacrifice: "sad" (present). || 92 ||
"But my intention is this: 'I shall approach this lady as my wife.'"
Having thus dispatched the Gandharva, he then approaches her.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "jāyām" (his wife) as follows: "Aham" (I). The meaning of the construction of the sentence is: "I am approaching this wife of mine who is staying with me, her husband; you should grant me leave for that. He then introduces the passage beginning with "athainām" (then her) as follows: "Evam" (Thus). The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is the absence of any obstruction to the embrace immediately after the Gandharva had departed. ||93||
The husband embraces his wife for the sake of the desired conception of an embryo.
By the recitation of the mantra "I am He," we two have become identical with the deity.
O Goddess, one should undertake ritual action for the sake of accomplishing the birth of a virtuous son.
Both you and I, having come together, shall deposit our seed in the womb.
He states this attainment (*abhipatti*) with the words "abhīṣṭa" (desired). He shows the mantra for the embrace with the words "amo'hamiti.

He explains the meaning of "tāv ehi" and so forth with the word "tau. Anticipating the doubt as to what this commencement of action is, he explains the meaning of "saha" and so forth with the words "tvaṃ ca. || 94 || 99 ||
And he has stated the fruit of discharging semen for the sake of obtaining a male son.
Immediately after reciting the mantra, he should say to her: "May you sport [with me]. || 96 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "puṃse putrāya" (for the male child) as follows: "The semen... etc. Showing the meaning of the word *atha* (then) found in the subsequent sentence, he introduces the mantra for the parting [of the wife's thighs]: "By the recitation of the mantra... etc. The meaning is that after embracing his wife, he should mutter the mantra for the purpose of separating her thighs by means of the recitation of the mantra beginning with "amo'ham" (I am he). || 96 ||
He carefully separates the wife's thighs by means of a mantra.
And let this wound on your thighs be observed with the words, "May you two be separated. (97)

He explains the words beginning with *asyāḥ*: "he causes to separate" (*vihāpayati*), which means "he causes to disjoin. The meaning is "by means of the mantra beginning with *vijihīthām*. The meaning is "by way of performing the subjugation through effort. Here too, the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) is not intended to be expressed.
He states the meaning of the term *dyāvāpṛthivī*: "of the two thighs" (*ūrvoḥ*). This [term] *dyāvāpṛthivī* is an address to the two thighs.
The connection is "let [it] be saluted. The ellipsis to be supplied is "the performance of the injunction regarding the word 'vijihīthām' (may you two move apart). || 97 ||
This is the form of the causative (*ṇyanta*) of the root *vijihīti*, which has "motion" as its object.
Then, with the mantra, he should stroke her three times with his hand in the natural direction.
Then, reciting the mantra "Viṣṇu," you should request that wife [to step forward].

Having first stated the manner in which the verbal form "vihāpayati" arises, he explains its meaning with the words "of the root *vijihī*. He analyzes the phrase "three times each" and so forth. Regarding the word "mantrataḥ": it means from the top of the head down to the feet in the natural order (*anuloma*).
The word "atha" signifies that this follows immediately after the rite concerning cattle (*paśukarma*). He states that mantra for the wiping (*anumārjana*): "the mantra *maśram*" || 98 || 99 ||
Establishment, the purpose of the conceptualization, and likewise the eightfold division of the members [of the syllogism].
May he bring about beautiful forms for my son.

Regarding how the naturally established womb (*yonis*) is conceptualized therein, he says: "the justification" (*samarthanam*). This means the bringing about of capacity at the birth of a son. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Tvaṣṭṛ": "Tvaṣṭṛ," etc. Anticipating the objection—"What is the role of Tvaṣṭṛ in the forms being produced part by part from the body of one's own wife?"—he says: "of the son," etc. (Verse 100).
And here, the deity of the new moon day (darśāha) is called Sinīvālī.
She is called Pṛthuṣṭuti because she is the extensive praise (pṛthustuti). || 101 ||

He explains the meaning of the word *sinīvālī* found in the mantra beginning with "Conceive a fetus" (*garbhaṃ dhehi*). He says: "The new moon. Regarding the phrase "O broad-tressed one" (*pṛthuṣṭuke*) in the mantra "Conceive a fetus, O broad-tressed one," he states this in order to dispel the doubt that some other deity might be the one being addressed. || 101 ||
The two Aśvins, adorned with lotus garlands, have properly deposited the embryo within you.
In this context, the two Aśvins are to be understood as the sun and the moon.

He takes the portion beginning with "The Aśvins [are] your embryo" (garbha te aśvinau). Regarding the word "embryo" (garbham), he explains the term "Aśvins" by distinguishing them from the well-known [divine] Aśvins. Regarding the words "Sūrya... and so on, it is stated that since the aforementioned nature of the [divine] Aśvins might be suspected to apply everywhere, the word "here" (iha) is used. 102.
For those two, garlanded with rays of light, are indeed renowned throughout the world. || 103 ||
Gold is light and immortal; O auspicious one, that [light] is my veil.
By means of those two, the Aśvins churned the nectar of immortality in ancient times.

He states the reason for that: "By their own rays" (*svaraśmi*). Since those two, the Sun and the Moon, are garlanded with their own rays, they are established in the world as the Aśvins; thus, the connection is that the Sun and Moon are specified as being "garlanded with lotuses" (*puṣkarasrajau*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the force of the qualification. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "golden" (*hiraṇmayī*): "Gold" (*hiraṇyam*) [is the meaning]. || 103 ||
Just as the Aśvins with great effort churned forth the embryo, so [did they do].
Likewise, they assumed that form for birth in the tenth month.

He analyzes the passage beginning with "that" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the two Aśvins": it indicates that because the embryo is equal to nectar (*amṛta*), one must exert effort [for its protection].
This is expressed by the word "through effort" (*prayatnāt*). || 105 ||
Just as the earth contains fire within it, or as the sky is filled with light by Indra.
Just as the wind is seen to be the embryo of the quarters, performing the action of loosening.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "yathā" (as). Regarding "yathā": he explains the meaning of the word "indra" by [the phrase] "bhānunā" (by the light). He explains "vāyum" (wind) by [the phrase] "na" (not). || 106 ||
Having pronounced my own name, I likewise place the embryo within you.
Or the husband, reciting the mantra, should utter her name.

Stating two meanings for the word *asau* (this one), he explains the manner of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) with the words "ātmeti" (the Self). The meaning is that [the husband] should recite the mantra, "I place the embryo in you," as if the earth and other elements were the womb (*garbha*) of fire and so forth. The completion of the sentence is that while reciting it, the husband should take the name of his wife, saying, "This one [is her name]. This is the construction of the second half of the verse. || 107 ||
Then, the mother should slowly sprinkle water over her as she is about to give birth.
Just as the wind causes a lotus pond to quiver and move. || 108 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "sopyantīm" (to her who is about to give birth) as follows: "by means of the mantra," which means by means of the mantra beginning with "yathā vāyuḥ" (as the wind). The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is the immediate succession following the completion of the tenth month, starting from the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*). The word "eṣa" (this) refers to the husband. [The phrase] "for the sake of removing pain" [is used]. (Note: Variants *adis* and *gatoyaṃ* appear in manuscripts *ka* and *kha*; *dṛṣṭaścalana* appears in manuscript *ga*.)

3, Page 930] 4 Brāhmaṇam], accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
2065. It was stated "gradually. He explains the mantra for sprinkling: "Vāyu... [The wind], shaking everything, [is like] a lotus pond—
And it does not even move me; such is the meaning. || 108 ||
Just as the wind, though moving everywhere, does not disturb a lotus pond;
In that same way, may your embryo move with ease and cause you no harm. 109.

He restates the intended portion of the example with the words "yathā" (just as). The phrase "of that [cognition]" (*tasyāḥ*) is to be supplied after "kṣatiṃ" (damage). He explains the passage beginning with "eva" (indeed) with the words "tadvat" (in the same way). || 109 ||
May the womb bring you comfort along with the fetus and the placenta;
for this path of the fetus was indeed previously made obstructed by a bolt. (110)

He states the meaning of "saha" and so forth: "garbhastvām" (the womb [received] you). The particle "ava" has the sense of "sukhayann" (gladdening). He analyzes "indrasya" and so forth: "vraja" (the cow-pen). By "purā" (formerly), the time of creation or the time of conception is stated. [This refers to] the bolt of the path of the womb.
Or rather, the word "hi" has the sense of establishing a well-known fact. || 110 ||
O Indra, quickly strike down that womb-barrier.
After the fetus has emerged, that which subsequently comes forth from the birth canal. || 111 ||
A thin strip of flesh, similar [in shape], is called an *sāvare*.
And here, Prāṇa is to be understood as Indra; therefore, he alone is the one who is prayed to.
He explains *argalam*: "The placenta" (*jarāyu*). The meaning is: "Having broken the path that is obstructed by a bolt, make it a path free of obstructions.

Regarding the passage beginning with "by the embryo" (*garbheṇa*), he analyzes the word *avaram*. "The embryo" (*garbha*): the word "equal" (*samā*) is to be supplied after "by the embryo. Its connection is with the preceding phrase "she brings it forth" (*nirjahī*). Although the first occurrence of the word "Indra" refers to the embryo, he states what the referent of the second one is: "And the vital breath" (*prāṇaśca*).

The phrase "here" refers to the statement in the sentence. The reason for this is given as "that very one. Since, in the passage "him Indra," it is the vital breath (prāṇa) alone that is sought after by the wife, the meaning is that the word "Indra" applies to that very [breath] alone. || 111 || 112 ||
Then, when the prince was born, his father placed him upon his lap.
For, having established the sacred fire, another well-known purpose follows.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "When [the son] is born" (*jāte 'gnim*) and so forth. Regarding the word "born" (*jāte*): the word *atha* (then) signifies that the rite of birth (*jātakarman*) occurs immediately after the birth. "Lord" (*pati*) means the nourisher; "father" (*pitā*) means the progenitor. The syntactical connection is: "having established [the fire], he offers oblations. The particle *hi* (for/indeed) serves to indicate the presence of the *āvasathya* (domestic) fire. When there was the possibility of needing an explanation for the passage beginning with "In a bronze vessel, the speckled butter" (*kaṃse pṛṣadājyam*), it was stated that the meaning is well-known (*prasiddhārtha*). ||113||
Clarified butter mixed with curd is designated as *pṛṣadājya*.
Then, having combined and gathered together the *pṛṣadājya* according to the mantra, || 114 ||
In the expression "he offers repeatedly" (*upaghātaṃ juhoti*), the suffix *ṇamul* is desired in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*).
Saying "upahatya, upahatya," one should cast oblations of speckled butter (pṛṣadājya). || 115 ||
He announces the *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter), saying "Clarified butter" (*ghṛtam*). He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "having mixed" (*saṃnīya*) as "having made into one.

Having mixed the clarified butter and the curd together, and having placed it in a bronze vessel before him, he subsequently takes portions of the *pṛṣadājya* repeatedly with the mantras to be recited hereafter.
259 [Vol. 3, page 931] 2066 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Sixth Chapter]
The meaning is "having called. How is its repetition expressed? To that he says: "by means of the suffix *ṇamul*. It manifests constant recurrence (*ābhīkṣṇya*).

Regarding the word "upahatya," intending that it is a genitive in the sense of the object (*karman*), he states the meaning of the phrase "he offers the speckled butter" (*pṛṣadājyasya juhoti*) as follows: "the speckled butter" (*pṛṣadājya*). || 114 || 111 ||
"May I dwell here in my own home among men according to my desire;
may I always be known by the name Sahasra, with a thousand voices. (116)

He explains that mantra: "May I nourish" (*puṣyāsam*). Here, the connection is: "In my own home, may I nourish a thousand of men at will and perpetually. He states the reason for the restriction to a thousand there: "Of the much" (*bahoḥ*) || 116 ||
Thus, as you grow up here, O son, you shall consider the continuity of your lineage.
"You shall perform the dedication of the sacrificial animal and other offerings for me within my lineage. || 117 ||
He states the meaning of *dāntikam* with the word "thus" (*evam*). He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "of this" (*asya*) with the words "in the lineage" (*saṃtatau*).
The connection is: "You, increasing in my lineage. The explanation of the term *upasandyām* is "in the lineage"; the ellipsis to be supplied is "the lineage of cattle and so forth. || 117 ||
It does not require an explanation at all, because its meaning is already clear.
Let the passage beginning with "mayi prāṇān" be understood by oneself. || 118 ||
He states that [the scripture] does not depend upon an explanation: "Not at all," [verse 118].
Then, having placed his right ear against his own mouth, he—
For one should indeed utter "vāk, vāk" three times; thus it is called the Trayī Vāk (the Triple Speech).

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then for him" (athāsya) as follows: "Then" (atha). The meaning of the word "then" is immediate succession to the birth-rite (jātakarman). || 119 ||
May this triple Veda enter you through the path of the ear for the sake of your highest good.
Sarasvatī is praised here with the verse beginning, "That breast of yours... (yaste stanaḥ).

He explains the intention of Janaka as he says "Speech, speech" three times into the right ear of his son: "The Veda is Speech. He explains the purport of the passage beginning with "That breast of thine," etc., with the words "That which is thine. Here, the phrase "in this" refers to the context of the son's drinking from the breast. || 120 ||
"May the son possess the attainment of noble qualities"—thus it is said.
Śaśaya is to be understood as doubt (saṃśaya), and śaya is said to be the fruit (phala). || 121 ||
He states the fruit of the praise: "Exalted," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "by means of the infant’s drinking from the breast. He explains the words: "saśaya" (doubtful).

In that regard, having entered the mother’s breast, He sustains all beings as the object of their enjoyment; thus, the meaning is that He is the cause of the subsistence of all living creatures by becoming food. Explaining the meaning of the word *vāryāṇi*, he connects it with the sentence: "the gods and so forth. He explains the phrase beginning with *tam* (referring to "by which you prosper") as follows: [it is for] "drinking. The word *mama* (my) is connected to both instances. || 129 || 126 ||
Then, with the mantra "Ilāsī," he respectfully addressed the mother of the son.

Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

Now he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "athāsyā" (then of her): "ilā'si" (you are Ilā). The word "atha" (then) signifies the immediate sequence following the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) for the giving of the breast. The statement "ilā'si" is an expression of the wife’s worthiness of praise: she is a deity-like being who is the offspring of Mitra and Varuṇa, and who, as the sustainer of life, has produced a virtuous son for me. He prays that she may possess living sons; such are you.

He states that even for himself, his wife is the cause for the company of the son of the world (lokyaputra), saying "She who [gave] us... This refers to the relationship with Ilā. He states the fruit of the consecration of the wife (*bhāryābhimantraṇa*) by means of the mantra whose meaning has been explained: "Excellent" (*sādhu*). It is a praiseworthy and virtuous act (*sādhukarma*) consisting of the proper nurturing of the son. || 127 ||
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

For the sake of the attainment of the meaning of the Madhukāṇḍa according to its nature.

Having raised the doubt as to why the first two lineages are specified by males while the third is specified by a female, he states the intended meaning of the commentary beginning with "due to the predominance of the female" (*strīprādhānyāt*). it did not originate thus from Brahmā himself, and therefore it is called "Svayambhū" (Self-existent).
Regarding the phrase "Brahmā, the Self-Existent" (*brahma svayaṃbhū*), he states the reason for employing the word *svayaṃbhu* with respect to Brahman: "from another," [verse 9].
The knowledge of others arises from the Veda by relying on numerous means.
Therefore, because he is by nature the self that is the Veda, he indeed consists of all knowledge.

Explaining the meaning of the word *brahman*, he establishes its independence from a teacher. Regarding the phrase "of others": it means that for others, there is an abundance of means such as extensive hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth; however, the Supreme Self—Brahman characterized by the Veda—has no dependence on a teacher, because He consists of all knowledge. || 10 ||
"Although he is the controller of all," and so forth; nevertheless, I have spoken previously [to the contrary].
The Veda and whatever exists, moving or unmoving, is indeed the Supreme Deity.

He states the mark (*liṅga*) for the Supreme Being’s identity with that [all-knowing nature] by saying "of all. The meaning is that mastery and so forth are not established without being composed of omniscience. The word "also" (*api*) implies that His omniscience is well-known even in other scriptural passages (*śruti*), such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and so on.

Anticipating the objection that if the Supreme Being—conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Veda—is designated by the word "Brahman," then non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost due to the distinction between the adjunct and its substrate, he says:
"By others," so [it is said]. || 11 ||

Since the Veda, though its internal distinctions are conceptually constructed, establishes the Self, other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are also possible for that purpose; thus, there is the exclusion of connection with anything else.

Anticipating the objection that [the Self] is not established by perception and other means of knowledge, he says: "By the threefold... For its cognition cannot be attained through perception and so forth, as it is unfit for such means;
therefore, the seeker of liberation attains fulfillment only by knowing his own true nature as taught by the Veda as the Self, according to such scriptural passages as "Only by knowing Him...
To clarify non-duality, he qualifies "fulfillment" with the words "kārya... (verse 13).
Because [the father] says, "You have been seen," they give a name to this child as soon as he is born.
How indeed can one attain the Supreme Brahman by means of the Veda as one's very self? || 14 ||
He states another argument for the idea that the realization of the Supreme occurs through the Veda which constitutes His own nature: "You are the Veda" (vedo 'si).

The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is that the Veda, being the very self [of the Lord], makes known His essential nature. He expresses the intention of those who give the name "Veda" to a newborn infant by saying: "O you whose self is the Veda" (vedātman). || 14 ||
For in all the Vāji branches, indeed, [the lineages] begin with Āsurāyaṇa.
Let it be observed that these sages of the lineage are indeed equal until the final conclusion. || 15 ||

Having explained the meaning of the word "Brahmā" in the phrase *brahma svayaṃbhū*, he states the intermediate distinction residing within the two preceding lineages: "In the Vāji recensions. In all fifteen of those [recensions], the sages of the two lineages appear according to the order of their textual recitation.

The meaning is that those [lineages] beginning with Yaṇa and ending with Brahman, known as the Vedas, are identical up to Āsurāyaṇa; however, prior to him, they differ branch by branch, extending down to humans in both cases, because of the scriptural statement regarding their difference. The first *hi* (for) indicates that the identity of the lineage-sages is well-known among teachers.
The second *hi* indicates that such a commonality is capable of being experienced according to the textual recitation. || 15 ||
For these very Yajus formulas were indeed proclaimed by Āditya.
Therefore, the wise correctly call them the Ādityas. || 16 ||
In the passage "These [verses] belong to the Ādityas," the solar nature of the *yajus* mantras is heard; he establishes that with the words "by the Sun.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that it is well known in the Purāṇas that the *yajus* were proclaimed by him (the Sun) and obtained by Yājñavalkya within the Vājasaneya branch. || 16 ||
This tradition has thus come down from the Veda itself, which is the very soul of the Vedas.
[He taught] all [the sages], beginning with Parameṣṭhin, down to human beings through the traditional lineage. || 17 ||
For this reason as well, he states that they have the Sun as their essence: "He is the Veda," and so forth. For he, Hiraṇyagarbha, is the self of the Vedas;
from him comes the tradition of knowledge (vidyā-saṃpradāya) for Parameṣṭhin. Therefore, this tradition has come down by succession to all [the sages] beginning with him.
Consequently, the meaning is that the Yajus formulas have the Sun as their essence. The word "evam" (thus) refers to the statement of the sequence as studied in the Vaṃśabrāhmaṇa. || 17 ||
The supreme Brahman is unconditioned and free from all defects.
This which shines as residing in the sun is the supreme form of the Vedas.

It is not only they who possess the nature of the Sun; rather, it belongs to the entire Veda as well, because of its well-known character as consisting of the threefold knowledge (trayī). Thus he says:

Even that Brahman which has perished does not perish within the Sun.
Then, by that very [means], the great seers find it after having performed austerities. || 19 ||

In that very context, he states another reason: "It is destroyed," and so forth. "At the end of the age, the great seers, having been authorized by the Self-born One, recovered through austerity the Vedas along with the Itihāsas that had disappeared."
The meaning is that such scriptural passages as these constitute the authority here. || 19 ||
Starting from Vedabrahman, the lineage of all the followers of the Vedic branches remains one and undivided, extending down to the son of Sāṃjīvī.

Thus has been spoken this discourse on the non-dual Self, which possesses the fragrance of the logic of the *māyā-śūnya* [or the *ājya-śūnya*] like a blossoming lotus;
it is variegated with sixfold chapters, frequented by the bees that are the lords of ascetics, and filled with the honey of the sage [Madhva].
This garland of verses, bound together by knots of meaning, having for its subject the Unconditioned and for its fruit the realization of the Truth, and strung upon the excellent thread of love—
may it follow the Lord Viṣṇu’s stainless and unborn state, just as the Gaṅgā follows Śambhu. || 22 ||

Now, one might suspect that this *Vārttika* was composed by an unreliable author because it was undertaken for the sake of fame, gain, and honor; therefore, since it has not attained widespread acceptance through the adoption of the learned (*śiṣṭas*), the labor of the author of the *Vārttika* would be in vain.

Anticipating this objection, he states [the following] to show that under the pretext of composing the *Vārttika*, his intended aim was the contemplation of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, and not fame and so forth—so how could there be room for the aforementioned suspicion of fault?
Thus it is said: for here the status of this *Vārttika* as a garland (*mālā*) that serves as a means of worship for the venerable Bhagavatpāda is established.
In that regard, it is one in which the very sentences expressing non-duality—which have been explained according to the method stated in the six chapters—are the fully blossomed lotuses;
for a garland is not possible without flowers, and yet there are no other flowers here [than these]. And that [garland] is composed of abundant, faultless reasoning (*nyāya*).

For one who possesses fragrance does not accept a garland devoid of scent; nor is there any other fragrance in a lotus composed of words, beyond the principle of its own constituent materials, [just as there is no scent] in the stalks known by the names *madhu*, *muni*, and *akhila*.

Indeed, a beautiful garland fashioned from three diverse sections is not observed to be as pleasing when constructed using lotuses alone. *Suresvaracharya-krita Bṛhadaranyakopanisad-bhasya-vartika*, Sixth Chapter. [Vol. 3, p. 937] 2072. [The garland] is variegated by the three [sections]; for a garland composed of lotuses alone is not seen to be so charming.

Nor are there other sections here [in this work], yet it has been devotedly cultivated by the firm bees that are the wandering mendicants who are supreme *paramahaṃsas*. Indeed, for those observing a garland from a distance, it is not possible to ascertain the fragrance residing within it without the attendance of bees;
nor are other bees conceivable here, [for this is] the commentary known as the *Vārttika*, consisting of the original twelve thousand verses.

Endowed with the fruit of supreme bliss characterized by the direct realization of Brahman, it enters the path of adoption for those who possess discernment. That Supreme Brahman—which is the object of supreme love, whose nature is supreme bliss, and which is unconditioned—is itself, when variegated by ignorance, denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) and is the cause of all. That same [Brahman], conditioned by the five unquintuplicated elements, is the *sūtra* (the thread). The garland that has been fashioned, being endowed with such a *sūtra*, is certainly not a garland without a thread.

It deserves to be highly esteemed, and no other sūtra applies here; for this [work], following the essential purport (*tātparya*) that the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is the goal to be attained by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), serves as its ornament. Indeed, even a garland endowed with every excellence cannot be fruitful unless it is offered as an ornament to some preeminent person; nor can there be an ornament elsewhere apart from the state of being the Blessed One.

The construction is: "It must be considered thus. He provides an illustration for the fact that the garland under discussion follows the feet of the Blessed One with total intent. "Like the Gaṅgā" means:

The meaning is that the garland under discussion, being unfit for any adventitious person other than the Blessed One's feet as previously shown, follows only those. [This is stated] in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa].
