The nectar of awakening arises from the effort born of compassion for those suffering who seek liberation; it is produced by the nails of the reasoning and words of the ocean of wisdom, with faith as its sole guide, and stability as its pillar.
I bow to my stainless guru named Vedhas, born of the lineage of Atri, by drinking from whom those seeking liberation—freed from the torrent of birth and death—attained final release. 23.

Now, one might object: "Surely the teachers were already saluted at the beginning of the treatise, and its fruit—characterized by the completion of the work—has already been realized; therefore, a salutation to them at the end should not be performed, as it would be fruitless. Anticipating this doubt, the author salutes his teacher, considering that a salutation to the teacher at the end, just as at the beginning, must be prescribed to illuminate the fact that [the work] is a means for attaining knowledge. He says: "Whose wisdom..."—meaning, the wisdom of that Blessed One, the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakṛt), is itself...

Because it lacks a further shore, the ocean must be churned; therefore, reasoning is the instrument and sound is the means, and by means of the churning-stick consisting of these, I must produce the nectar of knowledge—the cause of liberation sought by those desiring release—for no other has the power to do so. Thus, with the extremely firm rope of the conviction in the scriptures, and through the support of the pillar called "Stability" belonging to this very Blessed One, I have shown compassion toward those suffering seekers of liberation.

Having drunk the nectar called "Awakening" (bodha), which is produced through the effort of contemplation (*rūpa-yatna*), and having obtained it by means of service (*śuśrūṣā*) and other practices, many seekers of liberation—freed from the stream of birth and so forth—have attained liberation; for that [nectar] is free from all defects and stands manifest like Hiraṇyagarbha himself. "I salute my own guru, who is the foremost among the learned and the pride of his lineage. His wisdom (*yat-prajñā*) is itself an ocean.

and he whose "yatna" (effort) is compassion alone toward those who are seekers of liberation and yet suffering, is such; and he whose wisdom is... [the remainder of the passage].

The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that which arises from trust (*viśvāsa*), from reasoning (*yukti*), from words (*śabda*), and from the nails (*nakha*); it is that which consists solely of faith (*śraddhā*) and is the sole refuge (*sannatraka*); it is that which is the pillar of stability (*sthairyastambha*); and it is the effort born of compassion for those suffering in their desire for liberation (*mumukṣuduḥkhita-kṛpāyatna*). From that arises the nectar called awakening (*bodhākhyam amṛtam*). Regarding the term *vaidhobhidham*:

he who ordains (*vidadhāti*) is the Creator (*vedhāḥ*), the Supreme Lord; his name is Śaṅkara. That [nectar] has him as its designation. One should bow with speech, body, and mind to that most venerable one, Bhavānī.
The connection. || 23 ||

My venerable teacher alone has composed this pure commentary on the Upanishads, which brings welfare to the virtuous and is illuminated by various systems of reasoning, because its intent is the non-dual unity of the Self.
Having removed the defects of fallacious reasoning from the Upaniṣads based on the Kaṇva recension, I have composed this Vārtika concerning them in brief, by the power of faith alone. (24)

Having set aside the arguments regarding [the Upaniṣads] being composed by untrustworthy persons and lacking a traditional lineage, he concludes his composition of the *Vārttika* with the words beginning "yām" (which...). The syntactical connection is as follows: "This *Vārttika* has been composed for that commentary (*vṛtti*) which our teacher wrote upon the Upaniṣads belonging to the Kāṇva recension. This is because, through a thorough investigation of the Vedāntas' ultimate purport toward the non-duality of the Self, [he treats] the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* based on the Kāṇva branch...

Under the guise of commenting on the *Kaṇṇāmadheya Upaniṣad*, the Guru composed a commentary (*vṛtti*) upon all the Upaniṣads; therefore, considering that it is profound and requires the *Vārtika* for its full understanding, he says: "Of the Veda-heads" (*vedaśirasām*). He further states: "Bringing joy to the virtuous" (*sajjanaśaṅkarīm*), meaning that because it brings about the unsurpassed human goal for those people who are virtuous—namely, those endowed with the fourfold qualifications—the commentary is faultless.

He demonstrates its freedom from defects both in terms of word and meaning by saying "suvimalām" (extremely pure). He states that it is faultless because it is devoid of the instruments of logic such as frivolous talk (*jalpa*) and mere disputation (*vāda*), by saying "nānā" (various). He further states that it is without defect because it refutes the opposing positions that obstruct the path to the highest good (*śreyaḥ*), by saying "dustarka" (bad reasoning). Thus, this *Vārttika* has been composed out of faith toward such a treatise, and not out of mere intellectual ability.

He speaks of the necessity [of this work]. "Merely by way of faith" (*śraddhāmātra*): in this *vārttika*, he clarifies both the brevity of the text and the richness of its meaning for the sake of engaging the listener. "By means of a summary" (*samāsāt*): it is said "merely" in order to express that the Blessed One, the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself, possesses the capacity to compose such a commentary, and not anyone else. In this verse, everything that was stated under the pretext of the *Kāṇva Upaniṣad* is to be understood in accordance with what has been said here.
This is the Veda. || 24 ||

The Sixth Chapter [Adhyāya] in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, composed by the venerable Sureśvarācārya, disciple of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya*).
The eighth chapter according to the sequence of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. || 8 ||

In order to make it known—based on such scriptural passages as "He who has supreme devotion for the Lord"—that the knowledge of Brahman belongs only to one possessed of unsurpassed devotion to the Guru and not to others, he again pays homage to the Guru with the words "From the mountain" (ā śailāt). Here, the venerable author of the Commentary (Śaṅkara) describes himself as the Sun and his disciples as its rays; thus, by being situated between the mountains of sunrise and sunset, he encompasses all people.

The multitude of those seeking liberation, who were under the authority of this Blessed One, became free from the darkness of false ignorance, pervaded by the disciples of that Lord—Sanandanācārya and others—who were radiant with the rays of exceedingly clear fame; and because of the rays known as "knowledge" (jñāna) emitted by that Guru, which reached as far as the sun, the sun itself was eclipsed and acted like the moon. Indeed, the rays of fame of the disciples of the author of the Bhāṣya pervade the entire world.
Having approached the preeminent men appointed here and there who traverse the [entire] circle, they dispel the ignorance residing therein;

yet the rays of knowledge of the blessed Commentator further ascend to the earth, the heavens, and the intermediate space, destroying the darkness everywhere— salutations in three ways to that blessed Sun, the Author of the Commentary, who bears the illustrious name of Śaṅkara.
The connection [of the verse] is as follows: the word "always" (sada) illuminates the excellence of devotion and faith, for it is preceded by these that an act of salutation bears fruit.

Whatever variation in the wording may be observed here due to our own dullness or other causes, that should somehow be understood as intended, because for those who know it, the established rule is that it is like the Vedic meters.

who bears a body consisting of supreme bliss and perfect knowledge.
Salutations to the Guru, who is the sun for the lotus of the essence of the three Vedas, and who is most capable of destroying the darkness of the night of opposing views.

This commentary, which takes refuge in the reality of things through its supreme excellence in the expansion of various modes of inquiry that have cast away the doubts of fallacious reasoning by the force of a multitude of countless logical saws;
and which is profound with deep, hidden expressions rendered firm by the weight of constant remembrance of the pair of feet of Śrī Ānanda.
May this joy, composed by Nandajñāna, bestow delight upon the virtuous in the world. || 5 ||

It is a vast ocean of jewels of grammar, possessing great crocodiles in the form of extensive treatises on verses that are firm with waves of various logical methods, and a flood of waters consisting of investigations into the Śrauta and Smārta traditions.
Victorious is this ocean of Vārtikas, the crest-jewel of the Upanishads, who is the preeminent and singular ground for the manifestation of the glory of the nectar of inward consciousness.
Thus composed and established, this *Śāstraprakāśikā*, following the words of the Lord of the Gods, has been offered by us unto Puruṣottama.
Thus, O seekers of liberation, if you desire to taste the essential nectar of the Vārttika, please study this commentary, the Śāstraprakāśikā.
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya in the commentary on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Vārtika-Ṭīkā. || 5 ||

[This work] possesses a face of beautiful syllables as complete as mountains; it is radiant with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) strewn with a multitude of excellent jewels that are collections of sound reasoning, and it has eyes and ears free from defects.
